## Critical Notes

Faint handwritten pencil notations are visible in the upper right-hand corner of the page:

**Book VII, Hymn 21**
**Book VII, Hymn 18**

<note>These archival markings refer to specific sections of the Rig Veda. "VII" denotes the Seventh Mandala (Book), a collection of hymns traditionally attributed to the sage Vashistha and his family. Hymn 18 is particularly famous for describing the "Battle of the Ten Kings," a pivotal historical-mythological conflict.</note>

<meta>This page begins the Preface to Volume III of Max Müller’s edition of the Rig-veda. It follows the formal dedication to the Directors of the East-India Company, who funded the publication. This preface marks a transition from the administrative front matter to the scholarly justification and historical context of the work.</meta>

# PREFACE.

---

In laying before the public the third volume of my edition of the **Rig-veda** and its Commentary by **Sáyana Áchárya**, <note>Sáyana Áchárya was a 14th-century scholar whose massive commentary, the *Mádhavíya Vedártha Prakásha*, is considered the most comprehensive traditional interpretation of the Rig-veda.</note> it gives me much pleasure to acknowledge the increasing interest which of late years has been evinced by the most eminent scholars in England, in India, and on the continent, with regard to these ancient remnants of the sacred poetry of the **Brahmans**. <note>The priestly and scholarly class in traditional Indian society.</note> Their importance for **Sanskrit** literature had been felt ever since **Sir William Jones**, **Colebrooke**, and **F. Rosen** informed us of their existence, and gave us the first specimens of their contents; <note>These three men were foundational figures in Western Orientalism: Jones (the "father" of Indo-European linguistics), Colebrooke (the first great Sanskrit scholar), and Rosen (who published the first few hymns in 1838).</note> and no one acquainted with the later literature of India, the epic poems, the law-books, the systems of philosophy, could fail to see that our knowledge of the historical growth of the Indian mind must remain incomplete until we had gained an insight into that period of literature which precedes **Vyása** and **Valmíki**, **Manu** and **Jaimini**, <note>Vyása is the legendary compiler of the Vedas and Mahabharata; Valmíki is the author of the Ramayana; Manu is the traditional lawgiver; and Jaimini is the founder of the Mimamsa school of philosophy.</note> and to which the poets, the lawgivers, and philosophers of India point with common consent as the highest authority for their inspirations, their belief, and their institutions. **Sanskrit** literature without the **Veda** was like Greek literature without **Homer**, like Arabic literature without the **Koran**, like English without **Shakespear**.

But as the study of **Sanskrit** owes its permanent interest chiefly to the fact that the ancient language of India has been proved to be most intimately connected with the classical languages of Europe, and that in it has been found the key to the most secret archives of the history of language in general, the **Veda** would never have engaged the serious attention of a large class of scholars, if this ancient literary relic had not been found to shed the most unexpected light on the darkest periods in the history of the most prominent nations of antiquity. The religious traditions of the **Persians** or the **Zoroastrians** have been traced back to their source in the **Veda**. Many of the most obscure grammatical forms in the arrow-headed inscriptions of **Darius** and **Xerxes** have <note>original: "arrow-headed inscriptions" — refers to Cuneiform inscriptions. Müller is highlighting how the older Sanskrit found in the Vedas helped scholars decipher and understand the grammar of Old Persian and other ancient languages.</note>

<summary>Friedrich Max Müller introduces the third volume of his Rig-veda edition, arguing that the Vedas are the essential foundation for understanding Indian history, literature, and the shared linguistic heritage of Europe and Asia.</summary>
<keywords>Rig-veda, Sáyana Áchárya, Indo-European linguistics, Sanskrit literature, ancient history, comparative philology</keywords>

--- Page 12 ---
<meta>This page continues Max Müller’s preface to the third volume of the Rig-veda. On the previous page, Müller argued that to understand Indian history and philosophy, one must look back to the period before the great epics and law-books, to the age of the Vedas themselves.</meta>

# PREFACE.

->vi<-
->d<-

...have been deciphered by means of the **Veda**. <note>The Vedas are the oldest sacred scriptures of Hinduism, written in an archaic form of Sanskrit.</note> The mythology of Greece and Italy, and even of Germany and Iceland, has suddenly taken on a new appearance and an understandable meaning by being compared with the poetic language of the **Veda**. Even social institutions, local customs, and common proverbs found in the later history of the **Aryan** <note>original: "Arian"; Müller uses this term to refer to the broad family of Indo-European peoples, including Indians, Persians, Greeks, Romans, and Germans.</note> nations have received unexpected explanations through the simple poetry of the **Veda**. In this way, the **Veda**—even though it is not yet fully known in its entirety—has gained an importance that no other literary work from India could ever claim. We can rest assured that as long as humanity treasures the records of its "family history" in the broadest sense of the word, these simple songs will keep their place among the most precious records of ancient history.

There is one group of readers who might have been disappointed: those who study ancient literature more for its poetic beauty than its historical value. Those who expected the **Veda** to contain elaborate songs like the odes of **Pindar** <note>An ancient Greek poet famous for his complex and grand choral lyrics.</note> or the vague and misty atmosphere of **Ossian** <note>A cycle of epic poems published in the 18th century, claimed to be translated from ancient Scottish Gaelic sources.</note> will find very little that meets their expectations. However, the true historian values genuine, ancient facts; to him, a corroded copper **As** <note>A low-value bronze coin used during the Roman Republic.</note> of the Roman Republic is more valuable than a gold imperial medal of the finest craftsmanship. What the philosopher **Schelling** <note>Friedrich Wilhelm Joseph Schelling (1775–1854), a major German philosopher.</note> says regarding the gods of the later **Hindu pantheon**—as they are represented to us in the **Mahábhárata**, the poems of **Kálidása**, and the **Puráṇas** <note>The Mahábhárata is a massive epic; Kálidása was a premier classical poet and playwright; the Puráṇas are texts detailing myths and genealogies. These represent a much later stage of Indian religion than the Vedas.</note>—applies to all historical facts: “Whether they are hideous or not, they stand before us and therefore require a rational explanation.”*

But it has been an even greater pleasure for me during the many years spent preparing this critical edition—not only of the text of the **Rig-veda** but also of its **Commentary** by **Sáyana Áchárya** <note>A 14th-century scholar whose massive work, the *Mádhavíya Vedártha Prakásha*, provides the traditional interpretation of the Rig-veda.</note>—to observe how the belief is becoming more and more widespread that an accurate and scholarly knowledge of the **Veda** could never have been achieved without this **Commentary**. At first, there was much debate about the value of **Sáyana** and whether it was necessary to publish a critical edition of his work. It seemed to me that his strengths and weaknesses would be so obvious to anyone who studied him honestly that I did not think I needed to defend him against his critics or "save" him from his over-enthusiastic supporters. While we all admired the quick insight and brilliant guesswork shown by some famous scholars who tried to figure out the meaning of these ancient hymns without the help of the tradition which—

***

\* Schelling’s *Philosophy of Mythology*, p. 24.

<summary>Müller explains that the Rig-veda is essential for understanding the origins of Indo-European ("Aryan") mythology and culture. He also defends the necessity of using Sáyana’s traditional commentary to accurately interpret these ancient texts, despite early scholarly skepticism.</summary>
<keywords>Comparative Mythology, Indo-European history, Sáyana Áchárya, Rig-veda, Schelling, historical value vs poetic value</keywords>

--- Page 13 ---
<meta>This page continues Max Müller’s preface to the third volume of the Rig-Veda. Here, Müller evaluates the methods used by previous scholars and the 14th-century commentator Sāyaṇa, debating whether we should seek the original meaning of the hymns or the later traditional interpretation provided by the priesthood.</meta>

## Preface

->vii<-

<term>Sáyaṇa</term> <note>A 14th-century scholar and minister in the Vijayanagara Empire whose commentary is the most influential traditional interpretation of the Vedas.</note> embodied in his Commentary—and though a work like that of the late **M. Langlois** <note>Simon Alexandre Langlois (1788–1854), a French scholar who produced an early, though sometimes criticized, complete translation of the Rig-Veda.</note>, who actually published a complete translation of the <term>Veda</term> <note>The most ancient sacred scriptures of India.</note> at a time when most scholars were content with deciphering a few lines, will always excite our admiration by the boldness, the perseverance, and the undoubted ingenuity which it displays—yet before the tribunal of a more severe scholarship such works could not be approved; and it begins to be recognised that the errors which they propagated have proved so mischievous as to outweigh the many right guesses which no doubt they contained.

It would have been equally wrong, however, to consider <term>Sáyaṇa’s</term> Commentary as an infallible authority with regard to the interpretation of the <term>Veda</term>. <term>Sáyaṇa</term> gives the traditional, but not the original, sense of the <term>Vaidik</term> <note>Relating to the Vedas.</note> hymns. These hymns—originally popular songs, short prayers and thanks-givings, sometimes true, genuine, and even sublime, but frequently childish, vulgar, and obscure—were invested by the <term>Brahmans</term> <note>The priestly class of ancient India.</note> with the character of an inspired revelation, and made the basis of a complete system of dogmatic theology. If therefore we wish to know how the <term>Brahmans</term>, from the time of the composition of the first <term>Brāhmaṇa</term> <note>Later prose works that explain Vedic rituals and provide theological myths.</note> to the present day, understood and interpreted the hymns of their ancient <term>Rishis</term> <note>The ancient poet-seers who are believed to have first "heard" or composed the sacred hymns.</note>, we ought to translate them in strict accordance with <term>Sáyaṇa’s</term> gloss. This is the object which **Professor Wilson** <note>Horace Hayman Wilson (1786–1860), a renowned English orientalist who translated the Rig-Veda following the traditional Indian perspective.</note> has always kept in view in his translation of the <term>Veda</term>; and for the history of religion, which in India, as elsewhere, represents the gradual corruption of simple truth into hierarchical dogmatism and philosophical hallucination, his work will always remain the most trustworthy guide. Nor could it be said, that the tradition of the <term>Brahmans</term>, which <term>Sáyaṇa</term> embodied in his work, after the lapse of at least three thousand years, had changed the character of the whole of the <term>Rig-veda</term>. By far the greater part of these hymns is so simple and straightforward, that there can be no doubt that their original meaning was exactly the same as their traditional interpretation. But no religion, no poetry, no law, no language, can resist the wear and tear of thirty centuries; and in the <term>Veda</term>, as in other works, handed down to us from a very remote antiquity, the sharp edges of primitive thought, the delicate features of a young language, the fresh hue of unconscious poetry, have been washed away by the successive waves of what we call tradition, whether we look upon it as a principle of growth or decay. To restore the primitive outlines of the <term>Vaidik</term> period of thought will be a work of great

We must be able to translate our feelings and ideas into their language at the same time that we translate their poems and prayers into our own. We must not despair even where their words seem meaningless and their ideas barren or wild. What seems at first childish may at a happier moment disclose a sublime simplicity, and even in helpless expressions we may recognise aspirations after some high and noble idea. When the scholar has done his work, the poet and philosopher must take it up and finish it. Let the scholar collect, collate, sift, and reject—let him say what is possible or not according to the laws of the <term>Vaidik</term> <note>Relating to the Vedas, the oldest scriptures of Hinduism.</note> language—let him study the commentaries, the <term>Sūtras</term> <note>Manuals of ritual and legal rules written in a concise, aphoristic style.</note>, the <term>Brāhmaṇas</term> <note>Ancient prose texts that explain the myths and rituals associated with the Vedic hymns.</note>, and even later works, in order to exhaust all the sources from which information can be derived. He must not despise the tradition of the <term>Brahmans</term> <note>The priestly class of ancient India.</note>, even where their misconceptions and the causes of their misconceptions are palpable. 

To know what a passage cannot mean is frequently the key to its real meaning; and whatever reasons may be pleaded for declining a careful perusal of the traditional interpretations of <term>Yāska</term> <note>An ancient Sanskrit grammarian and etymologist, author of the Nirukta.</note> or <term>Sāyaṇa</term> <note>A 14th-century scholar whose commentary on the Rig-Veda is the most influential traditional interpretation.</note>, they can all be traced back to an ill-concealed <note>original: "argumentum paupertatis"</note> ‘argument of poverty’ <note>A Latin phrase used here to suggest that scholars who ignore traditional commentaries do so because they lack the resources or patience to study them, rather than because the texts are useless.</note>. Not a corner in the <term>Brāhmaṇas</term>, the <term>Sūtras</term>, <term>Yāska</term>, and <term>Sāyaṇa</term> should be left unexplored before we venture to propose a rendering of our own. <term>Sāyaṇa</term>, though the most modern, is on the whole the most sober interpreter. Most of his etymological absurdities must be placed to <term>Yāska’s</term> account, and the optional renderings which he allows for metaphysical, theological, or ceremonial purposes, are mostly due to his regard for the <term>Brāhmaṇas</term>. 

These <term>Brāhmaṇas</term>, though nearest in time to the hymns of the <term>Rig-veda</term>, indulge in the most frivolous and ill-judged interpretations. When the ancient <term>Rishi</term> <note>An inspired poet or sage who composed the Vedic hymns.</note> exclaims with a troubled heart, ‘Who is the greatest of the gods? Who shall first be praised by our songs?’ <note>A reference to the famous Rig-Veda hymn 10.121, where each verse ends with the question "To which god (Kasmai devāya) shall we offer our oblation?"</note>—the author of the <term>Brāhmaṇa</term> sees in the interrogative pronoun ‘Who’ <note>The Sanskrit word is "Ka."</note> some divine name, a place is allotted in the sacrificial invocations to a god ‘Who,’ and hymns addressed to him are called ‘Who-ish’ <note>original: "Kāya," meaning related to the god Ka.</note> hymns. To make such misunderstandings possible, we must assume a considerable interval between the composition of the hymns and the <term>Brāhmaṇas</term>. <header>PREFACE. ix</header>

## Preface

...authors of the even later **Niruktas** <note>Ancient treatises on the etymological interpretation and explanation of the Vedas.</note> were deceived by etymological fictions, and both conspired to mislead later and more sensible commentators, such as **Sāyaṇa**, through the weight of their authority. Where **Sāyaṇa** has no authority to mislead him, his Commentary is at least rational; however, his traditional scholastic notions would never allow him to accept the free interpretation that a comparative study of these venerable documents forces upon the unprejudiced scholar. We must, therefore, discover for ourselves the real vestiges of these ancient poets; and if we follow them cautiously, we shall find that with some effort we are still able to walk in their footsteps. We shall feel that we are brought face to face and mind to mind with men who are still intelligible to us, once we have freed ourselves from our modern conceits. We shall not succeed always: words, verses, indeed whole hymns in the **Rig-veda**, will and must remain a mystery to us. But where we can breathe new life into those early relics of thought and devotion, we shall have before us a more genuine antiquity than in all the inscriptions of Egypt or Nineveh; not only old names and dates, kingdoms and battles, but old thoughts, old hopes, old faith, and old errors—the "Human Being" <note>Müller uses the word 'Man' in the universal sense of human nature and history.</note> altogether—old now, but then young and fresh, simple and real in his prayers and in his praises.

How the **Veda** should be interpreted, and how **Sāyaṇa’s** Commentary should be used for that purpose, has lately been shown in a work by M. Adolphe Regnier, “*A Study of the Idiom of the Vedas and the Origins of the Sanskrit Language, First Part, Paris 1855*.” <note>Original title: “Étude sur l’idiome des Védas et les origines de la Langue Sanscrite, Première Partie, Paris 1855.”</note> I may be allowed to quote from this excellent essay the following passage, which lays down with fairness and exactness the principles which ought to be followed by every student of the **Veda**. 

<note>The following is translated from the original French.</note> “I add to the text of the hymns that of the commentary of **Sāyaṇa Āchārya** <note>Āchārya is a title meaning "distinguished teacher" or "spiritual guide."</note>, whom I shall follow in his interpretation wherever it seems to me that logic and grammar permit; every time that I adopt an opinion other than his, I shall give the reasons for it: first, to properly establish the meaning, because in a matter often so obscure, one must always first know the opinion of the Indians themselves; then, because these scholia <note>Ancient explanatory notes or commentaries written in the margins or between lines of a manuscript.</note> will give us the opportunity to become acquainted with some of the most common interpretive habits of the commentators. All those who have had the good fortune to follow the course of Mr. Eugène Burnouf <note>A pioneering French scholar of Sanskrit and Buddhism (1801–1852) who significantly influenced Müller.</note> know what importance he attached to the explanation of the commentaries. The best means, according to him, of ensuring and hastening progress and of accustoming oneself to the difficulties of the language, was to familiarize oneself early...”

## Preface Text

"...at the right hour with the method and style of the grammarians—a style often highly abstract, where synthetic modes of expression are frequently pushed to an extreme." <note>original French: "heure avec la méthode et le style des grammairiens, style souvent très-abstrait et où les procédés d'expression synthétique sont poussés fréquemment à l'excès."</note>

Even if the author had not paid this tribute to the memory of **Eugène Burnouf** <note>A pioneering French scholar of Sanskrit and Buddhism who was Müller’s teacher.</note>, the accuracy and painstaking minuteness of his work would have shown that he belonged to Burnouf’s school; and it is pleasing to see how the spirit of that eminent scholar seems still to be alive in that brilliant senate of learning of which he once formed so illustrious a member, when we read that the French Academy has proposed as one of its last prizes—

> “A commentary, specifically exegetical and grammatical, either on a continuous section or a selection of hymns from the **Rig-veda**, in which care shall be taken to always present and discuss—where appropriate, even if not adopted—the opinion of the commentator **Sāyaṇa Āchārya**.” <note>original French: “Un commentaire particulièrement exégétique et grammatical, soit sur une partie suivie, soit sur un choix d’hymnes du Rig-véda, où l’on aura soin d’exposer toujours et de discuter, s’il y a lieu, même quand on ne l’adoptera pas, l’opinion du commentateur Sáyana Áchárya.”</note>

Such a prize, while it gives a sanction to my work, for which I cannot sufficiently express my gratitude, will, it is to be hoped, act as an encouragement, and bring some of our young Sanskrit scholars toward that line of study which Burnouf pointed out to all of his pupils, as the most sure to lead to real and lasting results.

After what has been stated in the prefaces to the first and second volumes, I have little to add with regard to the manuscripts which I used for the third volume. There is one notice which I lately received from the **Rev. Dr. Stevenson** <note>An early British scholar and missionary in India, known for his work on the Sama-Veda.</note>, the distinguished editor and translator of the **Sama-veda**, and which I subjoin here in confirmation of my views on the local origin of the three families of the manuscripts of **Sāyaṇa’s** Commentary.

> “As I see you have formed a particular family of the two manuscripts **B 1.** and **B 2.**, I may as well mention to you all I have learnt of their history. **B 1.** was procured at **Pune** from a **Vakil** <note>An agent, attorney, or legal representative.</note>, who procured it from the family of the **Guru** <note>Spiritual teacher or counselor.</note> of the late **Peshwa** <note>The hereditary prime minister of the Maratha Empire, who held de facto power.</note>; at least, so he said; and, as the family was poor, and no one else likely to have such a work, there is no reason to discredit his story. It is, as you will see, written by two different scribes, the greater part in what we at Bombay call <term>Kayasthi script</term> <note>The handwriting style used by the Kayasthas, a community traditionally employed as clerks and administrators in Gujarat and North India.</note>, the handwriting of **Kayasthas** from the province of **Gujarat**. The letters in this portion are very deep. The rest is written by a **Deccani Brahman** in what we call the <term>Dakshani script</term> <note>Literally 'Southern script,' the style of Devanagari used by Brahmans in the Deccan region of central India.</note>, and not so deep as the other. This difference is discernible even in the Cave inscriptions in the old character.
> 
> “**B 2.** was copied for **Mr. Burnouf** from that manuscript by a **Pune Brahman**, whom I got to transcribe it for him.”

## Commentary (Mudgala's Abridgment)

->Salutation to the holy Ganesha!<-

> Om. Salutation to You, whose form is Being, Consciousness, and Bliss, who is eternal and pure, whose nature is inward consciousness, and who has become the world.
> Salutation to you, O Ganesha, the remover of obstacles.
> Salutation to you, O Sarasvati; be firm in the awakening of knowledge.
> Having reflected upon the previous commentary on the **Rig-Veda** <term>Bahvricha: an ancient name for the Rig-Veda, meaning "the many-versed"</term> from all sides,
> This work has been extracted with easy understanding by one who considers the original to be profound.

->Just as butter is extracted from milk and gold from sand,<-
->So has this essence been extracted for the accomplishment of understanding for living beings.<-
->By Mudgala of the Mudgalya lineage, through his own experience and well-refined intellect,<-
->This most excellent essence has been extracted as it truly is, by a capable seeker.<-

The state of being a mere "bearer of a burden" for one who lacks the meaning of the Veda is stated in the **Science of Etymology** <term>Nirukta: one of the six Vedangas or auxiliary sciences of the Veda, focusing on word origins</term>: "This man is like a pillar... who does not understand..." <note>A reference to the famous verse: "The man who has studied the Veda but does not understand its meaning is like a pillar, a mere bearer of a burden."</note> Having studied the Veda, the meaning of the Veda must be known. As it is said: Vedic and traditional rites should be performed; through the performance of the duties prescribed by one's own **branch** <term>Shakha: a specific tradition or school of Veda recitation</term> with the abandonment of the fruits of action, purification of the mind will occur. Through purification of the mind, knowledge of the Self will surely arise. For that reason, knowledge of the meaning of the Veda must certainly be achieved.

There are five branches of the Rig-Veda: the Ashvalayani, the Shankhayani, the Shakala, the Bashkala, and the Manduka. Among them, in the **Shakala Collection**, there are ten **Circles** <term>Mandalas: the ten primary books of the Rig-Veda</term>. In the first Circle, there are twenty-four **Sections** <term>Anuvakas: smaller thematic blocks within a Mandala</term>. In the first Section, there are three **Hymns** <term>Suktas: individual hymns</term>. These are revealed for the proper understanding of the deities, the poetic meters, and the seers. There, the hymn beginning "I praise Agni" <note>original: अग्निमीळे (Agni-mīḷe), the very first words of the Rig-Veda</note> is the first hymn, consisting of nine verses. The seer is named Madhuchandas, son of Vishvamitra. The meter is Gayatri; the deity is Agni.

Om, salutation to the holy Ganapati. Om.

When I began this edition, I thought the whole of it would be completed in three or four volumes, and I now find that the first three volumes contain hardly more than half of the whole work. I must confess that I could have wished that the ancient poets of the Veda and their Indian commentators had been less diffuse; for though I believe that no edition of any author in Sanskrit or any other language, for which manuscripts had first to be copied, others to be collated, innumerable references to be verified, and an index to be made of every word, has ever been brought out so rapidly as this edition of the Rig-Veda, yet I feel that ten years of my life are gone, and I know not whether I shall have sufficient time left to finish a work which I once undertook perhaps with too

He includes a sample of Sāyaṇa's word-by-word commentary on the very first verse of the Rig-Veda to illustrate the traditional Indian exegetical style.</summary>

->**PREFACE.**<-
<meta>visible bleed-through from the following page</meta>

much confidence. Yet even if I should not see the completion of this work, I should not be sorry for the time that I have spent on it; and nothing will ever induce me to change the principles which I have hitherto followed, and to give a hasty copy of a **manuscript** <note>original: "MS."</note>, instead of a critical edition of the text and commentary of the **Rig-veda** <term>Rig-veda: The "Knowledge of Verses," the oldest and most sacred collection of ancient Sanskrit hymns, dating back to the second millennium BCE</term>. I have had again for this volume the valuable assistance of my learned friend Dr. Aufrecht <note>Theodor Aufrecht (1822–1907), a distinguished German Indologist and philologist</note>, and I sincerely regret that I shall no longer enjoy this advantage, as much of the correctness and accuracy of the last volumes was due to his conscientious cooperation, joined to the kind assistance which I have never failed to receive from my honoured friend Professor H. H. Wilson <note>Horace Hayman Wilson, the first Boden Professor of Sanskrit at Oxford</note>.

I have to express my deep obligation to the Court of Directors of the Honourable the **East-India-Company**, under the chairmanship of Colonel Sykes, and to the Board of Control <note>The government body overseeing the East India Company’s affairs</note>, under the presidency of the Right Honourable Vernon Smith, for having sanctioned the continuation of this work, and granted funds necessary for its completion—an act of enlightened liberality, which will be applauded by all persons interested in the history of India and in the history of mankind, and by which one of the most important monuments of antiquity will be rescued from oblivion and restored in its integrity.

**M. M.** <note>Max Müller</note>

**OXFORD, June 5, 1856.**

## Critical Notes

-> **Book IV.** <- <note>original: "Maṇḍala IV."</note>

Page 1. line 4. (IV. 1, 1.) **In the hymn to Vāmadeva** <note>original: "vāmadevye"</note> in Manuscript B, written by a second hand <note>original: "secunda manu"</note>. **To Vāmadeva** <note>original: "vāmadeve"</note> in MSS A and B. **Of Vāmadeva** <note>original: "vāmadevasya"</note> in MS Ca. **Vāmadeva** <note>original: "vāmadeva"</note> in MS C. Compare the rules of the grammarian Pāṇini <term>Pāṇini: The ancient Indian linguist whose work standardized Sanskrit grammar</term>, Book IV, Chapter 2, Rule 9.

P. 2. l. 5. (IV. 1, 1.) **Indeed, at those sacrifices** <note>original: "tannadyajñeṣu"</note> in MSS A and C. **Thus, indeed, in those Vedas** <note>original: "tannadevaṃ tannahvedeṣu"</note> in MS B.

P. 2. l. 21. (IV. 1, 2.) **To the praisers** <note>original: "stotṝn"</note> in MS Ca. **To the human gods** <note>original: "nṛdevān"</note> in MS A. **To the gods** <note>original: "devān"</note> in MS B. **To the praising gods** <note>original: "stotṛdevān"</note> in MS C.

P. 4. l. 24. (IV. 1, 5.) **Giver of the highest fruit** <note>original: "atyantaphalapradaḥ"</note> in MSS A and B. **Giver of the most desired highest fruit** <note>original: "atyantamabhīpsitaphalapradaḥ"</note> in MS C.

P. 5. l. 1. (IV. 1, 5.) **The suffix *kanaj* used by grammatical substitution** <note>original: "rātērthavyatyayena kānaj"</note> in MSS A and B. **The suffix *shānach* used with the intensive prefix *yaṅ-luk* by substitution** <note>original: "rāteryaṅkuki vyatyayena śānac"</note> in MS C.

P. 6. l. 1. (IV. 1, 7.) **Wrapped or covered by his own brilliance** <note>original: "svatejasā parivītaḥ pariveṣṭitaḥ"</note> in MS C. **Wrapped** <note>original: "parivītaḥ"</note> in MSS A and B.

P. 7. l. 4. (IV. 1, 9.) **Having caused to be given** <note>original: "dāpayitvā"</note> in MSS A and B. **Having given** <note>original: "dattvā"</note> in MS C.

P. 8. l. 14. (IV. 1, 12.) **Worthy of praise** <note>original: "vipaṇyaṃ"</note>. The manuscripts have "vipaṇyāṃ" <note>the manuscripts use a long 'ā'</note>, but the commentator Sāyaṇa <term>Sāyaṇa: The 14th-century scholar whose commentary is the standard guide for interpreting the Vedas</term> must have read it as **vipaṇyaṃ**.

P. 11. l. 27. (IV. 1, 18.) **In the back-regions of the animal** <note>original: "paśvā pṛṣṭadeśeṣu"</note> in MS C. **In the various regions of the animal** <note>original: "paśvā pṛthagdeśeṣu"</note> in MSS A and B.

P. 13. l. 5. (IV. 1, 20.) After the name **Jātavedas** <term>Jātavedas: An epithet of the fire-god Agni, meaning 'one who knows all created beings'</term>, MS Ca adds: **Or, he is called Jātavedas because creatures find him.** <note>original: "jātānyenaṃ vindaṃtīti vā jātavedāḥ"</note>

P. 16. l. 8. (IV. 2, 6.) **The Talavakāra school says 'Khatavān' means wealth** <note>original: "khatavāndhnadhanānīti talavakāra uktaṃ"</note> in MS C. **'Khatavān' means finding wealth, the letter 'va' was said** <note>original: "khatavān dhanavitvāvakāra ukta"</note> in MS A; omitted in B. The word **Khatavān** has been repeated by editorial conjecture.

P. 18. l. 12. (IV. 2, 9.) **Destruction of sin** <note>original: "āhṛnaranaṃ pāpaṃ"</note> in MS B. MSS A and C omit the word **sin** <note>original: "pāpaṃ"</note>.

P. 18. l. 23. (IV. 2, 10.) **Of the incomplete** <note>original: "asāmastasya"</note> in MS C. **Of whom we should be** <note>original: "asāma yasya"</note> in MSS A and B. The readings of MS A 2, belonging to the scholar Colebrooke, in verse 13—originally left out in Aa (the manuscript sent to me by Mr. Hall)—seem to prove that A 2 is a copy of Aa. See also the notes for Book IV, Hymn 4, Verse 4.

P. 27. l. 25. (IV. 3, 6.) **With what word would you speak?** <note>original: "katkayā brūyāḥ"</note> in MSS A and C. **With what word would you speak of sin?** <note>original: "katpāpaṃ kayā brūyāḥ"</note> in MS B.

P. 29. l. 21. (IV. 3, 9.) **Thus 'jāḥ' means offspring, those to the kinswoman by reason of...** <note>original: "iti jāḥ prajāstā jāmayeṇa nimittena"</note> in MSS A and B. **Thus 'jāḥ' means offspring, those by reason of the fire, the non-dying...** <note>original: "iti jāḥ prajāstāmamayeṇājāmarakhani-nimittena"</note> in MS C.

P. 31. l. 3. (IV. 3, 12.) **Being encouraged** <note>original: "protsāhyamānaḥ"</note> in MSS B and C. **Being seized** <note>original: "pragṛhyamānaḥ"</note> in MS A.

P. 31. l. 12. (IV. 3, 13.) **Of the neighbor** <note>original: "prātiveśyasya"</note> inserted from MS C. **Of the person** <note>original: "janasya"</note> in MS B.

P. 32. l. 25. (IV. 3, 16.) **Mysteries mean things to be understood, secrets** <note>original: "niṇyāni neyārthāni gūḍhāni"</note> in MS C. **Mysteries mean secrets** <note>original: "niṇyā gūḍhāni"</note> in MS B; missing in MS A.

P. 33. l. 27. (IV. 4, 1.) **With the hottest, with the darkest, or with the very hottest** <note>original: "tapiṣṭhaistamastamaistapiṣṭhatamairiti vā"</note> in MS A, and in a manuscript of the Nirukta <term>Nirukta: An ancient treatise on Vedic etymology</term> located in Paris, where **with the very sharpest** <note>original: "tṛpratamaiḥ"</note> is given as a marginal note. Roth's edition has: **With the hottest, with the darkest, with the very sharpest, or with the very crushed.** So has MS B, only using slightly different spellings for "hottest." MS C has: **With the hottest, with the darkest, or with the very hottest.**

P. 35. l. 18. (IV. 4, 4.) **Or makes non-giving to the enemy** <note>original: "arātimadānaṃ vā kurute"</note> is missing <note>original: "deest"</note> in MS B.

## Critical Notes

**P. 36. l. 3. (IV. 4, 5.)** "kin, to a kinsman, a relative, enemies of the self" <note>original: "jāmi jāmiṃ bandhuṃ svadhuśatrūn"</note> in MS A. "kin, to a kinsman, enemies of relatives" <note>original: "jāmijāmiṃ bāndhuśatrūn"</note> in MS C. "to a kinsman, a relative, to one who is not a kinsman, not a relative—such enemies" <note>original: "jāmiṃ bandhumajāmimabandhuṃ etādṛśān śatrūn"</note> in MS B.

**P. 38. l. 12. (IV. 4, 9.)** "He serves" <note>original: "paricarati"</note> in MSS A and B. "Indeed, the praiser serves" <note>original: "paricaratyeva stotā"</note> in MS C.

**P. 41. l. 8. (IV. 4, 14.)** The word "or" <note>original: "vā"</note> before "strengths" <note>original: "vājān"</note> inserted by conjecture.

**P. 41. l. 11. (IV. 4, 14.)** "explained" <note>original: "pratipāditaṃ"</note> in MSS A and B. "requested" <note>original: "prārthitaṃ"</note> in MS C.

**P. 41. l. 21. (IV. 4, 15.)** After "we would serve" <note>original: "paricarema"</note>, MS Ca has "or the potential mood used for the past: we served" <note>original: "bhūte vā liṅ | paryacarāma"</note>.

**P. 42. l. 23. (IV. 5, 1.)** "by the force of the word 'two'" <note>original: "sāmarthyādviriti"</note> in MS C. "by capability, the rule" <note>original: "sāmarthyādvidhiriti"</note> in MSS A and B.

**P. 43. l. 9. (IV. 5, 1.)** "like a worm—like a bank" <note>original: "krimiva—kūlamiva"</note> in MSS A, B, and C; it seems to be a marginal note.

**P. 43. l. 17. (IV. 15, 3.)** "modes" <note>original: "prakārāṃ"</note> in MS C. "another mode" <note>original: "prakārāntaraṃ"</note> in MSS A and B.

**P. 43. l. 19. (IV. 15, 3.)** "being led" <note>original: "nīyamānaḥ"</note> in MS C. "placed" <note>original: "sthāpitaḥ"</note> in MS B; omitted in MS A.

**P. 44. l. 15. (IV. 5, 4.)** "those who are haters" <note>original: "ye dveṣṭāraḥ"</note> is a conjecture. MSS A and C have "haters" after "firm things" <note>original: "sthirāṇi"</note>. MS B omits it, but gives "haters" <note>original: "dveṣṭṝn"</note> after "of the knowing one" <note>original: "jānataḥ"</note>.

**P. 45. l. 24. (IV. 5, 7.)** "equal, of one form for all" <note>original: "samānaṃ sarveṣāmekarūpaṃ"</note>. MSS A, B, and C have "of one form for all, equal."

**P. 46. l. 5. (IV. 5, 7.)** "This is an elliptical simile" <term>elliptical simile: A Sanskrit poetic figure (luptopamā) where a comparison is implied rather than fully stated</term>. MSS A, B, and C have "this elliptical simile."

**P. 46. l. 7. (IV. 5, 7.)** "by lights and so forth" <note>original: "jyotīrādibhi"</note> in MS C. "light, the sun" <note>original: "jyotirāditya"</note> in MSS A and B.

**P. 46. l. 9. (IV. 5, 7.)** "manifested by the gods of this [earth]" <note>original: "ārupitaṃ devairainamasyā"</note> in MS A. "manifested, established, worshiped by the gods" <note>original: "ārupitaṃ āropitaṃ devainamasyaṃ"</note> in MS B. "manifested, established, by the gods..." <note>original: "ārupitaṃ āropitaṃ devairuyā"</note> in MS C.

**P. 48. l. 12. (IV. 5, 12.)** "to be given" <note>original: "dātavyaṃ"</note> in MSS A and B. "that is to be sung" <note>original: "tadgātavyaṃ"</note> in MS C.

**P. 49. l. 1. (IV. 5, 13.)** After "you will protect" <note>original: "pāliyisyaḥ"</note>, MS Ca has "or, those standing in the place of a wife" <note>original: "patnīsthāniyā vā"</note>.

**P. 49. l. 9. (IV. 5, 14.)** "by the hymn" <note>original: "ukthena"</note> in MSS A, B, and C. "in destruction" <note>original: "ucchedane"</note> in MS Ca.

**P. 50. l. 9. (IV. 6, 1.)** "In this place, what is the explanation of the basic part?" <note>original: "ityatra prakṛtyaṃśonuvādaḥ kaḥ"</note> in MS Ca. "In this place, the recitation of the part of the action" <note>original: "ityatra kṛtyaṃśonuvākaḥ"</note> in MSS A, B, and C.

**P. 56. l. 11. (IV. 7, 3.)** "The producer, the maker of growth" <note>original: "prabhāvakaṃ vṛddheḥ kartāraṃ"</note> in MS C. "The initiator" <note>original: "prāraṃbhakaṃ"</note> in MS B. MS A gives no explanation.

**P. 58. l. 4. (IV. 7, 7.)** The word "in the place" <note>original: "sthāne"</note> after "in the abode" <note>original: "dhāmani"</note> inserted from MS C.

**P. 59. l. 9. (IV. 7, 9.)** "you, the sacrifice" <note>original: "yajñaṃ tvāṃ"</note> in MSS B and C. "or whatever" <note>original: "yadyadvā"</note> in MS A.

**P. 59. l. 10. (IV. 7, 9.)** "the cause of production" <note>original: "jananahetuṃ"</note>. "the producer cause" <note>original: "janakahetuṃ"</note> in MSS A and C. "the cause of causes" <note>original: "hetukahetuṃ"</note> in MS B.

**P. 63. l. 24. (IV. 9, 5.)** "the Brahman priest of you" <note>original: "brahmā vo"</note>. "the Brahman priest indeed" <note>original: "brahmā tvo"</note> in MSS A and B. "the Brahman priest..." <note>original: "brahmā gho"</note> in MS C.

**P. 63. l. 25. (IV. 9, 5.)** The word "or" <note>original: "vā"</note> before "assembly-priest" <note>original: "sadasyo"</note> added from MS C.

**P. 68. l. 10. (IV. 11, 1.)** "Auspicious: to be honored" <note>original: "bhadraṃ bhajanīyaṃ"</note> in MS C; omitted in MS A. "Auspicious: blessed" <note>original: "bhadraṃ maṃgalaṃ"</note> in MS B: see also Hymn 10, verse 1.

**P. 71. l. 9. (IV. 12, 1.)** The word "meter" <note>original: "chandaḥ"</note> supplied. "Traishtubha" <note>original: "taidubhaṃ"</note> in MS C. "Traishtubha" <note>original: "taidubho"</note> in MSS A and B.

**P. 71. l. 18. (IV. 12, 1.)** "by the producer" <note>original: "bhāvukena"</note> in MS Ca. "by the destroyer" <note>original: "lopakena"</note> in MS A. "by the gratifier" <note>original: "toṣakeṇa"</note> in MSS B and C.

**P. 72. l. 4. (IV. 12, 2.)** The word "who" <note>original: "yo"</note> after "serving" <note>original: "paricaran"</note> inserted by conjecture. MS C has "he" <note>original: "sa"</note>.

**P. 74. l. 18. (IV. 13, 2.)** "The measured one, conscious of the day" <note>original: "miṃto’hrabhimānī"</note> added from MS C. MS B has only "measured" <note>original: "mito"</note>.

**P. 75. l. 2. (IV. 13, 3.)** "Not releasing" <note>original: "avimuṃcaṃtaḥ"</note> in MSS B and C. "Not restraining" <note>original: "aviṃsaṃyataḥ"</note> in MS A; probably meant for "unrestrained."

**P. 75. l. 10. (IV. 13, 4.)** "For the purpose of taking the essence which maintains the world" <note>original: "jagannirvōhātmakasya rasasyādānārthaṃ"</note>. MSS A and C: "For the purpose of taking that which maintains the world." MS B: "For the purpose of giving that which maintains the world." MS Ca: "For the purpose of taking the essence, which is of the nature of the maintenance of the world."

**P. 75. l. 12. (IV. 13, 4.)** "Cutting down" <note>original: "savṛścvan"</note> in MS C. "Cutting down" <note>original: "savṛścan"</note> in MSS A and B.

**P. 76. l. 2. (IV. 13, 5.)** "united with the firmament" <note>original: "nākena samavetaḥ"</note> in MSS A and C. "united with light" <note>original: "dyutena samavetaḥ"</note> in MS B.

**P. 78. l. 3. (IV. 15, 1.)** The word "of this" <note>original: "asya"</note> after "by the two subsequent [verses]" <note>original: "parābhyāṃ"</note> in MSS A, B, and C.

**P. 78. l. 25. (IV. 15, 2.)** "He goes around" <note>original: "paryaiti"</note> in MSS A, B, and C. "He goes around" <note>original: "pariyāti"</note> in the Aitareya Brahmana <term>Aitareya Brahmana: An ancient prose text explaining the rituals associated with the Rig Veda</term>.

## Critical Notes

**P. 175. l. 9. (IV. 34, 10.)** "striving for strength, powerful" <note>original: "vājayataṃ balavaṃtaṃ"</note> in MS B. "striving for strength, making an effort" <note>original: "vājayantamavayaṃtaṃ"</note> in MS C. "possessing strength" <note>original: "vājavataṃ"</note> in MS A.

**P. 175. l. 11. (IV. 34, 10.)** "to give" <note>original: "dātuṃ"</note> in MS Ca. "give" <note>original: "datta"</note> in MS B. "let him give" <note>original: "dadātu"</note> in MS A. "give ye" <note>original: "dadāta"</note> in MS C.

**P. 175. l. 12. (IV. 34, 10.)** "wealth" <note>original: "rayiṃ"</note> after "give" in MS C. "sage" <note>original: "ṛṣiṃ"</note> in MS A; omitted in MS B.

**P. 175. l. 19. (IV. 34, 11.)** "subsequent" <note>original: "aparakā"</note> in MSS A and B. "departed" <note>original: "apagatā"</note> in MS C.

**P. 175. l. 21. (IV. 34, 11.)** After "you rejoice" <note>original: "saṃmadatha"</note>, the phrase "and so you rejoice with the Maruts <note>The Maruts are storm deities who accompany Indra.</note>" <note>original: "tathā ca marudbhiḥ saṃmadatha"</note> should be added. MS B has "you rejoice; with the Maruts, the kings, the shining ones, etc." <note>original: "saṃmadatha | marudbhiḥ rājabhiḥ rājamānaiḥ etc."</note>

**P. 177. l. 2. (IV. 35, 3.)** From "now that fire" <note>original: "atha so'gniḥ"</note> to "you of skilled hands" <note>original: "kuśalahastā yūyaṃ"</note> is taken from MS C. MS B gives the following commentary: 
> "O Vajas <note>The Vajas or Ribhus are divine artisans who achieved immortality through their skill.</note>, having beautiful hands, O Ribhus, you made the chalice into four; and having done so, O friend Agni <note>The god of fire.</note>, through the grace of the word 'all-pervading,' he said, he spoke, 'drinking of the Soma' <note>Soma is the sacred ritual drink of the Vedic people.</note>. Then you, of the nature of immortality <note>original: "amṛtatvāmaraṇadharmakasya"</note>, etc."

**P. 179. l. 8. (IV. 36, 9.)** "possessing the third gift of Soma" <note>original: "somadānavantaṃ tṛtīyaṃ"</note> in MSS A and B. "that which is the third gift of Soma" <note>original: "somadānavantaṃ yattṛtīyaṃ"</note> in MS Ca.

**P. 179. l. 10. (IV. 36, 9.)** "possessing the sprinkling" <note>original: "paripecanavantaṃ"</note> in MSS A and B. "possessing the cooking" <note>original: "paripaktvanavantaṃ"</note> in MS Ca.

**P. 181. l. 24. (IV. 36, 6.)** "joined with praise" <note>original: "stutyā yukto"</note> in MS C. "by praise" <note>original: "stutyā"</note> in MS A. "worthy of praise" <note>original: "stutyo"</note> in MS B.

**P. 184. l. 5. (IV. 37, 2.)** "for skill, for effort" <note>original: "dakṣāyotsāhāya"</note> in MS C. "for skill, for strength" <note>original: "dakṣāya balāya"</note> in MS B. "for skill, for joy" <note>original: "dakṣāyolhādāya"</note> in MS A.

**P. 188. l. 13. (IV. 38, 4.)** After "of the sacrificer" <note>original: "yajamānasya"</note>, MS Ca has "'Knower' <note>original: "jñāpa"</note> is an epithet for the deity; it means 'one who has become known today.'"

**P. 189. l. 9. (IV. 38, 6.)** Instead of "shining white" <note>original: "śubhrā"</note>, Sāyaṇa <note>The most famous 14th-century commentator on the Rig Veda.</note> explains "well-supported" <note>original: "subhrā"</note>.

**P. 190. l. 10. (IV. 38, 9.)** "The overpowering speed, or the defeat of others—or both" <note>original: "abhibhavinīṃ jūtiṃ parābhibhūtimityubhayaṃ vā"</note>—"The overpowering speed, the defeat of others, the one who knows—or" <note>original: "abhibhavinīṃ jūtiṃ parābhibhūtiṃ cetukaṃ yaṃ vā"</note> in MS A. "...the one who knows, or" <note>original: "cetukaṃ ya"</note> in MS B1 (or "ve" in MS B). "The overpowering speed, the defeat of others, the one who knows—or both" <note>original: "abhibhavatīṃ jūtiṃ parābhibhūtiṃ cetukamubhayaṃ vā"</note> in MS Ca.

**P. 191. l. 13. (IV. 39, 1.)** "fodder" <note>original: "ghāsaṃ"</note> in MS C. "morsel" <note>original: "grāsaṃ"</note> in MSS A and Ca. "dwelling" <note>original: "vāsaṃ"</note> in MSS Aa and B.

**P. 191. l. 13. (IV. 39, 1.)** "illuminating" <note>original: "vivāsayantīḥ"</note> in MSS A, B, and Ca.

**P. 191. l. 15. (IV. 39, 1.)** After "of them" <note>original: "tāsāṃ"</note>, MSS A and Ca have "ghe" (or "ye"). MS B omits several words.

**P. 191. l. 24. (IV. 39, 2.)** "the star which" <note>original: "tārakaṃ yaṃ"</note> in MSS A and Ca. "the one who causes to cross over/savior" <note>original: "tāriyitāraṃ"</note> in MS B.

**P. 192. l. 16. (IV. 39, 4.)** "That which we thought" <note>original: "yattadanmanmahi"</note>—"That indeed we thought" <note>original: "tedanmanmahi"</note> in MSS A and Ca. "What we thought" <note>original: "yadanmanmahi"</note> in MS B.

**P. 194. l. 11. (IV. 40, 2.)** "He sits with speed" <note>original: "turaṇyasat"</note>. "He sits with haste" <note>original: "tvarayā sīdati"</note> added from MS B. "Thus, he sits with speed" <note>original: "iti turaṇyasat"</note> supplied by conjecture.

**P. 194. l. 21. (IV. 40, 3.)** "having followed after" <note>original: "vānusṛtya"</note>—"vānusṛga" in MS A; "cānusṛt" in MS C; "vānu" in MS B.

**P. 194. l. 24. (IV. 40, 3.)** After "like a hawk" <note>original: "śyenasyeva"</note>, MS Ca adds "of that deity."

**P. 195. l. 7. (IV. 40, 4.)** "in the region of the armpit" <note>original: "kakṣapradeśe"</note> in MS C. "in the region of the side" <note>original: "kakṣipradeśe"</note> in MS A. "in the region of the belly" <note>original: "kukṣipradeśe"</note> in MS B: cf. Rig Veda I. 117, 22.

**P. 195. l. 8. (IV. 40, 4.)** "he hastens to go" <note>original: "tvarayati gaṃtuṃ"</note>—"he hastens of the one going" <note>original: "tvarayati gaṃtuḥ"</note> in MS C. "to hasten to go" <note>original: "tvarayitu gaṃtu"</note> in MS A. "having gone, they go" <note>original: "gatvaṃtuṃ yaṃti"</note> in MS B.

**P. 195. l. 24. (IV. 40, 5.)** "situated in the form of the mind" <note>original: "cittarūpasthitaḥ"</note> in MS C. "cittaparūpasthitaḥ" in MS A. "ciṃttanupasthitaḥ" in MS B. "situated in the heart" <note>original: "hṛdi sthitaḥ"</note> in MS Ca.

**P. 195. l. 26. (IV. 40, 5.)** "one who should be worshipped by making into one, the Supreme Soul <note>Paramatman: the ultimate reality or self in Hindu philosophy.</note> to be explained" <note>original: "ekīkutyopāsyaḥ paramātmamaṃtaṃpratipādyaḥ"</note> in MS C. "...having unified the Supreme Soul..." in MS Aa. "...making into one, explained between each other..." in MS A. "unified, explaining the Supreme Soul between one another" <note>original: "ekīkṛtaṃ parasparaparamātmamaṃtaṃpratipādyaḥ"</note> in MS B.

**P. 196. l. 10. (IV. 40, 5.)** "The sacrifice" <note>original: "yajño" - nominative</note>—"The sacrifice" <note>original: "yajñaṃ" - accusative</note> in MSS A, B, and C.

**P. 197. l. 4. (IV. 41, 1.)** "Possessing the oblation, joined with the offering, etc." MS B has "Possessing the oblation, joined with the offering, immortal; immortal by the characteristic of not decaying, free from death; the invoker <note>hotā</note>, not like the sacrificial fire which is the means of attaining heaven."

**P. 197. l. 6. (IV. 41, 1.)** "spoken, uttered" <note>original: "ukta uditaḥ"</note> in MS C. "spoken in what is beneficial" <note>original: "uktaṃ hite"</note> in MS A. "spoken by what is mentioned" <note>original: "uktaḥ abhihitena"</note> in MS B.

**P. 198. l. 10. (IV. 41, 4.)** After "injurious" <note>original: "hiṃsakaḥ"</note>, MSS A and C have "of enemies." MS B omits the whole passage.

**P. 199. l. 1. (IV. 41, 6.)** "in the son, in his son" <note>original: "tanaye tatputre"</note> in MSS A and C. "in the son, in the grandson" <note>original: "tanaye pautre"</note> in MS B.

**P. 199. l. 5. (IV. 41, 6.)** "in wandering around" <note>original: "paritakane"</note>—"paritanake" in MSS A, B, and C. "in wandering around, in going" <note>original: "paritakame gamane"</note> in MS Ca.

It highlights differences in terminology regarding deities like the Ribhus and Agni, and philosophical concepts like the Supreme Soul (Paramatman).</summary>

<meta>This page continues the critical apparatus (Varietas Lectionis) for Book IV of the Rig Veda, specifically hymns 41 through 45. It documents variations in Sāyaṇa’s commentary across manuscripts A, B, C, and Ca, referencing page and line numbers from Max Müller's edition.</meta>

## Critical Notes

->**VARIANT READINGS.**<-

**P. 199. l. 24. (IV. 41, 8.)** "Bounteous ones, the givers of beautiful fruits" <note>original: "sudānū śobhanaphaladātārau"</note> added from MS B.

**P. 199. l. 25. (IV. 41, 8.)** After "desiring" <note>original: "kāmayamānāḥ"</note>, MS A has "for the lotus" <note>original: "padmaye"</note>, MS B "for what is to be reached" <note>original: "yadmayaḥ"</note>, and MS C "for the five" <note>original: "pañcaye"</note>. MS Ca omits it. "Of the five" <note>original: "pañcayo"</note> is a conjecture, or perhaps "of the steps" <note>original: "padānayo"</note>.

**P. 199. l. 25. (IV. 41, 8.)** "For help, for protection" <note>original: "avase rakṣaṇāya"</note> inserted in MS B after "of the five."

**P. 199. l. 27. (IV. 41, 8.)** "Lords of the mind" <note>original: "manasa īśvarā"</note> in MSS A and C. "Lords of the mind" <note>original: "manasā iṣāḥ (i.e., manasa īṣāḥ)"</note> in MS B.

**P. 200. l. 7. (IV. 41, 9.)** "The wealthy owner" <note>original: "dhinikaṃ svāminaṃ"</note> in MS C. "The supreme among masters" <note>original: "adhikaṃ svāmināṃ"</note> in MSS A and B.

**P. 200. l. 15. (IV. 41, 10.)** "Of the nature of a collection of chariots" <note>original: "rathasamūhasvarūpasya"</note> in MS C. "Of the form of a chariot" <note>original: "ratharūpasya"</note> in MSS A and B.

**P. 200. l. 16. (IV. 41, 10.)** "By yourself, personally, and without effort" <note>original: "tvanātmanā svayamevāprayatnena"</note> from MS C.

**P. 200. l. 17. (IV. 41, 10.)** "Help ye" <note>original: "avataṃ"</note> in MSS A and B. "Be ye" <note>original: "bhavataṃ"</note> in MS C.

**P. 200. l. 25. (IV. 41, 11.)** Before "in the winning of strength" <note>original: "vājasātau"</note>, MS B has "then, in our own..." <note>original: "tato'smadīye"</note>.

**P. 201. l. 15. (IV. 42, 1.)** "By the distinction of earth and heaven" <note>original: "kṣitisvargabhedena"</note>. MSS A, B, and C read "the earth, by the distinction of heaven" <note>original: "kṣitiḥ svargabhedena"</note>.

**P. 202. l. 11. (IV. 42, 3.)** From "even those, I myself" <note>original: "te'pyahameva"</note> to "heaven and earth" <note>original: "dyāvāpṛthivyau"</note> is supplied from MS Ca; it is left out in MS A. MS B has: "I have supported the two shining realms, the two worlds of heaven and earth. Furthermore, like the wise artisan-god Tvashtri <note>The divine builder of the cosmos</note> or the Lord of Creatures Prajapati, I set in motion all the worlds" <note>original: "rajasī rājamāne rodasī dyāvāpṛthivyau dhārayaṃ ca dhṛtavānasmi | kiṃca vidvān tvaṣṭeva prajāpatiriva viśvā sarvāṇi bhuvanāni samerayaṃ | prerayāmi"</note>.

**P. 202. l. 20. (IV. 42, 4.)** "Possessing Truth, endowed with the sacrifice" <note>original: "ṛtāvā yajñavān"</note> in MS Ca.

**P. 202. l. 21. (IV. 42, 4.)** "Only for my sake" <note>original: "madarthameva"</note> in MS C. "Capable indeed" <note>original: "samarthameva"</note> in MSS A and B.

**P. 203. l. 6. (IV. 42, 5.)** "I am the defeater of others" <note>original: "pareṣāmabhibhāvito'haṃ"</note> in MSS A and C. "I am the subduer of others" <note>original: "anyeṣāmabhibhāvuko'haṃ"</note> in MS B.

**P. 204. l. 1. (IV. 42, 7.)** "Enclosed and unenclosed" <note>original: "vṛtānāvṛtān"</note> in MS B. "Enclosed, covered" <note>original: "vṛtānācchannān"</note> in MSS A and C.

**P. 204. l. 2. (IV. 42, 7.)** "Those joined to water" <note>original: "apsaṃdhān"</note> in MS C. "Those born in water" <note>original: "apsutān"</note> in MS A. "The clouds, born in water" <note>original: "meghān apsutān"</note> in MS B.

**P. 204. l. 8. (IV. 42, 8.)** "Seeing the kingdom without a king, through the desire for Purukutsa" <note>original: "arājakaṃ dṛṣṭvā rāṣṭraṃ purukutsasya lipsayā"</note> in MS B. "That which was kingless" <note>original: "yatpāvarājakaṃ"</note> in MS Ca.

**P. 204. l. 9. (IV. 42, 8.)** "They spoke again" <note>original: "punaḥ procuḥ"</note> in MSS A and C. "They replied" <note>original: "pratiprocuḥ"</note> in MS B.

**P. 204. l. 24. (IV. 42, 9.)** "He gratified" <note>original: "aprīṇayat"</note> in MS C. "He gratifies" <note>original: "prīṇayati"</note> in MSS A and B.

**P. 205. l. 6. (IV. 42, 10.)** "We are the sharers of you two" <note>original: "yuvāṃ saṃbhaktāro vayaṃ"</note> in MS C. "You... we" <note>original: "yuvāṃ so vayaṃ"</note> in MS A. "We are the sharers of the oblations" <note>original: "haviṣāṃ saṃbhaktāro vayaṃ"</note> in MS B.

**P. 205. l. 13. (IV. 43, 1.)** "In the morning prayer and the Ashvina litany, at the Ashvina rite" <note>original: "prātaranuvākāśvinaśastrayorāśvine"</note> in MS C. "In the morning prayer and the Ashvina season" <note>original: "prātaranuvākāśvine ṛtau"</note> in MSS A and B.

**P. 205. l. 23. (IV. 43, 1.)** "May we prosper or may we attain" <note>original: "śreyasema āyayema vā"</note>. "May we prosper or may we rest" <note>original: "śreyasema śayema vā"</note> in MS A. "Or may we prosper" <note>original: "śreyasema vā"</note> in MS C. "May we attain prosperity" <note>original: "śreyasemāśayema vā"</note> in MS B. The last reading explains "may we prosper" <note>original: "śreyāma"</note> through "may we attain" <note>original: "āśayema"</note> from the root *shang* <note>original: "śaṅ"</note>. However, Sāyaṇa <note>The primary commentator used in this edition</note> seems to give two different etymologies of "may we prosper" <note>original: "śreyāma"</note>, either from the root *shri* <note>to resort to</note> or from the root *shi* <note>to sharpen</note>.

**P. 206. l. 6. (IV. 43, 2.)** "May he be gracious to us" <note>original: "mṛḷayedasmān"</note> in MSS A and C. "May he give us happiness" <note>original: "sukhayedasmān"</note> in MS B. Sāyaṇa frequently explains the root *mrid* <note>original: "mṛḍ"</note> as "he makes happy" <note>original: "sukhayati"</note>.

**P. 207. l. 23. (IV. 43, 6.)** "Understanders, goers" <note>original: "vetāro gaṃtāro"</note> in MS Ca.

**P. 208. l. 10. (IV. 43, 7.)** "The singer of praise" <note>original: "garitāraṃ"</note> found only in MS A.

**P. 208. l. 22. (IV. 44, 1.)** "Of the cow" <note>original: "goḥ"</note>—"of the cows" <note>original: "gavāṃ"</note> in MS Ca.

**P. 209. l. 7. (IV. 44, 2.)** After "an interchange of grammatical case" <note>original: "vibhakti-vyatyayaḥ"</note>, MSS A and C have "for the fuel" <note>original: "samidhe"</note>, while MS Ca has "in prosperity" <note>original: "samṛddhe"</note>.

**P. 209. l. 10. (IV. 44, 2.)** "They carry" or "they cause to carry" <note>original: "vahaṃti vāhayaṃti"</note> in MS Ca.

**P. 210. l. 11. (IV. 44, 5.)** "The sacrificers desiring" <note>original: "icchaṃto yajamānāḥ"</note> in MS C. "Desiring" <note>original: "icchamānāḥ"</note> in MSS A and B.

**P. 211. l. 15. (IV. 45, 1.)** Sāyaṇa has omitted "they are joined" <note>original: "yujyaṃte"</note>; MS B reads "they are joined to the ridge of the shining sun, across the two ridges, on the elevated place" <note>original: "dyotamānasyādityasya sānu yujyaṃte vi sānvau samucchritapradeśe"</note> etc.

**P. 211. l. 17. (IV. 45, 1.)** "Various provisions, foods" <note>original: "vividhāḥ pṛkṣāso'nnāni"</note>. MSS A and C leave out "provisions, foods" <note>original: "pṛkṣāso'nnāni"</note>. MS B gives the entire passage in this way: "Various, pairs, arranged in three ways, this food, eating, trees, foods" <note>original: "vividhāḥ mithunā tredhā vihitaṃ yāta idamannam-aśanaṃ vṛkṣāsaḥ annāni"</note>.

It highlights differences in word choice, grammatical interpretations by Sāyaṇa, and instances where one manuscript preserves a longer explanation than others.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the critical apparatus (Variant Readings) for the Fourth Mandala of the Rig Veda. It specifically covers Suktas 15 through 24, documenting discrepancies in the commentary of Sāyaṇa as found in various manuscripts (labeled A, B, C, Ca, etc.). The page numbers refer to Max Müller's standard edition of the text.</meta>

## Critical Notes

->**VARIANT READINGS.**<-

**P. 79. l. 13. (IV. 15, 4.)** **"Sātyahavya"** <note>original: "sātyahavyo," a proper name</note> || **"Satyēhavya"** in MS C. **"Smṛtyahavya"** in MS Ca. **"Satyatyahanya"** in MS B. **"Atyahanya"** in MS A.

**P. 79. l. 14. (IV. 15, 4.)** **"He caused to sacrifice"** <note>original: "ayīyajaditi"</note> || **"He sacrificed"** <note>original: "yīyaja iti"</note> in MS C. **"He might sacrifice"** <note>original: "yīyajata iti"</note> in MS A. **"He sacrificed in the sacrifice"** <note>original: "yīyajo yajñe iti"</note> in MS B.

**P. 79. l. 22. (IV. 15, 5.)** **"By this, of the sacrificer"** <note>original: "etena yajamānasya"</note> in MSS A and B. **"By this, the sacrificer"** <note>original: "anena yajamānaḥ"</note> in MS C.

**P. 82. l. 3. (IV. 16, 2.)** **"Nearby, just as men release horses"** <note>original: "samīpe aśvāmanunṣyā yathā muñcanti"</note> || **"Nearby, just as men release five"** <note>original: "samīpe pañcāva manuṣyā yathā muñcanti"</note> in MS A. **"Nearby, just as men release horses, they release horses"** <note>original: "samīpe aśvāva manuṣyā yathā aśvāmmuñcanti"</note> in MS C. **"Properly, just as men release horses"** <note>original: "samīcena manuṣyā yathā āśvāmmuñcanti"</note> in MS B.

**P. 83. l. 24. (IV. 16, 6.)** **"Even the mountain or the cloud; 'horse' is a name for a cloud"** <note>original: "parvatamapi meghaṃ vā | aśveti meghanāmaitat"</note> || **"The mountain or the cloud; a name for a cloud"** in MSS A and C. **"The mountain, the cloud, the mountain, thus a name for a cloud"** in MS B. **"Even the mountain or the cloud"** in MS Ca.

**P. 84. l. 10. (IV. 16, 7.)** **"Became"** <note>original: "babhūya"</note> || **"Became"** <note>original: "babhūva"</note> in MSS A and B. **"Was"** <note>original: "ḍabhūḥ"</note> in MS C.

**P. 85. l. 1. (IV. 16, 9.)** **"Thus for the men"** <note>original: "iti nṛmyaḥ"</note> in MSS A and C. **"Thus kind to men"** <note>original: "iti nṛmaṇāḥ"</note> in MS B. It ought to be **"kind to men."**

**P. 89. l. 3. (IV. 16, 17.)** **"Haste"** <note>original: "javodhi"</note> in MSS A, B, and C.

**P. 91. l. 2. (IV. 17, 1.)** **"Thou art great"** <note>original: "tvaṃ mahāँ iti"</note> added by conjecture. The second <term>Viniyoga</term> <note>the liturgical application of a verse</note> is only given by MS C.

**P. 92. l. 18. (IV. 17, 4.)** **"Without destruction"** <note>original: "vināśarahitaṃ"</note> in MS Ca. **"Without thought"** <note>original: "vicārarahitaṃ"</note> in MSS A and C. **"Without falling away"** <note>original: "vicyutirahitaṃ"</note> in MS B.

**P. 98. l. 2. (IV. 17, 16.)** From **"being thus"** <note>original: "evambhūtaṃ"</note> to **"this is the meaning"** <note>original: "ityarthaḥ"</note> is only found in MS C. MS B has: **"We do not abandon, but rather worship, Indra who is the vessel, the support, for the sake of protection... this is the meaning."** <note>original: "kośamādhārabhūtamidramavate rakṣaṇārtha nācyavigrāmaḥ na tyajāmaḥ bhajema ityarthaḥ . ."</note>

**P. 101. l. 24. (IV. 18, 3.)** **"He spoke after"** <note>original: "anvabravīt"</note> || **"He spoke to"** <note>original: "anubravīt"</note> in MS B. **"Let him speak to"** <note>original: "anubravītu"</note> in MSS A and C.

**P. 103. l. 10. (IV. 18, 6.)** **"By that which was extracted by the teacher"** <note>original: "pratipādakoddhṛtena"</note> in MSS A, B, and C.

**P. 103. l. 24. (IV. 18, 7.)** **"Sin"** <note>original: "pāpaṃ"</note> after **"in the form of the murder of a Brahmin"** <note>original: "brahmahatyārūpaṃ"</note> supplied by conjecture.

**P. 108. l. 5. (IV. 19, 2.)** **"Rivers"** <note>original: "nadīḥ"</note> in MS C. **"Waters, of them"** <note>original: "āpaḥ tāsāṃ"</note> in MS B; omitted in MS A.

**P. 112. l. 21. (IV. 20, 2.)** **"Having targeted"** <note>original: "abhilakṣīkṛtya"</note> in MS C. **"Aiming at"** <note>original: "abhilakṣya"</note> in MS B. **"Having turned toward"** <note>original: "abhimukhīkṛtya"</note> in MS A.

**P. 113. l. 25. (IV. 20, 5.)** **"Like"** <note>original: "iva"</note> after **"heroic man"** <note>original: "vīrapuruṣa"</note> added from MS B. **"Who"** <note>original: "yo"</note> added by conjecture.

**P. 114. l. 12. (IV. 20, 6.)** **"Emerging, gone out"** <note>original: "nṛṣṭaṃ nirgataṃ"</note> in MSS A, B, C, and Ca. The usual explanation would be **"fully attained"** <note>original: "nitarāṃ prāptaṃ"</note> or **"pervaded"** <note>original: "vyāptaṃ"</note>.

**P. 114. l. 19. (IV. 20, 7.)** **"The hinderer"** <note>original: "vārayitā"</note> in MSS A and B. **"The preventer"** <note>original: "nivārayitā"</note> in MS C.

**P. 119. l. 10. (IV. 21, 7.)** **"That which he serves"** <note>original: "sevata iti yat tat"</note> in MSS B and C. **"As far as he serves"** <note>original: "sevata iti yāvat"</note> in MS A.

**P. 121. l. 15. (IV. 22, 1.)** **"And the sacrifice, oblation, and so forth"** <note>original: "yajñahavirādikaṃ ca"</note> || **"And that oblation and so forth"** <note>original: "yat havirādikaṃ ca"</note> in MSS A and B. **"And whichever oblation and so forth"** <note>original: "yacca havirādikaṃ ca"</note> in MS C.

**P. 125. l. 10. (IV. 22, 10.)** **"Give to me"** <note>original: "upamāhi dehi"</note> in MS C. **"Brought near, closely connected"** <note>original: "upamāhi upasaṃśliṣṭa"</note> in MSS A and B.

**P. 126. l. 8. (IV. 23, 1.)** **"Of whom"** <note>original: "kasya"</note> after **"of the one performing the burnt offering"** <note>original: "homa-niṣpādakasya"</note> added by conjecture.

**P. 131. l. 2. (IV. 24, 1.)** **"Possessed of supreme sovereignty"** <note>original: "paramaiśvaryayuktaṃ"</note> || **"Supreme sovereignty"** <note>original: "paramaiśvaryaṃ"</note> in MSS A, B, and C.

**P. 132. l. 10. (IV. 24, 4.)** **"Not like then are some lucky ones"** <note>original: "tadānīmiva neme kecana bhāgyavanto"</note> in MS C. <note>The readings in MSS A and B for this line are corrupted and unclear.</note>

**P. 133. l. 3. (IV. 24, 6.)** MS Ca has **"truly indeed"** <note>original: "satyameva"</note> after the word **"thus"** <note>original: "itthā"</note>.

**P. 133. l. 5. (IV. 24, 6.)** The <term>Pada</term> <note>word-by-word</note> manuscripts have **"not discerning"** <note>original: "avivenan"</note> in the text. The <term>Samhitā</term> <note>continuous recitation</note> manuscripts S. 2 and 3 have **"not discerning him indeed"** <note>original: "avivenaṃ tamit"</note>; S. 1 has **"him who does not discern"** <note>original: "avivenantamit"</note>. The commentator Sāyaṇa read it as **"not discerning"** <note>original: "avivenaṃ"</note>.

**P. 133. l. 16. (IV. 24, 7.)** **"Signifying food"** <note>original: "annavācī"</note> in MS A. **"Signifying parched barley"** <note>original: "ata bhṛṣṭayavavācī"</note> in MS C. The entire passage is omitted in MS B.

**P. 134. l. 10. (IV. 24, 9.)** **"You were not sold by me"** <note>original: "na vikrītastvaṃ mayā"</note> in MS C. **"He did not sell before"** <note>original: "na sa vikrītavānpurā"</note> in MSS A and B. **"Not sold by myself"** <note>original: "na vikrītaḥ svayaṃ mayā"</note> in MS Ca.

**P. 134. l. 12. (IV. 24, 9.)** **"Crooked"** <note>original: "vakraṃ"</note> in MS B. **"To speak"** <note>original: "vaktuṃ"</note> in MS A. **"Of the buyer"** <note>original: "kretuḥ"</note> in MS C.

**P. 134. l. 13. (IV. 24, 9.)** **"If made"** <note>original: "cetkṛto"</note> || variants of the same spelling found in MSS C, A, Ca, B, and Aa.

<summary>This page catalogs scholarly variant readings for the Rig Veda, Mandala IV, hymns 15-24, noting differences in word choice and phrasing across several historical manuscripts.</summary>
<keywords>Rig Veda, Sāyaṇa, manuscript variants, Vedic Sanskrit, philology, textual criticism, Indra, sacrifice</keywords>

--- Page 26 ---
<meta>This page continues the "Varietas Lectionis" (Variant Readings) for the Fourth Mandala (Book) of the Rigveda, specifically covering the commentary of Sāyaṇa. The notes track differences between several key manuscripts, primarily those labeled A, B, C, and Ca, as well as references to other Vedic texts like the Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa. This section covers hymns 24 through 33.</meta>

### Page xviii

->**VARIANT READINGS.**<-

**P. 134. l. 13. (IV. 24, 9.)** **"Then, after deliberating on the value of this, a decision is made"** <note>original: "atha mūlyārthamatasyāṃvicāryaiva niścīyaḥ"</note> in MS A. **"Then, even without deliberating on the value of this, a decision..."** <note>original: "atha mūlyārthamatasyāmavicāryaiva niścayaḥ"</note> in MS B. **"Then, after indeed deliberating on the value from this, having decided..."** <note>original: "atha mūlyārthamatasyāt vicāryaiva tu niṇīyaḥ"</note> in MS Ca. MS C reads: **"From this"** <note>original: "metasyāt"</note>.

**P. 134. l. 14. (IV. 24, 9.)** **"Thus so"** <note>original: "ityevaṃ"</note> in MS C. **"Others"** <note>original: "anyeva"</note> in MS A. **"By another"** <note>original: "anyena"</note> in MS B.

**P. 134. l. 17. (IV. 24, 9.)** **"Thus this"** <note>original: "ityayaṃ"</note> in MSS A and C. **"Uttered"** <note>original: "īritaṃ"</note> in MS B.

**P. 135. l. 2. (IV. 24, 10.)** **"With praises"** <note>original: "stutibhiḥ"</note> is missing in MSS A and B.

**P. 135. l. 24. (IV. 25, 1.)** **"He prays for satisfaction. He praises Indra"** <note>original: "tarpaṣāya īṭṭe | indraṃ stauti"</note> in MS C. **"He prays for what is to be offered. He is Indra"** <note>original: "arpaṇīya īṭṭe | sa indraḥ"</note> in MS A. **"He prays for the offering. He entreats that Indra"** <note>original: "arpaṇāya īṭṭe | yācate sa indraḥ"</note> in MS B.

**P. 137. l. 1. (IV. 25, 4.)** **"Supporting/Holding"** <note>original: "dhārayan"</note> in MS C. **"Supporting"** <note>original: "dhārayat"</note> in MSS A and B. Compare with *Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa* 1.4.2.2 and 1.5.1.8.

**P. 137. l. 14. (IV. 25, 5.)** **"Mindful, one desiring praise regarding the gods"** <note>original: "manāyurdevaviṣayastutikāmaśca"</note> in MS C. **"Mindful, meaning the sacrificer who is focused in mind"** <note>original: "manāyumanoyukto yajamānaḥ"</note> in MS B; this is omitted in MS A.

**P. 137. l. 15. (IV. 25, 5.)** **"Well-protecting: a good protector"** <note>original: "suprāvīḥ suṣṭu prāvitā"</note>. MS Aa reads: **"Well-advancing: one who carries forward the oblation well"** <note>original: "suprācīḥ havi suṣṭu prā yitā"</note>. MS A reads: **"Well-advancing: a good advancer."** MS C reads: **"Well-advancing: one who satisfies well with oblations."** MS B reads: **"Well-protecting: one who causes to protect well."**

**P. 139. l. 14. (IV. 26, 1.)** **"I, Vamadeva, became Manu"** <note>original: "vāmadevo manurabhavaṃ"</note> in MSS A and C. **"Vamadeva or Indra became Manu"** <note>original: "vāmadevaḥ indro vā manurabhavaṃ"</note> in MS B.

**P. 139. l. 16. (IV. 26, 1.)** The text from **"The son of Arjuna"** <note>original: "ārjuneyaṃ"</note> down to **"I alone am memory"** <note>original: "smṛtirahumevāsmi"</note> is supplied from MS C; it is omitted in MSS A and B. MS B places the passage **"Furthermore, I adorn the son of Arjuna, Kutsa; I, the wise seer Ushanas, look upon me as Shukra"** after the phrase **"Thus it is said."**

**P. 140. l. 11. (IV. 26, 3.)** **"I scattered and destroyed"** <note>original: "vyairaṃ śvadhvaṃsayaṃ"</note> in MS B. **"I scattered and sent forth"** <note>original: "vyairaṃ prairayaṃ"</note> in MS C. **"I scattered..."** <note>original: "vyairaṃ yaṃ"</note> (fragmentary) in MS A.

**P. 142. l. 21. (IV. 27, 1.)** **"Meaning: they protected me. Now, like a hawk, I have flown out with speed. Having emerged from the body, and knowing my unconditioned self, I have gone forth"** <note>original: "māmarakṣannityarthaḥ | athādhunā śyenaḥ śyenavatsthito'haṃ javasā vegena niradīyaṃ | śarī-rānnirgataṃ | anāvaraṇātmānaṃ jānannirgato'smītyarthaḥ"</note> in MS C. **"Meaning: they protected me. Thereafter, being a hawk, I emerged from the womb with speed"** in MS B. The entire explanation after **"Meaning: they protected me"** is omitted in MS A.

**P. 144. l. 14. (IV. 27, 5.)** **"Of King Soma"** <note>original: "somarājasya"</note> in MSS A and C. **"Of Soma"** <note>original: "somasya"</note> in MS B.

**P. 145. l. 22. (IV. 28, 3.)** **"All [feminine] / All [neuter]"** <note>original: "sarvāṃ sarvāṇi"</note> in MSS A and C. MS B has a clerical error **"Shavim"** for **"All."** Sāyaṇa <note>The 14th-century commentator</note> read it as "all."

**P. 150. l. 22. (IV. 30, 7.)** **"Why, exceedingly"** <note>original: "kimityatyantaṃ"</note> in MSS A and C. **"Exceedingly"** <note>original: "atyantaṃ"</note> in MS B.

**P. 159. l. 7. (IV. 31, 15.)** Before the phrase **"Our best,"** MSS A and B include **"Therefore you"** <note>original: "tasmā tttvaṃ"</note>, while Ca has a truncated version.

**P. 164. l. 7. (IV. 32, 19.)** The commentary to this verse is only provided in MSS B and Ca. MS A has: **"Having left aside [the verse] 'Ten of your jars,' as already stated."**

**P. 165. l. 15. (IV. 32, 24.)** **"In the sacrifices"** <note>original: "yāmeṣu yajñeṣu"</note> in MS B. **"In the journeys/movements"** <note>original: "yāmeṣu gamaneṣu"</note> in MS Ca. **"In the journeys"** <note>original: "yāmeṣu"</note> in MS A.

**P. 167. l. 4. (IV. 33, 2.)** The text from **"By the appearance"** to **"by actions"** is taken from MS Ca. MS B reads: **"Attending by appearance, serving by appearance, with marvelous skills, with the power of one's own actions, the food..."** MS A reads: **"Attending, by serving, by appearance, pervaded by appearance, or rather for the sake of food for the gods like Indra and others..."**

**P. 167. l. 6. (IV. 33, 2.)** **"Because it was said that one attains the status of a god through youth, the sense is that there is unity with the gods"** <note>original: "yuvaśā karveti devaprāmeruktekāntatvena devairakatvādibhāvaḥ"</note> in MS A. MS B ends with **"such is the intent."** MS Ca reads: **"Because the status of a god was mentioned through youth, the sense is they were called such by the gods."**

**P. 167. l. 8. (IV. 33, 2.)** **"By the fallen/shaken"** <note>original: "manāyai cyutena"</note> in MS A. **"For the sake of the mind"** <note>original: "manāyai matikṛte"</note> in MS Ca.

**P. 167. l. 18. (IV. 33, 3.)** **"Possessing good fear/danger(?)"** <note>original: "subhayaḥ"</note> in MSS A and B. **"Of good existence/well-being"** <note>original: "subhavaḥ"</note> in MS Ca.

**P. 168. l. 2. (IV. 33, 4.)** After **"that which they did,"** MS Ca adds: **"Does it mean they covered the limbs of the dead cow with skin and joined its flesh together?"**

**P. 168. l. 13. (IV. 33, 5.)** **"By the statement of attaining godhood, then among them, one is the eldest"** <note>original: "devatvaprāpyuktyena devatvena tadā teṣu madhye eko jyeṣṭhaḥ"</note> in MSS A and B. MS Ca reads: **"Upon the statement of attaining godhood, the eldest..."**

**P. 168. l. 15. (IV. 33, 5.)** **"The next younger and the youngest is Vaja"** <note>original: "tadavaro kaniṣṭho vājaḥ"</note> in MS B. MS Ca reads: **"The younger than him, and then even younger than that."** This is omitted in MS A.

<summary>This page lists variant readings for Sāyaṇa's commentary on the Rigveda, Mandala 4, Suktas 24–33, noting differences in phrasing and omissions across several manuscripts. It highlights technical disputes regarding the status of the Ribhus and the symbolic rebirth of the sage Vamadeva.</summary>

## Critical Notes

...thus it is heard that they should cause the eating. It seems that **the spotted ones** <note>original: "pṛṣāsaḥ"</note> as **foods**, just as **are joined** appeared before, was inserted in MS B from the margin. **"Which is ordained in three ways: this food, eating, and drinking; let them cause [us] to eat, thus it is heard"** in MS Ca. **"And here, ordained in three ways: this food, eating, and drinking; let them cause [us] to eat, thus it is heard"** in MS A.

**P. 213. l. 16. (IV. 45, 6.)** **"They with their arms"** <note>original: "te bāhubhiḥ"</note> in MSS A, B, and C.

**P. 213. l. 17. (IV. 45, 6.)** **"Destroying"** <note>original: "dhvaṃsayanto"</note> inserted from MS Ca., which reads after **rays:** **"They, with arms, with well-known lights, those two [gods] who possess curds, shaking, let them destroy the darknesses"** etc.

**P. 220. l. 4. (IV. 49, 2.)** **"In the lovely mouth, beautiful, pleasant. || In the lovely mouth, the Soma"** in MS A. **"In the lovely mouth, the Soma"** in MS B1. **"O Indra and Brihaspati, beautiful, pleasant"** in MS B4 (added by a second hand). MS Ca. omits the whole passage.

**P. 220. l. 12. (IV. 49, 3.)** **"Related || Related [one]"** in MSS A, B, and C. See the Sanskrit lexicon **Amara-kosha II. 2, 5.**

**P. 221. l. 21. (IV. 50, 1.)** **"To the pleasant-tongued one, the gladdening-tongued one, the delighting-tongued one, to him"** in MS Ca. **"To the pleasant-tongued one, to him"** in MSS A and C. **"The pleasant-tongued one: he whose tongue is pleasant is the pleasant-tongued one; to him"** in MS B.

**P. 222. l. 3. (IV. 50, 2.)** **"They dwell near"** in MSS A and C2. **"They dwell near"** <note>spelled with a long 'ā'</note> in MS B. **"They cause to dwell near"** <note>a causative verb form</note> in MS Ca.

**P. 227. l. 25. (IV. 51, 3.)** After **"in the middle of the universe"**, MS Ca. reads **"within the interior of the darkness"**.

**P. 228. l. 9. (IV. 51, 4.)** **"Those two, also in that region"** in MS B. **"Those two [feminine], also in that region"** in MS A. **"Which two, also in that region"** in MS Ca.

**P. 229. l. 3. (IV. 51, 6.)** **"The two boundaries"** in MSS A and B. **"The two eyes"** in MS Ca.

**P. 229. l. 4. (IV. 51, 6.)** **"Just as [plural] || Just as [singular]"** in MSS A, B, and C.

**P. 229. l. 12. (IV. 51, 7.)** **"They are indeed helpful"** in MS Ca. **"They are helpful by their own nature"** in MS A. **"Wandering..."** <note>original: "°cāriṇyaḥ"</note> in MS B.

**P. 229. l. 24. (IV. 51, 8.)** **"Due to the lack of separation from a region of uniform appearance"** in MS Ca.

**P. 229. l. 25. (IV. 51, 8.)** **"The priest, the bird, etc."** in MS Ca. **"The priest, the will, etc."** in MS A. **"The priest, etc."** in MS B.

**P. 230. l. 2. (IV. 51, 8.)** **"Due to the occasion and the helpfulness"** in MSS A and B. **"Due to being the agent of expansion"** in MS Ca.

**P. 230. l. 9. (IV. 51, 9.)** **"Of uninjured color"** <note>original: "ahiṃsitavarṇī"</note> taken from MS Ca.

**P. 231. l. 3. (IV. 51, 11.)** **"Shining forth, having various lights"** in MS Ca.

**P. 232. l. 9. (IV. 52, 4.)** **"Being separated"** in MSS B and C. **"Being joined"** in MS A.

**P. 232. l. 22. (IV. 52, 6.)** **"Following, after"** taken from MS Ca.; omitted in MSS A, B, and C2. MS B has **"follow, protect"** written by a second hand.

**P. 232. l. 24. (IV. 52, 7.)** The **ritual application** <note>term: viniyoga; instructions on how a verse is used in a ceremony</note> is given in MS Ca. only.

**P. 235. l. 11. (IV. 53, 5.)** **"Between the earth, not"** in MSS A and B. **"Between, it is the earth"** in MS Ca. **Yāska, in the etymological commentary Nirukta II. 10: "It is between the earth"** <note>original: "antarā kṣāntaṃ bhavati"</note>.

**P. 235. l. 17. (IV. 53, 5.)** **"The three heavens named Indra, Prajapati, and Satya"** in MS Ca. **"The three of Agni, of heaven, named Indra, Prajapati, and Satya"** in MS A. **"The three heavens named Agni, Indra, and Prajapati"** in MS B.

**P. 238. l. 2. (IV. 54, 3.)** **"Sinless, without evil"** in MS B.

**P. 238. l. 12. (IV. 54, 4.)** **"May he not perish; may he not be harmed"** in MSS A and B. **"May he not perish; may he not be harmed"** <note>the scribe used a different verb voice (ātmanepada) here</note> in MS Ca.

**P. 238. l. 13. (IV. 54, 4.)** **"'Of the divine,' in the locative || 'Of the divine,' in different bases"** in MSS A, B, and C2. **"In the divine locative"** in MS Ca.

**P. 238. l. 16. (IV. 54, 4.)** **"Which, who || who"** in MS B. **"whom"** in MS Ca. **"yī"** <note>illegible or corrupt</note> in MS A.

**P. 238. l. 17. (IV. 54, 4.)** **"Impels, he impels"** in MS B.

**P. 239. l. 1. (IV. 54, 5.)** **"Going [to] you"** in MSS A and C. **"Living beings going by you"** in MS B.

**P. 239. l. 24. (IV. 55, 1.)** The whole passage from **"And who is the protector..."** to **"the one who wards off"** is taken from MS Ca.

**P. 240. l. 5. (IV. 55, 1.)** **"'Co-ordinate' because of the common reference"** in MSS A and C2. **"'In proximity' means that which is co-ordinate"** in MS B. **"On account of the rule 'When followed by a co-ordinate vocative...' (Pāṇini 8.1.73), because of the prohibition of treating the word as if it were non-existent"** in MS Ca.
