## Hymn Text
**What will you say, O Agni, as you grow strong upon your altars? What will you say to the Wind, the powerful, the seeker of splendor? What to the Wanderer, to the Truthful One, to the Earth? What, O Agni, to Rudra, the slayer of men?** ॥ ६ ॥

**Word-by-word Analysis:**
**What | upon the altars | growing | O Agni | what | to the Wind | to the very powerful | to the seeker of splendor | to the wanderer | to the truthful one | to the earth | will you speak | what | O Agni | to Rudra | to the slayer of men.** ॥ ६ ॥

---

## Commentary (Sayana)
O Agni, you who are **growing** <note>original: vṛdhasānaḥ</note>—increasing in strength through offerings of clarified butter and other oblations—upon the various **sacrificial altars** <note>original: dhiṣṇyāsu</note>, what will you say [on our behalf]? What will you say to **the Wind** <note>original: vātāya</note>, who possesses **mighty strength** <note>original: pratavase</note>, who is a **seeker of splendor** <note>original: śubhaṃye</note>, and who is a **wanderer** <note>original: parijmane</note> traveling everywhere? What will you say to the **Truthful One** <note>original: nāsatyāya</note>—the leader of truth, or one in whom no untruth exists? Or to the Earth <note>original: kṣe</note>? <note>Commentary continues on next page</note>

<vocab>
- Agni: The God of Fire, who acts as a messenger between humans and gods.
- Varuna: The guardian of cosmic law and the punisher of sins.
- Mitra: A solar deity associated with friendships, contracts, and the day.
- Aryaman: A solar deity representing chivalry and the rules of society.
- Bhaga: The deity of fortune, wealth, and destiny.
- Dhishnyas: The small auxiliary fire-altars in the sacrificial arena.
- Nasatya: An epithet for the Ashvin twins, the divine physicians.
- Rudra: A fierce deity associated with storms and destruction, the precursor to Shiva.
- Agas: A term for moral transgression or sin.
</vocab>

## Commentary (Sayana)
<note>Conclusion of commentary on Rig Veda 4.3.6</note>
...to the god of wind <note>original: Vāyave</note>. Alternatively, the text may mean "to the two Nasatyas" <note>the Ashvins, the twin physicians of the gods</note>, involving a change in grammatical number. Regarding the word **Earth** <note>original: kṣe</note>: this refers to the ground, for living beings dwell <note>original: kṣiyanti</note> upon it. Regarding that **Earth**, how <note>original: kat</note> could you speak of our failings? O Agni, how could you speak of our sin <note>original: āgas</note> to the god **Rudra**, who is the **slayer of men** <note>original: nṛghne</note>—specifically those men who are sinners?

Regarding the term **thriving** <note>original: vṛdhasānaḥ</note>: this is derived from the root meaning 'to increase' <note>original: vṛdh</note>. The term **glory-seeking** <note>original: śubhaṃye</note> refers to one who attains splendor; the grammatical structure preserves the accusative case ending. The word for **Earth** <note>original: kṣe</note> comes from the root meaning 'to dwell.' The word **slayer of men** <note>original: nṛghne</note> uses the root for 'striking' or 'killing' <note>original: han</note> and is formed in a way common to Vedic grammar.

## Hymn Text
**How, O Agni, will you speak to the great Pushan, the bringer of prosperity? How to Rudra, the well-sacrificed giver of oblations? How to the wide-striding Vishnu? What will you say of our sin? What will you say to the Great Destroyer, the Autumn?** ॥ ७ ॥

**Word-by-word Analysis:**
**How | to the great | to the sustainer of prosperity | to Pushan | how | to Rudra | to the one worthy of worship | to the giver of oblations | how | to Vishnu | to the wide-striding | the seed (sin) | will you speak | what | O Agni | to the arrow (or Autumn) | to the great.** ॥ ७ ॥

---

## Commentary (Sayana)
O Agni, for what reason or by what cause would you speak of our sin to the god named **Pushan**, who is **great** and the **sustainer of prosperity** <note>original: puṣṭimbharāya</note>? How would you speak of it to **Rudra**, who is **well-worshipped** <note>original: sumakhāya</note>—meaning one who receives excellent sacrifices—and who is the **giver of oblations** <note>original: havirdas</note>? In this context, Agni himself acts as the giver of oblations to the gods, or perhaps Rudra is so called because he gives the results of the Svishtakrit sacrifice.

Furthermore, how would you speak of our **sin** <note>original: retaḥ</note>—here meaning that which causes destruction—to **Vishnu**, who is **wide-striding** <note>original: urugāyāya</note>, meaning he who is praised by many or possesses vast fame? And what would you say to the **Great Arrow** <note>original: śarave bṛhatyai</note>? The word **Arrow** <note>original: śara</note> refers here to the **Autumn** <note>original: śarad</note>, for the autumn "shatters" or "ripens" the crops. Alternatively, it refers to the goddess of destruction, **Nirriti**, who strikes down life. What would you say of our failings to that great Autumn or to that Great Destruction?

The term **sustainer of prosperity** <note>original: puṣṭimbhara</note> is derived from the root meaning 'to bear or nourish' <note>original: bhṛ</note>. The word **giver of oblations** <note>original: havirdas</note> carries a specific Vedic accent on the final syllable. The word **arrow** or **autumn** <note>original: śaru</note> comes from the root meaning 'to injure' or 'to shatter' <note>original: śṝ</note>, indicating the season's power to harvest or destroy.

<header>Mandala 4, Anuvaka 1, Sukta 3] || Third Book (Ashtaka) || 29</header>

## Hymn Text

-> **How shall you answer the host of the Maruts, the followers of Truth? How shall you respond to the great Sun when you are questioned? How will you answer Aditi, the infinite, or the swift Wind? O Agni, Knower of all created beings, you who are wise, accomplish our worship among the gods of heaven.** ॥ ८ ॥ <-

---

## Commentary (Sayana)

O Agni, for what reason <note>original: kathā</note> would you speak <note>original: pratibrūyāḥ</note> of my sin <note>original: āgas</note> to the **Maruts** <note>the storm gods</note>, who are the followers of **Truth** <note>original: ṛtāya</note> and who constitute a host of power? Being **questioned** <note>original: pṛcchyamānaḥ</note> by him, how would you speak to the great, mighty **Sun** <note>original: sūre</note>? Likewise, how would you answer the goddess **Aditi** <note>mother of the gods</note> or the swift-moving **Wind** <note>original: vāyave</note>? [Alternatively, the text refers to Agni answering for the sake of one who is not miserly and is swift]. Since this is so, O Agni, **Knower of all created beings** <note>original: jātavedas</note>, you who are **wise** <note>original: cikitvān</note> and know all things, **accomplish** <note>original: sādha</note> the worship of the shining gods of **Heaven** <note>original: divaḥ</note>. Or, accomplish the task of carrying the sacrifice to the heavenly world.

**Technical Note on the word "Sun"** <note>original: sūre</note>: In Vedic grammar, certain case endings are optional; here, the dative ending for "to the Sun" takes a unique form. 
**Technical Note on "Being Questioned"** <note>original: pṛcchyamānaḥ</note>: This comes from the root meaning 'to ask' <note>original: pracch</note>; it is a passive form where the vowels shift according to specific grammatical rules. 
**Technical Note on "Accomplish"** <note>original: sādha</note>: This comes from the root meaning 'to succeed' or 'to complete'; it is used here in the imperative mood to request the god to finalize the ritual.

---

-> ॥ Here begins the Ninth Verse ॥ <-

## Hymn Text

**Through Truth I praise the constant Truth: the milk of the cow. Though she is raw, O Agni, she contains the sweet, cooked milk. Though she is black, she nourishes with white food, with that milk which is for all people and is the source of immortality.** ॥ ९ ॥

-> **Through Truth | the Truth | constant | I praise | — | of the cow | raw | together | sweet-tasting | cooked | O Agni | black | being | with white | with food | this | for people/immortal | with milk | she nourishes.** ॥ ९ ॥ <-

---

## Commentary (Sayana)

O **Agni**, through the **Truth** <note>original: ṛtena</note>—the true performed sacrifice—I **praise** <note>original: īḷe</note> the **milk** <note>original: payas</note> of the **cow** <note>original: goḥ</note>, which is the constant, underlying water of immortality. The hidden meaning is: "I ask you for the cow’s milk for the sake of the ritual offerings." This cow, though she is **raw** <note>original: āmā; meaning unheated/living</note>, holds <note>original: sacā</note> within her the **cooked** <note>original: pakvam</note> milk which possesses **sweetness** <note>original: madhumat</note>. Even if she is **black** <note>original: kṛṣṇā</note> in color, this cow **nourishes** <note>original: pīpāya</note> us with **white** <note>original: ruśatā</note> **food** <note>original: dhāsinā</note> that sustains all living beings. This milk is **for all people** <note>original: jāmaryeṇa; literally 'born for men'</note> and is the cause of non-death <note>original: amaryeṇa</note>. It is your greatness, Agni, that you transform forms in this way.

**Technical Note on "Nourishes"** <note>original: pīpāya</note>: This is a specific Vedic form of the root meaning 'to swell' or 'to overflow,' describing how the cow’s udder provides abundance.

## Hymn Text (Word-by-word analysis for Verse 10)

With clarified butter | indeed | surely | the Bull | even | anointed | the Hero | Agni | with milk | from the back |
not-quivering | he moved | the sustainer of vitality | the Showerer | the bright [fluid] | he milked | the dappled one | from the udder ॥ 10 ॥

---

## Commentary by Sayana

The **Bull** <note>original: vṛṣabhaḥ</note>, the showerer of desired rewards, the **Hero** <note>original: pumān</note>, the most excellent—that Agni is **anointed** <note>original: aktaḥ</note>, or sprinkled, with **clarified butter** <note>original: ghṛtena</note>, which is the essence of truth, and with supporting, nourishing **milk** <note>original: payasā</note>. The particles *hi*, *ṣma*, and *cit* are used here as rhythmic fillers. Agni, the **sustainer of vitality** <note>original: vayodhāḥ</note> or giver of food, remained **steady** <note>original: aspandamānaḥ</note>, staying in one place, yet he **moved** <note>original: acarat</note>; that is, he moves everywhere through his radiant light. Likewise, the **Showerer** <note>original: vṛṣā</note> of rain, the dappled **Sun** <note>original: pṛśniḥ</note>, **milked** <note>original: duduhe</note> the bright fluid or milk from the **udder** <note>original: ūdhaḥ</note>, representing the mid-air or the clouds.

**Technical Notes:** **Anointed** <note>original: aktaḥ</note> is derived from the root *añj* (to manifest, smear, or move). **Milked** <note>original: duduhe</note> is a double-transitive verb here. **Udder** <note>original: ūdhaḥ</note> is treated as the direct object of the action.

## Hymn Text (Verse 11)

Breaking the mountain with clarified butter, the Angirases shouted together with the cows. The heroic leaders sat happily around the Dawn; the Sun became visible when Agni was born. ॥ ११ ॥

**Word-by-word analysis:**
With clarified butter | the mountain | apart | they were | breaking | together | the Angirases | they shouted | with the cows |
happiness | the leaders | around | they sat | the Dawn | manifest | the Sun | became | being born | Agni ॥ ११ ॥

---

## Commentary by Sayana

The **Angirases** <note>a group of celestial seers including figures like Medhatithi</note>, by means of **clarified butter** <note>original: ghṛtena</note>—representing the power of the sacrifice—were **breaking** <note>original: bhidantaḥ</note> or splitting the **mountain** <note>original: adrim</note> that confined the cows of light. They **cast it aside** <note>original: vyasan</note>. Consequently, they **shouted together** <note>original: sam navanta</note> or joined with the recovered **cows**. The **heroic leaders** <note>original: naraḥ</note>, who lead the ritual acts, **sat around** <note>original: pari sadan</note> or reached the goddess **Dawn** <note>original: uṣasam</note> with **happiness** <note>original: śunam</note>. Then, the **Sun** <note>original: svaḥ</note> also became visible to all. All of this occurred when you, **Agni**, were **born** <note>original: jāte</note> through the act of ritual churning.

**Technical Note:** **Cast aside** <note>original: vyasan</note> is a verb form indicating the act of throwing or scattering.

<vocab>
- **Agni**: The deity of fire, central to the Vedic sacrifice and seen as a messenger between humans and gods.
- **Angiras**: A semi-divine family of priests/seers credited with finding the lost light (cows) in Vedic mythology.
- **Clarified Butter (Ghruta)**: Melted butter used in offerings; symbolizes light, truth, and the fuel of the ritual fire.
- **Bull (Vrushan)**: A common metaphor for Agni or Indra, signifying strength, virility, and the "showering" of blessings.
- **Sun (Surya/Svar)**: The ultimate source of light, often appearing in the Veda after the ritual birth of Agni.
- **Dawn (Ushas)**: The goddess who precedes the sun; her appearance marks the success of the morning ritual.
- **Milk (Payas)**: Symbolizes both the physical offering and the cosmic fluids of rain and life-force.
- **Mountain (Adri)**: In Vedic myth, the "rock" or cave where the Panis (demons) hid the cows (rays of light or rain).
</vocab>

### Book 3, Page 31. Mandala 4, Chapter 1, Hymn 3.

## Commentary (Sayana) — Conclusion of Verse 12
Joined with these flowing **waters** <note>original: arṇobhir-udakaiḥ</note>, the **divine** <note>original: devīḥ</note> rivers, by means of the **sacrifice** <note>original: ṛtena</note> or through the truth, being ever-moving, should flow **forever** <note>original: sadam-it</note> to their destination. An illustration is given: **Like a horse** <note>original: vājī na</note>. Just as a horse goes forward when **urged** <note>original: prastubhānaḥ</note> or encouraged in races, so do the waters. 

**Technical Notes:** **Waters** <note>original: āpaḥ</note> is derived from the root *āp* (to pervade or reach). It uses the suffix *kvip* in the sense of an action. **Urged** <note>original: prastubhānaḥ</note> comes from the root *stubh*, which refers to the act of praising or chanting.

## Hymn Text (RV 4.3.13)
O Agni, never go to the **sacrifice** <note>original: yakṣam</note> of the **injurer** <note>original: huraḥ</note>, nor to that of the **harmful neighbor** <note>original: veśasya praminataḥ</note>, nor to that of a **kinsman** <note>original: āpeḥ</note>.
O Agni, do not accept the **oblation** <note>original: vṛṇam</note> of a **crooked brother** <note>original: bhrātur-anṛjoḥ</note>. May we not **enjoy** <note>original: bhujema</note> the **wealth** <note>original: dakṣam</note> of a friend who is a **foe** <note>original: ripoḥ</note>. ॥ 13 ॥

### Word-by-Word Analysis (Pada-patha)
Not | of anyone | the sacrifice | always | indeed | of the injurer | go | not | of the neighbor | of the harmful | not | of the kinsman |
not | of the brother | O Agni | of the crooked | the oblation | desire | not | of the friend | the wealth | of the foe | may we enjoy ॥ 13 ॥

## Commentary (Sayana)
O Agni, do not **ever go** <note>original: mā gāḥ</note> to the **sacrifice** <note>original: yakṣam</note> of any living being who is our **injurer** <note>original: huraḥ</note>. Never go there at any time. Do not go to the sacrifice of a **neighbor** <note>original: veśasya</note> who is **harmful** <note>original: praminataḥ</note>. Likewise, do not go to the sacrifice of a **kinsman** <note>original: āpeḥ</note>—meaning a relative other than ourselves. Furthermore, do not **desire** <note>original: mā veḥ</note> the **oblation** <note>original: vṛṇam</note>, which is like a debt to be given, from a **brother** <note>original: bhrātuḥ</note> who is **crooked** <note>original: anṛjoḥ</note> or deceitful in heart. Similarly, may we not **enjoy** <note>original: mā bhujema</note> the **wealth** <note>original: dakṣam</note> or power capable of enjoyment belonging to a **foe** <note>original: ripoḥ</note> who acts like a friend. Instead, may we only enjoy the wealth given by you.

**Technical Notes:** **Injurer** <note>original: huraḥ</note> is from the root *hvṛ* (to bend or strike). **May we enjoy** <note>original: bhujema</note> is from the root *bhuj* (to protect or eat); it is used here in the potential mood (benedictive) with a specific Vedic grammatical variation in the ending.

<meta>This page concludes the analysis of Verse 14 and provides the complete text and commentary for Verse 15 and the first half of Verse 16 of Mandala 4, Hymn 3. It continues the theme of invoking Agni's favor through specific prayers and explores the mystical origins of the Angiras clan.</meta>

## Hymn Text

Slay the **demon** <note>original: rakṣo</note>, even if it be **great** <note>original: mahi</note>, or **growing** <note>original: vāवृधānam</note>, or already **mighty** <note>original: vṛddhaṃ</note>, which acts as an **obstructor** <note>original: bādhakam</note>. ॥ 14 ॥

---

-> ॥ Now for the Fifteenth Verse ॥ <-

O **Agni** <note>the Fire-God</note>, be **well-disposed** <note>original: sumanāḥ</note> toward us through these **hymns** <note>original: arkaiḥ</note>; O **Hero** <note>original: śūra</note>, touch our **sacrificial foods** <note>original: vājān</note> through these **prayers** <note>original: manmabhiḥ</note>. And, O **Angiras** <note>a sacred title for Agni</note>, accept our **sacred prayers** <note>original: brahmāṇi</note>; may the **divine-reaching** <note>original: devavātā</note> **praise** <note>original: śastiḥ</note> strengthen you. ॥ 15 ॥

**Word-by-Word Analysis:**
Through these | be | well-disposed | O Agni | through hymns | these | touch | through prayers | O Hero | sacrificial foods |
And | sacred prayers | O Angiras | accept | together | your | praise | divine-reaching | strengthen. ॥ 15 ॥

---

-> ॥ Now for the Sixteenth Verse ॥ <-

O **Creator** <note>original: vedho</note>, for you who are the **knower** <note>original: viduṣe</note>, I have spoken these all-pervading **secret words** <note>original: niṇyā vacāṃsi</note> and **insightful sayings** <note>original: kāvyāni</note>; as a **wise sage** <note>original: vipraḥ</note>, I have proclaimed them with **prayers** <note>original: matibhiḥ</note> and **hymns** <note>original: ukthaiḥ</note>. ॥ 16 ॥

**Word-by-Word Analysis:**
These | all | for the knower | for you | O Creator | reaching the goal | O Agni | secret | words |
sayings | for the wise poet | insightful poems | I have proclaimed | with prayers | the wise sage | with hymns. ॥ 16 ॥

---

## Commentary (Sayana)

**[Regarding Verse 14]:**
In the combined text <note>original: saṃhitā</note>, there is a specific grammatical change of the 'n' sound to 'ṇ' because of the preceding letters. The word for **protecting** <note>original: rarakṣāṇaḥ</note> is derived from the root *rakṣ* (to protect). The word **slay** <note>original: jahi</note> comes from the root *han* (meaning to strike or kill); in the imperative mood, the root *han* is replaced by *ja*. According to technical rules of grammar, the usual dropping of the suffix does not occur here.

**[Regarding Verse 15]:**
**O Agni**, through these **hymns** <note>original: arkaiḥ</note> of mine—which are weapons of praise—be **well-disposed** <note>possessing a beautiful mind</note>. **O Hero**, through our **prayers** <note>original: manmabhiḥ</note>, **touch** or accept **these** sacrificial foods of ours. Furthermore, he is addressed as **Angiras**. This title applies to Agni because he "goes toward" <note>original: angati</note> the oblations. Alternatively, the sacred teaching <note>original: brāhmaṇa</note> states: "Those which were glowing embers <note>original: angārāḥ</note> became the Angirases." Because Agni is the cause or source of these Angiras sages, he is called Angiras. This is supported by another verse: "Those who are the sons of Angiras were born from Agni" <note>original: Rig Veda 10.62.5</note>. O such an Agni, **accept** and enjoy our **sacred prayers**. The **praise** which is **divine-reaching**—meaning it has gone forth to praise the gods—should **strengthen** <note>original: saṃjareta</note> you.

**Technical Note:** The word **touch** <note>original: spṛśa</note> comes from the root *spṛś* (to touch). **Divine-reaching** <note>original: devavātā</note> is derived from the root *vā* (to go). It is a compound where the "divine" element refers to the destination of the praise.

**[Regarding Verse 16]:**
**O Creator** <note>original: vedho</note>, you who are the disposer or ordainer. **O Agni**, for you who are the **knower**—one who possesses knowledge of the sacrificial acts—and a **wise poet** <note>original: kavaye</note> who sees beyond the surface, I have spoken these things. These include: **goal-reaching** <note>original: nīthāni</note> words that bring about results; **secret** <note>original: niṇyā</note> words; and **sayings** <note>original: nivacanāni</note> that must be spoken clearly. These are **insightful poems** <note>original: kāvyāni</note> created by wise sages. All these **words** and sentences...

<note>The text continues on the next page, further explaining the nature of these poetic utterances.</note>

<summary>This page concludes the prayer to Agni to destroy obstacles and presents a request for the deity to accept specific hymns and sacrificial foods. It highlights Agni's identity as the source of the Angiras sages and the "knower" of secret, poetic wisdom.</summary>

<keywords>Agni, Angiras, secret wisdom (niṇyā), prayer (manman), hymns (arka), sage (vipra), sacrifice, Vedic grammar, Sayana's commentary</keywords>

<meta>This page concludes the commentary on Verse 16 of the third hymn and begins the fourth hymn of the fourth Mandala. The previous page detailed the sage's "secret words" and insightful prayers offered to Agni, the all-knowing creator. This new section shifts focus to Agni's role as the "Slayer of Demons" (Rakshohan), utilizing a more martial and protective tone.</meta>

Accompanied by these **prayers** <note>original: matibhiḥ</note> that are worthy of contemplation, by **songs of praise** <note>original: stotraiḥ</note>, and **recitations** <note>original: śastraiḥ</note>, I, the wise sage, have proclaimed [this]. I have spoken. The meaning is: may you enjoy these offerings.

-> ॥ Thus ends the twenty-second Varga of the fourth chapter of the third book (Ashtaka) ॥ <-

---

The fourth hymn, beginning with **"Spread forth"** <note>original: kṛṇuṣva</note>, consists of fifteen verses. Its **Seer** <note>the rishi, or inspired composer</note> is Vamadeva, its **meter** is Trishtubh <note>a rhythmic structure of 11 syllables per line</note>, and its **deity** is Agni in his form as the **Slayer of Demons** <note>original: rakṣohā</note>. The **Anukramanika** <note>an ancient index of the Vedas</note> states: "The five verses starting with 'Spread forth' are demon-slaying." These verses are used during the **morning recitation** <note>Prātaranuvāka</note> and the ritual for the **Ashvin twins** <note>Aśvina-śastra</note>. Specifically, in the **Pravargya** ceremony <note>a ritual centered on a heated milk offering</note>, the five verses beginning with "Spread forth your power" are prescribed. This is indicated in the sacred manuals: "The five starting with 'Spread forth your power, like a wide net...'" (Asvalayana Shrauta Sutra 4.6).

---

## Hymn Text

-> ॥ Here is the first verse ॥ <-

**Spread forth** <note>original: kṛṇuṣva</note> your **power** <note>original: pājaḥ</note> like a **wide net** <note>original: prasitiṃ na pṛthvīṃ</note>; go like a **mighty king** <note>original: rājeva amavām</note> with his **elephant** <note>original: ibhena</note>. Moving along your **swift path** <note>original: tṛṣvīm anu prasitim</note>, you are the **archer** <note>original: astā asi</note>; pierce the **demons** <note>original: rakṣasaḥ</note> with your **hottest** <note>original: tapiṣṭhaiḥ</note> shafts. ॥ 1 ॥

**[Pada-patha]**
Spread | power | net | like | wide | go | king-like | mighty | with elephant |
swift | following | path | moving | archer | you are | pierce | demons | with hottest ॥ 1 ॥

---

## Commentary (Sayana)

O Agni, <term>krunushva</term> [make or extend] your <term>pajah</term> [a mass of brilliance]. An illustration is provided: <term>prasitim na</term>. Just as a hunter spreads a <term>pṛthvīm</term> [wide] and extensive <term>prasitim</term>—a snare or net <note>derived from the root meaning 'to be bound together'</note>—in the dense forest to catch birds, so too should you extend your great strength to destroy the demons. Accompanied by an <term>ibhena</term> [a fearless mass of brilliance], <term>yahi</term> [go forth] to slay the demons.

Another illustration follows: <term>rajeva</term> [like a king]. Just as an <term>amavan</term> king—where 'Ama' can mean an attendant or minister, thus one who possesses them; or 'Ama' refers to a disease or affliction, meaning he is like a disease to his enemies—just as a king goes against the enemy's force mounted on an <term>ibhena</term> [an elephant], so do you. Furthermore, following your <term>tṛṣvīm</term> [swift] and <term>prasitim</term> [excellent army or continuous movement], <term>dunanah</term> [moving toward or pursuing], you are the <term>asta</term> [the thrower or archer] who strikes down enemies. With your <term>tapishthaih</term> [most burning or hottest] rays, <term>vidhya</term> [pierce or strike] the <term>rakshasah</term> [demons].

The **Nirukta** <note>Yaska's ancient etymological dictionary</note> explains this verse as follows:
> "Spread your power; power comes from the concept of protecting. Like a wide net; 'prasiti' is from the root 'to bind,' meaning a thread or a snare. Go like a king who has ministers, or who has neighbors, or who is personally powerful, or with a fearless group, or with an elephant. Moving along a swift 'prasiti'; 'trishvi' is a word for swift, from the roots for 'crossing' or 'hurrying.' You are the archer, pierce the demons with your hottest, most burning shafts." (Nirukta 6.12)

---

<vocab>
- **Vamadeva**: The ancient sage (Rishi) credited with receiving this hymn.
- **Agni**: The fire god, here invoked specifically for protection against dark forces.
- **Trishtubh**: A classical Vedic meter consisting of 44 syllables.
- **Pajah**: A word meaning strength, power, or a mass of light.
- **Prasiti**: A complex term meaning a net, a snare, or a continuous forward movement.
- **Ibha**: Usually means an elephant, but interpreted by commentators as "fearless" or "powerful."
- **Nirukta**: One of the six Vedangas (limbs of the Veda) dealing with etymology.
</vocab>

Sayana provides linguistic analysis and quotes the Nirukta to clarify the martial and protective metaphors used in the prayer.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the commentary on the fourth hymn of the fourth Mandala. The top section concludes the grammatical analysis of terms from the first verse, specifically the verb meaning "to do" or "to harm" (kṛvi), before moving into the second and third verses of the hymn to Agni as the Slayer of Demons.</meta>

The root <term>kṛvi</term> means to do harm. In the <term>imperative mood</term> <note>original: loṭi</note>, the suffix "u" is added according to the rule for verbs like "dhinv" and "kṛṇv." It takes the <term>middle voice</term> <note>original: ātmanepada</note> by way of exception. The accent of the <term>affix</term> <note>original: vikaraṇa</note>, although it is "sati-śiṣṭa" <note>a technical term for a later-occurring grammatical rule</note>, does not override the accent of the personal ending. Thus, the accent remains on the ending.

-> ॥ Now the second verse ॥ <-

## Hymn Text

**Your wandering [rays] fall swiftly; touch [the enemies] with your bold [might], O shining one. Release your heats, O Agni, with your flame, like falling sparks; unhindered, scatter your firebrands everywhere.** ॥ 2 ॥

**Your** <note>original: tava</note> । **wandering [rays]** <note>original: bhramāsaḥ</note> । **swiftly** <note>original: āśu-yā</note> । **fall** <note>original: patanti</note> । **upon** <note>original: anu</note> । **touch/burn** <note>original: spṛśa</note> । **with bold [might]** <note>original: dhṛṣatā</note> । **intensely shining** <note>original: śośucānaḥ</note> ।
**heats** <note>original: tapūṃṣi</note> । **O Agni** <note>original: agne</note> । **with the flame/ladle** <note>original: juhvā</note> । **falling sparks/birds** <note>original: pataṅgān</note> । **unhindered** <note>original: asanditaḥ</note> । **specially** <note>original: vi</note> । **release** <note>original: sṛja</note> । **everywhere** <note>original: viśvak</note> । **firebrands** <note>original: ulkāḥ</note> ॥ 2 ॥

---

## Commentary (Sayana)

O **Agni**, **your wandering** <note>moving</note> rays, which possess **swift motion**, **fall**; they spread in all directions. You, being **intensely shining**, **touch**—that is, burn—the enemies in succession with your **bold** mass of light, which is capable of overpowering others. 

He now describes the method of burning: You, being **unhindered** <note>not blocked by enemies</note>, **release** three things: your **heats** <note>the light that causes heat</note>, your **falling sparks** <note>literally "pataṅgān," which can mean birds or flying sparks</note>, and your **firebrands**. You release these **everywhere** <note>in all directions</note> with your **flame**. <note>The word "juhū" usually refers to a sacrificial ladle, but Sayana glosses it here as "jvalā" or flame, into which offerings are poured.</note>

**Grammatical Analysis:**
For the word **āśuyā** <note>swiftly</note>, the case-ending is replaced by "yāj" according to the rule for Vedic substitutions. For **dhṛṣatā** <note>with boldness</note>, the root is "dhṛṣ" <note>to dare/overpower</note> from the 10th class; the accent falls on the case-ending. For **juhvā** <note>with the flame/ladle</note>, the word is derived from the root "hu" <note>to sacrifice</note> with doubling and lengthening; the accent follows the rule for semi-vowels. For **asanditaḥ** <note>unhindered</note>, it comes from the root "do" <note>to cut/bind</note> with a negative prefix, meaning "not cut off" or "not restrained."

---

-> ॥ Now the third verse ॥ <-

## Hymn Text

**Send forth your spies, you who are swiftest; be the unhindered protector of these people. May no one, whether far or near, O Agni, who intends evil, overpower us or your power.** ॥ 3 ॥

**Against** <note>original: prati</note> । **spies/rays** <note>original: spaśaḥ</note> । **specially** <note>original: vi</note> । **release** <note>original: sṛja</note> । **swiftest** <note>original: tūrṇi-tamaḥ</note> । **become** <note>original: bhava</note> । **protector** <note>original: pāyuḥ</note> । **people/subjects** <note>original: viśaḥ</note> । **of this** <note>original: asyāḥ</note> । **unhindered** <note>original: adabdhaḥ</note> ।
**who** <note>original: yaḥ</note> । **our/us** <note>original: naḥ</note> । **at a distance** <note>original: dūre</note> । **evil-intending** <note>original: agha-śaṃsaḥ</note> । **who** <note>original: yaḥ</note> । **near** <note>original: anti</note> । **O Agni** <note>original: agne</note> । **may no one** <note>original: mākiḥ</note> । **your** <note>original: te</note> । **pain/power** <note>original: vyathiḥ</note> । **towards** <note>original: ā</note> । **overpower** <note>original: dadharṣīt</note> ॥ 3 ॥

---

## Commentary (Sayana)

O **Agni**, you who are the **swiftest**, **send forth** your **spies** <note>original: spaśaḥ</note>. These are your rays which afflict others, or they are like secret agents sent to distinguish between truth and falsehood. Direct them especially toward the enemies. You, being **unhindered** <note>unharmed by anyone</note>, **become** the **protector** <note>guardian</note> of **these people**, meaning our clans and subjects. Why is this protection needed? [Because...]

<meta>This page continues the grammatical commentary for Rig Veda, Mandala 4, Hymn 4, Verse 3, focusing on Agni’s protection against those who speak or wish evil, before proceeding to the full text and explanation of Verses 4 and 5.</meta>

...as for the expectation of the word "near," the text says: [Protect] us from that one who is a speaker of evil <note>original: agha-śaṃsaḥ</note>. A speaker of evil is one whose desire or recitation is of a sinful nature. Because such an evil-speaker stands near us, you should be the protector from both kinds of distress. Furthermore, let no <note>original: mākir</note> demon belonging to you <insert>or attacking you</insert> dare to trouble or oppress us. The meaning is: let no one cause our defeat. 

Regarding the word **near** <note>original: anti</note>: there is a loss of the "ka" sound from the word *antika* (near), and the first syllable takes the high tone <note>original: ādyudāttatvaṃ</note>. **O Agni**: because it is at the start of a verse-quarter, it retains its initial high tone. **No one** <note>original: mākiṣṭa</note>: in the combined text <note>original: saṃhitā</note>, the "s" changes to "ṣ" due to its position within the verse-line. **Dared** <note>original: dadharṣīt</note>: from the root *dhṛṣ* meaning "to assault." In the <term>imperative mood</term> <note>original: laṅi</note>, the "śap" marker is replaced by "śyu" frequently in Vedic usage. The vowel "i" is added to the ending, and the word takes a low tone <note>original: nighātaḥ</note>.

---

->॥ Now the Fourth Verse ॥<-

## Hymn Text

**Rise up, O Agni, spread yourself out; burn down the enemies, O you of sharp weapons! O kindled one, whoever creates hostility toward us, burn him down like dry timber.** ॥ 4 ॥

**Rise** । **O Agni** । **stand** । **toward** । **out** । **spread** । **down** । **the enemies** । **burn** । **O sharp-weaponed one** ।
**Who** । **our** । **hostility** । **O kindled one** । **has made** । **downward** । **him** । **burn** । **timber** । **as** । **dry** ॥ 4 ॥

## Commentary (Sayana)

**O sharp-weaponed one** <note>original: tigmahete</note>: one whose flames <note>original: jvālā</note> are sharp weapons. O **Agni** of such a nature, rise up. Be ready for the purpose of **slaying demons** <note>original: rakṣohananārtha</note>. Spread yourself out toward the enemies. Expand the mass of your flames. With those masses of splendor, **burn down** the enemies—that is, burn them completely. 

O **kindled one** <note>original: samidhāna</note>, O Agni who shines by means of fuel, whatever man creates **hostility** <note>original: arāti</note> toward **us**—the word "hostility" here refers to the state of being an enemy or the act of not giving—**burn** that man down so he is cast **downward**. 

A comparison is given: **like dry timber** <note>original: atasaṃ na śuṣkam</note>. Just as you burn dry, un-moist wood, burn him in the same way.

Regarding **burn** <note>original: oṣatāt</note>: from the root *uṣ* meaning "to burn." In the <term>imperative mood</term>, the ending "hi" is replaced by "tāt." **Burn** <note>original: dhakṣi</note>: from the root *dah*. In the imperative, the "śap" marker is dropped in Vedic usage. The "h" changes to "ḍ" and then through further grammatical rules of sound-change, it becomes "kṣ." It carries a low tone.

**Be upright, pierce [the enemies]; reveal the divine powers, O Agni. Slacken the strong [bows] of the demon-driven; destroy the enemies, whether kin or stranger.** ॥ 5 ॥

**Upright** । **be** । **toward** । **pierce** । **above** । **from us** । **manifest** । **make** । **divine [powers]** । **O Agni** ।
**Down** । **the firm [bows]** । **slacken** । **of the demon-driven** । **the kin** । **the non-kin** । **forth** । **destroy** । **enemies** ॥ 5 ॥

## Commentary (Sayana)

O **Agni, be upright**. Be ready for the purpose of slaying demons. From us, [pierce] those who are superior—

<meta>This page continues the commentary on the Rig Veda, specifically finishing the explanation for Mandala 4, Hymn 4, Verse 5, and providing the full text and detailed commentary for Verse 6. This marks the transition from Varga 23 to Varga 24 within the fourth chapter of the third book (Ashtaka).</meta>

# 36 || Rig Veda || Book 3, Chapter 4, Section 24

## Commentary (Sayana)
Pierce the demons. Strike each one individually. **And reveal** <note>original: āviṣkṛṇuṣva</note> your divine splendors. Manifest them. Having done these three things, **loosen** <note>original: avatanuhi</note> the firm and strong bows of the **sorcerers** <note>original: yātujūnām</note>—those who rush to cause pain and distress to living beings. Make their bows unstrung. Furthermore, **strike down** <note>original: pramṛṇīhi</note> the **kin and the stranger** <note>original: jāmim ajāmim</note>, meaning your related and unrelated enemies. Kill them. Alternatively, "kin" refers to one who was struck before, and "stranger" to one not previously struck; kill such enemies. Do not hesitate, thinking, "this one has already been hit." 

Regarding the word **reveal** <note>original: āviṣkṛṇuṣva</note>: in the combined text, the "s" changes to "ṣ" because it follows a specific vowel sound <note>original: idudupadhasya</note>. **Loosen** <note>original: tanuhi</note>: from the root *tan* (to stretch); in the <term>imperative mood</term> <note>original: loṭ</note>, the suffix "hi" is not dropped, which is an occasional feature of Vedic grammar. **Of the sorcerers** <note>original: yātujūnām</note>: from the root *ju* (to move); it uses a specific suffix <note>original: kvip</note> and a long vowel, with an added "n" sound characteristic of Vedic Sanskrit. **Strike down** <note>original: mṛṇīhi</note>: from the root *mṛṅ* (to abandon life/kill). It includes a causative sense ("to make them die") and uses a specific grammatical marker <note>original: śnā</note> for the imperative mood. The word carries a low tone <note>original: nighātaḥ</note>.

-> ॥ Thus ends the twenty-third section (varga) of the fourth chapter of the third [Ashtaka] ॥ <-

---

## Hymn Text
-> ॥ Now the Sixth Verse ॥ <-

**O youngest Agni, he understands your benevolence who approaches you and offers a hymn of praise for the Great One. For this worshiper, may you, the Lord, shine particularly upon his home with many fine days, wealth, and splendors.** ॥ 6 ॥

**Word-by-word (Pada-patha):**
**He** । **your** । **understands** । **benevolence** । **O youngest one** । **who** । **approaches** । **for the Great One (Brahman)** । **a hymn/path** । **offers** ।
**All** । **for him** । **fine days** । **wealth** । **splendors** । **the Lord** । **particularly** । **the doors (home)** । **toward** । **let him shine** ॥ 6 ॥

---

## Commentary (Sayana)
**O youngest one** <note>original: yaviṣṭha</note>: O most youthful Agni. Alternatively, "he who most excellently mixes the oblations for the gods." **He** who is a man that **approaches** <note>original: īvate</note> you—moving toward you for the sake of reaching welfare—and **offers** <note>original: airat</note> or directs a **hymn** <note>original: gātum</note> (that which is sung or recited) **for the Great One** <note>original: brahmaṇe</note> (referring to you, Agni, who are vast/all-encompassing); such a man **understands** <note>original: jānāti</note> your **benevolence** <note>original: sumatim</note>. This means he obtains your graceful and kind-hearted intellect. 

For this sacrificer who has created this hymn, may you, **the Lord** <note>original: aryaḥ</note> (the master of sacrifices), **shine particularly** <note>original: vi dyaut</note> toward his **doors** <note>original: duraḥ</note> (meaning his home). Grant him **all fine days** <note>original: viśvāni sudināni</note> (auspicious days), **wealth** <note>original: rāyaḥ</note> (riches such as cattle, which "give" milk), and **splendors** <note>original: dyumnāni</note> (shining things like gold and jewels). 

Some scholars suggest a different sentence structure: For the sacrificer who offers the hymn, all days become auspicious and prosperous. Wealth (cattle) and splendors (gold) come to him. That sacrificer, the **Lord** (performer of the rites), then **shines particularly** in his own home. 

Regarding **approaches** <note>original: īvate</note>: from the root *ī* (to go); it uses a suffix denoting possession. **Offers** <note>original: airat</note>: from the root *īr* (to move/set in motion); because it is linked to the word "who," it does not take a low tone. **Lord** <note>original: aryaḥ</note>: from the root *ṛ* (to go/reach); it is a form meaning "master" or "lord."

<note>
**Youngest** (yaviṣṭha): A common title for Agni because the sacrificial fire is "reborn" and made young every time it is freshly kindled.
**Benevolence** (sumati): Literally "good-mindedness," representing the god's favor toward the worshiper.
**Hymn** (gātu): While it can mean "path," the commentator here identifies it as a song of praise (stotra).
**Splendor** (dyumna): Refers to glory but also tangible wealth that "shines," like precious metals.
**Lord** (arya): A title of respect; here it can refer to Agni as the master of the rite or the human patron of the sacrifice.
**Sorcerer** (yātudhāna): Malevolent beings or humans using harmful magic, whom Agni is asked to disarm.
**Fuel** (samidh): The wood used to sustain the sacred fire.
</note>

<keywords>Agni, Sayana's commentary, Yaviṣṭha, Sumati, wealth, Yātudhāna (sorcerers), ritual hymns, Vedic grammar, Arya (lord)</keywords>

In the Vedic <term>aorist tense</term> <note>original: luṅ</note>, it takes the <term>active voice</term> <note>original: parasmaipada</note> marker. -> ॥ The Seventh Verse ॥ <-

## Hymn Text

**Let that man, O Agni, be fortunate and a bountiful giver, who seeks to please you with constant oblations or with hymns of praise. In his own life and in his home, let every day be truly auspicious for him; may his sacrifice be successful.** ॥ 7 ॥

**Word-for-Word Breakdown:**
He | indeed | O Agni | let be | fortunate | bountiful giver | who | you | with constant | oblation | who | with hymns | seeks to please | in his own | life | in the home | all | indeed | for him | good days | that | let it be | sacrifice ॥ 7 ॥

## Commentary (Sayana)

O Agni, that man who **seeks to please** <note>original: piprīṣati</note> you—desiring to gratify you—with a **constant oblation** <note>original: nityena haviṣā</note>, meaning the daily *Agnihotra* and other rituals performed throughout one's life; and he who seeks to please you with **hymns of praise** <note>original: ukthaiḥ</note> or recitations; let that very man be **fortunate** <note>original: subhagaḥ</note>, meaning one who possesses beautiful wealth or prosperity. Let him also be a **bountiful giver** <note>original: sudānuḥ</note>, endowed with the habit of making fine offerings.

Furthermore, let him remain in his **home** <note>original: duroṇe</note>—which is sometimes interpreted as the "difficult to attain" <note>original: duravane</note> state—throughout his **own life** <note>original: sve āyuṣi</note> consisting of a full hundred years. For this **sacrificer** <note>original: yajamānāya</note>, let **all days** <note>original: viśvā sudinā</note> be "good days" or beautiful days. May his **sacrifice** <note>original: iṣṭiḥ</note> be **effective** <note>original: asat</note>; that is, may it be capable of producing the desired fruits.

**Grammatical Notes:**
**Seeks to please** <note>original: piprīṣati</note>: from the root *prīñ* (to please or satisfy). The <term>desiderative suffix</term> <note>original: san</note> is added to indicate "desire." **Let it be** <note>original: asat</note>: from the root *as* (to be), using the <term>subjunctive mood</term> <note>original: leṭ</note> with an added "a" sound. **Sacrifice** <note>original: iṣṭiḥ</note>: formed with a specific suffix <note>original: ktin</note> that carries the high accent.

In the *Ukhāsambharaṇīya* sacrifice, the verse "I worship your [benevolence]" is used as the **offering prayer** <note>original: yājyā</note>. This is indicated in the ritual manuals: "I worship your benevolence, let the sound [reach] hither..." beginning with these actions (Asvalayana Shrauta Sutra 4.1).

## Hymn Text

**I worship your benevolence, which is loud and turned toward us; let this, my song, sound forth to you. With good horses and good chariots, may we honor you; may they maintain powers for us through the passing days.** ॥ 8 ॥

**Word-for-Word Breakdown:**
I worship | your | benevolence | loud | hither-turned | together | you | beloved | let it sound | this | song | having good horses | you | having good chariots | let us honor | in us | powers | let them maintain | along | days ॥ 8 ॥

## Commentary (Sayana)

O Agni, I **worship** <note>original: arcāmi</note> or praise your **benevolence** <note>original: sumatim</note>, which is your beautiful, grace-bestowing intellect. This **song** <note>original: gīḥ</note> or speech being uttered is **beloved** <note>original: vavātā</note> as it reaches you again and again. Let it **sound forth** <note>original: jaratām</note>—meaning let it praise you—**loudly** <note>original: ghoṣi</note> and **turned toward us** <note>original: arvāk</note>, or facing you.

We also, being possessed of **good horses** <note>original: svaśvāḥ</note> and **good chariots** <note>original: surathāḥ</note>—this is an <term>illustrative term</term> <note>original: upalakṣaṇam</note> implying we are accompanied by sons, grandsons, and so on—**let us honor** <note>original: marjayema</note> you. We adorn...

## Commentary (Sayana)
[Continuation of Verse 8 commentary]

...we may perform. That is to say, we should serve. But you, **day after day** <note>original: anvaham</note>, should maintain **strengths** <note>original: kṣatrāṇi</note>—meaning wealth—within us. Please bestow them upon us.

**Grammatical Notes:**
**The sounding one** <note>original: ghoṣi</note>: Derived from the root *ghuṣ* (to sound). This is the <term>optative mood</term> <note>original: liṅ</note> in the causative form. The vowel lengthening <note>original: vṛddhi</note> is a specific Vedic variation.

->॥ The Ninth Verse ॥<-

## Hymn Text

**May a man approach you here with much devotion by himself, O dispeller of darkness, who shines day after day. With happy minds, let us serve you while we play, having taken for ourselves the riches of the people.** ॥ 9 ॥

**Padapatha:**
Here । you । much । [approach] । may move । toward । by self । O dispeller of darkness । the shining one । following । the days ।
playing । you । well-minded । may we serve । toward । riches । having stood over । of the people ॥ 9 ॥

## Commentary (Sayana)

O **Agni**, **here** <note>original: iha</note>—meaning either in this rite of destroying demons or in this world—a man **by himself** <note>original: tmana</note> should **approach** <note>original: upacaret</note> or serve you **frequently** <note>original: bhūri</note>, as you are the one **shining** <note>original: dīdivāṃsam</note> **day after day** <note>original: anu dyūn</note> and you are the **dispeller of darkness** <note>original: doṣāvasta</note> (both day and night). Therefore, by your grace, may we **take for ourselves** <note>original: abhitastivāsaḥ</note> the **riches** <note>original: dyumnā</note> of our enemies. Consequently, may we **serve you** <note>original: tvāṃ sapema</note> while being **joyful** <note>original: krīḷantaḥ</note>—playing with our sons and grandsons in our own homes—and being **well-minded** <note>original: sumanasaḥ</note> or benevolent.

Alternatively, **Dispeller of darkness** <note>original: doṣāvastaḥ</note> is an address: O you who cover or ward off the darkness created by the night.

**Grammatical Notes:**
**By himself** <note>original: tmana</note>: The word *ātman* (self) loses its initial 'ā' and takes the instrumental case ending. **Dispeller of darkness** <note>original: doṣāvastaḥ</note>: In the interpretation as a compound (Night-Day), the accent follows the rules for compound words. In the interpretation as a direct address (Vocative), it takes the accent on the first syllable because it occurs at the start of a verse section. **We may serve** <note>original: sapema</note>: From the root *ṣap* (to connect/serve) in the <term>optative mood</term>.

...goes, you become his savior and protector from all sins and difficulties. And whatever man offers to you **hospitality** <note>original: ātithyam</note>—that is, worship worthy of a guest—in the proper sequence of human groups, you become a friend to that man by granting him the appropriate fruits of his actions.

**Grammatical Notes:**
**Approaches** <note>original: upayāti</note>: This is a compound formed by a specific grammatical division <note>original: yoga-vibhāga</note>. Because the suffix <note>original: tip</note> is a 'pit' marker, the accent falls on the root. As it follows a verb, the accent is dropped. **Hospitality** <note>original: ātithyam</note>: Formed from the word for 'guest' <note>original: atithi</note> with a specific suffix <note>original: ñya</note>. The accent follows the suffix. **May he enjoy/offer** <note>original: jujoṣat</note>: A form of the root meaning 'to please' <note>original: joṣayate</note> in the <term>imperfect tense</term> <note>original: laṅ</note>. In Vedic usage, the 'shapa' suffix is replaced. The 'ni' marker is dropped because the suffix is treated as an <term>aorist-like</term> <note>original: ārdhadhātuka</note> form.

## Hymn Text
-> ॥ The Eleventh Verse ॥ <-

**I break the great [enemies] through kinship with my words; that [wisdom] has come down to me from my father Gotama. O invoker, O youngest one, O wise one, O dweller of the home, take notice of this speech of ours.** ॥ 11 ॥

**Word-by-word breakdown (Padapatha):**
The great । I break । kinship । with words । that । me । from father । from Gotama । following । has come ।
you । us । of this । of speech । notice । O invoker । O youngest । O wise one । O dweller of the home ॥ 11 ॥

---

## Commentary (Sayana)

O **invoker** <note>original: hotar</note> who calls the gods, O **youngest** <note>original: yaviṣṭha</note>, O Agni of **beautiful wisdom** <note>original: sukrato</note>: through these **words** <note>original: vacobhiḥ</note>—the hymns of praise composed for your sake—this **kinship** <note>original: bandhutā</note> or brotherly bond has arisen. Through that kinship, I **break** <note>original: rujāmi / bhanajmi</note> the **great** <note>original: maho</note> demons. That very speech, consisting of praise, **has come down** <note>original: anviyāya</note> to me, Vamadeva <note>The traditional seer of this book</note>, from my **father** and progenitor, the sage **Gotama**. You, who are a **dweller of the home** <note>original: damūnāḥ</note>—meaning one with a controlled mind, or one who bestows gifts, or the destroyer of enemies—**take notice** <note>original: cikiddhi</note> of this speech of ours, which consists of this sentence of praise. That is, please understand it.

**Grammatical Notes:**
**Notice** <note>original: cikiddhi</note>: From the root *kit* (to know/perceive). It belongs to the <term>third conjugation</term> <note>original: juhotyādi</note>. This is the form for the <term>imperative mood</term> <note>original: loṭ</note>. **O Invoker** <note>original: hotaḥ</note>: Because it stands at the beginning of a poetic foot, it retains the initial accent according to the rules of the sixth chapter of Panini. The following two vocatives, however, are treated as having no accent because they are in grammatical agreement with the first and do not start a new foot.

<meta>This page concludes the commentary on verse 12 and provides the full text and commentary for verse 13 of the 4th Hymn in the 4th Book (Mandala) of the Rig Veda. ## Commentary (Sayana) — Continued from previous page

**O wise one** <note>original: amūra</note>, you who are un-bewildered and all-knowing. Or, **O Agni**, you of unimpeded movement, the **sleepless ones** <note>original: asvapnajaḥ</note>—meaning the watchful ones. They are the **swift** <note>original: taraṇyaḥ</note>, those who naturally move constantly, or those who carry one across difficulties. They are **very kind** <note>original: suśevāḥ</note>, bestowing great happiness; **tireless** <note>original: atandrāso</note>, never lazy and always diligent; **non-harming** <note>original: avṛkā</note>; **un-confused** <note>original: adhamisthāḥ</note>; and **moving together** <note>original: sadhryañcaḥ</note> in unison with one another. May those rays of yours, being protectors, having settled within our bodies <note>original: niṣadyā</note>, guard us. May they protect us.

**Grammatical Notes:**
**Sleepless** <note>original: asvapnajaḥ</note>: Formed from the root for sleep with a specific suffix <note>original: najing</note>; the internal vowel change is a Vedic variation. **Moving together** <note>original: sadhryañcaḥ</note>: Formed from the word for 'together' <note>original: saha</note> and the root 'to move' <note>original: añc</note>. The word 'together' is replaced by 'sadhri', and the accentuation follows the rules for Vedic compounds. **Wise** <note>original: amūra</note>: Derived from the root for 'confusion' <note>original: muh</note> with a Vedic substitution of 'r' for 'dh', or alternatively from the root meaning 'to bind' <note>original: mūṅ</note>.

-> ॥ The Thirteenth Verse ॥ <-

## Hymn Text

**Those protectors of yours, O Agni, who, seeing the son of Mamata, protected him from misfortune though he was blind; the all-knowing one protected those who do good deeds; the enemies who wished to harm him could not do so.** ॥ 13 ॥

**Word-by-word breakdown:**
**Those** <note>original: ye</note> । **Protectors** <note>original: pāyavaḥ</note> । **The son of Mamata** <note>original: māmateyam</note> । **Your** <note>original: te</note> । **O Agni** <note>original: agne</note> । **Seeing** <note>original: paśyantaḥ</note> । **The blind one** <note>original: andham</note> । **From misfortune** <note>original: duritāt</note> । **Protected** <note>original: arakṣan</note> ।
**He protected** <note>original: rarakṣa</note> । **Them** <note>original: tān</note> । **The doers of good deeds** <note>original: sukṛtaḥ</note> । **The all-knowing one** <note>original: viśvavedāḥ</note> । **Wishing to harm** <note>original: dipsantaḥ</note> । **Indeed** <note>original: it</note> । **The enemies** <note>original: ripavaḥ</note> । **Not** <note>original: na</note> । **Surely** <note>original: aha</note> । **They harmed** <note>original: debhuḥ</note> ॥ 13 ॥

---

## Commentary (Sayana)

Regarding this, there is an ancient legendary story <note>original: aitihāsikī kathā</note>. Brihaspati, the younger brother of the sage Uchathya, desired Uchathya's pregnant wife, who was named Mamata. As he intended to place his seed within her, the embryo already dwelling in the womb spoke to the seed: "Do not cast your seed here; I am already dwelling here." Being thus addressed, Brihaspati, his desire obstructed, cursed the embryo: "May you enter into 'Long Darkness' <note>meaning: blindness</note>." Consequently, she gave birth to a son named **Dirghatamas** <note>literally: "Long Darkness"</note>. To remove his blindness, he praised Agni and thereby obtained vision.

This verse describes that event. **O Agni**, those rays of yours who are the **protectors** <note>original: pāyavo</note>, seeing with a compassionate gaze that "this one is blind," protected the **son of Mamata** <note>original: māmateyam</note>—the blind Dirghatamas—from **misfortune** <note>original: duritāt</note>, which refers to the curse of blindness. They protected him by restoring his sight. You, the **possessor of all knowledge** <note>original: viśvavedāḥ</note>, protected those rays who performed the beautiful deed of granting him eyes. The success of that protection is described: the **enemies** <note>original: ripavaḥ</note> who **desired to harm** <note>original: dipsantaḥ</note> or overpower him, surely could not harm this Dirghatamas.

**Grammatical Notes:**
**Son of Mamata** <note>original: māmateyaṃ</note>: Formed with a suffix <note>original: dhak</note> used to denote offspring of a female. **Wishing to harm** <note>original: dipsantaḥ</note>: From the root meaning 'to deceive or harm' <note>original: dambh</note>, using the desiderative form where the initial vowel changes to 'i'. **They harmed** <note>original: debhuḥ</note>: A perfect tense form of the root 'to harm', where the internal vowel is elided due to specific grammatical markers.

<vocab>
**Protectors** <note>original: pāyavaḥ</note>: The guarding rays of Agni.
**Son of Mamata** <note>original: māmateyam</note>: Referring to the sage Dirghatamas.
**All-knowing** <note>original: viśvavedāḥ</note>: An epithet of Agni, the possessor of all wisdom.
**Enemies** <note>original: ripavaḥ</note>: Those who sought to injure the sage.
**Misfortune** <note>original: duritāt</note>: Specifically referring here to the "difficulty" of congenital blindness.
**Dirghatamas** <note>original: dīrghatamā</note>: A famous Vedic seer born blind due to a curse, later healed by Agni.
</vocab>

<summary>This page discusses the protective nature of Agni's rays, recounting the legend of the sage Dirghatamas who was born blind due to Brihaspati's curse but regained his sight through Agni's grace.</summary>
<keywords>Agni, Dirghatamas, Mamata, Brihaspati, blindness, protection, Vedic legend, rays of light</keywords>

# Book 4. Chapter 1. Hymn 4. || Third Volume || 41

## Hymn Text

-> ॥ The Fourteenth Verse ॥ <-

Through you, we, sharing in your wealth <note>original: sadhanyas</note> and protected by you, may we attain nourishments <note>original: vājān</note> under your guidance. O protector of truth <note>original: satyatāte</note>, destroy both types of enemies <note>original: śaṃsā; meaning those near and far</note>, and act in due order <note>original: anuṣṭhuyā</note>, O you of bold movement! ॥ 14 ॥

**Word-for-word analysis:**
Through-you | we | sharing-in-wealth | protected-by-you | your | under-guidance | may-we-attain | nourishments | both | enemies | destroy | O-protector-of-truth | in-due-order | act | O-you-of-bold-movement ॥ 14 ॥

---

## Commentary (Sayana)

**O you of bold movement** <note>original: ahrayāṇa</note>: One whose movement is not shameful <note>interpretive note: "bold" or "unabashed"</note>. The ancient etymologist **Yaska** defines this as "one whose vehicle or progress is not withheld." To such a one, O Agni, we who are your singers, having become **sharers of common wealth** <note>original: sadhanyas</note> by your grace, and being **protected by you** <note>original: tva-ūtaḥ</note>, may we attain **nourishments** <note>original: vājān</note> or foods under your **guidance** <note>original: praṇītī</note>—that is, by your direction or permission. 

**O protector of truth** <note>original: satyatāte</note>: This refers to one who extends truth, or one in whom the sacrifice <note>term: satya; here referring to the true rite or sacrifice</note> is performed. O protector of truth, **destroy** <note>original: sūdaya</note> or kill **both** <note>original: ubhā</note> the **enemies** <note>original: śaṃsā</note>—meaning the close and the distant malicious ones. **In due order** <note>original: anuṣṭhuyā</note>: Do this sequentially. **Act** <note>original: kṛṇuhi</note>: Carry out the purpose described in this hymn.

**Grammatical Notes:**
**Sharing in wealth** <note>original: sadhanyas</note>: The word for wealth <note>original: dhana</note> takes a specific Vedic suffix <note>original: van-pā-vi</note> to indicate possession. **In due order** <note>original: anuṣṭhuyā</note>: This uses a rare Vedic case ending where a standard suffix is replaced to indicate the "order" of action. **Bold movement** <note>original: ahrayāṇa</note>: Derived from the root for "shame" <note>original: hrī</note>; the grammatical structure follows Vedic rules for verb formation and vowel changes.

---

## Hymn Text

-> ॥ The Fifteenth Verse ॥ <-

O Agni, with this fuel <note>original: samidhā; also implying a prayer</note> may we serve you; accept the hymn of praise being recited. Burn the godless demons <note>original: rakṣasaḥ</note>, and protect us, O you who are honored by friends <note>original: mitramaho</note>, from the malicious, from the censurer, and from blame. ॥ 15 ॥

**Word-for-word analysis:**
With-this | your | O-Agni | with-fuel | may-we-serve | accept | hymn | being-recited | take-hold-of | burn | the-godless | demons | protect | us | from-the-malicious | from-the-censurer | O-honored-by-friends | from-blame ॥ 15 ॥

---

## Commentary (Sayana)

O Agni, **with this** <note>original: ayā</note> bright **fuel** <note>original: samidhā</note>, which can also mean this radiant praise, **may we serve** <note>original: vidhema</note> or worship you. **Accept** <note>original: prati gṛbhāya</note>—take hold of—this **hymn** <note>original: stomam</note> which is **being recited** <note>original: śasyamānam</note> by us. 

**The godless** <note>original: aśaṃsaḥ</note>: Those who do not praise <note>original: śaṃsanti</note> the gods, meaning the wicked or non-believers. **Burn** <note>original: daha</note> those **demons** <note>original: rakṣasaḥ</note>; turn them to ashes. **O you who are honored by friends** <note>original: mitramaho</note>: O Agni, you who are worthy of worship by your friends, **protect** <note>original: pāhi</note> us from the **malicious** <note>original: druhaḥ</note>, from the **censurer** <note>original: nidaḥ</note> who speaks ill of us, and from **blame** <note>original: avadyāt</note> or public reproach.

**Grammatical Notes:**
**Accept** <note>original: gṛbhāya</note>: A Vedic variation of the imperative "to take" <note>root: grah</note> with a specific suffix <note>original: śāyac</note> and a consonant change <note>h to bh</note>. **Protect** <note>original: pāhi</note>: In this Vedic context, the accent is maintained because it begins a new thought within the sentence. **Censurer** <note>original: nidaḥ</note>: Derived from the root meaning "to despise" or "to blame" <note>original: nidi</note>.

# Rig Veda || Book 3. Chapter 5. Group 1. || 42

Due to the non-permanence of the rules of grammatical augment <note>original: āgamānuśāsana</note>, there is an absence of the 'num' augment. Regarding the word *sāveka-ac*, there is an acute accent <note>term: udātta; the high-pitched Vedic accent</note> on the case ending. Regarding *avadyāt*: the 'yat' suffix is applied according to the rule "avadyapaṇya." According to the rule of Panini 6.2.156, the final syllable has the acute accent. In the combined text <note>term: saṃhitā</note> of the phrase "Mitramaho avadyāt," the 'e' vowel maintains its original form <note>original: prakṛtibhāva</note> before 'a'.

->॥ Thus ends the twenty-fifth verse-group in the fourth chapter of the third book ॥<-

By illuminating the meaning of the Vedas, dispelling the darkness of the heart, may Vidyatirtha-Maheshwara <note>The guru or deity invoked by the commentator Sayana</note> grant the four goals of human life <note>term: puruṣārtha; refers to Dharma (duty), Artha (prosperity), Kama (pleasure), and Moksha (liberation)</note>.

Thus ends the fourth chapter in the third book of the "Illumination of the Meaning of the Vedas" (Madhaviya Vedartha-Prakasha), a commentary on the Rig Veda collection composed by the great teacher Sayana, the chief pillar of the empire of the illustrious King Vira Bukka, the Supreme Lord of Kings and promoter of the Vedic path.

---

->॥ Salutations to the holy Lord Ganesha ॥<-

To Him whose breath is the Vedas, who created the entire world from the Vedas—I bow to that Vidyatirtha-Maheshwara.

In the first section <note>term: anuvāka</note> of the fourth Book <note>term: maṇḍala</note>, there are ten hymns. The fifth hymn, beginning with "To Vaishvanara," consists of fifteen verses. Its seer is Vamadeva, its meter is Trishtubh <note>term: triṣṭubh; a Vedic meter of 44 syllables</note>, and its deity is Agni in his form as Vaishvanara <note>term: vaiśvānara; "belonging to all men," the universal fire</note>. According to the Index <note>original: anukramaṇikā</note>: "To Vaishvanara is Vaishvanara-themed." The ritual application is determined by its characteristic marks <note>original: laiṅgika</note>.

->॥ Here begins the First Verse ॥<-

## Hymn Text
With one mind, how may we offer great light to the bounteous Agni Vaishvanara? Like a supporting pillar, he held up the firmament with his vast, flawless power of conveyance. ॥ 1 ॥

**Word-for-word analysis:**
To-Vaishvanara | to-the-bounteous | with-one-mind | how | may-we-worship | to-Agni | great | light | with-flawless | with-vast | with-conveyance | up | he-supported | like-a-pillar | as-it-were | the-firmament ॥ 1 ॥

---

## Commentary (Sayana)
**With one mind** <note>original: sajoṣāḥ</note>: Being of the same mind or shared affection, we—the priests and the sacrificer. **To Vaishvanara**: To the one related to all men <note>original: viśvānara-saṃbandhine</note>, who bears this name. **To the bounteous** <note>original: mīḷhuṣe</note>: To the pourer or giver of desired rain and other blessings. **Great light**: To the God Agni who shines with a vast light. **How** <note>original: kathā</note>: In what way or by what means. **May we worship** <note>original: dāśema</note>: May we give. By implication, this refers to offering the sacrificial oblation <note>original: havis</note>.

[Commentary on Verse 1 continued]

...is understood. Alternatively, the phrase "singers of the great" <note>original: bṛhadgā</note> should be connected to what follows. It was asked, "How shall we worship?" <note>original: kathā dāśema</note>. If one asks what the greatness is in that worship, it is explained here: That Agni, who is both great and shining, supports the heavens with his complete and massive body—the physical form he carries. By his power, he pervades the celestial realm. An analogy is provided: "Like a supporting pillar" <note>original: upaminnarodhaḥ</note>. A pillar <note>term: upamit; a post or stay used in construction</note> is something placed nearby to support; just as a pillar supports beams to prevent a thatched roof from collapsing, so does Agni support the sky. Alternatively, he supports the heavens by means of the hymn <note>term: stotra</note> consisting of recited verses <note>term: uktha</note> which carry the rewards of the sacrifice. The word *stabhāyat* (supports) comes from the root *stambhu*; in the Vedic dialect, it takes a specific grammatical form <note>note: Sayana explains the Vedic linguistic variation of the 'shayaj' affix and the absence of the 'at' augment</note>. To what is this compared? "Like a pillar near the water" or "like a riverbank."

-> ॥ Now the Second Verse ॥ <-

## Hymn Text

Do not revile him, the God who possesses the sacrificial food <note>term: svadhāvān; one who has "svadhā" or inherent power/food</note> and has given this gift to me, a mortal. He is the wise <note>original: gṛtsa</note>, the immortal, the one of perfect intellect, the fire belonging to all men <note>term: vaiśvānara; Agni in his aspect as the common fire of humanity</note>, the most heroic leader, the great Agni, for the sake of the simple <note>note: or "the one of ripe wisdom"</note> ॥ 2 ॥

**Word-for-word analysis:**
Do not; revile; who; this; to me; gift; God; gave; to a mortal; possessing food; for the simple/wise; wise; immortal; possessing perfect intellect; belonging to all men; most heroic; great; Fire (Agni) ॥ 2 ॥

---

## Commentary (Sayana)

O priests <note>term: hotṛ; the primary reciter of the Rig Veda in a sacrifice</note>, do not revile this Agni Vaishvanara. Do not speak ill of him; the meaning is that you should praise him. That shining God, Agni, being possessed of the food consisting of the oblations we have offered, gave this wealth—in the manner it is currently being given—to me, the sacrificer <note>term: yajamāna</note>, who is a mortal of mature wisdom <note>note: Sayana interprets "pāka" (simple/immature) here as "paripakva-prajñā" or ripe wisdom</note>. He is further described: "Wise" <note>original: gṛtsa; a name for the wise</note>, "Immortal" by his very nature, "Possessing perfect intellect" or specific wisdom, "Belonging to all men" because he is led by all people into the various sacrificial fires, the "Greatest leader" who brings forth rewards, and "Great" <note>original: yahva; a synonym for great</note>. The essence is: praise such an Agni who is characterized by these qualities ॥

-> ॥ Now the Third Verse ॥ <-

## Hymn Text

The twice-great <note>original: dvibarhā; existing in two worlds, heaven and earth</note>, the great, the sharp-flamed, the possessor of thousandfold seed, the bull, the powerful—finding the hidden tracks of the cow, Agni has spoken the sacred song <note>original: manīṣā</note> to me ॥ 3 ॥

**Word-for-word analysis:**
Sacred song; twice-great; great; sharp-flamed; thousandfold-seed; bull; powerful; track; like; of a cow; hidden; finding; Agni; to me; forth; indeed; [particle]; spoke; wisdom/song ॥ 3 ॥

<vocab>
**Universal Fire** (Vaiśvānara): Agni as the fire present in all humans and the cosmos.
**Gift** (Rāti): Specifically refers to the wealth or spiritual insight granted by the deity.
**Possessing Food** (Svadhāvān): Carrying the sacrificial offerings or possessing inherent power.
**Wise** (Gṛtsa): A term denoting cleverness or meditative insight.
**Great** (Yahva): A Vedic term for vastness or majesty.
**Twice-great** (Dvibarhā): Expanding or existing in two realms, usually heaven and earth.
**Sharp-flamed** (Tigmabhṛṣṭi): Having intense, pointed radiance.
**For the simple** (Pākāya): This word can mean "for the immature" (needing guidance) or, as Sayana interprets, "for the one of ripe wisdom."
</vocab>

<meta>This page concludes the commentary for Rig Veda Mandala 4, Sukta 5, Verse 3, and provides the full text and commentary for Verse 4, and the start of Verse 5. It continues the theme of Agni as a divine judge who distinguishes between the wise and the sinful.</meta>

## Commentary (Sayana)
[Fragment from previous verse]

Agni exists in two places <note>original: dvibarhā; referring to the mid-region/atmosphere and the highest heaven</note>, he is sharp-rayed <note>original: tigma-bhṛṣṭiḥ</note> and possesses a thousand-fold essence. The word "seed" <note>original: retaḥ</note> here signifies essence or power; thus, he is of great essence. He is the "bull" <note>note: a common Vedic metaphor for a powerful male deity</note> who showers worshippers with their desires and possesses much wealth. Such is Agni, who knows the "footstep of the cow" <note>note: a metaphor for a deeply hidden secret or a lost path of wisdom</note> which is concealed like the tracks of a lost cow. The word for "wisdom" <note>term: manīṣā</note> is used here to mean that which is to be known. Knowing that great, venerable, and desired chant <note>term: sāma</note> of ours, may he speak it forth. Indeed, let him proclaim it.

-> ॥ Now the Fourth Verse ॥ <-

## Hymn Text
May Agni, the sharp-toothed, consume them with his most intense heat—he who is the giver of good wealth. May he consume those who violate the fixed and beloved laws of the wise Varuna and Mitra. ॥ 4 ॥

**Word-by-word Analysis:**
May—them—Agni—consume—sharp-toothed—with most intense—heat—who—possesses good wealth—violate—those who—of Varuna—the law/domain—beloved—of Mitra—the wise—fixed. ॥ 4 ॥

---

## Commentary (Sayana)
That Agni, who possesses "good wealth" <note>original: surādhāḥ</note>, being "sharp-toothed" <note>original: tigma-jambha</note>, may he consume <note>original: babhasat</note> those who surround [the sacrifice with ill intent], using his heat which intensely scorches enemies. The meaning is: let him burn them. <note>note: Sayana derives the word "babhasat" from a root meaning both to threaten and to shine, explaining the specific Vedic grammatical mood (let) used here</note>. Who are those he should consume? He explains: those who "violate" <note>original: pra minanti; to diminish or injure</note> the "laws" <note>term: dhāma; can refer to divine decrees, seats of power, or sacrificial acts</note> of Mitra and Varuna. These laws are "wise," "beloved," and "fixed" <note>original: dhruva</note>.

---

-> ॥ Now the Fifth Verse ॥ <-

## Hymn Text
Like brotherless women wandering aimlessly, or like wives who deceive their husbands and are of evil conduct—those who are sinful, untruthful, and false have created for themselves this deep place [of ruin]. ॥ 5 ॥

**Word-by-word Analysis:**
Brotherless—like—women—wandering—husband-deceiving—like—wives—evil-behaving—sinful—being—untruthful—false—this—place—they created—deep. ॥ 5 ॥

---

## Commentary (Sayana)
"Brotherless" <note>original: abhrātaraḥ</note> refers to women who lack brothers or family protectors. "Like women" <note>original: yoṣaṇo na</note> refers to those whose husbands have passed away. <note>note: Sāyana points out a specific Vedic linguistic variation where a long vowel is shortened in this context</note>. Just as such women might leave their husband’s home to return to their father’s home, so do these people wander <note>original: vyantaḥ</note> away, abandoning the path of sacrifice and following the wrong path. Likewise, "like wives who deceive their husbands" <note>original: patiripo na janayaḥ</note>...

<summary>This page contains Agni’s role as a protector of cosmic law (Rita). He is asked to consume those who violate the sacred decrees of Mitra and Varuna, with the text comparing sinners to socially unprotected or deceitful women who have strayed from the path of righteousness.</summary>

<meta>This page concludes the commentary for Rig Veda Mandala 4, Sukta 5, Verse 5, and provides the full text and commentary for Verse 6 and the beginning of Verse 7. It marks the completion of the first "Varga" (a traditional verse-grouping) within this hymn. The theme shifts from the punishment of the wicked to a plea for divine wealth and purification.</meta>

## Commentary (Sayana) — Continued from Verse 5

Those who are "husband-haters" <note>original: pati-dviṣaḥ; used here as a metaphor for those who turn away from their protector or lord</note> are like women of "evil conduct" <note>original: durevāḥ</note> or wicked behavior. Because they are "sinners" <note>original: pāpāsaḥ</note>, they are "untruthful" <note>original: anṛtāḥ</note>—meaning they lack mental truth—and "false" <note>original: asatyāḥ</note>—meaning they lack truth in their speech. Because they do not worship Agni with either mind or speech, they have "generated" <note>original: ajanata</note> for themselves this well-known "deep, bottomless place" <note>original: gabhīram agādhaṃ padaṃ</note>, which is the "station of hell" <note>original: narakasthānam</note>. It is they who bring such a state into existence. <note>The commentator notes a technical grammatical point: the verb 'ajanata' is a specific Vedic form signifying the creation or production of this state of being.</note>

->॥ This ends the First Varga of the Fifth Hymn in the Third Octave ॥<-

---

## Hymn Text
->॥ Now the Sixth Verse ॥<-

O Agni, the Purifier, give to me—who am humble yet do not neglect my duty—this great and thinkable wealth, like one handing over a heavy burden. May you provide that deep and mighty abundance, which overcomes enemies, is accompanied by food, and is seven-fold in nature. ॥ 6 ॥

> This | for me | Agni | to the humble | Purifier | to the one who does not neglect | heavy | burden | like | thought/wealth |
> great | give | by the overcomer [of enemies] | deep | mighty | surface/back | with food | seven-fold ॥ 6 ॥

---

## Commentary (Sayana)
O **Purifier** <note>original: pāvaka</note>, you who are the cleansing Agni! To me, who am **humble** <note>original: kiyate; literally 'small' or 'limited'</note>, and to one who **does not neglect** <note>original: aminnate; meaning one who does not injure or abandon the sacred rites</note> your service, please **give** <note>original: dadhāya</note> this well-known, **great** and abundant **thinkable** wealth <note>term: manma; usually 'thought' or 'prayer', but interpreted here by Sayana as 'wealth to be meditated upon'</note>. 

He uses a comparison: **like a heavy burden** <note>original: guruṃ bharaṃ na</note>. Just as one might hand over a weight they can no longer carry, or as one entrusts a significant load to another, give this to me. This wealth is further described: it is given **by the overcomer** <note>original: dhṛṣatā</note> who strikes down enemies; it is **deep** <note>original: gabhīram</note>, meaning it cannot be easily fathomed or exhausted by others; it is **mighty** <note>original: yahvam</note> and possesses a **surface** <note>original: pṛṣṭhaṃ</note> or form that is worthy of being touched. 

Finally, it is **seven-fold** <note>term: saptadhātu; 'having seven elements'</note>. According to sacred scripture <note>original: śruteḥ</note>, this refers to the "seven domestic animals and seven wild animals." The request is for Agni to grant such comprehensive wealth. Alternatively, the phrase **like a heavy burden** could be interpreted as: "Just as one gives another's burden to someone else to carry, give us the wealth that is meant to be given."

---

## Hymn Text
->॥ Now the Seventh Verse ॥<-

May our purifying thought, along with the appropriate ritual, quickly reach that same Universal One, who is uniform for all. On the surface of the earth, may Agni’s beautiful and ageless form be revealed, even as the multicolored clouds shine in the sky. ॥ 7 ॥

> Him | indeed | now | precisely | with equal mind | the same | towards | through ritual | purifying | thought | may reach |
> of the earth | on the skin | upon | beautiful | of the multicolored [sky/cow] | of Agni | the form | ageless | moving ॥ 7 ॥

---

## Commentary (Sayana)
The sage Yaska <note>a famous ancient scholar of Vedic etymology</note> has stated that the three forms of Fire—terrestrial fire, lightning in the mid-region, and the Sun in the heavens—are all designated by the term **Universal One** <term>Vaiśvānara: Agni in his cosmic aspect as 'belonging to all men'</term> depending on the context. Here, the Universal One is praised in the form of the Sun. 

May our **thought** <note>original: dhītiḥ</note>—our prayer and meditation—which is **purifying** <note>original: punatī</note> (cleansing us of sins), **quickly** <note>original: nveva</note> **reach** <note>original: aśyāḥ</note> or attain **Him** <note>original: tam it</note>, the Universal One who resides in the high heavens. He is **the same** <note>original: samānam</note> because he appears in one uniform form to all beings. Our prayer is **with equal mind** <note>original: samanā</note>, meaning it is consistent and fit for his greatness, and it is performed **through ritual** <note>original: ṛtvā</note> or actions that are appropriate for him.

<summary>This page concludes the description of the fate of the untruthful, who create their own hell, and begins a prayer to Agni for "seven-fold" wealth and cosmic purification. Agni is addressed as the Universal One (Vaishvanara), linking the ritual fire to the celestial sun.</summary>
