<meta>This page continues the commentary on the sixteenth hymn of the fourth Mandala of the Rigveda. The previous page concluded the discussion on verse 5 and 6, where Indra's majesty was described as surpassing heaven and earth, and his role in releasing the waters was established. This page moves into the specific myths of the slaying of Vritra and the recovery of the cattle with the help of Sarama and the Angiras sages.</meta>

94 || Rig Veda || [Book 3. Chapter 5. Section 14.]

## Hymn Text

-> ॥ Now the Seventh Verse ॥ <-

**You struck down Vritra, who had encompassed the waters; the conscious Earth protected your thunderbolt. O brave and daring one, becoming the lord through your strength, you set the celestial waters in motion.** ॥ 7 ॥

**Waters** <note>apaḥ</note> । **Vritra** <note>vṛtram</note> । **The encloser** <note>vavrivāṃsam</note> । **Away/Down** <note>parā</note> । **Struck** <note>ahan</note> । **Forward** <note>pra</note> । **Protected/Favored** <note>āvat</note> । **Your** <note>te</note> । **Thunderbolt** <note>vajram</note> । **Earth** <note>pṛthivī</note> । **Conscious** <note>sacetāḥ</note> ॥
**Forward** <note>pra</note> । **Waters/Streams** <note>arṇāṃsi</note> । **Celestial/Oceanic** <note>samudriyāṇi</note> । **Set in motion** <note>ainoḥ</note> । **Lord** <note>patiḥ</note> । **Becoming** <note>bhavan</note> । **With strength** <note>śavasā</note> । **O Brave one** <note>śūra</note> । **O Daring one** <note>dhṛṣṇo</note> ॥ 7 ॥

---

## Commentary (Sayana)

O **Indra**, [you who are] the protector of the worlds from demons and other threats, your **thunderbolt** <note>original: vajram</note> **struck down** <note>original: parāhan</note> the cloud called **Vritra**, who was the **encloser** or coverer of the **waters** characterized by rain. The **Earth**, being **conscious** <note>original: sacetāḥ; endowed with awareness</note>, was in union with you [during this act]. O **daring** <note>original: dhṛṣṇo</note> and **brave** <note>original: śūra</note> Indra, while **becoming the lord** or protector of the worlds through your own **strength** <note>original: śavasā</note>, you were the **mover** <note>original: prainoḥ</note> of the **celestial waters** <note>original: samudriyāṇi arṇāṃsi</note>—those waters which reside in the firmament.

---

## Hymn Text

-> ॥ Now the Eighth Verse ॥ <-

**O much-invoked one, when you split the mountain for the waters, the ancient [path] became manifest to you through Sarama. Being praised by the Angirases, and breaking open the cow-pens, you—our leader—grant us abundant food.** ॥ 8 ॥

**Waters** <note>apaḥ</note> । **When** <note>yat</note> । **Mountain** <note>adrim</note> । **O much-invoked one** <note>puruhūta</note> । **Split** <note>dardaiḥ</note> । **Manifest** <note>āviḥ</note> । **Became** <note>bhuvat</note> । **Sarama** <note>saramā</note> । **Ancient** <note>pūrvyam</note> । **To you** <note>te</note> ॥
**He** <note>saḥ</note> । **Our** <note>naḥ</note> । **Leader** <note>netā</note> । **Food/Wealth** <note>vājam</note> । **Towards** <note>ā</note> । **Grant/Reveal** <note>darṣi</note> । **Abundant** <note>bhūri</note> । **Cow-pens/Clouds** <note>gotrā</note> । **Breaking open** <note>rujan</note> । **By the Angirases** <note>aṅgiraḥbhiḥ</note> । **Being praised** <note>gṛṇānaḥ</note> ॥ 8 ॥

---

## Commentary (Sayana)

O **much-invoked** Indra, called upon by many, **when** you **split** the **mountain** <note>original: adrim; here meaning the cloud</note> for the sake of the **waters** intended for rain, **Sarama** <note>the divine hound of the gods</note> **made manifest** <note>original: āvirbhuvat</note> to **you** the **ancient** wealth of cattle that had been stolen by the Panis <note>demons who hoarded the world's light/cattle</note>. While **being praised** <note>original: gṛṇānaḥ</note> by the **Angiras** sages, you **break open** the **cow-pens** <note>original: gotrā; referring to the clouds which hold the waters like pens hold cows</note>. You are the **leader** who brings us to **abundant food** <note>original: bhūrim vājam</note>; as such, you have **bestowed your favor** <note>original: ādarṣi; shown care or respect</note> upon us.

-> ॥ Now the Ninth Verse ॥ <-

**Toward the wise poet, who is minded toward men, who is praying for the cattle in the contest for light—O Bounteous Lord, do you move with your aids. In the battle for glory, the deceptive, prayerless Dasyu was cast down.** ॥ 9 ॥

**Toward** <note>achā</note> । **Wise poet** <note>kavim</note> । **Minded toward men** <note>nṛ-manāḥ</note> । **Cattle** <note>gāḥ</note> । **In the prayer/praise** <note>abhiṣṭau</note> । **In the winning of light** <note>svaḥ-sātā</note> । **O Bounteous one** <note>maghavan</note> । **Praying/Seeking** <note>nādhamānam</note> ॥

95 || Rig Veda || [Book 4. Chapter 2. Section 16.]

## Commentary (Sayana)
[Continuation of commentary on RV 4.16.9]

O **Maghavan** <term>Maghavan: The Bountiful; a title of Indra referring to his possession of sacred wealth</term>, Indra, who is **mindful of men** <note>original: nṛmāṇāḥ; one who is thought of or worshipped by men</note>. You **approached** <note>original: accha gāḥ; went toward</note> the **wise** <note>original: kaviṃ</note> **Kutsa**. Furthermore, in the **bestowal of heavenly light** <note>original: svarṣātā; for the sake of giving the wealth of heaven</note>, while approaching the wise one [Kutsa], you **impelled** him with **protections** <note>original: ūtibhiḥ</note>—protections consisting of the removal of calamities caused by enemies—toward Kutsa, who was **beseeching** <note>original: nādhamānaṃ</note> you for the sake of battle.

The **Abrahma** <term>Abrahma: One who lacks a priest or is devoid of faith in Vedic rituals</term> is the one who possesses **guile** <note>original: māyāvān; deceptive</note>. A specific priest who knows all the ritual actions performed by the other priests and grants permission is called a "Brahma." One who does not have such a person is an "Abrahma"—meaning one who lacks faith in the ritual acts prescribed by the Vedas. The **Dasyu** <term>Dasyu: An enemy of the Vedic people, often described as godless or ritual-less</term>, who was the enemy of Kutsa, was **destroyed** <note>original: nyartaṃ; perished</note> in the **invocation of wealth** <note>original: dyumnahūtau</note>—the battle in which wealth <note>dyumnam</note> is the goal of the calling <note>hūtiḥ</note>. This means that Indra, having been called by Kutsa, killed his enemy.

---
-> ॥ Now the Tenth Verse ॥ <-

## Hymn Text
**Come to the home with a mind intent on slaying the Dasyu; may Kutsa be intensely desirous of your friendship. Sit down together in your own place, being of identical form; may the woman who knows the Truth distinguish between the two of you.** ॥ 10 ॥

**Word-for-word analysis:**
**Come** <note>ā</note> । **Slayer of the Dasyu** <note>dasyu-ghnā</note> । **With a mind** <note>manasā</note> । **Go/Come** <note>yāhi</note> । **Home** <note>astam</note> । **May he be** <note>bhuvat</note> । **Your** <note>te</note> । **Kutsa** <note>kutsaḥ</note> । **In friendship** <note>sakhye</note> । **Intensely desiring** <note>ni-kāmaḥ</note> ॥
**In own** <note>sve</note> । **Place/Source** <note>yonau</note> । **Down** <note>ni</note> । **Sit [you two]** <note>sadatam</note> । **Of identical form** <note>sa-rūpā</note> । **Apart/Distinguish** <note>vi</note> । **You two** <note>vām</note> । **May she discern/doubt** <note>cikitsat</note> । **Knower of Truth** <note>ṛta-cit</note> । **Indeed** <note>ha</note> । **Woman** <note>nārī</note> ॥ 10 ॥

---

## Commentary (Sayana)
A certain legend is heard regarding this. There was a royal sage named Katharuru. His son was a royal sage named Kutsa. Once, wishing to fight with enemies but being himself powerless in battle, he called upon Indra to slay the enemies. That Indra came to Kutsa's house and killed his enemies. Afterward, out of great affection, a friendship was formed between the two. After the friendship was established, Indra brought him to his own home. There, Shachi <note>Indra's wife</note>, having come to receive Indra and seeing the two of them looking exactly alike, became confused and felt doubt, as she lacked the discrimination to tell: "Is this Indra or is this Kutsa?" The meaning appearing through this legend is presented here.

O Indra, with a **mind** <note>original: manasā</note> intent on being a **slayer of the Dasyu** <note>original: dasyughnā</note>, **come** <note>original: āyāhi</note> to the **home** <note>original: astaṃ</note>—"Astam" is a name for a house. <note>original: āyāhi is a prayer in the imperative used here for the past tense</note>. And Kutsa **became** <note>original: bhuvat</note> **intensely desiring** <note>original: nikāmo</note> of your **friendship** <note>original: sakhye</note>. Then, you two **sat down** <note>original: niṣadataṃ</note> in your **own place** <note>original: sve yonau</note>. The **woman** <note>original: nārī</note>, Indra's wife Shachi, who **perceives the Truth** <note>original: ṛtacit</note>, was **perplexed** <note>original: vicikitsat; felt doubt</note> by **you two** <note>original: vām</note> who were of **identical form** <note>original: sarūpā</note>.

-> ॥ Thus ends the eighteenth Varga of the fifth Adhyaya of the third Ashtaka ॥ <-

<summary>This page concludes the story of Indra's intervention for Sage Kutsa, ending with a famous myth where Kutsa becomes so much like Indra in appearance that even Indra's wife, Shachi, cannot distinguish between them.</summary>
<keywords>Indra, Kutsa, Shachi, Dasyu, friendship, identical form, Abrahma, Varga 18, Mandala 4</keywords>

96 || Rig Veda || [Book 4. Chapter 5. Section 19.]

->॥ Now the Eleventh Verse ॥<-

## Hymn Text
You go with **Kutsa** <term>Kutsa: A legendary king-sage and friend of Indra</term> on the same chariot, desiring to protect him, O striker [of enemies], you who are the master of the two horses swift as the **wind** <note>original: vātasyeva; like the wind</note>. While the wise one [Kutsa] wishes to harness the two straight-going horses to the chariot as if seeking a prize, he shall be empowered on that day to cross over [danger] ॥ 11 ॥

**Word-for-word breakdown**
You go | with Kutsa | on the same chariot | desiring to protect | the striker | of the wind [like] | two horses | the master |
the two straight-going | a prize | like | to be seized | wishing to harness | the wise one | when | on the day | for crossing over | shall be empowered ॥ 11 ॥

---

## Commentary (Sayana)
O **Indra**, you are **desiring to protect** <note>original: avasyuḥ; wishing for the protection of Kutsa; a grammatical form expressing desire</note> Kutsa. You are the **striker** <note>original: todaḥ; one who torments or strikes enemies</note> and the **lord** of the two wind-swift horses. **With Kutsa**, the royal sage of that name, you **go on the same chariot.** The term **to be seized** <note>original: gadhyam; derived from the root 'grah', to take</note> refers to that which is graspable. The **Nirukta** <term>Nirukta: Yaska’s ancient Sanskrit text on etymology and philology</term> cites this verse: "Wishing to harness the straight-going horses like a prize to be seized." Like one seeking food or a prize, Kutsa harnesses the straight-going horses to his own chariot. The **wise** <note>original: kaviḥ; the learned or poetic</note> Kutsa, on **whatever day** <note>original: yat ahan; on which day</note> he **is empowered** for the sake of **crossing over** <note>original: pāryāya; to cross over or escape from calamity</note>, on that very day you go with Kutsa on the same chariot. This connects with the previous statement.

->॥ Now the Twelfth Verse ॥<-

## Hymn Text
For **Kutsa**, you struck down **Shushna** <term>Shushna: A 'hissing' demon of drought defeated by Indra</term>, the joyless one; at the beginning of the day, you struck **Kuyava** <term>Kuyava: A demon whose name implies 'bad harvest'</term> and thousands [of others] instantly. Destroy the **Dasyus** <term>Dasyu: Hostile, non-sacrificing enemies</term> with the **Kutsa-like weapon** <note>original: kutsyena; the thunderbolt associated with Kutsa</note>; tear away the wheel of the **Sun** <note>original: sūraḥ; of the stimulator, the Sun</note> in the encounter ॥ 12 ॥

**Word-for-word breakdown**
For Kutsa | Shushna | the joyless | down | you struck | at the beginning | of the day | Kuyava | thousands |
instantly | the Dasyus | forth | destroy | with the Kutsa-like [weapon] | forth | of the Sun | the wheel | tear away | in the encounter ॥ 12 ॥

---

## Commentary (Sayana)
The meaning established in the verse "**Shushna and Pipru...**" <note>original: Rig Veda 1.103.8</note> is further clarified by these two verses beginning with "For Kutsa." O Indra, for the sake of **Kutsa**, you **struck down** <note>original: nibarhīḥ; you killed</note> the demon named **Shushna**, who is **joyless** <note>original: aśuṣam; devoid of happiness or 'shusha'</note>. Likewise, **at the beginning of the day** <note>original: prapitve ahnaḥ; in the forenoon</note>, you killed the demon named **Kuyava**. Furthermore, with **thousands**—meaning with many followers—**instantly**, at the same time you killed Kuyava, **destroy** <note>original: pramṛṇa; kill! (used here in the sense of a past action)</note> the **Dasyus**, the enemies, with the **Kutsa-like weapon.** The word **Kutsya** is a name for the **Vajra** <term>Vajra: Indra's celestial thunderbolt</term>. Thus, with that bolt, you killed them. Also, you **tore away** the **wheel** of the Sun, the stimulator, **in the encounter** <note>original: abhīke; in proximity or in battle</note>, meaning you severed it completely.

<summary>This page describes Indra’s close alliance with the sage Kutsa, depicting them riding together on a chariot to defeat the demons Shushna and Kuyava. It highlights Indra’s power to manipulate the elements, such as his command over wind-like horses and his ability to seize the wheel of the Sun during battle.</summary>

## Hymn Text

## Commentary (Sayana)
O Indra, you killed the demon named **Pipru** and the demon named **Mrigaya**, who was **swelling** <note>original: prushnuvāṃsaṃ; increased or grown powerful</note> with pride. Furthermore, you **surrendered** them—meaning you brought them under the control—of the King named **Rijishvan**, who is the son of Vidathin. You **struck down** <note>original: ni-vapaḥ; killed or scattered</note> **fifty thousand** demons of **dark** color. Likewise, as **old age** <note>original: jarimā</note> destroys the body or a specific form <note>original: atkaṃ na; like a garment or a body</note>, you **tore through** the cities and fortresses of the demon Shambara.

->॥ Now the Fourteenth Verse ॥<-

## Hymn Text
Placing your body near the **Sun** <term>Surya: The Sun god</term>, your immortal form became clearly visible. Like a **wild elephant** <note>original: mṛgo na hastī; literally "the beast with a hand"</note> consuming the strength [of others], you are like a fearsome lion bearing your weapons ॥ 14 ॥

**Word-for-word breakdown:**

## Commentary (Sayana)
O Indra, **when** you were **placing** or holding your **body** in the **vicinity** of the Sun—the great animator—then your **immortal** and deathless **form** was **clearly known** or specifically recognized by those who understand. The meaning is this: while all other forms become dim or overshadowed in the presence of the Sun, Indra's form is not like that; rather, his beauty shines even more brilliantly near the Sun. Moreover, O Indra, like a specific type of beast, the **elephant**, you are **consuming** or burning the strength of your enemies. **Bearing** your **weapons**, such as the thunderbolt <term>Vajra: Indra's primary weapon, often associated with a lightning bolt</term>, you became **fearsome** and terrifying like a **lion**.

## Hymn Text

-> **Verse 15 (Word-for-word Breakdown)** <-

Indra | desires | wealth-seeking | they went | in the battle for heaven | like | at the pressing [of Soma] | desiring |
seeking protection | praising | with hymns | home | like | delightful | beautiful to look upon | nourishment ॥ 15 ॥

## Commentary (Sayana)

**Desires** <note>original: kāmāḥ</note> refers to the singers who, desiring the removal of the fear of demons and other dangers, seek Indra. These singers are **wealth-seeking** <note>original: vasuyantaḥ</note>, meaning they desire riches such as cattle. They **went** <note>original: agman</note> toward Indra, who possesses supreme lordship. <note>original: agaman; the commentator notes this is a Vedic 'lung' or aorist tense used in the sense of the present tense 'they go'</note>. 

What kind of singers are they? Like those who are **desiring** victory in a **battle for heaven** <note>original: svaḥ-mīḷhe; literally "where the sun or heaven is the prize"</note>, they are **desiring** <note>original: cakānāḥ</note> or requesting [the god's presence] at the **pressing** <note>original: savane</note>, which is the sacrificial rite. They are **seeking protection** <note>original: avasyavaḥ</note>, desiring food, and **praising** <note>original: śaśamānāsaḥ</note> him with **hymns** <note>original: ukthaiḥ</note>. Then, this Indra becomes **like a home** <note>original: oko na</note>—a place of residence or refuge—for the singers. He is **delightful** <note>original: raṇvā</note> and **beautiful to look upon** <note>original: sudṛśīva</note>, appearing like the goddess Lakshmi <note>The goddess of fortune and beauty</note>.

Furthermore, Indra is **one whose wealth is desirable** <note>original: spārhā-rādhāḥ</note>. To a **singer** <note>original: jaritre</note> **like me** <note>original: māvate</note>, he **quickly** <note>original: makṣu</note> **brings** <note>original: bharati</note>—or fetches—**strength** <note>term: Vaja; usually refers to food or strength gained through sacrifice</note> that is **graspable** <note>original: gadhyam; something that should be taken or joined with</note>. Therefore, O **sacrificers** <term>Yajamana: The patrons who fund and participate in the Vedic ritual</term>, let us **call** <note>original: huvema</note> upon that Indra for you, in such a way that it constitutes a **good invocation** <note>original: su-havam</note>.

# Mandala 4. Chapter 2. Hymn 16. || Third Book || 89

<note>This section concludes the commentary for Verse 17</note>
...In the confusing battle, may the sharp and piercing thunderbolt fall <note>original: pātaati - let it fall</note> [upon our enemies]. O noble Lord <term>Indra|The king of the gods and deity of storms and war</term>, if ever a terrible and fearful clash of war should occur with our enemies, then at that time be the guardian of our bodies. You have indeed recognized us and acted as our protector against our foes.

---

## Hymn Text

-> ॥ Now the Eighteenth Verse ॥ <-

May you be the protector of Vamadeva’s prayers; may you be a friend without malice in the winning of wealth. Following your superior wisdom, we have come; O you of great praise, may you be with the singer for all time. ॥ 18 ॥

**Word-for-word Breakdown:**
Become | the protector | of Vamadeva | of the prayers | become | a friend | without malice | in the winning of wealth |
you | following | superior wisdom | we have come | of great praise | for the singer | for all time | may you be ॥ 18 ॥

## Commentary (Sayana)

O Indra, may you become the protector of the prayers <note>original: dhīnām - referring here to ritual acts or meditations</note> belonging to me, the seer named <term>Vāmadeva|The Rishi or sage to whom this fourth book of the Rig Veda is traditionally attributed</term>. Being harmless and without malice, become my friend and companion in the winning of wealth <note>original: vājasātau - also implies the "winning of war"</note>. O Indra, we have come to you, looking toward your superior wisdom and excellence. May you, who are characterized by great praise, always remain with the singer of your hymns through great songs of glorification.

---

## Hymn Text

-> ॥ Now the Nineteenth Verse ॥ <-

O Indra, with these men who seek you, and with the wealthy patrons, O Lord of Wealth, in every battle; shining like the heavens with riches, overcoming the enemy, may we rejoice through the nights and many autumns. ॥ 19 ॥

**Word-for-word Breakdown:**
With these | with men | Indra | desiring you | you | with the wealthy patrons | O Lord of Wealth | in every | battle |
the heavens | like | with riches | overcoming | being | the enemy | nights | may we rejoice | autumns | and | many ॥ 19 ॥

## Commentary (Sayana)

O <term>Maghavan|An epithet of Indra meaning "The Generous" or "Lord of Riches"</term> Indra, in every battle, we—the sacrificers—along with these men (our sons, grandsons, and attendants) who desire you for the sake of victory, and along with the wealthy patrons who possess the riches intended for the sacrificial offerings, pray to you. Just as the heavens are bright, may we be brilliant with our wealth. Overcoming our enemies, may we rejoice and praise you through all the nights and for many, many <term>autumns|The word 'śaradaḥ' (autumns) is used here to mean 'years'</term>. The meaning is that the sacrificers gladden Indra with their hymns at all times and across all seasons.

<summary>This page concludes the 16th hymn of the 4th Mandala, featuring prayers by the sage Vamadeva for Indra's protection in battle and for a long, prosperous life of ritual worship lasting many years.</summary>

<meta>This page concludes the 16th hymn (Sukta) of the 4th Mandala and provides the liturgical introduction to the 17th hymn. It marks the transition from Varga 20 to Varga 21 within the 5th Chapter (Adhyaya) of the 3rd Book (Ashtaka) of the Rig Veda.</meta>

# Rig Veda || Book 3. Chapter 5. Varga 21. || 90

## Hymn Text
-> ॥ Now the Twentieth Verse ॥ <-

Thus for Indra, the powerful showerer of blessings, the <term>Bhrigus|A legendary family of ancient sages known for their skill in crafting, often compared to master chariot-makers</term> have fashioned this prayer, just as one crafts a chariot. May he never distance himself from our friendship; may he be our fierce protector and the guardian of our bodies. ॥ 20 ॥

**Word-for-word Breakdown:**
Thus | indeed | for Indra | for the showerer of benefits | for the powerful | the sacred prayer | we have made | the Bhrigus | like | a chariot |
now | even | so that | our | friendship | may he [not] separate | may he be | our | fierce | protector | guardian of the body ॥ 20 ॥

---

## Commentary (Sayana)
Just as Indra should not separate or distance himself <note>original: vi-yauṣat - let him not separate</note> from our friendly ritual acts, and just as the fierce, radiant Indra, the protector of our bodies, should become our guardian—even so, in that manner, we the sacrificers have fashioned <note>original: akarma - we have performed or made</note> this sacred hymn <note>original: brahma - prayer or song of praise</note> for Indra, the <term>Vrishabha|The Bull; a common Vedic metaphor for a deity who "showers" or rains down strength and fulfillment of desires</term>, the eternally youthful and powerful one. 

In this, there is an illustration: "like the Bhrigus making a chariot." Just as the radiant master-craftsmen (the Bhrigus) build a chariot, so do we build this hymn. The meaning is that the worshippers praise Indra so that he may grant them the fruits they desire.

---

## Hymn Text
-> ॥ Now the Twenty-First Verse ॥ <-

O Indra, now being praised by the ancients and now being celebrated by us, cause food to swell for the singer like the flowing rivers. O Lord of the tawny steeds, a new prayer has been fashioned for you; through this wisdom, may we always be masters of chariots and your eternal servants. ॥ 21 ॥

**Word-for-word Breakdown:**
Now | praised | Indra | now | being celebrated | food/nourishment | for the singer | rivers | like | cause to swell | 
it has been made | for you | O Lord of tawny steeds | prayer | new | through wisdom | may we be | masters of chariots | eternal servants ॥ 21 ॥

---

## Commentary (Sayana)
O Indra, you who were quickly praised by the ancient seers and are now being quickly celebrated by us, make food <note>original: iṣam - nourishment or sacrificial offerings</note> swell and increase <note>original: pīpeḥ - cause to overflow</note> for me, the singer, just as the moving rivers overflow their banks. O <term>Harivan|Lord of the tawny horses; Indra is traditionally described as riding a chariot pulled by two golden-colored steeds named Hari</term>, this newer and fresher prayer has been made for you by us. Through this praise, which is the form of our intellect, may we always be "masters of chariots" <note>meaning: wealthy and victorious</note> and always remain your devotees, or those who offer the nourishment of the sacrificial butter for your sake.

-> ॥ Thus ends the twentieth Varga of the fifth Adhyaya in the third Ashtaka ॥ <-

---

## Commentary (Intro to Sukta 17)
The seventh hymn, beginning with "You are great, O Indra," consists of twenty-one verses. Regarding this, the <term>Anukramani|The ancient systematic index of the Vedas providing the poet, meter, and deity for each hymn</term> states: "The hymn 'You are great' contains one verse in the <term>Ekapada Viraj|A specific Vedic meter consisting of a single line of ten syllables</term> meter beginning 'In the Asikni,' while the remaining twenty verses are in the <term>Trishtubh|A meter consisting of four lines of eleven syllables each</term> meter. The deity is Indra." 

In the ritual context, this hymn is recited during the <term>Nishkevalya|A specific cup-offering or chant dedicated exclusively to Indra</term> ceremony on the eighth day of the "Ten Nights" <note>original: Daśarātra - a major ten-day sacrificial cycle</note> festival.

<note>The vocabulary below summarizes key terms used in the manuscript's internal glossary.</note>
- **Indra**: The chief deity of the Rig Veda, king of the gods.
- **Vrishabha**: Literally "Bull," representing strength and the pouring forth of rain/blessings.
- **Bhrigu**: A family of semi-divine sages often associated with fire and craftsmanship.
- **Brahma-akarma**: The act of composing or performing a sacred prayer.
- **Tanupa**: A title meaning "protector of the body" or the physical self.
- **Harivan**: "Possessing tawny steeds," a standard epithet for Indra.
- **Navya Brahma**: A "new prayer," indicating the continuous creative tradition of the seers.
- **Dhiya**: With prayer, intellect, or meditative insight.
- **Nishkevalya**: A specific ritual chant belonging solely to Indra during the Soma sacrifice.

<meta>This page continues the transition into the 17th hymn (Sukta) of the 4th Mandala. It provides the ritual application (viniyoga) for the hymn and presents the first two verses with their linguistic breakdown (Pada Patha) and the classical commentary by Sayana.</meta>

# Rig Veda || Book 3. Chapter 5. Varga 21. || 91

**Ritual Application:**
The use of this hymn is prescribed as follows: As noted in the liturgical texts, the verse "You, O Indra, are great..." <note>original: tvaṃ mahāṃ indra tubhyam</note> is used for the <term>Nishkevalya|A specific chant or recitation performed by the Hotri priest during the midday libation of the Soma sacrifice</term>. Additionally, the same verse is the invocatory prayer <note>original: anuvākyā</note> for the offering of the sacrificial cake <term>Pashupurodasha|A grain-offering made during the animal sacrifice ritual</term> dedicated to Indra in his aspect as the slayer of Vritra.

---

->॥ Here is the First Verse ॥<-

## Hymn Text

**You are great, O Indra; to you the earth and the heaven acknowledge sovereign power through your greatness. Having slain the obstructor <note>Vritra</note> by your might, you released the rivers that had been swallowed by the dragon.** ॥ 1 ॥

**Word-for-word Breakdown:**
You | great | Indra | to you | indeed | the earth | acknowledge | sovereign power | by greatness | recognized | the heaven |
You | the obstructor | by might | having slain | released | the rivers | by the dragon | swallowed ॥ 1 ॥

---

## Commentary (Sayana)

O **Indra**, **you** are **great** or all-pervading. The **earth** <note>original: kṣāḥ; a name for the earth</note>, being endowed with **greatness** <note>original: maṃhanā</note>, has **acknowledged** <note>original: anu-manyata</note> or granted permission to **your** **sovereign power** <note>original: kṣatram</note>—that is, your strength—for **your** sake alone. Likewise, the **heaven** acknowledged your strength. 

O Indra, **having slain** <note>original: jaghanvān</note> the demon named **Vritra**, who was the "obstructor" or "coverer" of the worlds, by **your might**, you furthermore **released** <note>original: asṛjaḥ</note> the **rivers** which were being **swallowed** <note>original: jayasānān</note> or grasped by the **dragon** <note>original: ahinā</note>, which is another name for Vritra. 

---

->॥ Now the Second Verse ॥<-

## Hymn Text

**At your radiance, at your birth, the heaven trembled; the earth trembled through fear of your own wrath. The mighty mountains were moved; the waterless tracts were moistened; the waters flowed forth.** ॥ 2 ॥

**Word-for-word Breakdown:**
Of you | of the radiant | at the birth | trembled | heaven | trembled | earth | through fear | of your own | of the wrath |
mighty | being firm | the mountains | were moved | the waterless tracts | cause to flow | the waters ॥ 2 ॥

---

## Commentary (Sayana)

O **Indra**, when **you**, the **radiant** one, were **born**, the **heaven** <note>the mid-air or celestial realm</note> **trembled** <note>original: arejat</note> due to the **fear** produced by **your own** **wrath** <note>original: manyuḥ; here used in the sense of anger or intense spirit</note>. The **earth**, too, was **trembling**. 

The **mighty** <note>original: subhvaḥ</note> **mountains** <note>original: parvatāsaḥ; Sayana interprets these as clouds in this context</note>, which were previously held in check by you for the sake of providing rain for the crops, were **moved** <note>original: ārdēn; meaning they were shaken or they destroyed the thirst of living beings</note>. Furthermore, the clouds **caused the waters** to reach the **waterless tracts** <note>original: dhanvāni; deserts or dry regions</note>.

<summary>This page presents the first two verses of Mandala 4, Sukta 17, describing Indra's cosmic birth and his victory over the dragon Vritra, which releases the cosmic waters and causes the earth and sky to tremble in awe.</summary>
<keywords>Indra, Vritra, Ahi, Earth and Heaven, Sayanacharya, Rig Veda commentary, Vedic ritual, dragon-slayer</keywords>

# Rig Veda || Book 3. Chapter 5. Varga 21. || 92

## Hymn Text

-> ॥ The Third Verse ॥ <-

**He split the mountain by his strength, hurling the thunderbolt, manifesting his power, and exerting his might. Exhilarated, he slew the obstructor <note>Vritra</note> with his thunderbolt; then the waters, their captor being slain, flowed forth with speed.** ॥ 3 ॥

---

### Pada Patha

He split | the mountain | by strength | the thunderbolt | hurling | manifestation | exerting might | power |
He slew | the obstructor | by the thunderbolt | exhilarated | flowing | the waters | with speed | their captor being slain ॥ 3 ॥

---

## Commentary (Sayana)

**Exerting his might** <note>original: sahasānaḥ</note>, which is the power to overcome enemies, and **manifesting his power** <note>original: āviṣkṛvāṇaḥ</note> or brilliance, **Indra**, **hurling the thunderbolt** <note>original: vajramiṣṇan</note> or directing the weapon, **split** <note>original: bhinat</note> the **mountain** <note>original: girim</note>—referring to the mass of clouds—**by his strength** <note>original: śavasā</note> or force. Furthermore, **exhilarated** <note>original: mandasānaḥ</note> by the Soma juice, Indra **slew** <note>original: vadhīt</note> or destroyed the demon named **Vritra** <note>the 'Obstructor'</note> **with his thunderbolt** <note>term: Vajra|Indra's signature weapon, often representing lightning</note>. Consequently, the **waters** <note>original: āpaḥ</note> that had been enveloped by Vritra became those **whose captor was slain** <note>original: hatavṛṣṇīḥ</note>. This means the "bull" or showerer, Vritra, who held them back, was killed. Once he was slain, being without further obstruction, they **flowed** <note>original: saran</note> or moved **with speed** <note>original: javasā</note> or velocity.

---

## Hymn Text

-> ॥ The Fourth Verse ॥ <-

**Heaven, your progenitor, deemed himself a hero; the creator of Indra was a most skillful worker. He who begot the heavenly one, the wielder of the good thunderbolt, who is immovable from his place, like the greatness of the earth.** ॥ 4 ॥

---

### Pada Patha

With good sons | your | progenitor | thought | Heaven | of Indra | the creator | most skillful worker | became |
Who | him | begot | heavenly | with a good thunderbolt | immovable | from his place | like | the earth ॥ 4 ॥

---

## Commentary (Sayana)

O Indra, **he who** <note>referring to Prajapati</note> **begot** <note>original: jajāna</note> **him**, meaning **you**, who are **heavenly** <note>original: svaryam</note> or worthy of being praised by the priests, who possess a **good thunderbolt** <note>original: suvajram</note>, and who are **immovable** <note>original: anapacyutam</note> or without destruction from your own **place** <note>original: sadasaḥ</note> known as heaven. The word **like** <note>original: na</note> is used here for comparison or conjunction. You are endowed with the **greatness** <note>original: bhūma</note> or vastness of the earth. **Heaven** <note>original: dyauḥ</note>, the shining **progenitor** or father of yours, who is <term>Prajapati|The 'Lord of Progeny', often identified in the Brahmanas as the father or creator of the gods</term>, **thought** <note>original: manyata</note> to himself, "I am one who has a **good son** <note>original: suvīraḥ</note>." Moreover, the **creator of Indra**, Prajapati, **became** <note>original: bhūt</note> a **most skillful worker** <note>original: svapastamaḥ</note> or one of exceedingly beautiful deeds for having produced such a son.

---

## Hymn Text

-> ॥ The Fifth Verse ॥ <-

**He who alone, by his will, moves the earth, the king of all people, Indra, who is invoked by many. All follow him with joy, the giver, the divine, the praised, the wealthy one.** ॥ 5 ॥

<vocab>
- Indra: Chief deity of the Rig Veda, slayer of Vritra.
- Vritra: The demonic serpent or cloud-dragon that holds back the rain.
- Vajra: The thunderbolt, Indra's weapon.
- Prajapati: The creator deity identified as Indra's father in this commentary.
- Shavas: Strength or raw power.
- Ojas: Vitality or the inherent brilliance of a deity.
- Maghavan: A common title for Indra, meaning 'the generous' or 'the wealthy one'.
- Janita: Progenitor or father.
- Apaḥ: The cosmic or terrestrial waters.
</vocab>

## Hymn Text

-> म० ४. अ० २. सू० १७. <-

**He who alone moves the earth, the king of the tribes, the much-invoked Indra; truly all rejoice in him, the gift of the god, who celebrates the bountiful ones.** ॥ 5 ॥

He | alone | indeed | moves | forth | the earth | king | of the tribes | much-invoked | Indra | truth | him | after | all | rejoice | the gift | of the god | of the praising one | of the bountiful one ॥ 5 ॥

## Commentary (Sayana)

The **king**, the lord of all subjects or people <note>term: kṛṣṭī|referring to the various tribes or agricultural people under divine protection</note>, the **much-invoked** <note>original: puruhūta</note> who is called upon by many—he is the one chief among the gods. This **Indra** thoroughly destroys <note>original: pracyāvayati</note> or drives away the fear that has arisen from enemies. **All** the sacrificers—following after this Indra, the shining deity who provides refuge—truly **rejoice** and offer praise for the **gift** or liberality <note>original: rātim</note> of the **bountiful** one <note>original: maghonaḥ</note>, which refers to the one who possesses the wealth of the oblations.

The word *sacā* in this context means "truly" or "together." Truly, they became abundant. Furthermore, the **delights** <note>original: madāsaḥ</note>, which are the intoxicating Soma juices, became **most exhilarating** to this **great** Indra. O **Indra**, you **became** the **Lord of Wealth** <note>original: vasupatiḥ</note>. Not merely a lord of wealth, but the master **of all riches** such as cattle and other possessions. O Indra, you **uphold** or support **all the tribes** of praisers with your **wisdom** <note>original: adhiyā</note> or your intellect, specifically when wealth is being sought.

## Rig Veda || [Book 3. Chapter 5. Verse 22.]

Toward the slopes, directed at the serpent <note>original: ahim</note> named Vritra, the demon who was lying there blocking the waters, you struck him down with your thunderbolt <note>original: vajra</note>. You have cut him to pieces.

The verse "The slayer of many, the bold..." <note>original: sacāhāṇam dādhṛṣim</note> is used as the invitatory prayer <note>term: anuvākyā|a verse recited by the Hotri priest to invite a deity to accept an offering</note> for the animal sacrifice to Indra, the slayer of Vritra. This is indicated in the Ashvalayana Shrauta Sutra <note>original: Ā. 3. 8.</note>: "The slayer of many, the bold, the impeller, Indra, the boundless, the much-invoked, the dweller."

---

-> ॥ This is the eighth verse of the hymn ॥ <-

## Hymn Text

**The slayer of many, the bold, the impeller, Indra, the great, the boundless, the showerer of boons, the well-armed;**
**Who is the slayer of Vritra, the winner and giver of food, the bountiful one, the giver of riches, the gracious giver.** ॥ 8 ॥

**Word-by-word breakdown:**
The-slayer-of-many | the-bold | the-impeller | Indra | the-great | the-boundless | the-showerer | the-well-armed |
The-slayer | who | Vritra | the-winner | and | food | the-giver | riches | the-possessor-of-wealth | the-gracious-giver ॥ 8 ॥

---

## Commentary (Sayana)

**The slayer of many** <note>original: sacāhāṇam</note> means the destroyer of numerous enemies. **The bold** <note>original: dādhṛṣim</note> means the one who is exceedingly courageous. **The impeller** <note>original: tugram</note> comes from a root meaning to incite; it refers to the one who drives or impels his enemies. **The great** <note>original: mahām</note> is the eminent one, and **the boundless** <note>original: apāram</note> means one without limit, implying he is beyond destruction. **The showerer** <note>term: vṛṣabha|literally 'bull', but in a Vedic context, it refers to a deity who 'showers' or rains down rewards and boons upon worshippers</note> is the one who pours out desired things. We, the singers of praise, worship this **Indra** who is equipped with a **beautiful thunderbolt**. 

This Indra is the **slayer** or the one who strikes down the demon named **Vritra**. **And also** <note>original: utāpi</note>, this Indra is the **winner** and **giver of food** <note>original: vājam</note>. This **bountiful one** <note>term: Maghavan|a common title for Indra meaning 'The Generous' or 'Lord of Riches'</note>, who possesses magnificent wealth, is the **giver of riches**. We praise that Indra—this connects back to the beginning of the verse. 

<note>A grammatical note: In this verse, the accusative case is used for these titles instead of the genitive case, following specific rules of Paninian grammar regarding nouns ending in specific suffixes when used with certain verbal forms.</note>

---

-> ॥ Now the ninth verse ॥ <-

## Hymn Text

**He drives away the gathered enemies; he who alone is renowned in battles as the bountiful one;**
**He brings the food that he wins; may we be dear to him in his friendship.** ॥ 9 ॥

**Word-by-word breakdown:**
He | the-enemies | drives-away | the-gathered-ones | who | in-battles | the-bountiful-one | is-heard-of | alone |
He | food | brings | which | he-wins | of-him | dear-ones | in-friendship | may-we-be ॥ 9 ॥

---

## Commentary (Sayana)

This **bountiful Indra**, who is wealthy in riches, **is heard of** or renowned as the **sole** chief hero **in battles**. This Indra **drives away** or destroys the **gathered** <note>original: samīcīḥ</note> **enemies** <note>original: vṛtaḥ</note>. Here, the "enemies" are those who surround or "cover" <note>original: vṛṇvanti</note> the world to conceal it. Whatever **food** or strength **he wins** for the sake of the sacrificer, he **brings** or sustains that food to give it to the sacrificer. May we, the singers of praise, be **dear** to such an Indra and remain **in his friendship**.

<vocab>Indra: King of the gods and deity of rain and battle, Vritra: The 'Enveloper,' a dragon/demon representing drought or chaos, Maghavan: The bountiful patron (Indra), Suvajra: He who holds the good thunderbolt, Vaja: Food, strength, or the prize of battle, Sacahana: One who slays many at once, Dadhrishi: Bold or courageous, Tugra: The one who incites or impels, Vrishabha: The bull or the one who showers boons, Suradhas: Gracious giver of wealth, Aji: Battle or race</vocab>

# Mandala 4. Adhyaya 2. Sukta 17. || Third Ashtaka || 95

-> ॥ This is the tenth verse ॥ <-

## Hymn Text
**He is renowned as conquering, and as slaying; and in battle he wins the cattle.**
**When Indra makes his wrath real, the whole world—both the fixed and the moving—trembles in fear of him.** ॥ 10 ॥

**Word-by-word breakdown:**
This-one | is-heard-of | then | conquering | and | slaying | this-one | and | forth | makes | through-battle | the-cattle |
When | real | he-makes | wrath | Indra | the-whole | the-firm | fears | the-moving | from-him ॥ 10 ॥

---

## Commentary (Sayana)
Furthermore, this Indra, conquering—that is, defeating his enemies—is "heard of" <note>original: śṛṇve</note>; he is famous everywhere. And also, as he is slaying—killing his enemies—his fame is heard everywhere. And also, through war—by means of battle—he "wins" or brings forth the cattle <note>original: gāḥ</note>, taking the livestock away from the enemy. Moreover, when Indra makes his "wrath" <note>original: manyum</note> or anger "real" <note>original: satyam</note>, meaning he makes it effective in the sense of appearing clearly, at that time the whole world—both the "firm" <note>original: dṛḷham</note>, referring to stationary things like mountains, and the "moving" <note>original: ejat</note>, referring to living, mobile beings—fears <note>original: bhayate</note> this Indra. It is terrified of him.

-> ॥ This is the eleventh verse ॥ <-

## Hymn Text
**Indra won the cattle, he won the gold, he won the horses—he, the generous one, who indeed won many [armies].**
**With these men, the most heroic leader, through his powers, is the divider of riches and the gatherer of wealth.** ॥ 11 ॥

**Word-by-word breakdown:**
Completely | Indra | the-cattle | won | completely | gold | completely | the-horses | the-generous-one | who | indeed | many |
With-these | men | the-most-heroic-leader | of-this | through-powers | of-riches | the-divider | the-gatherer | and | of-wealth ॥ 11 ॥

---

## Commentary (Sayana)
He who is indeed the generous and wealthy <note>original: maghavā</note> Indra, has "won" <note>original: samajayat</note>—meaning he has completely defeated and seized—the cattle belonging to the demons <note>original: asurāṇām</note>. Moreover, he won the gold—the beneficial and beautiful riches belonging to the enemy. Likewise, he won the horses—the herds of horses belonging to the enemy. Likewise, he won many <note>original: pūrvīḥ</note>—meaning numerous—enemy armies. The sense is that Indra, having defeated all enemies, took away all their wealth, such as their cattle.

Through his "powers" <note>original: śākaiḥ</note> or capabilities, he is the "most heroic leader" <note>original: nṛtamaḥ</note>, the supreme director who manages the captured cattle. That Indra, when praised by "these men" <note>original: nṛbhiḥ</note>—referring to the singers or worshippers—becomes the "divider" <note>original: vibhaktā</note> of this "riches" <note>original: rāyaḥ</note>, the wealth consisting of cattle and other goods. This means he is the giver who distributes the portions to those who praise him. Furthermore, he is the "gatherer" <note>original: saṃbharaḥ</note> and the sustainer or holder of wealth <note>original: vasvaḥ</note>.

<summary>These verses describe Indra's terrifying power over the entire world and his role as a victorious warrior who seizes cattle, gold, and horses from enemies to distribute them among his worshippers.</summary>
<keywords>Indra, manyu (wrath), cattle (wealth), gold, horses, maghava (generous), nrtama (heroic leader), spoils of war, distribution of wealth</keywords>

## Hymn Text
**How much [knowledge or power] does Indra indeed learn from his mother? How much from his father, the progenitor who begot him?**
**He who repeatedly impels his own vigor, like the wind driven by thundering clouds.** ॥ 12 ॥

**Word-by-word breakdown:**
How much | indeed | Indra | upon | goes (learns) | from the mother | how much | from the father | from the progenitor | who | begot |
who | of this | vigor | repeatedly | impels | wind | like | driven | with thundering | clouds ॥ 12 ॥

---

## Commentary (Sayana)
Which Indra acquires or "goes toward" <note>original: adhigacchati</note> how much strength from the presence of his mother, the one who gave birth? How much strength does he acquire from the presence of his father? Which Indra, from the progenitor—that is, from the Lord of Creatures <note>term: Prajapati|a Vedic deity presiding over procreation and the protector of life</note>—brought forth <note>original: ajanayat</note> this visible world? Which Indra, from that same Lord of Creatures, repeatedly impels or drives the vigor <note>original: śuṣmam</note> of this world? Just as the wind <note>original: vātaḥ</note> is driven or impelled by roaring, thundering clouds, so too is that Indra impelled by the praisers and called for the purpose of providing the sacrificial offerings.

---

## Hymn Text
**You make the one who is wasting away into one who is not wasting away. The Bounteous Lord drives away the gathered dust.**
**A destroyer like the heaven with its thunderbolt, may the Bounteous Lord place the singer in wealth.** ॥ 13 ॥

**Word-by-word breakdown:**
Wasting away | you | non-wasting | make | impels (drives) | dust | the Bounteous Lord | gathered |
the destroyer | thunderbolt-possessing-like | heaven | and | the singer | the Bounteous Lord | in wealth | may place ॥ 13 ॥

## Commentary (Sayana)
The Bounteous Lord <note>term: Maghavan|an epithet of Indra meaning 'the generous' or 'possessor of gifts'</note>, who is the master of riches, makes "you"—meaning a single person who is "wasting away" <note>original: kṣiyantaṃ</note> due to a lack of wealth—into one who is "not wasting away" through the gift of riches. The meaning is that a certain destitute man, having praised Indra, became abundant in wealth. Like the heaven <note>original: dyauḥ</note> or the atmosphere which, possessing a thunderbolt <note>original: aśani</note>, is a "destroyer" <note>original: vibhañjanuḥ</note> of enemies, the Bounteous Indra drives away the "gathered dust" <note>original: reṇum</note>, which refers here to sin <note>original: pāpam</note>, from the vicinity of the singer. And furthermore, the Bounteous Indra places—or has placed—the singer in "wealth" <note>original: vasau</note>.

# 97 || Rig Veda || Mandala 4. Adhyaya 2. Sukta 17. ] ->॥ Third Ashtaka ॥<- 97

## Hymn Text

**He impelled the wheel of the Sun; he stayed Etasha as he was rushing [to battle]. In the depths of the light, in the womb of this atmosphere, the dark [cloud], moving subtly, sprinkles him.** ॥ 14 ॥

**Word-by-word breakdown:**
This [Indra] | the wheel | impelled | of the Sun | down | Etasha | stayed | rushing | 
toward | the dark [cloud] | him [Indra] | moving subtly | sprinkles | of light | in the foundation | of the atmosphere | of this | in the womb ॥ 14 ॥

---

## Commentary (Sayana)

Regarding the half-verse "He impelled Etasha who was contending with the Sun" <note>original: praitashaṃ sūrye paspṛdhānam; Rig Veda 1.61.15</note>, an ancient legend was previously suggested. Here, in the first half of the verse beginning "He [impelled] the wheel," that same story is indicated. There was a certain king named Shvabhna. He worshipped the Sun <note>term: Surya|the solar deity</note> to obtain a son. The Sun himself was born there as his son and engaged in a battle with a great sage named Etasha. At that time, the sage prayed to Indra for victory in the battle. Indra, being praised by him, protected the sage from the battle involving the Sun, who had become the son of Shvabhna. 

"This Indra" impelled or sent forth the wheel, which is the weapon of the Sun. He "stayed" <note>original: nyarīramat</note> or restrained the sage named Etasha, who was "rushing" or moving toward the battle. "The dark one" refers to a dark-colored cloud <note>term: Megha|a rain cloud</note>. Moving in a subtle or "crooked" <note>original: kuṭilaṃ</note> manner, it "sprinkles" <note>original: āsiñcati</note> or refreshes Indra, who is situated in the atmosphere—the "womb" or place of "this water" <note>original: rajas|often meaning mist or atmosphere, here interpreted as water</note>—at the very foundation of the light. The meaning is that Indra protected the one who was terrified by the wheel and other weapons sent by the enemies.

---

## Hymn Text

**Word-by-word breakdown:**

## Commentary (Sayana)

This verse consists of a single line and is connected to the previous verse as an illustration. In the "dark night" <note>original: asiknyām</note>, just as a "sacrificer" <note>term: Yajamana|the person who sponsors and pays for the sacrifice</note> or a "Hotar priest" <note>term: Hota|the chief priest who recites the Rig Veda verses</note> sprinkles or pours offerings of Soma onto the fire <note>the grammar uses the first case 'priest' to mean the second case 'onto the priest-fire'</note>, in the same way, the cloud sprinkles Indra.

# 98 || Rig Veda || [Ashtaka 3. Adhyaya 5. Varga 24.]

## Commentary (Sayana) - Continued
<note>This is the conclusion of the explanation for Verse 16</note>
...the showerer <note>original: vṛṣaṇam</note> of desires, the giver of a wife, and one whose protection is undiminishing. This means he is a constant protector. Such is Indra, whom we "draw toward us" or cause to come here. An analogy is provided: "from a well" <note>original: avate</note>. The word **avata** is a name for a well, as seen in the ancient word-lists where **avata, avaṭa,** and **krivi** are listed as synonyms for a well. **Like a bucket** <note>original: kośam na</note> refers to a vessel used for drawing water. Just as men draw a bucket into a well to fill it with water, in the same way, we "draw" Indra toward us [with our prayers].

-> || Now the Seventeenth [Verse] || <-

## Hymn Text
**Be our savior, appearing as our kinsman; the overseer and comforter of those who offer Soma. A friend, a father, the most fatherly of fathers, the creator of this world, the bestower of vital strength to the one who desires [it].** ॥ 17 ॥

**Word-by-word breakdown:**
Savior | our | be | appearing | kinsman | overseer | comforter | of the Soma-offerers | friend | father | most fatherly | of fathers | creator | of this | indeed | world | to the one who desires | bestower of strength ॥ 17 ॥

## Commentary (Sayana)
O **Indra**, you who are our **kinsman**, who are **seen** by all as a protector—**be our savior** or protector. Furthermore, you are the **overseer** (the one who looks upon us) and the **comforter** (the one who gives happiness) to the **Soma-offerers**, meaning the patrons of the sacrifice. You are a **friend**, possessing a fame equal to the Lord of Progeny <note>term: Prajapati|the creator deity in Vedic thought</note>. You are a **father** or protector. You are not just a protector, but the **most fatherly among fathers** (the greatest among all protectors). You are the **creator** of this **world**—the heavenly realm and others—and for the singer who **desires** those realms, you are the **bestower of vital strength** <note>term: Vayas|typically refers to food or the energy derived from it</note>. Be the one who grants us sustenance.

---

-> || Now the Eighteenth [Verse] || <-

## Hymn Text
**Be the protector of those who desire your friendship; O Indra, being praised as a friend, bestow strength upon the one who lauds you. For we, O Indra, hard-pressed [by foes], call upon you, honoring you with these ritual acts of praise.** ॥ 18 ॥

**Word-by-word breakdown:**
of those desiring friendship | protector | be | friend | being praised | Indra | for the praiser | strength | bestow | we | indeed | toward | you | have called | hard-pressed | with these | ritual acts | honoring | Indra ॥ 18 ॥

## Commentary (Sayana)
O **Indra**, **be the protector** of us who **desire your friendship**. Likewise, **being praised** by us, **be a friend**. O **Indra, bestow strength** (food) upon me, the one **who lauds you**. O **Indra**, we who are **hard-pressed** (beset by troubles or enemies), **indeed** we **call upon you**. How so? By **honoring you** with **these** visible **ritual acts** <note>original: śamībhiḥ</note> consisting of hymns of praise.

<note>
The term "śami" refers to sacrificial labor or effort, which Sayana interprets here as the "work" of composing and reciting hymns.
</note>

<meta>This page follows page 98, which concluded the commentary on Verse 18 of Mandala 4, Sukta 17. This page presents the final two verses (19 and 20) of the hymn, providing the ritual context, the original verse, the word-by-word breakdown, and Sayana’s detailed medieval commentary.</meta>

# 99 || Rig Veda || [Mandala 4. Anuvaka 2. Sukta 17.]

The verse "Praised be Indra" <note>original: stuta indra iti</note> is used as the offering prayer <note>original: yājyā</note> for the sacrificial cake <note>original: puroḍāśa</note> dedicated to Indra, the slayer of the demon Vritra. This is indicated in the ritual manuals: "Praised be Indra, the bountiful, when he [slays] the Vritras... Indra is the true sovereign" <note>Ashvalayana Shrauta Sutra 3. 8.</note>.

->॥ This is the Nineteenth Verse of the Hymn ॥<-

## Hymn Text

**Praised be Indra, the Bountiful, when he alone slays many irresistible enemies. Dear to him is the singer, in whose refuge neither gods nor mortals interfere.** ॥ 19 ॥

---

**Praised | Indra | the Bountiful | when | indeed | enemies | many | alone | irresistible | slays |**
**his | dear | singer | in whose | refuge | no one | gods | interfere | nor | mortals** ॥ 19 ॥

## Commentary (Sayana)

**When** <note>original: yaddha</note> indeed the **Bountiful** <note>original: maghavā</note> Indra—the one who possesses great wealth—is **praised** by us, then Indra **alone** <note>original: eko'sahāya</note>, without any assistance, **slays** <note>original: hanti</note> or destroys **many** <note>original: bhūrīṇi</note> **irresistible** <note>original: apratīni</note>—meaning those who cannot be approached or opposed—**enemies** <note>original: vṛtrā</note> or obstacles. Furthermore, the **singer** <note>original: jaritā</note> or praiser of this Indra becomes **dear** <note>original: priyaḥ</note> to him. In the **refuge** <note>original: śarman</note> or protection of this Indra, where the singer remains, the **gods** <note>original: devāḥ</note> do **not interfere** <note>original: nakirvārayante</note> or offer prevention, **nor** do **mortals** <note>original: martāḥ</note> offer any prevention or obstruction.

---

In the ritual known as the *Agnimaruta Shastra*, the verse "Thus to us, Indra" <note>original: evā na indra iti</note> is the concluding verse <note>original: paridhānīyā</note>. This is indicated in the manual: "One should conclude with: 'Thus may Indra, the Bountiful, the loud-sounding...'" <note>Ashvalayana Shrauta Sutra 5. 20.</note>.

->॥ This is the Twentieth Verse of the Hymn ॥<-

## Hymn Text

**Thus may the Bountiful Indra—the loud-sounding, the sustainer of people, the unopposed—make our desires true. You, the king of all living beings, bestow upon us that great glory which is to be given to the singer.** ॥ 20 ॥

---

**Thus | our | Indra | the Bountiful | loud-sounding | may he make | true | sustainer of people | unopposed |**
**you | king | of those born | bestow | in us | over | glory | great | which | to the singer** ॥ 20 ॥

## Commentary (Sayana)

The word **loud-sounding** <note>original: virapśī</note> refers to one who makes many kinds of sounds (is mighty). The **sustainer of people** <note>original: carṣaṇīdhr̥t</note> is the one who supports all subjects. The **unopposed** <note>original: anarvā</note> is one who is not reached or overcome by any adversary. May such a **Bountiful** <note>original: maghavā</note> Indra, being praised thus by us, **make** <note>original: karat</note> or fulfill **our** <note>original: naḥ</note> **true** <note>original: satyā</note> and desired fruits of sacrifice. O Indra, **you** are the **king** or lord of **all living beings** <note>original: januṣām</note>. Therefore, **bestow** <note>original: dhehi</note> or place **in us** <note>original: asme</note>, in great measure, that **great** <note>original: māhinam</note> **glory** <note>original: śravas</note> or fame which is meant to be granted to the **singer** <note>original: jaritre</note>. This verse "Thus may Indra, the Bountiful, the loud-sounding" is also discussed in the Brahmanas <note>Aitareya Brahmana 3. 38.</note>.

## Commentary (Sayana)

The eighth hymn, beginning with "This is the path" <note>original: ayaṃ panthāḥ</note>, consists of thirteen verses and is composed in the Trishtubh meter <note>A Vedic meter of 44 syllables</note>. According to the Index <note>original: Anukramanika</note>: "The seven verses starting 'This is the path' are a dialogue between Indra, Aditi, and Vamadeva." Since the rule states that the one who speaks is the Seer <note>original: rishi</note> and the one addressed is the Deity <note>original: devata</note>, the specific seer and deity should be understood for each verse. In this hymn, a certain legend in the form of a dialogue between Indra, Aditi, and Vamadeva is suggested by the following verses:

> The great sage Vamadeva, endowed with divine knowledge even while lying in the womb, 
> resolved: "I shall not be born from the mother's birth canal in the usual way, 
> but rather through her side." Knowing this intention, the mother, 
> for the sake of peace, meditated upon the goddess Shachi and Aditi, the mother of Indra. 
> Then Aditi, accompanied by Indra, approached the pregnant mother. 
> Aditi, Indra, and Vamadeva then engaged in a dialogue. 
> This story is indicated by the mention of a "dialogue" in the ritual rules. 
> Because the specific speakers are not explicitly named in the traditional instructions, 
> the distinction between speakers must be understood from the context of the meaning. 
> Indra, Aditi, and the Sage converse in this hymn. 
> In the first verse, Indra <note>original: Shatakratu, "He of a hundred powers"</note> speaks to Vamadeva, 
> who has been lying in the womb for a long time without emerging. 
> The next five half-verses are spoken by the sage. 
> The seven half-verses beginning "Not indeed of him" <note>original: na hī nvasya</note> are the words of Aditi. 
> The five verses starting "The young mother" <note>original: mamaccana tvā yuvatiḥ</note> belong to the Sage. 
> Vamadeva speaks the final verse to ward off misfortune. 
> Thus, the distinction of speakers is determined by the sense; this is the teaching of the experts. 
> Because the meaning is clear through careful consideration, it was not explicitly stated in the primary instructions. 
> It is explained here for the purpose of correctly identifying the Seer and the Deity.

-> ॥ The First Verse ॥ <-

## Hymn Text

**This is the ancient, well-found path by which all the gods were born into being. By this same path, let him be born as he grows great; let him not bring his mother to death in that manner.** ॥ 1 ॥

**Pada Patha:**

**This | path | well-found | ancient | from which | gods | were born | all |**
**from this | indeed | [let him] | be born | the grown-one | not | mother | in that manner | to destruction | may he lead.** ॥ 1 ॥

<vocab>
<term>Indra</term>: The king of the gods and the primary deity of the Rig Veda.
<term>Aditi</term>: The personification of the infinite and mother of the principal gods (Adityas).
<term>Vamadeva</term>: The sage to whom the fourth book of the Rig Veda is attributed; famous for his prenatal wisdom.
<term>Samvada</term>: A dialogue or conversation, a specific genre of Vedic hymns.
<term>Garbha</term>: The womb or the fetus/embryo within it.
<term>Traistubha</term>: The Trishtubh meter, common in the Rig Veda, consisting of four lines of eleven syllables each.
<term>Anukramanika</term>: Ancient systematic indices or catalogs of the Rig Veda's hymns, authors, and meters.
</vocab>

Sayana's commentary provides the narrative framework for Vamadeva's miraculous birth and identifies the speakers of the upcoming dialogue.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the commentary on the 18th hymn of the fourth Mandala of the Rig Veda. It transitions from the general description of the "ancient path" of birth to the specific dialogue where the sage Vamadeva, speaking from the womb, refuses a natural birth. It also introduces Indra’s actions immediately following his extraordinary birth.</meta>

# 101 || Third Book [Ashtaka] || [Mandala 4. Chapter 2. Hymn 18.]

This ancient and beginningless path <note>original: purāṇo'nādirayaṃ</note>, which is perceived directly, is the way consisting of passage through the womb <note>original: yonirgamana-rūpo mārgo</note>. It is followed in succession by all who are being born. Since all the gods were born from this same womb-path, and all humans are born from it—what more needs to be said? Even from this very path, the well-grown embryo <note>original: pravṛddho garbhaḥ</note> Vamadeva should have been born in the normal way. However, he says: "Let me not cause this mother of mine to fall," meaning to die <note>original: mā kṛḥ; mā karotu... maraṇāyetyarthaḥ</note>.

---

## Hymn Text

-> ॥ The Second Verse ॥ <-

**"I will not go out by this [path]; it is a difficult passage. I will emerge crosswise from the side. Many deeds, as yet unperformed, are to be done by me; I must fight with one, and I must consult with another."** ॥ 2 ॥

**Word-by-word Analysis [Pada-patha]:**
**Not | I | from here | out | go | difficult to traverse | this | crosswise | from the side | out | go |**
**Many | my | unperformed | deeds to be done | I shall fight | with one | together | with one | I shall question.** ॥ 2 ॥

## Commentary (Sayana)

Vamadeva speaks thus to Indra: I will not go out from this womb-path. This way of exiting the womb is difficult to traverse <note>original: durga-ha; duḥkhena grāhyaṃ</note>; it is not to be reached. Rather, I shall emerge crosswise from the side <note>original: tiraścataḥ pārśvāt</note>. This means: "I, not having exited from the usual place, shall emerge by breaking through the side." Not only is this act being done by me—an act unperformed by others—but there are also many other deeds to be performed. For that purpose, I shall fight with one who is a disputing rival, and I shall thoroughly question another who is a seeker of knowledge.

---

## Hymn Text

-> ॥ The Third Verse ॥ <-

102 || Rig Veda || [Book 3, Chapter 5, Varga 25]

The commentator now avoids attributing "wrongdoing" to the sage and instead explains Indra’s own "inappropriate" actions through the second half of the previous verse. Indra, while being invited into the house of Tvashtri <note>The divine craftsman of the gods</note>, drank the Soma <note>The sacred sacrificial nectar</note> belonging to the one who had prepared the juice <note>original: sutavataḥ</note>, which was purchased with great wealth. He performed the drinking of the Soma by force <note>original: balātkāreṇa</note>. This story—how Tvashtri, whose son had been killed, brought the Soma—is elaborated upon in great detail in the section of the Taittiriya Samhita (2.4.12) beginning with the words "Tvashtri, having lost his son..."

-> ॥ Now the Fourth Verse ॥ <-

**What extraordinary deed will he perform, he whom his mother bore for a thousand months and many autumns? For there is certainly no one equal to him among those already born, nor among those yet to be born.** ॥ 4 ॥

**Word-by-word Analysis [Pada-patha]:**
**What | he | extraordinary | shall perform | whom | a thousand | months | bore | autumns | and | many |**
**Not | indeed | of him | an equal | exists | among | the born | and | those | to be born.** ॥ 4 ॥

---

## Commentary (Sayana)

Aditi <note>The mother of the gods</note> bore this Indra for a thousand—meaning many—months, and for many autumns, meaning years. This form of the word <note>original: jabhāra</note> is derived from the root meaning "to bear." The sense is that Indra, while remaining in the womb, caused Aditi distress for many years. 

Regarding such a being, it is asked: What "extraordinary" <note>original: rdhak; meaning a unique or contrasting action</note> deed will he do? It implies he will do everything. Aditi, the mother of Indra, not tolerating this challenge to Indra's greatness, speaks toward the sage Vamadeva: "O Vamadeva, among those already produced <note>born</note>, there is indeed no 'counter-measure' or equal to this Indra." The word **nu** is used here to fill the meter of the verse. "Furthermore, even among those gods and others who are 'to be born' <note>original: janitvāḥ; those who will be generated in the future</note>, there is no equal to this Indra."

**being born.** ॥ 5 ॥

## Commentary (Sayana)

In a "secret place" <note>original: guhā</note>, meaning a cave-like birthing chamber, the mother Aditi—perceiving the newly born Indra "as if he were a disgrace" <note>original: avadyamiva; perhaps due to the unusual nature of his birth or his overwhelming power</note>—placed him or hid him. He was already "filled with vital power" <note>original: nyuṣṭam; endowed with great strength</note>. 

Then, immediately upon being born, Indra stood up by himself, "donning his garment" <note>term: atka; a robe or armor of light/splendor</note>. As he was being born, he completely "filled the two worlds" <note>term: rodasī; the spatial duality of Heaven and Earth</note>.

## Hymn Text

-> ॥ Now the Sixth Verse ॥ <-

**These waters flow, making a bubbling sound, like righteous women calling out to one another. Ask them: what is this they are saying? Which mountain-barrier are the waters breaking through?** ॥ 6 ॥

**Word-by-word Analysis [Pada-patha]:**
**These | flow | making a bubbling sound | like those possessing truth | calling out together |**
**These | [ask] particularly | ask | what | this | they say | what | waters | mountain | barrier | break.** ॥ 6 ॥

---

## Commentary (Sayana)

The waters are described as **making a bubbling sound** <note>original: "alalabhavantīḥ"; an onomatopoeic description of the sound "alala"</note> and **like righteous women** <note>original: "ṛtāvarīḥ"; those associated with the cosmic order (Rta)</note>. These rivers, **calling out together** with a great variety of sounds due to the joy arising from the proclamation of Indra's greatness, **flow** or move forward. 

The text then addresses the Rishi <note>the sage Vamadeva</note>: "O Sage, **ask** these rivers particularly, inquire of them: **what is this they are saying** as they murmur? What is the meaning of their sound?" When one reflects on this, the answer is that their sound is a proclamation of Indra's majestic power. 

Furthermore, **what mountain** or cloud-barrier <note>original: "adrim"</note>—acting as an enclosing **fence**—do the **waters break through**? The implication is that the waters themselves do not break any cloud; rather, it is my son Indra who breaks the cloud that was obstructing the waters and sets them in motion.

## Commentary (Sayana)

The mother of the gods, Aditi, speaks here, anticipating the thought of the sage Vamadeva—who might suggest that when Indra slew the demon Vritra, he incurred the eternal sin of "Brahmin-slaying" <note>original: "brahmahatyā"; Vritra was sometimes considered the son of a priest, making his death a religious transgression</note>. 

Regarding the **invocatory formulas** <note>term: "Nivids" (invocatory mantras used in rituals, specifically the Marutvatiya Shastra, to praise the Maruts and Indra)</note>: these are certain words used to express the praise of Indra. What do these **formulas say** regarding this Indra, who is thought to have incurred sin due to the killing of Vritra? Do they speak of his guilt? If one considers him free from sin, then the formulas...

...[the waters] praise him. How can Indra be free from sin <note>referring to the myth of Indra's guilt after killing Vritra</note>? ## Commentary (Sayana)

With the remainder of the hymn, the Sage praises Indra. O Indra, **even while reckless** <note>original: "mamaccana"; meaning intoxicated with joy or heedless</note>—that is, acting without care—the **youthful woman**, your mother Aditi, **cast you away** <note>original: "parāsa"</note>. While still in the birthing-chamber, he warded off the demoness and stood up with great excellence.

## Commentary (Sayana)
**A cow that has calved once** <note>original: "gṛṣṭiḥ"</note>: Just as a cow that has given birth for the first time brings forth her calf, so did the mother of Indra, Aditi, **bring forth** <note>original: "sasūva"</note> Indra for the purpose of **wandering** <note>original: "carathāya"</note> according to his own will. What kind of Indra was he? He was **ancient** <note>original: "sthaviram"</note>, meaning matured in age; **strong** <note>original: "tavāgām"</note>, possessing great power; **unassailable** <note>original: "anādhṛṣyam"</note> by any enemies; **vigorous** <note>original: "vṛṣabham"</note>, capable of showering blessings like a bull; **powerful** <note>original: "tumram"</note>, an impeller of actions; and **unlicked** <note>original: "arīḷham"</note>, meaning he was not overcome or subdued by his foes. He was **desiring** <note>original: "icchamānam"</note> for **himself** <note>original: "svayam"</note> a **path** <note>original: "gātum"</note> for his own **body** <note>original: "tanve"</note>, choosing to walk his own way without depending on others.

<meta>This page concludes the commentary on Rig Veda 4.18.12 and provides the full text and explanation for verse 13. It marks the completion of the Fifth Chapter (Adhyaya) of the Third Book (Ashtaka). The previous page discussed Indra’s birth and his relationship with his mother, Aditi.</meta>

"Grabbing by the feet" <note>original: "pādagṛhya"</note> means that you seized him by his feet and struck him down with great force. For this reason, what other god besides you made your own **mother** <note>original: "mātaram"</note> a **widow** <note>original: "vidhavām"</note> (rendered without a husband because of the slaying of the father)? ## Hymn Text
**In my state of destitution, I cooked the entrails of a dog; among the gods, I found no consoler. I beheld my wife being dishonored; then the hawk brought the honey to me.** ॥ 13 ॥

**Padapatha:**
**In destitution | of a dog | the entrails | I cooked | Not | among the gods | I found | a consoler | I beheld | my wife | being dishonored | Then | for me | the hawk | honey | brought.** ॥ 13 ॥

---

## Commentary (Sayana)
With this verse, the Sage Vamadeva describes the excellence of Indra by pointing to his own previous state of extreme poverty. I, Vamadeva, being in a state of **destitution** <note>original: "avatyā"</note>—meaning a total lack of the means of livelihood—**cooked** <note>original: "pece"</note> the **entrails** <note>original: "āntrāṇi"</note> or the internal organs of a **dog** <note>original: "śunaḥ"</note>. Among the shining **gods** <note>original: "deveṣu"</note> such as Agni and the others, I **did not find** <note>original: "na vivide"</note> any **consoler** <note>original: "marḍitāram"</note> or anyone who could grant me happiness, except for Indra. Furthermore, I **beheld** <note>original: "apaśyam"</note> my own **wife** <note>original: "jāyām"</note> being **dishonored** <note>original: "amahīyamānām"</note>, or rather, appearing joyless and miserable due to hunger. **Then** <note>original: "adha"</note>, immediately after that time of distress, Indra—moving as swiftly as a **hawk** <note>original: "śyenaḥ"</note>—**brought** <note>original: "ājabhāra"</note> to **me** <note>original: "me"</note> **honey** <note>original: "madhu"</note>, which refers to sweet, life-giving water or sustenance.

-> ॥ Thus ends the twenty-sixth Varga of the fifth Adhyaya of the third Ashtaka ॥ <-

By the light of the meaning of the Veda, dispelling the darkness of the heart, may the Supreme Lord Vidyatirtha grant the four goals of human life <note>The Purusharthas: Dharma (Duty), Artha (Prosperity), Kama (Desire), and Moksha (Liberation)</note>.

Thus concludes the fifth chapter (Adhyaya) of the third book (Ashtaka) in the "Illumination of the Meaning of the Veda," a commentary on the Rig Veda Samhita composed by the great teacher Sayana, the minister of the empire of the illustrious King Bukka, the supreme king of kings and upholder of the Vedic path.

->॥ Salutations to the Illustrious Lord Ganesha ॥<-

I bow to that Great Lord of Knowledge <note>original: "Vidyātīrtha-maheśvara"</note>, whose breath is the Vedas, and who created the entire universe from those Vedas.

## Hymn Text

->॥ Here is the first verse ॥<-

**Thus, O Indra, wielder of the thunderbolt, here all the gods—well-invoked and protecting—and both the great Heaven and Earth, choose you alone, the grown and majestic, for the slaying of Vritra.** ॥ 1 ॥

**Word-by-word analysis (Pada-patha):**
**Thus | you | O Indra | O wielder of the thunderbolt | here | all | gods | well-invoking | protectors | great | both | Heaven and Earth | grown | majestic | you alone | indeed | they choose | for the slaying of Vritra.** ॥ 1 ॥

---

->॥ Now the second verse ॥<-

**Like the aged, the gods released [you]; you became the sovereign ruler, O Indra, true in your essence. You struck the serpent that lay around [the waters]; you carved out paths for the life-giving rivers.** ॥ 2 ॥

**Word-by-word analysis (Pada-patha):**
**Down | they released | the aged | like | the gods | you became | sovereign ruler | O Indra | of true essence | you struck | the serpent | lying around | the waters | forth | the paths | you carved | giving life to all.** ॥ 2 ॥

---

## Commentary (Sayana)

In the second section <note>original: "anuvāka"</note> of the fourth cycle <note>original: "maṇḍala"</note>, eight hymns have been explained. The ninth hymn, beginning with **"Thus, O Indra"** <note>original: "evā tvāmindra"</note>, consists of eleven verses. According to the general definitions of this cycle, **Vamadeva** is the Seer <note>original: "ṛṣi"</note>. By the standard rules of the text, **Trishtubh** is the meter <note>original: "chhandas"</note>, and **Indra** is the deity <note>original: "devatā"</note>. This is confirmed by the Index <note>original: "Anukramaṇī"</note> which states: "Thus, [a hymn of] eleven [verses]." In the **Agnishtoma** sacrifice <term>Agnishtoma: A fundamental five-day Soma sacrifice</term>, during the Midday pressing, this hymn is used in the recitation for the deity **Maitravaruna**. This is indicated in the ritual manual: "The offering verses are 'Thus, O Indra, may you be with us' and 'O Indra, well-minded and close at hand'" <note>Ashvalayana Shrauta Sutra 5.16</note>. Furthermore, on the first day of the six-day ritual <note>original: "pṛṣṭhya-abhilava-ṣaḍaha"</note>, this is the first of three "rebound hymns" <note>original: "saṃpāta-sūktāni"</note> used in place of the regular hymn for Maitravaruna. This is noted: "Thus, O Indra, what Indra [is] to us" <note>Ashvalayana Shrauta Sutra 7.5</note>.

**[Verse 1 Commentary]**
"Here" <note>original: "atra"</note> means in this sacrifice. "Wielder of the thunderbolt" <note>original: "vajrin"</note> is an address to Indra. "Well-invoked" <note>original: "suhavāsaḥ"</note> means those possessing beautiful calls. "Protectors" <note>original: "ūmāḥ"</note> means guardians. "All the gods" <note>original: "viśve devāsaḥ"</note> refers to the entire divine assembly. "Both Heaven and Earth" <note>original: "ubhe rodasī"</note> refers to the sky and the earth. In this manner, they "choose you alone" <note>original: "tvāmekam-it ni-vṛṇate"</note>—meaning they serve or honor you completely—for the "slaying of Vritra" <note>original: "vṛtra-hatye"</note>, for the purpose of killing the demon Vritra. You are described as "Great" <note>original: "mahāṃ"</note>, meaning abundant or vast; "Grown" <note>original: "vṛddhaṃ"</note>, one who has increased through divine qualities; and "Majestic" <note>original: "ṛṣvaṃ"</note>, meaning beautiful or worthy of being seen.
