<meta>This page continues the translation of Mandala 4, Hymn 19 of the Rig Veda. It completes the commentary on the second verse and provides the text and explanation for the third and fourth verses. The previous page introduced the hymn as a composition of the seer Vamadeva, focusing on Indra's heroic deeds.</meta>

O Indra, the gods—like aged fathers releasing their young sons—impelled you for the destruction of the demon. Then, O Indra, you who dwell in truth became the sovereign ruler of all the worlds. You struck the serpent Vritra <note>original: "ahi"</note>, who lay coiled around the waters. You carved out the flowing paths of the rivers that nourish all. The meaning is this: Indra, having slain Vritra, sets in motion the waters that were obstructed by him, allowing them to flow as currents.

---

-> ॥ Here is the third verse ॥ <-

## Hymn Text
**O Indra, with your thunderbolt you shattered the serpent as he lay across the seven rivers—that serpent who was never satiated, who lay limp and senseless, unconscious and deep in slumber, at the joint of the seasons.** ॥ 3 ॥

**Word-by-word analysis (Pada-patha):**
**Unsatiated | limp | senseless | unconscious | soundly sleeping | O Indra | seven | toward | rivers | lying across | the serpent | with the thunderbolt | shattered | at the joint.** ॥ 3 ॥

## Commentary (Sayana)
O Indra, you shattered Vritra the serpent with your thunderbolt at the "joint" <note>original: "aparvan"; here referring to the transition of the full moon</note>. This serpent is described as unsatiated in his enjoyments, with limp limbs, difficult to perceive, knowing nothing, and sleeping soundly. He lay obstructing the seven rivers <note>original: "sapta pravataḥ"</note> which are prone to flowing. That Vritra was slain on the full moon is supported by the Taittiriya Scripture <note>original: "Taittirīya Saṃhitā 2.5.2.5"</note>, which states: "Indeed, they strike him on the full moon; they let him swell on the new moon."

---

-> ॥ Here is the fourth verse ॥ <-

## Hymn Text
**With his might, Indra agitated the foundation of the parched sky like the wind agitates water with its power. Desiring strength, he cast down the firm clouds and struck off the peaks of the mountains.** ॥ 4 ॥

**Word-by-word analysis (Pada-patha):**
**He agitated | with might | the parched | foundation | water | like | the wind | with powers | Indra | the firm | down | he cast | desiring | strength | down | he struck | the peaks | of the mountains.** ॥ 4 ॥

## Commentary (Sayana)
Indra, endowed with supreme lordship, used his strength <note>original: "śavasā"</note> to crush the atmosphere <note>original: "budhnam"</note> which had been parched or depleted of water <note>original: "kṣāmam"</note>. An analogy is provided: just as the wind <note>original: "vātaḥ"</note> agitates the water with its great forces, so did Indra. Furthermore, Indra, desiring to manifest his power, cast down or shattered the firm and steady clouds <note>original: "dr̥ḷhāni"</note>. He also struck off the peaks <note>original: "kakubhaḥ"</note>—or figuratively, the "wings"—of the mountains <note>In Vedic mythology, mountains were once believed to have wings until Indra severed them to make the earth stable</note>, breaking them completely.

<summary>This page describes Indra’s violent destruction of the drought-serpent Vritra and his subsequent liberation of the waters. It uses vivid imagery of the thunderbolt shattering clouds and mountains to explain natural phenomena like rain and storms.</summary>
<keywords>Indra, Vritra, Vajra (Thunderbolt), Seven Rivers, Sayana's Commentary, Vedic Mythology, Atmospheric phenomena, Taittiriya Samhita</keywords>

# Mandala 4, Anuvaka 2, Hymn 19. | Third Ashtaka, Page 109

## Hymn Text

**Like mothers gazing upon a child, the stones <note>The Maruts, Indra's storm-deity companions</note> have looked toward you; like chariots, they have moved forth together. O Indra, you satisfied the flowing rivers; you struck the surging waves of the clouds and released the waters that were held captive.** ॥ 5 ॥

> **Word-by-word analysis (Pada-patha):**
> Toward | forth | they looked | mothers | like | a child | chariots | like | forth | they went | together | the stones.
> You satisfied | spreading | you struck | the waves | you | the obstructed | you released | Indra | the rivers.** ॥ 5 ॥

---

## Commentary (Sayana)

O Indra, the stones—meaning the Maruts—looked toward you as mothers <note>original: "janayaḥ"</note> look upon a child <note>original: "garbham"</note> or a son. They approached you. Furthermore, like chariots <note>original: "rathāḥ"</note> that are swift in their movement, they went forth together with you for the purpose of slaying Vritra. O Indra, you satisfied the spreading rivers; you filled them with waters. Likewise, you struck <note>original: "ubjaḥ"</note> the waves of the clouds. And so, you released the rivers <note>original: "sindhūn"</note> that had been held back or covered by Vritra.

-> ॥ This concludes the first section (varga) of the sixth chapter of the third book ॥ <-

## Hymn Text

-> ॥ Here is the sixth verse ॥ <-

**You made the great earth, which nourishes all, yield its abundance for the sake of Turviti and Vayya. With food, you calmed the surging flow; O Indra, you made the rivers easy to cross.** ॥ 6 ॥

> **Word-by-word analysis (Pada-patha):**
> You | the great | earth | nourishing all | for Turviti | for Vayya | yielding.
> You calmed | with food | surging | the flow | easy to cross | you made | Indra | the rivers.** ॥ 6 ॥

---

## Commentary (Sayana)

O Indra, for the king named Turviti and for the one named Vayya, you made the great earth <note>original: "avanim"</note>—which nourishes all—yield her desired rewards. With food <note>original: "namasā"</note>, you calmed the surging, moving flow of the waters. The meaning is that Indra makes the earth rich with food and water. Furthermore, O Indra, you made the waters <note>original: "sindhūn"</note> easy to cross <note>original: "sutaraṇān"</note>; you made them so that they could be crossed with ease.

# Rig Veda — Book 3, Chapter 6, Section 2
### Page 110

Indra, who is the destroyer of the billowing enemies <note>referring to clouds or rivals</note>, is like an army that shatters the riverbanks. He made the young women—who are the rivers, the knowers of the divine law <note>original: "ritajña"</note>, and the mothers of the truth—swell with water. **The Unmarried Ones** <note>original: "agruva"</note> is a name for these rivers. He made these forward-flowing rivers overflow. He also filled the desert places and the parched uplands with rain. Furthermore, he satisfied the thirsty men who were traveling on the path of ignorance. Additionally, Indra liberated the **wives of demons** <note>original: "damsupatni"; referring to the waters or women held captive by the "taming" or oppressive Asuras</note>. He also milked—meaning he made fruitful—the **sterile** cows that had ceased to give birth. The sense is that Indra released the cows whose offspring had been blocked by the suffering caused by demons, making them fertile once again.

---

## Hymn Text
->॥ Here is the eighth verse ॥<-

**Praised by many dawns and through many autumns, Indra, having slain Vritra, set the rivers free. He pierced the rivers that were hemmed in and held captive, so they might flow along the path of the earth.** ॥ 8 ॥

**[Word-by-word analysis]**
Many | dawns | and | autumns | praised | Vritra | having slain | he released | forth | the rivers |
hemmed in | he pierced | held captive | the flowing rivers | Indra | to impel/for the purpose of flowing | by the earth. ॥ 8 ॥

---

## Commentary (Sayana)

Indra, who had been swallowed by the darkness, having slain the demon named Vritra, created or released **many** <note>original: "purvih"</note> dawns and many autumns—meaning the years themselves. He created them specifically. Likewise, he released the waters that had been covered by Vritra. Furthermore, he pierced the **flowing rivers** <note>original: "sira"</note>—"Sira" is another name for rivers—which were **hemmed in** on all sides within the clouds and **held captive** by Vritra. He did this so they might **flow** <note>original: "savitave"</note> along the path of the **earth** <note>original: "prithivya"</note>.

---

## Hymn Text
->॥ Here is the ninth verse ॥<-

**O Lord of the Bay Horses, you rescued the son of the unmarried woman from his dwelling, where he was being eaten by ants. The blind one regained his sight; taking hold of the serpent, he emerged. The one who was in the broken jar moved his limbs.** ॥ 9 ॥

**[Word-by-word analysis]**
By ants | the son | of the unmarried woman | not giving (being eaten) | from the dwelling | O Lord of the Bay Horses | toward | you brought |
forth | the blind one | he saw | the serpent | taking hold | out | he became | the one in the broken jar | together | they moved | the limbs. ॥ 9 ॥

---

## Commentary (Sayana)

O Indra, Lord of the Bay Horses <note>original: "harivah"</note>, you rescued the son of **Agru** <note>Agru is interpreted here as a proper name or as an "unmarried woman" who abandoned her child</note>. You brought him out from his **dwelling**, which was an **anthill**, where he was being eaten by **ants** <note>original: "vamribhih"</note> or termites. While being rescued by Indra, the son of Agru, who was previously **blind**, specifically **saw** the serpent. Then he emerged; he went out from the anthill. **The one in the broken jar** <note>original: "ukhacchit"; interpreted as the one who breaks out of a container or the anthill itself</note> <unclear>...</unclear>

## Commentary (Sayana)
<note>Continued from previous page for Rig Veda 4.20.9 regarding the myth of the abandoned son healed by Indra</note>

The various joints of the limbs, which had been severed and scattered inside the "pot" <note>original: "ukhā"</note> of the anthill, were all loose and disconnected. However, they were then brought back together. The sense is that the limbs of the son, which had been weakened and pulled apart by the small ants <note>original: "upajihvikā"</note>, were rejoined and restored by the power of Indra.

---

## Hymn Text
->॥ Verse 10 ॥<-

**O wise Indra, the inspired singer, who knows your nature, proclaims your ancient heroic deeds to you, the all-knowing one. He tells of how you performed those manly, self-inspired, and human-benefiting works, O King.** ॥ 10 ॥

**Pada-patha (Word-by-word break):**
Forth | your | ancient | heroic deeds | the inspired singer | knowing well | speaks | to the one who knows | works |
just as | manly/powerful deeds | self-inspired | works | O King | benefiting men | you have performed. ॥ 10 ॥

## Commentary (Sayana)

O King <note>original: "rājan"</note>, who are Indra, the performer of the sacrifice: just as you have performed <note>original: "viveshīḥ"</note> your **powerful deeds** <note>original: "vṛṣṇyāni"</note> which are capable of showering benefits, which are **self-inspired** <note>original: "svagūrtā"</note>—meaning they arose from your own will—and which are **beneficial to men** <note>original: "naryā"</note>, so too does the inspired singer <note>original: "vipra"</note> speak of them. This sage, Vamadeva, knowing your nature completely, proclaims <note>original: "pra... āha"</note> your **ancient** <note>original: "pūrvāṇi"</note> **achievements** <note>original: "karaṇāni"</note> and your **works** <note>original: "karāṃsi"</note> to you, who are **all-knowing** <note>original: "viduṣe"</note>.

---

## Hymn Text
->॥ Verse 11 ॥<-

**Now, O Indra, being praised by the ancients and now being lauded by us, make nourishment swell for the singer like mountain rivers. O Lord of the Bay Horses, a new prayer has been fashioned for you; through this wisdom, may we always be masters of chariots and givers of offerings.** ॥ 11 ॥

**Pada-patha (Word-by-word break):**
Now | praised | O Indra | now | being lauded | food/nourishment | for the singer | rivers | like | make swell |
has been made | for you | O Lord of the Bay Horses | prayer/hymn | new | through wisdom | may we be | masters of chariots | always-giving. ॥ 11 ॥

## Commentary (Sayana)

O **Indra**, you who were **praised** <note>original: "stutaḥ"</note> **now** (and in the past) by the ancient Rishis, and are **now** being **lauded** <note>original: "gṛṇānaḥ"</note> by us: **make swell** <note>original: "pīpeḥ"</note> or increase the **nourishment** <note>original: "iṣam"</note> and food **for the singer** <note>original: "jaritre"</note>—meaning for me, the invoker. Let this food flow **like rivers** <note>original: "nadyo na"</note> coming from the mountains. O **Lord of the Bay Horses** <note>original: "harivo"</note>, a **new** <note>original: "navyam"</note> **prayer** <note>original: "brahma"</note> or hymn **has been made** <note>original: "akāri"</note> by us for you. Through this **wisdom** <note>original: "dhiyā"</note> consisting of praise, may we **become** <note>original: "syāma"</note> **masters of chariots** <note>original: "rathyo"</note> and **always-giving** <note>original: "sadāsāḥ"</note>—meaning those who constantly worship you and provide oblations of food for your sake.

->॥ This ends the second section (Varga) of the sixth chapter of the third book (Ashtaka) ॥<-

## Critical Notes
<note>Introductory notes for Hymn 21</note>

The tenth hymn, beginning with **"Ā na indra"** (Come to us, O Indra), consists of eleven verses. The Seer (Rishi) is Vamadeva, the meter is Trishtubh, and the deity is Indra. This is noted in the Index <note>original: "Anukramanika"</note> by the phrase "Ā na." During the six-day ritual cycles (Prishthya and Abhiplava), on the first day, this hymn is used in the specific recitation known as the Nishkevalya Shastra.

<vocab>
- <term>vṛṣṇyāni</term>: Manly or powerful deeds; often implies the power to "shower" or fertilize like rain.
- <term>vipra</term>: A sage or inspired poet who possesses inner vision.
- <term>indra</term>: The king of the gods in the Rig Veda, associated with thunder, rain, and heroism.
- <term>vāmadeva</term>: The ancestral sage to whom the fourth book (Mandala) of the Rig Veda is attributed.
- <term>brahma</term>: In this context, it refers to the sacred word, prayer, or hymn of praise.
- <term>harivaḥ</term>: An epithet for Indra, meaning "possessor of the Hari horses" (usually translated as bay or golden-tawny horses).
- <term>jaritre</term>: The one who sings or invokes the deity during a sacrifice.
- <term>iṣam</term>: Strength, vitality, or food-offering.
- <term>adrinadī</term>: A mountain river, used here as a metaphor for an abundant, rushing flow of blessings.
</vocab>

<summary>This page concludes Sukta 20 with prayers for Indra to provide nourishment like rushing rivers and highlights the poet's role in proclaiming Indra's ancient deeds. It also introduces Sukta 21, detailing its ritual use and authorship by the sage Vamadeva.</summary>
<keywords>Indra, Vamadeva, heroic deeds, nourishment, bay horses, Varga conclusion, Nishkevalya Shastra, Vedic ritual</keywords>

<meta>The previous page concluded the commentary on Mandala 4, Hymn 20. This page begins a new section, Mandala 3, Hymn 37, which is dedicated to Indra. The header confirms we are now in the Third Ashtaka (Book), Sixth Adhyaya (Chapter), Third Varga (Section).</meta>

112 ॥ Rig Veda ॥ [ Book 3. Chapter 6. Section 3. ]

It has been prescribed in the liturgical manuals: **"A na indra"** (Come to us, Indra) is the *Nishkevalya* <note>A specific recitation dedicated to Indra during the midday libation</note> Shastra recitation (Ashvalayana Shrauta Sutra 7. 5.). This hymn is also a "Sampata" hymn <note>A 'falling together' or 'attainment' hymn used for specific ritual effects</note> used in the *Mahavrata* ceremony <note>A major Vedic rite performed at the end of the year</note>. Similarly, it is prescribed in the Fifth Aranyaka: **"A na indro durad a na asad"** is the *Sampata* (Aitareya Aranyaka 5. 8.).

->॥ Here begins the First Verse ॥<-

## Hymn Text

May Indra come to us from afar, may he come from near; may the fierce one, the fulfiller of desires, come for our protection. May the leader of men, with the thunderbolt in his arm, together with his most powerful companions, be the conqueror of attacking enemies in the meeting of battles. ॥ 1 ॥

**Pada-patha (Word-by-word break):**
Towards | us | Indra | from afar | towards | us | from near | fulfiller of desires | for protection | may he come | the fierce |
with the most powerful [Maruts] | the leader of men | thunderbolt-armed | in the meeting | in battles | the conqueror | those who attack. ॥ 1 ॥

---

## Commentary (Sayana)

May Indra—the fierce one and the **fulfiller of desires** <note>original: "abhiṣṭikṛt"</note> belonging to the sacrificer—come from afar for our protection. Let him arrive. Furthermore, may he also come to us from near <note>original: "āsāt"</note>, from close by, for our protection. What is his nature? He is the **conqueror** <note>original: "turvaṇiḥ"</note> or destroyer of enemies when there is a **meeting** <note>original: "saṃge"</note> or encounter with foes in **battles** <note>original: "samatsu"</note>. He is the **thunderbolt-armed** <note>original: "vajrabāhuḥ"</note>, the **leader of men** <note>original: "nṛpatiḥ"</note>—the protector of human beings—and he is joined by his **most powerful** <note>original: "ojiṣṭhebhiḥ"</note> companions, meaning the extremely radiant Maruts <note>Storm deities who are Indra's constant companions</note>.

->॥ Now the Second Verse ॥<-

## Hymn Text

May Indra, facing toward us, come with his bay horses for our protection and for our wealth. May the thunderbolt-wielder, the bountiful, the mighty one, stand over this sacrifice of ours in the winning of the prize. ॥ 2 ॥

**Pada-patha (Word-by-word break):**
Towards | us | Indra | with his bay horses | may he come | toward | facing us | for protection | for wealth | and |
may he stand | the thunderbolt-wielder | the bountiful | the mighty | this | sacrifice | following | our | in the winning of the prize. ॥ 2 ॥

---

## Commentary (Sayana)

May Indra, being **facing toward us** <note>original: "arvācīnaḥ"</note>, come toward us <note>original: "accha"</note> with his **bay horses** <note>original: "haribhiḥ"</note> for our **protection** <note>original: "avase"</note> and for our **wealth** <note>original: "rādhase"</note>. Furthermore, may the **thunderbolt-wielder** <note>original: "vajrī"</note>, the **bountiful** <note>original: "maghavā"</note>, and the **mighty** <note>original: "virapśī"</note>—for "Virapshi" is listed among the synonyms for "great"—stand over <note>original: "tiṣṭhāti"</note> this sacrifice of ours. This occurs when we have reached the **winning of the prize** <note>original: "vajasātau"</note>, meaning the battle with the Asuras <note>original: "asurādibhiḥ"</note> and others who obstruct our work. Let him stand there, intending for this sacrifice.

->॥ Now the Third Verse ॥<-

## Hymn Text

O thunderbolt-wielder, Indra, placing this sacrifice of ours before you, you grant us our sacrificial will. Just as a horseman wins a race, may we, through you, win the prize of wealth in the contest. ॥ 3 ॥

<vocab>
**Indra** (Indra): The King of the Gods and god of storms and war.
**Durat** (from afar): Signifies Indra's ability to hear prayers from any distance.
**Asat** (from near): Signifies Indra's immediate presence.
**Vajrabahu** (thunderbolt-armed): Indra's primary weapon is the *Vajra*.
**Samatsu** (in battles): The Vedic life often involved conflicts where Indra's aid was sought.
**Maghava** (bountiful/wealthy): A common epithet for Indra as the giver of rewards.
**Virapshi** (great/mighty): Implies vastness or overwhelming power.
**Vajasati** (winning of wealth/war-prize): Literally "the conquest of food/strength," often referring to battle-spoils.
**Kratu** (sacrifice/will): Can mean either the physical ritual or the mental intention behind it.
</vocab>

<meta>This page continues the translation of Mandala 4, Hymn 20. Note that the previous page's metadata mentioned Mandala 3, Hymn 37, but the current source text is clearly marked as Mandala 4, Hymn 20, which is dedicated to Indra. This page covers the end of Mantra 3, and the full text and commentary for Mantras 4 and 5.</meta>

[Mandala 4. Adhyaya 2. Sukta 20.] ॥ Third Ashtaka ॥ 113

## Hymn Text

-> [Conclusion of Mantra 3] <-

This | sacrifice | you | our | Indra | in front | placing | you will gain | rite | our | like a hunter | thunderbolt-wielder | for gain | of riches | by you | we | of the enemy | battle | may we win. ॥ 3 ॥

---

## Commentary (Sayana)

O **Indra**, you, **placing us in front** <note>original: "puro dadhat"; meaning giving us priority or leadership</note>, will favor **our rite**, this **sacrifice** currently being performed. Furthermore, like a **hunter** <note>original: "shvaghni", literally "dog-killer," a term for a hunter or a gambler</note> seeking deer, O **wielder of the thunderbolt** <note>original: "vajrin"</note>, with **your** help, may **we**—your praisers—**win the battle** against the **enemy** <note>original: "aryaḥ", interpreted here as the foe</note> for the **gain of riches** such as cattle and other wealth. May we be completely victorious.

In the *Agnishtoma* sacrifice, during the midday libation (*madhyandina-savana*), the verse starting with **"Ushannu ghu nah"** is the offering prayer (*yājyā*) for the Maitravaruna priest. This is also indicated in the ritual manuals: "The verse 'Ushannu ghu nah sumana upake' is the offering prayer" <note>Ashvalayana Shrauta Sutra 5. 16.</note>.

-> ॥ This is the fourth verse of the hymn ॥ <-

## Hymn Text

Desiring us indeed, well-disposed and nearby, O self-powerful one, drink now of the well-pressed Soma. O Indra, drink of the offered sweet juice; may you be thoroughly delighted by the food and the *Prishtya* chants. ॥ 4 ॥

**Word-by-word breakdown:**
Desiring | indeed | indeed | to us | well-disposed | nearby | of Soma | now | well-pressed | O self-powerful | drink | Indra | offered | of the sweet | thoroughly | with the food | may you rejoice | with the Prishtya. ॥ 4 ॥

---

## Commentary (Sayana)

O **self-powerful one** <note>original: "svadhavah"; one possessing food or inherent power</note>, O Indra, you who are **well-disposed** (possessing a gracious mind), being **nearby** to **us**, and **desiring** us greatly, **drink** <note>original: "pāḥ"</note> **now** (quickly) of the **Soma** juice which is **well-pressed** and **offered** (duly prepared) and is **sweet** (intoxicating). By the **Soma-food** <note>original: "andhasā"</note> that has been drunk and by the **Prishtya**—this term **Prishtya** refers to the *Stotra* (hymn of praise) chanted by the Udgatar priests during the midday libation—associated with it, **may you be thoroughly delighted** <note>original: "sam-mamadaḥ"</note>.

-> ॥ Now the fifth verse ॥ <-

## Hymn Text

He who is loudly praised by the new seers, like a tree full of ripe fruit, like a victorious warrior skilled with weapons; like a young man thinking of a young woman, I call upon that much-invoked Indra. ॥ 5 ॥

**Word-by-word breakdown:**
Thoroughly | who | is praised | by seers | new | tree | like | ripe | weapon-skilled | like | conqueror | young man | like | young woman | towards | thinking | towards | I call | much-invoked | Indra. ॥ 5 ॥

---

## Commentary (Sayana)

Like a **tree** <note>original: "vṛkṣo na"</note> that is **ripe** with fruit. Here, the word *srini* (sickle/hook) refers to a weapon; by it, any weapon is implied. Like a **conqueror** who is a heroic man **skilled with weapons** and victorious over enemies; **who** (Indra) is **variously praised** <note>original: "vi rarapshe"</note> by **new** (modern) **seers**. I, the singer, **call upon** that **Indra** who is **invoked by many**, just as a **young man** yearns for and **thinks of a young woman**...

<term>Prishtya (पृष्ट्य)</term>: A specialized form of chanting used in Vedic rituals, specifically during the midday libations, involving complex musical arrangements of the Samaveda.

<term>Madhyandina-savana (माध्यंदिनसवन)</term>: The second of the three daily Soma pressings/offerings, performed at noon and primarily dedicated to Indra.

The commentary explains the liturgical use of these verses in the Agnishtoma sacrifice and uses vivid metaphors, like a ripe fruit tree and a yearning lover, to describe Indra's bounty and the worshiper's devotion.</summary>

[Sayana concludes the commentary on Verse 5:] ...targeting [the deity], he speaks specifically. "I speak specifically" means "I praise." In this context, an illustration is provided: just as a mortal man, recognizing "this woman is mine," approaches his wife, so too [does the singer approach the deity].

## Hymn Text
->॥ Now the Sixth Verse ॥<-
Like a mountain, self-powerful and great is Indra, born from of old for overpowering strength, the fierce one. He, the formidable one, struck the great thunderbolt like [pouring] a vessel overflowing with wealth. ॥ 6 ॥

**Word-by-word breakdown:**
Like | a mountain | who | self-powerful | great | Indra | from of old | indeed | for strength | born | fierce | the striker | the thunderbolt | great | like | formidable | like | a vessel | with wealth | sent forth. ॥ 6 ॥

## Commentary (Sayana)
"Like a mountain" <note>original: "giriḥ"</note> means like a hill. "Self-powerful" <note>original: "svatavān"</note> means naturally augmented or powerful by his own nature. "Great" <note>original: "ṛṣvaḥ"</note> means vast; the word *Rishva* is listed in the ancient lexicons <note>the Nighantu</note> as a synonym for both "great" (*mahat*) and "the sacred word" (*brahma*). That **Indra**, who is "fierce" <note>original: "ugra"</note> or full of energy, was "born" or manifested "from of old" <note>original: "sanādeva"</note>—that is, from a long time ago—for the "overpowering" <note>original: "sahase"</note> or defeat of enemies. He is "formidable" <note>original: "bhīmaḥ"</note> because he inspires fear in his foes. That Indra "struck" <note>original: "ādartā"</note>—meaning he hit or discharged—the "great" <note>original: "sthaviram"</note> "thunderbolt" <note>original: "vajram"</note>. The poet uses a comparison: just as one might tip a "vessel" <note>original: "kośam"</note> to pour out water, Indra [discharged the weapon] which was "sent forth" <note>original: "nṛṣṭam/nisṛṣṭam"</note> with "wealth" <note>original: "vasunā"</note>, meaning with radiant energy or power. In this verse, the particle "na" is used both for comparison ("like") and as a conjunction ("and").

---

## Hymn Text
->॥ Now the Seventh Verse ॥<-
By birth, there is indeed no restrainer of you; there is no one to snatch away your gift of bounty. O powerful and fierce one, showering [blessings], O you who are invoked by many, grant us wealth! ॥ 7 ॥

**Word-by-word breakdown:**
Not | of whom | restrainer | by birth | indeed | is | not | of the gift | snatcher | of bounty | showering | O powerful one | O fierce one | to us | grant | O you invoked by many | wealth. ॥ 7 ॥

## Commentary (Sayana)
O **Indra**, by your "birth" <note>original: "januṣā"</note>—that is, by your very nature—there is "truly" <note>original: "nu"</note> no "restrainer" <note>original: "vartī"</note> who can ward you off or stop you. Regarding your "bounty" <note>original: "maghasya"</note>, which is the wealth you give that facilitates "sacrificial rites" <note>original: "rādhasaḥ"</note>, there is no "snatcher" <note>original: "amarītā"</note> or person capable of destroying it. O "powerful one" <note>original: "taviṣīvaḥ"</note>, you who possess great strength and luster; O "fierce" <note>original: "ugra"</note> lord; O "invoked by many" <note>original: "puruhūta"</note>—you who are called upon by many worshippers—you are the "showerer" <note>original: "udvṛṣāṇaḥ"</note> who rains down the fulfillment of our desires. "Grant" <note>original: "daddhi"</note> or give to "us" <note>original: "asmabhyam"</note>, your praisers, "wealth" <note>original: "rāyaḥ"</note> consisting of cattle and other riches.

## Hymn Text
->॥ Now the Eighth Verse ॥<-
I behold the wealth of the domain of the people, and you are the one who opens the fold of the cattle; O leader of men, you are the winner in battles, the lord who brings us abundant treasure. ॥ 8 ॥

## Hymn Text

<note>RV 4.20.8 (continued from previous page)</note>
I rule over. Of wealth. Of the home. Of the people. And. The enclosure. The opener. You are. Of cows.
The guide of men. In battles. The great one. Of wealth. A heap. The bringer. You are. Abundant. ॥ 8 ॥

## Commentary (Sayana)

O Indra, you rule over <note>original: "īkṣe"</note>—that is, you look after—the wealth and the homes <note>original: "kṣayasya"</note> of the people <note>original: "carṣaṇīnām"</note>. Furthermore, you are the opener <note>original: "apavartā"</note> of the cow-pens. The meaning is that you are the one who releases the cows from the demons who obstruct them. Moreover, O Indra, you are the guide of men <note>original: "śikṣānaraḥ"</note> because you are the ruler of the wise through your instruction. In battles <note>original: "samitheṣu"</note>, you are the great one who wields weapons. You are the bringer <note>original: "abhinetā"</note> who causes one to obtain a vast heap of wealth. ॥ 8 ॥

## Hymn Text

-> || Now the Ninth Verse || <-

<note>RV 4.20.9</note>
By what power is he heard, he who is most wise? By which power does the lofty one frequently perform any deeds? He is the great destroyer of sin for the giver of oblations; he bestows wealth upon the singer. ॥ 9 ॥

**Word-by-word Analysis:**
By what. That. Is heard. By power. Most wise. By which. He performs. Frequently. Any. Indeed. Lofty. Abundant. For the giver. The great destroyer. Sin. Toward. He places. Wealth. For the singer. ॥ 9 ॥

---

## Commentary (Sayana)

**The most wise** <note>original: "śaciṣṭhaḥ"</note> means the one who is exceedingly intelligent. **"That"** <note>original: "tat"</note> represents Indra (though the grammatical gender varies here). By **what power** <note>original: "kayā śacyā"</note>—that is, by what wisdom—is he **heard** <note>original: "śṛṇve"</note>? The word *Shachi* is a synonym for wisdom. The **lofty** <note>original: "ṛṣvaḥ"</note> or great Indra, by which wisdom does he **frequently** <note>original: "muhu"</note> **perform** <note>original: "kṛṇoti"</note> **any** <note>original: "kā cit"</note> deeds? That Indra becomes the **great destroyer** <note>original: "vicayiṣṭhaḥ"</note> or the one who completely removes the **abundant** <note>original: "puru"</note> **sin** <note>original: "aṃhaḥ"</note> of the **giver** <note>original: "dāśuṣe"</note>, the sacrificer who has offered oblations. Furthermore, he **places** <note>original: "dadhāti"</note> or gives **wealth** <note>original: "draviṇam"</note>, characterized by cattle and other riches, to the **singer** <note>original: "jaritre"</note> or the one who offers praise. ॥ 9 ॥

---

## Hymn Text

-> || Now the Tenth Verse || <-

<note>RV 4.20.10</note>
Do not harm us; bring [wealth] to us. Grant us that; for you are able to give much to the one who offers oblations. In this new, praised hymn, we shall proclaim Indra, offering our praise. ॥ 10 ॥

**Word-by-word Analysis:**
Do not. Us. Harm. Toward. Bring. Grant. That. Us. [Preverb for giving]. For the giver. To give. Abundant. Which. Yours. In the new. In the gift. In the praised. In this. Yours. In the hymn. [Preverb for proclaiming]. We speak. We. Indra. Praising. ॥ 10 ॥

---

## Commentary (Sayana)

O Indra, **do not harm us** <note>original: "mā no madhīḥ"</note>. Do not injure us. Instead, **bring** <note>original: "ābhara"</note> for us; be our nourisher. O Indra, **that** wealth of **yours** which is **abundant** <note>original: "bhūri"</note> and which suffices **to give** <note>original: "dātave"</note> to the **giver** <note>original: "dāśuṣe"</note>—the sacrificer who has offered oblations—having gathered that wealth, **grant** <note>original: "daddhi"</note> it to us. Give it. O Indra, we who are praising you...

<vocab>
Indra: the king of the gods in Vedic tradition; charshani: the active people or human subjects; shachi: power, often interpreted by Sayana as wisdom or skill; dravinam: wealth, usually in the form of livestock; uktha: a recited hymn or song of praise.
</vocab>

The eleventh hymn, beginning with "May Indra come," consists of eleven verses. It was revealed to the seer Vamadeva, is composed in the <term>Trishtubh</term> meter <note>A Vedic meter of 44 syllables</note>, and is dedicated to Indra. This is confirmed by the Index <note>original: "Anukramani"</note> which states: "May Indra come." In the six-day ritual cycles known as the <term>Prishthya</term> and <term>Abhilava</term>, this hymn is used as the <term>Nividdhaniya</term> <note>a specific placement for a sacrificial formula</note> on the first day. This is also indicated in the liturgical manuals: "May Indra come for our help" is the hymn for the <term>Marutvatiya</term> section <note>A libation offered to Indra accompanied by the Maruts</note>. [Asvalayana Shrauta Sutra 7. 5. 1].

## Hymn Text

May Indra come to us for protection and for help; praised here, may the hero be with us in joy. Increasing in strength, he whose powers are ancient and many—like heaven, may he nourish his overcoming sovereignty. ॥ 1 ॥

**Padapatha:**
May. Come. Indra. For protection. For help. Our. Here. Praised. Joy-sharing. May be. Hero.
Increasing. Strengths. Whose. Many. Heaven. Like. Sovereignty. Overcoming. May [he] nourish. ॥ 1 ॥

## Commentary (Sayana)

May that Indra come near <note>original: "upāyātu"</note> for our protection <note>original: "rakṣaṇāya"</note>. May this Indra, who is praised <note>original: "stutaḥ"</note> here in this sacrifice, who is a hero <note>original: "śūraḥ"</note> of great valor, and who is increasing <note>original: "vavṛdhānaḥ"</note> in stature, be one who rejoices with us <note>original: "sadhamādastu"</note>. The powers <note>original: "taviṣīḥ"</note> or strengths of this Indra are many <note>original: "pūrvīḥ"</note> and ancient. Just as the shining <note>original: "dyotamānaḥ"</note> sun in heaven, may Indra nourish <note>original: "puṣyāt"</note> his own sovereignty <note>original: "kṣatram"</note> or strength, which overcomes the power of others. This connects back to the beginning: may such an Indra come near.

## Hymn Text

Praise the manly powers of him here, the very glorious, the giver of much wealth to men. His wisdom is like a lightning flash; the sovereign, the overcomer, the deliverer, he stands above all people. ॥ 2 ॥

<vocab>
Indra: The king of the gods and deity of storms and war.
Vamadeva: The primary seer (Rishi) of the fourth book of the Rig Veda.
Trishtubh: A common Vedic meter with four lines of eleven syllables each.
Nishkevalya: A specific chant for Indra performed at the midday sacrifice.
Marutvatiya: A ritual part of the Soma sacrifice involving Indra and the Maruts (storm gods).
Tavishi: Spiritual or physical strength and power.
Shura: A hero or warrior.
Sadhamada: A companion in a feast or sacrifice; one who shares in the joy.
Ashtaka/Adhyaya/Varga: Traditional divisions used to organize the text of the Rig Veda.
</vocab>

## Hymn Text

<note>Rig Veda 4.21.2 Pada-patha — Word-for-word breakdown</note>
His. Indeed. Here. Praise. Manly powers. Of much glory. Of much wealth. Leaders.
Whose. Power. Worthy of the assembly. As. Sovereign. Overpowering. Rescuing. Over. Is. The people. ॥ 2 ॥

---

## Commentary (Sayana)

**Of much glory** <note>original: "tuvidyumnasya"</note> means one of great fame; **of much wealth** <note>original: "tuvirādhaso"</note> means one possessing great riches. **His indeed** <note>original: "tasyet"</note>—that is, of that very Indra—you must **praise** <note>original: "stavatha"</note> the **manly powers** <note>original: "vṛṣṇyāni"</note>, which are the heroic **leaders** <note>original: "nṝn"</note>, the Maruts <note>The storm gods who accompany Indra</note>. O praisers, do this in this sacrifice. He is **overpowering** <note>original: "sāhvān"</note>, meaning he defeats his enemies, and a **rescuer** <note>original: "tarutro"</note>, meaning he delivers us from calamities. **Whose** <note>original: "yasyendrasya"</note>—that is, Indra's—**power** <note>original: "kratuḥ"</note> or action **is over** <note>original: "abhyasti"</note> or overcomes the **people** <note>original: "kṛṣṭīḥ"</note> belonging to the enemy. An illustration is given: **As a sovereign worthy of the assembly** <note>original: "vidathyo na samrāṭ"</note>. This means like a universal ruler who is worthy of the assembly <note>original: "vidatha"</note> or sacrifice, and who is the lord of all worlds. The phrase "his manly powers" from earlier is connected here as well.

---

## Hymn Text

-> ॥ Now the Third Verse ॥ <-

May Indra come to us from heaven, or from the earth; may he come quickly from the sea or from the watery firmament. May he come from the sun-lit realm for our protection, accompanied by the Maruts; or from the distant region, or from the dwelling of the waters. ॥ 3 ॥

<note>Rig Veda 4.21.3 Pada-patha — Word-for-word breakdown</note>
Toward. Let him come. Indra. From heaven. Toward. From earth. Quickly. From the sea. And. Or. From the watery firmament.
From the sun-lit realm. For protection. Our. Attended by the Maruts. Distant. Or. From the dwelling. Of the water. ॥ 3 ॥

---

## Commentary (Sayana)

**Attended by the Maruts** <note>original: "marutvān"</note>, meaning accompanied by the storm-gods, may **Indra** **come** <note>original: "ā yātu"</note> for **our protection** <note>original: "no'vse"</note>. Let him come **from heaven** <note>original: "divaḥ"</note>, the celestial world, and **from the earth** <note>original: "pṛthivyā"</note>, the terrestrial world; let him come **quickly** <note>original: "makṣu"</note>. **And or** <note>original: "uta vā"</note>—alternatively—let him come **from the sea** <note>original: "samudrāt"</note>, which here refers to the atmosphere. "Sea" is a name for the atmosphere, as it is listed among such names in the ancient lexicons <note>e.g., the Nighantu</note>. Or let him come **from the watery firmament** <note>original: "purīṣāt"</note>. The word *purisha* is a name for water, as seen in the lexical lists alongside terms like *madhu* and *pippala*. Let him come **from the sun-lit realm** <note>original: "svarṇarāt"</note>, which is the world where the sun <note>original: "svaḥ"</note> is the man <note>original: "naraḥ"</note> or leader. **Or from the distant region** <note>original: "parāvato vā"</note>, let him come from afar. Let him come **from the dwelling of the water** <note>original: "ṛtasya sadanāt"</note>, which is the world of the clouds. In this context, *rita* is interpreted as water.

---

## Hymn Text

-> ॥ Now the Fourth Verse ॥ <-

Him who rules over thick wealth and great riches—that Indra indeed let us praise in the assemblies. He who conquers alongside the Wind in the battles for cattle, and boldly leads us toward better things. ॥ 4 ॥

<note>Rig Veda 4.21.4 Pada-patha — Word-for-word breakdown</note>
Of the thick. Of wealth. Of the great. Who. Rules. Him. Indeed. Let us praise. In the assemblies. Indra.
Who. With the Wind. Conquers. In the cattle-possessing (battles). Forward. Boldly. Leads. Better wealth. Toward. ॥ 4 ॥

---

## Commentary (Sayana)

**Who** <note>original: "yaḥ"</note>, namely Indra, **rules** <note>original: "īśe"</note> over **thick** <note>original: "sthūrasya"</note> or substantial and **great** <note>original: "bṛhato"</note> or vast **wealth** <note>original: "rāyaḥ"</note>. This occurs **in the assemblies** <note>original: "vidatheṣu"</note> or sacrifices; *vidatha* is a name for a sacrifice. **Him indeed** <note>original: "tam u"</note>—that very Indra—let us, the praisers, **praise** <note>original: "stavāma"</note>. **Who**, Indra...

--- Page 184 ---
<meta>This page concludes the commentary for Rig Veda, Mandala 4, Sukta 21, Verse 4, and provides the full text and commentary for Verses 5 and 6. It follows the previous page's discussion on Indra's power to grant wealth and victory. This section is part of the 3rd Ashtaka, 6th Adhyaya, 6th Varga.</meta>

Through **Vayu** <term>Vāyu: the god of wind, interpreted here as the vital breath or strength</term> who is the form of life-force, he conquers and triumphs over enemies in armies possessing cattle. The **bold** <note>original: dhṛṣṇuḥ</note> and courageous Indra leads his praisers toward **excellent wealth** <note>original: vasyas; literally "better," referring to cattle and other riches</note>. The previous sentence connects here: "Let us praise that very Indra."

---

## Hymn Text

-> ॥ Now the Fifth Verse ॥ <-

He who supports the heavens, generating **speech** <note>original: vācam; often interpreted as the sound of thunder or ritual prayer</note> for the sake of sacrifice; may the Priest, sought by many and adorned with hymns, bring Indra into our sacrificial chambers. ॥ 5 ॥

**Padapatha:**
He. Who. To heaven. Supporting. Sends forth. Speech. Generating. To sacrifice. 
Adorned. Sought by many. With hymns. [Particle of invitation]. Indra. May he make. In the chambers. The Priest. ॥ 5 ॥

## Commentary (Sayana)

**Supporting** <note>original: upastabhāyan</note> means propping up the worlds. **Generating speech** means producing the sound of thunder or the speech required for the sacrifice. **Adorned** <note>original: cañjasānaḥ</note> means being perfected or prepared; the sage Yaska defines this term as the act of perfecting. Indra is **sought by many** <note>original: puruvāraḥ</note> because he is to be enjoyed or honored by many through **hymns** <note>original: ukthaiḥ</note> which are specific ritual recitations. 

In the word **heaven** <note>original: namasi</note>, the term *namas* is used here as a name for food. He sends or impels **food**—the means of sacrifice—to the sacrificers who have given him oblations. The inner meaning is this: Indra, being satisfied by the oblation, provides food by means of rain, and through that food, the sacrifice is performed once again. May our **Priest** <term>Hotṛ: the invoker priest who recites the Rig Vedic verses</term> make that Indra turn toward us within our **sacrificial houses** <note>original: sadaneṣu</note>.

-> ॥ Thus ends the fifth Varga in the sixth Adhyaya of the third Ashtaka ॥ <-

---

## Hymn Text

-> ॥ Now the Sixth Verse ॥ <-

When they, desiring prayer, seeking the moving ones, and sitting [near] the **Rock** <note>original: adrim; an epithet for Indra as the crusher of enemies</note> in the dwelling of the **son of Ushij**; the Priest of the house, who is difficult to consume, and who is our great **bearer** <note>original: vahniḥ</note> in the protected places. ॥ 6 ॥

**Padapatha:**
Through prayer. If. Desiring prayer. The moving ones. Sitting. The rock. Of the son of Ushij. In the dwelling. 
[Particle of approach]. Difficult to consume. Of the house. The priest. Who. Our. Great. In protected places. The bearer. ॥ 6 ॥

## Commentary (Sayana)

**Desiring prayer** <note>original: dhiṣayantaḥ</note> means those who desire to offer praise directed toward Indra. **Of the son of Ushij** <note>original: auśijasya</note> refers to the sacrificer or patron who is the descendant of Ushij (the "desirous one"). In the **dwelling** <note>original: gohe/gṛhe</note> of that patron, the people are **sitting** <note>original: sardantaḥ</note>. 

The **Rock** <note>original: adrim</note> refers to Indra, so called because he "strikes down" <note>original: āhṇāti</note> his enemies. When these people approach Indra through **prayer** <note>original: dhiṣā</note> or praise, then may that Indra come. He is the **bearer** <note>original: vahniḥ</note> who is great in our **protected places** <note>original: saṃvaraṇeṣu</note> or battle-grounds against enemies...

<vocab>
Indra: The king of the gods and the primary deity of this hymn, associated with thunder, rain, and battle.
Vayu: The god of the wind, often associated with Indra as his companion or strength.
Hota: The "Invoker" priest who recites the verses of the Rig Veda to invite the gods to the sacrifice.
Aushija: A patronymic name; "son of Ushij." Ushij represents "desire," often referring to a lineage of wise sacrificers.
Adri: Literally "mountain" or "rock," but used here as an epithet for Indra's unshakeable strength or his role as a "crusher."
</vocab>

<summary>This page describes Indra as the cosmic supporter who provides rain and food in exchange for sacrifice. It highlights the role of the priest (Hota) and the patron (Aushija) in inviting Indra to the sacrificial hall through prayer.</summary>

<meta>This page concludes the commentary on Verse 6 and provides the full text and scholarly explanation for Verses 7 and 8 of Hymn 21. It continues the theme of Indra’s immense power and his presence in both the ritual space and the hearts of his worshipers.</meta>

In times of constraint, the "Carrier" <note>original: vahnir; usually referring to the priest who carries the oblation or the fire itself</note> is the one who understands. For the sacrificer dwelling in his house, Indra—the invoker, the one whose wrath is difficult to withstand, the Great One—becomes manifest. May he come to us.

---

## Hymn Text
-> ॥ Now the Seventh Verse ॥ <-

Truly, when the strength of the Showerer <note>original: vṛṣṇaḥ; literally "the bull," a common epithet for Indra as a source of fertility and power</note>, the son of the Supporter, attaches itself to the worshiper for the sake of the prize; when it manifests in the secret place of the worshiper, or when it is directed toward the ritual, for the attainment of desires, or for joy. ॥ 7 ॥

**Word-for-Word Analysis:**
Truly. When. [Particle of emphasis]. Of the son of the Supporter. Of the Showerer. Attaches. Strength. For the worshiper. For the prize. 
In the secret place. When. [Particle of emphasis]. Of the worshiper. In the dwelling. Forth. When. For the ritual. Forth. For the attainment. For joy. ॥ 7 ॥

## Commentary (Sayana)

**Of the son of the Supporter:** The term *Bharvara* refers to **Prajapati** <term>Prajāpati: the "Lord of Progeny" or Creator deity in Vedic mythology</term>, who is the sustainer of the world. His son is *Bhārvara* <note>original: bhārvarasya; here identifying Indra as the offspring or a form of the Creator</note>. The **strength** <note>original: śuṣmaḥ</note> of this Indra, who showers down the fulfillment of desires, serves or "attaches itself" to the sacrificer who offers praise. This is **truly** <note>original: sacā</note> so. 

That this power prevails in the **secret place** <note>original: guhā</note>, meaning the cave-like heart of the worshiper, is a truth. That it prevails in the **dwelling** <note>original: gohe</note> or house of the worshiper for the sake of the **ritual** <note>original: dhiye</note> is also a truth. Furthermore, that this strength is effective for the **attainment** <note>original: aryase</note> of one's goals and for **joy** <note>original: madāya</note> is a truth. The essential meaning is that Indra’s power constantly protects the worshiper.

---

## Hymn Text
-> ॥ Now the Eighth Verse ॥ <-

When he throws open the enclosures of the mountain and invigorates the flow of the waters with their currents; when the wise, with focused minds, bring him for the sake of nourishment, he finds the wild kine in the dwelling. ॥ 8 ॥

**Word-for-Word Analysis:**
Apart. When. Enclosures. Of the mountain. He threw open. With waters. He invigorates. Of the waters. The speeds.
He finds. The Gaura-deer. The Gavaya-ox. In the dwelling. If/When. For the sake of food. The wise. They bring. ॥ 8 ॥

## Commentary (Sayana)

It is a known truth that Indra **threw open** <note>original: vivṛṇe</note> the **enclosures** or doors of the **mountain** <note>original: parvatasya; here interpreted as the clouds which "imprison" the rain</note>. He **invigorates** or swells the **speed** and flow of the waters with rain. When the **wise** <note>original: sudhyaḥ</note>, those sacrificers who perform good deeds, **bring** or invite Indra for the sake of obtaining **food** <note>original: vājāya</note>, then he finds or bestows both the **Gaura** <term>Gaura: a species of wild reddish deer or bison found in the forest</term> and the **Gavaya** <term>Gavaya: the gayal or forest ox</term> within the **dwelling** of the worshiper. All these acts are connected to the word "truly" from the previous verse.

---

## Ritual Application

In the **Abhyudayeshti** <term>Abhyudayeṣṭi: a specific sacrificial rite performed for prosperity or when a special celestial alignment occurs</term>, the verse beginning "Your auspicious hand..." is used as the concluding prayer for Indra the Giver. This is indicated in the **Ashvalayana Shrauta Sutra** <term>Āśvalāyana Śrauta Sūtra: a manual of ritual instructions for priests of the Rig Veda</term>: "Long is your hook... your hand is auspicious, and your arms are well-made" (Asv. 3. 13).

<vocab>
**Indra**: The king of the gods, associated with thunder, rain, and war.
**Prajapati**: The Lord of Creatures, often identified as the supreme creator in later Vedic thought.
**Parvata**: Literally "mountain," but in the Rig Veda, it frequently serves as a metaphor for the rain-clouds.
**Yajamana**: The patron or sacrificer who pays for and benefits from the ritual.
**Vaja**: A multi-layered term meaning food, strength, wealth, or the "prize" won in a race or battle.
</vocab>

It concludes with specific ritual instructions for using these verses to ensure prosperity.</summary>
<keywords>Indra, Prajapati, rain-clouds, heart/cave (guha), Gaura and Gavaya, Abhyudayeshti ritual, Ashvalayana Srauta Sutra</keywords>

<meta>This page continues the text and commentary of the 17th Hymn (Sūkta) of the 4th Mandala of the Rig Veda. It transitions from the description of Indra's inherent power to a direct plea for his generosity and a record of his historical victory over the demon Vritra.</meta>

-> ॥ This is the Ninth Verse of the Hymn ॥ <-

## Hymn Text
Auspicious are your hands, O Indra, well-wrought; indeed, your palms are the bestowers of wealth to the one who praises you. What is your reason for sitting still? Why do you not exhilarate us? Why do you not rejoice in giving to us? ॥ 9 ॥

---

**Auspicious. Your. Hands. Well-wrought. And. Palms. Bestowers. To the one who praises. Wealth. Indra. What. Your. Sitting-down. Why. Indeed. Us. Exhilarate. Why. Not. Greatly. Rejoice. To give. ॥ 9 ॥**

## Commentary (Sayana)

O **Indra**, **your** two **hands** <note>original: hastā</note> are **auspicious**, meaning they bring good fortune and welfare. They are **well-wrought**, meaning they perform beautiful and effective deeds. **And also** <note>original: utāpi</note>, your **palms** <note>original: pāṇī</note> are the **bestowers** of **wealth** <note>original: rādhas</note> to the **worshiper** who offers praise. O Indra, **what** is your **sitting-down** <note>original: niṣattiḥ; referring to a state of inaction or delay</note>? That is, what is the reason for your staying still? **Why** do you **not exhilarate** <note>original: mamatsi</note> **us**? Why do you not cause us to be intoxicated with joy? **Why** and for what reason do you not **rejoice** greatly **to give** us wealth? Why are you not filled with delight to bestow these gifts?

This verse is used as the consecration prayer <term>Yājyā: a sacrificial prayer recited while the offering is poured into the fire</term> for the animal sacrifice dedicated to Indra, the Slayer of Vritra. This is indicated in the ritual manuals: "Indra is the true sovereign of wealth... (Rig Veda 4.17.10)" as cited in **Ashvalayana Shrauta Sutra 3. 13.**

---

-> ॥ This is the Tenth Verse of the Hymn ॥ <-

## Hymn Text
Thus Indra, the true, the sovereign of wealth, the slayer of Vritra, created wide space for the human worshiper. O much-praised one, empower us with riches; may I enjoy your divine protection. ॥ 10 ॥

---

**Thus. Of wealth. Indra. True. Sovereign. Slayer. Vritra. Wide space. For the human. Created. O much-praised. Through the rite. Us. Empower. Of riches. May I enjoy. Your. Protection. Divine. ॥ 10 ॥**

## Commentary (Sayana)

**Thus**, in the manner described, being praised, the **true** one, the **sovereign** <term>Samrāṭ: an emperor or supreme ruler</term> of **wealth**, the **slayer** of the demon named **Vritra**, that Indra **created** **wide space** <note>original: varivaḥ; often interpreted as room, freedom, or abundance</note> for the **human** worshiper <note>original: pūrave; referring to the descendants of Puru or humanity in general</note>. This means he bestows wealth. 

O **much-praised one** <note>original: puruṣṭuta</note>, praised by many worshipers, through this **rite** <note>original: ṛtvā</note> which is the cause of our praise, you **empower** **us** with **riches**. Give them to us. **May I enjoy**—meaning may I partake in—your **divine protection** <note>original: avasaḥ</note>, which is associated with the gods. Here, "protection" implies the gift of food. <note>original: karmaṇi ṣaṣṭhī; a grammatical note stating that the genitive case "avasaḥ" is used here to denote the object of enjoyment</note>.

---

-> ॥ Now the Eleventh Verse ॥ <-

## Hymn Text
Now praised, O Indra, now being sung, swell the nourishment for the singer like the rivers. A new prayer has been made for you, O Lord of the Bay Horses; through our devotion, may we always be masters of chariots. ॥ 11 ॥

<vocab>
Indra: The King of the Gods, known for his strength and generosity.
Vritra: The drought-demon who imprisoned the waters, slain by Indra.
Radhas: Riches, success, or the bounty resulting from a sacrifice.
Samrat: A supreme ruler; one who rules over other kings.
Varivas: "Wide room" or "freedom"; metaphorically, the removal of distress and the granting of wealth.
Purushtuta: An epithet meaning "one who is praised by many."
Pani: Specifically the palms of the hands.
Hasta: The hands or forearms.
</vocab>

<summary>This page contains verses 9-11 of Hymn 17, where the poet addresses Indra's physical capacity to give, his historical victory over Vritra, and a plea for immediate divine nourishment and future prosperity.</summary>
<keywords>Indra, Vritra, wealth, hands of god, sovereignty, protection, human worshiper, sacrifice, Sanskrit commentary</keywords>

## Hymn Text (RV 4.21.11 fragment)

<note>This is the conclusion of the 21st hymn, featuring both the continuous Samhitā text and the word-by-word Padapāṭha breakdown.</note>

Now! Praised, O Indra, now being lauded, [bring] food to the singer as rivers [overflow]. 
O Lord of the Bay Horses, a new prayer has been made for you. Through our devotion, may we always be masters of chariots and victors in battle. ॥ 11 ॥

---

## Commentary (Sayana)

**This was explained previously.** <note>Referring to the detailed linguistic breakdown of verse 11 provided on the preceding page.</note>

**॥ This concludes the sixth section of the sixth chapter of the third book ॥**
**॥ This concludes the second sub-section (Anuvāka) of the fourth book (Maṇḍala) ॥**

In this, the third sub-section, there are eleven hymns. The first of these, beginning with "What Indra [has enjoyed]," consists of eleven verses. Its Seer is **Vāmadeva**, its meter is **Triṣṭubh** <note>a rhythmic meter of 11 syllables per line</note>, and its deity is **Indra**. This is noted in the Index. In the six-day sacrificial rituals called the *Pṛṣṭhya* and *Abhilava*, during the midday pressing of the Soma, this is the second "confluence" hymn <term>Sampāta-sūkta: a hymn believed to 'fall together' or coincide with specific ritual powers</term> used in the recitation for the gods Mitra and Varuna. This is indicated in the ritual manuals: "Thus to you, Indra... What Indra..." (Āśvalāyana Śrauta Sūtra 7.5).

---

## Hymn Text

-> ॥ Here is the first verse [of Hymn 22] ॥ <-

<note>Rig Veda 4.22.1</note>
What Indra has enjoyed and what he desires, may the Great and Mighty one perform that for us. 
The prayer, the praise, the Soma, and the recited hymns—he who goes holding the stone [thunderbolt] by his strength. ॥ 1 ॥

**Word-by-word Analysis (Padapāṭha)**
What . for us . Indra . has enjoyed . what . and . he desires . that . for us . Great . may he perform . Mighty . indeed . 
Prayer . praise . Lord of Wealth . Soma . recited hymns . who . stone . by strength . bearing . goes ॥ 1 ॥

---

## Commentary (Sayana)

**Indra enjoys** <note>original: jujuṣe</note> our sacrifice, characterized by offerings and food. The **Great** and **Mighty** Indra **desires** <note>original: vaṣṭi</note> the sacrificial offerings. The word "Cit" is used here in the sense of "and." The **Lord of Wealth** <note>original: Maghavā; an epithet of Indra</note> should accept four things: the **prayer** <note>original: brahma; interpreted here as sacrificial food like the rice cake</note>, the **praise** <note>original: stoma; a collection of chants</note>, the **Soma** <note>the sacred pressed juice</note>, and the **recited hymns** <note>original: ukthā; specifically the Shastra hymns recited by the Hotri priest</note>. Let him accept them. The word **stone** <note>original: aśman</note> refers to the **Vajra** <note>Indra's thunderbolt weapon</note>. That Indra who **goes** forth, **bearing** the thunderbolt and endowed with **strength**, may he accept our offerings—this connects to the previous statement.

---

## Hymn Text

-> ॥ Now the second verse ॥ <-

<note>Rig Veda 4.22.2</note>
The Bull, hurling the bull-like four-edged [weapon], the fierce one, most heroic in his arms, the powerful. 
For the sake of beauty, he approached the Paruṣṇī [river], heating it; he whose joints he enveloped for the sake of friendship. ॥ 2 ॥

**Word-by-word Analysis (Padapāṭha)**
Bull . bull-like . four-edged . hurling . fierce . with arms . most manly . powerful .
For beauty . Paruṣṇī . heating . wool . whose . joints . for friendship . he enveloped ॥ 2 ॥

---
<vocab>
Indra: King of the gods and deity of storms/war.
Vamadeva: The primary Rishi (seer) of the 4th Book of the Rig Veda.
Trishtubh: A common Vedic meter of 44 syllables.
Vajra (Ashman): Indra's legendary thunderbolt weapon.
Parushni: An ancient name for the Ravi River in modern-day Punjab.
</vocab>

It describes Indra as a powerful warrior bearing a four-edged thunderbolt who visits the Parushni river.</summary>

## Commentary (Sāyaṇa) — Continued from previous page
[Rig Veda 4.17.2]
Indra—the showerer of desires, who causes rain by splitting the clouds, holding the four-edged <note>original: *caturaśriṃ*, meaning a thunderbolt with four corners or rays</note> thunderbolt in his arms to hurl at his enemies—possesses uplifted power. As the supreme leader and one full of action, he enjoys the **Paruṣṇī** <note>a sacred river in the Punjab, modern-day Ravi</note>, which covers the land and flows from the mountains, for his own glory. He has enveloped the different regions of this river for the sake of friendship <note>performing friendly or beneficial acts</note>.

## Hymn Text
->॥ Here is the third verse ॥<-

The shining God, the most divine of gods, upon being born with great food-offerings and great strengths, holding the desirable thunderbolt in both arms, made the heaven and the earth tremble with his power. ॥ 3 ॥

**Word-for-word analysis:**
Who; God; most-divine; being born; great; with food-offerings; with great [strengths]; and; with strengths; holding; the thunderbolt; in two arms; the desiring; heaven; with power; he shook; forth; earth. ॥ 3 ॥

## Commentary (Sāyaṇa)
Indra, the shining and most generous god <note>original: *devatamo*, the greatest giver</note>, upon being born, became endowed with great food-offerings and great strengths. This Indra, holding the desirable thunderbolt in his hands, made both the heaven and the earth tremble with his might.

## Hymn Text
->॥ Here is the fourth verse ॥<-

All the heights and the many depths, heaven and earth trembled at the birth of the Great One. The powerful one supports the parents of the sun; like men, the winds howl in the atmosphere. ॥ 4 ॥

**Word-for-word analysis:**
All; heights; depths; and; many; heaven; from the Great One; at birth; trembled; earth; [and]; the parents; he supports; the powerful one; [and]; of the sun; like men; in the atmosphere; howl; the winds. ॥ 4 ॥

## Commentary (Sāyaṇa)
All the **heights** <term>rodhāṃsi: elevated regions such as mountains</term> and the many **depths** <term>pravataḥ: slopes or low-lying areas like oceans</term>, as well as heaven and earth, trembled at the birth of Indra because of his greatness. Furthermore, the powerful Indra supports the "parents of the traveler" <note>original: *goḥ mātara*, referring to heaven and earth as the parents of the Sun</note>. Like men, the winds driven by Indra howl loudly in the atmosphere.

## Hymn Text
O Indra, those great deeds of yours, the mighty one, are truly to be proclaimed in all the Soma-pressings <note>original: *savaneṣu*, referring to the morning, midday, and evening ritual offerings</note>. When, O brave and daring hero, having become bold, you struck the serpent-demon <note>original: *ahim*, the "snake" or "dragon" Vritra who obstructed the waters</note> with your bold thunderbolt and strength. ॥ 5 ॥

**Word-for-word analysis:**
Those; indeed; your; Indra; of the great; great [deeds]; in all; indeed; Soma-pressings; are to be proclaimed; when; O hero; O daring one; with boldness; having become bold; the serpent; with the thunderbolt; with strength; you struck. ॥ 5 ॥

## Commentary (Sāyaṇa)
O **Indra**, the deeds of **yours**, who are **great** and powerful, are indeed **great**. In **all Soma-pressings**—such as the morning libations and others—your deeds are **to be proclaimed** <note>original: *pravācyā*, worthy of being spoken of by the chanters</note>, meaning they are worthy of praise. O **daring one**, O courageous **heroic Indra**, you who **support** and maintain the worlds, you who are endowed with **strength**, have **struck** and killed **Vritra**, the demon <note>original: *ahim*, the serpent-like asura</note>, with your **thunderbolt** which overpowers others. The phrase "you struck" <note>original: *aviveṣīḥ*</note> is synonymous with the act of slaying. The connection to the previous sentence is that these deeds, starting with this victory, are truly great.

## Hymn Text
O Indra of many strengths <note>original: *tuvinṛmṇa*, possessing abundant wealth or power</note>, all those deeds of yours are truly realized. The milch-cows <note>original: *dhenavaḥ*, often a metaphor for rain-clouds</note> flow forth from the udder for the showerer of benefits. And then, O Indra of vigorous mind, the rivers, fearing you, have run forth with great speed. ॥ 6 ॥

**Word-for-word analysis:**
Those; indeed; your; true; O one of many strengths; all; forth; the milch-cows; flow; for the showerer; from the udder; then; indeed; from you; O one of vigorous mind; fearing; forth; the rivers; with speed; have moved. ॥ 6 ॥

## Commentary (Sāyaṇa)
O **Indra of many strengths**, all **those** deeds of **yours** quickly become **true** <note>meaning they are manifest and unfailing</note>. O Indra, out of fear of **you**, the **showerer** of desires, the **milch-cows** <note>the cows or the clouds</note> **flow forth** with milk—or rain—from their **udders**. Furthermore, O **Indra of vigorous mind** who intends to shower blessings, the **rivers** <note>original: *sindhavaḥ*</note>, being **afraid** of you, have **run forth with speed**. They indeed move with great intensity.

## Hymn Text (Word-for-word analysis for Verse 7)

The hymns; indeed; your; O Lord of the bay horses <note>original: *harivaḥ*, an epithet for Indra referring to his golden-brown horses</note>; those; indeed; divine [rivers]; with protections; O Indra; they praise; the sisters; when; them; following; forth; you released; those who were bound; long; following; the bond; to flow at will. ॥ 7 ॥

---

## Commentary (Sāyaṇa) on Verse 7

O **Indra**, **when** <note>original: *yat-yadā*</note> you **released** <note>original: *pra mucaḥ*</note> those who were **bound** <note>original: *baddhadhānāḥ*</note> by the demon Vritra—referring to **these rivers** <note>original: *sīmanu*</note>—from their **long** and excessive **bond** <note>original: *prasitim*</note> so that they might **flow at will** <note>original: *syandayadhyai*</note>, then a great event occurred. O **Lord of the bay horses**, at that very moment of liberation, **those** well-known **divine sisters** <note>original: *devīḥ swasāraḥ*</note>—a term here meaning the **rivers**—**praise** you <note>original: *stavante*</note> because of the **protections** <note>original: *avobhiḥ*</note> you provided. The meaning is that through your acts of filling the riverbeds and other deeds, people are inspired to praise Indra.

->॥ Now the eighth verse ॥<-

## Hymn Text (Verse 8)

The Soma-stalk has been pressed; the intoxicating juice flows like a river. May the power of the priest’s ritual labor draw you here. May the hands of the radiant worshiper draw you toward us, like a swift driver pulling the reins of a strong horse. ॥ 8 ॥

**Word-for-word analysis:**
Has been pressed; the Soma-stalk; intoxicating; like; a river; toward; you; the ritual labor; of the one performing the rite; the power; toward us; of the radiant one; the hands; swift; like; the reins; of great strength; of the horse. ॥ 8 ॥

---

## Commentary (Sāyaṇa) on Verse 8

O **Indra**, the **intoxicating Soma-stalk** <note>original: *madyo’ṃśuḥ*</note> **has been pressed** <note>original: *pipīḷe*</note>, meaning the juice has been extracted for the ritual. The word **like** <note>original: *na*</note> here signifies "now" or "indeed." **Indeed, now** the **flowing** Soma juice, like a **river** <note>original: *sindhuḥ*</note>, should **draw you** <note>original: *ā-yamyāḥ*</note> toward us. May the **power** <note>original: *śaktiḥ*</note> and the **ritual labor** <note>original: *śamī*</note> of the **radiant** <note>original: *suṣucānasya*</note> and **praising** worshiper draw you **toward us**. The poet provides a **comparison** <note>original: *dṛṣṭāntaḥ*</note>: just as a **swift** charioteer pulls the **reins** <note>original: *raśmim*</note> of a **horse** <note>original: *goḥ*</note> that possesses **great strength** <note>original: *tuvyojasam*</note> or firmness, so should our prayers pull you to this sacrifice.

->॥ Now the ninth verse ॥<-

## Hymn Text (Verse 9)

O Overpowering One, grant us the most abundant, greatest, and most excellent heroic strengths. Together with us, subdue our enemies so they are easy to strike; strike down the weapon of the mortal who seeks to harm us. ॥ 9 ॥

**Word-for-word analysis:**
To us; most abundant; make; greatest; heroic strengths; together; O Overpowering One; powers; for us; enemies; easy to strike; subdue; strike; the weapon; of the attacker; of the mortal. ॥ 9 ॥

---

## Commentary (Sāyaṇa) on Verse 9

O **Indra**, you who are the **Overpowering One** <note>original: *sahure*, one who endures and conquers</note>, **always** <note>original: *sacā*</note> **grant to us** <note>original: *asme kṛṇuhi*</note> **heroic strengths** <note>original: *nṛmṇāni*</note> that are **most abundant** <note>original: *varṣiṣṭhā*</note>, **greatest** <note>original: *jyeṣṭhā*</note>, and most excellent. Grant us **powers** <note>original: *sahāṃsi*</note> that can overcome our foes.

<vocab>
- **Indra**: The King of the Gods and the primary deity of this hymn.
- **Harivah**: "Lord of the Bay Horses," a title emphasizing Indra's chariot and speed.
- **Soma**: A sacred ritual drink made from the *Anshu* (stalk) of a plant, offered to gods.
- **Pipile**: A technical term for the crushing or squeezing of the Soma plant.
- **Sahure**: "The Conqueror" or "Overpowering," highlighting Indra's endurance.
- **Nrimnani**: Heroic deeds or the vital strength required to perform them.
- **Vritra**: The demon of drought and obstruction; also used generally for "enemies" or "obstacles."
</vocab>

## Commentary (Sāyaṇa)

**Make** <note>original: *kṛṇuhi*</note>. Do. ## Commentary (Sāyaṇa)

O **Indra**, **listen** <note>original: *śṛṇuhi*</note> **well** <note>original: *su*</note> specifically to **our** <note>original: *asmākam*</note> own praises. Likewise, O **Indra**, **provide** <note>original: *upamāhi*</note>—give—to us **wonderful** <note>original: *citrān*</note> and desirable **riches** <note>original: *vājān*</note> <note>Literally 'vāja' refers to strength or food-wealth gained in battle.</note>. ## Commentary (Sāyaṇa)

This verse has been explained previously <note>This is a recurring concluding verse (khila) used by the Rishi Vamadeva to end several of his hymns.</note>.

-> ॥ Thus ends the eighth section of the sixth chapter of the third book ॥ <-

The second hymn, beginning with "By what greatness" <note>original: *kathā mahā*</note>, consists of eleven verses. The **Seer** <note>original: *ṛṣi*</note> is **Vamadeva**, the **meter** is **Trishtubh**, and the **deity** is **Indra**. Alternatively, the three verses starting with "Of the Truth indeed" <note>original: *ṛtasya hi*</note> have **Truth** <note>original: *ṛta*</note> <note>The cosmic order</note> as their deity. So it is stated in the Index <note>original: *Anukramani*</note>: "By what [greatness]; the last three may have the Goddesses of Truth as their deity." In the **Abhijit** rite <note>a specific 'Victory' sacrifice</note> during the ten-night ceremony, on the first day at the **midday libation** <note>original: *mādhyaṃdinasavana*</note>, this is the third "concordant hymn" used in the recitation for Mitra and Varuna. It is indicated in the ritual manual: "By what greatness Indra... he who alone broke the cities" <note>Ashvalayana Shrauta Sutra 7.5</note>. In the **Mahavrata** <note>Great Vow</note> ceremony, in the litany for the Self, this is also used. As indicated by the teacher **Shaunaka** in the **Fifth Aranyaka**: "By what greatness he prospered, for which priest..." <note>Aitareya Aranyaka 5.8</note>.

<meta>This page continues the liturgical commentary of the Rig Veda. 126 || Rig Veda || [Ashtaka 3, Adhyaya 6, Varga 9]

-> ॥ Here is the first [verse] ॥ <-

## Hymn Text

**How has the Great One increased? By which priest’s sacrifice, [he] who is pleased, [comes] towards the Soma from the overflowing udder?**
**Drinking, desiring, and enjoying the food, the exalted one bore [the drink] for the sake of shining wealth. ॥ 1 ॥**

How; Great; increased; whose; of the priest; sacrifice; enjoying; towards; Soma; udder;
Drinking; desiring; enjoying; food; bore; exalted; for the shining; for wealth. ॥ 1 ॥

---

## Commentary (Sāyaṇa)

**How** <note>original: *kathā*</note>—in what way or by what means—did our inspired praise **increase** <note>original: *avṛdhat*</note> **Indra** <note>The king of the gods and the primary recipient of the Soma offering.</note>, who is already **Great** <note>original: *mahān*</note> and grown by his own qualities? The poet implies that his majesty is so immense that it is a wonder that human praise can add to it at all. Furthermore, that same Indra, **enjoying** <note>original: *juṣāṇaḥ*</note>—being pleased—whose **sacrifice** <note>original: *yajñam*</note> of **which** <note>original: *kasya*</note> **priest** <note>original: *hotuḥ*</note> (the patron of the ritual) might he **approach** <note>original: *abhi*</note>? <note>The commentator notes that since the prefix 'abhi' is present, a verb of movement like 'approach' must be understood.</note> Moreover, **drinking** and tasting the **Soma**-food, which is like an **overflowing udder** <note>original: *ūdhaḥ*; Sāyaṇa explains this as the 'raised' or 'abundant' Soma ready for the ritual</note>, the **exalted** <note>original: *ṛṣvaḥ*</note> Indra **desiring** that divine food and **enjoying** it, **bore** <note>original: *vavakṣe*</note>—that is, he carries and holds the consumed food in his belly—for the sake of granting **shining wealth** <note>original: *śucate dhanāya*</note> such as gold. Through these two statements, the poet reveals that Indra’s character and deeds are beyond human comprehension.

---

-> ॥ Now the second ॥ <-

## Hymn Text

**Who is the hero that attained his joint-revelry? Who has reached him through good thoughts?**
**When is his wonderful [wealth] perceived? When will he, through protection, be for the growth of the worshipper who sacrifices? ॥ 2 ॥**

Who; his; hero; joint-revelry; attained; reached; with good thoughts; who; his;
When; his; wonderful; perceived; when; with protection; for growth; [he] will be; of the worshipper; of the sacrificer. ॥ 2 ॥

---

## Commentary (Sāyaṇa)

**Who** among men, being a **hero** <note>original: *vīraḥ*; one who overcomes enemies or leads the chanting</note>, **attained** <note>original: *āpa*</note> the **joint-revelry** <note>original: *sadhamādam*</note> related to this Indra? <note>Sāyaṇa interprets 'joint-revelry' as either the 'battle' where gods and men fight together or the 'communal drinking' of Soma.</note> And who **reaches** <note>original: *sam ānaṃśa*</note> him through **good thoughts** <note>original: *sumatibhiḥ*</note>—that is, through beautiful and gracious intentions? **When** <note>original: *kad/kat*</note> is the **wonderful** <note>original: *citram*</note> and desirable wealth of this Indra **perceived** <note>original: *cikite*</note>? The meaning is that no one knows the exact time he chooses to bestow his gifts. Furthermore, **when** will he **be** <note>original: *bhuvat*</note> present with his **protection** <note>original: *ūtī*</note> for the **growth** <note>original: *vṛdhe*</note> of the **worshipper** <note>original: *śaśamānasya*</note> who offers the **sacrifice** <note>original: *yajyoḥ*</note>?

<vocab>
- <term>Indra</term>: The primary deity addressed in these verses, known for his strength and love of Soma.
- <term>Soma</term>: The sacred ritual drink, often compared to milk from an udder or described as "food" for the gods.
- <term>Yajña</term>: The sacrificial ritual that forms the core of Vedic religious practice.
- <term>Hotṛ</term>: The priest responsible for reciting the verses of the Rig Veda during the ritual.
- <term>Sadhamāda</term>: A term for "joint-revelry" or "festivity," which the commentator links to both battle and the ritual feast.
- <term>Sumati</term>: Divine benevolence or the "right-mindedness" of the worshipper that attracts the god's favor.
- <term>Ūdhas</term>: Literally "udder," used here metaphorically to describe the abundance of the Soma juice.
- <term>Śaśamāna</term>: A technical term for the person actively engaged in praising the deity or performing the ritual.
</vocab>

<keywords>Indra, Soma ritual, Sāyaṇa commentary, Vedic sacrifice, priest, divine wealth, joint-revelry</keywords>

## Hymn Text

-> ॥ Now, the Third [Verse] ॥ <-

How does Indra hear the one who calls upon him? How, while hearing, does he recognize the protections needed by this person? What are his many ancient gifts? How do they speak of him as the fulfiller of the singer's needs? ॥ 3 ॥

How; hears; the one being called; Indra; how; hearing; protections; his; knows;
What; his; ancient; gifts <note>original: *upamatayaḥ*, literally 'comparisons' or 'approximations', interpreted by the commentator as 'acts of giving'.</note>; indeed; how; him; they call; the fulfiller; for the singer. ॥ 3 ॥

## Commentary (Sāyaṇa)

How—in what manner—does **Indra**, who possesses supreme lordship, **hear** the singer who is **calling** <note>original: *hūyamānaṃ*</note> upon him? While **hearing** the hymns, **how** does he **know**—or recognize—the **protections** <note>original: *avasāṃ*</note> belonging to **this** singer? Furthermore, **what** <note>original: *kā ha*</note> are the **ancient** <note>original: *pūrvīḥ*</note> **gifts** belonging to **this** Indra? (The sense is: what sort of gifts are they?). And **how** do they **speak** of **him**, Indra, as the **fulfiller** <note>original: *papuriṃ*</note> of the desires belonging to the **singer** <note>original: *jaritre*</note>?

## Hymn Text

-> ॥ Now, the Fourth [Verse] ॥ <-

How shall the worshiper, though beset by distress, attain wealth through his efforts and meditation? May the shining God become the knower of my sacred hymns, once he has accepted the food and is pleased with us. ॥ 4 ॥

How; beset by distress; the one striving; his; may reach; unto; wealth; meditating;
God; may be; knower; my; of truths; food <note>original: *namaḥ*, usually meaning 'homage', but here interpreted as the sacrificial food.</note>; having accepted; unto; when; he is pleased. ॥ 4 ॥

## Commentary (Sāyaṇa)

How does the sacrificer, who is **beset by distress** <note>original: *sabādhaḥ*</note> (meaning the pain caused by enemies), **striving** <note>original: *śaśamānaḥ*</note> with praise for Indra, and **meditating** <note>original: *dīdhyānaḥ*</note>—shining through his ritual acts—**attain wealth** consisting of cattle and riches belonging to **this** Indra? When Indra, **having accepted** the **food** <note>original: *namaḥ*</note> characterized by the oblation, **is pleased** with me, then may the **shining** <note>original: *devo*</note> Indra **become** an intensive **knower** <note>original: *navedā*</note> of **my** **sacred hymns** <note>original: *ṛtānāṃ*</note>. <note>The commentator notes that the particle 'na' here signifies intensity or excellence rather than negation.</note>

How and when, at the breaking of this dawn, did the God enjoy the friendship of a mortal? How was his friendship given to those friends who have directed their well-harnessed desire toward him? ॥ 5 ॥

How; when; of this; of the dawn; at the breaking; God; of the mortal; friendship; enjoyed;
How; when; his; friendship; to the friends; who; in him; desire; well-harnessed; have stretched. ॥ 5 ॥
