# Rig Veda [3.6.10]

## Commentary (Sāyaṇa)
<note>This is the conclusion of the commentary for Verse 5</note>

The shining god Indra—at the break of this dawn, how and in what manner does he enjoy the **friendship** <note>original: *sakhyam*, the act of being a friend</note> belonging to the mortal worshiper? Those singers who have extended the desirable **oblation** <note>original: *haviḥ*</note> and the hymn, which are well-connected to this Indra—when might his friendship for these singing friends come to be?

->॥ Thus ends the ninth varga in the sixth chapter of the third book ॥<-

---

## Hymn Text
->॥ Now, the Sixth [Verse] ॥<-

**Samhita Patha:**
What then is this friendship for your friends? When, indeed, shall we proclaim your brotherhood? For the sake of splendor, the appearance of this fair-looking one is a creation like the sun, most wonderful, extending to the cow. ॥ 6 ॥

**Pada Patha:**
What । then । ... । friendship । for friends । When । indeed । your । brotherhood । proclaim ।
For splendor । of the fair-looking । body/form । of him । creation । sun । like । most wonderful । for food/strength । ... । cow ॥ 6 ॥

## Commentary (Sāyaṇa)
O Indra, what kind of **friendship**—your act of being a friend—shall we, the sacrificers, proclaim to your **friends**, the singers? It is a friendship that overcomes enemies. And when, indeed, shall we proclaim your **brotherhood** <note>original: *bhrātram*, the duty or act of a brother</note>? The efforts of this Indra, who is beautiful to behold, exist for the **splendor** <note>original: *śriye*</note>—that is, for the welfare of all the singers. Like the **sun** <note>original: *svar*, translated here as Surya</note>, which is most beautiful to see, the **body** of Indra, the goer, is most wonderful to behold and is sought after by all for the sake of **food** <note>original: *iṣe*</note> and strength.

---

## Hymn Text
->॥ Now, the Seventh [Verse] ॥<-

**Samhita Patha:**
Desiring to slay the deceitful, godless destroyer, he whets his sharp weapons to strike. Where the punisher of debts drives away the unknown dawns in the distance, [there our debts are felt]. ॥ 7 ॥

**Pada Patha:**
The deceitful । desiring to slay । the destroyer । the godless । whets । sharp । for the strike । weapons/army ।
Debts । even । where । the punisher of debts । like । ... । in the distance । unknown । dawns । drives away ॥ 7 ॥

## Commentary (Sāyaṇa)
This Indra, desiring to **slay** the **destroyer** <note>original: *dhvarasam*, a female demon or rakshasi</note> who practices **deceit** <note>original: *duham*</note> and is **godless** <note>original: *anindrām*, literally "one who does not acknowledge Indra"</note>, **whets** his **sharp weapons** <note>original: *anīkā*, which can mean 'points', 'faces', or 'armies'</note> excessively for the purpose of striking her. In those days marked by the dawns where **debts** <note>original: *ṛṇā*, meaning moral, ritual, or financial obligations</note> trouble us—those dawns that are **unknown** and far away—he, as the **punisher of debts**, drives them away...

<summary>These verses explore the relationship between the deity Indra and his devotees, framing it as both a "friendship" and "brotherhood," while also depicting Indra as a warrior who sharpens his weapons to destroy godless, deceitful forces.</summary>

...[with] strength raised high, he is the slayer of debt <note>original: *rinasya hanta*, one who destroys or removes debt/sin</note>. Indra is the one who goes [against enemies]. He crushed <note>original: *abadhat*, tormented or pressed down</note> those who were unknown and unexperienced in the distance.

In the **Rtapeya** <note>A specific type of Soma sacrifice where 'Rita' or Truth is 'drunk' or celebrated</note> ceremony, performed over a single day, during the recitations for the gods Maruts and Indra <note>original: *marutvatiya-nishkevalya-shastrayoh*</note>, these two verses beginning with "For of Truth..." are to be recited in order before the insertion of the **Nivid** <note>A short sacrificial formula or invocation</note>. ## Hymn Text
For the streams of Truth are many; the wisdom of Truth destroys sins. The sound of Truth, awakening and radiant, has pierced the deaf ears of man. ॥ 8 ॥

**Word-by-Word Breakdown:**
Of Truth | indeed | streams/waters | are | many | of Truth | wisdom/prayer | sins/evils | destroys | of Truth | sound/praise | deaf | pierced | ears | awakening | radiant | of man ॥ 8 ॥

## Commentary (Sāyaṇa)
In this context, the word **Truth** <term>Rita: A central Vedic concept referring to the Cosmic Order, the Law of Nature, the Truth, or the Sacrifice itself</term> refers to either the god Indra, the Sun-god <note>Aditya</note>, Truth, or the Sacrifice.

There are **many** <note>original: *purvih*</note> **streams** <note>original: *shurudhah*, which Sayana glosses as *apah* or waters</note> belonging to the God of Truth. Indeed, they exist. The **wisdom** <note>original: *dhitih*, meaning insight or the prayer born of it</note> concerning this God of Truth **destroys** <note>original: *hanti*</note> all **sins** <note>original: *vrijinani*, those evils that ought to be avoided</note>. The **sound** <note>original: *shlokah*, a hymn of praise</note> of this God of Truth **pierced** <note>original: *tatarda*, meaning to open or penetrate</note> the **deaf ears** of the man <note>original: *ayoh*, the mortal sacrificer</note>. What is this sound like? It is **awakening** <note>original: *budhanah*, becoming conscious</note> and **radiant** <note>original: *shuchamanah*, shining brightly</note>.

->॥ Now, the ninth [verse] ॥<-

## Hymn Text
Strong are the foundations of Truth; many and delightful are its forms for the sake of beauty. Through Truth, they have desired abundant food; through Truth, the cows have entered into the Truth. ॥ 9 ॥

**Word-by-Word Breakdown:**
Of Truth | strong/firm | foundations | are | many | delightful/moon-like | for beauty | forms | through Truth | long/abundant | they desired | food/strength | through Truth | cows | Truth | entered ॥ 9 ॥

## Commentary (Sāyaṇa)
**For the sake of beauty** <note>original: *vapushe*, used here to mean 'for the one who possesses a beautiful body'</note>, there **are** many **strong** <note>original: *drilha*, firm</note> **foundations** <note>original: *dharunani*, that which supports</note> belonging to the God of Truth. These **forms** <note>original: *vapunshi*</note> are **many** and **delightful** <note>original: *chandra*, pleasing like the moon</note>. Through the power of the God of **Truth**, the worshipers **desire** <note>original: *ishananta*</note> **abundant** <note>original: *dirgham*, literally 'long' or 'great'</note> **food** <note>original: *prikshah*</note>. Through **Truth** (the God), the **cows** have **entered** into the **Truth**—meaning they have entered the sacrifice as the ritual fee <note>original: *dakshina*</note>. Alternatively, this means the **rays of light** <note>also called *gavah*</note> have entered into the **water** <note>another meaning of *Rita*</note>.

## Hymn Text

-> ॥ The Tenth Verse ॥ <-

He who upholds the **Truth** <note>original: *ṛta*, refers to the cosmic order or the sacrifice</note> attains the **Truth**; the power of **Truth** is swift and desires the waters. The broad and deep Heaven and Earth belong to **Truth**; these two milch-cows yield their bounty in the highest place for the sake of **Truth**. ॥ 10 ॥

**Word-by-Word Breakdown**
Truth | upholding | Truth | indeed | wins | of Truth | power | swift | and | desiring water | for Truth | the broad | many | the deep | for Truth | the two milch-cows | in the highest | yield ॥ 10 ॥

---

## Commentary (Sāyaṇa)

The worshiper <note>original: *stotā*</note> who controls or influences the God of **Truth** <term>Ṛtadevam: Sāyaṇa personifies the cosmic order (Ṛta) as a deity here</term> by means of his praises, wins or enjoys the favor of that very God of **Truth**. The strength or power belonging to this God is swift-moving and seeks to bring forth water <note>original: *jalakāma*, desiring water/rain</note>. The vast and deep Heaven and Earth <note>original: *dyāvāpṛthivyau*</note> exist for the sake of the God of **Truth**. These two, which nourish all beings like milch-cows, yield their essence in the most excellent, highest place for that same God.

## Sukta Introduction

The third hymn <note>referring to its place in this specific section of the Rig Veda</note> begins with the words "What good praise..." <note>original: *kā suṣṭutiḥ*</note>. It contains eleven verses and is attributed to the seer **Vāmadeva**. It is addressed to the god **Indra**. The tenth verse is in the **Anuṣṭubh** meter <note>8 syllables per line</note>, while the remaining verses are in the **Triṣṭubh** meter <note>11 syllables per line</note>. As stated in the Index: "The hymn 'What good praise' ends with an Anuṣṭubh." The ritual application <term>viniyoga: the specific point in a ceremony where a verse is recited</term> is determined by its subject matter.

---

## Hymn Text

-> ॥ The First Verse ॥ <-

What excellent praise shall bring the **Son of Strength**, **Indra**, toward us for the sake of wealth? For that Hero is indeed the giver of riches to the one who praises him; He is the Lord of Cattle, the one who removes all obstacles, O people! ॥ 1 ॥

**Word-by-Word Breakdown**
What | excellent praise | of strength | the son | Indra | hither-turned | for wealth | shall bring | the giver | indeed | the hero | to the praiser | riches | He | the lord of cattle | the remover of obstacles | for us | O people ॥ 1 ॥

<vocab>
ऋतम् (Ṛta) - The cosmic order, truth, or the regulated process of the sacrifice.
इन्द्र (Indra) - The king of the gods, associated with storms, strength, and the protection of the righteous.
वामदेव (Vāmadeva) - An ancient sage (Rishi) to whom most hymns of the Fourth Mandala are attributed.
त्रिष्टुप् (Triṣṭubh) - A common Vedic meter consisting of four lines of eleven syllables each.
अनुष्टुप् (Anuṣṭubh) - A Vedic meter consisting of four lines of eight syllables each.
शवसः सूनुम् (Śavasaḥ Sūnum) - "Son of Strength," a frequent epithet for Indra, emphasizing his powerful nature.
</vocab>

## Commentary (Sayana) - Continued from previous page (Verse 1)
What sort of excellent praise <note>original: *suṣṭutiḥ*</note> can turn the son of strength <note>original: *śavasaḥ sūnum*, the son of power</note>—meaning the exceedingly powerful one—Indra, who possesses supreme sovereignty, toward us <note>original: *arvācīnam*</note> so that he may give us wealth <note>original: **rādhase**</note>? O men <note>original: **janāso**, O worshipers</note>, he is the hero <note>original: **vīro**, the courageous one</note>, the lord of cattle <note>original: **gopatiḥ**, the protector of cattle and other forms of wealth</note>. That Indra is indeed the giver <note>original: **dadirhi**</note> of riches <note>original: **vasūni**</note> belonging to those who would withhold them <note>original: **niḥṣidhām**, referring to enemies who do not sacrifice</note> to those who praise him <note>original: **gṛṇate**</note>, namely, to us.

## Hymn Text (Samhita)
He is to be invoked in the slaying of Vritra; he is to be praised; he is the well-lauded Indra, whose gifts are true. He, the liberal one, bestows wealth upon the mortal who seeks prayer and presses the Soma in battle. ॥ 2 ॥

## Commentary (Sayana)
That Indra is to be invoked <note>original: **havya**</note> in the "slaying of Vritra" <note>original: **vṛtrahatye**, a term often used to mean battle or the overcoming of obstacles</note> during the course of a conflict <note>original: **yāman**</note>. That Indra is worthy of praise <note>original: **īḍyaḥ**</note>. When that Indra is well-praised <note>original: **suṣṭutaḥ**</note>, he becomes one whose gifts are true <note>original: **satyarādhā**, meaning his promise of wealth to the sacrificer is unfailing</note>. The liberal one <note>original: **maghavā**, a title for Indra as the possessor of riches</note>, that Indra, bestows <note>original: **ādhāt**, gives from all sides</note> wealth <note>original: **varivo**, a specific Vedic word for riches or wide space</note> upon the mortal <note>original: **martyāya**, the human worshiper</note> who desires to offer a hymn <note>original: **brahmaṇyate**</note> and who presses the Soma juice <note>original: **suṣvaye**</note> for the sacrifice.

-> || Now the Third Verse || <-

## Hymn Text (Samhita)
Men call upon him in battle; sacrificing their own bodies, they make him their protector. When both parties meet in conflict and approach the giver, men do so for the gain of sons and grandsons. ॥ 3 ॥

## Padapatha
Him | indeed | men | [prefix] call | in battle | having offered up | bodies | they make | protector |
mutually | when | the giver | both | approach | men | of offspring | of a descendant | in the gain ॥ 3 ॥

## Commentary (Sayana)
Men <note>original: **naro**, the leaders or worshipers</note> call upon <note>original: **vi hvayante**, make various invocations to</note> that very Indra in battle <note>original: **samīke**</note>. The sacrificers, offering up <note>original: **ririkvāṃsaḥ**, dedicating or purging through austerity</note> their own bodies <note>original: **tanvaḥ**</note>, make <note>original: **kṛṇvata**</note> that Indra their protector <note>original: **trām**</note>. When <note>original: **yat**</note> both groups <note>original: **ubhayāsaḥ**, referring to both the sacrificers and the chanters</note> meet together <note>original: **mithaḥ**</note> and approach Indra, the bestower of gifts <note>original: **tyāgam**, the one who performs the act of giving</note>, they do so for a purpose. These men make Indra their protector when the cause is the acquisition <note>original: **sātau**</note> of sons <note>original: **tokasya**</note> and grandsons <note>original: **tanayasya**</note>.

<note>The vocabulary section below defines key terms used in the Sanskrit text above.</note>

*   **Indra:** The king of the gods and the primary deity of the atmosphere and battle.
*   **Vritrahatya:** Literally "the killing of Vritra" (the demon of drought), used here as a general term for war or struggle.
*   **Maghavan:** A common epithet for Indra meaning "The Generous" or "The Liberal One."
*   **Varivas:** A Vedic term that can mean "wealth," "treasure," or "freedom and wide space."
*   **Samika:** A term for a meeting, specifically a meeting in battle or a clash.
*   **Toka and Tanaya:** Traditional terms for children and grandchildren, representing the continuity of the family line.
*   **Sati:** The act of gaining, obtaining, or winning something (like booty or offspring).

## Hymn Text

<vocab>
- **human tribes** (kṣitayaḥ): people or men, often referring to the settled clans.
- **acquisition of floods** (arṇasāti): the winning of water or battles fought specifically for water rights.

- **sacrificial cake** (puroḷāśa): a primary vegetable offering in Vedic ritual made from grain.

- **for the sake of sacrifice** (yajadhyai): an archaic dative form meaning "to sacrifice."
- **Bull** (vṛṣabha): a common title for Indra, symbolizing his virility and his power to "shower" or rain down blessings.
- **water/flood** (arṇa): literally "the moving thing," a term for water.
</vocab>

१३४ || Rig Veda || [A. 3. Adh. 6. V. 12.]

...should look at him. Then his, Indra's wife, in the <term>house</term> <note>original: *durone*, the sacrificial hall</note>, by the <term>Soma-pressers</term> <note>original: *somasudbhiḥ*, the priests who extract the juice</note> who possess the Soma, he is sharpened or made keen. ## Hymn Text

-> ॥ Now the Ninth Verse ॥ <-

With a great [commodity] he traded for a small price; returning, he said, "This is unsold." He did not yield the small for the large. The weak and the skilled alike fulfill the contract. ॥ 9 ॥

### Padapatha
With a great | commodity | he traded | smaller | not | sold | I desired | again | returning |
he | with a great | smaller | not | he yielded | the weak | the skilled | out | they milk (fulfill) | the | word (contract) ॥ 9 ॥

## Commentary (Sayana)

Regarding these two verses, certain traditional verses <note>original: *ślokāḥ*</note> are recited by the ancient teachers who knew the tradition. They are written here:

> He who accepts a small price for a great commodity, returning to the buyer, says, "This was not actually sold by me."
> Speaking thus, he desires the completion of the price. That seller should not yield the great commodity for the small price [until the price is right].
> He does not obtain the wealth if it was sold previously; it should be exactly according to the agreement made between them at the time, and not otherwise.
> If an agreement was made that "this is indeed a sale," then the decision is reached only after considering the matter for the sake of the price.
> If such an agreement was made, then the price is fulfilled. Therefore, thinking "I must make an agreement first," the Sage Vamadeva, having subdued Indra with a great hymn, made an agreement while "selling" him, saying "Who [will buy] this [Indra]?"

And so, the meaning of this Rig-verse is found in the phrase <term>with a greater commodity for a price</term>. The following meaning is presented: Someone traded or obtained a very small <term>price</term> <note>original: *vasram*, wealth or value</note> for a great commodity. Returning to the buyer, that seller, saying "this was not sold by me," <term>desired</term> <note>original: *akāniṣam*</note> the completion of the price. (The verb is used in the first person here by grammatical variation). That seller did not <term>yield</term> <note>original: *narirecīt*, did not empty or surrender</note> the commodity for that smaller price. That is, he does not yet accept the deal. Both the <term>weak</term> <note>original: *dīnāḥ*, those lacking power</note> and the <term>skilled</term> <note>original: *dakṣāḥ*, those who are capable</note> "milk" or fulfill the <term>word</term> <note>original: *vāṇam*, the contract or speech</note>. They receive exactly what was agreed upon at the time of the purchase.

---

## Hymn Text

-> ॥ Now the Tenth Verse ॥ <-

Who will buy this Indra of mine for ten cows? When he has slain the <term>Vritras</term>, then let him give him back to me. ॥ 10 ॥

### Padapatha
Who | this | with ten | my | Indra | buys | with cows |
when | the Vritras (enemies) | he shall slay | then | him | to me | again | giving ॥ 10 ॥

<vocab>
- **Wealth/Price** (vasram): The value or money exchanged in a deal.
- **Smaller** (kanīyas): A lesser amount or value.
- **Cows** (dhenu): In the Vedic ritual context, cows were the standard unit of value or "currency."
- **Vritra** (Vṛtra): The demonic force of obstruction slain by Indra; here used in the plural to mean enemies or obstacles.
- **Vamadeva** (Vāmadeva): The ancient seer (Rishi) who composed this hymn.
- **Indra** (Indra): The king of the gods, who is being metaphorically "sold" for the price of a ritual offering.
</vocab>

## Commentary (Sayana)
Who buys this Indra of mine, who is my own, with ten <term>cows</term> <note>original: *dhenubhiḥ*; Sayana interprets these as ten satisfying songs of praise</note>? Who makes the purchase? ## Commentary (Sayana)
**Previously explained.** <note>Sayana often omits detailed commentary for verses that have appeared and been explained in earlier sections of the Rig Veda.</note>

->॥ Thus ends the twelfth section of the sixth chapter in the third book ॥<-

The fourth hymn, beginning with "Who today," has eight verses. The seer is Vamadeva, the meter is <term>Trishtubh</term> <note>a poetic meter of four lines, each with eleven syllables</note>, and the deity is Indra. This is confirmed by the Index <note>original: *Anukramani*</note>, which says: "The eight verses beginning with 'Who today'." In the <term>Dasharatra</term> <note>a ten-night sacrificial ritual</note>, on the fourth day, during the midday libation, when the chant is increased, this hymn should be inserted after the starting verse of the Maitravaruna priest's recitation. It is stated in the ritual manuals: "When the chant increases: 'Who today, O heroic men'" (Ashvalayana Shrauta Sutra 7.12).

---

## Hymn Text
->॥ First Verse of Hymn 25 ॥<-

<note>Rig Veda 4.25.1</note>
Who today, being a friend to men and desiring the gods, has lovingly sought the friendship of Indra? Or who, having pressed the <term>Soma</term> while the fire is kindled, prays to him for great, ultimate protection? ॥ 1 ॥

**Word-for-word breakdown:**
Who | today | friend to men | desiring the gods | longing | Indra's | friendship | has enjoyed |
Who | or | for great | protection | ultimate | well-kindled | in the fire | having pressed Soma | prays ॥ 1 ॥

---

## Commentary (Sayana)
Today, on this day, who is that <term>heroic man</term> <note>original: *naryo*; one who is helpful to men</note>, desiring the gods and longing for them, who has enjoyed Indra's friendship? That is, who serves him? Furthermore, who is the sacrificer who has pressed the Soma, and while the fire is well-kindled and blazing, prays to Indra for great, increased, and <term>ultimate</term> <note>original: *paryaya*; protection that allows one to cross over difficulties</note> protection or satisfaction? He praises Indra.

<vocab>
**Indra**: The king of the gods and deity of storms and war.
**Vamadeva**: The ancient sage to whom the fourth book of the Rig Veda is attributed.
**Trishtubh**: A common Vedic meter used for invocations of power.
**Dasharatra**: A major ten-day ritual sequence within the Vedic sacrificial calendar.
**Sutasoma**: One who has prepared and extracted the sacred Soma juice.
**Sakhya**: The intimate bond of friendship between a devotee and a deity.
**Narya**: A term meaning "manly" or "friendly to mankind," often applied to gods or noble patrons.
</vocab>

# ॥ Rig Veda ॥ [Book 3, Chapter 6, Section 13]

## Hymn Text
Who bows with words of praise to the one who deserves the <term>Soma</term> <note>A ritual drink offered to the gods</note>? Who, being devoted, becomes his? Who is clothed in <term>cows</term> <note>original: *usrāḥ*; also interpreted as rays of light</note>? Who desires the alliance of Indra? Who his friendship? Who his brotherhood? Who seeks the sage's protection? ॥ 2 ॥

> Who | bows | with a word | for the Soma-worthy | devoted | or | becomes | wears | cows |
> Who | Indra's | alliance | who | friendship | who | brotherhood | desires | for the sage | who | for protection ॥ 2 ॥

---

## Commentary (Sayana)
Which sacrificer bows down—meaning, who humbles himself—to Indra, the one worthy of the Soma juice, through speech in the form of a hymn? Or who is devoted to Indra, meaning who is desirous of praising him? Who is "clothed" in the cows given by Indra—meaning who possesses or maintains them? Who desires the "alliance" or help of Indra? Who desires his friendship? Who desires "brotherhood," or a brotherly relationship? Who exists for the "protection" or the satisfaction of the far-seeing Indra? This is the implied question.

---

-> ॥ Now the Third Verse ॥ <-

## Hymn Text
Who chooses the protection of the gods today? Who prays to the <term>Adityas</term> <note>The solar deities, sons of the goddess Aditi</note>, to <term>Aditi</term> <note>The goddess representing the infinite and the mother of the gods</note>, and to the light? For which man do the <term>Ashvins</term> <note>The twin horsemen, physicians of the gods</note>, Indra, and Agni drink the juice of the pressed Soma with a focused mind? ॥ 3 ॥

> Who | of the gods | protection | today | chooses | who | the Adityas | Aditi | light | prays to |
> Of whom | the Ashvins | Indra | Agni | of the pressed | of the juice | drink | with a mind | focused ॥ 3 ॥

---

## Commentary (Sayana)
On this day, which sacrificer chooses or prays for the protection of the "shining ones," such as Indra and the other gods? Who asks the Aditya deities, the mother of the gods Aditi, and for "light"—which here refers to water? For which sacrificer do the two Ashvins, Indra, and Agni—being pleased by the mind's praise—drink the Soma juice? The term "focused mind" <note>original: *avivena*</note> means with a mind that is not wavering, or as desired. They drink the juice of the Soma that has been pressed out.

To that man, <term>Agni Bharata</term> <note>Agni, either as the fire of the Bharata tribe or the "bearer" of the oblation</note> shall grant protection; he shall long see the sun rising high. This is for him who says, "Let us press the Soma for Indra," for the Hero, the manly, the most manly among men. ॥ 4 ॥

> For him | Agni | Bharata | protection | shall grant | long | shall see | the sun | up | rising |
> Who | for Indra | let us press | thus | says | for the Hero | for the manly | for the most manly | of men ॥ 4 ॥

<vocab>

# Mandala 4, Section 3, Hymn 25 | The Third Book (Ashtaka)

## Commentary (Sayana)
<note>This section concludes the explanation of verse 4, which asks which gods will accept the sacrifice.</note>
**Bharata** <note>original: *bhārataḥ*</note> refers to <term>Agni</term> <note>The god of fire and messenger to the gods</note> as the "bearer" of the oblation. According to the *Vajasaneyaka* scripture, he is called "Bharata" because he supports all creatures by becoming the vital breath. May this Agni grant **happiness** <note>original: *śarma*</note> or shelter to that <term>Yajamana</term> <note>The patron or person performing the sacrifice</note>. Furthermore, may this Agni see—meaning allow the sacrificer to see—the rising sun for a long time. This refers to the sacrificer who says, "Let us press the <term>Soma</term> juice for Indra." To what kind of Indra? To the **Leader**, the one who is beneficial to men, and the **most heroic** among all those who lead mankind.

---

## Hymn Text
->॥ Now the Fifth Verse ॥<-

Neither the many nor the few harm him; <term>Aditi</term> <note>The mother of the gods, representing the infinite</note> grants him wide protection. Dear to Indra is the one who performs good deeds; dear is the one who desires to praise him; dear is the one who is attentive; and dear to him is the one who offers the Soma juice. ॥ 5 ॥

> Not | him | do they harm | the many | nor | the few | wide | for him | Aditi | happiness | may she grant |
> Dear | the good-doer | dear | in Indra | the prayerful | dear | the attentive | dear | his | the Soma-offerer ॥ 5 ॥

---

## Commentary (Sayana)
Neither **the few** <note>original: *dabhrā*</note> nor even **the many** enemies **harm** <note>original: *jinanti*</note> or strike that sacrificer. This connects to the previous verse: it refers to the one who says, "Let us press Soma for Indra." **Aditi**, the mother of Indra, shall **grant** <note>original: *yaṃsat*</note> **wide** or extensive **happiness** to this sacrificer. Furthermore, the **good-doer**—the one who performs beautiful sacrifices and rituals—becomes **dear** to Indra. The **prayerful** <note>original: *manāyuḥ*</note>, who desires to offer hymns of praise regarding Indra, becomes dear to him. The **attentive** one—the sacrificer who approaches or serves well—is dear to this Indra. Finally, the **Soma-offerer**—the one possessing the Soma juice—is dear to this Indra.

->॥ Thus ends the thirteenth group (Varga) in the sixth chapter of the third book. ॥<-

---

## Hymn Text
->॥ Now the Sixth Verse ॥<-

This hero, the conqueror of enemies, makes the exclusive offering of the Soma-presser his own. He is no relative, no friend, and no kinsman to the one who does not press the juice; he is difficult to reach and the punisher of those who do not worship. ॥ 6 ॥

> The attentive | the quick-conqueror | this | hero | of the presser | the cooked offering | he makes | exclusive | Indra |
> Not | of the non-presser | relative | not | friend | not | kinsman | difficult to reach | the destroyer | indeed | of the speechless ॥ 6 ॥

---

## Commentary (Sayana)
**The quick-conqueror** <note>original: *prāśuṣāṭ*</note> means the one who rapidly overcomes his enemies. This **heroic** and powerful Indra **makes the exclusive** or special **cooked offering** <note>original: *paktim*</note>—which belongs to the **presser** <note>the sacrificer who extracts the Soma juice</note>—his own. Furthermore, Indra is **not a relative** <note>original: *āpiḥ*</note> who pervades the life of the **non-presser** <note>the one who fails to perform the sacrifice</note>. Indra is **not a friend** to the non-sacrificer, nor is he a **kinsman**...

# Rig Veda | Book 3, Chapter 6, Group 15

[Indra] is not obtained by such a person. Moreover, he is difficult to reach; he acts as a destroyer toward the man who does not approach him and is without speech, meaning one who offers no praise.

---

-> ॥ Now the Seventh Verse ॥ <-

## Hymn Text

Indra, the drinker of the pressed juice, does not accept friendship with the wealthy miser who does not press the Soma. He seizes his wealth and strikes down the one who gives nothing; he belongs exclusively to the one who presses the juice and cooks the offerings. ॥ 7 ॥

**Not | the wealthy | with the miser | friendship | Indra | the non-presser | the juice-drinker | together | accepts |**
**Away | his | wealth | he seizes | he strikes | the useless | completely | for the presser | for the cook | exclusive | he became ॥ 7 ॥**

---

## Commentary (Sayana)

Indra, the **drinker of the pressed juice** <note>original: *sutapā*</note>, who drinks the <term>Soma</term> <note>A sacred ritual drink made from a pressed plant</note> that has been prepared, does not accept or praise **friendship** <note>original: *sakhyam*</note> with a **wealthy** <note>original: *revatā*</note> <term>Pani</term> <note>A term for a greedy person or merchant-miser who hoards wealth without using it for sacrifice</note>. Such a person is a **non-presser** <note>original: *asunvatā*</note>, meaning a non-sacrificer who does not perform the pressing of the Soma. This means Indra does not approve of him. 

Furthermore, he **seizes** <note>original: *ākhidati*</note> or takes away the **useless** <note>original: *nagnam*, literally "naked"</note> **wealth** <note>original: *vedaḥ*</note>—which can also refer to knowledge—of this non-sacrificer. He **strikes** <note>original: *hanti*</note> or destroys it as well. Moreover, he becomes **exclusive** <note>original: *kevalaḥ*</note>, meaning unique and fully present, for the **presser** <note>original: *suṣvaye*</note> who extracts the Soma juice and the **cook** <note>original: *paktaye*</note> who prepares the sacrificial food offerings.

---

-> ॥ Now the Eighth Verse ॥ <-

## Hymn Text

The high, the low, and the middle-placed call upon Indra; those who go forth and those who stay at home call upon Indra. Those who dwell in peace and those who fight in battle, the leaders of men desiring spoils, they all call upon Indra. ॥ 8 ॥

**Indra | the high | the low | the middle ones | Indra | the going | the settled | Indra |**
**Indra | the dwelling | and | the fighting | Indra | the men | desiring spoils | they call ॥ 8 ॥**

---

## Commentary (Sayana)

People who are **high** <note>distinguished or superior</note>, **low** <note>humble or inferior</note>, and those in the **middle** call upon—meaning they invoke—Indra. Those who are **going forth** <note>original: *yāntaḥ*</note> to accomplish a task invoke Indra; those who are **settled** <note>original: *avasitāsaḥ*</note> or residing at home invoke him. People **dwelling** <note>original: *kṣiyantaḥ*</note> in their houses call upon Indra. And also, those who are **fighting** <note>original: *yudhyamānāḥ*</note> in battle invoke Indra for the sake of victory. The **leaders** <note>original: *naraḥ*</note> or leading men, **desiring spoils** <note>original: *vājayantaḥ*, also meaning desiring food or strength</note>, all call upon Indra.

-> **॥ Thus ends the fourteenth group (Varga) in the sixth chapter of the third book ॥** <-

## Introductory Commentary (Sukta 26)

The fifth hymn [of this section], beginning with **"I was Manu"** <note>original: *ahaṃ manuḥ*</note>, consists of seven verses and is attributed to the seer **Vamadeva**. Regarding this, the index of contents states: with the first three of these seven verses, the seer praised himself as if he were Indra, or Indra praised himself [through the Rishi].

<vocab>
Indra (King of the gods), Pani (A miserly non-sacrificer), Sakhyam (Friendship), Soma (The ritual libation), Yajamana (The patron of the sacrifice), Vamadeva (The sage/Rishi), Ashtaka (One of eight major books), Adhyaya (Chapter), Varga (A small group of verses)
</vocab>

<summary>This page concludes Hymn 25, emphasizing that Indra rejects the friendship of wealthy misers (Panis) in favor of active sacrificers, and notes how Indra is invoked by all people regardless of rank or situation. It then introduces Hymn 26, where the sage Vamadeva speaks in the first person, identifying himself with the divine.</summary>

[Page] 139
# Mandala 4, Anuvaka 3, Sukta 26 | Third Book

Regarding the **Praise of the Hawk** <note>original: *śyena-stuti*</note>: In this section, beginning with the words "I was Manu," the seer **Vamadeva** <note>The primary poet-sage of this book of the Rig Veda</note> praises himself in the form of **Indra** <note>The King of the Gods</note> across three verses. Alternatively, it is Indra himself praising his own nature. Therefore, in the view where these are Vamadeva’s words, Vamadeva is the **Rishi** <note>seer/author</note> and Indra is the **Devata** <note>the deity being addressed</note>. In the view where these are Indra’s words, Indra is both the Rishi and the **Paramatman** <note>The Supreme Soul/Absolute Reality</note> is the deity. The meter is **Trishtup** <note>A Vedic meter consisting of four lines of eleven syllables each</note>. For the remaining verses of this hymn and the subsequent hymn, Vamadeva is the Rishi, and they praise the **Brahman** <note>The ultimate, impersonal reality</note> in the form of a beautiful-winged bird <note>original: *suparṇa*</note>; thus, the Supreme Brahman is their deity. 

In the **one-day sacrifice** <note>original: *ekāha*</note> known as the **Shyena-yaga** <note>An 'eagle sacrifice' performed for specific goals</note>, during the **midday libation** <note>original: *mādhyandina-savana*</note>, this hymn is used for the **Marutvatiya** offering. This is indicated in the ritual manuals: "One who practices magic should sacrifice with the two 'Swift Hawk' hymns, beginning with 'I was Manu' and 'While yet within the womb'" <note>Aśvalāyana Śrauta Sūtra 9. 7</note>.

-> ॥ Here is the First Verse ॥ <-

## Hymn Text

I was **Manu** and I became the **Sun**; I am the wise seer **Kakshivan**. I favor **Kutsa**, the son of Arjuni; I am the poet **Ushana**—behold me! ॥ 1 ॥

**I | Manu | became | Sun | and | I | Kakshivan | seer | am | wise |**
**I | Kutsa | son of Arjuni | down | favor | I | poet | Ushana | behold | me ॥ 1 ॥**

---

## Commentary (Sayana)

With these first three verses, Vamadeva, while still dwelling **within the womb** <note>referring to his miraculous enlightenment before birth</note>, having attained the knowledge of ultimate truth, describes his own experience of **Universal Selfhood** <note>original: *sarvātmya*; the realization that one is identical with all things</note> by showing himself in the forms of Manu and others.

He says: "I, Vamadeva, **became Manu** <note>The progenitor of humanity</note>. I am **Prajapati**, the thinker of all. I alone am the **Sun** <note>original: *sūrya*</note>, the **Savita** who impels everyone. I alone am the wise and learned seer named **Kakshivan**, the son of **Dirghatamas**. I **favor** <note>original: *nyṛñje*, explained as *ni-tarāṃ prasādayāmi*</note>—that is, I bestow my complete grace upon—the seer named **Kutsa**, the son of **Arjuni**. I alone am the seer named **Ushana**, the 'Poet' of transcendent vision." 

What is mentioned here are just examples; the meaning is that from the perspective of the **Ultimate Truth** <note>original: *paramārtha-dṛṣṭyā*</note>, "I am indeed everything." O people, **behold me** who is the soul of all! The implication is: "You too should experience your own true nature in this same way."

-> ॥ Now the Second Verse ॥ <-

## Hymn Text

I gave the **earth** to the **noble** man; I gave **rain** to the mortal who offers oblations. I led the loudly lowing **waters**; the **gods** followed my will. ॥ 2 ॥

**I | earth | gave | to the noble | I | rain | to the offering | to the mortal |**
**I | waters | led | loudly lowing | my | gods | following | intent | went ॥ 2 ॥**

---

## Commentary (Sayana)

I, Vamadeva (or Indra), **gave the earth**—the wide ground—to **Manu** <note>here referring to the noble/Aryan man</note>. I have bestowed it. For the **mortal** man, the **sacrificer** <note>original: *yajamāna*</note> who possesses the offerings, I gave the gift of **rain** for the growth of crops and other resources...

<summary>This page introduces Sukta 26, where the Rishi Vamadeva realizes his identity with the entire universe (Sarvātmya). He identifies himself as Manu, the Sun, and various ancient sages, asserting his role as the divine provider of earth and rain.</summary>
<keywords>Vamadeva, Indra, Manu, Surya, Kakshivan, Kutsa, Ushana, Universal Selfhood, Sarvātmya, rain, sacrifice, Rig Veda commentary</keywords>

...I alone gave the water. Furthermore, I led the roaring <note>original: *vāvaśānāḥ*</note> waters. I caused them to reach every region. The gods, such as Varuna and others, followed my will <note>original: *ketam*</note>, my intent. They continue to follow it.

-> ॥ Now the Third Verse ॥ <-

## Hymn Text
Rejoicing in the exhilaration [of Soma], I shattered at once the ninety-nine fortresses of **Shambara**; and the hundredth I made a dwelling-place, when in the sacrifice of all, I protected **Divodasa** who is **Atithigva**. ॥ 3 ॥

**I. fortresses. rejoicing. apart. shattered. nine. at once. ninety. of Shambara.**
**the hundredth. a dwelling-place. in the sacrifice of all. Divodasa. Atithigva. when. I protected.** ॥ 3 ॥

---

## Commentary (Sayana)
I—either the sage Vamadeva or the god Indra—rejoicing in the **Soma** <note>The sacred ritual drink</note>, destroyed ninety-nine fortresses <note>original: *puraḥ*</note> belonging to the demon <note>original: *asura*</note> named **Shambara** simultaneously. The hundredth fortress, which completed the hundred, I made into a place fit for the king named **Divodasa** to enter and dwell in. When I protected the royal seer Divodasa—who is called **Atithigva** because he is one who "approaches guests" <note>original: *atithīnām-abhigantāram*</note>—at the sacrifice of all <note>original: *sarvatātā*</note>, it was then that I shattered those fortresses. This connects back to the earlier statement.

---

-> ॥ Now the Fourth Verse ॥ <-

## Hymn Text
May that bird, O **Maruts**, be pre-eminent over all birds; may the hawk, swift-flying, be superior to all hawks; for with a wheel-less self-power, the beautiful-winged one brought the oblation, favored by the gods, to **Manu**. ॥ 4 ॥

**forward. well. that. from birds. O Maruts. bird. let it be. forward. hawk. from hawks. swift-flying.**
**with the wheel-less. when. by self-power. the beautiful-winged one. oblation. brought. to Manu. favored by the gods.** ॥ 4 ॥

---

## Commentary (Sayana)
From this verse onwards, the **Hawk** <note>original: *śyena*</note> is praised. O Maruts—you who are birds swift like the winds—let that famous bird called the Hawk be pre-eminent <note>original: *pra su astu*</note> among all birds. Moreover, let this swift-flying hawk be superior to all other hawks of excellent flight. When the **Suparna** <note>the beautiful-winged one</note> brought the oblation—which is the Soma—to **Manu** <note>the progenitor of mankind</note> to be enjoyed by the gods, he brought it from the celestial realm. He did so by a wheel-less power <note>original: *achakrayā svadhayā*</note>, which refers to his own nature or a wheel-less chariot. We know that the word <term>svadhā</term> can mean "chariot" from other Vedic passages, such as "standing in a wheel-less *svadha*" (Rig Veda 10.27.19).

## Hymn Text

-> ॥ Now the Fifth Verse ॥ <-

When the bird, startling [the guards], brought [the Soma] from that place, he was released upon the wide path [of the sky], moving with the speed of thought. The hawk went quickly with the honey-sweet Soma, and here the hawk gained his fame. ॥ 5 ॥

**Word-for-word breakdown:**
**brought. if. the bird. from there. startling. by the path. wide. swift as thought. was released.**
**quickly. went. with the honey. of the Soma. and. fame. gained. the hawk. here.** ॥ 5 ॥

## Commentary (Sayana)

When <note>original: *yadi*</note> the **bird**, the **hawk**, frightening the keepers of the Soma <note>original: *vevijānaḥ*</note>, **brought** <note>original: *bharat*</note> the Soma from that heaven, he was **released** <note>original: *asarji*</note>—meaning he was united—with the **wide path** of the atmosphere, moving with a **speed like that of the mind**. He **went** <note>original: *yayau*</note> **quickly** with the **honey-sweet** food consisting of **Soma**. **And also**, **here** in this world, the **hawk** <note>meaning the "fair-winged one" or *suparṇa*</note> **gained** <note>original: *vivide*</note> the **fame** or glory resulting from the act of bringing the Soma.

---

## Hymn Text

-> ॥ Now the Sixth Verse ॥ <-

The straight-flying hawk, holding the stalk, a bird from afar [brought] the delightful exhilaration; the hawk brought the Soma, grasping it firmly, accompanied by the gods, taking it from that highest heaven. ॥ 6 ॥

**Word-for-word breakdown:**
**straight-flying. the hawk. holding. the stalk. from afar. the bird. delightful. exhilaration.**
**Soma. brought. grasping firmly. accompanied by gods. from heaven. from that. highest. having taken.** ॥ 6 ॥

---

## Commentary (Sayana)

The **straight-flying** hawk <note>original: *ṛjīpī*</note>, **holding** or supporting the **stalk** <note>original: *aṃśu*</note> of the Soma from **afar**, being a **hawk** of praiseworthy flight, **accompanied by the gods**, a **bird** <note>original: *śakunaḥ*</note> **taking** the **delightful**, praiseworthy, and **intoxicating** Soma **from that highest heaven**, and **grasping it firmly** <note>original: *dadahṛvāṇaḥ*</note>, he **brought** <note>original: *bharat*</note> it.

---

## Hymn Text

-> ॥ Now the Seventh Verse ॥ <-

Having taken it, the hawk brought the Soma, a thousand pressings and ten thousand together; here, the wise **Purandhi** left behind the enemies <note>or "the illiberal"</note> in the exhilaration of the Soma. ॥ 7 ॥

**Word-for-word breakdown:**
**having taken. the hawk. brought. Soma. a thousand. pressings. ten thousand. and. together.**
**here. Purandhi. left behind. enemies. in the exhilaration. of the Soma. the foolish. the wise.** ॥ 7 ॥

---

## Commentary (Sayana)

The **hawk**, the bird of praiseworthy flight, **brought** a **thousand**—the number one thousand—of the **pressings** <note>original: *savān*</note> or sacrifices...
<margin>VOL. III. 00</margin>

<note>The term *Purandhi* in this context often refers to a deity of abundance or wisdom who assists in the ritual or the retrieval of Soma. The "enemies" or "illiberal ones" (*arātīḥ*) represent those who do not offer sacrifices.</note>

<summary>This page describes the divine hawk's successful retrieval of the Soma plant from the highest heaven. It emphasizes the hawk's incredible speed, its victory over the celestial guards, and the resulting abundance of Soma pressings available for ritual use.</summary>

<meta>This page concludes the commentary on Hymn 26 and begins Hymn 27 of the Fourth Book (Mandala) of the Rig Veda. It marks the transition between the 15th and 16th sections (Vargas) of the 6th chapter (Adhyaya) in the 3rd Book (Ashtaka) of the overall collection. The text focuses on the famous "Hymn of the Hawk," where the seer Vamadeva describes his spiritual liberation while still in the womb.</meta>

... [the hawk] brought **ten thousand** <note>original: *ayutam*</note>, meaning a count of ten thousand or an innumerable amount. **Together** <note>original: *sākam*</note> with that, taking the **Soma**—which is characterized as the divine food—he **brought** it. He carried it away; he fetched it. When this Soma had been brought, **Purandhi** <note>a title meaning "bearer of cities" or "wise one"</note>—who is the wise, non-deluded Indra of many deeds—being in the **exhilaration** <note>original: *made*</note> or joy belonging to the Soma, **abandoned** the **foolish** <note>original: *mūrā*</note> **enemies** <note>original: *arātīḥ*</note>. He left them behind; the meaning is that he struck them down. The word for "enemy" here is in the feminine gender.

->॥ This ends the fifteenth varga of the sixth chapter of the third book ॥<-

**"In the womb indeed"** <note>original: *garbhe nu*</note> begins the sixth hymn of five verses. The **Seer** <note>original: *Rishi*</note> is **Vamadeva**, and the **meter** is **Trishtubh** <note>a rhythmic pattern of 11 syllables per line</note>. The final verse is in the **Shakvari** meter, consisting of fifty-six syllables. The **deity** is the **Hawk** <note>original: *Shyena*</note>. Since it was mentioned in the previous hymn that there are eight verses, the deity of the last verse could also be Indra. Thus, the index <note>original: *Anukramani*</note> states: **"In the womb indeed... five verses, the last is Shakvari."** This hymn is used during the recitation of the <term>Nishkevalya Shastra</term> <note>a specific ritual chant performed during the midday Soma sacrifice</note>. The ritual formula was cited previously.

---

## Hymn Text

->॥ Here is the first verse ॥<-

While still in the **womb**, I **knew** all the **births** of these **gods** in their proper order. A **hundred iron fortresses** guarded me; **then**, as a **hawk**, I flew forth with **speed**. ॥ 1 ॥

**Word-by-word analysis (Pada Patha):**
**In the womb. indeed. being. according to. of these. I knew. I. of the gods. births. all.**
**A hundred. me. fortresses. made of iron. guarded. then. the hawk. with speed. out. I flew.** ॥ 1 ॥

---

## Commentary (Sayana)

Regarding this, the following verse is recited: "Taking on the form of a hawk, he emerged from the womb through the power of Yoga." The Seer <note>Vamadeva</note>, while lying in the womb, says: **"In the womb indeed."** While still **being** <note>original: *san*</note> in the very **womb**, I, Vamadeva, **knew** <note>original: *anvavedam*</note>—I understood in successive order—**all the births** or origins of **these gods** such as Indra and the others. The meaning is: "I knew that all the gods were born from the Supreme Self." Before this realization, a **hundred**—meaning many—**iron** <note>original: *āyasīḥ*</note>, or unbreakable, **fortresses**, which are the physical bodies, **guarded me**. They protected me; the meaning is they guarded me so that I would not know the Self as distinct from the body. **Then**, now, **as a hawk**—staying like a hawk—I **flew forth** <note>original: *niradīyam*</note> with **speed** or velocity. Having known the unconditioned Self, I have emerged from the body. In the section of the <term>Aitareya Aranyaka</term> [2.25] starting with "This one is first in the person...", this meaning is fully established by the passage: "Vamadeva, lying even in the womb, spoke thus."

---

## Hymn Text

->॥ Now the second verse ॥<-

Indeed, he did not carry me away according to his **pleasure**; he excelled in **power** and **valor**. Then the **wise one** <note>original: *purandhiḥ*</note> left the **enemies** behind, and as he **sped forward**, he crossed over the **winds**. ॥ 2 ॥

<vocab>
- Vamadeva: A famous Vedic sage (Rishi) credited with most of the fourth book of the Rig Veda.
- Hawk (Shyena): A powerful symbol in the Vedas representing the soul's flight or the fetching of divine nectar (Soma) from heaven.
- Iron fortresses (Ayasi purah): A metaphor for the physical body or the cycle of rebirth that "imprisons" the soul.
- Births of the gods (Janimani): The cosmic origins and manifestations of divine powers.
- Aitareya Aranyaka: An ancient philosophical text that interprets this specific verse as a moment of prenatal enlightenment.
</vocab>

<summary>This page features the famous declaration of the sage Vamadeva, who attained spiritual enlightenment while still in the womb. He describes breaking free from the "iron fortresses" of physical existence with the speed and power of a divine hawk.</summary>
<keywords>Vamadeva, Hawk, prenatal enlightenment, iron fortresses, Soma, Indra, rebirth, Aitareya Aranyaka</keywords>

## Commentary (Sayana)

**Conclusion of Commentary on Verse 2**
That womb did **not indeed take away** the **pleasure** <note>original: *joṣam*</note> or the sufficiency of me, Vamadeva. The meaning is that even while dwelling in the womb, I did not experience delusion. Rather, I **overcame** <note>original: *abhyabhavam*</note> this **misery** <note>original: *īm*</note> of staying in the womb through **sharp strength** <note>original: *tvakṣasā*</note>, which is the power of my spiritual knowledge. He, the **Bountiful One** <note>original: *purandhiḥ*</note>—the inner controller of all and the supporter of the "cities" (the bodies)—**abandoned** or destroyed the **enemies** <note>original: *arātīḥ*</note> residing in the womb. Furthermore, **growing** <note>original: *bhūśuvānaḥ*</note> into the full Supreme Self, he **crossed over** the **winds** <note>the vital airs or forces</note> that cause pain in the womb.

**Commentary on Verse 3**
**Then** <note>original: *adha*</note>, at the time of bringing the Soma, **when** the **Hawk** made a **downward sound** or scream from **heaven**; and **when** the Soma-guardians **bore** <note>original: *ūhuḥ*</note> or scattered this **Bountiful** Soma away from this Hawk; and **when** the archer named **Krishanu**, a guardian of Soma, wishing to move with the **speed of mind**, **shot** the **bowstring** from the end of his bow—he indeed released an arrow at this Hawk. As the <term>Brahmana</term> <note>a prose commentary on the Vedas</note> says: "Shooting after it, Krishanu, the Soma-guardian, cut off a claw of its left foot." The connection to the next verse is: when the Soma-guardians acted in this way, then the Hawk brought the Soma.

**Commentary on Verse 4 (beginning)**
The **straight-flying** <note>original: *ṛjipyaḥ*</note> Hawk, for whom **Indra** is the protector, brought [the Soma] from the **great height**...

<vocab>
- श्येन (Syena): Falcon or Hawk; in this context, it represents the divine force or the bird that fetches the sacred Soma from heaven.
- वामदेव (Vamadeva): The Rishi (Seer) of this hymn who realizes his divinity while in the womb.
- सोम (Soma): The sacred plant/drink of the Vedic sacrifice, often guarded by celestial beings.
- कृशानु (Krishanu): A celestial archer who guards the Soma and attempts to shoot the Hawk.
- पुरंधि (Puramdhi): A complex term meaning "city-bearer" or "bountiful"; here applied to Soma or the inner Self.
- भुज्यु (Bhujyu): A king's son who was rescued by the Ashvins (divine twins); used here as a comparison for being rescued or brought safely.
</vocab>

## Commentary (Sayana)
<note>Continuing from the previous verse</note>
He brought this Soma from the celestial world <note>original: *dyulokād*</note> situated above. An illustration is provided: just as the **Ashvins** <note>the twin divine physicians</note> brought the king named **Bhujyu** from a place protected by **Indra**, so too was the Soma brought. Then, at that time, during the journey <note>original: *yāmani*</note> in battle, a feather <note>original: *parṇam*</note> of the bird fell, having been struck by the weapons of **Krishanu** <note>the celestial guardian of Soma</note> who had intercepted the bird's path. It fell.

## Hymn Text
Now, may the **Bountiful One** <note>original: *maghavā*, an epithet of Indra</note> take the bright **Soma juice** <note>original: *andhaḥ*</note>, which is in the white vessel, mixed with the products of the cow <note>milk</note>, and swelling with strength; it is offered by the **Adhvaryu priests** <note>the priests responsible for the physical ritual</note>. May the **Hero** <note>Indra</note> take it to drink for the sake of exhilaration; may he take it to drink for the sake of exhilaration. ॥ 5 ॥

## Padapāṭha
Now | White | Vessel | With cows <note>milk</note> | Mixed | Swelling | Bountiful | Bright | Juice |
By Adhvaryus | Offered | Of the sweet | This | Indra | For exhilaration | Towards | May he take | To drink | Hero | For exhilaration | Towards | May he take | To drink. ॥ 5 ॥

## Commentary (Sayana)
Now, the heroic and powerful **Indra** <note>Maghavan</note> should take the Soma-food <note>original: *andhaḥ*</note>—which is bright and full of essence, contained in a white or shining vessel, mixed or sprinkled with the milk of the cow, and currently increasing in potency—offered by the **Adhvaryu priests**. He should take this sweet Soma juice to drink for the purpose of exhilaration or joy <note>original: *madāya*</note>. The repetition <note>of "for exhilaration, may he take it to drink"</note> is intended to show great respect and emphasis.

The seventh Sukta (Hymn 28), beginning with the words "With you as ally," consists of five verses. It is seen by the Seer **Vamadeva** and is composed in the **Trishtubh** meter. The deities addressed are **Indra** and **Soma** together. The application <note>original: *viniyoga*</note> of the hymn is determined by its characteristic marks <note>used in rituals involving both deities</note>.

## Hymn Text
Through your **alliance** <note>original: *sakhyasya*, friendship</note>, O **Soma**, and with you as his **ally** <note>original: *yujā*</note>, **Indra** made the flowing waters for **Manu** <note>the ancestral father of humanity</note>; he slew the **Serpent** <note>original: *ahim*, referring to the demon Vritra</note> and sent the **Seven Rivers** flowing; he opened the outlets that were closed like sealed cavities. ॥ 1 ॥

## Padapāṭha
With you | As ally | Your | That | Soma | In friendship | Indra | Waters | For Manu | Flowing | Made |
Slew | Serpent | Sent flowing | Seven | Rivers | Back | Opened | Closed | Like | Outlets. ॥ 1 ॥

## Commentary (Sayana)
O **Soma**, when your friendship <note>alliance</note> existed, **Indra**, with you as his companion or helper, made the waters—which are characterized by rain and have a natural tendency to flow—available for **Manu** <note>mankind</note>. He performed this act.

<vocab>
- **Soma**: The sacred ritual drink and the deity embodying it.
- **Indra**: The king of the gods, often associated with thunder and rain.
- **Maghavan**: "The Generous One," a common title for Indra.
- **Adhvaryu**: The priest who handles the manual preparation of the sacrifice.
- **Manu**: The archetypal human or first man in Vedic thought.
- **Ahi**: "The Serpent," a name for Vritra, the demon of drought who imprisoned the waters.
- **Seven Rivers**: The Sapta Sindhu, the primary rivers of the Vedic landscape.
</vocab>

## Commentary (Sayana) - Verse 1 (Continued)

Moreover, he struck the **Serpent** <note>original: *ahi*</note>, the demon Vritra. He killed him. He set in motion the **seven** <note>original: *sapta*</note> flowing **rivers** <note>original: *sindhūn*</note>, the waters. He released them. Even though they were as if concealed—hidden and obscured by Vritra. The word "as if" <note>original: *iva*</note> here also functions as "and." He opened the **hollows** <note>original: *khāni*</note>, which are the gates of the streams. He threw them open.

## Hymn Text - Verse 2

-> || Now the Second Verse || <-

With you as his ally, O **Soma** <note>original: *indo*</note>, **Indra** instantly and with force struck off the **wheel of the Sun** <note>original: *sūryasya cakram*</note>. Situated high upon the great ridge of the sky, the wheel that moves through all life was taken away from the great deceiver. ॥ 2 ॥

**Word-by-Word Analysis —**
With you | As ally | Down | Struck | Of the Sun | Indra | Wheel | With force | Instantly | O Soma |
Upon | Ridge | Great | Revolving | Of the great | Deceiver | Away | All-pervading life | Was taken. ॥ 2 ॥

---

## Commentary (Sayana) - Verse 2

O **Soma** <note>original: *indo*</note>, **Indra** instantly, with **you** as his **ally** <note>original: *yujā*</note> or helper, struck off <note>original: *nikhidat*</note> with overwhelming **force** one **wheel** belonging to the stimulator, the **Sun** <note>Savitṛ</note>, from his chariot which previously had two wheels. What was this wheel like? It was **revolving** <note>original: *vartamānam*</note> **upon** the **great ridge** <note>original: *snunā bṛhatā*</note> of the vast mid-air. Furthermore, the **all-pervading** wheel belonging to the **great deceiver**—the Sun—**was taken away**. It was carried off by Indra.

## Hymn Text - Verse 3

-> || Now the Third Verse || <-

Indra struck and Agni burned the **enemies** <note>original: *dasyūn*</note>, O Soma, in the battle before **midday** <note>original: *madhyaṃdināt*</note>. In the difficult place, in the stronghold, he destroyed many of them with force and weapons, as if they were travelers being struck down by a purposeful act. ॥ 3 ॥

**Word-by-Word Analysis —**
Struck | Indra | Burned | Agni | O Soma | Before | Enemies | Midday | In battle |
In difficult access | In the stronghold | By act | Like | Of those going | Many | With force | With weapons | Struck down. ॥ 3 ॥

## Commentary (Sayana) - Verse 3

O **Soma**, in **battle** <note>original: *abhīke*</note>, **Indra struck** the **Dasyus** <note>the term <term>Dasyu</term> refers to the chaotic enemies or demons opposed to the divine order</note>. He killed them. **Agni** <note>the Fire-god</note> **burned** some of these enemies. What was the state of Indra and Agni? They had gained strength from drinking you in the morning, **before midday**. He **destroyed** <note>original: *nibarhīt*</note> **many** and indeed **all** of the demons as they were **going** or fleeing, using his overwhelming **force**. An illustration is provided: just as a thief greedy for wealth might kill travelers <note>original: *yātām*</note> going along their path to achieve his own purpose <note>original: *kratvā na*</note> while they are in a **difficult place** <note>original: *durge*</note> or a **stronghold** <note>original: *duroṇe*</note> where it is impossible to protect them, so did Indra strike them down.

## Hymn Text

-> ॥ Now the Fourth Verse ॥ <-

O **Indra** <note>The king of the gods and deity of storms and war</note>, you have scattered the **Dasyus** <note>original: *dasyūn*; the enemies of the Vedic people, often described as godless or chaotic</note> in all directions, making them low and abject. You have rendered the **Dasa** <note>A term for enemies or servile tribes</note> people inglorious and without praise. [O Indra and Soma,] restrain them; strike down the enemies; through your weapons of destruction, let us find retribution and honor. ॥ 4 ॥

**Word-by-Word Analysis —**
Scattered | Entirely | Low/Abject | Indra | Enemies (Dasyus) | People | Dasa | You made | Unglorified | 
Restrain | Strike down | Low | Enemies | Let me find | Retribution/Honor | With weapons of destruction. ॥ 4 ॥

---

## Commentary (Sayana)

O Indra, you have **made** <note>original: *akṛṇoḥ*</note> these **Dasyus low** and **scattered in all directions**, meaning you have deprived them of all their limbs and status. Furthermore, you made the **Dasa** people—those who are devoid of ritual actions—**unglorified**, meaning they are now despised. O **Indra and Soma** <note>The dual deity addressed here</note>, may you both **restrain** the enemies. **Strike them down**; that is, kill them utterly. Moreover, through the **weapons** or blows dealt to those enemies, let me **find honor** <note>original: *apacitim*; Sayana interprets this as "worship" or "respect" from the people</note> among the people.

---

## Hymn Text

-> ॥ Now the Fifth Verse ॥ <-

Truly, O **Bounteous Ones** <note>original: *maghavānā*; refers to Indra and Soma as dispensers of wealth</note>, you both performed that great deed: Indra and Soma, you broke open the great mountain-pen of the **cows**. The hidden [treasures] were released; even the earth was cleft as you forced them open. ॥ 5 ॥

**Word-by-Word Analysis —**
Thus | Truly | O Bounteous Ones | You two | That [deed] | Indra | and | Soma | Great enclosure | Born from the waters (cloud) | Of the cow | 
Completely | Cleft/Broke | The hidden things | By the consumer | They released | The earth | Even | Cleft/Tearing through. ॥ 5 ॥

---

## Commentary (Sayana)

O **Soma**, you and the Moon—meaning both of you together—**broke open** <note>original: *ādarhatam*</note> the **great** <note>original: *urvam*</note> mountain-pen, which is the **water-born** <note>original: *abjam*; referring to the clouds</note> mass, and the herd of **cows**. The groups of cows that were **hidden** or covered by the **Panis** <note>A class of demons who stole and hid the celestial cows/light</note> were **released** <note>original: *riricyuḥ*; emptied out</note> by your **consuming power** <note>original: *aṣṇā*; the strength that devours the enemies</note> which also broke through the lands of the Panis. O **Bounteous Ones**, Indra and Soma, you who are the destroyers of enemies, whatever you did in this manner is **truly** the truth.

## Hymn Text

The eighth hymn, beginning with **"Come to us, O Praised One,"** consists of five verses. It was seen by the seer **Vamadeva**. It is in the **Trishtubh** meter and is dedicated to **Indra**. The "Anukramanika" <note>An ancient index of Vedic hymns</note> confirms this. Its ritual application is determined by the characteristic signs found within the verses.

-> ॥ Therein the First Verse ॥ <-

Come to us, O **Indra**, you who are praised with strengths and aid. Come with your **haris** <note>original: *haribhiḥ*; the tawny horses of Indra</note>, rejoicing in our offerings. Even from afar, hear our many prayers, O you whose gifts are true, as you are lauded with our songs of praise. ॥ 1 ॥

<vocab>
**Indra**: The primary heroic god of the Rig Veda, associated with thunder and strength. 
**Soma**: The sacred ritual drink and the deity associated with it. 
**Vamadeva**: The primary seer (Rishi) of the 4th Book (Mandala) of the Rig Veda. 
**Dasyu**: A term for enemies of the Vedic order, often interpreted as dark or demonic forces. 
**Pani**: Mythical miserly demons who hide the cows (representing light or rain). 
**Maghavan**: "The Bounteous One," a frequent title for Indra. 
**Sukta**: A Vedic hymn. 
**Varga**: A small section or "class" of verses. 
**Anukramanika**: Traditional indices providing metadata about the hymns.
</vocab>

### Mandala 4. Section 2. Hymn 29. || Third Volume || 147

## Hymn Text
<note>RV 4.29.1 (Continuation of the Word-by-Word Breakdown)</note>
Come | to us | O praised one | near | with food | with protection | Indra | go | with your golden horses | being delighted |
beyond | even | the enemy's | libations | many | with hymns | being lauded | O you of true wealth. ॥ 1 ॥

---

## Commentary (Sayana)
O **Indra**, you who are **praised**, come **with food** <note>original: *vājebhiḥ*; implying both sacrificial offerings and the strength they provide</note>. The term **beyond even** <note>original: *tiraścit*</note> signifies "having reached" or "passing through." **Yaska** <note>An ancient linguist and etymologist</note> explains in the **Nighantu 3.20** that this refers to "attaining." Come **near** to our many **full libations** <note>original: *purūṇi savanā*; the three-times-daily offerings of Soma juice</note> for our **protection**, coming with your **horses** <note>original: *haribhiḥ*; specifically Indra's two bay or golden steeds</note>. What is his nature? He is **delighted** <note>original: *mandasāno*</note>, he is the **lord** <note>original: *aryaḥ*</note>, and he is **lauded** <note>original: *gṛṇānaḥ*</note> by our **hymns** <note>original: *āṅgūṣebhiḥ*</note>. He is **one whose wealth is true** <note>original: *satyarādhāḥ*; meaning his gifts and blessings are real and eternal, unlike worldly illusions</note>.

---

## Hymn Text
<note>RV 4.29.2</note>
-> ॥ Now the Second Verse ॥ <-
Truly, the wise one who is helpful to men comes, being called to the sacrifice by the priests who press the juice. He of the fine horses, who is fearless, thinking [of the sacrifice], rejoices together with the heroes. ॥ 2 ॥

<note>Word-by-Word Analysis</note>
Come | truly | [particle] | he goes | helpful to men | the wise one | being called | by the pressers | near | the sacrifice |
of fine horses | who | fearless | thinking | by those who press | he rejoices | together | [particle] | with heroes. ॥ 2 ॥

---

## Commentary (Sayana)
**Helpful to men** <note>original: *naryo*</note> means beneficial to human beings. The **wise one** <note>original: *cikitvān*</note> is he who knows all things. Being **called** <note>original: *hūyamāna*</note> by the **pressers** <note>original: *sotṛbhiḥ*</note>—the priests who extract the Soma juice—may **Indra come** toward **our sacrifice**. The words **truly** <note>original: *hi sma*</note> are used here to complete the poetic meter. He has **fine horses** <note>original: *svaśvaḥ*</note> and is **fearless** <note>original: *abhīru*</note> by nature. Being **lauded** <note>original: *manyamānaḥ*</note> by the sacrificers who press the juice, that Indra **rejoices** <note>original: *sammadati*</note> together with the **heroes**, who are the **Maruts** <note>The storm-deities and Indra's constant companions in battle</note>. The phrase "May he come" is understood from the previous verse.

---

## Hymn Text
<note>RV 4.29.3</note>
-> ॥ Now the Third Verse ॥ <-
Make his ears hear; let him be strengthened; following the favorable direction, let him be delighted. Showering [blessings] for the sake of wealth, the mighty Indra will make for us good crossings and freedom from fear. ॥ 3 ॥

<note>Word-by-Word Analysis</note>
Make hear | [particle] | his | ears | to strengthen | favorable | following | forward | direction | to delight |
showering | for wealth | the mighty one | he makes | for us | Indra | good crossings | freedom from fear | and. ॥ 3 ॥

---

## Commentary (Sayana)
O singer, **make [these hymns] heard** <note>original: *āvaya*</note> by **his**—Indra's—**ears**. In order to **strengthen** <note>original: *vājayadhyai*</note> Indra and to greatly **delight him** <note>original: *mandayadhyai*</note> along the **favorable directions** <note>original: *juṣṭām anu diśam*</note> which he frequents in all quarters. The word **it** is a filler for the meter. He is **showering** <note>original: *udvavṛṣāṇaḥ*</note>, meaning he is being sprinkled with Soma juice, and he is **mighty** <note>original: *tuviṣmān*</note>—

# Rig Veda 
### [Ashtaka 3, Adhyaya 6, Varga 18]

...may **Indra** grant us, for the sake of our **prosperity** <note>original: *rādhase*; referring to wealth gained through sacrificial success</note>, **excellent crossings** <note>original: *sutīrthā*; auspicious paths or safe fords through difficulty</note> and **fearlessness** <note>original: *abhayam*</note>. May he do so.

-> ॥ Now the Fourth Verse ॥ <-

## Hymn Text

**Truly he is the one who goes toward the seeker for protection, even to the wise one who is calling and praising him in this manner; he, the thunderbolt-handed, who in his own person places thousands and hundreds of swift horses upon the yoke.** ॥ 4 ॥

**Toward | He | Who | Goes | The seeker | For protection | In this manner | The wise one | Calling | Praising |**
**Near | In his own person | Placing | On the yoke | Swift (horses) | Thousands | Hundreds | Thunderbolt-handed.** ॥ 4 ॥

---

## Commentary (Sayana)

The **thunderbolt-handed** <note>original: *vajrabāhuḥ*; describing Indra’s characteristic weapon, the Vajra</note> Indra, placing **thousands** and **hundreds** of **swift horses** <note>original: *āśūn*; literally 'fast-movers'</note> that are under his own control upon the **yoke** <note>original: *dhuri*; the part of the chariot that bears the weight and pull</note> of his chariot, becomes the **one who goes** <note>original: *gantā*</note> **directly** <note>original: *acchā*</note> toward the **wise** <note>original: *vipram*; the inspired poet-priest</note> **sacrificer** who is **seeking** <note>original: *nādhamānam*</note> help, **calling** <note>original: *havamānam*</note> upon him, and **praising** <note>original: *gṛṇantam*</note> him in this way for the sake of **protection** <note>original: *ūtī*</note>. This connects to the previous verse: May that Indra grant us safe passage and freedom from fear.

---

-> ॥ Now the Fifth Verse ॥ <-

## Hymn Text

**O Maghavan, O Indra, protected by you, may we be the wise ones, the singers who praise you, sharing in the wealth of the Great Heaven, which is to be invoked and provides much nourishment.** ॥ 5 ॥

**Protected by you | O Maghavan | Indra | Wise ones | We | Yours | May be | Singers | Praising |**
**Partakers | Of the Great Heaven | Of wealth | To be invoked | For the giving | Of much nourishment.** ॥ 5 ॥

---

## Commentary (Sayana)

O **Maghavan** <note>original: *maghavan*; a common epithet for Indra meaning 'Lord of Munificence'</note>, O Indra, being **protected by you** <note>original: *tvātāḥ*</note>, may **we**—the **wise ones** <note>original: *viprāḥ*</note> and **praisers** <note>original: *sūrayaḥ*</note> who are **lauding** <note>original: *gṛṇantaḥ*</note> you—become **partakers** <note>original: *bhejānāsaḥ*</note> when you decide on the **giving** <note>original: *davane*</note> of the **wealth** <note>original: *rāyaḥ*</note> belonging to the **Great Heaven** <note>original: *bṛhaddivasya*; signifying the vast radiant realm</note>. This wealth is **to be praised** <note>original: *ākayyasya*</note> from all sides and provides **much nourishment** <note>original: *purukṣoḥ*; can also mean 'great fame' or 'abundant food'</note>. May we possess this.

-> ॥ Thus ends the eighteenth varga of the sixth adhyaya of the third book ॥ <-

## Critical Notes

The ninth hymn, beginning with "There is no one [but Indra]" <note>original: *nakir indra*; this refers to the start of Rig Veda 4.30</note>, contains twenty-four verses and is seen by the seer **Vamadeva**. The meter is **Gayatri**, though the eighth and the twenty-fourth verses are in the **Anushtubh** meter. **Indra** is the deity. The triplet of verses beginning with "Even from heaven" <note>original: *divaś cin na*</note> is dedicated to both the deity **Ushas** (the Dawn) and Indra. As it is stated in the **Anukramani** <note>An ancient index/catalogue of the Rig Veda</note>: "The hymn 'Nakir' has twenty-four verses; the triplet 'divas cit' is for Ushas; the meter is Gayatri, with the eighth and the final being Anushtubh..."

M. 4. A. 3. S. 30.] || Third Ashtaka || 149

Regarding this hymn: In the **Atiratra** <note>A specific type of Soma sacrifice that lasts through the entire night</note>, during the third **round** <note>original: *paryāya*; a sequence of recitations</note>, this hymn is used as the final part of the **Maitravaruna-shastra** <note>The specific litany recited by the Maitravaruna priest</note>. As it is indicated in the ritual manuals: "One should conclude with 'None is superior to you, O Indra'." <note>Reference to the Asvalayana Shrauta Sutra 6. 4.</note>

---

## Hymn Text

->॥ Here begins the first verse ॥<-

**None is superior to you, O Indra; no one is greater than you, O Slayer of Vritra. Truly, there is no one else such as you are. ॥ 1 ॥**

->॥ Now the second verse ॥<-

**Truly, all the peoples follow you, revolving like wheels follow a chariot. Truly, you are great and famous. ॥ 2 ॥**

->॥ Now the third verse ॥<-

**Indeed, all the gods fought with you as their strength, O Indra, when you struck down the enemies throughout the days and nights. ॥ 3 ॥**

->॥ Now the fourth verse ॥<-

**And when, for the sake of the oppressed and for Kutsa as he fought, you, O Indra, stole the wheel of the Sun. ॥ 4 ॥**

---

## Commentary (Sayana)

**No one | Indra | Than you | Superior | Not | Greater | Is | Slayer of Vritra | No one | Truly | As | You ॥ 1 ॥**

O **Slayer of Vritra** <note>original: *vṛtrahan*; a title for Indra referring to his defeat of the demon of drought, Vritra</note>, O Indra, destroyer of the demon Vritra. In this world, not even one person is **superior** or more excellent **than you**. There is not even one who is **greater** <note>original: *jyāyān*; more praiseworthy or older in status</note> than you. O **Indra**, just as you are famous in the world, there is **truly no one** else like that. The meaning is that no one in the world is equal to Indra.

->॥ Now the second verse ॥<-

**Truly | Your | Following | Peoples | All | Like wheels | They turned | Truly | Great | You are | Famous ॥ 2 ॥**

O **Indra**, the **peoples** <note>original: *kṛṣṭayaḥ*; referring to the five tribes of men or mankind in general</note>, making you their aim, **truly follow** you. Here an example is given: like **all** the **wheels** <note>original: *cakreva*; like the wheels of a cart</note>. Just as wheels follow the movement of a chariot, so do they follow you. O **Indra**, you are **great** and **truly famous** <note>original: *śrutaḥ*; literally 'heard of' or renowned</note> due to your many qualities.

->॥ Now the third verse ॥<-

**All | Even | Indeed | Through this strength | You | Gods | Indra | They fought | When | Days | At night | You struck down ॥ 3 ॥**

O **Indra**, **all** the **gods** who desired to conquer the demons, having obtained **you** as their help and **strength** <note>original: *anā*; interpreted here as 'vital breath' or 'power'</note>, **fought** against the demons. This is **because** you **struck down** the enemies completely during the **days** and **nights**. Therefore, the statement "they fought" is connected to your support.

->॥ Now the fourth verse ॥<-

**When | And | For the oppressed | Wheel | For Kutsa | Fighting | You stole | Indra | The Sun ॥ 4 ॥**

<term>Indra</term> (The King of the Gods, wielder of the thunderbolt); <term>Vritrahan</term> (Slayer of Vritra, the personification of drought); <term>Krishtayah</term> (The farming peoples or tribes of humanity); <term>Kutsa</term> (A favorite sage and warrior of Indra); <term>Surya</term> (The Sun God); <term>Atiratra</term> (An all-night Vedic sacrifice); <term>Maitravarunashastra</term> (A specific recitation by the Maitravaruna priest).

...And in whichever battle, O Indra, for the sake of the oppressed and for Kutsa—who was providing aid—you stole the sun-related wheel from the Sun while he was fighting. The meaning is that you took it away. In that battle, you protected Etasha with your divine powers <note>original: *śacībhiḥ*; refers here to Indra's powerful deeds in war</note>. This connects to the text that follows.

## Hymn Text
**And when you alone fought all the raging adversaries, O Indra, you struck down the attackers. ॥ 5 ॥**

**Word-for-word analysis:**
And when | the gods <note>original: *devān*; here interpreted by the commentator as 'adversaries' or 'demons'</note> | raging | all | you fought | alone | truly | you | Indra | the attackers | killed ॥ 5 ॥

## Commentary (Sayana)
O Indra, you were truly alone, without any assistants. In whichever battle you fought all the **raging** <note>original: *r̥ghāyataḥ*; those who are violent or oppressive</note> beings—namely the Rakshasas <note>demons or malevolent spirits</note> who were oppressing the gods—you alone fought them. Likewise, you **struck down** or destroyed the **attackers** <note>original: *vanūn*; those who seek to injure</note>.

-> ## ॥ Here begins the sixth verse ॥ <-

## Hymn Text
**And when, for the sake of a mortal, you checked the Sun, O Indra, you protected Etasha with your divine powers. ॥ 6 ॥**

**Word-for-word analysis:**
And when | also | for a mortal | [filler] | you checked | Indra | the Sun | [forth] | protected | with divine powers | Etasha ॥ 6 ॥

## Commentary (Sayana)
And in whichever battle, O Indra, you **checked** or hindered the **Sun** for the sake of a **mortal**—the sage named Etasha. (The word *kam* is a poetic filler). At that time, through your **divine powers** <note>original: *śacībhiḥ*; interpreted here as battle-actions</note>, you **protected** the sage named Etasha. You guarded him with great excellence.

## Hymn Text
**Are you not then, O Slayer of Vritra, most wrathful, O Bountiful One? Right here, you struck down the son of Danu. ॥ 7 ॥**

What | then | also | you are | Slayer of Vritra | Bountiful One | most wrathful | here | indeed | the son of Danu | [towards] | struck down ॥ 7 ॥

## Commentary (Sayana)
O **Slayer of Vritra** <note>original: *vr̥trahan*; the one who destroys the darkness that covers the world</note>, O **Bountiful One** <note>original: *maghavan*; the lord of wealth</note>, O Indra! Immediately after that, are you not **most wrathful**? (The word *kim* indicates a question). You become exceedingly angry. **Right here** in this mid-air, you **struck down** <note>original: *ātiraḥ*; harmed or destroyed from all sides</note> **the son of Danu** <note>original: *danum*; referring to Vritra, the son of the goddess Danu</note>.

## Hymn Text
