<header>|| Mandala 4, Hymn 35, Verse 35 || Third Ashtaka || 177</header>

"O **Ribhus**, you **made the vessel fourfold** <note>original: camasaṃ caturdhā vyakṛṇota</note>. You fashioned it so. And having done so, you said, '**O Friend**—meaning Agni, who has become a friend—**favor us and accept this Soma-drink**.' Thus you spoke. Then **that Agni spoke to you** in return. He said: 'O **Vajas and Ribhus, with skillful hands** <note>original: suhastāḥ</note>, you have **traversed the path** to the immortal, deathless heaven.' **What is that immortality?** It is reaching the **host** or assembly of the gods, such as Indra and the others."

->॥ Now the Fourth Verse ॥<-

## Hymn Text
**Of what was this vessel made, which by your wisdom you made into four? Now, O priests, press the libation for joy; O Ribhus, drink of the sweet Soma-juice. ॥ 4 ॥**

**Of what made | Indeed | Vessel | This | Was | Which | By wisdom | Four | Made |**
**Now | Press | Libation | For joy | Drink | O Ribhus | Of the sweet | Soma-related ॥ 4 ॥**

---

## Commentary (Sayana)
**Of what was it made?** What was the nature of **this vessel?** The word **indeed** <note>original: svit</note> here indicates a question. **Which** vessel, originally being one, you **made into four** by your **wisdom**—that is, by the skillful work associated with wise poets <note>original: kāvyena; implying both poetic inspiration and technical mastery</note>. **Now**, at this time, O priests, **press the libation**—the Soma-juice is called 'libation' because it is pressed out—**for joy** and exhilaration. O **Ribhus**, you also **drink** the sweet, pleasant juice **of the Soma**.

---

->॥ Now the Fifth Verse ॥<-

## Hymn Text
**By your skill, you made your parents young again; by your skill, you made the vessel for the gods to drink; by your skill, O Ribhus who possess wealth as jewels, you fashioned the two swift horses that carry Indra. ॥ 5 ॥**

**By skill | Made | Parents | Young | By skill | Made | Vessel | For the gods to drink |**
**By skill | Two horses | Swift | Fashioned | Carrying Indra | O Ribhus | Wealth-jeweled ॥ 5 ॥**

---

## Commentary (Sayana)
O **you who possess wealth as jewels** <note>original: vājaratnāḥ; meaning those who possess lovely Soma-food as their treasure</note>, O **Ribhus**, you **made** your **parents** (mother and father) **young** once more through your **skill** <note>original: śacyā; referring to their divine power or ritual action</note>. Likewise, by your **skill**, you **made the vessel** fit **for the gods to drink**—meaning you divided the single cup into four. You also **fashioned the two horses** <note>original: hari; the golden steeds of Indra</note> through your craft of carving. What kind of **horses**? They are **swift** <note>original: dhanutarā; those who travel quickly</note> and are the **carriers of Indra**.

->॥ Thus ends the fifth Varga of the seventh Adhyaya in the third Ashtaka ॥<-

## Hymn Text
**O Vajas, for that man who presses the sharp Soma-libation for exhilaration at the decline of the days, O Ribhus, you showerers of blessings, being delighted, fashion wealth that includes many heroic sons. ॥ 6 ॥**

**Who | For you | Presses | At the decline | Of days | Sharp | O Vajas | Libation | For exhilaration |**
**For him | Wealth | O Ribhus | Including all heroes | Fashion | O showerers | Being delighted ॥ 6 ॥**

## Commentary (Sayana)
O **Ribhus** and **Vajas**—those who possess food or strength—**for you**, for your sake, **whoever** (the patron of the sacrifice) **at the decline of days** <note>original: abhipitve; interpreted here as the time when the day "falls away" or concludes</note>, meaning at the third Soma-pressing of the day, **presses the sharp**, highly flavorful **libation**—the Soma which is "pressed" <note>the word 'savana' comes from the root 'su', to press</note>—**for exhilaration**, for that man, O **showerers** of blessings <note>original: vṛṣaṇaḥ; literally "bulls," a term for those who rain down rewards</note>, being **delighted** or joyful, **fashion**—meaning provide or create—**wealth** that is **inclusive of all heroes**, which refers to wealth accompanied by many sons and brave progeny.

---

-> ॥ Now the Seventh Verse ॥ <-

## Hymn Text
**O Lord of the bay horses, you drank the morning libation; the midday libation was yours alone. Now drink together with the Ribhus, the givers of riches, whom you, O Indra, made your friends through their skillful work. ॥ 7 ॥**

**In the morning | Pressed | You drank | O Lord of bay horses | Midday | Libation | Exclusively | Yours |**
**Together | With the Ribhus | Drink | Bestowers of jewels | Friends | Whom | Indra | You made | By good work ॥ 7 ॥**

---

## Commentary (Sayana)
O **Lord of the bay horses** <note>original: haryaśva; Indra, who is pulled by two tawny or greenish-gold horses</note>, **in the morning**, at the first pressing, **you drank** the **pressed** Soma. The **midday libation** was **exclusively yours**; it belonged to you alone and no others. Since the first two pressings are assigned separately, the third pressing remains. In this third pressing, **drink together with the Ribhus**, who are the **bestowers of jewels** or delightful gifts. O **Indra**, these are the Ribhus **whom you made** your **friends** because of their **skillful work**—their beautiful and holy deeds.

---

-> ॥ Now the Eighth Verse ॥ <-

## Hymn Text
**You who became gods through your good work and sit in heaven like eagles, bestow upon us riches, O sons of strength; O sons of Sudhanvan, you have become immortal. ॥ 8 ॥**

**They | Riches | Bestow | Of strength | O sons | O sons of Sudhanvan | Became | Immortals ॥ 8 ॥**

## Commentary (Sayana)
O **Ribhus, you who became gods** through your **good work**—your beautiful, sacrificial deeds. **Like eagles**—meaning those with praiseworthy movement or like specific birds of prey—you **sat** or took your place **upon the heavens**, the celestial realm. O...

<header>Mandala 4. Sukta 4. Verse 36.] || The Third Ashtaka || Page 119</header>

O grandsons of strength, you who are powerful, grant us wealth and jewels. Bestow it upon us! O sons of Sudhanvan <note>The Ribhus are often called 'Saudhanvana' after their father, Sudhanvan</note>, you have become immortal gods.

---

## Hymn Text (RV 4.36.9)

-> ॥ Now the Ninth Verse ॥ <-

**Since you made the third libation a bestower of jewels through your skillful work and clever hands, O Ribhus, now drink this poured-out Soma together with all your exhilarating senses. ॥ 9 ॥**

**Pada-patha (Word-by-word):**
**Since | Third | Libation | Bestowing jewels | You made | Through good work | Skillful-handed |**
**That | O Ribhus | Poured out | For you | This | Together | With exhilarating | Senses | Drink ॥ 9 ॥**

## Commentary (Sayana)

O **skillful-handed** <note>original: suhastāḥ; having beautiful or capable hands</note> Ribhus, because you **made**—meaning you perfectly accomplished—**the third libation** <note>the evening Soma offering</note> to be a **bestower of jewels** <note>original: ratnadheyam; similar to the giving of delightful Soma</note> through your **desire for good work** <note>original: svapasyā</note>, therefore, **drink** this **poured-out** Soma-juice belonging to **you**. Drink it **together** with your **exhilarating senses**. <note>Sayana notes: although the mouth is the primary instrument for drinking, the eyes and ears are also said to "drink" figuratively because they find satisfaction in seeing and hearing the ritual.</note>

-> ॥ This concludes the sixth section (Varga) of the seventh chapter (Adhyaya) of the third book (Ashtaka) ॥ <-

---

## Hymn Text (RV 4.37.1)

The fourth hymn, beginning with **"Born horseless,"** consists of nine verses and is dedicated to the Ribhus. The Seer <note>Rishi</note> is Vamadeva. According to the general rules of poetic meter, the final verse is in the *Trishtubh* meter (11 syllables per line), while the remaining verses are in the *Jagati* meter (12 syllables per line). The **Index of Hymns** <note>original: Anukramanika</note> confirms: "The hymn 'Born horseless' ends in a Trishtubh." In the *Abhijit* sacrifice, on the third day, this hymn to the Ribhus is recited during the ritual for All-Gods <note>original: Vaishvadeva-shastra</note>. This is indicated in the ritual manuals: "The Vaishvadeva hymn begins with 'Born horseless from afar'" (Ashvalayana Shrauta Sutra 9.7).

-> ॥ Now the First Verse ॥ <-

**Born horseless, without reins, the praiseworthy three-wheeled chariot rolls across the atmosphere. This is the great proclamation of your divine power, O Ribhus, that you nourish both heaven and earth. ॥ 1 ॥**

**Pada-patha (Word-by-word):**
**Horseless | Born | Without reins | Praiseworthy | Chariot | Three-wheeled | Around | Turns | Atmosphere |**
**Great | That | Your | Divine | Proclamation | Heaven | O Ribhus | Earth | Which | And | You nourish ॥ 1 ॥**

## Commentary (Sayana)

O **Ribhus**, the **chariot** belonging to the Ashvins, which was crafted by you, has **become**—or was created—**horseless**, meaning it functions without needing horses to pull it. Similarly, it is **without reins** <note>original: anabhīśuḥ; lacking the leather straps for control</note>, yet it is **praiseworthy** and possesses **three wheels**. In this state, it **rolls across** or wanders through the **atmosphere** <note>original: rajaḥ</note>. This act of creating such a chariot is **your great proclamation**—a magnificent declaration of **your divine** skill and power. Furthermore, it is a great deed **that you nourish** or support both **heaven and earth**.

<term>Ribhus (ऋभवः)</term>: A group of three brothers (Ribhu, Vibhvan, and Vaja) who were human artisans but attained divinity through their miraculous skills, such as making a chariot for the Ashvins and dividing one sacrificial cup into four.

<term>Third Libation (तृतीय सवन)</term>: The Soma sacrifice is divided into three sessions (morning, midday, and evening). The Ribhus are specifically invited to the third, evening session.

<summary>This page concludes the 36th hymn and begins the 37th hymn of the Rig Veda's fourth Mandala. It highlights the divine craftsmanship of the Ribhus, specifically their creation of a miraculous, horseless, three-wheeled chariot that traverses the sky.</summary>

<header>|| Rig Veda || [Book 3, Chapter 7, Section 7]</header>

...the proclamation of your divine nature. And by that work through which you nourish <note>original: puṣyatha; to make strong or flourishing</note> both the heavens and the earth.

-> ॥ Now the Second Verse ॥ <-

## Hymn Text
**The chariot which you, the wise ones, fashioned—smooth-rolling and unswerving—using only the meditation of your minds; O Vajas and Ribhus, we now invite you to the drinking of this sacred libation. ॥ 2 ॥**

---

**Pada-patha (Word-by-word):**
**Chariot | which | they made | well-rolling | wise-minded | unswerving | mind | from/over | by meditation |**
**them | (particle) | now | this | of libation | for drinking | (towards) | you | O Vajas | O Ribhus | we make known (invite) ॥ 2 ॥**

## Commentary (Sayana)
The **wise-minded** <note>original: sucetasaḥ; those with beautiful or clear consciousness</note> **Ribhus** made a **well-rolling** chariot—one with smooth-turning wheels—that was **unswerving** <note>original: avihvarantam; literally "not crooked" or steady</note>. They **made** this **quickly** <note>original: nu</note> through the **meditation of the mind** alone, without physical effort. **Them**—the word "u" here is used for emphasis—to **them**, O **Vajas** and **Ribhus**, we **make known** <note>original: vedayāmasi; we invite or announce</note> that you are called to **you** for the **drinking of this libation** <note>original: savanasya pītaye</note>, this Soma juice.

-> ॥ Now the Third Verse ॥ <-

## Hymn Text
**That greatness of yours, O Vajas and Ribhus, became a celebrated wonder among the gods; for you took your parents, who were aged and worn out by time, and fashioned them into youth once more so they might walk freely. ॥ 3 ॥**

---

**Pada-patha (Word-by-word):**
**That | your | O Vajas | O Ribhus | well-proclaimed | among gods | O Vibhus | became | greatness |**
**Aged | (particle) | being | parents | old-worn | again | young | for walking | you fashioned ॥ 3 ॥**

## Commentary (Sayana)
O **Vajas**, **Ribhus**, and **Vibhus** <note>The Ribhus are three brothers: Ribhu, Vibhu, and Vaja; the plural address covers them all</note>, **that greatness** <note>original: mahitvanam</note> of **yours** **became** something **well-proclaimed** <note>original: supravācanam; worth speaking of highly</note> **among the gods**. What was that deed? He explains: Your **parents**, though they were **aged** and **worn out by time** <note>original: sanājurā; decayed by old age</note>, **you fashioned** <note>original: takṣatha; crafted or remodeled</note> into being **young again** for the purpose of **walking** <note>original: carathāya; to move about at will</note> as they pleased.

-> ॥ Now the Fourth Verse ॥ <-

## Hymn Text
**You made the one cup into four; you brought forth the cow from the hide through your sacred acts. Then you attained immortality among the gods; O Vajas and Ribhus, that work of yours is worthy of praise. ॥ 4 ॥**

**Pada-patha (Word-by-word):**
**One | (divided) | made | cup | fourfold | (out of) | from skin | cow | you brought forth | by prayers/acts |**
**Then | among gods | immortality | attained | quickly | O Vajas | O Ribhus | that | your | worthy of praise ॥ 4 ॥**

<header>Mandala 4, Adhyaya 4, Sukta 36. || The Third Ashtaka || 181</header>

## Commentary (Sayana)
[Continuation from the previous page for Rig Veda 4.36.4]

O **Ribhus** <note>The Ribhus are three brothers—Ribhu, Vibhu, and Vaja—who were mortal artisans but became gods through their skill.</note>, you made the one vessel—which was a single means of drinking—into four parts <note>original: catuḥ-śākhaṃ; literally "four-branched"</note>. You fashioned it into a four-fold object. Likewise, through your sacred works and deeds, you fashioned <note>original: nirariṇīta; prepared or refined</note> a new cow from a hide. Because of these deeds, you attained immortality among the gods. O **Vajas**, O **Ribhus**, that work of yours is celebrated. The word **śruṇīti** <note>shruniti</note> is a synonym for "quick"; thus, your work is primarily and quickly praiseworthy.

---
->॥ Now the Fifth Verse ॥<-

## Hymn Text
**May that wealth, which brings the highest fame, come from the Ribhus—that wealth which the leaders, famous for their strength, brought into being. Fashioned by the Vibhus, it is highly praised in the sacrifices; O shining gods, whatever you protect becomes all-seeing. ॥ 5 ॥**

### Pada-patha (Word-by-word)
**From the Ribhus | wealth | bringing the highest fame | famous for strength | which | they generated | the leaders |**
**fashioned by the Vibhus | in the sacrifices | highly praiseworthy | which | O gods | you protect | he | all-seeing ॥ 5 ॥**

## Commentary (Sayana)
**From the Ribhus** <note>original: ṛbhutaḥ</note>, may there be **wealth** <note>original: rayiḥ</note> for us, which possesses the **highest fame** <note>original: prathama-śravas-tamaḥ; literally "first among those heard of," meaning primary food or reputation</note>. The **leaders**, the Ribhus who are **famous for their strength** <note>original: vāja-śrutāso; vāja can mean both "strength" and "food"</note>, are the ones who **generated** or produced this wealth. **Fashioned by the Vibhus** <note>Vibhu is one of the three Ribhu brothers</note>, refers to the sacrificial cup or the chariot of the Ashvins that was crafted with skill; this object is **highly praiseworthy** during the **sacrifices** <note>original: vidatheṣu; assemblies or sacrificial rituals</note>. O **shining gods** <note>original: devāso</note>, whichever chariot or cup you **protect**, that object becomes **all-seeing** <note>original: vicarsaniḥ</note>, meaning it observes various things or is worthy of being seen by all.

---
->॥ Thus ends the seventh section (varga) of the seventh chapter (adhyaya) in the third book (ashtaka) ॥<-

**He becomes energetic and swift; he is a seer through his inspired speech; he is a valiant hero, a striker of enemies in battles, difficult to overcome. He holds the nourishment of wealth and great vigor—he whom Vaja, Vibhvan, and the Ribhus have favored. ॥ 6 ॥**

He is a **seer** <note>original: ṛṣiḥ; one who knows that which is beyond the senses</note> and is endowed with **inspired speech** or praise. He is a **hero**, meaning he is valiant and is a **striker** or destroyer of his enemies. He himself is **difficult to overcome** in **battles**. He **holds** or possesses the **nourishment of wealth** and **great vigor** <note>original: suvīryam; the quality of having good sons or heroic strength</note>. That man whom **Vaja**... <note>Text continues to the next page</note>

# Rig Veda 
### [Book 4. Chapter 3. Group 8.]

Vibhu and the **Ribhus** <note>The three brothers: Ribhu, Vibhu, and Vaja</note> have manifested and protected [the sacrifice]; this is how it occurs. The use of the plural in the final part of the previous verse is intended to include all three brothers, as the name "Ribhu" is commonly used to refer to the group as a whole.

---

-> ॥ Now the Seventh Verse ॥ <-

## Hymn Text
A most excellent and beautiful form has been bestowed upon you; O **Vajas**, O **Ribhus**, delight in this hymn of praise. For you are steady, wise, and learned sages; we make ourselves known to you through this sacred prayer. ॥ 7 ॥

**Word-by-word Breakdown:**
Most excellent | your | form | upon | bestowed | beautiful | hymn | O Vajas | O Ribhus | that | delight in |
Steady | for | you are | poets/sages | learned | those | you | with this | sacred prayer | [we] make known ॥ 7 ॥

---

## Commentary (Sayana)
A most excellent, and therefore highly **beautiful** <note>original: darśatam; "worthy of being seen"</note>, **form** <note>original: peśo; shape or appearance</note> has been bestowed upon you. Therefore, O **Vajas** and **Ribhus**, delight in this **hymn of praise** <note>original: stomaḥ</note> which has been prepared by us. That is, accept it. You who are **steady** <note>original: dhīrāso; wise or firm-minded</note>, famous **poets** <note>original: kavayo; seers or inspired thinkers</note>, and **learned** <note>original: vipaścitaḥ; those who know the inspired word</note>—we make ourselves known to you through **this sacred prayer** <note>original: enā brahmaṇā</note> in the form of a recitation. Alternatively, the meaning is: those whom the learned praisers (as described) laud, those [gods] we announce and make known through this prayer.

---

-> ॥ Now the Eighth Verse ॥ <-

## Hymn Text
You, who are all-knowing, grant us all human enjoyments from these prayers; O **Ribhus**, fashion for us a bright strength and the highest wealth that overcomes the power of the mighty, and grant us food. ॥ 8 ॥

**Word-by-word Breakdown:**
You | for us | from the prayers | from | knowing | all | human | enjoyments |
Bright | strength | overcoming the mighty | highest | [towards] | us | wealth | O Ribhus | fashion | [towards] | food/life-force ॥ 8 ॥

---

## Commentary (Sayana)
O **Ribhus**, you, for our sake, through these **prayers** <note>original: dhiṣaṇābhyaḥ; here interpreted as "praises" or "intelligences"</note> which act as the cause—<note>The word "pari" here acts as a marker for the fifth case (ablative).</note>—or perhaps, knowing all **human enjoyments** <note>original: naryāṇi bhojanāni</note> that are even greater than our own thoughts, provide them to us. Furthermore, O **Ribhus**, fashion for us **bright** <note>original: dyumantam; shining, perhaps referring to gold</note> and **powerful strength** <note>original: vājam</note>, and **wealth** <note>original: rayim</note> that is the best and capable of drying up <note>original: śoṣakam</note> even the strongest enemies, along with **food** <note>original: vayaḥ</note>.

---

-> ॥ Now the Ninth Verse ॥ <-

## Hymn Text
Granting us here progeny and here wealth, fashion for us here fame accompanied by heroes; O **Ribhus**, give us that wonderful strength by which we may surpass all others. ॥ 9 ॥

## Hymn Text

> Here | offspring | here | wealth | bestowing | here | a horse <note>original: arvaḥ; often used here to signify "speed" or "fame"</note> | with heroes | fashion | for us |
> By which | we | may be distinguished | beyond | others | that | strength | wonderful | O Ribhus | give | to us ॥ 9 ॥

## Commentary (Sayana)

O **Ribhus**, bestowing your favor upon us at this sacrifice, fashion <note>original: takṣata; "carve" or "create," reflecting their status as artisans</note> offspring for us in the form of sons and grandsons. Accomplish this. Right here at this sacrifice, fashion wealth. Also, right here at this sacrifice, fashion fame <note>original: arvaḥ</note> accompanied by heroes <note>original: vīravat</note>, meaning sons and servants. Furthermore, O **Ribhus**, give us that wonderful and desirable strength <note>original: vājam; also means food or plenty</note> by which we may be distinguished and known as superior to others who are our equals. Give it to us.

-> **॥ Thus ends the eighth group of the seventh chapter of the third book ॥** <-

## Hymn Text (Sukta 37)

**The fifth hymn of this section, beginning with "Come to us, O Vajas," consists of eight verses. It is seen by the Rishi Vamadeva and addressed to the Ribhus. The meter is Trishtubh <note>a meter of 44 syllables</note>. However, the last four verses—starting from the fifth—are in the Anushtubh meter <note>a meter of 32 syllables</note>. This is confirmed by the Index of Verses: "Come to us consists of eight verses, with four being Anushtubh." In the ritual of the "Divided Ten-Nights" <note>original: Vyūḍha Daśarātra</note>, on the sixth day, during the recitation for the All-Gods <note>original: Vaiśvadeva-śastra</note>, the first four verses are to be recited. This is indicated in the ritual manuals: "Come to us, O Vajas, the thirteen verses for the Ribhus and these four" (Ashvalayana Shrauta Sutra 8.8).**

-> **॥ Here is the first verse ॥** <-

Come to us, O **Vajas**, to the sacrifice, O **Ribhukshas** <note>the eldest of the three Ribhus</note>; O Gods, come by the paths traveled by the gods. Just as you sustain the sacrifice among these human subjects of **Manu** <note>the ancestral father of humanity</note> on the auspicious days of the calendar, O delightful ones, [come to us]. ॥ 1 ॥

> Come | to us | O Vajas | to the sacrifice | O Ribhukshas | Gods | come | by paths | traveled by the gods |
> Just as | the sacrifice | of Manu | among subjects | these | you sustain | O delightful ones | on auspicious days | of the days ॥ 1 ॥

---

## Commentary (Sayana)

O **Vajas**, O **Ribhukshas**, O **Ribhus**, O Gods, come to our **sacrifice** <note>original: adhvaram</note>. Approach. Come by the paths that are to be traveled by the gods. Just as you, O delightful **Ribhus**, sustain our sacrifice during the auspicious days of the year among these subjects belonging to **Manu**—that is, among the sacrificing people—in the same way that you come and create auspiciousness, please come to our sacrifice.

---

## Hymn Text

-> **॥ Now the second verse ॥** <-

May these sacrifices be for your heart and mind; today, may the offerings, adorned with clarified butter, reach you. The pressed [Soma juices], full and invigorating, are offered to you; once drunk, may they gladden you for the sake of wisdom and skill. ॥ 2 ॥

> These | for you | for the heart | for the mind | may they be | sacrifices | pleasing | today | adorned with butter | they have gone |
> Forth | for you | pressed [juices] | invigorating | full | for wisdom | for skill | may they gladden | [once] drunk ॥ 2 ॥

<meta>This page continues the commentary on the hymns dedicated to the Ribhus (divine artisans) in the third book of the Rig Veda. It concludes the explanation of the previous verse regarding the Soma offering and provides the text and commentary for verses 3 and 4 of the 60th Sukta.</meta>

# 184 || Rig Veda || [Book 3, Chapter 3, Section 9]

Today, on this day of sacrifice, let these very sacrifices—which are the means of performing the rite—and the Soma juices be for your heart <note>original: hṛde</note>, meaning for the satisfaction of your heart and mind. Let them be so. Today, on this day, may the sufficient Soma juices, which have a brilliant form because they are mixed with clarifying substances <note>original: ghṛta-nirṇijaḥ; literally 'clothed in ghee'</note>, go forth. May they reach your heart. The pressed Soma juices, filling the bowls, are offered for your sake. Alternatively, this may be a form of the root *harya*, meaning "to desire"; they intensely desire you. For the sake of the ritual season <note>original: ṛta</note>, for the sake of the holy work, and for your skillful energy <note>original: dakṣāya</note>, may these drinks gladden you. May they make you rejoice.

---

## Hymn Text

-> ॥ Now the third verse ॥ <-

Just as the sacrificial food, which is appointed by the gods and travels to the three daily libations, is offered to you, so the hymn of praise is given to you, O **Vajas**, O **Ribhukshanas** <note>The three Ribhu brothers are Ribhu, Vibhu, and Vaja; 'Ribhukshanas' is a title for the eldest or the group</note>. I offer the Soma to you among the people who reside near the place of worship, just as the ancestral priest **Manu** did, in the presence of the gods of great light ॥ 3 ॥

**अ॒दा॒यम् । दे॒वऽहि॑तम् । यथ॑ । व॒: । स्तोम॑: । वाजा॒: । ऋ॒भु॒क्ष॒ण॒: । द॒दे । व॒: ।**
**जु॒ह्वे । म॒नु॒ष्वत् । उ॒प॑रासु । वि॒क्षु । यु॒ष्मे इति॑ । सचा॑ । बृ॒हत्ऽदि॑वेषु । सोम॑म् ॥ 3 ॥**

-> ॥ Now the fourth verse ॥ <-

May you be possessors of sturdy horses and shining chariots; be those with metal helmets <note>original: ayaḥ-śiprāḥ; 'shipra' can mean jaws or the visor of a helmet</note>, O energetic ones, wearing beautiful neck-ornaments. O sons of **Indra**, O grandsons of strength, let this sacrificial food be known among the gods for your delight ॥ 4 ॥

**पी॒वः॑ऽअश्वा॒: । शुच॑त्ऽरथाः । हि । भू॒त । अय॑:ऽशिप्र॒ा: । वाजि॑नः । सु॒ऽनिष्का॑: ।**
**इन्द्र॑स्य । सू॒नो इति॑ । शव॑सः । न॒पा॒तः॒ । अनु॑ । व॒: । चे॒ति॒ । अ॒मिय॑म् । मदा॑य ॥ 4 ॥**

---

## Commentary (Sayana)

Regarding the word *adāyam*: it refers to the sacrificial food called **Soma** which goes to the three daily libations <note>original: savana-traya</note>. It is "appointed by the gods" <note>original: deva-hitam</note>, meaning it is beneficial to the gods or ordained by them. This refers specifically to the offering at the third libation. Just as that food supports you, O **Vajas**, O **Ribhukshanas**, and just as the hymn of praise <note>original: stomaḥ</note> supports you among the *uparāsu*—meaning those people <note>original: vikṣu</note> who delight in staying near the place of sacrifice—so do I. Among the gods of great light <note>original: bṛhad-diveṣu</note>, I offer <note>original: juhve</note> the Soma for your sake, together with the other offerings, just as the ancient sacrificer **Manu** did <note>original: manuṣvat</note>.

O energetic **Ribhus**, be "owners of fat horses" <note>original: pīvo-aśvāḥ</note>, meaning those whose horses are well-fed and strong. Likewise, be "owners of shining chariots" and "metal-jawed" <note>original: ayaḥ-śiprāḥ</note>. The word *śipra* refers to either the jaws or the nose; thus, they have jaws or helmets as strong as metal. Be "well-ornamented" <note>original: suniṣkāḥ</note>, possessing beautiful wealth or golden neck-rings. O sons of **Indra**—meaning you are to be protected by him like sons—and O grandsons of strength <note>original: śavaso napātaḥ</note>, meaning powerful ones, let this sacrificial food <note>original: amiyam</note> belonging to the third libation be known and recognized among the gods for your intoxication and delight.

-> ॥ Now the fifth verse ॥ <-

## Hymn Text
O Ribhukshanas <note>original: ṛbhukṣaṇaḥ; a title for the Ribhus, the celestial artisans</note>, we invoke the shining wealth that brings power in battle—the most vigorous companion, possessed of Indra’s strength, the greatest of givers, and accompanied by horses ॥ 5 ॥

**Pada-patha:**
**ऋभुम् । ऋ॒भुक्ष॑णः । र॒यिम् । वाजे॑ । वा॒जिन्ऽत॑मम् । यु॒जम् । इन्द्र॑ऽस्वन्तम् । ह॒वा॒म॒हे॒ । सदा॑ऽसा॒तम॑म् । अ॒श्विन॑म् ॥ ५ ॥**

---

## Commentary (Sayana)
O **Ribhukshanas** <note>the elder Ribhu brothers</note>, I invoke your group. I call upon the **shining wealth** <note>original: ṛbhum rayim</note>, which takes the form of riches. Because you are the cause of such wealth, you are addressed by that name. I call for that which is **most powerful** <note>original: vājintamam</note> in **battle** <note>original: vāje</note>, a **companion** <note>original: yujam</note> joined to one another, **possessing Indra’s strength** <note>original: indrasvantaṃ</note>—meaning possessing great power or associated with Indra—the **best of givers** <note>original: sadāsātamam</note> at all times, and **provided with horses** <note>original: aśvinam</note>. I **invoke** <note>original: havāmahe</note> you all ॥

-> ॥ Thus ends the ninth section (varga) of the seventh chapter of the third book ॥ <-

-> ॥ Now the sixth verse ॥ <-

## Hymn Text
O Ribhus, that mortal whom you and Indra protect, he indeed shall prevail. Through his sacred thoughts and prayers, he shall be a winner at the sacrifice, and he shall be foremost with his swift horse ॥ 6 ॥

**Pada-patha:**
**सः । इत् । ऋ॒भवः॑ । यम् । अव॑थ । यू॒यम् । इन्द्रः॑ । च॒ । मर्त्य॑म् । सः । धी॒भिः । अ॒स्तु । स॒नि॒ता । मेध॑ऽसाता । सः । अर्व॑ता ॥ ६ ॥**

---

## Commentary (Sayana)
O **Ribhus**, that **mortal whom you and Indra protect** <note>original: avatha</note>, **he indeed** <note>original: sa it</note> shall be the one. The meaning is that no one else can be superior to him. He alone shall be the **winner** <note>original: sanitā</note> or possessor through **sacred prayers** <note>original: dhībhiḥ</note>. In the **battle for wisdom or sacrifice** <note>original: medhasātā</note>, let him alone be joined **with a horse** <note>original: arvatā</note> that is swift ॥

-> ॥ Now the seventh verse ॥ <-

## Hymn Text
O Vajas, O Ribhukshanas, clearly show us the paths for the sake of the sacrifice. O wise ones, having been praised, may you enable us to cross over all the regions of the earth ॥ 7 ॥

**Pada-patha:**
**वि । नः॒ । वाजाः॑ । ऋ॒भुक्ष॑णः । प॒थः । चि॒त॒न॒ । यष्ट॑वे । अ॒स्मभ्य॑म् । सू॒र॒यः॒ । स्तु॒ताः । विश्वाः॑ । आ॒शाः । त॒री॒षणि॑ ॥ ७ ॥**

---

## Commentary (Sayana)
O **Vajas**, O **Ribhukshanas** <note>names of the Ribhu brothers used as vocatives</note>, **clearly reveal** <note>original: vi-citana</note> for **us** <note>original: naḥ</note> the **paths** <note>original: pathaḥ</note> of the sacrifice so that we may **perform the ritual** <note>original: yaṣṭave</note>. O **wise ones** <note>original: sūrayaḥ; meaning the gods or the patrons</note>, being **praised** by us...

<margin>
VOL. III. 3 B
</margin>

<note>The vocabulary below defines the key terms used in the verses above.</note>
- **Ribhu** <term>ṛbhu</term>: A class of deities who were originally humans but became divine celestial artisans.
- **Ribhukshanas** <term>ṛbhukṣaṇaḥ</term>: An epithet for the Ribhus or Indra; literally, the "lords of the Ribhus."
- **Wealth** <term>rayim</term>: Refers to both material treasure and spiritual abundance.
- **Most powerful** <term>vājintamam</term>: Extremely vigorous or strong, especially in a competitive or martial context.
- **Winner** <term>sanita</term>: One who gains, wins, or bestows rewards.
- **In the sacrifice** <term>medhasāta</term>: Literally "in the acquisition of wisdom," often used to refer to the performance of a sacrifice or a spiritual battle.
- **To sacrifice** <term>yaṣṭave</term>: The ritual act of worship or offering.
- **Wise men** <term>sūrayaḥ</term>: Refers to the enlightened patrons of the ritual or the gods themselves.

The commentary by Sayana explains the attributes of the Ribhus as bestowers of strength and success in worship.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the commentary on the 37th hymn of the 4th book of the Rig Veda, concluding the praises for the Ribhus, and begins the 38th hymn dedicated to Dadhikra, the divine horse. It transitions from the 10th to the 11th section (varga) of the 7th chapter (adhyaya) in the 3rd volume (ashtaka).</meta>

१८४ ॥ Rig Veda ॥ [A. 3. A. 7. V. 11.

...perceive. Make us perceive. The meaning is: make us wise. O wise patrons <note>original: sūrayaḥ</note>, being praised by us, grant us the ability to cross <note>original: tarīṣaṇi</note> through all regions <note>original: viśvā āśāḥ</note>—that is, all directions. The word "grant" is to be supplied to complete the sense ॥

---

## Hymn Text

-> ॥ Now the eighth verse ॥ <-

**O Vajas, O Ribhukshanas <note>titles for the Ribhus</note>, O Indra, and O Nasatyas <note>the twin Ashvins</note>! Proclaim for us that abundant wealth, along with horses, for the sake of the people, and for the giving of riches ॥ 8 ॥**

**Pada-patha:**
**तं । नः॒ । वाजाः॒ । ऋ॒भु॒क्ष॒णः॒ । इन्द्र॑ । नास॑त्या । र॒यिम् ।**
**सं । अश्व॑म् । च॒र्ष॒णिऽभ्यः॑ । आ । पु॒रु । शस्त॑ । म॒घत्त॑ये ॥ ८ ॥**

## Commentary (Sayana)

Concluding the praise with this verse, the poet prays for his desired goal. O **Vajas**, O **Ribhukshanas** <note>the Ribhus</note>, O **Indra**, O **Nasatyas** <note>the Ashvins</note>—all of you, for us, for the **people** <note>original: carṣaṇibhyaḥ; meaning the humans who are praising</note>, proclaim that **abundant** <note>original: puru</note> **wealth** <note>original: rayim</note>, and abundant **horses** <note>original: aśvam</note>, for the **giving of riches** <note>original: maghattaye</note>. Make a complete proclamation of this bestowal ॥

-> ॥ Thus ends the tenth section (varga) of the seventh chapter of the third book ॥ <-

---

The sixth hymn of this section, beginning with "Uto hi vam," consists of ten verses. The Seer <note>original: rishi; the inspired poet-sage</note> is Vamadeva. The meter is **Trishtubh** <note>a Vedic meter of 11 syllables per line</note>. The deity is **Dadhikra** <note>the divine horse, a personification of the morning sun or royal power</note>. The first verse is addressed to **Heaven and Earth**. Regarding this, the Index <note>original: Anukramanika</note> states: "*Uto hi* consists of ten verses for Dadhikra, with Heaven and Earth as the deities of the first." Its ritual application is determined by the characteristics of the deities mentioned in the verses ॥

---

## Hymn Text

-> ॥ Therein, the first verse ॥ <-

**And indeed, your ancient gifts exist, which Trasadasyu <note>a famous king of the Puru tribe</note> bestowed upon the Purus in their time of distress. You two gave the winner of fields, the winner of fertile lands, a slayer for the Dasyus <note>enemies of the Vedic people</note>, a fierce subduer ॥ 1 ॥**

**Pada-patha:**
**उ॒तो इति॑ । हि । वाम् । दा॒त्रा । संति॑ । पू॒र्वा । या । पू॒रुऽभ्यः॑ । त्र॒स॒दस्युः॑ । नि॒ऽतो॒शे ।**
**क्षेत्र॑ऽसाम् । द॒दथुः॑ । उ॒र्व॒राऽसाम् । घ॒नम् । दस्यु॑ऽभ्यः । अ॒भिऽभू॑तिम् । उ॒ग्रम् ॥ १ ॥**

## Commentary (Sayana)

The word **Uto** is a filler used for the meter. Although Heaven and Earth are not explicitly named in this verse, they are the ones to be addressed. O Heaven and Earth, from you two, there are **ancient** <note>original: pūrvā; meaning old or filling</note> **gifts** <note>original: dātrā; acts of giving</note> that were obtained by **Trasadasyu**, the son of Purukutsa. These are the riches which King Trasadasyu **bestowed** <note>original: nitośe; gave or poured out</note> upon the **Purus** <note>the seekers or the human tribe</note>. You gave him a **winner of fields** <note>original: kṣetrasām; a horse that conquers all lands</note>. Likewise, you gave him a **winner of fertile land** <note>original: urvarāsām; a son who wins land rich in crops</note>.

<summary>This page concludes the 37th hymn with a prayer for wealth and horses from the Ribhus and Indra, and begins the 38th hymn celebrating the divine horse Dadhikra and the legendary generosity of King Trasadasyu.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the commentary of Sayana on the 38th hymn of the 4th Mandala of the Rig Veda, which is dedicated to Dadhikra, the divine horse. The previous page concluded the 37th hymn (to the Ribhus) and began the first verse of the 38th hymn.</meta>

# Mandala 4. Section 4. Hymn 38. ] || Third Volume || 177

...and you two gave a dense <note>original: ghanam</note> weapon for the sake of slaying the Dasyus <note>original: dasyubhyo; the enemies or outsiders</note>. What kind of weapon? One that overcomes <note>original: abhibhūtim</note>, an overcomer, possessing uplifted strength. Alternatively, the latter half of the verse is a single sentence: You two gave wealth as described and a son. You two are the givers. The meaning is: may you two give those same things to me as well ॥

-> || Now the second verse || <-

## Hymn Text
**And you two gave the swift one <note>original: vājinam</note>, the repeller of many, Dadhikra, who watches over all people; the straight-going hawk, the radiant-bodied, the rapid, who is to be celebrated like a hero, like a king <note>original: nṛpatim</note> who leads men ॥ 2 ॥**

### Pada-patha
**And । the swift । the-repeller-of-many । Dadhikra । indeed । you-two-gave । watcher-over-all-people ।**
**straight-going । the hawk । the-radiant-bodied । the rapid । the-one-to-be-celebrated । of the foe । the-leader-of-men । like । the hero ॥ 2 ॥**

---

## Commentary (Sayana)
**And** <note>original: utāpi</note> also you gave the **swift one**, meaning the one possessing speed. Or, the god in the form of a horse, for Dadhikra is the name of Agni <note>the fire god</note> in the form of a horse. This horse-form of Agni is recorded in the Brahmana <note>ritual text</note>: "That Agni, having become a horse, rushed forth." **The repeller of many** means the one who holds back many enemies. **Dadhikra** is so called because he carries food <note>original: dadhadannam</note> and moves <note>original: krāmati</note>. To that god of this name—the word **u** is a particle for filling the meter—who is the **watcher over all people**, meaning all the people to be protected or the humans who are his servants are his. **Straight-going** <note>original: ṛjipyam</note> means he who attains or moves in a straight line. To him, the **hawk**, meaning one with a praiseworthy gait; the **radiant-bodied** <note>original: muṣitapsuṃ</note>, meaning one of shining form; the **rapid**, meaning pervasive and quick-moving; and who is **to be celebrated** <note>original: carkṛtyam</note> repeatedly by the foe; who is like a **hero**, like a **king** <note>original: nṛpatim</note> who rules men—to such a god, Heaven and Earth <note>original: dyāvāpṛthivyau</note> gave [him] or support [him] ॥

---

-> || Now the third verse || <-

## Hymn Text
**Whom all people celebrate <note>original: madati</note> with joy as he rushes like [water] down a slope; [the horse] who is eager with his feet like a hero seeking glory <note>original: medhayuṃ</note>, speeding like a chariot, rushing like the wind ॥ 3 ॥**

### Pada-patha
**Whom । everywhere । after । as-if-down-a-slope । rushing । every । person । celebrates । rejoicing ॥**
**with-feet । eager । glory-seeking । like । the hero । chariot-speeding । the-wind-like । rushing ॥ 3 ॥**

---

## Commentary (Sayana)
**Whom**, that is Dadhikra, **every person** <note>original: viśvaḥ pūruḥ</note>, every human being, **rejoicing** or making others rejoice, **celebrates** or praises. The connection is: Heaven and Earth gave that god. That god is further described: **everywhere** <note>original: sīm</note>, following **as if down a slope**, moving like water rushing down a steep path; **with his feet** <note>original: padbhiḥ</note>, meaning with his hooves, **eager** to cross over the directions. An illustration is given: **like a hero seeking glory** <note>original: medhayuṃ na śūram</note>, like a warrior desiring battle. Alternatively, like one desiring the sequence of a sacrifice <note>original: medha</note>, such as wealth. **Chariot-speeding**, meaning one who goes by chariot, **rushing like the wind**...

<summary>This page contains the commentary on Rig Veda 4.38.2-3, praising the divine horse Dadhikra. He is described as a swift, hawk-like manifestation of Agni, granted by Heaven and Earth to protect people and defeat enemies.</summary>
<keywords>Dadhikra, Agni, divine horse, Sayana, Vamadeva, Dasyu, king, hawk, wind metaphor</keywords>

<meta>This page continues the commentary of Sayana on the 38th hymn of the 4th Mandala of the Rig Veda, dedicated to Dadhikra, the divine horse. The previous page (197) was discussing Verse 3, describing how Dadhikra is praised by all people, comparing him to the wind or the elements.</meta>

...like the swift-moving wind <note>original: vāyumiva</note>. The meaning is that just as all people praise the waters and the wind which are characterized by the aforementioned qualities, so they established <note>original: dadhuḥ</note> or praised this god.

---

-> ॥ Now the Fourth Verse ॥ <-

## Hymn Text
Who indeed, seizing the prize <note>original: gadhyā; literally 'that which is to be mixed or grasped,' referring to booty or fame</note> in battles <note>original: samatsu</note>, moves as a great bestower, going among the cattle; manifest in his power, perceiving wisdom <note>original: vidathā</note>, he bypasses distress <note>original: aratim</note> for the sake of the human <note>original: āyoḥ</note> worshiper ॥ 4 ॥

### Pada-patha
Who । indeed । seizing । the-prize । in-battles । the-bestower । moves । among-the-cattle । going ।
manifest-in-power । wisdom-rites । perceiving । beyond । distress । around । the-waters । of-the-human ॥ 4 ॥

## Commentary (Sayana)
**Who indeed** refers to that god who, **seizing the prize** <note>original: gadhyā</note>, meaning the rewards to be mixed or shared. The *Nirukta* <note>an ancient text on etymology</note> defines this as "the act of mixing." He is one who holds back or secures these rewards in **battles** <note>original: samatsu</note>. He is a **bestower** <note>original: sanutaraḥ</note>, one who shares out wealth, and he moves **among the cattle** <note>original: goṣu</note>, meaning either in all directions or for the sake of cattle. He is **manifest in power** <note>original: āvirbhuñjīkaḥ</note>, meaning his means of action are visible, or he is virile. He **perceives** <note>original: nicikyat</note>—a word denoting the act of seeing—and understands the **wisdom-rites** <note>original: vidathā</note> that must be known. He **bypasses** <note>original: paritiraścarati</note> or overcomes **distress** <note>original: aratim</note>, which refers to a lack of joy, sorrow, or an approaching enemy. For whom does he do this? For the **human** <note>original: āyoḥ</note> worshiper or the sacrificer who is diligent in his work.

---

-> ॥ Now the Fifth Verse ॥ <-

## Hymn Text
And indeed, people cry out after him in battles, as if after a thief <note>original: tāyum</note> who has snatched a garment; like a hungry hawk <note>original: śyenam</note> swooping down, he rushes toward glory <note>original: śravaḥ</note> and the cattle-rich herd ॥ 5 ॥

### Pada-patha
And । indeed । him । the-garment-snatcher । like । a-thief । after । they-cry-out । the-people । in-battles ।
downward । moving । the-hungry । like । a-hawk । glory । and । toward । cattle-possessing । and । the-herd ॥ 5 ॥

## Commentary (Sayana)
**And indeed** <note>original: uta sma</note> even him, Dadhikra, in **battles** <note>original: bhareṣu</note>, **people** <note>original: kṣitayaḥ</note> cry out after him **like a thief who snatches a garment** <note>original: vastramathiṃ tāyuṃ na</note>. Just as people shout when they see a thief who has stolen clothes, so do the enemies cry out when they see him. Furthermore, **swooping down** <note>original: nīcā ayamānam</note>, he is **like a hungry hawk** <note>original: jasuriṃ na śyenam</note>. Just as other birds flee when they see a hungry hawk, so do the enemies. He moves **toward** <note>original: accha</note> **glory** <note>original: śravaḥ</note>, which can mean food or fame, **and the cattle-rich herd**. The connection is that they cry out as he rushes toward these things. For the word "garment-snatcher," one should consult the *Nirukta* (4.24) for further etymological detail.

-> ॥ Thus ends the eleventh Varga of the seventh Adhyaya in the third Ashtaka ॥ <-

## Hymn Text

-> ॥ Now the Sixth Verse ॥ <-

And also, rushing foremost among these <note>original: āsu; referring to the battle lines</note>, he moves repeatedly with the ranks of the chariots. Creating a garland <note>original: srajam</note>, like a horse prized by the people <note>original: janyaḥ</note>, beautiful to look upon, licking the dust and biting the bit <note>original: kiraṇam</note> ॥ 6 ॥

**Word-by-word Analysis:**
And | indeed | among-these | foremost | rushing | repeatedly | moves | with-ranks | of-chariots |
A-garland | creating | belonging-to-people | like | beautiful | dust | licking | the-bit | biting ॥ 6 ॥

---

-> ॥ Now the Seventh Verse ॥ <-

And also that powerful one <note>original: vājī</note>, the conqueror, follower of the Law <note>original: ṛtāvā</note>, obedient with his body in the encounter of battle <note>original: samarye</note>. Speeding among the swift-moving hosts, going straight <note>original: ṛjīṣyaḥ</note>, he scatters the dust over his brows, tossing it up ॥ 7 ॥

**Word-by-word Analysis:**
And | that | powerful-one | conqueror | follower-of-truth | desiring-to-obey | with-body | in-battle-encounter |
swiftly | among-those-going | speeding | straight-going | over | the-two-brows | scatters | dust | tossing-up ॥ 7 ॥

-> ॥ Now the Eighth Verse ॥ <-

And also, like the thunder of the sky, his enemies tremble when he charges <note>original: cyutnayataḥ; literally 'shaking' or 'dropping' like rain-clouds</note> at the attackers. When he has fought against a thousand, he becomes difficult to resist <note>original: duvartuḥ</note>, fearsome, moving straight forward ॥ 8 ॥

**Word-by-word Analysis:**
And | indeed | his | thunder-like | of-heaven | charging | the-attackers | tremble |
when | a-thousand | against | towards | he-fought | difficult-to-resist | indeed | he-becomes | fearsome | moving-straight ॥ 8 ॥

---

## Commentary by Sayana

**[Commentary on Verse 6]**
**And also** <note>original: uta sma</note> furthermore, **wishing to rush** <note>original: sariṣyan</note> into the demon armies, being the **foremost** <note>original: prathamaḥ</note>—meaning the most excellent or the chief—and being joined **with the ranks of chariots** <note>original: rathānāṃ śreṇibhiḥ</note> or rows of vehicles, **he moves repeatedly** <note>original: niveveti</note>. This means he moves intensely or runs here and there. To what is he compared? It is said: **A garland** <note>original: srajam</note>. A garland is an ornament <note>original: sragalaṅkṛtiḥ</note> so called because it "creates" or produces a beautiful form. **Creating** <note>original: kṛṇvānaḥ</note> that ornament, he is **like a horse prized by people** <note>original: janyo na</note>, meaning a horse that is beneficial to men. He is **beautiful** <note>original: śubhvā</note>, meaning he looks very fine. **Biting** <note>original: dadaśvān</note> the **bit** <note>original: kiraṇam</note> which is placed in his mouth, he is **repeatedly licking** <note>original: rerihat</note> the **dust** <note>original: reṇum</note> produced by the striking of his own hooves.

**[Commentary on Verse 7]**
**And also** <note>original: uta</note> furthermore, **that** <note>original: sya</note> horse described with the aforementioned characteristics, the **powerful one** <note>original: vājī</note> who possesses great speed or movement, is a **conqueror** <note>original: sahuriḥ</note> in **battle** <note>original: samarye</note>, meaning he has a nature that overcomes enemies. He is a **follower of the Law** <note>original: ṛtāvā</note>, meaning one who possesses truth, or <gloss>alternatively</gloss> one who possesses limbs like hooves. **Desiring to obey with his body** <note>original: tanvā śuśrūṣamāṇaḥ</note>, meaning he attends with his own physical form. **Among the swift-moving** <note>original: turaṃ yatīṣu</note> demon armies, he is **speeding** <note>original: turayan</note> or causing others to hurry. Being **straight-going** <note>original: ṛjīṣyaḥ</note>, he **scatters** <note>original: kirate</note> the **dust** <note>original: reṇum</note> **over his brows** <note>original: bhruvor adhi</note>, **tossing it up** <note>original: ṛñjan</note> or making the dust fly as he organizes his movement.

**[Commentary on Verse 8]**
<meta>The commentary for the eighth verse begins here and will continue onto the next page.</meta>

## Critical Notes
- The bottom of the page contains the volume and signatures: **VOL. III. 3 C**
- Verse 6 notes: The term <term>srajam</term> (garland) is glossed by Sayana as <term>sragalaṅkṛtiḥ</term> (the ornament of a garland). This suggests the horse is so beautiful he seems to be wearing or creating an ornamental wreath as he runs.
- Verse 8: The Samhita text <term>cutnayato</term> (charging/shaking) is a specific orthography for the more common <term>cyutnayato</term>, which often refers to rain dropping from clouds, comparing the horse's charge to a storm.

The commentary explains his physical actions, such as biting the bit and kicking up dust over his eyes, symbolizing his intense focus and power.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the translation of Rig Veda Mandala 4, Hymn 38. The previous page ended mid-sentence in the commentary for Verse 8, describing the fearsome nature of Dadhikra (the divine horse). This page completes that commentary and translates Verses 9 and 10, which conclude the hymn. The text follows the commentary of Sayana, a 14th-century scholar.</meta>

...fearsome <note>original: bhīmaḥ</note>. And also, indeed, just like the thunder of the sounding sky-lightning, the attackers—the demons <note>original: asurāḥ</note>—are afraid of this deity called Dadhikra when he strikes them down. They fear him. Furthermore, when he has fought against a thousand on all sides, then, preparing himself, he becomes a cause of fear and is irresistible <note>original: duvartuḥ; difficult to ward off</note>.

---

-> ॥ Now the Ninth Verse ॥ <-

## Hymn Text

And also, people praise the speed <note>original: jūtiḥ</note> of this swift one, the one who fulfills the people’s needs <note>original: kṛṣṭipraḥ</note> and overcomes enemies. And they say of him, as they move through the encounter of battle: "Dadhikra has rushed forward with thousands!" ॥ 9 ॥

**Word-by-word Analysis:**
And | indeed | of-him | praise | people | the-speed | filler-of-people | the-overcoming-power | of-the-swift-one |
And | him | they-say | in-battle-encounter | going-through | forward | Dadhikra | has-rushed | with-thousands ॥ 9 ॥

---

## Commentary (Sayana)

And also, indeed, people praise both the overcoming power and the speed <note>original: jūtim</note> of this Dadhikravan. They extol him. What is his nature? He is the "filler of people" <note>original: kṛṣṭipraḥ</note>; the word *krishti* refers to human beings, and he satisfies them. He is "swift" <note>original: āśuḥ</note>, meaning he is pervasive or fast-moving. And also, people moving in various directions in the encounter of battle <note>original: samithe</note> say of him: "This deity Dadhikra, surrounded by thousands of followers, has rushed forward," meaning he has gone ahead of us to strike others. Alternatively, they say this: the enemies are defeated while Dadhikra goes with thousands.

Regarding the ritual use: having performed the sacrifice with the wooden ladle <note>original: pavineṣṭvā</note>, this verse is the offering prayer for Dadhikravan. Thus it is indicated in the manuals:
> "I have made mention of Dadhikravan... Dadhikra with his strength [has pervaded] the five peoples."

<note>original reference: Ashvalayana Shrauta Sutra 2. 10.</note>

---

-> ॥ This is the Tenth Verse ॥ <-

## Hymn Text

Dadhikra with his strength <note>original: śavasā</note> has extended over the five peoples <note>original: pañca kṛṣṭīḥ</note>, just as the Sun with his light extends over the waters. May the powerful horse <note>original: vājī arvā</note>, the winner of thousands and hundreds, mingle these words of ours with sweetness <note>original: madhvā</note> ॥ 10 ॥

**Word-by-word Analysis:**
Fully | Dadhikra | with-strength | the-five | peoples | Sun-like | with-light | the-waters | has-extended |
winner-of-thousands | winner-of-hundreds | the-powerful | horse | may-he-mingle | with-sweetness | completely | these | words ॥ 10 ॥

---

## Commentary (Sayana)

That deity Dadhikra, who by his might <note>original: śavasā</note> has pervaded the "five peoples"—referring to the five classes of beings: gods, humans, asuras <note>demons</note>, rakshasas <note>spirits</note>, and ancestors <note>pitṛs</note>; or alternatively, the four castes with the Nishadas <note>forest-dwellers</note> as the fifth—just as the Sun with his brilliance covers the world, so does he extend over the waters. He is the winner of thousands and hundreds...

<vocab>
**Dadhikra**: The divine stallion, often a metaphor for the sun or martial energy.
**Juti**: Rapid movement or divine inspiration.
**Krishti**: Literally "ploughed fields," used here to mean settled people or tribes.
**Samitha**: A meeting, specifically a confrontation or battle.
**Shavas**: Heroic strength or sacrificial power.
**Vaji / Arvan**: Terms for a swift, powerful horse or a warrior.
**Madhva**: With honey or sweetness, representing the delight of the gods.
</vocab>

...and he is the giver of thousands, the prize-winning steed <note>original: vājī</note>, full of speed and skilled in heroic deeds. May he join them together.

->॥ Thus ends the twelfth section of the seventh chapter in the third book ॥<-

---

The seventh hymn, beginning with "the swift Dadhikra," consists of six verses. The first five are in the *Trishtubh* meter <note>a Vedic meter with four lines of eleven syllables each</note>, and the sixth is in the *Anushtubh* meter <note>a Vedic meter with four lines of eight syllables each</note>. The Seer is Vamadeva. Because it was mentioned in the previous hymn, this one is also dedicated to Dadhikra <note>the divine horse, often identified with the morning sun</note>. As the Index states: "The swift one, six verses, the last being Anushtubh." The application of the hymn follows its internal markers.

->॥ There, the first verse ॥<-

## Hymn Text

Let us now praise the swift Dadhikra; let us celebrate him from Heaven and Earth. May the brightening Dawns urge me on; may they deliver us across all difficulties. ॥ 1 ॥

**Word-by-word Analysis:**
Swift | Dadhikra | him | indeed | now | let-us-praise | of-Heaven | of-Earth | and | let-us-celebrate | 
brightening | me | Dawns | let-them-urge-on | distress | all | difficulties | let-them-cross-over ॥ 1 ॥

---

## Commentary (Sayana)

Let us now quickly praise that same deity, the swift-moving <note>original: āśum</note> Dadhikra. And furthermore, let us repeatedly offer <note>original: carkurāma; from a root meaning to scatter or mention repeatedly</note> praise, which is like fodder for him, from the direction of both Heaven and Earth. May the Dawns <note>the Uṣas goddesses</note>, who brighten the world and dispel the darkness, urge me on. May they protect my rewards. May they carry us across <note>original: atiparṣan</note> all difficult paths and troubles. Even though these are mantras dedicated to a specific deity, the praise of other deities <note>like the Dawns</note> is not contradictory because they occupy a subordinate position in the invocation.

---

->॥ Now the second verse ॥<-

## Hymn Text

I perform the great praise of the steed, the fulfiller of rituals, the horse Dadhikravan, desired by many and showering blessings; whom Mitra and Varuna, the deliverers, gave to the Puru people for their benefit, shining like fire. ॥ 2 ॥

**Word-by-word Analysis:**
Great | I-perform-repeatedly | of-the-steed | filler-of-rituals | of-Dadhikravan | desired-by-many | of-the-showering-one | 
whom | to-the-Puru-people | shining | like | Fire | they-gave | Mitra-and-Varuna | the-deliverer ॥ 2 ॥

---

## Commentary (Sayana)

Being a "filler of rituals" <note>original: kratuprāḥ; one who completes the sacrificial acts</note>, I perform the praise <note>original: carkurmi; I do it intensely</note> of the great, swift-moving steed Dadhikravan, who is desired by many <note>original: puruvārasya</note> and is a "showering one" <note>original: vṛṣṇaḥ; one who rains down benefits</note>. O Mitra and Varuna <note>the dual deities of cosmic order and water/friendship</note>, you two hold and have given this deliverer <note>original: taturṇim; one who helps cross over obstacles</note>, who stands shining like the fire, to the Puru people <note>an ancient Vedic tribe</note> for their benefit.

<vocab>
- <term>Dadhikrā</term> (Dadhikrā): A personification of the morning sun as a divine horse.
- <term>Vamadeva</term> (Vāmadeva): The Rishi <note>inspired sage</note> of the fourth Mandala.
- <term>Mitra-Varuna</term> (Mitrā-Varuṇā): The dual deity Mitra and Varuna, representing the sun/law and the ocean/judgment.
- <term>Trishtubh</term> (Triṣṭubh): A Vedic meter of 44 syllables.
- <term>Anushtubh</term> (Anuṣṭubh): A Vedic meter of 32 syllables.
- <term>Carkurama</term> (Carkurāma): An intensive form of the verb, meaning to praise or scatter repeatedly.
- <term>Taturṇi</term> (Taturṇi): Delivering, rescuing, or helping one to cross over difficulties.
</vocab>

## Hymn Text

## Commentary (Sayana)

The worshipper who, at the dawning of light <note>original: prabhāte</note> when the ritual fire is kindled, has performed <note>original: akārṣīt</note> the praise of the horse—the pervasive <note>original: vyāptasya</note> Dadhikra—may Aditi, who is associated with Mitra and Varuna (the presiding deities of day and night), and who represents the indivisible <note>original: akhaṇḍanīyo</note> nature of Dadhikra, make that worshipper sinless <note>original: anāgasam</note>.

We meditate upon <note>original: stumaḥ</note> that which is the auspicious <note>original: bhadram</note> name and form of the great deity Dadhikra, who brings food <note>original: iṣaḥ</note> and strength <note>original: ūrjaḥ</note>, and who is the very self of the Maruts (the singers of praise). Furthermore, we call upon Varuna and the other deities who receive offerings in this ritual for our protection and well-being <note>original: kṣemāya</note>.

Just as people call upon Indra, so do "both" (meaning two groups of people or two opposing sides), rising up and preparing for battle or similar efforts, and approaching the sacrifice—that is, beginning and proceeding with the sacred ritual—loudly call upon <note>original: āhvayanti</note> this Dadhikra. You, Mitra and Varuna, have given to the mortal man this horse-shaped deity, who is the impeller <note>original: prerakam</note> or purifier <note>original: sūdanam</note>... <note>Text continues on next page</note>

<meta>This page concludes the commentary on the 39th hymn of the 4th Book (Mandala) of the Rig Veda and introduces the 40th hymn. It continues the theme of praising Dadhikra, the divine horse, who is associated with the morning sun and ritual purification.</meta>

...O Mitra and Varuna, may you two sustain the divine Dadhikra for our sake. Here, the word "both" <note>original: "ubhaye"</note> should be understood as referring to two types of participants in the ritual: the chanters and the reciters.

The verse "I have celebrated Dadhikravan..." <note>original: "dadhikravno akarisham"</note> is the invitatory prayer for the purification rite. It is noted in the ritual manuals: "I have celebrated Dadhikravan; Dadhikra has pervaded the five classes of men with his strength" <note>Ashvalayana Shrauta Sutra 2.12</note>. This verse is also recited during the ritual consumption of curd-drops <note>original: "dadhi-drapsa-bhakshana"</note>, as indicated in the text: "They consume the curd-drops in the Agnidhriya fire-hall while reciting 'I have celebrated Dadhikravan...'" <note>Ashvalayana Shrauta Sutra 6.12</note>.

## Hymn Text
-> ॥ This is the Sixth Verse ॥ <-

I have celebrated the praise of Dadhikravan, the victorious, the swift horse. May he make our mouths fragrant; may he prolong our lives. ॥ 6 ॥

**Word-by-word Analysis:**
Of-Dadhikra | I-have-made (praise) | of-the-victorious | of-the-horse | of-the-swift | 
fragrant | our | mouths | may-he-make | may-he-forward | our | lives | increase ॥ 6 ॥

## Commentary (Sayana)
I have performed <note>original: "akarisham"</note> the praise of the deity Dadhikravan. I do this for the victorious <note>original: "jishnu"</note>, the all-pervading horse who is swift <note>original: "vajin"</note>. May that deity make our mouths—meaning our senses such as sight and speech—fragrant <note>original: "surabhi"</note>, which implies making them pure and pleasant. May he also prolong <note>original: "pratarishat"</note> our lives; the prefix "pra" with the root "tri" here signifies "to increase" or "to extend."

-> ॥ Thus ends the thirteenth section (Varga) of the seventh chapter (Adhyaya) of the third book (Ashtaka) ॥ <-

The eighth hymn <note>Hymn 40</note>, beginning with "Of Dadhikravan indeed," consists of five verses. It was revealed to the seer Vamadeva and is dedicated to Dadhikra. The first verse is in the <term>Trishtubh meter (a rhythmic structure of 11 syllables per line)</term>, while the remaining verses are in the <term>Jagati meter (12 syllables per line)</term>. The final verse, "The swan seated in the light," is specifically dedicated to the Sun god (Surya). The index of the Veda states: "Dadhikravan has five verses; the last four are Jagati, and the final one is dedicated to Surya." The application of this hymn follows its literal meaning.

## Hymn Text

->॥ Now the Second Verse ॥<-

The swift goer, the sustainer, the seeker of light, dwells among the worshippers; desiring food, he hastens at the time of Dawn. Truth-abiding, the moving one, the fleet-footed, the bird-like leaper—may Dadhikravan generate food, strength, and heaven for us. ॥ 2 ॥

**Word-by-word Analysis:**
The-Goer | the-sustainer | the-seeker-of-light | he-who-sits-among-worshippers | 
desiring-renown-or-food | food/offerings | of-the-Dawn | he-who-hastens-to-sit | 
the-true | the-moving-one | the-highly-swift | the-bird-like-leaper | 
Dadhikravan | food | strength | heaven | may-he-generate ॥ 2 ॥

---

## Commentary (Sayana)

**The Goer** <note>original: "sattva"</note> refers to one who moves. **The sustainer** <note>original: "bharishah"</note> is one who is skilled in supporting or nourishing. **The seeker of light** <note>original: "gavishah"</note> is the impeller or the seeker of the "cows" <note>a Vedic metaphor for rays of light or wealth</note>. **He sits among the worshippers** <note>original: "duvanyasat"</note>: those who desire to perform service or worship are called "duvanyas"; he resides among them. This occurs at the **time of the Dawn** <note>original: "ishah ushasah"</note>, meaning the period associated with the goddess of morning. Alternatively, "ishah" can mean one who is sought after.

**He desires food** <note>original: "shravasyat"</note> or desires renown. Furthermore, **he hastens to sit** <note>original: "turanyasat"</note>, meaning he takes his place with great speed. He is **Truth-abiding** <note>original: "satyah"</note>, manifesting among those who are true. He is the **moving one** <note>original: "druvah"</note>, the goer. He is **fleet-footed** <note>original: "drubarah"</note>, possessing superior velocity. He is the **bird-like leaper** <note>original: "patangarah"</note>: a "patanga" is one who moves by falling or leaping forward like a bird; one who possesses that movement is "patangarah." May the deity **Dadhikravan**, described by these characteristics, **generate** <note>original: "janat"</note> or produce for us **food** <note>original: "isham"</note>, **strength** <note>original: "urjam"</note>, and **heaven** <note>original: "svah"</note>.

---

## Hymn Text

->॥ Now the Third Verse ॥<-

And truly, when he runs, when he hastens, the wind blows after the flight of this intensely eager deity as if following the wing of a bird. Like a hawk rushing to its nest, they gather around the flank of Dadhikravan, who brings strength and carries us across. ॥ 3 ॥

**Word-by-word Analysis:**
And | indeed | of-him | of-the-running | of-the-hastening | 
wing/feather | like | of-a-bird | after | blows | of-the-intensely-eager | 
of-a-hawk-like | rushing | the-flank/chest | around | 
Dadhikravan | with | strength | of-the-one-who-carries-across ॥ 3 ॥

---

## Commentary (Sayana)

**And truly** <note>original: "uta sma"</note>, furthermore, of this deity who is **running** <note>original: "dravatah"</note> and **hastening** <note>original: "turanyatah"</note>. The speed of this **intensely eager** <note>original: "pragardhinah"</note> deity—one who intensely desires his goal—is such that just as other birds fly **following the wing** <note>original: "parnam na"</note> or the flight of a moving **bird** <note>original: "veh"</note>, so too does every swift-moving person blow or move after him. This means he is the swiftest of all.

Furthermore, he is **rushing** <note>original: "dhrajatah"</note> and **carrying across** <note>original: "tarichatah"</note>, meaning he enables others to cross over difficulties <note>this verb here includes a causative sense</note>. Just as one might approach the **flank** <note>original: "ankasam"</note>—referring to the chest or the place where the feet rest—**of a hawk** <note>original: "shyenasyeva"</note>, people gather **around** <note>original: "pari"</note> him from all sides. They unite **with strength** <note>original: "urja"</note> for the sake of obtaining food or power. The sense is that they move together in a great assembly.

<vocab>
- Dadhikravan: A divine horse, often identified with the sun or the power of prayer.
- Ushas: The Goddess of Dawn.
- Shyena: A hawk or eagle, a common Vedic symbol for swift divine descent.
- Urj: Vitality, strength, or the essence of nourishment.
- Padapatha: The "word-for-word" recitation of the Veda where each word is isolated.
</vocab>

<meta>This page concludes the 40th hymn of the 4th Book (Mandala) of the Rig Veda. ## Hymn Text
-> ॥ Now the Fourth Verse ॥ <-

And that spirited one <note>the divine horse Dadhikravan</note> hastens like a whip, bound at the neck, at the withers, and in the mouth. Dadhikra, following the sacred work and increasing in strength, moves swiftly along the windings of the paths. ॥ 4 ॥

**Word-by-word Analysis:**
And | that | spirited-one | whip/speed | he-causes-to-hasten | in-the-neck | bound | at-the-withers | in-the-mouth | 
divine-will/work | Dadhikra | following | increasing-in-strength | of-the-paths | windings/curves | following | he-moves-repeatedly ॥ 4 ॥

---

## Commentary (Sayana)
"And also" <note>original: "utapapi ca"</note> refers to that spirited deity in the form of a horse. He is **bound at the neck**—the instrument of swallowing—and **at the withers** <note>the ridge between the shoulder blades</note>, and **in the mouth** or face. For a horse that is harnessed, it is natural for the ropes and bindings to be in these specific places. Even while thus bound, he **hastens like a whip** <note>original: "kshipanim"</note>, meaning he causes himself to move with great speed. 

Furthermore, this deity **Dadhikra**, following **"Kratu"** <term>Kratu: specifically refers here to sacrificial action or divine intelligence</term>, becomes immensely powerful and **moves through the windings** <note>the "crooked" or "curved" parts</note> of the paths. He travels everywhere with great intensity. The word "apani-phanat" is a frequentative form of the root *phan*, meaning "to go." One should also consider the explanation in the **Nirukta** <note>Yaska's ancient Vedic etymology text, 2.28</note> which states: "Also that spirited one," and so forth.

---

Regarding the ritual use: During the **Dasharatra** <note>a ten-day soma sacrifice</note>, on the sixth day, at the third libation, in the recitation dedicated to Mitra and Varuna, the verse beginning with **"The Swan dwelling in purity"** <note>Verse 5</note> is used. The ritual manual states: "Having performed the invocation, he should ascend the 'difficult-ascent' <note>original: "durohanam", a specific mounting of the sacrificial chant</note> with the verse 'The Swan dwelling in purity,' reciting it by quarter-verse and then by half-verse." <note>Ashvalayana Shrauta Sutra 8.2</note>

The sage Shounaka mentions its use in domestic or personal practice: "A person who is pure, by chanting the verse 'The Swan dwelling in purity' while looking at the sun at the time of death, attains the eternal abode of Brahman." <note>Rig-vidhana 2.13</note>

---

## Hymn Text
-> ॥ Now the Fifth Verse ॥ <-

The **Swan** dwelling in purity <note>the sky or light</note>, the **Vasu** <note>pervader</note> dwelling in the atmosphere, the **Priest** dwelling at the altar, the **Guest** dwelling in the house; dwelling in men, dwelling in the best [gods], dwelling in truth <note>or the sacrifice</note>, dwelling in the sky; born of water, born of light, born of truth, born of mountains—he is the Truth. ॥ 5 ॥

**Word-by-word Analysis:**
The-Swan | dwelling-in-purity | the-Vasu | dwelling-in-the-atmosphere | the-Priest | dwelling-at-the-altar | the-Guest | dwelling-in-the-house | 
dwelling-in-men | dwelling-in-the-best | dwelling-in-truth | dwelling-in-the-sky | born-of-water | born-of-light/cows | born-of-truth | born-of-mountains | the-Truth ॥ 5 ॥

---

## Commentary (Sayana)
Through this solar verse <note>a verse dedicated to Surya, the Sun</note>, it is established that the **Golden Person** <term>Hiranmayah Purushah: The divine being described in the Upanishads as residing within the solar disc with golden hair and beard</term> is the deity who presides over the sun. He is also the **Supreme Soul** (Paramatman) who resides within the hearts of all living beings, and he is the **Supreme Brahman** who is free from all limiting conditions. All of these are essentially one and the same. 

**The Swan** (Hamsah): The root *han* means "to go." He is the one who goes everywhere at all times. As stated in the Upanishadic texts, "I am He," this identifies the individual soul with the universal...

<meta>This page continues the exposition of the 40th hymn of the 4th Book, specifically the final verse (4.40.5), which is a profound philosophical statement identifying the divine horse/sun with all aspects of existence. It then transitions into the 41st hymn, a prayer addressed to the dual deity Indra-Varuna.</meta>

## Commentary (Sayana)
<note>Continuing the analysis of verse 5, the "Hamsavati" mantra</note> 
The term "dwelling in the home" <note>original: "pastyah"</note> refers to the Sun <note>original: "Aditya"</note> who is the subject of the Supreme Soul mantra. He sits in the pure, shining heaven; thus he is called **the dweller in purity** <note>original: "shuchishat"</note>. This is supported by the scripture <note>the Upanishads/Brahmanas</note> stating, "Now, that light which shines above this heaven..." By this, the Sun's position in the celestial realm is established.

The commentator then explains that he is also the Wind <note>original: "Vayu"</note> in the middle region. He is the **Vasuh** <note>the "Attainer" or "Dweller"</note>, the one who causes everyone to dwell, and he is the "dweller in the atmosphere" because he moves through the mid-air. 

Next, his form as the sacrificial fire on earth is described. He is the **Invoker** <note>original: "hota"</note> who calls the gods or performs the sacrifice. He is the **dweller on the altar** <note>original: "vedishat"</note>, residing on the sacrificial ground in forms such as the "Householder's Fire" <note>original: "Garhapatya"</note>. He is the **guest** <note>original: "atithi"</note>, who like a guest is always worthy of worship. He is the **dweller in the house** <note>original: "duronasat"</note>. "Durona" is a name for a house; he stays there as the means for cooking and other domestic needs. By this, his nature as the secular/domestic fire is expressed.

He is the **dweller among men** <note>original: "nrishat"</note>. He resides within human beings in the form of consciousness. By this, his nature as the **Supreme Soul** <term>Paramatma: the universal or absolute spirit</term> is expressed.

Once again, his solar nature is stated: he is the **dweller in the exalted place** <note>original: "varasat"</note>. He sits in the "Vara" or the choice, excellent solar disk. Indeed, the scripture says, "That is the most excellent of seats in which he, being seated, shines." He is the **dweller in truth** <note>original: "ritasat"</note>; "Rita" means Truth, Brahman, or Sacrifice. He is the **dweller in the void** <note>original: "vyomasat"</note>; "Vyoma" refers to the atmosphere or sky where the Wind resides.

Now, concerning the Sun again: He is **born of the waters** <note>original: "abja"</note>, for he indeed rises from the midst of the waters <note>the ocean</note>. He is **born of the cows/rays** <note>original: "goja"</note>, born among the rays of light. He is **born of Truth** <note>original: "rita-ja"</note>; because he is visible to everyone, he is born of the manifest truth. Unlike deities like Indra, he is not beyond perception. Alternatively, this may mean he is born in the waters in the form of lightning or the undersea fire. He is **born of the mountain** <note>original: "adrija"</note>, rising from the eastern mountain.

Thus, this great-souled Sun is the Truth—the unshakeable, foundational reality of Brahman. He is indeed of that form. This nature of the Sun is confirmed in the **Aitareya Brahmana (4.20)** <note>an ancient prose text explaining Rigvedic rituals</note> which states: "The Swan sitting in the purity... this is indeed the Swan sitting in the purity."

->॥ Thus ends the fourteenth Varga of the seventh Adhyaya in the third [Ashtaka] ॥<-

**The ninth hymn, beginning with "Indra, who among you," consists of eleven verses, is seen by the seer Vamadeva, is in the Trishtubh metre, and is addressed to the dual deity Indra-Varuna.** 

According to the Index <note>original: "Anukramanika"</note>: "Indra, who among you" is eleven verses to Indra-Varuna. In the "Abhishravika" libations of the Third Pressing <note>the evening ritual</note>, during the recitations of the Maitravaruna priest, these two hymns (starting with "Indra, who among you") are used to supplement the chants when the praise-songs are expanded. This is indicated in the ritual manuals <note>original: "Ashvalayana Shrauta Sutra 7.9"</note>.

->॥ Here begins the first verse ॥<-

## Hymn Text
Indra and Varuna! Who has obtained your favor? What hymn, accompanied by oblations, is like a deathless invoker? Which prayer of ours, filled with wisdom and accompanied by prostrations, shall touch your heart, O Indra and Varuna? ॥ 1 ॥

## Commentary (Padapatha)
Indra | who | of-you-two | Varuna | favor/happiness | has-attained | hymn | possessing-oblation | deathless | like | invoker |
which | of-you-two | in-the-heart | possessing-wisdom | from-us | spoken | shall-touch | Indra-Varuna | possessing-reverence ॥ 1 ॥

---

<vocab>
- Aditya: The Sun deity, often viewed as the physical manifestation of the divine.
- Shuchishat: "Dwelling in the bright/pure," referring to the Sun in the sky.
- Duronasat: "Dwelling in the house," referring to the domestic fire used for daily life.
- Rita: A central Vedic concept meaning "Cosmic Order," "Truth," or "Sacred Law."
- Aitareya Brahmana: One of the oldest prose explanations of the Rig Veda's rituals.
- Vamadeva: The ancestral seer (Rishi) of the entire 4th Book of the Rig Veda.
- Indra-Varuna: A dual deity representing the combined powers of the warrior-king (Indra) and the moral judge/cosmic king (Varuna).
- Stoma: A specific type of chanted hymn or "praise-song."
- Hota: The priest responsible for reciting the Rig Vedic verses and inviting the gods to the sacrifice.
- Kratuman: Someone possessing "Kratu," which implies both spiritual wisdom and the sacrificial will to act.
</vocab>

<summary>This page concludes the famous "Hamsavati" mantra, which identifies the Sun with the Universal Soul (Brahman) across all planes of existence. It then introduces a new hymn addressed to Indra and Varuna, focusing on whose prayer can best reach the hearts of these two powerful gods.</summary>
<keywords>Sun deity, Brahman, Universal Soul, Agni, Vayu, Indra-Varuna, Vamadeva, Vedic ritual, Cosmic Order, consciousness</keywords>
