<meta>This page continues the commentary on the hymns of the fourth book of the Rig Veda. The previous page introduced Hymn 46, dedicated to the dual deity Indra-Vayu. This page provides the text and commentary for verses 3 through 6, discussing the arrival of the deities in their golden chariot to partake in the Soma sacrifice.</meta>

Page 215
Mandala 4. Chapter 5. Hymn 46. || The Third Ashtaka || <note>The Rig Veda is traditionally divided into eight 'Ashtakas' or 'eighths' for study and memorization.</note>

Indra became the owner of the fourth part, while Vayu received three parts; so say the collectors of the fourth part. Following this example, Indra became like a charioteer and won the race. <note>original: "tantu-rīya-bhāg-indro-abhavat..." citing Aitareya Brahmana 2.25. This ancient story explains why Vayu often receives a larger share of certain offerings than Indra.</note>

---

## Hymn Text
-> ॥ Verse Three ॥ <-

**O Indra and Vayu, may a thousand bay horses bring you both to the food, for the drinking of Soma. || 3 ||**

**ā | vām | sahasram | harayaḥ | indravāyū iti | abhi | prayaḥ | vahantu | soma-pītaye || 3 ||** <note>This is the 'Pada-patha' or word-for-word breakdown of the verse, used to ensure every syllable is preserved correctly.</note>

## Commentary (Sayana)
O Indra and Vayu, a thousand horses <note>original: "harayaḥ"</note>—the term 'Hari' here refers generally to horses—are hurrying you toward the food <note>original: "prayaḥ"</note>, which is the sacrificial offering. May they bring you here for the drinking of the Soma.

---

## Hymn Text
-> ॥ Verse Four ॥ <-

**O Indra and Vayu, you surely ascend the golden-framed chariot that touches the heavens and belongs to the auspicious sacrifice. || 4 ||**

**ratham | hiraṇya-vandhuram | indravāyū iti | su-adhvaram | ā | hi | sthāthaḥ | divi-spṛśam || 4 ||**

## Commentary (Sayana)
O Indra and Vayu, you have surely ascended <note>original: "āsthātho hi"</note> the chariot. This chariot has a frame or seat-base made of gold <note>original: "hiraṇya-vandhuram"</note>, it touches the heavenly world, and it is present at the well-performed sacrifice <note>original: "svadhvaram"</note>. The sense is: since you are already seated in your chariot, please come here. Alternatively, it can be interpreted as: "You ascend the chariot to come to the beautiful ritual."

The triad of verses starting with "By the chariot, broadly..." is used on the fifth day of the Ten-Night sacrifice <note>term: Dasharatra (a prominent ten-day Vedic ritual sequence)</note> during the Indra-Vayu portion of the Prauga litany <note>term: Prauga-shastra (a specific series of recitations dedicated to several deities during the morning Soma-pressing)</note>. This is indicated in the ritual manuals: **"By the chariot of broad power, many wise ones..."** <note>original: "rathena pṛthupājasā..." citing Ashvalayana Shrauta Sutra 7.12.</note>

---

## Hymn Text
-> ॥ This is the first verse of the triad and the fifth of the hymn ॥ <-

**With your chariot of vast power, go to the donor; O Indra and Vayu, come here! || 5 ||**

**rathena | pṛthu-pājasā | dāśvāṃsam | upa | gacchatam | indravāyū iti | iha | ā | gatam || 5 ||**

## Commentary (Sayana)
O Indra and Vayu, with your chariot of great strength <note>original: "pṛthupājasā"</note>, go toward the donor <note>original: "dāśvāṃsam"</note>, who is the patron of this sacrifice. For his sake, come here; arrive at this ritual.

---

## Hymn Text
-> ॥ Verse Six ॥ <-

**O Indra and Vayu, this Soma is pressed; drink it in the house of the donor, in joyful company with the gods. || 6 ||**

**indravāyū iti | ayam | sutaḥ | tam | devebhiḥ | sa-joṣasā | pibatam | dāśuṣaḥ | gṛhe || 6 ||**

## Commentary (Sayana)
O Indra and Vayu, this Soma juice has been pressed <note>original: "sutaḥ"</note>. Drink that Soma in the sacrificial hall <note>original: "gṛhe"</note> of the giver of oblations, being in the company of the other gods and sharing a common joy <note>original: "sajoṣasā"</note> with them.

<meta>This page concludes Hymn 47 of the Fourth Book (Mandala) and introduces Hymn 48. It follows the commentary on Indra and Vayu’s arrival at the sacrifice. We are currently in the Third 'Ashtaka' (the Great Eighths) of the Rig Veda, specifically in the Seventh Chapter of that section.</meta>

# Rig Veda
## Book 4, Chapter 7, Group 23

### Hymn Text (RV 4.47.7)

-> ॥ Verse Seven ॥ <-

**May your journey end here, O Indra and Vayu, and may the unyoking of your horses be here. May you both stay here for the drinking of the Soma. || 7 ||**

**Word-for-word breakdown:**
**iha | pra-yāṇam | astu | vām | indravāyū iti | vi-mocanam | iha | vām | soma-pītaye || 7 ||**

---

### Commentary (Sayana)

O **Indra and Vayu**, may your **journey** <note>original: "prayāṇam"</note> or arrival lead to this sacrifice. **In this very sacrifice, may the unyoking of your horses** <note>original: "vimocanam-aśvānām"</note> **be for you both to drink the Soma.** Although the phrases "journey" and "unyoking" effectively point to the same goal—their arrival—the repetition is used to show great respect and hospitality <note>original: "ādarāt punar-vacanam," indicating that repeating a request is a sign of earnestness in Vedic Sanskrit</note>.

-> ॥ Thus ends the twenty-second group of the seventh chapter of the third book ॥ <-

---

**"O Vayu, the bright..."** <note>original: "vāyo śukra"</note> begins the second hymn of this section (Hymn 48). It consists of four verses composed in the Anushtubh meter <note>Anushtubh is a rhythmic structure of 32 syllables</note>. The seer is Vamadeva, and the hymn is dedicated to Indra and Vayu. The first verse is dedicated solely to Vayu. According to the Verse Index <note>original: "Anukramanika"</note>: **"The four verses beginning with 'O Vayu' are in the Anushtubh meter and addressed to Vayu."** The application of the hymn in rituals is determined by its characteristics. The first verse is the first of a triplet for Vayu recited during the 'Prauga-shastra' <note>a specific morning litany</note> on the fourth day of the 'Dasharatra' <note>a ten-day sacrificial session</note>. This is confirmed in the ritual manuals: **"O Vayu, the bright [Soma] is offered to you..."** <note>original: citing Ashvalayana Shrauta Sutra 7.11</note>.

### Hymn Text (RV 4.48.1)

-> ॥ Verse One ॥ <-

**O Vayu, the bright Soma is offered to you; it is the best of the sweets, offered during the rites for seeking heaven. O God, come for the drinking of Soma with your team of horses, for you are most desirable. || 1 ||**

**Word-for-word breakdown:**
**vāyo iti | śukraḥ | ayāmi | te | madhvaḥ | agram | divi-iṣṭiṣu |**
**ā | yāhi | soma-pītaye | spārhaḥ | deva | niyutvatā || 1 ||**

---

### Commentary (Sayana)

O **Vayu**, for **you**, the **bright** <note>original: "śukraḥ," meaning purified through the ritual</note> and **sweet Soma juice** <note>original: "madhvaḥ"</note> **is offered** <note>original: "ayāmi," meaning it is brought forward or presented</note> by me before all others. For what purpose? During the **sacrifices seeking heaven** <note>original: "diviṣṭiṣu"</note>. O **Lord Vayu**, you who are **desirable** <note>original: "spārhaḥ"</note>, **come** with your **team of horses** <note>The 'Niyuts' are the specific horses that pull Vayu's chariot</note> for the **drinking of the Soma**.

The triplet beginning with **"Indra and..."** <note>original: "indraś ca"</note> is the second part of the Indra-Vayu offering on the fourth day of the ten-day sacrifice. This is also noted in the manuals: **"Indra and Vayu, you both deserve the drinking of these Somas, O wise and powerful ones."** <note>original: citing Ashvalayana Shrauta Sutra 7.11</note>.

---

### Hymn Text (RV 4.48.2)

-> ॥ Verse Two of the Hymn ॥ <-

**Indra and Vayu, you both deserve to drink of these Somas; for the offerings go toward you together, like waters flowing down a slope. || 2 ||**

<summary>This page concludes a hymn to Indra and Vayu with a welcoming prayer and begins Hymn 48, describing the offering of purified Soma and Vayu's arrival on his chariot pulled by his Niyut horses.</summary>
<keywords>Indra, Vayu, Soma, Vamadeva, Anushtubh meter, Niyut horses, Dasharatra sacrifice, Prauga-shastra, Vedic ritual</keywords>

# Rig Veda
## Book 4, Chapter 5, Hymn 48

### Hymn Text (RV 4.48.2)

**Indra and Vayu, you both are worthy of drinking these Somas. For these drops of Soma indeed flow to you, just as waters flow together toward a low place. || 2 ||**

**Word-for-word breakdown:**
**Indra | and | O Vayu | of these | Somas | the drinking | you both deserve | you two | indeed | go | the drops | low place | waters | like | together. || 2 ||**

---

### Commentary (Sayana)

O **Vayu**, you and **Indra** <note>original: "indraśca"</note> are worthy of **drinking** <note>original: "pītiṃ pānam"</note> these prepared Somas. For indeed, the **Soma drops** <note>original: "indavaḥ"</note> go to you; they reach you. Just as **waters** <note>original: "āpaḥ"</note> flow **together** <note>original: "sadhyak"</note> toward a **low-lying area** <note>original: "nimnaṃ khātapradeśam"</note>, in the same way, all the Somas go to you both.

---

### Hymn Text

-> ॥ Verse Three ॥ <-

**Vayu and Indra, the mighty ones, O lords of strength! You who possess the Niyut horses, come here for our protection and for the drinking of the Soma, seated together upon the same chariot. || 3 ||**

**Word-for-word breakdown:**
**Vayu | Indra | and | mighty | on the same chariot | of strength | O two lords | having steeds | our | for protection | come | for the drinking of Soma. || 3 ||**

---

### Commentary (Sayana)

O **Vayu** and **Indra**, O **lords of strength** <note>original: "śavasaspatī," meaning masters of power</note>, you two are **mighty** <note>original: "śuṣmiṇā"</note> and possess the horses known as **Niyuts** <note>term: Niyuts — the specific team of horses that pull Vayu's chariot</note>. Having mounted the **same chariot** <note>original: "saratham"</note>, come to us. Come for our **protection** <note>original: "ūtaye"</note> and for the **drinking of the Soma**. Alternatively, this can be understood as two distinct requests: "Mount the same chariot" and "come here."

---

### Hymn Text

-> ॥ Verse Four ॥ <-

**O leaders, O Indra and Vayu, who bear the sacrifice! Those steeds of yours which are desired by many, grant them to us, the patrons who have offered the oblation. || 4 ||**

**Word-for-word breakdown:**
**Which | your | are | desired by many | steeds | for the giver | O two leaders | to us | those | bearers of the sacrifice | Indra and Vayu | bestow. || 4 ||**

---

### Commentary (Sayana)

O **leaders** <note>original: "narā," meaning guides or heroes</note>, O **Indra and Vayu**, you who are the **bearers of the sacrifice** <note>original: "yajñavāhasā"</note>! Those **steeds** <note>original: "niyutaḥ"</note> which are **desired by many** <note>original: "puruspṛho"</note>, grant them to **us** <note>original: "asme"</note>, the patrons who have offered the **oblation** <note>original: "dāśuṣe havirdattavate"</note>. Grant them for my sake.

---

### Critical Notes

-> ॥ Thus ends the twenty-third group of the seventh chapter of the third book ॥ <-

**Introduction to Hymn 49:**
The third hymn, beginning with **"Drink the oblations"** <note>original: "vihi hotrā"</note>, consists of five verses. It is composed by the seer **Vamadeva** and is addressed to **Vayu**. According to the **Verse Index** <note>original: "Anukramanika"</note>: "The five verses beginning with 'Vihi' are addressed to Vayu." The ritual application <note>original: "viniyoga"</note> is determined by the characteristics of the text. The first verse is used on the **fourth day of the Ten-Night sacrifice** <note>term: Dasharatra — a prominent ten-day Vedic ritual cycle</note>.

## Hymn Text
**This hymn, beginning with "This for you both," consists of six verses. Furthermore, the **hymn of praise** <note>original: "uktham," a specific type of recited liturgical chant</note> which produces **joy** <note>original: "made," exhilaration or intoxication from the ritual</note> **is being recited**.

<note>
The "mouths" of the gods are symbolically the sacrificial fire through which they receive offerings. In this verse, the poet Vamadeva is inviting two major figures of the Vedic pantheon: Indra (the king of gods) and Brihaspati (the high priest of the gods).

In the sacrifice dedicated to Indra and Brihaspati <note>term: "aindrābārhaspatyām-iṣṭau," a specific ritual offering made to these two deities together</note>, this verse serves as the offering prayer <note>term: "yājyā"</note> following the third invitatory verse <note>term: "anuvākyā"</note> which begins "O Indra..." <note>original: "ā na indra"</note>. # Mandala 4. Hymn 5. Verse 50. || Third Book || 221

## Commentary (Sayana)
O Indra and Brihaspati, you two, in the house of the giver—the patron <note>term: "yajamāna," the person commissioning the sacrifice</note> who offers the oblation—are "abiding in that home" <note>original: "tadokasā," meaning those who have that very house as their residence</note>. Being so, drink the Soma. Having drunk, grant us exhilaration.

->॥ This ends the twenty-fifth section of the seventh chapter of the third book. ॥<-

The fifth hymn, beginning with **"He who supported,"** consists of eleven verses. The seer is Vamadeva <note>term: "ārṣam," the sage to whom the hymn was revealed</note>. The meter is Trishtubh <note>term: "traiṣṭubham," a meter of 44 syllables</note>, except for the tenth verse which is Jagati <note>term: "jagatī," a meter of 48 syllables</note>. The tenth and eleventh verses are dedicated to the dual deity Indra-Brihaspati; the remaining nine are dedicated to Brihaspati alone. The index of the Rig Veda states: **"The hymn 'He who supported' has eleven verses; it belongs to Brihaspati; the last two are for Indra [and Brihaspati], and the penultimate is in the Jagati meter."**

In the "Abhiplavika" rituals <note>term: "ābhiplavikeṣu," a type of six-day Soma sacrifice</note>, specifically during the third pressing of the Soma <note>term: "tṛtīyasavane"</note>, this hymn is inserted by the "Brahmanacchamsin" priest <note>term: "brāhmaṇācchamsinaḥ," one of the assistants to the main priest</note> to increase the praise-hymn. Thus it is said in the ritual manual: **"He who supported; He who is the breaker of the rock" (Ashvalayana Shrauta Sutra 7.9).** In the initial sacrifice dedicated to Brihaspati <note>term: "bṛhaspatisavane"</note>, this hymn is used as the introductory chant for the Marutvatiya and Nishkevalya offerings. This is indicated by the manual: **"He who supported; With his moving gait" (Ashvalayana Shrauta Sutra 9.9).**

---

## Hymn Text
->॥ Now, the First Verse ॥<-

He who supported with might the ends of the earth, Brihaspati, abiding in three places, with a roar—him the ancient seers, shining and wise, placed in front, he of the delightful tongue. ॥ 1 ॥

**[Padapatha]**
He | supported | with might | apart | of the earth | the ends | Brihaspati | abiding in three places | with a roar | him | the ancients | seers | shining | in front | the wise | placed | delightful-tongue ॥ 1 ॥

---

## Commentary (Sayana)
That **Brihaspati**—the deity who is the protector of the "Great" (either the Supreme Being or the Sacrifice)—**with might** and strength, **the ends of the earth** (meaning the ten directions), he **supported** them in various ways or regulated them. He is **abiding in three places** <note>original: "triṣadhasthaḥ," existing in the three realms: earth, atmosphere, and heaven</note>. He did this **with a roar**, or a sound saying "Stand thus!" **Him**, that deity, the **ancient seers**—those who can see beyond the reach of the senses—the **shining**, **wise** patrons and priests, **placed in front** through their praises and rituals. He is **of the delightful tongue** <note>original: "mandrajihvam," interpreted by Sayana as having a tongue that either causes exhilaration (mādana) or bestows joy (modana)</note>.

---

## Hymn Text
->॥ Now, the Second Verse ॥<-

Those of moving gait, rejoicing in the well-known [Brihaspati], who has extended himself toward us; protect, O Brihaspati, his spotted, moving, uninjured, vast source. ॥ 2 ॥

**[Padapatha]**
Moving-gaits | the well-known | rejoicing | Brihaspati | toward | those | us | has extended | spotted | moving | uninjured | vast | Brihaspati | protect | his | source ॥ 2 ॥

<vocab>
Brihaspati: The Lord of Prayer, often associated with the planet Jupiter and sacred speech.
Indra: The King of the Gods, associated with storms and war.
Vamadeva: The primary seer (Rishi) of the fourth book of the Rig Veda.
Trishtubh: A common Vedic meter of four lines, each with eleven syllables.
Jagati: A Vedic meter of four lines, each with twelve syllables.
Yajamāna: The patron who pays for and benefits from the Vedic sacrifice.
Triṣadhastha: Abiding in three places (heaven, mid-air, and earth).
Mandrajihva: Having a pleasant, soft, or intoxicating voice/tongue.
</vocab>

# Rig Veda || Book 3. Chapter 7. Section 26.

O **Brihaspati**, [those whose] **shaking movement** <note>original: "dhunetayaḥ"</note>—that is, those whose movement or progress causes the enemies to tremble—such officiating priests belonging to **us**, while **gladdening** or praising you, who possess **excellent wisdom**, **stand around** or offer themselves. **May you protect the source** <note>original: "yonim"</note> of these [priests], which is the sacrifice, or [protect] me, the patron of the sacrifice. The nature of this **source is specified**: it is **flecked** <note>original: "pṛṣantam"</note> or sprinkling rewards, **gliding** by nature, **undamaged**, and **vast**.

**The two verses beginning with "O Brihaspati, that which..." are the invitatory hymns <note>term: "anuvākye," verses recited to invite a deity</note> for the offering of the omentum and the sacrificial cake <note>term: "vapāpuroḍāśa," two specific parts of an animal sacrifice</note> in the rite dedicated to Brihaspati. This is indicated by the ritual manual: "Brihaspati, that which is the furthest distance—these two verses" <note>reference: Ashvalayana Shrauta Sutra 3.7</note>.**

---

## Hymn Text

-> ॥ This is the third verse ॥ <-

**O Brihaspati, from that furthest distance, those who touch the Sacred Law have come and sat down for you. For you, the wells dug out and milked by the stones drip the sweet juice, overflowing in every direction. ॥ ३ ॥**

**Brihaspati | which | furthest | distance | from that | towards | for you | touchers of the Sacred Law | down | sat. |**
**For you | dug out | wells | stone-milked | of the sweet juice | drip | all around | abundance. ॥ ३ ॥**

---

## Commentary (Sayana)

**O Brihaspati, there exists that well-known, most excellent, and extremely remote dwelling called heaven. Or, by a change of gender in the grammar, it refers to the "highest place." From that place, or from this region here, those who touch the Sacred Law <note>term: "ṛtaspṛśo," those who perform or contact the sacrifice</note>—referring to your horses—have come and sat down <note>original: "niṣeduḥ"</note> below you. For your sake, the wells are dug out. This is a condensed comparison <note>term: "luptopamā," a poetic figure where the "like" is implied</note>: just as dug-out wells overflow on all sides, in the same way, the Soma juices—which are "milked by the stones" <note>original: "adridugdhāḥ," meaning pressed by the ritual grinding stones</note>—drip the sweet nectar so that there is abundance, or rather, so that there is a loud sound of chanting.**

---

## Hymn Text

-> ॥ Now the fourth verse ॥ <-

**Brihaspati, first coming into being from the great light in the highest heaven, seven-mouthed and multi-born, with a roar and seven rays, he blew away the darknesses. ॥ ४ ॥**

**Brihaspati | first | being born | of the great | light | in the highest | heaven. |**
**Seven-mouthed | many-born | with a roar | away | seven-rayed | blew | the darknesses. ॥ ४ ॥**

---

## Commentary (Sayana)

**This Brihaspati is the deity who presides over the sacred mantras. Being first born or manifested in the highest, unsurpassed heaven <note>original: "vyoman," the sky or celestial ether</note> of the great and shining sun; being "seven-mouthed," which means his mouth consists of the seven Vedic meters <note>note: the Seven Meters are Gayatri, Ushnih, Anushtubh, Brihati, Pankti, Trishtubh, and Jagati</note>; being "multi-born," or produced in many ways; with a roar or sound; and being "seven-rayed," which means having the nature of moving...** [continues]

# Rig Veda || Book 4. Chapter 5. Section 50. || Third Ashtaka <note>term: "Ashtaka," one of the eight major divisions of the Rig Veda</note> || 223

## Commentary (Sayana - continued from previous page)
Radiant with light, he drove away the darkness. The word "drives" <note>original: "dhamati"</note> is defined as a verb of movement in the *Nirukta* <note>term: "Nirukta," the ancient Sanskrit science of etymology</note>. He moves in various directions; this means he destroys the darkness.

->|| This is the fifth verse ||<-

## Hymn Text
**With the praise-singing and radiant troop, he shattered the enclosure of Vala with a roar. Brihaspati drove out the lowing cows, who provide the offerings, while crying out in triumph. ॥ ५ ॥**

**He | with the praise-singing [troop] | he | with the radiant | troop | Vala | shattered | the cave-breaker | with a roar |**
**Brihaspati | the cows | the offering-pourers | crying out | lowing | out | drove. ॥ ५ ॥**

---

## Commentary (Sayana)
That **Brihaspati**, along with the **praise-singing** <note>original: "suṣṭubhā"</note>—those possessing beautiful hymns—and the **radiant** <note>original: "ṛkvatā"</note> or luminous **troop** <note>original: "gaṇena"</note> of the Angirasas <note>note: the Angirasas are a group of celestial seers associated with Brihaspati</note>, and with a **roar** or loud sound, **shattered Vala**. The word "cave-breaker" <note>original: "phaliga"</note> is derived from a root meaning to split or divide; thus it refers to the one who moves through the splitting of the mountain [the demon Vala]. He shattered the demon named Vala. The second use of the word "he" <note>original: "saḥ"</note> in the verse is for grammatical completion. That same deity, while **crying out** or making a loud sound, **drove out** the **cows** <note>original: "usriyā"</note>. These cows are described as "flowing with enjoyments" or "offering-pourers" <note>original: "havyasūdaḥ"</note> because they provide the milk and butter used in sacrifices. They were **lowing** <note>original: "vāvaśatīḥ"</note>, or making a sound, as he opened the enclosure.

->|| This concludes the twenty-sixth section (Varga) of the seventh chapter (Adhyaya) of the third book (Ashtaka) ||<-

The verse "Thus to the father..." is used as the sacrificial recitation <note>term: "yājyā," a verse recited while the offering is poured into the fire</note> for the butter offering in the animal sacrifice dedicated to Brihaspati. This is indicated by the ritual manual: "Thus to the father, the all-god, the showerer... to all the Maruts today for all protection" <note>reference: Ashvalayana Shrauta Sutra 3.7.1</note>. In the *Agnishtoma* sacrifice <note>term: "Agnishtoma," a major five-day Soma sacrifice</note>, this same verse is used as an additional recitation <note>term: "dhāyyā"</note> during the hymn to All the Gods. The ritual rule states: "Thus to the father, the all-god, the showerer... let noble thoughts come to us from every side" <note>reference: Ashvalayana Shrauta Sutra 5.18</note>.

->|| This is the sixth verse ||<-

## Hymn Text
**Thus to the Father, the All-God, the showerer of blessings, let us serve with sacrifices, with reverence, and with offerings. O Brihaspati, may we be blessed with good offspring and heroic sons, and may we become masters of riches. ॥ ६ ॥**

**Thus | to the Father | to the All-God | to the showerer | with sacrifices | let us serve | with reverence | with offerings |**
**Brihaspati | possessing good offspring | possessing heroes | we | may we be | masters | of riches. ॥ ६ ॥**

---

## Commentary (Sayana)
To the **Father**, meaning the protector, who is the **All-God** <note>original: "viśvadevāya"</note> because he embodies all the deities. Since all deities are established through mantras, and Brihaspati is the presiding lord of mantras, he is identified with all gods. Alternatively, the word "God" <note>original: "deva"</note> signifies praise; thus, he is "one to be praised by all." To him, the **showerer** <note>original: "vṛṣṇe"</note> of rewards, to this deity Brihaspati, let us **serve** or worship in the manner described, using **sacrifices** and their means, **offerings** such as clarified butter and cooked grains, and **reverence** <note>original: "namasā"</note> in the form of praise. **O Brihaspati**, may **we**, possessing **good offspring** <note>original: "suprajāḥ"</note> (excellent sons) and **heroic sons** <note>original: "vīravantaḥ"</note> (endowed with strength), **become masters of riches** or wealth.

<vocab>
- Brihaspati (Bṛhaspati): Deity of prayer, wisdom, and the priesthood.
- Vala (Vala): A demon who imprisoned the celestial cows (representing light/water) in a cave.
- Phaliga (Phaliga): A container, cloud, or mountain enclosure; here referring to Vala’s stronghold.
- Usriya (Usriyā): Luminous cows, often a metaphor for the first rays of dawn or the elements of sacrifice.
- Viśvadeva (Viśvadeva): "All-God"; a title implying the deity contains the powers of all others.
- Suprajāḥ (Suprajāḥ): The blessing of having a virtuous and healthy family.
- Vīravantaḥ (Vīravantaḥ): Having sons or companions who are heroes/warriors.
- Rayīṇām (Rayīṇām): Material and spiritual wealth or prosperity.
</vocab>

# Rig Veda || Ashtaka 3. Adhyaya 7. Varga 27. || 224

## Hymn Text

-> ॥ The Seventh Verse ॥ <-

**That king alone, by his power and valor, stands superior over all hostile forces, who well-nourishes Brihaspati, who praises him and honors him as the first recipient of honor. ॥ ७ ॥**

**He | indeed | the king | against | hostile forces | all | with power | stands | over | with valor |**
**Brihaspati | who | well-nourished | supports | praises | bows | the first-sharer. ॥ ७ ॥**

---

## Commentary (Sayana)

Regarding this triad of verses starting here, the *Brahmana* <note>original: "Aitareya Brahmana 8.26"</note> states that it is a "praise of the domestic priest" <note>term: "Purohita," the royal chaplain or priest who advises the king</note>. Alternatively, since this hymn (excluding two verses) is dedicated to Brihaspati, it may be viewed as a praise of Brihaspati himself. 

**That king alone**—whether he is a consecrated monarch or simply one who shines with authority—**stands superior** over **all hostile forces**. Here, "hostile forces" <note>original: "pratijanyāni"</note> refers to enemy armies in battle or the territories of adversaries. He overcomes them through **power** <note>original: "śuṣmeṇa"</note>, meaning strength, and **valor** <note>original: "vīryeṇa"</note>, meaning physical prowess. 

The text asks: Who is this king? It is he **who supports Brihaspati**—the "protector of the great" or the aforementioned domestic priest—and keeps him **well-nourished** through offerings, food, and clothing. He **praises** him and **bows** to him, making him the **first-sharer** <note>original: "pūrvabhājam"</note>, meaning he grants the priest his portion before all others. The one who acts in this way is the one who stands victorious.

---

## Hymn Text

-> ॥ The Eighth Verse ॥ <-

**He dwells well-established in his own home; for him, the Earth yields her bounty at all times. To that king, the subjects bow down of their own accord, before whom the Priest walks first. ॥ ८ ॥**

**He | indeed | dwells | well-established | home | in his own | for him | the Earth | yields | at all times |**
**for him | the subjects | of their own accord | indeed | bow | in whom | the Priest | for the king | first | goes. ॥ ८ ॥**

---

## Commentary (Sayana)

**He indeed dwells** or resides **well-established**, being thoroughly satisfied, within **his own home**. Such a king remains prosperous and unhindered, living in comfort. For him, **the Earth** <note>original: "Iḷā"</note> **yields her bounty** or increases her fruits **at all times**. 

To that king, the **subjects** or the common people **bow down of their own accord**. This means they remain submissive and pay their taxes or tributes voluntarily, without the king having to use a rod of punishment. This happens in the case of a **king** before whom the **Priest** <note>term: "Brahma," the high priest or spiritual guide</note> **walks first**—meaning the priest is honored as the foremost authority and is present to guide him.

---

## Hymn Text

-> ॥ The Ninth Verse ॥ <-

**Unopposed, he wins riches, both from enemies and from his own kin. To the king who provides prosperity to the Priest, the gods grant their protection. ॥ ९ ॥**

<vocab>Brihaspati (Lord of Prayer/Sacred Speech), Purohita (Domestic Priest), Ila (the Earth/Goddess of Nourishment), Brahma (Priest/Spiritual Guide), Raja (King), Pratijanyani (Enemy forces), Aitareya Brahmana (An ancient Vedic prose text explaining rituals)</vocab>

<summary>This page describes the political and spiritual benefits of a king supporting a domestic priest (Purohita), asserting that such a king will be victorious in war and loved by his subjects. It uses Brihaspati as the divine archetype for the priestly role in the royal court.</summary>
<keywords>royal priest, kingship, military victory, social order, Brihaspati, prosperity, taxation, Vedic ritual, Aitareya Brahmana</keywords>

# Rig Veda || Ashtaka 3. Adhyaya 7. Varga 27. || 225

## Hymn Text

**[RV 4.50.9 Word-for-Word Breakdown continued]**

**Unopposed | He wins | completely | riches | from enemies | and | those | from his own kin |**
**For the seeker of protection | who | wealth | grants | for the Priest | the King | him | protect | the Gods. ॥ ९ ॥**

---

## Commentary (Sayana)

That King, being **unopposed** <note>original: "apratītaḥ"</note>—meaning not countered by others—completely **wins** those **riches** which belong to **enemies** <note>original: "prati-janyāni"</note>, meaning rival peoples, and **also** those riches belonging to **his own kin** <note>original: "sa-janyā"</note>. 

The **King** who **grants** or gives **wealth** <note>original: "varivaḥ"</note> to the **Priest** <note>original: "brahmaṇe"</note>—either a Brahman desiring to please him or to Brihaspati himself—and who seeks to protect the one **seeking protection** <note>original: "avasyave"</note> (referring to one who is destitute or desiring safety), such a king becomes great in the manner described. The **Gods protect** <note>original: "avanti"</note>—or guard—that very king.

The verse beginning with "Indra and the Soma" (Verse 10) serves as the "Recitation of Departure" <note>term: "Prasthita-yajya," a prayer recited when offerings are being poured</note> for the **Assistant Priest** <note>term: "Brahmanacchamsin," a specific priest associated with the Brahman</note> during the **Third Libation** <note>term: "Tritiya-savana," the final of three daily Soma pressings</note>. This is indicated in the ritual manuals: "O Brihaspati, you and Indra drink the Soma... may they bring you here, swift-moving" <note>original: "Ashvalayana Shrauta Sutra 5.5"</note>. The text of that verse follows:

---

## Hymn Text

**[RV 4.50.10]**

**O Brihaspati, may you and Indra drink the Soma in this sacrifice, rejoicing, O you givers of wealth; may the drops of Soma enter you, being well-pervading; grant to us wealth consisting of all heroes. ॥ १० ॥**

**[RV 4.50.10 Word-for-Word Breakdown]**

**Indra | and | Soma | drink | O Brihaspati | in this | sacrifice | rejoicing | givers of wealth |**
**To | both of you | may they enter | drops | well-pervading | to us | wealth | all-heroic | down | grant. ॥ १० ॥**

---

## Commentary (Sayana)

**O Brihaspati**, may **you and Indra drink the Soma**. What is the nature of you two? You are **rejoicing** in **this sacrifice**, and you are **givers of wealth** <note>original: "vṛṣaṇvasū," literally those whose wealth rains down like a bull's strength</note>, meaning those who provide wealth to the sacrificers. 

May the **drops** of **Soma enter you**—that is, enter the bodies of you both. These drops are **well-pervading** <note>original: "svābhuvaḥ"</note>, meaning they are capable of spreading through the entire body. **Grant to us wealth** that is **all-heroic**, meaning it is accompanied by many sons and followers. Give it to us.

**O Brihaspati, O Indra, prosper us; may that favor of yours remain with us; protect our thoughts and awaken our wisdom; exhaust the hostilities of the enemy and the attacker. ॥ ११ ॥**

**[RV 4.50.11 Word-for-Word Breakdown]**

**O Brihaspati | O Indra | prosper | us | together | that | of you both | favor | let it be | in us |**
**Protect | thoughts | awaken | wisdoms | exhaust | of the enemy | of the attackers | hostilities. ॥ ११ ॥**

---

## Commentary (Sayana)

**O Brihaspati, O Indra**, you two **prosper us**—make us grow and make us great. May **that favor**, which is your compassionate mindset, **remain with us**—stay together with us. **Protect** our **thoughts** <note>original: "dhiyaḥ"</note>, meaning our religious actions. <unclear>...</unclear>

...protect us. Lead us to the other side. Awaken those **thoughts** <note>original: "purandhīḥ"</note>—meaning the praises or prayers by which the "city" of the body is established—and rouse them. # Mandala 4. Anuvaka 5. Sukta 51. || Third Book || 227

## Commentary (Sayana) - Continued from previous page
This very <note>original: "idam u"</note> light seen before us, which is to be praised by us and is world-renowned, is most abundant and **full of radiance** <note>original: "vayunavat"</note>. This term is derived from the root *vī*, meaning the act of shining; thus, it means possessing excellent beauty. Alternatively, the word *vayuna* refers to **knowledge** <note>original: "prajñā"</note>; thus, it means possessed of knowledge, or the one who makes all things known. What kind of light? It stood in the East, rising out of the **darkness** <note>original: "tamas"</note>. This being so, truly the Dawns, who are the daughters of the Sun <note>original: "divaḥ," or the Sky/Heaven</note>, as they shine forth, provide the **power of movement** <note>original: "gātum"</note>—that is, the ability to perform activities like walking—to the people, specifically the sacrificers.

---

-> ॥ Now the second verse ॥ <-

## Hymn Text
The wonderful Dawns have stood in the East, like **sacrificial posts** <term>Svaru: a ceremonial wooden post to which the sacrificial animal is tied</term> set up at sacrifices. Shining and purifying, they have thrown open the doors of the **enclosure of darkness**. ॥ 2 ॥

**Word-by-word breakdown (Pada-patha):**
They stood. Truly. Wonderful. The Dawns. In the East. Fixed, like. Sacrificial posts. In the sacrifices.
Open. Truly. Of the enclosure. Of the darkness. The doors. Shining. They have reached/opened. Bright. Purifiers. ॥ 2 ॥

## Commentary (Sayana)
The wonderful—meaning worthy of being gazed upon—Dawns have stood in the eastern direction. They remain there; the sense is that they have pervaded that region. A comparison is given: like **sacrificial posts** <note>original: "svaravaḥ"</note> that are fixed or planted during sacrifices. Just as those posts shine in front of the altar, so do the Dawns. Although the word *svaru* technically refers to the first chip of wood that falls when carving the sacrificial post <note>original: "yūpa"</note>, here it refers to the post itself. This is understood because of the word "fixed" <note>original: "mita"</note> and because similar usage is seen in phrases like "posts possessing rings." These Dawns, bright and purifying—meaning they cleanse the world—have opened the doors of the **enclosure of darkness** <note>original: "vrajaya tamasaḥ"</note>, which acts as an obstruction. They have uncovered it.

---

-> ॥ Now the third verse ॥ <-

## Hymn Text
Shining today, may the wealthy Dawns rouse the **liberal givers** <term>Bhojas: generous patrons of the sacrifice</term> for the bestowal of wealth. Let the **stingy ones** <term>Panis: those who withhold wealth or do not sacrifice; often identified with merchants</term> sleep unawakened in the midst of the **thick darkness**. ॥ 3 ॥

**Word-by-word breakdown (Pada-patha):**
Shining. Today. They rouse. The liberal givers. For the giving of wealth. The Dawns. Wealthy.
In the unlovely. Within. The Panis. Let them sleep. Unawakened. Of the darkness. In the very middle. ॥ 3 ॥

## Commentary (Sayana)
On this day, the wealthy Dawns, who drive away the darkness, rouse or awaken the **Bhojas**—the sacrificers who provide food and gifts—so that they may bestow wealth such as the **Soma juice** <note>original: "rādhodeyāya"</note>. In the "unlovely" <note>original: "acitre"</note>, meaning the center of extremely thick darkness, let the **Panis**—the traders who act as non-givers—remain sleeping, without being awakened.

## Rig Veda: Book 3, Chapter 8, Section 1

## Commentary (Sayana)
Protect us. Lead us across to the other shore. Awaken <note>original: "jigṛtaṃ"</note> the praises <note>original: "purandhīḥ"</note>—those thoughts by which the "city" of the body <note>original: "pura"</note> is sustained or established. Wake up! May you two [the Ashvins] destroy <note>original: "jazastaṃ"</note> the powerful, profound enemies <note>original: "arātīḥ"</note> of us who are your sharers or devotees <note>original: "vanuṣām"</note>. Fight them; that is to say, make them perish. In Vedic grammar, the word *arāti* (enemy/hostility) is feminine. Having thus concluded the praise, the seer prayed for his desired goal.

**Of the seventh chapter in the third book of the Rig Veda.**

## Book 4, Chapter 5, Hymn 51. The Third Ashtaka.

## Commentary (Sayana)

This visible light <note>original: "idam"</note>, which is to be praised by us and is famous among all, is extremely abundant <note>original: "purutamam"</note> and possesses wisdom or light <note>original: "vayuṇavat"</note>. This word is derived from a root meaning "to shine"; thus, it means "having excellent light." Alternatively, "vayuna" is a name for wisdom <note>original: "prajñā-nāma"</note>. In this sense, it means "endowed with wisdom" or "the one who makes everything known." What kind of light is this? It has risen <note>original: "udasthāt"</note> in the east, out of the darkness. This being so, truly <note>original: "nūnam"</note> the Dawns—who are the daughters of the Sun <note>original: "divaḥ"</note> or stand in the place of daughters—shining forth, create for people (specifically the sacrificers) the ability to move about and perform their various activities.

---

## Hymn Text

->॥ Now the Second Verse ॥<-

The wonderful Dawns have stood in the east, like sacrificial posts set up at the rituals. Shining forth, the bright and purifying ones have opened the doors of the fold of darkness. ॥ 2 ॥

**Word-by-word Analysis:**
The wonderful <note>original: "citrāḥ"</note> Dawns <note>original: "uṣasaḥ"</note> have stood <note>original: "asthuḥ"</note> in the east <note>original: "purastāt"</note>, like <note>original: "iva"</note> sacrificial posts <note>original: "svaravaḥ"</note> set up <note>original: "mitāḥ"</note> at the sacrifices <note>original: "adhvareṣu"</note>. They have opened <note>original: "avran"</note> wide <note>original: "vi"</note> the doors <note>original: "dvārā"</note> of the fold <note>original: "vrajasya"</note> of darkness <note>original: "tamasaḥ"</note>, being bright <note>original: "śucayaḥ"</note> and purifying <note>original: "pāvakāḥ"</note> as they shine <note>original: "ucchantiḥ"</note>. ॥ 2 ॥

## Commentary (Sayana)

The wonderful and beautiful Dawns have taken their place <note>original: "asthuḥ"</note> in the eastern direction. That is to say, they have spread out. A comparison <note>term: dṛṣṭānta (an illustration or simile)</note> is provided: like sacrificial posts <note>term: svaru (traditionally a chip of wood from the post, but here the post itself)</note> that are fixed in the ground <note>original: "khātāḥ"</note> during sacrifices. Just as those posts shine in front of the altar, so do the Dawns. Although the word *svaru* usually refers to the first chip of wood that falls when carving the sacrificial post—as it is said in the ritual texts, "the first chip that falls should be made into the *svaru*"—here it refers to the entire post. This is understood because they are described as "fixed" <note>original: "mita"</note> and because other Vedic passages describe "the sacrificial posts with their head-pieces." These bright and purifying Dawns have opened wide <note>original: "vyavṛṇvan"</note> the doors of the darkness that encloses or obstructs <note>original: "vrajasya"</note> the world.

---

## Hymn Text

->॥ Now the Third Verse ॥<-

Shining today, may the wealthy Dawns awaken the liberal patrons for the giving of gifts. In the midst of the unsightly darkness, let the stingy merchants sleep without waking. ॥ 3 ॥

**Word-by-word Analysis:**
Shining <note>original: "ucchantiḥ"</note> today <note>original: "adya"</note>, may the wealthy <note>original: "maghonīḥ"</note> Dawns <note>original: "uṣasaḥ"</note> awaken <note>original: "citayanta"</note> the liberal patrons <note>original: "bhojān"</note> for the giving of wealth <note>original: "rādho-deyāya"</note>. Within <note>original: "antaḥ"</note> the unsightly <note>original: "acitre"</note> darkness, in the very middle <note>original: "vi-madhye"</note> of the gloom <note>original: "tamasaḥ"</note>, let the stingy ones <note>term: paṇayaḥ (the Panis, a class of beings known for withholding wealth)</note> sleep <note>original: "sasantu"</note>, remaining unawakened <note>original: "abudhyamānāḥ"</note>. ॥ 3 ॥

## Commentary (Sayana)

Today, on this day, as they shine and dispel the darkness, the wealthy <note>original: "maghonīḥ"</note> Dawns awaken the liberal patrons—those sacrificers who provide food—to give wealth such as the Soma juice. In the "unsightly" <note>original: "acitre"</note> darkness—meaning the extremely deep gloom that is not fit to be seen—let the *Panis* <note>note: These are compared to greedy merchants who do not give anything in sacrifice.</note> remain sleeping without waking up.

<note>
The imagery here contrasts the "liberal givers" (bhojan), who wake up with the Dawn to perform sacrifices, with the "stingy ones" (panis), who are left behind in the darkness. The Dawn is not just a physical light but a moral force that distinguishes between the generous and the miserly.
</note>

<summary>This page contains Sayana's commentary on Rig Veda 4.51, verses 2 and 3, where the Dawns are compared to sacrificial posts and are asked to awaken the generous patrons while leaving the stingy Panis in darkness.</summary>
<keywords>Ushas, Dawn, Sayana, sacrificial post, Svaru, Panis, generosity, darkness, Vedic ritual</keywords>

<meta>This page continues the translation of Rig Veda, Mandala 4, Hymn 51, dedicated to Ushas (the Dawn). It follows the previous page's discussion of the first three verses and here covers verses 4, 5, and the beginning of verse 6. ## Hymn Text

-> ॥ Now the Fourth Verse ॥ <-

May that ancient or new journeying-vehicle of yours, O divine Dawns, be with us many times today; that vehicle by which you, O wealthy ones, shone forth wealthily upon the nine-fold <term>Navagva</term>, the ten-fold <term>Dashagva</term>, and the seven-mouthed <term>Angiras</term>. ॥ 4 ॥

-> Word-by-word Analysis <-

Many times <note>original: "kuvit"</note>; that <note>original: "saḥ"</note>; divine ones <note>original: "devīḥ"</note>; ancient <note>original: "sanayaḥ"</note>; new <note>original: "navaḥ"</note>; or <note>original: "vā"</note>; journey/vehicle <note>original: "yāmaḥ"</note>; may it be <note>original: "babhūyāt"</note>; O Dawns <note>original: "uṣasaḥ"</note>; of you/for you <note>original: "vaḥ"</note>; today <note>original: "adya"</note>; by which <note>original: "yena"</note>; for the nine-fold ones <note>original: "navagve"</note>; for the Angiras <note>original: "aṅgire"</note>; for the ten-fold ones <note>original: "daśagve"</note>; for the seven-mouthed <note>original: "saptāsye"</note>; O wealthy ones <note>original: "revatīḥ"</note>; wealthily/brilliantly <note>original: "revat"</note>; indeed <note>original: "ūṣu"</note>. ॥ 4 ॥

---

## Commentary (Sayana)

O **divine, shining Dawns**, may that **ancient** or **new journeying-vehicle** <note>original: "yāmaḥ"</note>—the chariot that is the means of your movement—**be present many times** <note>original: "kuvit"</note> on this coming day. The meaning is: may it arrive. By **which** chariot, O **wealthy ones**, you have shone forth the light of dawn for the **Angiras** group—specifically for the **Navagvas** (those who sacrifice for nine months), the **Dashagvas** (those who sacrifice for ten months), and the **seven-mouthed** <note>original: "saptāsye"</note> ones, meaning those whose mouths are endowed with the seven poetic meters <note>original: "sapta-cchando-yukta-mukhe"</note>. This refers to those two specific groups and all others belonging to the clan of the Angirases. As it is said elsewhere: "The Navagva and the Dashagva are the best of the Angirases" (Rig Veda 10.62.6). You have shone **wealthily** <note>original: "revat"</note>, which means in a way that is faultless and grand.

---

## Hymn Text

-> ॥ Now the Fifth Verse ॥ <-

For you, O divine Dawns, travel around all worlds instantly with horses yoked by the Sacred Law, awakening the sleeping living being—both the biped and the quadruped—to move about for their daily life. ॥ 5 ॥

-> Word-by-word Analysis <-

You <note>original: "yūyam"</note>; indeed <note>original: "hi"</note>; divine ones <note>original: "devīḥ"</note>; with those yoked by the Sacred Law <note>original: "ṛta-yug-bhiḥ"</note>; horses <note>original: "aśvaiḥ"</note>; around <note>original: "pari"</note>; travel <note>original: "pra-yātha"</note>; worlds <note>original: "bhuvanāni"</note>; instantly <note>original: "sadyaḥ"</note>; awakening <note>original: "pra-bodhayantīḥ"</note>; O Dawns <note>original: "uṣasaḥ"</note>; the sleeping one <note>original: "sasantam"</note>; biped <note>original: "dvipāt"</note>; quadruped <note>original: "catuṣpāt"</note>; for movement/activity <note>original: "carathāya"</note>; the living being <note>original: "jīvam"</note>. ॥ 5 ॥

---

## Commentary (Sayana)

O **shining, divine Dawns**, **indeed** you **travel around** all **worlds instantly** with **horses yoked by the Sacred Law** <note>original: "ṛtayugbhiḥ"</note>—meaning horses that are harnessed to bring the light to the sacrifice. While doing so, what are you doing? You are **awakening** the **sleeping** <note>original: "sasantam"</note> **living beings**, characterized as **bipeds** (humans) and **quadrupeds** (cattle and animals), for the purpose of **movement**—that is, for their daily business and behavior.

-> ॥ Thus ends the first Varga in the eighth Adhyaya of the third Ashtaka ॥ <-

---

## Hymn Text

-> ॥ Now the Sixth Verse ॥ <-

Where is the ancient one among them? Which one is she? By which of them did they establish the arrangements of the <term>Rbhus</term>? When the bright Dawns move in their glory, they are not distinguished; they look alike and are unaging. ॥ 6 ॥

-> Word-by-word Analysis <-

Where <note>original: "kva"</note>; [particle of inquiry] <note>original: "svit"</note>; of these <note>original: "āsām"</note>; which one <note>original: "katamā"</note>; ancient <note>original: "purāṇī"</note>; by which <note>original: "yayā"</note>; arrangements/ordinances <note>original: "vi-dhānā"</note>; they established <note>original: "vi-dadhuḥ"</note>; of the Rbhus <note>original: "ṛbhūṇām"</note>; glory/beauty <note>original: "śubham"</note>; which <note>original: "yat"</note>; bright <note>original: "śubhrāḥ"</note>; Dawns <note>original: "uṣasaḥ"</note>; move <note>original: "caranti"</note>; not <note>original: "na"</note>; [prefix for distinction] <note>original: "vi"</note>; are known/distinguished <note>original: "jñāyante"</note>; looking alike <note>original: "sa-dṛśīḥ"</note>; unaging <note>original: "ajuryāḥ"</note>. ॥ 6 ॥

<summary>This page describes the Goddesses of Dawn (Ushas) as they awaken the world and travel in chariots to bless ancient sage-clans like the Angirases. It emphasizes the Dawns' role in transitioning the world from sleep to activity and notes their eternal, unchanging nature.</summary>
<keywords>Ushas, Dawn, Angiras, Navagva, Dashagva, Ṛta (Sacred Law), Rbhus, Vedic sacrifice, Sanskrit commentary</keywords>

<meta>This page continues the commentary on Rig Veda, Mandala 4, Hymn 51. It begins with the conclusion of the explanation for Verse 6, then presents the full text and commentary for Verse 7 and the start of Verse 8. The discussion continues to focus on the nature of the Dawns (Ushas) as both ancient and eternally new, and their role in the sacrificial ritual.</meta>

## Commentary (Sayana - Fragment from Verse 6)

Among these Dawns, where indeed has she gone today? Which one is the **ancient** <note>original: "purāṇī"</note> one? She, by whom the **Rbhus** <note>divine artisans in Vedic mythology</note> performed the **regulations** <note>original: "vidhānā"</note>—the fashioning of the sacrificial cups and other such works. Or rather, the bright, radiant Dawns perform **beauty** <note>original: "śubhaṃ"</note>, creating splendor and light; they are **un-aging** <note>original: "ajūryā"</note>, not decaying, and eternally new, so they cannot be distinguished. Because they are **similar** <note>original: "sadṛśīḥ"</note>, having one and the same form on all days, it is not known which are today’s and which are those of old. This similarity of the Dawns—"Similar today, similar indeed tomorrow"—is established in another verse <note>Rig Veda 1.123.8</note>.

---

-> || Now the Seventh Verse || <-

## Hymn Text

Indeed, those auspicious Dawns were present of old, possessing glory through their approach, born of the cosmic order and truthful; in whom the sacrificer, striving with hymns, praising and reciting, obtained wealth instantly. ॥ 7 ॥

Those <note>original: "tāḥ"</note>; indeed <note>original: "gha"</note>; those <note>original: "tāḥ"</note>; auspicious <note>original: "bhadrāḥ"</note>; Dawns <note>original: "uṣasaḥ"</note>; of old <note>original: "purā"</note>; were <note>original: "āsuḥ"</note>; possessing glory through approach <note>original: "abhiṣṭi-dyumnāḥ"</note>; born of the cosmic order and truthful <note>original: "ṛtajāta-satyāḥ"</note>; in whom <note>original: "yāsu"</note>; the sacrificer <note>original: "ījānaḥ"</note>; striving <note>original: "śaśamānaḥ"</note>; with hymns <note>original: "ukthaiḥ"</note>; praising <note>original: "stuvan"</note>; reciting <note>original: "śaṃsan"</note>; wealth <note>original: "draviṇam"</note>; instantly <note>original: "sadyaḥ"</note>; obtained <note>original: "āpa"</note>. ॥ 7 ॥

## Commentary (Sayana)

**Those indeed**: the word "indeed" <note>original: "gha"</note> is used for emphasis or fame. Those helpful, **auspicious**—meaning beautiful or worthy of praise—**Dawns were present of old**. They possess **glory through their approach** <note>original: "abhiṣṭi-dyumnāḥ"</note>, meaning wealth is obtained simply by their arrival. They are **born of the cosmic order and truthful** <note>original: "ṛtajāta-satyāḥ"</note>, meaning they are born for the sake of the **Rita** <note>the sacred cosmic order or the sacrifice</note> and their rewards are unfailing. In the presence of these Dawns, the one **performing the sacrifice** <note>original: "ījānaḥ"</note>, **striving** with **hymns** <note>original: "uktha"</note>, **praising** with chants, and **reciting** the sacrificial verses, **obtains wealth instantly**. The connection is that such Dawns are truly auspicious.

---

-> || Now the Eighth Verse || <-

## Hymn Text

They move hither from the east, alike from every side, spreading out from the same place; the goddesses of the cosmic order, waking from the seat of sacrifice, the Dawns are praised like the release of cattle. ॥ 8 ॥

Those <note>original: "tāḥ"</note>; hither <note>original: "ā"</note>; move <note>original: "caranti"</note>; alike <note>original: "samanā"</note>; from the east <note>original: "purastāt"</note>; from the same [place] <note>original: "samānataḥ"</note>; alike <note>original: "samanā"</note>; spreading <note>original: "paprathānāḥ"</note>; of the cosmic order <note>original: "ṛtasya"</note>; goddesses <note>original: "devīḥ"</note>; from the seat <note>original: "sadasaḥ"</note>; waking <note>original: "budhānāḥ"</note>; of cattle <note>original: "gavām"</note>; like <note>original: "na"</note>; releases <note>original: "sargāḥ"</note>; Dawns <note>original: "uṣasaḥ"</note>; are praised <note>original: "jarante"</note>. ॥ 8 ॥

## Commentary (Sayana)

**Those Dawns move** hither from all sides. They are **alike** <note>original: "samanā"</note>—equal in all directions—coming **from the east**, the forward direction. They come **from the same place**, meaning from the mid-air or atmosphere, **spreading** themselves everywhere. They are the **goddesses of the cosmic order** <note>original: "ṛtasya devīḥ"</note>. They are **waking** <note>original: "budhānāḥ"</note> the **seat** of the sacrifice—meaning they awaken the priests and the patrons present there. <note>The grammatical form here implies a causative meaning: "causing to wake."</note> Such magnificent Dawns **are praised** <note>original: "jarante"</note>. They are like the **release of cattle**...

<summary>This page describes the Dawns as eternally recurring deities who bring immediate wealth to sacrificers and awaken the ritual assembly from the east, comparing their appearance to the release of cattle from a pen.</summary>
<keywords>Ushas, Dawns, Sayana, Rbhu, sacrifice, Rita, cosmic order, wealth, hymns, cattle metaphor</keywords>

--- Page 298 ---
<meta>This page continues the commentary on Rig Veda, Mandala 4, Hymn 51, focusing on the transition from Verse 8 to the final three verses of the hymn (9-11). It follows the previous discussion regarding the repetitive yet ever-fresh nature of the Dawns.</meta>

...like the release of waters; like the out-pouring of cows <note>original: "gavāṃ sargā" — a common Vedic metaphor for rays of light being released like cattle from a pen</note>, so are the rays. As it is heard in scripture: **"The rays are like the release of waters"** <note>Rig Veda 4.52.5</note>. Just as those waters and rays are praised everywhere because of their constant connection to the world and their helpfulness, so too are these Dawns praised.

---

->॥ Now the Ninth Verse ॥<-

## Hymn Text
Those very Dawns move together, similar and uniform, of un-decaying color. Hiding the dark, vast void with their shining bodies, they are radiant, pure, and glowing. ॥ 9 ॥

**Word-for-word analysis:**
Those <note>original: "tāḥ"</note> ; indeed <note>original: "it"</note> ; now <note>original: "nu"</note> ; truly <note>original: "eva"</note> ; together <note>original: "samanā"</note> ; uniform <note>original: "samānīḥ"</note> ; of un-decaying/infinite color <note>original: "amīta-varṇāḥ"</note> ; Dawns <note>original: "uṣasaḥ"</note> ; move <note>original: "caranti"</note> ; hiding <note>original: "gūhentīḥ"</note> ; the vast void <note>original: "abhvam"</note> ; the dark <note>original: "asitam"</note> ; with glowing <note>original: "ruśadbhiḥ"</note> ; bright <note>original: "śukrāḥ"</note> ; bodies <note>original: "tanubhiḥ"</note> ; pure <note>original: "śucayaḥ"</note> ; shining <note>original: "rucānāḥ"</note>. ॥ 9 ॥

## Commentary (Sayana)
Those very Dawns—the word *it* is a particle used for emphasis. Now, *together* means in one way or uniformly. *Uniform* means they possess the same form. *Of un-decaying color* means their colors are either un-harmed or infinite. These Dawns move everywhere. What are they doing? They are hiding the **vast void** <note>original: "abhvam" — Sayana identifies this as a word for "great" or "immense"</note>. This refers to the immense, black form of night. They conceal this darkness with their **glowing bodies**—their own physical forms which are bright, radiant, pure, and shining, or rather, making everything else shine.

---

->॥ Now the Tenth Verse ॥<-

## Hymn Text
O Daughters of Heaven, shining forth, grant us wealth accompanied by offspring, O Goddesses. Awaking from a pleasant state to meet you, may we become masters of heroic strength. ॥ 10 ॥

**Word-for-word analysis:**
Wealth <note>original: "rayim"</note> ; of Heaven <note>original: "divaḥ"</note> ; Daughters <note>original: "duhitaraḥ"</note> ; shining forth <note>original: "vibhātīḥ"</note> ; possessing offspring <note>original: "prajā-vantam"</note> ; grant <note>original: "yacchata"</note> ; among us <note>original: "asmāsu"</note> ; Goddesses <note>original: "devīḥ"</note> ; from a pleasant state <note>original: "syonāt"</note> ; toward <note>original: "ā"</note> ; you <note>original: "vaḥ"</note> ; awaking <note>original: "prati-budhyamānāḥ"</note> ; of heroic strength <note>original: "su-vīryasya"</note> ; masters <note>original: "patayaḥ"</note> ; may we be <note>original: "syāma"</note>. ॥ 10 ॥

## Commentary (Sayana)
O **Daughters of Heaven** <note>the Dawns are poetically described as the daughters of the shining Sun or the Sky</note>, who shine forth or perform a special kind of illumination: grant unto us **wealth** <note>original: "rayim"</note> that is accompanied by children and grand-children. O Goddesses, awaking from a **pleasant state** <note>original: "syonāt" — refers to the comfort of sleep or a happy home</note> to greet you, may we be the masters and protectors of wealth that includes heroic sons and strength.

<note>Ritual application note:</note>
One should recite the verse starting with "That of yours, Heaven..." at the moment of **daybreak** <note>original: "vyuṣṭāyām"</note>.

->॥ The Eleventh Verse ॥<-

## Hymn Text
O Daughters of Heaven, shining forth, I, the beacon of the sacrifice, announce that beauty of yours, O Dawns. May we be famous among the people; may Heaven and the divine Earth grant us that. ॥ 11 ॥

<summary>This page concludes the 51st hymn of Mandala 4, praising the Dawns for their ability to dispel the vast darkness of night and requesting blessings of wealth, offspring, and fame for the sacrificers.</summary>

--- Page 299 ---
<meta>This page concludes the final verse of Hymn 51 and introduces the first two verses of Hymn 52 in the fourth Book (Mandala) of the Rig Veda. It continues the theme of praising the Dawns (Ushas), focusing on their role in the morning ritual and their relationship with the Sun, the Night, and the twin gods, the Ashvins.</meta>

## Hymn Text (RV 4.51.11 conclusion)

**That [blessing], O Daughters of Heaven, O Dawns, who shine forth, I invoke.**
**I, whose signal is the sacrifice, [pray that] we may be possessors of fame among the people.**
**May Heaven and the divine Earth grant us that. ॥ 11 ॥**

**Word-for-word analysis:**
**That** <note>original: "tat"</note> ; **of you** <note>original: "vaḥ"</note> ; **of Heaven** <note>original: "divaḥ"</note> ; **Daughters** <note>original: "duhitaḥ"</note> ; **shining forth** <note>original: "vibhātīḥ"</note> ; **near/unto** <note>original: "upa"</note> ; **I speak/invoke** <note>original: "bruve"</note> ; **O Dawns** <note>original: "uṣasaḥ"</note> ; **whose signal is the sacrifice** <note>original: "yajñaketuḥ"</note> ; **we** <note>original: "vayaṃ"</note> ; **may we be** <note>original: "syāma"</note> ; **possessing fame/glory** <note>original: "yaśasaṃ"</note> ; **among people** <note>original: "janeṣu"</note> ; **that** <note>original: "tat"</note> ; **Heaven** <note>original: "dyauḥ"</note> ; **and** <note>original: "ca"</note> ; **may they grant** <note>original: "dhattāṃ"</note> ; **Earth** <note>original: "pṛthivī"</note> ; **and** <note>original: "ca"</note> ; **divine** <note>original: "devī"</note>. ॥ 11 ॥

---

## Commentary (Sayana)

O Daughters of Heaven, O Dawns, I invoke you who are shining forth for the reward that will be described in the first part of the second half of the verse. I, who am "one whose signal is the sacrifice" <note>original: "yajñaketuḥ" — meaning the ritual itself is the sign or indicator of the poet's intent</note>, approach and speak to you. Then, the poet speaks in the plural: "We, the praisers, among our equals, may we be the masters of fame, glory, or wealth." May Heaven and the divine Earth grant and sustain that fame.

->**॥ Thus ends the second section (varga) of the eighth chapter (adhyaya) of the third book (ashtaka) ॥**<-

The seventh hymn, beginning with "Prati ṣya," contains seven verses in the Gayatri meter <note>a sacred poetic rhythm of three lines with eight syllables each</note> and is dedicated to the goddess Dawn (Ushas). The Index <note>original: "Anukramani"</note> states: "*Prati ṣvā*, seven, Gayatri." This hymn is intended to be recited during the morning litany <note>original: "Prataranuvaka"</note> in the Dawn-ritual, and specifically during the invocation to the twin gods of the morning, the Ashvins <note>original: "Ashvina-shastra"</note>, in the Gayatri section. This is indicated in the ritual manuals <note>Ashvalayana Shrauta Sutra 4.14</note>: "Then the dawn-hymn: *Prati ṣvā sūnarī*."

->**॥ Here is the First Verse ॥**<-

## Hymn Text (RV 4.52.1)

**She, the noble leader, the mother of all, shining out around her sister [the Night],**
**the Daughter of Heaven has been seen. ॥ 1 ॥**

**Word-for-word analysis:**
**Towards** <note>original: "prati"</note> ; **She** <note>original: "ṣvā/sā"</note> ; **noble leader** <note>original: "sūnarī"</note> ; **mother/generator** <note>original: "janī"</note> ; **shining out/dispelling darkness** <note>original: "vyucchantī"</note> ; **around** <note>original: "pari"</note> ; **of the sister** <note>original: "svasuḥ"</note> ; **of Heaven** <note>original: "divaḥ"</note> ; **has been seen** <note>original: "adarśi"</note> ; **Daughter** <note>original: "duhitā"</note>. ॥ 1 ॥

---

## Commentary (Sayana)

"She" <note>original: "svā"</note> is the one being praised. She is a "noble leader" <note>original: "sūnarī"</note> because she excellently guides living beings, and she is the "mother" <note>original: "janī"</note> because she produces the fruits or rewards of actions. She shines out "around her sister" <note>original: "svasuḥ"</note>, meaning she appears at the conclusion of the Night, who is like a sister to her. It is said elsewhere in the Rig Veda (1.124.8): "The sister [Dawn] yields to her elder sister [Night]." Ushas, the daughter of the shining Sun or Heaven, is now seen by everyone.

->**॥ Now the Second Verse ॥**<-

## Hymn Text (RV 4.52.2)

**Like a mare, wonderful and bright, the mother of the rays, the observer of Truth,**
**Dawn has become the friend of the Ashvins. ॥ 2 ॥**

**Word-for-word analysis:**
**A mare** <note>original: "aśvā"</note> ; **like** <note>original: "iva"</note> ; **wonderful/to be looked at** <note>original: "citrā"</note> ; **bright/shining** <note>original: "aruṣī"</note> ; **mother** <note>original: "mātā"</note> ; **of the cows/rays** <note>original: "gavām"</note> ; **possessing Truth/Order** <note>original: "ṛtāvarī"</note> ; **friend** <note>original: "sakhā"</note> ; **has become** <note>original: "abhūt"</note> ; **of the two Ashvins** <note>original: "aśvinoḥ"</note> ; **Dawn** <note>original: "uṣāḥ"</note>. ॥ 2 ॥

---

## Commentary (Sayana)

Like a "mare" <note>original: "aśveva"</note>, she is "wonderful" or worthy of being noticed and "bright" or glowing. She is the "mother" or creator of the "cows," which here refers to the rays of light. She is "the observer of Truth" <note>original: "ṛtāvarī"</note>, meaning she is associated with the sacred sacrifice. Dawn has become the "friend" of the twin Ashvins, meaning she shares the same renown and is praised alongside them. Because the Ashvins and the Dawn are praised together in the ritual, they are considered to have a mutual friendship.

<summary>This page concludes Hymn 51 with a prayer for fame and divine protection, and begins Hymn 52, which personifies the Dawn (Ushas) as a noble leader and a sister to the Night. The commentary explains the ritual context of these verses and Dawn's mythological friendship with the Ashvins.</summary>
<keywords>Ushas, Dawn, Ashvins, Gayatri meter, Sayana, Rig Veda, Vedic ritual, morning litany, daughters of heaven, Rita (Truth/Order)</keywords>

->॥ Now the Third Verse ॥<-

## Hymn Text
**And you are the friend of the Ashvins <note>The Ashvins are the twin physicians of the gods who travel in a golden chariot before the dawn.</note>; and you are the mother of the cows; and, O Dawn, you rule over wealth.** ॥ 3 ॥
<note>RV 4.52.3</note>

**And** <note>original: "uta"</note> ; **friend** <note>original: "sakhā"</note> ; **you are** <note>original: "asi"</note> ; **of the two Ashvins** <note>original: "aśvinoff"</note> ; **and** <note>original: "uta"</note> ; **mother** <note>original: "mātā"</note> ; **of the cows** <note>original: "gavām"</note> ; **you are** <note>original: "asi"</note> ; **and** <note>original: "uta"</note> ; **O Dawn** <note>original: "uṣaḥ"</note> ; **of wealth** <note>original: "vasvaḥ"</note> ; **you rule** <note>original: "īśiṣe"</note>. ॥ 3 ॥

---

## Commentary (Sayana)
And further, you are the friend of the Ashvins. And also, you are the mother of the "cows" <note>original: "gavām" — here interpreted as the rays of light</note>. And further, O Dawn, you rule over—meaning you are the mistress of—wealth and riches.

---

->॥ Now the Fourth Verse ॥<-

## Hymn Text
**O you who drive away hatred, O wise one, O bringer of joyful truths! We have awakened to greet you with our hymns.** ॥ 4 ॥
<note>RV 4.52.4</note>

**Driving away hatred** <note>original: "yavayaddveṣasam"</note> ; **you** <note>original: "tvā"</note> ; **O wise/knowing one** <note>original: "cikitvit"</note> ; **O bringer of joyful truths** <note>original: "sūnṛtāvari"</note> ; **towards/in response** <note>original: "prati"</note> ; **with hymns** <note>original: "stomaiḥ"</note> ; **we have awakened** <note>original: "abhūtsmahi"</note>. ॥ 4 ॥

---

## Commentary (Sayana)
**Driving away hatred** <note>original: "yāvayaddveṣasaṃ"</note>: This refers to the Dawn who separates or removes enemies and those who harbor hatred. Alternatively, it means those who hate are pushed aside. For indeed, enemies who are ready to strike in the night flee during the time of dawn. We address **you**, who are **wise** <note>original: "cikित्वित्" — making things known</note>, O **bringer of joyful truths** <note>original: "sūnṛtāvari"</note>. "Sunrita" is a name for speech; you who possess such speech, O Goddess, we **awaken in response** to you with **hymns** or songs of praise. The meaning is: "we praise you."

---

->॥ Now the Fifth Verse ॥<-

## Hymn Text
**Her auspicious rays have appeared like herds of cows let loose. Dawn has filled the wide expanse.** ॥ 5 ॥
<note>RV 4.52.5</note>

**Towards/in response** <note>original: "prati"</note> ; **auspicious** <note>original: "bhadrāḥ"</note> ; **they have appeared** <note>original: "ahrakṣata"</note> ; **of cows** <note>original: "gavām"</note> ; **herds/bursts** <note>original: "sargāḥ"</note> ; **like** <note>original: "na"</note> ; **rays** <note>original: "raśmayaḥ"</note> ; **hither** <note>original: "ā"</note> ; **Dawn** <note>original: "uṣāḥ"</note> ; **has filled** <note>original: "aprāḥ"</note> ; **wide** <note>original: "uru"</note> ; **space/movement** <note>original: "jrayāḥ"</note>. ॥ 5 ॥

---

## Commentary (Sayana)
The **auspicious** and praiseworthy rays **have appeared**; they are clearly seen. Like the **bursts of cows** <note>Sayana glosses "gavām" here as "udakānām," meaning the gushing streams of water</note>, this Dawn has **filled** the **wide expanse** with great light.

---

->॥ Now the Sixth Verse ॥<-

## Hymn Text
**O radiant one, you who fill [the world], you have uncovered the darkness with your light. O Dawn, favor our ritual food.** ॥ 6 ॥
<note>RV 4.52.6</note>

**Filling** <note>original: "āpaprūṣī"</note> ; **O radiant one** <note>original: "vibhāvari"</note> ; **apart/away** <note>original: "vi"</note> ; **you have uncovered/removed** <note>original: "āvaḥ"</note> ; **with light** <note>original: "jyotiṣā"</note> ; **darkness** <note>original: "tamaḥ"</note> ; **O Dawn** <note>original: "uṣaḥ"</note> ; **along/after** <note>original: "anu"</note> ; **ritual food/nature** <note>original: "svadhām"</note> ; **favor/protect** <note>original: "ava"</note>. ॥ 6 ॥

---

## Commentary (Sayana)
O **radiant one**, O shining Dawn, you who are **filling** the world with your brilliance, you have **uncovered** or removed the **darkness** with your **light**. Furthermore, **favor** or protect the **ritual food** <note>original: "svadhā" — food in the form of an offering</note> that follows your appearance.

The verse beginning "You spread over the sky" <note>original: "ā dyāṃ tanoṣi"</note> is the recitation for the Dawns during the offerings to the gods. This is indicated in the ritual manuals: "You spread over the sky with your rays, bringing desirable nourishment..." <note>Aśvalāyana Śrauta Sūtra 1. 16.</note>

<meta>This page transitions from the end of a hymn to the Dawn (Ushas) into a new hymn dedicated to the solar deity Savitr. It includes the ritual instructions for the hymn's use in Vedic sacrifices and detailed linguistic analysis by the 14th-century commentator Sayana.</meta>

## Hymn Text

-> ॥ This is the seventh verse ॥ <-

**You overspread the sky with your rays, and the vast, beloved mid-air, O Dawn, with your bright light.** ॥ 7 ॥

**Towards/Over** <note>original: "ā"</note> ; **the sky** <note>original: "dyām"</note> ; **you spread** <note>original: "tanoṣi"</note> ; **with rays** <note>original: "raśmibhiḥ"</note> ; **towards/over** <note>original: "ā"</note> ; **the mid-air** <note>original: "antarikṣam"</note> ; **vast** <note>original: "uru"</note> ; **beloved** <note>original: "priyam"</note> ; **O Dawn** <note>original: "uṣaḥ"</note> ; **with bright** <note>original: "śukreṇa"</note> ; **with light** <note>original: "śociṣā"</note>. ॥ 7 ॥

---

## Commentary (Sayana)

O Dawn <term>Ushas; the goddess of the morning</term>, you spread over the sky or heaven with your rays. You spread over the vast, wide, and beloved mid-air with your rays. You perform this action being endowed with bright and shining light.

-> ॥ Thus ends the third varga <note>a small sub-section of verses</note> in the eighth chapter of the third book ॥ <-

The hymn beginning with the words "That [wealth] of the god" <note>original: "tad devasya"</note> consists of seven verses. It is the eighth hymn of this section, seen by the Seer <term>Rishi; a divinely inspired poet-sage</term> Vamadeva. It is composed in the Jagati meter <note>a Vedic meter of 48 syllables</note> and is dedicated to the deity Savitr <term>The Solar deity representing the impelling force of the sun</term>. The ancient Index <note>Anukramani</note> states: "The hymn to Savitr beginning 'That [wealth] of the god' is in the Jagati meter." Regarding its ritual application: in the third day of the *Abhiplava* ceremony, during the litany to the All-Gods <note>Vaishvadeva-shastra</note>, this hymn to Savitr is recited. This is indicated in the ritual manuals: "The three verses 'That [wealth] of the god' and 'With ghee, heaven and earth' [are used]." <note>original reference: Ashvalayana Shrauta Sutra 7.7</note>.

---

## Hymn Text

-> ॥ Now the first verse ॥ <-

**We pray for that great, desirable wealth of the divine Savitr, the wise one who possesses vital strength; with which he himself bestows a dwelling upon the giver of offerings. May that great god rise for us throughout the nights.** ॥ 1 ॥

**That** <note>original: "tat"</note> ; **of the god** <note>original: "devasya"</note> ; **of Savitr** <note>original: "savituḥ"</note> ; **desirable/to be chosen** <note>original: "vāryam"</note> ; **great** <note>original: "mahat"</note> ; **we choose/pray for** <note>original: "vṛṇīmahe"</note> ; **of the one with vital force** <note>original: "asurasya"</note> ; **of the wise one** <note>original: "pracetasaḥ"</note> ;
**dwelling/protection** <note>original: "chardiḥ"</note> ; **by which** <note>original: "yena"</note> ; **to the giver** <note>original: "dāśuṣe"</note> ; **he bestows** <note>original: "yacchati"</note> ; **by himself** <note>original: "tmanā"</note> ; **that** <note>original: "tat"</note> ; **to us** <note>original: "naḥ"</note> ; **great** <note>original: "mahān"</note> ; **up** <note>original: "ut"</note> ; **may he go/rise** <note>original: "ayān"</note> ; **the god** <note>original: "devaḥ"</note> ; **with the nights** <note>original: "aktubhiḥ"</note>. ॥ 1 ॥

---

## Commentary (Sayana)

We pray for and request that wealth which is "desirable" (worthy of being chosen) and "great" (venerable) belonging to the god Savitr, the impeller of all. The word **Asura** here means "one who possesses the strength of an Asura" <note>original: "asurabala"; in the early Vedas, Asura refers to divine power rather than a demon</note>. He is **Pracetas**, meaning one of excellent intellect. This refers back to the God. By which wealth he himself bestows a **Chardis**—this is a name for a house or dwelling—meaning the collection of wealth characterized by a home, upon the sacrificer who has given oblations. May that great god Savitr rise up for us through the **nights** <note>original: "aktubhiḥ"</note>. This term also implies the days; it means may he rise for us during all days and at all times. Alternatively, "Chardis" can be a name for light/splendor; in that case, the prayer is: may that light rise up for us.

---

## Hymn Text

-> ॥ Now the second verse ॥ <-

**The upholder of heaven, the lord of the world, the wise one puts on his golden mantle. The far-seeing Savitr, spreading out and filling the wide space, has generated praiseworthy happiness.** ॥ 2 ॥

<vocab>
- Ushas: Goddess of Dawn
- Savita: The Solar deity (Savitr)
- Asura: Here used in the sense of 'mighty' or 'possessing vital force'
- Pracetas: Wise, attentive
- Chardis: Protection, house
- Vamadeva: The Rishi (seer) of the hymn
- Jagati: A meter consisting of four lines of 12 syllables each
- Savicha: Dedicated to Savitr
</vocab>

## Hymn Text

<note>Rig Veda 4.53.2 (Word-by-word analysis)</note>
**Of heaven** | **sustainer** | **of the world** | **Lord of creatures** | **golden** | **mantle** | **towards** | **he puts on** | **the wise** | **far-seeing** | **spreading out** | **filling** | **broadly** | **he has generated** | **Savitr** | **happiness** | **praiseworthy** ॥ 2 ॥

---

-> ॥ Now the third verse ॥ <-

<note>Rig Veda 4.53.3 (Connected text)</note>
The divine one has filled the celestial and earthly regions; he creates a song of praise for his own function. Savitr has stretched out his arms at his impulse, settling the world and setting it in motion through the days and nights. ॥ 3 ॥

<note>Rig Veda 4.53.3 (Word-by-word analysis)</note>
**He has filled** | **the regions** | **celestial** | **earthly** | **praise/song** | **the god** | **he makes** | **for his own** | **function/law** | **forth** | **the two arms** | **he has stretched** | **Savitr** | **at the impulse** | **settling** | **impelling** | **through the nights/days** | **the world** ॥ 3 ॥

---

<note>Rig Veda 4.53.4 (Connected text)</note>
Watching over the worlds, the undeceivable god Savitr protects the sacred laws. He has stretched out his arms for the creatures of the world; he, whose laws are firm, rules over the great path. ॥ 4 ॥

<note>Rig Veda 4.53.4 (Word-by-word analysis)</note>
**Undeceivable** | **the worlds** | **watching over** | **the laws** | **the god** | **Savitr** | **around** | **he protects** | **forth** | **he has stretched** | **the two arms** | **of the world** | **for the creatures** | **whose laws are firm** | **of the great** | **path** | **he rules** ॥ 4 ॥

---

## Commentary (Sayana)

<note>Commentary on Rig Veda 4.53.2</note>
He is the **sustainer** <note>original: "dhartā"</note> **of heaven** <note>the celestial realm</note>. Not only of heaven, but also the **Lord of creatures** <term>Prajāpati; a title for a creator or protector deity</term> and the sustainer **of the world**, the entire universe. He protects the creatures through the manifestation of light and rain. The **wise** and learned god **puts on** <note>covers himself with</note> a **golden mantle** <term>drāpi; refers to a cloak or protective armor, here signifying the sun's brilliant golden light</term> at every sunrise. That same **far-seeing** god, who sees in various ways, **has generated** or produced **broad** and abundant **happiness** which is **praiseworthy**, while **spreading out** and **filling** the universe with his famous splendor.

<note>Commentary on Rig Veda 4.53.3</note>
This god, Savitr, **has filled** with his own light the **celestial** and **earthly regions** <term>rajāṃsi; the various realms or "dusts" of the universe</term>. Indeed, there are three heavens and three earths, for it is heard in the scriptures: "Sustaining the three earths and also the three heavens" <note>quoting Rig Veda 2.27.8</note>. The god **makes** or creates a **praise** or hymn **for his own function** <note>original: "dharmaṇe"</note>, meaning for his own support. **Savitr**, at the moment of his **impulse** <note>original: "savīmani"</note> or command, **has stretched out** <note>extended</note> his own **two arms**. What is he doing? He is **settling** the **world** by establishing everyone in their respective duties, and **impelling** them to action through his **splendors** <note>original: "aktubhiḥ"</note>. Alternatively, the word "aktubhiḥ" is a name for the night; thus, it means he does this through all nights and days, at all times.

## Critical Notes
- The commentator quotes **Rig Veda 2.27.8** ("Sustaining the three earths and also the three heavens") to justify the plural use of "regions" as referring to the Vedic cosmology of triple worlds.
- The verb **asrāk** <note>he stretched</note> is interpreted by the commentator as "extending" or "wiping forth."
- The term **aktubhiḥ** has a dual interpretation: either "with rays of light" or "by the nights/days," indicating the cyclical nature of the sun's influence.

<vocab>
**Savitā**: The solar deity, specifically representing the sun before sunrise or the stimulating power behind the sun.
**Prajāpatiḥ**: Lord of Progeny; a title used here to emphasize the sun's role in sustaining life.
**Drāpi**: A mantle or cloak; metaphorically, the golden atmosphere or light that clothes the sun.
**Vichakṣaṇa**: Far-seeing or all-seeing; a common epithet for solar deities who observe all human deeds from above.
**Savīmani**: From the root *su* (to impel); the divine "push" or command that starts the day.
**Dhṛtavrataḥ**: One whose laws or "vows" are fixed; referring to the unchanging regularity of natural laws (Rta).
</vocab>
