The commentary by Sayana explains the sun's movement as a divine extension of arms that establishes the laws of day and night.</summary>
<keywords>Savitr, Rig Veda, Sayana, solar deity, Vedic cosmology, Prajapati, golden mantle, divine law</keywords>

<header>Mandala 4. Adhyaya 5. Sukta 53. ] || Third Book || 235</header>

## Commentary (Sayana) - Verse 4 (Continued)

The deity Savitr, who is undeceivable—meaning he cannot be harmed by others—illuminates and brightens the worlds and protects the <term>vratāni</term> <note>sacred laws or habitual duties</note> of all living creatures. He has stretched out <note>original: "prasārāyati"</note> his two arms for the benefit of the inhabitants of the world. This means he grants permission for everyone to engage in their respective tasks, as all activities are dependent upon the Sun. Indeed, the sacred scripture <note>Śruti</note> states: "Savitr is truly the lord of impulses" <note>original: "Savitā vai prasavānāmīśa iti hi śrutiḥ"</note>. He, whose laws are firm <note>original: "dhṛtavrataḥ"</note>, performs his role in this way and rules over the great path of the world.

---

## Hymn Text - Verse 5

-> ॥ Now the Fifth Verse ॥ <-

Thrice the mid-region Savitr [encompasses] by his greatness; he is the all-pervading lord of the three realms and the three luminous spheres. He reaches the three heavens and the three earths; by his three laws, he protects us by his own nature. ॥ 5 ॥

**Word-by-word Analysis:**
Thrice | the mid-region | Savitr | by greatness | three | realms | all-pervading | three | luminous spheres | three | heavens | earths | three | reaches | by three | laws | towards | us | protects | by his own nature ॥ 5 ॥

---

## Commentary (Sayana) - Verse 5

This Savitr encompasses the mid-region <term>antarikṣa</term> <note>the space between heaven and earth</note>, which is divided into three parts. The mid-region is called such because it remains between the earth and the heavens. Being all-pervading, he reaches or fills it by his greatness. These three divisions of the atmosphere are the realms of <term>Vayu</term> <note>the wind</note>, <term>Vidyut</term> <note>lightning</note>, and <term>Varuna</term> <note>the god of cosmic order</note>, as confirmed by the scripture: "He enters the world of Vayu, the world of Varuna," and so on.

He also reaches the three <term>rajas</term> <note>realms or spaces</note> which are coloring or illuminating in nature—namely the earth, the mid-region, and the heavens. Note that earlier the specific subdivisions of the mid-region were mentioned, but here they are mentioned in a general sense, so there is no repetition. He reaches the three <term>rocanā</term> <note>luminous spheres</note> by acting as the master of the three places of the shining Agni (Fire), Vayu (Wind), and Aditya (the Sun). 

Furthermore, the subdivisions of heaven and earth are described: He reaches the three heavens known as the realms of Indra, Prajapati, and Satya. Likewise, he reaches the three earths, referring to the internal divisions of the terrestrial realm. In this way, the deity who pervades everything protects us with his three <term>vratas</term> <note>divine laws expressed as seasons</note>—specifically the seasons of heat, rain, and frost—acting through his own benevolent will. May he protect and guard us.

---

## Hymn Text - Verse 6

-> ॥ Now the Sixth Verse ॥ <-

Of great benevolence, the impeller, the one who gives rest, the ruler of both the moving and the stationary; may that divine Savitr grant us protection and a triple-layered shelter for our dwelling, [saving us] from sin. ॥ 6 ॥

**Word-by-word Analysis:**
Greatly benevolent | the impeller | one who gives rest | of the moving | of the stationary | of both | who | the ruler | he | our | god | Savitr | protection | may he grant | for us | for the dwelling | triple-layered | from sin ॥ 6 ॥

<vocab>
<term>Savitā</term> — The deity Savitr (The Impeller or the Sun in its creative aspect)
<term>Antarikṣa</term> — The mid-region or atmospheric level of the universe
<term>Rajas</term> — The regions or realms (often described as a threefold division of space)
<term>Rocana</term> — Luminous spheres or bright celestial realms
<term>Vrata</term> — Divine laws, ordinances, or the seasonal cycles of nature
<term>Sumna</term> — Happiness, favor, or benevolence
<term>Prasavitā</term> — The generator or the one who impels all actions
<term>Niveśanā</term> — One who brings rest or provides a place to dwell
<term>Śarma</term> — Protection, shelter, or refuge
<term>Trivarūtha</term> — Triple-layered or providing protection in three ways (often interpreted as physical, mental, and spiritual)
</vocab>

<summary>This page describes the cosmic reach of the solar deity Savitr, who governs the threefold divisions of the earth, atmosphere, and heavens. He is portrayed as the benevolent protector who establishes the laws of the seasons and provides shelter for all living beings, both moving and stationary.</summary>

## Commentary (Sayana)
He who possesses great happiness <note>original: "bṛhat-sumnaḥ," interpreted as either abundant wealth or great bliss</note>, the Impeller <note>Savitr</note>, the one who permits all actions and is the ultimate destination for everyone. He is the ruler of both the moving world <term>jagat</term> and the stationary <term>tasthivāṃs</term>. May that great divine Savitr grant us shelter <note>original: "śarma"</note>. What kind of shelter? One that is "triple-layered" <note>original: "tri-varūtham," referring to protection in the three stations or realms: earth, atmosphere, and heaven</note>. Let this be for the destruction of our sins <note>original: "aṃhasaḥ kṣayāya"</note>.

In the ritual for the purchase of King Soma <note>the "Rāja-kraya" ceremony</note>, the verse "The god has come" <note>original: "āgan deva"</note> is to be recited as an invitatory prayer. This is indicated in the ritual manuals: "The god has come; let him increase the dwelling with the seasons"—one should pause at this half-verse <note>Aśvalāyana Śrauta Sūtra 4.4</note>.

---

->॥ This is the Seventh Verse ॥<-

## Hymn Text
The divine Savitr has come along with the seasons; may he increase our dwelling and grant us food accompanied by good offspring. May he invigorate us by night and by day; may he bestow upon us wealth characterized by many descendants. ॥ 7 ॥

**Padapatha:**
Toward | has come | the God | with the seasons | let him increase | the dwelling | let him place | for us | Savitr | with good offspring | food |
He | us | by nights | by days | and | let him invigorate | possessing offspring | wealth | in us | completely | let him reach ॥ 7 ॥

## Commentary (Sayana)
**The divine Savitr has come along with the seasons.** Let him arrive <note>grammatical note: "āgan" is a Vedic aorist form of the root "gam," to go/come</note>. Furthermore, **let him increase**—that is, cause to grow—our **dwelling** <note>original: "kṣayam," meaning house or abode</note>. May he **grant**—give—to **us food** <note>original: "iṣam"</note> joined with **good offspring** such as excellent sons. May **he** himself **invigorate** or please **us by nights and by days**—meaning throughout all days. May he **completely reach** or bestow **wealth possessing offspring** among **us**.

->॥ This concludes the fourth section (varga) of the eighth chapter (adhyaya) of the third book (ashtaka) ॥<-

---

## Commentary (Intro to Sukta 54)
The ninth hymn of this section, beginning with "The god has appeared" <note>original: "abhūd devaḥ"</note>, consists of six verses. The seer is Vamadeva, and the deity is Savitr. The final verse is in the <term>Triṣṭubh</term> meter <note>11 syllables per line</note>; the remaining verses, according to the general definition of the meter, are in <term>Jagatī</term> <note>12 syllables per line</note>. Thus the Index <note>Anukramaṇikā</note> states: "The god has appeared; six verses, ending in Trishtubh." 

In the <term>Agniṣṭoma</term> sacrifice, during the litany to the All-Gods <note>Vaiśvadeva-śastra</note>, this hymn is used for the insertion of the Savitr-invocation. As the manual says: "The god has appeared with one and with ten..." <note>Aśvalāyana Śrauta Sūtra 5.18</note>. The first verse is the invitatory prayer for the cup of Savitr. As the manual says: "They proceed with the cup of Savitr: 'The god Savitr has appeared, now to be praised by us...'" <note>Aśvalāyana Śrauta Sūtra 5.18</note>.

->॥ This is the First Verse ॥<-

## Hymn Text
The divine Savitr has appeared; he is now to be praised by us. At this time of the day, he is to be invoked by men. He who distributes treasures to the descendants of Manu <note>humanity</note>, may he bestow the most excellent wealth upon us here. ॥ 1 ॥

<summary>This page concludes the 53rd hymn with a prayer for seasonal prosperity and begins the 54th hymn, which establishes Savitr as the distributor of treasures to humanity during ritual sacrifices.</summary>
<keywords>Savitr, Vamadeva, Agnishtoma sacrifice, seasonal rituals, prosperity, offspring, Vedic meters, Jagati, Trishtubh</keywords>

<meta>This page continues the text and commentary for Mandala 4, Sukta 54 of the Rig Veda. The previous page (236) concluded the discussion on Hymn 53, also dedicated to Savitr. This page begins the new hymn, focusing on Savitr’s role as the distributor of wealth and the granter of immortality to the gods and long life to humans.</meta>

Mandal 4. Anuvaka 5. Sukta 54. || Third Ashtaka || 237

## Hymn Text

The divine Savitr has appeared; he is to be praised by us now. He is to be invoked and spoken of by men <note>meaning the officiating priests</note>. He who distributes treasures to humans, may he, being worthy, grant us the most excellent wealth. ॥ 1 ॥

**Padapatha:**
Savitr | was | the god | to be praised | now | for us | now | he was invoked | to be spoken of | by men |
who | treasures | distributes | for humans | excellent | for us | worthy | wealth | as | granting ॥ 1 ॥

---

## Commentary (Sayana)

That Savitr, the god, has appeared <note>original: "abhūt"; he has become manifest</note>. Therefore, now <note>original: "nu"; quickly</note> he becomes one to be praised <note>worthy of our adoration</note> by us. Now, at the time of the sacrifice, during the third libation <note>original: "tṛtīya-savana"</note>, he is to be spoken of <note>original: "upavācyaḥ"</note>—that is, praised—by men, our own officiating priests. That god, who distributes lovely treasures <note>original: "ratnā"</note>—pleasing wealth—to humans, the children of Manu, for the sake of the <term>yajamāna</term> <note>the patron of the sacrifice</note>; may that god grant us the most excellent and praiseworthy wealth, characterized by cattle and other possessions, in this ritual. This means he should give it. Thus, he has become one to be praised and spoken of.

---

->॥ Now the Second Verse ॥<-

## Hymn Text

For you, first among the gods worthy of sacrifice, grant immortality—the most excellent portion. Thereafter, O Savitr, you unfold for humans, for the sake of the donors <note>the givers of oblations</note>, successive lives. ॥ 2 ॥

**Padapatha:**
To the gods | for | first | worthy of sacrifice | immortality | you grant | portion | highest |
then | indeed | to the giver | O Savitr | you | unfold | successive | lives | for humans ॥ 2 ॥

---

## Commentary (Sayana)

First, indeed, for the gods. The word "hi" <note>indeed</note> indicates a well-known fact. To the gods who are worthy of sacrifice <note>original: "yajñiyebhyaḥ"</note>, you grant <note>original: "suvasi"; you permit or authorize</note> immortality <note>original: "amṛtatvam"</note>—the means to it—which is the highest, most excellent portion, characterized by the Soma juice and other offerings. Immediately after that <note>original: "ād-it"</note>, O Savitr, you unfold <note>original: "vyurṇuṣe"; you reveal or manifest</note> for the donor <note>original: "dāmānam"</note>, the one who gives the oblations. For humans, the <term>yajamānas</term>, you unfold "successive lives" <note>original: "anūcīnā jīvitā"</note>—lives that follow in a sequence, such as fathers, sons, and grandsons. This is the meaning of the sequence. Such lives you unfold afterward.

---

->॥ Now the Third Verse ॥<-

## Hymn Text

Whatever [sin] we have committed through lack of wisdom against the divine folk, through our feeble strength, through pride, or through our human nature—O Savitr, among both gods and humans, declare us sinless here. ॥ 3 ॥

**Padapatha:**
In lack of wisdom | what | we have done | in the divine | folk | by feeble | powers | by abundance | through human nature |
among gods | and | O Savitr | among humans | and | you | us | here | grant | sinless ॥ 3 ॥

---

## Commentary (Sayana)

O Savitr, whatever [sin] we have committed through lack of wisdom <note>original: "acittī"; through ignorance</note> against the divine folk—that is, against the gods or against you—whether through our feeble strength, or through our children and officiating priests who are not strong, or through "abundance" <note>original: "prabhūtī"; meaning the intoxication of power or wealth</note>. That is to say, through the pride of sovereignty. Human-

---
<vocab>
Savitr (सविता): The solar deity as the "Impeller" or stimulator of life and ritual.
Yajamāna (यजमान): The patron or host of the Vedic sacrifice who pays for the ritual and receives its primary benefits.
Padapatha (पदपाठ): The "word-by-word" version of the Vedic text used to ensure perfect preservation of every syllable.
Amṛtatvam (अमृतत्वम्): Immortality; in the Vedas, this is often linked to the drinking of Soma or being granted a place among the gods.
Yajñiya (यज्ञिय): Holy, or specifically "worthy of receiving a share of the sacrifice."
</vocab>

The commentary emphasizes Savitr's role in establishing the order of life for humans (successive generations) and his power to forgive sins committed through ignorance or pride.</summary>

# Rig Veda

## Book 4, Hymn 54, Verses 4–5

...and because of our human nature, whatever sin <note>original: "āgas"</note> we have committed. Not only have we erred against you, but whatever we have done out of ignorance against other gods or fellow humans—may you, in this ritual, declare us sinless <note>original: "anāgasaḥ"</note>. Please grant your permission.

In the offerings to the "God-Impelling" <note>original: "deva-suvām"</note> deities, the verse beginning with "The divine Savitr's [work] is not to be obstructed" serves as the sacrificial offering verse <note>original: "yājyā"</note>. This is indicated in the Ashvalayana Shrauta Sutra (4.11.1): "The divine Savitr's... that is the first for Brihaspati."

->॥ This is the Fourth Verse ॥<-

## Hymn Text

The divine Savitr's work is not to be obstructed; in such a way he shall support the entire world. In the expanse of the earth and in the height of heaven, he of the beautiful fingers impels; that is his Truth. ॥ 4 ॥

**Word-by-word Analysis:**
Not | to be obstructed | of Savitr | the divine | that | in which way | the whole | world | he will support |
that | of the earth | in the expanse | [and] | he of the beautiful fingers | in the height | of heaven | impels | Truth |
of him | that ॥ 4 ॥

---

## Commentary (Sayana)

The work of the divine god Savitr is "not to be obstructed" <note>original: "na pramiye"</note>; it should not be frustrated or diminished. It is not something that can be harmed. <note>Grammar note: The "ken" suffix is used here to denote "worthy of action."</note> Alternatively, the word "divine" <note>original: "daivyasya"</note> is in the genitive case, implying "concerning divine action." 

Why is it indestructible? He explains: "In such a way he shall support the entire world." The work consisting of supporting the universe is not to be obstructed. Likewise, he who has "beautiful fingers" <note>original: "svanguriḥ"</note>—referring to the hands characterized by beautiful rays—impels life both in the "expanse" <note>original: "variman"</note> of the earth (the particle *ā* here means "and") and in the "height" <note>original: "varshman"</note> of the sky. This mentioned work of the god is "Truth" <note>original: "satyam"</note>, meaning it is unshakeable and absolute.

->॥ Now the Fifth Verse ॥<-

## Hymn Text

With Indra as the chief, you impel us from the great mountains toward dwellings that possess homes. Just as they moved through the air, so they stood still according to your command, O Savitr. ॥ 5 ॥

**Word-by-word Analysis:**
Indra as the chief | from the great | mountains | dwellings | for these | you impel | possessing homes |
in whatever way | flying/moving | they were held | in that very way | they stood | O Savitr | for the command | of you ॥ 5 ॥

---

## Commentary (Sayana)

O Savitr, "with Indra as the chief" <note>original: "indrajyeshṭhān"</note>—meaning either you yourself are Indra possessed of supreme lordship, or Indra is the eldest and most worshipful among those you lead. You "impel" <note>original: "suvasi"</note> or inspire us, who are even greater than the "great mountains." Furthermore, for "these" patrons of the sacrifice <note>the <term>yajamānas</term></note>, you provide "dwellings" <note>original: "kshayan"</note> such as villages and cities, which are "possessing homes" <note>original: "pastyāvataḥ"</note>... <note>Text cuts off at bottom of page</note>

<summary>This page explains Savitr’s role as the cosmic maintainer whose divine laws are indestructible across heaven and earth, and as the provider of secure homes for worshippers.</summary>
<keywords>Savitr, Indra, Truth (Satya), divine law, dwellings, Ashvalayana Shrauta Sutra, cosmic order</keywords>

--- Page 307 ---
<meta>This page continues from the previous commentary on Sukta 54, concluding the final verse of that hymn and introducing Sukta 55. The transition involves shifting from the worship of Savitr (the solar impeller) to a broader invocation of the All-Gods (Vishvedevas).</meta>

...you impel. You urge. Just as those traveling <note>referring to birds or moving beings</note> are held back or guided by you, in that same way, never overstepping your command <note>original: "savāya"</note>, they remain steadfast.

---

-> ॥ Now the Sixth Verse ॥ <-

## Hymn Text
Those who, O worthy Savitr, day after day, bring forth good fortune through your impulsions;
May Indra, Heaven and Earth, the River with the waters, and Aditi with the Adityas, grant us protection. ॥ 6 ॥

**Word-by-word Analysis:**
Those | your | O worthy one | Savitr | impulsions | day by day | good fortune | bring forth |
Indra | Heaven and Earth | the River | with the waters | with the Adityas | us | Aditi | protection | may grant ॥ 6 ॥

## Commentary (Sayana)
"Those" refers to the sacrificers. O Savitr, for your sake, there are **impulsions** <note>original: "savāsaḥ"</note>, meaning the Soma offerings. Here, the first case is used in place of the second <note>a grammatical substitution in Vedic Sanskrit</note>, meaning "the Soma juices." Alternatively, "impulsions" refers to the three daily ritual sessions—morning, noon, and evening—during which they press the Soma. Not only on a single day, but **day by day**, every day, they **bring forth** <note>original: "āsuvanti"</note> or produce **good fortune**. For them, and for us, **may Indra grant protection** <note>original: "śarma yansat"</note>. May he bestow it. Furthermore, **Heaven and Earth**, as well as the deity presiding over the **River** <note>original: "Sindhu"</note>, and **Aditi** along with the **Adityas** <note>solar deities, sons of Aditi</note>, **may they grant protection**. Although this is a hymn to Savitr, it is not contradictory to mention and pray to Indra and other gods as well.

---

-> ॥ This concludes the fifth group (varga) of the eighth chapter of the third book (ashtaka) ॥ <-

The tenth hymn, beginning with "Who is your protector," has ten verses. The seer is Vamadeva, and the deities are the All-Gods <note>original: "Vishvedevas"</note>. According to the general rules of the Index <note>original: "Anukramani"</note>, the eighth, ninth, and tenth verses are in the Gayatri meter, while the rest are in Trishtubh meter. As it is stated: "Who [is your protector] is ten [verses], dedicated to the All-Gods, ending with three Gayatris." The ritual application is determined by the internal markers of the text.

---

-> ॥ Therein, the First Verse ॥ <-

## Hymn Text
Who is your protector, O Vasus? Who is your defender? O Heaven and Earth, and Aditi, be our refuge;
O Varuna and Mitra, who among mortals gives wealth to you during the sacrifice, O Gods? ॥ 1 ॥

**Word-by-word Analysis:**
Who | your | protector | O Vasus | who | defender | Heaven and Earth | Aditi | and | be [for] | us |
more powerful | O Varuna | O Mitra | from a mortal | who | your | in the sacrifice | wealth | gives | O Gods ॥ 1 ॥

## Commentary (Sayana)
O **Vasus** <note>a class of eight deities representing aspects of nature</note>, you who cause all to dwell, **who is your protector**? The implication is that since you are the Vasus, you yourselves are the protectors. And who is the **defender** <note>original: "varūtā"</note>, the one who is chosen or who shares? Alternatively, among you, who is the god who protects and who is the one who wards off suffering? O **Heaven and Earth**, **be [refuge]** for us. Protect us. O **Aditi**, the indivisible one. This also refers to Heaven and <note>text continues on next page</note>

<vocab>
- सवितृ (Savitṛ): The "Impeller," a solar deity representing the divine motive power of the sun.
- इन्द्र (Indra): The king of the gods and deity of rain and thunder.
- द्यावापृथिवी (Dyāvāpṛthivī): The compound deity of Heaven and Earth.
- अदिते (Adite): Aditi, the mother of the gods, representing the boundless or infinite.
- वसवः (Vasavaḥ): The Vasus, a group of eight elemental gods (Fire, Earth, Air, etc.).
- वरुण (Varuṇa): The deity of the cosmic order and the waters.
- मित्र (Mitra): The deity of friendship, contracts, and the morning sun.
- सौभगम् (Saubhagam): Prosperity or good fortune.
- शर्म (Śarma): Shelter, protection, or the bliss resulting from it.
- अध्वर (Adhvara): A sacrifice or ritual, literally "that which is not injurious."
</vocab>

It then introduces the 55th hymn, dedicated to the All-Gods (Vishvedevas), beginning an inquiry into the nature of divine protection.</summary>

--- Page 308 ---
<meta>This page continues the commentary on the final part of Verse 1 of the 55th Hymn, which transitions from a general invocation to a specific plea for protection by Mitra and Varuna. It then introduces Verse 2, which praises the eternal orderers of the universe, and begins the commentary for Verse 3, focusing on the goddess Aditi.</meta>

...serves as an adjective for the Earth <note>referring to the previous verse's structure</note>. There is a variation in grammatical number here. If this were a separate invocation of a deity, the accent would not be lowered <note>original: "nighāta"</note>. According to the rule that a previous address is treated as if non-existent, this would be at the start of a verse-foot. This is similar to the phrasing in **"O Aditi, Mitra, and Varuna, have mercy" (Rig Veda 2.27.14)** or **"Adityas, Rudras, Vasus, the generous givers" (Rig Veda 10.66.12)**. If it is treated as an adjective, then because of its shared grammatical relationship <note>original: "sāmānādhikaranya"</note>, the accent is lowered as in the phrase **"O Agni, O Purifier, with your brilliance" (Rig Veda 5.26.1)**. Therefore, it is a modifier for the phrase "Heaven and Earth." O Varuna, O Mitra, may you both protect us from the powerful mortal, from the human assailant. O Gods, in your sacrifice <note>original: "adhvara"</note>, who bestows <note>original: "dhāti"</note> the wealth? Or, who among you holds the wealth?

---

-> ॥ Now the Second Verse ॥ <-

## Hymn Text
Those who, while worshiping the ancient establishments, drive away the darkness; the un-deluded separators of sorrow;
The eternal orderers, those of true thoughts, the wonderful ones to behold, have established our desires and they shine. ॥ 2 ॥

**Word-by-word Analysis**
Those | who | establishments | ancient | worshiping | away | when | they drive away | the separators | the un-deluded |
The orderers | away | for you <note>or "they"</note> | established | the eternal ones | those of true thoughts | they shine | the wonderful ones ॥ 2 ॥

## Commentary (Sayana)
Those gods who **worship** or bestow upon their praisers the **ancient** <note>original: "pūrvyāṇi"</note> **establishments** <note>original: "dhāmāni"</note>, meaning the sacred places or stations. And those who are **separators** <note>original: "viyotāraḥ"</note>, meaning those who separate or remove us from sorrows—the **un-deluded** <note>original: "amūrāḥ"</note> ones—they **drive away** the darkness. These gods, the **orderers** <note>original: "vidhātāraḥ"</note> who bring about the fruits of our actions, being **eternal** <note>original: "ajasrāḥ"</note>, **establish** or perform that which we desire. Furthermore, those of **true thoughts** <note>original: "ṛtadhītayaḥ"</note>, whose actions are truth, the **wonderful ones** <note>original: "dasmāḥ"</note> who are beautiful to behold, they **shine** <note>original: "rurucanta"</note>.

---

-> ॥ Now the Third Verse ॥ <-

## Hymn Text
I praise the goddess Aditi, the one to be approached by all, the flowing River, with hymns for her friendship;
So that both Day and Night, the dawn and the dark, may protect us and act toward us without malice. ॥ 3 ॥

**Word-by-word Analysis**
Forth | the one to be approached | Aditi | the River | with hymns | well-being | I praise | for friendship | the goddess |
Both | so that | us | the two days | protection | the Dawn and the Night | may they act | the un-deceived ॥ 3 ॥

## Commentary (Sayana)
The one **to be approached** <note>original: "pastyām"</note> or reached by all; **Aditi**, the non-deficient mother of the gods; that **goddess**; the **River** <note>original: "Sindhu"</note>, the deity who flows or presides over the rivers; the goddess named **Well-being** <note>original: "Svasti"</note>, who provides a happy residence; I **praise** <note>original: "īḷe"</note> her with **hymns** <note>original: "arkaiḥ"</note> or sacred mantras, for the sake of her **friendship** or favor—

<vocab>
**Aditi**: The "Boundless" mother of the gods, representing the infinite.
**Mitra**: The solar deity of friendship and contracts.
**Varuna**: The deity of cosmic order and the waters.
**Dhama (Establishments)**: Refers to divine laws, stations, or sacred locations.
**Rtadhiti**: Possessing thoughts or prayers directed toward the cosmic Truth (Rta).
**Pastya**: A term for a dwelling or someone who is frequently visited/sought.
**Sindhu**: Both the Indus River and the general concept of a flowing goddess.
**Nipata**: Protection or a falling/landing toward someone.
</vocab>

<meta>This page continues the commentary on the final part of Verse 3 of the 55th Hymn, which transitions from praising the goddesses of Dawn and Night to an invocation for general protection. It then introduces and provides the commentary for Verse 4, focusing on the paths shown by Aryaman, Varuna, and Agni, and the protection of Indra and Vishnu. It continues with Verse 5, invoking Parvata, the Maruts, and Bhaga for protection from human-born sin, and begins the text for Verse 6.</meta>

...I praise. I praise both "days"—meaning Heaven and Earth—so that they may protect us, and preserve us well. May Ushas and Nakta <note>Dawn and Night</note>, the presiding deities of day and night, who are invincible and undeceived, perform our desired purpose <note>The Sanskrit text implies "what is sought" or the fruit of the ritual</note>.

---

## Hymn Text

-> ॥ Now the Fourth Verse ॥ <-

**May Aryaman and Varuna distinguish the path, and Agni, the lord of offerings, the easy way to prosperity.**
**O Indra and Vishnu, being praised with human-like songs, grant us powerful protection and a secure shelter. ॥ 4 ॥**

May distinguish | Aryaman | Varuna | the path | the offering | the lord | prosperity | the way | Agni |
Indra and Vishnu <note>dual deity</note> | human-like | indeed | well | being praised | protection | to us | grant | powerful | shelter ॥ 4 ॥

## Commentary (Sayana)

The god Aryaman distinguishes <note>original: "vicheti," meaning to perceive or make known</note> our path, specifically the path of sacrifice. Likewise, Varuna distinguishes the same. Agni, the lord or protector of the "offering" <note>original: "iṣu," here interpreted as the sacrificial food</note>, makes known the happy way or the path to the heavenly realms. O Indra and Vishnu, being "well praised" <note>original: "su ṣu stavānā"</note> with hymns suited for humans, grant to us a "shelter" <note>original: "varūtha," meaning choice or excellent</note> that is "powerful" <note>original: "amavat," filled with strength</note> and "human-filled" <note>original: "nṛvat," meaning accompanied by men or descendants</note>, which is to say, grant us a home or happiness.

---

## Hymn Text

-> ॥ Now the Fifth Verse ॥ <-

**I seek the protections of Parvata and the Maruts, and of the divine protector Bhaga.**
**May the Lord protect us from human-born distress, and may Mitra guard us with his friendship. ॥ 5 ॥**

Towards | of Parvata | of the Maruts | protections | of the god | of the protector | I seek | of Bhaga |
May he protect | the Lord | human-born | from distress | us | Mitra | from friendship <note>or "from a friend's [wrong]"</note> | and | us | may he guard ॥ 5 ॥

## Commentary (Sayana)

I "seek" <note>original: "āvi," here interpreted as "ā-vṛṇe," I choose or invoke</note> the "protections" <note>original: "avāṃsi"</note> of the god named Parvata, who is a friend of Indra, and of the Maruts <note>the Storm Gods</note>, and of the divine protector <note>original: "chātuḥ"</note> Bhaga. Furthermore, may the Lord <note>original: "patiḥ," referring to Varuna</note> "protect" <note>original: "pāt"</note> us from "distress" <note>original: "aṃhasaḥ," sin or calamity</note> arising from "human relations" <note>original: "janyāt," pertaining to people or kin</note>. And also, may Mitra guard us with a spirit of "friendship" <note>original: "mitriyāt"</note>.

-> ॥ Thus ends the sixth group (varga) of the eighth chapter of the third book (ashtaka) ॥ <-

**Like those seeking wealth in the crossing of the ocean, the rivers have flowed toward the glowing heat. ॥ 6 ॥**

<summary>This page contains verses 4 and 5 of Rig Veda Hymn 4.55 with Sayana's commentary, focusing on the deities Aryaman, Varuna, Agni, Indra, Vishnu, and Mitra as protectors of the sacrificial path and guardians against human-born sin.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the commentary on Mandala 3, Sukta 54 of the Rig Veda. It concludes the explanation of Verse 6 and provides the text and commentary for Verses 7, 8, and 9. The focus remains on the interconnectedness of cosmic deities and the efficacy of the sacrificial ritual.</meta>

## Hymn Text
### Verse 6 (Continued - Word-by-Word Analysis)
**Now | Heaven and Earth | with | the Serpent | of the Deep | may one praise | the two goddesses | also with these | desired objects |**
**the ocean | as | in the moving together | desiring gain | resounding like the heat | the rivers | away | they have uncovered ॥ 6 ॥**

## Commentary (Sayana)
O **Heaven and Earth** <note>original: "rodasī"</note>, may one praise you both quickly <note>original: "nu"</note> along with the god named the **Serpent of the Deep** <note>original: "ahina budhnyena"</note>, on account of these attainable and desired objects. I praise them. Like those who desire to obtain wealth <note>original: "saniṣyavaḥ"</note> in the act of moving together—that is, traveling across the middle of the ocean—praise the ocean itself, so do we praise. Because these gods "uncovered" <note>original: "apavṛn"</note> or opened up the rivers, which have resounding sounds like the heat of the ritual <note>original: "gharmasvarasaḥ"</note>. This is spoken as if of someone absent. Alternatively, it is a blessing: "May those gods uncover the rivers." Therefore, the connection is: "Thus, I praise."

---

->॥ Now the Seventh Verse ॥<-

## Hymn Text
### Verse 7
**May the divine Aditi protect us along with the gods; may the protecting god, being watchful, guard us.**
**Indeed, we are not able to violate the nourishment of Mitra, of Varuna, nor the summit of Agni. ॥ 7 ॥**

**with the gods | our | the divine | Aditi | down | may she protect | the god | the protector | may he guard | not being careless |**
**not indeed | of Mitra | of Varuna | the nourishment | we are able | to violate | the summit | of Agni ॥ 7 ॥**

## Commentary (Sayana)
May the **divine Aditi** <note>original: "aditirdevī"</note>, the mother of the gods who is not deficient, protect us together with the other gods such as Mitra and the rest. Likewise, may the **Protector** <note>original: "trātā"</note> god—meaning Indra—guard us while being **watchful** <note>original: "aprayuchan," meaning not being careless</note>. Furthermore, we are not **able** <note>original: "arhāmasi"</note> to **violate** <note>original: "pramiyam," meaning to harm or diminish</note> the **nourishment** <note>original: "dhāsim"</note> consisting of the Soma and other offerings belonging to Mitra, Varuna, and the **summit** <note>original: "sānu," the high point or surface</note> of Agni. Rather, the meaning is that we are capable only of increasing these offerings through the performance of the ritual.

---

->॥ Now the Eighth Verse ॥<-

## Hymn Text
### Verse 8
**Agni rules over the collection of wealth; Agni rules over great good fortune. May he grant those to us. ॥ 8 ॥**

**Agni | rules | over the collection of wealth | Agni | of great | good fortune | those | to us | may he grant ॥ 8 ॥**

## Commentary (Sayana)
The god **Agni** rules <note>original: "īśe"</note> over the **collection of wealth** <note>original: "vasvavyasya"</note>; he has the power to give it. Likewise, Agni rules over great **good fortune** <note>original: "saubhagagasya"</note> or prosperity. Therefore, may he **grant** <note>original: "rāsate"</note>—that is, give—those riches and that good fortune to us.

---

->॥ Now the Ninth Verse ॥<-

## Hymn Text
### Verse 9
**O Bountiful Dawn, bringer of pleasant truths, bring many desirable things to us, O you who are rich in food. ॥ 9 ॥**

**O Dawn | O Bountiful One | hither | bring | O bringer of pleasant truths | desirable things | many | to us | O you who are rich in food ॥ 9 ॥**

O **Ushas** <note>original: "uṣo", the Goddess of Dawn</note>, O wealthy one <note>original: "maghoni"</note>, O you who take pride in pleasant and truthful speech <note>original: "sūnṛte"</note>, O goddess possessing food <note>original: "vājinīvati"</note>, bring us many desirable <note>original: "vāryā"</note> riches. Procure them for us.

## Hymn Text
### Verse 10
**May Savita, Bhaga, Varuna, Mitra, and Aryaman do that well for us. May Indra come to us with bounty. ॥ 10 ॥**

**Word-by-word Analysis (Pada-patha):**
**That | Well | Our | Savita | Bhaga | Varuna | Mitra | Aryaman | Indra | Our | With bounty | Toward | May he come ॥ 10 ॥**

---

## Commentary (Sayana)
With whatever bounty <note>original: "rādhasā"</note> or wealth Savita, Bhaga, Varuna, Mitra, Aryaman, and Indra each come—that is, arrive at the sacrifice—may those gods provide that bounty/wealth to us very well <note>original: "su suṣṭhu"</note>. This is the implied completion of the sentence.

->॥ Thus ends the seventh section of the eighth chapter of the third book ॥<-

The hymn beginning "The Great Heaven and Earth" <note>original: "mahī dyāvāpṛthivī"</note> is the eleventh hymn of the section, consisting of seven verses. The Seer (Rishi) is **Vamadeva**, and the deity is **Heaven and Earth** <note>original: "dyāvāpṛthivyam"</note> as a dual pair. As stated previously, because the preceding hymn ended in a *Gayatri* meter, the first three verses here are also in the *Gayatri* meter, while the remaining ones are in the *Trishtubh* meter. The Ancient Index <note>original: "Anukramaṇikā"</note> states: "The Great seven, to Heaven and Earth." 

In the ritual context of the "Expanded Ten-Day Sacrifice" <note>original: "vyūḍhe daśarātre"</note>, on the fifth day, during the recitation for the Universal Gods <note>original: "vaiśvadeva-śastra"</note>, the first four verses of this hymn to Heaven and Earth are used as the foundational verses <note>original: "nividdhānīyaṃ"</note>. This is indicated in the liturgical manual: "The four verses 'The Great Heaven and Earth' and 'The Ribhus, Vibhvan'..." <note>original: "Āśvalāyana Śrauta Sūtra 8. 8"</note>.

->॥ There, the First Verse ॥<-

## Hymn Text
### Verse 1
**May the great Heaven and Earth here at the highest [sacrifice] be endowed with light through the shining hymns.**
**Because the Great Two, measuring out the most excellent [space], stayed firm, the Sprinkler roars with his spreading movements. ॥ 1 ॥**

**Word-by-word Analysis (Pada-patha):**
**Great | Heaven and Earth | Here | At the highest | With light | May they be | With the shining | With hymns |**
**Since | Him/Everywhere | At the most excellent | The Great Two | Measuring out | Roaring | Indeed | The Sprinkler | With spreading | With movements ॥ 1 ॥**

---

## Commentary (Sayana)
In this sacrifice, may the **Great** <note>original: "mahī"</note> and most excellent **Heaven and Earth** <note>original: "dyāvāpṛthivī"</note> be joined with light <note>original: "rucā"</note> and with shining <note>original: "śucayadbhir"</note> hymns <note>original: "arkaiḥ"</note>—which are the means of worship—or with sacrificial offerings like Soma. Because <note>original: "yat"</note> the great Heaven and Earth, while measuring out and establishing the most excellent and widest space, the **Sprinkler** <note>original: "ukṣā", the fertilizing rain-god Parjanya</note> roars <note>original: "ruvati"</note> or makes a sound along with the **Maruts** <note>original: "evaiḥ", the storm-gods</note> or the moving clouds. The word "ha" is a filler. Therefore, the connection is: "May they be exalted."

->॥ Now the Second Verse ॥<-

## Hymn Text
### Verse 2
**The two goddesses, with the adorable gods, worshipful, stand unceasingly, being sprinkled [with butter].**
**Upholders of the Cosmic Order, yielding the fruits of Order, mothers of the gods, the leaders of the sacrifice, with shining hymns. ॥ 2 ॥**

<vocab>
- **Savita** (Savitā): The Solar deity, the Impeller who rouses life.
- **Heaven and Earth** (Dyāvāpṛthivī): Revered as the primeval parents of all beings.
- **Vamadeva** (Vāmadeva): The ancient Seer (Rishi) of the fourth book of the Rig Veda.
- **The Sprinkler** (Ukṣā): A term for the rain-god or a bull, symbolizing the fertilizing power of the storm.
- **Bounty** (Rādhas): Specifically the wealth or success gained through a correctly performed ritual.
- **Upholders of Order** (Ṛtāvarī): Those who maintain *Rita*, the natural and moral law of the cosmos.
</vocab>

## Hymn Text (Rig Veda 3.54.2-4)

---

<note>Analysis of the words for Rig Veda 3.54.2 (Continued from previous page)</note>
The two divine ones <note>original: "devī iti"</note> | with the gods | worthy of worship <note>original: "yajate iti"</note> | by those deserving of sacrifice | not injuring <note>original: "aminatī iti"</note> | they two stood | sprinkling/moistening <note>original: "ukṣamāṇe iti"</note> |
possessing clarified butter <note>original: "ghṛtavarī iti ghṛtavarī"</note> | not failing/not harming | having gods as children <note>original: "devaputre iti devaputre"</note> | of the sacrifice | the two leaders <note>original: "netrī iti"</note> |
with the shining/cleansing | chants/hymns ॥ 2 ॥

## Commentary (Sayana)

**The two divine ones** <note>original: "devī"</note> refers to the Goddesses (Heaven and Earth). They are **worthy of worship** <note>original: "yajate"</note> by those performing sacrifices. They are **not injuring** <note>original: "aminatī"</note>, meaning they do not harm living beings. They are **sprinkling** <note>original: "ukṣamāṇe"</note>, meaning they shower down rain and moisture. They are **possessing clarified butter** <note>original: "ghṛtavarī"</note>, and they are **not failing/harming** <note>original: "aduhrau"</note>, meaning they do not commit any treachery or withhold their bounty. They are the **parents of the gods** <note>original: "devaputre"</note> because they produced the various deities. They are the **leaders of the sacrifice** <note>original: "yajñasya netrī"</note> because they carry out and support the ritual. These two, **Heaven and Earth**, together **with the gods** who are **worthy of worship**, and joined by the **shining chants** <note>original: "arkaiḥ"</note>—which are the mantras or the offerings that purify—**they stood** <note>original: "tasthatuḥ"</note>. This means they remain or abide in their respective roles.

---

## Hymn Text

->॥ Now the Third Verse ॥<-

**He indeed was skillful in his works among all beings, he who generated these two, Heaven and Earth. The wise one, by his power, set in motion those two wide, deep, well-established, and unsupported regions. ॥ 3 ॥**

<note>Word-by-word Analysis (3.54.3)</note>
He | indeed | skillful in works | among beings | was | who | these | Heaven and Earth | generated |
wide | deep | the two regions/worlds | well-established | without a beam/support | wise | by power/skill |
completely | set in motion ॥ 3 ॥

## Commentary (Sayana)

**He indeed**—referring to the Creator (Prajapati)—possessing **skillful works** <note>original: "svapāḥ"</note> or performing beautiful actions, **was among the beings** <note>original: "bhuvaneṣvāsa"</note>, meaning he exists as the supreme. He is the one **who generated these two, Heaven and Earth**. Furthermore, he is the **wise one** <note>original: "dhīraḥ"</note> who, through his **skillful power** <note>original: "śacyā"</note>, **set in motion** <note>original: "samairat"</note> or perfectly impelled these two worlds. These worlds are described as **wide** <note>original: "urvī"</note>, **deep** <note>original: "gambhīre"</note> and unshakeable, **well-established** <note>original: "sumeke"</note> with a beautiful form, and **unsupported** <note>original: "avaṃśe"</note>, meaning they are without a central pillar or beam in the mid-air. He who did this is truly the one of "good works."

---

## Hymn Text

->॥ Now the Fourth Verse ॥<-

**Now, O Heaven and Earth, may you both, being in harmony and desiring our offering, protect us quickly with great shelters and with the gods who have their wives. Wide-reaching and pervasive, you are worthy of worship; protect us! By our holy thought, may we always be masters of chariots and winners of wealth. ॥ 4 ॥**

<note>Word-by-word Analysis (3.54.4)</note>
Now | Heaven and Earth | with great | us | with protections/shelters | with those having wives | desiring food/offering | in harmony |
wide-reaching | all/pervading | worthy of worship | down | protect | by holy thought | may we be | masters of chariots | always winning ॥ 4 ॥

## Commentary (Sayana)

O **Heaven and Earth** <note>original: "rodasī"</note>, **now** <note>original: "nu"</note> quickly **protect us** <note>original: "ni pātaṃ"</note> thoroughly. Do so along with the **great** <note>original: "bṛhadbhiḥ"</note> and vast **protections** <note>original: "varūthaiḥ"</note>—which refer to either houses or wealth—and alongside the gods **who have their wives** <note>original: "patnīvadbhiḥ"</note>. You two, **desiring our food/offering** <note>original: "iṣayantī"</note> and being **in harmony** <note>original: "sajoṣāḥ"</note> with one another, are **wide-reaching** <note>original: "urūcī"</note> and **pervade everything** <note>original: "viśve"</note>. Being **worthy of worship**, protect us. The phrase starting with "By our holy thought" <note>original: "dhiyā..."</note> has been explained previously <note>referring to a recurring prayer for becoming masters of wealth and chariots through divine favor</note>.

---

<vocab>
**Heaven and Earth** (Rodasī / Dyāvāpṛthivyau): The dual deity representing the cosmic parents of all things.
**Skillful in work** (Svapāḥ): An epithet for the Creator, highlighting the precision of the natural world.
**Worthy of worship** (Yajatra): Entities or gods to whom sacrifices are rightfully offered.
**Not injuring** (Aminatī): The benevolent nature of the Earth and Sky toward living creatures.
**Sprinkling** (Ukṣamāṇe): The act of the Sky providing rain and the Earth providing nourishment.
**Shelter/Protection** (Varūtha): Can refer to physical protection, a home, or the security provided by wealth.
</vocab>

The triplet of verses beginning with "Toward you two..." <note>original: "pra vām ityādi"</note> is in the Gayatri meter. It is to be inserted during the Recitation to the All-Gods <term>Vaishvadeva-shastra: a specific liturgical recitation performed during a Soma sacrifice</term> within the Ten-Night Ceremony <note>original: "daśarātre"</note>. This is indicated in the ritual manuals: "The two triplets beginning 'Toward you two, O great Heaven and Earth...'" <note>original: "pra vāṃ mahi dyavī iti tṛcau"; reference: Ashvalayana Shrauta Sutra 8.11</note>.

## Hymn Text

-> ॥ The fifth verse of the first hymn in this triplet ॥ <-

**Toward you two, O great Heaven and Earth, we bring forward great praise; O pure ones, we approach you for glorification. ॥ 5 ॥**

**Toward | you two | great | Heaven and Earth | unto | near | praise | we bring | pure ones | near | for glorification ॥ 5 ॥**

## Commentary (Sayana)

O Heaven and Earth <note>original: "dyāvāpṛthivyau"</note>, you who are **luminous** <note>original: "dyavī"</note>, we **bring** <note>original: "bharāmahe"</note> or thoroughly prepare a **great** <note>original: "mahi"</note> and abundant **praise** <note>original: "upastutim"</note> for **you two** <note>original: "vām"</note>. O **pure** <note>original: "śucī"</note> and bright ones, we **approach** <note>original: "upagacchāmaḥ"</note> you in order **to glorify** <note>original: "praśastaye"</note> you. <note>The commentator notes that since the prefix "upa" (near/toward) is present, a verb of motion like "we approach" must be understood.</note>

---

## Hymn Text

-> ॥ Now the sixth verse ॥ <-

**Purifying each other with your own bodies, you shine through your own strength; you two have upheld the Eternal Law from of old. ॥ 6 ॥**

**Purifying | with the body | mutually | with your own | with strength | you two shine | you two uphold | from of old | the Eternal Law ॥ 6 ॥**

## Commentary (Sayana)

O goddesses, **purifying** <note>original: "punāne"</note> or cleansing the sacrifice or the sacrificer, you **shine** <note>original: "rājathaḥ"</note> through your own **bodies** <note>original: "tanvā"</note> and your **own strength** <note>original: "svena dakṣeṇa"</note> **mutually** <note>original: "mithaḥ"</note>, each individually. Alternatively, it means you purify **each other** <note>original: "mithaḥ"</note> with parts of your own bodies: Heaven purifies the Earth with its rain, and the Earth purifies Heaven through the effects of the moon and smoke. You **uphold** <note>original: "ūhyāthe"</note> or carry the **Eternal Law** <note>original: "ṛtam"</note>—meaning the sacrifice—**from of old** <note>original: "sanāt"</note>, or at all times.

---

## Hymn Text

-> ॥ Now the seventh verse ॥ <-

**The two great ones, fulfilling the seeker's wish, crossing over, fulfilling the Law, you have sat down around the sacrifice. ॥ 7 ॥**

**Great ones | of the friend | fulfilling | crossing | fulfilling | the Law | around | the sacrifice | you two sat down ॥ 7 ॥**

## Commentary (Sayana)

The **great** <note>original: "mahī"</note> Heaven and Earth, **fulfilling** <note>original: "sādhayaḥ"</note> the desires of the **friend** <note>original: "mitrasya"</note>—that is, the worshipper—**crossing over** <note>original: "taranti"</note> or enabling one to cross difficulties, and **fulfilling** <note>original: "pipratī"</note> or providing **the Law** <note>original: "ṛtam"</note>—here interpreted as food <note>original: "annam"</note>—you **sat down** <note>original: "niṣedathuḥ"</note> **around** <note>original: "pari"</note> or took refuge in the **sacrifice** <note>original: "yajñam"</note>.

-> ॥ Thus ends the eighth section of the eighth chapter of the third book ॥ <-

## Introductory Notes for Sukta 57

The twelfth hymn, beginning with "By the Lord of the Field..." <note>original: "kṣetrasya patinā"</note> was seen by the seer Vamadeva. The first, fourth, sixth, and seventh verses are in the Anushtubh meter <note>a meter of four quarters with 8 syllables each</note>. The fifth verse is Pura-ushnih <note>a meter where the first quarter has 12 syllables and the rest have 8</note>. The remaining three verses are in the Trishtubh meter <note>four quarters of 11 syllables each</note>. The first three verses are dedicated to the deity "Lord of the Field" <note>original: "kṣetrapati"</note>, the fourth is to the deity named Suna...

<vocab>
- Dyavaprithivya: The dual deity representing Heaven and Earth.
- Dyavi: Luminous or shining ones.
- Punane: The act of purifying or cleansing.
- Ritam: A central Vedic concept meaning Cosmic Order, Truth, or the Sacrifice itself; Sayana also glosses it as "food."
- Kshetrasya Pati: The tutelary deity of the soil or "Lord of the Field."
- Vamadeva: The ancient sage (Rishi) to whom the fourth book of the Rig Veda is attributed.
- Anushtubh / Ushnik / Trishtubh: Common rhythmic meters used in Vedic poetry.
</vocab>

<meta>This page transitions from the general hymns to Heaven and Earth into a specific agricultural hymn dedicated to the Lord of the Field (Kshetrapati). It provides the liturgical context for the hymn's use in plowing rituals and sacrificial ceremonies before detailing the first two verses and their scholarly commentary.</meta>

# Rig Veda [Ashtaka 3, Adhyaya 8, Varga 9]

The eighth verse belongs to the deities of the plow <term>Shunasira: personifications of the plow and the plowshare</term>; the sixth and seventh verses are dedicated to the Furrow <term>Sita: the personified furrow of a plowed field</term>. Thus it is stated in the Index <note>original: "Anukramanika"</note>: 
"Of the eight verses concerning the field, three are for the Lord of the Field, one for the plow, the following is in the *Pura-ushnih* meter, the last is for the Plow-deities, the penultimate for the Furrow; those two are in the *Anushtubh* meter, as are the first and fourth verses." 
When plowing a field, one should offer an oblation or recite this entire hymn verse by verse. Thus it is instructed: "One should offer or recite 'With the Lord of the Field' verse by verse" <note>reference: Grihya Sutra 2.10.1</note>. In the *Aptoryama* sacrifice <term>Aptoryama: a specific variation of the Soma sacrifice</term>, there are four additional recitations <note>original: "atirikta-ukthya"</note> following the Ashvin-litany. The first of these is the concluding verse. It is instructed: "'With the Lord of the Field' is the concluding verse" <note>reference: Ashvalayana Shrauta Sutra 9.11.1</note>.

---

## Hymn Text

-> ॥ The First Verse ॥ <-

**With the Lord of the Field as our helper, we shall be victorious. May he nourish our cattle and horses; may he be gracious to us in such a state. ॥ 1 ॥**

**Pada-patha (Word-by-word):**
Of the field । with the Lord । we । as with a helper । we conquer ।
cow । horse । nourisher । near । he । us । may he be gracious । in such [a state] ॥ 1 ॥

---

## Commentary (Sayana)

We, the sacrificers <note>original: "yajamānaḥ"</note>, through the **Lord of the Field** <note>original: "kshetrasya patinā"</note>—who is a divine being. Some say this Lord of the Field is the god Rudra, others say he is Agni, or he may be a distinct deity who is simply called the Master of the Field. **As with a helper** <note>original: "hitena-iva"</note>: the word "iva" (as if) here implies emphasis; he is the one who truly benefits all living beings. Alternatively, it means "as with a friend." Just as one achieves their goal with the help of a friend, so do we. **We shall be victorious** <note>original: "jayāmasi"</note>: we conquer or successfully cultivate the field. May that god **bring** <note>an implied verb from the prefix 'ā'</note> wealth consisting of **cattle and horses** to **nourish** us. That same god **is gracious to us** <note>original: "mṛḷāti"</note>, meaning he grants us happiness, when it comes to granting the aforementioned wealth. One should look to the *Nirukta* <note>ancient etymological text, 10.15</note> for the explanation of the phrase "Lord of the Field."

In the additional recitations for the deity Mitra-Varuna during the *Aptoryama* sacrifice, the following is the concluding verse. It is instructed: "'O Lord of the Field, a wave of sweetness' is the concluding verse" <note>reference: Ashvalayana Shrauta Sutra 9.11.1</note>.

---

## Hymn Text

-> ॥ The Second Verse ॥ <-

**O Lord of the Field, like a cow yielding milk, pour forth for us a wave full of sweetness, dripping with honey, like well-clarified butter. May the lords of Truth be gracious to us. ॥ 2 ॥**

**Pada-patha (Word-by-word):**
Of the field । O Lord । full of sweetness । a wave । like a cow । milk । among us । pour forth ।
honey-dripping । like clarified butter । well-purified । of Truth । us । the lords । may they be gracious ॥ 2 ॥

<meta>This page continues the commentary on the agricultural hymns of the Rig Veda, specifically moving from the general blessings of the Lord of the Field to specific invocations for environmental sweetness and the practical tools of farming like the plow and oxen. It concludes the discussion on verse 2 and covers verses 3 and 4 of Sukta 57.</meta>

### Mandala 4. Hymn 5. Verse 57. ]    ॥ Third Ashtaka ॥    247

## Commentary (Sayana)
[Conclusion of commentary on RV 4.57.2]

O **Lord of the Field**, may you **pour forth** for us an **overflowing wave** full of **sweetness**, just as a **cow yields milk**. <note>original: "dhenuḥ paya iva"</note> The phrase **"dripping with sweetness"** refers to water that is as **pure as clarified butter** <term>Ghrita: Ghee or clarified butter, used in rituals and symbolized as a source of life</term>; this is an **analogy**. This means the water should be of such a quality. May the lords of the clarified butter, or of the sacrifice, or of the water, **be gracious to us** <note>original: "mṛḷayantu"</note>—that is, make us happy. Alternatively, regarding the grammar of "clarified butter," may they provide it to us; for here, the root for "being gracious" <note>original: "mṛḷ"</note> acts as a verb of giving.

For the priest known as the *Brahmanacchamsin*, this is the concluding verse in the *Ukthya* sacrifice. The verse beginning **"May the herbs be sweet, the heavens, the waters"** is the concluding verse, as indicated in the ritual manuals <note>reference: Ashvalayana Shrauta Sutra 9.11</note>.

---

## Hymn Text
-> ॥ The Third Verse ॥ <-

**May the herbs be sweet; may the heavens, the waters, and the mid-air be sweet for us. May the Lord of the Field be sweet for us; may we follow him, remaining unharmed. ॥ 3 ॥**

**Pada-patha (Word-by-word):**
Full of sweetness । herbs । heavens । waters । full of sweetness । for us । may it be । mid-air ।
of the field । the Lord । full of sweetness । for us । may he be । unharmed । following । him । may we move ॥ 3 ॥

## Commentary (Sayana)

May the **herbs**—meaning crops like rice and millet—**be sweet** <note>original: "madhumatīḥ"</note> for us. Likewise, the **heavens** <note>original: "dyāvaḥ"</note>; the plural is used here appropriately because it is said there are "three heavens." Likewise, may the **waters** and the **mid-air** <term>Antariksha: the space between heaven and earth</term> **be sweet for us**. Furthermore, may the **Lord of the Field** also **be sweet for us**. Being **unharmed**—meaning not being injured by others—may we **follow** or move along happily after **this** Lord of the Field.

---

## Hymn Text
-> ॥ The Fourth Verse ॥ <-

**May the draft-animals work happily; may the men work happily; may the plow furrow happily. May the leather straps be fastened happily; swing the goad happily. ॥ 4 ॥**

**Pada-patha (Word-by-word):**
Happily । draft-animals । happily । men । happily । may it plow । the plow ।
happily । leather straps । may they be bound । happily । the goad । up । swing ॥ 4 ॥

## Commentary (Sayana)

May the **draft-animals** <note>original: "vāhāḥ"</note>, the oxen, work **happily** <note>original: "śunam"</note>. This word *shunam* is a synonym for happiness or prosperity. The meaning is "may they carry [the load] in a way that happiness ensues." Likewise, may the **men**, the leaders and farmers, perform their work **happily**. So too, may the **plow** <note>original: "lāṅgalam"</note> **furrow happily**. May the **leather straps**, the harnesses made of leather, **be bound happily**. **Swing**—or urge forward—the **goad** <note>original: "aṣṭrām"</note> **happily**. The deity named **Shuna** is one of two, often identified as **Vayu** <term>Vayu: The Vedic god of Wind and vitality</term>, the god who brings happiness. It is through his grace that all this happens, and thus he is praised here in accordance with the sacred scriptures.

In the *Shunasiriya* festival, this verse serves as the invitatory and offering prayer for the oblation dedicated to the deities **Shunasira**. As noted in the ritual manuals: "O Shunasira, may you enjoy this speech; may our plowshares [be favorable] to us." <note>reference: Ashvalayana Shrauta Sutra 2.20</note>

-> ॥ The Fifth Verse ॥ <-

## Hymn Text
**O Shunasira, may you both enjoy this speech; and with that nourishment which you have created in the heavens, sprinkle this earth. ॥ 5 ॥**

**Padapatha (Word-by-word):**
Shunasira । this । speech । may you both enjoy । which । in heaven । you both have made । nourishment (or water) । with that । this [earth] । sprinkle ॥ 5 ॥

---

## Commentary (Sayana)
According to the sage **Shaunaka**, Shuna is the deity of the sky. Therefore, **Shuna** is **Indra** <term>Indra: The king of the gods, often associated with rain and the power that breaks open the clouds</term> and **Sira** is **Vayu** <term>Vayu: The god of wind</term>. Alternatively, the scholar **Yaska** suggests: "**Shuna** is Vayu (from its movement in the atmosphere) and **Sira** is **Aditya** (the Sun, from its constant moving across the sky)." <note>original: Nirukta 9.40</note>. 

O Shunasira, you two should enjoy my speech that is about to be uttered. With that water/nourishment <note>original: "payas"</note> which you have established in the heavens, sprinkle this earth.

-> ॥ The Sixth Verse ॥ <-

## Hymn Text
**O auspicious Furrow, be turned toward us; O Sita, we praise you, so that you may be well-portioned for us, so that you may be fruitful for us. ॥ 6 ॥**

**Padapatha (Word-by-word):**
Turned toward us । O auspicious one । be । O Sita (Furrow) । we praise । you । so that । for us । well-portioned/fortunate । you may be । so that । for us । fruitful । you may be ॥ 6 ॥

---

## Commentary (Sayana)
O auspicious **Sita** <term>Sita: Literally 'the furrow' made by a plow, personified here as a goddess of agriculture and fertility</term>, may you be turned toward us <note>original: "arvaci"</note>. We praise you—that is, we offer hymns to you. We praise you so that you may become a source of beautiful wealth for us, and so that you may become the provider of excellent fruits (crops).

-> ॥ The Seventh Verse ॥ <-

## Hymn Text
**May Indra take hold of the Furrow; may Pushan guide her. May she, flowing with nourishment, milk for us year after year. ॥ 7 ॥**

**Padapatha (Word-by-word):**
Indra । the Furrow । may he take hold of । her । Pushan । may he guide/uphold । she । for us । full of nourishment । may she milk । year । after year ॥ 7 ॥

## Commentary (Sayana)
May the god **Indra** take firm hold of **Sita**, the wooden beam that holds the furrow. May the god **Pushan** <term>Pushan: A solar deity who acts as a protector of cattle and a guide for paths, ensuring the plow stays its course</term> guide or support that Furrow.

## Commentary (Sayana - Introduction to Sukta 58)
The thirteenth hymn, beginning with "From the ocean the wave," consists of eleven verses. The final verse is in the *Jagati* meter, and the rest are in the *Trishtubh* meter. The deity is either Agni, Surya, Agni-Cow-Ghee, or simply a praise of Ghee <term>Ghrita: clarified butter, central to Vedic offerings</term>. The Seer (Rishi) is **Vamadeva**. 

The Index <note>original: "Anukramani"</note> states: "The eleven verses beginning 'From the ocean the wave' are addressed to Agni; the end is in Jagati; it is alternatively addressed to the Sun, or the Waters, or the Cow, or it is a praise of Ghee." 

This hymn is used as the *Ajya-shastra* <term>Ajya: an invocation involving clarified butter</term> on the day of the Equinox (*Vishuvat*). Thus the ritual manual says: "The Ajya-shastra is 'From the ocean the wave...'" <note>original: Ashvalayana Shrauta Sutra 8.6</note>. Furthermore, in the ten-night sacrifice <note>original: "Dasharatra"</note>, on the seventh day, this same hymn is used for the Ajya invocation, as noted: "Now the meters... 'From the ocean the wave' is the Ajya." <note>original: Ashvalayana Shrauta Sutra 8.9</note>.

---

->॥ The First Verse ॥<-

**Padapatha (Word-by-word):**
From the ocean । the wave । honey-filled (sweet) । up । it rose । near । with the stalk (Soma) । together । immortality । it reached ।
of the ghee । the name । secret । which । exists । the tongue । of the gods । of immortality । the navel ॥ 1 ॥

<meta>This page continues the commentary on the first verse of Rig Veda 4.58 and provides the text and commentary for verses 2 and 3. This hymn, known as the "Ghee Hymn" (Ghrita Sukta), is highly philosophical and symbolic, comparing the ritual offering of clarified butter (ghee) to cosmic forces like the sun, fire, and the soul.</meta>

## Commentary (Sayana)
<note>This is the conclusion of the commentary for Verse 1</note>
Because it flows from water, it is called lightning-fire <note>original: "vaidyuto-agniḥ"</note>. From that, a wave <note>original: "ūrmiḥ"</note>—like a surging mass of sweetness or a cluster of sweet fruits—has arisen or ascended. Alternatively, a juice that produces waves has arisen from the lightning. Or, the wave of water has arisen from the "ocean" <note>original: "samudrāt"</note>, which refers to the Sun, since the scripture says "rain is born from the Sun." Or, the ocean refers to the atmosphere from which water arises. Or, the ocean refers to the udder <note>original: "vāmṛdhasaḥ"</note> from which the bright milk-juice flows. 

This interpretation applies equally if we take "ocean" to mean clarified butter <term>Ghrita: clarified butter, the essential liquid offering in Vedic fire sacrifices</term>. Although butter comes from milk, it is spoken of as coming from the udder here in a figurative sense. The rest of the sentence is the same for all five possible interpretations (Agni, the Sun, etc.). Through the radiant ray, a person attains immortality <note>original: "amṛtatvaṃ"</note> or liberation <term>Moksha: the release from the cycle of rebirth</term>. I proclaim the secret name <note>original: "guhyaṃ nāma"</note> of this radiant butter—this milk-substance—which is the means of reverent bowing. That name serves as the tongue of the gods <note>original: "devānāṃ jihvā"</note> for tasting, and it is the "navel" or the binding point of immortality. This dual nature is what is meant by the "name" of ghee. This should be applied to all the verses according to whichever interpretation one follows.

---

->**॥ Now the Second Verse ॥**<-

## Hymn Text
**We shall proclaim the name of the clarified butter; in this sacrifice, we shall sustain it with our bows of reverence. May the Great Priest <note>original: "Brahmā"</note> hear this praise as it is recited. The four-horned, golden-hued deity has poured this forth. ॥ 2 ॥**

**Word-by-word breakdown:**
We । name । forth । we shall speak । of the clarified butter । in this । sacrifice । we shall sustain । with bows of reverence । 
toward । the Great Priest । may he hear । being recited । the four-horned । he poured forth । the golden-hued । this ॥ 2 ॥

## Commentary (Sayana)
We, the sacrificers, proclaim <note>original: "pra bravāma"</note> or praise the name of the ghee. In this sacrifice, we sustain it with bows of reverence or with sacrificial offerings <note>original: "havirbhir vā"</note>. May **Brahma**, the all-pervading deity, hear <note>original: "upaśṛṇavat"</note> this praise as it is being chanted. **Four-horned** <note>original: "catuḥśṛṅgaḥ"</note>: this refers to one who has four horns in the form of the four Vedas <term>Vedas: the four primary collections of ancient sacred hymns (Rig, Yajur, Sama, and Atharva)</term>. This is the interpretation for the Sun or Agni. In other contexts, the word "horn" should be explained according to the etymological derivations given by the sage Yaska. The **Golden-hued** <note>original: "gauraḥ"</note> or reddish-colored deity pours forth <note>original: "avamīt"</note>, meaning he emits or carries out this ritual, or perhaps the world itself.

<meta>
This page continues the extensive commentary by Sayana on the "Ghee Hymn" (Rig Veda 4.58). ## Commentary (Sayana)

<note>This section provides a multi-layered explanation of Verse 3: "Four are his horns, three are his feet..."</note>

Although this hymn can be explained in five different ways because it is dedicated to five deities including Fire <term>Agni: the god of fire and the ritual altar</term> and the Sun <term>Surya: the solar deity</term>, it is explained here primarily in relation to the sacrificial Fire and the Sun, following the methods established in the *Nirukta* <note>The Nirukta is an ancient Vedic treatise on etymology and philology</note>.

In the context of the sacrificial Fire, the **four horns** represent the four Vedas <note>original: "catvāro vedāḥ"</note>. Although the sage Apastamba states that "the sacrifice is performed with three Vedas" <note>original: "tribhirvedairvidhīyate", referring to the Rig, Yajur, and Sama Vedas</note>, the Atharvaveda is included here because it describes the entirety of the rituals without depending on others, thus making four "horns." 

The **three feet** represent the three daily extraction ceremonies <term>Savanas: the morning, midday, and evening pressings of the Soma juice</term>. They are called "feet" because they are the means by which the ritual progresses. 

The **two heads** refer to the *Brahmodana* and the *Pravargya* rites <note>These are specific ritual offerings within the larger Vedic ceremony</note>. This is said in reference to the primary importance of the *Ishti* and *Soma* sacrifices. 

The **seven hands** are the seven poetic meters <term>Chandas: the rhythmic structures of Vedic hymns, such as Gayatri or Trishtubh</term>. Just as hands are the primary tools for performing an action, these meters are the primary means of pleasing the gods. 

**Bound in three ways** means he is bound by the three types of texts: the Mantras, the ritual manuals <note>original: "kalpa"</note>, and the explanatory prose <note>original: "brāhmaṇa"</note>. His "binding" refers to how the ritual is accomplished through these. 

The **Bull** <note>original: "vṛṣabhaḥ"</note> is the "showerer" of the fruits of the sacrifice. He **roars** <note>original: "roravīti"</note>, meaning he makes a great sound. He cries out through the sounds produced by the *Rik*, *Yajur*, and *Saman* chants, which take the form of weapons, sacrifices, and praises. In this way, the **Great God has entered into mortals**. The "entry" is a metaphorical way of saying the god is manifested through the mortal sacrificers. The sage Yaska also explained this, stating "The Four Horns are the Vedas" <note>original: "vedā vā eta uktāḥ"; Nirukta 13.7</note>. That explanation should be kept in mind.

---

Now, the verse is explained from the perspective of the **Sun**:
The **four horns** of the Sun are the four cardinal directions. These are metaphorically called "horns" because they are the means of his movement. 
His **three feet** are the three Vedas. They are "feet" because they are the means of his motion across the sky. This is supported by the scripture which says: "The god moves in the heavens in the morning with the *Riks*... the Sun proceeds not empty of the three Vedas." 
The **two heads** are Day and Night. 
The **seven hands** are the seven rays of the sun, or perhaps the seven hands are the seasons—six distinct seasons and one common one. 
**Bound in three ways** refers to being connected to the three realms (Earth, Atmosphere, and Heaven) in the forms of Fire, Air, and Sun. Or, he is bound by the three seasons known as Summer, the Rains, and Winter. 
The **Bull**, the showerer of rain, **roars** by making the sound of thunder and falling rain. That **Great God entered mortals** as their inner controller. For the scripture says: "The Sun is the soul of all that moves and stays" <note>original: "sūrya ātmā jagatastasthuṣaśca"; Rig Veda 1.115.1</note>. This interpretation can also be applied to water and other elements.

The **Grammarians** <note>original: "śābdikāstu"</note>, however, explain this in terms of the "Word-Absolute" <term>Shabda-Brahman: the concept of ultimate reality manifested as sound/speech</term>. They explain that the **four horns** are the four types of words: **Nouns**, **Verbs**, **Prefixes**, and **Particles** <note>original: "nāmākhyāte copasarganipātāśca"</note>. Others interpret it in yet other ways. All of these views should be considered here.

---

-> ॥ Now the Fourth Verse ॥ <-

## Hymn Text

The gods found the ghee <note>original: "ghṛtam"</note> which was hidden in three places by the Panis <term>Panis: mythical demons or hoarders who steal the cows of light</term>, concealed within the Cow. Indra created one part, the Sun created one part, and the gods fashioned one part from the Vena <note>original: "venāt"</note> through their own inherent power. ॥ 4 ॥

<vocab>
Yajña (Sacrifice), Sūrya (Sun), Śabdabrahman (Word-Absolute), Nirukta (Etymology), Vṛṣabha (Bull/Showerer), Ghṛta (Clarified Butter/Ghee), Catvāri Śṛṅgā (Four Horns), Nāmākhyāta (Nouns and Verbs), Upasarga (Prefixes), Nipāta (Particles)
</vocab>

२५२ || Rig Veda || [Book 3. Chapter 8. Section 11.]

## Hymn Text

-> **Verse 4 (Word-by-word Analysis)** <-
Threefold | placed | by the Panis | being hidden | in the cow | the gods | the ghee | found.
Indra | one | Surya | one | produced | from the Loving One | one | by self-power | out | they fashioned. || 4 ||

---

## Commentary (Sayana)

The gods <note>original: "devāso"</note> found the clarified butter <term>Ghrita: the sacred essence of offerings, representing both physical butter and spiritual clarity</term>, which was a shining or liquid substance placed <note>original: "hitam"</note> and hidden <note>original: "guhyamānam"</note> by the Panis <term>Panis: a class of demons who hoard the world's treasures, such as cows or light</term> within the cows in three forms—namely, as milk, curd, and butter. From these, Indra produced one part (milk); the Sun <term>Surya: the solar deity</term> produced one part; and the gods fashioned one part of the ghee from the "Loving One" <note>Vena, which the commentator identifies here as either the brilliant Fire (Agni) or the Mind-possessing Wind (Vayu)</note> through the means of the sacrificial food or ritual power <note>original: "svadhayā"</note>. Thus, the gods brought it forth.

---

-> **|| Now the Fifth Verse ||** <-

## Hymn Text

These flow from the ocean of the heart, a hundred-fold path, not to be perceived by the enemy.
I behold the streams of ghee; the golden reed is in the midst of them. || 5 ||

-> **(Word-by-word Analysis)** <-
These | flow | from the heart | from the ocean | hundred-pathed | by the enemy | not | to be perceived.
Of the ghee | the streams | I | behold | golden | the reed | in the middle | of them. || 5 ||

---

## Commentary (Sayana)

These waters or streams of ghee flow <note>original: "arṣanti"</note>—they fall downward. Possessing a hundred-fold path <note>original: "śatavrajā", meaning unlimited movement</note>, they flow from the "ocean of the heart" <note>original: "hṛdyāt samudrāt"</note>, which refers to the atmospheric ocean or the depths of the soul. They flow in such a way that they are not visible <note>original: "navacakṣe"</note> to the enemy <term>Vritra: the demonic "Enveloper" who obstructs the flow of waters and light</term>.

The seer says: I behold <note>original: "abhicākaśīmi"</note> those streams of ghee. Where are they? It is explained: the "Golden Reed" <term>Vetasa: literally a cane or reed; here representing the lightning-fire or the primordial Agni</term> exists in the midst of these waters. By the final line, "I behold the streams of ghee," the poet refers to the Fire of the sacrifice, the Fire of the lightning, or the Sun himself as the witness.

-> **|| Thus ends the tenth section of the eighth chapter of the third book ||** <-

## Commentary (Sayana)

Upon this Fire, the streams of ghee flow perfectly <note>original: "samyak sravanti"</note>. Like what? Like rivers...

- Ghrita (ghṛta): clarified butter, brilliance, spiritual essence
- Pani (paṇi): a class of demons, hoarders of light/cattle
- Vetasa (vetasa): the golden reed, identifying Agni (Fire) in the waters
- Samudra (samudra): ocean, celestial waters, the heart's depth
- Arshanti (arṣanti): they flow or move rapidly
- Chakashimi (cākaśīmi): I behold or I illuminate
- Hiranyaya (hiraṇyaya): golden or made of light
- Ripu (ripu): enemy, deceiver, or one who obstructs
</vocab>

## Hymn Text

## Commentary (Sayana)
From a flowing river, like waters in a sloping place <note>original: "pravaṇavati deśe"</note>, the "fast-moving" <note>original: "śūghanāsaḥ"</note> streams fall. The terms *āśru* and *śru* are synonyms for "quick" according to the Etymology <term>Nirukta: the ancient science of Vedic interpretation and linguistics</term>. The great <note>original: "yahvāḥ"</note> streams of ghee, with a velocity surpassing the wind <note>original: "vātapramiyo"</note>, fall upon the fire. 

In the interpretation where ghee signifies "water," the word "like" <note>original: "iva"</note> in the phrase "like a river" is considered redundant. In that case, the meaning is: from the atmosphere, which is the source of flowing, these described streams of water fall to the earth. 

Furthermore, the mass of ghee, breaking through the barriers <note>original: "kāṣṭhāḥ"</note> that constitute the ritual boundaries <term>Paridhi: the green wood sticks placed around the sacrificial fire to contain it</term>, becomes increased or "swelling" with its liquid waves. In the water interpretation, it means breaking through the quarters of the sky where the water was held, and swelling with its billows. An illustration is provided: like a "shining horse" <note>original: "aruṣo na vājī"</note> moving with pride. Just as such a horse breaks through obstacles and surges forward, so does the ghee.

---

->॥ Now the Eighth Verse ॥<-

## Hymn Text
The beautiful, smiling streams of ghee approach the Fire, like wives to a gathering. They reach the kindling wood, and the Knower of All Beings, being pleased, desires them. || 8 ||

**Word-by-word Analysis:**
Towards | they flow | as if to a gathering | women | beautiful | smiling | Agni | of ghee | the streams | the fuel | they reach | these | being pleased | he desires | the Knower of All Beings. || 8 ||

---

## Commentary (Sayana)
The streams of ghee approach this Fire as women <note>original: "yoṣāḥ"</note> of the same mind <note>original: "samanamanaskā"</note> approach a husband at a gathering <note>original: "samane"</note>. They bow towards him; they immerse themselves in him. What are these streams like? They are "beautiful" <note>original: "kalyāṇyo"</note>, having auspicious forms...

## Commentary (Sayana) - Conclusion of Verse 8
Smiling <note>original: "smayamānāso"</note>, meaning laughing. Furthermore, those streams, truly illuminating the kindling, reach or pervade <note>original: "nasanta"</note> it. The Knower of Births <note>original: "jātavedāḥ"</note>, who is precious and worthy of being sought, being pleased and honoring those very streams, desires <note>original: "haryati"</note> them. In the interpretation where the word "ghee" <note>original: "ghṛta"</note> refers to water, then the terms "Agni" and "Jatavedas" refer to the lightning-fire or the Sun. The streams of water flow toward and reach that deity. He, in turn, desires them.

## Hymn Text
->॥ Now the Ninth Verse ॥<-

Like maidens anointing themselves with ornaments to go to a wedding, I behold the streams of ghee. Where the Soma is pressed, where the sacrifice is performed, there the streams of ghee flow. || 9 ||

**Word-by-word Analysis:**
Like maidens | to a wedding | to go | [intensifier] | ornaments | anointing | toward | I behold |
where | Soma | is pressed | where | the sacrifice | of ghee | the streams | toward | that | they flow. || 9 ||

## Commentary (Sayana)
Like maidens <note>original: "kanyā iva"</note>, meaning unmarried young girls. Just as they, to go to a wedding <note>original: "vahatūm"</note>—that is, to go to a husband—anoint themselves <note>original: "añjānāḥ"</note> with ornaments <note>original: "añji"</note> or a brilliant luster, manifesting their beauty; so do I behold the streams of ghee. Like those girls, they manifest their own characteristic form while going toward the fire—whether the terrestrial sacrificial fire, the lightning, or the Sun—who acts as their husband. It is well known that the terrestrial and lightning fires are kindled and intensified by ghee and water respectively. Furthermore, those streams flow toward <note>original: "pavante"</note> and reach that <term>yajña</term> <note>ritual sacrifice</note> wherever the Soma is pressed or whenever a sacrifice is extended.

## Hymn Text
->॥ Now the Tenth Verse ॥<-

Flow toward the beautiful praise and the prize of cattle; bestow auspicious riches upon us. Lead this sacrifice to the gods for us; the streams of ghee flow in a sweet manner. || 10 ||

**Word-by-word Analysis:**
Toward | flow | the beautiful praise | of cattle | the prize | in us | auspicious | riches | bestow |
this | sacrifice | lead | O gods | our | of ghee | the streams | sweetly | they flow. || 10 ||

## Commentary (Sayana)
O my <term>ṛtvij</term> <note>sacrificial priests</note>, flow toward <note>original: "abhyarṣata"</note> the prize <note>original: "ājim"</note> consisting of herds of cattle or related to cattle; that is, approach it or cause it to approach. Reach the beautiful praise. Here, by the word "cattle" <note>original: "go"</note>, waters or cows are meant, and their assembly is intended. Bestow <note>original: "dhatta"</note> or establish auspicious and praiseworthy riches in us, the patrons of the sacrifice. Indeed, the fruit of the ritual is obtained through such praise. Furthermore, lead this <term>yajña</term> <note>sacrifice</note> of ours to the deities, the gods who are to be worshipped here. The streams of ghee flow <note>original: "pavante"</note> in a way that is "filled with sweetness" <note>original: "madhumat"</note> or nectar-like.
