## Commentary (Sayana)

The phrase "In your domain" <note>original: "dhāman te"</note> is the first verse of the following hymn and is employed during both the commencement and the conclusion of the ritual study of the Vedas. This is indicated by the citation of the opening words "In your domain is the universe..." followed by the phrase "two verses" in the *Ashvalayana Household Sutras* <note>original: "Āśvalāyana Gṛhya Sūtra 3.5"</note>.

---

## Hymn Text

-> ॥ This is the eleventh verse ॥ <-

The whole world is rested upon your domain; it is within the ocean, within the heart, and within life. In the gathering of the waters, in the meeting place of battle, wherever it is brought forth—may we attain that wave of yours, which is full of sweetness. || 11 ||

-> **[Word-by-word Analysis]** <-

Domain | your | the whole | world | upon | rested | within | the ocean | the heart | within | life | of the waters | in the face | in the meeting | which | brought forth | that | may we attain | full of sweetness | your | wave || 11 ||

---

## Commentary (Sayana)

In your **domain** <note>original: "dhāman"</note>, meaning in the place of your light, the **whole world is established**. You exist **within the ocean** in the form of the submarine fire <note>the mythical fire beneath the sea</note>; you exist **within the heart** of all living beings as the <term>Vaiśvānara</term> <note>the "Universal Fire" of digestion and consciousness</note>; and you exist in **life** as the nourishment for all creatures. Alternatively, "life" <note>original: "āyuṣi"</note> may be an adjective for "heart," as life is sustained by the digestive fire. In the **face of the waters**, you exist as the fire of lightning, and in the **meeting**, meaning in battle, you exist as the fire of heroism. Thus, your power exists in all these places. In that domain, whatever **wave**—whether in the form of ghee or the essence of water—is **brought forth** or established, may we **attain** or pervade **that** sweetness-filled essence of **yours**.

-> ॥ This is the eleventh section of the eighth chapter of the third book ॥ <-

In this way, the illustrious Prime Minister Sayana, who bears the weight of the empire of King Bukka, and who has attained the glory of all-knowingness through the grace of his teacher Vidyatirtha, has completed this commentary.

Sayana, the knower of the essence of all scriptures, in this work titled "The Radiance of the Meaning of the Veda" <note>original: "Vedārtha Prakāśa"</note>, has clearly explained the Fourth Mandala of the Rig Veda. This Mandala was envisioned by the Seer <term>Vāmadeva</term>. It consists of fifty-eight hymns and is composed of five hundred and eighty-nine verses. He has explained this for the sake of easy understanding; let those who are free from malice behold it.

-> ॥ The Fourth Mandala is concluded ॥ <-

## Commentary (Sayana)

-> **|| The Rig Veda ||** <-

-> **|| Now begins the Fifth Book ||** <-

**He whose breath is the Vedas, and who from the Vedas fashioned the entire world; I salute that Maheshvara, the sacred site of knowledge.** <note>original: "vidyātīrthamaheśvaraṃ". This is a traditional opening invocation used by the commentator Sayana, honoring his spiritual teacher and the Supreme Lord as the source of all wisdom.</note>

In this Fifth Book, belonging to the clan of **Atri** <note>original: "ātreye"</note>, there are six sub-sections. In the first sub-section, there are fourteen hymns. Among these, the first hymn begins with the words "Agni has been awakened" <note>original: "abodhyagniḥ"</note> and consists of twelve verses. The ancient index <note>the Anukramani</note> states: "The twelve verses beginning with 'Agni has been awakened' were seen by the sages Budha and Gavishthira." According to the general rule for this Fifth Book, unless otherwise specified, the family name of the sages should be understood as being of the **Atri** lineage. Therefore, the two sages are Budha and Gavishthira, both descendants of Atri. By the rule of default, the meter is <term>Trishtubh</term> <note>a rhythmic structure consisting of four lines of eleven syllables each</note>. Following the rule for the start of a book, the deity is **Agni** <note>the god of Fire</note>. These first four hymns are used in the Atreya ritual, specifically during the chanting of the Ashwin-shastra in the Trishtubh meter. This is indicated in the ritual manuals: "The four hymns starting with 'Agni has been awakened'..." <note>original: "Āśvalāyana Śrauta Sūtra 4.13"</note>. Additionally, the first three verses are used during the rituals for the commencement and conclusion of the annual study of the Vedas.

---

## Hymn Text

-> || This is the first verse || <-

Agni has been awakened by the fuel of men; he stands facing the approaching Dawn like a cow returning home. Like young birds <note>original: "yahvāḥ"</note> flying up from the branches of a tree, his glowing rays spread forth toward the firmament. || 1 ||

**Word-by-word Analysis**
Awakened | Agni | by fuel | of men | toward | like a cow | approaching | Dawn | like young birds | forth | branches | flying up | forth | rays of light | spread | the firmament | toward || 1 ||

---

## Commentary (Sayana)

This Agni has been **awakened**—meaning he has become fully ignited—by the **fuel** provided by the priests and others. He is compared to a **cow**; just as one wakes up to attend to the cow for the morning milking, Agni awakens to face the **Dawn** as it arrives in the morning. Furthermore, the **rays of light** or the flames of the awakened Agni **spread forth** toward the **firmament** <note>the sky or atmosphere</note>. They are like great **branches** <note>original: "vayāḥ"</note> of trees or like young birds leaving the branches and flying upward, rising from their resting place to move toward the heavens.

---

## Hymn Text

-> || Now the second verse || <-

The Priest <note>the Hotar</note> has been awakened to sacrifice to the gods; Agni has stood up at dawn with a benevolent mind. When he is well-kindled, his gleaming splendor is seen; this Great Deity has been released from the darkness. || 2 ||

## Mandala 5. Hymn 1. Verse 1-4. || The Third Ashtaka || 257

## Hymn Text

**[Verse 2 - Word-for-Word Analysis]**

## Commentary (Sayana)

This **invoker** <note>original: "hotā", the priest who chants the invitations to the gods</note>, Agni, the one who completes the oblation, has been awakened to sacrifice to the gods who are to be worshipped. That Agni, at the time of dawn, being **good-minded**—that is, possessing a mind intent on favoring the **sacrificer** <note>original: "yajamāna", the patron who sponsors the ritual</note>—has stood upward. He rises up. The **bright**, shining **strength** of this kindled one, which is defined by his flames, is seen. It is visible. Then, the great deity, being in such a state, was **released from darkness**, from the blinding gloom.

-> || Now the Third Verse || <-

## Hymn Text

**[Verse 3 - Continuous Chant]**
When he has swallowed the rope of the collective world, the pure Agni, anointed with pure rays;
Then the sacrificial gift is joined, seeking nourishment; being upright, he drank from the ladles. || 3 ||

**[Verse 3 - Word-for-Word Analysis]**
When | him | of the collective | the rope | swallowed/seized | [thus] | pure | anointed | with pure | rays [literally: cows] | Agni | then | the sacrificial gift | is joined | seeking food | stretched out | upright | drank | with the ladles. || 3 ||

## Commentary (Sayana)

**When** <note>original: "yat"</note> this Agni **swallows** or seizes the **rope** <note>original: "raśanā"</note> of the collective world—the darkness which, like a cord, binds and obstructs all activity—it means he becomes fully kindled. At that time, the **pure**, radiant Agni reveals the entire world with his **pure rays** <note>original: "gobhiḥ", literally 'cows', a common Vedic metaphor for beams of light</note>. **Immediately after** <note>original: "āt"</note>, the **sacrificial gift** <note>original: "dakṣiṇā"</note>, which is the expanded stream of clarified butter <note>ghee</note> seeking to provide food for the gods, is **joined** or prepared. Alternatively, the "Dakshina" refers to the highly increased stream of ghee being readied. Agni, being **upright** and elevated, **drank** that stream—which is spread out above him—using the **sacrificial ladles** <note>original: "juhūbhiḥ", the specific wooden spoons used to pour offerings into the fire</note>.

Towards Agni, the minds of those seeking the gods move together, as eyes move toward the sun;

**[Verse 4 - Word-for-Word Analysis]**
Agni | towards | of those seeking the gods | the minds | like eyes | toward the sun | together | move | when | him | well-born/urged | the two Dawns [Day and Night] | of different forms | white | the horse/strong one | is born | at the beginning | of days. || 4 ||

---

## Commentary (Sayana)

The minds of the **sacrificers**, who desire the gods for themselves, **move toward** or focus upon the god **Agni**. The meaning is that they meditate on when this Agni will grow strong for the sake of the gods who are to be worshipped. This is **as eyes** of all living beings move toward the **sun**. When this Agni, along with the **Dawn** and her **different form** <note>referring to the alternating pair of Day and Night, or perhaps Heaven and Earth</note>...

<meta>This page continues the commentary on the hymns of the Rig Veda. [Page 258]
# Rig Veda | Book 3. Chapter 8. Section 12.

Heaven and Earth produce him; at that time, the white, brilliantly colored, powerful, and swift Agni <note>original: "vājī", meaning strong or possessing speed/power</note> is born at the time of dawn. That is to say, he increases.

---

-> ॥ Now the Fifth Verse ॥ <-

## Hymn Text
For he was born, the noble one, at the beginning of the days; placed among the auspicious woods, the red-shining one. In every house, holding the seven treasures, Agni the invoker, the most efficient sacrificer, has sat down. || 5 ||

**Word-for-Word Analysis:**
Was born | indeed | the noble/to-be-produced | at the beginning | of days | placed | in the auspicious [places] | the red-shining [one] | in the woods | in house and house | seven | treasures | holding | Agni | the invoker | down | sat | the most worshipful. || 5 ||

## Commentary (Sayana)
This Agni, the noble one who is to be produced, was born at the time of dawn. That is, he appeared. Afterward, in the beneficial woods—the fuel-wood from which fire is born—he is placed, shining as the red one. Then, in house after house—meaning in various sacrificial halls—he holds the seven **treasures** <note>original: "ratnā"; Sayana explains these are either the seven lovely flames of fire or seven types of wealth for the sacrificer</note>. Agni, acting as the **invoker** <note>original: "hotṛ", the priest who chants the invitations to the gods</note> who performs the oblation, being the most worshipful, has sat down. He remains seated.

If a rumor arises that a **sacrificer** <note>original: "yajamāna", the patron of the ritual</note> has died while he is actually still alive, then the "Fragrant Offering" <term>Surabhimati Ishti: a specific corrective ritual involving sweet-smelling substances</term> should be performed. In that rite, this verse is used as the invitatory prayer. It is indicated in the **Aitareya Brahmana** <note>original: "Ai. Brā. 7.9"</note>:
> "Agni the invoker has sat down, the most worshipful, to perfectly facilitate our worship of the gods today."

---

-> ॥ This is the Sixth Verse ॥ <-

## Hymn Text
Agni the invoker has sat down, the most worshipful, in the lap of the Mother, in that fragrant place. The youth, the sage, present in many places, the follower of Truth, the supporter of the people, kindled in their midst. || 6 ||

**Word-for-Word Analysis:**
Agni | the invoker | down | sat | the most worshipful | in the lap | of the Mother | in the fragrant | indeed | place | the youth | the sage | present in many places | the follower of Truth | the supporter | of the people | and | in the middle | kindled. || 6 ||

## Commentary (Sayana)
This Agni, being the invoker who performs the oblation and being the most worshipful, has sat down. Where? It is explained: in the lap—the bosom—of the **Mother** <note>original: "mātuḥ"; interpreted here as the Earth, the creator of all</note>. Specifically, in the fragrant place—the place characterized by the sacrificial altar <note>original: "vedi"</note>, which is filled with the fragrance of clarified butter and other offerings.

Furthermore, he is the **youth** <note>original: "yuvā"; eternally young or newly kindled</note>, the **sage** <note>original: "kaviḥ"; the wise poet</note>, and is **present in many places** <note>original: "puruniṣṭhaḥ"</note>. He is the **follower of Truth** <note>original: "ṛtāvā"; one who possesses or follows the cosmic law/sacrifice</note> and the supporter of all. Being such, he remains kindled in the midst of the **people** <note>original: "kṛṣṭīnām"; specifically the officiating priests and the sacrificers</note>.

Mandala 5. Chapter 1. Hymn 1. | **Third Ashtaka** | Page 259

-> ॥ Now the Seventh Verse ॥ <-

## Hymn Text
They quickly praise that inspired sage with salutations, Agni, the one who is efficient in the rites and the invoker. He who has extended Heaven and Earth with clarified butter—the priests always purify that swift one with clarified butter. || 7 ||

**Word-for-Word Analysis:**
Forth | indeed | that | inspired sage | in the rites | efficient | Agni | the invoker | they praise | with salutations.
Extensively | who | stretched out | Heaven and Earth | with clarified butter | always | they purify | the swift one | with clarified butter. || 7 ||

---

## Commentary (Sayana)
They quickly praise <note>original: "īḷate"</note> that Agni with hymns of praise. What is he like? He is a **sage** <note>original: "vipra", meaning wise or meditatively inspired</note>, efficient in producing results during the rites, and the **invoker** <note>original: "hotṛ"</note> who carries out the offering. This god is the one who extended <note>original: "atatan"</note> the two worlds, **Heaven and Earth** <note>original: "rodasī"</note>, with water. This is because the oblation thrown into the fire produces rain through the sun. Alternatively, he extended the heavens with the true sacrificial offering, and the earth with the resulting rewards like rain. The sacrificers always purify or tend to this swift god, who possesses food and strength, using water or clarified butter <note>original: "ghṛta", also known as ghee</note>. They serve him.

-> ॥ Now the Eighth Verse ॥ <-

## Hymn Text
The one to be cleansed is purified in his own place, the friend of the house, praised by the wise, our auspicious guest. The thousand-horned bull of such power; O Agni, you surpass all others by your might. || 8 ||

**Word-for-Word Analysis:**
To be cleansed | is purified | in his own [place] | friend of the house | praised by the wise | guest | auspicious | to us.
Thousand-horned | bull | of such power | all | O Agni | by might | forth | you are [surpassing] | others. || 8 ||

---

## Commentary (Sayana)
This Agni, who is **worthy of being cleansed** <note>original: "mārjālyaḥ"</note>, is purified and tended to in his own place, the sacrificial altar. What is he like? He is a **friend of the house** <note>original: "damūnās", meaning one whose mind is generous or self-controlled</note>, highly praised and extolled by wise poets. He is our **guest** <note>original: "atithi"</note>, worthy of worship like a visitor, and he is a bringer of happiness. He is the **thousand-horned** <note>original: "sahasraśṛṅgaḥ"</note>—meaning he possesses countless flames—and he is a **bull** <note>original: "vṛṣabhaḥ"</note> because he rains down rewards. He possesses "that" power—meaning his strength is the very essence of all known power. Now, the poet addresses him directly: O Agni, you surpass <note>original: "prāsi"</note> all other beings besides yourself by your sheer strength. This means you either defeat them or you have the power to pervade everything.

-> ॥ Now the Ninth Verse ॥ <-

## Hymn Text
O Agni, you immediately surpass all others, you for whom you have become most beautiful and visible. Worthy of praise, wonderful to look upon, radiant, the dear guest of human people. || 9 ||

# Rig Veda Sanhita
### Ashtaka 3, Adhyaya 4, Varga 13 | Page 260

## Hymn Text

**[Word-for-Word Analysis for Verse 9]**

Worthy of praise | having a beautiful form | possessing luster | beloved | of the people | guest | human || 9 ||

-> ॥ Now the Tenth Verse ॥ <-

O youngest Agni, the people bring offerings to you from near and also from afar. Recognize the high-minded praise of the one who lauds you most; for your protection, O Agni, is great, auspicious, and vast. || 10 ||

**[Word-for-Word Analysis for Verse 10]**
To you | they bring | the people | O youngest one | an offering | O Agni | from near <note>The text reads 'artita', but is understood as 'antitaḥ'</note> | [toward] | and | from afar |
[Toward] | of the one who praises most | the high-minded praise | recognize | great | your | O Agni | mighty | protection | auspicious || 10 ||

---

-> ॥ Now the Eleventh Verse ॥ <-

O radiant one, today mount your radiant chariot, O Agni, along with the adorable gods, entirely. Knowing the paths through the wide atmosphere, bring the gods here to eat the oblation. || 11 ||

**[Word-for-Word Analysis for Verse 11]**
[Toward] | today | the chariot | O radiant one | the radiant [one] | O Agni | stand/mount | with the adorable ones | completely | [the end] |
Knowing | of the paths | the wide | atmosphere | [toward] | here | the gods | for the eating of the oblation | bring || 11 ||

---

## Commentary (Sayana)

O Agni, having reached the sacrifice, you immediately <note>original: "sadyas"</note> go beyond others who are like you. You surpass them. You become manifest for the sake of the one to whom you have become most beautiful. Furthermore, you are one to be praised <note>original: "īḷenyaḥ"</note>, the one who gives form or radiance <note>original: "vapuṣyaḥ"</note>, the one possessing special luster <note>original: "vibhāvā"</note>, the beloved of all living beings, and the worshipful guest <note>original: "atithiḥ"</note> of human subjects.

-> ॥ Now the Tenth Verse ॥ <-

O most youthful <note>original: "yaviṣṭha", a common epithet for Agni as he is reborn at every fire-kindling</note> Agni, human beings <note>original: "kṣitayaḥ"</note> provide for you. What do they provide? An offering <note>original: "bali", a term for a religious gift or tribute</note> consisting of worship and oblations from nearby <note>original: "antitaḥ"</note> and also from afar. The word "ā" is used here in the sense of "and." Furthermore, recognize <note>original: "ā-cikiddhi"</note> the praise <note>original: "sumatim"</note> of the one who praises you excessively. O Agni, the happiness or protection <note>original: "śarma"</note> to be given by you to us is vast, great, and worthy of praise.

-> ॥ Now the Eleventh Verse ॥ <-

O radiant Agni <note>original: "bhānumo"</note>, today on this day of sacrifice, mount <note>original: "ātiṣṭha"</note> the radiant chariot which is well-proportioned in all its parts, along with the gods who are to be worshipped <note>original: "yajatebhiḥ"</note>. You, who have full knowledge of the gods to be worshipped, bring <note>original: "vaksi"</note> the gods here to this place through the paths of the divine sacrifice, through the vast atmosphere, so that they may eat the oblation <note>original: "havira-adyāya"</note>.

---

## Critical Notes

- **Accents:** The text uses standard Vedic accents: a horizontal line below for the low tone <note>original: "anudatta"</note> and a vertical line above for the moving tone <note>original: "svarita"</note>.
- **Lexical Variant:** In verse 10, the printed text shows **अर्तित** (*artita*), but the commentator Sayana clarifies it as **अन्तितः** (*antitaḥ*, meaning "from nearby"), which is the standard reading in most versions of the Rig Veda.
- **Phonetics:** The specific Vedic letter **ळ** (a retroflex 'l' sound) is used in the word **ईळेन्यः** (*īḷenyaḥ*). This is a characteristic sound of the Rig Veda, often replacing the 'd' sound when it occurs between two vowels.
- **Notation:** In verse 11, the numeral **१** (one) placed after the word **उ॒र्वि** (*urvi*) indicates a specific pitch modulation or "trembling" <note>term: "kampa", a specialized vocal technique in Vedic chanting</note> used to mark certain phonetic conditions.

It emphasizes Agni's role as the divine intermediary who receives offerings from humans and invites the celestial beings to the ritual feast.</summary>

## Hymn Text

-> ॥ Now the Twelfth Verse ॥ <-

We have uttered a song of praise to the wise, the sacrificial, the powerful, the showering <note>original: "vṛṣṇe," implying one who rains down blessings</note> Agni. Gavishthira <note>The Rishi or seer of this hymn</note> has offered this praise with reverence to Agni, like a wide-reaching jewel set in the sky. || 12 ||

**[Word-for-Word Analysis]**

Gavishthira | With reverence | Praise | In Agni | In the sky | Like | A jewel | Wide-reaching | He has placed/offered || 12 ||

## Commentary (Sayana)

We, the descendants of Atri, have spoken this song of praise—which is full of adoration—to the wise, the one worthy of sacrifice, the powerful bestower of rewards, the youthful Agni. Now the Rishi refers to himself in the third person to conclude the praise. This Rishi, Gavishthira, has offered this praise, accompanied by prostration or offerings of clarified butter, to Agni. He has placed it there just like the sun <note>original: "adityam"</note>, which is a wide-moving, shining jewel in the sky.

-> ॥ Thus ends the thirteenth Varga of the eighth [Adhyaya] of the third Ashtaka ॥ <-

The second hymn, beginning with "The young mother," consists of twelve verses. The Rishi <note>seer</note> is Kumara, the son of Atri, or Vrisha, the son of Jana, or both. However, for the two verses "Who is this?" <note>verse 3-4</note>, the Rishi is specifically Vrisha, not Kumara. The final verse is in the *Shakvari* meter (56 syllables), while the remaining verses are in the *Trishtubh* meter. The deity is Agni. According to the Index <note>original: "Anukramanika"</note>: "The boy [is the theme], Kumara or Vrisha Jana are the seers, or both; it ends with a Shakvari verse; for the two verses starting 'Who is this,' it is only Vrisha." The use of this hymn in the Morning Prayer and the Litany to the Ashvins was mentioned previously along with the first hymn.

## Hymn Text

-> ॥ First Verse of the Second Hymn ॥ <-

The youthful mother carries the boy in secret, held closely; she does not yield him to the father. People see his face <note>original: "anīkam," also meaning brilliance or array</note> before them, not fading, placed in the fire-stick <note>original: "aratau," referring to the wood used to churn fire</note>. || 1 ||

**[Word-for-Word Analysis]**

The face/brilliance | Of him | Not | Fading | The people | Before/In front | They see | Placed | In the fire-stick || 1 ||

## Commentary (Sayana)

A legend from the *Shakhayana Brahmana* <note>An ancient priestly commentary</note> is told here. There was a king named Tryaruna, son of Trivrishan, of the Ikshvaku dynasty. The sage Vrisha Jana was his domestic priest <note>original: "purohita"</note>. It is said that the priests used to hold the reins of the chariots to protect them. While Tryaruna was driving, the priest Vrisha held the reins. A boy playing in the path was struck by the wheel of the chariot. The boy was cut by the wheel and died. The priest said, "You are the killer..."

<meta>This page continues the commentary by Sayana on the second hymn of the Fifth Mandala. ## Commentary (Sayana)

The King and the priest argued further. The King said, "You are the killer of this boy, not I." The priest replied, "Because you were the driver and controller of the chariot's speed, he was killed by you." The King retorted, "Since you are the owner and master of the chariot, you are the slayer." Thus disputing, they went to the Ikshvakus <note>a famous solar dynasty of kings and elders</note> to ask for a judgment. They asked the Ikshvakus, "By whom was this twice-born <note>Brahmin</note> boy slain?" They replied that the driver, named Vrisha, was the slayer.

Then Vrisha, using the *Varsha-Saman* <note>a sacred musical chant named after him</note>, brought the boy back to life. Having told that story, another tradition is also recounted. Because the Ikshvakus spoke out of bias or passion against the seer <note>Rishi</note>, calling him a killer, the glow and power <note>original: "tejas"</note> of the ritual fire departed from their homes. In their houses, cooking and other essential fire-tasks could no longer be performed. They pondered the cause: "Because we called Vrisha a child-killer, the fire’s heat has left us. Let us call Vrisha back." Thinking thus, they invited the seer back with great respect.

When he arrived quickly, the heat of their fire returned. By singing the *Varsha-Saman*, he desired it to be as it was before. While singing, the seer saw the personified sin of "Brahmin-killing" <note>original: "brahmahatya"</note> which had arisen from the incident, attached to the wife of King Trasadasyu. She had taken the form of a demoness <note>original: "pishacha"</note>, and having taken the fire's heat, she was staying in the King's bedding. Seeing this clearly, the seer appeased that heat with his chant and subsequently reunited it with the fire. Then, the fire became endowed with its glow once more, and cooking and other tasks proceeded as before.

This version is told by the *Shatyayana* school; the version from the *Tandya* school is also mentioned. Vrisha was the domestic priest <note>Purohita</note> of King Trasadasyu. While the King was driving the chariot, he accidentally cut down a Brahmin boy with the chariot wheel. The King said to Vrisha: "Because you are my priest, this sin of passion falls on me; you must remove it." That seer then revived the boy using the *Varsha-Saman*.

The "mother" who produces the boy is a young woman <note>original: "yuvati"</note>. She carries the boy, who was struck by the wheel and hidden in a secret place <note>original: "guha," a cave or secret spot</note> on the path. She does not give him back to his father, the one who begot him. Alternatively, the "mother" is the Earth, the creator of all, who holds the boy hidden within a secret place and does not return him to the father. People do not see his face or form <note>original: "anikam"</note> because it has been harmed. Instead, they see him placed in a joyless, remote place. Or perhaps this revived boy, Vrisha, speaks of himself directly. Or a singer <note>original: "jaro"</note>, having revived him, speaks. 

Alternatively, because the hymn is dedicated to Agni <note>the Fire-god</note>, the "boy" refers to Agni. The "mother" is the young fire-stick <note>original: "arani"</note> which produces the fire. She holds him hidden and secret and does not give him to the "father," the sacrificer who initiates the rite. People do not see the burning, consuming heat of this Agni, but they see him placed within the fire-sticks.

</vocab>

## Hymn Text

**Mandala 5, Section 1, Hymn 2. (Anukramani - 2)**

->**Word-by-Word Analysis**<-

Whom. This. You. O young woman. Child. Destructive demoness. You carry. The Great Queen. Gave birth.
For many. Indeed. Fetus. Years. He grew. I saw. Born. When. Brought forth. The mother. || 2 ||

---

## Commentary (Sayana)

In this context, because the Fire-God <note>original: "Agni"</note> is being produced or "born" through the ritual, he is referred to by the word "Child" <note>original: "Kumara"</note>. 

Addressing the woman, the seer asks: "O young woman, why do you carry this child as if you were a destructive demoness <note>original: "peshi" / "pishacika"</note>?" This refers to a legend where the sage Vrisha speaks of the king's wife concealing the glow of the fire. He implies that because she did not truly "give birth" to it (produce it through ritual), her holding it is improper. 

The "Great Queen" <note>original: "Mahishi"</note> refers to the great and worshipful fire-drill <note>original: "arani," the wooden tool used to churn fire</note> which actually gave birth to him. He explains further: The fetus—referring to the potential fire residing within the wood—grew for many "years" <note>original: "sharadah," literally autumns</note> or long periods. "And I saw him," the seer says, "when his mother, the fire-drill, finally brought him forth." 

In the context of the Prince <note>referring back to the boy in the legend</note>: "O young woman, O Lady of the Earth, why do you carry this child like a demoness?" The rest of the verse should be applied to the birth of the prince. Similarly, in the following verses, the meaning should be interpreted appropriately as referring both to the Fire-God and to the life-force of the boy.

->**|| The Third Verse ||**<-

## Hymn Text

I saw the gold-toothed one, bright in color, from a distance in the field, shaping his weapons. 
Giving him the immortal, all-pervading offering—what can those who have no Indra and no sacred hymns do to me? || 3 ||

->**Word-by-Word Analysis**<-

Gold-toothed. Bright-colored. From a distance. From the field. I saw. Weapons. Shaping.
Giving. To him. Immortal. All-pervading. What. Me. Those without Indra. Do. Hymnless ones. || 3 ||

---

## Commentary (Sayana)

The seer Vrisha says: "I saw the Fire-God from a distance in the 'field' <note>referring to the sacrificial ground</note>." He describes the fire as "gold-toothed," meaning its flames are like teeth made of gold, and "bright-colored" due to its glowing appearance. The fire is "shaping his weapons," which refers to the sparks and leaping flames that look like tools or arms.

The seer continues: "I am the giver of the immortal offering <note>original: "amritam," referring to the nectar of the gods or the clarified butter</note> or the means to immortality, which is the all-pervading oblation and song of praise." 

Regarding the phrase "those without Indra": Indra represents supreme power, and here it signifies the Fire-God in his majestic form. Those who are "without Indra" are those who do not perform sacrifices. The seer asks: "What can those who do not worship or sing hymns of praise do to harm me?" Since he is protected by the fire he has restored, he is beyond their reach.

->**|| The Fourth Verse ||**<-

## Hymn Text

I saw him from the field, moving in secret, shining greatly like a happy herd.
They did not grasp him, for he has been born, even when the grey ones become young women. || 4 ||

->**Word-by-Word Analysis**<-

From the field. I saw. In secret. Moving. Happy. Herd. Like. Greatly. Shining.
Not. Those. They grasped. Was born. For. He. The grey ones. Indeed. Young women. They become. || 4 ||

## Hymn Text

## Hymn Text
The enemies have hidden the King of those who dwell, the dwelling place of all people, among the mortals. Let the sacred prayers of the Sage release him. Let the revilers themselves become deserving of revilement. ॥ 6 ॥

## Commentary (Sayana)
The "King of those who dwell" refers to the master of all living beings. He is the "dwelling place of people" because the Fire-God, as described previously, is the refuge of all. The enemies have hidden <note>original: "nidadhuḥ"</note> him; they have failed to protect him among the mortal worlds. Let the sacred prayers or hymns of the sage Vrisha—who is here called "the unperceived" <note>original: "aceḥ," referring to his hidden or subtle power</note>—release that child, the Fire-God. Alternatively, let the prayers of the Sage release the boy. Or, regarding the Sage's prayers for the unperceived one <note>grammatically identifying "Sage" and "unperceived"</note>, let them release the child. May those who insult us become themselves objects of insult by us. Relying on the phrase "the prayers of the Sage," even Vrisha should be considered unperceived <note>Text continues to next page</note>

In the ritual known as the "Sudden Pressing" <note>original: "añjaḥsava"</note>, during the worship of the Offering-Fire <note>original: "āhavanīya"</note>, this verse regarding Shunahshepa is used. The Sacred Prose <note>original: "Brāhmaṇa"</note> states: "Shunahshepa, being bound, worshipped the Offering-Fire; he was released from a thousand [bonds]" <note>original: Aitareya Brahmana 7.19</note>.

->॥ This is the seventh verse ॥<-

## Hymn Text

You released **Shunahshepa** <note>A legendary seer whose name literally means "Dog-tail"</note> from the **sacrificial post**, though he was **bound** by a **thousand** [ties]; for he indeed was stilled <note>original: "ashamiṣṭa," meaning he became quiet or offered praise</note>. Even so, O **Agni**, release the **bonds** from us, O **Wise Priest**, having **seated** yourself here. ॥ 7 ॥

### Word-by-Word Analysis
Shunahshepa. Indeed. Bound. From a thousand. From the sacrificial post. You released. He was stilled. For. He.
Even so. From us. O Agni. [Away]. Release. The bonds. O Invoking Priest. O Wise One. Here. Indeed. Having sat down. ॥ 7 ॥

---

## Commentary (Sayana)

O **Agni**, you **released the seer Shunahshepa**, who was intensely **bound** <note>original: "niditam"</note>, from the **sacrificial post** which was of **a thousand** <note>meaning many-sided or having many ropes</note> forms. You set him free. The word "**Chit**" is a filler word. In the traditional recitation <note>original: "saṃhitā"</note>, the name "**Shunahshepa**" is positioned with its components rearranged. **That seer indeed was stilled**; he became peaceful. Or, since he "stilled" (meaning he offered praise, as this is a term for the act of praising), you therefore released him. **Even so**, in that same way, **release the bonds** from us. O **Priest** <note>original: "hotar"</note>, O **Conscious Agni**, stay **here** upon the altar <note>original: "vedyām"</note> having **seated** yourself.

->॥ Now, the eighth verse ॥<-

## Hymn Text

Being **angry**, you indeed **moved away from me**. But the **guardian of the vows** of the **gods** told me. **Indra**, the **knowing one**, indeed **observed** you; guided **by him**, O **Agni**, I have **come** to you. ॥ 8 ॥

### Word-by-Word Analysis
Being angry. Away. Indeed. From me. You moved. [Forward]. To me. Of the gods. Guardian of vows. Told.
Indra. Knowing. [After/Indeed]. For. You. Saw. By him. I. O Agni. Instructed. [Toward]. I have come. ॥ 8 ॥

---

## Commentary (Sayana)

O **Agni**, you, **being angry** <note>original: "hṛṇīyamānaḥ"</note>, **moved away from me**. You indeed departed. <note>The word "ayaiḥ" (you moved) comes from the root 'i' meaning to go, with specific grammatical changes common in Vedic Sanskrit where the 'a' of the suffix changes to 'e'.</note> To **me**, **Indra**, the **guardian of the ritual vows** <note>original: "vratapāḥ"</note> of the **gods**, **told** [where you were]. He, being **wise**, **observed** (saw) **you**. **Instructed by him**, O **Agni, I have come** to you. Thus says the seer Vrisha.

<vocab>
- <term>Shunahshepa (शुनःशेप)</term>: A famous Vedic figure who was nearly sacrificed by his father but saved by the gods after praying to Agni, Varuna, and others.
- <term>Agni (अग्नि)</term>: The God of Fire, the primary mediator between gods and humans.
- <term>Indra (इन्द्र)</term>: The King of the Gods, often depicted as a heroic warrior and protector.
- <term>Vratapa (व्रतपा)</term>: A title meaning "Guardian of Vows" or "Protector of Rites," ensuring sacred laws are followed.
- <term>Yupa (यूप)</term>: The sacrificial post to which the victim or offering was symbolically or literally tied.
- <term>Pasha (पाश)</term>: Ropes, fetters, or the spiritual bonds of sin and mortality.
- <term>Aitareya Brahmana (ऐतरेय ब्राह्मण)</term>: An ancient prose commentary on the Rig Veda detailing ritual procedures and myths.
</vocab>

<summary>This page covers verses 7 and 8 of the hymn, detailing the liberation of Shunahshepa from his bonds and the reconciliation of the seer Vrisha with Agni through Indra's guidance.</summary>
<keywords>Shunahshepa, Agni, Indra, sacrificial post, bonds, Vratapa, Aitareya Brahmana, ritual release, Vrisha</keywords>

<meta>This page continues the third Mandala of the Rig Veda, transitioning into the fifteenth section (Varga) of the fourth lesson (Adhyaya). While the previous page discussed the release of the seer Shunahshepa, this page focuses on the cosmic power of the fire-god Agni to dispel darkness and demonic illusions, and the poet's act of crafting a hymn as a spiritual vehicle.</meta>

->**॥ The Ninth Verse ॥**<-

## Hymn Text

**Agni** shines abroad with **great light**; through his **might**, he makes **all things manifest**. He overcomes **undivine illusions** <note>original: "māyāḥ," supernatural powers or deceptive magic</note> that are **evil-moving**, and he **sharpens** his flames like **horns** to **pierce** the **demons** <note>original: "rakṣase," malevolent spirits</note>. ॥ 9 ॥

---

**Word-by-Word Analysis**

Abroad. With light. With great. Shines. Agni. Manifest. All [things]. He makes. Through [his] might.
Forward. Undivine. Illusions. He overcomes. Evil-moving. He sharpens. Horns. For the demon. For piercing. ॥ 9 ॥

## Commentary (Sayana)

This **Agni shines** <note>original: "vi bhāti," shines intensely or specifically</note> with **great brilliance** or heat. Being such, through his own **might** or greatness, he **makes manifest**—that is, he reveals—**all** existing **objects**. **Agni**, thus grown powerful, **overcomes** the **undivine**, demonic **illusions** <note>original: "māyāḥ"</note> which are **evil-moving** <note>original: "durevāḥ," difficult to approach or causing misery</note>. He subdues them. Furthermore, he **sharpens** his **horns**—or rather, he sharpens his destructive flames which resemble horns. For what purpose? **To pierce** or destroy the **demon**. As the ancient etymologist Yaska says: "He pierces the demon with his horn to destroy it" <note>Nirukta 4.18; Nirukta is the ancient Vedic science of etymology</note>. ॥ 9 ॥

---

->**॥ The Tenth Verse ॥**<-

## Hymn Text

And may the **roaring sounds** of **Agni** be in **heaven**, possessing **sharp weapons** to **slay** the **demons**. Even in his **exhilaration**, his **glows** **crush** [the enemies]; the **undivine** **obstructors** do **not** **restrain** him. ॥ 10 ॥

---

**Word-by-Word Analysis**

And. Roaring [flames]. In heaven. Let them be. Of Agni. Sharp-weaponed. For the demon. For slaying. Indeed.
In exhilaration. Even. His. [Forward]. They crush. Glows. Not. They restrain. Obstructors. Undivine. ॥ 10 ॥

## Commentary (Sayana)

Furthermore, let the **roaring** or sounding **flames** of **Agni appear in heaven** <note>the sky or celestial realm</note>. For what purpose? These flames, acting as **sharp weapons**, are **to slay the demons**. The particle "u" is a rhythmic filler. Even in **exhilaration** <note>original: "made," the joy of the ritual or the Soma-press</note>, the **glows** or angers of **Agni** intensely **crush** or break the demons. The **undivine** armies of the demons, who act as **obstructors** on all sides, do **not restrain** or ward him off. ॥ 10 ॥

---

->**॥ The Eleventh Verse ॥**<-

## Hymn Text

O **many-born** one <note>original: "tuvijāta," born in many places or of great power</note>, I, the **wise poet**, have **fashioned** this **hymn** for **you**, as a **skilled craftsman** fashions a **chariot**. If **you**, O **divine Agni**, should **accept** it, may we **win** the **heavenly waters** through **this**. ॥ 11 ॥

---

**Word-by-Word Analysis**

This. For you. Hymn. O many-born. The wise poet. A chariot. Like. A steady [craftsman]. Of good works. I have fashioned.
If. Indeed. O Agni. [Towards]. You. O Divine. You should accept. Possessing the light of heaven. Waters. Through this. May we win. ॥ 11 ॥

## Commentary (Sayana)

O **Agni**, who are **many-born**, I, the **wise poet**, **have fashioned** <note>original: "atakṣam," carved or constructed</note> **this hymn** <note>original: "stoma," song of praise</note> for **you**. I have done this **like a steady** or skillful **craftsman** of **good works** fashions a **chariot**. **If you**, O **divine** one, **accept** this hymn with favor, then **through this** act of worship, **may we win** the **waters** that **possess the light of heaven** <note>original: "svarvatīḥ," celestial or sun-filled</note>. ॥ 11 ॥

It ends with the poet comparing the composition of a sacred hymn to the careful craftsmanship of a chariot, intended to win divine favor and celestial rewards.</summary>

<meta>This page concludes the second hymn (Sukta) and begins the third hymn of the Fifth Mandala of the Rig Veda. It continues the commentary by Sayana (a 14th-century scholar) on the nature of Agni, the fire-god, transitioning from Agni as a powerful protector to Agni as a universal deity who embodies the qualities of other major gods like Varuna and Mitra.</meta>

## Commentary (Sayana) — Continued from previous page (RV 5.2.11)

O Agni, you who have attained many forms <note>original: "tuvijāta," born in many ways or of great power</note>, I—the wise singer of praises—have fashioned <note>original: "atakṣam," carved or constructed, like a carpenter</note> this hymn for you, just as a skillful craftsman builds a **chariot**. O Divine Agni, if you truly **delight** in this hymn, then through it may we obtain the **waters** that possess the light of heaven <note>original: "svarvatīḥ," associated with Svar, the celestial realm</note> and provide us with protection.

---

## Hymn Text

-> ॥ The Twelfth Verse ॥ <-

**Broad-necked, the Bull, growing strong, he drives together the wealth of the enemy without a rival. The immortals said this of this Agni: "May he grant peace to Manu who possesses the sacred grass; may he grant peace to Manu who possesses the oblation." ॥ 12 ॥**

**Broad-necked. The Bull. Growing strong. Without a rival. Of the enemy. Together. He drives. Wealth.**
**Thus. This. Agni. The immortals. They said. To the one with sacred grass. To Manu. Peace. May he grant.**
**To the one with the oblation. To Manu. Peace. May he grant. ॥ 12 ॥**

---

## Commentary (Sayana)

**Broad-necked** <note>original: "tuvigrīvaḥ"</note> means one with many flames or a massive neck of fire. He is the **Bull** because he showers down the fulfillment of desires. **Growing strong**, Agni **drives together**—that is, he secures or joins—the **wealth** of the **enemy** <note>original: "aryaḥ," often referring to a rival or hostile person</note> in a way that is **without a rival** <note>original: "aśatru," without enemies or obstacles</note>. The other **immortal** gods **said this** very thing about Agni. Because he is such a powerful deity, **may he grant peace**—meaning happiness—to **Manu** <note>The ancestral father of humanity; here used for the human sacrificer</note> who **possesses the sacred grass** <note>original: "barhiṣmate," one who has prepared the ritual seat for the gods</note>. Also, **may he grant peace** to the one **possessing the oblation** <note>original: "haviṣmate," the worshiper offering food into the fire</note>.

-> ॥ Thus ends the fifteenth section (Varga) of the eighth lesson (Adhyaya) of the third Book (Ashtaka) ॥ <-

---

## Sukta Introduction

The third hymn, beginning with "**You, Agni, are Varuna**" <note>original: "tvam agne varuṇa"</note>, consists of twelve verses. Its **Seer** <note>original: "Rishi," the inspired poet to whom the hymn was revealed</note> is Vasushruta, a descendant of Atri. The **meter** is <term>Trishtubh</term> <note>a Vedic meter of 4 lines with 11 syllables each</note>, and the deity is Agni. This is noted in the ancient index: "You, Agni, Vasushruta." Its ritual use in the "Morning Litany" and the "Ashvina Weapon" <note>specific parts of the Soma sacrifice</note> has already been mentioned in the section beginning with "Agni has been awakened."

---

## Hymn Text

-> ॥ The First Verse ॥ <-

**You, Agni, are Varuna when you are born; you become Mitra when you are kindled. In you, O Son of Strength, are all the gods; you are Indra for the mortal who gives. ॥ 1 ॥**

**You. Agni. Varuna. You are born. When. You. Mitra. You become. When. Kindled.**
**In you. Thus. All. Of strength. O Son. Gods. You. Indra. To the giver. To the mortal. ॥ 1 ॥**

---

## Commentary (Sayana)

O **Agni**, **you** yourself are **Varuna** <note>The god of the night sky and cosmic law</note>, who wards off darkness and presides over the night, **when** you **are born** <note>as the ritual fire is first lit</note>. Furthermore, **you** are **Mitra** <note>The god of friendship and the day</note>, the protector from destruction who presides over the day, **when** you are **kindled**. This means that as soon as you are produced, you remove the darkness, and when you are fully grown, you become the benefactor of all. **In you**, O **Son of Strength** <note>A common title for Agni, as fire is produced by the "strength" of rubbing sticks</note>, are **all**... <note>The commentary breaks off here at the end of the page</note>

<summary>This page concludes the second hymn of Mandala 5 with a prayer for Agni's protection and then begins the third hymn, which identifies Agni as a composite deity embodying Varuna, Mitra, and Indra.</summary>
<keywords>Agni, Varuna, Mitra, Manu, Trishtubh meter, Vasushruta, Vedic sacrifice, ritual wealth, Son of Strength</keywords>

--- Page 336 ---
<meta>This page continues the commentary by the 14th-century scholar Sayana on Rig Veda Mandala 5, Sukta 3. It concludes the explanation of Verse 1, which identifies Agni with various deities, and provides the text and commentary for Verses 2 and 3. These verses highlight Agni’s role in marriage rituals and his manifestation as lightning in the atmosphere.</meta>

...all the gods are present within him. This is because they live through that oblation. Indeed, the sacred scripture <note>original: "śruteḥ," referring to the Vedas</note> says that the gods, being afraid, entered into Agni. O **Son of Strength** <note>original: "sahasasputra," a common title for Agni because fire is produced by the "strength" of friction when rubbing sticks together</note>! Furthermore, you are Indra, the master, for the mortal sacrificer who gives the oblation.

Regarding the butter-offering on the fourth day of a wedding, there is the verse "You are Aryaman." This is indicated in the *Asvalayana Gṛhya Sutra* (1.4.1): "The verse 'You are Aryaman when [you are the name] of maidens' is used for the fourth offering in a wedding."

->॥ This is the Second Verse ॥<-

## Hymn Text
**You become Aryaman when you take the secret name of the maidens, O Lord of Self-Power. They anoint you like a well-placed friend with the products of the cow, when you make the husband and wife of one mind. ॥ 2 ॥**

**You. Aryaman. You become. When. Of the maidens. Name. O Lord of Self-Power. Secret. You bear. They anoint. Friend. Well-placed. Like. With cows. When. Husband and wife. Of one mind. You make. ॥ 2 ॥**

---

## Commentary (Sayana)
O Agni, you are **Aryaman** <note>The solar deity of hospitality and marriage</note>. You are the regulator of all. When <note>original: "yat," since</note> you are related to the maidens. Furthermore, O **Lord of Self-Power** <note>original: "svadhāvan," one possessing the sacrificial food or inherent power</note>, you bear a **secret** name that should be kept hidden; that name is **Vaishvanara** <note>original: "vaiśvānara," the Fire belonging to all men</note>. Like a **well-placed**—meaning well-established—**friend**, they **anoint** you with the **products of the cow**. Here, the word "cow" is used to mean its derivatives, such as milk and clarified butter. Because <note>original: "yat," since</note> you make the **husband and wife** possess **one mind** <note>original: "samanasā," in total harmony</note>.

->॥ Now the Third Verse ॥<-

## Hymn Text
**For your glory, the Maruts purified you, O Rudra, when your birth was beautiful and wondrous. When the highest step of Vishnu was established, through that you protect the secret name of the waters. ॥ 3 ॥**

**Of you. For glory. The Maruts. They purified. O Rudra. When. Your. Birth. Beautiful. Wondrous. Step. Which. Of Vishnu. Highest. Established. Through that. You protect. Secret. Name. Of the cows. ॥ 3 ॥**

---

## Commentary (Sayana)
This verse describes the **atmospheric form** of Agni <note>Agni as lightning</note>. O Agni, for your **glory**—that is, for your arrival—the **Maruts** <note>The storm-gods</note> purified the waters in the atmosphere. O **Rudra** <note>Sayana explains this as Agni in his fierce form as the "roarer" through rain</note>, your **birth** in the form of lightning is **beautiful**, meaning it is to be approached, and **wondrous**, meaning it is to be admired. If one asks how this happens, it is explained: the **highest** and **secret**—meaning inaccessible—**step** of **Vishnu**, the all-pervading god, was **established**. By this, the "atmosphere" is meant. As it is said in the *Brahmana* text, "Because it is like the middle step of Vishnu, therefore they do not see the atmosphere." Through that, you **protect** the **secret name** of the **cows**, which here refers to the **waters** <note>In Vedic imagery, clouds are often called "cows" and rain is their "milk"</note>.

## Hymn Text
**By your glory, O beautiful God, the gods, holding many [treasures], attain immortality. Men have sat down around this Agni, the invoker, distributing offerings and desiring [blessings], for the sake of the praising mortal. ॥ 4 ॥**

**By your. Glory. Beautiful-to-look-at. O God. The gods. Many. Holding. Immortality. They attain.
The invoker. Agni. Men. Down. They have sat. Distributing. Desiring. Praise. Of the living man [the sacrificer]. ॥ 4 ॥**

---

## Commentary (Sayana)
O Divine Agni <note>original: "devāgne"</note>, through your beauty—that is, your prosperity—the gods such as Indra and others, holding much <note>meaning, having great affection for you</note>, attain <term>immortality</term> <note>original: "amṛtaṃ," the state of deathlessness or the divine nectar</note>. Men—specifically the officiating priests—have sat down around Agni, the <term>Invoker</term> <note>original: "hotāram," the priest who recites the hymns and calls the gods</note>, to serve him. What are they doing? They are distributing the <term>oblation</term> <note>original: "havis," the sacrificial offering</note> for the sake of the "living man" <note>original: "āyoḥ," interpreted here as the human sacrificer</note> who desires the fruit of the praise.

->॥ This is the Fifth Verse ॥<-

## Hymn Text
**There is no invoker older than you, O Agni, nor one more skilled in sacrifice; none is beyond you in wisdom, O Master of Self-Power. The clan to whom you become a guest, O God, shall overcome [all other] mortals through sacrifice. ॥ 5 ॥**

**Not. Than you. Invoker. Older. O Agni. Better at sacrificing. Not. With wisdom. Beyond. Is. O Master of Self-Power.
Of the clan. And. To whose. Guest. You become. He. Through sacrifice. Shall overcome. O God. Mortals. ॥ 5 ॥**

---

## Commentary (Sayana)
O Agni, there is no other <term>Invoker</term> <note>Hotar</note> who is "older" <note>original: "pūrvaḥ," meaning either the one who fills/satisfies or the ancient one</note> or a better sacrificer than you. There is no one beyond you or superior to you even in future times in terms of wisdom or hymns <note>original: "kāvyaiḥ"</note>. O God, O **Master of Self-Power** <note>original: "svadhāvaḥ," one possessing the sacrificial food or inherent strength</note>, in whichever clan or for whichever priest you become a guest <note>meaning you are honored like a prestigious guest</note>, that person will, through the power of the sacrifice, overcome or strike down the mortals who hate us. Alternatively, it means he will properly provide for the mortals who serve him.

**We. O Agni. May we conquer. Protected by you. Seeking wealth. With the oblation. Awakening.

...May we obtain wealth. What kind of people are we? We are those who desire riches <note>original: "vasumyavaḥ"</note>, and by awakening you with the sacrificial offering, may we conquer our enemies in battle. ## Hymn Text

->॥ The Seventh Verse ॥<-

**Whoever brings offense or sin upon us, place that evil upon that malicious speaker. O wise Agni, strike down this curse; strike him down who harms us with double-dealing. ॥ 7 ॥**

Whoever. Us. Offense. Upon. Sin. Brings. Place. Indeed. Evil. Upon-the-malicious-speaker. Place. 
Strike. O Wise One. Curse. This. O Agni. Who. Us. Harms. With-the-double. ॥ 7 ॥

## Commentary (Sayana)

Whichever mortal brings offense <note>original: "āgaḥ," a mistake or transgression</note> or sin <note>original: "enaḥ"</note> upon us, let Agni place that very evil upon that malicious speaker <note>original: "aghaśamse," one who speaks or plots evil</note>. Let Agni give it back to him. The word "Indeed" <note>original: "it"</note> is a filler for the meter. The meaning is: whatever offense someone commits against me, Agni does the same to him. 

Now the poet speaks directly to the god: O Agni, strike down this curse <note>original: "abhiśastim," a public accusation or a magical curse</note>. Since the word "who" appears later in the verse, we should interpret "this" as "this curser." Strike down the one who harms or obstructs us with "the double" <note>original: "dvayena," which Sayana interprets as the twofold burden of the aforementioned offense and sin</note>.

## Hymn Text

->॥ The Eighth Verse ॥<-

**O God, the ancients, making you their messenger at the dawning of this night, worshipped you with oblations. When you go to the gathering of riches, O Agni, you are kindled as a God by mortals and by the Vasus. ॥ 8 ॥**

You. Of this. At the dawning. O God. The ancients. Messenger. Making. They worshipped. With oblations. 
In the gathering. When. O Agni. You go. Of riches. God. By mortals. By the Vasus. Being kindled. ॥ 8 ॥

## Commentary (Sayana)

O Agni, at the dawning of this night <note>original: "asyā vyuṣi," meaning when the dawn has fully broken</note>, the ancient sacrificers of old, making you the messenger <note>original: "dūtam," the one who conveys the sacrifice to the gods</note> and the one who impels the gods, worshipped you by means of sacrificial offerings. When there is a gathering or a bringing together of riches <note>original: "rayīṇām," here interpreted as the wealth of the sacrificial materials</note>, O Agni, you go there. You are the shining God, being kindled <note>original: "idhyamānaḥ"</note> by mortals—the human officiating priests—and by the <term>Vasus</term> <note>original: "vasubhiḥ," a class of deities associated with the elements, but here also meaning "the indwellers"</note>.

<meta>This page continues the translation of Mandala 5, Sukta 3, dedicated to Agni. The previous page concluded the commentary on Verse 8. ## Hymn Text

-> ॥ The Ninth Verse ॥ <-

**Deliver the father, O Son of Strength; being wise, separate him from evil—he who as a son serves you. O wise Agni, when will you look upon us? O Knower of the Eternal Order, when will you set us on the right path? ॥ 9 ॥**

Deliver. The father. Separate. Being wise. The son. Who. You. Of strength. O Son. Serves.
When. O Wise One. Upon. You look. Us. O Agni. When. Knower of the Eternal Order. You will set on the right path. ॥ 9 ॥

---

## Commentary (Sayana)

O **Son of Strength** <note>original: "sahasas sūno," an epithet for Agni because fire is produced by the forceful friction of wood-sticks</note>, O Agni, **deliver** <note>original: "avaspṛdhi," meaning to rescue or bring across</note> us. **Separate** <note>original: "yodhi"</note> us from sin. The **son** who serves as your worshiper, knowing you as his **father** and protector, **serves** <note>original: "ūhe"</note> you by carrying the oblation. The Sage speaks of himself here in the third person. 

As it will be said later:
> Agni, the bearer of oblations, the undecaying, is our father. <note>original: "havyavāḷagnirajaraḥ pitā naḥ" — Rig Veda 5.4.2</note>

Alternatively, the relationship of father and son is inverted here: Deliver and protect the worshiper who acts like a **father** to you <note>the sacrificer "gives birth" to the ritual fire</note>, and you, Agni, are like the **son** who must always be protected. 

As the scripture says:
> You become the son of him who serves you. <note>original: "tvaṃ putro bhavasi yaste'vidhat" — Rig Veda 2.1.9</note>

O **Wise One** <note>original: "cikitvaḥ," the conscious or mindful one</note>, O Agni, **when** will you **look upon us**? And **when**, O **Knower of the Eternal Order** <note>original: "ṛtacit," one who perceives the Truth or the Law of the sacrifice</note>, you who are the perceiver of the sacrifice or the waters, will you **set us on the right path**? That is, guide us through the virtuous way.

---

## Hymn Text

-> ॥ The Tenth Verse ॥ <-

**The father, O Dweller, bestows your many names with praise, if you take pleasure in that. Often Agni, the God, desiring the offering through his might, bestows happiness as he grows. ॥ 10 ॥**

Many. Name. Praising. Bestows. The father. O Dweller. If. That. You take pleasure in.
Often. The God. Through might. Desiring. Happiness. Agni. Bestows. Growing. ॥ 10 ॥

---

## Commentary (Sayana)

While **praising** your **many** abundant names, he **bestows** them; he holds them. By extension, this means he holds the oblation. Or, he holds the abundant oblation called "name" in order to give it. You are the **father** and protector, O **Dweller** <note>original: "vaso," a title for Agni meaning the Abode or the one who causes all to dwell</note>. **If** you **take pleasure in that** oblation, you enjoy it. **Often** <note>original: "kuvit"</note> the **God**, Agni, who is full of **might**, is **desiring** <note>original: "cakānaḥ"</note> the many oblations of the worshiper. Alternatively, using the possessive case for the action: **Agni**, while **growing** <note>original: "vavṛdhānaḥ"</note> or making the worshiper grow, **bestows happiness** <note>original: "sumnam vanate"</note>—he grants peace and joy.

---

## Hymn Text

-> ॥ The Eleventh Verse ॥ <-

**Indeed, O Agni, most youthful one, you carry the singer across all difficulties. Thieves have been hidden, and those people who are enemies and of unknown intent have become crooked... ॥ 11 ॥**

<summary>This page discusses verses 9 and 10 of Rig Veda 5.3, emphasizing the intimate, reciprocal father-son relationship between Agni and his worshipers. Agni is invoked as the "Son of Strength" and the "Knower of Eternal Order" to guide the faithful and provide happiness.</summary>

<meta>This page transitions from the end of the second hymn (Sukta 2) to the beginning of the third hymn (Sukta 3) in the fifth book (Mandala) of the Rig Veda. It continues the themes of divine protection against enemies and the transition into a new ritual cycle, specifically the morning litany.</meta>

## Hymn Text

<note>Rig Veda 5.2.11 - Word-by-word analysis (Padapatha)</note>
You | indeed | the singer | O youngest one | all | O Agni | difficulties | across | carry | thieves | have been seen <note>or "fled"</note> | enemies | people | of unknown intent | crooked | have become. ॥ 11 ॥

---

## Commentary (Sayana)

O dear one, Lord Agni, O **youngest** <note>original: "yaviṣṭha" — Agni is called the youngest because he is reborn every time the sacrificial fire is freshly lit</note>, carry the **singer** <note>original: "jaritāram" — the one who chants the praises</note> across **all difficulties** <note>original: "duritāni" — literally "difficult paths" or sins</note> to show your favor. The **thieves** and robbers have been **seen** <note>original: "adṛdhran" — interpreted by Sayana as being visible and thus unable to hide, or being driven away</note>. The **enemies**, those people who have become our foes and whose **intent is unknown** <note>original: "ajñāta-ketāḥ" — those whose signs or purposes are not recognized</note>, and those who are **crooked** <note>original: "vṛjinā" — those who are harmful or deceptive</note>, have been kept far away from us.

---

## Hymn Text

-> ॥ The Twelfth Verse ॥ <-
<note>Rig Veda 5.2.12 - Standard recitation (Samhitapatha)</note>
**These paths of praise have turned toward you; to the Bountiful One, even this sin was spoken. May this Agni, as he grows, not deliver us to the slanderer, nor to the one who wishes us harm. ॥ 12 ॥**

<note>Rig Veda 5.2.12 - Word-by-word analysis (Padapatha)</note>
These | paths | toward you | have become | to the Bountiful One | or | that | indeed | sin | was spoken | not | indeed | this | Agni | to the slanderer | us | not | to the injurer | growing | away | give. ॥ 12 ॥

---

## Commentary (Sayana)

These **paths** <note>original: "yāmāsaḥ" — meaning the moving or progressing hymns of praise</note> have turned **toward you**. Alternatively, to the **Bountiful One** <note>original: "vasave" — an epithet of Agni as the source of wealth</note>, this **sin** <note>original: "āgaḥ"</note> was **spoken**. I have spoken to Agni: "The very act of begging 'give this to me' is itself a sin." <note>Sayana suggests that for a high-minded devotee, the necessity of asking for material things feels like a moral failing</note>. Or, it refers to the sin committed by our enemies that has been reported to the god. Furthermore, may this Agni, **growing** larger through our songs of praise, **not deliver** us to the **slanderer** <note>original: "abhishastaye" — one who speaks ill or accuses falsely</note>, nor should he give us up to the **injurer** who seeks to harm us.

-> ॥ This concludes the seventeenth section (varga) of the eighth chapter (adhyaya) of the third book (ashtaka) ॥ <-

---

## Hymn Text

The fourth hymn of the fifth book, beginning with "You, O Agni," consists of eleven verses. It was seen by the Sage **Vasuśruta**, a descendant of **Atri**. It is composed in the **Trishtubh** meter <note>a poetic meter of 44 syllables</note> and is dedicated to **Agni**. As mentioned previously, it is used in the morning litany and the ceremonies of the Twin Physicians (Ashvins).

-> ॥ The First Verse ॥ <-
<note>Rig Veda 5.3.1 - Standard recitation (Samhitapatha)</note>
**You, O Agni, the Lord of Riches, I gladden at the sacrifices, O King! With you, as we strive for strength, may we conquer; may we overcome the assaults of mortal men. ॥ 1 ॥**

<note>Rig Veda 5.3.1 - Word-by-word analysis (Padapatha)</note>
You | O Agni | Lord of Riches | of riches | toward | forth | I gladden | in the sacrifices | O King | with you | strength | seeking strength | may we conquer | over | may we be | the attacks | of mortals. ॥ 1 ॥

---

## Commentary (Sayana)

O Agni, you are the **Lord of Riches** <note>original: "vasupatiṃ vasūnām"</note>. The word "riches" is repeated to show the great abundance of your wealth and your total mastery over it.

<vocab>
**yaviṣṭha** — youngest or most youthful, an epithet of Agni because he is newly made;
**duritā** — difficulties or sins;
**stenāḥ** — thieves;
**vasuśruta** — "He who is heard as wealth," the name of the Sage who authored this hymn;
**ātreya** — a descendant of the great Sage Atri;
**traiṣṭubha** — a meter with four lines of eleven syllables each;
**āgneya** — a hymn or ritual directed specifically toward Agni;
**vasupati** — the master or lord of treasures;
**vṛjinā** — crooked, deceptive, or those to be avoided.
</vocab>

# Mandala 5. Chapter 1. Hymn 4. | Third Octet | Page 273

...I praise you, the master of many riches, during the sacrificial rites. O King <note>original: "rājan" — a common title for Agni as the ruler or director of the sacrifice</note>, with you being favorable, may we, desiring sustenance, win strength. Furthermore, may we overcome the advancing armies of mortals <note>original: "pṛtanyatīḥ" — refers to hostile forces or opposing armies</note>.

This verse is used as the consecration prayer <note>original: "yājyā" — the verse recited at the moment the offering is poured into the fire</note> for the Lord of the House during the *Patni-samyaja* <note>original: "patnīsaṃyāje" — a ritual dedicated to the wives of the gods</note> in the Full and New Moon sacrifices. As stated in the ritual manuals: "Agni, the bearer of oblations, ageless, our father..." (*Ashvalayana Shrauta Sutra* 1.10). This same verse is also used for Agni in the *Devasuva* <note>original: "devasuvāṃ" — specific oblations to "god-impelling" deities</note> offerings. As stated: "Agni, the bearer of oblations, ageless, our father, and you, O Soma, according to our desire..." (*Ashvalayana Shrauta Sutra* 4.11).

->॥ This is the Second Verse ॥<-

## Hymn Text
**Agni, the bearer of oblations, the ageless one, is our father; he is all-pervading, radiant, and beautiful to behold for us. Shine with excellent household fires upon the sacrificial foods; and measure out for us, in our direction, glorious wealth. ॥ 2 ॥**

**[Word-by-word analysis]**
The oblation-bearer | Agni | ageless | father | our | all-pervading | radiant | beautiful to behold | for us | with excellent household fires | together | sacrificial foods | shine | toward us | together | measure out | glorious wealth ॥ 2 ॥

---

## Commentary (Sayana)
May this Agni, the bearer of oblations <note>original: "havyavāt"</note> and the ageless one <note>original: "ajaraḥ"</note>—the one who never decays—be our father. Furthermore, may he be all-pervading <note>original: "vibhuḥ"</note>, radiant, and beautiful to behold <note>original: "sudṛśīkaḥ"</note> for us. Now the text speaks directly to the deity: O Agni, shine brightly <note>original: "sam didīhi"</note> upon the foods or firewood accompanied by excellent household fires <note>original: "sugārhapatyāḥ"</note>. Or, grant them to us. Toward us, measure out <note>original: "sam mimīhi"</note> foods or fame <note>original: "śravāṃsi"</note>.

->॥ Now the Third Verse ॥<-

## Hymn Text
**The Sage of the people, the Lord of the People of human kind, the pure, the purifier, the butter-backed Agni—him, the Invoker, you establish for the knowledge of all. He wins desirable things among the gods. ॥ 3 ॥**

**[Word-by-word analysis]**
Of the people | the Sage | the Lord of the People | of human kind | the pure | the purifier | the butter-backed | Agni | down | the Invoker | for the knowledge of all | you establish | he | among the gods | wins | desirable things ॥ 3 ॥

---

## Commentary (Sayana)
O priests, establish <note>original: "ni dadhidhve" — to place or hold firmly in the ritual seat</note> Agni, the Lord of the People <note>original: "viśpatiṃ"</note> of human subjects—the protector or master of all human-form creatures—the Sage <note>original: "kaviṃ"</note> or wise one, the pure, the radiant, the purifier <note>original: "pāvakaṃ"</note> who cleanses others, whose body is characterized by a back of clarified butter <note>original: "ghṛtapṛṣṭham"</note> (referring to his flames being fed by ghee, or his upper portion being covered in it), the Invoker <note>original: "hotāraṃ"</note> who performs the sacrifice, the knower of everything <note>original: "viśvavidaṃ"</note>. That deity, among the gods, wins <note>original: "vanate"</note> or obtains desirable riches for our sake; or, he himself enjoys the desirable oblations <note>original: "havīṃṣi"</note>.

# Rig Veda | [Book 3. Chapter 8. Section 19.]

## Hymn Text

-> ॥ Now the Fourth Verse ॥ <-

**Rejoice, O Agni, in harmony with the sacrificial food, striving alongside the rays of the sun. Rejoice, O Knower of All Births <note>original: "jātavedas" — a title for Agni meaning he who knows all created beings</note>, in our kindling-wood; bring the gods here for the eating of the oblation. ॥ 4 ॥**

**Pada Patha:**
Rejoice | O Agni | with the sacrificial food | in harmony | striving | with the rays | of the sun |
Rejoice | our | kindling-wood | O Knower of All Births | bring | and | the gods | for the eating of the oblation | you carry ॥ 4 ॥

---

## Commentary (Sayana)

O **Agni, rejoice**; that is, accept this praise. **With the sacrificial food** <note>original: "iḷayā"</note>, meaning with the earth characterized by the sacrificial altar, or with speech, be of **one harmony** or equal affection. Likewise, **striving alongside the rays of the sun**, making your effort at the time of dawn. Furthermore, O **Knower of All Births**, O Agni who knows all that is born, **rejoice in our kindling-wood**. Accept it. **Bring the gods here for the eating of the oblation**, that they may consume the offering. You **carry** <note>original: "vakṣi" — from the root 'vah', to carry</note> that oblation to them.

Now, this verse is the invitation prayer <note>original: "anuvākyā"</note> for the "Maker of Good Sacrifice" <note>term: "sviṣṭakṛt" — a specific aspect of Agni who corrects errors in the ritual</note> during the Purificatory Sacrifice <note>original: "pavitreṣṭyāṃ"</note>. This is indicated in the ritual manuals: "Agni, the domestic friend, rejoice... for great prosperity," these are the two verses for the final offerings (*Ashvalayana Shrauta Sutra* 2.12). Even in the offering of the seven-layered cake to the Maruts <note>original: "marudbhyaḥ puroḍāśaṃ saptakapālam"</note>, this is the invitation prayer for the *Svishtakrit* offering: "Those Maruts who are like swift horses... Agni, the domestic friend, rejoice" (*Ashvalayana Shrauta Sutra* 2.17).

---

## Hymn Text

-> ॥ This is the Fifth Verse ॥ <-

**The beloved domestic friend, the guest in the home—O Wise One, come to this sacrifice of ours. O Agni, having struck down all attackers, bring to us the sustenance of those who act as enemies. ॥ 5 ॥**

**Pada Patha:**
The beloved | the domestic friend | the guest | in the home | this | our | sacrifice | unto | come | O Wise One |
All | O Agni | attackers | having struck down | those acting as enemies | bring | sustenance ॥ 5 ॥

---

## Commentary (Sayana)

**The beloved**, meaning the one who is sufficient; **the domestic friend** <note>original: "damūnā" — meaning one whose mind is focused on giving, or one who is self-controlled</note>; and being **worshipful like a guest**, **come unto this sacrifice of ours**. Approach it. **O Wise One**, you who are knowing; O **Agni, having struck down all attackers**, all those who assault us, **bring the sustenance**, the food or wealth, of **those who act as enemies**. Bring it to us. Regarding the word "guest," the ancient etymological text states: "He is a guest because he goes toward the houses" (*Nirukta* 4.5).

-> ॥ Thus ends the eighteenth section of the eighth chapter of the third octet ॥ <-

---

## Hymn Text

-> ॥ Now the Sixth Verse ॥ <-

**With your weapon, drive away the enemy <note>original: "dasyu" — refers to spiritual or physical enemies who do not perform sacrifices</note>, creating strength for your own body. Since you, O Son of Strength, rescue the gods, O Agni, protect us, the most heroic, in the struggle for wealth. ॥ 6 ॥**

# Mandala 5. Anuvaka 1. Sukta 4. ] || Third Ashtaka || 275

## Hymn Text

**Drive away the destroyer <note>original: "dasyu" — often referring to enemies of the ritual or chaotic forces</note> with your weapon, creating vigor for your own body. Since you satisfy the gods, O Son of Strength <note>original: "sahasa-putra" — a common epithet for Agni, born from the strength of friction</note>, O Agni, best of leaders, protect us in battle. ॥ 6 ॥**

---

**Pada Patha:**
With the weapon | the destroyer | away | indeed | drive | vigor | creating | for the body | your own |
You satisfy | since | of strength | O Son | the gods | he | O Agni | protect | O best of leaders | in battle | us ॥ 6 ॥

## Commentary (Sayana)

O Agni, with your weapon <note>original: "vadhena"</note>, **drive away** and utterly destroy the **destroyer** who consumes or harms. The word "hi" is used here for poetic emphasis. **Creating vigor** <note>original: "vayaḥ" — meaning food or vital energy</note> for your **own body**. Alternatively, it means providing food for the worshiper, who is like a son to you. Because you, O **Son of Strength**, **satisfy** <note>original: "piparṣi"</note> or please the **gods**, therefore, O Agni, you who are the **best of leaders**, **protect us in battle** or during the struggle for spoils.

---

-> ॥ Now the Seventh Verse ॥ <-

## Hymn Text

**O Agni, may we serve you with hymns of praise; O Purifier <note>original: "pāvaka"</note> of auspicious light, may we serve you with oblations. Bestow upon us wealth that is desired by all; grant us all forms of riches. ॥ 7 ॥**

---

**Pada Patha:**
We | you | O Agni | with hymns | may we serve | we | with oblations | O Purifier | O you of auspicious light |
To us | wealth | desired by all | together | bring | to us | all | riches | place ॥ 7 ॥

## Commentary (Sayana)

O **Agni, we serve** or worship **you with hymns** <note>original: "ukthaiḥ" — specifically the "shastra" or recited portions of the ritual</note>. We also **serve you with oblations** <note>original: "havyaiḥ"</note> of ghee and grain. O **Purifier**, O you of **auspicious light**, **bring** or cause us to attain **wealth** that is **desired by all** people. **Place** or establish within **us all** varieties of **riches**.

---

-> ॥ Now the Eighth Verse ॥ <-

## Hymn Text

**O Agni, accept our sacrifice; O Son of Strength, who dwells in the three regions <note>term: "triṣadhastha" — refers to Agni's presence in the three worlds: earth as fire, atmosphere as lightning, and sky as the sun</note>, accept our oblation. May we be doers of good deeds among the gods; protect us with your triple-shielded shelter. ॥ 8 ॥**

---

**Pada Patha:**
Our | O Agni | sacrifice | accept | of strength | O Son | O dweller in the three regions | oblation |
We | among the gods | doers of good deeds | may we be | with shelter | us | triple-shielded | protect ॥ 8 ॥

## Commentary (Sayana)

O **Agni, accept** and enjoy **our sacrifice** <note>original: "adhvara" — literally "the non-injured," a term for a flawlessly performed ritual</note>. O **Son of Strength**, O you who **dwells in the three regions** <note>original: "triṣadhastha"</note>, namely the earth, atmosphere, and heavens, accept our **oblation**. Alternatively, "sacrifice" and "oblation" can be read together as "the unharmed offering." May **we**, the worshippers, **be doers of good deeds** <note>original: "sukṛtaḥ"</note> or creators of spiritual merit <note>original: "apūrva"</note> among the gods. **Protect us** with **triple-shielded shelter** <note>original: "trivarūthena"</note>. This refers to happiness that is threefold (perhaps mental, vocal, and physical) or a house with three layers of protection.

<summary>In these verses, Agni is praised as a powerful protector who destroys enemies, a purifier who grants universal wealth, and a triple-shielded refuge dwelling in the three worlds.</summary>

# Rig Veda || Ashtaka 3. Adhyaya 8. Varga 19.

## Hymn Text

-> ॥ Now the Ninth Verse ॥ <-

**O Knower of All Beings, carry us across all difficult paths; as if across a river by a boat, transport us beyond our troubles. O Agni, praised by our minds like the sage Atri, be the protector of our bodies. ॥ 9 ॥**

---

**Word-by-word Analysis (Pada Patha):**
All | us | difficult paths | O Knower of All Beings |
A river | as | by a boat | troubles | across | carry |
O Agni | like Atri | with the mind | being praised | our | be mindful | protector | of bodies ॥ 9 ॥

---

## Commentary (Sayana)

O **Knower of All Beings** <note>original: "jātavedas"</note>, **carry us across** all **difficult paths** <note>original: "durgahā"</note>—those which are hard to traverse or experiences full of suffering. **Transport us beyond our troubles** <note>original: "duritānyatipariṣi"</note>. He provides an analogy: **as if across a river by a boat** <note>original: "sindhuṃ na nāvā"</note>, just as a boatman carries someone across water. O **Agni**, being **praised** by **our prayer** or hymn **like the sage Atri** was, **be mindful** <note>original: "bodhi"</note> or aware of us, and become the **protector of our bodies** <note>original: "tanūnām avitā"</note>.

In the ritual for those desiring a son <note>term: "Putrakameshti" — a Vedic sacrifice performed by those wishing to conceive children</note>, this verse serves as the principal recitation for the offering. This is indicated in the ritual manuals: "He who thinks of you with a prayerful heart, O Agni of most abundant fame..." <note>reference: Ashvalayana Shrauta Sutra 2. 10</note>.

---

## Hymn Text

-> ॥ Now the Tenth Verse ॥ <-

**I, a mortal, call upon you, the Immortal, thinking of you with a praising heart. O Knower of All Beings, bestow glory upon us; O Agni, may I attain immortality through my children. ॥ 10 ॥**

---

**Word-by-word Analysis (Pada Patha):**
Who | you | with the heart | praising | thinking |
Immortal | mortal | call repeatedly |
O Knower of All Beings | glory | in us | bestow |
Through children | O Agni | immortality | may I attain ॥ 10 ॥

---

## Commentary (Sayana)

**I, a mortal** <note>original: "martya" — one subject to the law of death</note>, **call repeatedly** <note>original: "johavīmi"</note> and with great intensity upon **you, the Immortal** <note>original: "amartyam"</note> or the one who is deathless. I do this while **thinking** of you or praising you **with a praising heart**—a heart focused on songs of glory. Alternatively, the word **praising** <note>original: "kīriṇā"</note> refers to the hymn itself; thus, "with a mind joined to the hymn." O **Knower of All Beings, bestow glory** (wealth or distinguished progeny) **upon us**. O **Agni**, through such **children**, **may I attain immortality** <note>original: "amṛtatvam"</note>. Here, immortality is defined as "the characteristic of an unbroken lineage" <note>original: "santatyaviccheda"</note>. Indeed, the sacred texts state: "A man is reborn in the form of his child; that is his immortality, O mortal" <note>reference: A citation from the Brahmanas/Shruti regarding lineage</note>.

In that same ritual for a son, this verse beginning with "To whom you..." is the invitatory prayer <note>term: "Anuvakya" — a verse used to invite a specific deity to receive an offering</note> for Agni as the "Possessor of Sons." This is indicated by the manual: "To whom you, O Knower of Beings, grant success... he who thinks of you with a praising heart" <note>reference: Ashvalayana Shrauta Sutra 2. 10</note>.

<note>
The word "Jatavedas" is a primary epithet for Agni, signifying his omniscience regarding all created things. The sage Atri is the traditional seer of this fifth book (Mandala) of the Rig Veda.
</note>
