**Introduction to the Fifth Hymn:**
The fifth hymn, beginning with "To the well-kindled," consists of eleven verses. It was revealed to the seer Vasushruta, a descendant of Atri. The meter is Gayatri, and the deities addressed are the Kindling Sticks <note>original: "Idhma"</note> and others. This is designated as an *Apri* hymn <note>term: "Apri-sukta" — a special category of propitiatory hymns used in the preliminary stages of a Vedic sacrifice</note>. It is noted that this specific version omits the form of Agni known as *Tanunapat* <note>original: "tanūnapādvārjitaṃ"</note>. According to the ritual manuals, these verses are to be used in the preliminary offerings of the animal sacrifice.

->॥ The First Verse ॥<-

**To the well-kindled flame, offer the intense clarified butter; to Agni, the Knower of All Beings. ॥ 1 ॥**

**Word-by-word Analysis (Pada-patha):**
To the well-kindled | to the flame | clarified butter | intense | offer | to Agni | to the Knower of All Beings ॥ 1 ॥

->॥ Now the Second Verse ॥<-

**Narashansa, the inviolable, speeds this sacrifice; for he is the wise sage with sweet hands. ॥ 2 ॥**

**Word-by-word Analysis (Pada-patha):**
Narashansa <note>Agni as "The Praise of Men"</note> | well-speeds | this | sacrifice | inviolable | the wise sage | for | with sweet hands ॥ 2 ॥

---

## Commentary (Sayana)

**For that well-doer (5. 4. 11):** O **Knower of All Beings** <note>original: "jātavedas"</note>, O Agni, for whichever **well-doer**—the patron of the sacrifice who performs good deeds—you **make** or have made a **place** that is **blissful** or full of happiness. The particle **u** is used here simply to fill the meter. Alternatively, it means you make the place blissful through your light <note>original: "ālokena"</note>. May you do this through your grace. That patron then **attains** a state of **well-being** <note>original: "svasti"</note> that is imperishable, and **wealth** characterized by having many **horses**, many **sons**, and **heroes** (representing strength or brave descendants), as well as many **cattle**.

**To the well-kindled (5. 5. 1):** To Agni who is **well-kindled**—meaning perfectly ignited—and who possesses the name **Flame** <note>original: "shochishe"</note> or brilliance, **offer** the **clarified butter** (ghee). This offering should be **intense** <note>original: "tīvram"</note>, meaning abundant. This is for **Agni**, who possesses qualities such as "going forward," and who is the **Knower of All Beings** or the "possessor of wealth" <note>original: "jātavedase"</note>.

**Narashansa (5. 5. 2):** **Narashansa** refers to Agni as the one "to be praised by men" <note>original: "naraiḥ shaṃsanīyaḥ"</note>. He **speeds** or perfectly prepares **this sacrifice** or this offering. That deity is **inviolable**—he cannot be harmed by anyone. He is a **wise sage** <note>original: "kavi"</note> or one of great intelligence, and he is **sweet-handed**, meaning his hands are associated with the sweetness of the offerings or he holds the sweet oblations.

---

## Critical Notes
*   **5. 4. 11:** This verse concludes the 19th Varga of the 3rd Ashtaka.
*   **5. 5:** This is an *Apri* hymn. These hymns follow a strict order of deities representing different aspects of the sacrificial fire. This version by the Atri family is unique because it features *Narashansa* but excludes *Tanunapat*, which is usually the second deity invoked in such hymns.
*   The page footer marks this as part of **VOLUME III.** of the edited series.

# Rig-Veda — Book 3, Chapter 4, Section 21

## Hymn Text

-> ॥ The Third Verse ॥ <-

**O Agni, being praised, bring Indra—the marvelous and beloved—here to this sacrifice with pleasant chariots for our protection. ॥ 3 ॥**

**Word-by-word Analysis (Pada-patha):**
Praised | O Agni | [particle for motion] | bring | Indra | marvelous/bright | here | beloved | with pleasant | chariots | for protection ॥ 3 ॥

---

## Commentary (Sayana)

O **Agni, being praised** <note>original: "īḷitaḥ"</note> and lauded by us, **bring Indra**, the **marvelous** or adorable one who is **beloved**, **here to this sacrifice with pleasant** or comfortable **chariots for our protection** <note>original: "ūtaye"</note> and preservation.

---

## Hymn Text

-> ॥ The Fourth Verse ॥ <-

**O you who are soft as wool, spread yourself wide; the singers have sounded their hymns. O radiant one, be present for our gain. ॥ 4 ॥**

**Word-by-word Analysis (Pada-patha):**
Soft as wool | [particle for expansion] | spread out | [particle for direction] | hymns/singers | have sounded | be | for us | O radiant one | for gain ॥ 4 ॥

---

## Commentary (Sayana)

O **soft as wool** <note>term: "ūrṇamradā" — an epithet describing the sacred grass as having the softness of a woolen blanket</note>, O **sacred grass** <note>term: "Barhis" — the ritual grass spread on the altar as a seat for the gods</note>, **spread yourself wide**. Expand yourself. The **singers** <note>original: "arkāḥ"</note> **have sounded their hymns**; they are praising you. O **radiant one** <note>original: "śubhra"</note>, **be** present for **our gain**—either for the acquisition of wealth or for the bestowing of it.

---

## Hymn Text

-> ॥ The Fifth Verse ॥ <-

**O divine doors, open yourselves wide; be easy to pass through for our protection. Abundantly fulfill the sacrifice. ॥ 5 ॥**

**Word-by-word Analysis (Pada-patha):**
Divine | doors | [particle for opening] | open yourselves | easy to pass through | for us | for protection | abundantly | sacrifice | fulfill ॥ 5 ॥

---

## Commentary (Sayana)

O **doors** of the sacrificial hall, you who are **divine**, **open yourselves wide**. Become separated <note>interpretive: "viriakta," meaning to open up the entrance</note>. Being **easy to pass through**, providing a good means of entry **for our protection**, **abundantly fulfill the sacrifice** <note>original: "pṛṇītana"</note>. This means either to fill the sacrificer with desires or to fulfill the sacrifice itself with its intended rewards.

-> ॥ Thus ends the twentieth section (Varga) of the third book (Ashtaka) ॥ <-

---

## Hymn Text

-> ॥ The Sixth Verse ॥ <-

**The two goddesses of Night and Dawn, of beautiful form, increasers of strength, the two mighty mothers of the Cosmic Order—we pray to them. ॥ 6 ॥**

**Word-by-word Analysis (Pada-patha):**
Of beautiful form | increasers of strength | mighty | of the Cosmic Order | the two mothers | Night | Dawn | we pray to ॥ 6 ॥

---

## Commentary (Sayana)

O goddesses who preside over the day and the night, you are **of beautiful form** or possess lovely limbs. You are **increasers of strength** <note>original: "vayo-vṛdhā," interpreted here as food or vitality</note>. You are the **mighty mothers** or creators **of the Cosmic Order** <note>term: "Ṛta" — the fundamental law of the universe, often associated with the sacrifice or with the life-giving waters</note>. Of these two, **we pray to** the goddess of **Night** <note>original: "doṣām"</note> and the goddess of **Dawn** <note>original: "uṣasam"</note>; that is, we offer them our praise.

# Rig-Veda — Mandala 5, Hymn 5, Section 1
## Page 279

-> ॥ The Seventh Verse ॥ <-

## Hymn Text
**Praised for their movement like the wind, the two Divine Invokers of mankind, come to this sacrifice of ours. ॥ 7 ॥**

**Word-by-word Analysis (Pada-patha):**
Of the wind | in the path | praised | divine | invokers | of man | this | our | sacrifice | [particle for motion] | come ॥ 7 ॥

---

## Commentary (Sayana)
**In the path of the wind.** This is a hidden comparison <note>original: "luptopamā"</note>. It means they are praised by us to move with a speed similar to the wind. Alternatively, it means those who travel through the atmosphere <note>original: "antarikṣe"</note>, which is the place of the wind's movement. You two, the **Divine Invokers** <note>term: "daivyā hotārā" — divine counterparts to the human priests who invite the gods to the ritual</note> who emerged from Agni (Fire) and Aditya (the Sun), who invite the gods: **come to this sacrifice of ours**, belonging to man. The phrase "of man, our sacrifice" uses two genitive cases in different relations <note>original: "vyadhikaraṇe ṣaṣṭhyau"</note>, meaning: "to the sacrifice of us, the sacrificers."

---

-> ॥ The Eighth Verse ॥ <-

## Hymn Text
**May Ila, Sarasvati, and Mahi—the three goddesses who bring delight and are unfailing—sit upon the sacred grass. ॥ 8 ॥**

**Word-by-word Analysis (Pada-patha):**
Ila | Sarasvati | Mahi | three | goddesses | delight-bringing | sacred grass | may they sit | unfailing ॥ 8 ॥

---

## Commentary (Sayana)
**Ila** is the Earth. **Sarasvati**: "Saras" means water, and from that comes "Sarasvan," the wind; his wife is Sarasvati. **Mahi** is the "Great One," also known as **Bharati**, the wife of Bharat—the Sun <note>original: "ādityasya patnī"</note>. Although her name (Bharati) is not explicitly mentioned here, she is understood because these three are always seen together and the text mentions the number "three." Alternatively, these are the goddesses of Speech <note>original: "vāgdevyaḥ"</note> residing in the three realms: Earth, Atmosphere, and Heaven. These goddesses are **delight-bringing** (causataries of happiness) and **unfailing** (non-harming). May they **sit upon the sacred grass** <note>term: "Barhis" — the carpet of grass prepared for the gods' seating</note>.

---

-> ॥ The Ninth Verse ॥ <-

## Hymn Text
**O Tvashtr, being auspicious, come here; you are all-pervading in nourishment and by your own self. Protect us in every sacrifice. ॥ 9 ॥**

**Word-by-word Analysis (Pada-patha):**
Auspicious | O Tvashtr | here | [particle for motion] | come | all-pervading | in nourishment | and | by self | in sacrifice-after-sacrifice | us | [particle for upward/excellent] | protect ॥ 9 ॥

---

## Commentary (Sayana)
O **divine Tvashtr** <note>term: "Tvaṣṭṛ" — the divine artisan or architect of forms</note>, being **auspicious** (bestower of happiness), **come here** to our sacrifice. You are **all-pervading** and expansive in the act of **nourishment**. Having come **by your own self** (voluntarily), **protect us** excellently in **every sacrifice**.

<note>Ritual Note: The text mentions a specific ritual procedure here. In the Agnihotra, if the second offering spills or drips, one should place a fuel stick while reciting the next verse ("Where you know..."). This is indicated in the ritual manuals (Ashvalayana Shrauta Sutra 3.11).</note>

---

-> ॥ The Tenth Verse ॥ <-

## Hymn Text
**O Lord of the Forest, where you know the secret names of the gods, there convey our offerings. ॥ 10 ॥**

**Word-by-word Analysis (Pada-patha):**
Where | you know | O Lord of the Forest | of the gods | secret | names | there | offerings | cause to go ॥ 10 ॥

---

The commentary provides ritual context for correcting mistakes during the Agnihotra sacrifice.</summary>

# Rig-Veda — Mandala 5, Hymn 5 & 6
## Page 280

### ॥ Rig-Veda ॥ [Book 3. Chapter 8. Section 22.]

## Commentary (Sayana)

O **Vanaspati** <note>term: Vanaspati — literally 'Lord of the Forest'; here it refers to the deity presiding over the wooden sacrificial post</note>, in whatever place you know the secret, hidden names and forms of the gods, lead the offerings there. Make them reach their destination.

->॥ The Eleventh Verse ॥<-

---

## Hymn Text

**Svāhā to Agni and Varuna! Svāhā to Indra and the Maruts! Svāhā to the gods, the offering! ॥ 11 ॥**

**Word-by-word Analysis (Pada-patha):**
Svāhā | to Agni | to Varuna | Svāhā | to Indra | to the Maruts | Svāhā | to the gods | the offering ॥ 11 ॥

---

## Commentary (Sayana)

The "All-Gods" <note>term: Viśvedevāḥ — a collective group of deities</note> are headed by Agni. To those gods, I make this offering with the word "Svāhā" <note>term: Svāhā — a ritual exclamation used when casting offerings into the sacred fire; it signifies the consecration of the gift</note>. The meaning is: "I make it well-offered." This is a praise of the act of Svāhā-consecration.

->॥ Thus ends the twenty-first section (varga) of the eighth chapter of the third book (ashtaka) ॥<-

**"I think of that Agni"** — so begins the sixth hymn, consisting of ten verses. It was revealed to the seer **Vasushruta**; it is dedicated to the god Agni and is composed in the **Pankti** meter <note>term: Pankti — a poetic meter consisting of five lines, usually with eight syllables each</note>. The Index (Anukramani) states: **"Agni, I think of him—ten verses in Pankti."** In the morning litany <note>term: Prātar-anuvaka — the first ritual recitation of the day</note> during the Agni-related rites, and in the liturgy of the Ashvins (Ashvina-shastra), this hymn is used. This is indicated by the ritual manual: **"I think of that Agni—in the Pankti meter" (Ashvalayana Shrauta Sutra 4.13).** Furthermore, on the middle day of the Ashvamedha <note>term: Ashvamedha — the Royal Horse Sacrifice</note>, this is used as the 'Clarified Butter Litany' (Ajya-shastra). It is recorded: **"I think of that Agni—the Ajya liturgy follows on the single-day rite" (Ashvalayana 10.10).** In the initial 'Abhilavika' rituals, the first three verses serve as the response for the priest Maitravaruna: **"I think of that Agni who is the source of wealth, O Agni, bring us abundant riches" (Ashvalayana 7.8).**

->॥ Herein the First Verse ॥<-

---

## Hymn Text

**I think of that Agni who is the source of wealth, to whom the milch-cows return as to their home.**
**To whom the swift horses return as to their home, to whom the constant prize-winners return as to their home. Bring food to the praisers! ॥ 1 ॥**

<note>RV 5.6.1</note>

**Word-by-word Analysis (Pada-patha):**
Agni | him | I think | who | the source of wealth | the home | whom | they go | the milch-cows |
the home | the horses | the swift | the home | the constant | the prize-winners | food | to the praisers | [particle for bringing] | bring ॥ 1 ॥

---

## Commentary (Sayana)

I think of that Agni; I praise him. That Agni who is **Vasu** <note>term: Vasu — a name for Agni meaning 'the dweller' or 'the provider of shelter'</note>, the one who causes all to dwell. He is the **home** (Astam), the place of refuge for all beings. The **milch-cows** go to him to be satisfied. The **swift-moving horses** also go to him as to a home. Likewise, the **constant prize-winners**—the patrons and sacrificers who possess food in the form of offerings—go to him as their shelter. O Agni, bring food and nourishment to us, the singers of your praise.

->॥ Now the Second Verse ॥<-

---

## Hymn Text

**That Agni is the source of wealth, whom I praise, to whom the milch-cows come together.**
**To whom the swift-running horses come together, to whom the well-born wise men come together. Bring food to the praisers! ॥ 2 ॥**

<note>RV 5.6.2</note>

---

<summary>This page concludes the Āprī hymn (ritual invocations) and begins a new series of hymns to Agni, where the god is depicted as a central home or refuge to which all creatures—cows, horses, and wise men—return at the end of the day or ritual.</summary>
<keywords>Agni, Vanaspati, Svāhā, Vasushruta, Pankti meter, sacrificial post, morning litany, Vasu, cows and horses as symbols of wealth</keywords>

# Rig-Veda — Mandala 5, Hymn 6
## Page 241

### [Book 3. Chapter 8. Section 22. Hymn 6.]

-> २ <-

## The Sacred Verse (Word-by-word Analysis)
**He | Agni | who | the source of wealth | is praised | together | whom | come toward | the cows | together | the horses | swift-running | together | the well-born | the wise men | strength | to the praisers | [thou] | bring ॥ 2 ॥**

---

## Commentary (Sayana)
That Agni is indeed the one who is praised as the "source of wealth" <note>original: "vasu"; this refers to Agni as an inhabitant of the world or a provider of dwellings</note>. The cows come together toward him for the sake of the ritual offering. The swift-running horses and the well-born, wise, and meditative men also gather toward him. Therefore, [O Agni], bring strength and food to those who offer these hymns of praise.

---

-> **॥ Now the Third Verse ॥** <-

## The Sacred Verse
**Agni indeed gives a spirited [gift] to the people, he who is all-seeing.**
**Agni, for the sake of wealth, [gives] that which is all-pervading; he, being pleased, moves toward the desirable. Bring strength to the praisers! ॥ 3 ॥**

### Word-by-word Analysis (Pada-patha)
Agni | indeed | the spirited/strong | to the people | gives | the all-seeing |
Agni | for wealth | the all-pervading | he | pleased | goes/bestows | the desirable | strength | to the praisers | [thou] | bring ॥ 3 ॥

---

## Commentary (Sayana)
Agni indeed gives to the "people" <note>original: "vishe"; here referring to the one performing the sacrifice</note> a "spirited" <note>term: vajina — this can mean a son endowed with food, a horse, or simply sacrificial food</note> gift. He is "all-seeing" <note>term: vishvacharshani — meaning his eyes are on all people, or he is worshiped by all</note>. To the one desiring wealth, Agni bestows that which is "all-pervading" <note>original: "swabhuvam"; excellence that spreads everywhere</note> and "desirable" <note>original: "varyam"; that which is chosen by all</note>. Being pleased with the sacrifice, he moves or directs these gifts toward the worshiper. The final phrase "bring strength to the praisers" follows the previous pattern.

---

In the ritual context of the *Abhiplavika* ceremonies <note>term: Abhiplavika — a specific six-day ritual cycle within the Vedic Soma sacrifice</note>, during the third daily pressing of the Soma juice, the first two verses of this triplet (starting with "O Agni, let us kindle you") are used. This is indicated in the ritual manuals which state: "O Agni, let us kindle you..." and "Both the very bright with clarified butter..." <note>original: "A te agne idhimahyu..." referencing the Ashvalayana Shrauta Sutra 7.8</note>.

-> **॥ Of that triplet, here is the first, which is the fourth of the hymn ॥** <-

## The Sacred Verse
**O Agni, let us kindle you, the radiant, the divine, the ageless.**
**When your most praiseworthy fuel shines in the heavens, bring strength to the praisers! ॥ 4 ॥**

### Word-by-word Analysis (Pada-patha)
Toward | you | O Agni | let us kindle | the radiant | divine | the ageless |
When | indeed | that | your | most praiseworthy | fuel | shines | in the heaven | strength | to the praisers | [thou] | bring ॥ 4 ॥

---

## Commentary (Sayana)
O Divine Agni, we "kindle" <note>original: "idhimahi"; to light or intensify the flame</note> you from all sides—you who are "radiant" <note>original: "dyumantam"; full of light</note> and "ageless" <note>term: ajara — undecaying or ever-young</note>. When indeed your "fuel" <note>original: "samid"; the wood used to feed the flame</note>, which is most "praiseworthy" <note>original: "paniyasi"; worthy of great hymns</note>, shines brightly in the "heavens" <note>original: "dyavi"; the celestial realm</note>, then bring strength to us who praise you.

<note>
**Technical Terms Summary:**
**Agni**: The deity of the Sacred Fire, the mediator between gods and humans.
**Vasu**: A class of gods, or a term for one who provides a home/wealth.
**Dhenu**: The cow, representing physical and spiritual nourishment.
**Vajina**: Derived from 'vaja' (strength/food); refers to anything potent, like a horse or a strong son.
**Stotri**: The priest or poet who composes and recites the hymns of praise.
**Ish**: A multifaceted word for food, vital strength, or the sacrificial meal.
**Vishvacharshani**: An epithet of Agni meaning "All-seeing" or "belonging to all people."
**Ajara**: Ageless; fire is considered 'ever-young' because it is reborn each time it is kindled.
</note>

<summary>This page contains verses 2 through 4 of Hymn 6 in the fifth Mandala, where Agni is praised as a provider of wealth, cows, and strength to his worshipers. The text describes the kindling of the ageless fire and its light reaching into the heavens during the ritual.</summary>
<keywords>Agni, Rig-Veda, Sayana, Mandala 5, Vedic ritual, sacrifice, wealth, strength, light, Abhiplavika</keywords>

<meta>This page continues the commentary on the 6th Hymn of the 5th Mandala of the Rig-Veda. The previous page discussed verses 2, 3, and 4, focusing on Agni as the source of wealth and the gatherer of cows, horses, and wise men. This page moves into the final verses of the hymn, specifically verses 5, 6, and 7, transitioning from Section (Varga) 22 to 23 of the 8th Chapter of the 3rd Book (Ashtaka).</meta>

# Rig-Veda — Mandala 5, Hymn 6
## Page 282

### [Book 3. Chapter 8. Section 23.]

-> ॥ Now the Fifth Verse ॥ <-

## The Sacred Verse
**O Agni, with a sacred verse, the oblation is offered to you, the Lord of bright radiance.**
**O beautifully shining one, O destroyer [of foes], O Lord of the people, O bearer of oblations, to you it is offered. Bring nourishment to the praisers! ॥ 5 ॥**

### Word-by-word Analysis (Pada-patha)
Toward | you | O Agni | with a sacred verse | the oblation | of the bright | of the radiance | O Lord |
O beautifully shining | O destroyer | O Lord of the people | O bearer of oblations | to you | is offered | nourishment | to the praisers | [thou] | bring ॥ 5 ॥

---

## Commentary (Sayana)
O **Lord of radiance** <note>original: "shochisho pate"</note>, meaning the master of light, O Agni; to **you**, the **bright** <note>original: "shukrasya"</note> or shining one, the **oblation is offered** along with a **sacred verse** <note>original: "richa"</note> or mantra. O **beautifully shining** <note>original: "sushchandra"</note> one—one who gladdens greatly or one who possesses beautiful gold—O **destroyer** <note>original: "dasma"</note> who causes the destruction of enemies, O **Lord of the people** <note>original: "vishpate"</note> who protects the subjects or progeny, O **bearer of oblations** <note>original: "havyavat"</note> who carries the sacrificial offerings. The term **nourishment** <note>original: "isham"</note> has been explained in previous verses.

-> ॥ This concludes the twenty-second section of the eighth chapter of the third book. ॥ <-

---

-> ॥ Now the Sixth Verse ॥ <-

## The Sacred Verse
**Indeed, those fires among the fires nourish every desirable thing.**
**They are impelled; they pervade; they desire nourishment. Continuously, bring nourishment to the praisers! ॥ 6 ॥**

### Word-by-word Analysis (Pada-patha)
Indeed | those | fires | among the fires | every | nourish | desirable thing |
They | are impelled | they | pervade | they | desire nourishment | continuously | nourishment | to the praisers | [thou] | bring ॥ 6 ॥

---

## Commentary (Sayana)
**Indeed they nourish** <note>original: "pro pushyanti"</note>; **those** <note>original: "tye"</note> refers to the fires placed upon the **altars** <note>term: dhishnya — specific consecrated mounds or hearths for sacrificial fires</note> among the sacred **fires** such as the **Householder’s fire** <note>term: garhapatya — the primary, perpetually maintained fire of a Vedic household</note> and others. Alternatively, it means that common worldly fires nourish all **desirable** <note>original: "varyam"</note> or sought-after wealth when placed within the Vedic fires. **Those** fires **are impelled** <note>original: "hinvire"</note>, meaning they please or are satisfied. They **pervade** <note>original: "invire"</note>, meaning they spread through the ritual space. **They desire nourishment** <note>original: "ishayanti"</note>, meaning they seek the sacrificial food. **Continuously** <note>original: "anushak"</note> means in an uninterrupted or connected manner. In this context, although there are many fires, the singular is used to refer to the general nature of Agni.

---

-> ॥ Now the Seventh Verse ॥ <-

## The Sacred Verse
**O Agni, those rays of yours, vigorous and great, increase;**
**They who, with the speed of hooves, stir the stalls of the cattle. Bring nourishment to the praisers! ॥ 7 ॥**

### Word-by-word Analysis (Pada-patha)
Your | those | O Agni | rays | greatly | increase | vigorous |

## Commentary (Sayana)

O **Agni**, bring <note>original: "ābhara"</note> to **us, the praisers**, **new**—meaning either recently composed praises or brand new—**nourishment** <note>original: "ishah"</note> consisting of food as previously described, and **good dwellings** <note>original: "sukshitīh"</note>, which can also mean good offspring. **May we**, who **honor** <note>original: "ānrichuh"</note> or worship **you in every house** <note>original: "dame-dame"</note>—meaning in all sacrificial halls—**be** those who have **you as our messenger** <note>original: "tvādūtāsah"</note>, the one who indicates or brings the results of the sacrifice. May we become prosperous. Alternatively, the phrase "in every house" can be linked to "may we be."

In the ritual of the *Abhisravika Ukthya* sacrifices, during the third pressing of the Soma, this is the third verse of the optional triplet <note>original: "stotriya-tricha"</note>. The ritual rule <note>original: "sūtra"</note> has been stated previously.

[Page 264]

|| Rig Veda || [Mandala 5, Adhyaya 1, Varga 24]

In the manner already described, they have joined <note>original: "ajuh"</note>—that is, they approach—Agni with songs of praise and sacrifices, or with the oblations that are the means of sacrifice. Having done so, they restrain <note>original: "yamuh"</note> or establish him. This means they worship him with oblations. In this way, the descendants of Atri <note>the Atreyas</note> refer to themselves in the third person. Regarding the word "ajuryam," it is a compound where the verb is repeated to indicate the continuity of the action. Furthermore, may he bestow upon **us** heroic power <note>original: "suviryam"</note>, meaning excellent sons and so on, and also wealth in horses <note>original: "ashvyam"</note>. One who possesses swift horses is "ashvya"; the state of possessing them is "ashvyam." May he uphold that as well.

->|| Thus ends the twenty-third Varga of the eighth Adhyaya of the third Book ||<-

The seventh hymn, beginning with "Friends, together for you" <note>original: "sakhayah sam vah"</note>, consists of ten verses. The seer is Isha, a descendant of Atri. The final verse is in the **Pankti** metre <note>a Vedic metre with five lines of eight syllables</note>, while the remaining verses are in the **Anushtubh** metre <note>a metre with four lines of eight syllables</note>, according to the rule for defining the ends of such groups. Thus it is recorded in the Index: "Sakhayah, by Isha, ending in Pankti." In the morning recitation <note>original: "prataranuvaka"</note>, specifically in the section dedicated to Agni in the Anushtubh metre, and in the ritual of the Ashvin deities, this entire hymn is used, except for the last verse. This is indicated in the ritual manual: "The hymns 'Sakhayah sam vasvam' and 'Agne havishmantah'..." (Asvalayana Shrauta Sutra 4.13).

## Hymn Text

->|| First Verse ||<-

**O friends, together [bring] for yourselves a perfect offering and praise to Agni, to the most excellent among the peoples, the grandson of strength, the powerful one. || 1 ||**

**Friends | Together | For you | Perfect | Offering | Praise | And | To Agni |**
**To the most excellent | Of the peoples | Of strength | To the grandson | To the powerful one || 1 ||**

---

## Commentary (Sayana)

O **friends** <note>original: "sakhayah"</note>, you who are the officiating priests <note>original: "ritvijah"</note>, prepare <note>an appropriate verb like "prepare" is supplied to complete the sense of the prefix "sam"</note> for **yourselves**. Furthermore, prepare a **perfect** <note>well-directed</note> **offering** <note>original: "isham"</note> of food and a **praise**-song <note>original: "stotram"</note> for **Agni**, who is **most excellent**—meaning greatly increased or supreme—for the sake of the **peoples** or the sacrificers. To him who is the **grandson of strength** <note>original: "urjo naptre," a title for Agni because he is generated through the "strength" of rubbing fire-sticks</note>, meaning he who does not allow strength to fall, or is its son; to that **powerful one**, perform the service.

**The worthy | Indeed | Whom | They kindle | They bring to life together | Creatures || 2 ||**

## [Book 5. Chapter 1. Hymn 7.] || Third Volume || 295

### Commentary by Sāyaṇa
<note>This concludes the explanation for Rig Veda 5.7.2</note>
The leaders <note>original: "naro"</note>, being the sacrificial priests <note>original: "ṛtvijaḥ"</note>, find delight. In the seat of man <note>original: "nṛṣadane"</note>—that is, in the sacrificial hall—they kindle him even while they are worthy <note>original: "arhantaścit"</note>. The word "cit" here is used in the sense of honor; being honorable or honoring him, they light the fire and make it shine. For that purpose, living beings <note>original: "jantavaḥ"</note> or creatures produce him from the fire-sticks <note>original: "araṇyāṃ"</note>. The phrase "wherever" <note>original: "kuha"</note> relates to this connection.

---

### Hymn Text
->|| Now the Third Verse ||<-
<note>RV 5.7.3</note>
When we win the strengths <note>original: "iṣo"</note>, and when we win the offerings of men, then he takes up the ray of truth <note>original: "ṛtasya raśmim"</note> through the power of his radiance. || 3 ||

**Word-by-Word Analysis:**
Together | When | Strengths | We win | Together | Offerings | Of men |
And | Of radiance | With power | Of truth / Sacrifice | The ray | Toward | He takes || 3 ||

### Commentary by Sāyaṇa
Whenever we win or partake in strengths <note>original: "iṣo"</note>—meaning food or energies—and when Agni enjoys the offerings <note>original: "havyā"</note> of us humans, then, through the strength and capacity of his shining food, he takes the ray <note>original: "raśmim"</note> that seizes the water <note>original: "ṛtasya"</note>. This means Agni has accepted the brilliance that produces results. Alternatively, he accepts the praise <note>original: "stavam"</note> which, like a ray, takes hold of the sacrifice <note>original: "ṛtasya"</note>.

---

### Hymn Text
->|| Now the Fourth Verse ||<-
<note>RV 5.7.4</note>
He indeed creates a signal <note>original: "ketum"</note> even in the night for the man who sits afar, when the Purifier <note>original: "pāvakaḥ"</note>, the ageless one, utterly consumes the lords of the forest <note>original: "vanaspatīn"</note>. || 4 ||

**Word-by-Word Analysis:**
He | Indeed | Creates | A signal | Toward | Night | Even | Afar | Toward | For one who sits |
The Purifier | When | Lords of the forest (trees) | Utterly | Indeed | Consumes | The ageless one || 4 ||

### Commentary by Sāyaṇa
That Agni indeed <note>original: "sa sma"</note> makes a signal <note>original: "ketum"</note>—a sign of knowledge—all around. To whom? It is said: even <note>original: "cit"</note> in the night, and <note>original: "ā"</note> to the man who remains at a distance. When does this happen? Whenever this Agni, the Purifier <note>original: "pāvakaḥ"</note>, being ageless <note>original: "ajaro"</note>—meaning undecaying or invincible—completely consumes <note>original: "pra sma mināti"</note> the trees or the fuel. The word "sma" is used here to complete the meter.

<note>RV 3.29.7</note>

**Word-by-Word Analysis:**

---

## Commentary by Sāyaṇa

**In whose service** <note>original: "veṣaṇe"</note>—meaning in the attendance upon Agni—on the paths of the sacrifice, the *Adhvaryu* priests offer "sweat" <note>original: "svedam"</note>, which refers to the downward-flowing clarified butter <note>original: "ājyam"</note>. At that time, the streams of butter surely climb <note>original: "abhiruruhuraha"</note> or ascend upon this Agni. The word "aha" is used here for emphasis. They are like **self-born abundance** <note>original: "svajanyaṃ bhūma"</note>—"abundance" refers to offspring that becomes many. They climb him **like backs** <note>original: "pṛṣṭhāiva"</note>, just as sons climb upon the back of a father. This is the comparison.

-> ॥ Thus ends the twenty-fourth section (Varga) of the eighth chapter (Adhyaya) in the third book (Ashtaka) ॥ <-

**Whom (Agni) who is greatly desired** <note>original: "puruspṛhaṃ"</note> by many, the mortal sacrificer **finds** <note>original: "vidat"</note> or knows, for the sake of the **maintenance of the universe** <note>original: "viśvasya dhārase"</note> or the pervasiveness of all. He is the **sweetener** <note>original: "svādanaṃ"</note> or the one who makes the food of the ancestors <note>original: "pitṝṇām"</note> particularly delicious. He is the **builder of the home** <note>original: "astatātitam"</note>, the one who creates a residence in your house, for the sake of the **living man** <note>original: "āyave"</note>—meaning for the sake of the sacrificer or for the sake of food.

**For he indeed** <note>original: "sa hi ṣma"</note>—that Agni indeed—**consumes** <note>original: "dāti"</note> the wood and grass that have taken hold <note>original: "ākṣitaṃ"</note> in a **desert** <note>original: "dhanva"</note> or waterless region. He cuts them apart on all sides; that is to say, he burns them. He is a **reaper** <note>original: "dātā"</note>, a cutter of grass and wood, **like an animal** <note>original: "paśun"</note>. Just as an animal gradually consumes a patch of grass, so does he. He is **golden-bearded** <note>original: "hiriśmaśru"</note> or possesses a beard of golden flame; **bright-toothed** <note>original: "śucidan"</note> or possessing shining teeth; and **tawny** <note>original: "babhru"</note>, becoming tall or great. This means he is mighty. He possesses **unyielding strength** <note>original: "anibhṛtataviṣi"</note>, or power that cannot be suppressed.

<vocab>
- Agni: The deity of fire, central to these ritual verses.
- Veṣaṇa: Service or attendance <note>original: "paricaryā"</note> during a ritual.
- Adhvaryu: The priest responsible for the physical details of the sacrifice.
- Puruspṛha: An epithet meaning "longed for by many."
- Hiriśmaśru: "Golden-bearded," describing the yellow-orange hue of fire's flames.
- Śucidan: "Bright-toothed," metaphorically describing the sparks or the consuming edge of the fire.
- Anibhṛtataviṣi: Possessing strength <note>original: "taviṣi"</note> that is not held back or diminished.
</vocab>

## Hymn Text

-> ॥ Now the Eighth Verse ॥ <-
<note>Rig Veda 5.7.8</note>

Radiant indeed is he to whom the seeker goes forth as to a flame, or like an axe <note>original: "svadhitiḥ"</note> that moves swiftly. The mother, capable of good birthing, has brought forth the active one, since he has attained his portion of the sacrifice. || 8 ||

**Word-by-word Analysis:**
Radiant | indeed | to whom | like-a-flame | forth | like-an-axe | moves |
well-birthing | brought forth | mother | active | when | attained | share || 8 ||

## Commentary (Sāyaṇa)

This fire is **radiant** <note>original: "śuciḥ"</note>, meaning he is truly glowing. To this fire, the sacrificer **goes forth** <note>original: "prarīyate"</note> as if to a flame to offer the oblation. Alternatively, the word "sma" is a filler word. "Radiant to whom"—the fourth case is used here in the sense of the first case <note>interpretive note: a grammatical shift in Vedic Sanskrit where "to whom" implies "he who is"</note>. He is radiant like an animal that eats grass <note>original: "acivat"</note>. Just as an animal goes about eating grass, so too does Agni move while consuming offerings. **Like an axe** <note>original: "svadhitiḥ"</note>, he moves as if cutting through things. The **mother** <note>original: "mātā"</note>, which is the fire-drill stick <term>arani: the wooden tool used to churn fire</term>, who is **well-birthing** <note>original: "suṣūḥ"</note>, **brought forth** <note>original: "asūta"</note> the one who is **active** <note>original: "krāṇā"</note>, meaning the one who performs the work that benefits the world. **Since** <note>original: "yat"</note>—or "the one who"—this fire **attained** <note>original: "ānaśe"</note> his **share** <note>original: "bhagam"</note>, meaning the food of the oblation.

---

## Hymn Text

-> ॥ Now the Ninth Verse ॥ <-
<note>Rig Veda 5.7.9</note>

O Agni, you who are fed on clarified butter, whatever happiness exists for you as the sustainer, bestow that glory and fame upon these mortals; establish favor within their minds. || 9 ||

**Word-by-word Analysis:**
Toward | who | your | butter-fed | O Agni | happiness | is | for the sustainer |
toward | these | glory | and | fame | toward | mind | among mortals | bestow || 9 ||

## Commentary (Sāyaṇa)

O **butter-fed** one <note>original: "sarpirāsute"</note>—O Agni, whose food is the clarified butter called *ghṛta*—**you who** <note>original: "yaḥ"</note> are present everywhere, to **you** <note>original: "te"</note>, the **sustainer** <note>original: "dhāyase"</note> or nourisher of all, there **is happiness** <note>original: "śam asti"</note> or peace resulting from this praise. If that is so, then **bestow** <note>original: "ādhāḥ"</note> or establish **glory** <note>original: "dyumnam"</note> or renown **among these mortals** <note>original: "eṣu martyeṣu"</note>, the singers who are to be enriched. **And also** <note>original: "uta"</note> bestow **fame** <note>original: "śravaḥ"</note>, which refers to food. Bestow also **favor** <note>original: "cittam"</note>, meaning your own graceful disposition toward us.

<meta>This page concludes the commentary on the 25th Varga (group of verses) of the third Ashtaka and begins the 8th Hymn of the 5th Mandala of the Rig Veda. The previous page discussed the final verses of the 7th Hymn, focusing on Agni’s birth from the fire-sticks. This page transitions into the 8th Hymn, which is also dedicated to Agni and attributed to the seer Isha Atreya.</meta>

In this manner, through the described method, the fire-born one [brings] the hymn, which is the means of meditation. To the one who is not of Agni <note>original: "agnivyatiriktĕra," meaning a non-sacrificer</note>, he is unassailable, or rather, as the creator, I take the cattle that you are to give—meaning the Rishi [seer] takes them. He takes, or he should take. Immediately after taking them, let the flames of Agni overcome the enemies <note>original: "dasyūn," refers to those who do not sacrifice</note> who do not satisfy or give. Let him thoroughly overcome the desiring opponents. The repetition is for the sake of emphasis.
->॥ This concludes the twenty-fifth group (Varga) of the eighth chapter of the third book (Ashtaka) ॥<-

The eighth hymn, beginning with "To you, Agni" <note>original: "tvām agne"</note>, consists of seven verses. It was seen by the seer Isha, a descendant of Atri. The meter is Jagati, and the deity is Agni. The Index <note>the Anukramani, a traditional catalog of Vedic hymns</note> states: "To you, Agni, seven Jagati verses." This hymn is used in the Morning Recitation <note>original: "Prātaranuvāka"</note>, in the ritual for Agni, in the Jagati meter, and in the litany to the Ashvins <note>original: "Āśvina-śastra"</note>. Thus says the rule-book: "The protector of the people, to you, O Agni, the seekers of Truth..." <note>original: "janasya gopāstvām agna ṛtāyavaḥ"; Ashvalayana Shrauta Sutra 4.13</note>.

->॥ Here follows the first verse ॥<-

## Hymn Text

To you, O Agni, those desiring Truth have kindled, you the ancient one, for their protection, O you born of strength. You who are greatly delightful, worthy of worship, all-sustaining, the friend of the house, the lord of the home, the one to be chosen. || 1 ||

**Word-by-word Analysis:**
To you | O Agni | Truth-desiring | well | kindled | the ancient | the ancient ones | for protection | strength-produced | many-delighting | worship-worthy | all-sustaining | domestic-minded | house-lord | desirable || 1 ||

---

## Commentary (Sayana)

O **produced by strength** <note>original: "sahas-kṛta"</note>, Agni who is the creator of power, the **ancient ones** <note>original: "pratnāsaḥ"</note>—the seers of old—who are **desiring the sacrifice** <note>original: "ṛtāyavo," those seeking the cosmic order or "Rita"</note> have **kindled** you well, you who are the **ancient one**, for the sake of **protection** or self-preservation. What kind of Agni are you? **Greatly delightful** <note>original: "puruścandram"</note>—possessing much wealth or being exceedingly pleasing. **Worthy of worship** <note>original: "yajataṃ"</note>—one who should be sacrificed to. **All-sustaining** <note>original: "viśvadhāyasaṃ"</note>—possessing much food or nourishment. **Domestic-minded** <note>original: "damūnasam"</note>—one whose mind is focused on giving, or a resident of the home. **Lord of the house** <note>original: "gṛhapatiṃ"</note>—the protector of the sacrificer’s home. **Desirable** <note>original: "vareṇyaṃ"</note>—worthy of being chosen.

[The seeker] of riches, the one who performs good labor <note>original: "suśamīṇam," referring to one who conducts sacrifices well</note>, the provider of good happiness, the well-protecting one, and the consumer of aging things—meaning the one who pervades old trees or consumes stagnant waters.

For that rite, the verse beginning "To you, O Agni, the human [tribes]" is the sacrificial prayer <note>original: "yājyā"</note>. This is indicated in the liturgy: "To you, O Agni, the human tribes pray, O Agni, come for the feast" (*Aitareya Brāhmaṇa* 7. 6.).

## Commentary (Sayana)

O **Agni, the auspicious one** <note>original: "subhaga," meaning one of beautiful wealth</note>, **to you the human tribes**—all the people belonging to humanity—**pray**; they praise you. What is your nature? You are the **knower of the sacrificial invocations** <note>original: "hotrāvidam," one who knows the offerings or those who recite them</note>, the **discerner** who distinguishes between the good and the bad, and the **greatest bestower of riches**—the giver of the most delightful wealth. You **dwell in the secret place** <note>original: "guhā santam," refers to Agni hiding in the "cave" of the forest or the "cave" of the human heart</note> always, you are **visible to all**, and you possess **many sounds** <note>original: "tuviṣvaṇasam," referring to the loud crackling of the ritual fire</note>. You are an **excellent sacrificer** and you are **clothed in clarified butter** <note>original: "ghṛtaśriyam," meaning one who takes refuge in or is beautified by the poured butter offerings</note>.

## Commentary (Sayana)

O **Agni**, you, being **many-formed** <note>original: "pururūpaḥ," referring to his various manifestations in different ritual fires</note>, **provide strength** or nourishment <note>original: "vayo," meaning food or life-force</note> **to every person**—that is, to every sacrificing worshiper—**as in ancient times**. O **one praised by many**, you **rule over** or become the master of **many foods**, such as the sacrificial cakes and offerings <note>original: "caru-puroḍāśādīni"</note>, through your divine **power**. Your famous **brilliance** <note>original: "tviṣiḥ"</note> **cannot be overcome** by others while you are **growing in strength** <note>original: "tiviṣyāṇasya," from the root 'tiviṣ' meaning to shine or be powerful</note>.

## Commentary (Sayana)

O **youngest one** <note>original: "yaviṣṭhya," an epithet for Agni because he is newly kindled for every sacrifice</note>, the **gods** have **made you**, who are **well-kindled, the messenger** and the **carrier of oblations** <term>Havyavāhana: the aspect of Fire that specifically transports offerings to the gods</term>. Among the three ritual fires, it is the Carrier of Oblations who was first appointed by the gods as their messenger, as confirmed by sacred scripture: "The carrier of oblations belongs to the gods." Furthermore, the **gods and humans** have **established you** as the **brilliant eye**—meaning the all-illuminating one who functions like a physical eye—which **impels the mind**. You are **wide-moving** <note>original: "urujrayasam," possessing great speed or reach</note>, **born of clarified butter** <note>original: "ghṛtayoni," meaning ghee is the cause or source of your flame</note>, and you are **invoked** through rituals. It is the mind that is truly guided by this divine "eye."

### Mandala 5. Anuvaka 1. Sukta 8. ] || Third Ashtaka || 291

## Commentary (Sayana)

O **Agni**, the ancient <note>original: "pradivaḥ"</note> sacrificers <note>those performing the ritual, original: "yajamānāḥ"</note> who desire happiness <note>original: "sumnayavaḥ"</note> have kindled you—who are offered with clarified butter—well, using excellent fuel <note>original: "suṣamidhā"</note>. That is to say, they have lit you perfectly. As you are **growing** in strength and are sprinkled or moistened <note>original: "ukṣitaḥ"</note> by the essences of plants, you spread over the earthly trees. Alternatively, the term "earthly" <note>original: "pārthiva"</note> may be an adjective describing your victory or expansion. You preside over the earthly offerings such as the cooked rice <term>Charu: an oblation of rice or barley boiled with milk or water</term> and the sacrificial cakes <term>Purodasha: a heap of ground seeds or a cake offered in fire</term>. You exist, manifesting yourself through these ritual elements.

-> ॥ Thus ends the twenty-sixth section <term>Varga: a small subdivision of a Vedic chapter</term> of the eighth chapter of the third book ॥ <-

May the Great Lord Vidyatirtha <note>Sayana’s spiritual teacher, often invoked as an incarnation of the deity Maheshvara (Shiva)</note>, who removes the darkness of the heart by the light of the Veda’s meaning, grant the four goals of human life <term>Purusharthas: the four aims of human existence: Dharma (virtue), Artha (purpose/wealth), Kama (pleasure), and Moksha (liberation)</term>.

Thus ends the eighth chapter <term>Adhyaya</term> in the third book <term>Ashtaka</term> of the "Light of the Veda’s Meaning" <note>original: "Vedartha-prakasha"</note>, the commentary on the Rig Veda collection composed by Sayanacharya. Sayana served as the prime minister of the empire of the illustrious King Vira Bukka <note>Vira Bukka Raya I (reigned 1356–1377), a founding sovereign of the Vijayanagara Empire</note>, the supreme lord of kings and the promoter of the Vedic path.

In the fifth Book <term>Mandala: one of the ten primary 'circles' or books of the Rig Veda</term>, in the first Recitation <term>Anuvaka: a sub-division of a Vedic book</term>, the first eight hymns have been explained. The ninth hymn, beginning with **"You, O Agni, possessing oblations"** <note>original: "tvām agne haviṣmanta"</note>, contains seven verses and was seen by the Seer <term>Rishi: the inspired poet-sage</term> Gaya, a descendant of Atri. The seventh and fifth verses are in the Pankti meter <note>a meter consisting of five segments of eight syllables</note>; the remaining verses are in the Anushtubh meter <note>the standard four-line meter of eight syllables per line</note>. The deity is Agni. Thus it is indexed in the Ritual Directory <term>Anukramani: the traditional index of Vedic authors, meters, and deities</term>: **"You, O Agni... Gaya... the last and the fifth are Pankti"**. In the Morning Litany <term>Prataranuvaka: the first ritual recitation of the day</term> and the Litany for the Twin Gods <term>Ashvinashastra: a recitation dedicated to the Ashvins</term>, these two hymns starting with this one are to be recited. This is indicated in the ritual manual: **"The hymn 'You, O Agni, possessing oblations' (Ashvalayana Shrauta Sutra 4.13)"**.

## Hymn Text

**You, O Agni, the divine one, mortals possessing oblations invoke.**
**I consider you the Knower of all beings; may you bring the offerings in due order. || 1 ||**

## Commentary (Sayana)

O **Agni, you, the divine** <note>original: "devam", the shining one</note>, **mortals** <note>original: "martāso"</note> **possessing oblations** <note>original: "haviṣmanto", those equipped with the materials for sacrifice</note> **invoke** <note>original: "īḷate"</note>. That is, they praise you. And I consider you the **Knower of all beings** <note>original: "jātavedasam"</note>. He is called the "Knower of all beings" because he knows all created things, whether moving or stationary. Or, he is "the one known by all things," meaning all stationary and moving things know him. Alternatively, the word **veda** refers to wealth; "Knower of all beings" is he in whom all wealth <note>original: "vedas"</note> is found <note>original: "jāta"</note>. To such a **you**...

<meta>This page continues the grammatical commentary on Rig Veda, Mandala 4, Hymn 1. Note: The previous page provided in the prompt mentioned Mandala 5, but the current OCR header and text clearly identify this as Mandala 4, Sukta 1. ## Commentary (Sayana)

**I consider** <note>original: "manye"</note>. That is, **I praise**. The root *man* is used here in the sense of "to praise," because verbal roots can have multiple meanings. You, [O Agni], **carry** <note>original: "vakṣi"</note> the **oblations** <note>original: "havyā"</note>, which are the means of the sacrifice, **continuously** <note>original: "ānuṣak"</note> or in an uninterrupted manner.

**Those possessing oblations** <note>original: "haviṣmantaḥ"</note>: The word *havis* (oblation) ends with the *is* suffix from the *Unadi* rules; therefore, the accent falls on the final syllable. The suffix *matup* <term>matup: a grammatical suffix meaning 'possessing' or 'containing'</term> is added to indicate "that which belongs to this." According to the rule "the letters *t* and *s* before a *matvartha* suffix," the word takes the *bha* designation <term>bha-sangya: a technical grammatical status that prevents certain internal sound changes</term>, which explains why the *s* does not change into *r*. Since the *matup* suffix and the case ending are unaccented, the original suffix's accent remains.

**The divine** <note>original: "devam"</note>: The word *deva* is accented on the final syllable because it ends with the *ach* suffix.

**Mortals** <note>original: "marta-saḥ"</note>: Derived from the root *mṛ* (to leave life/die). The suffix *tan* is added by the rule beginning with "asi-hasi-mṛ." It undergoes vowel strengthening (guna). The case ending *jas* receives the *asuk* augment. Because of the *n* marker in the suffix, the accent is on the first syllable.

**They praise** <note>original: "īḷate"</note>: From the root *īḍ* (to praise). The class-suffix *shap* is deleted because it belongs to the *Adadi* group. In the middle voice (Atmanepada), the ending *jhe* is replaced. Here, following the tradition of Vedic recitation, the letter *ḍ* is pronounced as *ḷ* <note>original: "ळकार"</note>. Because the suffix is unaccented, the root accent would normally prevail, but it becomes unaccented (nighata) due to the rules of the eighth chapter of Panini's grammar.

**I consider** <note>original: "manye"</note>: The suffix *shyan* is marked with *n*, causing the accent to fall on the first syllable.

**You** <note>original: "tvā"</note>: From the root *yu* (to mix). The word *yuṣmad* (you) ends in the suffix *madik* and is accented on the final syllable. By the rule "tva and ma in the singular," the portion up to the letter *m* is replaced by *tva*. By Panini’s rule 7.2.87, the vowel becomes long. When two vowels merge, the resulting vowel is accented. However, by the rule "all [pronouns] are unaccented when not at the start of a verse-foot," it becomes unaccented.

**The knower of all births** <note>original: "jātavedasam"</note>: From the root *jan* (to be born). The suffix *kta* is added. The augment *i* is prohibited. The root *jan* changes its vowel to *ā*. The suffix *kta* is accented on the final syllable. The word *vedas* is also accented on the first syllable because it ends in the *asun* suffix. If treated as a "Karma-dharaya" compound, the first member retains its original accent. If treated as a "Bahuvrihi" compound, the rule "in a Bahuvrihi, the first member remains in its natural form" applies.

**Oblations** <note>original: "havyā"</note>: In the sense of "worthy of being invoked," the suffix *ya* is added. It is a neuter form. The plural ending is replaced by *shi*, which is then deleted in the Vedic style. By the rules of suffixes, the *num* augment and lengthening occur. The final syllable is accented.

**You carry** <note>original: "vakṣi"</note>: From the root *vah* (to carry/convey). The second-person singular suffix *sip* is added. The class-suffix *shap* is deleted. Various sound changes (dhatva, katva, shatva) occur to the root. Since the suffix is unaccented, the root would normally be accented on the first syllable, but it loses its accent (nighata) due to its position in the sentence.

**Continuously** <note>original: "ānuṣak"</note>: From the prefix *anu* and the root *sañj*. The suffix *kvip* is added. The nasal *n* is dropped and the consonant changes to a *k* sound. The *s* of the root changes to *ṣ* because of the preceding prefix. The vowel lengthening is a Vedic variation. The second part of the compound retains its natural accent.

---

## Hymn Text

-> ॥ Now the second verse ॥ <-

**Agni is the Invoker <term>Hotr: the priest who recites the Rig Veda</term> of the worshiping household that has strewn the sacred grass. To him the sacrifices proceed together, as do the seekers of glory with their strengths.** ॥ २ ॥

<vocab>
Agni: the fire god, Hotr: the invoking priest, Jatavedas: knower of all beings, Vriktabarhis: one who has prepared the sacred grass for ritual, Anushak: continuously, Matup: a possessive suffix, Nighata: the loss of accent in a verb, Havya: sacrificial offerings
</vocab>

# Mandala 5. Chapter 1. Hymn 9. 

### Fourth Book (Ashtaka), Page 295

## Hymn Text

**Agni** is the **Invoker** of the **generous giver**, in the **dwelling** where the **sacred grass is clipped**. Toward him the **sacrifices** proceed together; toward him the **offerings** proceed, **seeking protection**. [Verse 2]

-> **Word-by-Word Analysis (Padapatha)** <-

**Agni**; the **Invoker**; of the **generous giver**; of the **dwelling**; of the **one who has clipped the sacred grass**; **together**; the **sacrifices**; **proceed**; **him**; **together**; the **offerings**; **seeking protection**. [Verse 2]

---

## Commentary (Sayana)

Toward which Agni **all the sacrifices** <note>original: "yajñāsaḥ"</note> go or gather together. **Seeking protection** <note>original: "avasyavo"</note>—that is, those securing great fame for the sacrificer—the **offerings** <note>original: "vājāso"</note> reach and proceed toward Agni. Agni, described in this way, becomes the **Invoker** <note>original: "hotā"</note>, the one who calls the gods for the sacrifice of that **generous** <note>original: "dāsvataḥ"</note> patron who gives oblations. This patron is further described as **one who has clipped the sacred grass** <note>original: "vṛktabarhiṣaḥ"</note>. This refers to the one by whom the *Darpha* grass (used for the altar) has been cut and prepared. In his **dwelling** <note>original: "kṣayasya"</note>—so called because the rewards and means of reaching heaven "dwell" or reside within the sacrifice—Agni performs his office.

**Grammatical Notes:**
**Of the generous giver** <note>original: "dāsvataḥ"</note>: Derived from the root *dā* (to give) with the suffix *asun*. The suffix *matup* <term>matup: a possessive suffix meaning 'possessing'</term> follows, and the *m* changes to *v* because of the preceding vowel. The accent is on the first syllable.
**Of the dwelling** <note>original: "kṣayasya"</note>: From the root *kṣi* (to dwell or move). It refers to a residence and carries the primary accent on the first syllable.
**Of the one who has clipped the grass** <note>original: "vṛktabarhiṣaḥ"</note>: From the root *vṛj* (to exclude), which here by extension means "to cut" or "to shear." This is a compound word <term>bahuvrīhi: a compound where the whole refers to an external object, here the sacrificer</term>, preserving the original accent of the first word.
**Sacrifices** <note>original: "yajñāsaḥ"</note>: The word *yajña* (sacrifice) is formed with the suffix *naṅ* and has the accent on the final syllable.
**They proceed** <note>original: "caranti"</note>: From the root *car* (to move). It loses its accent due to the rules of verbal conjugation in a sentence, though the presence of the relative pronoun "whom" prevents total loss of accent in some contexts.
**Offerings** <note>original: "vājāso"</note>: Derived from the root *vaj*. In Vedic usage, the accent can shift to the first syllable.
**Seeking protection** <note>original: "avasyavuḥ"</note>: Formed from a word meaning "desiring one's own protection" using the *kyac* suffix. The accent falls on the final syllable.

-> **The Third Verse** <-

And indeed, him whom the **two fire-sticks** produced like a **new-born infant**—the **supporter** of the **human tribes**, **Agni**, the **performer of beautiful sacrifices**. [Verse 3]

-> **Word-by-Word Analysis (Padapatha)** <-

**And**; **indeed**; **whom**; **infant**; **like**; **new**; **produced**; **the two fire-sticks**; **the supporter**; **of the human**; **tribes**; **Agni**; **the performer of beautiful sacrifices**. [Verse 3]

---

Moreover, the **two fire-sticks** <note>original: "araṇī"</note>—the wooden blocks used to churn fire—**produced** <note>original: "janiṣṭa"</note> Agni. They produced him **like a new-born infant** <note>original: "śiśuṃ yathā"</note> for the sake of the **human** <note>original: "mānuṣīṇāṃ"</note> **tribes** <note>original: "viśāṃ"</note> (those born of Manu). He is the **supporter** <note>original: "dhartāraṃ"</note> because he nourishes the physical elements of the body through the cooking of food and sacrificial offerings. He is the **performer of beautiful sacrifices** <note>original: "svadhvaraṃ"</note>. The meaning is that the fire-sticks created Agni to sustain and nourish all people.

**Grammatical Notes:**
**Infant** <note>original: "śiśuṃ"</note>: From the root *śo* (to sharpen/thin). Through a complex process of vowel changes and doubling the root, it becomes *śiśu*. It is accented on the first syllable.
**Like** <note>original: "yathā"</note>: In this position at the end of a foot, it is entirely unaccented.
**Produced** <note>original: "janiṣṭa"</note>: From the root *jan* (to be born). <unclear>The text cuts off here during the explanation of the verbal tense.</unclear>

# ॥ Rig Veda ॥ [Book 4. Chapter 1. Section 1.]

...the Aorist tense <note>original: "luṅ"</note>. Due to Vedic usage, there is an exchange of the tense-suffix. **The two fire-sticks** <note>original: "araṇī"</note>: Derived from the root *ṛ* (to go). With the suffix *ani*, the initial syllable is accented. Agni "goes" or arises from these two, hence they are called *araṇī*. Even though the suffix *ani* usually denotes the starting point of an action <term>apādāna</term>, here it is established as an exceptional form according to the rules of Pāṇini <note>referencing Pāṇini 3.4.75</note>. **Of the human** <note>original: "mānuṣīṇām"</note>: Derived from *Manu* with suffixes indicating "born of." The initial syllable is accented. **Of the people** <note>original: "viśām"</note>: From the root *viś* (to enter). The case ending is accented. **The well-performed sacrifice** <note>original: "svadhvaram"</note>: From the root *dhvṛ* (to injure). A sacrifice <term>adhvara</term> is that in which there is no "dhara" or injury/interruption. In this compound, the final syllable is accented.

---

-> ॥ Now the Fourth Verse ॥ <-

## Hymn Text
And truly, you are difficult to seize, like the offspring of those who move crookedly; you, O Agni, who consume many forests, like a beast in the pasture. ॥ 4 ॥

-> **Word-by-Word Analysis** <-
And; truly; difficult to seize; the son/offspring; like; of the crooked-moving ones; many; who; consumer; are; forests; O Agni; beast; like; in the pasture. ॥ 4 ॥

---

## Commentary (Sayana)
**And truly** <note>original: "uta sma"</note>: furthermore. **Of the crooked-moving ones** <note>original: "hvāryāṇām"</note>: of snakes that move in a winding fashion. Alternatively, it refers to horses that move with a specific curved or leaping gait. **Like the son** <note>original: "putro na"</note>: like a young snake or an untrained young horse. **You are difficult to seize** <note>original: "durgṛbhīyase"</note>: you are caught with great difficulty. O Agni, **you who** <note>original: "yas tvaṃ"</note> become the **consumer** <note>original: "dagdhā asi"</note> of **many forests** <note>original: "puru vanā"</note>. How is this so? **Like a beast** <note>original: "paśur na"</note> in the **pasture** <note>original: "yavase"</note>. The meaning is this: just as a beast suffering from extreme hunger, when released into a field of grass, consumes everything in its path, so do you consume the woods.

**Grammatical Notes:**
**Difficult to seize** <note>original: "durgṛbhīyase"</note>: From the root *grah* (to take/seize). It uses the passive suffix *yak*. In the Vedas, there is a frequent insertion of the vowel *i*. The sound *h* changes to *bh* according to Vedic rules. **Of the crooked-moving ones** <note>original: "hvāryāṇām"</note>: From the root *hvṛ* (to be crooked). The vowel is lengthened, and it carries a specific swinging pitch <term>svarita</term>. **Many** <note>original: "puru"</note>: From the root *pṛ* (to fill/protect). The suffix *ku* is applied, and the vowel changes to *u*. **You are** <note>original: "asi"</note>: Since it follows a relative pronoun, it does not lose its accent.

---

-> ॥ Now the Fifth Verse ॥ <-

## Hymn Text
Then indeed, his smoky flames rise up together in unison, when I place him upon the altar; he blows like a smelter in the sky, he whets his flame like a smith. ॥ 5 ॥

-> **Word-by-Word Analysis** <-
Then; indeed; whose; flames; together; well; go; smoky; when; him; I; placed; in the heaven/altar; up; like a blower; blows; whets; the smelter; as/like. ॥ 5 ॥

<vocab>
- Agni: The sacred fire deity, central to Vedic ritual.
- Araṇī: Two wooden sticks (usually from the Ficus religiosa or Acacia catechu) rubbed together to produce the sacrificial fire.
- Adhvara: A term for sacrifice, literally meaning "that which is not injurious" or "uninterrupted."
- Hvārya: Descriptive of a crooked or winding movement, often applied to snakes or galloping horses.
- Yavasa: Fresh grass or pastureland where animals graze.
- Dhmātṛ: A smelter or metal-worker who uses a bellows to blow on a fire to increase its heat.
- Arci: A ray of light or a tongue of flame.
</vocab>

## Commentary (Sayana)
<note>This section concludes the explanation of Rig Veda 5.9.5 from the previous page.</note>

**And further** <note>original: "adha sma api ca"</note>: additionally, of the **smoky one** <note>original: "dhūminaḥ"</note>, meaning of that Agni whose **flames** <note>original: "arcayaḥ"</note> or rays **unite well** <note>original: "samyak saṃyanti"</note>, reaching everywhere. He is spread in **three places** <note>original: "citas tisṛṣu sthāneṣu"</note>, meaning he pervades the three regions of the sky, the atmosphere, and the earth. When he **puffs himself up** <note>original: "īm ayam ātmānam upadhamati"</note> or increases his own form, then the flames go out in all directions. How is this done? **Like a smelter** <note>original: "dhmāteva"</note>. Just as a **blacksmith** <note>original: "karmāraḥ"</note> increases the fire using **bellows** <note>original: "bhastrā-ādibhiḥ"</note>, in the same way, Agni increases himself. Furthermore, just as in the presence of a smelter, the fire being blown upon **sharpens itself** <note>original: "śiśīte"</note> or becomes intense, so does Agni sharpen his own form. The word **aha** is merely used to fill the meter <term>pādapūraṇa</term>.

**They go** <note>original: "yanti"</note>: From the root *iṇ* (to go). Due to the connection with the word "who" <note>original: "yat"</note>, there is no loss of accent <term>nighāta</term>. **He puffs** <note>original: "dhamati"</note>: From the root *dhmā* (to blow or to connect with fire). According to the rules of grammar, *dhmā* becomes *dhama*. As before, there is no loss of accent. **He sharpens** <note>original: "śiśīte"</note>: From the root *śo* (to thin or sharpen). It takes the Middle voice <term>ātmanepada</term> as an exception. In the Vedic dialect <term>chandas</term>, the class-marker is dropped <term>ślu</term>. The vowel changes to *ā* before certain suffixes, and the root is reduplicated. The vowel of the reduplicated syllable becomes *i*. Because it follows a verb form, the accent is not lost.

---

## Hymn Text

-> || Now the Sixth Verse || <-

Through your protections, O Agni, and through the praises of Mitra, may we overcome the misfortunes caused by mortals, as if they were hateful enemies. ॥ 6 ॥

**Word-by-Word Analysis:**
Your; I; O Agni; through protections; of Mitra; and; through praises; of hatred-joined; like; misfortunes; may we overcome; of mortals. ॥ 6 ॥

---

## Commentary (Sayana)

O **Agni**, through **your protections** <note>original: "tava ūtibhiḥ"</note>, the acts of guarding performed by you who are a **friend** <note>original: "mitrasya"</note> to all, and through **praises** <note>original: "praśastibhiḥ"</note>, the hymns of glorification performed by us—may we **overcome** <note>original: "turyāma"</note> or cross over the **misfortunes** <note>original: "duritā"</note>, the sinful deeds and difficulties caused by **mortals** <note>original: "martyānām"</note> who are our enemies, just **as** <note>original: "na"</note> one overcomes **hateful** <note>original: "dveṣoyutaḥ"</note> foes. The meaning is this: through your protection and through the hymns related to you, may I overcome both external and internal enemies.

**Through protections** <note>original: "ūtibhiḥ"</note>: From the root *av* (to protect or favor). It takes the suffix *ktin*. By specific grammatical rules <note>referencing Pāṇini and Unadi rules</note>, the internal vowel is lengthened, and the final accent is fixed. **Through praises** <note>original: "praśastibhiḥ"</note>: From the root *śaṃs* (to praise) with the suffix *ktin*. The initial syllable of the prefix takes the accent. **Joined with hatred** <note>original: "dveṣoyutaḥ"</note>: From the root *dviṣ* (to dislike/hate). It uses the suffix *asun* to form the noun "hatred," combined with the root *yu* (to mix/join). The compound follows the standard accentuation for verbal derivatives. **May we overcome** <note>original: "turyāma"</note>: From the root *tṛ* (to cross over or float). It is in the **Potential mood** <term>liṅ</term> expressing a prayer or wish. Through various Vedic grammatical transformations <term>śapaḥ luk</term> and vowel changes <term>utva</term>, the form *turyāma* is achieved. The accent remains on the mood-marker, and it is not suppressed because it does not follow a word in the same poetic foot.

<vocab>
- Agni (अग्नि): The divine fire, mediator between gods and men.
- Mitra (मित्र): Often a solar deity, but here interpreted by Sayana as "friend to all."
- Protections (ऊति - ūti): Divine aid, guarding, or favoring the worshiper.
- Praises (प्रशस्ति - praśasti): Glorification or hymns of excellence.
- Misfortunes (दुरित - durita): Literally "difficult paths," referring to sins, troubles, or calamities.
- Overcome (तुर्याम - turyāma): To cross over a river or to transcend a difficulty.
- Mortals (मर्त्य - martya): Human beings, here specifically referring to human enemies.
- Blacksmith (ध्मातृ/कर्मार - dhmātṛ/karmāra): Used as a simile for how Agni fans his own flames.
</vocab>

<summary>This page concludes the description of Agni's self-intensifying power using the simile of a blacksmith's bellows and begins a prayer for protection. The worshiper asks Agni and Mitra to help them overcome human-induced troubles and "cross over" life's difficulties through divine aid and sacred hymns.</summary>

->॥ Seventh Verse ॥<-

## Hymn Text
O powerful Agni, bring that wealth to us, the leaders [of the sacrifice]. May he drive away [our enemies], may he nourish [us], may he be there for the winning of strength, and be there for our increase in battles. ॥ 7 ॥

O Agni. To us. Toward. Men. Wealth. O powerful one. Bring. 
He. May he drive away. He. May he nourish. May he be. Of strength. For the winning. And. Be. In battles. Our. For growth. ॥ 7 ॥

---

## Commentary (Sayana)
O **powerful Agni** <note>original: "agne sahasvo"</note>, O mighty one! The **men** <note>original: "naro"</note>, who are the leaders of the oblations, [ask]: **bring to us that wealth** <note>original: "no'smākaṃ taṃ rayiṃ"</note>. Bring toward us that wealth which is famous in the world, characterized by cattle and other riches. The aforementioned **Agni, may he drive away** <note>original: "so'gniḥ kṣepayat"</note>; let him drive away our enemies. **May that Agni nourish** <note>original: "so'gniḥ poṣayat"</note>; let him nourish us. **For the winning** <note>original: "sātaye"</note> or the acquisition of **strength** <note>original: "vajasya"</note> or food, **may he be** <note>original: "bhuvat"</note>; let him exist for that purpose. **And also** <note>original: "uta"</note>, O Agni, **in battles** <note>original: "pṛtsu"</note>, meaning in wars, **be there for our growth** <note>original: "no'smākaṃ vṛdhe"</note> or for our prosperity. The meaning is: for the sake of victory over enemies in battle, you should bring about prosperity.

**Powerful** <note>original: "sahvas"</note>: From the root *ṣah* (to prevail or endure). With the suffix *asun*. Strength is called *sahas* because one prevails over enemies with it. It takes the possessive suffix *matup*. The *m* changes to *v* because it follows an *a* sound. The final *s* becomes *ru* in the vocative case in Vedic usage. The word loses its accent <term>nighāta</term> because it is a vocative following another word. **May he drive away** <note>original: "kṣepayat"</note>: From the root *kṣip* (to throw or impel). It is the causal form in the Let mood (Vedic subjunctive). There is an elision of the final *i*. The *a* augment is added. **May he nourish** <note>original: "poṣayat"</note>: From the root *puṣ* (to nourish). **May he be** <note>original: "bhuvat"</note>: From the root *bhū* (to be). The guna change is prohibited by specific rules. **Be** <note>original: "edhi"</note>: From the root *as* (to be). In the imperative mood, it undergoes specific transformations to become *edhi*. It loses its accent. **In battles** <note>original: "pṛtsu"</note>: The word *pṛtanā* (army/battle) is substituted with *pṛd* based on grammatical rules.

->॥ Thus ends the first section (Varga) of the first chapter in the fourth book ॥<-

The tenth hymn, beginning with "O Agni, most powerful," consists of seven verses. The Seer <term>rishi</term> and other designations are as before <note>Gaya of the Atri family</note>. The fourth and seventh verses are in the Pankti meter. The index states: "O Agni, most powerful, the last and fourth are Pankti."

Agni. Most powerful. Bring. Splendor. To us. Master of stones.
Forth. Us. With wealth. Far-reaching. Carve/Prepare. For strength. A path. ॥ 1 ॥

O **Agni**, bring the **most powerful** <note>original: "ojiṣṭham"</note> or mightiest **splendor** <note>original: "dyumnam"</note>. This refers to wealth that shines <note>original: "dyotate"</note> everywhere in the form of bracelets, crowns, and so on...

<meta>This page continues the commentary on Rig Veda, Mandala 5, Hymn 10. It concludes the grammatical analysis of Verse 1 and provides the text and commentary for Verse 2. It maintains continuity from the previous page's discussion of Agni's role in providing wealth and strength.</meta>

Mandala 5. Chapter 1. Hymn 10.] || Fourth Book (Ashtaka) || 299

## Commentary (Sayana)
[Conclusion of commentary on Mandala 5, Hymn 10, Verse 1]

Thus, **splendor** <note>original: "dyumnaṃ"</note> means wealth. **Bring to us** <note>original: "asmabhyam-ābhara"</note>; fetch it. O **Adhrigu** <note>original: "adhrigo"</note>, you of unrestrained movement! One whose movement <note>original: "gamanaṃ"</note> is unrestrained <note>original: "adhṛtam"</note> or unhindered. Alternatively, one whose rays <note>original: "gāvo rasmayo"</note> are unrestrained. This is the address to him. Join **us** <note>original: "no"</note> with **all-encompassing wealth** <note>original: "parīṇasā rāyā"</note>—that is, wealth that is pervasive on all sides. For the **gain of food** <note>original: "vājāya"</note>, **engrave** <note>original: "ratsi"</note>—meaning create or prepare—a **path** <note>original: "panthāṃ"</note>, a way that serves as the means for food to reach me.

**Most powerful** <note>original: "ojiṣṭhaṃ"</note>: Derived from the root meaning 'to be straight or honest.' By applying the technical grammatical rules <note>original: "ubje-rbalo-paśca"</note>, the word *ojas* (strength) is formed. To this, the suffix indicating possession is added, followed by the superlative suffix *isthan*. After the elision of certain technical markers, we arrive at the word, which carries the primary accent on the first syllable. **Splendor** <note>original: "dyumnaṃ"</note>: From the root *dyut* (to shine), the suffix *nak* is added and the letter *m* is substituted as the final part of the base. By the rules of accentuation, the accent falls on the final syllable. **Adhrigu** <note>original: "adhrigo"</note>: Here, the word *adhṛta* (unrestrained) is replaced by the form *adhri*. The word for 'ray' or 'cow' <note>original: "go"</note> undergoes a vowel shortening as it is the secondary member of a compound. As a vocative, it loses its accent. **All-encompassing** <note>original: "parīṇasā"</note>: The root *ṇas* usually means 'to be crooked,' but here it means 'to pervade,' as roots often have multiple meanings. It uses a specific suffix to indicate the state or action. The prefix *pari* indicates 'reaching all around.' Although it is a compound, a specific rule for Vedic phonetics causes the *n* to change to *ṇ*. There is a technical debate here regarding whether the prefix rules apply, but the commentator concludes that the change is justified by the general Vedic flexibility. The vowel in the prefix is lengthened, and the compound preserves the original accent of the first member. **Engrave** <note>original: "ratsi"</note>: From the root *rad* (to scratch or engrave). It belongs to the *bhū* class of verbs. The typical class-sign is dropped in Vedic usage. As it stands at the beginning of a poetic foot, it retains its accent. **Path** <note>original: "panthāṃ"</note>: This is the accusative singular. The nasal sound is dropped according to Vedic usage. The accent falls on the first syllable.

---
->॥ Now, the second [verse] ॥<-

## Hymn Text
O wonderful Agni, you [grant] us, through our sacrifice and the greatness of your skill. Through your deeds, you reached divine power, like Mitra, the worshipful one. ॥ 2 ॥

**Word-by-word Breakdown (Pada Patha):**
You. To us. O Agni. O wonderful one. Through action. Of skill. Through greatness.
In you. Divine power. Toward. He reached. Through deeds. Mitra. Like. Worthy of sacrifice. ॥ 2 ॥

---

## Commentary (Sayana)
O **wonderful Agni** <note>original: "agne adbhuta"</note>, you who are a marvel to all because of your extraordinary power! Being pleased with **us** <note>original: "no"</note> by our **action** <note>original: "kratvā"</note>—the performance of sacrifices and other rituals—[grant us] the **greatness** <note>original: "maṃhanā"</note>, which means the giving, of **skill** <note>original: "dakṣasya"</note>, meaning strength or wealth. This "giving" is implied to complete the sentence. Because **divine power** <note>original: "asuryam"</note>, or lordly strength, has **ascended** <note>original: "āruhat"</note> into **you** <note>original: "tve"</note>, you are **worthy of sacrifice** <note>original: "yajñiyo"</note> like **Mitra** <note>original: "mitro na"</note> (the Sun). Through your **deeds** <note>original: "krāṇā"</note>, which involve the removal of demons who destroy the sacrifice—

<vocab>
- Agni: The Vedic deity of fire and the mediator between gods and humans.
- Adbhuta: Wonderful, mysterious; often used to describe Agni's unique nature.
- Kratu: Sacrificial action, wisdom, or the mental power behind a rite.
- Daksha: Skill, dexterity, or the power of will.
- Maṃhanā: Greatness, often interpreted in the context of generous giving.
- Asurya: Divine or lordly power (before the term 'Asura' took on a purely negative connotation).
- Mitra: A major solar deity representing friendship and contracts; often paired with Varuna.
- Yajñiya: Fit for sacrifice; holy.
- Sayana: The 14th-century scholar whose commentary is the standard for understanding the Vedas.
</vocab>
