# Book 5, Chapter 2, Hymn 29 ] || Fourth Ashtaka || 343

---

## Hymn Text

-> ॥ Here is the fifth verse ॥ <-

**Then by [your] power, O Generous One, all the gods granted the drinking of Soma to you; when you made the falling, forward-moving bay horses of the Sun stay behind for Etasa.** ॥ ५ ॥

-> [ Word-by-word Analysis ] <-
Then. By power. O Generous One <note>original: maghavan</note>. To you. The gods. In order. All. Gave. The drinking of Soma.
When. Of the Sun. The bay horses. Falling. In front. Being. Behind. For Etasa. Made. ॥ ५ ॥

---

## Commentary (Sayana)

Furthermore, O **Generous One** <note>original: maghavan</note>, O wealthy Indra, **by power** <note>original: kratvā</note>—that is, by your ritual action—**all the gods**, the shining ones like Agni and others, **granted** <note>original: anudaduḥ</note>—gave in proper order—**the drinking of Soma** <note>original: somapeyam</note> to you and for your sake. The meaning is that from that time forward, Indra became superior to all the gods. This is also heard in the sacred texts: "He, having become great, said to the deities, 'Take out an extra portion for me,'" and so on.

O Indra, **when** you **made** <note>original: kaḥ; an archaic form of akārṣīḥ</note> the **bay horses** <note>original: haritaḥ</note>—the mares belonging to the Sun—which were **falling** (arriving) and **moving in front**, to become **behind** <note>original: uparāḥ</note>—that is, having their speed stopped or slowed—for the sake of the sage named **Etasa**. For Etasa held a competition with the Sun, who is the son of Svashva. This is also mentioned in another Vedic passage:
> Indra helped the sacrificer Etasa when he was contending in a horse-race with the Sun. <note>original: Rig Veda 1.61.15</note>

-> ॥ Thus ends the twenty-third section <term>Varga</term> of the first chapter of the fourth book ॥ <-

---

## Hymn Text

-> ॥ Here is the sixth verse ॥ <-

**When the Generous One shattered his ninety and nine strongholds at once with the thunderbolt, the Maruts sang to Indra in the place of assembly; with the Trishtubh hymn, he struck the sky.** ॥ ६ ॥

-> [ Word-by-word Analysis ] <-
Nine. When. His. Ninety. And. Strongholds <note>original: bhogān</note>. At once. With the thunderbolt. The Generous One. Shattered.
They sing. To Indra. The Maruts. In the place of assembly. With the Trishtubh. With the word. He struck. The sky. ॥ ६ ॥

---

## Commentary (Sayana)

**When** the **Generous One**, the wealthy Indra, **shattered**—meaning split or destroyed—**at once** with his **thunderbolt** <note>original: vajreṇa</note> the **ninety and nine strongholds** <note>original: bhogān</note> belonging to **him** (meaning the demon Shambara). The word "strongholds" <note>original: bhogān</note> is used here to mean cities, as indicated by its specific accentuation. 

At that time, the **Maruts** <note>the storm-gods</note> **sang** to **Indra** as he stood in the **place of assembly** <note>original: sadhasthe</note>—which refers either to a common location or the battlefield—with a **hymn** <note>original: vacasā</note> in the form of a praise-song composed in the **Trishtubh** <note>a meter consisting of four lines of eleven syllables</note> meter. Indra, having been praised in this way, **struck**—meaning distressed or attacked—the **sky** <note>original: dyām</note>, which here refers to the shining demon named Shambara, using the powerful mantra recited by the great ones.

<vocab>
- Maghavan: An epithet for Indra meaning "the bountiful" or "the wealthy one."
- Soma: A sacred ritual drink offered to the gods.
- Etasa: A mythical figure or horse associated with the Sun, often aided by Indra in myths.
- Shambara: A powerful demon <term>Asura</term> in Vedic mythology known for possessing many fortresses.
- Trishtubh: One of the most common poetic meters in the Rig Veda.
- Maruts: A group of storm deities who are the constant companions and warriors of Indra.
</vocab>

## Rig Veda || [Book 4, Chapter 1, Section 24] || Page 344

---

## Hymn Text

-> ॥ Here is the seventh verse ॥ <-

**The friend [Agni] for his friend [Indra] quickly cooked three hundred buffaloes by his [Indra’s] power. At once, Indra drank three lakes <note>ritual vessels</note> of pressed Soma for the slaying of Vritra.** ॥ ७ ॥

-> [ Word-by-word Analysis ] <-
The friend. For the friend. Cooked. Quickly. Agni. His. By power. Buffaloes. Three. Hundreds.
Three. At once. Indra. Of Manu <note>the first man/sacrificer</note>. Lakes <note>vessels</note>. Pressed. He drank. For the slaying of Vritra. Soma. ॥ ७ ॥

---

## Commentary (Sayana)

**Agni**, who is the friend and ally of Indra, **quickly cooked**—that is, prepared—**three hundred** in number of **buffaloes** <note>original: mahiṣāṇām paśūnām</note> as sacrificial animals. This was done **for his friend** <note>original: sakhye</note>, meaning for Indra who is his ally, and by the **power** <note>original: kratvā</note> or ritual action of Indra which served as the cause. Furthermore, **Indra**, who is possessed of supreme lordship, **drank** at the very same time <note>original: sākam</note> the **pressed Soma** which was contained in **three lakes** <note>original: sarāṃsi</note>. 

In this context, the word "lakes" refers to the three specific ritual vessels named the <term>Putabhrit</term> <note>the "purified-bearer" jar</note>, the <term>Adhavaniya</term> <note>the "cleansing" jar</note>, and the <term>Dronakalasha</term> <note>the "wooden" jar</note>. These were related to **Manu** <note>meaning they were provided by the human sacrificer</note>. He drank this for the purpose of **the slaying of Vritra** <note>original: vṛtra-hatyāya</note>.

---

## Hymn Text

-> ॥ Here is the eighth verse ॥ <-

**When you ate the meat of three hundred buffaloes, and when you, O Bountiful One, drank the three lakes of Soma-juice, all the gods called out to Indra—as if calling a champion—when he struck down the Serpent.** ॥ ८ ॥

-> [ Word-by-word Analysis ] <-
Three. When. Hundreds. Of buffaloes. Meat. [You] ate. Three. Lakes. The Bountiful One. Soma-containing. [You] drank.
A champion <note>or worker/hero</note>. Like. All. They called. The gods. For a burden <note>strength for battle</note>. To Indra. When. The serpent. He struck. ॥ ८ ॥

---

## Commentary (Sayana)

O **Indra**, **when** <note>original: yat</note> you **ate** the **meat** <note>original: māṃsāni</note> of **three hundred buffaloes**... <note>The word *aghaḥ* is a specific Vedic form of the verb "to eat."</note> And **when** you, the **Bountiful One** <note>original: maghavā</note>—possessor of great wealth—**drank** the **three lakes** consisting of Soma. **When** Indra **struck down** the serpent **Vritra**, then **all the gods** **called out** to **Indra** for the "burden" <note>original: bharam</note>, meaning they called him to battle, fully invigorated by the drinking of Soma. 

The text provides a comparison: **like a champion** <note>original: kāraṃ na</note>. Just as a master calls upon a skilled worker or servant to perform a task, so the gods called upon Indra.

<margin>The Sage Usanas' Praise</margin>
The beginning of the next hymn in the "Marutvatiya" section is mentioned here: "When Usanas with the powerful ones..." It is stated that one should perform sacrifice while thinking of oneself as if swallowed by poison, using the praise of Usanas. This is noted in the ritual manuals <note>original: Āśvalāyana Śrauta Sūtra 9. 5.</note>.

# Mandala 5. Anuvaka 2. Sukta 29. || The Fourth Eight-Part Volume || Page 345

## Commentary (Sayana) on Verse 9

When, O Indra, you and the sage **Ushana** <note>original: uśanā kāvyaśca; a famous ancient seer and advisor to the gods and asuras</note> went to the **home** of the seer **Kutsa** with **horses** that were **powerful**—possessing the nature of overcoming others—and **swift**—meaning they were moving rapidly—at that time, O Indra, you were **winning** <note>original: vanvānaḥ; meaning destroying or conquering</note> the enemies in this moment. You **went** on the **same chariot**, meaning a single shared vehicle, along with **Kutsa** and the other **gods**. Furthermore, you **struck** <note>original: avanoḥ; killed or harmed</note> the demon named **Shushna**. Indeed, you truly destroyed him.

-> ॥ Here is the Tenth Verse ॥ <-

## Hymn Text (Verse 10)

**You tore away one wheel of the Sun; the other you made free for Kutsa to go forward. You struck the speechless barbarians with your weapon; in the place of battle, you struck down those of hostile speech.** ॥ १० ॥

**Word-by-word Analysis:**
Tore away | One | Wheel | You tore away | Of the Sun | For Kutsa | The other | Wealth/Room | To go | He made | Struck | 
The speechless | The barbarians/enemies | He struck | With the weapon | Down | In the place of battle | He struck down | Of hostile speech || १० ॥

## Commentary (Sayana) on Verse 10

O Indra, previously you **tore away**—meaning you separated—**one wheel** of the **Sun**, who usually possesses two wheels. The **other** single wheel you **made**—meaning you performed the action—so that **Kutsa** could obtain **wealth** <note>original: varivaḥ; often used to mean "wide space" or "freedom," here interpreted as "wealth"</note> or the ability **to go** forward. Furthermore, you **struck** <note>original: amṛṇah; killed or injured</note> the **barbarians** <note>original: dasyūn; the Dasyus, enemies of the Vedic people</note> who were **speechless** <note>original: anāsaḥ; literally "without a mouth/face." Sayana interprets this as "voiceless" or "speechless" because the word for mouth implies the capacity for speech</note> with your **weapon**, the thunderbolt <note>original: vajreṇam</note>. In the **place of battle** <note>original: duryoṇe; also meaning "at home" or "in a dwelling"</note>, you **struck down** or utterly cut to pieces those of **hostile speech** <note>original: mṛdhravācaḥ; those whose power of speech is injured or who speak harmfully</note>. The two different words for "struck" <note>original: amṛṇo and nyavṛṇak</note> are used together here to show emphasis and respect for the act.

O Indra, the **hymns** belonging to me, the seer named **Gauriviti**, **increased** you. May they continue to increase your strength. You **subdued**—meaning you brought under control—the demon named **Pipru** for the sake of the son of **Vidathin**, who is known by the name **Rijishvan**. O Indra, a certain seer named **Rijishvan** **brought you** toward himself for the sake of **friendship**...

<gloss>
- **Indra**: The king of the gods and the primary deity of the Rig Veda.
- **Ushana**: A sage-priest known for his wisdom and association with the chariot of Indra.
- **Kutsa**: A favorite protégé of Indra, often depicted riding in Indra's own chariot.
- **Shushna**: A demon of drought or "the hissing one" defeated by Indra.
- **Dasyu**: A term for enemies or hostile tribes who do not follow the Vedic rituals.
- **Anas**: Interpreted by the commentator as "speechless" or "without proper mouths," but often translated by modern scholars as "noseless."
- **Mridhravach**: Having "spoiled" or "stammering" speech; a derogatory term for enemies.
- **Gauriviti**: The seer (Rishi) to whom this specific part of the hymn is attributed.
- **Pipru**: A demon or enemy chief subdued by Indra.
- **Rijishvan**: A seer, son of Vidathin, who was aided by Indra against Pipru.
- **Stomas**: Formal ritual hymns of praise.
</gloss>

# || Rig Veda || [Book 4, Hymn 1, Section 25]

## Commentary (Sayana)
Indra, for the sake of companionship, has made you <note>referring to the sacrificer or Agni</note> his own, as you cook the offerings—the sacrificial cakes and other items. You have brought him face to face. Furthermore, you have drunk the Soma belonging to this person who has the remains of the sacrifice. Through the nights...

Regarding the **Dashapeya** <note>A specific ritual involving the drinking of Soma by ten priests</note> day, in the ritual of the **Marutvatiya** <note>Offerings made to Indra accompanied by the Maruts, the storm gods</note>, the hymn beginning with **Navagvasah** is the introductory verse. It is so indicated in the liturgical texts: **"The Navagvas, having pressed the Soma, to Indra... indeed when with the friend-like Navagvas," these are the first of the two recited verses. (Ashvalayana Shrauta Sutra 9.3).**

## Hymn Text
The **Navagvas** <note>The "nine-month" seers</note>, having pressed the Soma, and the **Dashagvas** <note>The "ten-month" seers</note> worship **Indra** with prayers. Like leaders, the praising **Angirases** opened the wide cave of the cows, even though it was covered [by the demon]. ॥ 12 ॥

## Commentary (Sayana)
**The Navagvas:** Those who attained their goal and departed after performing a session of sacrifice for nine months are the Navagvas. Those who departed after completing ten months are the Dashagvas. Both of these types of **Angirases** <note>A family of semi-divine fire-priests who helped Indra recover the stolen cows of light</note>, being **pressers of Soma**, **worship Indra** with **prayers**—with hymns that are worthy of worship. They praise him.

Likewise, the **praising leaders**, the Angirases, **opened** <note>original: apāvrṇvan; meaning uncovered or threw open</note> **that** famous and vast **herd of cattle** <note>original: gavyam cit; a group related to cows</note> which was **covered**—hidden away by the demon **Vala** <note>original: valenāsurēṇācchāditavantam; the demon who personifies the enclosure of the light/rain</note> in many places.

In the one-day sacrifice called **Parikri**, for the rituals of the Marutvatiya and Nishkevalya, the two verses beginning with **Kadho nu te** are the introductory hymns. It is indicated: **"How now may I serve you, knowing... these two verses." (Ashvalayana Shrauta Sutra 9.5).**

->॥ Here is the Thirteenth Verse ॥<-

O Indra, you who are <term>Aparitah</term> <note>original: "shatrubhir-aparigatah" - not surrounded or overcome by enemies</note>, you have performed all these visible and pervasive worlds and deeds through your own heroic power which is inherent in you from birth. ## Commentary (Sayana)

O <term>Shavistha</term> <note>Most powerful or most heroic</note> Indra, we have composed these new, modern songs of praise for you today. O Indra, please accept and enjoy these <term>Brahmani</term> <note>prayers</note> being performed by us. I am a wise person of good deeds, and <term>Vasoyu</term> <note>original: "dhanakāmo" - one who desires wealth</note>. I have fashioned these prayers like <term>Bhadra</term> <note>beautiful or pleasing</note> garments that are well-made, or like a craftsman builds a chariot. 

<note>Sayana explains the metaphors here: The comparison to **garments** is used because hymns are meant to be "worn" or accepted by the god, just as one accepts fine clothes. The comparison to a **chariot** is used because the hymn is the vehicle that brings the god to the sacrifice. The poet's intention is: "Accept these prayers and grant me wealth."</note>

### ३४८ ॥ Rig Veda ॥ [Book 4. Chapter 1. Section 26.]

## Hymn Text
**Where is that hero? Who has seen Indra traveling in his fine-wheeled chariot with his two bay horses? He, the wielder of the thunderbolt, seeking the one who has pressed the Soma, comes to that dwelling with protection, he who is invoked by many with wealth.** ॥ १ ॥

-> ॥ Therein, the First [Verse] ॥ <-

**Where? | That | Hero | Who? | Saw | Indra | Fine-wheeled chariot | Traveling | With two bay horses |**
**Who | With wealth | Thunderbolt-wielder | Pressed-Soma | Seeking | That | Dwelling | Comer | Invoked by many | With protection ॥ १ ॥**

---

## Commentary (Sayana)
The hymn beginning with **"Where is that hero"** <note>original: "kva sya vīra"</note> comprises fifteen verses and is the thirtieth hymn of this section. According to the <term>Anukramani</term> <note>The ancient index of Vedic hymns</note>: **"Where is that hero—Babhru is the seer, and King Rinamchaya is also praised here."** The <term>Rishi</term> <note>inspired seer/composer</note> is Babhru of the Atri clan. Since the metre is not otherwise specified, it is <term>Trishtubh</term> <note>a classic Vedic metre of 44 syllables</note>. Indra is the deity. A king named Rinamchaya is also praised in certain parts; therefore, he is also considered a deity of the hymn. In the one-day ritual called <term>Tivrasoma</term>, this hymn is used as the <term>Nivid-dhana</term> <note>a specific placement of verses within the Marutvatiya litany</note>. This is indicated in the ritual manuals: "One desiring food should use 'Where is that hero' in the Tivrasoma ritual" (Ashvalayana Shrauta Sutra 9.7).

The **Thunderbolt-wielder** <note>original: "Vajrī"</note> is Indra, who is **invoked by many**. Seeking the worshipper who has **pressed the Soma** juice, and bringing **wealth** to be given, he becomes the **comer** to **that** worshipper's **dwelling** for the sake of **protection**. Where is **that hero**, the valiant Indra? He is described as having a **fine-wheeled chariot**. This means a chariot whose axle-holes are well-crafted. Alternatively, **"Sukha"** <note>translated here as "fine" or "comfortable"</note> might mean that which "digs" or marks the ground well—referring to such a chariot. The etymologist <term>Yaska</term> notes in the <term>Nirukta</term> (3.13): "Sukha (happiness/well-being) comes from 'su-kha' (good axle-hole); 'kha' (hole) again comes from 'khan' (to dig)." **Who has seen** Indra **traveling** with his **two bay horses**, which are his specific vehicles? Who has beheld him?

---

## Hymn Text
**I have seen his station, the hidden and mighty place of the Creator; seeking him, I followed. I asked others too, and they said to me: "We, the wise leaders of men, have reached Indra."** ॥ २ ॥

-> ॥ Now the Second [Verse] ॥ <-

**Down | I saw | Station | His | Hidden | Mighty | Of the placer/creator | After | I went | Seeking |**
**I asked | Others | And | They | To me | Said | Indra | Men/Leaders | Having become wise | We reached ॥ २ ॥**

---

## Commentary (Sayana)
**I saw** <note>original: "avācacakṣaṃ"</note> the **station** or place of this Indra. What kind of place? It was **hidden** <note>original: "sasvaḥ"</note>, concealed, and **mighty** or exalted. Furthermore, **seeking** or searching for Indra, I **followed after** <note>original: "anv-āyam"</note> the station of this Indra, who is the **Creator** <note>original: "nidhātuḥ"</note> or the one who establishes all things in their place. I also **asked others**, namely other wise men on the path, about Indra. Those who were questioned **said to me**—and what they said is this: "We, the **leaders** of the sacrifices, **having become wise** <note>original: "bubudhānā"</note> and desiring to know, **have reached** <note>original: "ashema"</note> Indra." Even though Indra exists, if he is difficult to find...

[Mandala 5. Anuvaka 2. Sukta 30.] || The Fourth Book || 349

Desiring to know where he should go, [the seer] inquired about Indra’s nature. Having been told that Indra is easily accessible to those who ask, he perceived the remainder of the hymn for the purpose of attaining Indra's presence.

->॥ Now, the Third [Verse] ॥<-

## Hymn Text

**Now let us proclaim, at the pressing of the Soma, those deeds of yours, O Indra, which you have performed and which you have favored for our sake. Let the one who does not know come to know, and let the one who knows listen; this wealthy Lord, followed by all his armies, approaches.** ॥ ३ ॥

---

**Proclaim | Now | We | At the pressing | Which | Your | Deeds | Indra | Let us speak | Which | Our | Favored ॥**
**Let him know | The unknowing | Let him hear | And | The knowing | Approaches | This | Wealthy one | Followed by all armies ॥ ३ ॥**

## Commentary (Sayana)

O **Indra**, whatever **deeds** <note>original: "kṛtāni karmāṇi"</note> of yours exist, **now**, today, **we**, the chanters, while the **Soma is pressed** <note>original: "sute"</note>, **proclaim** those deeds excellently. Furthermore, **those** deeds which you **favored** <note>original: "jujoṣaḥ"</note> or performed **for our sake**, let the person who is **unknowing**—who was previously ignorant of these acts—**know** them. And let the **knowing** person **hear** them as well. Or, it may mean: let the man who knows listen and then cause the unknowing man to hear them. **This Indra**, who is **wealthy** <note>original: "maghavā"</note> and **followed by all his armies**, knowing [the devotion of the seekers], **approaches** <note>original: "vahate"</note> those who know and listen. <note>Sayana notes a grammatical shift here: "vyatyayena kartṛ-pratyayaḥ," indicating a substitution of the active verbal suffix.</note> He causes them to attain their desires.

---

->॥ Now, the Fourth [Verse] ॥<-

## Hymn Text

**O Indra, as soon as you were born, you made your mind steady. Alone, you truly go forth to battle even against many. With your might, you split open even the rock; you found the hidden herd of the cows, the dawn-rays.** ॥ ४ ॥

---

**Steady | Mind | You made | Born | Indra | You go | Truly | Alone | For battle | Many | Even ॥**
**The rock | Even | With might | You split | Open | You found | Of the cows | The enclosure | Of the dawn-rays ॥ ४ ॥**

## Commentary (Sayana)

O **Indra**, as soon as you were **born**, you **made** your **mind** <note>original: "manaḥ"</note> **steady** and unshakeable. That is to say, you resolved: "I shall conquer all the strongest enemies." Furthermore, O Indra, **alone** and without any other help, you **go** forth **for battle** even against **many** demons and foes. Moreover, with your **might**, you **split open** <note>original: "vididyutaḥ"</note> even the **rock**—the mountain that was concealing the cows. Additionally, you **found** or obtained the **enclosure** <note>original: "ūrvam"</note> of the **cows** <note>original: "ustriyāṇām"</note>, those milch-cows that yield their milk.

<note>The "rock" and "enclosure of cows" refers to the famous Vedic myth of the Vala demon, who hid the cows (often symbolizing light or wealth) in a cave, which Indra then split open to restore them to the world.</note>

## || Rig Veda || [Book 4. Chapter 1. Varga 27.]

## Hymn Text

-> ॥ Now, the Fifth [Verse] ॥ <-

**When you, O Indra, the most excellent, were born in the highest beyond, bearing a name that is far-famed even in the distance—from that very moment the gods were struck with fear of you. Indra conquered all the waters that were held captive by the Dasa.** ॥ ५ ॥

-> Word-for-Word Breakdown <-

**Beyond | When | You | Highest | Were born | In the distance | Worthy of being heard | Name | Bearing |
From that | Indeed | Indra | Feared | The gods | All | Waters | Conquered | Having the Dasa as their master ॥ ५ ॥**

## Commentary (Sayana)

When, O **Indra**, being **beyond** <note>original: "paraḥ"</note>—situated in the region above—you, the **highest** <note>original: "paramaḥ"</note> or most excellent, **were born** <note>original: "ājaniṣṭhāḥ"</note> from all sides, **bearing** or holding a **name** <note>original: "nāma"</note> that is **worthy of being heard** <note>original: "śrutyaṃ"</note> even in a **far-off distance** <note>original: "parāvati"</note>... <note>The rest of the verse is spoken in the third person.</note> **From that** moment onward, the **gods** <note>original: "devāḥ"</note>—the shining ones like Agni and others—**feared** <note>original: "abhayanta"</note> Indra. **Indra conquered** and brought under his control **all the waters**. What kind of waters? Those **having the Dasa as their master** <note>original: "dāsapatnīḥ"</note>, meaning those waters of which the Dasa Vritra was the lord or protector.

---
-> ॥ This concludes the twenty-sixth Varga of the first [chapter] of the fourth [Ashtaka] ॥ <note>A Varga is a small subsection of the Vedic text, used for recitation and study.</note>

## Hymn Text

-> ॥ Now, the Sixth [Verse] ॥ <-

**For you alone, these Maruts, who bring delightful joy, chant the sacred hymn and press the Soma-nectar. Indra, through his wondrous powers, has overcome the serpent who was harassing the gods and lying across the waters—the wily one.** ॥ ६ ॥

-> Word-for-Word Breakdown <-

**For you | Indeed | These | Maruts | Bringing joy | Chant | The hymn | Press | The nectar |
The serpent | Harassing | The waters | Lying across | Forth | With powers | The wily one | Overcame | Indra ॥ ६ ॥**

## Commentary (Sayana)

**These Maruts**. They are called **Maruts** <note>original: "marutaḥ"</note> because they "run and speak greatly"—these are the praisers. They are **bringers of joy** <note>original: "suśevāḥ"</note>; being "possessors of beautiful happiness," meaning they produce excellent happiness through their songs of praise. O Indra, **for you alone** they **chant** the **hymn** <note>original: "arkam"</note>—the song worthy of being honored. They perform the praise. They **press** the **nectar** <note>original: "andhaḥ"</note>, which refers to the food that is the Soma-juice; they perform the extraction. **Indra**, who is possessed of supreme sovereignty, **overcame** <note>original: "prasakṣat"</note> the **serpent** <note>original: "ahim"</note> Vritra with his own **powers** <term>Maya: creative, miraculous, or illusory power</term>. What kind of serpent? One who was **harassing** <note>original: "ohānam"</note> or obstructing the gods, who was **lying across** the **waters**, covering them, and who was **wily** <note>original: "māyinam"</note> or full of deceit.

## Hymn Text

-> ॥ Now, the Seventh [Verse] ॥ <-

**O Bounteous Lord, scattering the enemies from your very birth, and desiring the cows, you moved with speed. You struck off the head of the Dasa Namuchi when you wished to make a path for Manu.** ॥ ७ ॥

## Hymn Text

**[Verse 7 - Word-for-Word Breakdown]**

-> || Now, the Eighth [Verse] || <-

**For you made me your companion, O Indra, even as you were crushing the head of the servant Namuchi; while the whizzing stone was turning, Heaven and Earth were propelled by the Maruts like two wheels.** ॥ ८ ॥

**Word-for-Word Breakdown:**
**Companion | For | Me | You made | Then | Indeed | O Indra | The head | Of the servant | Of Namuchi | Crushing | The stone | Even | Whizzing | Turning | Forth | Like two wheels | Heaven and Earth | With the Maruts** ॥ ८ ॥

-> || Now, the Ninth [Verse] || <-

**The servant made women his weapons; what can his powerless armies do to me? For he <note>Indra</note> perceived his two "milch-cows" <note>likely meaning Namuchi's sustaining sources or wives</note> within; then Indra went forth to do battle with the Dasyu.** ॥ ९ ॥

**Word-for-Word Breakdown:**
**Women | For | The servant | Weapons | Made | What | To me | Can they do | Powerless | His | Armies | Within | For | He perceived | Both | His | Two milch-cows | Then | Near | Forth | He went | For battle | The Dasyu | Indra** ॥ ९ ॥

## Commentary (Sayana)

**[Verse 7]**
O **Generous One** <note>original: "maghavan"</note>—O wealthy Indra—**being well-praised** <note>original: "saṃcakānaḥ"</note> by us... <note>The word "saṃcakānaḥ" comes from the root 'kā' meaning 'to sound' or 'to praise' with the prefix 'sam'.</note> ...**driving away** or destroying the **gift-obstructer** <note>original: "dānam"</note>—the demon Vritra who hinders the gods—**with the thunderbolt** <note>original: "gavā"</note> <note>literally "with the cow," but interpreted here as the weapon made of bone or the "shining one"</note>, you **thoroughly struck** <note>original: "su vyahan"</note> the **enemies** <note>original: "mṛdhaḥ"</note>—the demons and followers of Vritra—**from birth** <note>original: "januṣā"</note>. This means Indra’s enemies existed from the very moment of his birth. O Indra, in this battle, **desiring** a **path** <note>original: "gātum"</note> or happiness **for Manu** <note>original: "manave"</note>—referring to me <note>the seer</note> whose cattle were stolen by Namuchi—**when you turned** or crushed the **head** <note>original: "śiraḥ"</note> belonging to the demon named **Namuchi** <note>original: "namuceḥ"</note>, the "Oppressor," then you destroyed all enemies. This connects to the previous statement.

**[Verse 8]**
O Indra, while you were **crushing** or pulverizing the **head** of the **servant** <note>original: "dāsasya"</note> Namuchi, the demon, while the **whizzing** <note>original: "svaryam"</note> or sounding **stone** <note>original: "aśmānam"</note>—which was **turning** or spinning like a cloud—**then indeed** <note>original: "ādit"</note> immediately after, you **made me** your **companion** <note>original: "yujam"</note> or friend. You truly did this. At that time, with the **Maruts** <note>original: "marudbhiḥ"</note>—the storm gods—as your helpers, **Heaven and Earth** <note>original: "rodasī"</note> **were** like **two wheels** <note>original: "cakriye-iva"</note> propelled forward. <note>Since an adverbial prefix is used without a verb, the appropriate action "were propelled" is understood.</note>

**[Verse 9]**
The **servant** Namuchi, the oppressor demon, **made women** <note>original: "striyaḥ"</note> his **weapons** <note>original: "āyudhāni"</note> or instruments of war. He sent them forth to fight against Indra. [Indra thought:] "What can **his**—this demon's—**powerless** <note>original: "abalāḥ"</note> **armies** do to me?" For Indra **perceived** <note>original: "akhyat"</note> or saw **both** of **his**—the demon's—**milch-cows** <note>original: "dhene"</note> <note>referring to two sources of strength, perhaps streams or wives</note> hidden **within**. Then **Indra** **went forth** to **battle** with the **Dasyu** <note>original: "dasyum"</note> or the destructive demon.

<vocab>
**Indra**: The king of the gods and deity of storms.
**Maghavan**: A title for Indra meaning "The Generous" or "Possessor of Wealth."
**Namuchi**: A specific demon (*asura*) known for being difficult to kill.
**Asura**: A powerful, often chaotic or demonic being in Vedic mythology.
**Marut**: The storm-deities who are the companions and warriors of Indra.
**Rodasi**: A dual term referring to the union of Heaven and Earth.
**Vajra**: Indra’s primary weapon, the thunderbolt.
**Vritra**: The "Obstructor," the great serpent-demon of drought.
**Ayudha**: A weapon or tool used in battle.
**Dasyu**: A class of beings seen as enemies of the gods and of the ritual order.
</vocab>

## Commentary (Sayana)

[Ending of commentary for Verse 9]
Thinking, "What can these weak, female-formed armies do to me?" Indra perceived within the house both of this demon’s <term>Dasyu<note>A term used in the Vedas for enemies of the gods or those who do not perform the Vedic sacrifices; often identified with demons or hostile tribes.</note></term> pleasing and beautiful wives. He surely confined them within the residence. Immediately after this, Indra went forth to do battle with the demon Namuchi.

## Hymn Text

-> ॥ Now, the Tenth [Verse] ॥ <-

**When the cows were separated here and there from their calves, they lowed together; Indra joined them back together through his powers when the well-pressed Somas exhilarated him.** ॥ १० ॥

**Word-for-Word Breakdown:**
**Together | They lowed | Here and there | With calves | Separated | When | They were | Together | Those | Indra | Joined | Of this [sage] | By powers | When | Him | Somas | Well-pressed | They exhilarated** ॥ १० ॥

## Commentary (Sayana)

When the cows were separated or detached from their calves—at this time, the cows that had been stolen from all sides by Namuchi lowed together <note>original: "samanvanta"</note> in various places. When the Somas—which were excellently pressed by the sage named Babhru—exhilarated <note>original: "amamandan"</note> this Indra, then Indra, accompanied by the powerful Maruts <note>storm deities who assist Indra</note>, joined those cows belonging to Babhru (which had been stolen by Namuchi) back with their calves.

## Hymn Text

-> ॥ Now, the Eleventh [Verse] ॥ <-

**When the Somas pressed by Babhru exhilarated him, the Bull roared loudly in the dwellings; the Fort-Destroyer, Indra, having drunk of this, gave back the milk-yielding cows.** ॥ ११ ॥

**Word-for-Word Breakdown:**
**When | Him | Somas | Pressed by Babhru | Exhilarated | He roared loudly | The Bull | In the dwellings | The Fort-Destroyer | Having drunk | Indra | Of this | Back | Of the cows | He gave | Of the milk-yielding ones** ॥ ११ ॥

## Commentary (Sayana)

When the Somas pressed by the sage Babhru exhilarated this Indra, then the Bull—the showerer of desires, Indra—roared loudly <note>original: "aroraravīt"</note> in the midst of the battles. The Fort-Destroyer <note>original: "puramdaraḥ", a title for Indra as the breaker of enemy strongholds</note>, Indra, having drunk this Soma, gave back the cows that pour out milk <note>original: "usriyāṇām"</note>. He gave them back to the sage Babhru.

## Hymn Text

**Word-for-Word Breakdown (Verse 12):**
**Auspicious | this | the Rushamas | O Agni | they did | of cows | four | giving | thousands | of Rinamchaya | presented | gifts | we have accepted | of the best of leaders | of men** ॥ १२ ॥

---

-> ॥ Now, the Thirteenth [Verse] ॥ <-

**The Rushamas, O Agni, send me to my home well-adorned, along with thousands of cows; the strong, pressed Soma juices exhilarated Indra at the dawning of the encompassing night.** ॥ १३ ॥

**Word-for-Word Breakdown:**
**Well-adorned | me | the traveler/poet | they send | home | of cows | with thousands | the Rushamas | O Agni | strong | Indra | they exhilarated | the pressed [Somas] | of the night | at the dawning | of the encompassing [night]** ॥ १३ ॥

---

-> ॥ Now, the Fourteenth [Verse] ॥ <-

**That encompassing night dawned for King Rinamchaya of the Rushamas; like a swift, spirited horse being urged on, four thousand brown [cows] were gained.** ॥ १४ ॥

**Word-for-Word Breakdown:**
**It dawned | that | night | encompassing | which | for Rinamchaya | for the King | of the Rushamas | horse | like | spirited | swift | being urged | brown | four | he gained | thousands** ॥ १४ ॥

---

## Commentary (Sayana)

<term>Rushama<note>A historical tribe or region mentioned in the Rig Veda, known for their association with King Rinamchaya.</note></term> refers to a specific region or people. Here, the word Rushamas refers to the people living there. The Rushamas, who are the servants of the King named <term>Rinamchaya<note>Literally "One who removes or collects debts"; here, the name of a generous royal patron.</note></term>, O Agni, have performed this auspicious and beneficial act. In what manner? By giving me four—that is, the number four—thousand cows. The meaning is that although the wealth is given by the King, it is the royal officers who actually deliver the gift. Among the leaders of men, from the most excellent leader King Rinamchaya, we have accepted <note>original: "prati agrabheshma"</note> these presented gifts of wealth in the form of cattle. The plural "we" is used as a mark of honor for the speaker.

O Agni, the Rushamas—the servants of Rinamchaya—send me <note>the poet Babhru</note> back to my home <note>original: "astam"</note> well-adorned, refined with ornaments and clothing, and accompanied by thousands of cows. Immediately following this, the strong and flavorful Soma juices, pressed by me after I had obtained such great wealth, exhilarated Indra at the flushing or dawning of the night. The term <term>paritakmyā<note>From 'pari' (around) and 'tak' (to rush or move); interpreted by Sayana as the night that moves or covers all beings in darkness.</note></term> refers to the night, because it moves around or encompasses all beings with darkness. At the "dawning" <note>original: "vyuṣṭau"</note> of that night means at the time of dawn. The Somas made Indra joyful. The implication is that immediately after receiving the cows, the poet performed a sacrifice to Indra with Soma juices.

## Hymn Text

**We have received, O Agni, four thousand cattle from the Rushamas; we sages have accepted the vessel which was heated for the sacrifice, made of metal.** ॥ १५ ॥

**Four-thousand | of cattle | animals | in return | we have received | among the Rushamas | O Agni | the heat-vessel (Gharma) | indeed | heated | for the ritual | which | was | made of metal | that | indeed | we took | sages.** ॥ १५ ॥

## Commentary (Sayana)

O **Agni**, we have received **four thousand** of the **cattle**—referring here to the animal species in general—among the people known as the **Rushamas**. For the sake of the **sacrifice** <note>original: pravrije; the Pravargya ceremony</note>, the **heated**, beautiful-colored **heat-vessel** <note>original: gharma; the Mahavira pot used to offer hot milk</note> which was **made of metal** <note>original: ayasmayaḥ; Sayana interprets this as "made of gold" in a ritual context</note>, that vessel for milking we **sages**, the wise ones, have **taken** from the Rushamas.

## Critical Notes

The seventeenth hymn, beginning with **"Indra for the chariot"** (*Indro rathāya*), contains thirteen verses. The <term>Rishi<note>The inspired poet or seer to whom the hymn was revealed.</note></term> is Avasyu Atreya. The meter is Trishtubh. The deity is Indra. However, for the lines "And may you both come" and "When he indeed," the deities are optionally Kutsa and Ushanas. In the verse "Indra and Kutsa being carried," the deities are both Indra and Kutsa. This is according to the Index (*Anukramani*): "Indra for the chariot, thirteen verses, Avasyu; the lines beginning 'And may you both' are for Kutsa and Ushanas, or the whole verse is for Indra and Kutsa." The ritual application of these verses is determined by their specific content.

->॥ In that hymn, the first [verse] ॥<-

## Hymn Text

**Indra makes a downward path for the chariot which the Generous One has mounted, seeking plunder. Like a cowherd [separating] the herds of cattle, he, the unharmed guardian, goes first, desiring to win [wealth].** ॥ १ ॥

**Word-for-Word Breakdown:**
**Indra | for the chariot | a downward path | makes | which | he mounted | the Generous One (Maghavan) | seeking plunder | herds | like | of cattle | away | he drives/separates | the guardian | unharmed | he goes | first | desiring to win.** ॥ १ ॥

<meta>This page continues the commentary on the 31st Hymn of the 5th Book (Mandala) of the Rig Veda. The previous page discussed the arrival of Indra on his chariot. This page completes the first verse's commentary and provides the full text and explanation for the second and third verses, focusing on Indra's role as a provider of wives, wealth, and light.</meta>

## Commentary (Sayana)
[Continuation of commentary on Verse 1]

The <term>bountiful<note>original: Maghavā; referring to Indra as the possessor and bestower of great wealth</note></term> Indra, desiring food for the one who desires it, makes a downward path for the chariot he stands upon. Furthermore, just as a **shepherd** <note>original: gopāḥ</note> drives herds of cattle, he drives away the armies of the enemy. Being **unharmed**—meaning he himself is not injured by enemies—the **foremost** of the gods, the chief Indra, **moves** forward, desiring the wealth of his foes.

---

## Hymn Text
-> ॥ Now, the Second [Verse] ॥ <-

**Run toward us, O Lord of the Bay Horses! Do not turn away from us. O Giver of tawny wealth, be favorable to us. Indeed, O Indra, there is nothing better than you; you make even the wifeless to have wives.** ॥ २ ॥

**[Word-for-Word Breakdown]**
**Toward | forward | run | O Lord of the Bay Horses | not | turn away | O Giver of tawny wealth | toward | us | be favorable | for not | than you | O Indra | better | other | is | the wifeless | even | those with wives | you make.** ॥ २ ॥

## Commentary (Sayana)

O **Lord of the Bay Horses**, Indra, you must **run toward** us; go toward us with great speed. But **do not turn away** from us. The root *venati* refers to the act of desiring or loving; do not be without desire for us. Furthermore, O **Giver of tawny wealth** <note>original: Piśaṅgarāte; referring to gold or the reddish-brown color of cattle</note>, O Indra of manifold riches, **be favorable** to us; serve us. Additionally, O Indra, **there is nothing** else **better** or more beneficial **than you**. There is no other collection of wealth that exists. You **make** even the **wifeless**—those who have no women—to be **possessors of wives**.

---

## Hymn Text
-> ॥ Now, the Third [Verse] ॥ <-

**When the Might was born from Might, Indra assigned all the powers. He urged forward the easy-milking cows from within the enclosure; with light, he rolled away the covering darkness.** ॥ ३ ॥

**[Word-for-Word Breakdown]**
**Up | when | Might | from Might | toward | was born | he assigns | Indra | powers/wealth | all | forward | he urged | the easy-milking cows | the enclosure | within | away | with light | he rolled | darkness | covering.** ॥ ३ ॥

## Commentary (Sayana)

Alternatively, when the **Might** <note>original: sahaḥ; the power associated with the sun's brilliance</note> belonging to the sun **was born** from the **might** of the dawn—appearing above it—then Indra **assigns all powers**—that is, all forms of wealth—to the sacrificers. The word "power" <note>original: indriyāṇi</note> is here a name for wealth. He **urged forward** the **easy-milking cows** who were forcefully confined **within** the **enclosure** <note>original: vavre; the mountain or cave where the cows were hidden</note>. **With** his **light**, he **rolled away** or removed the **covering darkness** that had enveloped everything.

## Hymn Text

-> ॥ Now, the Fourth [Verse] ॥ <-

**The Anus fashioned your chariot for the horse; Tvashtṛ, O Much-invoked, fashioned your brilliant thunderbolt. The priests, magnifying Indra with songs, strengthened him for the slaying of the serpent.** ॥ ४ ॥

**Pada-patha:**
The Anus | your | chariot | for the horse | fashioned | Tvashtṛ | thunderbolt | O Much-invoked | brilliant | the priests | Indra | magnifying | with songs | strengthened | for the serpent | for slaying | indeed. ॥ ४ ॥

---

## Commentary (Sayana)

O <term>Much-invoked<note>original: puruhūta; an epithet for Indra as he who is called upon by many worshippers</note></term> Indra, the **Anus**—meaning either men or the <term>Ribhus<note>a group of three brothers who were mortal artisans elevated to divinity for their skill</note></term>—**fashioned** your **chariot**, which is perfectly suited for your horses. Furthermore, **Tvashtṛ** <note>the divine architect and smith of the gods</note> made your **thunderbolt** <note>original: vajra</note> **brilliant** and shining. Also, the <term>priests<note>original: brahmāṇaḥ; here referring to the Angirases or the mighty Maruts who serve as Indra's companions</note></term>, worshiping and honoring Indra, **strengthened** him with **songs** of praise <note>original: arkaiḥ</note> so that he might be empowered for the **slaying** of the **serpent** <note>original: ahaye; referring to Vritra, the demon of drought who obstructs the waters</note>.

---

## Hymn Text

-> ॥ Now, the Fifth [Verse] ॥ <-

**When the showers of praise for the Showerer, O Indra, the pressing stones and the Boundless were in harmony, then the unhorsed and chariotless ones, sent by Indra, overcame the enemies.** ॥ ५ ॥

**Pada-patha:**
For the Showerer | when | your | the showers | song | offered | Indra | pressing stones | Boundless | in harmony | unhorsed | who | wheels | chariotless | sent by Indra | against | turned | the enemies. ॥ ५ ॥

---

## Commentary (Sayana)

O **Indra**, when the <term>showers<note>original: vṛṣaṇaḥ; a play on words where the Maruts are "showering" praise upon Indra, the "Showerer" of blessings</note></term>, the Maruts, **offered** a **song** of praise to **you**, the **Showerer** of all desires, then the <term>pressing stones<note>original: grāvāṇaḥ; the stones used to crush the Soma plant</note></term> and <term>the Boundless<note>original: aditiḥ; interpreted here as the "invincible" or "unbroken" stones</note></term> became **harmonious** and joined together in the ritual. The **unhorsed** and **chariotless** <term>shining ones<note>original: pavayaḥ; referring to the Maruts who move with purifying speed</note></term>, having been **sent by Indra**, **overcame** the **enemies** <note>original: dasyūn; the demonic forces or human foes</note>, turning against them and subduing them.

-> ॥ This ends the twenty-ninth Varga of the first Adhyaya of the fourth [Ashtaka] ॥ <-

---

## Hymn Text

-> ॥ Now, the Sixth [Verse] ॥ <-

**I proclaim your ancient deeds, O Bountiful One, and the new ones you have done. O Mighty One, you who sustain both Heaven and Earth, winning the waters for Manu, wondrous with gifts.** ॥ ६ ॥

**Pada-patha:**
Forth | your | ancient | deeds | I proclaim | forth | new | O Bountiful One | which | you have done | O Mighty One | when | you sustain | Heaven and Earth | both | winning | the waters | for Manu | wondrous with gifts. ॥ ६ ॥

<vocab>
- **Much-invoked** (puruhūta): One who is called upon by many; a primary title of Indra.
- **Ribhus** (ṛbhavaḥ): Divine artisans known for their craftsmanship, specifically for Indra's chariot.
- **Tvashtṛ** (tvaṣṭā): The divine architect/smith who forged the thunderbolt.
- **Thunderbolt** (vajram): Indra's primary weapon, symbolizing the lightning bolt.
- **Songs** (arkaiḥ): Hymns or chants that possess the power to increase the strength of the gods.
- **Maruts** (marutaḥ): The storm gods and companions of Indra, often described as a youthful, militant band.
- **Pressing stones** (grāvāṇaḥ): Large stones used in the Vedic sacrifice to press the juice from the Soma stalks.
- **Enemies** (dasyu): Those who do not sacrifice or follow the cosmic law; often depicted as dark, chaotic forces.
- **Bountiful One** (maghavan): A common name for Indra as the generous dispenser of rewards.
- **Heaven and Earth** (rodasī): The dual world-halves, often described as parents or a vessel sustained by Indra.
</vocab>

<summary>This page describes how divine and human agents collaborate to empower Indra, featuring the crafting of his chariot and thunderbolt, and his victory over the Dasyus supported by the Maruts. It emphasizes the power of hymns and sacrificial ritual to sustain the god's strength and his role as the protector of Manu (humanity).</summary>

<keywords>Indra, Maruts, Tvashtr, Ribhus, Vajra, Dasyu, Soma sacrifice, Vedic ritual, Heaven and Earth, Manu</keywords>

## Commentary (Sayana) - Continued from previous page

O Indra, I proclaim <note>original: pravochaṃ</note> your ancient <note>original: pūrvāṇi</note> deeds <note>original: karmāṇi</note>. I proclaim your new <note>original: nūtanā</note> deeds. O Maghavan <note>the "Bountiful One," a common title for Indra</note>, the meaning is: I proclaim those deeds which you have performed. O Powerful One <note>original: śaktīvaḥ</note>, you who possess power <note>shakti, which can refer to his thunderbolt or his sacrificial activity</note>; you who, while conquering and subduing both heaven and earth <note>original: rodasi</note>, bear <note>original: vibharāḥ</note> and distribute the waters for **Manu** <note>the progenitor of the human race</note>. What is the nature of these waters? They are of varied brightness <note>original: dānu-citrāḥ</note> and gleaming.

---

## Hymn Text
-> ॥ Now, the Seventh [Verse] ॥ <-

**O Sage, that is indeed your deed, when you, O Skillful one, struck the Serpent and manifested your strength. You seized the illusions of Shushna, and as you approached the battle, you drove away the Dasyus.** ॥ ७ ॥

**That | indeed | now | your | deed | O Skillful one | O Sage | the serpent | when | slaying | strength | you | manifested | of Shushna | even | around | illusions | you seized | the approach | going | away | the Dasyus | you drove.** ॥ ७ ॥

## Commentary (Sayana)
O Skillful One <note>original: dasma; one who is beautiful or worthy of being seen</note>, O wise and learned Indra, in this world, while slaying or destroying the serpent <note>original: ahi; the demon Vritra who blocks the rain</note>, the strength <note>original: ojaḥ</note> and power you manifested <note>original: amimīthāḥ</note> is truly your own great deed <note>original: karaṇam</note>. Furthermore, you seized <note>original: paryagṛbhṇāḥ</note> the illusions <note>original: māyāḥ; the magical or deceptive powers</note> belonging to the demon named **Shushna**. O Indra, as you reached the battle <note>original: prapitvam</note> or came near to the enemy, you drove away <note>original: apāsedhaḥ</note> or repelled the **Dasyus** <note>the enemies of the divine order, often depicted as demons or lawless tribes</note>.

---

## Hymn Text
-> ॥ Now, the Eighth [Verse] ॥ <-

**O Indra, for the sake of Yadu and Turvasha, you caused the waters, which yield like good milch-cows, to rest on the far bank. You brought the powerful Kutsa, and you struck down Shushna; when the gods and Ushana joined you both.** ॥ ८ ॥

**You | the waters | for Yadu | for Turvasha | caused to rest | yielding well | the bank | Indra | powerful | un-traversed | you brought | indeed | Kutsa | together | indeed | when | you both | Ushana | joined | the gods.** ॥ ८ ॥

## Commentary (Sayana)
O Indra, on the far bank <note>original: pāre</note> of the rivers—having become great—you caused the waters <note>original: apaḥ</note>, which yield well <note>original: sudughāḥ; literally "milking well," providing for plants and trees</note>, to rest <note>original: aramayaḥ</note> or settle for the sake of the king named **Yadu** and the king named **Turvasha**. O Indra, you and **Kutsa** <note>a human protégé of Indra</note> together encountered the fierce and unyielding Shushna. Then, having slain Shushna, you brought <note>original: avahaḥ</note> Kutsa back to his home. Alternatively, **Ushana**—the descendant of Bhrigu—and the other **gods** <note>original: devāḥ</note> joined <note>original: samarenta</note> or united with both of you, Indra and Kutsa.

## Hymn Text

-> ॥ Now, the Ninth [Verse] ॥ <-

**May the swift horses carry Indra and Kutsa, riding together in their chariot, even to the ear [of the worshiper]. May you two blow away the demon Shushna from his dwelling and remove the darkness from the heart of the generous giver.** ॥ ९ ॥

-> Padapatha (Word-for-Word Break) <-

**Indra and Kutsa | being carried | by chariot | towards | you two | horses | even | in the ear | may they carry | out | him | down | you two blow | out | from the common dwelling | of the generous giver | from the heart | you two ward off | darkness.** ॥ ९ ॥

---

## Commentary (Sayana)

O **Indra and Kutsa** <note>original: indrākutsā; a dual invocation of the god Indra and the royal sage Kutsa, who are often depicted riding together</note>, who are being **carried** in a chariot, may your **horses** <note>original: atyāḥ; literally "the swift ones"</note> **carry** you **even to the ear**—meaning to the side of the listener or the sacrificer who performs the hymns. Furthermore, may you two **blow away** <note>original: nirdhamathaḥ</note> **this** <note>original: sīm</note> demon **Shushna** <note>original: śuṣṇāsura; a demon of drought whose name means "the dryer"</note> who has entered **down** into the waters. You must drive him **out from his own place**. You two **ward off** the **darkness** of ignorance and the resulting sins from the **heart** of the **generous giver** <note>original: maghona; the patron or sacrificer who provides the offerings</note>.

---

## Hymn Text

-> ॥ Now, the Tenth [Verse] ॥ <-

**The wise seeker of help reached the horses, well-yoked and swift as the wind. Here, O Indra, all your friends, the Maruts, have increased your strength with their sacred prayers.** ॥ १० ॥

-> Padapatha (Word-for-Word Break) <-

**Of the wind | yoked | well-yoked | indeed | horses | the wise one | indeed | this one | reached | seeking help | all | your | here | Maruts | friends | O Indra | sacred prayers | strength | they increased.** ॥ १० ॥

---

## Commentary (Sayana)

**The wise one** <note>original: kaviścit</note> named Avatsyu, who is the seer of this mantra and **seeker of help**, **reached** the **horses** which are **yoked** with the speed of **the wind** and are **well-yoked** <note>easy to control or harness</note>. O **Indra**, **all** of your **friends**, the many **Maruts** <note>storm deities who accompany Indra into battle</note> who are also the praisers, **have increased** your **strength** <note>original: taviṣīm</note> in this world through their **sacred prayers** <note>original: brahmāṇi; hymns or spiritual formulas</note>.

-> ॥ Thus ends the thirtieth section (Varga) of the first chapter (Adhyaya) of the fourth Book (Ashtaka) ॥ <-

---

## Hymn Text

-> ॥ Now, the Eleventh [Verse] ॥ <-

**He made the Sun's chariot, which was behind and struggling, go in front during the race. Etasha bears the wheel; he completes the work, and placing us in the lead, he will grant us wisdom.** ॥ ११ ॥

-> Padapatha (Word-for-Word Break) <-

**The Sun | indeed | chariot | in the race | in front | he made | behind | struggling | he bears | the wheel | Etasha | together | he completes | in front | placing | he will grant | wisdom | to us.** ॥ ११ ॥

### Mandala 5, Chapter 2, Hymn 31 | Fourth Book | Page 359

## Commentary (Sayana) — Verse 11 (Conclusion)

**Indra** is in the *paritakmyā* <note>original: paritakmyāyāṃ; often interpreted as a night journey or a decisive battle</note>, meaning in the **battle**. A battle is called *paritakmyā* because "fear goes all around it." Together with the sage named **Etasha**, Indra made the fast-moving **chariot** belonging even to the **Sun** become **still**—that is, he brought its movement to an end. He did this for the sake of Etasha. <note>The grammar shows a change in case endings here.</note> **Indra** took **one wheel** from the chariot of the Sun. With **that wheel**, he **strikes down** or destroys the demons. Furthermore, **placing us at the front**—meaning honoring us—may he **participate in** and bless **our sacrifice**.

---

## Hymn Text — Verse 12

-> ॥ Now, the Twelfth Verse ॥ <-

**O people, this Indra has come to see you, seeking his friend who has pressed the Soma juice. The pressing stone, speaking aloud, rests upon the altar, where the Adhvaryu priests move with speed.** ॥ १२ ॥

**Word-for-Word Break (Pada-patha):**
Towards | this | O people | to see | has come | Indra | friend | who has pressed Soma | desiring | speaking | pressing stone | down | altar | rests upon | whose | quick | Adhvaryu priests | move. ॥ १२ ॥

## Commentary (Sayana) — Verse 12

O **people**, this **Indra** has **come** here **to see** you. He comes **desiring** or seeking the **sacrificer** <note>original: yajamānam</note> who is his **friend** and who has **pressed the Soma** <note>original: sutasomam; Soma is a sacred ritual drink</note> for him. The **pressing stone** <note>original: grāvā; the stone used to crush the Soma stalks</note> makes a **sound** and **rests upon the altar**. It is the stone for which the **Adhvaryu priests** <note>term: Adhvaryu; the priests responsible for the physical movements and manual duties of the ritual</note> **move** with **speed** <note>original: jīram; meaning quickness or impulse</note> to perform the pressing.

---

## Hymn Text — Verse 13

-> ॥ Now, the Thirteenth Verse ॥ <-

**O Immortal One, those mortals who have truly longed for you—let them not encounter evil. Support the sacrificers and grant strength to those people among whom we may be yours.** ॥ १३ ॥

**Word-for-Word Break (Pada-patha):**
Those | have longed for | have longed for | indeed | those | mortals | O Immortal | not | those | evil | towards | encounter | support | the sacrificers | and | in them | place | strength | in people | in whom | we | may be. ॥ १३ ॥

## Commentary (Sayana) — Verse 13

O **Indra**, those **mortals** <note>original: martāḥ; human beings subject to death</note> who, for the sake of wealth, **have longed for** you—and let them **quickly** long for you again—O **Immortal** <note>original: amṛta; one who does not die</note> Indra, let **those people** **not encounter** or fall into **evil** <note>original: aṃhaḥ; meaning sin, distress, or calamity</note>. <note>The phrase "mo" is a combination of particles used here to mean "not."</note> **And** also, **support** or favor **the sacrificers**. O Indra, **place strength** and power **among those people** in whose midst we, the singers, **may be yours** <note>that is, we wish to be counted as your own devotees</note>.

-> ॥ Thus ends the twenty-first section (Varga) of the first chapter (Adhyaya) of the fourth book (Ashtaka) ॥ <-

<summary>This page concludes a hymn to Indra, describing his mythological feat of taking a wheel from the Sun's chariot to assist the sage Etasha and his arrival at the ritual ground to reward the Soma-pressers.</summary>
<keywords>Indra, Etasha, Sun's chariot, Soma, Adhvaryu priests, pressing stones, immortality, strength, protection from evil</keywords>

### 360 || Rig Veda || Mandala 4, Anuvaka 1, Varga 32

The 18th hymn, consisting of twelve verses, begins with the phrase "He split" <note>original: ardardṛt</note>. The **Rishi** <term>Rishi: a divinely inspired poet or seer to whom the Vedic hymns were revealed</term> is named **Gātu**. The **metre** is **Trishtubh** <note>a Vedic meter of 4 lines with 11 syllables each</note>. The **deity** addressed is **Indra**. As stated in the *Anukramani* <note>a traditional index of the Rig Veda</note>: "He split, twelve, Gatu." The ritual application (vinyoga) has been explained previously.

---

## Hymn Text

-> ॥ Now, the First Verse ॥ <-
**You split the spring and released the openings; you set free the water-bearing clouds that were held bound. O Indra, when you opened the great mountain, you released the streams and struck down the son of Danu.** ॥ १ ॥

**Word-for-Word Break (Pada-patha):**
Split | the spring | released | [prefix] | openings | you | water-bearing [clouds] | held-bound | set free.
The great | O Indra | mountain | [prefix] | when | open | you | released | [prefix] | streams | [prefix] | the son of Danu | struck. ॥ १ ॥

---

## Commentary (Sayana)

O **Indra**, you **split** the **spring**—meaning the cloud that trickles with water. After that, you **released** the **openings**, which are the exit points for the waters of the cloud. Furthermore, you **set free** or let flow the **water-bearing clouds** that were **held bound** or obstructed. <note>The commentator notes that the verb *ramṇāti* here signifies the act of releasing or making flow.</note> O Indra, you **opened** the **great** and vast **mountain** (the cloud) and **released** the **streams** of water. Moreover, you **struck down** the **son of Danu** <note>original: dānava; referring to the demon Vritra</note>, who is the demon Vritra, or the cloud that gives water. 

In this context, the **Nirukta** <term>Nirukta: Yaska's ancient treatise on etymology and the meaning of Vedic words</term> states: "He split the spring. A spring (*utsa*) is called so because it 'sits up' (*utsadanāt*), 'flows up' (*utsandanāt*), or 'moistens' (*unnattervā*). You released its openings, you released the water-bearing ones..." (Nirukta 10.9).

---

## Hymn Text

-> ॥ Now, the Second Verse ॥ <-
**O wielder of the thunderbolt, you released the springs that were bound during the seasons; you moved the udder of the mountain. Having struck the serpent that was lying extended, O Indra, you took up your great might.** ॥ २ ॥

**Word-for-Word Break (Pada-patha):**
You | the springs | according to seasons | held-bound | moved | the udder | of the mountain | O wielder of the thunderbolt.
The serpent | even | [particle] | extended | lying | having struck | O Indra | might | you took up. ॥ २ ॥

---

## Commentary (Sayana)

O **wielder of the thunderbolt**, O **Indra**, during the **seasons** <note>specifically the rainy seasons</note>, you released the **springs** (the clouds) that were being **held bound** or obstructed. <note>The commentary implies the completion of the thought: "you freed them from their bonds."</note> Furthermore, you **moved** the **udder**—referring to the strength or the water—of the **mountain** (the cloud). O Indra, you of soaring power, you **struck** the **serpent** <note>original: ahi; the dragon/serpent Vritra</note> who was **lying** down, **extended** in the waters. O Indra, you then **took up** or held your **might** (strength). This means that after the slaying of Vritra, Indra's fame became known throughout the world.

<summary>This page contains the opening of Hymn 18 of the 4th Mandala, where Indra is praised for splitting the clouds (metaphorically called mountains or springs) and slaying the serpent Vritra to release the waters. Sayana provides etymological support from the Nirukta to explain the celestial nature of these "springs" and "mountains."</summary>

<keywords>Indra, Vritra, Gatu, Trishtubh, cloud metaphors, Vala, Nirukta, Vedic sacrifice, rain deity, Danava, Ahi</keywords>

## 361 || Rig Veda || Mandala 5, Anuvaka 2, Sukta 32

## Hymn Text

-> ॥ Now, the Third Verse ॥ <-

**With his mighty powers, Indra struck the weapon of that great, wild beast; he, who alone considered himself without a rival, was then surpassed by another more powerful than himself.** ॥ ३ ॥

**Word-for-Word Break (Pada-patha):**
That | indeed | great | [prefix] | wild beast | weapon | struck | with powers | Indra |
who | alone | indeed | without rival | considering | then | from him | another | was born | more powerful. ॥ ३ ॥

---

## Commentary (Sayana)

[Indra] struck out the weapon with speed and strength through Vritra. From the body of Vritra, another great demon appeared. After killing Vritra first, Indra then killed the second one named **Shushna** <term>Shushna: a demon of drought, whose name implies "the one who withers" or "scorches"</term>; the Rishi <term>Rishi: a seer or composer of the sacred hymns</term> celebrates Indra with these subsequent verses. **Indra** struck the **weapon** belonging to that **wild beast** <note>original: mṛgasya</note>—referring to the demon Vritra who moves swiftly like a wild animal—with his own **powers** or strengths. He destroyed it completely. He who is **alone** and without assistance, **considering** himself to be **without a rival** <note>original: apratiḥ</note>—at that time, **from him** (Vritra), **another** demon who was **more powerful** or more grown **appeared**. ॥ ३ ॥

---

## Hymn Text

-> ॥ Now, the Fourth Verse ॥ <-

**The wielder of the thunderbolt, with his bolt, struck down Shushna—that son of the mist who was rejoicing in his own power, growing strong in the darkness; Indra struck the fury of that Danava.** ॥ ४ ॥

**Word-for-Word Break (Pada-patha):**
That | indeed | of them | with self-power | rejoicing | of the mist | son/protector | well-growing | going in darkness |
striker of the rain-cloud | of the Danava | fury | with the thunderbolt | the wielder of the thunderbolt | [prefix] | struck | Shushna. ॥ ४ ॥

---

## Commentary (Sayana)

**Rejoicing** in the **self-power** or food of these living beings—meaning he was consuming the food of all creatures himself—he was the **protector** <note>original: napātaṃ</note> of the **mist** or the cloud capable of sprinkling. Here, the word *napat* refers to a "protector" or "governor." This is supported by the Brahmana <term>Brahmana: ancient texts explaining Vedic rituals and mythology</term> which states: "Breath is indeed the protector of the body, for it protects the limbs" <note>original: prāṇo vai tanunapātsa hi tanvaḥ pāti</note>. He was **well-growing** and **going into darkness** or gloom. [Indra] struck down that Vritra. The **wielder of the thunderbolt**, Indra, who is the **striker of the rain-cloud**, struck with his own weapon, the **thunderbolt**, the **fury** of the **Danava** <term>Danava: a class of demons, descendants of the goddess Danu</term>. Here, the word "fury" (bhāma) refers to the demon Shushna who was born from that fury. He **struck** that **Shushna**; he killed him. ॥ ४ ॥

---

## Hymn Text

-> ॥ Now, the Fifth Verse ॥ <-

**By his wise acts, Indra discovered the vital spot of that one who sat concealed and deemed himself immortal...** ॥ ५ ॥

<vocab>
इन्द्र (Indra): King of the gods, the celestial hero of the Rig Veda.
वृत्र (Vritra): The "Enveloper," the primary demonic antagonist of Indra who blocks the waters.
शुष्ण (Shushna): The "Scorcher," a demon representing drought.
वज्र (Vajra): Indra's divine weapon, often identified as the thunderbolt.
स्वधा (Svadha): Self-power, nature, or the sacrificial food.
नपात् (Napat): Usually means "grandson" or "descendant," but here interpreted by Sayana as "protector."
</vocab>

## 362 || Rig Veda || Mandala 4, Anuvaka 1, Varga 33

## Hymn Text

<note>Rig Veda 4.17.5 — Word-for-Word Break (Pada-patha)</note>
That | indeed | his | with powers | seated | without vital spots | found | indeed | his | vital spot | which | him | well-striking | in the offering | of the exhilaration | desiring to fight | in darkness | in the dwelling | placed. ॥ ५ ॥

---

->॥ Now, the Sixth Verse ॥<-

**That one indeed, who was lying thus, the Katpaya, increasing in the sunless darkness—at him, Indra, the bull, exhilarated by the pressed Soma, having raised his weapon, struck from on high.** ॥ ६ ॥

<note>Rig Veda 4.17.6</note>

**That | indeed | thus | Katpaya | lying | in sunless | darkness | increasing | that | indeed | rejoicing | the bull | of the pressed [Soma] | on high | Indra | having raised [the weapon] | struck.** ॥ ६ ॥

---

->॥ Now, the Seventh Verse ॥<-

**When Indra raised his unassailable power, the intended weapon, against the great Danava; when he struck him at the hurling of the thunderbolt, he made him the lowest of every living creature.** ॥ ७ ॥

<note>Rig Veda 4.17.7</note>

**Up | when | Indra | for the great | Danava | weapon | raised | power | unassailable | when | him | of the thunderbolt | in the hurling | he struck | of every | creature | the lowest | he made.** ॥ ७ ॥

---

## Commentary (Sayana)

<note>Commentary for Verse 5</note>
Of this Vritra <term>Vritra: the primary antagonist of Indra, a demon who personifies drought and encompasses the waters</term>, who considered himself to be without a vital point <note>original: amarmaṇaḥ</note>, you, O Indra, with your wisdom and insight <note>original: kratubhiḥ</note>, knew the vital spot <note>original: marma</note>—the place where, if pierced, one dies. Even though he was seated there, you recognized it. When the exhilarating <note>original: madasya</note> Soma <term>Soma: a sacred ritual drink believed to provide strength and inspiration to the gods</term> was offered in abundance, you, O powerful Indra, placed this Vritra—who was desiring to fight—into the destructive <note>original: hārmye</note> darkness. This means that out of fear of Indra, Vritra entered the darkness.

<note>Commentary for Verse 6</note>
Rejoicing in the pressed Soma, Indra, the showerer of desires <note>original: vṛṣabhaḥ</note>, raised his thunderbolt <note>original: vajram</note> on high and struck that very demon Vritra. In what state was the demon? He was lying in the mid-space as **Katpaya** <term>Katpaya: an epithet explained by the commentator as "one whose water is only slightly pleasant," referring to the demon's hoarding of the rains</term>, increasing in the sunless darkness where no light reaches. The repetition of the word "that" <note>original: tyaṃ cit</note> is for the purpose of completing the poetic meter.

->॥ This marks the end of the thirty-second Varga of the first Adhyaya of the fourth Mandala ॥<-

<note>Commentary for Verse 7</note>
When Indra raised his thunderbolt <note>original: vadhar</note>—which is the unassailable power <note>original: sahaḥ</note> that overcomes enemies and is resisted by none—against the great **Danava** <term>Danava: a class of demons, descendants of Danu; here refers to Vritra</term>... when at the great hurling of the thunderbolt...

<vocab>
Vritra (the demon of drought), Indra (the king of gods), Soma (the ritual drink), Vajra (Indra's thunderbolt), Danava (a demon), Marma (a vital or vulnerable point), Katpaya (an epithet for Vritra), Sahas (overwhelming power), Prabhriti (an offering or a hurling)
</vocab>

It emphasizes Indra's empowerment through the Soma sacrifice and his use of the unassailable thunderbolt.</summary>

# 363 || Rig Veda || Mandala 5, Adhyaya 2, Sukta 32

...exists. <note>original: "सति" (sati)</note>. In the formation of the word *hvayoh*, there is the substitution of the letter 'bh'. <note>A grammatical point regarding the Vedic Sanskrit root</note>. He struck <note>original: "ददाभ" (dadābha)</note> this Vritra; then, he made him the lowest and most degraded <note>original: "अधमं" (adhamaṃ)</note> of every living creature or being.

---

## Hymn Text

->॥ Now, the Eighth Verse ॥<-

**The powerful [Indra] struck that one—the cloud-encompassing [Vritra] who lay drinking the sweet [waters], unquenchable and covering all. With a great weapon, he struck the footless, immeasurable, and vile-tongued [demon] down in the place of battle.** ॥ ८ ॥

<note>Rig Veda 5.32.8</note>

->**Word-for-Word Break**<-

That | indeed | water-encompassing | sweet-drinking | lying | unquenchable | the coverer | great | struck | the powerful | footless | immeasurable | with a great | weapon | down | in the place of battle | struck down | the vile-tongued. ॥ ८ ॥

---

## Commentary (Sayana)

The **powerful** <note>original: "उग्र" (ugra)</note> Indra, whose strength is uplifted, **struck** <note>original: "आर्दत्" (ārdat)</note> or took hold of **that** very Vritra. What was he like? He was **water-encompassing** <note>original: "अर्णं" (arṇam)</note>, meaning he remained **lying** down, having obstructed the flowing waters or the clouds. He was a **drinker of sweetness** <note>original: "मधुपं" (madhupaṃ)</note>, the protector or consumer of the "honey" of the waters. He was **unquenchable** <note>original: "असिन्वं" (asinvaṃ)</note>, meaning one who casts down his rivals. <note>Sayana notes this form comes from the root 'as' - to throw</note>. He is called the **coverer** <note>original: "वव्रं" (vavraṃ)</note> because he covers or shrouds everything. As the **Taittiriya Samhita (2.5.2.2)** states: <note>original: "स इमाँल्लोकानवृणोत्त्वृत्रस्य वृत्रत्वं"</note> "He covered these worlds; that is why Vritra is called Vritra [the Enveloper]."

Following that, Indra, in the **place of battle** <note>original: "दुर्योणे" (duryoṇe)</note>, with a **great** and mighty **weapon**—the thunderbolt—struck down Vritra, who was **footless** <note>original: "अपादं" (apādaṃ)</note>, **immeasurable** <note>original: "अत्रं" (atram)</note> or without limit, and **vile-tongued** <note>original: "मृध्रवाचं" (mṛdhravācam)</note>, meaning his organ of speech was destroyed or he was overcome by gasping. <note>original: "जृंभाभिभूत" (jṛmbhābhibhūta)</note>. The **Taittiriya Samhita (2.5.2.4)** notes: "From him, as he was gasping, Agni and Soma went out, or rather, the out-breath and in-breath left him."

---

## Hymn Text

->॥ Now, the Ninth Verse ॥<-

**Who can restrain his drying power and strength? Alone and unopposed, he carries away the wealth [of enemies]. Even these two goddesses [Heaven and Earth] move away in fear of this Indra’s shattering might.** ॥ ९ ॥

<note>Rig Veda 5.32.9</note>

->**Word-for-Word Break**<-

Who | his | drying power | strength | restrains | alone | wealth | carries | unopposed | these | indeed | his | of the shattering | indeed | the two goddesses | of Indra | of the might | through fear | move away. ॥ ९ ॥

---

## Commentary (Sayana)

**Who can restrain** <note>original: "को वराते" (ko varāte)</note> or ward off the **drying power** <note>original: "शुष्मं" (śuṣmaṃ)</note> and the **strength** <note>original: "तविषीं" (taviṣīṃ)</note> belonging to **this Indra**? <note>Sayana notes that although 'Shushma' is masculine, it functions here as a descriptor of power</note>. Being **unopposed** <note>original: "अप्रतीतः" (apratītaḥ)</note>, not countered by anyone, Indra **alone**, without any helper, **carries** or takes away the **wealth** and riches of his enemies. Even **these two goddesses** <note>original: "देवी" (devī)</note>, the shining **Heaven and Earth**, **indeed move away** <note>original: "जिहाते" (jihāte)</note> or tremble out of **fear** of **this** Indra's **shattering** <note>original: "जर्यसो" (jaryaso)</note> **might**...

<summary>This page describes Indra's violent defeat of the demon Vritra, portrayed here as a "covering" entity that obstructed the world's waters. It also highlights Indra's peerless power, which causes even Heaven and Earth to recoil in fear.</summary>
<keywords>Indra, Vritra, water, thunderbolt, Heaven and Earth, Taittiriya Samhita, Vedic Sanskrit, battle imagery, divine power</keywords>

...they flee out of **fear** <note>original: "भियसा" (bhiyasa)</note> arising from the **power** <note>original: "ओजसः" (ojasaḥ)</note> belonging to this swift Indra. They **depart** <note>original: "जिहाते" (jihāte)</note>, meaning they move or tremble.

## Hymn Text
**The divine Heaven, the self-sustainer, bows down before this Indra; the Earth, the path, yields to him like a loving woman. When he joins all his might with these subjects, the people bow down in obedience to the powerful one.** ॥ १० ॥

**Down | for him | the divine | self-sustainer | bows | for Indra | the path | like one desiring | yields | together | when | power | he joins | all | by these | following | for the powerful one | the people | bow.** ॥ १० ॥

## Commentary (Sayana)
The **self-sustainer** <note>original: "स्वधितिः" (svadhitiḥ)</note>, meaning the one supported by her own nature, the **divine** and shining Heaven, **bows down** <note>original: "निजिहीते" (nijihīte)</note> before this Indra; she moves into a lower position. The **path** <note>original: "गातुः" (gātuḥ)</note>, meaning the Earth, **yields** <note>original: "येमे" (yeme)</note> or restrains herself for Indra **like a loving woman** <note>original: "उशतीव" (uśatīva)</note> who desires a man. This means she becomes ready to be employed by him according to his will. Whenever Indra **joins** <note>original: "संयुवते" (saṃyuvate)</note> or unites his **all-encompassing power** <note>original: "विश्वम् ओजः" (viśvam ojaḥ)</note> with **these** <note>original: "आभिः" (ābhiḥ)</note> subjects, it means Indra has placed his own strength within all creatures. Then, the **people** <note>original: "क्षितयः" (kṣitayaḥ)</note>, which is a <term>synonym for humans</term>, acting in accordance with his will, **bow down** <note>original: "नमन्त" (namanta)</note> or prostrate themselves before the **powerful** <note>original: "स्वधावने" (svadhāvane)</note> Indra.

---

-> ॥ Now, the Eleventh Verse ॥ <-

## Hymn Text
**I hear that you alone, the protector of the good, the one born for the five races, are glorious among all people. My people, seeking fulfillment, have grasped that newest Indra, calling him by night and by day.** ॥ ११ ॥

**Sole | indeed | you | protector of the good | for the five races | born | I hear | glorious | among men | him | my | have grasped | seeking fulfillment | newest | at night | by day | calling | Indra.** ॥ ११ ॥

## Commentary (Sayana)
O Indra, among **all men** <note>original: "जनेषु" (janeṣu)</note>, I, the seer of this mantra, **hear** from the chief sages that **you** are the **sole** <note>original: "एकम्" (ekam)</note> or primary one. What are you like? You are the **protector of the good** <note>original: "सत्पतिम्" (satpatim)</note>, the guardian of virtuous people; you are **born for the five races** <note>original: "पाञ्चजन्यम्" (pāñcajanyam)</note>, meaning you are beneficial to the five classes of humans; and you are **glorious** <note>original: "यशसम्" (yaśasam)</note>, full of fame. My subjects, who are **seeking fulfillment** <note>original: "आशसः" (āśasaḥ)</note> of their desires and **calling** <note>original: "हवमानासः" (havamānāsaḥ)</note> or praising you **at night** <note>original: "दोषा" (doṣā)</note> and **by day** <note>original: "वस्तोः" (vastoḥ)</note>, **have grasped** <note>original: "जगृभ्रे" (jagṛbhre)</note>—meaning they should take hold of or accept—that Indra who is **newest** <note>original: "नविष्ठम्" (naviṣṭham)</note>, or most exceedingly praiseworthy.

---

-> ॥ Now, the Twelfth Verse ॥ <-

## Hymn Text
**For thus I hear of you, who in due season, directs wealth to the wise. Why, Indra, do your priest-friends withhold their praise, they who have placed their desire in you?** ॥ १२ ॥

## Hymn Text

<note>RV 5.33.12</note>
**Even thus, indeed, I hear of you guiding [beings] according to the seasons, giving wealth to the sages. What do your friends, the sages, grasp [from you], O Indra—those who have placed their desire in you?** ॥ १२ ॥

**Even thus | indeed | you | seasonally | guiding | wealth | to the sages | giving | I hear | what | your | sages | grasp | friends | who | in you | placed | desire | Indra.** ॥ १२ ॥

---

## Commentary (Sayana)

**Even thus** <note>original: "एवैवमुक्तप्रकारेण"</note>, in the manner just described, I **hear** <note>original: "शृणोमि"</note> or perceive you, O Indra, **guiding** or impelling all living creatures **seasonally** <note>original: "ऋतुथा" (ṛtutha)</note>, meaning at the proper time, and **giving wealth** <note>original: "मघा ददतं"</note> to the **sages** <note>original: "विप्रेभ्यः"</note> who praise you. This truth seems almost unreal in its greatness. O Indra, **what do they grasp** <note>original: "किं गृहते"</note> from you? That is, what reward are your **friends**, the great **sages** <note>original: "ब्रह्माणो"</note> and praisers, receiving from you—those **who have placed** <note>original: "निदधुः"</note> their heart's **desire** <note>original: "कामं"</note> **in you** <note>original: "त्वाया"</note>? The sense is that the Sage speaks this because of a delay in his desires being fulfilled.

->॥ Thus ends the thirty-third group (Varga) of the first chapter in the fourth book ॥<-
->॥ Thus ends the second section (Anuvaka) of the fifth Mandala ॥<-

**By the light of the Veda’s meaning, removing the darkness of the heart, may Vidyatirtha-Maheshvara grant the four goals of human life.** <note>The "four goals" (Purusharthas) are Duty, Prosperity, Pleasure, and Liberation. Vidyatirtha-Maheshvara was Sāyaṇa’s spiritual teacher, often identified with the Supreme Lord.</note>

Thus, in the "Light of the Veda's Meaning" composed by Sāyaṇa, the minister of King Bukka, the protector of the Vedic path and supreme lord of kings, **the first chapter of the fourth book is completed.**

---

->**॥ Salutations to Lord Ganesha ॥**<-

**I bow to Vidyatirtha-Maheshvara, whose breath is the Vedas, and who created the entire world from the Vedas.**
**Having explained the first chapter in the fourth book, the wise Sāyaṇa, capable of interpretation, now desires to explain the second.**

In this third section (Anuvaka) of the fifth Mandala of the Sage Atri, there are twelve hymns. Among them, the first hymn, beginning with **"The great [one]..."** <note>original: "महि मह" (mahi maha)</note>, has ten verses. The Sage is Samvarana, the son of Prajapati. The deity is Indra. The metre is Trishtup <note>A Vedic metre of 4 lines with 11 syllables each</note>. This is recorded in the Index <note>Anukramani</note> as: "The ten verses of Samvarana, son of Prajapati." Its ritual use is determined by its content.
