# Rig Veda — Book 4, Chapter 2, Varga 1

## Hymn Text

-> **I meditate upon the great, for the Great, the Powerful; for the leaders, for Indra, in this manner, for the powerful and for the weak.** <-
-> **He who, when praised, recognizes the good-will for this person in the winning of spoils, among the people in the assembly.** ॥ १ ॥

---

## Commentary (Sayana)

I, the seer Samvarana—being myself extremely weak <note>original: "अतव्यान" (atavyān)</note>, as it were—meditate upon, illuminate, or manifest a great and abundant hymn for the great and powerful Indra in the manner about to be described. For what purpose? For the **strength** <note>original: "तवसे" (tavase)</note> of our **men** <note>original: "नॄन्" (nṝn)</note>, meaning our people. Alternatively, it may mean for the sake of overpowering our enemies. To that end, for our own strength. 

That Indra—who, when praised for the sake of obtaining **food** or **spoils** <note>original: "वाजसातौ" (vājasātau)</note> in the midst of battle for this person (the worshipper)—recognizes or grants **good-will** <note>original: "सुमतिम्" (sumatim)</note>. He does this in the company of mortals, or with the Maruts <term>storm-gods</term> who fight alongside him, or among those worthy of the battlefield.

---

-> ॥ Now the second verse ॥ <-

**O Indra, you who are mindful of us through hymns, O Showerer, to yoke the horses [from the] clouds.**
**Those [hymns] which you, O Maghavan, have carried according to your pleasure, approach and excel the people.** ॥ २ ॥

-> **He | you | us | Indra | being mindful | through hymns | of the horses | O Showerer | to yoke | [from] clouds.** <-
-> **Which | thus | O Maghavan | according to | pleasure | carried | towards | forth | [approach] | people.** ॥ २ ॥

## Commentary (Sayana)

O **Showerer** <note>original: "वृषन्" (vṛṣan), a common epithet for Indra as a pourer of boons</note>, Indra, you are that famous one. Being mindful of us and considering us through our **hymns** <note>original: "अर्कैः" (arkaiḥ)</note> which are the means of our worship, you should yoke the horses to be joined to your chariot. The word **clouds** <note>original: "अभ्रेः" (abhreḥ)</note> suggests you act with the power of the storm. O **Maghavan** <term>the Bounteous One</term>, those hymns which you have carried or accepted according to your pleasure—with those as the cause, approach our people and **excel** <note>original: "सक्षि" (sakṣi)</note> or overcome our adversaries.

---

-> ॥ Now the third verse ॥ <-

**O Mighty Indra, those who are not joined with you do not surpass you from our side, due to their lack of prayer.**
**Mount that chariot, O wielder of the thunderbolt; you guide the reins, O God, you who have excellent horses.** ॥ ३ ॥

-> **Not | your | that | Indra | towards | from us | O Mighty One | unjoined | lack of prayer | when | they are.** <-
-> **Stand | chariot | upon | that | thunderbolt-in-hand | [hither] | reins | O God | you guide | having good horses.** ॥ ३ ॥

## Commentary (Sayana)

O **Mighty** <note>original: "ऋष्व" (ṛṣva)</note> Indra, those who are other than your devotees—those who are **unjoined** <note>original: "अयुक्तासः" (ayuktāsaḥ)</note> or not united with you in worship—cannot surpass you. This is because of their **lack of prayer** <note>original: "अब्रह्मता" (abrahmata)</note>, meaning they possess no sacred hymns or devotion.

---

<summary>This page contains the first three verses of Mandala 4, Hymn 21, where the poet Vamadeva (or Samvarana in the commentary) invokes Indra’s strength and asks him to yoke his horses and attend the sacrifice, noting that those without prayer cannot reach him.</summary>
<keywords>Indra, Vamadeva, Sayana’s commentary, Maghavan, prayer (Brahma), hymns (Arka), ritual strength, Rig Veda Mandala 4</keywords>

<page-num>367</page-num>
# Rig Veda — Book 5, Hymn 33

...they became **without prayer** <note>original: "अब्रह्मता" (abrahmatā)</note>. **Prayer** <note>original: "ब्रह्म" (brahma)</note> refers to the "expanded" or "great" ritual action. Because they lack that, those men are not yours. Therefore, mount that famous chariot to come to our sacrifice. O Indra, you who hold the thunderbolt in your hand <term>Vajrahasta<gloss>an epithet of Indra as the wielder of the lightning bolt</gloss></term>, mount the chariot for which you yourself control the reins to be yoked.

---

## Hymn Text

-> ॥ Now the fourth verse ॥ <-

**Abundant are your hymns of praise, O Indra; fighting in the fertile fields for the sake of the cow, you acted.**
**You fashioned a path even for the Sun in his own abode; O Showerer, you destroyed the very name of the Dasa in battles.** ॥ ४ ॥

**Word-for-Word Analysis**
**Abundant | which | your | Indra | are | hymns | for the cow | you acted | in fertile fields | fighting |**
**he fashioned | for the sun | even | abode | in his own | the showerer | in battles | of the Dasa | the name | even** ॥ ४ ॥

## Commentary (Sayana)

O Indra, whenever there are **abundant** <note>original: "पुरूणि" (purūṇi)</note> **hymns of praise** <note>original: "शस्त्राणि" (śastrāṇi)</note> belonging to you, then—in the **fertile lands** <note>original: "उर्वरासु" (urvarāsu)</note> which are filled with grain—you act for the sake of the **cow** <note>meaning: the waters of the rain</note> by fighting and destroying those who obstruct the waters. Where do you do this? You **fashion** or accomplish this for the **Sun** in the Sun’s own **abode** or station. Being a **Showerer** <note>original: "वृषा" (vṛṣā), meaning one who rains down blessings or water</note>, you even destroy the very name of the demon named **Dasa** <term>Dasa<gloss>a class of beings or an individual demon who opposes the gods and obstructs the rain</gloss></term> in **battles** <note>original: "समत्सु" (samatsu)</note>. This means you utterly annihilate him.

---

## Hymn Text

-> ॥ Now the fifth verse ॥ <-

**We are yours, O Indra, and those men who have produced strength, and the chariots that have set out.**
**May the hero come to us, O you of serpent-like might; like the god Bhaga, he is to be invoked, beautiful during the offerings.** ॥ ५ ॥

**Word-for-Word Analysis**
**We | yours | those | Indra | who | and | men | strength | producing | set out | and | chariots |**
**to | us | may he come | O you of serpent-might | the hero | Bhaga | like | to be invoked | in the offerings | beautiful** ॥ ५ ॥

## Commentary (Sayana)

O Indra, those **men** who are the leaders of the ritual—the priests and the sacrificers—we are they, and we are yours. What kind of people are we? We are those **producing strength** <note>original: "शर्धः" (śardhaḥ)</note> through our songs of praise, and we are like swift **chariots** that have arrived to perform the offering to you. Furthermore, O **Ahishushma** <term>Ahishushma<gloss>one whose strength is all-pervading like a serpent's movement, or who possesses the heat/breath of a dragon</gloss></term>, by your grace, may the beautiful **hero** <note>original: "सत्वा" (satvā), referring to a protector or follower</note>—who is worthy of praise and joins us—come to us in battles or in sacrifices. He is **like Bhaga** <note>the god of fortune and share</note>, being desirable and worthy of invocation. Just as the god Bhaga comes to help us, may this heroic strength or follower come to us during the **offerings** <note>original: "प्रभृथेषु" (prabhṛtheṣu)</note>.

-> ॥ Thus ends the first group of the second chapter of the fourth book. ॥ <-

<summary>This page contains the translation and commentary for Rig Veda 5.33.4-5, focusing on Indra's role as a warrior who secures fertile land and rain by defeating the Dasa demons, and a request for divine favor and heroic strength compared to the god Bhaga.</summary>
<keywords>Indra, Sayana, Dasa, Bhaga, Ahishushma, Vedic sacrifice, fertile fields, rain-god, Rig Veda Mandala 5</keywords>

# Rig Veda — Book 4, Hymn 37 (continued)

-> ॥ Now the sixth verse ॥ <-

## Hymn Text
**Your power, O Indra, is worthy of being sought; for strength is indeed in you, O most heroic, immortal one.**
**Clothed in your own radiance, grant us white-gleaming wealth; I praise the gift of the sovereign, of him who possesses great riches.** ॥ ६ ॥

**Word-for-Word Analysis (Pada-patha):**
**Worthy of contact | Indra | your | [it] | for | power | riches | and | most heroic/dancing | immortal |**
**He | to us | white/shining | being clothed | wealth | grant | I praise | of the Lord | the gift | of the one with abundant wealth** ॥ ६ ॥

---

## Commentary (Sayana)
O **Indra**, your **power** <note>original: "ओजः" (ojas)</note>, which is **worthy of contact** <note>original: "पप्रुक्षेण्यं" (praprukshenyam)</note> or worshipful, is indeed within you. This means it is under your control. O **immortal one**, you who are **most manly** <term>Nritamanah<gloss>Literally "the most dancing," used here to mean the most active or heroic in the ritual or battle</gloss></term>, you who are **clothed** in your own radiance as you cover the world, grant us **riches** <note>original: "नृम्णानि" (nṛmṇāni)</note>—the word "and" <note>original: "च" (ca)</note> is used here in anticipation of what follows—and give us **wealth** that is **white-colored** <note>original: "एनीम्" (enīm)</note> or gleaming. And I **praise** <note>original: "प्रस्तुषे" (prastuṣe)</note> the **gift** given by the **Lord** <note>original: "अर्ये" (arye)</note> who is the **master of abundant wealth**.

---

-> ॥ Now the seventh verse ॥ <-

## Hymn Text
**Even so, O Indra, protect us with your aids; protect the chanting poets, O Hero.**
**And in the winning of the prize, satisfy yourself with the sweet, well-pressed, lovely Soma-juice.** ॥ ७ ॥

**Word-for-Word Analysis (Pada-patha):**
**Even so | us | Indra | with aids | protect | guard | the chanting | O Hero | the poets/makers |**
**And also | the skin [vessel] | giving | in the winning of the prize | satisfy [yourself] | of the honey-sweet | of the well-pressed | of the lovely** ॥ ७ ॥

---

## Commentary (Sayana)
O **heroic Indra**, in **this very way** <note>original: "एवैवं" (evaivaṃ)</note>, **protect** and **guard** us, the **poets** <term>Karun<gloss>the makers or performers of the sacrifice</gloss></term> who are **chanting** your praises, by means of your **aids** or protections. **And also**, in the **winning of the prize** <note>original: "वाजसातौ" (vājasātau)</note>—meaning in battle—**satisfy** yourself with the **lovely**, **honey-sweet** <note>original: "मध्वः" (madhvaḥ)</note> **Soma juice** that has been **well-pressed**. The commentary explains that you should "please your soul" with the juice that is presented. The grammatical form used for "honey-sweet" <note>genitive case used for accusative</note> implies: "Drink the Soma characterized by these qualities." Alternatively, it means "Satisfy yourself by the drinking of such Soma."

---

-> ॥ Now the eighth verse ॥ <-

## Hymn Text
**And may those ten white horses of the patron Trasadasyu, the son of Purukutsa, as they are being given, carry me.**
**May I always be associated with the sacred acts of this son of Girikshit.** ॥ ८ ॥

**Word-for-Word Analysis (Pada-patha):**
**And | those | me | of the son of Purukutsa | of the patron | of Trasadasyu | having gold/treasures | being given |**
**let them carry | me | ten | white | of him | of the son of Girikshit | with the sacred acts | now | I am associated** ॥ ८ ॥

<note>This verse begins a famous section praising the generosity of King Trasadasyu and the speed of the divine horse Dadhikra.</note>

<vocab>
Indra: The king of the gods and god of thunder; Ojas: Inner power or spiritual luster; Rayi: Wealth, often referring to cattle or spiritual abundance; Soma: The sacred ritual drink; Vajasati: The acquisition of strength or the winning of rewards in battle; Trasadasyu: A famous Vedic king known for his generosity; Paurukutsa: Son of King Purukutsa; Karu: A poet-priest or "maker" of hymns.
</vocab>

<header>Mandala 5, Hymn 33, Verse 33.] || Fourth Ashtaka || 369</header>

## Commentary (Sayana)
<note>Continued from the previous page for Rig Veda 5.33.8</note>

**Trasadasyu**, **Vidatha**, and **Dhunya** are the three kings mentioned. They have released horses and wealth for the sake of giving. **And also those** <note>original: "उताप च त्ये" (utāpa ca tye)</note> [gifts] are for **me**. Here, the second grammatical case is used in the sense of the fourth case, meaning "unto me." **Being given** <note>original: "रराणाः" (rarāṇāḥ)</note>; this is a form of the verb *rā* (to give) in the perfect participle. It means "having been granted." 

May the **white-colored** <note>original: "श्येतासः" (śyetāsaḥ)</note> horses of **Trasadasyu**—who is the son of Purukutsa <note>original: "पौरुकुत्स्यस्य" (paurukutsyasya)</note>, a wise instigator, a possessor of gold, a royal seer, and a descendant of the Girikshit lineage—carry me or bring these gifts to me. And I, through my **labors** <note>original: "ऋतुभिः" (ṛtubhiḥ)</note>—meaning ritual acts such as yoking the chariot or performing sacrifices—shall **quickly attain** <note>original: "नु सक्षे" (nu sakṣe)</note> or reach the goal.

---

-> || Now the Ninth Verse || <-

## Hymn Text
And those red horses of Vidatha, the son of Marutashva, bestowed at the distribution, their wealth earned through sacred work; he, bestowing thousands upon me, has granted an ornament for the body, as a master brings honor. ॥ ९ ॥

**Word-for-Word Analysis (Pada-patha):**
**And | those | me | of the son of Marutashva | red [horses] | whose wealth is earned by ritual | of Vidatha | in the gift |**
**Thousands | me | flowing/moving | giving | in succession | the master | for the body | as | he honored/granted** ॥ ९ ॥

## Commentary (Sayana)
**And also** <note>original: "उतापि च" (utāpi ca)</note> **those** horses of **Vidatha**, the king who is the son of **Marutashva**—one who possesses horses with the speed of the Maruts <term>Marutashva<gloss>Literally "having the horses of the Maruts (storm gods)," signifying extreme speed</gloss></term>. His horses are **red-colored** <note>original: "शोणाः" (śoṇāḥ)</note> and their **wealth is earned by ritual** <note>original: "क्रत्वामघासः" (kratvāmaghāsaḥ)</note>, meaning they are worthy of being honored for their swift movement during the rite. These horses are employed in the **gift** <note>original: "रातौ" (rātau)</note> or the act of distribution to carry me. 

Furthermore, the **master** <note>original: "अर्यः" (aryaḥ)</note> or the worshipful patron, granting to **me**—here the sixth case is used for the fourth, meaning "for me, the worshipful one"—**thousands** of immeasurable riches, and **bestowing** <note>original: "ददानः" (dadānaḥ)</note> them as they flow toward me, he **granted** <note>original: "अर्चत्" (arcat)</note> an **ornament** <note>original: "आनुकम्" (ānukam)</note> for the **decoration of the body** <note>original: "वपुषे" (vapuṣe)</note>. The word "as" <note>original: "न" (na)</note> here also functions as "and."

---

-> || Now the Tenth Verse || <-

## Hymn Text
And those [riches] of Dhunya, the son of Lakshmana, have reached me—pleasing, beautiful in brilliance, and well-directed; like cows moving toward the pen, these great riches have been presented to the seer Samvarana. ॥ १० ॥

**Word-for-Word Analysis (Pada-patha):**
**And | those | me | of Dhunya | reached/cherished | of the son of Lakshmana | beautifully brilliant | striving/directed |**
**Great | riches | of Samvarana | of the seer | the pen | like | cows | presented | even | they went** ॥ १० ॥

## Commentary (Sayana)
**And also** those **riches** <note>original: "रायो" (rāyo)</note> belonging to **Dhunya**, the king who is the **son of Lakshmana** <note>original: "लक्ष्मण्यस्य" (lakṣmaṇyasya)</note>, have **reached me** <note>original: "मा जुष्टा" (mā juṣṭā)</note>. These are **beautifully brilliant** <note>original: "सुरुचः" (surucaḥ)</note> and are **striving** <note>original: "यतानाः" (yatānāḥ)</note> or being carried toward me. These **great** <note>original: "महा" (mahā)</note> **riches**, having been **presented** <note>original: "प्रयता" (prayatā)</note> as gifts...

<note>Commentary for Verse 10 continues on the next page.</note>

Trasadasyu (त्रसदस्यु), Vidatha (विदथ), Dhunya (धुन्य), Marutashva (मारुताश्व), Lakshmanya (लक्ष्मण्य), Kratu (क्रतु - ritual/work), Magha (मघा - wealth), Rati (राति - gift), Raya (राय - riches)
</vocab>

<meta>This page transitions from the conclusion of Hymn 33 in the fifth Mandala (book) of the Rig Veda to the beginning of Hymn 34. <page-num>370</page-num>
<header>|| Rig Veda || [Book 4, Chapter 2, Section 3.]</header>

<note>This first paragraph concludes the commentary on the final verse of the previous hymn, where the sage describes receiving gifts from royal patrons.</note>

...of the sage Samvarana, they have **approached** <note>original: "अपित्मन" (apigman)</note>; meaning they have arrived at my home. This is the implied meaning. **Like cows to a pen** <note>original: "व्रजं न गावो" (vrajaṃ na gāvo)</note>—the gifts are compared to cattle returning to their stall. Alternatively, the word "na" can mean "and," implying that both the horses and the cows have reached my pen. It is noted in the introduction to this section <note>Anuvaka 1.2</note> that in hymns dedicated to Indra, praises for the Maruts (storm deities) and the generosity of kings are common and not contradictory.

-> || Thus ends the second group (Varga) of the second chapter (Adhyaya) in the fourth book (Ashtaka) || <-

**"Unto him without a born enemy"** <note>original: "अजातशत्रुम्" (ajātashatrum)</note>—this marks the second hymn of this section, consisting of nine verses. It is attributed to the seer Samvarana, the son of Prajapati, and is dedicated to Indra. The ninth verse is in the Trishtubh meter <term>Trishtubh: a Vedic meter of 44 syllables</term>, while the rest are in the Jagati meter <term>Jagati: a Vedic meter of 48 syllables</term>, following the general rule that hymns ending in Trishtubh are primarily Jagati. The ritual application of this hymn follows the specific markers within the text.

---

## Hymn Text

-> || Here is the first verse || <-

Unto him without a born enemy, the unaging, the heavenly one, the immeasurable sacrificial food follows his nature. Press the Soma, cook the offerings for the carrier of prayer, for the one praised by many, establish the work further. ॥ १ ॥

**Word-for-Word Analysis**
**Unto him without a born enemy | the unaging | the heavenly | follows | nature | immeasurable | the destroyer | reaches | press | cook | for the carrier of prayer | for the one praised by many | further | establish.** ॥ १ ॥

## Commentary (Sayana)

**Unto him without a born enemy** <note>original: "अजातशत्रुं" (ajātashatruṃ)</note>: One who has no enemies yet born to challenge him. **The destroyer** <note>original: "दस्मं" (dasmam)</note>: The one who causes the destruction of his enemies. **The unaging** <note>original: "अजरा" (ajarā)</note>: One who does not decay or diminish. **The heavenly** <note>original: "स्वर्वती" (svarvatī)</note>: Possessing the light of heaven. **The immeasurable** <note>original: "अमिता" (amitā)</note>: Boundless. **The sacrificial food** <note>original: "स्वधा" (svadhā)</note>: The oblation or food offered in the ritual **reaches** <note>original: "अन्वीयते" (anvīyate)</note> or follows him. 

For that purpose, O priests, **press the Soma** <note>original: "सुनोतन" (sunotana)</note>; extract the sacred juice. **Cook** <note>original: "पचत" (pacata)</note> the rice-cakes and other offerings. For whom? For **the carrier of prayer** <note>original: "ब्रह्मवाहसे" (brahmavāhase)</note>, meaning Indra, who carries or receives the great hymns of praise. For the **one praised by many** <note>original: "पुरुष्टुताय" (puruṣṭutāya)</note>. **Establish** <note>original: "दधातन" (dadhātana)</note> the ritual work that is appropriate for each of you **further** <note>original: "प्रतरं" (prataraṃ)</note> or most excellently.

---

## Hymn Text

-> || Now the second verse || <-

He who filled his belly with Soma, the wealthy lord rejoiced in the sweet food. When, to strike the beast, he of the great weapon held the thousand-pointed bolt, [along with] the desiring Ushana. ॥ २ ॥

**Word-for-Word Analysis**
**Completely | who | with Soma | the belly | filled | rejoiced | the wealthy lord | of the sweet | food | when | him | for the beast | to strike | the great weapon | thousand-pointed | the desiring one | the weapon | held.** ॥ २ ॥

## Commentary (Sayana)

**He**, the **wealthy lord** <note>original: "मघवा" (maghavā - an epithet of Indra)</note>, **completely filled** <note>original: "आ अपिप्रात" (ā apiprāta)</note> his **belly** with **Soma**. He **rejoiced** <note>original: "अमन्दत" (amandata)</note> or was satisfied by the drinking of the **sweet food** <note>original: "मध्वो अन्धसः" (madhvo andhasaḥ)</note>, the Soma juice. 

**When** <note>original: "यत्" (yat)</note> he intended **to strike** <note>original: "हंतवे" (hantave)</note> the demon named **the beast** <note>original: "मृगाय" (mṛgāya)</note>, he **held** <note>original: "यमत्" (yamat)</note> or aimed his **weapon** <note>original: "वधं" (vadhaṃ)</note>, the thunderbolt. This **great weapon** <note>original: "महावधो" (mahāvadho)</note> is **thousand-pointed** <note>original: "सहस्रभृष्टि" (sahasrabhrishti)</note>, meaning it possesses immeasurable brilliance and power. He did this while **desiring** <note>original: "उशना" (ushanā)</note> to destroy the enemy, or perhaps in the company of the sage **Ushanas**. It was then that he filled himself and rejoiced.

<summary>This page concludes the previous section's commentary on royal gifts and begins Hymn 34 of Mandala 5. It introduces Indra as a god without enemies who receives Soma and prepares to strike the demon Mriga with his thousand-pointed thunderbolt.</summary>
<keywords>Indra, Samvarana, Soma sacrifice, Vajra, thunderbolt, Mriga demon, Sayana commentary, Rig Veda Mandala 5, Vedic meter, Jagati</keywords>

<meta>This page continues the third Anuvaka (section) of the fifth Mandala (book) of the Rig Veda. It covers verses 3 and 4 of Hymn 34, which is dedicated to Indra. The previous page introduced the hymn's focus on Indra's power to distinguish between the pious sacrificer and the stingy non-believer.</meta>

<page-num>311</page-num>
<header>Mandala 5, Anuvaka 3, Hymn 34.] || Fourth Ashtaka ||</header>

->|| Here is the third verse ||<-

## Hymn Text

He who for this [Indra] in **the heat of the sun** <note>original: "घ्रंसे" (ghraṃse)</note> or in **the udder** <note>original: "ऊधनि" (ūdhani)</note> presses the Soma, he becomes **radiant** <note>original: "द्युमाँ" (dyumān)</note> throughout the days. The Mighty One drives away the **self-adorner** <note>original: "ततनुष्टिं" (tatanuṣṭiṃ)</note>, even he who is wealthy, who is a **friend of the wicked** <note>original: "कवासखः" (kavāsakhaḥ)</note>. || 3 ||

**Word-for-Word Breakdown:**
He; for him [Indra]; in the sun’s heat; or; and; he; in the udder; Soma; presses; becomes; radiant; indeed;
away-away; the Mighty One; the self-adorner; drives; the self-beautifier; the wealthy one; who; friend-of-the-wicked. || 3 ||

---

## Commentary (Sayana)

Whichever sacrificer presses the Soma for this Indra in **the sun's heat** <note>original: "घ्रंसे" (ghraṃse)</note>—this refers to the day. The word *ghraṃsa* is used because light is held within it. Or, whichever sacrificer presses Soma in **the udder** <note>original: "ऊधनि" (ūdhani)</note>. The word *ūdhas* (udder) refers to the night, either because it is "raised up" or because of the similarity between the flow of milk and the moisture of the night. Whether in the day or the night, the one who presses Soma becomes **radiant** <note>original: "द्युमान्" (dyumān)</note> or full of light. The word **indeed** <note>original: "अह" (aha)</note> is used for emphasis. Furthermore, the **Mighty One** <note>original: "शक्रः" (shakraḥ)</note>, this powerful Indra, drives away the **self-adorner** <note>original: "ततनुष्टिं" (tatanuṣṭiṃ)</note>. This refers to one who "stretches" (desires) only to satisfy his own cravings rather than performing the continuous sequence of religious duties. He drives away that **self-beautifier** <note>original: "तनूशुभं" (tanūshubhaṃ)</note>, one whose body is beautiful only with ornaments for his own sake but who does not sacrifice. The repetition of the word **away** <note>original: "अप" (apa)</note> is for poetic completion. The **Wealthy One** <note>original: "मघवा" (maghavā)</note> Indra also drives away the one who is a **friend of the wicked** <note>original: "कवासखः" (kavāsakhaḥ)</note>, meaning a companion to vile people.

---

->|| Here is the fourth verse ||<-

## Hymn Text

He whose father he killed, whose mother, whose brother, the Mighty One does not flee from him in distress. He surely seeks the **offerings** <note>original: "प्रयता" (prayatā)</note> of this one who **sets things right** <note>original: "यतंकरः" (yataṃkaraḥ)</note>; the **source of wealth** <note>original: "वस्व आाकरः" (vasva ākaraḥ)</note> does not flee from **sin** <note>original: "किल्बिषात्" (kilbiṣāt)</note>. || 4 ||

**Word-for-Word Breakdown:**
Whose; he killed; father; whose; mother; whose; the Mighty One; brother; not; distressed; flees;
seeks; surely; indeed; of this; offerings; the one who restrains/orders; not; from sin; flees; of wealth; the source. || 4 ||

---

## Commentary (Sayana)

The **Mighty One** <note>original: "शक्रो" (shakraḥ)</note>, this powerful Indra, may have killed the father of a person who does not sacrifice. He may have killed the mother, or the brother. Even so, Indra does **not flee** <note>original: "नेषते" (neṣate)</note>—meaning he does not fear or move away—from such a person if they turn to him. Rather, he **surely seeks** <note>original: "वेतीदु" (vetīdu)</note> the offerings given by this person once they are properly dedicated. This means that after disciplining the non-sacrificer, Indra engages him in the ritual. He is the **one who sets things right** <note>original: "यतंकरो" (yataṃkarao)</note> or the maker of restraint, and the **source of wealth** <note>original: "वस्वो... आकर" (vasvo... ākara)</note> who brings riches forward. He **does not flee** <note>original: "नेषते" (neṣate)</note> from the **sin** <note>original: "किल्बिषात्" (kilbiṣāt)</note> associated with the act of killing [those who oppose him]. Indra’s destruction of those who do not praise him is well-known in the sacred scriptures, such as the passages: "Indra gave the **Yatis** <term>Yatis: a group of ancient ascetics who, in this myth, failed to worship Indra correctly</term> to the **Salavrikas** <term>Salavrikas: literally 'mountain-wolves' or hyenas; mythical creatures that devour those rejected by the gods</term>," and "He threw the **Paulomas** <note>original: "पौलोमान्" (paulomān), a class of demons</note> into the atmosphere and the **Kalakanjas** <note>original: "कालकांज्यान" (kālakāñjyāna), another demonic group</note> upon the earth."

<summary>These verses describe Indra's role as a stern judge who punishes those who refuse to sacrifice (the 'self-adorners') while rewarding those who offer Soma day or night. The commentary highlights Indra's fearsome reputation for destroying non-believers, even their families, to establish the sacrificial order.</summary>
<keywords>Indra, Soma, Sacrifice, Ghramsa, Udhan, Yatis, Salavrikas, Paulomas, Sayana, Rig Veda 5.34</keywords>

<meta>This page continues the translation of the Rig Veda, Mandala 5, Hymn 34, dedicated to Indra. The previous page covered verses 3 and 4, discussing how Indra distinguishes between the devoted sacrificer and the selfish non-believer. This page transitions from Varga (section) 3 into Varga 4 of the second Adhyaya (chapter) of the fourth Ashtaka (book).</meta>

<page-num>372</page-num>
<header>|| Rig Veda || [Chapter 4, Section 2, Varga 4] </header>

## Hymn Text

-> || Now the Fifth [Verse] || <-

Not with five or ten does he wish to begin an undertaking; he does not associate with the **non-presser** <note>original: "असुन्वता" (asunvatā); referring to one who does not perform the Soma sacrifice</note>, even if that person **prospers** <note>original: "पुष्यता" (puṣyatā)</note>. The **Shaker** <note>original: "धुनिः" (dhuniḥ); one who causes enemies to tremble</note> overcomes or even kills that [non-sacrificer] in that way; he admits the **god-seeker** <note>original: "देवयुं" (devayuṃ)</note> into a **stall full of cattle** <note>original: "गोमति व्रजे" (gomati vraje)</note>. || 5 ||

**Word-for-Word Analysis:**
Not. With five. With ten. He wishes. To begin. Not. With the non-presser. He associates. With the prospering one. Even.
He overcomes. Or. Indeed. In that way. He kills. Or. The Shaker. Toward. The god-seeker. He causes to share. In the cow-containing. In the stall. || 5 ||

---

## Commentary (Sayana)

This Indra **does not wish** <note>original: "न वष्टि" (na vaṣṭi)</note> for an undertaking or a support for killing enemies through **five or ten** assistants. The meaning is that he does not require help. Alternatively, he does not desire the effort begun by this [non-sacrificer] through five or ten means other than the sacrifice. He **does not associate** <note>original: "न सचते" (na sacate)</note> with the **non-presser** <note>one who does not perform the ritual extraction of Soma</note>, **even if he is prospering** <note>original: "पुष्यता चन" (puṣyatā cana)</note> by nourishing his children and others. This means he does not reach the one who does not press Soma, the one who does not sacrifice, and the one who does not nourish the gods. It is not merely a lack of reaching him, but rather **he overcomes** <note>original: "जिनाति वा" (jināti vā)</note> him. The word "or" <note>original: "वा" (vā)</note> here functions as "and." He also defeats him. The word **indeed** <note>original: "इत्" (it)</note> is a filler for the meter. The **Shaker** <note>original: "धुनिः" (dhuniḥ)</note>, who makes his enemies tremble, **kills** that non-sacrificer **in that way** <note>original: "अमुया" (amuyā)</note>. However, he **causes the god-seeker** <note>original: "देवयुं" (devayuṃ)</note>—the sacrificer who desires the god Indra—**to share in the stall full of cattle** <note>original: "गोमति व्रजे आभजति" (gomati vraje ābhajati)</note>. This means he connects the sacrificer with wealth in the form of livestock.

-> || Thus ends the third Varga in the second [chapter] of the fourth [Ashtaka] || <-

---

## Hymn Text

-> || Now the Sixth [Verse] || <-

The **Thinner of enemies** <note>original: "वितवक्षणः" (vitavakṣaṇaḥ)</note> in **battle** <note>original: "समृतौ" (samṛtau)</note>, who **attaches the chariot wheel**; he is **averse** <note>original: "विषुणः" (viṣuṇaḥ)</note> to the non-presser and the **strengthener** <note>original: "वृधः" (vṛdhaḥ)</note> of the presser. Indra, the **subduer** <note>original: "दमिता" (damitā)</note> of all, the **Terrifier** <note>original: "विभीषणो" (vibhīṣaṇo)</note>, the **Noble One** <note>original: "आर्यः" (āryaḥ)</note>, leads the **Servant** <note>original: "दासं" (dāsaṃ)</note> as he wills. || 6 ||

**Word-for-Word Analysis:**
The Thinner [of enemies]. In battle. The attacher of the wheel. Of the non-presser. Averse. Of the presser. The strengthener.
Indra. Of all. The subduer. The Terrifier. According to his will. He leads. The Servant. The Noble One. || 6 ||

---

## Commentary (Sayana)

In **battle** <note>original: "समृतौ" (samṛtau)</note>, he is the **Thinner** <note>original: "वितवक्षणो" (vitavakṣaṇo)</note>, specifically the one who makes the bodies of enemies thin [by killing them]. For that purpose, he is the **attacher of the chariot wheel** <note>original: "चक्रमासजो" (cakramāsajo)</note>. He is **averse** <note>original: "विषुणः" (viṣuṇaḥ)</note>—having his face turned away—from the **non-presser** <note>the non-sacrificer</note>. He is the **strengthener** <note>original: "वृधो" (vṛdho)</note>, the one who increases the prosperity, of the **presser** <note>the sacrificer</note>. Indra is the **subduer** <note>original: "दमिता" (damitā)</note> or teacher of all, the **Terrifier** <note>original: "विभीषणो" (vibhīṣaṇo)</note> or generator of fear, and the **Noble** <note>original: "आर्यः" (āryaḥ)</note> master. He **leads** <note>original: "नयति" (nayati)</note> the **Servant** <note>original: "दासं" (dāsaṃ)</note>—the person performing the work of a servant or enemy—under his own control **as he wills** <note>original: "यथावशं" (yathāvaśam)</note>.

---

## Hymn Text

-> || Now the Seventh [Verse] || <-

He drives away the **sustenance** <note>original: "भोजनं" (bhojanaṃ)</note> of the **Miser** <note>original: "पणेः" (paṇeḥ)</note> for **plunder** <note>original: "मुषे" (muṣe)</note>; he distributes **delightful wealth** <note>original: "सूनरं वसु" (sūnaraṃ vasu)</note> to the **giver** <note>original: "दाशुषे" (dāśuṣe)</note>. Not even in a **fortress** <note>original: "दुर्गे" (durge)</note> is any person held safe, who has **angered** <note>original: "अचुक्रुधत्" (acukrudhat)</note> his **power** <note>original: "तविषीं" (taviṣīṃ)</note>. || 7 ||

<vocab>
<term>Indra</term>: The chief Vedic deity, god of thunder, rain, and war.
<term>Asunvat</term>: A person who does not "press" the Soma plant, representing those who refuse to participate in the sacred rituals.
<term>Sunvat</term>: The sacrificer who extracts the Soma juice as an offering.
<term>Yajamana</term>: The patron or beneficiary of the Vedic sacrifice.
<term>Dasa</term>: Often translated as "servant" or "slave," in the Rig Veda it refers to enemies of the Aryas or non-sacrificers.
<term>Arya</term>: "Noble" or "honorable," referring to those who follow the Vedic way of life and perform sacrifices.
<term>Pani</term>: A class of mythological figures characterized as stingy, wealthy misers who withhold cattle and offerings from the gods.
</vocab>

<summary>This page describes Indra as a self-sufficient warrior who does not need allies to conquer his enemies. He is depicted as a stern judge who punishes non-sacrificers (Asunvat/Dasa) while rewarding his devotees (Sunvat/Arya) with cattle and wealth stolen from misers (Panis).</summary>
<keywords>Indra, Soma sacrifice, Arya, Dasa, Pani, wealth, divine justice, battle, Vedic ritual</keywords>

--- Page 441 ---
<meta>This page continues from the previous discussion of Indra’s role as the divine distributor of wealth. It concludes the commentary on verse 7, which describes how Indra takes from the hoarding merchant (Pani) to give to the devout sacrificer. It then presents verse 8, focusing on Indra's judgment between rivals and his alliance with the faithful, and begins verse 9, which introduces a patron from the lineage of Agnivesha.</meta>

## Hymn Text
->Mandala 5, Sukta 34<-

**॥ Word-for-Word Analysis ॥**
Together. This [Indra]. Of the merchant. Drives away. The food. For theft. Away. To the giver. Distributes. Excellent. Wealth. 
In difficulty. Even. Is held. Everyone. Toward. Many. People. Who. His. Might. Provoked. || 7 ||

---

## Commentary (Sayana)
This Indra drives away—meaning he goes toward and seizes—the food, wealth, or grain of the **Pani** <note>original: "पणेः" (paṇeḥ); referring to a stingy merchant or non-believer who hoards wealth without sacrificing</note>, who is like a greedy miser who does not give. Having gone and taken it, he distributes it to the **giver** <note>original: "दाशुषे" (dāśuṣe)</note>, the sacrificer who offers oblations. He gives him **excellent** <note>original: "सूनरं" (sūnaraṃ)</note> or beautiful human wealth. The meaning is that he drags wealth away from the non-sacrificer and presents it to the sacrificer.

Not only does he provide the merchant's wealth, but every giving person is **supported** <note>original: "आध्रियते" (ādhriyate); established or sustained</note> by him even in **difficulties** <note>original: "दुर्गे" (durge)</note> or calamities where one can only travel with great pain. The final part of the verse connects back: Indra drives away [the wealth] of that merchant who **provoked** <note>original: "अचुक्रुधत्" (acukrudhat)</note> Indra’s **might** <note>original: "तविषीं" (taviṣīṃ)</note> or strength by failing to perform the ordained rituals. Alternatively, it means that every person who has provoked his might is held or restrained by Indra even in difficult situations. The particle *cana* <note>original: "चनेत्येकपदम्"</note> is treated as a single word according to the traditional school of recitation.

---

## Hymn Text
->॥ Now the Eighth [Verse] ॥<-

**When Maghavan Indra recognizes the two people, both wealthy and possessing universal strength, in the matter of the bright cattle; he makes the other his ally, he the Shaker, and with his warriors, the Agitator releases the herd of cows. || 8 ||**

->**॥ Word-for-Word Analysis ॥**<-
Together. When. Two people. Well-wealthy. Universal-strength. Recognized. Indra. The Generous. Among cows. Bright.
Ally. Indeed. Another. Made. The Trembler. Out. This. Cow-herd. Releases. With warriors. The Shaker. || 8 ||

---

## Commentary (Sayana)
Indra **recognizes** <note>original: "समवेत्" (samavet)</note> or understands. Or, when there are **two people** <note>original: "जनौ" (janau)</note> who are mutual rivals, both possessing **excellent wealth** <note>original: "सुधनौ" (sudhanau)</note> and **universal strength** <note>original: "विश्वशर्धसौ" (viśvaśardhasau)</note> or great enthusiasm—the wealthy Indra, in the matter of the **bright cows** <note>original: "गोषु शुभ्रिषु" (goṣu śubhriṣu)</note> which serve as the cause of the conflict, makes the **other** (the sacrificer) his **ally** <note>original: "युजं" (yujaṃ)</note> or companion. 

Indra is the **Trembler** <note>original: "प्रवेपनी" (pravepanī)</note>, the one who makes his enemies shake. He **releases** <note>original: "उत् सृजते" (ut sṛjate)</note> the group of cows for this [sacrificer] along with his **warriors** <note>original: "सत्वभिः" (satvabhiḥ)</note>, identified here as the **Maruts** <note>the storm gods who accompany Indra</note>. He is called the **Shaker** <note>original: "धुनिः" (dhuniḥ)</note> because he causes the clouds to tremble. The meaning is: whether it be a sacrificer or a non-sacrificer, Indra knows them both; recognizing the cause regarding the cows, he bestows the herd upon the [sacrificing] person.

---

## Hymn Text
->॥ Now the Ninth [Verse] ॥<-

**I praise the pure descendant of Agnivesha, the winner of a thousand, the highest banner of the noble, O Agni; for him the flowing waters swell, and in him let there be power, forceful and brilliant. || 9 ||**

->**॥ Word-for-Word Analysis ॥**<-
Winner of a thousand. Descendant of Agnivesha. I praise. Pure. O Agni. Highest. Banner. Of the noble.
For him. Waters. Flowing together. Swell. In him. Power. Forceful. Brilliant. Let it be. || 9 ||

---

## Commentary (Sayana)
I praise the **son of Agnivesha** <note>original: "आग्निवेशिम्" (āgniveśim)</note>, who is pure and the giver of uncounted wealth. The Sage prays in this verse... the son of Prajapati... <note>Page ends; commentary continues on next page.</note>

<vocab>
**Maghavan** (मघवा): An epithet of Indra meaning "the Generous" or "Possessor of Bounties."
**Pani** (पणि): A class of demons or stingy humans who hoard wealth and refuse to sacrifice to the gods.
**Yajamana** (यजमान): The patron or performer of the Vedic sacrifice.
**Maruts** (मरुत्): The storm gods and constant companions of Indra in battle.
**Dhuni** (धुनि): "The Shaker" or "The Roarer," referring to Indra's power over clouds and enemies.
</vocab>

<summary>This page concludes the description of Indra's justice in seizing wealth from the stingy Pani and awarding it to the faithful. It emphasizes Indra's role as a "Shaker" who chooses the sacrificer as his ally in battles over cattle and introduces a praise for a patron named Agniveshi.</summary>

<meta>This page concludes the commentary on Mandala 5, Sukta 34, and introduces Sukta 35. It maintains continuity from the previous discussion regarding the royal patron Shaci and transitions into a new set of prayers for Indra's protection and wisdom.</meta>

# Rig Veda — Book 4, Chapter 2, Section 5

The wise one. I, the noble one, praise Shaci, the royal sage <term>Rajarsi: a king who has attained the status of a seer through spiritual merit</term>, who is the son of Agnivesha and a giver of thousands—meaning one who bestows infinite wealth. I praise; I laud him. O Agni <note>original: "अग्ने" (agne); here, the commentator explains this is addressed to Indra, but using qualities associated with Agni, the fire god</note>, what is this patron like? He is exemplary, a beacon <note>original: "केतुं" (ketuṃ); a signal or mark of distinction</note>, meaning he is renowned. For him, the flowing waters move perfectly and nourish him. For that king, may there be power and wealth, accompanied by strength, bright and shining.

-> ॥ Thus ends the fourth section (Varga) in the second chapter of the fourth book. ॥ <-

The third hymn, beginning with "That which is your most effective" <note>original: "यस्ते साधिष्ठ" (yaste sādhiṣṭha)</note>, consists of eight verses. The Seer (Rishi) is Prabhūvasu of the Angiras lineage. The final verse is in the **Pankti** metre; according to the technical rule regarding hymns ending in a Pankti, the remaining verses are in the **Anushtubh** metre. The deity is **Indra**. This is recorded in the Index: "The eight verses starting with *yaste*, by Prabhūvasu Āṅgirasa, ending in Pankti." 

The ritual application <term>Viniyoga: the specific use of a verse in a Vedic ceremony</term> is determined by the textual context. In the *Abhistavika* praises of the *Ukthya* sacrifice during the third pressing, the first triplet (three verses) is an optional corresponding chant for the *Achhavaka* priest. This is indicated in the Ashvalayana Shrauta Sutra (7.8): "That which is your most effective for protection..." and "Young poet, breaker of forts..." Furthermore, in the ritual days known as *Svarasaman*, the first triplets serve as the corresponding chants. Six Anushtubh verses starting with "That which is your most effective for protection" are specified in the Ashvalayana Shrauta Sutra (8.5).

---

## Hymn Text

-> ॥ Here is the first verse ॥ <-

That which is your **most effective** for **protection**, O **Indra**, that **wisdom**, bring to us; [that which] **overcomes all people**, is **victorious**, and is **invincible** in **battles**. ॥ 1 ॥

> That | which | your | most effective | for protection | Indra | wisdom | that | [bring] near | bear/bring |
> for us | overcoming people | victorious | in battles | difficult to overcome ॥ 1 ॥

## Commentary (Sayana)

O Indra, whatever wisdom <note>original: "क्रतुः" (kratuḥ); can refer to sacrificial action, mental power, or divine will</note> or ritual action of yours is most effective—meaning it is the most powerful means of achieving results—bring that to us for our protection. What is this wisdom like? It is that which overcomes all men <note>original: "चर्षणीसहं" (carṣaṇīsahaṃ)</note>, is pure or bestows gifts <note>original: "सस्निं" (sasniṃ)</note>, and is invincible or cannot be surpassed by others in battles.

---

## Hymn Text

-> ॥ Now the second verse ॥ <-

Whether, O **Indra**, you have **four**, or whether, O **Hero**, there are **three**, or whether the protection of the **five tribes**, bring that well to us. ॥ 2 ॥

> Whether | Indra | your | four | whether | Hero | are | three |
> whether | or | five | of the tribes | protection | that | well | to us | [bring] near | bear/bring ॥ 2 ॥

<summary>This page concludes Sukta 34 with a blessing for the patron Shaci and begins Sukta 35, a prayer by Rishi Prabhūvasu asking Indra to bring his most effective protection and wisdom to the people.</summary>
<keywords>Indra, Shaci, Prabhūvasu Āṅgirasa, Kratu (wisdom/will), Pankti metre, Anushtubh metre, protection, five tribes, Ashvalayana Shrauta Sutra</keywords>

<meta>This page continues the commentary on Rig Veda, Mandala 5, Sukta 35. The previous page introduced the hymn as being revealed to the Rishi Prabhūvasu Āṅgirasa, dedicated to Indra. # Mandala 5, Anuvaka 3, Hymn 35 || Fourth Book ||

O Indra, your protections <note>original: "ऊतयः" (ūtayaḥ)</note> which are established among the four castes <term>Varnas: the four social classes of Vedic society</term> and those which, O Hero, exist in the three worlds. Or—taking the word "or" to mean "and"—the five protections belonging to the five tribes <term>Pancha-janas: the five groups of people frequently referenced in the Rig Veda</term>; bring all that excellent protection <note>original: "अवो" (avo)</note> well to us. Bring it here.

---

-> ॥ Now the Third Verse ॥ <-

## Hymn Text

We invoke that desirable protection of yours, O most bountiful one. For you were born with a rushing force, O Indra, overcoming all with your pervading powers. ॥ 3 ॥

**We | invoke | that | protection | desirable | of the most bountiful |**
**With a rushing force | for | you were born | with pervading powers | Indra | overcoming ॥ 3 ॥**

## Commentary (Sayana)

O Indra, we invoke <note>original: "आहूमहे" (āhūmahe)</note> your protection—or your arrival—which is desirable, for you are the greatest showerer <note>original: "वृषंतमस्य" (vṛṣantamasya); one who pours down rewards like rain</note> of fruits. O Indra, you who move with the speed of rain <note>original: "वृषजूतिः" (vṛṣajūtiḥ)</note> and who are the swiftest overcomer or destroyer of enemies; you truly manifest <note>original: "जज्ञिषे" (jajñiṣe)</note> protection through your pervading powers, which are as pervasive as the light or the waters. We call upon those protections. Alternatively: having the gait of a bull, you have come to the sacrifice today and produced the fruit of the ritual; therefore, we call for your protection.

---

-> ॥ Now the Fourth Verse ॥ <-

## Hymn Text

For you are the showerer; you were born for the sake of prosperity. Your strength is a showering force. Your mind is self-governing and bold, O Indra, and your manly power is all-conquering. ॥ 4 ॥

**Showerer | for | you are | for prosperity | you were born | showering | your | strength |**
**Self-governing | your | bold | mind | together | I | Indra | manly power ॥ 4 ॥**

## Commentary (Sayana)

O Indra, for the prosperity <note>original: "राधसे" (rādhase)</note> of the sacrificers, you are indeed the showerer. You are the bestower of the fruits of the ritual. Or, you are truly the showerer, and you are born for the sake of bestowing wealth. Your strength <note>original: "शवः" (śavaḥ)</note> is a showering force. Your mind is self-governing <note>original: "स्वक्षत्रं" (svakṣatram)</note>, meaning your power is under your own control, and it is bold, capable of overwhelming opponents. O Indra, your manly power <note>original: "पौंस्यं" (pauṃsyam)</note> is that which destroys the gathered hosts of the enemy.

---

-> ॥ Now the Fifth Verse ॥ <-

## Hymn Text

O Indra, master of power, you who possess a hundred wisdoms, drive down with all your chariots toward that mortal who... ॥ 5 ॥

**You | that | Indra | mortal | ...**

<summary>This page contains verses 3 and 4 of Sukta 35, where the poet invokes Indra's protection and praises his inherent strength, self-governing mind, and ability to bestow wealth upon the five tribes.</summary>
<keywords>Indra, Vṛṣantama, protection (avah), five tribes (pancha-janas), prosperity (radhas), manly power (paumsya), Sayana, Rig Veda commentary</keywords>

# Rig Veda [Book 4, Chapter 2, Section 6]

## Hymn Text (Word-by-word breakdown)
<note>RV 6.32.5</note>

To that | To that | Indra | mortal | acting as an enemy | O wielder of the thunderbolt |
With all-pervading chariots | O performer of a hundred rites | thus | performer of a hundred rites | down | come | of power | O Lord ॥ 5 ॥

---

## Commentary (Sayana)
O **Indra**, to that mortal who acts with enmity or desires to be an enemy—O **wielder of the thunderbolt** <note>original: "अद्रिवो" (adrivo); referring to the Vajra or stone weapon</note>, O Indra—with a chariot that pervades everywhere <note>original: "सर्वरथा" (sarvarathā)</note>—O **performer of a hundred rites** <note>original: "शतक्रतो" (śatakrato); one of Indra's primary titles signifying immense power or many sacrifices</note>, O **Lord of power** <note>original: "शवसस्पते" (śavasaspate)</note>, Indra, come down. Come down specifically to overcome him.

-> ॥ Thus ends the fifth section in the second chapter of the fourth book ॥ <-

## Hymn Text
<note>RV 6.33.1</note>
-> ॥ Now the Sixth Verse ॥ <-

**You indeed, O greatest slayer of Vritra, the people who have prepared the sacrificial grass,**
**the fierce and ancient one among the many, they call for the winning of strength. ॥ 6 ॥**

### Word-by-word breakdown
You | indeed | O greatest slayer of Vritra | people | those who have prepared the sacrificial grass |
fierce | among many | ancient | they call | for the winning of strength ॥ 6 ॥

---

## Commentary (Sayana)
O **greatest slayer of Vritra** <note>original: "वृत्रहन्तम" (vṛtrahantama)</note>, most excellent destroyer of enemies, O Indra, you alone do the people <note>original: "जनासो" (janāso)</note> call upon—those **who have prepared the sacrificial grass** <note>original: "वृक्तबर्हिष" (vṛktabarhiṣa); those who have spread the sacred Darbha grass on the altar, meaning they have commenced the sacrifice</note>. They call upon the **fierce** one of heightened strength, who is the **ancient** one existing among **many** subjects, for the **winning of strength** <note>original: "वाजसातये" (vājassātaye); meaning for battle or for the attainment of food and booty</note>. They invoke you.

---

## Hymn Text
<note>RV 6.33.2</note>
-> ॥ Now the Seventh Verse ॥ <-

**O Indra, protect our invincible chariot that goes in front in battles,**
**that moves with followers and seeks booty in every contest. ॥ 7 ॥**

### Word-by-word breakdown
Our | Indra | invincible | going in front | in battles |
going together | in every wealth | desiring booty | protect | chariot ॥ 7 ॥

---

## Commentary (Sayana)
O **Indra**, protect <note>original: "अव" (ava)</note> **our chariot** <note>original: "रथं" (rathaṃ); interpreted here as either the physical vehicle or a son who is swift and capable</note>. What kind of chariot? One that is **invincible** or difficult for enemies to overcome; one **going in front** in battles, leading the way; one **going together** with followers or attendants; and one **desiring booty** <note>original: "वाजयंतं" (vājayantaṃ)</note> or seeking battle and wealth in **every contest** <note>original: "धने धने" (dhane dhane); literally "in wealth after wealth," referring to the prizes of war</note>.

---

## Hymn Text
<note>RV 6.33.3</note>
-> ॥ Now the Eighth Verse ॥ <-

**O Indra, prosper our chariot; protect us with wisdom.**
**O most powerful one, may we establish glory in heaven; in heaven we contemplate the hymn. ॥ 8 ॥**

# Mandala 5, Hymn 36 | The Fourth Book | Page 399

## Hymn Text (RV 5.35.8 - Word-by-word breakdown)

Ours | O Indra | hither | come | our | chariot | protect | with wisdom |
we | O most powerful | choice [wealth] | in heaven | fame | we may place | in heaven | praise | we meditate ॥ 8 ॥

---

## Commentary (Sayana)

O **Indra**, come to us, remaining as our protector alone. Having arrived, protect our chariot with your excellent wisdom <note>original: "पुरंध्या" (purandhyā); glossed as "shobhana-buddhyā" or beautiful intellect</note>. And we, O **most powerful one** <note>original: "शविष्ठ" (śaviṣṭha); most exceedingly strong</note>, by your grace, may we place "choice" fame or food <note>original: "श्रवः" (śravaḥ); can mean both reputation and sacrificial food</note> in the shining heaven—that is, within you. Likewise, we perform—or meditate upon—this hymn of praise <note>original: "स्तोमं" (stoma); a sacrificial song</note> for you in heaven.

-> ॥ This ends the sixth section in the second chapter of the fourth book ॥ <-

The fourth hymn in this section, beginning with "May he come," consists of six verses. The **Seer** <note>original: "ऋषि" (ṛṣi); the poet-sage who "saw" the mantra</note> is **Prabhuvasu**, of the lineage of **Angiras**. The third verse is in the **Jagati** meter <note>48 syllables</note>, while the remaining verses, being unstated, are in the **Trishtubh** meter <note>44 syllables</note>. The deity is **Indra**. As stated in the index: "May he come, six verses, the third is Jagati." Its ritual application follows its thematic characteristics.

---

## Hymn Text (RV 5.36.1)

-> ॥ The First Verse ॥ <-

**May that Indra come, he who knows how to grant the wealth of the Vasus, the giver of riches.**
**Like an archer wandering the desert, or like a thirsty bull, desiring the draught, let him drink the pressed Soma juice. ॥ 1 ॥**

**Word-by-word breakdown:**
He | hither | may come | Indra | who | of the Vasus | knows | to give | giver | of riches |
desert-wandering | like | a bull | thirsty | desiring | let him drink | pressed | Soma-stalk [juice] ॥ 1 ॥

---

## Commentary (Sayana)

May that **Indra** come toward our sacrifice. He is the god who knows how to grant the riches <note>original: "वसूनां" (vasūnām); wealth or the treasures of the Vasu-gods</note>—the grammar here uses the sixth case to denote the object. He is the giver, or one whose mind is set on giving wealth. A comparison for his arrival is given: like an archer <note>original: "धन्वचरः" (dhanvacaraḥ)</note> traveling with a bow, or like a bull <note>original: "वंसगः" (vaṃsagaḥ)</note> with a desirable gait who is extremely thirsty and full of desire, let him drink this pressed **Soma** juice <note>original: "अंशुम्" (aṃśum); literally "the stalk," referring to the juice extracted from the plant</note>.

# Mandala 10, Hymn 42 | The Eighth Book | Page 314

### Header: || Rig Veda || [Book 8, Chapter 4, Hymn 2, Section 7]

The term refers to the jaws <note>original: "शिप्रा" (śiprā); can refer to the jaws, cheeks, or the visor of a helmet</note>, yet the repetition of the word for jaws should not be seen as improper. May the Soma <note>the sacred sacrificial nectar</note> reach or ascend into the well-formed or clenched jaws. It does not "climb" upon the back of the mountain; that is, it does not remain there. Alternatively, the word "not" <note>original: "na"</note> used earlier can imply a comparison: like Soma on the mountain's peak. Just as it flows there with confidence, so too here. O radiant King Indra, following you—along with that <note>The grammar implies "with the song"</note>—all of us, like those tending to horses with grass, please you with our songs and praises. Let us rejoice, O much-invoked Indra, you who are called upon in many ways by many people.

---

-> ॥ Now the Third Verse ॥ <-

**Like a rotating wheel, O much-invoked one, my mind trembles with fear of the ignorant, O wielder of the stone. From the chariot, may the singer, O ever-increasing one, quickly praise you, O bounteous one, who possesses many riches.** ॥ 3 ॥

**Word-by-word Breakdown**
Wheel | Like | Rotating | O much-invoked one | Trembles | Mind | Fear | My | Of the ignorant | Indeed | O wielder of the stone | From the chariot | Above | You | Singer | O ever-increasing one | Surely | Now | May he praise | O bounteous one | Possessing many riches ॥ 3 ॥

## Commentary (Sayana)
O **much-invoked** <note>original: "puruhūta"</note> Indra, called upon by many, and O **wielder of the stone** <note>original: "adrivaḥ"; referring to the thunderbolt or the Soma-pressing stone</note>, my mind trembles with fear because of the "ignorant" <note>original: "amateḥ"; those who do not know or acknowledge the gods</note>. It shakes like a **rotating wheel** moving upon the ground. Because of this, the **singer** <note>original: "jaritā"</note>—the seer of this hymn who is **ever-increasing** in devotion and **possessing many riches**—situated above the chariot, will surely and quickly praise you, O **bounteous** <note>original: "maghavan"</note> Indra. 

---

-> ॥ Now the Fourth Verse ॥ <-

**This singer, like the pressing-stone, sends forth his voice to you, O Indra, while seeking great rewards. O bounteous one, grant us riches with your left hand; and with your right, O wielder of the bay horses, do not turn away from us.** ॥ 4 ॥

**Word-by-word Breakdown**
This | Like a pressing-stone | Singer | To you | O Indra | Sends forth | Voice | Great | Seeking | Forth | With the left [hand] | O bounteous one | You grant | Riches | Forth | From the right [hand] | O wielder of the bay horses | Do not | Turn away ॥ 4 ॥

## Commentary (Sayana)
This **singer** <note>original: "jaritā"</note> is like the **pressing-stone** <note>original: "grāva"</note> used to extract Soma. Just as the stone produces the sacred juice, he "sends forth" his voice and praise to you, O Indra. He does this while **seeking great rewards** <note>original: "āśuṣāṇaḥ"; quickly enjoying or attaining the fruits of the ritual</note>. O **bounteous one**, grant us **riches** <note>original: "rāyaḥ"</note> with your left hand; and it is understood that you should also grant them with your right. O **wielder of the bay horses** <note>original: "harivaḥ"</note>, do not be "without desire" <note>original: "mā vi venaḥ"; do not turn away or become indifferent to our prayer</note>.

<summary>This page contains the commentary for Rig Veda 10.42.3-4, where the poet-sage expresses anxiety toward the "ignorant" and urges Indra to provide wealth and protection, using the metaphor of a pressing-stone for the act of praise.</summary>
<keywords>Indra, Soma, pressing-stone, Maghavan, Jarita, wealth, Rig Veda commentary, Sayana</keywords>

### Header: [Mandala 5, Hymn 37, Verse 37.] || The Fourth Book ||

-> ॥ Now the Fifth Verse ॥ <-

## Hymn Text

**May the potent showerer, the Heaven, increase you, the potent showerer; you are carried by the two potent bay horses. So, as the potent showerer with the potent chariot, O fair-jawed one, O you of potent deeds, O potent wielder of the thunderbolt, sustain us in battle.** ॥ 5 ॥

**Potent showerer | you | potent showerer | may increase | Heaven | potent showerer | by the two potent ones | you are carried | by the two bay horses |
He | us | potent showerer | of the potent chariot | O fair-jawed one | O you of potent deeds | O potent one | O wielder of the thunderbolt |
In battle | sustain** ॥ 5 ॥

---

## Commentary (Sayana)

O **Indra**, may the **potent showerer** <note>original: "vṛṣā" (vṛṣā); here referring to the one who rains down blessings</note>, the shining **Heaven** <note>original: "dyauḥ"; the commentator notes this can also represent "shining praise" derived from the root meaning to shine</note>, increase you. May it increase you, the **potent showerer** <note>original: "vṛṣaṇam"</note> who fulfills all desires. You, the potent one, are **carried** <note>original: "vahase"</note> toward the sacrifice by the two **potent** <note>original: "vṛṣabhyām"</note> **bay horses** <note>original: "haribhyām"</note>. O **fair-jawed one** <note>original: "suśipra"; referring to well-formed cheeks or jaws</note>, O you of **potent deeds** <note>original: "vṛṣakrato"</note>, O **thunderbolt-wielder** <note>original: "vajrin"</note> Indra, being yourself potent and possessing a **potent chariot** <note>original: "vṛṣaratha"</note>, **sustain** <note>original: "dhāḥ"</note> us in **battle** <note>original: "bhare"</note>—which is the "bearing" of arms—or in the sacrifice which sustains us.

---

-> ॥ Now the Sixth Verse ॥ <-

## Hymn Text

**He who bestowed the two spirited red horses, he the master of riches, accompanied by three hundred, has been declared. To this young Shrutaratha, may the people bow with service, and may the Maruts also be favorable.** ॥ 6 ॥

**He | the two red ones | the two spirited ones | the master of riches | by three | hundreds | being accompanied | he bestowed |
To the young | together | to him | the people | may they bow | to Shrutaratha | the Maruts | with service** ॥ 6 ॥

---

## Commentary (Sayana)

This verse is a **praise of the gift** <note>original: "dāna-stuti"</note> given by King **Shrutaratha**. **He**, the king, who is the **master of riches** <note>original: "vājinīvān"</note> and who possesses the famous chariot (**Shrutaratha**), **bestowed** <note>original: "adiṣṭa"</note> **two red** <note>original: "rohitau"</note> **spirited horses** <note>original: "vājinau"</note> along with the stated number of **three hundred** cows or pieces of wealth. To this **young** <note>original: "yūne"</note> king, who is ever-youthful or who mingles with all, let all **people** <note>original: "kṣitayaḥ"</note> **bow down** <note>original: "samnamantām"</note> in greeting with **service** <note>original: "duvoyā"</note>. The mention of the **Maruts** <note>original: "marutaḥ"</note> is an address to the Storm Gods who are the helpers of Indra.

-> ॥ Thus ends the seventh section of the second chapter of the fourth book ॥ <-

# || Rig Veda || [Book 4, Chapter 2, Group 8]

-> ॥ Here is the First Verse ॥ <-

## Hymn Text
He strives with the brilliance of the sun, being invoked, his back glistening with clarified butter, moving gracefully. For him, the unfailing Dawns shall shine—for the one who says, "Let us press the Soma for Indra!" ॥ 1 ॥

> Together | with brilliance | he strives | of the sun | being invoked | butter-backed | moving gracefully |
> For him | unfailing | Dawns | [shall] shine | who | for Indra | let us press | [thus] | says ॥ 1 ॥

---

## Commentary (Sayana)
Being invoked everywhere along with the brilliance—the light—of the sun... <note>original: "karmaṇi kartṛ-pratyayaḥ"; a grammatical note indicating a passive construction used in an active sense</note>. The fire <note>original: "Agni"</note>, whose flames are ignited and whose "back" is covered with clarified butter <note>original: "ghṛta-pṛṣṭhaḥ"</note>, or whose surface is coated with ghee, and who moves gracefully, exerts himself well. Indeed, the sacrificial fires are kindled at the time of sunrise. For this reason, the patron <term>Yajamana|The sponsor of the Vedic sacrifice</term> who speaks to the executive priest <term>Adhvaryu|The priest responsible for the physical manual labor of the ritual</term> saying, "Let us press the Soma for Indra," for that patron, the unfailing <note>original: "amṛdhrāḥ"; unharming or persistent</note> Dawns <note>original: "Uṣasaḥ"</note> shall shine. The meaning is: for the one who says, "The fire is kindled at sunrise, therefore let us perform the Soma sacrifice," his days become truly auspicious.

---

-> ॥ Now the Second Verse ॥ <-

## Hymn Text
With the fire kindled, possessing wealth, the sacred grass spread, the pressing-stones ready, and the Soma pressed—he sings. The stones of him who speaks make a desirable sound, as the priest approaches the water with the oblation. ॥ 2 ॥

> Kindled-fire | possessing wealth | spread-grass | ready-stones | pressed-soma | he sings |
> Stones | whose | desirable | speak | priest | with oblation | down [to] | the river/water ॥ 2 ॥

---

## Commentary (Sayana)
This patron, having the fire kindled and the sacred grass <term>barhis|The sacrificial grass spread on the altar as a seat for the deities</term> laid out, obtains wealth <note>original: "vanavat"; he shares in or possesses</note>. With the pressing-stones <note>original: "grāvāṇaḥ"</note> employed and the Soma juice extracted, he sings or praises. The pressing-stones of that priest <note>original: "Adhvaryu"</note> utter a desirable or moving sound; that priest then approaches the water <note>original: "sindhum"; here referring to the ceremonial waters or the "Pannejani" waters used in the rite</note> along with the oblation.

---

-> ॥ Now the Third Verse ॥ <-

## Hymn Text
This bride comes seeking a husband, he who will carry her as a vigorous queen. Out of a desire for glory, his chariot shall thunder and roll across many thousands. ॥ 3 ॥

> Bride | this | husband | desiring | goes | who | her | carries | queen | vigorous |
> Toward | his | from desire for glory | chariot | toward | and | will sound | many | thousands | around | will turn ॥ 3 ॥

<vocab>
**Bhanu** (भानु) - light or ray; **Ghritaprishtha** (घृतपृष्ठ) - having a back of ghee; **Amridhra** (अमृध्रा) - unharming or unfailing; **Ushas** (उषस्) - the Dawn goddess; **Adhvaryu** (अध्वर्यु) - the ritual priest; **Yajamana** (यजमान) - the patron of the sacrifice; **Gravana** (ग्रावाण) - stones used to crush the Soma plant; **Ishira** (इषिर) - quick, vigorous, or desirable; **Vadhu** (वधू) - a bride; **Mahishi** (महिषी) - a consecrated queen; **Shravasyat** (श्रवस्यात्) - seeking fame or glory.
</vocab>

# || Rig Veda || [Book 4, Chapter 2, Group 8]

This wife <note>Indra’s wife, Indrani</note>, the queen of Indra, desiring her husband—desiring him who has set out for the journey of the sacrifice—comes forward. She follows him. When Indra carries this queen with his swift-moving horses, may the patron <term>Yajamana|The sponsor of the sacrifice</term> be seated upon Indra’s chariot, facing towards us. He desires food. And he shouts aloud; he makes a celebratory sound. He brings about and obtains thousands upon thousands of riches in every direction. The phrases "may he be facing" and "may he shout" refer to this same prosperity.

---

-> ॥ Here is the Fourth Verse ॥ <-

## Hymn Text
That king does not waver in whom Indra drinks the sharp Soma mixed with milk. With his brave followers, he drives forth and slays the obstacle; he dwells among the people, a lucky man, nourishing his renown. ॥ 4 ॥

**Word-by-word Analysis:**
Not | that | king | wavers | in whom | Indra | the sharp | Soma | drinks | cow-friended <note>original: "go-sakhāyam"; refers to Soma mixed with milk</note> |
Forth | with brave followers | he drives | he slays | the obstacle <note>original: "Vṛtram"; the demon Vritra or a general enemy</note> | he dwells | among the people | fortunate | his name | nourishing ॥ 4 ॥

---

## Commentary (Sayana)
That king does not waver; he does not become agitated or fearful. In the sacrifice of this king, Indra drinks the sharp Soma, which is intoxicating and "cow-friended." This is a technical use of language where the source material <note>original: "vikāre prakṛti-śabdaḥ"</note>—the cow—is used to mean its products, like milk, which are mixed into the drink. That king, accompanied by his brave followers or attendants <note>original: "satvanaiḥ"</note>, drives forward in all directions. He slays "Vritra," which can mean either the personification of sin or a physical enemy. He moves among the people, or alternatively, he dwells securely in his residences. He is "fortunate" <note>original: "subhagaḥ"</note>, meaning one possessed of beautiful happiness, while nourishing his "name"—which refers either to his reputation or to the wealth and praises offered to Indra.

---

-> ॥ Here is the Fifth Verse ॥ <-

## Hymn Text
May he prosper in peace, may he be superior in acquisition; may he conquer both the contending hosts. May he be dear to the Sun and dear to Agni, he who has pressed the Soma and gives it to Indra. ॥ 5 ॥

**Word-by-word Analysis:**
May he nourish | in peace | over | acquisition | may he be | both | hosts | contending | well | may he conquer |
Dear | to the Sun | dear | to Agni | may he be | who | for Indra | with pressed Soma | gives ॥ 5 ॥

---

## Commentary (Sayana)
May he nourish or increase his horses and possessions. In "peace" <term>Kshema|The preservation of wealth already acquired</term> and in "acquisition" <term>Yoga|The attainment of what is not yet possessed</term>, may he be superior. The prefix "over" <note>original: "abhi"</note> either emphasizes the verb or suggests he becomes a powerful lord. Furthermore, may he conquer both "contending hosts." This refers to the regulated cycle of Day and Night <note>original: "ahorātre"</note>; may he master them so they become comfortable and beneficial for him. Additionally, that patron becomes dear to the Sun and dear to the Fire <note>original: "Agnau"</note>—specifically the one who, having pressed the Soma juice, offers it to Indra.

---

# || Rig Veda || [Book 4, Chapter 2, Group 9]

This sixth hymn, beginning with "Uroṣṭa," contains five verses. It is attributed to the sage Airāṣma, composed in the Anushtubh meter, and dedicated to the god Indra. The Anukramani <note>the ancient Vedic index</note> notes: "Uroṣṭa is in the Anushtubh meter." The application of the hymn is determined by its characteristic marks <term>lingika|usage based on the divine attributes mentioned in the text</term>.

-> ॥ Here is the First Verse ॥ <-

## Hymn Text

Wide, O Indra, is your gift of wealth, O performer of a hundred acts.
Now then, O observer of all people, increase our glories and provide excellent riches. ॥ 1 ॥

**Word-by-word Analysis:**
Wide | your | Indra | of wealth | extensive | gift | O performer of a hundred acts <note>original: "śatakrato"; often referring to Indra’s many powers or sacrifices</note> |
Now | our | O observer of all people <note>original: "viśvacarṣaṇe"</note> | glories | excellent wealth | and | increase ॥ 1 ॥

---

## Commentary (Sayana)

O **Indra**, O **Shatakratu** <note>original: "śatakrato"; he of a hundred deeds</note>, the **gift** or act of giving of **your** "wide" or abundant **wealth** is **extensive** and great. **Now, for this reason**, grant **to us**, O **Vishvacharshane** <note>original: "viśvacarṣaṇe"; he who watches over all people</note>, O Indra who possesses beautiful wealth—here, the word **'kshah'** is a synonym for wealth—**increase** or bestow upon us **glories**, which is to say, many forms of riches.

---

-> ॥ Now the Second Verse ॥ <-

## Hymn Text

Since you, O most powerful Indra, possess that famous food,
It spreads abroad as the most widely heard of fame, golden-hued and insurmountable. ॥ 2 ॥

**Word-by-word Analysis:**
Since | indeed | Indra | famous | food | O most powerful | you possess |
It spreads | most widely heard | golden-colored | insurmountable ॥ 2 ॥

---

## Commentary (Sayana)

O **Indra**, O **Shavishtha** <note>original: "śaviṣṭha"; most mighty</note>, **since** you **possess** or grant that **food which is famous** and worthy of being heard about everywhere—note that the word for food, **'isha'**, is used here in the neuter gender—O **golden-hued Indra**, that food **spreads** or increases. In what way? It is **the most widely heard**, meaning its fame is to be celebrated everywhere. It spreads as that which is **insurmountable**, possessing the qualities described above.

---

-> ॥ Now the Third Verse ॥ <-

## Hymn Text

## Commentary (Sayana)
...rules. The term *mehanā* <note>original: "mehanā"</note> refers to that which is honorable or worthy of praise. ## Commentary (Sayana)
And also, O **Slayer of Vritra** <note>original: "vṛtrahan"; an epithet for Indra</note>, bring to us the wealth or strength of this certain indescribable or greatly increased giver. Bring it to us, your own people. The repetition of "for us" is intended to show earnestness or respect. O Indra, bring near the wealth <note>Sayana interprets "nṛmaṇā" here as "nṛmṇāṃ," meaning riches</note>. O Indra, because you desire wealth for us, you act with a benevolent mind toward us.

## Hymn Text
->॥ Here is the Fifth Verse ॥<-

## Commentary (Sayana)
O **Indra, Lord of a hundred acts** <note>original: "śatakrato"; referring to Indra's numerous ritual sacrifices or powers</note>, with these "approaches" or protections of yours, may we quickly become prosperous <note>Sayana adds "prosperous" to complete the sense</note>. O Indra, while in your shelter <note>original: "śarman"</note>—which means your happiness or protection—may we be well-guarded. ## Commentary (Introduction to Hymn 40)
The seventh hymn, beginning with **"Yadindra cicceti,"** consists of five verses. It is attributed to the seer Atri, son of Atri <note>original: "atrirātreya"</note>, and is dedicated to Indra. The final verse is in the Pankti meter; the remaining verses are in the Anushtubh meter, following the definition for Pankti-ended sequences. The **Anukramani** <note>the ancient Vedic index</note> states: "Yadindra is in the Pankti-ended meter." In the *Abhiplavika* rituals <note>a type of six-day Soma sacrifice</note>, specifically during the *Ukthya* rites of the third pressing, the first triplet <note>three verses</note> may optionally be used as the *Stotriya* <note>chant</note> for the *Acchavaka* priest. This is indicated in the ritual manuals: "Yadindra citra mehanā yaste sādhiṣṭho’vase" <note>Ashvalayana Shrauta Sutra 7.8</note>.

## Commentary (Sayana)

**To him indeed**, to this very Indra, the **poetic** <note>original: "kāvyaṃ"</note> work—that which relates to the poet or singer—or perhaps "that which is to be sounded" (from the root *ku* meaning 'to sound'), the **word**, and the **hymn** <note>original: "uktham"</note> or weapon of praise, is **to be recited**. Because of this, **to him**, to that very Indra who is the **carrier of the great prayer** <note>original: "brahmavāhase"; the one who bears or receives the matured prayer</note>, the **singers** <note>original: "arcayaḥ"; referring to those of the Archi lineage</note> **increase** the **songs** or praises. The **singers beautify** <note>original: "śumbhanti"</note> or illuminate the **songs**. The repetition of these words is for the sake of showing great respect.

## Critical Notes

<note>Introductory commentary for Hymn 40</note>

**"Come with the stones"** <note>original: "ā yāhy adribhiḥ"</note> is the eighth hymn, consisting of nine verses. Here is the **index of contents** <term>Anukramani|A systematic index of Vedic hymns providing the poet, meter, and deity</term>. The hymn beginning with "Come" <note>original: "ā yāhi"</note> has nine verses. The first is in the **Ushnih** meter; the last is in the **Anushtubh** meter. In the middle, there is a verse dedicated to the Sun <note>original: "Saurī"</note>; there is an ancient story regarding this because the Sun is the deity of the praise-action. The seer <term>Rishi|An inspired poet or sage of the Vedic hymns</term> of the entire hymn, by general definition, is Atri, specifically the sage **Archis**. The first three verses are in the **Ushnih** meter <note>A poetic meter of 28 syllables</note>. The fifth and ninth verses are in the **Anushtubh** meter <note>A meter of 32 syllables</note>. The remaining four are in the **Trishtubh** meter <note>A meter of 44 syllables</note>. Because the sage Atri is being praised, the sixth and following verses have **Atri** as their deity and were seen by the sage Archis. The fifth verse is dedicated to the deity **Surya** (the Sun). The rest are dedicated to **Indra**. This is used on the third day of the **Dasharatra** <note>A ten-night sacrificial ritual</note>.

## || Rig-Veda || [Book 4, Chapter 2, Section 11]

## Hymn Text

->॥ 1 ॥<-
Come, O Indra, with the pressing-stones; drink the pressed Soma, O Lord of Soma! O powerful one, O Indra, with the powerful [Maruts], O greatest slayer of Vritra. ॥ 1 ॥
<note>RV 6.044.22</note>

**Word-by-word Analysis:**
Come | Come | with the stones | the pressed [juice] | the Soma | O Lord of Soma | drink | O powerful one | O Indra | with the powerful ones | O greatest slayer of Vritra ॥ 1 ॥

---

->॥ 2 ॥<-
Powerful is the pressing-stone; powerful is the exhilaration; powerful is this pressed Soma. O powerful Indra, with the powerful [Maruts], O greatest slayer of Vritra. ॥ 2 ॥
<note>RV 6.044.23</note>

**Word-by-word Analysis:**
Powerful | the pressing-stone | powerful | the exhilaration | powerful | the Soma | this | pressed | O powerful one | O Indra | with the powerful ones | O greatest slayer of Vritra ॥ 2 ॥

---

->॥ 3 ॥<-
As a powerful one, I call upon you, the powerful one, O wielder of the thunderbolt, with your various aids. O powerful Indra, with the powerful [Maruts], O greatest slayer of Vritra. ॥ 3 ॥
<note>RV 6.044.24</note>

**Word-by-word Analysis:**
Powerful [the caller] | you | the powerful [Indra] | I call | O wielder of the thunderbolt | with various/wonderful | with aids/protections | O powerful one | O Indra | with the powerful ones | O greatest slayer of Vritra ॥ 3 ॥

---

## Commentary (Sayana)

This first triplet <note>original: "tṛca"; a group of three verses</note> is the fifth part of the *Prauga-shastra* <note>a specific litany recited during the morning libation</note> dedicated to Indra. This is indicated in the ritual manuals: "Come with the stones, with all the gods." <note>A reference to the Ashvalayana Shrauta Sutra 1.10</note>. This triplet is also used during the *Mahavrata* rite <note>an important seasonal festival</note> within the collection of eighty verses in the *Ushnih* meter.

->॥ Commentary on the First Verse ॥<-

O **Indra**, **come**! Approach our sacrifice. Having arrived, O **Lord of Soma** <note>original: "somapate"; the master or protector of the Soma juice</note>, O Indra, **drink the Soma** that has been **pressed** <note>original: "sutam"</note> by the **stones** <note>original: "adribhiḥ"; referring to the stones used to crush the Soma stalks</note>. O **powerful one** <note>original: "vṛṣan"; literally "the bull," but interpreted here as the "showerer of rewards"</note>, O **greatest slayer of Vritra** <note>original: "vṛtrahantama"; the one who is most excellent at destroying enemies or the demon of drought</note>, come and drink with the **powerful ones** <note>original: "vṛṣabhiḥ"</note>, referring to the Maruts <note>storm deities</note> who also shower rewards.

->॥ Commentary on the Second Verse ॥<-

The **pressing-stone** <note>original: "grāvā"</note>, which is the instrument for extraction, is **powerful** <note>original: "vṛṣā"</note>, meaning it showers forth the Soma juice or brings about rewards. The **exhilaration** <note>original: "madaḥ"</note> produced by drinking the Soma is also **powerful**. **This** very **pressed Soma** is **powerful**. Drink that Soma with the **powerful** ones <note>the Maruts</note>.

->॥ Commentary on the Third Verse ॥<-

O **wielder of the thunderbolt** <note>original: "vajrin"</note>, O Indra, I, the **powerful one** <note>original: "vṛṣā"; here referring to the human sacrificer as the "pourer" of the juice</note>, **call upon** <note>original: "huve"</note> **you**, the **powerful one** <note>original: "vṛṣaṇam"</note>. For what purpose? For the sake of your **various** <note>original: "citrābhiḥ"; wonderful or desirable</note> **aids** <note>original: "ūtibhiḥ"; protections or helps</note>. The rest of the meaning is as previously explained.
