### [ Mandala 5, Anuvaka 3, Hymn 40 ] || Fourth Ashtaka || 387

The verse beginning "Owner of the Soma-residue, wielder of the thunderbolt" <note>original: "ṛjīṣī vajrī..."</note> is the offering-prayer <note>term: yājyā; a verse recited by the Hotri priest while the oblation is poured</note> for the priest known as the *Brahmanacchamsin*. It is specifically indicated in the ritual manuals: "The offering-prayer is 'Owner of the Soma-residue, wielder of the thunderbolt, the bull-like lord, the overcomer of the swift'" <note>original: "ṛjīṣī vajrī vṛṣabhasturāṣāḍiti yājyā"; quoting Ashvalayana Shrauta Sutra 5.16</note>.

->॥ This is the Fourth Verse ॥<-

## Hymn Text

The owner of the Soma-residue, wielder of the thunderbolt, the bull-like lord, the overcomer of the swift, the powerful king, slayer of Vritra, and drinker of Soma—yoking his two bay horses, may Indra come here to us and rejoice at the midday libation. ॥ 4 ॥

**Word-by-word Analysis:**
Owner of the residue | wielder of the thunderbolt | bull-like lord | overcomer of the swift | powerful | king | slayer of Vritra | drinker of Soma | yoking | with his two bay horses | hither | may he come | toward us | in the midday | libation | may he rejoice | Indra ॥ 4 ॥

---

## Commentary (Sayana)

**Owner of the Soma-residue:** <note>term: ṛjīṣī</note>. In the first two libations of the day, the Soma juice is pressed. The "residue" <note>term: ṛjīṣa</note> is the Soma plant after its primary juice has been extracted. This residue is then refreshed with water and pressed again for the third libation. One who possesses this is called the "Owner of the Residue." **Wielder of the thunderbolt:** possessor of the *Vajra* weapon. **Bull-like lord:** one who showers or bestows rewards. **Overcomer of the swift:** one who withstands or defeats enemies who are rushing or swift. **Powerful:** full of strength. **King:** the lord of all. **Slayer of Vritra:** the killer of the demon of obstruction. **Drinker of Soma:** the consumer of the Soma juice. May Indra, who possesses such great majesty, yoke his chariot with his two bay horses and **come hither** toward us. **At the midday libation:** <note>term: mādhyaṃdina savana; the second of the three daily Soma pressings</note>, may Indra **rejoice** or be exhilarated by the Soma juice.

---

->॥ Now the Fifth Verse ॥<-

## Hymn Text

When, O Sun, Svarbhanu of the Asura race pierced you with darkness, all the worlds appeared like one who is lost, not knowing the way. ॥ 5 ॥

**Word-by-word Analysis:**
When | you | O Sun | Svarbhanu | with darkness | pierced | the Asura | one not knowing the place | like | bewildered/lost | the worlds | appeared/were seen ॥ 5 ॥

---

## Commentary (Sayana)

With this verse and the three following it, the deeds of the **Atris** <note>a famous family of Vedic sages</note> are celebrated. **O Sun:** O god who impels all. **When** the **Asura**—either a son of the demon Asura or a "remover of life"—named **Svarbhanu pierced** or covered you with **darkness** created by his magic, then **all the worlds** <note>original: "bhuvanāni"</note> appeared as if they were **bewildered**. Just as a person in a strange place who does **not know the way** <note>original: "akṣetravit"</note> becomes confused and lost, so too did all living beings become terrified and confused by the sudden darkness of the eclipse.

->॥ This ends the 11th Section (Varga) of the 2nd Chapter (Adhyaya) of the 4th [Ashtaka] ॥<-

---

->॥ Now the Sixth Verse ॥<-

## Hymn Text

O Indra, when you struck down the magical arts of Svarbhanu which were operating below the heavens, Atri found the Sun, which had been hidden by the unholy darkness, through the fourth prayer. ॥ 6 ॥

# 388
### Rig Veda || Ashtaka 4, Adhyaya 2, Varga 12

## Commentary (Sayana)

<note>Continuing from the previous page's discussion of verse 6</note> After the bewilderment of the world, whatever magical illusions <note>original: "māyāḥ"</note> belonged to the demon <note>term: asura; a powerful, often chaotic being in Vedic myth</note> Svarbhanu, Indra struck them all down. What were these illusions like? They were existing below the shining Sun in heaven; the sense is that they were unable to actually obscure the Sun from above. 

Now follows an indirect reference to the Sage Atri. The Sun was hidden by a lawless darkness—"lawless" <note>original: "apavratena"</note> because darkness is an obstruction that prevents the performance of sacred rites. Through the "fourth prayer" <note>term: turiya brahma; a specific ritual formula or the fourth in a series of mantras</note>, which is identified with the formula "The Brahman of the pressing stones," Atri quickly found the Sun. That is, he obtained the means to remove the covering or found the pure Sun itself. This prayer is called the "fourth" in relation to the three preceding mantras. By removing one part of the illusion with each of the first three mantras, he drove away even the deep, hidden darkness with the fourth mantra.

->॥ This is the Seventh Verse ॥<-

## Hymn Text

"Let not the malevolent one, out of greed, devour me through terrifying darkness, for I am yours, O Atri! You are Mitra, whose gifts are true; may both you and King Varuna protect me here." ॥ 7 ॥

**Word-by-word Analysis:**
Not | me | this one | your | being | O Atri | through greed | the malevolent one | through fear | down | may he swallow | you | Mitra | are | of true wealth | those two | me | here | may they protect | Varuna | and | the King ॥ 7 ॥

---

## Commentary (Sayana)

These are the words of the Sun himself. "O Atri, let not the malevolent demon <note>original: "dugdhaḥ"</note>, who seeks to harm through the desire for another's possessions, swallow me down in this state—me, who belongs to you—by using the darkness that produces fear. Furthermore, O Friend <note>note: The Sun addresses Atri as 'Mitra' (Friend), which is also the name of a solar deity</note>, you are Mitra; you are a protector from destruction. You possess true wealth. May both you and King Varuna protect me here." Alternatively, it may be understood that Atri himself is being addressed as the god Mitra, who together with Varuna is asked for protection.

->॥ This is the Eighth Verse ॥<-

## Hymn Text

The Sage-Priest <note>term: Brahmā; the priest who oversees the ritual and protects it from errors</note>, yoking the pressing stones and worshipping the gods with reverence, seeking to please them with praise—Atri established the eye of the Sun in heaven and swept away the magical illusions of Svarbhanu. ॥ 8 ॥

**Word-by-word Analysis:**
The pressing stones | the Brahman | yoking | worshipping | with praise | the gods | with reverence | seeking to please | Atri | of the Sun | in heaven | the eye | [prefix] | established | of Svarbhanu | away | the magical illusions | he milked/swept away ॥ 8 ॥

---

## Commentary (Sayana)

The Brahman priest, namely Atri, seeking to please the gods with the prayer "protect us here," yoked the stones for the purpose of pressing <note>original: "abhiṣava"; the ritual extraction of Soma juice</note>... <note>The text ends mid-sentence as the page concludes</note>

<summary>Sage Atri uses a "fourth prayer" and ritual pressing stones to dispel the darkness of the demon Svarbhanu, successfully restoring the Sun to its place in heaven at the Sun's own plea.</summary>
<keywords>Atri, Svarbhanu, solar eclipse, Turiya Brahma, Mitra, Varuna, ritual restoration, pressing stones, Vedic myth</keywords>

<meta>This page concludes the commentary on the myth of the solar eclipse in Sukta 40, where the Sage Atri and Indra restore the Sun. It then transitions to Sukta 41, a hymn dedicated to the "All-Gods" (Vishvedevas), beginning with an invocation to Mitra and Varuna.</meta>

# 389
### Mandala 5, Sukta 41, Verse 1 || Ashtaka 4

## Commentary (Sayana)
<note>Continued commentary on Rig Veda 5.40.8 regarding the restoration of the Sun</note>

The phrase "the person yoking" <note>original: "jāno yuñjan"</note> means one who is pressing the <term>Soma</term><note>The sacred ritual drink offered to the gods</note> for the sake of Indra. Similarly, "with a hymn" <note>original: "kīriṇā"</note>—the word *kīri* refers to a prayer or hymn of praise that is "scattered" or broadcasted. By worshipping the gods with such hymns and mantras <note>original: "namasā"</note>, the sage placed the "eye" of the Sun—the all-pervading solar disc that impels everything—back into the sky and mid-air. This means he made it free from darkness. 

The text then clarifies: the magical illusions <note>original: "māyāḥ"</note> of the demon named <term>Svarbhanu</term><note>The Vedic demon responsible for eclipses</note>. These "illusions" are powers that dwell within the demon and bewilder others. As it is said, "By the fourth prayer" <note>original: "turīyeṇa brahmaṇā"</note>, Indra, aided by Atri, struck down and warded off those illusions. 

Alternatively, the third line can be explained as follows: regarding the Sun's light which was previously covered in heaven, Atri removed that obstruction and "placed the eye," meaning he witnessed the gathering together of the solar light once the blockage was gone. This covering of the Sun by Svarbhanu's magic is also mentioned in the *Haridravaka* <note>An ancient lost branch of the Veda</note>: 

"Svarbhanu, the <term>asura</term><note>A powerful, often chaotic celestial being</note>, pierced the Sun with darkness. The gods sought a remedy for him. When they struck off the first layer of darkness, it became a black cow; the second layer became a reddish cow; the third became a white cow; and when they cut away the last piece that remained..." and so on.

---

-> ॥ This is the Ninth Verse ॥ <-

## Hymn Text
<note>Rig Veda 5.40.9</note>

The Sun which Svarbhanu, the asura, had pierced with darkness—only the descendants of Atri found it; indeed, no others were able to do so. ॥ 9 ॥

**Word-by-word Analysis:**
Which | indeed | Sun | Svarbhanu | with darkness | pierced | the asura | the Atris | that [Sun] | subsequently | found | not | indeed | others | were able. ॥ 9 ॥

---

## Commentary (Sayana)

The poet repeats the description of this miraculous power: **"The Sun which..."** This verse is self-explanatory. The descendants of Atri found the Sun. Through the sequence of sacrifices for Indra, the praise of deities, and prostrations, they gradually resisted the darkness and regained the Sun. Truly, others were not able to find it.

-> ॥ This ends the twelfth Varga of the second Adhyaya in the fourth Ashtaka ॥ <-

---

## Commentary (Sayana)
<note>Introductory commentary for Sukta 41</note>

The ninth hymn of twenty verses, beginning **"Who indeed of you..."** <note>original: "ko nu vām"</note>, was seen by the Sage Atri, son of Bhauma. The sixteenth and seventeenth verses are in the *Atijagati* metre; the twentieth is in the *Ekapada Viraj* metre; the remaining seventeen are in the *Trishtubh* metre. The deities are the **Vishvedevas** <note>The "All-Gods," a collective group of Vedic deities</note>. As the Index <note>original: "Anukramani"</note> states: "The hymn 'Who indeed' has twenty verses and is addressed to the All-Gods; the sixteenth and following are *Atijagati*, and the final is *Ekapada*." The ritual application is determined by the specific markers in the verses.

-> ॥ Here is the first verse ॥ <-

## Hymn Text
<note>Rig Veda 5.41.1</note>

Who among you, O Mitra and Varuna, moving according to the Eternal Law, protects us from heaven or from the great earthly realm? In the seat of the Law, may you protect us for the sacrifice, like those who guard the cattle or our strengths. ॥ 1 ॥

---

<vocab>
- Svarbhānu: The demon of eclipse who "possesses the light of heaven."
- Atri: A legendary sage credited with unique ritual powers over light.
- Asura: A class of powerful beings; in this context, a demonic figure.
- Soma: The ritual nectar that empowers both gods and priests.
- Mitra-Varuṇa: Dual deities representing friendship/oaths and cosmic order.
- Turīya Brahma: The "fourth prayer," a specific high-potency ritual formula.
- Vishvedevas: The collective assembly of all the gods.
</vocab>

# 390 || Rig Veda || Book 4, Chapter 2, Varga 13

## Hymn Text

Who | indeed | of you two | O Mitra and Varuna | seeking the Law | from heaven | or | the great | of the earth | or | gods | of the Law | or | in the seat | may you two sit | for us | for the master of the sacrifice | or | having cattle | like | strengths. || 1 ||

---

->|| Now the second verse ||<-

May they—Mitra, Varuna, Aryaman, Ayu, Indra, Ribhuksha, and the Maruts—accept us; those who with bows (reverence) offer a well-purified hymn of praise to the bountiful Rudra, in harmony. || 2 ||

They | us | Mitra | Varuna | Aryaman | Ayu | Indra | Ribhuksha | Maruts | may they accept |
With bows | or | who | offer | well-purified | hymn of praise | to Rudra | to the bountiful | harmonious. || 2 ||

---

->|| Now the third verse ||<-

I invoke you two, the most excellent Ashvins, in the path of the wind and the abundance of the chariot; and to the Lord <note>original: "asurāya"</note> of Heaven, offer a prayer like sacrificial food for the one to be worshipped. || 3 ||

I | you two | most excellent | Ashvins | to invoke | of the wind | in the path | of the chariot | in the abundance |
And | or | of heaven | to the Lord | prayer | forth | like sacrificial foods | for the one to be worshipped | do you bring. || 3 ||

---

## Commentary (Sayana)

O divine Mitra and Varuna, who indeed <note>original: "kaḥ nu"</note> among the sacrificers desiring the rite <note>original: "ṛtāyan"</note> would be capable? <note>Sayana implies that the poet is uniquely capable of this worship.</note> Therefore, it has been performed by me alone. In the "seat of heaven," in the place belonging to the celestial world; and in the "seat of the great earth," and in the seat of the atmosphere which produces the earth—for the cause is often named by its effect. In these three places, may you two protect <note>original: "cāsīthāṃ"</note> us. The word "or" <note>original: "vā"</note> here is used in the sense of "and." Furthermore, to us and to the giver of the oblation, grant strengths <note>original: "vājān"</note>—that is, foods such as milk and curd that come from cattle—just as you provide those things, so protect us. Alternatively, the word "like" <note>original: "na"</note> acts as a conjunction, meaning: "Give us both cattle and strengths."

May those gods—Mitra and the others—accept <note>original: "juṣanta"</note> our well-purified hymn of praise <note>original: "suvṛktiṃ stomaṃ"</note>, which is a prayer that wards off sin, or may they accept it along with our oblations <note>original: "namobhir vā"</note>. Those who "offer" <note>original: "dadhate"</note> are those who maintain this described prayer. Gods are of two kinds: those who receive hymns and those who receive oblations. Here, the recipients of hymns are mentioned. "Ayu" <note>original: "āyuḥ"</note> refers to <term>Vayu</term><note>The god of the wind</note> because he is in constant motion. Then the <term>Maruts</term><note>The storm deities and companions of Indra</note> are distinguished as a separate group. "To the bountiful Rudra" <note>original: "rudrāya mīḷhuṣe"</note>: here the dative case <note>meaning "to/for"</note> is used in place of the instrumental case <note>meaning "with"</note>. The term "harmonious" <note>original: "sajoṣāḥ"</note> means being pleased together with Rudra. This refers to the Maruts, because they are known as the sons of Rudra. Some scholars, however, say that "harmonious with Rudra" is an adjective describing all the deities beginning with Mitra.

By this third verse, the Ashvins and Rudra are addressed. O Ashvins <note>original: "ashvinā"</note>, you who are the "most excellent" <note>original: "yeṣṭhā"</note> or the best guides of desires, I invoke you two...

---

# 391 || Fourth Book || 391

In the path of the wind. Due to the similarity of their functions, the term "righteous" is understood. When the horse, which moves with a speed equal to the wind, is acquired, and when there is a reason for the chariot’s strength, I invoke <note>original: "huve"</note>—that is, I am able to call upon you. Alternatively, it means: when there is a cause for the nourishment of the chariot, which is the means of your swift movement like the wind. Moreover <note>original: "uta vā"</note>, O officiating priests, bring forth <note>original: "prabharadhvam"</note>—that is, perform—a thoughtful hymn <note>original: "manma"</note> for the Divine Lord <note>original: "asurāya"</note> of the shining heavens. 

<note>The term "asura" here is used in its ancient Vedic sense of "powerful lord" or "divine being." Sayana offers two interpretations: it refers either to Rudra as the "taker of life-breath" (prāṇāpahartre) or to the Sun or Wind as the "giver of life-breath" (prāṇadātre).</note>

The hymn is for the one who facilitates the sacrifice <note>original: "yajyave"</note>. Bring the offerings, which are characterized by the sacrificial food <note>original: "andhāṃsīva"</note>, and the hymn of praise.

---

-> || Now the fourth verse || <-

## Hymn Text
The celestial overcomer, he who has the Kanva sages as his invokers, gathered from the heavens, the Wind and Agni who are of one mind; Pushan and Bhaga, the nourishers of all, have come to the offering like horses to a race—they who possess the swiftest steeds. || 4 ||

**Word-by-word breakdown:**
Forth | the overcomer | celestial | having the Kanvas as invokers | gathered | from heaven | of one mind | the Wind | Agni |
Pushan | Bhaga | at the offering | all-sustaining | a race | like | they have gone | having the swiftest horses. || 4 ||

## Commentary (Sayana)
Here the deities are those mentioned in the verse. The connection is with the phrase "they have gone forth." The **overcomer** <note>original: "sakṣaṇim"</note> is one who serves the sacrifice or conquers enemies. **Celestial** means belonging to heaven. **He who has the Kanvas as his invokers** <note>original: "kaṇvahotā"</note> refers to one whose callers are the Kanva sages or the wise. **Gathered** <note>original: "citaḥ"</note> means spread across the three regions (earth, atmosphere, and heaven). He is **of one mind** <note>original: "sajoṣāḥ"</note> with the Sun—meaning they have the same movement or same affection. **Wind** refers to the Vayu as previously described, along with **Agni**, **Pushan** (the nourisher), and the deity named **Bhaga**. All these gods, described as **all-sustaining** <note>original: "viśvabhojā"</note>—meaning they protect the world or carry all across—being the **best among those possessing swift horses**, have **gone forth** to this offering <note>original: "prabhṛthe"</note> as if to a **race** or battle.

---

-> || Now the fifth verse || <-

## Hymn Text
Bring forth for yourselves wealth with yoked horses; for the attainment of riches and for protection, let the prayer be established. The invoker of the son of Ushij is very gracious in his ways—those which are your paths, O swift Maruts. || 5 ||

**Word-by-word breakdown:**
Forth | for you | wealth | with yoked horses | bring forth | of wealth | for the attainment | for protection | let be established | the prayer |
Very gracious | with ways | of the son of Ushij | the invoker | which | your | paths | Maruts | of the swift. || 5 ||

## Commentary (Sayana)
O Maruts, do you **bring forth**—that is, provide—**wealth** accompanied by horses, or a son worthy of horses. For the sake of seeking or obtaining **riches** such as cattle and horses; **for protection** <note>original: "avase"</note>. Here, the word "avas" is a name for food.

<note>The commentary for verse 5 breaks off here and continues on the next page.</note>

<vocab>
- **Overcomer** (sakṣaṇiḥ): A term for a deity who either overcomes obstacles or actively participates in the ritual.
- **Kanva-invoker** (kaṇvahotā): Refers to the Kanva family of rishis, famous for their Vedic hymns.
- **All-sustaining** (viśvabhojāḥ): A title for gods who provide nourishment or protection to the entire universe.
- **Offering** (prabhṛtha): The act of bringing the sacrificial materials forward.
- **Son of Ushij** (auśijasya): Usually refers to the sage Kakshivat, a famous poet of the Rig Veda.
- **Maruts**: The storm deities, often described as a troop of young warriors.
</vocab>

It emphasizes the speed and power of these deities, comparing their arrival at the sacrifice to horses entering a race, and begins a prayer to the Maruts for wealth and protection.</summary>

# 392 || Fourth Book || 392

<header>|| Rig Veda || [Book 4, Chapter 2, Section 14]</header>

The singer <note>original: "dhih"</note> should perform this praise to obtain food or to protect the wealth already gained. He holds the praise in his heart. Like the priest Kakshivat, the son of Ushij, he becomes very blissful <note>original: "sushevah"</note> through desires that move with great speed or horses that serve as the means of travel. "Shevam" is a name for happiness; may he be truly happy. O Maruts <note>storm-deities who accompany Indra</note>, may it be done with those horses or desires of yours, you who are ever-speeding <note>original: "turana"</note>.

-> || Thus ends the thirteenth section (varga) in the second chapter of the fourth book || <-

The sixth verse, beginning with "Pra vo vayum," is used as the offering prayer <term>yajya<note>A specific verse recited at the moment the sacrificial offering is cast into the fire.</note></term> for the sacrifice of an animal dedicated to the Wind-god <term>Vayu</term>. This is indicated in the Ashvalayana Shrauta Sutra (3.8). The text is as follows:

---

## Hymn Text

-> **Verse 6** <-
Prepare the Wind <note>Vayu</note> for yourselves, the one who yokes the chariot; praise the divine, wise one, the praiser, with hymns. May the seekers of the gods, the observers of Truth, the bountiful wives <note>of the gods</note>, established in their dwellings, be here for our holy work. || 6 ||

-> **Word-by-word Analysis** <-
Forth | for you | the Wind | chariot-yoking | make | forth | the divine | the wise | the praiser | with hymns | seeking the gods | Truth-serving | bountiful-ones | dwelling in houses | our | here | wives | for the holy work | have placed (arrived). || 6 ||

---

## Commentary (Sayana)

O my officiating priests <term>Ritvija<note>The various types of priests who perform the Vedic rituals.</note></term>, prepare <note>original: "krnudhvam"</note> for yourselves the **Wind-god** <note>Vayu</note>, who is **yoked to the chariot** <note>original: "rathayujam"</note> to travel to the sacrifice. With **hymns** <note>original: "arkaih"</note>, which are the means of worship, praise the **shining** <note>original: "devam"</note> and **wise** <note>original: "vipram"</note> one—the one who specifically fulfills desires or is worshipful like a sage—the **praiseworthy** one <note>original: "panitaram"</note> who bestows the fruits of the ritual. Furthermore, may the **wives of the gods** <note>original: "patnih"</note>, who are **seekers of the gods** <note>original: "ishudhyavah"</note>, who **serve the sacrifice** <note>original: "ritasapah"</note>, who are **bountiful** <note>original: "purandhih"</note> or of beautiful form, and who are **praiseworthy** <note>original: "vastvih"</note>, have **arrived** <note>original: "adhuh"</note> here at this sacrifice for **our holy work** <note>original: "dhiye"</note>, so that the ritual may be completed.

---

-> || Now the seventh verse || <-

## Hymn Text

-> **Verse 7** <-
To you both, the great ones, I bring the offering with worshipful, powerful songs and with hymns from the heavens that inspire thought. Dawn and Night, like two wise women, bring the whole sacrifice for the mortal man. || 7 ||

-> **Word-by-word Analysis** <-
Near-forth | to you | I bring (offering) | with worshipful | with strengths | forth | the great (two) | from heaven | with thought-inspiring | with hymns | Dawn-and-Night | wise (two) like | all | hither | indeed | they two bring | for the mortal | the sacrifice. || 7 ||

## Commentary (Sayana)

O **Dawn and Night** <note>original: "ushasanakta"</note>, the twin goddesses presiding over day and night! You are **great** <note>original: "yahvi"</note>. Along with the other **worshipful** <note>original: "vandyebhih"</note> gods, **from the heavens** <note>original: "divah"</note>—that is, from the atmosphere or from every region—**I bring near** to you both <note>original: "upapraishe"</note> the sacrificial offering <note>original: "havih"</note>. [I do this] with **powerful songs** <note>original: "shushaih"</note> that bring happiness and with **thought-inspiring** <note>original: "chitayadbhih"</note>—

<meta>This page continues the commentary on Rig Veda, Mandala 5, Sukta 41, which is part of a series of hymns dedicated to the "All-Gods" (Vishvedevas). The previous page concluded the discussion on the seventh verse. ...I bring [you] near with praises and hymns. O mentioned deities, like two who know all that is to be done <note>original: "kartavyajātam"</note>, bring the sacrifice to the mortal worshiper. The word "ha" <note>a Sanskrit particle</note> is used here as a filler for the meter. Or, as some scholars say, terms like "Pushair" and others ending in the third-case plural are adjectives qualifying "Vandyebhir" <note>meaning "those to be praised"</note>.

---

## Hymn Text

->|| Eighth Verse ||<-

I praise you, the leaders who possess nourishment; [I praise] the Lord of the Dwelling <term>Vāstoṣpati<note>The tutelary deity of the home or the physical foundation of the house.</note></term> and the divine Artisan <term>Tvaṣṭṛ<note>The heavenly builder or fashioner of forms in Vedic mythology.</note></term>, being delighted. May the wealthy and harmonious Goddess of Speech <term>Dhiṣaṇā<note>A goddess associated with inspiration, sacred speech, and sometimes the earth.</note></term> be honored with salutations, along with the Lords of the Forest <note>trees</note> and the Herbs, for the attainment of wealth. || 8 ||

**Word-by-word Analysis:**
Towards | you all | I praise | possessing nourishment | leaders | of the dwelling | the Lord | the Artisan | being delighted | wealthy | harmonious | the Goddess of Speech | with salutations | the Lords of the Forest | the Herbs | of wealth | in the pursuit. || 8 ||

---

## Commentary (Sayana)

I worship <note>original: "abhipūjayāmi"</note> **you**, the leaders of ritual acts who **possess nourishment** <note>original: "poṣyāvato"</note>, meaning those who have many people to support and nourish. I praise you. Who are you? It is explained: I am the one giving the offering and sporting or rejoicing <note>original: "rarāṇaḥ"</note> with hymns, honoring **the Lord of the Dwelling** and **the Artisan**. The **Goddess of Speech** <note>original: "dhiṣaṇā"</note>—this is a name for the deity of Voice—is **wealthy** <note>bestowing riches</note> and **harmonious**, meaning she moves with or pleases the other gods. <margin>These words are in the first case but used here in the sense of the second case (as objects of worship).</margin> The connection is: I worship this described Goddess of Speech, the trees, and the herbs along with salutations. For what purpose? **In the pursuit of wealth**, to obtain riches.

---

## Hymn Text

->|| Ninth Verse ||<-

For our offspring and our descendants, may the mountains be easy to access—those who, like heroes, are the dwellers of the world. May the worshipful Sun, praised by all, always increase our prayer; he is helpful to men when he is sought. || 9 ||

**Word-by-word Analysis:**
For offspring | our | for descendants | the mountains | may they be | easy to access | who | dwellers | like | heroes | the praised | the reaching | worshipful | always | our | may he increase | our | prayer/praise | helpful to men | in the seeking. || 9 ||

---

## Commentary (Sayana)

**The mountains** <note>original: "parvatāḥ"</note> refer to the actual mountains or the clouds which are full of water. May they be **easy to access** <note>original: "svaitavaḥ"</note>, meaning of good movement, for the purpose of **giving** <note>original: "tuje"</note> to our **offspring** <note>original: "tane"</note>. Alternatively, "tane" refers to a son. <margin>The fourth case is used here in the sense of the sixth case (possessive).</margin> The meaning is: for the gift of a son. Or, may they be so for **our offspring** (the son) and for the "tana" (the grandson). What are these mountains or clouds like? **They who**, like **heroes**, are the **dwellers** <note>original: "vasavo"</note> or those who cause the world to dwell in stability. Furthermore, may the **worshipful** Sun <note>original: "ādityaḥ"</note>—who is **praised** by all and is **reaching** <note>original: "āpnaḥ"</note> or attainable by all—**always increase our prayer**, our hymn of praise. This deity is **helpful to men** <note>original: "naryo"</note> and does this when he is **sought** <note>original: "abhiṣṭau"</note>, meaning when we approach him or seek his presence.

- Tvaṣṭṛ: The divine smith or carpenter who fashions the forms of all living beings.
- Dhiṣaṇā: A goddess representing meditative or liturgical speech.
- Narya: An epithet meaning "manly," "heroic," or "beneficial to mankind."
- Tana: A Vedic term for a descendant or offspring, often specifically a grandson.

## Hymn Text

-> ॥ The Tenth Verse ॥ <-

I have praised the offspring of the showerer <note>original: "vṛṣṇaḥ", referring here to the rain-cloud or the sun</note>, the womb of the earth, the child of the waters, with a cleansing hymn. Agni, with hair of flame <note>original: "śociṣ-keśaḥ"</note>, does not roar in anger at the singer with his powerful rays, but rather he consumes the forests. ॥ 10 ॥

**Word-by-word Analysis:**
Of the showerer | I have praised | of the earth | the womb | the gathered one | the offspring | of the waters | with a cleansing hymn |
He sings | Agni | to the mover [the singer] | not | with roars/powers | he whose hair is flame | down | he consumes | the forests. ॥ 10 ॥

---

## Commentary (Sayana)

Regarding "of the earth" <note>original: "bhūmyasya"</note>: the "earth" here refers to the atmosphere. He who is worthy of that place, such is the showerer of rain, the cloud-god Parjanya.
Or, "of the earth" may refer to the literal ground, as Agni provides the rain necessary for it. The **offspring** <note>original: "napātam"</note> of the waters, the protector dwelling within the clouds as lightning, is Agni. I have praised him with a **cleansing hymn** <note>original: "suvṛkti"</note>, which is a ritual act of praise characterized by the avoidance of sin. He is "the gathered one" <note>original: "citaḥ"</note> because he is built up or extended in places where darkness has been dispelled. Toward me, the "mover" or the singer, he **does not roar** <note>original: "na gṛṇīte"</note> with his **powers** <note>original: "śūṣaiḥ"</note> or comfortable rays; that is, he does not show anger. Instead, being **flame-haired** <note>original: "śociṣ-keśaḥ"</note>, having rays of brilliant light, he **consumes** <note>original: "niriṇāti"</note> the forests. He destroys them, which is to say, he burns them.

-> ॥ Thus ends the fourteenth section of the second chapter of the fourth book ॥ <-

---

## Hymn Text

-> ॥ The Eleventh Verse ॥ <-

In what manner shall we speak [our praise] to the great sons of Rudra <term>the Maruts<note>Vibrant storm deities who accompany Indra or Rudra.</note></term>? What [hymn] shall we speak for wealth to the wise <term>Bhaga<note>A solar deity representing fortune and prosperity.</note></term>? May the waters and the herbs protect us, and the heavens, the forests, and the mountains whose hair is the trees. ॥ 11 ॥

**Word-by-word Analysis:**
In what manner | to the great | to the sons of Rudra | let us speak | what | for wealth | to the wise | to Bhaga |
The waters | the herbs | and | us | may they protect | the heaven | the forests | the mountains | those whose hair is trees. ॥ 11 ॥

---

## Commentary (Sayana)

We, the seers, **in what manner** <note>original: "kathā"</note> shall we **speak** our praises to the **great sons of Rudra** <note>original: "rudriyāya"</note>, the troop of Maruts? **What** song of praise shall we speak for the **attainment of wealth** to the god named **Bhaga**, who **knows all things**? Furthermore, may the deities of the **waters**, the **herbs**, the deity of **heaven**, the **forests**, and the **mountains whose hair is the trees**—those who have trees standing in the place of hair—may all these mentioned deities **protect us**.

---

## Hymn Text

-> ॥ The Twelfth Verse ॥ <-

May the Lord of Strength hear our songs—he who crosses the clouds, the swift, the all-pervading. May the bright waters hear us, like [watchmen] guarding a city, from all sides of the ladle-bearing priest's pressing stone. ॥ 12 ॥

**Word-by-word Analysis:**
May he hear | us | of strength | the Lord | the songs | he | the cloud-crosser | swift | the all-pervading |
May they hear | the waters | the cities | like | bright | around | the ladles | of the great | of the pressing stone. ॥ 12 ॥

[Mandala 5, Anuvaka 3, Hymn 41] || Fourth Ashtaka || 395

## Hymn Text

May the **Lord of Strengths** <note>original: "ūrjāṃ patiḥ", likely referring to the Wind-god Vāyu</note> hear our songs; he who belongs to the clouds, moves within the clouds, and is most swift to cross the sky. May the active, all-pervading one and the waters cleanse us—the waters which are bright like ancient garments, flowing from around the expanding rock <note>original: "adreḥ", which can mean either a mountain or a rain-cloud</note>. ॥ 12 ॥

**Word-by-word Analysis:**
May he hear | our | of strengths | the Lord | the songs | he | of the cloud | dwelling in the cloud | most swift to cross |
active | moving all around | may they cleanse | the waters | cities [or ancient ones] | like | bright | around | flowing | of the expanding | rock. ॥ 12 ॥

---

## Commentary (Sayana)

May he hear our songs of praise. Who? **Vāyu**, the wind, who is the **Lord of Strengths** <note>original: "ūrjāṃ"</note> or powers. Alternatively, he is the Lord of nourishments. The pervasiveness of Vāyu, when identified with the **Life-breath** <note>original: "prāṇa"</note>, is well known in the sacred texts. As the scripture says: "The Creator fashioned all this as food for the Breath." He is "of the cloud" because he dwells and moves within the atmosphere. He is "most swift to cross" the distance to be traveled, and he is "all-pervading," moving everywhere. Furthermore, may the **waters** <note>original: "āpaḥ"</note> cleanse our songs. What are these waters like? They are like "bright cities" or "shining ancient things," flowing from all sides of the expanding "rock"—which refers here to either a cloud or a mountain.

---

-> ॥ The Thirteenth Verse ॥ <-

## Hymn Text

O great ones, take notice! We who hold the desirable offering speak of your paths, O skillful ones. Even the well-formed birds <note>original: "vayaścana", here interpreted by Sayana as the Maruts appearing as swift movers</note> come toward us, following the mortal with their weapons for his protection <note>or "following the mortal enemy with weapons to strike him"</note>. ॥ 13 ॥

**Word-by-word Analysis:**
Know | indeed | now | O great ones | ye | your | ways | let us speak | O skillful/beautiful ones | the desirable [offering] | holding |
birds | even | well-formed | toward | toward | they go | with beauty | the mortal | followed | with weapons. ॥ 13 ॥

---

## Commentary (Sayana)

O great **Maruts** <note>storm deities</note>, quickly **know** <note>original: "vid"</note> or take notice of this hymn. O **skillful ones** <note>original: "dasmāḥ", beautiful or effective ones</note>, we speak praise to you—we who are travelers on your paths, who serve you, and who hold or provide the choice offering. Alternatively, it means: "Ye who come to our sacrifice, take notice." (The word *cit* is a filler). These Maruts, appearing as "birds" or swift-moving beings, being well-formed and fully grown, come toward us. What do they do? Accompanied by beauty, they approach, and with their **weapons** <note>original: "vadhasnaiḥ"</note>, they ward off or strike the mortal enemy who has come against us.

---

-> ॥ The Fourteenth Verse ॥ <-

## Hymn Text

I speak to the divine and the earthly births, and to the waters, for the one who provides good wealth. May the heavens and our songs increase for delight; and may our gains increase in the flood of the waters. ॥ 14 ॥

**Word-by-word Analysis:**
Toward | divine | earthly | births | waters | and | toward | for the wealth-giver | I have spoken |
may they increase | heavens | songs | for delight | and | may they increase | gains | in the flood. ॥ 14 ॥

---

## Commentary (Sayana)

The "divine births" <note>original: "daivyāni janma"</note> refer to things related to the gods, and the "earthly births" <note>original: "pārthivāni"</note> refer to things related to the earth, and the waters—

-> ॥ Rig-Veda ॥ [Ashtaka 4, Adhyaya 2, Varga 16] <-

I speak <note>original: "vocam"</note> this prayer for the host of the **Maruts** <note>The Maruts are the storm-deities, companions of Indra, known for their collective power</note>, those of the auspicious sacrifice. May the songs of praise increase. May the shining heavens, which reveal the truths they contain and possess delight or gold <note>original: "candrāyāḥ", referring to the golden or pleasing light of the sky</note>, increase. May the flowing rivers, joined by the Maruts through the gift of water, increase and become prosperous.

---

-> ॥ Verse Fifteen ॥ <-

## Hymn Text

At every step <note>original: "pade-pade"</note>, my **hymn of praise** <note>term: "jariman" (praise/hymn)</note> is established. Or she, the powerful one, who is the **protectress** <note>term: "varūtrī" (preventer of calamities)</note> through her guarding powers. May the Great Mother, the **Earth** <note>original: "rasā", here referring to the moisture-rich earth or the personified goddess</note>, attend to us along with the wise ones—she who is straight-handed and a giver of favor. ॥ 15 ॥

**Word-by-word Analysis:**
At every step | my | hymn | down | is placed | the protectress | or | the powerful | who | with guards | and |
may she attend | the Mother | the Great | the Earth | us | together with | the wise ones | straight-handed | a giver of favor. ॥ 15 ॥

---

## Commentary (Sayana)

The word **hymn** <note>original: "jarimā"</note> means my song of praise; it is established or performed at every step, which is to say, at every moment upon the earth. And she who is **powerful** <note>original: "śakrā"</note>, through her acts of guarding, becomes the **protectress** <note>original: "varūtrī"</note> who wards off our misfortunes. The word "or" <note>original: "vā"</note> here is used in the sense of "and."

May the **Mother**, the creator of all, the **Great** and venerable **Earth** <note>original: "rasā", the essence-filled one</note>, attend to or favor our praise. Alternatively, once she is praised, may she accompany us. The word "together with" <note>original: "smat"</note> implies excellence. She is pleased through the service of the **excellent wise ones** <note>original: "sūribhiḥ", the inspired poets or priests</note>. May she be **straight-handed** <note>original: "ṛjuhastaḥ"</note>, meaning her hands are moved by a favorable intent toward us, and may she be a **giver of favor** <note>original: "ṛjuvaniḥ"</note>, bestowing auspicious gifts.

-> ॥ This ends the fifteenth section (varga) of the second chapter of the fourth book ॥ <-

-> ॥ Verse Sixteen ॥ <-

## Hymn Text

In what manner shall we serve with our salutation the **bountiful givers** <note>term: "sudānu" (generous givers)</note>, the Maruts, when the inviting address is made? The famous Maruts, when the address is made? May the **Serpent of the Deep** <note>term: "ahirbudhnya" (the dragon or serpent of the celestial foundations)</note> not deliver us to injury; may he be the winner of our near-approaching offerings. ॥ 16 ॥

**Word-by-word Analysis:**
In what manner | shall we serve | with salutation | the bountiful givers | in this way | the Maruts | in the inviting address | the famous | the Maruts | in the inviting address |
not | us | the serpent | of the deep | to injury | may he deliver | of us | may he be | the winner of near-offerings. ॥ 16 ॥

---

## Commentary (Sayana)

In what manner or by what means shall we serve or worship the **Maruts**, who are **bountiful givers**, using either songs of salutation or offerings of food? When this specific inviting address is made toward them, how shall we serve those Maruts? The implication is that they are difficult to propitiate.

<vocab>
- jariman: praise/hymn (according to Sayana)
- varūtrī: protectress/preventer of calamities
- Marut: the storm gods, sons of Rudra
- Ahirbudhnya: the serpent of the foundations/depths, a deity of the atmosphere
- ṛjuhasta: straight-handed/favorable-handed
- sudānu: bountiful givers
- acchokti: inviting address
</vocab>

How? They become those who possess excellent food. In the presence of me, whose praise consists of approaching with speech; or rather, when there is an approaching speech—a hymn—for the sake of me who possesses excellent food, in what way shall we worship the **Maruts**? <note>The repetition in the original Sanskrit is for the sake of showing deep reverence.</note> May the god **Ahirbudhnya** <note>term: "Ahirbudhnya" (The Serpent of the Deep); a deity of the celestial depths or the atmospheric horizon</note> not deliver us to the injurer. Let him not place us in the power of one who seeks to harm. May that god be for us a slayer of enemies <note>original: "upamātivaniḥ"</note>.

## Hymn Text
Thus indeed for **offspring** accompanied by **cattle**, O Gods, the mortal worships you; O Gods, the mortal worships you.
Towards the auspicious support of this body [may she look]; may **Nirṛti** <note>Nirṛti is typically the goddess of decay and destruction; here, the poet asks her to consume old age itself</note> consume even old age for me. ॥ 17 ॥

**Word-by-word Analysis:**
Thus | indeed | now | for offspring | accompanied by cattle | O Gods | worships | the mortal | you | (towards) |
O Gods | worships | the mortal | you |
towards | auspicious | of the body | support | of this | old age | even | for me | Nirṛti | may she consume. ॥ 17 ॥

## Commentary (Sayana)
O Gods <note>original: "devāso"</note>, thus indeed, the mortal man—the sacrificer—quickly worships or seeks you for the sake of offspring that is accompanied by cattle. The repetition "O Gods" is for the sake of reverence. In this sacrifice, may the deity Nirṛti provide auspicious food <note>original: "dhāsim"</note> for this body of mine—meaning for the son who has been favored by the gods. May she also consume <note>original: "jayasīt"</note> or overcome old age.

->॥ Verse Eighteen ॥<-

## Hymn Text
That **benevolence** of yours, O Gods, and that invigorating food, O **Vasus**, may we obtain through the praise of the cow.
May that divine one, the generous giver, the comforter, hastening toward us, come for our welfare. ॥ 18 ॥

**Word-by-word Analysis:**
That | your | O Gods | benevolence | invigorating | food | may we obtain | O Vasus | by praise | of the cow |
She | us | the generous giver | comforting | the Goddess | towards | hastening | for welfare | may she come. ॥ 18 ॥

## Commentary (Sayana)
O Gods, O **Vasus** <note>A class of deities representing the elemental spheres of existence</note> who cause all to dwell: may we obtain that well-known **benevolence** <note>term: "sumati" (goodwill or right-thinking)</note> of yours, which is the means of producing good thoughts. The connection between food and thought is well known from sacred texts like the Upanishads: "The mind, my dear, consists of food" <note>original: "anna-mayaṃ hi somya manaḥ"; a famous quote from the Chāndogya Upaniṣad 6.5.4 implying that physical nourishment sustains mental clarity</note>. May we obtain invigorating food <note>original: "iṣam"</note>, such as milk and curds, through the praise of the cow. May that goddess come to us for our happiness or welfare <note>original: "suvitāya"</note>. The deity is further described as a generous giver <note>original: "sudānuḥ"</note>, one who is comforting or merciful <note>original: "mṛḷayantī"</note>, and one who hastens toward us.

<vocab>
**Maruts**: Storm deities; **Ahirbudhnya**: Serpent of the Deep; **Nirṛti**: Goddess of destruction/decay; **Vasus**: The 'Bright' or 'Good' ones; **Sumati**: Benevolence or favor; **Sudānu**: One who gives well; **Mṛḷayantī**: Comforting/Merciful.
</vocab>

[ऋ० ४. अ० २. व० १७.] || Rig Veda || 398

-> ॥ Verse Nineteen ॥ <-

## Hymn Text

May **Ila**, the mother of the herd, along with the **rivers**, praise us; or may **Urvashi** praise us.
May Urvashi, whose light is great, being praised and covering [the sacrificer], praise us for the sake of the offering of the mortal man. ॥ 19 ॥

---

**Word-by-word Analysis:**
Praise | us | Ila | of the herd | mother | along with | rivers | Urvashi | or | may she praise |
Urvashi | or | of great light | being praised | covering | of the offering | of the mortal man. ॥ 19 ॥

## Commentary (Sayana)

May she praise us—meaning, may she favor us—**Ila**, who is the Earth <note>original: "bhūmi"</note> and the creator or mother of the multitude of cattle. Alternatively, they say Ila is the daughter of **Manu** taking the form of a cow. Or, Ila is the "speech of the middle realm" <note>atmospheric speech, often associated with lightning or thunder</note>, the creator of the host of **Maruts** <note>storm deities</note>. Or **Urvashi** is the speech of the middle realm. May she praise us along with the rivers like the **Ganges** and others. The word *smat* is stated to be a term for "praiseworthy" or "excellent." May she praise with excellence. 

Or otherwise, may Urvashi, who possesses abundant light and is being praised—meaning she is sounding out and praising our ritual act—cover whom? The mortal man <note>original: "āyu"</note>, the human sacrificer. With what? By the giving of the power of the offering or the giving of water. The <term>Nirukta</term> <note>Yaska's ancient treatise on etymology and semantics</note> states (11.49) that this refers to "the power or the water of the offering." Alternatively, it means she covers or protects the mortal who possesses the means of striking or offering. ॥

-> ॥ Verse Twenty ॥ <-

## Hymn Text

May [the gods] accompany us for the prosperity of **Urjavya**. ॥ 20 ॥

---

**Word-by-word Analysis:**
May they accompany | us | for the prosperity | of [the king named] Urjavya. ॥ 20 ॥

## Commentary (Sayana)

May they accompany or serve us in relation to the prosperity of the one who nourishes us, the king named **Urjavya**. By implication, the "assembly of gods" is understood as the subject. Alternatively, Urvashi or the host of Maruts is understood here, as they were the subjects of the preceding context. ॥

## Commentary (Sayana)
<note>Introduction to the next Hymn (Hymn 10 of this section / Sukta 59 overall)</note>

**The tenth hymn, beginning with "Pro Shantama," consists of eighteen verses. Its seer is Atri, the son of Bhumi; its meter is Trishtubh.** Since the previous hymn was said to be dedicated to the "All-gods" <note>term: "Vaishvadeva"; a category of hymns addressed to the pantheon of deities collectively</note>, this one is also dedicated to the All-gods. However, the eleventh verse, "Praise him well," is dedicated to **Rudra**. According to the index of verses, the seventeenth and eighteenth verses are in the "one-footed" meter, and the one before the last is also "one-footed." The index states: **"The hymn 'Pro Shantama' is for the All-gods; the eleventh is for Rudra."** The application of these verses in ritual is determined by their specific marks or signs.

-> ॥ Verse One of the Hymn ॥ <-

## Hymn Text

May **Varuna**, **Mitra**, **Bhaga**, and **Aditi** truly hear our most peaceful prayers and hymns through our portion.
May the one of dappled origin, the one who possesses the five priests, hear us—the **Asura** <note>In the Vedas, "Asura" is a title for powerful divine beings, often meaning "Lord" or "Life-giver," before it later came to mean "demon" in post-Vedic literature</note> who is of unswerving path and the source of happiness. ॥ 1 ॥

<vocab>
- **Ila**: Representing Earth, the mother of cattle, or the sacred speech of the atmosphere.
- **Urvashi**: A celestial being or nymph, here interpreted as lightning or atmospheric sound.
- **Maruts**: The storm-gods who accompany Indra.
- **Nirukta**: An ancient text used to explain the difficult vocabulary of the Vedas.
- **Yajamana**: The person who sponsors and benefits from the Vedic sacrifice.
- **Vaishvadeva**: A hymn or ritual dedicated to all the gods collectively.
- **Atri, son of Bhumi**: The sage (Rishi) to whom this hymn is attributed.
- **Raudri**: A verse or hymn specifically addressed to the god Rudra.
- **Varuna**: The guardian of cosmic order and the lord of the waters.
- **Mitra**: The solar deity of friendship, contracts, and the day.
- **Bhaga**: The god of fortune, wealth, and destiny.
- **Aditi**: The infinite mother of the gods, representing freedom and the vast sky.
</vocab>

<meta>The previous page (398) concluded the commentary for the 41st hymn of the 5th Mandala, specifically discussing the goddess Urvashi and the "speech of the middle realm." This page (399) begins the 42nd hymn of the 5th Mandala, which is a collection of prayers dedicated to various deities including Varuna, Mitra, Aditi, and the Wind-god (Vayu).</meta>

M. 5. A. 3. S. 42. ] || Fourth Ashtaka || 399

## Hymn Text

### [Verse 1]
**Word-by-word Analysis:**
Truly | most peaceful | Varuna | sacrificial act | song | Mitra | Bhaga | Aditi | now | may it reach | 
He whose source is the rain | the five-fold priest | let him hear | he whose path is unimpeded | the giver of life | the source of bliss. ॥ 1 ॥

## Commentary (Sayana)

**[On Verse 1]:**
May the most peaceful—meaning extremely joy-giving—song, which is speech in the form of praise, now truly and unfailingly reach **Varuna**, **Mitra**, **Bhaga**, and **Aditi**, along with the sacrificial act <note>original: "dīdhitī"</note> characterized by the pouring of oblations. 

Furthermore, let **Vayu** (the Wind-god) hear. He is described as having "the rain as his source" <note>original: "pṛṣadyoniḥ"; inhabiting the atmosphere where rain originates</note>. He is the "Five-fold Priest" <note>original: "pañcahotā"</note> because he is the facilitator of the five types of internal breath-offerings, such as the *Prana* and *Apana* <note>the vital life forces</note>. Alternatively, "Five-fold Priest" is simply a name for Vayu, as the sacred texts <note>original: "śruteḥ"</note> say: "Vayu is the five-fold priest, he is the breath." 

He is also "he whose path is unimpeded" <note>original: "atūrtapanthāḥ"; his movement cannot be harmed or stopped</note>, the "Asura" <note>original: "asuraḥ"; here used in the ancient sense of "giver of life-force" or "powerful lord"</note>, and the "source of bliss" <note>original: "mayobhuḥ"</note> or the abode of happiness. Let Vayu, possessed of these qualities, hear our hymn.

---

### [Verse 2]
-> **Now the second verse** <-

**Sacred Text:**
May **Aditi** accept my hymn, as a mother her son, as something dear to the heart and very kind; 
That sacred prayer, dear to the gods and established by them, which I bring to **Mitra** and **Varuna**, and which is the source of bliss. ॥ 2 ॥

**Word-by-word Analysis:**
Towards | my | hymn | Aditi | may she accept | son | like | mother | heart-pleasing | very kind | 
sacred prayer | dear | established for the gods | which | is | I | Mitra | Varuna | which | source of bliss. ॥ 2 ॥

## Commentary (Sayana)

**[On Verse 2]:**
May the goddess **Aditi** accept <note>original: "pratijagṛbhyāt"</note> my hymn or song of praise. She should do so "as a mother accepts her son"—meaning, just as a mother embraces her own child and is filled with satisfaction, so should she. 

What is this hymn like? It is "heart-pleasing" <note>original: "hṛdyam"</note> and "very kind" <note>original: "suśevam"</note>, meaning it brings beautiful happiness. These two descriptions apply to both the hymn and the child. Furthermore, that sacred prayer <note>original: "brahma"</note>, consisting of the collection of mantras, which is dear, which is to be obtained by the gods, and which is the means of happiness—"I bring that to **Mitra** and **Varuna**." (This concludes the sentence). 

Alternatively, the meaning is: I uphold that ritual work <note>original: "karma"</note> in the form of sacrifice, which is described as "sacred prayer" and is directed toward Mitra and Varuna, the deities presiding over the Day and Night.

---

### [Verse 3]
**Ritual Context:**
The verse beginning "Stir up" <note>original: "udīraya"</note> is the recitation for the offering <note>original: "yājyā"</note> of the omentum <note>original: "vapā"; the fatty tissue</note> of the animal sacrifice dedicated to **Savitar** during the eleven-animal rite. It is noted in the ritual manuals: "Stir up the wisest of the wise, Bhaga, the prayer, the distributors of wealth, the giver of plenty—these two verses" (**Ashvalayana Shrauta Sutra 3.7**). Thus it is said.

-> **This is the third verse** <-

**Sacred Text:**
Stir up the wisest of the wise; anoint him with honey and with clarified butter; 
May the divine **Savitar** grant us treasures that are ready, well-placed, and glittering. ॥ 3 ॥

**Word-by-word Analysis:**
Upward | stir | wisest | of the wise | upward | him | towards | with honey | with clarified butter | 
He | to us | treasures | ready | well-placed | glittering | divine | Savitar | may he grant. ॥ 3 ॥

<meta>This page continues the commentary on the final verse of the previous section and provides the full text and explanation for verses 4 and 5 of Rigveda Mandala 4, Sukta 31. This corresponds to the 2nd Adhyaya of the 4th Ashtaka, ending at the 17th Varga.</meta>

## Commentary (Sayana) - Continued
By this verse, Savitr <note>the solar deity representing the impelling force of the sun</note> is also praised. O officiating priests, raise up <note>original: "udīraya"; meaning to elevate or cause to reach upward</note> this Agni-Savitr who stands before us, the most visionary of all seers. This means you should gladden him. Anoint <note>original: "abhyunnatta"; meaning to moisten or saturate</note> this god with sweet Soma juice and with clarified butter. This means you should satisfy him. May that god, Savitr, grant <note>original: "suvāti"</note> us riches suitable for our dwellings—such as cattle and other wealth—which are beneficial and delightful as gold.

---

-> ॥ Now the Fourth Verse ॥ <-

## Hymn Text
O Indra, lead us together with a noble mind and with cattle; together with the wise ones, O Lord of the Bay Horses, and with well-being. Together with the sacred prayer which is beneficial to the gods, and with the favor of the gods who are worthy of sacrifice. ॥ 4 ॥

**Word-by-word Analysis:**
Together | O Indra | us | with mind | lead | with cattle | together | with the wise ones | O Lord of the Bay Horses | together | with well-being | 
together | with the prayer | which is beneficial to the gods | which | exists | together | of the gods | with the favor | of those worthy of sacrifice ॥ 4 ॥

---

## Commentary (Sayana)
O Indra, lead us <note>original: "neṣi"</note> together with an excellent mind and with cows. This means: cause cows to be given to us. This sense of "leading to us" applies to all the following terms. O Lord of the Bay Horses <note>original: "harivaḥ"; Indra is traditionally drawn by two tawny or bay steeds</note>, lead us together with the "Sūris"—referring to either wise sons or the officiating priests. Likewise, lead us with "svasti"—meaning safety or well-being. Lead us with "brahman"—meaning abundant food <note>Sayana often glosses 'brahman' as food in a sacrificial context</note>; specifically that which is beneficial to the gods. Furthermore, lead us with the "sumati"—the favor or graceful will—of the gods who are worthy of sacrifice.

---

-> ॥ Now the Fifth Verse ॥ <-

## Hymn Text
The divine Bhaga, Savitr, and Amsha, the master of wealth; Indra, the conqueror of the demon Vritra and of riches; Rbhukshan, Vaja, and also Purandhi—may these immortals, hastening to us, protect us. ॥ 5 ॥

**Word-by-word Analysis:**
The god | Bhaga | Savitr | of wealth | Amsha | Indra | of Vritra | the conqueror | of riches | 
Rbhukshan | Vaja | and | also | Purandhi | may they protect | us | the immortals | the hastening ones ॥ 5 ॥

---

## Commentary (Sayana)
The deities in this verse are mentioned by their characteristics. The god Bhaga, Savitr, and Amsha <note>identified here as a form of Tvashtr, the divine artisan</note> who is the master of wealth. Also, Indra, the slayer of the demon Vritra. These gods are the "conquerors" <note>original: "sañjitaḥ"</note> of various riches. Then there are the three Rbhus: Rbhukshan (referring to Rbhu) and Vaja. Also Purandhi <note>a deity of abundance or wisdom</note>, who is described here as "one of many thoughts" or "highly wise." May these gods—Bhaga and the others—who are immortal <note>original: "amṛtāsaḥ"</note> and who are "hastening" <note>original: "turāsaḥ"</note> toward our sacrifice, protect us.

-> ॥ Thus ends the seventeenth Varga in the second Adhyaya of the fourth Ashtaka ॥ <-

# Mandala 5. Adhyaya 3. Hymn 42. | The Fourth Ashtaka

->॥ Now the Sixth Verse ॥<-

## Hymn Text
Let us proclaim the deeds of the one accompanied by the Maruts <note>original: "marutvat"; the storm-gods who are Indra's companions</note>, the irresistible, the victorious, and the unaging. O Bountiful Lord <note>original: "maghavan"; an epithet of Indra as the generous provider</note>, neither the men of old, nor those of later times, nor anyone recent, has ever attained the limit of your heroic power. ॥ 6 ॥

**Word-by-word Analysis:**
Of the one with the Maruts | of the irresistible | of the victorious | of the unaging | forth | let us speak | the deeds |
not | your | the ancients | O Bountiful Lord | not | the later ones | not | heroic power | recent | anyone | at all | attained ॥ 6 ॥

---

## Commentary (Sayana)
We, the sacrificers, should proclaim—that is, make widely known—the heroic deeds of Indra, who is accompanied by the Maruts. What is his nature? He is irresistible <note>original: "apratīta"</note>, meaning he never retreats in battle. Not only that, he is victorious <note>original: "jiṣṇu"</note> by his very nature and unaging <note>original: "ajuryata"</note>, which means he remains forever young. Now the deity is addressed directly: O Bountiful Indra, the men of old did not reach the extent of your valor. Nor did those who followed after. To say even more: no one in the present, no matter how extraordinary, attains your heroic power.

---

->॥ Now the Seventh Verse ॥<-

## Hymn Text
Praise the foremost bestower of jewels <note>original: "ratnadheya"</note>, Brihaspati <note>the Lord of Prayer or Sacred Speech</note>, the winner of riches. He is the most benevolent to the one who recites and praises; he comes as the possesser of vast wealth to the one who calls upon him repeatedly. ॥ 7 ॥

**Word-by-word Analysis:**
Towards | praise | the foremost | the bestower of jewels | Brihaspati | the winner | of riches |
who | for the one who recites | for the one who praises | the most benevolent | possessor of vast wealth | came | the one calling repeatedly ॥ 7 ॥

---

## Commentary (Sayana)
O inner soul, praise the divine Brihaspati. He is the foremost <note>original: "prathama"</note>, meaning the most excellent. He is the bestower of delightful wealth and the winner <note>original: "sanitṛ"</note> of riches consisting of sacrificial offerings. Alternatively, "jewels" refers to gems and pearls, while "wealth" here refers to cattle and other livestock. Praise Brihaspati, the Lord <note>term: Brihaspati | from 'bṛhat' (great prayer) and 'pati' (lord); the deity presiding over sacred speech</note>. He is the one who becomes the most benevolent <note>original: "śambhaviṣṭha"</note> or the greatest source of happiness for the sacrificer who recites hymns <note>original: "śastra"</note> and chants melodies <note>original: "sāman"</note>. He, being the possessor of abundant riches <note>original: "puruvasu"</note>, comes to the sacrificer who calls out to him.

---

->॥ Now the Eighth Verse ॥<-

## Hymn Text
O Brihaspati, may the patrons <note>original: "maghavanaḥ"; the wealthy sponsors of the sacrifice</note>, following along with your protections, remain uninjured and blessed with brave sons. Those who give horses, or indeed give cows, those who give garments—may wealth and fortune abide in them. ॥ 8 ॥

<meta>This page concludes the commentary on Verse 8 of Hymn 50 in the Fourth Mandala of the Rig Veda and provides the full text and commentary for Verses 9 and 10. The text continues the praise of Brihaspati (the Lord of Prayer) and introduces an invocation to the Maruts (the Storm-gods) to protect the sacrifice from those who are stingy or hostile to sacred rites.</meta>

## Hymn Text

<note>Rig Veda 4.50.8 (Word-by-word analysis continuation)</note>
By your | protections | those joined | unharmed | O Brihaspati | the bountiful | with noble sons |
who | horse-givers | and | or | are | cow-givers | who | garment-givers | fortunate | in them | wealth ॥ 8 ॥

---

## Commentary (Sayana)

O **Brihaspati**, those who are **joined** <note>original: "sacamānāḥ"</note> with your **protections** remain **unharmed**. They become **bountiful** <note>original: "maghavāno"; wealthy patrons</note> and possessors of **noble sons**. Among those who, favored by you, **are** the givers of many **horses**, **or** indeed the **givers of cows**, and those who are **givers of garments** and are **fortunate**—in all of **them**, let **wealth** be established. This is the remaining sense of the prayer.

---

-> ॥ Now the Ninth Verse ॥ <-

## Hymn Text

<note>Rig Veda 4.50.9</note>
Make the wealth of these vanish—those who consume without giving to us despite our hymns. Drive the lawless, who flourish in this world and hate sacred prayer, away from the light of the sun. ॥ 9 ॥

**Word-by-word Analysis:**
Of these | wealth | make | vanishing | who | enjoy | without giving | to us | with hymns |
the lawless | in the world | flourishing | the prayer-haters | from the sun | drive away ॥ 9 ॥

---

## Commentary (Sayana)

**Make** the **wealth** of **these** (the enemies to be described) **vanishing** <note>original: "visarmāṇam"; scattering or disappearing</note>. O **Brahmanaspati** <note>another name for Brihaspati, the Lord of Prayer</note>, who are "these" people? He explains: **those who enjoy** their riches **without giving** anything **to us**, who are distinguished by our **hymns** <note>original: "ukthaiḥ"; specifically the "shastra" recitations used in the ritual</note>. Those who are **lawless** <note>original: "apavratān"; those who have turned away from the sacred duties</note>, who are **flourishing** in this human **world**, and who are **haters of prayer** <note>original: "brahmadviṣo"; those who hate the Brahmins or the sacred mantras</note>—**drive them away from the sun**. This means to separate them from the light and place them in darkness.

---

-> ॥ Now the Tenth Verse ॥ <-

## Hymn Text

<note>Rig Veda 4.50.10</note>
If one brings demons into the feast of the gods, O Maruts, strike him down with your wheel-less chariots. Strike him who mocks the holy labor of the diligent, while he himself sweats only for empty desires. ॥ 10 ॥

**Word-by-word Analysis:**
Who | brings | demons | in the feast of the gods | with wheel-less (chariots) | him | O Maruts | strike down |
who | your | holy labor | of the diligent | mocks | empty | desires | pursues | sweating ॥ 10 ॥

---

## Commentary (Sayana)

**He who**, as a sacrificer, **brings** powerful **demons** <note>original: "rakṣaso"</note> into the **feast of the gods** <note>original: "devavītau"; the sacrifice where gods receive their portion</note>. This refers to a person who, by performing the ritual incorrectly, makes it "asuric" (demonic) rather than divine. **O Maruts** <note>the Storm-gods, brothers of Indra</note>, **strike down** that sacrificer with your **wheel-less** chariots. Cast him utterly into darkness. Alternatively, "wheel-less" may be connected to the previous phrase; "wheels" here could refer to the physical limbs. Thus, one who is repeatedly without limbs <unclear>...</unclear>

[The priest] attains [the gods] through the primary offerings alone. For a sacred rite, when performed with all its parts, reaches the gods. And whoever might revile your work—that is, the work of praise belonging to me, the one striving <note>original: "śaśamānasya"</note>—whoever reviles the Vedic rites such as the **Jyotishtoma** <note>A foundational seven-day Soma sacrifice</note>, and instead pursues trivial, perishable desires like the enjoyments born of agriculture and worldly labor, exhausting himself and "sweating" <note>original: "siṣvidānaḥ"; implying worldly toil versus sacred effort</note>; or, if he makes those desirable enjoyments among you seem trivial...

## Hymn Text

->॥ Now the Eleventh Verse ॥<-
Praise him, the one with the good arrows and the good bow, who rules over every medicine. Worship **Rudra** for great benevolence; with prostrations, honor the divine, mighty one. ॥ 11 ॥

**Word-by-word Analysis:**
Him | indeed | praise | who | [has] good arrows | [has] a good bow | who | of all | rules | medicine |
worship | for great | benevolence | Rudra | with prostrations | the divine | the mighty | honor ॥ 11 ॥

---

## Commentary (Sayana)

O Soul, praise that very **Rudra**. Offer your praise. He is the one who possesses **excellent arrows** and an **excellent bow**. This excellence refers to his ability to slay those who oppose the divine order. He is also the one who **rules** as the master of **all medicine** <note>original: "bheṣajasya"</note> or healing remedies. Because there is no medicine other than the Lord for the pacifying of physical or worldly afflictions, and because he is uniquely connected to healing, he is the master of medicine.

As the scripture says:
> "I hear that you are the greatest physician among physicians." <note>original: "bhiṣaktamaṃ tvā bhiṣajāṃ śṛṇomi"; Rig Veda 2.33.4</note>

Furthermore, worship that same Rudra—the god who releases us from the "threefold suffering" <note>Traditional Indian philosophy categorizes suffering as: 1. Internal (body/mind), 2. External (other beings), and 3. Divine/Natural forces</note> or from sin—for the sake of **great benevolence** or goodness of mind. It is well known that peace of mind is achieved through the adoration of the Lord. Moreover, with **prostrations**—either through sacrificial offerings or physical bows—honor the shining god, the **mighty one** <term>Asura: In this ancient context, 'Asura' does not mean a demon, but a powerful, life-giving divinity</term>. Or, "Asura" may mean the giver of the life-breath. Serve him.

---

## Hymn Text

->॥ Now the Twelfth Verse ॥<-

**Word-by-word Analysis:**
The domestic ones | the active ones | who | [have] skillful hands | of the showerer | the wives | the rivers | fashioned by Vibhvan |
Saraswati | Brihaddiva | and | Raka | making [us] see | grant abundance | the bright ones ॥ 12 ॥

---

## Commentary (Sayana)

In this verse, the deities are addressed by their characteristics. **Domestic ones** <note>original: "damūnasaḥ"</note> refers to those with a mind for giving, or a controlled mind. They are **active** <note>original: "apasaḥ"</note>, meaning they possess beautiful works such as the creation of sacred ladles, horses, or chariots. Therefore, they are **skillful-handed**, possessing expert hands, who...

<meta>This page continues the commentary on the Vedic goddesses and transitions into the praise of Indra and Parjanya (the Rain God). Note: While the header mentions Mandala 4, the content belongs to Mandala 5, Sukta 41. The previous page ended with an invocation of various deities; this page concludes the description of the river goddesses and the semi-divine Ribhus before focusing on the celestial waters.</meta>

The Ribhus <note>semi-divine celestial artisans</note> are present, along with the wives—meaning the protectors—of the mighty Indra, the showerer of blessings. These wives are the roaring rivers, such as the Ganges and others, who were fashioned by Vibhvan <note>the middle of the three Ribhu brothers</note>. There is also the river named Sarasvati—the Goddess of Speech—and Brihaddiva of great radiance, and the goddess Raka <note>the deity associated with the full moon</note>. May these goddesses, who grant our desires <note>original: "daśasyantyaḥ"</note>, be bright and auspicious. May they desire wealth for us.

---

-> ॥ Now the Thirteenth Verse ॥ <-

## Hymn Text
I bring forth an excellent, newer song of wisdom, currently being born, for the great one who provides good shelter. He, the striker, who fashioned this water for us while shaping forms in the streams of his daughter. ॥ 13 ॥

**Word-by-word Analysis:**
Forth | well | for the great | for the one providing good shelter | wisdom | song | I bring | newer | being born |
Who | the striker | of the daughter | in the streams | forms | shaping | fashioned | this [water] | for us ॥ 13 ॥

---

## Commentary (Sayana)
I perfectly bring forth—meaning I compose and offer—a song of **wisdom** <note>original: "medhām"</note>, a prayer being held in the mind. This is intended for the great one, the **provider of good shelter** <note>original: "suśaraṇāya"</note>, referring to either Indra or Parjanya <note>the God of Rain</note>, or perhaps a state of great happiness. What kind of song is it? It is **newer** <note>original: "navyasīm"</note>, meaning more worthy of praise, or **presently being born**—meaning it is brand new. That deity, whether Indra or Parjanya, is the **striker** <note>original: "āhunā"</note> or the pourer of rain. For the sake of his **daughter** <note>referring to the Earth, who is often poetically described as the daughter of the sky or the rain</note>, he creates **forms** within the **streams** <note>the riverbeds or channels</note> and fashions **this water** for us.

---

-> ॥ Now the Fourteenth Verse ॥ <-

## Hymn Text
O singer, may your excellent praise now reach the thundering, roaring Lord of Nourishment. He, who possesses clouds and water, moves forward, sprinkling Heaven and Earth with lightning. ॥ 14 ॥

**Word-by-word Analysis:**
Forth | excellent praise | the thundering | the roaring | of nourishment | the lord | O singer | now | may it reach |
Who | cloud-bearing | water-bearing | moves forward | forth | with lightning | Heaven and Earth | sprinkling ॥ 14 ॥

---

## Commentary (Sayana)
In this verse, Parjanya <note>the personified rain cloud</note> is praised. O singer <note>original: "jaritaḥ"; the one who chants the hymn</note>, may your **excellent praise** truly reach or pervade the deity. He is the **thundering** one, the one making the **roaring** sound produced by the falling rain, and the **Lord of nourishment** <note>original: "iḷaḥ"</note>, which refers to both food and the water that produces it. This Parjanya is **cloud-bearing** <note>original: "abdimān"; here 'abdi' refers to the cloud that gives water</note> and **water-bearing**. As he moves forward, he is **sprinkling** both **Heaven and Earth** <note>original: "rodasī"</note> with his flashes of lightning.

<term>Ribhus (Ṛbhavaḥ)</term> — A group of three brothers (Ribhu, Vibhvan, and Vaja) who were mortal artisans but became divine through their skill, often associated with the sun's rays and the fashioning of sacred objects.
<term>Parjanya (Parjanyaḥ)</term> — The Vedic deity of rain and thunder, often depicted as a bull or a provider of life-giving waters.
<term>Rodasi (Rodasī)</term> — A dual term referring to the cosmic pair of Heaven (Dyaus) and Earth (Prithvi).

[Mandala 5, Anuvaka 3, Hymn 42] || Fourth Book || 405

-> || Now the Fifteenth Verse || <-

## Hymn Text
May this **hymn** <note>original: "stomaḥ"</note> reach toward the **Marut troop** <note>the storm deities</note>, toward the sons of **Rudra** <note>the fierce Vedic storm-god</note>, the youthful and vigorous. My desire calls out for **wealth** <note>original: "rāye"</note>; may it be well. O tireless one, praise those who possess **dappled horses** <note>original: "pṛṣadaśvān"; refers to the Maruts whose chariots are drawn by spotted deer or horses</note>. ॥ 15 ॥

**Word-by-word Analysis:**
This | hymn | relating to the Maruts | troop | toward | of Rudra | sons | youthful/vigorous | out | may it reach |
desire | for wealth | calls | may [it] | well-being | near | praise | having dappled horses | tireless ॥ 15 ॥

---

## Commentary (Sayana)
This hymn, which I have prepared, should reach toward the Marut troop—the strength of the storm gods. Having praised them as a collective, the seer now speaks of them as individuals. They are the "sons of Rudra"; the fact that they are considered the children of Rudra has been mentioned many times. "Youthful" <note>original: "yuvan-yūn"</note> refers to those who are energetic or mixers of strength. The poet addresses his own mind: "O mind, pervade them." The "desire" or holy resolve calls for wealth—specifically, non-perishing well-being. Because of this, approach and praise those who possess dappled horses and who travel to the sacrifice.

---

-> || Now the Sixteenth Verse || <-

## Hymn Text
May this hymn reach **Earth**, the **Atmosphere**, the **Trees**, and the **Plants** for the sake of wealth. May every single **god** be easily invoked for me. May Mother Earth never place us in a state of **ill-will** <note>original: "durmatau"; refers to misfortune or a bad state of mind</note>. ॥ 16 ॥

**Word-by-word Analysis:**
Forth | this | hymn | Earth | Atmosphere | Trees | Plants | for wealth | may reach |
God by god | easily invoked | may be | for me | not | us | mother | Earth | in ill-will | may she place ॥ 16 ॥

---

## Commentary (Sayana)
May this hymn or praise reach the deities starting with Earth. For what purpose? For wealth. May every single god be "easy to call" <note>original: "suhavaḥ"</note> for my sake; let them be responsive to my invocation. May Earth, who is the mother and creator of all things, or who is called "Mother" because she measures out everything, never place us in "ill-will." That is, let her not leave us in a state of misfortune or bad disposition.

---

-> || Now the Seventeenth Verse || <-

## Hymn Text
O **Gods**, may we be in the wide, **unobstructed** space. ॥ 17 ॥

**Word-by-word Analysis:**
In the wide | O Gods | in the unobstructed | may we be ॥ 17 ॥

---

## Commentary (Sayana)
O Gods, may we exist within your vast, great, and entirely unobstructed happiness. May we remain there, free from all confinement.

It emphasizes the relationship between the storm gods (Maruts) and their father Rudra, ending with a plea for existence in a state of "wide, unobstructed" well-being.</summary>

[Rig Veda — Ashtaka 4, Adhyaya 2, Varga 20] 406

->॥ The Eighteenth Verse ॥<-

## Hymn Text
May we come into contact with the **Ashvins** <note>the divine twin horsemen and healers</note> through their **new protection** <note>original: "avasa nūtanena"</note>, which brings happiness and provides excellent guidance. Bring to us **wealth** <note>original: "rayim"</note>, as well as **heroic sons** <note>original: "vīrān"</note>, and all **immortal fortunes**. ॥ 18 ॥

**Word-by-word Analysis:**
Together | with the Ashvins | protection | with new | happiness-producing | with good guidance | may we go |
Near | to us | wealth | bring | and | also | heroic sons | near | all | immortal | fortunes ॥ 18 ॥

---

## Commentary (Sayana)
May we be joined with the protection of the Ashvins—a protection that is "new," meaning it has not been experienced by others before. This protection is **happiness-producing** <note>original: "mayobhuvā"</note>, meaning it causes comfort to arise, and is characterized by excellent guidance. O **Immortal Ones** <note>original: "amṛtā"; referring to the Ashvins who do not die</note>, bring to us **wealth** or riches. And also bring **heroic sons**—sons possessed of great valor. Bring all forms of **good fortune** as well.

->॥ Thus ends the nineteenth section of the second chapter of the fourth book ॥<-

---

The eleventh hymn of this section, beginning with "**The milch-cows**" <note>original: "ā dhenava"</note>, contains seventeen verses. It was revealed to the seer **Ache** <note>Ache-rishi</note> and is composed in the **Trishtubh** meter <note>a rhythmic cycle of 44 syllables</note>, dedicated to the **All-gods** <note>original: "viśvadeva"</note>. Regarding its ritual application: it is used during the "Grandson of Waters" <note>original: "aponaptriya"</note> ceremony when the special **Ekadhana** water-jars are being carried toward the sacrificial fire-hall. It is the first verse to be recited in that context, as indicated in the ritual manuals: "The milch-cows with their milk, for the sake of the swift..." <note>original citation from the Ashvalayana Shrauta Sutra 5.1</note>.

->॥ The First Verse of the Hymn ॥<-

## Hymn Text
May the **milch-cows** <note>symbolizing the rivers or waters</note> come near to us with their **milk** <note>symbolizing sweetness or life-force</note>, moving swiftly toward their goal, and never failing. For the sake of **great wealth**, the **sage** <note>original: "vipraḥ"</note>, the worshipper who causes happiness, calls out repeatedly to the **seven** great ones. ॥ 1 ॥

**Word-by-word Analysis:**
Near | the milch-cows | with milk | swift-moving | not-neglecting | near | us | may they go | with sweetness |
for great | wealth | the great [ones] | seven | the sage | happiness-producing | the worshipper | calls repeatedly ॥ 1 ॥

---

## Commentary (Sayana)
The **milch-cows** here refer to the **rivers** that nourish us. They are accompanied by **sweetness**—that is, sweet water or essence. They are **swift-moving** <note>original: "tūrṇyarthāḥ"</note> in their journey. The ancient scholar Yaska defines "artha" in this context as derived from the root for "going." They are **not neglecting** or not harming us as they approach. To obtain **great wealth**, the **sage**—one who is especially pleasing to the gods—and the **worshipper** <note>original: "jaritā"</note> **calls out repeatedly** <note>original: "johavīti"; a frequentative verb indicating intensity</note>. He calls to the **seven** great ones, who are the seven moving rivers. These are the Ganges and others mentioned in the famous "Hymn to the Rivers" <note>referencing Rig Veda 10.75.5</note>, as there the count of seven is primary. He calls to these rivers because they are **bringers of happiness**.

<summary>This page concludes a prayer to the Ashvins for protection and wealth, then introduces a new hymn dedicated to the Waters (Rivers), highlighting their role in sacrificial rituals and their identification as the "Seven Rivers."</summary>
<keywords>Ashvins, Sayana, Vedic ritual, Seven Rivers, Aponaptriya, wealth, protection, milch-cows, water deities</keywords>
