[Rig Veda — Book 4, Chapter 3] 407

## Hymn Text

-> ॥ The Second Verse ॥ <-

I desire to turn toward us **Heaven** and **Earth** <note>original: "dyāvā-pṛthivī"</note>, who are never-failing, with a **fine hymn** <note>original: "suṣṭutyā"</note> and with **reverence** <note>original: "namasā"</note> for the sake of **nourishment** <note>original: "vājāya"</note>. May the **Father** and the **Mother**, sweet-spoken and with **skillful hands**, protect us with **glory** in every **battle** <note>original: "bhare-bhare"</note>. ॥ 2 ॥

---

Toward | with a fine hymn | with reverence | to turn | Heaven | for nourishment | Earth | never-failing |
Father | Mother | sweet-spoken | with skillful hands | in every battle | us | glorious | may they protect ॥ 2 ॥

## Commentary (Sayana)

I desire to turn toward us **Heaven and Earth**, who are free from harm or destruction, through a **fine hymn**—that is, an excellent song of praise—and with **reverence**, meaning with the sacrificial offering. This is for the sake of **nourishment** <note>original: "vājāya"</note>, which refers to food and other sustenance; indeed, the sacred scripture <note>the Brahmana texts</note> says "food is indeed *vāja*." The **Father** is the sky (Heaven), who acts as the protector, and the **Mother** is the Earth, who acts as the creator. They are **sweet-spoken**, meaning they utter pleasant or truthful words, and have **skillful hands** <note>original: "suhastā"</note> because they bestow desired gifts with beautiful hands. These two descriptions apply to both deities. May these two **glorious** ones, Heaven and Earth, **protect** us in **every battle**, which refers to either literal conflicts or to the various sacrificial rites.

---

## Hymn Text

-> ॥ The Third Verse ॥ <-

O **officiating priests** <note>original: "adhvaryavaḥ"</note>, having prepared the **sweet juices**, offer the **delightful**, **bright** Soma to **Vayu** <note>the god of the wind</note>. Like the **Hotri priest** <note>original: "hotā-iva"; the primary invoker</note>, O God, drink first of this **mead** <note>original: "madhvaḥ"</note> for our sake; we have given it to you for your **exhilaration**. ॥ 3 ॥

---

Officiating priests | having prepared | sweet juices | toward | to Vayu | bring forth | delightful | bright |
Like the Hotri | our | first | drink | of this | God | of the mead | we have given | your | for exhilaration ॥ 3 ॥

## Commentary (Sayana)

O **Adhvaryu priests**, you who are engaged in the sacrifice <note>original: "adhvaram yuñjānā"</note> and who have **prepared the sweet juices**—meaning the Soma juice, clarified butter, and other offerings—bring forth and provide the **delightful** and **bright**, shining Soma specifically for **Vayu** first. And O Vayu, just as the **Hotri priest** drinks first during a ritual, in the same way, for our sake, **drink** <note>original: "pāhi"</note> of this Soma **first**, before the other gods. O **divine** Vayu, we **give** <note>original: "rarima"</note> this sweet Soma juice for your **exhilaration** or joy. The tradition that Vayu receives the first drink has been explained many times in the scriptures.

---

## Hymn Text

-> ॥ The Fourth Verse ॥ <-

The **ten fingers** <note>original: "daśa kṣipo"; literally "the ten throwers"</note> and the two arms yoke the **pressing-stone** <note>original: "adriṃ"</note> of the Soma; they are the two **preparers** <note>original: "śamitārā"</note> with **skillful hands**. He of the **good hands** <note>the priest</note> has milked the **bright juice** of the mead from the **mountain-dwelling** stalk, which makes a **splashing sound** <note>original: "caniścadat"</note> as it flows. ॥ 4 ॥

---

Ten | fingers | they yoke | two arms | the stone | of the Soma | which | two preparers | with skillful hands |
of the mead | juice | with good hands | mountain-dwelling | splashing | he milked | bright | the stalk ॥ 4 ॥

[Rig Veda — Book 4, Chapter 2] 408

## Commentary (Sayana)
[Continuation of commentary on verse 4]

Since the pressing of the plant is being described here, **Soma** is the deity. Alternatively, the deity is **Indra**. The **ten throwers** <note>original: "daśa kṣipo"</note>, meaning the ten fingers, **unite with** <note>original: "yuñjate"</note> or grasp the **pressing stone** <note>original: "adrim"</note>. Or rather, they become joined with one another in the act. The two arms of the **Adhvaryu** <note>the priest responsible for the physical ritual</note> join with the pressing stone. These two arms—which have **skillful hands** <note>original: "suhastā"</note> and are the "slayers" or preparers of the Soma—engage in the pressing. The Adhvaryu, possessing **beautiful fingers** <note>original: "sugabhastiḥ"</note>, brings delight <note>The commentator notes the grammatical form "aniṣvada" is a Vedic variant of "cadi," meaning to delight</note> as he extracts the **mountain-dwelling** <note>original: "giriṣṭhāṃ"</note> juice of the sweet Soma—so called because the plant grows on mountains or stays in an elevated place. He **milked** <note>original: "duduhe"</note> or extracted it. That **Soma stalk** <note>original: "aṃśuḥ"</note> has yielded its bright, pure juice. Alternatively, the sentence may be read: the Adhvaryu with skillful hands has milked the sweet juice of the pervading Soma stalk.

---

## Hymn Text
-> ॥ The Fifth Verse ॥ <-

Soma has been pressed for you, who enjoy it, for **ritual action**, for **strength**, and for **great exhilaration**. O **Indra**, being invoked, hitch your two beloved **bay horses** to the **chariot** which is well-yoked, and turn them **toward us**. ॥ 5 ॥

**Word-by-word analysis (Pada-patha):**
Pressed | for you | for the one who enjoys | Soma | for ritual action | for strength | for great | for exhilaration |
The two bay horses | in the chariot | well-yoked | in the joining | toward us | Indra | beloved | make | being invoked ॥ 5 ॥

---

## Commentary (Sayana)
O **Indra**, for **you** who **enjoy** the offering, the **Soma has been pressed** <note>original: "asāvi"</note>. For what purpose? For **ritual action** <note>original: "kratve"</note>, such as the slaying of the demon Vritra, for **strength** <note>original: "dakṣāya"</note>, and for **great exhilaration** <note>original: "mādāya"</note>. Because this is so, O **Indra**, as you are **being invoked** by us, join your **beloved bay horses**—who are fastened to a **sturdy yoke** <note>original: "sudhurā"</note>—to the **chariot** fit for the journey, and **make** that chariot turn **toward us**.

-> ॥ This ends the twentieth section (Varga) of the second chapter (Adhyaya) of the fourth book (Ashtaka) ॥ <-

---

## Hymn Text
-> ॥ The Sixth Verse ॥ <-

O **Agni**, with one mind with us, bring the great **Aramati** <note>the goddess of Devotion or Earth</note> and the divine **Gna** <note>a goddess of speech or offerings</note>, who is like a cow, with reverence and offered oblations. For the **exhilaration** of the **honey-sweet juice**, bring the **great one** who **knows the Truth** through the **paths traveled by the gods**. ॥ 6 ॥

**Word-by-word analysis (Pada-patha):**
Toward | us | the great | Aramati | with one mind | Gna | the goddess | with reverence | who is given oblations |
Of the honey | for exhilaration | the great | who knows the Truth | toward | Agni | bring | by the paths | traveled by the gods ॥ 6 ॥

---

## Commentary (Sayana)
Addressing Agni here, because the goddess **Gna** is to be invited through him, the deity of this verse is either Agni or Gna. O **Agni**, being **with one mind** <note>original: "sajoṣā"</note> or pleased together with us, bring the **divine Gna**, the deity of this name who is to be approached by all. **Yaska** <note>the ancient etymologist</note> states in his lexicon that the words *Mena* and *Gna* are names for women [or goddesses]. For our sake, via the **paths** to be traveled by the gods...

<meta>This page continues the commentary by Sayana on the 43rd hymn of the 5th Mandala. It completes the explanation for verse 6, then provides the text and commentary for verses 7 and 8. [Rig Veda — Book 5, Chapter 3] 409

...bring her facing us. What kind of goddess is she? The **Great** <note>original: "mahī"</note> **Devotion** <note>original: "aramatim"</note>, who is all-pervading or moves everywhere, along with **praise** <note>original: "namasā"</note>, she who has **prepared oblations** <note>original: "rātahavyāṃ"</note>—meaning her desire is for the given offerings. For what purpose? For the **exhilaration** <note>original: "madāya"</note> of the sweet Soma. Furthermore, she is **mighty** <note>original: "bṛhatīm"</note> and **knower of the ritual truth** <note>original: "ṛtajñām"</note>, one who recognizes the sacrifice. 

In the **Pravargya** ritual <note>a preliminary Vedic ceremony</note>, while the **Mahavira** <note>the large earthenware pot used to heat milk and ghee</note> is being anointed, the verse "They anoint him..." is recited. This is indicated in the ritual manuals: "They anoint him while spreading, like a sage... during the anointing" (Asvalayana Shrauta Sutra 4.6).

---

## Hymn Text

-> ॥ The Seventh Verse ॥ <-

They **anoint** him—the wise priests, as if spreading him out—as they heat the one who possesses the **sacrificial fat** <note>original: "vapāvantam"</note> with fire. Like a **beloved son** <note>original: "preṣṭhaḥ putraḥ"</note> in his **father's lap** <note>original: "pituḥ upasi"</note>, the **hot vessel** <note>original: "gharmaḥ"</note>, desiring the sacrifice, has been placed upon the Fire. ॥ 7 ॥

### Pada-patha
They anoint | him | spreading | like | the wise [priests] | possessing the omentum | like | with fire | heating | of the father | like | the son | in the lap | most beloved | [particle of completion] | the hot vessel | the fire | desiring the rite | has been placed ॥ 7 ॥

## Commentary (Sayana)

The wise and intelligent priests—the Adhvaryu and others—now anoint that **Gharma** <note>the ritual vessel</note> as they spread the ritual. The word "like" <note>original: "na"</note> here is used in the sense of "now" or for comparison. Just as they heat a **fatty animal** <note>original: "vapāvantam"</note> in the fire during a sacrifice, they heat the vessel with fire. Like a most beloved son sitting in the lap of a father, the **Gharma** (the Mahavira pot) sits upon the fire. Indeed, the ancient scriptures say: "It is called 'Gharma' because it was heated." Seeking the **sacrifice** <note>original: "ṛtayant"</note>, it has been placed upon the fire. The metaphor of the father and son is used here to illustrate how the vessel sits comfortably and securely, without cracking or bursting.

---

## Hymn Text

-> ॥ The Eighth Verse ॥ <-

May our **great, mighty, and most auspicious song** <note>original: "gīḥ"</note> go forth like a **messenger** <note>original: "dūtaḥ"</note> to call the **Ashvins**. O producers of happiness, come hither in your **single chariot**; come to the **treasure** <note>the Soma</note> like the **linchpin** <note>original: "āṇiḥ"</note> to the **hub of the wheel** <note>original: "nābhim"</note>. ॥ 8 ॥

### Pada-patha
Towards | great | mighty | most peaceful | song | messenger | like | to go | O Ashvins | to call | happiness-producing | having a single chariot | hither | come | towards | the treasure | the axle-load | the linchpin | like | the hub ॥ 8 ॥

## Commentary (Sayana)

May our praise go **towards** <note>original: "accha"</note> the Ashvins to **call them** <note>original: "huvadhyai"</note>. May it travel like a messenger who goes to invite a guest. The song is described as: **venerable** <note>original: "mahī"</note>, **great** <note>original: "bṛhatī"</note>, and **most peaceful** <note>original: "śantamā"</note>—yielding the highest happiness. O Ashvins, you who bring forth happiness and travel together in the same chariot, come toward the **stored Soma** <note>original: "nidhi"</note>, which has been placed for you. Come hither. Just as the **linchpin** <note>original: "āṇiḥ"</note>—the small pin at the end of the axle—is essential to the **hub** <note>original: "nābhim"</note>...

<vocab>
अश्विन् (Aśvin): Twin deities who are the physicians of the gods, often appearing at dawn.
घर्म (Gharma): Both the name of the hot milk offering and the earthen pot (Mahavira) used to prepare it.
महावीर (Mahāvīra): "The Great Hero," the specific name for the reinforced clay pot used in the Pravargya.
वपावन् (Vapāvan): Literally "possessing the omentum" (sacrificial fat), used here to compare the vessel's heating to the cooking of a fatty offering.
ऋत्विज् (Ṛtvij): A general term for the various priests who perform the Vedic sacrifice.
प्रवर्ग्य (Pravargya): A mystic ritual performed as a preliminary to the Soma sacrifice, symbolizing the restoration of the head of the sacrifice.
निधि (Nidhi): "Treasure" or "deposit," here referring to the Soma juice that has been prepared and set aside.
</vocab>

...like. Just as a **wheel-hub** <note>original: "nābhi"</note> without a **linchpin** <note>original: "niṣkīlā"</note> cannot support the movement of a chariot, in the same way, the **Soma** juice, when separated from you two <note>referring to the twin Ashvins from the previous verse</note>, does not carry forth the sacrifice. This illustration is given to make this principle known.

## Hymn Text

->॥ The Ninth Verse ॥<-

I have **directed** <note>original: "adikṣi"</note> an **utterance of homage** to the powerful, the swift **Pushan**, and also to **Vayu**; they two who, through **wealth**, are the **stimulators of thoughts**, and who are themselves the **givers of strength**. ॥ 9 ॥

| **tavyasaḥ** | of the powerful |
| **namaḥ-uktim** | the utterance of homage |
| **turasya** | of the swift |
| **aham** | I |
| **pūṣṇaḥ** | of Pushan |

| **vāyoḥ** | of Vayu |

## Commentary (Sayana)

**I**, the seer of this hymn, **direct**—meaning I present or declare—an **utterance of homage** (a word of salutation or a hymn of praise) to the god **Pushan**, the "Nourisher" who possesses excellent strength and is swift in his actions. This applies to the deity described by these qualities, and **also to Vayu**, the god of wind, described by similar characteristics. 

Who are these two? **Pushan and Vayu** are the **stimulators of thoughts** by means of **wealth** (acting as the cause, in the form of the sacrificial oblation). Alternatively, the word for **wealth** <note>original: "rādhasā"</note> is used here in the third grammatical case but carries the meaning of the sixth case; thus, they are the "stimulators of wealth and of thoughts." These two are also the stimulators of **strength** (meaning either food or success in battle). The text implies: "May you two, by your own nature, be the **givers of wealth** for the purpose of inspiring others."

---

## Hymn Text

->॥ The Tenth Verse ॥<-

O **Jatavedas**, being **invoked**, bring all the **Maruts** with their **names** and their **forms**. O all you **Maruts**, come to the **sacrifice**, to the **singer's** words and **beautiful praise**; all of you, come with **protection**. ॥ 10 ॥

**Padapatha:**

| :--- | :--- |

| **marutaḥ** | the Maruts [storm gods] |
| **vakṣi** | bring |
| **viśvān** | all |
| **ā** | [towards/prefix] |
| **rūpebhiḥ** | by forms |
| **jāta-vedaḥ** | O Knower of Beings (Agni) |
| **huvānaḥ** | being invoked |
| **yajñam** | the sacrifice |
| **giraḥ** | the words |
| **jarituḥ** | of the singer |
| **su-stutim** | the beautiful praise |

| **ganta** | come |
| **marutaḥ** | O Maruts |
| **viśve** | all |
| **ūtī** | with protection |

## Commentary (Sayana)

O **Jatavedas** <note>a title for Agni, the fire god, meaning "knower of all created beings" or "knower of wisdom"</note>, while being **invoked** by us, **bring** here **all the Maruts**—the storm gods who share in the hymns and the offerings—according to their **names**, such as those characterized by Indra or Varuna. Bring them also with their **forms**, which are distinguished by having a "thousand eyes" or "holding the thunderbolt" in their hands. 

Furthermore, O **Maruts**, all of you **come** toward our **sacrifice** (or the oblation related to the sacrifice), toward the **words** (the spoken praises) of the **singer**, and the **beautiful praise** which results in auspicious rewards. <note>The commentator notes that "praise" is used in the singular because it is a single unified prayer, while "words" is plural because it is made of many parts.</note> All of you, come together with your **protection** or your saving help.

<vocab>
- <term>Pushan (Pūṣan)</term>: A solar deity representing the nourishing power of the sun and the protector of travelers.
- <term>Vayu (Vāyu)</term>: The personification of the wind and the breath of the cosmos.
- <term>Maruts (Marutaḥ)</term>: A group of storm deities, often described as the sons of Rudra and the brilliant, spear-wielding companions of Indra.
- <term>Jatavedas (Jātavedas)</term>: A common epithet for Agni (the ritual fire), meaning "he who knows all births" or "the possessor of all knowledge."
- <term>Soma</term>: The sacred ritual drink pressed from a plant, offered to the gods to grant them strength and exhilaration.
</vocab>

<meta>This page continues the commentary on Rig Veda, Mandala 5, Hymn (Sukta) 43. The previous page concluded the discussion on the tenth verse. This page contains the text, word-analysis (Padapatha), and Sayana’s commentary for the eleventh and twelfth verses of the same hymn. Mandala 5. Anuvaka 3. Sukta 43.] || Fourth Ashtaka || 411

The eleventh verse, beginning with "May she from heaven," is the second verse in the triplet dedicated to **Sarasvati** <note>A Vedic goddess representing both a sacred river and the power of speech/wisdom</note> used during the **Prauga Shastra** <note>A specific recitation by the Hotri priest</note> on the ninth day of the **Dasharatra** <note>A ten-day ritual sequence</note> rite. This is indicated in the ritual manuals: "May Sarasvati from the heaven, from the great mountain... she who leads us to better things." (Ashvalayana Shrauta Sutra 7.11). The text follows:

## Hymn Text

-> ११ <-
May the worshipful **Sarasvati** come to our **sacrifice** from the **heaven**, or from the **great mountain**. May the **divine** one, being **pleased**, she who is **turned toward the clarified butter**, hear our **pleasant speech**, she who is **desiring** it. ॥ 11 ॥

**Hither | our | from heaven | from the great | from the mountain | hither | Sarasvati | the worshipful | may she go | the sacrifice |**
**the invocation | the divine | being pleased | turned toward butter | pleasant | our | speech | desiring | may she hear ॥ 11 ॥**

---

## Commentary (Sayana)

May the **worshipful** goddess **Sarasvati**, who is worthy of sacrifice, come **hither** to our sacrifice from the shining **heaven** (the celestial world). Likewise, may she come from the **great mountain**—referring either to the cloud in the atmosphere which "fills" or "pleases" like a mountain, or the high peaks. By this, she is identified as the **Middle Voice** <note>original: "mādhyamikī vāk"; in Vedic thought, speech exists in three levels—celestial, atmospheric/thunder, and human. The "Middle Voice" is the thunder/speech of the mid-regions</note>. Alternatively, "great mountain" acts as a description of "heaven," as the Vedas say there are three heavens and three earths. In this second view, the word "hither" is repeated for emphasis.

May the **divine Sarasvati**, **being pleased** by and enjoying our praise, and being **turned toward the clarified butter** <note>original: "ghṛtācī"; can also mean "turned toward water"</note>, **hear our pleasant** and joy-giving **speech** (hymn of praise), for she is **desiring** and loving toward it.

-> || Now the Twelfth Verse || <-

## Hymn Text

-> १२ <-
Place the **wise** one, the **blue-backed**, the **great Brihaspati** upon the **seat**. We shall **serve** him who sits at his **source**, who **shines** within the **house**, who is **gold-colored** and **ruddy**. ॥ 12 ॥

**Hither | the wise | the blue-backed | the great | Brihaspati | upon the seat | place [ye] |**
**sitting at the source | in the house | hither | the shining | gold-colored | the ruddy | we shall serve ॥ 12 ॥**

---

## Commentary (Sayana)

This verse is dedicated to **Brihaspati** <note>The "Lord of Prayer" and the priest of the gods</note>. O **priests** <note>original: "ṛtvijaḥ"</note>, **place Brihaspati**, the divine lord of the great prayer <term>Mantra: a sacred formula or hymn</term>, **upon the seat** in our sacrificial hall. What kind of god is he? He is the **wise one** (the performer of various works), **blue-backed** (having smooth or beautiful limbs), and **great**. We, the priests and the patrons, shall **serve** and honor him.

He is further described: **sitting at the source** (resting in his proper place on the altar), **shining** all around within the **house** (the sacrificial hall), **gold-colored**, and **ruddy** (shining brightly).

Alternatively, this hymn is dedicated to **Agni** <note>The god of fire</note>. **Brihaspati** is a name used for Agni here because he is the "lord of the great (expanded) ritual." This is supported by descriptions like **blue-backed**, which refers to the blue-tinted smoke of the fire, and his being seated in the house and his golden-ruddy color—all of which are characteristic signs of **Agni**.

<summary>This page contains verses 11 and 12 of Rig Veda 5.43, providing ritual instructions, the original text, and Sayana's commentary focusing on the goddess Sarasvati as atmospheric speech and Brihaspati, who is also interpreted as the sacrificial fire, Agni.</summary>
<keywords>Sarasvati, Brihaspati, Agni, Prauga Shastra, Middle Voice, sacrificial ritual, Veda commentary, Sayana</keywords>

## Hymn Text

-> ॥ Now the thirteenth verse ॥ <-

May the supporter of all, the one of great light, come here; rejoicing and being called with all protections. Wearing the moving flames among the plants, unharmed, the triple-horned bull, the bestower of food and strength. ॥ 13 ॥

**Hither | Supporter of all | Of great light | Rejoicing | With all | To come | With protections | Being called |**
**Moving flames | Wearing | Plants | Unharmed | Triple-horned | Bull | Bestower of food ॥ 13 ॥**

---

## Commentary (Sayana)

This and the following two verses are attributed to the sage **Atri** <note>One of the seven great Vedic seers (Rishis)</note>. May **Agni** <note>The Fire God</note> come to our sacrifice. He is the **supporter of all** <note>original: "dharṣisi"</note>, the one who sustains everything. He is of **great light** <note>original: "bṛhaddivaḥ"</note>, possessing abundant radiance. **Rejoicing** <note>original: "rarāṇo"</note>, he delights in the ritual and grants our desires. He is **being called** <note>original: "huvāna"</note> along with **all protections** <note>original: "viśvebhir omebhiḥ"</note>. He is **wearing** <note>original: "vasāno"</note> his **moving flames** <note>original: "grā"</note> among the **plants** <note>original: "oṣadhiṣu"</note>. He is **unharmed** <note>original: "amṛdhro"</note>, meaning he is never struck down or extinguished. He is **triple-horned** <note>original: "tridhātuśṛṅgaḥ"</note>—this refers to his elevated flames which appear in three colors: red, white, and black. He is the **bull** <note>original: "vṛṣabho"</note> because he showers blessings upon us, and he is the **bestower of food** <note>original: "vayodhā"</note> or the sustainer of the clarified butter offerings.

---

## Hymn Text

-> ॥ Now the fourteenth verse ॥ <-

In the mother’s highest place, in the bright spot of the human sacrificer, the praisers, the touchers of the oblation, have arrived. Giving offerings with reverence, they cleanse the delightful, newly-born Agni, as humans might clean a child for its dwelling. ॥ 14 ॥

**Of the mother | In the place | In the highest | In the bright | Of the human | The praisers | The touchers of the oblation | Have gone |**
**Delightful | With reverence | Given-offerings | The newly-born | They cleanse | Humans | As if | For a dwelling ॥ 14 ॥**

---

## Commentary (Sayana)

For the **human** <note>original: "āyoḥ"</note> sacrificer, the **praisers** <note>original: "vipanyavaḥ"</note>—this is a name for the singers, such as the **Hotri** <note>The priest who recites the hymns of the Rig Veda</note> priests—and the **touchers of the oblation** <note>original: "rāspirāsaḥ"</note> have arrived. The word *raśpirāsaḥ* refers to those who handle the sacrificial ladles (juhu) which touch the ritual food. These priests have **gone** <note>original: "agman"</note> to the **bright**, **highest place** <note>original: "śukre parame pade"</note> of the **mother** <note>original: "mātuḥ"</note>, which refers to the Earth or specifically the **North Altar** <note>original: "uttaravedi"</note>. There, they **cleanse** <note>original: "mṛjanti"</note> or purify the **newly-born** <note>original: "śiprum"</note> Agni, who is **delightful** <note>original: "suśevyam"</note> and beneficial for happiness. They do this for his **dwelling** <note>original: "vāse"</note> in the ritual, having **given offerings** <note>original: "rātahavyā"</note> and accompanied by **reverence** <note>original: "namasā"</note> or songs of praise. A comparison is given: **as humans** <note>original: "āyavo na"</note> in the world might clean a child or a person to prepare them for a dwelling place, so do the priests prepare the fire.

---

## Hymn Text

-> ॥ Now the fifteenth verse ॥ <-

Great strength to you, O great Agni! The couple, aging with prayer, attend to you. May every god be easy to invoke for me; may Mother Earth not hold us in ill-will. ॥ 15 ॥

---

<vocab>
- **dharṣisi**: Supporter or holder of all things.
- **bṛhaddivaḥ**: Possessing the vast light of the heavens.
- **rarāṇaḥ**: One who is joyful or bestows gifts freely.
- **omebhiḥ**: Through various forms of divine protection.
- **amṛdhraḥ**: Unfailing, imperishable, or one who cannot be harmed.
- **tridhātuśṛṅgaḥ**: Having three types of "horns" (the distinct colors/parts of a flame).
- **vayodhāः**: The giver of nourishment, strength, or life-force.
- **mātuṣpade**: Literally "in the mother's step/place," identifying the sacrificial altar as a spot on Mother Earth.
- **vipanyavaḥ**: Learned singers or priests who chant praises.
- **rāspirāsaḥ**: Priests whose ritual tools touch the sacrificial offerings.
- **suśevyam**: Highly enjoyable, kind, or easy to serve.
- **śiprum**: Usually refers to a chin or jaw, but here interpreted as the "newly born" fire or the "radiant" one.
- **āyavaḥ**: Men, particularly the mortal human beings involved in the sacrifice.
</vocab>

The final verse is a prayer for strength, divine accessibility, and the favor of Mother Earth.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the translation of the Rig Veda, Mandala 5, Sukta 43, providing the final three verses (15–17) and the commentary by the scholar Sayana. It then transitions to the introduction and first verse of Sukta 44, marking a shift in both authorship and ritual application.</meta>

## Hymn Text

-> Mandala 5, Anuvaka 3, Hymn 43 <-

Abundant food for you, the Great One, O Agni, is offered by those worn by ritual labor. Linked as couples, they serve you. May every god be easy to invoke for me. May our Mother Earth never hold ill-will toward us. ॥ 15 ॥

---

## Commentary (Sayana)

**Abundant** <note>original: "bṛhat"</note> means plentiful food <note>original: "vayaḥ"</note>. **O Agni**, for you who are **Great**, those **worn by ritual labor** <note>original: "dhiyājuraḥ"</note>—meaning those whose bodies are aged or spent through the performance of sacred work—**linked as couples** <note>original: "mithunāso"</note>, together with their wives, **serve** <note>original: "sacante"</note> or worship you. This is supported by the scriptural revelation <note>term: "Sruti" - sacred revealed text</note> which states: "The husband and wife should both establish the sacred fire." Indeed, in the sixth chapter of the *Adhikara-adhyaya* <note>The "Chapter on Qualifications" in Mimamsa philosophy</note>, it is established that a woman has the right to perform fire rituals, provided she does so alongside her husband. The rest of the verse is understood from previous explanations. ॥

---

## Hymn Text

-> ॥ Now the sixteenth verse ॥ <-

May we be in a wide place, O Gods, free from oppression. ॥ 16 ॥
> **In a wide place | O Gods | Free from oppression | May we be ॥ 16 ॥**

-> ॥ Now the seventeenth verse ॥ <-

Together with the newest, joy-giving protection of the **Ashvins** <note>The twin divine physicians</note>, and under their excellent guidance, may we move forward. Bring to us wealth and heroic sons; bring all immortal blessings. ॥ 17 ॥
> **Together | Of the Ashvins | With protection | Newest | Joy-giving | Under good guidance | May we move | Bring | To us | Wealth | Bring | And | Heroic sons | Bring | All | Immortal | Blessings ॥ 17 ॥**

**These two verses have been explained.**

-> ॥ Thus ends the twenty-second section (varga) of the second chapter (adhyaya) of the fourth book (ashtaka) ॥ <-

---

## Commentary (Sayana - Introduction to Sukta 44)

The twelfth hymn, beginning with "**As of old**" <note>original: "tam pratnathā"</note>, contains fifteen verses. The Seer <note>term: "Rishi" - the inspired poet to whom the hymn was revealed</note> is named **Avatsara**, who belongs to the **Kashyapa** clan. In those specific verses where other names like Sadapruna, Bahuvrikta, and others are heard, those individuals are also considered joint authors. The fourteenth and fifteenth verses are in the **Trishtubh** meter <note>44 syllables</note>; the remaining verses, according to the rule that the end of a section concludes with a Trishtubh, are in the **Jagati** meter <note>48 syllables</note>. The deities of this hymn are the **Vishve Devah** <note>The "All-Gods" or the collective pantheon</note>. 

The index of hymns <note>term: "Anukramani"</note> states: "The hymn 'As of old' has fifteen verses; the seer is Avatsara the Kashyapa; other seers are also seen here through specific marks; the last two are Trishtubh." In the **Vajapeya** sacrifice <note>A prestigious "Drink of Strength" ritual</note>, during the additional **Ukthya** stage, the first thirteen verses of this hymn are to be recited. It is noted in the ritual manuals: "Having recited thirteen of the verses starting with 'As of old' and leaving one, he should perform the *Durohana* ascent." (Asvalayana Shrauta Sutra 9.9). ॥

---

## Hymn Text (Sukta 44)

-> ॥ Therein the first verse ॥ <-

As of old, as in former times, as in all ways, so now—to that Eldest One, who sits upon the sacred grass, who finds the light of heaven, who faces his worshipers; to Him you must milk the strength of the prayer, for He is the swift winner of battles in whom you find your strength. ॥ 1 ॥

<vocab>
- अग्नि (Agni): Deity of fire
- अश्विन् (Ashvins): Twin Vedic deities of healing and light
- अवत्सार (Avatsara): The seer (Rishi) of this hymn, from the Kashyapa family
- विश्वे देवाः (Vishve Devah): The collective group of all Vedic deities
- वाजपेय (Vajapeya): A high-status Soma sacrifice involving chariot races
- दूरोहण (Durohana): A complex ritual recitation technique involving "climbing" and "descending" through the verses
- त्रयस्त्रिंश (Trayastrimsha): The thirty-three primary deities of the Vedic pantheon
- जगती (Jagati): A Vedic meter consisting of four lines of 12 syllables each
- त्रिष्टुभ् (Trishtubh): A Vedic meter consisting of four lines of 11 syllables each
</vocab>

<keywords>Agni, Ashvins, Avatsara Kashyapa, women's ritual rights, Vajapeya sacrifice, Jagati meter, Vishve Devah, Durohana ritual</keywords>

<meta>This page concludes the commentary for the first verse of Rig Veda, Mandala 4, Sukta 5, and provides the text and partial commentary for the second verse. The discussion focuses on the ritual application of these verses during the Soma sacrifice and provides a word-for-word breakdown of Indra's attributes.</meta>

## Hymn Text

-> **Word-for-Word Breakdown - Verse 1** <-

Him | in the ancient way | in the former way | in every way | in this way | of greatest rank | seated on the sacred grass | finding the light of heaven | facing toward us | the gathering of strength | to milk or draw out | with a song | the swift one | conquering | following | in which praises | you grow. ॥ १ ॥

---

## Commentary (Sayana)

It is said that this verse and the one following are addressed to the god Indra. The experts provide the ritual justification <note>term: "viniyoga" - the specific ritual use of a verse</note> for this: the verse "Him in the ancient way..." is designated for use during the drawing of the *Shukra* and *Manthin* vessels <note>Two specific vessels of Soma juice used in the morning libation, representing the Sun and Moon</note>. These vessels are associated with Indra. When the priest recites praises to Indra, the *Shukra* and *Manthin* vessels become "endowed with the chant" <note>original: "ukthavantau"</note>. As the *Aitareya Brahmana* (3.7) <note>A sacred prose text explaining the significance of the Rig Veda's hymns</note> states: "By that which is addressed to Indra, he recites; thus the Shukra and Manthin vessels possess the chant."

There is also a formal command <note>term: "sampraiṣa" - a ritual instruction from one priest to another</note> from the Adhvaryu priest: "Morning by morning, for the morning pressing of the Soma with the *Shukra* vessel, send forth the honey-dripping Somas set out for Indra" (*Shatapatha Brahmana* 4.2.1.23). Similarly, the command of the director <note>term: "Prashastr" - a priest who gives instructions</note> is: "May the Hotar priest worship Indra at the morning pressing..." (Ashvalayana Shrauta Sutra 5.5). The verse used for offering the Soma is also addressed to Indra: "This is your honey-like Soma" (Ashvalayana 5.5). Therefore, the hymn is clearly for Indra.

The commentary on the words follows: "Him" refers to Indra. **In the ancient way** <note>original: "pratnathā"</note> means like the ancient sacrificers. **In the former way** means like our ancestors. **In every way** means like all living beings. **In this way** means like the sacrificers present right now. Just as they obtained rewards through praising Indra, so too—O inner Self <note>Sayana suggests the poet is addressing his own soul here</note>—you also: **Of greatest rank** <note>original: "jyeṣṭhatātim"</note>, the eldest; **Seated on the sacred grass** <note>original: "barhiṣadam"</note>, sitting on the sacrificial Barhis grass; **Finding the light of heaven** <note>original: "svavidam"</note>, the all-knowing one or the one who allows everyone to reach heaven; **Facing toward us** <note>original: "pratīcīnam"</note>, turning his face toward us; **The gathering** <note>original: "vṛjanam"</note>—this word is a name for strength, referring here to the one who possesses strength; the swift-moving or pervasive one; **Conquering**, the one who overcomes all. You **milk** <note>original: "dohase"</note> or draw out from this Indra all your desires always, by the means of a **song** <note>original: "girā"</note> or praise. This is the command to the inner Self. **In which** praises **you grow**—that is, you become great, or you make Indra grow through the praise. The use of the plural "in which" <note>original: "yāsu"</note> is a grammatical variation.

---

-> ॥ Now the Second Verse ॥ <-

## Hymn Text

For glory, the beautiful waters of the cloud, which, shining in heaven, he urges from the heights for the one who does not impel. You are a good protector, O wise one, not to be deceived; beyond delusions, you were present through the Eternal Truth, which is your name. ॥ २ ॥

-> **Word-for-Word Breakdown** <-

For glory | beautiful to see | of the cloud | which | heaven | shining | of the heights | to the non-impeller | good protector | you are | not | to be deceived | O wise one | beyond | by delusions | in Truth | you were | name | your ॥ २ ॥

---

## Commentary (Sayana)

O Indra, **shining in heaven** <note>original: "svaḥ virocamānaḥ"</note>—that is, shining in the sky—you, **to the non-impeller** <note>original: "acodate" - Sayana notes the dative case is used here in place of the genitive 'of the non-impeller'</note>, meaning for the one who does not urge. **Of the cloud** <note>original: "uparasya"</note>, referring to that which belongs to the cloud. **Beautiful to see** <note>original: "sudṛśīḥ"</note>, those beautifully shining waters which exist; among all the **heights** <note>original: "kakubhām"</note> or directions, **for glory** <note>original: "śriye"</note>—the sense is that you should be the impeller for the refuge of all living beings. O **wise one** <note>original: "sukrato"</note>, you who perform good deeds such as providing rain, you **are a good protector** <note>original: "sugopāḥ"</note>, a fine guardian of all creatures. Therefore, you are **not to be deceived** <note>original: "na dabhāya"</note>...

# Mandala 5, Anuvaka 3, Hymn 44. || Fourth Eighth || 415

You do not exist for the purpose of deceptive destruction of living beings. You do not prevail in such a way. And you, existing beyond all illusions <note>original: "māyābhira-āsurībhiḥ" - refers to the deceptive or creative powers often associated with powerful beings</note>, are stationed beyond all deceptions. This is because your name—which is to say, your very form—resides in the world of truth <note>original: "satya-loke"</note>.

---

## Hymn Text

->|| Now the Third Verse ||<-

The truthful oblation he attends, the enduring and supporting [offering], he of unimpeded path. He is the Invoker-priest, the bearer of strength. Gliding forward along the sacred grass, the showerer [of blessings], tender, in the midst [of the plants], youthful, ageless, placed among the spreading vegetation. ॥ ३ ॥

**Word-for-Word Breakdown**

Truthful | oblation | attends | existing/enduring | and | supporting | and | of unimpeded path | He | Invoker-priest | bearer of strength |
gliding forward | along | sacred grass | showerer | tender/youthful | in the middle | youth | ageless | among spreading plants | placed. ॥ ३ ॥

## Commentary (Sayana)

This verse is addressed to Agni <note>The God of Fire</note>, as indicated by signs such as his role as the "Invoker-priest" <note>term: "hotṛtva"</note> and his "youthfulness." This Agni constantly attends to—that is, serves—the oblation consisting of clarified butter and other offerings. What kind of oblation? It is "truthful" <note>original: "sat"</note>; because it is a means to achieve real results, the offering itself is called real.

It is also "supporting" <note>original: "dhātu"</note>, the sustainer of everything. Because the oblation being offered serves as a means for rain through the mediation of the Sun, and by that rain, offspring are produced, the offering is the sustainer. As it is said: "The oblation cast into the fire reaches the Sun; from the Sun comes rain, from rain comes food, and from food come living beings" <note>A famous verse from the Laws of Manu (3.76) explaining the cosmic cycle of the sacrifice</note>.

He is of <term>unimpeded path</term> <note>original: "ariṣṭagātuḥ"</note>, meaning his movement is uninjured. Since his movement results in the completion of the sacrifice and the attainment of its fruits, he is called unimpeded. The text explains this: He is indeed the <term>Invoker-priest</term> who performs the sacrifice; the <term>bearer of strength</term> <note>original: "sahobhariḥ"</note>, the sustainer of power; <term>gliding forward along the sacred grass</term>, moving exceedingly well; the <term>showerer</term> <note>original: "vṛṣā"</note>, the one who showers results. He is <term>tender</term> <note>original: "śiṣnuḥ"</note>, meaning one who must be protected or one who is not yet fully grown; <term>youthful</term>, the mixer of all things; <term>ageless</term>, free from decay; and <term>placed among the spreading vegetation</term> <note>original: "visruhā"</note>, established in the midst of the herbs and plants. Such a being attends to the sacrifice.

---

## Hymn Text

->|| Now the Fourth Verse ||<-

These well-yoked [rays] go forth on the journey for your seeking, directed downward for that [sacrificer], to be guided, increasers of Truth. With well-guiding, all-ruling reins, the Krivi-spirit steals the names in the depths. ॥ ४ ॥

**Word-for-Word Breakdown**

Forth | for you | these | well-yoked | on the journey | for seeking | downward | for that one | to be guided | increasers of Truth |
with well-guiding [reins] | with all-ruling [reins] | with reins/rays | Krivi | names | in the depth | steals. ॥ ४ ॥

## Commentary (Sayana)

This verse is addressed to the Sun <note>Surya</note>. These "well-yoked" <note>term: "suyujaḥ"</note> rays are well-connected to one another. On their "journey," they go "downward" for the "seeking" or desiring [of the sacrifice]. They are "to be guided" <note>original: "yamyā"</note>—meaning they are fit to go toward the sacrificer. Alternatively, the term refers to the Sun as the Controller <note>original: "Yama"</note>, and these are his rays. They are also the "increasers of Truth" <note>original: "ṛtāvṛdhaḥ"</note>, the expanders of the sacrifice. This Sun, with "well-guiding" and "all-ruling" "reins"—that is, his rays... <note>The commentary on this page ends mid-sentence</note>

<vocab>
अरिष्टगातुः (unimpeded movement), सहोभरिः (bearer of strength), प्रसस्राणः (gliding forward), वृषा (showerer/virile), शिश्नुः (tender/youthful), अजरः (ageless), विस्रुहा (spreading plants), सुयुजः (well-yoked/rays), ऋतावृधः (increasers of Truth/Sacrifice), अभीशुभिः (with reins/rays)
</vocab>

[Page 416]

# Mandala 5, Ashtaka 4, Adhyaya 2, Varga 24.

With his rays, the "Doer" <note>original: "kriviḥ" - a term Sayana interprets here as "the creator/doer," though it can also refer to a historical tribe</note> takes away <note>original: "muṣāyati" - literally 'steals' or 'robs'</note> the waters from the low-lying regions of the earth. Alternatively, this may mean that for the sake of the sacrifice, these well-yoked horses of Agni travel in his chariot to the place of worship. The rest of the meaning is similar: Agni, acting like a creator, takes the oblations—which are characterized by his flames—in the sloping sacrificial ground.

->|| Now the Fifth Verse ||<-

## Hymn Text
Accepting the Soma-offering repeatedly with the sacrificial woods, he who possesses the branches <note>Soma stalks</note> is melodious among those of focused hearts. You shine among the sustainers of the hymns, O you of straight songs; increase the protective ones <note>original: "patnīḥ" - refers to the plants or flames</note> toward the living at the sacrifice. ॥ ५ ॥

**Word-for-Word Breakdown**
Repeatedly grasping | with the woods (sacrificial acts) | the pressed juice | the one with branches | among those with intent hearts | melodious | among the sustainers of the hymns | O you of straight songs | you shine | increase | the wives/protectors | toward | the living | at the sacrifice. ॥ ५ ॥

---

## Commentary (Sayana)
O Agni, you of beautiful praise-songs <note><term>ṛjugātha</term>: one whose chants are straight or harmonious</note>, through the sacrifices performed with wood products <note>original: "tarubhiḥ"</note>, you grasp the juice extracted from the pressed Soma. You take up the Soma plants, which possess many branches <note>original: "vayākinam" - referring to the creepers or stalks of the Soma plant</note>, amidst the praises that capture the heart. As you move beautifully or offer beautiful songs, you shine among the "Sustainers of Speech" <note><term>dhāravākeṣu</term>: the priests and patrons who 'hold' or sustain the sacred chants</note>. Furthermore, at the sacrifice <note><term>adhvare</term></note>, you who are the giver of life to all <note>original: "jīvaḥ"</note>, please increase or nourish the "wives"—meaning the protecting plants or the sacrificial flames—on behalf of the living.

->|| Thus ends the twenty-third section (Varga) of the second chapter (Adhyaya) in the fourth book (Ashtaka). ||<-

->|| Now the Sixth Verse ||<-

## Hymn Text
Just as he is seen, so is he described; they have established their form in the waters with success through their splendor. Give us great, wide-reaching victory, and vast, heroic, unwavering strength. ॥ ६ ॥

**Word-for-Word Breakdown**
Just as | indeed | he is seen | so | he is described | together | with splendor | they have established | with success/perfection | in the waters | hither | great | to us | wide-reaching | wide | victory | vast | heroic | unwavering | strength. ॥ ६ ॥

---

## Commentary (Sayana)
This verse is addressed to the **All-Gods** <note><term>vaiśvadevī</term>: a hymn or verse dedicated to the Viśvedevas, the collective pantheon</note>. 

"Just as he is seen"—meaning, in whatever form the deity appears—"so is he described." This implies that the gods are praised exactly as they are perceived by the seer, rather than relying on the reports of others. Because of their splendor <note>original: "chāyayā"</note> which is achieving or perfecting <note>original: "sidhrayā"</note>, they have established their own form or praise within the pervasive hymns <note>Sayana interprets "waters" here as "pervasive praises"</note>. May those gods grant us a great, worshipful, and abundant wealth...

...granting us abundant victory and speed, and offspring who are great, mighty, and of excellent strength; and may he grant us undiminished, overpowering might and strength.

## Hymn Text
The wise poet, the traveler, the one with a wife, goes indeed beyond all rivals with a mind focused on the gathering. May he, who is the master of his own wealth, grant us protection, guarding our radiant home from every side. ॥ ७ ॥

> **Word-for-Word Breakdown**
> Goes | the traveler | possessing a wife | indeed | beyond | rivals | with an assembly-seeking | mind | the sun-like | the wise poet |
> the radiant | guarding | around | from all sides | the home | our | protection | may he grant | having his own wealth ॥ ७ ॥

## Commentary (Sayana)
This verse is addressed to the Sun <note>original: "saurī"</note>. The god Surya is the traveler <note>original: "ayuḥ"</note>, and he is "one with a wife" <note>original: "janivān"</note> because the Dawn <note>original: "uṣā"</note> is his wife. The word "indeed" <note>original: "vai"</note> indicates a well-known fact. The "wise poet" <note>original: "kaviḥ"</note>, who sees beyond ordinary limits, goes beyond all rivals or battles with a mind that seeks the assembly <note>original: "samaryatā manasā"</note>. This means he surpasses the Mandeha demons <note>A class of demons in Hindu mythology said to attack the sun at dawn and dusk</note> in order to fight them. May we attend to him who guards the "radiant" <note>original: "ghṛsaṃ"</note> "home" <note>original: "gayam" — referring to either the house or the mid-space of the atmosphere</note> from every side. May that god, being the master of his own wealth <note>original: "svāvasuḥ"</note>, grant us <term>sharma</term> <note>happiness or protection</note> in its entirety.

---

-> ॥ Now the Eighth Verse ॥ <-

## Hymn Text
By the banner of this great traveler, the worshiper approaches you who are praised by the Rishis, in those hymns where your name resides. Whatever desire was placed in him, may he find it through sacrificial work; he who carries himself [the sun/fire] shall make things fitting. ॥ ८ ॥

> **Word-for-Word Breakdown**
> The greater | of this | traveler | by the banner | the one praised by Rishis | he approaches | in which | name | your |
> in whatever | was placed | that | through sacrificial work | may he find | who | indeed | himself | carries | he | fitting | shall make ॥ ८ ॥

## Commentary (Sayana)
This verse is addressed to either Agni or the Sun. O God, the sacrificer approaches you, the exceedingly great one, by the "banner" <note>original: "ketunā" — a sign or intellect</note> of this "traveler" <note>original: "yatunasya," from the root 'yat' meaning motion</note>. This refers to the sun as the traveler, distinguished by the indicator of his rising. You are "praised by the Rishis" <note>original: "ṛṣisvaram"</note>. By what means does he approach? Through those hymns in which your "name"—meaning your form or the act of bowing to you—is present. 

Alternatively, it means he approaches you, who are distinguished by your "banner" or act of dispelling the darkness. In whatever desire <note>the mind is implied here</note> the worshiper has "placed" his intent, may he "find" <note>attain</note> that desire through "sacrificial work" <note>original: "apasyayā"</note> such as the offering of oblations and the singing of praises.

...he finds [it]. He who, of his own accord and unprompted by others, by his own wisdom carries or supports the fruit of the ritual, may he perform it abundantly. The word "does" is implied here. ## Hymn Text
The foremost praise has reached the ocean of these libations; the sacrifice does not perish in which these prayers are extended. Here, the heart's desire of the singer Kakvana does not tremble, where the prayer is found connected to the Pure One. ॥ ९ ॥

---

The ocean | of these | down | has reached | the foremost | not | perishes | the sacrifice | in which | extended |
here | not | the heart's desire | of Kakvana | trembles | where | the prayer | is found | bound to the Pure One ॥ ९ ॥

## Commentary (Sayana)
This verse is also addressed to the Sun <note>original: "saurī"</note>. Our "foremost" <note>original: "agrimā"</note> or most excellent praise has reached the **ocean** <note>original: "samudram"</note>, which refers to the Sun, who is the final destination of all prayers, just as the ocean is the destination of rivers. Alternatively, the "ocean" refers to the relationship of the praise offered by these people or priests. The **sacrifice** <note>original: "savanam"</note>—the sacred place or time where the Soma juice is pressed—**does not perish** <note>original: "na riṣyati"</note>; it is not harmed but rather prospers. This is a sacrifice **in which** the hymns are **extended** <note>original: "āyatā"</note> or spread out. In this sacrificer's house, the **heart's desire** <note>original: "hādi"</note> belonging to the heart of **Kakvana** <note>the name of the singer or praiser</note> **does not tremble** <note>original: "na rejate"</note>. This means it does not waver or prove false. Where the **prayer** <note>original: "matiḥ"</note> is **bound to the Pure One** <note>original: "pūtabandhanī"</note>, meaning it is firmly connected to the pure Sun, there the singer's desire remains steady.

->॥ Now the Tenth Verse ॥<-

## Hymn Text
With the insights of Kshetra, Manasa, Evavada, Yajata, Sadhri, and Avatsara, let us satisfy with beautiful rays the strongest strength, the portion intended for the wise. ॥ १० ॥

---

He | for | of Kshetra | of Manasa | with the insights | of Evavada | of Yajata | of Sadhri |
of Avatsara | let us satisfy | with rays | the strongest | strength | of the wise | even | the portion ॥ १० ॥

## Commentary (Sayana)
This verse is also addressed to the Sun. He, the god Savita, is indeed to be praised by all, for he fulfills all desires. The word "for/indeed" <note>original: "hi"</note> indicates a well-known truth in both worldly and Vedic traditions. From him—as it is stated that other sages have also perceived the truth—[we receive]. The names mentioned—Kshetra, Manasa, Evavada, Yajata, Sadhri, and Avatsara—refer to specific sages <note>Rishis</note>. Through the **beautiful insights** <note>original: "raśmibhiḥ cittibhiḥ"</note> of these sages and our own, let us **satisfy** <note>original: "smṛṇavāma"</note> or fill. What shall we fill? The **strongest strength** <note>original: "śaviṣṭhaṃ vājam"</note>, meaning exceptionally powerful food; as the scripture says: "Strength is indeed food" <note>original: "annaṃ vai vājaḥ"</note>. We, including Kshetra and the other sages, satisfy the **portion** <note>original: "ardham"</note> or the half that is to be attained by the **wise** <note>original: "viduṣām"</note> or the learned.

->॥ Thus ends the twenty-fourth Varga in the second Adhyaya of the fourth Ashtaka ॥<-

# Hymn 44 (Continued)
### Mandala 5, Anuvaka 3, Hymn 44 | The Fourth Book | Page 419

## Hymn Text

->|| Now the Eleventh Verse ||<-

The exhilaration of this [libation] for the worshipful, wise, and all-desirable [Soma] is like a falcon; it is the infinite, the filler of the stomach. Mutually encouraging one another to go forward, they know the vessel that provides the drink, the protector, to be near at hand. ॥ ११ ॥

**Word-by-Word Analysis**
The falcon | of these | the infinite | the girth-filler | exhilaration | of the all-desirable | of the worshipful | of the wise | mutually | one another | they encourage | to go | they know | the vessel | the protective drink | near | they ॥ ११ ॥

---

->|| Now the Twelfth Verse ||<-

The ever-generous, the worshipful one has struck down the enemies; he with active arms, the knower of sacred revelation, the traverser, is with you all. He attains both desirable states and shines brightly when he honors the divine host with well-prepared hymns. ॥ १२ ॥

**Word-by-Word Analysis**
The ever-generous | the worshipful | down | the enemies | has struck | with active arms | the knower of revelation | the traverser | your | with | both | he | desirable things | toward | goes | shines | and | when | him | the host | honors | with well-prepared [hymns] ॥ १२ ॥

---

->|| Now the Thirteenth Verse ||<-

The bearer of the pressed juice, the protector of the righteous for the sacrificer, is the udder of all [blessings]; he is the drawer-up of prayers. Bearing [blessings] like a cow with its milk, reciting the sacred words, he does not fall into sleep but stays alert. ॥ १३ ॥

**Word-by-Word Analysis**
The juice-bearer | of the sacrificer | the protector of the righteous | of all | the udder | he | of prayers | the drawer-up | bearing | the cow | like the milk | in the sacred ceremony | the milk | reciting | toward | goes | not | sleeping ॥ १३ ॥

## Commentary (Sayana)

**This verse is dedicated to the Exhilaration <note>original: "madadevatya," referring to the personified joy of the Soma juice</note>. For the three sages—Vishvavara and his companions—the exhilaration of these waters, which take the form of the Soma juice, is like a falcon <note>original: "śyenaḥ"</note>. This means its movement is praiseworthy, going quickly to the presence of the one who drinks it. It is infinite <note>original: "aditiḥ"</note>, meaning it is not meager but exceedingly abundant, and it is "girth-filling" <note>original: "kakṣyaḥ"</note>, meaning it fills the belly of the partaker. These sages, such as Vishvavara, being engaged in the rite, mutually encourage one another to go and obtain the Soma to drink it—they ask for permission from one another. They know the vessel <note>original: "viṣāṇam," interpreted here as the distributor of exhilaration</note> and the protective drink <note>original: "paripānam"</note> to be near at hand; they know it or they obtain it.**

---

**"Ever-generous" <note>original: "sadāpṛṇaḥ"</note> is the name of a person who is always disposed toward giving. He is "worshipful" <note>original: "yajataḥ"</note>, a performer of sacrifice. "With active arms" <note>original: "bāhuvṛktaḥ"</note> refers to one whose arms have performed the sacred duty of preparing the ritual ground. "Knower of revelation" <note>original: "śrutavit"</note> is one who knows the Vedas, and "the traverser" <note>original: "taryaḥ"</note> is another epithet. Although these five descriptions are given, they refer to the sage in relation to the others, and thus the singular verb is used. That sage strikes down <note>original: "vadhīt"</note> or destroys the enemies <note>original: "dviṣaḥ"</note> while in your company—meaning he is aided by you. That sage attains <note>original: "pratyeti"</note> both "desirable things" <note>original: "varā"</note>, referring to the rewards of both this world and the next. He shines <note>original: "bhāti"</note> because he honors this host <note>original: "gaṇam"</note>, the company of gods, with "well-prepared hymns" <note>original: "suprayāvabhiḥ"</note>, which are songs that effectively mix and reach the divine. It is for this reason that he is said to shine.**

## Commentary (Sayana)
[Continuation from previous page for Rig Veda 5.44.13]

The sage named **Sutambhara** <note>literally "the bearer of the pressed juice"</note>, who carries out the sacrifice for me, the sacrificer Avatsara, is the protector of the existing fruits of the ritual. He acts as the priest <note>Sanskrit: *hotā*</note>. He is the "udder" <note>source of nourishment</note> of all prayers and actions, meaning he raises the fruits of the ritual to their highest point and ensures they reach their goal. Like a **cow** <note>Sanskrit: *dhenu*</note> carrying milk for its calf, he carries the ritual essence. This essence is supported by his strength. Reciting the sacred words in their proper sequence, and not falling into sleep—remaining constantly vigilant—he continues his study and remembrance. This is how the sage Avatsara describes him; such is the character of Sutambhara.

---

## Hymn Text
-> ॥ Now the Fourteenth Verse ॥ <-
The sacred hymns desire him who stays awake; the chants approach him who stays awake. To him who stays awake, this Soma speaks, saying: "I have made my home in your friendship." ॥ १४ ॥

**Padapatha:**
He | who | stays awake | him | the hymns | desire | he | who | stays awake | him | indeed | the chants | go to |
he | who | stays awake | him | this | Soma | says | your | I | am | in friendship | settled. ॥ १४ ॥

## Commentary (Sayana)
Whichever deity remains always wakeful and vigilant in the house, the hymns <note>Sanskrit: *ṛcaḥ*, representing all sacred knowledge</note> desire him. And to him who stays awake, the chants <note>Sanskrit: *sāmāni*, the songs of praise</note> approach. To the one who remains vigilant, this pressed Soma juice speaks, saying: "Please accept me." O Agni <note>the god of fire</note>, in the friendship—the mutual well-wishing—of such a person, I am **settled in my place** <note>Sanskrit: *nyokāḥ*, meaning one who has a permanent or fixed residence</note>.

## Introductory Commentary (Anuvaka 4)
Now begins the fourth Anuvaka, which contains twelve hymns. The first hymn, beginning with the words "Vida diva" <note>Know the Heaven</note>, consists of eleven verses. The sage <note>Rishi</note> is named Sadaprina. The meter is Trishtubh. This hymn is dedicated to the **All-gods** <note>Sanskrit: *Vaiśvadeva*</note>, as indicated by the traditional markers. The index of the Veda notes: "Vida, eleven verses, Sadaprina." Its ritual application is determined by the specific characteristics found within the text.

<meta>This page transitions to Hymn 45 of the Fifth Book of the Rig Veda. While the previous page focused on the vigilance of the ritualist (Sutambhara), this hymn moves into the cosmic realm, describing the dawn of light, the breaking of the celestial mountain, and the restoration of order by the gods and the ancestral sages.</meta>

-> ॥ Now the First Verse ॥ <-

## Hymn Text

With the knowledge of heaven, releasing the mountain with hymns, the rays of the approaching Dawn have gone forth. The divine one has uncovered the darkness-filled enclosures and has opened the gates of human activity from the celestial world. ॥ १ ॥

**Word-for-Word Breakdown:**
With knowledge | of heaven | releasing | the mountain | with hymns | of the approaching | Dawn | the rays | have gone |
back | he has drawn | the darkness-enclosures | up | the light | from | he has gone | wide | the doors | for humanity | the God | has opened. ॥ १ ॥

---

## Commentary (Sayana)

The deities of this verse are identified by their characteristics as Indra and others. This verse describes how Indra released the **cows** <note>original: "gāḥ", referring to both literal cattle and the rays of light</note> that had been stolen by the **Panis** <note>a group of demonic beings who hoarded the light/wealth</note> and hidden beneath the mountain.

**With knowledge**: Indra made it known—he discovered the hidden cows. How? By **releasing** <note>original: "viṣyan", meaning throwing or discharging</note> his **mountain**-breaking thunderbolt <note>original: "adri", literally "rock" but interpreted here as the thunderbolt</note> upon the captors, triggered by the **hymns** or prayers of the **Angirases** <note>the ancestral fire-priests of Vedic tradition</note>.

Then, the **rays** <note>original: "arcinaḥ"</note> belonging to the **approaching Dawn** went forth; they spread everywhere. He **uncovered** the **darkness-enclosures** <note>original: "vrajinīḥ", interpreted as nights thick with shadows</note>. The Sun, whose nature it is to move through the heavens, **arose**. Having done this, the **divine** Sun **opened wide** the **doors** of **human** activity. By removing the darkness, he made it possible for humans to perform their daily tasks and rituals.

---

-> ॥ Now the Second Verse ॥ <-

## Hymn Text

The Sun manifests his beauty like a splendid form; the Mother of the cows, knowing her path, has come from the vastness. The rivers whose waters flow through the desert have their banks eroded by the flood; the sky has become firm, like a well-set pillar. ॥ २ ॥

**Word-for-Word Breakdown:**
Wide | the Sun | beauty | like | splendor | manifests | from | the vastness | of the cows | the Mother | knowing | has come |
flowing-through-the-desert | the rivers | eating-the-banks-with-water | a pillar-like | well-fixed | has become firm | the sky. ॥ २ ॥

---

## Commentary (Sayana)

The divine **Sun manifests** <note>original: "visāt", meaning to divide or reveal</note> his **beauty** or light. The phrase **like a splendid form** <note>original: "amatim na śriyam"</note> is explained as follows: just as physical objects like pots or cloths attain various colors and forms when light hits them, the Sun reveals the beauty of the world.

Likewise, the **Mother of the cows**—who is the **Dawn** <note>Ushas</note>—comes from the **vast** atmosphere. She arrives **knowing** that the Sun is about to rise and that it is her duty to dispel the darkness.

Furthermore, the **rivers** are described as **flowing through the desert** <note>original: "dhanvarṇasaḥ"</note>. This means their waters are in constant motion. They are **eroding the banks** <note>original: "khādoarṇaḥ", literally "eating the banks with water"</note>, showing the power of the flowing current. Additionally, by the command of the Sun, the **sky** has been made **firm**, standing steady **like a well-fixed pillar** that supports a house. All these natural stabilities and movements occur under the divine order of the rising Sun.

---

</vocab>

## Hymn Text
For this hymn, the child of the mountain, the birth of the great ones, for the ancient one; the mountain yields, the heaven achieves its purpose, as those who serve the gods exhaust themselves in their labors. ॥ ३ ॥

**For this | hymn | of the mountain | the child | of the great ones | the birth | for the ancient | apart | the mountain | yields | achieves | heaven | serving | exhausting | the ground/labors. ॥ ३ ॥**

## Commentary (Sayana)
For this, my **hymn** <note>original: "ukthāya", a song of praise</note>, the **child of the mountain**—referring to the water held within the mountain-like <term>cloud (megha)</term>—moves or is set in motion. Indra causes it to flow. For what purpose? For the **birth** or production of **great** praises for the **ancient** one <note>referring to Indra or the ancestral tradition</note>. This is repeated for emphasis: the **mountain** (the cloud) yields or parts. And **heaven achieves** the purpose, which is the bringing of rain. Those who **serve** the gods from all sides—the **Angirases** <note>the semi-divine ancestral fire-priests</note>—**exhaust themselves** <note>original: "dasayanta", meaning to spend or wear out</note> or exert themselves greatly through their ritual actions upon the sacrificial ground.

->॥ Now the Fourth Verse ॥<-

## Hymn Text
With well-spoken words beloved by the gods, I call upon Indra and Agni for our protection. For with hymns, the wise ones, skilled in sacrifice, serving the gods like the Maruts, perform the worship. ॥ ४ ॥

---

**With well-spoken words | of you | with words | beloved by the gods | Indra | now | Agni | for protection | to call | with hymns | indeed | (particle) | the wise | skilled in sacrifice | serving | the Maruts | they worship. ॥ ४ ॥**

## Commentary (Sayana)
O Indra, O Agni! <note>The Sanskrit uses a dual form for each name, acknowledging them as a pair</note>. Even though the word is separated in the middle, this is a poetic license of the Vedas. O **Indra and Agni**, I call upon **you** <note>original: "vaḥ", a plural pronoun used here for the dual pair</note> with **well-spoken words** <term>sukta (hymns of good praise)</term> that reveal your auspicious qualities and are **beloved by the gods**, for the sake of **protecting** us. I call you **quickly** <note>original: "nu"</note>. Indeed, with these **hymns**, the **wise ones**—the learned ancient sages—who are **skilled in sacrifice**, perform the worship. They are **serving** or attending the gods through praise and are **like the Maruts** <note>the storm-gods known for their swiftness</note> because they are diligent and swift in their ritual duties. They **worship** or honor the gods. <note>The words "hi" and "sma" are used here as grammatical fillers to complete the meter</note>.

## Hymn Text
Come, let us now be of good thought today; let us cast away misfortune more broadly. Let us place hatreds far away and move forward toward the one who performs the sacrifice. ॥ ५ ॥

---

<summary>This page describes the ritual's power to release rain from the clouds (the 'mountain') and calls upon Indra and Agni to protect the worshippers. It emphasizes the role of the ancient Angiras priests and the modern sacrificers in maintaining cosmic order through "well-spoken words."</summary>

<meta>This page continues the commentary on Rig Veda, Mandala 5, Hymn 45. The previous page discussed the Angirases (ancestral fire-priests) and their ritual efforts to bring the dawn and release the waters. This section concludes the fifth verse and provides the full text and explanation for the sixth and seventh verses, focusing on the myth of the stolen cattle and the power of sacred speech.</meta>

This is the declaration of the <term>Angirases</term> <note>original: "aṅgirasāṃ vādaḥ"; the Angirases are a semi-divine family of priests</note>. Today, on this day of sacrifice, let us come quickly. Let us become those of good intellect and performers of noble deeds. Let us utterly destroy our enemies. "More greatly" <note>original: "varīyaḥ"</note> means exceedingly. That is what is being said. Let us place the hatreds—the enemies of the <term>sacrificer</term> <note>original: "yajamāna"; the person for whom the ritual is performed</note>—far away. Alternatively, the word "far away" <note>original: "sanutar"</note> can mean "hidden." This distinguishes the current request from previous ones: earlier, the destruction of manifest enemies was mentioned; now, it refers to those who are concealed. For that purpose, let us go toward the sacrificer, moving forward to the one who always nourishes, like <term>Avatsara</term> <note>a celebrated seer in Vedic lore</note>.

O friends, let us perform this prayer which, like a mother, opens the stall of the cattle; by which <term>Manu</term> <note>the archetypal human ancestor</note> conquered the jawless one, and by which the wandering merchant obtained the filling water. ॥ ६ ॥

## Commentary (Sayana)

This is also a statement by the Angirases. **Come** means approach. Having come, **let us perform the prayer** <note>original: "dhiyaṃ... kṛṇavāma"</note>, meaning the song of praise. **O friends** is the address the Angirases use for one another. This **prayer**, acting like a **mother** or creator of the cattle, **opened the stall** <note>original: "vrajam"</note>—the enclosure of the cows that had been stolen by the <term>Panis</term> <note>demons who hoarded the world's light and cattle in a cave</note>. And **by which** prayer **Manu conquered the jawless** <note>original: "viśipram"</note> enemy. Alternatively, "Manu" refers to Indra, the "thinker" of all, and "the jawless one" refers to the demon **Vritra**. Indra conquered him through the power of our prayer characterized by these hymns. Also, **by which** prayer the **merchant**—referring to the seer <term>Kakshivan</term> who, like a merchant, desired great results from small ritual acts—wandering in search of water, **obtained the filling water**. This refers to the tradition where the <term>Ashvins</term> <note>divine twins</note> provided a "storehouse of honey" for the merchant <term>Dirghashravas</term>, the son of Ushij (as heard in Rig Veda 1.112.11).

Here, the rock held in the hand roared; worshipping with it, the <term>Navagvas</term> completed the ten months. Following the path of Truth, <term>Sarama</term> found the cattle; the Angiras made all things true. ॥ ७ ॥

## Commentary (Sayana)

**Here**, in this sacrifice, the stone used for pressing the <term>Soma</term> juice, being **held in the hand** and struck, **roared**. The root "nu" means to make a sound—

<meta>This page concludes the commentary on Rig Veda Mandala 4, Sukta 2, Verse 7, and provides the full text and commentary for Verse 8 and the beginning of Verse 9. ## Commentary (Sayana)
<note>This concludes the explanation for Verse 7 from the previous page</note>

The word refers only to the sound produced. "He made them cry out" <note>original: "aśrandayat"</note>. By means of the pressing-stone and the extraction of the <term>Soma</term> juice, the **Navagvas** <note>a sub-group of the Angirases who completed their rite in nine months</note> performed their duties for ten months. Those <term>Angirases</term> who followed the ritual for nine months are called Navagvas. They worshiped and praised Indra. Alternatively, there are those Angirases who performed the ritual for ten months, and others who were Navagvas; all of them worshiped Indra with this sound. There is a scriptural basis for this: "The Navagvas, having pressed the Soma, [praised] Indra" (**Rig Veda 5.29.12**). 

The word **Ritam** <note>original: "ṛtam"</note> refers to either the Truth or the sacrifice. **Sarama**, who is the personification of the "moving" speech of the Angirases, or the "divine hound" sent by Indra to find the cattle, attained that Truth. She found the cows that had been stolen and hidden by the <term>Panis</term> <note>a group of demons or mythical hoarders who stole the light/cattle</note>. The Angiras made all things—characterized by the accumulation of wealth and the like—truly "true" <note>meaning he made them manifest or real through his ritual action</note>.

---

## Hymn Text
->|| Now the Eighth Verse ||<-

When all the Angirases sang together with the cows at the dawning of this great [Dawn], their spring [of milk] was enjoyed in the highest place of assembly; Sarama found the cows through the path of Truth. ॥ ८ ॥

**Word-by-Word Analysis:**
**vifve** (All) । **asyāḥ** (of this) । **vi-uṣi** (at the dawning) । **māhināyāḥ** (of the great/magnificent) । **sam** (together) । **yat** (when) । **gobhiḥ** (with the cows) । **aṅgirasaḥ** (the Angirases) । **navanta** (shouted/sang) ।
**utsaḥ** (the spring/fountain) । **āsām** (of these) । **parame** (in the highest) । **sadha-sthe** (in the place of assembly) । **ṛtasya** (of Truth/Order) । **pathā** (by the path) । **saramā** (Sarama) । **vidat** (found) । **gāḥ** (the cows) ॥ ८ ॥

---

## Commentary (Sayana)

**All** <note>original: "viśve"</note> the Angirases, when the **dawning** <note>original: "vyuṣi"</note> of **this** worshipful **Dawn** <note>original: "uṣaso"</note> occurred—that is, when the darkness concealing the cattle was removed—they **sang together** with the cows. At that time, the **spring** <note>original: "utsaḥ"</note> of these cows, which is the flow of their milk and other products, became available for use in the **highest** excellent **place of assembly**, which refers to the sacrifice. 

Through the **path** of **Truth** <note>original: "ṛtasya"</note>—the path of cosmic order—**Sarama**, interpreted either as "speech" or the "divine hound," **found** the hidden cows. She obtained them. 
Alternatively, the "spring" refers to a fountain of water located in the "highest place of assembly," which is the hidden cave where the cows were kept. In this sense, it refers to a "hole" or "opening." Thus, Sarama found the cows by following the path of the water of Truth.

---

## Hymn Text
->|| Now the Ninth Verse ||<-

Let the Sun, with his seven horses, come to the field which is his for his long journey; like a swift hawk let him fly toward the food; youthful, a seer, let him shine while moving among the cattle. ॥ ९ ॥

**Word-by-Word Analysis:**
**ā** (towards/hither) । **sūryaḥ** (the Sun) । **yātu** (let him come) । **sapta-aśvaḥ** (having seven horses) । **kṣetram** (to the field) । **yat** (which) । **asya** (his) । **urviyā** (extensively) । **dīrgha-yāthe** (on the long journey) ।
**raghuḥ** (swift) । **śyenaḥ** (hawk) । **patayat** (let him fly) । **andhaḥ** (the food/juice) । **acha** (towards) । **yuvā** (youthful) । **kaviḥ** (the seer/poet) । **dīdayat** (let him shine) । **goṣu** (among the cattle/rays) । **gachan** (moving) ॥ ९ ॥

---

## Commentary (Sayana)

**Surya** is the god who impels everyone. He possesses **seven horses**, or horses that have the nature of creeping/moving. Let him **come** toward us. Because the **field** of this Sun, in his **long journey**... <note>Commentary continues on next page</note>

<vocab>
- **Angirases**: A group of semi-divine ancestral priests who assist Indra.
- **Navagvas**: A specific class of Angirases associated with a nine-month sacrificial cycle.
- **Sarama**: The messenger of Indra, often depicted as a dog, who tracks the stolen cows of light.
- **Ritam**: The fundamental cosmic order, truth, or the regulated ritual of sacrifice.
- **Surya**: The Sun god, the celestial form of fire.
- **Saptashva**: A name for the Sun, meaning "one with seven horses" (representing the seven rays or days).
- **Vyushi**: The specific moment of the dawning of light.

[Continuation of commentary on verse 9]
The destination is in the "vast" <note>original: *urviyā uru*</note> and exceedingly abundant space. That same deity, "swift of motion" <note>original: *raghu-laghu-gamanaḥ*</note>, like a **hawk** <note>original: *śyenaḥ*</note> of praiseworthy flight, descends toward the intended oblation. He arrives. Being "youthful" <note>original: *yuvā*</note>, the mixer of all things, and a "sage" <note>original: *kaviḥ*</note> who sees beyond, he moves among the "cows" <note>symbolizing rays of light</note> and shines in their midst. ## Hymn Text

-> ॥ Now the Tenth Verse ॥ <-

**The Sun has ascended the bright ocean, when he yoked his bay horses with smooth backs. Like a boat upon the water, the sages have led him; the waters, spreading over everything, have stood facing him.** ॥ १० ॥

**Word-by-word analysis (Pada-patha):**
The Sun; has ascended; the bright; ocean; he yoked; when; the bay horses; smooth-backed; out; like; a boat; they led; the wise; spreading; the waters; facing; stood. ॥ १० ॥

---

## Commentary (Sayana)

The Sun deity has ascended toward the "bright ocean" <note>original: *śukram arṇas*</note>, which refers to the waters or the atmospheric expanse. He manifests everywhere. Because—or at which time—he yoked the "bay horses" <note>original: *haritaḥ*</note> with "smooth backs" <note>original: *vītapṛṣṭhāḥ*</note> to his chariot, then the "wise" <note>original: *dhīrāḥ*</note>—the intelligent sacrificers and others—led that Sun just as one leads a **boat** <note>original: *nāvam*</note> through water. At that time, the waters, "spreading" or giving their consent from all sides, stood facing him or turned toward him.

## Hymn Text

-> ॥ Now the Eleventh Verse ॥ <-

**I offer your prayer in the waters, the giver of light, by which the Navagvas crossed the ten months. Through this prayer may we be protected by the gods; through this prayer may we cross over evil.** ॥ ११ ॥

**Word-by-word analysis (Pada-patha):**
The prayer; your; in the waters; I hold; the giver of light; by which; they crossed; ten; months; the Navagvas; through this; prayer; may we be; protected by the gods; through this; prayer; may we cross; beyond; evil. ॥ ११ ॥

---

## Commentary (Sayana)

O Gods, I "hold" <note>original: *dadhiṣe*</note> or perform your "prayer" <note>original: *dhiyam*</note>—the hymn of praise—which is offered in the presence of the waters and is the "giver of heaven" <note>original: *svarṣām*</note> or the granter of all things. <note>The verb form used is a middle voice variation</note>. By which "prayer" or ritual action the **Navagvas** <note>a sub-group of the ancestral Angiras priests</note> "crossed ten months" <note>referring to a sacrificial session lasting ten months</note> and completed their duties. Through this prayer, may we be **protected by the gods** <note>original: *devagopāḥ*</note>. Through this prayer, may we thoroughly "cross over" <note>original: *tuturyāma*</note> "evil" <note>original: *aṃhaḥ*</note> or sin.

## Introductory Notes for Sukta 47

The second hymn, beginning with "Like a horse" <note>original: *hayo na*</note>, consists of eight verses and was revealed to the seer **Pratikshetra**. The eighth and second verses are in the **Trishtubh** meter <note>4 lines of 11 syllables</note>; the remaining six are in the **Jagati** meter <note>4 lines of 12 syllables</note>. The first six verses are dedicated to the Universal Gods (Vishvedevas), while the seventh and eighth verses are dedicated to the **Devapatnis** (the wives of the gods). Similarly—

<vocab>
- **Surya (Sūrya):** The Sun God, often depicted as the soul of the universe.
- **Arnas (Arṇas):** Water, flood, or the celestial sea.
- **Navagvas (Navagvāḥ):** "Those who go in nine"; a mythical group of priests who performed sacrifices for nine or ten months.
- **Dhi (Dhī):** Thought, prayer, ritual action, or meditation.
- **Devagopa (Devagopā):** One who is guarded or protected by the divine powers.
- **Amhas (Aṃhaḥ):** Distress, constriction, or the moral concept of sin.
- **Pratikshetra (Pratikshetra):** The name of the Rishi (sage) who "saw" or composed this particular hymn.
</vocab>
