# Rig Veda #

### Book 4, Chapter 2, Section 28 ###

The introductory note states: "The horse," "The two horses," "The protector"—the last two verses are a praise of the wives of the gods. The last verse is in the Trishtup meter, as is the second. The ritual application of the hymn follows its indicative marks.

---

## Hymn Text

-> ॥ Now the First Verse ॥ <-

**Like a wise horse, I have yoked myself to the pole of the sacrifice by my own will. I bear that pole which carries us across and seeks divine protection. I do not desire to be released from it, nor do I wish to turn back. The wise leader, knowing the paths, shall lead us along the straight road.** ॥ १ ॥

**Word-by-word analysis (Pada-patha):**
A horse; like; wise; I have yoked; myself; at the pole; that; I bear; the crossing; seeking protection; not; of this; I desire; the release; not; the turning; again; again; wise; of the path; the leader; straight; he shall lead. ॥ १ ॥

## Commentary (Sayana)

Like a horse <note>original: *hayo na*</note>, the all-knowing <note>original: *vidvān*</note> priest—here the seer Prati-kshatra—has yoked himself by his own will, unprompted by others, to the "pole" <note>the yoke or burden</note> consisting of the sacrifice. I—whether acting as the <term>Adhvaryu</term> <note>the priest in charge of the physical ritual</note> or the <term>Hota</term> <note>the reciter of hymns</note>—bear that pole which is the "great crosser" <note>original: *prataraṇīm*</note>, enabling us to cross over difficulties, and the granter of protection. I do not desire the "release" <note>original: *vimučam*</note> or abandonment of this sacrificial burden, nor do I wish to turn back from it. If one asks, "Who will guide me in this burden?", it is answered: the all-knowing "inner controller" <note>the divine guide within</note>, who is the "leader" <note>original: *pura-etā*</note> going in front, will lead the paths of the sacrifice along the "straight" <note>original: *ṛju*</note> or uncrooked way.

---

## Hymn Text

-> ॥ Now the Second Verse ॥ <-

**O Agni, Indra, Varuna! In this way, O Gods, and the host of Maruts, grant us strength! And O Vishnu! May both the Ashvins, Rudra, and the Divine Wives, along with Pushan, Bhaga, and Sarasvati, be pleased with our sacrifice.** ॥ २ ॥

**Word-by-word analysis (Pada-patha):**
O Agni; Indra; Varuna; thus; O Gods; the host; forth; grant; O Maruts; and; O Vishnu; both; the Ashvins; Rudra; and; the Divine Wives; Pushan; Bhaga; Sarasvati; may they be pleased. ॥ २ ॥

## Commentary (Sayana)

O Agni, Indra, and Varuna! Thus, O Gods, grant us "strength" <note>original: *śardhas*</note> or power. <note>A grammatical note follows: in this recitation, since there is no word preceding them, these names at the start of the verse-line do not lose their emphasis or accent.</note> Furthermore, O Maruts—referring to the collective strength of the storm-gods—and O Vishnu, grant us that same strength. <note>Note: here the name "Vishnu" undergoes a change in accent because it is separated from the main verb by the word "uta" meaning "and".</note> Furthermore, may both the "truth-abiding" <term>Nasatyas</term> <note>the twin Ashvin gods of healing</note>, Rudra, and the "Divine Wives" <note>original: *gnāḥ*</note>—the female counterparts of the gods—along with Pushan, Bhaga, and Sarasvati, "be pleased" <note>original: *juṣanta*</note> with or serve our sacrifice and our praise.

<vocab>
- **Horse** (Haya): A metaphor for the energetic and disciplined priest.
- **Wise/All-knowing** (Vidvān): Referring both to the priest's ritual knowledge and the deity's omniscience.
- **Yoke/Burden** (Dhur): A technical term for the responsibility of the sacrifice; the "pole" of the ritual chariot.
- **Release/Untying** (Vimuc): Leaving the ritual before its completion.
- **Leader** (Pura-etā): One who walks in front to show the way.
- **Straight/Upright** (Ṛju): The correct, moral, and ritual path without errors.
- **O Agni** (Agne): Invocation to the God of Fire.
- **Strength/Host** (Śardhas): Can refer to physical power or the specific "host" of the Marut deities.
- **The Ashvins** (Nāsatyā): The twin Vedic gods of the dawn and medicine.
- **Divine females/Goddesses** (Gnāḥ): The wives of the gods who receive specific portions of the ritual.
- **Goddess Sarasvati** (Sarasvatī): The goddess of speech, inspiration, and the sacred river.
</vocab>

The second verse invokes a large assembly of deities—including Agni, Indra, the Ashvins, and the Divine Wives—to bless the ritual with strength.</summary>

### Book 5, Section 4, Hymn 46 ###
### Fourth Volume (Ashtaka 4) ###

-> || Now the Third Verse || <-

## Hymn Text
**Indra and Agni, Mitra and Varuna, Aditi, the Sun, the Earth, the Heaven, the Maruts, the Mountains, and the Waters; I invoke Vishnu, Pushan, Brahmanaspati, Bhaga, and Savitar for our protection.** ॥ ३ ॥

---

**Word-by-word analysis (Pada-patha):**
Indra and Agni; Mitra and Varuna; Aditi; the Sun; Earth; Heaven; the Maruts; Mountains; Waters; I invoke; Vishnu; Pushan; of Prayer (Brahman); the Lord (Patim); Bhaga; now; the Praiseworthy; Savitar; for protection. ॥ ३ ॥

## Commentary (Sayana)
I invoke or praise these fourteen deities, from Indra through to Savitar, for our protection <note>original: *ūtaye*</note>. The word "Svar" refers to the Sun <note>original: *Āditya*</note>, so called because he moves well or is self-shining.

-> || Now the Fourth Verse || <-

## Hymn Text
**And may Vishnu, and the Wind, the non-harming giver of wealth, and may Soma grant us happiness; and may the Ribhus, and the Ashvins for our wealth, and Tvashtar and Vibhvan grant us their favor.** ॥ ४ ॥

---

**Word-by-word analysis (Pada-patha):**
And; our; Vishnu; and; the Wind; non-harming; wealth-giver; and; Soma; happiness-granting; and; the Ribhus; and; for wealth; our; the two Ashvins; and; Tvashtar; and; Vibhvan; favor; they shall grant. ॥ ४ ॥

## Commentary (Sayana)
Moreover, may Vishnu, the all-pervading deity, grant us happiness <note>original: *mayas*</note>. May the Wind <note>original: *Vāta*</note>, being non-harming, also grant us happiness. Furthermore, may Soma, the giver of riches, grant us happiness. May the <term>Ribhus</term> <note>celestial artisans who gained immortality through their skill</note> favor us with wealth. May the two Ashvins, the deity Tvashtar, and Vibhvan <note>one of the three Ribhus</note> also grant their favor. The verb "favor" or "grant" should be applied individually to each of these deities.

---

-> || Now the Fifth Verse || <-

## Hymn Text
**And may that host of Maruts come to our dwelling, they who are worthy of worship, to sit upon the sacred grass; and may Brihaspati, Pushan, and also Varuna, Mitra, and Aryaman grant us a secure refuge.** ॥ ५ ॥

---

**Word-by-word analysis (Pada-patha):**
And; that; our; Marut-related; host; may it come; to the dwelling; worthy of worship; the sacred grass; to sit upon; Brihaspati; refuge; Pushan; and; our; may he grant; providing shelter; Varuna; Mitra; Aryaman. ॥ ५ ॥

## Commentary (Sayana)
Furthermore, may that "host" <note>original: *śardhas*</note>—meaning the strength or the assembly of the Maruts—come to us. Let them arrive at our dwelling.

<meta>This page continues the commentary on Mandala 5, Sukta 41 of the Rig Veda. While the previous verse concluded with an invocation of Brihaspati and Pushan for protection, this page expands the call to nature spirits (mountains and rivers) and the wives of the gods (Deva-patni), highlighting their roles in both the cosmic order and specific sacrificial rituals like the Patnisamyaja.</meta>

# Rig Veda #

### Volume 4, Chapter 2, Section 28 ###

What is that host of gods like? They are "dwellers in heaven" <note>original: *divikṣayam*</note>, existing in the celestial realm, and "worthy of worship" <note>original: *yajatam*</note>. The purpose of their arrival is then stated: "to sit upon the sacred grass" <note>original: *barhir-barhiṣyāsad*</note>. This means they come to sit and accept the oblation. Furthermore, may the god Brihaspati bestow "happiness" <note>original: *śarma*</note>—may he grant it. And may Pushan also grant it to us. What kind of happiness? "Protective" <note>original: *varūthyam*</note>. A *varūtha* is a house that wards off cold and wind; therefore, *varūthya* means that which is worthy of a home or provides shelter. Moreover, may all three deities—Varuna and the others—each grant us happiness.

-> || Now the Sixth Verse || <-

## Hymn Text
**And may those mountains, well-praised and of beautiful light, and the rivers, be for our protection. May Bhaga, the distributor of wealth, come with his power and aid; may Aditi of wide-reaching influence hear my invocation.** ॥ ६ ॥

**Word-by-word analysis (Pada-patha):**
And; those; our; mountains; well-praised; beautiful-lighted; rivers; for protection; may they be; Bhaga; distributor; with power; with aid; hither; may he come; wide-reaching; Aditi; may she hear; my; invocation. ॥ ६ ॥

---

## Commentary (Sayana)
And also, may those "mountains" <note>original: *parvatāḥ*</note>, the crags consisting of many parts, which are "well-praised" <note>original: *suśastayaḥ*</note> (meaning they have beautiful hymns of praise), and also those of "beautiful light" <note>original: *sudītayaḥ*</note> (meaning givers of good things), and the "rivers" <note>original: *nadyaśca*</note> be for our "protection" <note>original: *trāmaṇe*</note> or guarding. May the god "Bhaga" <note>original: *bhago devaḥ*</note>, being the "distributor" <note>original: *vibhaktā*</note> or giver of wealth, come hither along with "power" <note>original: *śavasā*</note> (meaning food or strength) and "aid" <note>original: *avasā*</note> (protection). May "Aditi" <note>original: *aditiḥ*</note>, the mother of the gods whose "influence is wide-reaching" <note>original: *uruvyacāḥ*</note> (meaning her lordship and pervasiveness are great), "hear" <note>original: *śrotu*</note> my "invocation" <note>original: *havam*</note>—either my praise or my calling.

Regarding the <term>Patnisamyaja</term> <note>a ritual offering made to the wives of the gods at the conclusion of a sacrifice</note>, there are two verses beginning "The wives of the gods..." <note>original: *devānām patnīḥ*</note> used as the invitatory and offering verses <note>original: *yājyānuvākyā*</note>. This is indicated in the *Ashvalayana Shrauta Sutra* (1.10): "The two verses: 'May the wives of the gods, longing, protect us...'" <note>original: *devānāṃ patnīruśatīravantu na iti dve*</note>. These same two verses are also used in the <term>Agni-maruta-shastra</term> <note>a specific litany recited at the end of the Soma sacrifice</note> along with the two verses beginning "I [invoke] Raka..." <note>original: *rākāmaham*</note>, as noted in the *Ashvalayana Shrauta Sutra* (5.20).

-> || Of those two, the first is the seventh in this hymn || <-

## Hymn Text
**May the wives of the gods, longing for us, protect us; may they help us to obtain progeny and to win wealth. Whether they dwell on the earth or within the waters, may those goddesses, who are easily invoked, grant us happiness.** ॥ ७ ॥

**Word-by-word analysis (Pada-patha):**
Of the gods; the wives; longing; may they protect; us; forward; may they protect; us; for progeny; for winning wealth; who; dwelling on earth; who; of the waters; also; in the function; those; us; goddesses; easily-invoked; happiness; grant. ॥ ७ ॥

---

## Commentary (Sayana)
The "wives of the gods" <note>original: *devānām patnyaḥ*</note> like Indra and others, being "longing" <note>original: *uśatyaḥ*</note>, that is, desiring our praise or our ritual...

## Commentary (Sayana)
[Continuation from previous page]

...may they protect us. May they guard us. Likewise, may they specifically protect us for the sake of our "strong son" <note>original: *tujaye*</note> and for the "attainment of food" <note>original: *vājasātaye*</note>—or perhaps for victory in battle. May they protect us excellently or come to us. Those who are "earthly" <note>original: *pārthivāsaḥ*</note>, related to the earth, and those who exist in the "function of the waters" <note>original: *apām vrate*</note> in the mid-air—O goddesses, you who are "well-invoked" <note>original: *suhavāḥ*</note> (meaning those of beautiful invitations), grant us happiness.

---

-> ॥ Now the Eighth Verse ॥ <-

## Hymn Text

**And may the divine wives, the goddesses, protect us—Indrani, Agnayi, and the radiant Ashvini. May Rodasi and Varunani hear us; may the goddesses partake of the oblation, as it is the season of the divine wives.** ॥ ८ ॥

**Word-by-word analysis (Pada-patha):**
And; the goddesses (wives); may they partake; the wives of the gods; Indrani; Agnayi; Ashvini; the radiant one; hither; Rodasi; Varunani; may she hear; may they partake; the goddesses; which; [is] the season; of the wives. ॥ ८ ॥

---

## Commentary (Sayana)

And also, may the **goddesses** <note>original: *gnāḥ*</note>, the women who are the **wives of the gods** <note>original: *devapatnīḥ*</note>—those whose husbands are the gods—may they **partake** <note>original: *vyantu*</note>, meaning consume the sacrificial offering. They are now listed individually. **Indrani** is the wife of Indra; **Agnayi** is the wife of Agni; **Ashvini** is the wife of the two Ashvins; and **Radiant** <note>original: *rāṭ*</note> means the one who is shining. 

Furthermore, **Rodasi**—the scholar Yaska states she is the wife of Rudra. If this is so, then in the passage "Rodasi with loosened locks" <note>RV 1.167.5</note>, the grammatical accents and vowel-joining rules should be applied here as they were there. Nevertheless, since the great sage Shakalya <note>The traditional editor of the word-for-word version of the Rig Veda</note> has analyzed the text in this way, it should be viewed exactly as he presented it. May **Varunani**, the wife of Varuna, **hear** the invocation from all sides. 

Moreover, may the **goddesses** <note>original: *devīḥ*</note> associated with the *Patni-samyaja* <term>Patni-samyaja: A specific ritual where offerings are made to the wives of the gods at the conclusion of a sacrifice</term> **partake** or consume the oblation. May those goddesses who preside over the **season** <note>original: *ṛtuḥ*</note> or appointed time of the **wives** <note>original: *janīnām*</note> (the spouses of the gods) also hear and partake. On this point, the Nirukta passage <note>Nirukta 12.46</note> stating "May the goddesses, the wives of the gods, partake" should be consulted for further clarity.

-> ॥ Thus ends the twenty-eighth Varga in the second Adhyaya of the fourth Ashtaka ॥ <-

---

By the light of the meaning of the Veda, dispelling the darkness of the heart, may Vidyatirtha-Maheshvara grant the four goals of human life. <note>The four goals are duty, prosperity, desire, and spiritual liberation.</note>

<meta>This page marks the beginning of the Third Chapter (Adhyaya) of the Fourth Book (Ashtaka) of the Rigveda. Having concluded the previous chapter's focus on the wives of the gods, we now move to a hymn dedicated to All-Gods (the Vishvedevas), beginning with an invocation to the Dawn.</meta>

-> ॥ Salutations to Holy Bharati <note>The goddess of speech and learning.</note> ॥ <-

**He whose breath is the Vedas, who from the Vedas created the entire world, I salute that Maheshvara, the sacred site of all knowledge.**

Now the third chapter begins. Within it, the third hymn, beginning with "Setting in motion" <note>original: *prayuñjatī*</note>, consists of seven verses composed by the seer Pratiratha in the Trishtubh meter. As it was previously stated that "This is indeed dedicated to all the gods," this hymn is also dedicated to the All-Gods <note>original: *vaiśvadeva*</note>. The Index <note>original: *Anukramaṇikā*</note> states: "The seven verses beginning with *prayuñjatī* are by Pratiratha." Its ritual application is determined by its characteristic marks <note>original: *laiṅgikaḥ*</note>.

---

## Hymn Text

-> ॥ Here is the First Verse ॥ <-

**Setting [all] in motion, she comes from the sky, making herself known—the Great Mother awakening her daughter. Seeking the gods, the ever-youthful and wise one comes, calling repeatedly to the Fathers at the place of sacrifice.** ॥ १ ॥

**Word-by-word analysis (Pada-patha):**
Setting in motion; from the sky; she comes; making herself known; Great; Mother; of the daughter; awakening; seeking [the gods]; young woman; the wise one; for the Fathers; hither; in the seat; calling repeatedly. ॥ १ ॥

---

## Commentary (Sayana)

This verse refers to the **Dawn** <note>original: *uṣasyā*</note>. **Setting in motion** <note>original: *prayuñjatī*</note> means she impels living beings toward their current tasks. She **comes** <note>original: *eti*</note> from the **sky** <note>original: *divaḥ*</note>. **Making herself known** <note>original: *bruvāṇā*</note> means she is being praised—here the active form is used in a passive sense. She is the **Great** <note>original: *mahī*</note> or mighty **Mother** <note>original: *mātā*</note>, the creator of light or of the gods. She is **awakening** <note>original: *bodhayantī*</note> her **daughter** <note>original: *duhituḥ*</note>, referring to the Earth. The Earth is metaphorically called her "daughter" because it depends on the Dawn for its sustenance. Alternatively, the "daughter" refers to the Sky itself. 

The fact that the Dawn is the daughter of the Sky is well-known from Vedic passages such as "Shine forth, O Daughter of Heaven." Elsewhere, it is said: "The Daughter of Heaven is the wife of the world" (**Rigveda 7.75.4**). From this, we understand that sometimes the Sky is born from the Dawn, and the Dawn from the Sky. Other teachers say, "Prajapati <note>The Creator Lord</note> longed for his own daughter; some say she was the Sky, others say she was the Dawn" (**Aitareya Brahmana 3.33**). A similar sign of this reversal of cause and effect is seen in the verse: "From Aditi, Daksha was born, and from Daksha, Aditi was born" <note>This highlights the cyclical nature of Vedic deities where parent and child can swap roles.</note>.

Furthermore, she is **seeking the gods** <note>original: *āvivāsantī*</note>, meaning she is attending to them. She is the **young woman** <note>original: *yuvatiḥ*</note> because she mixes with all or is eternally young. She is **wise** <note>original: *manīṣā*</note>, meaning she possesses or is the subject of praise. **For the Fathers** <note>original: *pitṛbhyaḥ*</note>—here the fifth case ending is used in the sense of the third case—meaning "with the Fathers" or the protector-gods. In the **seat** <note>original: *sadane*</note> or the sacrificial hall, she is **calling repeatedly** <note>original: *johuvānā*</note>, summoning them from all sides. Alternatively, she calls "for the Fathers," meaning for the sake of the patrons of the sacrifice <note>original: *yajamānas*</note> who protect the rituals, or those who protect by obtaining desired fruits for them.

<summary>This page introduces the third chapter of the fourth book, beginning a hymn to the All-Gods. The first verse describes the Dawn (Ushas) as a cosmic mother who awakens the earth and summons the gods to the sacrifice.</summary>

<keywords>Ushas, Dawn, Pratiratha, Sayana, Aitareya Brahmana, Aditi, Daksha, Vishvedevas, Vedic metaphor, Mother-Daughter relationship</keywords>

<meta>This page continues the translation of Mandala 5, Hymn 47 of the Rig Veda. The previous page introduced the first verse, which focused on the Dawn (Ushas). [M. 5. A. 4. S. 47.] || Fourth Book || 431

->॥ Here is the Second Verse ॥<-

## Hymn Text
Moving quickly, performing that work, reaching the navel of immortality; the infinite, wide paths travel around heaven and earth on every side. ॥ २ ॥

**Word-by-word analysis (Padapatha):**
Moving quickly; that; work; being set in motion; having stood; of immortality; the navel; infinite; wide; from every side; around; heaven and earth; they go; the paths. ॥ २ ॥

---

## Commentary (Sayana)
**Moving quickly** <note>original: *ajirāsaḥ*</note> means those who possess the quality of constant motion. The word <term>ajiri</term> <note>an ancient grammatical form</note> is used here to denote this speed. **Performing that work** means their primary activity is the act of illumination. **Being set in motion** <note>original: *īryamāṇāḥ*</note>, they go toward the **navel of immortality** <note>original: *amṛtasya nābhim*</note>, which refers to the sun’s orb—the great gatherer—or to the atmosphere, which is the "navel" or center of the waters <note>original: *amṛtasya udakasya*</note>. Having reached this, the **infinite** or boundless, **wide** and pervading **paths** <note>meaning the falling rays of light</note> **go** <note>original: *yanti*</note> **around heaven and earth** <note>original: *dyāvāpṛthivī pari*</note>, covering the sky, the earth, and the atmosphere **from every side**. The word **around** <note>original: *sīm*</note> is used here as a poetic filler to complete the sense of encompassment.

->॥ Here is the Third Verse ॥<-

## Hymn Text
The Bull, the Ocean, the Red Bird with beautiful wings, has entered the source of the ancient Father. Placed in the middle of heaven, the dappled Stone has strode out; he guards the two ends of the atmosphere. ॥ ३ ॥

**Word-by-word analysis (Padapatha):**
The Bull; the Ocean; the Red One; the Golden-winged Bird; of the ancient; the source; of the Father; hither; has entered; in the middle; of heaven; placed; the dappled; Stone; out; has strode; of the atmosphere; he guards; the two ends. ॥ ३ ॥

---

## Commentary (Sayana)
**This triplet of verses is dedicated to the Sun** <note>original: *sauriyo'yaṃ tṛcaḥ*</note>. **The Bull** <note>original: *ukṣā*</note> is the one who pours out water or fulfills desires. **The Ocean** <note>original: *samudraḥ*</note> is so called because he causes moisture to rise, or because the gods "rejoice" <note>original: *sammodante*</note> in him. He is the **Red One** <note>original: *aruṣaḥ*</note> because he shines brightly, and the **Golden-winged Bird** <note>original: *suparṇaḥ*</note> because his movement is graceful. He has **entered** the **source** <note>original: *yonim*</note> or the birthplace of the **ancient Father** <note>original: *pituḥ*</note>, referring to the atmosphere which protects and sustains the world. Afterward, he is **placed in the middle of heaven** as the **dappled one** <note>original: *pṛśniḥ*</note>—the Sun is called dappled because various colors reach him. He is the **Stone** <note>original: *aśmā*</note> because he pervades everything, or perhaps this is a metaphor comparing his strength and permanence to a stone. He **has strode out** across the two **ends of the atmosphere** <note>meaning the eastern and western horizons</note> and **guards** the world. He strides for the sake of protecting all living beings.

->॥ Here is the Fourth Verse ॥<-

## Hymn Text
Four of them bear him, desiring his welfare; ten nourish the infant so he may move. His three-fold cows travel in the highest [heavens], going instantly around the ends of the sky. ॥ ४ ॥

<vocab>
ajira: fast or moving quickly
amṛtasya nābhi: the navel or center of immortality (the Sun)
ukṣā: the pourer or bull (the Sun as a source of rain and life)
samudra: ocean (the Sun as a gatherer of waters)
suparṇa: the golden-winged bird (the Sun moving through the sky)
pṛśni: dappled or multicolored (the Sun)
aśmā: stone (the Sun as a solid or pervading force)
</vocab>

432 || Rig-Veda || [Book 4, Chapter 3, Verse 1]

## Hymn Text

<note>Rig-Veda 4.58.4 - Word-by-word Analysis (Padapatha)</note>
Four; him; carry; desiring security; ten; the fetus; for movement; they cause to suckle; threefold; highest; his; cows [rays]; of heaven; they wander; around; immediately; the ends. ॥ ४ ॥

---

## Commentary (Sayana)

Four priests, desiring security <note>original: *kṣemayantaḥ*, wishing for their own well-being</note> for themselves, carry this Sun; they support him with offerings and songs of praise. Furthermore, the ten directions <note>original: *daśa diśaḥ*</note> cause him—who is like a fetus <note>original: *garbham*</note> produced in their midst—to suckle so that he may move <note>original: *carase*</note>, which refers to his daily activity of rising and setting. The three-fold rays <note>original: *gāvaḥ*, literally "cows"</note> of this Sun—threefold because of the divisions of cold, heat, and rain—wander through the furthest reaches of heaven and the atmosphere <note>original: *divaḥ*</note> immediately after his rising.

---

-> ॥ Now the Fifth Verse ॥ <-

## Hymn Text

<note>Rig-Veda 4.58.5</note>
**O people, this form is the proclamation; where the rivers flow, the waters stay. Two carry him from the mother, others born here and there, twins and kinsmen.** ॥ ५ ॥

<note>Rig-Veda 4.58.5 - Word-by-word Analysis (Padapatha)</note>
This; form; proclamation; O people; they move; where; rivers; stood; waters; two; when; him; they carry; from the mother; others; here and there; born; twins; kinsmen. ॥ ५ ॥

---

## Commentary (Sayana)

O people <note>the priests</note>, this visible form <note>original: *vapuḥ*, the solar orb</note> standing before us is "the proclamation" <note>original: *nivacanam*</note>, meaning it is worthy of being praised. Relying on this orb, the rivers move and flow. The waters also stay in their place because they are dependent on the solar orb. The two <note>Day and Night</note> carry this Sun of the aforementioned characteristics. They are produced from the "Mother" <note>the atmosphere, which acts as the measurer or creator</note>, and are born again and again <note>original: *iheha jāte*</note> wherever the Sun appears. They are "twins" <note>original: *yamyā*</note> because they are paired or regulated, and they are "kinsmen" <note>original: *sabandhū*</note> because they possess equal strength and a common bond—the Sun is the single axis or "relative" that connects them both.

---

<note>Rig-Veda 4.58.6</note>
**They spread out prayers for him and ritual acts; mothers weave garments for the son. Rejoicing at the point of contact, the showering ones go toward the brides by the path of heaven.** ॥ ६ ॥

<note>Rig-Veda 4.58.6 - Word-by-word Analysis (Padapatha)</note>
Out; they spread; prayers; for him; ritual acts; garments; for the son; mothers; they weave; at the contact; showering ones; rejoicing; of heaven; by the path; the brides; they go; toward. ॥ ६ ॥

---

## Commentary (Sayana)

For this Sun, they spread out prayers <note>original: *dhiyaḥ*, hymns</note> and ritual acts <note>original: *apāṃsi*, sacred works</note>. They expand them...

<vocab>
- Aditya: The Sun as a celestial deity.
- Ritvij: The officiating priests of a Vedic sacrifice.
- Kshemayantah: Those seeking peace, security, or the preservation of what they have.
- Vapuh: A beautiful form, body, or the physical disk of the Sun.
- Nivachanam: That which is to be spoken of or proclaimed with praise.
- Ahoratre: The twin pair of Day and Night.
- Dhiyah: Sacred thoughts or prayers that guide the ritual.
- Apamsi: Diligent ritual actions or religious works.
</vocab>

## Commentary (Sayana)
[Continuation from previous page]

...the sacrificers. For the "son"—meaning the Sun, who is like a son—the "mothers," which refers to the Dawns <note>original: *uṣaso*</note> or the directions of space, weave <note>original: *vayanti*</note> garments. This means they produce dense rays of light <note>original: *tejāṃsi*</note> that resemble clothing. When there is contact or union <note>original: *upaprakṣe*</note> with the "sprinkler"—the Sun—then the rays, acting like joyful brides <note>original: *vadhvo*</note>, spread and move along the "path of the day," which is the Sun’s own route, facing the Sun as they move.

## Hymn Text

-> ॥ Now the Seventh Verse ॥ <-

**Let that be so, O Mitra and Varuna! Let that be so, O Agni! Let this praise be for our peace and the warding off of ill. May we reach a firm footing and stability. Salutations to the Great Heaven, the abode of all.** ॥ ७ ॥

**Word-by-word Analysis (Padapatha):**
That. Let be. Mitra-Varuna. That. Agni. Peace <note>original: *śam*</note>. Warding off <note>original: *yoḥ*</note>. For us. This. Let be. Praised. May we reach. A footing. And. Stability. Salutation. To heaven. To the great. To the abode. ॥ ७ ॥

## Commentary (Sayana)

The deities here are determined by the gender and context of the words. O Mitra and Varuna, may this hymn <note>original: *sūktaṃ*</note> be well-recited and praised. O Agni, let this hymn be well-praised. May this recitation bring us happiness <note>original: *śam*</note> and the separation or removal of sufferings <note>original: *yor*</note>. May we also attain a secure standing <note>original: *gādham*</note> and a foundation <note>original: *pratiṣṭhām*</note>—meaning an uninterrupted stability in our life. I offer salutations to the shining Sun, the great heaven, who is the shelter and abode of the entire universe.

## Hymn Text (Sukta 49)

The fourth hymn, beginning with "What for the dear," consists of five verses. The seer <note>original: *rishi*</note> is Pratibhanu, a descendant of Atri. The meter is Jagati <note>a Vedic meter of 48 syllables</note>. The deities are the All-Gods <note>original: *viśve devāḥ*</note>. The Index of the Veda states: "What... five verses, Pratibhanu, Jagati meter." In the fifth day of the *Abhiplava* <note>a specific six-day Soma ritual</note> ceremony, this hymn is used as the foundational text for the All-Gods recitation. This is indicated by the ritual manual: "What for the dear... is for the All-Gods" (Ashvalayana Shrauta Sutra 7.7.1).

-> ॥ Therein the First Verse ॥ <-

**What [praise] shall we contemplate for the dear abode, for him who possesses his own power and his own glory, for the Great One? When she [the lightning], possessing mysterious power, spreads the waters in the cloud of the immeasurable region.** ॥ १ ॥

**Word-by-word Analysis (Padapatha):**
What. [Particle]. For the dear. For the abode. We contemplate. For him with his own power. For him with his own glory. For the Great. We. Of the immeasurable. Of the region. When. In the cloud. [Particle]. Waters. Choosing/Encompassing. Spreads. Possessing mysterious power <note>original: *māyinī*</note>. ॥ १ ॥

## Commentary (Sayana)

This verse is a praise for Agni in the form of lightning. *Kadu*: When? The word *u* is a filler. For the "dear"—that which is beloved by all...

---
<vocab>
- **Mitra-Varuna**: A dual deity representing cosmic order, friendship, and justice.
- **Agni**: The god of fire, here specifically associated with lightning in the atmosphere.
- **Jagati**: A rhythmic meter used in Vedic poetry, consisting of four lines of twelve syllables each.
- **Vishve Devah**: "All-Gods" or the Universal Gods, a collective invocation of the divine pantheon.
- **Abhiplavika**: A standard liturgical period in the Soma sacrifice lasting six days.
- **Vaishvadeva**: Ritual acts or hymns dedicated specifically to the All-Gods.
- **Shastam**: Literally "recited" or "praised," referring to the formal chanting of Vedic verses.
</vocab>

# || Rig Veda || [Book 4, Chapter 3, Section 2]

## Commentary (Sāyaṇa)
[Conclusion of Verse 1]

Because he brings about rain and provides the materials for offerings, his universal popularity is well-known. To such a Power <note>original: *dhāmne*</note>—the energy of the lightning—is this praise directed. This is understood because the subsequent sentence will mention "spreading waters in the clouds." To what kind of power? To one who possesses his own strength <note>original: *svakṣatrāya*</note>, and his own food or glory <note>original: *svayaśase*</note>. Indeed, the entire movement of the universe belongs to him. When shall we honor <note>original: *manāmahe*</note> or praise this great, worshipful being? Since the following text uses feminine markers, the word "which" should be transformed into the feminine. That power of Agni, which is "untouched" <note>original: *āmā*</note>, extends throughout the middle region <note>original: *rajas*</note>, which is to be measured on all sides. Though the sky is immeasurable, it is measured by all as being "this much." Within the associated cloud, or above the cloud, she spreads the waters characterized as rain, covering or expanding them. This "power" is either the one being served or the "possessor of Maya" <note>original: *māyinī*</note>. *Maya* is a name for wisdom; thus, she is "possessed of wisdom." Alternatively, this may be interpreted as the "Voice of the Middle Region" <note>original: *mādhyamikī vāk*</note>—the thunder—which belongs to him.

---

## Hymn Text
-> ॥ Verse Two ॥ <-

**Those Dawns spread the infinite wisdom, which is to be carried by heroes, with a uniform covering of light throughout the world. The pious man drives away the retreating and following Dawns and prospers himself through the former ones.** ॥ २ ॥

**Word-by-word Analysis (Pada-patha):**
Those. Infinite. Wisdom <note>original: *vayunaṃ*</note>. Carried by heroes. With a uniform. Covering. Everywhere. To. The region. Waters. Facing away. Subsequent. Away. He drives. Forth. By the previous ones. He increases. God-seeking. Person. ॥ २ ॥

## Commentary (Sāyaṇa)

This verse refers to the Dawn <note>original: *uṣasyā*</note>. Those Dawns extend the infinite—what? The **wisdom** <note>original: *vayunaṃ*</note> or the manifestation of knowledge. What is its nature? It is **to be carried by heroes** <note>original: *vīravakṣaṇaṃ*</note>, meaning it is to be supported by the heroic officiating priests. Alternatively, it refers to that by which the "carriers of the work" (the performers of rituals) are impelled. Furthermore, with a **uniform** and single-formed **covering** <note>original: *vṛtayā*</note> of light, they spread across the entire **region** <note>original: *rajas*</note> or world. This being the case, the **pious man** <note>original: *devayuḥ*</note> who desires the gods **drives away** <note>original: *apejate*</note> or moves along the **retreating** <note>original: *apācīḥ*</note> Dawns and the **subsequent** <note>original: *aparāḥ*</note> or future ones. The second use of the word "away" <note>original: *apa*</note> is for poetic completion. Through **the previous ones** <note>original: *pūrvābhiḥ*</note>, he **prospers** <note>original: *pratirate*</note>. The root *tṛ* with the prefix *pra* means "to increase." Thus, he increases his own wisdom, or he himself grows in prosperity.

---

## Hymn Text
-> ॥ Verse Three ॥ <-

**With the pressing-stones, with the days and the nights, he sprinkles the most excellent thunderbolt in the wise one. Or he, whose hundred rays move in his own abode, rolling up the days and rolling them out.** ॥ ३ ॥

**Word-by-word Analysis (Pada-patha):**
Towards. By the pressing-stones. By the days. By the nights. The most excellent. The thunderbolt <note>original: *vajram*</note>. Towards. He sprinkles. In the wise one. A hundred. Or. Of whom. Moving. In his own. In the abode. Rolling together. Out. And. Rolling. The days. ॥ ३ ॥

## Commentary (Sāyaṇa)

In this verse, the first half refers to Indra, and the second half refers to the Sun as the soul of Indra. "He is invoked"—this phrase should be supplied. By what means?

<vocab>
- वयुन (Vayuna): Wisdom, knowledge, or the sacred order of the ritual.
- रजस् (Rajas): The middle region of the universe, often associated with the atmosphere or space.
- उषस् (Uṣas): The Dawn, personified as a goddess who brings light and drives away darkness.
- वज्र (Vajra): The thunderbolt, the primary weapon of Indra, representing divine power.
- ग्रावन् (Grāvan): The stones used in the Vedic ritual to press the Soma juice.
</vocab>

# Mandala 5. Hymn 48. Verse 48 [sic] || Fourth Ashtaka || 435

...by these days, which are constituted by the completed seasons and nights. This means they are produced [by him]. With such travelers <note>original: *yāvabhiḥ*</note>. Here, the word for the "means" is used to represent the "end." By means of the pressing [of Soma] which acts as the cause. Having arrived, being the Soma-drinker, when the deceptive Vritra <note>the demon of drought and chaos</note> is present, he hurls the most excellent, very wide thunderbolt <note>original: *vajra*</note> from all sides. He makes it shine. Moreover, the word "or" <note>original: *vā*</note> here means "and." Whose—that is, of the Sun who is identical to Indra—one hundred rays wander in his own home, the sky. What are they doing? Drawing together <note>original: *saṃvartayantaḥ*</note>, they destroy living beings. Or, drawing the days together, they set them in motion and turn them back; they make the days return and bring back those that have passed. This is because the depletion of the lifespan of living beings and the cycle of day and night depend on the heat and movement of the Sun.

---

->॥ The Fourth Verse ॥<-

## Hymn Text
I have beheld that path of his, like the edge of an axe; I have beheld the face of this form for our enjoyment. When he, along with us, provides a dwelling full of food, he bestows a delightful treasure upon the people called to the battle-sacrifice. ॥ 4 ॥

**Word-by-word Breakdown**
That. His. Path. Like an axe. Toward. Face. I have beheld. For enjoyment. Of this. Form.
Together. If/When. Like one possessing food. Dwelling. Treasure. He bestows. For the call to battle. For the people. ॥ 4 ॥

## Commentary (Sāyaṇa)
This verse is addressed to Agni. "That" well-known "path" <note>original: *rītiṃ*</note>—either his nature or his movement—of Agni, I see as if it were the "representative of an axe" <note>original: *parashoḥ pratinidhim*</note>. The meaning is: just as an axe accomplishes what its master desires, so does he. "The face"—the collection of rays—"of this form"—of this Sun who possesses form—I describe for the sake of "enjoyment" <note>original: *bhuje*</note> or experience. "If" <note>original: *yadi*</note>—because that god, being our companion, "bestows" or holds "delightful wealth"—"treasure" <note>original: *ratnaṃ*</note>—for the "people"—the sacrificer who calls him to the battle or the sacrifice—just like a "dwelling" <note>original: *kshayam*</note> that is "full of food" <note>original: *pitumantam*</note>. The meaning is that he gives both [food and wealth].

---

->॥ The Fifth Verse ॥<-

## Hymn Text
He, with his tongue, being four-faced, shines, clothed in beauty; like Varuna, he subdues the enemy. We do not know his greatness as a man; from him, Bhaga and Savitr grant desirable wealth. ॥ 5 ॥

**Word-by-word Breakdown**
He. With the tongue. Four-faced. Shines/Moves. Beautiful. Clothed. Varuna. Subduing. The enemy.
Not. His. We know. By human nature. We. From whom. Bhaga. Savitr. Grants. Desirable [wealth]. ॥ 5 ॥

## Commentary (Sāyaṇa)
That Agni, being "four-faced" <note>original: *caturanīkaḥ*</note>—that is, having flames spread in the four directions—"moves" <note>original: *cañjate*</note> with his tongue. He goes toward the clarified butter and other offerings. Or, being four-faced, he "adorns" <note>original: *cañjate*</note> himself with his tongue. Doing what?

<vocab>
**Season** <note>original: *ṛtu*</note>: the natural divisions of the year
**Thunderbolt** <note>original: *vajra*</note>: the primary weapon of Indra, used to strike down Vritra
**Solar deity / The Sun** <note>original: *āditya*</note>: the celestial form of light and heat
**Ray of light** <note>original: *raśmi*</note>: the "fingers" or "arms" of the sun reaching the earth
**Axe** <note>original: *paraśu*</note>: a sharp tool used here as a metaphor for the sharp, decisive power of fire or light
**Treasure** <note>original: *ratna*</note>: literally "that which is delightful," usually referring to wealth or spiritual gifts
**Savitr** <note>original: *savitṛ*</note>: the solar deity representing the impelling or creative power of the sun
**Varuna** <note>original: *varuṇa*</note>: the deity of cosmic order and the vast sky
**Four-faced** <note>original: *caturanīka*</note>: having four fronts or divisions, likely referring to fire spreading in all cardinal directions
</vocab>

The metaphors compare the deity's path to the sharpness of an axe and describe his "four-faced" nature as flames spreading in all directions.</summary>

# Rig Veda || Book 4. Chapter 3. Section 3.

Wearing beautiful, delightful splendor, the god Varuna, who is the dispeller of darkness, striving against and removing the enemy <note>original: *arim*</note>. We do not know him. That is to say, we do not know him who is possessed of manhood <note>original: *puruṣatvatā*</note> or the power to fulfill all desires. This is an abstract suffix indicating "fulfillment." ## Sukta Introduction
The fifth hymn, beginning with "The divine [Savitar] for you," consists of five verses. It is the work of the seer <term>Pratiprabha Ātreya</term> (the son of Atri). The meter is <term>Trishtubh</term> (a rhythmic cycle of 44 syllables), and it is dedicated to the <term>Vishvedevas</term> (the All-Gods). The Index <note>original: *anukramaṇikā*</note> states: "The divine [Savitar] for you" is by Pratiprabha, while the final verse is by Trinapani. The ritual application <note>original: *viniyoga*</note> follows the specific markers in the text.

---

## Hymn Text

->॥ Here is the first verse ॥<-

<note>RV 4.44.1</note>
**I approach the divine Savitar for you today, and Bhaga who distributes treasure to mankind.**
**O leaders, O Ashvins who enjoy much, I would turn you toward us day after day, desiring your friendship. ॥ 1 ॥**

**Word-by-word Breakdown**
**The divine. For you. Today. Savitar. Toward. I approach. Bhaga. And. Treasure. Distributing. To mankind.**
**Toward. You two. O Leaders. O Great-Enjoyers. I would turn. Day after day. Indeed. O Ashvins. Desiring friendship. ॥ 1 ॥**

## Commentary (Sayana)

I approach the divine <note>original: *devam*</note>, the shining Savitar, the one who permits all things, for you. This means "for you" <note>original: *tvām*</note>. Alternatively, this is a statement by the <term>Hotar</term> (priest): "For you, the sacrificers, for your sake, I approach <note>original: *eṣe*</note> now." And I approach the god Bhaga, the worshipful one, who distributes delightful <note>original: *ratnam*</note> oblation to the man, the sacrificer. Indeed, the distribution of wealth by Bhaga is well known, as the scripture <note>original: *śruti*</note> says: "May Bhaga distribute to you both," and "The divider of wealth and the bringer of riches" <note>Rig Veda 4.17.11</note>, and "Bhaga is the divider by his power" <note>Rig Veda 5.46.6</note>. Alternatively, the genitive case here is used in the sense of the dative: "distributing delightful wealth for the sake of the man (the sacrificer)." 

O leaders <note>original: *narā*</note>, O you who enjoy much <note>original: *purubhujā*</note>—meaning they enjoy many things—O <term>Ashvins</term> (the celestial twins), I turn you <note>original: *ā-vavṛtyām*</note> toward us every day, day after day. Seeking your friendship <note>original: *sakhiyan*</note>, meaning desiring the status of your friend. The word *chit* is used here for metrical completion.

---

## Hymn Text

->॥ Now the second verse ॥<-

<note>RV 4.44.2</note>
**Knowing the approach of the Lord, honor the divine Savitar with well-spoken hymns.**
**Knowing him well, one should address him with reverence, as he distributes the most excellent treasure to mankind. ॥ 2 ॥**

**Word-by-word Breakdown**
**Toward. The approach. Of the Lord (Asura). Knowing. With well-spoken hymns. The divine. Savitar. Honor.**
**Near. One should speak. With a bow (reverence). Knowing well. The most excellent. And. Treasure. Distributing. To mankind. ॥ 2 ॥**

# Mandala 5. Chapter 4. Hymn 49. || Fourth Book || 437

Knowing the return journey—the homecoming—of the sun-god <term>Savitar</term>, the expeller of enemies, serve the divine Savitar with hymns. O Inner Self, serve him! Furthermore, to mankind <note>original: *āyoḥ*</note>, he distributes the greatest jewel and wealth. This means he gives it. Knowing this, honor him with reverence <note>original: *namasā*</note> or with a sacrificial oblation. This means one should specifically meditate upon him. Alternatively, the sense is causative: making our needs known, may you, the worshiper, praise him.

---

## Hymn Text

->॥ Here is the third verse ॥<-

With his [tongue/flame], he partakes of choice things; <term>Pushan</term>, <term>Bhaga</term>, and the infinite <term>Aditi</term>; the Sun clothes himself in light. Indra, Vishnu, Varuna, Mitra, and Agni—the wonder-workers—create auspicious days. ॥ ३ ॥

**Word-for-word breakdown:**
With-his-tongue | he-partakes-of | choice-things | Pushan | Bhaga | Aditi | clothes-himself | the-Sun | Indra | Vishnu | Varuna | Mitra | Agni | days | auspicious | create | the-wonder-workers ॥ ३ ॥

## Commentary (Sayana)

This Agni [the Fire] partakes of things to be eaten <note>original: *adrayā*</note>. The word *adri* here uses a specific grammatical suffix <note>original: *uṇādi ktra*</note>. Or, that which eats is the "tongue" <note>original: *adrā*</note>. With that tongue, he partakes of <note>original: *dayate*</note> the choice pieces of wood. The verb *dayate* has many meanings, including "to burn." Thus, it means he burns them. By context, we understand this refers to Agni. Alternatively, he bestows <note>original: *dayate*</note> choice foods upon the patron of the sacrifice. The root *day* can mean giving, moving, destroying, or protecting.

What is the nature of this Fire? He is **Pushan**, the nourisher; he is **Bhaga**, the adorable one; he is **Aditi**, the indivisible one. Or perhaps all three—Pushan and the others—each bestow choice foods. **The Sun** <note>original: *usraḥ*</note> clothes <note>original: *vaste*</note> or covers himself, which by context refers to his rays of light. The five gods starting with Indra are **wonder-workers** <note>original: *dasmāḥ*</note>, beautiful to behold. They **create** <note>original: *janayanta*</note>—meaning they produce—**auspicious** <note>original: *bhadrā*</note> **days** <note>original: *ahāni*</note> for the coming sacrifice. The "auspiciousness" of these days consists specifically in them being characterized by sacrifice and the giving of gifts.

---

## Hymn Text

->॥ Here is the fourth verse ॥<-

May the irresistible <term>Savitar</term> grant us that shelter; may the rushing rivers follow after that. When I, the priest of the sacrifice, speak, may we be masters of wealth, possessing the treasures of strength. ॥ ४ ॥

**Word-for-word breakdown:**
That | to-us | irresistible | Savitar | shelter | that | rivers | rushing | follow | after-going | near | when | I-speak | of-the-sacrifice | the-priest | of-wealth | may-we-be | masters | possessing-treasures-of-strength ॥ ४ ॥

## Commentary (Sayana)

That famous **shelter** <note>original: *varūtham*</note>, meaning the choice wealth we desire, may the god **Savitar**—who is **irresistible** <note>original: *anarvā*</note> and not turned back by anyone—grant to **us**. Regarding that wealth, may the **rivers** <note>original: *sindhavaḥ*</note>, which are **rushing** <note>original: *iṣayantaḥ*</note> or flowing, **follow** <note>original: *anu gman*</note>. This means may they go toward the act of giving wealth.

---
<note>Bottom of page contains signature mark: VOL. III. 5 T</note>

<vocab>
- **Pushan (Pūṣā):** A solar deity who acts as a nourisher and protector of flocks and paths.
- **Bhaga (Bhagaḥ):** The god of fortune, destiny, and due inheritance.
- **Aditi (Aditiḥ):** The goddess of the infinite and boundless sky, mother of the gods.
- **Usra (Usraḥ):** Literally "the bright one," usually referring to the Sun or the Dawn.
- **Dasmāḥ (Dasmāḥ):** Accomplishers of wonderful deeds; often translated as "wonder-workers."
- **Anarvā (Anarvā):** One who has no enemy to check him; irresistible or unimpeded.
- **Savitar (Savitā):** The divine "Impeller" or solar deity representing the sun before sunrise.
- **Varūtham (Varūtham):** A place of protection, a shield, or metaphorically, the "shelter" of wealth.
- **Sindhavaḥ (Sindhavaḥ):** The flowing waters or rivers.
- **Vāja-ratnāḥ (Vājaratnāḥ):** Those who possess the prizes/jewels of strength or battle-booty.
</vocab>

Sayana's commentary clarifies the multi-functional roles of Agni and the sun-god in providing nourishment and protection.</summary>

# 438 || Rig Veda || [Book 4. Chapter 3. Section 4.]

Since I, the Invoker <note>original: *hotā*, the priest who recites the hymns</note>, speak thus while approaching the sacrifice <note>original: *adhvarasya*</note>, may the gods grant that wealth—this is the implied conclusion. Furthermore, may we become the masters of many kinds of riches <note>original: *rāyo*</note>. May we be delightful, or perhaps invigorated, by food and strength <note>original: *vājaratnā*</note>. Alternatively, the meaning is: because I offer this praise, may the god <term>Savitar</term> come to our protection <note>original: *varūtham*</note>. Therefore, may the rivers also follow after our protection or our sacrifice.

->॥ Here is the fifth verse ॥<-

## Hymn Text
Those who, speaking well-said words, offer food <note>original: *namaḥ*</note> to the <term>Vasus</term> <note>the 'Good Ones,' a class of deities representing elements of nature</note>, and to <term>Mitra</term> and <term>Varuna</term> in the home; may great wealth <note>original: *abhvam*</note> come to us. Grant us wide-reaching happiness. May we rejoice in the protection of Heaven and Earth. ॥ ५ ॥

**Word-for-word breakdown:**
Toward | those who | for the Vasus | quickly | indeed | food/reverence | in the home | to Mitra | to Varuna | speakers of well-said words | down | may it come | great wealth | create/make | wider [happiness] | of Heaven | of Earth | with protection | may we rejoice ॥ ५ ॥

---

## Commentary (Sayana)
Those sacrificers who provide food <note>original: *namaḥ*</note>—consisting of the five-fold offerings—speedily to the <term>Vasus</term>, the gods who dwell in the sacrifice; and those who are speakers of well-said words <note>hymns</note> to the gods <term>Mitra</term> and <term>Varuna</term>; to us, may great wealth or brilliance <note>original: *abhvam*</note> come. O Gods, create for these people a wider and greater happiness. May we rejoice or be gladdened by the protection of both Heaven and Earth.

->॥ Thus ends the third section in the third chapter of the fourth book ॥<-

The sixth hymn, beginning with "Every [mortal] of the Divine," consists of five verses. It was revealed to the sage <term>Svastyatreya</term>. It is addressed to the <term>Vishvedevas</term> <note>the "All-Gods" or the collective pantheon</note>. The fifth verse is in the <term>Pankti</term> meter <note>40 syllables</note>, while the first four are in the <term>Anushtubh</term> meter <note>32 syllables</note>. This is stated in the <term>Anukramani</term> <note>the traditional Vedic index</note>: "The hymn 'Vishvah' is by Svastyatreya and ends with a Pankti verse." 

In the ritual known as the <term>Prishthya Abhilava Shadaha</term> <note>a six-day sacrifice</note>, on the first day, during the recitation for the All-Gods, this hymn serves as the opening triplet. This is indicated in the *Ashvalayana Shrauta Sutra* (7.6): "The hymn 'Every [mortal] of the divine leader' is the first." This same hymn also serves as the opening for the recitation on the second, fourth, and sixth days of the <term>Abhilava</term> rituals, as it is noted: "Thus it is for the even-numbered days in the Abhilava."

->॥ Therein is the first verse ॥<-

## Hymn Text
Every mortal should choose the friendship of the divine leader. Every man seeks wealth; may he choose glory so that he may prosper. ॥ १ ॥

**Word-for-word breakdown:**
Every | of the divine | of the leader | mortal | should choose | friendship | every | for wealth | seeks | glory | should choose | for prospering ॥ १ ॥

# 439 || Rig Veda || [Book 4. Chapter 3. Section 4.]

Every person, every mortal, follows the leader, the god. This refers to <term>Savitar</term> <note>the solar deity representing the divine impulse and the transition of light</note>. One should choose his friendship. Every person desires wealth <note>original: *rāye*</note>. Through his grace, may every person choose glorious wealth from Savitar, sufficient for nourishment <note>original: *puṣyase*</note> or enough to provide complete prosperity.

---

## Hymn Text

-> ॥ Here is the second verse ॥ <-

O Divine Leader, those who are yours, and those who are able to offer these praises—with your riches, may we be united through your fellowship. Indeed, those to be honored, may we attain them with all our desires. ॥ २ ॥

**Word-for-word breakdown:**
They | your | O God | O Leader | who | and | these | for praising | they | with wealth | your | indeed | for honoring | may we be united | through fellowship. ॥ २ ॥

## Commentary (Sayana)

O Leader! O God! Those who are yours—meaning we, the <term>Yajamanas</term> <note>the patrons or sacrificers who institute the ritual</note>, and others—these <note>there is a grammatical shift in the case ending here</note> priests like the <term>Hotar</term> <note>the primary priest who recites the hymns</note> who are capable of praising <note>original: *anuśase*</note>, they also belong to you. 

Alternatively, the phrase "these" refers to other deities such as Indra, whom the priests are capable of praising in their proper order. Or perhaps, the intended meaning is that there is only one Great Soul <note>original: *mahānātmā*</note>, who is the Sun <note>original: *Sūrya*</note>; for as it is said, "He is the Soul of all that moves and stays," implying all other deities are included within him. The point is: it is not only those who specifically praise you. 

The connection is this: may both groups of us be united <note>original: *sacemahi*</note> with wealth <note>original: *rāyā*</note>. For they indeed are the ones to be honored <note>original: *āpṛce*</note>. <note>Grammatical note: The original Sanskrit uses the *ken* suffix to denote an action that ought to be done; it functions as an indeclinable, which is why the case ending is hidden.</note> May we be associated with or attain all our desires through fellowship <note>original: *sacathyaiḥ*</note>.

---

## Hymn Text

-> ॥ Here is the third verse ॥ <-

From here, serve the leading men, the guests; from here, [serve] the wives of the gods. May the expeller of enemies keep all those standing in our path far away. ॥ ३ ॥

**Word-for-word breakdown:**
From here | our | [prefix] | leaders | guests | from here | wives | serve/worship | far away | all | standing in the path | enemies | may [he] separate | the separator. ॥ ३ ॥

## Commentary (Sayana)

From here—meaning from within this sacrifice <note>the suffix *tasi* is used here to represent the necessary case for "in this"</note>—serve <note>original: *daśasyata*</note> or worship on all sides the "leaders" <note>original: *nṝn*</note> of us priests, and the "guests" <note>original: *atithīn*</note>, who are the gods worthy of being worshipped like honored guests. Also, from here in this sacrifice, serve the wives <note>original: *patnīḥ*</note> of the gods as well, by offering oblations and other ritual acts. 

Alternatively, the meaning is: O Gods, grant <note>original: *daśasyata*</note> to us these three things: leading sons and servants, guests, and wives. 

May the assembly of gods, or Savitar, who is the "Separator" <note>original: *yuyuviḥ*</note>—one who keeps things unmixed or drives things apart—keep far away <note>original: *yuyotu*</note> all enemies <note>original: *dviṣaḥ*</note> standing in the path <note>original: *patheṣṭhām*</note>, as well as any other haters.

<note>
Vocabulary Summary:
**Savitar**: The solar impeller.
**Wealth/Riches (Raya)**: Material and spiritual prosperity.
**Wives (Patnih)**: The female counterparts of the Vedic gods.
**Guests (Atithin)**: A metaphor for the gods arriving at the sacrifice.
**Worship/Serve (Dashasyata)**: To perform ritual service.
**Separator/Expeller (Yuyuvih)**: A title for a deity who removes obstacles or enemies.
</note>

It emphasizes the unity of the sacrificers with the divine through wealth and fellowship, and instructs the worship of both male deities and their divine wives to ensure the removal of enemies.</summary>
<keywords>Savitar, wealth, sacrifice, hospitality, wives of gods, protection, ritual priests, Surya, Vedic commentary</keywords>

# 440 || Rig Veda || [Book 4. Chapter 3. Section 5.]

## Hymn Text

-> ॥ Here is the fourth verse ॥ <-

When the carrier is led forward, like an animal to the wooden post, he who has a mind for men, whose home is filled with heroes, is the giver of wealth, like a skilled woman. ॥ ४ ॥

**Word-for-word breakdown:**
When | the carrier | led forward | runs | of the post | the animal |
having a mind for men | having a home of heroes | skilled | like a wise woman | the giver ॥ ४ ॥

---

## Commentary (Sayana)

In whichever sacrifice the carrier <note>original: *vahniḥ*; one who bears or carries the sacrifice</note> is led to the sacrificial post <note>original: *yūpaṃ*</note>, and the animal destined for the post <note>original: *droṇyaḥ*</note> goes toward that post; there, the god Savitar, who has a mind for the sacrificer <note>original: *nṛmaṇā*</note>, becomes the distributor of rewards. He is "one whose home is filled with heroes" <note>original: *vīrapastyaḥ*</note>, meaning his home <note>original: *pastyaṃ*</note> contains heroes such as priests, sacrificers, sons, and servants. Alternatively, it means he provides a home filled with sons and followers. He is the giver <note>original: *sanitā*</note>, being skilled <note>original: *arṇī*</note> like a wise or capable woman <note>original: *dhīrā-iva*</note>. Or perhaps, being skilled in the sacred rites, he becomes the giver while looking toward the sacrificial offerings.

---

## Hymn Text

-> ॥ Here is the fifth verse ॥ <-

O Divine Leader, this is your Lord of the Chariot, a blessing of wealth. For the sake of wealth, for peace, for well-being, we praise the desired one; we praise the one whom the gods praise. ॥ ५ ॥

**Word-for-word breakdown:**
This | your | O God | O Leader | Lord of the Chariot | blessing | wealth |
blessing | for wealth | blessing | for well-being | the desired | we praise | praised by gods | we praise ॥ ५ ॥

---

## Commentary (Sayana)

O Leader! O God Savitar! This "Lord of the Chariot" <note>original: *rathaspatiḥ*</note> of yours is the protector of all and the possessor of wealth to be given. <note>The scholar notes a grammatical omission of the possessive suffix here.</note> May he provide a blessing—this is the implied conclusion. And we, for the sake of wealth and for the sake of peace and well-being <note>original: *svastaye*; a state of "being well" or non-destruction</note>, we praise <note>original: *manāmahe*</note> this desired Savitar. We who are the praisers of the God, or the praisers of the gods, we offer our thoughts and hymns.

-> ॥ Thus ends the fifth section in the third chapter of the fourth book ॥ <-

---

## Introductory Commentary (Sukta 51)

The seventh hymn, beginning with the words **"Before the pressed [juice]"** <note>original: *agre sutasya*</note>, consists of fifteen verses. The Index of the <term>Atreya</term> <note>the lineage of the sage Atri</note> describes it as follows: **"The first four verses are in the Gayatri meter, followed by six in the Ushnik meter, then three in either Jagati or Trishtubh, and the final two are in the Anushtubh meter."** According to the general definition that the sage is the one from whom the knowledge flows, the Sage here is of the Atri family. Regarding the meters: the first four are <term>Gayatri</term> <note>a 24-syllable meter</note>; from the fifth onwards, six are <term>Ushnik</term> <note>a 28-syllable meter</note>; from the eleventh onwards, three are <term>Jagati</term> <note>a 48-syllable meter</note> or <term>Trishtubh</term> <note>a 44-syllable meter</note>; and the fourteenth and fifteenth are <term>Anushtubh</term> <note>a 32-syllable meter</note>. The deities are the **All-Gods** <note>original: *Viśve Devāḥ*; the collective pantheon</note>.

<vocab>
- <term>Savitar</term>: The solar deity representing the divine impulse and creative power.
- <term>Yupa</term>: The consecrated wooden post to which the sacrificial animal is tied.
- <term>Rathaspati</term>: Literally "Lord of the Chariot," a title for a protective deity.
- <term>Anukramanika</term>: An ancient systematic index of the Vedic hymns providing the poet, meter, and deity.
- <term>Meters</term>: The Rig Veda is composed in specific rhythmic structures; <term>Gayatri</term> is the most famous, often used for invitations to the gods.
</vocab>

<keywords>Savitar, sacrificial animal, wealth, prosperity, Gayatri meter, Ushnik meter, Atri lineage, All-Gods</keywords>

# 441 || Rig Veda || [Book 4. Chapter 4. Section 5.]

->॥ Here is the first verse ॥<-

## Hymn Text

O Agni, come for the drinking of the pressed juice, with all the protecting gods, for the giving of the oblation. ॥ १ ॥

**Word-for-word breakdown:**
O Agni | of the pressed juice | for the drinking | with all | with the protectors | come | with the gods | for the giving of the oblation ॥ १ ॥

---

## Commentary (Sayana)

O **Agni**, for the purpose of **drinking the pressed juice** <note>original: *sutasya pītaye*; the extracted Soma juice</note>, please **come** <note>original: *ā gahi*</note> together with **all the protectors** <note>original: *viśvair umebhiḥ*; refers to all the guardian deities</note> and the **gods** <note>original: *devebhiḥ*</note> such as Indra and others, for the **giving of our oblation** <note>original: *havyadātaye*</note>, or for the sake of the sacrificer who presents the offering.

---

->॥ Now the second verse ॥<-

## Hymn Text

O observers of Truth, come to the sacrifice; you whose laws are true, drink with the tongue of Agni. ॥ २ ॥

**Word-for-word breakdown:**
O observers of Truth | come | you whose laws are true | to the sacrifice | of Agni | drink | with the tongue ॥ २ ॥

---

## Commentary (Sayana)

O **observers of Truth** <note>original: *ṛtadhītayaḥ*; those whose praises are true or whose actions are unfailing</note>, O gods, **come** <note>original: *ā gata*</note> to our **sacrifice** <note>original: *adhvaram*</note>. Having arrived, O you **whose laws are true** <note>original: *satyadharmāṇaḥ*; upholders of the eternal order</note>, **drink** the clarified butter and Soma juice **with the tongue of Agni** <note>original: *agneḥ jihvayā*; the fire acts as the mouth of the gods, consuming the offerings</note>.

---

->॥ Now the third verse ॥<-

## Hymn Text

O wise and adorable one, come with the wise gods who arrive in the morning, for the drinking of the Soma. ॥ ३ ॥

**Word-for-word breakdown:**
With the wise ones | O wise one | O adorable one | with those who arrive in the morning | come | with the gods | for the drinking of the Soma ॥ ३ ॥

---

## Commentary (Sayana)

O **wise one** <note>original: *vipra*; the sage or the fulfiller of various desires</note>, O **adorable Agni** <note>original: *santya*; one worthy of being served</note>, please **come** <note>original: *ā gahi*</note> along with the **gods** who are **wise** and **arrive in the morning** <note>original: *prātaryāvabhiḥ*</note> at the time of sacrifice. For what purpose? **For the drinking of the Soma** <note>original: *somapītaye*</note>.

---

->॥ Now the fourth verse ॥<-

## Hymn Text

This Soma is pressed between the boards; it is poured into the vessel, dear to Indra and to Vayu. ॥ ४ ॥

**Word-for-word breakdown:**
This | Soma | between the boards | pressed | into the vessel | around | is poured | dear | to Indra | to Vayu ॥ ४ ॥

---

## Commentary (Sayana)

**This** present **Soma**, having been **pressed** <note>original: *suto*</note> between the two **pressing-boards** <note>original: *camū*</note>, **is poured** <note>original: *pari ṣicyate*</note> into the **vessel** <note>original: *amatre*</note> or cup. It is then filled. This juice is **dear** <note>original: *priyaḥ*</note> to **Indra and Vayu**. The phrase "O Indra and Vayu, come to drink it" is understood as remaining to be completed.

<note>Ritual Note: The verse "O Vayu, come hither" is the first of a triplet dedicated to Vayu in the Prauga-shastra recitation on the third day of the Prishtha sacrifice. This is indicated in the ritual manuals: "Vayu, come to drink the juice" is one, and "O Vayu, drink the auspicious [juices] from heaven" are two others (Ashvalayana Shrauta Sutra 7.10).</note>

### Vocabulary

*   **O Agni** <note>original: *Agne*</note>: The god of fire and mediator between gods and men.

*   **Vayu** <note>original: *Vāyu*</note>: The god of wind.

*   **For the giving of the oblation** <note>original: *havyadātaye*</note>: Referring to the act of sacrifice.
*   **Observers of truth/law** <note>original: *ṛtadhītayaḥ*</note>: Deities who maintain the cosmic order (Rita).
*   **Sacrifice** <note>original: *adhvaram*</note>: Specifically a "harm-less" or perfect ritual.
*   **With the tongue** <note>original: *jihvayā*</note>: Referring to Agni's flames.
*   **Arriving in the morning** <note>original: *prātaryāvabhiḥ*</note>: Deities associated with the dawn or early morning rites.
*   **Pressing-boards/vessel** <note>original: *camū*</note>: Ritual implements used to extract Soma.
*   **Prauga-shastra** <note>original: *praugaśastra*</note>: A specific morning recitation in the Vedic liturgy.

## Commentary by Sayana

**[Regarding Verse 5:]**
O **Vayu**, aiming for the **food** <note>original: *prayaḥ*; specifically the food known as Soma</note>, please **come here** <note>original: *āyāhi*</note> for the purpose of **eating** <note>original: *vītaye*</note>. Being **pleased** <note>original: *juṣāṇaḥ*</note>, come for the sake of the **giver of the oblation** <note>original: *havyadātaye*</note>, which means for the sacrificer. Having arrived, **drink** the **juice of the pressed plant** <note>original: *sutasyāndhaso*; the food characterized as Soma which has been extracted</note>.

-> ॥ Thus ends the fifth section in the third chapter of the fourth book ॥ <-

<note>This ritual note explains how these verses are used in a specific ceremony.</note>
On the third day of the **Prishtha sacrifice** <note>a complex six-day Soma sacrifice involving the singing of specific chants</note>, during the **Prauga Shastra** <note>a specific litany of seven triplets of verses recited by the Hotri priest</note>, in the section dedicated to Indra and Vayu, one should recite the two verses beginning with "Both Indra and...". One should form a triplet <note>original: *tṛca*</note> by repeating either the first or the second of those two verses. This is indicated in the **Ashvalayana Shrauta Sutra** <note>original: *Āśvalāyana Śrauta Sūtra* 9.10; a manual for Vedic rituals</note>: "Of the two verses, 'Both Indra and Vayu, of these pressed...', one or the other is recited twice."

**[Regarding Verse 6:]**
O **Vayu**, both you **and Indra** deserve the **drinking** <note>original: *pītim*</note> of **these** Soma juices which have been **pressed** <note>original: *sutānām*</note> and placed before you. Because this is so, therefore **partake** <note>original: *juṣethām*</note> of those Soma juices, you two who are **without harm** <note>original: *arepasau*; faultless or non-injurious</note>. For that purpose, the word "come" is understood—aiming for the **food** <note>original: *prayaḥ*</note> known as Soma. Or, the term implies "those who possess the nature of food."

**[Regarding Verse 7:]**
<note>The manuscript provides the word-for-word breakdown for Verse 7 but the specific verbal commentary concludes on the following page.</note>

## Commentary by Sayana
<note>This is the conclusion of the commentary for Verse 7 from the previous page.</note>

For Indra and Vayu, the **Soma juices** <note>original: *somāsaḥ*</note> are **mixed with curds** <note>original: *dadhyāśiraḥ*</note> and have been **pressed** <note>original: *sutāḥ*</note>. These juices, which take the form of food, go toward you, O Indra and Vayu, just as **rivers** <note>original: *sindhavaḥ*</note> flow into a **low-lying pit** <note>original: *nimnaṃ gartam*</note>.

On the third day of the sacrifice, during the recitation of the **Prauga litany** <note>term: *Prauga-shastra*; the second litany of the morning libation consisting of several triplets addressed to different deities</note>, this **triplet** <note>term: *tricha*; a unit of three verses</note> beginning with **"Together with all"** <note>original: *sajūr viśvebhiḥ*</note> is dedicated to the **All-Gods** <note>term: *vaishvadeva*; relating to the Vishvedevas or "All-the-Gods"</note>. This is indicated in the ritual manuals: "Together with all the gods and our dear ones..." <note>original: *sajūr viśvebhir devebhir uta naḥ priyā priyāsu*; citing Ashvalayana Shrauta Sutra 7.10</note>.

O **Agni**, being **together** <note>original: *sajūḥ*</note> with **all the gods** and being of **equal affection** <note>original: *samānaprītiḥ*</note> with the **Ashvins** <note>the divine twin physicians</note> and **Dawn**, **come here**. Just as your **flame** <note>original: *arcis*</note> delights in the sacrifice, or just as you delight in your own light, in that same way, **rejoice** <note>original: *raṇa*</note> in the **pressed** Soma juice.

### 444 || Rig Veda || [Book 4. Chapter 3. Section 9.]

On the sixth day of the **Prishthya sacrifice** <term>Pṛṣṭhya; a complex six-day ritual sequence</term>, during the recitation of the **litany to the All-Gods** <note>original: *vaiśvadeva-śastre*</note>, the triplet beginning with **"May well-being..."** <note>original: *svasti naḥ*</note> is used. This is indicated in the ritual manuals: "The triplet 'May the Ashvins and Bhaga fashion well-being for us' is for the All-Gods" <note>citing Ashvalayana Shrauta Sutra 8.1</note>. Similarly, in the **Brihaspati-sava** ritual, this triplet is used to introduce the "Nivid" <note>term: *Nivid*; a short sacrificial formula inserted into a hymn</note> for the All-Gods, as indicated by the manual: "The verse 'May the Ashvins and Bhaga fashion well-being for us' is for the All-Gods" <note>citing Ashvalayana Shrauta Sutra 9.5</note>.

---

## Hymn Text

-> ॥ The first verse of the triplet; the eleventh in the hymn ॥ <-

May the **Ashvins** and **Bhaga** fashion **well-being** for us; may the divine **Aditi**, who is **unresisted**, fashion well-being. May **Pushan**, the **Asura**, bestow well-being upon us; may **Heaven and Earth** grant well-being through their **noble wisdom**. ॥ ११ ॥

**Pada Patha:**
Well-being | for us | may they fashion | the two Ashvins | Bhaga | well-being | the divine | Aditi | unresisted |
well-being | Pushan | the Asura | may he bestow | for us | well-being | Heaven and Earth | through noble wisdom ॥ ११ ॥

## Commentary (Sayana)

May the two Ashvins fashion for us **well-being** <note>original: *svasti*; defined here as *avināśam*, "non-destruction" or safety</note>. May **Bhaga** <note>the god of fortune</note> also fashion well-being. Likewise, may the divine **Aditi** <note>the mother of the gods</note> fashion well-being. May **Pushan**, the **unresisted** <note>original: *anarvaṇaḥ*; one who is not opposed by others</note> and the **Asura** <note>original: *asuraḥ*; interpreted here as "the expeller of enemies" or "the giver of life-breaths and strength"</note>, bestow well-being upon us. Also, may **Heaven and Earth** <note>original: *dyāvāpṛthivyau*</note>, characterized by their **noble wisdom** <note>original: *su-cetunā*; excellent knowledge</note>, fashion well-being for us.

---

## Hymn Text

-> ॥ Now the twelfth verse ॥ <-

For **well-being**, we call upon **Vayu**; upon **Soma** for well-being, he who is the **protector of the world**. Upon **Brihaspati**, accompanied by **all the hosts**, for well-being; may the **Adityas** be for our well-being. ॥ १२ ॥

**Pada Patha:**
For well-being | Vayu | we call upon | Soma | well-being | of the world | who | the lord |
Brihaspati | with all hosts | for well-being | for well-being | the Adityas | may they be | for us ॥ १२ ॥

## Commentary (Sayana)

For the sake of **well-being** <note>original: *svastaye*; welfare or security</note>, we call upon **Vayu** <note>the wind god</note>; the meaning is that we praise him. We also call upon **Soma**. Soma is the **protector of the world** <note>original: *bhuvanasya patiḥ*</note> because the life of all the world is dependent upon Soma. Likewise, we praise **Brihaspati**, the protector of the **great ritual act or mantra** <note>original: *bṛhataḥ karmaṇo mantrasya pālayitāram*</note>, who is accompanied by **all the hosts** <note>original: *sarva-gaṇam*; with all the groups of deities</note>, for the sake of well-being. May the **Adityas** <note>the solar deities, sons of Aditi, such as Aruna and the others, often numbered as twelve</note> all be for our well-being.

If a person who has been consecrated for a **sacrificial session** <note>term: *satra*; a long-term ritual</note> falls ill, this triplet is used to introduce the **Nivid** formula in the litany to the All-Gods on that day. This is indicated: "One should place the Nivid in the *Svastya-veya* hymn" <note>citing Ashvalayana Shrauta Sutra 6.9</note>. It is explained in the commentary there that by the term *Svastya-veya*, this specific triplet is intended. Furthermore, this triplet should be chanted when there are bad omens or portents.

<vocab>
**Svasti:** Well-being, prosperity, or safety from harm.
**Ashvins:** Divine twin physicians of the gods, associated with healing and the transition from darkness to light.
**Bhaga:** A solar deity representing wealth, fortune, and the rightful share of prosperity.
**Aditi:** The boundless mother goddess, representing the infinite expanse and the mother of the primary deities.
**Pushan:** A solar deity who acts as a nourisher, protector of travelers, and guide of souls.
**Heaven and Earth (Dyavaprithivi):** The universal parents in Vedic thought, symbolizing the totality of the cosmos.
**Vayu:** The god of wind and the vital breath (Prana).
**Soma:** Both a sacred plant/juice used in rituals and the lunar deity; the source of immortality and strength.
**Brihaspati:** The "Lord of Prayer," the teacher and priest of the gods.
**Adityas:** A group of solar deities (sons of Aditi) who uphold the laws of the universe.
**Vaishvadeva-shastra:** A specific ritual recitation dedicated to the "All-Gods" (Vishvedevas).
</vocab>

Sayana's commentary explains the ritual application of these verses, particularly their use as a prayer for healing during long sacrificial sessions.</summary>

## Mandala 5. Chapter 4. Hymn 51. || Fourth Volume || 445

---

## Hymn Text

-> ॥ The Thirteenth Verse ॥ <-

May **all the gods** favor us today for **well-being**; may **Agni Vaishvanara**, the **Vasu**, favor us for well-being.
May the divine **Ribhus** favor us for well-being; may **Rudra** protect us with well-being from **sin**. ॥ १३ ॥

**Word-by-word analysis:**
All | gods | us | today | for well-being | Vaishvanara | Vasu | Agni | for well-being |
gods | may they favor | Ribhus | for well-being | well-being | us | Rudra | may he protect | from sin ॥ १३ ॥

---

## Commentary (Sayana)

May all the gods, every one of them, favor us today on this coming day for **well-being** <note>original: *svastaye*; interpreted as *kṣemāya*, prosperity or security</note>. **Vaishvanara**: he is called Vaishvanara because "all men lead him" <note>original: *viśve enaṃ narā nayantīti vaiśvānaraḥ*</note>. He is **Vasu**, the deity Agni who causes all things to dwell within him. The sage Shakapuni states, "This very Agni is Vaishvanara" <note>citing Nirukta 7.23</note>, according to Yaska. May he also favor us for well-being. May the divine Ribhus <term>Ribhus; three brothers who attained divinity through their craftsmanship</term> also favor us for well-being. May **Rudra**, the deity who "makes suffering weep or flee" <note>original: *duḥkhād-rāvayitā*; a traditional etymology for Rudra</note>, protect us from **sin** <note>original: *aṃhasaḥ*; evil or distress</note> with well-being.

---

## Hymn Text

-> ॥ The Fourteenth Verse ॥ <-

**Well-being**, O **Mitra and Varuna**! **Well-being**, O **Pathya Revati**!
**Well-being** for us, O **Indra and Agni**! **Well-being** for us, O **Aditi**, create! ॥ १४ ॥

**Word-by-word analysis:**
Well-being | Mitra-Varuna | well-being | Pathya | Revati |
well-being | us | Indra-Agni | [end of compound] | well-being | us | Aditi | create ॥ १४ ॥

---

## Commentary (Sayana)

O **Mitra and Varuna**, the two deities presiding over day and night, grant us well-being. O **Pathya**, O Goddess **Pathya-Svasti** <note>the personified goddess of the path or journey</note>. The **Path** <note>original: *panthā*</note> refers to the atmospheric way; she is the goddess who presides over the safety of those routes. O such a one, **Revati**, wealthy goddess, create well-being for us. May **Indra and Agni** individually create well-being for us. O Goddess **Aditi**, create well-being for us.

---

## Hymn Text

-> ॥ The Fifteenth Verse ॥ <-

May we follow the **path** for **well-being**, like the **Sun and Moon**.
May we meet again with the **giver**, the **non-injurer**, and the **one who knows**. ॥ १५ ॥

**Word-by-word analysis:**
Well-being | path | along | may we move | Sun and Moon | like |
again | with the giver | with the non-injurer | with the one who knows | together | may we go ॥ १५ ॥

---

## Commentary (Sayana)

May we move along the **path** with **well-being** or safety, just like the **Sun and Moon**. Just as those two move through the unsupported...

<meta>This page concludes the commentary on the final verse of Hymn 51 (the "Well-being" hymn) and introduces Hymn 52 of the 5th Mandala. It marks the transition between the 7th and 8th Varga (sections) of the 3rd Adhyaya (chapter) of the 4th Ashtaka (book).
