## Rig Veda || Chapter 4, Adhyaya 3, Varga 8 || Page 446

## Commentary (Sayana)
[Continuation from previous page regarding Hymn 51, Verse 15]

...moving on the path unmolested by demons and such. Furthermore, may we, while staying away from home, be united with our kinsmen—those who give us what we desire <note>original: "datta-abhimatam"</note>, who do not strike us with the anger of a long-delayed return, and who know and do not forget us, meaning they do not doubt who this person is who has returned after a long time, but rather recognize, "This is our own." This is the meaning.

Alternatively, the first half of the verse is the speech of those returning from a journey, and the second half is the speech of the kinsmen: "May we kinsmen unite with the traveler—he who grants us what he has earned, who does not strike us with the anger of the journey's hardships, and who approaches us with affection."

->॥ Thus ends the seventh section (Varga) of the third chapter (Adhyaya) of the fourth book (Ashtaka) ॥<-

---

The eighth hymn, beginning with "Prave Shyavashva," contains seventeen verses. According to the Index of Authors <note>the Anukramani</note>, the seer is Shyavashva of the Atri clan. This and the following ten hymns are dedicated to the **Maruts** <term>Maruts; the storm gods and companions of Indra, known for their brilliance and power</term>. The meters are varied: the sixth and seventeenth verses are in the *Pankti* meter <note>a meter consisting of five lines of eight syllables each</note>, while the remaining verses follow the rules of the *Anushtubh* meter. The ritual application is as previously stated.

->॥ Here begins the first verse ॥<-

## Hymn Text
**Samhita (RV 5.52.1):**
**O Shyavashva, boldly praise with hymns the Maruts, the singers; those who, receiving harmless food according to their self-power, rejoice—the gods worthy of sacrifice.**

**Word-by-word Analysis (Pada Patha):**
Praise | Shyavashva | boldly | chant | with the Maruts | with the singers |
who | the harmless | according to self-power | food | rejoice | worthy of sacrifice ॥ १ ॥

---

## Commentary (Sayana)
O Sage named **Shyavashva**, you who are **bold** <note>original: "dhṛṣṇu"</note>, praise the **Maruts** who are to be celebrated with hymns. <term>The instrumental case is used here in place of the accusative</term> <note>meaning "praise the Maruts" rather than "praise with the Maruts"</note>. In this way, the sage encourages himself. Alternatively, the patron of the sacrifice addresses the priest Shyavashva. Or, it means: praise with songs alongside other chanters who are like the Maruts.

These Maruts are **worthy of sacrifice**. **According to their self-power** <note>original: "anu-svadham"</note> means day by day. The word **Svadha** <term>Svadha; usually meaning 'self-power' or 'inherent nature', but here interpreted by Sayana as sacrificial food</term> refers to the offering of food in the form of oblations. Having obtained **harmless food** <note>original: "shravas", which Sayana often glosses as 'food' or 'wealth' rather than the modern 'fame'</note>, they **rejoice** or are exhilarated.

->॥ Now the second verse ॥<-

## Hymn Text
**Samhita (RV 5.52.2):**
**For they are the friends of constant strength, existing boldly; they, the powerful ones, protect all people throughout their journey by their own might.**

**Word-by-word Analysis (Pada Patha):**
They | indeed | of the constant | of strength | friends | they are | boldly |
they | in the journey | indeed | the powerful ones | by their own power | protect | always ॥ २ ॥

<vocab>
- **Shyavashva**: The seer (Rishi) of this Sukta.
- **Maruts**: The storm deities, sons of Rudra.
- **Boldly** (Dhṛṣṇuyā): Courageously or with strength.
- **Singers** (Ṛkvabhiḥ): Those who chant or the hymns themselves.
- **Self-power/Offering** (Svadhā): The inherent nature of the gods or the sacrificial food.
- **Food/Fame** (Śravaḥ): Derived from the root for "hearing," interpreted here as nourishment.
- **Worthy of sacrifice** (Yajñiyāḥ): Divine beings entitled to receive offerings.
</vocab>

## Commentary (Sayana) — Continued
<note>This concludes the commentary for Verse 2</note>
Indeed, they (the Maruts) are the companions of unwavering, unshakable strength <note>original: "shavasa"</note>. They exist for my benefit. They are bold <note>original: "dhrishnavah"</note>. And in their journey—the word "and" is implied here—they are courageous even in movement. By their own self-willed grace <note>original: "atmana-anugrahena"</note>, without even expecting any service from us in return, they protect many of us forever—our sons, servants, and others. They guard us.

---

## Hymn Text
-> ॥ The Third Verse ॥ <-

They, the swift ones, like bulls, leap across the nights. Now we praise the great glory of the Maruts in heaven and on earth. || 3 ||

**Word-by-word Analysis (Pada-patha):**
They | Swift ones | Like | Bulls <note>or "sprinklers"</note> | [leap across] | Leap across | Nights | Of the Maruts | Now | Great | In heaven | Earth | And | We praise. || 3 ||

## Commentary (Sayana)
Those Maruts are "swift" <term>syandrasah; meaning they have a nature to flow or move rapidly like water</term> and "sprinklers" <term>ukshanah; literally bulls, but used here to mean shedders of rain</term>. The word "like" <note>original: "na"</note> also carries the sense of "and." Because they are swifter than others, they "leap across the nights" <term>sharvarih; the nights, or the divisions of time</term>. They transcend them. This implies they are eternal. Because they are such, we "now" <note>original: "adha"</note> "praise" <note>original: "manmahe"</note> the "great" might or brilliance of the Maruts that exists in "heaven" <note>original: "divi"</note> and on "earth" <note>original: "kshma"</note>.

---

## Hymn Text
-> ॥ The Fourth Verse ॥ <-

Among the Maruts, let us place for you the hymn and the sacrifice with boldness. They, who throughout all human generations, protect the mortal from injury. || 4 ||

**Word-by-word Analysis (Pada-patha):**
Among the Maruts | For you | Let us place | Hymn | Sacrifice | And | Boldly | All | Who | Human | Generations | Protect | Mortal | From injury. || 4 ||

## Commentary (Sayana)
O priests <note>such as the Adhvaryu and Hotar</note>, for your benefit, "among the Maruts"—who are courageous—"place" <note>the text uses the first-person "let us place," but Sayana interprets this as an instruction to the priests</note> the "hymn" of praise and the "sacrifice"—meaning the oblation <note>original: "havis"</note> by which one worships. Why is this given? Because all those Maruts "protect" the "mortal"—the sacrificer who is subject to death—from "injury" or the one who wishes to harm. They do this "throughout all human generations" <note>original: "manusha yuga"</note>—meaning at all times.

---

## Hymn Text
-> ॥ The Fifth Verse ॥ <-

They who are worthy, the liberal givers, heroes of undiminished strength; sing a song of praise for the sacrifice, to the Maruts who deserve the sacrifice, the sons of heaven. || 5 ||

<vocab>
**Marut**: Storm deities; **Syandra**: Swift/flowing; **Ukshan**: Sprinkler or bull (representing fertility/rain); **Sharvari**: Night/time; **Stoma**: Hymn of praise; **Yajna**: Sacrifice or oblation; **Dhrishnu**: Courageous/impelling; **Martya**: Mortal/man; **Rish**: Injury/harm.
</vocab>

<meta>This page concludes the commentary on Verse 5 of the 52nd Hymn in the 5th Mandala of the Rig Veda and presents the full text and commentary for Verses 6 and 7. It marks the transition from the 8th to the 9th Varga (sub-section) of the 3rd Adhyaya (chapter).</meta>

# || Rig Veda || [Mandala 5. Adhyaya 3. Varga 9.]

## Hymn Text (Verse 5 - Word-by-word)

Worshipping | Those who | Bounteous | Leaders | Of complete strength | Forth | Sacrifice | To those worthy of sacrifice | Of the bright sky | Worship | To the Maruts || 5 ||

---

## Commentary (Sayana - Verse 5)

<note>This concludes the commentary for the fifth verse</note>
O Hotar-priest! O master of the self! Those Maruts who are "worshipping" <term>archantah; those who are themselves worthy of being praised</term>, "bounteous" <term>su-danavah; those who give excellent gifts</term>, and "leaders" <term>narah; leaders of ritual acts</term>, possess "complete strength" <term>asami-shavasah; meaning their power is not limited or partial, but full</term>. For those Maruts, who are "worthy of sacrifice" <term>yajniyebhyah</term> and who belong to the "bright sky" <term>divah; meaning the shining heavens</term>. <note>The commentator notes a grammatical variation here where cases or numbers may be swapped for poetic or archaic effect.</note> Or alternatively, the word for "heaven" is in the genitive case to indicate the object of the action. Therefore, "worship" <term>prarcha; meaning to honor or offer</term> the "sacrifice" <term>yajnam</term>, which here refers to the bright sacrificial oblation. Alternatively, the connection is that they have come "from the bright sky" or the mid-air.

-> || This ends the eighth Varga in the third Adhyaya of the fourth Book || <-

---

## Hymn Text (Verse 6)

-> || The Sixth Verse || <-

With golden ornaments, with weapons, the leaders, the mighty ones, have cast their spears. The lightning follows them, the Maruts, like sounding waters; their light has gone forth by itself from the sky. || 6 ||

**Word-by-word Analysis (Pada-patha):**
Towards | With golden ornaments | Towards | With a weapon | Leaders | Mighty | Spears | They have cast | Following | These | Indeed | Lightnings | Maruts | Like sounding [waters] | Light | Went forth | By itself | From the sky || 6 ||

---

## Commentary (Sayana - Verse 6)

The "leaders" <note>original: "narah"</note> of the rain, the "mighty" <term>rishvah; the great ones</term> Maruts, shine with "golden ornaments" <term>rukmatih; specifically, brilliant breastplates or jewelry</term>—it is understood here that they "shine." <note>The commentator explains that in Vedic Sanskrit, a prefix like 'a' can imply the accompanying action even if the verb is omitted.</note> Likewise, they shine with the "weapon" <note>original: "yudha"</note> used for striking. These great beings "have cast" <note>original: "asrikshata"</note> their "spears" <term>rishtih; a specific type of pointed weapon or lance</term>. They hurl them to pierce the clouds.

"Lightnings" <note>original: "vidyutah"</note> also "follow" <note>original: "anvah"</note> these Maruts, appearing "like sounding waters" <term>jarjhutira-iva</term>. The ancient dictionary <note>Nirukta 6.16</note> confirms that the word *jarjhutirah* refers to waters that make a sound. The "light" <note>original: "bhanuh"</note> or brilliance of the shining Marut-host has "gone forth" <note>original: "arta"</note> "by itself" <term>tmana; through their own inherent power</term> from the "sky" <note>original: "divah"</note>.

---

## Hymn Text (Verse 7)

-> || The Seventh Verse || <-

They who grew great, being of the earth; they who are in the wide atmosphere; or in the strength of the rivers, or in the gathering place of the great sky. || 7 ||

**Word-by-word Analysis (Pada-patha):**
Who | Grew | Of the earth | Who | In the wide | Atmosphere | Towards | In the strength/enclosure | Or | Of the rivers | In the gathering place | Or | Of the great | Sky || 7 ||

---

## Commentary (Sayana - Verse 7)

Those Maruts who "grew" <note>original: "vavridhanta"</note> while being "of the earth" <term>parthivah; connected to the terrestrial realm</term>. And those who grew in the "wide," great "atmosphere" <note>original: "antarikshe"</note>. The word "a" here is used in the sense of "and." They also grew in the "strength" <term>vrijane; meaning power or the enclosure</term> of the "rivers" <term>nadinam; those that flow with sound</term>.

[In the dwelling place of the] great <note>original: "maho mahato"</note> heaven <note>original: "divo dyulokasya"</note>, in the common assembly-place, they grew. The word "or" is used in both instances to convey the intended meaning. Thus, the Maruts, increasing everywhere, released their rain-spears <note>An ancient metaphor for lightning or raindrops</note> for the sake of rain—this connects to the preceding section.

-> ॥ The Eighth Verse ॥ <-

## Hymn Text
Praise the Marut host, true in power and wondrously great; and these leaders, for their splendor, have by themselves yoked their swift steeds. ॥ 8 ॥

**Pada-patha (Word-by-word Analysis):**
The host | of the Maruts | Up | Praise | True-powered | Wondrously great |
And | Indeed | These | For splendor | The leaders | Forth | Swift-moving | Yoked | By themselves ॥ 8 ॥

## Commentary (Sayana)
O praiser <note>original: "stotar"</note>, praise <note>original: "shamsa"</note> the **host** <term>shardhas; interpreted here as strength or a troop</term> of the Maruts. What is this host like? It is **true in power** <note>original: "satya-shavasam"</note>—meaning their speed and might are real—and **wondrously great** <term>rbhvasam; meaning greatly increased or magnificent</term>. **And also**, these **leaders** <term>narah; the Maruts as leaders of the rain</term> for the sake of **splendor** <term>shubhe; also implies "for the sake of water"</term> have **yoked** <note>original: "pra yujata"</note> their **swift** <term>syandra; meaning those that move rapidly, referring to their deer-steeds, the Prishatis</term> by **themselves** <note>original: "tmana"</note>—that is, by their own will and for the purpose of protecting the world.

---

-> ॥ The Ninth Verse ॥ <-

## Hymn Text
And indeed, they clothe themselves in wool by the Parushni river, seekers of purity; and with the rims of their chariots, they split the mountain by their might. ॥ 9 ॥

**Pada-patha (Word-by-word Analysis):**
And | Indeed | These | By the Parushni | Wool | Clothe themselves | Seekers of purity |
And | With the rim | Of chariots | The rock-cloud | They split | By might ॥ 9 ॥

## Commentary (Sayana)
**And also, these** Maruts exist **by the Parushni**, which is the name of a specific river. There, they **clothe themselves** in **wool**, which here refers to cleansing **lights** <term>shundhyavah; those that purify or radiant glows</term>. Furthermore, with the **rim** <term>pavya; the outer tire or edge of the wheel</term> of their **chariots**, they **split** the **rock** <term>adrim; this can mean a physical mountain or a "cloud-rock" that holds back water</term> through their inherent **might** or strength.

-> ॥ The Tenth Verse ॥ <-

<vocab>
- Marut: Storm deities, sons of Rudra, known for their collective strength and association with rain.
- Shardhas: Translated here as "host" or "troop," it signifies the collective power of the Marut group.
- Parushni: An ancient river mentioned in the Rig Veda, identified with the modern-day Ravi river in Punjab.
- Pavi: The metal rim or tire of a chariot wheel, often described as striking the clouds to release rain.
- Adri: Literally "rock" or "stone," but in the Rig Veda, it frequently serves as a metaphor for the heavy, solid-looking rain clouds.
- Yajna: A ritual sacrifice or offering made to the deities.

## Commentary (Sayana) - Verse 10 (concl.)

By means of the inner paths <note>original: "antasthayā"</note>, such as the openings of caves and crevices, and through favorable paths, these Maruts exist. With these four types of names or forms, they carry <term>ohate; meaning they bear or extend</term> the sacrifice <term>yajña</term>, which has been spread out for my sake. Alternatively, it means they carry the sacrifice along with these "names," which refer to the waters.

->॥ Thus ends the ninth section of the third chapter of the fourth book ॥<-

---

## Hymn Text - Verse 11

->॥ The Eleventh Verse ॥<-

**Now the leaders bear [the world] down; now, yoked in teams, they carry.**
**Now, though coming from the distant lands, their various forms are worthy to be seen. ॥ 11 ॥**

**Word-by-word Analysis:**
Now | The leaders | Down | They bear | Now | Yoked in teams | They carry |
Now | From distant lands | Thus | Indeed | Forms | Worthy to be seen ॥ 11 ॥

## Commentary (Sayana) - Verse 11

**Now** <note>original: "adhātha"</note>, the **leaders** <term>narah; referring to the Maruts as leaders who bring desired rain</term> **bear down** <note>original: "nyohate"</note>; they greatly support the world. **Now**, being those who **yoked** <term>niyutaḥ; those who join or harness themselves</term> themselves, they **carry** the burden of the clouds. **Now**, they are associated with **distant lands** <term>pārāvatāḥ; coming from "parāvat," a remote place</term>, meaning they are the supporters of the clouds even in distant regions like the atmosphere. In this stated manner, may their **forms** <term>rūpāṇi</term>, which are of many kinds and are to be honored, become **worthy to be seen** <note>original: "darśyā"</note> through their own activities <note>the storm and rain</note>—this is the implied conclusion of the sentence.

---

## Hymn Text - Verse 12

->॥ The Twelfth Verse ॥<-

**Praising with meters, desiring water, the singers moved the fountain.**
**They were not like thieves to me, but protectors, visible in their splendor. ॥ 12 ॥**

**Word-by-word Analysis:**
Praising with meters | Desiring water | The fountain | Toward | The singers | They moved |
They | To me | Someone | Not | Thieves | Protectors | Were | In appearance | In splendor ॥ 12 ॥

## Commentary (Sayana) - Verse 12

Those who are **praising with meters** <term>chandaḥ-stubhaḥ; those who chant using Vedic rhythms</term>, **desiring water** <term>kubhanyavaḥ</term>, and the **singers** <term>kīriṇaḥ</term>—these are the Maruts who **moved** <term>nṛtuḥ; meaning they led or acted</term> the **fountain** <term>utsam; a well or source of water</term> toward the thirsty Sage Gautama. This means they brought the song of praise to completion, or alternatively, it refers to those who are to be praised with meters. The word "stubhati" refers to the act of praising. Those who "desire water" are the pourers of rain-water. The word "kubhi" refers to the act of wetting or showering. 

The Maruts brought the well <note>This refers to a famous Vedic legend where the Maruts tilted a well to help the thirsty sage Gautama</note> for the sake of the singer Gautama to drink. Indeed, it has been said elsewhere: "They poured out the fountain for the thirsty Gautama" <note>Rig Veda 1.85.11</note>. The word for "moved" <note>original: "nṛtuḥ"</note> comes from the root meaning "to lead" or "to dance," referring here to the active movement of the Maruts. **To me**, those Maruts were **not** like **thieves** <term>tāyavaḥ; those who remain hidden or unseen</term> who are never to be seen. Instead, they were **protectors** <term>ūmāḥ</term>, visible in their **splendor** and appearance.

## Hymn Text
-> ॥ The Fourteenth Verse ॥ <-

**Towards the troop of Maruts, O Sage, come with a gift as a woman [comes to] a friend. O bold ones, praised with our prayers, come from heaven or [other worlds] with power. ॥ 14 ॥**

**Word-by-word Analysis:**
Towards | O Sage | Belonging to the Maruts | Troop | With a gift | A friend | Like | A woman |
From heaven | Or | O bold ones | With power | Praised | With prayers | Come ॥ 14 ॥

## Commentary (Sayana)
O **Sage**, [come] **towards** the **troop of Maruts** <term>marut-saṅgha</term>—the assembly of storm-gods—with a **gift** <note>original: "dānā"</note>, which refers to the offering of oblations <term>havir-dāna</term>, like a **woman** <note>original: "yoṣaṇā"</note> [approaches] a **friend** <note>original: "mitram"</note> or the sun-god Mitra. <note>Sayana explains "yoṣaṇā" as being derived from the root 'yu' (to join), meaning it refers to a "hymn of praise" that joins the worshiper to the deity.</note> With that praise, the phrase "come towards" is understood to complete the sense. The second half of the verse is a direct address by the Rishi. O **bold ones** <note>original: "dhṛṣṇavaḥ"</note>, you who are the overpowerers, come from **heaven** <term>dyu-loka</term> **or**—the word "or" implies—from the other two worlds <note>the earth and the atmosphere</note>. Being **praised** by our **prayers** <term>dhībhiḥ; our meditative hymns or intentions</term>, **come** <note>original: "iṣayayata"</note> with your **power** to the sacrifice.

## Hymn Text

-> ॥ The Sixteenth Verse ॥ <-

**The wise ones who, in the search for my kin, spoke to me of the Cow; they spoke of Prishni as the Mother.**
**And then those powerful ones spoke of the father, the mighty Rudra. ॥ 16 ॥**

**Word-by-word Analysis:**
Towards | Who | To me | In the search for kin | The Cow | Spoke | The wise ones | Prishni | Spoke | The Mother ॥
And then | The Father | The mighty | Rudra | Spoke | The powerful ones ॥ 16 ॥

## Commentary (Sayana)

Those Maruts who, when I was searching for my own kin <note>original: "bandhveṣe"</note>, being the **wise** stimulators, **spoke** to me of the **Cow**—referring either to the speech of the middle realm <term>madhyamikāṃ vācaṃ; the thunder</term> or the deity of the Cow. The rest of the sentence follows from the desire [of the Rishi]. The Rishi here repeats the words of the Maruts. Therefore, there is a loss of accent in the subsequent verbs because they are connected to the relative pronoun "who" <note>original: "yacchabdānvayānnighātaḥ"</note>. They **spoke** of **Prishni**, either the deity of the sky or the dappled cow, as the **Mother**. This is supported by the scripture: "From the milk of Prishni were the Maruts born." **And then**, those **powerful ones** <term>śikvasaḥ; those capable of great deeds</term> **spoke** of their **father**, the **mighty** <note>original: "is̲miṇam"; interpreted as one who is moving or possesses food</note> **Rudra**. The fact that the Maruts were accepted as sons by Rudra has been established many times in the texts.

## Hymn Text

-> ॥ The Seventeenth Verse ॥ <-

**The seven times seven, the powerful ones, gave me a hundred each.**
**Upon the Yamuna, I brighten the famous wealth of cattle; I brighten the wealth of horses. ॥ 17 ॥**

**Word-by-word Analysis:**
Seven | To me | Seven | The powerful ones | Each one | Hundreds | Gave ॥
Upon the Yamuna | Famous | Upwards | Wealth | Consisting of cattle | I polish | Downwards | Wealth | Consisting of horses | I polish ॥ 17 ॥

## Commentary (Sayana)

The **seven** groups of **seven** <note>original: "sapta sapta"</note>. This is based on the scripture: "The Maruts are indeed seven groups." It is well known in the Puranas that when the wind was in the womb of Aditi, Indra entered and split it into seven parts, and then split each of those into seven again; thus they became the forty-nine hosts of Maruts. These are the **powerful ones** <term>śākinaḥ; those capable of doing everything</term>. And to **me**, **each one** of those groups **gave hundreds** of herds of cattle and horses. Or, this may be expressed as a blessing: "May they give." That which was given by them was received **upon the Yamuna** river...

<vocab>मरुत् (Marut): The storm-gods, often described as a collective troop. </vocab>
<vocab>रुद्र (Rudra): The fierce father of the Maruts, associated with storms and healing. </vocab>
<vocab>पृश्नि (Prishni): The mother of the Maruts, often envisioned as a dappled cow representing the starry sky or rain clouds. </vocab>
<vocab>यमुना (Yamuna): One of the sacred rivers of India, where the Rishi receives his rewards. </vocab>
<vocab>शाकिन् (Shakin): Powerful or capable; used to describe the Maruts' divine abilities. </vocab>
<vocab>गव्य (Gavya): Relating to cattle; wealth in the form of cows. </vocab>
<vocab>अश्व्य (Ashvya): Relating to horses; wealth in the form of horses. </vocab>
<vocab>राधस् (Radhas): Wealth, bounty, or a gift resulting from sacrifice. </vocab>

# Mandala 5, Anuvaka 4, Sukta 53 ] || Fourth Ashtaka || 453

## Commentary (Sayana) — Continued from previous page
This [phrase] is a restatement of the locative case. In that context, I collect <note>original: "unmṛje"</note> the well-known wealth consisting of herds of cows or related to cows. Similarly, I collect <note>original: "nimṛje"</note> the wealth consisting of herds of horses or related to horses given by them.

->॥ This ends the tenth varga of the third chapter of the fourth ashtaka ॥<-

The ninth hymn, beginning with "Who knows the birth" <note>original: "ko veda jānam"</note>, consists of sixteen verses. The Seer is **Shyavashva**. The 1st, 5th, 10th, 11th, and 15th verses are in the **Kakubh** meter <term>Kakubh: A Vedic meter consisting of 8+12+8 syllables</term>. The 6th, 7th, 9th, 13th, 14th, and 16th are in the **Satobrihati** meter <term>Satobrihati: A meter of 12+8+12+8 syllables</term>. The 8th and 12th are in the **Gayatri** meter. The 2nd is in **Brihati**, the 3rd is in **Anustubh**, and the 4th is in **Pura-ushnih**. The **Maruts** are the deities. Thus it is stated in the *Anukramani* <note>The index of Vedic hymns</note>: "Who knows... sixteen verses, Kakubh, Brihati, Anustubh, Pura-ushnih, Kakubh, Satobrihati, Gayatri, Satobrihati, Kakubh, Gayatri, Satobrihati, Kakubh, and Satobrihati." The ritual application <term>viniyoga</term> is according to its characteristics.

---

## Hymn Text

->॥ The First Verse ॥<-

**Who knows the birth of these? Or who of old was present in the favors of the Maruts, when he yoked the spotted ones? ॥ 1 ॥**

**Word-by-word Analysis (Pada-patha):**
Who | knows | the birth | of these | who | or | of old | in the favors | was | of the Maruts | when | he yoked | the spotted ones ॥ 1 ॥

---

## Commentary (Sayana)

Of these || Regarding the Maruts: since they were introduced in the previous hymn and are the subject of subsequent reference, the word "of these" <note>original: "eṣām"</note> loses its primary accent. Who knows—which man truly understands—their **birth** or origin? Or who **of old**, in former times, **was** present in the **favors** or happiness of these Maruts? When—at the time—they **yoked** to their chariot the **spotted ones** <note>original: "kilāsyaḥ," referring to the Prishati, the spotted mares or deer of the Maruts</note>, who then knows their status, their signs of strength, and their blessings? The underlying thought is that because the Maruts move with the speed of the wind, they are beyond common human comprehension.

---

## Hymn Text

->॥ The Fourth Verse ॥<-

**Those who are self-luminous in their ornaments, in their daggers, in their garlands, in their golden disks, and in their bracelets; who are on their chariots and on their bows. ॥ 4 ॥**

**Word-by-word Analysis:**
Who | in ornaments | who | in daggers | self-luminous | in garlands | in golden disks | in bracelets |
those | on chariots | on bows ॥ 4 ॥

## Commentary (Sayana)

<note>This first paragraph concludes the explanation of verse 2 from the previous page.</note>
Who could hear the sound of their shout or the sound of their chariots? How and in what manner do they go? Who knows this? Or rather, how could other gods and beings follow them? For the sake of the "good-giver" <term>Sudase: A patron or a soul who offers well</term>, the rains, which act as kin and are all-pervading, have flowed down along with various types of food. They descend in due order.

**[On the Third Verse]**
The Seer <term>Rishi: The inspired poet-priest</term>, wishing to describe the manifestation of the Maruts through the two verses starting here, speaks as he beholds them appearing before him. "They," the Maruts, spoke to "me" <note>original: "me" / "mahyam"</note> in this manner. These are the Maruts who "came near" or reached me. By what means did they come? They came with "lights" <note>original: "dyubhiḥ"</note>, meaning with shining qualities, and with "steeds" <note>original: "vibhiḥ"</note>, which are the horses that carry them. For what purpose? For "joy" <note>original: "madāya"</note>, referring to the exhilaration born from drinking the Soma juice. 

He then recounts what they said: the "leaders" <note>original: "naro"</note> or guides, who are "heroes" <note>original: "maryā"</note> beneficial to mankind, and who are "stainless" <note>original: "arepaso"</note> or free from any taint. They said: "O Seer, beholding these—that is, looking upon us as we stand here with your own eyes—offer praise!" In this way, they urged him to praise them as he saw them.

**[On the Fourth Verse]**
With this verse, the Seer describes the physical form and equipment of the Maruts. O Maruts, those "self-luminous" ones of yours—possessing their own inherent light—are "in ornaments" <note>original: "añjiṣu"</note>, meaning they are the source of beauty in their decorations. They are also present in their "daggers" <note>original: "vāśīṣu"</note> or weapons, and in their "garlands" <note>original: "srakṣu"</note> or wreaths. They are in the "golden disks" <note>original: "rukmeṣu"</note> worn on their chests, and in the "bracelets" <note>original: "khādiṣu"</note> worn on their hands and feet. 

Regarding these bracelets, the sacred texts <note>the Vedas</note> say: "On their hands are bracelets" <note>original: "hasteṣu khādiśca," Rig Veda 1.168.3</note> and "Bracelets on their feet" <note>original: "patsu khādaḥ," Rig Veda 5.54.11</note>. Furthermore, they are "self-luminous" and "present" in their "chariots" and "bows." Another Vedic passage confirms this: "They are well-bowed, possessed of arrows, having good chariots, the sons of Prishni" <note>original: "sudhanvāna iṣumantaḥ surathāḥ pṛśnimātaraḥ," Rig Veda 5.57.2</note>. To all of those... <note>The commentary continues to the next page</note>

"We praise" is the implied verb here. Or, alternatively: those Maruts who are self-luminous <note>original: "svabhanavah"</note>, we shall become the seekers or the refuge for their ornaments <note>original: "anjisu"</note>, and their daggers <note>original: "vashishu"</note>. ## Hymn Text

-> ॥ The Fifth Verse ॥ <-

**O Maruts, you who give quickening life, I direct my thoughts toward your chariots for the sake of joy, just as the shining heavens appear when the rain is falling. ॥ 5 ॥**

**यु॒ष्माक॑म् (Your) । स्म॒ (filler particle) । रथा॑न् (chariots) । अनु॑ (following/toward) । मु॒दे (for joy) । द॒धे (I hold/place) । म॒रु॒तः॒ (O Maruts) । जी॒र॒ऽदा॒न॒वः॒ (O you of quickening gifts) ।**
**वृ॒ष्टी (in the rain) । द्यावः॑ (heavens/shining ones) । य॒तीः (going/moving) । इ॒व (like) ॥ 5 ॥**

## Commentary (Sayana)

O <term>Jiradanavah: Those whose gifts are quick or life-giving</term>, O Maruts, I direct my mind toward your chariots for "joy" <note>original: "mude"</note>, meaning for the sake of delight. "I hold" <note>original: "dadhe"</note> means I perform or sustain; by implication, this refers to the act of chanting praises. The word "sma" is a particle used to fill the meter. The connection is that the chariots are seen moving everywhere, like the "shining heavens" <note>original: "dyavah"</note> appearing through the falling rain.

-> ॥ Thus ends the eleventh section (varga) of the third chapter of the fourth book ॥ <-

In the <term>Kariri-ishti: A Vedic sacrifice performed specifically to bring rain</term>, three balls of flour/porridge are to be offered. For the second offering, the verse "A yam narah" (Verse 6) is used as the invitatory prayer. This is indicated in the ritual manuals:
> "The heroes, who are givers of good gifts, have shaken for the giver... they whose light is like lightning, the heroes whose spears are like stones."

<note>Ashvalayana Shrauta Sutra 2. 13.</note>

---

## Hymn Text

-> ॥ The Sixth Verse ॥ <-

**The heroic leaders, givers of good gifts, have shaken down the vessel of heaven for the one who offers. They release the rain-cloud over heaven and earth; the rains spread across the dry lands. ॥ 6 ॥**

**आ (from) । यम् (which) । नरः॑ (leaders/men) । सु॒ऽदा॒न॒वः॒ (good givers) । द॒दा॒शुषे॑ (for the giver/sacrificer) । दि॒वः (from heaven) । को॒शम् (vessel/cloud) । अ॒चु॒च्य॒वुः (have shaken/caused to fall) ।**
**वि (prefix for release) । पर्जन्यं॑ (rain-cloud) । सृ॒ज॑न्ति (they release) । रोद॑सी॒ (heaven and earth) । अनु॑ (along/following) । धन्व॑ना (over dry land/wasteland) । यन्ति (they go) । वृ॒ष्टयः॑ (the rains) ॥ 6 ॥**

## Commentary (Sayana)

The "leaders" <note>original: "narah"</note> are the Maruts, the guides. Being "good givers" <note>original: "sudanavah"</note>, they have shaken down the "vessel" <note>original: "kosham"</note>—this is a name for a cloud, which like a vessel holds the waters—from the "sky" <note>original: "divah"</note> or the mid-region. They do this for the sacrificer who has given offerings. They "release" <note>original: "vi srijanti"</note> the <term>Parjanya: The personified rain-cloud</term>, following the path of "heaven and earth" <note>original: "rodasi"</note>. Afterwards, the "rains" <note>original: "vrishtayah"</note>, the Maruts who provide rain, "go" or spread across the "dry lands" <note>original: "dhanvana"</note>, meaning they pervade everywhere with the water that travels to all places.

<vocab>
**Maruts:** Storm deities and companions of Indra. **Jiradanavah:** A title meaning those who give "quick" or "living" gifts (rain/vitality). **Kosha:** Literally a "pail" or "vessel," used here as a metaphor for a rain-cloud. **Parjanya:** The god of rain or the rain-cloud itself. **Rodasi:** A dual term referring to the pair of Heaven and Earth. **Kariri:** A specific sacrifice performed during droughts to invoke rain.
</vocab>

<summary>This page describes the Maruts as life-giving storm gods whose chariots bring joy and whose power releases the 'vessel of heaven' (the clouds) to bring rain. It also highlights the ritual use of these verses in the Kariri sacrifice for ending droughts.</summary>
<keywords>Maruts, rain-making, Kariri sacrifice, Parjanya, Vedic ritual, storm gods, Sayana commentary, heaven and earth</keywords>

## Rig Veda | Book 4, Chapter 3, Section 12

-> ॥ The Seventh Verse ॥ <-

## Hymn Text
**The rivers, breaking forth with their surging water, have flowed through the atmosphere like cows. Like swift horses at the end of their journey, when the colorful ones turn about. ॥ 7 ॥**

**त॒तृ॒दा॒नाः (Breaking forth) । सिन्ध॑वः (the rivers) । क्षोद॑सा (with surging water) । रजः॑ (the atmosphere) । प्र । स॒स्रुः॒ (flowed forth) । धेन॑वः (cows) । यथा (like) ।**
**स्य॒न्नाः (swift-moving) । अश्वाः॑ऽइव (like horses) । अध्व॑नः (of the path/journey) । विऽमो॑चने (at the release/end) । वि । यत् । वर्त॑न्ते (turn about) । ए॒न्यः॑ (the colorful/shining ones) ॥ 7 ॥**

---

## Commentary (Sayana)
The flowing waters <note>original: "sindhavah"</note>, breaking out or piercing through <note>original: "tatridanah"</note> from the clouds, the Maruts move through the atmosphere <note>original: "rajah"</note> together with the surging water <note>original: "kshodasa"</note>. They spread forth like newly-calved cows <note>original: "dhenavah"</note> who are sprinkling milk. Furthermore, another comparison is offered: they are like swift-moving horses <note>original: "syanna ashva"</note> when they travel toward the "release of the journey" <note>original: "adhva-vimochana"</note>, meaning the rest-point for men. This is the sense. Alternatively, the "shining ones" <note>original: "enyah"</note> refers to the rivers themselves. The rivers turn <note>original: "vi vartante"</note> in various directions, or they turn back and swell; that is, they increase in size. This refers back to the previous description of their actions.

-> ॥ The Eighth Verse ॥ <-

## Hymn Text
**Come, O Maruts, from heaven, from the atmosphere, and from this place nearby. Do not stay far away. ॥ 8 ॥**

**आ । या॒त॒ (Come) । म॒रु॒तः॒ (O Maruts) । दि॒वः (from heaven) । आ । अ॒न्तरि॑क्षात् (from the atmosphere) । अ॒मात् (from nearby/this world) । उ॒त (and also) ।**
**मा (not) । वः॒ (you) । स्था॒त॒ (stay/remain) । प॒रा॒ऽवतः॑ (in the distance) ॥ 8 ॥**

---

## Commentary (Sayana)
O Maruts, come from the most distant place, from the heavenly world <note>original: "divah"</note>. Likewise, come from the atmosphere <note>original: "antarikshat"</note>. And also <note>original: "uta"</note> come from "this" place <note>original: "amat"</note>, meaning from this world. The word "far distance" <note>original: "paravatah"</note> can also be applied here as: Do not remain in those far-off places like the heavenly world; do not make your dwelling there [instead of coming to us].

-> ॥ The Ninth Verse ॥ <-

## Hymn Text
**May the Rasa, the Anitabha, the Kubha, or the Krumu not delay you. May the Indus river not hold you back. May the Sarayu, rich in water, not stand in your way. Let your benevolence be with us alone. ॥ 9 ॥**

**मा (not) । वः॒ (you) । र॒सा (the Rasa river) । अ॒नित॑भा (the Anitabha river) । कु॒भा (the Kubha river) । क्रुमुः॑ (the Krumu river) । मा (not) । वः॒ (you) । सिन्धुः (the Indus) । नि । री॒र॒म॒त् (delay/stop) ।**
**मा (not) । वः॒ (you) । परि॑ । स्था॒त् (stand around/block) । स॒रयुः॑ (the Sarayu river) । पु॒री॒षिणी॑ (rich in water) । अ॒स्मे (with us) इति॑ । इत् (only) । सु॒म्नम् (happiness/benevolence) । अस्तु॒ (let it be) । वः॒ (your) ॥ 9 ॥**

---

## Commentary (Sayana)
O Maruts, may the <term>Rasa: the name of a river</term> not [delay] you. That "Rasa" is a river is confirmed in the <note>Nirukta 11.25</note>.

# Page 457
## Book 4, Chapter 3, Section 12

...Thus says the Nirukta <note>an ancient Vedic treatise on etymology and semantics</note>. "One possessing taste" <note>rasanavati</note> or "one possessing sound" <note>shabdavati</note>. Regarding the term **Anitabha** <note>a name for a river</note>: "Ita" means "attained," and "bha" means "light" or "lustre"; thus "itabha" is one who has attained light. "Anitabha" is the opposite of that <note>one who has not yet attained such light, or perhaps possesses a distinct, non-attained radiance</note>. May the river **Kubha** <note>the Kabul river</note>, which has a "wretched radiance" <note>kutsita-dipti</note>, not delay you <note>ma ni roramat</note>. May she not hold you back in a lowly place. May the **Krumu** <note>the Kurrum river</note> which moves everywhere, and the **Sindhu** <note>the Indus river</note> not delay you. Likewise, may the "water-rich" <note>purishini</note>—as "purisha" refers to water—river **Sarayu** also not stand around you <note>ma pari sthat</note>; that is, may she not obstruct your path. Let that "well-being" <note>sumnam</note>—the happiness born of your arrival—be only with us <note>asme it</note>; let that happiness which belongs to you be ours as well.

->॥ The Tenth Verse ॥<-

## Hymn Text
**I praise that host of your chariots, that brilliant Marut company of the newest [chariots]. The rains follow them. ॥ 10 ॥**

**Pada-patha:**
**तम् (That) । वः॒ (of you) । शर्ध॑म् (host/strength) । र॒थाना॑म् (of chariots) । त्वे॒षम् (brilliant) । ग॒णम् (company) । मारु॑तम् (of the Maruts) । नव्य॑सीनाम् (of the newest) । अनु॑ (following) । प्र (forth) । य॒न्ति॒ (go) । वृ॒ष्टयः॑ (the rains) ॥ 10 ॥**

---

## Commentary (Sayana)
The word "That" <note>tam</note> is connected to the "Marut company." I praise <note>stami—implied</note> that host or strength <note>shardham</note> of your <note>vah</note>—you who are the impellers—of the newest <note>navyasinam</note> chariots, and that brilliant <note>tvesham</note> company <note>ganam</note> of the Maruts. This is the meaning. Alternatively, it is a single sentence: "I praise your troop <note>ganam</note> which is the strength <note>shardham</note> of the swift-moving <note>ranhana-shilanam</note> chariots and the subduer of enemies." 

Now, the description shifts to the third person <note>paroksha-krita</note>: "The rains <note>vrishtayah</note> follow <note>anu pra yanti</note> you." They go forth with great force. Or, the Maruts who bring rain move along in a favorable, excellent way.

->॥ Thus ends the twelfth section (varga) in the third [chapter] of the fourth [book] ॥<-

->॥ The Eleventh Verse ॥<-

## Hymn Text
**Troop by troop of yours, company by company, group by group—we follow with beautiful praises and with prayers. ॥ 11 ॥**

**Pada-patha:**
**शर्ध॑ऽशर्धम् (Troop by troop) । वः॒ (of you) । ए॒षाम् (of these) । व्रात॑म्ऽव्रातम् (company by company) । ग॒णम्ऽग॑णम् (group by group) । सु॒ऽश॒स्तिऽभिः॑ (with beautiful praises) । अनु॑ (following) । क्रा॒मे॒म॒ (may we go/attain) । धी॒तिऽभिः॑ (with prayers) ॥ 11 ॥**

---

## Commentary (Sayana)
O Maruts! Of these groups of yours, may we follow <note>anu kramama</note> troop by troop <note>shardham shardham</note>—each specific strength; and company by company <note>vratam vratam</note>—where a "vrata" is an assembly of an indefinite number; and group by group <note>ganam ganam</note>—referring to the groups consisting of seven members each <note>the Maruts are traditionally grouped in sets of seven or seven-times-seven, making 49</note>. May we follow them with beautiful praises <note>sushastibhih</note> and with prayers <note>dhitibhih</note> or religious acts characterized by the offering of sacrificial food.

<vocab>
- **Marut** (मरुत्): Storm deities, often described as a military-like troop.
- **Shardha** (शर्ध): Strength, host, or a specific military-style unit.
- **Gana** (गण): A multitude or group; specifically here, the organized groups of seven Maruts.
- **Vrishti** (वृष्टि): Rain, the physical manifestation of the Maruts' arrival.
- **Vrata** (व्रात): A company or assembly of people/deities.
- **Sushasti** (सुशस्ति): "Fair praise" or "good hymn" used in rituals.
- **Dhiti** (धीति): Prayer, devotion, or the ritual act of offering oblations.
</vocab>

-> ॥ Now the Thirteenth [Verse] ॥ <-

**By which [favor] you bring grain and imperishable seed to the son and the descendant, grant that to us; that wealth which we beg of you, providing life to all and good fortune. ॥ 13 ॥**

## Commentary (Sayana)

O Maruts, with **which** <note>yena</note> compassionate mind you **bring** <note>vahahdve</note> or sustain **grain and seed** that is **imperishable** <note>akshitam; undiminished</note> for the **son** <note>tokaya</note> and for the **descendant** <note>tanayaya; the son's son or further offspring</note>, with that same intent **grant** <note>dhattana</note> that grain and seed to us. And that which we **beg** <note>imahe</note> or request of **you** <note>vah</note>—namely **wealth** <note>radhah</note> that encompasses **all life** <note>vishvayu; either belonging to all people or lasting a full lifetime</note> and **good fortune** <note>saubhagam</note>—grant that as well. This is how the words are connected.

## Hymn Text

-> ॥ Now the Fourteenth [Verse] ॥ <-

**May we pass beyond blame, leaving behind sin and enemies through your blessings; in the rain, may there be peace, health, waters, and medicine, O Maruts, in your company. ॥ 14 ॥**

-> **Beyond** | **may we go** | **of blame** | **across** | **with blessings** | **having left behind** | **sin** | **enemies.** <-

## Commentary (Sayana)

O Maruts, may we, **leaving behind** <note>hitva</note> or abandoning **sin** <note>avadyam; literally "that which is censurable"</note> through **blessings** <note>svastibhih</note> or states of well-being, **pass beyond** <note>ati iyama</note> the **blamers** <note>nidah</note> and the **enemies** <note>aratih</note> who have approached <note>tiras</note> us. Alternatively, "tiras" means "concealed." "May we pass beyond" means we should overcome or disregard them. By this, the removal of the undesirable is prayed for; in the following part, the attainment of the desired is stated. When the **rains** <note>vrishti</note> are sent by you, may there be **peace** <note>sham</note> or happiness, and **health** <note>yoh; the averting of misfortunes</note>, and the **waters** <note>apah</note>...

# Mandala 5, Adhyaya 4, Hymn 54. ] || Fourth Ashtaka || 459

## Commentary (Sayana)
<note>Continued from the previous page regarding Rig Veda 5.54.14</note>

The word "shasah" is used in place of the plural case-ending. The term "usri" <note>original: usri</note> refers to medicine or healing associated with cows. Although this word can be a name for water, because water was mentioned separately, here it refers to food <note>original: annam</note>, which is the result or effect of water. May we all obtain all of that together, O Maruts. Alternatively, it means: May the waters directed by you perform all that has been said. May we all be together; may we become your own people.

---

## Hymn Text
-> ॥ Now the Fifteenth ॥ <-

**The mortal whom you protect, O leader Maruts, becomes well-blessed by the gods and a great hero with noble sons. May we be yours. ॥ 15 ॥**

**Pada-patha:**
**Well-blessed by gods | Truly | Great | He becomes | Heroic | O Leaders | O Maruts | That | Mortal | Whom | You protect | May we be | Yours ॥ 15 ॥**

## Commentary (Sayana)

O Great One <note>original: samaha; a word meaning "praiseworthy"</note>. O honored assembly of Maruts, a person becomes "well-blessed by the gods" <note>original: sudevah</note>, meaning they are accompanied by the auspicious deities known as the Maruts. O leaders <note>original: narah</note>, O Maruts, that mortal becomes "heroic" <note>original: suvira</note>, endowed with excellent sons and progeny. This applies to whichever mortal you "protect" <note>original: chayadhve</note> or nourish. May we, who are such people, be yours—meaning, may we belong to you.

---

## Hymn Text
-> ॥ Now the Sixteenth ॥ <-

**Praise the generous ones at the sacrifice of this singer; let them rejoice like cows in the pasture. From wherever they go, call them like old friends; praise the desirous ones with your song. ॥ 16 ॥**

**Pada-patha:**
**Praise | The generous givers | Of the singer | Of this | At the journey | Let them rejoice | Cows | Like | In the pasture | From wherever | Old | Like | Friends | Towards | Call | With song | Praise | The desirous ones ॥ 16 ॥**

## Commentary (Sayana)

O Sage <note>original: rishi</note>, praise the "generous" <note>original: bhojan</note> Maruts—the givers—at the "journey" <note>original: yamani</note> or sacrifice of this "praiser" <note>original: stuvatah</note> (the patron of the sacrifice). "Like cows in the pasture" <note>original: gavo na yavase</note>: just as cows going to eat grass or fodder rejoice, so may the Maruts "rejoice" <note>original: ranan</note> at the sacrifice. From wherever the Maruts are traveling, "call them" <note>original: anu hvaya</note> like "old friends" <note>original: purvan sakhin-iva</note>. Praise the Maruts, who "desire" <note>original: kaminah</note> or love the hymns, with your "song" <note>original: gira</note> or speech.

-> ॥ Thus ends the thirteenth section (Varga) of the third chapter (Adhyaya) of the fourth book (Ashtaka) ॥ <-

---

## Critical Notes
**Regarding the hymn "Pra shardhaya":** This tenth hymn of the section, containing fifteen verses <note>Though sixteen are transcribed, the index notes fifteen, suggesting the final verse may be treated as a concluding benediction</note>, was seen by the Sage Shyavasva and is dedicated to the Maruts. The fourteenth verse is in the *Trishtubh* metre, while the rest are in the *Jagati* metre. The index <note>Anukramani</note> states: "The hymn 'Pra shardhaya' has fifteen verses in Jagati metre, with the penultimate verse being Trishtubh." The ritual application of this hymn follows its literal meaning. It is used as the offering prayer (Yajya) for the main deity in the sacrifice to Indra and the Maruts. As stated in the Sutras: "Having recited the verse to Indra, one should sacrifice with the verse to the Maruts, 'Pra shardhaya marutaya svabhanave...'" (Ashvalayana Shrauta Sutra 2.11).

<term>Marut</term>: Storm deities in the Vedas, often depicted as a troop of young warriors riding chariots and bringing rain.
<term>Sudeva</term>: Literally "having good gods," referring to a person who enjoys divine favor.
<term>Suvira</term>: "Having good heroes," traditionally interpreted as having strong, noble sons to carry on the family lineage.
<term>Jagati</term>: A classical Vedic metre consisting of four lines of 12 syllables each.
<term>Trishtubh</term>: The most common Vedic metre, consisting of four lines of 11 syllables each.
<term>Shyavasva</term>: A prominent Vedic seer (Rishi) of the Atri family.

It also provides the technical "Anukramani" data regarding the hymn's author, Shyavasva, its poetic meters, and its use in ancient fire sacrifices.</summary>
<keywords>Maruts, Shyavasva, Vedic sacrifice, Jagati metre, Trishtubh metre, Sayana commentary, Rig Veda 5.54, divine protection</keywords>

## Rig Veda || Book 4, Chapter 3, Section 14 || 460

## Hymn Text

-> ॥ This is the first verse of the hymn ॥ <-

**Bring forth this speech, born of the mind, to the self-luminous host of Maruts, the mountain-shakers. To those who celebrate the heat, who come from heaven, who receive the Prishtha offerings, and whose fame is radiant, offer great strength. ॥ 1 ॥**

**Pada-patha:**
**Bring forth | To the host | To the Maruts | To the self-luminous | This | Speech | Born of the mind | To the mountain-shakers | To those who celebrate the heat | From heaven | Come | To those receiving the Prishtha offerings | To those of radiant fame | Great | Strength | Offer ॥ 1 ॥**

---

## Commentary (Sayana)

The connection is: **Bring forth** <note>original: prānaja</note>. Bring this **speech** <note>original: vācam</note>, the praise being performed, to the **host** <note>original: śardhāya</note> or the strength belonging to the **Maruts** <note>original: mārutāya</note>. To the **self-luminous** <note>original: svabhānave</note>, meaning those whose light is under their own control. To the **mountain-shakers** <note>original: parvatacyute</note>, those who cause mountains to tremble or fall. To the **celebrators of heat** <note>original: gharmastubhe</note>, those who praise the sun or the ritual heat. To those **from heaven** <note>original: diva ā</note>, who come from the celestial realm. To the **receivers of Prishtha offerings** <note>original: pṛṣṭhayajvane</note>, those worshiped with the six <term>Prishtha stotras</term> <note>specific melodic chants used in high rituals</note> like the Rathantara and Brihat. To those of **radiant fame** <note>original: dyumnaśravase</note>, meaning those whose food or renown is shining. **Offer** <note>original: arcata</note>, or give, **great** <note>original: mahi</note> and abundant **strength** <note>original: nṛmṇam</note>, which refers to wealth in the form of sacrificial offerings.

In the <term>Kariri Ishti</term> <note>a Vedic sacrifice performed specifically to bring rain</note>, during the first offering of flour-balls, this verse is used as the invitatory prayer <note>original: yājyā</note>. This is indicated in the ritual manuals:
> "To your strength, O Maruts, who are heroes... (Asvalayana Shrauta Sutra 2.13)."

---

## Hymn Text

-> ॥ This is the second verse ॥ <-

**Your hosts, O Maruts, appear—mighty, seeking water, increasing food, yoking horses, and traveling everywhere. They join with the lightning; the cloud thunders; the waters sound out and fall upon the earth, traveling all around. ॥ 2 ॥**

**Pada-patha:**
**Forth | Your | O Maruts | Mighty | Seeking water | Food-increasing | Horse-yoking | Traveling everywhere | Together | With lightning | They place | Sounds | The cloud | Sound | Waters | On the earth | Traveling everywhere ॥ 2 ॥**

---

## Commentary (Sayana)

O **Maruts**, **your** <note>original: vaḥ</note> hosts **appear** <note>original: pra prādurbhavanti</note>. What kind of hosts? They are **mighty** <note>original: taviṣā</note>, meaning either glowing or great. They are **seeking water** <note>original: udanyava</note> for the protection of the world. They are **food-increasers** <note>original: vayovṛdho</note>, augmenters of nourishment. They are **horse-yokers** <note>original: aśvayujo</note>, those who harness horses to their chariots for travel. They are **traveling everywhere** <note>original: parijrayaḥ</note>, going in all directions. They **join with lightning** <note>original: vidyutā saṃdadhati</note>. At that time, the **cloud** <note>original: citaḥ</note>, which is spread across the three realms, or perhaps the Marut-host itself, **sounds out** <note>original: vāśati</note> or thunders. In this interpretation, it refers to the collective roar of the storm. Then the **waters**, **traveling everywhere**, **sound out** <note>original: svaranti</note> and fall down upon the **earth** <note>original: avanāvanyāṃ</note>.

The verse "With lightning-brilliance" <note>original: vidyunmahasa</note> is the invitatory prayer for the second flour-ball offering in the same Kariri ritual. It is indicated:
> "Men of lightning-brilliance, whose spears are stones, whose path is dark, golden-colored, well-winged... (Asvalayana Shrauta Sutra 2.13)."

Book 5, Chapter 4, Hymn 54.] || Fourth <term>Ashtaka</term> <note>One of the eight "eighths" or books into which the Rig Veda is traditionally divided.</note> || 461

## Hymn Text

**O Maruts, men who possess the luster of lightning, armed with stone weapons, brilliant as the wind, and shakers of mountains; you who repeatedly surround the waters with the sound of thunder, you are loud-sounding with your host, impetuous, and of exalted power. ॥ 3 ॥**

**Pada-patha:**
**With the luster of lightning | Men | With stone weapons | With the brilliance of the wind | Maruts | Shakers of mountains |
Of the waters | Indeed | Repeatedly | Towards | Surrounded by thunder | With loud-sounding companions | Impetuous |
Of exalted power ॥ 3 ॥**

---

## Commentary (Sayana)

**With the luster of lightning** <note>original: vidyunmahaso</note> means having a shining splendor. **Men** <note>original: naro</note> refers to those who are the "dancers" or bringers of rain and other benefits. **With stone weapons** <note>original: aśmadidyavo</note> refers to those whose weapons are pervasive, or weapons made of stone (hard like the thunderbolt). **Brilliant as the wind** <note>original: vātatviṣo</note> means those who have attained a great radiance. **Shakers of mountains** <note>original: parvatacyutaḥ</note> are those who cause mountains or clouds to fall. They are the **givers of water** <note>original: abdyā</note> <note>The commentator notes that "cit" is a filler word here.</note>. **Surrounded by thunder** <note>original: hrādunīvṛto</note> means those who set the thunderbolt in motion. **With loud-sounding companions** <note>original: stanayadamāḥ</note>; here the word *ama* signifies "togetherness" or "companionship," meaning they are a host accompanied by sound. **Impetuous** <note>original: rabhasā</note> means they are striving for the sake of rain. **Of exalted power** <note>original: udojasaḥ</note> means they possess uplifted strength. The Maruts appear in this way for the sake of providing rain.

---

-> ॥ Now the Fourth Verse ॥ <-

## Hymn Text

**O sons of Rudra, you traverse the nights; O powerful ones, you traverse the days; you traverse the atmosphere and the regions, O shakers. When you drive the clouds like ships, O Maruts, you pass through difficult places, and you are never harmed. ॥ 4 ॥**

**Pada-patha:**
**Traverse | The nights | Sons of Rudra | Traverse | The days | Powerful ones | Traverse | The atmosphere | Traverse | The regions | Shakers |
Traverse | When | The clouds | You drive | Like ships | Indeed | Just as | Traverse | Difficult places | Maruts | Not | Verily |
You are harmed ॥ 4 ॥**

---

## Commentary (Sayana)

O **Sons of Rudra** <note>original: rudrā</note>, O Maruts, you **traverse the nights** <note>original: aktūn vyajayatha</note>. This verb "traverse" or "conquer" is connected from the latter half of the verse to all the objects mentioned. This means you pass through them. You also **traverse the days**. O **powerful ones** <note>original: śikvasaḥ</note>, those capable of doing all things, you traverse the **atmosphere**. Likewise, you traverse the **regions** <note>original: rajāṃsi</note>. O **shakers** <note>original: dhūtayaḥ</note>, when you **drive** <note>original: ajatha</note> or move the **clouds** <note>original: ajñān</note>, just as **ships** <note>original: nāvaḥ</note> move across the sea, in that same way you traverse **difficult places** <note>original: durgāṇi</note> or the fortresses of enemies. O Maruts, **you are never harmed** <note>original: nāha riṣyatha</note>, meaning you are never injured.

---

-> ॥ Now the Fifth Verse ॥ <-

## Hymn Text

**O Maruts, that greatness of yours is worthy of song; the Sun has extended it far, like a long path. These Maruts, whose light is unseizable in their march, when they travel, they make even the mountain bend... ॥ 5 ॥**

462 || Rig Veda || [Book 4, Chapter 3, Section 15.]

## Hymn Text

<note>RV 5.54.5 (Pada-patha)</note>
**That | prowess | your | Maruts | greatness | long | has extended | the sun | like | the distance (yoking).**
**These (mares) | like | in their course | of unseized brilliance | not yielding water (or shaking) | when | down | you struck | the mountain. ॥ 5 ॥**

---

## Commentary (Sayana)

<note>Commentary on RV 5.54.5</note>
O Maruts, **that prowess** <note>original: tat vīryam</note>—your well-known strength—and your **greatness** <note>original: mahitvanam</note> has **extended** <note>original: tatāna</note> or spread very far. The poet offers an analogy: **like the sun** <note>original: sūryo na</note> spreads its light over a **distance** <note>original: yojanam</note>. Or perhaps **like these** <note>original: etā na</note> colored mares of the gods, who extend over a long journey; this is another comparison. These Maruts are **of unseized brilliance** <note>original: agribhīta-śociṣaḥ</note>, meaning their splendor cannot be overtaken. Alternatively, this phrase describes the Maruts themselves. O Maruts, you who possess such brilliance, you **struck down** <note>original: nyāyātana</note> the **mountain** <note>original: girim</note>—referring either to a physical mountain or a cloud—which was **not yielding water** <note>original: anabhra-sradām</note> (perhaps because the water was withheld by the <term>Panis</term> <note>A class of demons or mythical stingy figures who hide cows or water.</note>) or was not providing the horses stolen by them.

-> ॥ This concludes the fourteenth section (Varga) of the third chapter of the fourth book. ॥ <-

---

## Hymn Text

-> ॥ The Sixth Verse ॥ <-
<note>RV 5.54.6 (Samhita)</note>
**O Maruts, your host shines when you shake the tree like caterpillars (or shakers), O creators. Then lead us toward delight along a good path, O companions, just as the eye guides one who is walking. ॥ 6 ॥**

<note>RV 5.54.6 (Pada-patha)</note>
**Shines | the host | Maruts | when | the tree (cloud) | you shake | the tree | like caterpillars (or shakers) | creators.
Then | indeed | us | toward delight | companions | like the eye | one who is walking | along | you lead | on a good path. ॥ 6 ॥**

---

## Commentary (Sayana)

<note>Commentary on RV 5.54.6</note>
O **creators** <note>original: vedhasaḥ</note> of rain, O Maruts, your **host** <note>original: śardhaḥ</note> or assembly **shines** <note>original: abhrāji</note>. When you **shake** <note>original: moṣatha</note>—meaning you strike—the **tree** <note>original: vṛkṣam</note>, which here refers to the cloud (so called because it is "cut" or divided to release water). The poet says **like caterpillars** <note>original: kapanā-iva</note>. The word "iva" here is a comparison. It means either "shakers," or refers to wood-boring worms like weevils that consume a tree; just as they dismantle a tree, you dismantle the clouds. Furthermore, the word "sma" is a rhythmic filler. **Us** <note>original: naḥ</note> means "me," the singer. O you who have **mutual affection** <note>original: sajoṣasaḥ</note> for one another, **lead us** <note>original: anu neṣatha</note> toward **delight** <note>original: aramatim</note>—meaning enjoyment or wealth—along a **good path** <note>original: sugam</note>. The analogy given is **like the eye** <note>original: cakṣur-iva</note>; just as the eye becomes a leader by showing the way, you guide us similarly.

---

## Hymn Text

-> ॥ The Seventh Verse ॥ <-
<note>RV 5.54.7 (Samhita)</note>
**He is not conquered, O Maruts, he is not slain, he does not fail, he does not tremble, and he is not harmed. His riches do not perish, nor do his protections, whom you—whether a Seer or a King—bring to success. ॥ 7 ॥**

<note>RV 5.54.7 (Pada-patha)</note>
**Not | he | is conquered | Maruts | not | is slain | not | fails | not | trembles | not | is harmed.
Not | his | riches | perish (waste away) | not | protections | the Seer | or | whom | the King | or | you bring to success. ॥ 7 ॥**

## Commentary (Sayana) — Continued from previous page
<note>Commentary on Rig Veda 5.54.7</note>
O Maruts, that sage <note>original: ṛṣiṃ</note>—the seer of the mantras—or that Brahmana or king whom you well-praise and impel toward good deeds, he is **not conquered** <note>original: na jīyate</note>. He is not defeated by others. The word *jīyate* stems from roots meaning to conquer or to suffer loss of vitality. O Maruts, such a man is **not struck down** <note>original: na hanyate</note>; he is not harmed, nor is he excessively separated from his life-breaths. He does **not wither** <note>original: na sredhati</note>; he does not decay. He is **not pained** <note>original: na vyathate</note>, nor is he oppressed. He is **not injured** <note>original: na riṣyati</note>. The root *ṛch* indicates injury or obstruction. His **wealth** <note>original: rāyo</note> does not run dry, nor do your **protections** <note>original: utayo</note> ever fail him.

In the <term>Kariri sacrifice</term> <note>A Vedic ritual performed to bring rain.</note>, this verse serves as the consecration prayer <note>original: yājyā</note> for the third ritual cake. This is indicated in the liturgical texts: "With their teams, conquering in their journey..." <note>quoting Ashvalayana Shrauta Sutra 2.13</note>.

-> ॥ This is the eighth verse ॥ <-

## Hymn Text
### Samhita-patha
With their **teams**, **conquering on their journey**, like **leading men**, like **Aryaman**, the **Maruts** are our **water-vessels**. 
They **swell the fount** when the **mighty ones** have **sounded**; they **moisten** the **earth** with the **essence of the sweet (water)**. ॥ 8 ॥

### Pada-patha
**With-teams | conquering-on-the-journey | as-if | men | Aryaman | like | Maruts | water-vessel-ours |**
**they-swell | the-fount | when | the-mighty-ones | sounded | throughly | moisten | the-earth | of-the-sweet | with-the-essence.** ॥ 8 ॥

---

## Commentary (Sayana)
The Maruts, who possess teams of horses known as <term>Niyuts</term> <note>Niyutvantaḥ: specifically referring to the Maruts' horses.</note>, are those who separate or analyze all composite things. They are **leaders** <note>original: naro</note> appearing in human-like form. The term **with-teams** <note>original: niyutvantaḥ</note> generally refers to those possessing very swift horses. They are **conquering on their journey** like men who win their way. They are **like Aryaman** <note>original: aryamaṇo na</note>—meaning they are radiant like <term>Aryaman</term> <note>One of the Adityas, or solar deities, representing nobility and solar light.</note> and the other sun-gods. Such Maruts become **possessors of water-vessels** <note>original: kabandhinaḥ</note> (clouds). 

When these **mighty ones** <note>original: ināsaḥ</note> (the lords/Maruts) **swell** <note>original: pinvanti</note> the **fount** <note>original: utsam</note>—referring to a well or a low-lying cloud—they do so with water. When they **sound** <note>original: asvaran</note> (thunder) and when they **moisten** <note>original: vyundanti</note> the **earth** with the **essence** <note>original: andhasā</note> of the **sweet** <note>original: madhvo</note> honey-like water, it is then that this happens. Alternatively: when they sound, they swell the fount; then, as mighty lords, they moisten the earth with the essence.

<vocab>
Marutaḥ (मरुतः): Storm gods
Aryaman (अर्यमन्): A solar deity (Aditya) representing nobility.
Kabandhin (कबन्धिन): Literally 'having a headless trunk', but in Veda means a water-skin, vessel, or cloud.
Niyutvantaḥ (नियुत्वन्तः): Possessing teams of horses (Niyuts).

Andhasā (अन्धसा): With juice, food, or in this context, the nourishing water of the rain.
Utsam (उत्सम्): A fount, spring, or a cloud viewed as a source of water.

<meta>This page continues the translation of Rig Veda, Mandala 5, Hymn 54, dedicated to the Maruts (the storm gods). It concludes the commentary on verse 9, which describes how the earth, sky, and atmosphere adapt to the movement of the storm gods, and proceeds to verses 10 and 11, detailing their swift travel and their brilliant ornaments and weaponry.</meta>

464 || Rig Veda || [Book 4, Chapter 3, Section 16]

This **earth** <note>original: pṛthivī</note> becomes **full of slopes** <note>original: pravatvatī; implying a surface that facilitates easy movement</note> for the Maruts, for the sake of the Maruts' purpose. "Full of slopes" means having regions that are widely extended and expansive. Such she becomes. The meaning is that the entire earth becomes devoted to the Maruts; they pervade all of it. Likewise, the **heaven** <note>original: dyauḥ</note> also becomes "full of slopes" for those who travel with great force. That too is for the movement of the Maruts. Similarly, the **paths in the atmosphere** <note>original: antarikṣyāḥ pathyāḥ</note>, which are easy to traverse, become "full of slopes" for the Maruts. The **mountains** <note>original: parvatāḥ</note>—or the clouds—become "full of slopes," and the Maruts are **quick-givers** <note>original: jīradānavaḥ</note> because they cause the clouds to release rain quickly.

-> ॥ This is the tenth verse ॥ <-

## Hymn Text
### Samhita-patha
When, O **Maruts**, you of **shared strength**, with **beautiful hymns**, revel at the **rising of the sun**—O **leaders of heaven**!—your **horses** do not **slacken** as they **gallop**; immediately you reach the **end of this path**.

### Pada-patha
When | Maruts | shared-strength | beautiful-hymns | sun | rising | you-revel | heaven | leaders |
not | your | horses | slackening | indeed | galloping | immediately | of-this | path | end | you-reach || 10 ||

---

## Commentary (Sayana)

O Maruts, you who possess **shared strength** <note>original: sabharasaḥ</note> and are the **leaders of all** <note>original: svarkāḥ</note>, when the **sun has risen**—that is, when it has ascended at midday—you **revel** <note>original: madatha</note> with the <term>Soma</term> juice, O **leaders of the heavenly world**. This means when you desire to drink the Soma. At that time, your **horses**, while **galloping** <note>original: sisrataḥ</note>, do **not slacken** <note>original: na... śrathayanta</note> at all. They never grow weary. **Immediately** <note>original: sadyaḥ</note>, at that very moment, you **reach the end** <note>original: pāram aśnutha</note> of the path to the place of sacrifice. Alternatively, it means that when you are exhilarated by the Soma, your horses do not become exhausted, and you traverse the paths of all the three worlds.

-> ॥ This concludes the fifteenth section (varga) of the third chapter of the fourth book ॥ <-

O Maruts, on your **shoulders** <note>original: aṃseṣu</note>, **spears** <note>original: ṛṣṭayaḥ</note> or weapons are shining—this is the implied meaning. On your **feet** <note>original: patsu</note> are **rings** <note>original: khādayaḥ</note> or anklets. On your **chests** <note>original: vakṣaḥsu</note> are **golden ornaments** <note>original: rukmāḥ</note> or necklaces. On the **chariot** <note>original: rathe</note> are **beauties** <note>original: śubhaḥ; Sayana interprets this as sweet, shining waters</note>. Like **blazing fires**...

**Maruts** (Storm gods), **shared strength** (cooperative power), **beautiful hymns** (well-praised), **horses** (divine steeds), **galloping** (moving swiftly), **spears** (throwing weapons), **rings** (anklets/bracelets), **golden ornaments** (bright necklaces), **golden** (made of or shining like gold)

465 || Rig Veda || Fourth Octave (Ashtaka)

...the lightnings shine in their **grasp** <note>original: gabhastyoḥ</note> or in their hands. Upon their **heads** <note>original: śīrṣasu</note>, **golden** <note>original: hiraṇyayīḥ</note> **head-pieces** <note>original: śiprāḥ</note>—which are like turbans—are **spread out** <note>original: vitatāḥ</note>. The word "spread out" should be connected to each preceding description.

-> ॥ The Twelfth Verse ॥ <-

## Hymn Text

O Maruts, you shake that **firmament** whose **brilliance is unseizable**, and you shake the **bright fruit**; your **forces** unite and **shine intensely** when you, the **seekers of Truth**, sound a **widespread roar**. ॥ 12 ॥

-> That | firmament | moving-ones | unseizable-brilliance | <-
-> bright | fruit | Maruts | shake | <-
-> together | unite | forces | intensely-shining | when | <-
-> sound | roar | widespread | seekers-of-Truth ॥ 12 ॥ <-

## Commentary (Sayana)

O **Maruts**, you who are **movers** <note>original: aryaḥ</note>, you shake that well-known **firmament** <note>original: nākam; the place where there is no 'aka' or unhappiness—interpreted here as the Sun or the sky</note>. This firmament has **brilliance that cannot be seized** <note>original: agṛbhīta-śociṣam</note> or stolen by demons. You shake the **bright** <note>original: ruśat</note> **fruit** <note>original: pippalam</note>, which refers to the water [of the clouds]. You shake it in various ways <note>Sayana notes this verb takes two objects: the sky and the water</note>.

When your **forces** <note>original: vṛjanā</note> are **united** <note>original: samacyanta</note>, you become powerful through the oblations offered to you. Afterward, you **shine intensely** <note>original: atitviṣanta</note>. <note>Sayana notes a grammatical shift in person here</note>. Alternatively, when the forces of the demons are gathered, you sound a **roar** <note>original: ghoṣam</note> that causes fear and is **widespread** <note>original: vitatam</note>. You do this as **seekers of Truth** <note>original: ṛtāyavaḥ</note>, meaning those who desire to release the waters.

Or, the second half of the verse can be explained in terms of the priests and the sacrificer: When the **seekers of Truth** (the sacrificers) gather their **strengths** and offer **praise** (the roar), then, O Maruts, shake down the fruit of the rains.

---

-> ॥ The Thirteenth Verse ॥ <-

## Hymn Text

O **wise Maruts**, may we be masters of **wealth** **given by you**, which is **abounding in food** and fit for **chariots**; that wealth which does not **fail**, just as the **star** does not fail from **heaven**. O Maruts, may you cause **thousandfold** wealth to **delight** in us. ॥ 13 ॥

-> from-you-given | Maruts | wise-ones | wealth | <-
-> may-we-be | chariot-owners | food-abounding | <-
-> not | which | fails | the-star | like | <-
-> from-heaven | in-us | delight | Maruts | thousandfold ॥ 13 ॥ <-

## Commentary (Sayana)

O **Maruts of diverse wisdom** <note>original: vicetasaḥ</note>, may we **become** <note>original: syāma</note> the masters of **wealth** <note>original: rāyaḥ</note> that is **given by you** and **abounding in food** <note>original: vayasvataḥ</note>. Who are we? We are **chariot-owners** <note>original: rathyaḥ</note>.

This wealth given by you does not **fail** <note>original: yucchati</note>—it does not perish or fall away. Just as the **star** <note>original: tiṣyaḥ</note>—which Sayana identifies here as the **Sun** <note>original: ādityaḥ</note>—does not fall from the **heaven** <note>original: divaḥ</note>, so too may this wealth remain stable. O Maruts, make **thousandfold** <note>original: sahasriṇam</note> or immeasurable wealth **delight** <note>original: rāranta</note> or stay within **us** <note>original: asme</note>.

---
<vocab>
Marut: Storm deities, frequent subjects of the Rig Veda.
Naka: The firmament or heaven; Sayana etymologizes it as "na-aka" (no-unhappiness).
Pippala: Literally "fig" or "fruit," but used here as a metaphor for rain-water.
Rtayavah: Seekers of Rta (Cosmic Order/Truth), often referring to those performing rituals correctly.
Tisya: A celestial body; while often the star Sirius or a lunar mansion, Sayana glosses it here as the Sun to emphasize its fixed position.
Vayasvata: Possessed of 'vayas' (food, vigor, or bird-like swiftness).
</vocab>

466 || Rig Veda || Chapter 4. Section 3. Verse 17.

## Hymn Text

-> ॥ The Fourteenth Verse ॥ <-

O Maruts, you grant wealth that is accompanied by **desirable heroes**; you protect the **Seer** who is **skilled in sacred chants**. You bestow the **horse** and **nourishment** to the **bearer** of the sacrifice, and you grant a **sovereign** who possesses **joyous obedience**. ॥ 14 ॥

**You | Wealth | Maruts | Desirable-heroes | You | Seer | protect | Chant-skilled |**
**You | Horse | for-the-Bearer | Nourishment | You | grant | Sovereign | Obedient/Happy ॥ 14 ॥**

---

-> ॥ The Fifteenth Verse ॥ <-

I ask you for that **wealth**, O you who offer **immediate help**, by which we may **spread our influence** over men just as the **sun** spreads its light. O Maruts, delight in this **speech** of mine, so that by its **power** we may cross over a **hundred winters**. ॥ 15 ॥

**That | from you | I ask | Wealth | Immediate-help | By which | Sun | Like | Spread | Men | Over |**
**This | well | my | Maruts | delight in | Speech | By whose | we may cross | power | hundred | winters ॥ 15 ॥**

---

## Commentary (Sayana)

O **Maruts**, you grant **wealth** <note>original: rayim</note> that is **endowed with desirable heroes** <note>original: spārhāvīram</note>, meaning it is accompanied by sons, servants, and other brave attendants. O Maruts, you **protect** <note>original: avatha</note> the **Seer** <note>original: rishim</note> who is a **master of chants** <note>original: sāmavipram</note>—one who inspires the various melodies of the Saman, or a wise one accompanied by such chants. You bestow the **horse** <note>original: arvantam</note> and **food** <note>original: vājam</note> to the **bearer** <note>original: bharatāya</note>, referring to the Sage Shyavashva who "bears" or supports the gods through his offerings. O Maruts, you grant a **sovereign** <note>original: rājānam</note>—meaning a radiant master or perhaps a son—who is **obedient and happy** <note>original: śruṣṭimantam</note>.

O you of **immediate help** <note>original: sadyoūtayaḥ</note>—those whose protection is instantaneous or who arrive at once—I **ask** <note>original: yāmi</note> you for that **wealth** <note>original: draviṇam</note>. By that wealth, let us **spread our influence** <note>original: tatatnāma</note> over our sons, servants, and other men, just as the **Sun** <note>original: svar</note> spreads its rays. O Maruts, may you **rightly delight in** <note>original: su harayata</note> this **speech** <note>original: vacaḥ</note>, this hymn of praise being performed by me now. By the **power** <note>original: tarasā</note> of this prayer, may we **cross over** <note>original: tarema</note> **one hundred winters** <note>original: śataṃ himāḥ</note>. This is a prayer to live for a hundred years.

-> ॥ Thus ends the sixteenth section of the third chapter of the fourth octave ॥ <-

The eleventh hymn, beginning with "The worshipful ones" <note>original: prayajyavaḥ</note>, contains ten verses. It is seen by the Sage Shyavashva and is dedicated to the Maruts. The tenth verse is in the **Trishtubh** meter <note>a meter of 11 syllables per line</note>, while the remaining verses are in the **Jagati** meter <note>a meter of 12 syllables per line</note>. The Index <note>original: Anukramanika</note> states: "The worshipful ones; the last of the ten is Trishtubh." In the ritual of the sixth day of the **Abhiplava** festival <note>a six-day religious cycle</note>, this hymn is to be recited during the 'Agni-Maruta' litany as the portion dedicated to the Maruts. It is indicated in the ritual manuals: "The worshipful ones, this hymn..." <note>original: Ashvalayana Shrauta Sutra 7.9</note>.
