Mandala 5. Chapter 4. Hymn 55. || The Fourth Octave || 461

## Hymn Text

-> ॥ The First Verse ॥ <-

The **Maruts**, who sacrifice effectively, possessing **shining spears** and **golden plates** upon their chests, have taken unto themselves **great strength**. They move with **horses** that are **swift** and **easy to control**; their **chariots** follow their path for the sake of **glory**. ॥ 1 ॥

**Word-by-word Breakdown:**
**Effective-sacrificers | Maruts | Shining-spears | Great | Strength | They-have-taken | Golden-chested |**
**They-move | with-Horses | Easy-to-control | Swift | Glory | For-those-going | Following | Chariots | They-turned ॥ 1 ॥**

---

## Commentary (Sayana)

The **Maruts** <note>original: Marutaḥ</note>, who are **effective sacrificers** <note>original: prayajyavaḥ</note>—meaning they worship with excellence—and who possess **shining weapons** <note>original: bhrājadṛṣṭayo</note>, have taken up **great** <note>original: bṛhat</note> **strength** <note>original: vayo</note>, which can refer to their youthful vigor or abundant food. They are **golden-chested** <note>original: rukmavakṣaso</note>, meaning their chests are adorned as if with golden necklaces. These Maruts **move** <note>original: īyante</note> or are carried by **horses** <note>original: aśvair</note> that are **easy to control** <note>original: suyamebhiḥ</note> and **fast-moving** <note>original: āśubhiḥ</note>. Their **chariots** <note>original: rathā</note> **follow** <note>original: anvavṛtsata</note> behind the Maruts as they **travel** <note>original: yātām</note> toward the sacrificial water or toward their **glory** <note>original: śubhaṃ</note> in a beautiful manner.

---

## Hymn Text

-> ॥ The Second Verse ॥ <-

By **yourselves** you have taken up **strength**, just as you **know** it to be; O **great ones**, you **shine** widely and vastly. You have **measured** the **atmosphere** with your **might**; their **chariots** follow their path for the sake of **glory**. ॥ 2 ॥

**Word-by-word Breakdown:**
**Yourselves | You-have-taken | Strength | As | You-know | Vast | Great-ones | Widely | Shine |**
**And | Atmosphere | They-measured | With-might | Glory | For-those-going | Following | Chariots | They-turned ॥ 2 ॥**

---

## Commentary (Sayana)

O Maruts, you **yourselves** <note>original: svayam</note>, without any outside help, **take up** <note>original: dadhidhve</note>—or rather, create—your **strength** <note>original: taviṣīṃ</note> and power. You do this **as you know** <note>original: yathā vida</note>, implying your power is unhindered and known only to you. O **Great ones** <note>original: mahānto</note>, you **shine** <note>original: vi rājatha</note> as you pervade the **vast** <note>original: urviyā</note> regions. **And also** <note>original: utāpi</note>, you **measured** <note>original: vi mamire</note> or pervaded the **atmosphere** <note>original: antarīkṣam</note> with your **might** <note>original: ojasā</note>. The phrase regarding "glory" and "chariots" follows the same meaning as the previous verse.

---

## Hymn Text

-> ॥ The Third Verse ॥ <-

**Born together**, of **noble nature**, and **grown together**, these **heroes** have increased further and further for the sake of **glory**. Like the **shining rays** of the **sun**, their **chariots** follow their path for the sake of **glory**. ॥ 3 ॥

**Word-by-word Breakdown:**
**Together | Born | Noble-natured | Together | Grown | Glory | Even | Towards | Further | They-increased | Heroes |**
**Shining | Of-the-sun | Like | Rays | Glory | For-those-going | Following | Chariots | They-turned ॥ 3 ॥**

---

## Commentary (Sayana)

**Born together** <note>original: sākaṃ jātāḥ</note> means they were all produced at the same time. They are **noble-natured** <note>original: subhuvaḥ</note>, meaning they are excellent or great. Likewise, they have **together** <note>unclear: ...</note>

<term>Maruts: In Vedic mythology, these are the storm deities and sons of Rudra, often depicted as a unified troop of young warriors riding in golden chariots.</term>
<term>Rukma-vakshasah: Literally "gold on their chests." This refers to the golden breastplates or ornaments worn by the Maruts, symbolizing their brilliance and solar connection.</term>
<term>Tavishi: A specific Vedic term for physical or spiritual strength, often associated with the vital energy of the storm gods.</term>

<meta>This page continues the commentary on Hymn 55 of the 5th Mandala of the Rig Veda. Following the description of the Maruts' appearance and chariots, the text now focuses on their divine power, their ability to grant immortality, and their role as bringers of rain from the celestial "ocean."</meta>

# Rig Veda | Book 4. Chapter 3. Section 18.

[The Maruts], being sprinkled together <note>original: sakṛdevokṣitāḥ</note>, they who pour down rain, have grown and increased in every direction for the sake of beauty. The "men" <note>the Maruts are often called "Narāḥ," meaning heroic men or leaders</note>, leaders of sacred actions, are shining like the rays of the sun. The phrase "for the sake of glory" has been explained previously.

---

-> ॥ The Fourth Verse ॥ <-

**O Maruts, your greatness is worthy of being praised; it is as visible as the light of the sun. Moreover, place us in immortality; your chariots follow your path for the sake of glory. ॥ 4 ॥**

**Word-by-word Breakdown:**
**Truly | Praiseworthy | Your | Maruts | Greatness | Worthy-of-being-seen | Of-the-sun-like | Appearance |**
**Moreover | Us | In-immortality | Place | Glory | For-those-going | Following | Chariots | They-turned ॥ 4 ॥**

## Commentary (Sayana)

O **Maruts**, your **greatness** <term>mahitvanam | majesty or power</term> is **worthy of being praised** <note>original: ābhūṣeṇyam</note>. Furthermore, like the **appearance of the sun** <note>original: sūryasyeva cakṣaṇam</note>, your form is **worthy of being seen** <note>original: didṛkṣeṇyam</note> or beautiful to behold. **Moreover** <note>original: uto</note>, **place us** <note>original: dadhātana</note> in **immortality** <term>amṛtatve | the state of deathlessness</term>, which refers to liberation <note>Moksha</note> or reaching the heavenly realm <note>Svarga</note>. The remainder of the verse is the same as the previous ones.

Liturgical note: In the *Kārīrī* sacrifice <note>a ritual performed to bring rain</note>, the verse beginning with "Rise up" (Verse 5) is used as the invitatory prayer for the first offering.

---

-> ॥ The Fifth Verse ॥ <-

**O Maruts, you raise up the rain from the ocean; you, the possessors of water, cause the rain to fall. O destroyers of enemies, your cows never fail; your chariots follow your path for the sake of glory. ॥ 5 ॥**

**Word-by-word Breakdown:**
**Up | You-raise | Maruts | From-the-ocean | You | Rain | You-cause-to-fall | Possessors-of-water |**
**Not | Your | O-Destroyers | Fail | Cows | Glory | For-those-going | Following | Chariots | They-turned ॥ 5 ॥**

## Commentary (Sayana)

O **Maruts**, **you raise up** <note>original: udīrayatha</note> or send forth **the rain** from the **ocean** <note>original: samudrataḥ</note>, which here refers to the atmosphere or the sky as the source of water. The same idea is emphasized again: O **possessors of water** <term>purīṣiṇaḥ | derived from roots meaning to fill or to please</term>, you **cause the rain to fall**. O **destroyers** <term>dasrāḥ | beautiful ones or those who destroy enemies/drought</term>, **your cows** <note>original: dhenavaḥ</note>—meaning the clouds which nourish and please the world—**do not fail** <note>original: na upadasyanti</note>, meaning they never run dry.

-> ॥ Thus ends the 17th Section (Varga) of the 3rd Chapter of the 4th Part ॥ <-

---

-> ॥ The Sixth Verse ॥ <-

**When you have yoked the dappled deer to your poles, and have harnessed the golden-colored [horses]... you drive away all enemies, O Maruts... ॥ 6 ॥**

<meta>This page continues the commentary on the 55th Hymn (Sūkta) of the 5th Mandala of the Rig Veda. It completes the explanation of verse 6 and provides the full text and commentary for verses 7 and 8. The previous page detailed the Maruts' divine chariots and their ability to grant immortality.</meta>

[Mandala 5. Anuvaka 4. Sukta 55.] || Fourth Book || 469

**When | Horses | To-the-poles | Spotted-mares | You-yoked | Golden | Towards | Armor | You-loosened (put on) |**
**All | Indeed | Enemies | Maruts | You-cast-aside | Beauty | For-those-going | Following | Chariots | They-turned ॥ 6 ॥**

O **Maruts**, when you have **yoked** <note>original: ayugdhvam</note> the **horses** to the **poles** <term>dhūrṣu | the part of the chariot to which the animals are harnessed</term> of the chariots. What kind of horses? The **spotted mares** <term>pṛṣatīḥ | the characteristic dappled deer or mares of the Maruts</term>. It is traditionally said that "the spotted ones belong to the Maruts." These are mares of various colors, though the word for horse is used here. You have **put on** <note>original: pratyamuñcata</note> your **golden** <note>original: hiraṇyavarṇān</note> **armor** <term>atkān | robes or protective coverings</term>. Having done this, O Maruts, you **cast aside** <note>original: vyasyatha</note> **all** your **enemies** <note>original: spṛdhaḥ</note> in every battle. The phrase "for the sake of glory..." has already been explained <note>this refers to the recurring refrain at the end of every verse in this hymn</note>.

---

## Hymn Text
-> ॥ The Seventh Verse ॥ <-

**Neither the mountains nor the rivers obstruct you, wherever you have intended to go, O Maruts, you go there indeed. You traverse around both Heaven and Earth; your chariots follow your path for the sake of glory. ॥ 7 ॥**

### Word-by-word Analysis (Pada-patha)
Neither | Mountains | Neither | Rivers | They-obstruct | You | Where | You-intended | Maruts | You-go | Indeed | Truly | That |
And | Heaven-and-Earth | You-go | Around | Beauty | For-those-going | Following | Chariots | They-turned ॥ 7 ॥

---

## Commentary (Sayana)

O **Maruts**, the **mountains** <note>original: shiloccayāḥ, literally "heaps of stone"</note> do **not obstruct** you; let them not hold you back. Similarly, the **rivers** do not obstruct you. Rather, **wherever**—that is, in whatever place such as a sacrifice—**you have intended** <note>original: jānītha saṅkalpayatha, "you know or resolve"</note> to go, to **that** place **you go indeed** <note>original: gacchathaiva</note>. **And** furthermore, **you travel around** <note>original: parito yāthana</note> both **Heaven and Earth** <term>dyāvāpṛthivī | the cosmic pair of sky and land</term> for the purpose of bringing rain.

---

## Hymn Text
-> ॥ The Eighth Verse ॥ <-

**Whatever is ancient, O Maruts, and whatever is new; whatever is raised up [as praise], O Vasus, and whatever is recited; of all that, you are the knowers. Your chariots follow your path for the sake of glory. ॥ 8 ॥**

### Word-by-word Analysis (Pada-patha)
Whatever | Ancient | Maruts | Whatever | And | New | Whatever | Is-raised-up | Vasus | Whatever | And | Is-recited |
Of-all | That | You-are | Knowers | Beauty | For-those-going | Following | Chariots | They-turned ॥ 8 ॥

---

## Commentary (Sayana)

O **Maruts**, **whatever** ritual action is **ancient** <note>original: pūrvyam, performed in the past</note>, and **whatever** ritual action is **new** <note>performed in the present</note>; **whatever is raised up** <note>original: udyate</note>, meaning that which is lifted or attained through praise; and O **Vasus** <term>vasavaḥ | "the indwellers" or "shining ones," a name for the Maruts here</term>, **whatever is recited** <note>original: śasyate, the chanting of hymns</note>—of **all that** excellent work, you **are the knowers** <term>navedasaḥ | those who are mindful, witnesses, or conscious of the offerings</term>.

<meta>This page transitions from the end of the 52nd Hymn (Sūkta) to the beginning of the 53rd Hymn of the 5th Book (Maṇḍala). While the previous page provided in the prompt (page 469) discussed the 55th Hymn, this page (page 410) focuses on the Maruts—the storm deities—asking for their protection and the removal of sins. ## Hymn Text

-> ॥ The Ninth Verse ॥ <-

**Be gracious to us, O Maruts; do not strike us. Grant us abundant protection. Come to our praise and our friendship; the chariot-riders have turned toward us for the sake of glory. ॥ 9 ॥**

---

**Be-gracious | to-us | Maruts | do-not | strike | for-us | protection | abundant | grant |**
**To | the-praise | the-friendship | come | glory | for-those-going | following | chariot-riders | they-turned ॥ 9 ॥**

## Commentary (Sāyaṇa)

O **Maruts**, **be gracious** <term>mṛḷata | show mercy or make happy</term> to us. **Do not strike** <note>original: mā vadhiṣṭana</note> us; that is, do not kill us with the anger arising from our transgressions or faults. Instead, **grant** <note>original: vi yantana</note> **abundant** <note>original: bahulam</note>, very great **protection** <term>śarma | refuge or bliss</term> to us. Furthermore, **come to** <note>original: adhi gātana</note> our **praise** <note>original: stotra</note> and our **friendship** <note>original: sakhya</note>. The meaning is: establish a friendly bond with us who offer these songs of praise.

---

## Hymn Text

-> ॥ The Tenth Verse ॥ <-

**O Maruts, being praised, lead us toward better wealth and away from calamities. O you who are worthy of sacrifice, accept our offering of oblations; may we become masters of riches. ॥ 10 ॥**

---

**You | us | lead | better-wealth | toward | away-from | calamities (sins) | Maruts | being-praised |**
**Accept | our | oblation-offering | O-worthy-of-sacrifice | we | may-become | masters | of-riches ॥ 10 ॥**

## Commentary (Sāyaṇa)

O **Maruts**, **lead** us **toward** <note>original: accha</note> **better wealth** <term>vasyo | more excellent riches or a high station such as heaven</term>. Furthermore, **lead us away** <note>original: nirṇayata</note> **from calamities** <term>aṃhṛtibhyaḥ | sins or difficulties</term>, while you are **being praised** <note>original: gṛṇānāḥ</note> by us. <note>Sāyaṇa notes a grammatical point: here the active suffix is used in a passive sense.</note> O **worthy of sacrifice** <term>yajatrāḥ | those to whom sacrifices are offered</term>, **accept** <note>original: juṣadhvam</note> **our offering of oblations** <note>original: havyadātim</note>, our sacrifice filled with offerings. And **may we become masters** of many kinds of **riches** <note>original: rayīṇām</note>.

-> ॥ This concludes the eighteenth section (Varga) of the third chapter (Adhyāya) of the fourth book (Aṣṭaka) ॥ <-

## Critical Notes

**The twelfth hymn** <note>Sukta 53</note> beginning with the words "**The defiant host first**" <note>original: agre śardhantam</note> consists of nine verses. The seer (Ṛṣi) is Śyāvāśva, and it is dedicated to the Maruts. The third and seventh verses are in the *Satobṛhatī* meter, and the rest are in the *Bṛhatī* meter. This is confirmed by the Index <term>Anukramaṇikā | a traditional register of Vedic meters and authors</term>.

## Hymn Text

-> ॥ The First Verse ॥ <-

**Today, I call down the defiant host of the Maruts from the brightness of heaven—that army decorated with golden ornaments and jewelry. ॥ 1 ॥**

<vocab>
- **Maruts** (marutaḥ): The storm gods, often depicted as a youthful, decorative band of warriors.
- **Gracious** (mṛḷata): A plea for the gods to set aside their weapons and grant peace.
- **Calamities** (aṃhṛtibhyaḥ): Often interpreted as "sins" or the narrow, constricted states of suffering.
- **Śyāvāśva**: A famous Vedic seer associated with the Atri family.
- **Bṛhatī**: A Vedic meter consisting of 36 syllables.
</vocab>

## Hymn Text

-> **॥ Now begins the Fifty-Sixth Hymn ॥** <-

O Agni, I call here the mighty host, adorned with golden plates and ornaments. Today, I invoke the clans of the Maruts from the bright realm of heaven. ॥ 1 ॥

**Word-by-word Breakdown**
O-Agni | the-mighty | hither | the-host | adorned | with-golden-plates | with-ornaments | the-clans | today | of-the-Maruts | down | I-call | from-heaven | indeed | from-the-bright-realm | from ॥ 1 ॥

---

Just as you, O Agni, conceive in your heart, so may the seekers come to me. O you of formidable appearance, increase those who have come closest to your invocations. ॥ 2 ॥

**Word-by-word Breakdown**
Just-as | indeed | you-think | with-the-heart | that | indeed | to-me | they-have-gone | the-seekers | who | your | nearest | the-invocations | they-have-come | those | increase | O-you-of-formidable-appearance ॥ 2 ॥

---

Like the earth, abounding in gifts and struck [by rain], the joyous host comes toward us. O Maruts, your power is like a shaggy bear, or like a formidable, charging bull. ॥ 3 ॥

**Word-by-word Breakdown**
Like-one-abounding-in-gifts | the-earth | struck | rejoicing | comes | from-us | hither | a-bear | like | your | O-Maruts | powerful | strength | difficult-to-restrain | like-a-bull | formidable ॥ 3 ॥

---

## Commentary (Sāyaṇa)

O **Agni**, [I invoke] the **host** <term>gaṇam | the troop of Maruts</term> who are **mighty** <term>śardhantam | those who overcome enemies or are eager for the sacrifice</term>. What kind of host? One that is **adorned** <note>original: piṣṭam</note> with **golden plates** <term>rukmebhiḥ | shining golden breastplates</term> and **ornaments** <term>añjibhiḥ</term>. **Today**, on this day of sacrifice, I **call** <note>original: hvaye</note> the **clans of the Maruts** <note>original: marutāṃ viśaḥ</note> toward us. [I call them] **from the bright realm** <note>original: rocanāt</note> of **heaven** <note>original: divaḥ</note>. The word **from** <note>original: adhi</note> indicates the point of origin, and **indeed** <note>original: cit</note> is a filler word for poetic meter.

-> ॥ The Second Verse ॥ <-

O **Agni**, just as you **think in your heart** <note>original: hṛdā yathā cinmanyase</note>—where "indeed" (*cit*) implies honor—in whatever way you highly honor the Maruts and show them favor, **so may they** <note>original: tadit</note> **come** <note>original: jagmuḥ</note> to **me** for my sake. May these **seekers** <term>āśasaḥ | those who desire to help or those who strike down enemies</term> arrive. Furthermore, those Maruts who **come** <note>original: ā-gman</note> **nearest** <note>original: nediṣṭham</note> upon hearing **your invocations**, **increase** <note>original: vardha</note> them by providing the sacrificial offerings, O you of **formidable appearance** <term>bhīmasankāsha | looking terrifying because you do not tolerate delay</term>.

-> ॥ The Third Verse ॥ <-

Like the **earth** <note>original: pṛthivīva</note> which is **abounding in gifts** <term>mīḷhuṣmatī | having a powerful master or being rich in water</term> and **struck** <note>original: parāhatā</note> [by rain or by others]. Here, the word "earth" refers to the people dwelling upon it; just as a person who is oppressed seeks their master, so the host of Maruts comes to us. The **joyous** army of Maruts **comes** <note>original: aiti</note> toward **us**. O Maruts, **your** <note>original: vaḥ</note> **strength** <note>original: amaḥ</note> is like a **bear** <term>ṛkṣaḥ</term>...

<vocab>
- Maruts: Storm deities known for their collective power and golden ornaments.
- Agni: The sacrificial fire, acting here as an intermediary to call other gods.
- Rukma: Golden discs or plates worn on the chest by the Maruts.
- Bhashya: The traditional Sanskrit commentary, here by the scholar Sāyaṇa.
- Mīḷhuṣmatī: A complex term meaning "fertile," "reward-giving," or "moisture-rich."
</vocab>

<summary>This page introduces the 56th hymn of the Rig Veda's fifth book, where the poet asks Agni to summon the Maruts (storm gods) from heaven. The verses describe the Maruts' glittering golden appearance and their formidable, irresistible strength, comparing them to powerful animals like bears and bulls.</summary>
<keywords>Agni, Maruts, Rig Veda, Sāyaṇa, Vedic sacrifice, storm gods, golden ornaments, divine invocation</keywords>

## Hymn Text

-> ॥ Now the Fourth Verse ॥ <-
They who by their might strike down [enemies] effortlessly, like cattle that are hard to restrain. They cause the sounding stone, the mountain, the hill to tremble during their journeys. ॥ 4 ॥

**Word-by-word Breakdown (Pada-patha):**
Down | they | strike | by might | effortlessly | cattle | like | difficult to restrain |
the stone | indeed | sounding | the mountain | the hill | forth | they cause to tremble | by their journeys ॥ 4 ॥

---

## Commentary (Sāyaṇa)

Those **Maruts** who, by their own **might** <term>ojasā | strength</term>, **strike down** <term>niriṇanti | kill or injure</term> their enemies **effortlessly** <term>vṛthā | without any strain</term>, simply by their movement, like **cattle** <note>original: "gāvo na"</note> or horses that are **difficult to restrain** <term>durdhuraḥ | hard to yoke or check</term>. Those Maruts cause the **sounding** <term>svaryam | making a noise</term> **stone** <term>aśmānam | the pervasive cloud</term>, the **mountain** <term>parvatam | that which fills the world with water</term>, to tremble. The scholar Yāska defines "mountain" <note>original: "parvavān parvataḥ..."</note> as that which has joints or that which satisfies. <note>Nirukta 7.20</note>. They move such a **hill** <term>girim | a cloud</term>. Alternatively, "mountain" is the noun and "hill" is the adjective. A hill is called *giri* because it "swallows" the water <note>original: "nigirati udakam iti giriḥ"</note>. They **cause it to tremble** <term>pracyāvayanti</term> during their **journeys** <term>yāmabhiḥ | their travels</term> to make the waters flow out.

---

## Hymn Text

-> ॥ Now the Fifth Verse ॥ <-
Arise now with the hymns of these [Maruts] who have been strengthened [by praise]. I invoke the most abundant, the unprecedented host of Maruts, like a herd of cows. ॥ 5 ॥

**Word-by-word Breakdown (Pada-patha):**
Up | stand | now | of these | by hymns | well-anointed |
of the Maruts | the most abundant | unprecedented | of cows | like a herd | I call ॥ 5 ॥

---

## Commentary (Sāyaṇa)

O Maruts, **arise** <term>uttiṣṭha</term>. "You all arise" <note>original: "uttiṣṭhata"</note>. The singular is used here for the plural by grammatical substitution. Surely, by the **hymns** <term>stomalḥ | songs of praise</term> of these **well-anointed** <term>samukṣitānām | those who have been increased or grown</term> Maruts—or rather, "I invoke [them] with hymns." I **call** <term>hvaye</term> the **most abundant** <term>purutamam | very numerous</term>, **unprecedented** <term>apūrvyam | those who have no one prior to them</term> **host** <term>sargam | group</term> of Maruts, like a **herd of cows** <note>original: "gavām sargam"</note> or a flow of waters.

-> ॥ Thus ends the nineteenth section (Varga) of the third chapter (Adhyāya) of the first book (Aṣṭaka) ॥ <-

---

## Hymn Text

-> ॥ Now the Sixth Verse ॥ <-
Harness the ruddy mares to the chariot; harness the stallions to the chariots. Harness the two swift bay horses to the pole to carry you—the best carriers to the pole to carry you. ॥ 6 ॥

---

<vocab>
- Maruts: Deities of the storm and wind, often depicted as a troop of young warriors.
- Ojasā: By strength; a term often associated with the vital energy of gods.
- Aśmānam: Literally "stone," but in the Rig Veda, it often metaphorically refers to a cloud that holds the "stony" hail or the lightning-bolt.
- Parvataḥ: Mountain; also a common metaphor for the massive, solid-looking rain clouds.
- Stoma: A sacrificial hymn or song of praise used to empower the gods.
- Gavām sargam: A phrase that can mean a "herd of cattle" or a "release of waters," playing on the double meaning of *go* (cow/water/ray of light).
- Voḷhave: A Vedic grammatical form meaning "to carry" or "to draw" a chariot.
</vocab>

Mandal 5. Chapter 4. Hymn 56.] || Fourth Book || 493

## Hymn Text

**[RV 5.56.6 Word-by-word Breakdown — Continued]**
Yoke | indeed | the red mares | in the chariot | yoke | in the chariots | the reddish horses |
yoke | the two bay horses | swift-moving | at the pole | to bear | the best bearers | at the pole | to bear ॥ 6 ॥

---

**[RV 5.56.7]**
-> ॥ Now the Seventh Verse ॥ <-
And this spirited, red, loud-sounding [horse] has been placed here, visible to all. O Maruts, may he not cause delay in your journeys; urge him forward on the chariots. ॥ 7 ॥

**[RV 5.56.7 Word-by-word Breakdown]**
And | this | spirited | red | loud-sounding | here | [filler] | has been placed | visible |
not | your | in journeys | Maruts | delay | may he make | forth | him | on the chariots | urge ॥ 7 ॥

---

**[RV 5.56.8]**
-> ॥ Now the Eighth Verse ॥ <-
We now call upon the chariot of the Maruts, which seeks glory, upon which Rodasi, bearing delightful treasures, has taken her stand together with the Maruts. ॥ 8 ॥

**[RV 5.56.8 Word-by-word Breakdown]**
The chariot | now | belonging to the Maruts | we | seeking glory | [call] hither | we call |
hither | in which | she stood | delightful [waters] | bearing | together | among the Maruts | Rodasi ॥ 8 ॥

---

## Commentary (Sāyaṇa)

**[Commentary on RV 5.56.6]**
O **Maruts**, you **yoke** <term>yuṅgdhvam | join or harness</term> to your chariot—which is shared by all—the **red mares** <note>original: "aruṣīḥ"</note>, those that are shining. Likewise, **yoke** the **reddish-colored** <note>original: "rohitaḥ"</note> horses to your chariots. Yoke the two **bay horses** <note>original: "harī"</note>, who are **swift-moving** <note>original: "ajrirā"</note>, to the **pole** <note>original: "dhuri"</note> for the purpose of carrying the load. The instruction is repeated for emphasis. Yoke the **best bearers** <note>original: "vahiṣṭhā"</note>, the horses most capable of pulling, to the pole for the journey.

**[Commentary on RV 5.56.7]**
Furthermore, this **spirited** <term>vājī | possessing speed or strength</term> horse, who is **shining** <note>original: "aruṣaḥ"</note> and **loud-sounding** <term>tuviṣvaṇiḥ | making a great noise</term>, has now been **placed** <term>dhāyi | stationed or yoked</term> here, appearing **beautiful to behold** <note>original: "darśataḥ"</note>. By the word "red" <note>original: "aruṣaḥ"</note>, the "reddish" <note>original: "rohitaḥ"</note> horse is meant. Indeed, it has been said elsewhere: "The reddish horse carries you forward" <note>original: "pra śvo vahati rohitaḥ" | Rig Veda 1.39.6</note>. O Maruts, may that horse **not cause** <note>original: "mā karat"</note> any **delay** <note>original: "ciram"</note> in your **journeys** <note>original: "yāmeṣu"</note>. As for him who is joined to the chariot, **urge him forward** <note>original: "pracodata"</note>; drive him so that he does not linger.

**[Commentary on RV 5.56.8]**
We, the descendants of Atri, now **call upon** <note>original: "ā huvāmahe"</note> the **chariot of the Maruts** <term>mārutam ratham</term>, a vehicle that is swift by nature and **seeking glory** <term>śravasyum | desiring food or fame</term>. In this chariot, **Rodasi**—who is the wife of Rudra and the mother of the Maruts—has **taken her stand** <note>original: "ātasthau"</note> alongside the Maruts. She is **bearing** <note>original: "bibhratī"</note> **delightful** <note>original: "suraṇāni"</note> waters. Alternatively, if Rudra is understood as Vayu (the wind), then his wife is the deity of the middle region (the atmosphere); I call upon the chariot where she stays in the company of the Maruts.

<summary>This page details the yoking of various colored horses (red, reddish, and bay) to the Maruts' chariots and invokes the goddess Rodasi, who travels with the storm gods while carrying refreshing waters.</summary>

494 || Rigveda || [Book 4, Chapter 3, Group 21]

## Hymn Text

-> ॥ Now the Ninth Verse ॥ <-

I invoke that host of yours, beautiful on the chariot, fierce, and worthy of praise; in which [host] the well-born, fortunate, and liberal goddess <term>Mīḷhuṣī | the generous one, identified here as the wife of Rudra</term> is honored together with the Maruts. ॥ 9 ॥

-> **Word-by-word Breakdown** <-

That | your | host | beautiful on the chariot | fierce | worthy of praise | hither | I invoke |
in which | well-born | fortunate | she is honored | together | among the Maruts | the liberal goddess ॥ 9 ॥

---

## Commentary (Sāyaṇa)

O **Maruts**, **I invoke** <note>original: "āhuve"</note> **your host** <note>original: "śardhaṃ"</note>, your strength or assembly, which is **beautiful on the chariot**, **fierce** or bright, and **worthy of praise**. In **which** host the **well-born** (well-grown), **fortunate** (of great good fortune), and **liberal goddess** <note>original: "mīḷhuṣī"</note> is **honored** or worshipped **together with the Maruts**. Based on references such as "Most generous one, most auspicious one" <note>original: "mīḷhuṣṭama śivatama"</note>, we see that "The Generous One" <note>original: "Mīḷhvān"</note> refers to Rudra. His wife is **Mīḷhuṣī**. The teacher Apastamba also spoke of Rudra’s wife by the name Mīḷhuṣī: "With the later [verse] he invokes Ishana in the south; with common speech he invokes Mīḷhuṣī in the north, and Jayanta in the middle."

-> ॥ Thus ends the twentieth group in the third chapter of the fourth book ॥ <-
-> ॥ Thus ends the fourth lesson of the fifth mandala ॥ <-

**In the fifth lesson <term>anuvāka | a sub-section of the Vedic text</term>, there are sixteen hymns. Among them, the first hymn "Hither, O Rudras" <note>original: "ā rudrāso"</note> consists of eight verses composed by the seer Shyavashva and is dedicated to the Maruts. The seventh and eighth verses are in the Trishtubh meter <note>a meter with 11 syllables per line</note>, and the remaining six are in the Jagati meter <note>a meter with 12 syllables per line</note>. The Index <note>original: "Anukramaṇikā"</note> states: "The eight verses beginning 'Hither, O Rudras' contain two Trishtubhs." The ritual application is determined by the marks of the deities.**

-> ॥ There, the First Verse ॥ <-

O sons of Rudra <note>the Maruts</note>, accompanied by Indra, of one mind, having golden chariots—come for our well-being. This prayer of ours desires you, just as a thirsty man [longs] for the springs of heaven. ॥ 1 ॥

-> **Word-by-word Breakdown** <-

Hither | O sons of Rudra | accompanied by Indra | of one mind | golden chariots | for well-being | come |
this | your | from us | prayer | is desired | prayer | for a thirsty man | like | of heaven | the springs | for one desiring water ॥ 1 ॥

**O sons of Rudra**, children of the storm god, **accompanied by Indra** (your master), being of **one mind** (having equal affection for each other), and possessing **golden chariots**—**come** for **well-being** (for easy passage, or for the sacrifice which is the means to it). What is present here? It is said: **this prayer** (hymn of praise) **from us** (belonging to us) **desires** <note>original: "haryate"</note> you. Therefore, come.

<vocab>Maruts (Storm deities), Rudra (Father of the Maruts), Milhushi (Consort of Rudra), Shyavashva (The Sage/Rishi of this hymn), Trishtubh (11-syllable meter), Jagati (12-syllable meter), Anukramanika (Vedic index), Viniyoga (Ritual use), Indra (King of gods)</vocab>

<summary>This page concludes Hymn 56 of Mandala 5 with an invocation of the Marut host and the goddess Milhushi, then begins Hymn 57, where the seer Shyavashva invites the Maruts and Indra to the sacrifice, likening the soul's desire for the gods to a thirsty man seeking water.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the commentary on the hymns to the Maruts (the storm deities) in Mandala 5, Sukta 57. It completes the explanation for Verse 1 and provides the full text and commentary for Verses 2 and 3.</meta>

[Mandala 5, Chapter 5, Hymn 57] || Fourth Book || 455

...for the thirsty Sage Gotama who desired water, the springs of flowing water were sent by you from the sky <note>original: "divo"</note>, the world of light. In the same way, please come for our sake as well and grant us our desires. This is the meaning.

---

-> ॥ Now the Second Verse ॥ <-

## Hymn Text
Equipped with axes, equipped with spears, wise, with good bows, with arrows, and with quivers; you are provided with good horses, good chariots, O sons of Prishni! With good weapons, O Maruts, you go forth for the sake of prosperity. ॥ 2 ॥

**Word-by-word Breakdown:**
Equipped with axes | equipped with spears | wise | with good bows | with arrows | with quivers |
with good horses | you are | with good chariots | children of the dappled cow | with good weapons | O Maruts | you go forth | for prosperity ॥ 2 ॥

---

## Commentary (Sāyaṇa)
O **Maruts**, you are **equipped with axes** <note>original: "vāśīmantaḥ"</note>. The axe <note>original: "vāśī"</note> is a weapon used for carving; you possess such weapons. You are **equipped with spears** <note>original: "ṛṣṭimantaḥ"</note>; a spear <note>original: "ṛṣṭi"</note> is a type of dagger or blade. You possess these. This logic should be applied to all the following terms. You are **wise** <note>original: "manīṣiṇaḥ"</note>, meaning masters of the mind or high-spirited. You are **those with good bows**, **those with arrows**, and **those with quivers**. You **are provided with good horses** and **good chariots**. You are the **sons of Prishni** <term>Pṛśni | the earth-goddess or sky-cow, mother of the storm winds</term>. You are **equipped with good weapons**, including all types of arms like swords and battle-axes. Being such great souls, you **go forth** <note>original: "yāthana"</note> by your chariots for **prosperity** <note>original: "śubham"</note>, which refers to either a beautiful state or for the sake of bringing water.

---

-> ॥ Now the Third Verse ॥ <-

## Hymn Text
You shake the heavens and the mountains, [bringing] wealth to the giver of offerings. The forests bow down out of fear of your passage. You cause the earth to tremble, O sons of Prishni, when you, the fierce ones, have yoked the spotted deer for prosperity. ॥ 3 ॥

**Word-by-word Breakdown:**
You shake | the heavens | the mountains | to the giver | wealth | down | your | forests | they bow | at your passage | through fear |
you cause to tremble | the earth | O children of the dappled cow | for prosperity | when | O fierce ones | the spotted deer | you have yoked ॥ 3 ॥

---

## Commentary (Sāyaṇa)
O Maruts, you **shake** the **heavens** <note>original: "dyām"</note>—meaning the sky—and the **mountains** <note>original: "parvatān"</note>, which here refers to the clouds. You bring **wealth** <note>original: "vasu"</note> or treasures to the **giver** <note>original: "dāśuṣe"</note>, the sacrificer who offers the oblation. Out of **fear** of **your passage** or movement, the **forests**—the clusters of trees and plants—**bow down** <note>original: "ni jihate"</note>. This means they tremble greatly or bend low in praise. O **sons of Prishni**, for the sacred texts say, "The Maruts were born from the milk of Prishni." O Maruts, you **cause the earth to tremble** <note>original: "kopayatha"</note>; you agitate it with your heavy rains. O **fierce ones** <note>original: "uyā"; usually "ugrāḥ" in other editions</note>, you of unrestrained strength, **when** you **yoke** the **spotted deer** <term>pṛṣatīḥ | the female dappled deer that serve as the Maruts' mounts</term> that belong to you for the sake of **prosperity** (or water), then you cause the earth to tremble.

<vocab>
Marutaḥ (मरुतः) - Storm deities
Vāśī (वाशी) - An axe-like weapon
Ṛṣṭi (ऋष्टि) - Spear or dagger
Pṛśnimātaraḥ (पृश्निमातरः) - Having Prishni as mother
Dāśuṣe (दाशुषे) - For the donor/sacrificer
Vasu (वसु) - Wealth/Treasures
Pṛṣatīḥ (पृषतीः) - Dotted deer (the steeds of the Maruts)
</vocab>

476 || Rig Veda || [Book 1, Chapter 4, Section 22]

## Hymn Text

-> ॥ Now the Fourth Verse ॥ <-

With the brilliance of the wind, the Maruts are clothed in rain; like twins, they are identical in appearance and beautifully adorned. They possess tawny horses and ruddy horses; they are sinless, of great strength, and vast in their greatness like the sky. ॥ 4 ॥

**Word-by-word Breakdown:**
With the brilliance of the wind | the Maruts | clothed in rain | like twins | identical in appearance | beautifully adorned |
with tawny horses | with ruddy horses | sinless | of great strength | in greatness | like the sky | vast ॥ 4 ॥

---

-> ॥ Now the Fifth Verse ॥ <-

Abundant in water-drops, adorned with jewels, liberal givers, brilliant to behold, and with undiminished wealth; noble from their very birth, with golden plates upon their chests, these worshipful Maruts of the sky have partaken of the nectar. ॥ 5 ॥

**Word-by-word Breakdown:**
Abundant in water-drops | adorned with jewels | liberal givers | brilliant to behold | with undiminished wealth |
noble-born | from birth | with golden plates on the chest | of the sky | the worshipful ones | the nectar | by name | have partaken ॥ 5 ॥

---

-> ॥ Now the Sixth Verse ॥ <-

Spears rest upon your shoulders, O Maruts; power and might are placed in your arms. Manliness is on your heads, weapons are in your chariots; all your beauty is spread over your bodies. ॥ 6 ॥

---

## Commentary (Sāyaṇa)

**Verse 4:**
**With the brilliance of the wind** <note>original: "vātatviṣaḥ"</note> means they always possess a constant, far-reaching glow. **Clothed in rain** <note>original: "varṣanirṇijaḥ"</note> means they are the purifiers of the rain. Alternatively, the word "nirṇij" refers to a form or garment; thus, their very form is made of rain, meaning they are the givers of rain. **Like twins** <note>original: "yamā iva"</note> suggests they are like those born as pairs—they are **identical in appearance** <note>original: "susadṛśaḥ"</note>, being extremely similar to one another in strength and form. They are **beautifully adorned** <note>original: "supeśasaḥ"</note>. They possess **tawny horses** and **ruddy horses**. They are **sinless** <note>original: "arepasaḥ"</note>, meaning they are without fault. They are **of great strength** <note>original: "pratavakṣasaḥ"</note>, being those who greatly diminish or overcome their enemies. In their **greatness**, they are **vast like the sky** <note>original: "dyouriva"</note>, meaning they are as expansive as the mid-region or atmosphere. This description connects with the following verse regarding those who "have partaken of the name."

**Verse 5:**
**Abundant in water-drops** <note>original: "purudrupsāḥ"</note> means they possess a great quantity of water. They are **adorned with jewels** <note>original: "añjimantaḥ"</note> or ornaments. They are **liberal givers** <note>original: "sudānavaḥ"</note>, characterized by their excellent gifts. They are **brilliant to behold** <note>original: "tveṣasamdṛśaḥ"</note> and possess **undiminished wealth**. They are **noble from birth**, possessing the aforementioned qualities from the very moment of their manifestation. They have **golden plates upon their chests** <note>original: "rukmavakṣasaḥ"</note>, meaning their chests are adorned with golden necklaces or ornaments. These **worshipful** <note>original: "arkāḥ"</note> Maruts, coming from the **sky**, have **partaken of the nectar** <note>original: "amṛtaṃ nāma"</note>. Here, "nectar" refers to water, which is the means of immortality, or to the sacrificial oblation <note>original: "haviḥ"</note> which they have received.

---

## Critical Notes

-> ॥ This concludes the twenty-first Varga of the third Adhyaya of the first Ashtaka. ॥ <-

<vocab>
<term>Maruts</term> — The storm deities in Vedic mythology, often described as a troop of young warriors, the sons of Rudra and Prishni.
<term>Nirṇij</term> — A term that can mean a shining robe, a physical form, or the act of cleansing.
<term>Amṛta</term> — Literally "not-death" or immortality. In the Rig Veda, it often refers to the Soma juice, rain, or the divine food of the gods.
<term>Rukma</term> — A golden ornament or disc, often worn on the breast by the Maruts as a symbol of their solar brilliance.
<term>Varga</term> — A small section or paragraph-like division used in the Ashtaka system of Rig Veda organization.
</vocab>

## Hymn Text

### Verse 6 (Word-by-word Breakdown)

manly ornaments <note>original: "nṛmṇā"</note> | on the heads | weapons | in the chariots | [are] yours | all | your | beauty | over | the bodies | is spread ॥ 6 ॥

### Verse 7
-> ॥ Now the Seventh Verse ॥ <-
O Maruts, grant us wealth that includes cattle, horses, chariots, brave sons, and gold; O sons of Rudra, bring us prosperity; may I enjoy your divine protection. ॥ 7 ॥

**Word-by-word Breakdown:**
Possessing cattle | possessing horses | possessing chariots | with brave sons | possessing gold <note>literally "possessing the moon," meaning glittering gold</note> | wealth | O Maruts | give | to us |
glory | to us | make | O sons of Rudra | may I enjoy | your | protection | divine ॥ 7 ॥

### Verse 8
-> ॥ Now the Eighth Verse ॥ <-
O leaders, O Maruts, be gracious to us, you who are possessors of great wealth, immortal, and knowers of the Eternal Order; Truth-hearing, wise, youthful, great in voice, and vast in your power. ॥ 8 ॥

**Word-by-word Breakdown:**

## Commentary (Sāyaṇa)

**[On Verse 6]**
O Maruts, on your shoulders rest **spears** <note>original: "ṛṣṭayaḥ," a specific type of pointed weapon</note>, which are placed there. The word "placed" <note>original: "hitam"</note>, which appears later in the verse, should be applied here as well. The word "above" <note>original: "adhi"</note> functions as a locative marker. Likewise, in your arms is placed **vital strength** <note>original: "ojaḥ"</note>, which has the power to overcome enemies. This "vital strength" is considered the eighth constituent of the body <note>term: "asta-dhatu" (the eight bodily substances in traditional medicine)</note>. On your heads are placed **manly ornaments** <note>original: "nṛmṇāni"</note>, such as golden headbands or turbans. In your chariots are various **weapons**, the tools of war. All your **beauty** <note>original: "śrī," meaning luster or radiance</note> is established and spread over your bodies.

**[On Verse 7]**
O Maruts, give <note>original: "dada," here used as a command to "give"</note> to us **wealth** <note>original: "rādhaḥ," which refers to food or prosperity</note> that is accompanied by many cattle, many horses, chariots, and excellent, heroic sons, as well as glittering gold. <note>Note: The commentator observes that the verb is in the singular "give," though addressing multiple gods, a common Vedic grammatical variation</note>. O **sons of Rudra** <note>original: "rudriyāsaḥ"</note>, bring about our **glory** <note>original: "praśastim," meaning abundance or success</note>. May I partake in or enjoy your **protection** <note>original: "avasaḥ"</note>, which is **divine** and worthy of the gods.

**[On Verse 8]**
O **leaders** <note>original: "naraḥ," meaning guides or heroes</note>, O Maruts, **be gracious** to us. That is, make us happy or be favorable for our benefit. O you who possess **abundant wealth**, who are **immortal** by nature, and who are **knowers of the Eternal Order** <note>original: "ṛtajñāḥ," those who understand the cosmic Law or the ritual sacrifice</note>...

---

<meta>This page concludes the commentary for the 51st hymn (Sukta 51) and begins the 52nd hymn (Sukta 52) of the 5th Mandala of the Rig Veda. According to the traditional divisions, this section belongs to Book 4 (Ashtaka), Chapter 3 (Adhyaya), Section 23 (Varga). The commentary focuses on the transition from the general invocation of the gods to a specific hymn dedicated to the Maruts—the powerful storm deities—composed by the seer Shyavashva of the line of Atri.</meta>

... [You are] the knowers of the water or of the sacrifice. This means you are the performers. You are the upholders of truth <note>original: "satyabhṛtaḥ"</note>, known for providing results that are true and certain. You are wise, eternally youthful, and possessors of vast praises. You are exceedingly powerful in showering [blessings] or water when honored with oblations—O Maruts, be gracious to us.

->॥ This ends the twenty-second section in the third chapter of the fourth book. ॥<-

The second hymn of this section, beginning with the words "Tam u nunam," consists of eight verses. It was revealed to the sage <term>Shyavashva</term> <note>a renowned seer from the Atri family</note>. The meter is <term>Trishtubh</term> <note>a rhythmic structure consisting of four lines of eleven syllables each</note>, and the deity addressed is the host of <term>Maruts</term> <note>the storm gods who accompany Indra</note>. This is confirmed by the Index <note>original: "Anukramaṇī"</note>. Its ritual application is determined by the specific indications within the text.

---

## Hymn Text

->॥ Now the First Verse ॥<-

Now indeed, I praise that powerful host of Maruts with a new song; those who, possessing swift horses, move with overwhelming force, and who, as self-radiant rulers, hold power over the nectar of immortality <note>original: "amṛtasya," which Sāyaṇa interprets here as "water" or "rain"</note>. ॥ 1 ॥

> That | indeed | now | possessing power | of these | I praise | the host | of Maruts | with newest [songs] |
> who | possessing swift horses | with force | they move | and also | they rule | over the nectar | self-radiant ॥ 1 ॥

---

## Commentary (Sāyaṇa)

**[On Verse 1]**
I praise that very same host of Maruts previously mentioned. They are **possessing power** <note>original: "taviṣīmantaṃ"</note>, meaning they are full of light or strength. I praise them **now** with **new songs**. What kind of Maruts? Those who are **newest** <note>original: "navyasīnām"</note>; the commentator notes a grammatical variation here <note>original: "liṅgavyatyayaḥ"</note>, explaining it as those who are most worthy of being praised with fresh hymns. This refers to the Marut-host, where the individual Maruts are the members of the troop. What are they like? They are **possessing swift horses** and they **move** or proceed **with force** <note>original: "amavat"</note>, appearing as powerful beings. **And also**, they are the lords who **rule over the nectar**, meaning the water of the rains. They are **self-radiant**, meaning their brilliance is under their own control or they shine by their own light. I praise their host.

---

## Hymn Text

->॥ Now the Second Verse ॥<-

O wise priest, praise their powerful host, who wear rings on their hands, whose work is the shaking [of the world], who are possessors of secret knowledge, and who grant desired boons. Praise those leaders, the Maruts, who are the source of joy, and who are immeasurable in their greatness and abundant in wealth. ॥ 2 ॥

> Their | host | powerful | with rings on hands | whose work is shaking | possessing secret knowledge | giving desired things |
> source of joy | who | immeasurable | through greatness | praise | O wise one | possessing abundant wealth | leaders ॥ 2 ॥

---

## Commentary (Sāyaṇa)

**[On Verse 2]**
O wise priest <note>original: "vipra," referring to the Hotar or invoker</note>, **praise** <note>original: "vandasva"</note> that radiant host of Maruts. They are **powerful** <note>original: "tavasam"</note> and they are **wearing rings on their hands** <note>original: "khādihastam," referring to gold bracelets or quoits</note>. Their **work is shaking** <note>original: "dhunivratam," referring to the agitation of the trees and earth during a storm</note>. They are **possessors of secret knowledge** <note>original: "māyinam"</note> or wisdom, and they are **givers of desired wealth**. The connection here is: "O priest, offer your praise." These Maruts are the **source of joy** <note>original: "mayobhuvaḥ"</note> or the producers of happiness. They are **immeasurable** <note>original: "amitāḥ"</note> because of their **greatness**. Praise those **leaders** <note>original: "nṝn"</note> who possess **abundant wealth**.

<meta>This page continues the translation of the 5th Mandala of the Rig Veda, specifically the 58th hymn (Sukta) dedicated to the Maruts. The previous page likely concluded the second verse of this hymn. This page contains the third and fourth verses along with the commentary of the 14th-century scholar Sayana, followed by liturgical instructions for the use of these verses in specific Vedic sacrifices.</meta>

## Hymn Text

->॥ Now the Third Verse ॥<-

May the water-carriers <note>original: "udavāhāso," referring to the Maruts as bearers of rain clouds</note> come to you today, all those Maruts who stir the rain. O Maruts, this Agni <note>the god of fire</note> is well-kindled; O wise and eternally youthful ones, be pleased with this [offering]. ॥ 3 ॥

---

**Word-for-Word Analysis:**

May they come | to you | let them come | the water-carriers | today | the rain | who | all | Maruts | they stir |
This | which | Agni | O Maruts | is well-kindled | this | be pleased with | O wise ones | O youthful ones. ॥ 3 ॥

---

## Commentary (Sayana)

Those all-pervasive Maruts who stir and urge the rain—may those water-carriers come to you now, the priests and the patrons of the sacrifice. Now, the poet shifts to direct address: O Maruts, this well-known Agni has been properly kindled and made radiant; delight in this fire. O wise ones <note>original: "kavayaḥ," meaning those with foresight or poetic wisdom</note>, O youthful ones—you who are eternally young or who pervade everywhere.

---

## Hymn Text

->॥ Now the Fourth Verse ॥<-

O worshipful ones, produce for the people a king who is a driver [of enemies] and fashioned by Vibhva <note>one of the celestial artisans</note>. From you comes [a son] who is a striker with his fists and swift-armed; from you, O Maruts, comes one with excellent horses and great heroism. ॥ 4 ॥

---

**Word-for-Word Analysis:**

You | a king | a driver | for the people | fashioned by Vibhva | produce | O worshipful ones |
From you | comes | a striker with his fists | swift-armed | from you | with excellent horses | O Maruts | with great heroism. ॥ 4 ॥

---

## Commentary (Sayana)

O Maruts, for the person who performs the sacrifice <note>the "yajamana"</note>, produce a king—meaning a master or a shining son—who is a driver <note>original: "iryam," meaning one who impels or drives away enemies</note>. He should be "fashioned by Vibhva." Vibhva is the middle brother among the <term>Ribhus</term> <note>a group of three celestial brothers known for their extraordinary craftsmanship</note>. He is a skilled artisan. Therefore, the phrase means a son of exceedingly beautiful form, as if crafted by a divine artist. O worshipful ones, produce such a son. O Maruts, from your grace comes a son who is a "striker with his fists." The word "fist" here represents the entire arm; he is one who kills enemies through the strength of his own arms. This is further explained as "swift-armed," meaning one whose arms are impelled against enemies. Furthermore, from your grace comes a son with "excellent horses," meaning one who possesses many horses, and one who has "great heroism" or noble strength.

At the <term>Varunapraghasa</term> <note>the second of the four-monthly seasonal sacrifices</note>, the verse beginning **"Ara ive"** <note>"Like the spokes of a wheel..."</note> is used as the consecrating prayer <note>yajya</note> for the offering of curdled milk <note>amiksha</note> to the Maruts. This is indicated in the ritual manuals: **"Like the spokes, not the last... O Varuna, hear this plea of mine" (Ashvalayana Shrauta Sutra 2.17).** Similarly, in the <term>Ekadashina</term> <note>a ritual involving eleven animal victims</note> rite for the Maruts, this same verse serves as the prayer for the sacrificial cake. This is also indicated: **"Like the spokes, not the last... which are your blessings for the worshiper" (Ashvalayana Shrauta Sutra 3.7).**

<summary>This page translates verses 3 and 4 of Rig Veda 5.58, where the Maruts are invoked as rain-bringers and granters of heroic, well-formed sons, with Sayana's commentary explaining the divine craftsmanship of the Ribhus.</summary>
<keywords>Maruts, Agni, Ribhus, Vibhva, rain-bringers, heroic son, Varunapraghasa sacrifice, Vedic ritual, Sayana's commentary, Sanskrit translation</keywords>

<meta>This page continues the translation of the 5th Mandala of the Rig Veda, specifically the 58th hymn (Sukta) dedicated to the Maruts, the storm deities. The previous page concluded the commentary on Verse 4, which spoke of the Maruts granting heroic sons and kings to the people. This page presents Verses 5 and 6, which emphasize the perfect equality of the Maruts and the physical impact of their celestial procession on the natural world.</meta>

-> ॥ Now the Fifth Verse ॥ <-

## Hymn Text

Like spokes [of a wheel], none among them is last; like days, they are [all equal]. They are born in great splendor, accompanied by prayers. These sons of Prishni <note>the mother of the Maruts, often identified with the mottled earth or the rain-cloud</note> are equal to one another and most impetuous. By their own will, the Maruts have sprinkled [the earth]. ॥ 5 ॥

**Like spokes | indeed | not last | like days | forth-forth | they are born | accompanied by prayers | with greatness |**
**Of Prishni | sons | equal to each other | most impetuous | by their own | will | the Maruts | together | they have sprinkled. ॥ 5 ॥**

---

## Commentary (Sayana)

**Like spokes:** Just like the spokes of a chariot wheel <note>original: "ratha-śaṅkavaḥ"</note>, they are "not last" <note>original: "acaramāḥ"</note>, meaning none is inferior to the other. The sense is that they are all equal and were born at the very same time.

**Like days:** Just as all days are comprised of sixty *ghatikas* <note>a traditional Indian unit of time, approximately 24 minutes</note>, they are equal in their prowess and their majestic forms. Through these two metaphors—the spokes and the days—the poet establishes that there is no inequality among them.

Characterized in this way, they **emerge forth** with their "greatness" or splendors. The repetition of the word "forth" <note>original: "pra pra"</note> is used here to fill out the meter of the verse. They are **accompanied by prayers**, meaning they are not few in number. Alternatively, this may be an adjective for "greatness."

They are the **sons of Prishni**—Prishni being the "middle speech" in the form of a cow, or the atmosphere itself. They are **equal to one another** and possess **the greatest speed**. These Maruts of great dignity **have sprinkled** the earth with rain through their own **gracious intent**.

---

-> ॥ Now the Sixth Verse ॥ <-

## Hymn Text

O Maruts, when you go forth with your dappled steeds and your chariots with strong rims, the waters flow, the forests give way; let the ruddy bull, the sky, roar [for rain]. ॥ 6 ॥

**When | forth | you went | with dappled ones | with horses | with strong rims | Maruts | with chariots |**
**They flow | waters | they give way | forests | down | the ruddy | the bull | let him roar | the sky. ॥ 6 ॥**

---

## Commentary (Sayana)

O Maruts, **when you go forth** with your **dappled steeds**—the horses that serve as your means of transport. The word for "horse" here <note>original: "aśva"</note> is used as a general term for any vehicle or mount, which is why it appears in the masculine form. We see a similar usage in other verses, such as:
> "When you yoked the dappled mares to the poles..." <note>original: Rig Veda 5.55.6</note>

The terms "red-horsed" and "goat-horsed" are used in similar contexts. You go forth with **chariots** that have **strong rims** <note>original: "vīḷupavibhiḥ," meaning wheels with firm tires</note>. When the Maruts travel with these horses and chariots, then the **waters flow** or leak out. The **forests**, or groups of trees, **give way**; they are struck and broken by the sheer speed of the Maruts' movement.

The **ruddy** one—referring to the sun's rays—and the **bull** associated with them (the rain-cloud or *Parjanya* who pours the waters), let that shining **sky roar** downward to bring about the rain.

<summary>This page describes the Maruts as a perfectly equal brotherhood, likened to wheel spokes and days, and details how their chariot procession causes the waters to flow and the skies to thunder.</summary>
<keywords>Maruts, Prishni, equality, chariot, rain, Parjanya, atmospheric deities, Vedic metaphors</keywords>

<meta>This page continues the 5th Mandala of the Rig Veda, concluding Hymn 59 and beginning Hymn 60. Both hymns are dedicated to the Maruts, the storm-gods. The translation maintains continuity with the previous page's focus on the Maruts' divine power and their physical manifestation as storm phenomena.</meta>

## Hymn Text

-> ॥ Now the Seventh Verse ॥ <-

**The Earth expanded during their journey, for they placed their strength like a husband [places] his own offspring. The sons of Rudra yoked the winds as horses to the pole; they made the rain their sweat. ॥ 7 ॥**

**Expanded | during the journey | the Earth | indeed | of them | like a husband | the offspring | his own | certainly | strength | they placed |**
**The winds | for | the horses | to the pole | they yoked | the rain | sweat | they made | the sons of Rudra. ॥ 7 ॥**

---

## Commentary (Sayana)

**The Earth expanded:** During the **journey** or the movement of these Maruts, the **Earth** <note>original: "pṛthivī"</note>, even the ground itself, became wide and famous. The sense is that she became fit to receive the "offspring." These Maruts **placed** their **strength**, which in this context means water, just as a **husband** <note>original: "bhartā"</note> or protector in the world places the **offspring** or fetus within his wife. Thus, the water acts as the seed within the womb of the Earth.

**They yoked the winds:** Because they have **yoked** the **winds**, which are the travelers of the sky, like **horses** to the **pole** <note>original: "dhuri"</note> of their chariot, the **sons of Rudra** <note>term: Rudriyasah — a common epithet for the Maruts, identifying them as the children of the storm-god Rudra</note> produce the falling rain, which is described here as their **sweat**.

---

## Hymn Text

-> ॥ Now the Eighth Verse ॥ <-

**O men, O Maruts, have mercy on us, you who are of great wealth, immortal, and knowers of Truth. You who hear the truth, you who are seers, young, of great speech, and great in your sprinkling. ॥ 8 ॥**

**I invoke | O men | O Maruts | have mercy | on us | you of great wealth | O immortals | knowers of Truth |**
**Who hear the truth | O seers | O young ones | of great speech | greatly | sprinkling. ॥ 8 ॥**

**The eighth verse, "O men," is completed. ॥**

-> ॥ Thus ends the twenty-third section of the third chapter of the fourth book ॥ <-

## Introductory Notes (Sukta 60)

The third hymn [of this section], beginning with "To you who see," consists of eight verses. The Seer is **Shyavashva** <note>a prominent Vedic Rishi of the Atri family</note>, and the deity is the **Maruts**. The eighth verse is in the **Trishtup** meter <note>a meter of 44 syllables</note>, while the remaining seven are in the **Jagati** meter <note>a meter of 48 syllables</note>. The **Anukramanika** <note>an ancient index of Vedic hymns</note> states: "The hymn 'To you who see' ends with a Trishtup." The ritual application of this hymn is determined by its specific characteristics.

---

## Hymn Text

-> ॥ There, the First Verse ॥ <-

**I bring forth truth for Heaven and Earth, for your prosperity, to the Giver, to him who makes things visible. They sprinkle the horses as they cross through the atmosphere; they relax their own radiance with the floods. ॥ 1 ॥**

**Forth | for you | visible | he made | for prosperity | for the Giver | I pray | to Heaven | forth | for Earth | truth | I bring |**
**They sprinkle | the horses | they cross | through | the atmosphere | according to | their own | radiance | they relax | with the floods. ॥ 1 ॥**

<meta>This page is from the Max Müller edition of the Rig Veda with Sayana's commentary. It completes the explanation for hymn 5.59.1 and provides the full text and commentary for verse 2 and the start of verse 3. The previous page established the Maruts as powerful storm deities; this page continues that theme, comparing their movement to a heavy ship and their appearance to the rising sun.</meta>

### Page 492 || Rig Veda || [Book 4, Chapter 3, Section 24]

## Commentary (Sayana)
<note>This concludes the commentary on verse 5.59.1</note>
O Maruts, for you, for the sake of the well-attained giving of the oblation, the priest <note>original: "hotā"</note> has cried out—that is, he praises you. Or, he has cried out for you for the sake of well-attained giving. <note>The commentator notes that the word "akran" (cried out) is a past tense form used here with the meaning of the present tense.</note> O priest, praise the one who shines in the bright sky <note>original: "dyudeva"</note>; O Soul, praise him excellently. Furthermore, I prepare the praise of the Earth which has been heard. Both Heaven and Earth are recipients of the Maruts' influence because they serve as the foundation for them. Moreover, those Maruts moisten the "stones"—the clouds that contain a mass of water. They traverse the atmosphere, moving everywhere. They loosen their own radiance along with the ocean-clouds; they bring it into harmony with them.

---

-> ॥ Now the Second Verse ॥ <-

## Hymn Text
**Through fear of their approach, the Earth trembles like a full ship that wavers as it sails. Visible from afar, they are recognized by their movements; these leaders have exerted themselves within the great assembly for the sake of the sacrifice. ॥ 2 ॥**

**Pada-patha:**
**At their approach | of them | through fear | the Earth | trembles | ship | like | full | wavers | distressed | going |**
**visible from afar | who | are recognized | by their movements | within | for the great | assembly | have exerted | the leaders. ॥ 2 ॥**

---

## Commentary (Sayana)
**Of these:** Through fear of these Maruts, the **Earth** <note>original: "bhūmi"</note> **trembles** or shakes. It is **like a ship full** of living beings; just as such a vessel **wavers** and moves unsteadily while **going** through the water, being distressed by the waves. Both these terms—"wavering" and "going"—are adjectives describing the ship. **Visible from afar:** Although the Maruts are seen from a great distance, they **are recognized** by their **movements** or travels. These great Maruts, who are the **leaders** <note>original: "naraḥ"</note>, have **exerted** themselves **within** the space between Heaven and Earth for the **great assembly** <note>term: vidatha — an ancient Vedic term for a gathering, often for religious or sacrificial purposes</note> and for the sake of the great oblation.

---

-> ॥ Now the Third Verse ॥ <-

## Hymn Text
**For the sake of beauty, you wear an excellent head-dress like the horn of cows; like the Sun, you are the eye in the releasing of the mists. Like well-born, beautiful horses, you are graceful; O leaders, you reflect for glory like young men. ॥ 3 ॥**

**Pada-patha:**
**Of cows | like | for beauty | horn | excellent | the Sun | like | eye | of the mist | in the releasing |**
**horses | like | well-born | beautiful | you are | young men | like | for beauty | you reflect | the leaders. ॥ 3 ॥**

---

## Commentary (Sayana)
O Maruts, for the sake of **beauty** or splendor, you wear an **excellent** and superior **head-dress** <note>term: uṣṇīṣa — a turban or ritual head-wrap</note> or similar ornament, which is compared here to the **horn of cows**. **Like the Sun:** Just as the Sun, as the means of sight, holds his solar disk for the **releasing** of his radiance and light, so too do you, for the releasing of the rain-mists, possess light that illuminates everything...

<vocab>
मरुत् (Marut) — Storm deities, often described as a troop of young warriors.
भूमि (Bhūmi) — The Earth, personified as a goddess who reacts to the gods' movements.
नौ (Nau) — A boat or ship, used here in a rare Vedic metaphor for stability and movement.
यज्ञ (Yajña) — The central Vedic ritual of sacrifice and offering.
विदथ (Vidatha) — A communal assembly or sacrificial gathering of the tribe.
सूर्य (Sūrya) — The Sun god, the ultimate source of light and vision.
उष्णीष (Uṣṇīṣa) — A turban or head-dress, signifying status or festive preparation.
</vocab>

<summary>This page describes the awesome power of the Maruts (storm gods), whose approach makes the Earth tremble like a heavily laden ship at sea. It also highlights their beauty and radiance, comparing their ritual ornaments to horns and their light to the Sun.</summary>
<keywords>Maruts, Earth, Ship Metaphor, Sacrifice, Sun, Ornamentation, Vedic Ritual</keywords>

### Page 483 || Rig Veda || [Fourth Octad]

## Commentary (Sayana)
<note>This concludes the commentary on verse 3 from the previous page.</note>
...you support. You are like steeds, like horses, being well-formed <note>original: "subhavaḥ"</note>—that is, being present everywhere—and you are swift, beautiful, and pleasant to look upon. You are like mortals <note>original: "maryāḥ"</note>, like the human sacrificers. Just as they understand the sacrifice and other rites for the sake of glory, so you, O leaders <note>original: "naro"</note>, O Maruts <note>the storm deities</note>, strive for glory.

---

## Hymn Text

->॥ Now the Fourth Verse ॥<-

**Who among the great ones can attain your greatness? Who, O Maruts, your wisdom? Who indeed your heroic deeds? Truly, you shake the earth like a ray of light, when you prepare yourselves for the giving of good fortune. ॥ 4 ॥**

**Word-for-word text (Pada-patha):**
**Who | of you | the great things | of the great ones | up | attains | who | the wisdom | O Maruts | who | indeed | the heroic deeds |**
**You | indeed | the earth | a ray of light | like | shake | forward | when | you prepare yourselves | for good fortune | for the giving ॥ 4 ॥**

---

## Commentary (Sayana)

O Maruts, who among the sacrificers can attain <note>or "reach"</note> the great and excellent qualities of you, who are worshipful and great? And who, for that purpose, can attain the wisdom <note>original: "kāvyā"</note>—the poetic hymns of the sages—associated with you? Who indeed can reach your heroic deeds <note>original: "pauṃsyā"</note>? The repetition of "who" is for the sake of emphasis. 

Indeed, you shake the earth like a ray of light <note>original: "kiraṇam na"</note>. Just as you set the rays in motion for the sake of rain, so you shake the earth. Alternatively, the text means: you prepare the rain for the giving <note>original: "dāvane"</note> of well-attained wealth or rain-water. Because you act in this way, it is said that "he acts thus."

---

## Hymn Text

->॥ Now the Fifth Verse ॥<-

**Like horses, they are the shining ones, of the same lineage; like warriors, they have fought in the battles. Like vigorous young men, the leaders have grown strong; they obscure the eye of the Sun with their rains. ॥ 5 ॥**

**Word-for-word text (Pada-patha):**
**Horses | like | indeed | the shining ones | of the same lineage | warriors | like | fighters | forward | and | have fought |**
**Young men | like | well-growing | have grown strong | the leaders | of the Sun | the eye | forward | they obscure | by rains ॥ 5 ॥**

---

## Commentary (Sayana)

These Maruts are like horses because they move swiftly. They are the shining ones <note>original: "aruṣāsaḥ"</note> and are "of the same lineage" <note>original: "sabandhavaḥ"</note> because they have one common father, Rudra <note>the storm-god and father of the Maruts</note>, who binds them together, or because they are bound to one another by affection. Like warriors or soldiers who are fighters against enemies, they have indeed fought <note>original: "pra yuyudhuḥ"</note>—that is, they fight with great force.

Just as men grow in strength, so have these leaders <note>original: "naraḥ"</note>—who are either growing well themselves or causing others to grow—grown strong. These great souls, by means of their rains, obscure <note>original: "pra minanti"</note> the "eye of the Sun," which is the mass of light or the solar orb itself. This means they cover the sun with clouds.

<note>
**Technical Terms:**
- **Maruts:** The storm-deities, sons of Rudra, known for their collective power and beauty.
- **Rudra:** An early Vedic deity associated with storms and the father of the Maruts.
- **Yajamana:** The person who institutes or sponsors a Vedic sacrifice.
- **Kavya:** Wisdom or the inspired poetry of a seer (Kavi).
</note>

### || Rig Veda || [4th Octad, 3rd Lesson, 24th Section]

->॥ Now the Sixth Verse ॥<-

## Hymn Text

**Among them, none is the eldest, none the youngest, and none the middle-most; they have grown together in greatness. Well-born by their birth, children of the dappled cloud-mother <note>original: "pṛśnimātaro"</note>, O men <note>original: "maryāḥ"; here referring to the Maruts as heroic beings</note>, come to us from the heavens. ॥ 6 ॥**

**Word-for-word text (Pada-patha):**
**They | not-eldest | not-youngest | the piercers | not-middle-most | by greatness | thoroughly | have grown |**
**Well-born | by birth | children of Prisni | from heaven | O men | hither | to us | towards | come. ॥ 6 ॥**

---

## Commentary (Sayana)

Those Maruts are "not-eldest" <note>original: "ajyeṣṭhā"</note>, "not-youngest" <note>original: "akaniṣṭhāso"</note>, and "not-middle-most" <note>original: "amadhyamāso"</note>; they are all equal in every way. They are the "piercers" <note>original: "udbhidaḥ"</note>, meaning they are the destroyers of enemies. They have grown <note>original: "vivavṛdhuḥ"</note>—that is, they increase—through their "greatness" or splendor <note>original: "mahasā"</note>. 

You Maruts are "well-born" <note>original: "sujātāsaḥ"</note>, having come into being in an excellent manner, and by your "birth" <note>original: "januṣā"</note> you are "children of Prisni" <note>original: "pṛśnimātaraḥ"; Prisni is the dappled cow representing the earth or the clouds</note>. O "men" <note>original: "maryāḥ"</note>, you who are beneficial to human beings, come <note>original: "jigātana"</note> towards us from the vicinity of the heavens. Praise us from all sides, saying "this was performed well." 

<note>Sayana offers an alternative interpretation for the second half of the verse</note>: Alternatively, the second half of the verse is addressed directly to the priests. O heroic priests <note>original: "maryāḥ"</note>, you should approach <note>original: "ājigātana"</note> those Maruts who are well-born by birth and children of Prisni, as they have come from heaven; let them come toward us.

---

->॥ Now the Seventh Verse ॥<-

## Hymn Text

**Like birds <note>original: "vayo na"</note> in rows, they have filled the ends of the vast sky by their strength, from the ridge of the high heavens. Their horses <note>original: "aśvāsaḥ"</note> have shaken the moisture from the clouds, so that both <note>gods and men</note> may know. ॥ 7 ॥**

**Word-for-word text (Pada-patha):**
**Birds | like | who | rows | have filled | by strength | the ends | of heaven | of the great | of the ridge | from |**
**Horses | of these | both | as | they know | forward | of the mountain | the moisture-vapors | they have shaken. ॥ 7 ॥**

---

## Commentary (Sayana)

Those Maruts, who are like "birds" <note>original: "vayo na"</note> flying in "rows" or ranks <note>original: "śreṇīḥ"</note>, have "filled" or traversed <note>original: "paprūḥ"</note> the "ends" <note>perimeters</note> of the "heaven" <note>the atmosphere or the solar region</note> by their "strength" <note>original: "ojasā"</note>. They move all around the "ridge" <note>original: "sānunaḥ"</note> of the high, great circle of the sky. 

The "horses" of these Maruts have "shaken" <note>original: "acucyavuḥ"</note> or caused to fall the "moisture-vapors" <note>original: "nabhanūn"; derived from the root 'bhan' meaning to sound, similar to 'nabhas'</note> of the "mountain" <note>original: "parvatasya"; here used as a metaphor for the clouds</note>. They do this in such a way that "both" <note>original: "ubhaye"</note>—meaning both gods and men—"know" <note>original: "viduḥ"</note> or recognize it. 

The knowledge of men is well-known <note>as they see the rain</note>. The gods also "know" by the offering of the oblation in the *Agrayana* sacrifice <note>a harvest festival</note> once the rain has fallen. This realization of the gods regarding the completion of the rain is mentioned by the sage Ashvalayana: "When one is satisfied by the rain, one should sacrifice with the *Agrayana*... for the gods indeed say, 'He is surely satisfied with the rain, for he sacrifices with the *Agrayana*'" <note>original: "Ashvalayana Shrauta Sutra 2.9"</note>.

<vocab>
**Maruts** (storm deities), **ajyeṣṭhāḥ** (not older/none senior), **akaniṣṭhāsaḥ** (not younger/none junior), **pṛśnimātaraḥ** (children of the dappled cloud-cow Prisni), **marya** (heroic man/mortal), **śreṇī** (rows/organized lines), **ojas** (vital strength/power), **aśvāsaḥ** (horses/the winds of the storm), **nabhanūn** (waters or vapors released from clouds), **āgrāyaṇa** (the first-fruits sacrifice performed after the rainy season)
</vocab>

<summary>This page describes the Maruts as a unified brotherhood of equal status who fly through the sky like birds in formation. Their power releases rain from the clouds, an event celebrated by both humans and gods through the Agrayana harvest sacrifice.</summary>
<keywords>Maruts, equality, Prisni, rain cycle, Agrayana sacrifice, Ashvalayana, Vedic metaphors, storm deities</keywords>

[Page 495]
म० ५. अ० ५. सू० ६०.] ॥ Fourth Octad ॥ ४९५

-> ॥ Now the Eighth Verse ॥ <-

## Hymn Text

**May the Sky and the Infinite One <note>original: "aditiḥ"</note> create for our enjoyment; let the Dawns, bright with gifts, strive together. These Maruts, being praised by the seer, have shaken down the heavenly vessel <note>original: "kośam"; refers here to a rain-cloud</note> of Rudra. ॥ ८ ॥**

**Word-for-word text (Pada-patha):**
**May-create | the Sky | the Infinite | for enjoyment | for us | Together | the givers | the bright ones | the Dawns | may-they-strive |**
**Hither | they-have-shaken-down | the heavenly | vessel | these | O Seer | of Rudra | the Maruts | being-praised. ॥ ८ ॥**

---

## Commentary (Sayana)

For us, may "the Sky" <note>original: "dyauḥ"</note>, meaning the atmosphere, "create" <note>original: "mimātu"</note> or produce rain; let it make conditions favorable. What is the nature of the sky? It is "the Infinite" <note>original: "aditiḥ"</note>, meaning it is not meager or limited. Alternatively, may the Sky and the Earth (Aditi) create happiness. For what purpose? For "enjoyment" <note>original: "vītaye"</note>, which refers to the production or procreation of life. May "the Dawns" <note>original: "uṣasaḥ"</note>, who are "givers" <note>original: "dānūn"</note> of wonderful light, strive together. O "Seer" <note>original: "ṛṣe"</note>, the "Maruts" being praised by you—who are the sons of "Rudra"—have "shaken down" <note>original: "ācucyavuḥ"</note> or caused to flow "the heavenly vessel" <note>original: "divyaṃ kośam"</note>, which refers to the cloud filled with water. The verb used here <note>original: "ā-cyu"</note> implies a double action.

-> ॥ Thus ends the twenty-fourth section of the third lesson in the fourth [Octad] ॥ <-

The fourth hymn, beginning with "I praise Agni, the well-protecting," consists of eight verses and is seen by the Rishi Shyavashva. The seventh and eighth verses are in the Jagati meter <note>a meter of 48 syllables</note>, while the remaining six are in the Trishtubh meter <note>a meter of 44 syllables</note>. The deity addressed is either the Maruts or Agni-and-the-Maruts together. Alternatively, the hymn is dedicated to Agni up until the final two Jagati verses. The application of the hymn in ritual is according to its characteristics. The first verse is used as the invitation prayer <note>original: "yājyā"</note> for the kindling-verses in the Kariri sacrifice <note>a specific ritual performed to bring rain</note>. This is indicated in the ritual manuals: "I praise Agni, the well-protecting, with salutations" is the supporting verse <note>original: "dhāyyā"</note> (Asvalayana Srauta Sutra 2.13).

-> ॥ This is the First Verse ॥ <-

## Hymn Text

**I praise Agni, the well-protecting, with salutations; may he, being seated here and well-pleased, distinguish our work. Like with chariots seeking spoils, I bring forward the praise; going clockwise, may I increase the hymn of the Maruts. ॥ १ ॥**

**Word-for-word text (Pada-patha):**
**I-praise | Agni | the well-protecting | with salutations | here | being-seated | thoroughly | may-he-distinguish | the work | ours |**
**With chariots | like | forward | I-bring | seeking-spoils | going-clockwise | of the Maruts | the hymn | may-I-increase. ॥ १ ॥**

---

## Commentary (Sayana)

I, Shyavashva, "praise" <note>original: "īḷe"</note> "Agni" who is "well-protecting" <note>original: "svavasam"</note>—meaning protection is under his own control—with "salutations" or hymns. May he "distinguish" <note>original: "vi cayat"</note> or take notice of the "work" or ritual we have performed here, while "being seated" <note>original: "prasattaḥ"</note>—meaning he is well-pleased or has arrived at the sacrifice. Just as one reaches a desired goal "with chariots" <note>original: "rathairiva"</note>, I "bring forward" <note>original: "pra bhare"</note> or produce the hymns which act as the means of attainment. "Going clockwise" <note>original: "pradakṣiṇan"</note>, meaning proceeding in a favorable or respectful manner, "may I increase" <note>original: "ṛdhyām"</note> the "hymn" <note>original: "stomaṃ"</note> of the "Maruts."

<note>VOL. III. 6 H</note>

<vocab>
- मरुतः (Maruts): Storm deities, sons of Rudra, known for their collective power and bringing rain.
- अग्नि (Agni): The sacrificial Fire deity who acts as the intermediary between humans and gods.
- श्यावाश्व (Shyavashva): The Seer (Rishi) to whom these hymns were revealed.
- स्तोम (Stoma): A song or hymn of praise used in Vedic rituals.
- अदिति (Aditi): Representing infinite consciousness or the Earth; here invoked to provide bounty.
- कोश (Kosha): Literally a 'chest' or 'vessel,' used metaphorically for a rain-cloud.
- कारीरी (Kariri): A specialized Vedic sacrifice performed specifically to end drought and bring rain.
</vocab>

<keywords>Maruts, Agni, Shyavashva, rain ritual, Kariri sacrifice, Vedic meter, Aditi, Rudra's cloud</keywords>
