While the previous provided page discussed Hymn 60, this section focuses on the Maruts (storm deities) and their terrifying power over nature. We move from verse 2 through verse 4 of this hymn, focusing on the imagery of the Maruts' chariots and their spears.</meta>

[Page 466]
## Rig Veda ## [Book 5, Chapter 4, Section 25]

## Hymn Text

-> ॥ Now the Second Verse ॥ <-

Those Maruts, the sons of the Storm God <note>original: "rudrā"</note>, who have mounted their famous spotted deer <note>original: "pṛṣatīṣu"</note> and their easy-gliding chariots—before your fear, even the forests bow down, the earth herself trembles, and even the mountain shakes. ॥ २ ॥

**Word-for-word text (Pada-patha):**
**Hither | those-who | have-mounted | the spotted-deer | the famous-ones | the easy-gliding | the sons-of-Rudra | the Maruts | on-chariots |**
**The forests | even | the fierce-ones | they-bow-down | down | your | by-fear | the earth | even | trembles | the mountain | even. ॥ २ ॥**

---

## Commentary (Sayana)

Those Maruts who are the sons of Rudra <note>original: "rudra-putrā"</note> mount <note>original: "ā-tasthuḥ"</note> the "spotted deer" <note>original: "pṛṣatīṣu"</note>, which are the traditional mounts or vehicles of the Maruts. These deer are "famous" <note>original: "śrutāsu"</note> or well-known. They mount "easy-gliding" <note>original: "su-kheṣu"</note> chariots. Here, the word for "easy-gliding" <note>original: "kha"</note> refers to the sky or the space, but specifically here it means the holes <note>original: "chidram"</note> in the chariot's axle-hubs which are well-fitted, allowing for smooth movement. O "fierce ones" <note>original: "ugrā"</note> of intense strength, when you are mounted on your chariots, then even the "forests" <note>original: "vanā cit"</note> "bow down" <note>original: "ni jihate"</note> or bend low out of "fear" <note>original: "bhiyā"</note> of you. The "earth" <note>original: "pṛthivī cit"</note> also trembles, and even the "mountain" <note>original: "parvataścit"</note> trembles or shakes. The second half of this verse is addressed directly to the gods. In the first half, the priest indicates: "We shall increase the praise-song of those who act in this way."

In the *Kariri* sacrifice <note>a ritual performed to bring rain</note>, when offering a seven-layered cake to the Maruts, the phrase "Even the mountain..." is used as the sacrificial prayer <note>original: "yājyā"</note>. This is indicated in the liturgical manuals: "Even the mountain, though great and ancient, feared... (Ashvalayana Shrauta Sutra 2.13)."

---

## Hymn Text

-> ॥ This is the Third Verse ॥ <-

Even the mountain, though great and ancient, feared; even the ridge of the sky trembled at your roar. When you, O Maruts, armed with spears <note>original: "ṛṣṭimantaḥ"</note>, play together, you rush forward like waters moving toward a single point. ॥ ३ ॥

**Word-for-word text (Pada-patha):**
**The mountain | even | great | ancient | feared | the sky's | even | ridge | trembles | at-the-roar | your |**
**When | you-play | O Maruts | armed-with-spears | like-waters | together-moving | you-rush-forward. ॥ ३ ॥**

---

## Commentary (Sayana)

O Maruts, when your "roar" <note>original: "svane"</note>—that terrifying thunder—occurs, even the "mountain" <note>original: "parvataścit"</note>, though it is "great" <note>original: "mahi"</note> and "ancient" <note>original: "vṛddhaḥ"</note>, "feared" <note>original: "bibhāya"</note> or became afraid. Even the "ridge" <note>original: "sānu"</note> or the highest elevated region of the "sky" <note>original: "divaścit"</note>—the atmosphere—"trembles" <note>original: "rejate"</note>. Whenever you "play" <note>original: "krīḷatha"</note>, O Maruts, being "armed with spears" <note>original: "ṛṣṭimantaḥ"</note> or possessing weapons, you "rush forward" <note>original: "dhavadhve"</note> like "waters" <note>original: "āpa iva"</note> that are "moving together" <note>original: "sad hryañcaḥ"</note> or flowing toward the same goal.

---

## Hymn Text

-> ॥ Now the Fourth Verse ॥ <-

Like noble suitors <note>original: "varā iva"</note>, the divine ones have adorned their bodies with gold ornaments and with their own inherent powers. For the sake of beauty, the most excellent and powerful ones, together in their chariots, have placed glorious forms upon their persons. ॥ ४ ॥

<meta>This page continues the commentary and word-by-word analysis of Hymn 60 in the 5th Mandala of the Rig Veda. The previous page established the Maruts as fierce storm deities; here, the focus shifts to their shared splendor, their egalitarian nature, and their divine parentage.</meta>

[Mandala 5, Anuvaka 5, Hymn 60] || Fourth Ashtaka || 497

## Hymn Text

<note>Analysis of the word-by-word components (Pada-patha) for Rig Veda 5.60.4</note>
Like suitors | indeed | the wealthy ones | with gold ornaments | together | with their own powers | their bodies | they have adorned |
For beauty | the most excellent | the mighty ones | in their chariots | together | splendors | they have made | in their bodies ॥ 4 ॥

---

## Commentary (Sayana)

**Like suitors** <note>original: "varā iva"</note> refers to young men ready for marriage. Just as such **wealthy ones** <note>original: "raivatāso"</note> decorate **their bodies** with **gold** jewelry and perfumes <note>original: "svadhābhiḥ" - here interpreted by Sayana as water or cooling unguents</note>, so too do these Maruts. They are wealthy and they adorn their bodies with "gold" in the form of lightning and with "self-power" in the form of rain waters. For the sake of **beauty** or splendor, the **most excellent** and **mighty** Maruts have **made splendors** or held onto their brilliance **in their bodies** while gathered **together in their chariots**. The meaning is that, equipped with all ornaments and waters, they occupy their chariots and radiate light from their very forms.

-> || Now the Fifth Verse || <-

## Hymn Text

<note>Rig Veda 5.60.5</note>
None of them is the eldest, none the youngest; these brothers have grown together for prosperity. Their father is the youthful, noble-acting Rudra, and their mother is Prishni, who yields abundance and provides fair days for the Maruts. ॥ 5 ॥

> **None-eldest | none-youngest | these | together | brothers | they-have-grown | for-prosperity |**
> **Youthful | father | of-noble-work | Rudra | of-them | easy-to-milk | Prishni | fair-days | for-the-Maruts ॥ 5 ॥**

---

## Commentary (Sayana)

**None is eldest, none is youngest** <note>original: "ajyeṣṭhāso'kaniṣṭhāsaḥ"</note> means that among them, there is no hierarchy of older or younger; they were all born at the same time and possess equal strength. **These** Maruts, being **brothers** to one another, **have grown together** or prospered for the sake of **prosperity** <note>original: "saubhagāya"</note>. Their **father** is **Rudra**, who is eternally **youthful** and **of noble work**. Their mother is **Prishni** <note>represented as the dappled earth-cow</note>, who is **easy to milk** (abundant). She, along with Rudra, created **fair days** for the sake of the **Maruts**.

-> || Now the Sixth Verse || <-

## Hymn Text

<note>Rig Veda 5.60.6</note>
Whether you are in the highest heaven, O Maruts, or in the middle, or in the lowest, O blessed ones; from there, O Rudras, and also from here, O Agni, acknowledge this offering which we sacrifice. ॥ 6 ॥

> **Whether | in-the-highest | Maruts | in-the-middle | or | whether | or | in-the-lowest | O-blessed-ones | in-heaven | you-are |**
> **From-thence | our | O-Rudras | and | or | now | of-this | O-Agni | acknowledge | the-oblation | which | we-sacrifice ॥ 6 ॥**

---

## Commentary (Sayana)

O **Maruts**, **whether** you **are** in the **highest** or most excellent **heaven**, **or in the middle heaven, or in the lowest heaven**, O **blessed ones**. These three worlds are threefold—
<note>Text breaks off at the end of the page</note>

<summary>This page describes the Maruts as an egalitarian brotherhood of storm deities, born simultaneously and adorned with lightning-gold. It identifies their parents as the fierce god Rudra and the earth-cow Prishni, and begins an invocation for them to attend a sacrifice regardless of which layer of heaven they occupy.</summary>

<meta>This page concludes the commentary on verse 6 and provides the full text and explanation for verses 7 and 8 of Mandala 5, Hymn 60. The focus is on the collaborative relationship between Agni (the Fire-god) and the Maruts (the Storm-gods) as they descend from the highest heavens to receive offerings.</meta>

...From the scripture stating "the three heavens and the three earths," we understand the three-fold nature of the celestial realm. Therefore, from this triple-layered space, the phrase "come for our sake, O <term>Rudras</term> <note>original: "rudrāḥ"; the Maruts are frequently called the sons of Rudra</note>" is implied to complete the thought. "Or indeed" <note>original: "uta vā"</note>, even today, whatever sacrifice we perform and whatever oblation we cast into the fire, O Agni, you who are the knower of this oblation—be aware of it.

---

-> ॥ Now the Seventh Verse ॥ <-

## Hymn Text
When you, O **Agni**, and the **Maruts**, the **all-knowing ones**, travel from the **highest heaven** above the **ridges**,
May you all, **rejoicing**, **shakers of enemies**, and **destroyers of the injurious**, grant **precious wealth** to the **sacrificer** who **presses the Soma**. ॥ 7 ॥

**Word-by-word Analysis (Pada-patha):**
Agni | and | when | Maruts | all-knowing | heaven | you travel | highest | from/above | ridges |
they | rejoicing | shakers | destroyers of the injurious | precious-wealth | grant | to the sacrificer | who presses [Soma] ॥ 7 ॥

---

## Commentary (Sayana)
O **all-knowing** <note>original: "viśvavedasaḥ"; those who know all things or possess all wealth</note> Maruts! When you and **Agni** travel from the **highest** or most excellent **heaven**, moving over the **ridges** <note>original: "snubhiḥ"; literally the "peaks" or "surface" of the clouds/heavens</note>, it means you dwell in those high places. Alternatively, the word "ridges" can refer to **horses** that resemble mountain peaks; you travel by them. You all, **rejoicing** and being delighted by our hymns and oblations, being **shakers** <note>original: "dhunayaḥ"</note> who cause enemies to tremble, and being **destroyers of the injurious** <note>original: "riśādasaḥ"</note>—those who consume our enemies—grant **precious** and desirable **wealth** to the **sacrificer** who is currently **pressing** or extracting the Soma juice.

## Critical Notes
The eighth verse, "O Agni, with the Maruts," is the concluding prayer for the <term>Agnimaruta</term> <note>A specific ritual sequence involving both Agni and the Maruts</note> ceremony.
> O Agni, with the Maruts, the beautifying ones, the singers of hymns...
As indicated in the <term>Ashvalayana Shrauta Sutra</term> (5.20).

---

-> ॥ Now the Eighth Verse ॥ <-

## Hymn Text
O **Agni**, with the **Maruts** who bring **beauty**, who are **endowed with hymns**, drink the **Soma** while **rejoicing** with those who **resort to the troop**.
With the **purifying** ones, the **all-pervading** ones, the **vigorous** ones, O **Vaishvanara**, be **in union** with your **ancient banner**. ॥ 8 ॥

**Word-by-word Analysis (Pada-patha):**
Agni | with Maruts | beautifying | endowed with hymns | Soma | drink | rejoicing | resorting to the troop |
purifying | all-pervading | vigorous | Vaishvanara | with the ancient | banner | in union ॥ 8 ॥

---

## Commentary (Sayana)
O **Agni**, being in a state of **rejoicing**, drink the **Soma** juice together with the **Maruts**. What kind of Maruts? They are **beautifying** <note>original: "śubhayadbhiḥ"</note>, meaning they are either shining themselves or making others look beautiful. They are **endowed with hymns** <note>original: "ṛkvabhiḥ"</note>, worthy of praise. They are **resorting to the troop** <note>original: "gaṇaśribhiḥ"</note>, meaning they remain together in their celestial assembly. They are **purifying** <note>original: "pāvakebhiḥ"</note>, and **all-pervading** <note>original: "viśvaminvebhiḥ"</note>, meaning they satisfy the whole world with rain. They are **vigorous** or long-lived. O **Vaishvanara** <note>original: "vaiśvānara"; a title for Agni as "belonging to all men"</note>, you who are beneficial to all people, be **in union** with your **ancient banner** <note>original: "pradivā ketunā"</note>, which refers to your eternal mass of flames.

<meta>This page transitions from the end of the commentary on Sukta 60 to the beginning of Sukta 61 of the Fifth Mandala. It introduces a new hymn attributed to the Rishi Syavashva and provides a lengthy legendary narrative (itihasa) explaining the circumstances of the hymn's composition.</meta>

# Mandala 5, Anuvaka 5, Sukta 61 | The Fourth Book (Ashtaka)

## Anukramani (Introductory Notes)

The fifth <term>Sukta</term> <note>hymn</note>, beginning with the words **"Who are you, O heroes,"** consists of nineteen verses. According to the <term>Anukramani</term> <note>the ancient index of authors, meters, and deities</note>: **"Who are you"** has nineteen verses in the **Gayatri** meter; the <term>Rishi</term> <note>inspired seer/author</note> is Syavashva, the son of Archananas. The hymn praises the Maruts, but also mentions the kings Taranta and Purumilha (sons of Vidadashva), as well as Rathaviti (son of Dalbhya) and Taranta’s queen, Shashiyasi, out of gratitude for their gifts. The fifth verse is in the **Anushtubh** meter, the ninth is **Satobrihati**, and the rest are **Gayatri**. 

The first four verses are addressed to the **Maruts** <note>the storm deities</note>. The next four verses (starting with "She who...") are addressed to **Shashiyasi**, the wife of King Taranta. The verse "And let him speak to me..." is addressed to **Purumilha**. The verse "He who [gave] of my cows..." is addressed to King **Taranta**. The six verses beginning "Those who carry..." return to the **Maruts**. The final three verses (the <term>Tricha</term> <note>a triplet of verses</note>) are addressed to King **Rathaviti Dalbhya**. The ritual application is determined by the specific deity mentioned in each section.

---

## Commentary (Sayana)

Regarding this hymn, those who are experts in traditional history relate a marvelous ancient story: 

Long ago, the sage **Archananas**, a descendant of Atri, was chosen by King **Rathaviti** (the son of Dalbhya) to act as a priest in a long-running sacrifice. While performing the duties of the **Hotar** <note>the priest who recites the Rig Vedic hymns</note> at the widespread ritual, Archananas saw the king's daughter standing near her father. 

He asked for that daughter’s hand in marriage on behalf of his son, **Syavashva**. The King, intending to give her away, first asked his wife, "Shall we grant this?" When asked, the Queen replied: "How can you give her to him? Never before has a daughter of our lineage been given to anyone who is not himself a 'Seer' <note>original: "ṛṣaye"; a Mantric visionary</note>." 

Having decided this, the King refused Archananas. Thus, when the sacrifice was completed, Syavashva was rejected by the King. Filled with the hope of becoming worthy, the young <term>Brahmin</term> began to perform extremely severe penance. Remaining celibate and peaceful, he wandered as a mendicant. 

During his travels, he begged for alms from the virtuous Queen **Shashiyasi**, the wife of King Taranta. She went to her husband and said, "A great sage has arrived." Hearing this, the King told his wife, "Honor him well." With his permission, she gave Syavashva a herd of cows and many ornaments. King Taranta also gave him the wealth he desired and sent him to his younger brother, **Purumilha**, saying, "He too will honor you." 

Agreeing to the King's word, and having been shown the path by the Queen, Syavashva set off. While on the road, he saw the company of **Maruts** (the storm gods) arriving in identical forms, wishing to see him. Upon seeing them, the Brahmin was terrified. With his hair standing on end, he bowed with palms joined and, with a joyful heart, praised the delighted Maruts with special words. 

Having then obtained his heart's desire from the pleased Maruts, he became the "Seer" of this hymn, known as **Syavashva**. Afterward, he returned home, received a hundred cows from the King, and King Rathaviti (the son of Dalbhya), urged by the fact that Syavashva was now a true perceiver of mantras, gave him his daughter. 

This story involving Purumilha, Taranta, Queen Shashiyasi, Rathaviti Dalbhya, and the groups of Maruts is what is described in the hymn beginning with **"Who are you."**

->॥ The First Verse of the Hymn ॥<-

## Hymn Text

**Who are you, O heroes, the most excellent, who arrive one by one from the furthest distance? ॥ 1 ॥**

**Word-by-word Analysis (Pada-patha):**
Who | are | O heroes | most excellent | who | one-by-one | have arrived | from the most distant | distance ॥ 1 ॥

---

# Rig Veda | [Book 4, Chapter 3, Section 26]

O men, leaders, Maruts, most excellent, who are you? Where are you? Thus, because their true nature is not yet determined, the seer speaks in doubt. You who come one by one—from where? It is said: From the highest distance, from the extreme far-off land; that is to say, from the atmosphere.

---

## Hymn Text

-> ॥ Now the Second Verse ॥ <-

**Where are your horses? Where are the reins? How were you able? How did you travel? On the back is the seat; at the nostrils is the restraint. ॥ 2 ॥**

**Where । your । horses । Where । reins । How । able । How । travel । On the back । seat । nostrils । restraint ॥ 2 ॥**

## Commentary (Sayana)

O Maruts, from where are your horses? And where are the reins <note>original: "abhīśavaḥ", the binding ropes</note>? And how were you able <note>original: "śeka"</note> to travel so quickly? How <note>original: "kathā"</note> did you go? On the back—the back of the horses—is the seat <note>original: "sadaḥ", a saddle or place to sit</note>. It is indeed seen there. Likewise, at the nostrils <note>original: "nasoḥ"</note> is the restraint <note>original: "yamaḥ", a controller that prevents running away</note> which is seen in the nose of the animal. Therefore, by these signs of horses and equipment, you appear as though traveling swiftly; yet not having fully discerned your divinity, the seer asks: "Who are you?"

---

## Hymn Text

-> ॥ Now the Third Verse ॥ <-

**On the hindquarters is the whip of these; the leaders have spread the thighs, like women in the act of procreating a son. ॥ 3 ॥**

**On the hindquarters । whip । of these । wide । thighs । leaders । restrain । in the act of procreating a son । like । women ॥ 3 ॥**

## Commentary (Sayana)

On the hindquarters <note>original: "jaghane", the area to be struck</note> of these horses is the stimulator <note>original: "codaḥ", a whip or a specific wooden tool</note>. The meaning is that it exists there, striking them to ensure fast movement. The leaders <note>original: "naro", the Maruts</note> have spread the thighs <note>original: "sakthāni", the region of the limbs</note>. They restrain them. This means the limbs become wide apart due to rapid running. A comparison for this spreading is provided: like women <note>original: "janayaḥ", mothers of offspring</note> in the act of procreating a son. Just as women spread their thighs during the time of union for the sake of producing offspring, so do these limbs appear.

---

## Hymn Text

-> ॥ Now the Fourth Verse ॥ <-

**Go forth, O heroes, mortals, of auspicious birth; that you may be as those heated by fire. ॥ 4 ॥**

**Forth । heroes । go । mortals । of auspicious birth । heated by fire । that । you may be ॥ 4 ॥**

## Commentary (Sayana)

Seeing their desire to depart through signs such as the cracking of the whip, the seer says: O heroes <note>original: "vīrāso", the drivers away of enemies</note>! O mortals <note>original: "maryāso", those who are beneficial to mortal men</note>! O ones of auspicious birth <note>original: "bhadrajānayaḥ", those whose birth is praiseworthy; meaning the sons of Rudra</note>! May you be as those heated by fire <note>original: "agnitapaḥ"</note>, glowing like copper or other metals refined by fire. Or, alternatively: just as those scorched by fire flee quickly, so may you be.

<note>The commentator offers two interpretations for "agnitapaḥ": either the Maruts are glowing with divine brilliance, or they are moving with the speed of someone fleeing a fire.</note>

**Vocabulary**
- <term>Marutaḥ</term>: Storm-deities, the sons of Rudra and Prisni, known for their collective power and swift chariots.
- <term>Aśvāḥ</term>: Horses; specifically the swift steeds that pull the chariots of the gods.
- <term>Abhīśavaḥ</term>: Reins or bridles; the equipment used to guide the horses.
- <term>Jaghana</term>: The hindquarters or flanks of an animal.
- <term>Sakthāni</term>: Thighs or limbs.
- <term>Putrakṛthe</term>: In the act of procreating a son; a ritualistic or physical act of generation.
- <term>Bhadrajānayḥ</term>: Having an auspicious birth or noble origin; a reference to the divine parentage of the Maruts.
- <term>Agnitapaḥ</term>: Heated by fire or glowing like fire; representing either brilliance or extreme speed.

<summary>This page contains verses 2 through 4 of Hymn 61, where the seer Syavashva questions the Maruts about their horses and equipment, describing their swift and powerful movement using vivid physical metaphors. Sayana's commentary clarifies the technical terms for saddlery and provides a cultural context for the imagery used to describe the gods' speed.</summary>

# [Mandala 5, Chapter 5, Hymn 61] | The Fourth Ashtaka | Page 491

-> ॥ Now the Fifth Verse ॥ <-

## Hymn Text

**May she grant animal-wealth consisting of horses, and also cattle, and hundreds of sheep—she who extended her arm for the hero, who was praised by Śyāvāśva. ॥ 5 ॥**

**May grant । she । consisting of horses । animal-wealth । and also । consisting of cattle । hundred-sheep-possessing । by Śyāvāśva-praised । who । arm । for the hero । extended ॥ 5 ॥**

---

## Commentary (Sayana)

May she, the queen of Taranta, grant <note>original: "sanat"</note> to me. She gave. What did she give? **Animal-wealth** <note>original: "paśum"</note> consisting of horses <note>original: "aśvyam"</note>, or a herd of them. The word "animal" is used here in the singular to represent a class. **And also cattle** <note>original: "uta api ca gavyam"</note>, an animal-wealth consisting of a herd of cows, **and hundreds of sheep** <note>original: "śatāvayam"</note>, meaning wealth joined with many sheep. Who is this "she"? The text says: **Who** <note>original: "yā"</note> for the **hero** Taranta, who was **praised by Śyāvāśva** <note>original: "śyāvāśva-stutāya"</note> (by me), **extended** <note>original: "upababṛṃhat"</note> her own **arm** <note>original: "doḥ"</note> for the sake of an embrace. The meaning is that because she is the beloved of her husband, she is capable of giving great wealth.

-> ॥ This concludes the twenty-sixth section of the third chapter of the fourth book ॥ <-

-> ॥ Now the Sixth Verse ॥ <-

## Hymn Text

**Indeed, the woman Śaśīyasī is better and more wealthy than a man who does not worship the gods and is miserly. ॥ 6 ॥**

**And । indeed । woman । Śaśīyasī । than a man । becomes । wealthier । does not worship gods । miserly ॥ 6 ॥**

---

## Commentary (Sayana)

And also, this one woman **Śaśīyasī**. "Śaśīyasī" is the name of the queen. She is the woman. Alternatively, the word "and" <note>original: "uta"</note> is used here in the sense of "indeed." The meaning is that among women, she alone is to be praised. <note>Translator's note: Sāyaṇa here includes a grammatical note on the accentuation of the word "tvā" based on Vedic rules.</note> She **becomes wealthier** <note>original: "vasyasī"</note> or more excellent than a **man**. From what kind of man? It is said: **One who does not worship the gods** <note>original: "adevacaḥ"</note>. This refers to a person by whom the gods are not recognized or honored through praise and offerings. Therefore, she is better than the **miserly** <note>original: "arādhasaḥ"</note>. "Rādhas" means wealth; thus, one who lacks wealth fit for giving—in other words, a stingy person.

-> ॥ Now the Seventh Verse ॥ <-

## Hymn Text

**She who discerns the exhausted, the thirsty, and the desiring; she directs her mind toward the gods. ॥ 7 ॥**

**Discerning । who । knows । the exhausted । discerning । the thirsty । discerning । the desiring । toward the gods । makes । mind ॥ 7 ॥**

---

## Commentary (Sayana)

She, Śaśīyasī, **knows** or discerns the **exhausted** <note>original: "jasurim"</note>—one who is distressed. <note>The root "jas" refers to the act of striking or being exhausted.</note> She recognizes him. Likewise, she recognizes the **thirsty**, and she recognizes the **desiring** <note>original: "kāminam"</note>—one who longs for wealth and other things. The meaning is that out of compassion, she has given what was desired. **Toward the gods** <note>original: "devacā"</note> she **directs** <note>original: "kṛṇute"</note> her **mind**; she forms the intention to give for the sake of pleasing the gods. The one who does this is the "woman" referred to in the previous verse.

<vocab>
**Śyāvāśva:** The seer (Rishi) of this hymn.
**Taranta:** The king who, along with his queen, patronized the seer.
**Śaśīyasī:** The queen, praised here for her generosity and piety.
**Adevaca:** A technical term for one who neglects the gods or does not perform sacrifices.
**Jasuri:** Someone who is physically or mentally spent, often due to poverty or wandering.
**Kāmina:** One who has a specific need or desire, here implying a beggar or a seeking poet.
</vocab>

<summary>This page describes the generosity of Queen Śaśīyasī, who provides the sage Śyāvāśva with vast livestock. The commentary contrasts her virtuous, god-fearing nature with that of a miserly man who refuses to honor the gods or help those in need.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the commentary on Mandala 5, Hymn 61 of the Rig-Veda. The previous page introduced Queen Śaśīyasī and her husband King Taranta. This page focuses on the rewards given by the royal couple to the sage Śyāvaśva and the introduction of another patron, King Purumīḷha.</meta>

# Rig-Veda [Book 4, Chapter 3, Section 21]

->॥ Verse 8 ॥<-

## Hymn Text
**And even he who is but a half, the unpraised man—so I, the seeker, call him a miser. He is equal only in the payment of a debt. ॥ 8 ॥**

**And । indeed । half । unpraised । man । thus । I say । miser । he । in the payment of a debt । indeed । equal ॥ 8 ॥**

---

## Commentary (Sayana)
**And even** <note>original: "uta gha api ca"</note>. The word "gha" is a filler for the meter. **Half** <note>original: "nemaḥ"</note>. The Nirukta <note>An ancient Vedic dictionary and treatise on etymology</note> states that "tva" and "nema" mean "half." Because a husband and wife perform their sacred duties together as a single unit, they are considered one substance. This is supported by traditional Law-books <note>original: "smṛteḥ"</note> which state, "The wife is half of the body." 

Therefore, I, the **miser** <note>original: "paṇiḥ"</note>—meaning the singer or seeker—**call** <note>original: "bruve"</note> King Taranta, who is the **half** <note>original: "ardhabhūtaḥ"</note> of Queen Śaśīyasī, an **unpraised man** <note>original: "pumān astutaḥ"</note>. Although he has been praised many times, his virtues are so abundant that he remains effectively "unpraised" because words cannot exhaust his merits. He, Taranta, is **equal** <note>original: "samaḥ"</note> in the **payment of a debt** <note>original: "vairadeye"</note>. Here, "vaira" refers to heroes who inspire wealth or are generous givers; "deya" is the wealth that ought to be given by them. In the distribution of this wealth, he is equal—meaning he gives to everyone. The word "it" is a filler.

->॥ Verse 9 ॥<-

## Hymn Text
**And the young woman, rejoicing, spoke to me regarding the path; the two red horses carried [the chariot] toward Purumīḷha, the wise sage of long-lasting fame. ॥ 9 ॥**

**And । to me । spoke । young woman । rejoicing । toward । Śyāva [the seer] । path ॥**
**away । two red horses । for Purumīḷha । carried । for the wise sage । of long-lasting fame ॥ 9 ॥**

---

## Commentary (Sayana)
**And** <note>original: "uta"</note> also, for **me** <note>original: "me"</note>—meaning for Śyāvaśva—the **young woman** <note>original: "yuvatiḥ"</note> (Queen Śaśīyasī), who is in the bloom of her youth and **rejoicing** <note>original: "pratimamandhuṣī"</note>, **spoke** <note>original: "arapat"</note> or clearly explained the **path** <note>original: "varttanim"</note> or way. To whom was this path leading? To **Purumīḷha** <note>original: "purumīḷhāya"</note>, a king by that name whose house is vast. He is described as a **wise sage** <note>original: "viprāya"</note> of **long-lasting fame** <note>original: "dīrghayaśase"</note>, meaning one with abundant food or widespread glory. 

<note>Sayana notes a grammatical rule from Panini 2.3.14 regarding the dative case for an intended action.</note> 

The meaning is "in order to reach Purumīḷha." For that purpose, the **two red horses** <note>original: "rohitā"</note> given by Śaśīyasī **carried** <note>original: "viyematuḥ"</note> or held the chariot. The queen went ahead showing the way to Purumīḷha’s house, sitting in the chariot drawn by those horses. This connects to the previous idea that such a woman is a "better man" than a miserly man.

->॥ Verse 10 ॥<-

## Hymn Text
**Who gave to me a hundred cows, the son of Vidadashva, just as Taranta did, with great liberality. ॥ 10 ॥**

**Who । to me । of cows । hundred । the son of Vidadashva । just as । giving । Taranta । like । with liberality ॥ 10 ॥**

---

## Commentary (Sayana)
This verse is a praise of Purumīḷha. The **son of Vidadashva** <note>original: "vaidadaśviḥ"</note>, namely Purumīḷha, **who** <note>original: "yaḥ"</note> gave to **me** <note>original: "me"</note> a **hundred cows** <note>original: "dhenūnām śatam"</note> in the same **manner** <note>original: "yathā"</note> that Taranta did. He also **gave** <note>original: "dadat"</note> wealth with **liberality** <note>original: "maṃhanā"</note>, meaning through praiseworthy riches.

<summary>This page describes the seer Śyāvaśva’s journey from the court of King Taranta and Queen Śaśīyasī to that of King Purumīḷha. It emphasizes the generosity of these patrons, noting that the Queen herself showed the way and provided the horses for the journey.</summary>
<keywords>Śyāvaśva, Taranta, Śaśīyasī, Purumīḷha, generosity, Vedic patronage, red horses, cows, half-body (wife), Nirukta</keywords>

<meta>This page concludes the commentary on Verse 10 of Mandala 5, Hymn 61, and provides the full text and commentary for Verses 11 through 13. The previous page discussed the generosity of King Taranta and Queen Śaśīyasī. This page introduces a second patron, King Purumīḷha, before shifting focus back to the Maruts, the storm deities who are the primary subjects of this hymn.</meta>

...as if like Taranta. <note>original: "taranta iva"</note> Just as Taranta gave a hundred cows and many kinds of wealth, so too does the generous King Purumīḷha give; "I praise him" is the implied conclusion of the sentence.

->॥ This completes the twenty-seventh section (Varga) of the third chapter of the fourth book (Ashtaka) ॥<-

->॥ Verse 11 ॥<-

## Hymn Text
**They who are carried by swift steeds, drinking the intoxicating honey-mead, have established their glory here. ॥ 11 ॥**

**They । indeed । carry [themselves] । by swift [steeds] । drinking । the intoxicating । honey । here । glories । established ॥ 11 ॥**

---

## Commentary (Sayana)
Having now determined that these deities are indeed the <term>Maruts</term> <note>The storm gods, brothers who ride in chariots and accompany Indra</note>, the sage praises them for their world-renowned greatness. Those Maruts who are now carried or raised up by **swift steeds** <note>original: "āśubhiḥ"</note>—meaning fast-moving horses—what are they doing? They are **drinking the intoxicating honey-mead** <note>original: "madiraṃ madhu"</note>, which refers to the <term>Soma</term> juice. The commentator notes this Soma is held as "provisions for the journey" <note>original: "pātheyatvena"</note>. These Maruts **have established** <note>original: "dadhire"</note> their **glory** <note>original: "śravāṃsi"</note>—the fame produced by the songs of praise—in this place.

---

->॥ Verse 12 ॥<-

## Hymn Text
**By whose splendor both Heaven and Earth shine brilliantly as they ride in their chariots, like the sun high in the sky. ॥ 12 ॥**

**Of whom । by splendor । over । the two worlds । shine brilliantly । in chariots । [and] । in the sky । the golden sun । like । above ॥ 12 ॥**

---

## Commentary (Sayana)
By the **splendor** <note>original: "śriyā"</note> or beauty of these Maruts, the **two worlds** <note>original: "rodasī"</note>—referring to Heaven and Earth—are presided over. This is because these Maruts **shine brilliantly** in their **chariots**. The particle "ā" is used here in the sense of "and." To illustrate this, a comparison is given: they are like the **golden sun** <note>original: "rukmaḥ," literally a golden ornament or shining object</note>, the radiant <term>Aditya</term> <note>a solar deity</note>, high in the sky. Alternatively, the word "above" <note>original: "upari"</note> may be connected to the chariots, meaning they shine from atop their vehicles.

---

->॥ Verse 13 ॥<-

## Hymn Text
**That host of Maruts is youthful, with radiant chariots, blameless, traveling auspiciously, and irresistible. ॥ 13 ॥**

**Youthful । that । of the Maruts । host । with radiant chariots । blameless । traveling for beauty । irresistible ॥ 13 ॥**

---

## Commentary (Sayana)
That **host of Maruts** <note>original: "māruto gaṇaḥ"</note> is **youthful** <note>original: "yuvā"</note>, meaning they are either the "mixers of all things" or eternally young. They possess **radiant chariots** <note>original: "tveṣarathaḥ"</note> and are **blameless** <note>original: "anedyaḥ"</note>, meaning beyond reproach. They are **traveling auspiciously** <note>original: "śubhaṃyāvā"</note>, meaning they move with beauty or for the sake of prosperity. Finally, they are **irresistible** <note>original: "apratiṣkutaḥ"</note>, meaning they cannot be opposed or turned back. Such a magnificent host shines forth.

<summary>This page concludes the praise of human patrons Taranta and Purumīḷha before transitioning to a vivid description of the Maruts (storm gods) as a youthful, radiant, and unstoppable host traveling across the sky like the sun.</summary>

## Hymn Text

**Who truly knows of these [Maruts], where these Shakers rejoice? They are born of Eternal Order and are free from all taint. ॥ 14 ॥**

**Who । knows । truly । of these । and where । rejoice । the Shakers । born of Eternal Order । free from taint ॥ 14 ॥**

**You, O praiseworthy ones, are the leaders of the mortal man with this prayer; you are the listeners at the calls for the journey. ॥ 15 ॥**

**You । [to the] mortal । O praiseworthy ones । leaders । in this way । with prayer । listeners । at the calls for the journey ॥ 15 ॥**

---

**Those [Maruts], the eaters of enemies, worthy of sacrifice, and possessing much-gladdening wealth—may you turn toward us with desirable riches. ॥ 16 ॥**

**Those । [to] us । riches । desirable । much-gladdening । eaters of enemies । hither । worthy of sacrifice । turn [toward us] ॥ 16 ॥**

**Carry this, my song of praise, O Goddess of Night, to the son of Darbha; carry my words to him as a charioteer carries a traveler. ॥ 17 ॥**

**This । my । song of praise । O Night । to the son of Darbha । away । carry । words । O Goddess । like a charioteer ॥ 17 ॥**

## Commentary (Sayana)

॥ Verse 14 ॥
Who knows the place of these <term>Maruts</term> <note>The storm deities</note>? That is, who understands them? In what place do the **Shakers** <note>original: "dhūtayaḥ"</note>—those who cause their enemies to tremble—**rejoice** <note>original: "madanti"</note>? They are **born of Eternal Order** <note>original: "ṛtajātāḥ"</note>, meaning they were produced for the sake of the waters (rain) or appeared during the sacrifice. They are **free from taint** <note>original: "arepasaḥ"</note>, meaning they are without sin.

॥ Verse 15 ॥
O **praiseworthy ones** <note>original: "vipanyavaḥ"</note>, you Maruts who desire songs of praise: with **this prayer** <note>original: "itthā dhiyā"</note>—either this current thought of grace or this specific ritual act of praise—you are the **leaders** <note>original: "praṇetāraḥ"</note> who lead the **mortal** <note>original: "martaṃ"</note> sacrificer, whose nature is to die, toward his desired goal such as heaven. You are the **listeners** <note>original: "śrotāraḥ"</note> to the calls made **at the calls for the journey** <note>original: "yāmahūtiṣu"</note>. A "journey" <note>original: "yāmaḥ"</note> is a movement; thus, these are sacrifices in which there are calls for the sake of that movement. In those sacrifices, you hear the invocations.

-> ॥ This completes the twenty-eighth section (Varga) of the third chapter of the fourth book (Ashtaka) ॥ <-

॥ Verse 16 ॥
O **eaters of enemies** <note>original: "riśādasaḥ"</note>, you who consume those who wish to harm us; O **worthy of sacrifice** <note>original: "yajñiyāso"</note>; you who possess **much-gladdening** <note>original: "puruścandrāḥ"</note> wealth that brings great joy: may you **turn toward** <note>original: "ā vavṛttana"</note> us with **riches** <note>original: "vasūni"</note> that are suitable for dwelling and **desirable** <note>original: "kāmyā"</note>. This is not merely a request, but rather an expected praise of the Maruts' generosity.

॥ Verse 17 ॥
The teacher Śaunaka <note>An ancient authority on Vedic ritual and lineage</note> tells the story of the marriage between **Śyāvāśva**, who had attained the status of a <term>Rishi</term> <note>A divinely inspired seer</note>, and the daughter of **Rathavīti**. How so? When the Maruts had departed, the famous Śyāvāśva, the joy of the Citkula lineage, realized that the nature of a seer had manifested within himself. At that time, he mentally went toward the daughter of Rathavīti. He then spoke this truth—

<meta>This page continues the narrative from the previous page concerning the sage Śyāvāśva and King Rathavīti. The text concludes the introductory story explaining the context of the verses and then provides the translation and commentary for the final two verses of Hymn 61 (Mandala 5).</meta>

...identifying himself to Rathavīti. With the two verses beginning "Carry this, my song of praise," he appointed the Night as his messenger. Having understood the sage’s purpose and being prompted by the Goddess Night, the King approached the sage Arcanānas <note>The father of Śyāvāśva</note> to offer his daughter. Touching the sage's feet and standing humble with palms joined, he declared his name: "I am Rathavīti, son of Darbha." He continued, "Forgive me for previously rejecting you when you desired a union with my family. Salutations to you; O Holy One, do not be angry with me. You are the son of a sage, a sage yourself, and the father of a sage. Please, accept this daughter-in-law." Saying this, the King gave him a hundred horses and his well-adorned daughter to be his daughter-in-law. At the time of the wedding, the lord of men also gave a hundred horses, a thousand gifts for the daughter, and a thousand cows with much wealth. Then, the King went to the forest to perform penance.

[Sayana's Commentary on Verse 17 continues:] O **Urmyā** <note>original: "ūrmye"</note>, Goddess of Night—*Urmyā* is a name for the night—since I have become a **Seer of Mantras** <term>Mantra-dṛk</term> <note>One who "sees" or receives divine revelation</note> and have praised the <term>Maruts</term> <note>The storm deities</note>, carry this song of praise made for the Maruts to the son of Darbha, Śyāvāśva. Turn toward him and deliver it. For the sake of emphasis, he repeats: O Goddess Night, carry these songs of praise regarding the Maruts just as a **charioteer** <note>original: "rathīḥ"</note> carries intended wealth in a chariot and delivers it to the desired destination.

---

## Hymn Text

-> || Verse 18 || <-

**And also tell this of me: "In Rathavīti, where the Soma is pressed, my desire does not depart." ॥ 18 ॥**

**And । of me । tell [this] । thus । [where] Soma is pressed । in Rathavīti । not । desire । away । goes । of me ॥ 18 ॥**

## Commentary (Sayana)

O Urmyā, tell him this also on my behalf. Speak! What should be said? "In this way." How? "In King Rathavīti, who has performed the <term>Soma</term> sacrifice <note>The central ritual of the Vedic religion involving the pressing of the sacred Soma plant</note>, my desire—specifically for his daughter—does not depart; it does not cease." Tell him this.

---

## Hymn Text

-> || Verse 19 || <-

**This Rathavīti, the generous giver, dwells along the Gomati River, residing among the mountains. ॥ 19 ॥**

**This । dwells । Rathavīti । the generous giver । the Gomati [river] । along । in the mountains । residing ॥ 19 ॥**

## Commentary (Sayana)

After giving his daughter and fulfilling his duty, Rathavīti went to the forest to perform penance. Śyāvāśva, perceiving him through his **seer's vision** <note>original: "ārṣeṇa cakṣuṣā"</note>, spoke this verse: "This Rathavīti..."

This Rathavīti, the **generous giver** <term>Maghavā</term> <note>A title often used for Indra, but here applied to the king for his great liberality</note>, dwells along the **Gomati** <note>A river "abounding in cows/water"</note>, following the banks of the rivers. He resides in the mountains, specifically on the slopes of the **Himalayas** <note>original: "himavataḥ pṛṣṭhe"</note>.

# Rigveda
## [Ashtaka 4, Adhyaya 3, Varga 30]

The sixth hymn of this section, beginning with the words "By the Truth," consists of nine verses. It was revealed to the sage **Shrutavid** <note>original: "śrutavid"</note>, a descendant of the clan of Atri. The meter is **Trishtubh** <note>A Vedic meter of 44 syllables (4 lines of 11 syllables)</note>, and the deities addressed are **Mitra and Varuna**. The ancient index <note>The Anukramani</note> introduces it thus: "The nine verses beginning with 'By the Truth' by Shrutavid are for Mitra and Varuna." Because of the technical definition used in the index, this is the first of eleven hymns dedicated to Mitra and Varuna. The ritual application is determined by the specific marks within the text.

-> ॥ Here is the first verse ॥ <-

## Hymn Text

**By the Truth, the Truth is covered—that which is firm—there where they unyoke the horses of the Sun. Ten hundred rays stood together; I beheld that one, the most excellent form among the forms of the gods.** ॥ 1 ॥

---

**By the Truth . the Truth . covered . firm . of you two . of the Sun . where . they unyoke . the horses .**
**Ten . hundreds . together . they stood . that . one . of the gods . the best . of forms . I saw .** ॥ 1 ॥

---

## Commentary (Sayana)

The connection of the words is as follows: "I beheld the **firm** <note>original: "dhruvam"</note>, eternal, and true orb of the Sun, which was **covered by the Truth** <note>original: "ṛtena ṛtam apihitam"</note>," where "Truth" here refers to the waters of the atmosphere. This is the place where you two <note>Mitra and Varuna</note> reside. 

The residence of Mitra and Varuna within the solar orb is well-known in the Vedas, as seen in passages such as: **"The brilliant face of the gods has risen, the eye of Mitra, Varuna, and Agni"** <note>Rigveda 1.115.1</note>; **"O Varuna, the beautiful eye of you two gods rises"** <note>Rigveda 7.61.1</note>; and **"The eye of Mitra and Varuna..."** <note>Rigveda 7.63.1</note>. 

In that orb, the worshippers **unyoke the horses** <note>original: "vimucanty aśvān"</note>. This means they release the horses that were previously obstructed by the **Mandeha** <note>In Vedic mythology, these are a class of demons who attempt to swallow the sun every morning; they are dispersed by the prayers of brahmins</note> and other obstacles. Alternatively, it means the worshippers inspire the horses to run swiftly through their songs of praise. 

In that same orb, **ten hundred** <note>original: "daśa śatā"</note>—meaning a thousand—rays **stood together** <note>original: "saha tasthuḥ"</note>. I beheld that orb, which is the **best** <note>original: "śreṣṭham"</note> or most praiseworthy among the **forms** <note>original: "vapuṣām"</note> of the gods—that is, among luminous beings like the Fire-god (Agni). The word "forms" here refers to those possessing brilliance. Or, it may be interpreted as "the best of the bodies of the gods," since the solar orb serves as the physical body of the Sun. 

Alternatively, the phrase "of you two" <note>original: "vām"</note> refers to the fact that I saw the solar orb in your midst. This aligns with the sacred teaching that "the day belongs to Mitra" <note>original: "maitraṃ vā ahaḥ"</note>; because Mitra is identified with the Sun himself, the sage speaks of seeing this wondrous form.

-> ॥ Now the second verse ॥ <-

## Hymn Text

**O Mitra and Varuna, that majesty of yours is truly excellent! The firm-standing cows have yielded milk through the days. You two nourish all the streams of the gathering-place; the one wheel-rim of your chariot has rolled along.** ॥ 2 ॥

---

**That . well . of you two . Mitra and Varuna . majesty . firm . standing . by the days . they have yielded milk .**
**All . you two nourish . of the gathering-place . the cows/streams . along . of you two . one . wheel-rim . has rolled .** ॥ 2 ॥

---

## Commentary (Sayana)

O Mitra and Varuna, **that majesty** <note>original: "mahitvam"</note>—the greatness of you two—is **well** <note>original: "su"</note> or exceedingly praiseworthy.

<vocab>
- <term>Rita (Rita)</term>: Truth or Cosmic Order. Sayana often interprets this as "water" in the context of the sky covering the sun.
- <term>Mitra-Varuna (Mitra-Varuna)</term>: A dual deity representing the Day/Friendship (Mitra) and the Night/Moral Order (Varuna).
- <term>Mahitva (Mahitva)</term>: Majesty or greatness.
- <term>Surya (Surya)</term>: The Sun.
- <term>Vapush (Vapush)</term>: A "wondrous form" or "body."
- <term>Shrutavid (Shrutavid)</term>: "He who knows what is heard"; the Seer of this hymn.
- <term>Dhena (Dhena)</term>: Traditionally "milch-cows," but often used metaphorically for voices, prayers, or streams of water.
</vocab>

Sayana’s commentary explains the solar symbolism and the role of worshippers in unyoking the Sun's horses from demonic obstruction.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the commentary on the 62nd hymn of the fifth Mandala. It concludes the explanation of the second verse and provides the full text and commentary for the third and fourth verses. The previous page established that the hymn is addressed to the dual deity Mitra-Varuna and described the Sun's station in the heavens.</meta>

# Mandala 5, Adhyaya 5, Hymn 62 ] || Fourth Ashtaka || 497

What is that? It is being explained. The sun <note>original: "īmī", meaning the constant traveler and impeller of all</note> has "milked" the standing, stationary waters through the days associated with the rainy season. Furthermore, you two <note>Mitra and Varuna</note> cause all the "cows"—which here refer to the rays that gladden the worlds—of the sun <note>original: "svasara", meaning the one who moves by himself</note> to swell and increase. One of your chariot-rims <note>original: "pavi"</note> revolves without a rival. The word **pavi** refers to the rim of a wheel, according to the ancient scholar Yaska, but here, through a figure of speech <note>term: lakṣitā-lakṣaṇayā - where a part represents the whole</note>, it refers to the chariot itself, as a wheel rim cannot revolve on its own. One of your chariots follows in sequence, revolving in its proper order.

---

## Hymn Text
-> ॥ Now the third verse ॥ <-

**You two sustained the earth and the sky, O Mitra and Varuna, the sovereign kings, by your great powers. You make the plants grow, you make the cattle swell, and you send down the rain, O you whose gifts are swift!** ॥ 3 ॥

**Pada-patha:**
**You two sustained . the earth . and . the sky . O Mitra and Varuna, the sovereign kings . O Varuna . by great powers .**
**Make grow . the plants . make swell . the cattle . the hitherward . rain . send forth . O you whose gifts are swift .** ॥ 3 ॥

---

## Commentary (Sayana)
O **Mitra-rajana** <note>original: "mitrarājānā"</note>! This refers to the two of whom the praisers, who are like friends <note>Mitra</note>, are the masters or lords. O **Varuna**! The dual form is used here in relation to the other deity. Here, because it is at the beginning of a verse-quarter, the first word does not lose its accent. Regarding the word **Varuna**, according to the rule "the vocative is like the non-existent when it follows another word," it is treated as being at the very beginning of the line and thus retains its accent. However, another rule states that a vocative in apposition to a general term is treated differently; since "Varuna" is in apposition to "sovereign kings," it technically loses its accent as it follows the general term. 

O gods, by your great splendors and your own inherent powers, you have **sustained the earth** and also the **sky**. O gods, you two **make the plants grow** by providing rain. **Make the cattle swell**—that is, increase the herds of cows and other livestock. For that purpose, **send forth the rain**; impel it to fall downward, O **you whose gifts are swift** <note>original: "jīradānū", meaning those who give quickly</note>.

---

## Hymn Text
-> ॥ Now the fourth verse ॥ <-

**Let your well-yoked horses bring you; let the reins be held firm as they come hitherward. The shining robe of the clarified butter follows you; the rivers flow in the heights of heaven.** ॥ 4 ॥

**Pada-patha:**
**Hither . you two . the horses . well-yoked . let them carry . with controlled reins . hither . let them come . hitherward .**
**Of the clarified butter . the robe/form . after . it follows . you two . hither . the rivers . in the high heaven . they flow .** ॥ 4 ॥

---

## Commentary (Sayana)
O Mitra and Varuna, let the **horses**, being **well-yoked** to the chariot, **bring** the two of you here.

<meta>This page continues the commentary on the 62nd hymn of the fifth Mandala of the Rig Veda. It completes the explanation of verse 4 and provides the full text and commentary for verses 5 and 6. The previous page discussed the movements of the sun and the grace of Mitra and Varuna in regulating the waters and the cosmic order.</meta>

[Those whose] rays are controlled by the charioteer's hand descend downwards. The pure form <note>original: nirṇig</note> of the water or ghee follows your path. Furthermore, in the ancient heaven <note>original: pradivi, a name for ancient times or places</note>, the ancient rivers flow forth or approach by your grace.

---

## Hymn Text
-> ॥ Verse 5 ॥ <-
**Increasing the cosmic order and the renowned splendor, protecting the vast earth like the sacrificial grass is protected by the sacred formula; O Mitra and Varuna, you whose strength is firm, you sit upon your throne in the midst of the sacred offerings.** ॥ 5 ॥

**Pada-patha:**
**Increasing . the cosmic order . the renowned . splendor . the vast . Like . the sacrificial grass . by the sacred formula . protecting .**
**Possessing reverence . of firm strength . upon . the throne . Mitra . you two sit . Varuna . among the sacred offerings .**
**In the midst .** ॥ 5 ॥

---

## Commentary (Sayana)
Increasing the "renowned splendor" <note>original: amati - Sayana glosses this as a name for 'form' or the 'radiance of the body'</note>. They further increase this. The "sacrificial grass" <note>term: barhis - the grass matted for gods to sit upon during a sacrifice</note> represents the sacrifice itself. Just as the sacrifice is protected by the "sacred formula" <note>term: yajuṣ - a prose mantra from the Yajur Veda</note>, so too you protect the vast earth. O you who possess reverence <note>Sayana notes 'namasvanta' implies those full of food or bowing in respect</note>, O you of firm strength <note>original: dhṛtadakṣā</note>, O Mitra, O Varuna—you two, endowed with these qualities, sit in the midst of the "sacred offerings" <note>term: iḷāsu - the sacrificial grounds or the personified prayer/nourishment</note> upon the "throne" <note>original: garte</note> or the high seat of the chariot. The ancient scholar Yaska states that the word **garta** also refers to a chariot <note>Nirukta 3.5</note>. This is supported by the verse: "O Varuna and Mitra, you ascend the chariot-throne" <note>Rig Veda 5.62.8</note>.

-> ॥ This concludes the thirtieth Varga of the third Adhyaya in the fourth Ashtaka ॥ <-

---

## Hymn Text
-> ॥ Verse 6 ॥ <-
**With hands that are not stingy, protecting the well-doer from afar, you two, O Varuna, whom you protect in the midst of the sacred offerings; as shining kings, being honored, together you two uphold dominion and a palace with a thousand pillars.** ॥ 6 ॥

**Pada-patha:**
**With hands not stingy . for the well-doer . protecting from afar . whom . and . you two sit . Varuna . among the sacred offerings .**
**In the midst . two kings . dominion . being honored . thousand-pillared . you two uphold . together . both .** ॥ 6 ॥

---

## Commentary (Sayana)
"With hands that are not stingy" <note>original: akravihastā - literally 'non-bloody-handed', interpreted here as generous or liberal</note> means being heroes in giving. For whom? For the "well-doer," the one who performs beautiful hymns of praise. You are the "protectors from afar" <note>original: paraspā</note>, those who guard from above or from a distance. O Varuna <note>implying both Mitra and Varuna</note>, you both protect that sacrificer in the midst of the sacred offerings. Furthermore, you two, acting as "shining kings" and "being honored" <note>original: aharṇīyamānā - also meaning not being angry</note>, together uphold "dominion" <note>original: kṣatram - referring here to wealth or power</note> and a "thousand-pillared" house—meaning a mansion or palace supported by many pillars.

<meta>This page continues the commentary on the 62nd hymn of the fifth book (Mandala) of the Rig Veda. It concludes the explanation of verse 6, where the dual deities Mitra and Varuna are described as supporting the sacrificial order, and then presents verses 7 and 8 with their respective word-by-word breakdowns and commentaries.</meta>

...you two support. You hold [these] for the well-acting sacrificer. Or, you hold together both the sovereign power <note>original: kṣatra - royal authority or strength</note>, which is strength, and the chariot equipped with immeasurable pillars, for the sake of your arrival.

---

## Hymn Text

-> ॥ Verse 7 ॥ <-

**Golden-robed is its pillar; it shines in the sky like the lightning-whip that drives the clouds. Constructed in a blessed field or in fertile ground—may we enjoy the sweetness of this high seat.** ॥ 7 ॥

**Word-by-word analysis (Pada-patha):**
**Golden-robed . metal . its . pillar . [it] shines . in the sky . like the lightning-whip .**
**In a blessed . field . constructed . in a fertile [place] . or . may we enjoy . the sweetness . of the high seat.** ॥ 7 ॥

---

## Commentary (Sayana)

The chariot of these two is "golden-robed" <note>original: hiraṇyanirṇik</note>, meaning it has a golden form. The word "robe" <note>original: nirṇik</note> is a name for "form." The "pillar" <note>original: sthūṇā</note> or the pegs of this chariot are "metal" <note>original: ayaḥ - often referring to iron or bronze</note>. This is a name for gold here, or it means they are made of metal. Such a chariot shines in the sky, or the atmosphere. 

Like what? Like the "lightning-whip" <note>original: aśvājanī</note>. The "horses" <note>original: aśvā</note> are the clouds that pervade the sky. That which drives or moves them is the lightning—the lightning-whip. It shines in the sky just like that. Furthermore, the pillar—representing the sacrificial post <note>term: yūpa - the wooden post to which sacrificial animals were tied</note>—is established in a "blessed field," meaning a beautiful or praiseworthy place of sacrifice, or in a "fertile" <note>original: tilvila</note> place. The commentator explains "fertile" <note>root: til - to be unctuous/oily</note> as a land that is smooth or moist; this refers to the sacrificial ground made rich and "oily" by the offerings of clarified butter (ghee) and Soma. 

May we "enjoy" <note>original: sanema</note> the "sweetness" or the Soma-juice of the "high seat" <note>original: garta - here referring to the chariot floor or the throne</note> which is filled with honey-sweet offerings. This uses a grammatical case indicating the object of the action. Alternatively, it means: may we place the sweet Soma-juice upon the high seat of the chariot.

---

## Hymn Text

-> ॥ Verse 8 ॥ <-

**At the breaking of the dawn, at the rising of the sun, you mount the golden-formed high seat with its metal pillars, O Varuna, O Mitra; from there you look upon the infinite and the finite.** ॥ 8 ॥

**Word-by-word analysis (Pada-patha):**
**Golden-formed . of the dawn . at the breaking . metal-pillared . at the rising . of the sun .**
**[You two] mount . O Varuna . O Mitra . the high seat . from there . you behold . the infinite . the finite . and.** ॥ 8 ॥

---

## Commentary (Sayana)

"At the breaking of the dawn" means at the time of morning. "At the rising of the sun" describes the same time in another way. At that time, O Varuna, O Mitra, you two mount the "high seat" <note>original: garta</note>, which is the chariot, to reach the sacrifice. This chariot is "golden-formed" and has "metal pillars" <note>original: ayaḥ-sthūṇām</note>, meaning pegs made of metal. From that vantage point, you "behold" <note>look upon</note> the "infinite" <note>original: aditim - the indivisible earth or the goddess of the boundless</note> and the "finite" <note>original: ditim - the divided or limited, referring to subjects or offspring</note>.

---

## Critical Notes

In the Daksayana sacrifice <note>a specific ritual variation of the New and Full Moon sacrifice</note>, the ninth verse, "Which is established..." <note>original: yan-niṣṭhim</note>, is used as the consecration verse <note>term: yājyā - the verse recited when the offering is cast into the fire</note> for the offering to Mitra and Varuna on the second New Moon day. This is indicated in the ritual manuals: "O Mitra and Varuna, come to us... which is established... do not disregard us, O generous ones." <note>Reference to the Ashvalayana Shrauta Sutra</note>

<vocab>
- **Golden-robed / Golden-adorned** (hiraṇyanirṇik): A description of the radiant appearance of the gods' chariot.
- **Pillar or post** (sthūṇā): Structural elements of the chariot, compared here to the sacrificial post.
- **High seat / Chariot floor** (garta): The platform of the chariot where the gods sit; also interpreted as a throne.
- **Lightning-whip** (aśvājanī): A poetic metaphor where lightning is the whip that drives the "cloud-horses."
- **Sacred Field** (kṣetra): The ritual ground prepared for the gods.
- **Fertile / Smooth** (tilvila): Land enriched by ritual offerings like ghee and Soma.
- **The Finite / The Limited** (diti): Represents the manifested, divided world of creatures.
- **The Boundless / Infinite** (aditi): Represents the undivided, primordial source or the earth.
- **Of Mitra and Varuna** (maitravāruṇa): Ritual actions or offerings dedicated to this pair of deities.
</vocab>

<summary>This page describes Mitra and Varuna mounting their golden chariot at dawn. The verses use architectural metaphors—golden pillars and metal pegs—to describe the divine chariot and link it to the physical setting of the Vedic sacrifice.</summary>
<keywords>Mitra, Varuna, chariot, dawn, Aditi, Diti, sacrifice, golden-robed, lightning-whip, metal pillars</keywords>

## Hymn Text
-> Mandala 5, Hymn 62, Verse 9 <-

<note>original: इति ॥ मैत्रावरुणे पशौ हविष एषैव याज्या । सूचितं च । यद्बंहिष्ठं नातिविधे सुदानू हिरण्यगर्भः समवर्त्तताये । आ० ३. ८.। इति ॥ तत्पाठस्तु ॥</note>
In the ritual of the animal sacrifice dedicated to Mitra and Varuna, this very verse is used as the <term>yājyā</term> <note>the sacrificial prayer recited when the offering is cast into the fire</note>. This is indicated in the liturgical texts: "That which is most vast and impenetrable, O bounteous givers... (and) Hiranyagarbha appeared in the beginning..." (Ashvalayana Shrauta Sutra 3.8). The text of the verse follows:

**With that most vast and impenetrable shelter, O bounteous givers, protectors of the world—**
**With that, O Mitra and Varuna, protect us; may we, desiring to gain and conquer wealth, be successful.** ॥ 9 ॥

**Word-by-word analysis (Pada-patha):**
**That . most vast . [not] . to be pierced . O bounteous givers . [thus] bounteous givers . indestructible . shelter . of the world . protectors .**
**With that . us . O Mitra and Varuna . protect . desiring to gain . victorious . may we be .** ॥ 9 ॥

---

## Commentary (Sayana)

O **bounteous givers** <note>original: sudānū - fair givers</note>, O **protectors of the world**, you two hold that **most vast** or most abundant **indestructible** and uninterrupted **shelter** <note>original: śarma - can mean happiness, protection, or a house</note>, which is **impenetrable** <note>original: nātividhe - impossible to pierce or strike through</note>. Here, "shelter" is the quality being described. <note>The root is "vyadh," meaning to strike or pierce, combined with a suffix denoting possibility or necessity.</note> With **that** shelter, **protect us**. O **Mitra and Varuna**, may we be **desiring to gain** or distribute wealth, and **desiring to conquer** the riches of our enemies. May we **be** so.

-> ॥ Thus ends the twenty-first section (Varga) of the third chapter (Adhyaya) of the fourth book (Ashtaka) ॥ <-

---

Dispelling the darkness of the heart by the light of the meaning of the Vedas,
May Vidyatirtha Maheshvara <note>Sayana’s spiritual teacher, personified as the supreme deity</note> grant the four goals of human life <note>term: puruṣārtha - Virtue (Dharma), Wealth (Artha), Pleasure (Kama), and Liberation (Moksha)</note>.

**Thus ends the third chapter of the fourth Ashtaka in the "Light on the Meaning of the Veda," the commentary on the Rig Veda collection composed by the minister Sayana, the pillar of the empire of the great King Bukka I, the supreme lord of kings and promoter of the Vedic path.**

---

-> ॥ Salutations to the Goddess of Speech (Bharati) ॥ <-

I bow to Vidyatirtha Maheshvara, whose breath is the Vedas and who created the entire world from the Vedas.
The third chapter of the fourth Ashtaka has been clearly explained. Now, the fourth chapter will be explained by the teacher Sayana.

The seventh hymn, beginning with **"Protectors of the Truth"** <note>original: Ṛtasya gopā</note>, consists of seven verses. Here is the formal index <note>term: Anukramaṇikā</note>: **"The seven verses of 'Rtasya' are in the Jagati meter."** The Seer <note>term: Rishi - the inspired poet</note> is Arcanana, son of Atri. The meter is **Jagati** <note>a Vedic meter of 48 syllables</note>. According to the general definitions, the deities are **Mitra and Varuna**. Its ritual application is determined by the specific characteristics of the verses.

<meta>This page continues the Rig-Veda-Sanhita. Having concluded the ritual instructions for the previous hymn on the preceding page, we now begin the 63rd hymn of the Fifth Mandala, dedicated to the dual deities Mitra and Varuna. The text transitions into a series of prayers focused on their sovereignty over the heavens and their power to bring life-giving rain.</meta>

## Hymn Text

-> ॥ The First Verse ॥ <-

**Guardians of the Cosmic Order, you mount your chariot, you whose laws are true, in the highest heaven.**
**O Mitra and Varuna, for the worshiper whom you protect, for him you pour the honey-sweet rain from the sky.** ॥ 1 ॥

---

**Word-by-word analysis (Pada-patha):**
**Of the Order . guardians . upon . you two stand . the chariot . whose laws are true . in the highest . in the heaven .**
**Whom . [the worshiper] . O Mitra and Varuna . you protect . you two . for him . rain . honey-sweet . you pour . from the sky .** ॥ 1 ॥

## Commentary (Sayana)

O **guardians of the Cosmic Order** <note>original: ṛtasya - Sayana often glosses this as 'water' in rain-related contexts, but it fundamentally refers to the moral and cosmic law</note> and protectors, you who possess **true laws**, you **mount your chariot** to come to our sacrifice. Where? **In the highest heaven**, the unsurpassed sky. O **Mitra and Varuna, you** two **protect** the worshiper <note>original: yajamāna</note> **in this sacrifice**, and **for him**, the **rain** from the cloud **pours down honey-sweet water from the sky**. It sprinkles and nourishes him.

---

## Hymn Text

-> ॥ The Second Verse ॥ <-

**Sovereign lords of this world, you rule, O Mitra and Varuna, in the assembly, you who behold the light.**
**We pray to you for rain, for wealth, and for immortality; the thundering clouds move across heaven and earth.** ॥ 2 ॥

---

**Word-by-word analysis (Pada-patha):**
**Sovereign lords . of this . of the world . you rule . O Mitra and Varuna . in the assembly . beholding the light .**
**Rain . from you two . wealth . immortality . we pray . heaven and earth . across . they move . the thundering ones .** ॥ 2 ॥

## Commentary (Sayana)

O **Mitra and Varuna**, you are **sovereign lords** <note>original: samrājau - supreme rulers</note> who **rule** over **this world**. You are the masters. Being **beholders of the light** (heaven), you are the sovereigns **in the assembly** <note>original: vidathe - the sacrificial gathering or place of wisdom</note>. From **you**, we **pray for rain**, for **wealth** (specifically the wealth brought by rain), and for **immortality** <note>original: amṛtatvam - often interpreted as reaching the heavenly realms</note>. Your **thundering clouds** <note>Sayana notes these could also be interpreted as rays</note> **move across heaven and earth**, reaching everywhere. Alternatively, we pray for the triad of rain, wealth, and immortality.

---

## Hymn Text

-> ॥ The Third Verse ॥ <-

**Fierce sovereign lords, mighty bulls, lords of heaven and earth, O Mitra and Varuna, you who observe all—**
**You stand near with diverse clouds; you make the sky rain by the magic power of the Divine Spirit.** ॥ 3 ॥

---

**Word-by-word analysis (Pada-patha):**
**Sovereign lords . fierce . bulls . of heaven . lords . of earth . O Mitra and Varuna . observers of all .**
**[Thus] observers of all .**
**With diverse . clouds . near . you stand . the sound . the sky . you make rain . of the Divine Spirit . by the magic power .** ॥ 3 ॥

## Critical Notes

The commentary by Sayana explains these verses in the context of a sacrificial request for rain, prosperity, and heavenly life.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the translation of the Rig Veda, Fifth Mandala, Hymn 63. The previous page concluded with the second verse and the beginning of the third. ## Commentary (Sayana)
### [Conclusion of Commentary on Hymn 5.63.3]

You two are **sovereign rulers**, perfectly worshiped and of rising strength; you are the **showering ones** <note>original: vṛṣabhā - literally 'bulls', but used here to mean those who shower blessings or rain</note> who are the **lords of heaven** and the **lords of earth**, the **all-seeing** Mitra and Varuna. Being of such great majesty, you stand by the **song of praise** with the **wonderful clouds**. Afterward, you cause the **sky to rain** through the **mysterious power** <note>original: māyā - often refers to the divine capacity to create or transform</note> of **Parjanya**, the one who discharges the waters.

---

## Hymn Text
-> ॥ The Fourth Verse ॥ <-

**Your mysterious power, O Mitra and Varuna, is established in heaven; the Sun, the shining light, wanders as a wonderful weapon.**
**You hide him in the sky with the cloud and with rain; O Parjanya, the honey-sweet drops move forth.** ॥ 4 ॥

**Word-by-word analysis (Pada-patha):**
**Mysterious power . of you two . O Mitra and Varuna . in heaven . established . Sun . light . moves . wonderful . weapon .**
**Him . with the cloud . with rain . you hide . in heaven . O Parjanya . drops . honey-possessing . they move forth .** ॥ 4 ॥

## Commentary (Sayana)
O Mitra and Varuna, your **mysterious power** is **established in heaven**. What is this power of yours that is spoken of? The **Sun**, who is the stimulator of all things and the shining **light**, **moves** or wanders through the atmosphere as a **wonderful weapon**—admirable in form. It is called a "weapon" because it has the power to destroy enemies. **You two hide** <note>or 'protect'</note> that Sun **in the sky** by means of the **cloud** and the **rain**. O **Parjanya** <note>the deity of rain and thunder</note>, being impelled by you, Mitra and Varuna, the **honey-sweet drops** of rain are **moved forth**, or rather, those drops created by you go forth to the earth.

---

## Hymn Text
-> ॥ The Fifth Verse ॥ <-

**The Maruts harness their easy-gliding chariot for beauty, like a hero, O Mitra and Varuna, in the battles for cattle.**
**The thundering ones wander through the wonderful regions; O sovereign rulers, sprinkle us with the milk of heaven.** ॥ 5 ॥

**Word-by-word analysis (Pada-patha):**
**Chariot . they harness . the Maruts . for beauty . easy-gliding . hero . like . O Mitra and Varuna . in the desires for cattle .**
**Regions . wonderful . through . they wander . the thundering ones . of heaven . O sovereign rulers . with milk . us . sprinkle .** ॥ 5 ॥

## Commentary (Sayana)
O Mitra and Varuna, by your grace, the **Maruts** <note>storm deities who accompany Indra and are associated with thunder and wind</note> **harness** their **easy-gliding** chariot—one that is pleasant and well-constructed—**for beauty**, which here means for the purpose of bringing water. They do this **like a hero**; just as a warrior harnesses his chariot to go into battle, so do they. In <term>Gavishti</term> <note>literally 'the search for cattle,' a common Vedic metaphor for battle or the quest for the 'cows' of the sky, which represent light or rain-clouds</note>, these **thundering** ones wander through the **wonderful regions** or worlds. Therefore, joined with them, O <term>Sovereign rulers</term> <note>original: Samrājā - meaning supreme emperors of the cosmic order</note>, **sprinkle us** with the **milk** <note>meaning water</note> **from heaven**.

<summary>This page describes how Mitra and Varuna control the sun and clouds through their divine power (Maya) and highlights the role of the Maruts in bringing rain, equated here to "heavenly milk" or "honey-sweet drops."</summary>
<keywords>Mitra, Varuna, Parjanya, Maruts, rain, Maya, Sun, Gavishti, sovereign rulers, Rig Veda 5.63</keywords>

# Mandala 5, Hymn 63, Verse 6 — The Fourth Octave, Page 503

->॥ The Sixth Verse ॥<-

## Hymn Text

**O Mitra and Varuna, because of your favor, Parjanya <note>The personified rain-cloud or the deity of rain</note> utters a wonderful, brilliant, and food-providing voice. The Maruts <note>Storm-gods and companions of Indra</note> clothe themselves in clouds through their wise power; you two cause the red, sinless sky to rain.** ॥ 6 ॥

> **Voice . well . O Mitra and Varuna . possessing food . Parjanya . wonderful . speaks . brilliant .**
> **Clouds . they clothe . Maruts . well . through wise power . sky . you two cause to rain . the red . sinless .** ॥ 6 ॥

---

## Commentary (Sayana)

O **Mitra and Varuna**, by your grace, **Parjanya** (the cloud) **well** and properly **speaks**—that is, he makes the sound of thundering for the sake of rain. This **voice** (the thunder) is **food-providing** <note>original: irāvatīm - literally 'possessing liquid or food', meaning it leads to the growth of crops</note>, **wonderful** (worthy of being sought), and **brilliant**. Furthermore, the **Maruts well clothe** or cover the **clouds** through their own **wise power** <note>original: māyayā - refers here to their innate wisdom or creative skill</note>. And you two, along with Parjanya and the Maruts, cause the **red**-colored and **sinless** <note>original: arepasam - without stain or obstruction; here meaning the sky that is free from factors that prevent rain</note> **sky to rain**.

---

->॥ The Seventh Verse ॥<-

## Hymn Text

**O Mitra and Varuna, you wise ones, by your law you protect the religious observances through the wise power of the Spirit <note>original: asura - here referring to Parjanya as the one who drives away/discharges the clouds</note>. By Truth you rule over the entire world; you place the Sun in the sky as a wonderful chariot.** ॥ 7 ॥

> **By law . O Mitra and Varuna . O wise ones . observances . you two protect . of the Spirit . by the wise power .**
> **By Truth . the whole . world . you two rule . Sun . you two place . in the sky . wonderful . chariot .** ॥ 7 ॥

---

## Commentary (Sayana)

O **Mitra and Varuna**, you who are **wise**, you **protect** the **observances** (the sacrificial rituals and other duties) by your **law** <note>original: dharmaṇā - the cosmic and moral order manifested through actions like rain-giving</note> which supports the world. You do this through the **wise power** of the **Spirit** <note>original: asurasya - interpreted by the commentator here as Parjanya, who 'repels' or discharges the clouds</note>. By **Truth** <note>original: ṛtena - can mean the cosmic order, the sacrifice, or the waters</note>, you **rule over** (that is, you illuminate) the **entire world** and all living beings. For the benefit of the world, you **place** the **Sun**—who is like a **wonderful** or worshipful **chariot** because of his swift movement—within the **sky**.

->॥ Thus ends the first section (varga) of the fourth chapter (adhyaya) of the fourth octave (ashtaka) ॥<-

---

## Critical Notes

The eighth hymn, beginning with the words "**Unto Varuna...**" <note>original: varuṇaṃ vaḥ - the start of RV 5.64.1</note>, consists of seven verses. The seer is **Archananas**, and it is dedicated to **Mitra and Varuna**. According to the rules of verse endings, the meter is **Anustubh** <note>A meter of four quarters with eight syllables each</note>, while the final verse is in the **Pankti** meter <note>A meter of five quarters with eight syllables each</note>. This is confirmed by the Index <note>original: anukramaṇikā</note> which states: "Varuna is in the Pankti-end meter." Its ritual application is determined by its characteristic marks.

<meta>This page begins the translation of Mandala 5, Hymn 66 of the Rig Veda. The previous page concluded the commentary on Hymn 63. This new hymn shifts focus toward the joint invocation of Mitra and Varuna, emphasizing their role as protectors and guides to the heavenly realm.</meta>

# Rig Veda — Octave 4, Chapter 4, Section 2

<header>॥ Rig Veda ॥ [Ashtaka 4. Adhyaya 4. Varga 2.]</header>

## Hymn Text

-> ॥ The First Verse ॥ <-

**We invoke Varuna and Mitra, the destroyers of enemies, with a sacred hymn; they who encompass all like arms reaching around a cattle-pen, the leaders to the celestial light.** ॥ 1 ॥

**Varuna . of you two . the destroyer of enemies . with a hymn . Mitra . we invoke .**
**Around . like a cattle-fold . of the two arms . having gone . the leader to the light .** ॥ 1 ॥

---

## Commentary (Sayana)

Regarding the word **of you two** <note>original: 'vaḥ' - traditionally a plural 'you', but here used in place of the dual 'of you two' according to Vedic grammar</note>, it refers to the two deities, Mitra and Varuna. **The destroyer of enemies** <note>original: 'riśādasam' - from 'riś' (those who harm/enemies) and 'adas' (one who consumes/destroys)</note> means the one who prompts the destruction of those who wish us harm. **The leader to the light** <note>original: 'svarṇaram'</note> refers to the leader or guide to heaven; even though this word appears at the end of the verse, it applies to both deities. We **invoke** <note>original: 'havāmahe'</note> or call upon such a Varuna and a Mitra, who possesses these characteristics, with a **sacred hymn** <note>original: 'ṛcā' - a mantra of the Rig Veda</note>. Then, the metaphor is explained: **like a cattle-fold** <note>original: 'vrajeva'</note>, as if protecting a herd of cows, they are **having gone around** <note>original: 'pari-jaganvāṃsā'</note> or encompassing everything by the strength of their **two arms**.

---

## Hymn Text

-> ॥ The Second Verse ॥ <-

**O you two, with your wise hands, extend protection to this worshipper; for your venerable bliss is proclaimed throughout all the lands.** ॥ 2 ॥

**Those . two arms . with excellent wisdom . forward . extend . for this . for the worshipper .**
**Bliss . indeed . venerable . of you two . in all . lands . is proclaimed .** ॥ 2 ॥

---

## Commentary (Sayana)

**Those** <note>original: 'tā'</note> refers to you two; with your **arms** and with **excellent wisdom** <note>original: 'sucetunā'</note>—meaning you who possess great knowledge. Here, though the hands themselves are not "the knower," the quality of wisdom is attributed to them in praise. Alternatively, "those" could be a descriptor of the deities themselves as "the two wise ones." With your beautiful hands, **extend** <note>original: 'pra yantam'</note> or bestow the desired happiness **to this worshipper**—that is, to me who is singing your praises. The verb here should be understood in the causative sense <note>term: causative (ṇyartha) — a grammatical form where one causes an action to happen</note>, meaning "cause me to reach happiness." Your **venerable** <note>original: 'jāryam' - worthy of praise</note> **bliss** <note>original: 'śevam' - happiness</note>, which belongs to you or is created by you, **is proclaimed** <note>original: 'joguve'</note>—it goes forth or spreads across **all lands** or throughout the entire earth. The word for "proclaimed" is listed in ancient lexicons as a verb of motion, meaning it "reaches" everywhere, or it can mean "I loudly announce it everywhere."

---

## Hymn Text

-> ॥ The Third Verse ॥ <-

**May I now surely attain that goal, proceeding on the path of Mitra; may we abide in the refuge of this beloved, non-harming protector.** ॥ 3 ॥

**Which . now . I might attain . the goal . of Mitra . I might go . by the path .**
**Of this . of the beloved . in the refuge . of the non-harming . they abide .** ॥ 3 ॥

<vocab>
**Varuna**: The deity of cosmic order and the sky.
**Mitra**: The deity of friendship, oaths, and the morning light.
**Rcha**: A verse or mantra from the Rig Veda.
**Bahu**: Arm or hand, often symbolizing the power to protect or embrace.
**Svarnara**: A guide to the heavenly realm or the sun-lit world.
**Rishadasa**: A technical epithet meaning "consumer/destroyer of enemies."
**Ksha**: The earth or dwelling place.
**Jarya**: Something worthy of praise or old/venerable.
**Sheva**: Happiness, bliss, or auspiciousness.
</vocab>
