-> ॥ Now the Sixth Verse ॥ <-

## Hymn Text
**For your praiser is here; we remain in your beloved presence. Now listen to me! Come with your protections, O lords of strength! ॥ ६ ॥**

**Word-by-word Analysis:**
**asti** <note>is/exists</note> । **hi** <note>indeed</note> । **vām** <note>of you two</note> । **iha** <note>here</note> । **stotā** <note>the praiser</note> । **smasi** <note>we are</note> । **vām** <note>of you two</note> । **saṃ-dṛśi** <note>in the presence/sight</note> । **priye** <note>beloved/dear</note> ।
**nu** <note>now</note> । **śrutam** <note>listen/hear</note> । **me** <note>my (call)</note> । **ā** । **gatam** <note>come</note> । **avaḥ-bhiḥ** <note>with protections</note> । **vājinī-vasū** <note>O lords of strength/wealth</note> ॥ ६ ॥

## Commentary (Sayana)
O **Ashvins**, the **praiser** of you two, the sage Paura, **is indeed here**. He is present. O gods, may we **be** <note>original: "smasi"</note> in your **dear presence** or near your sight. For what purpose? For the sake of prosperity. **Now**, this day, **listen** to **my** invitation. Having heard it, **come** here. The poet asks: do you come in silence? No, he says: come **with protections** <note>original: "avobhiḥ"</note>, O **lords of strength** <note>original: "vājinīvasū"</note> or lords of food.

<vocab>
- **Ashvins** <term>Aśvinau</term>: Divine twin physicians of the Vedic gods, often associated with dawn and healing.
- **Chyavana** <term>Cyavana</term>: An ancient sage who became old and frail but was restored to youth and vitality by the Ashvins.
- **Covering** <term>vavri</term>: In this context, it refers to the physical "envelope" of the body, specifically the wrinkled skin or frail form of old age.
- **Cloak** <term>atka</term>: A garment or protective armor; used here as a metaphor for the body.
- **Lords of strength** <term>vājinīvasū</term>: An epithet for the Ashvins, meaning those who possess or dwell in wealth, food, or vital power.
- **Paura** <term>Paura</term>: The name of the seer (Rishi) or patron associated with this specific hymn.
</vocab>

<summary>This page describes the Ashvins' miraculous restoration of the sage Chyavana from old age to youth and contains a direct petition from the sage Paura for the gods' presence and protection.</summary>
<keywords>Ashvins, Chyavana, Paura, youth restoration, Vedic sacrifice, protection, Mandala 5</keywords>

## Hymn Text
Who among the many mortals has turned to you today? Which wise man, O you who are **borne by the prayers of the wise**? Who with sacrifices, O you who are **wealthy in horses**? ॥ ७ ॥

**Word-by-word Analysis:**
**kaḥ** <note>who</note> । **vām** <note>of you two</note> । **adya** <note>today</note> । **purūṇām** <note>among the many</note> । **ā** । **vavre** <note>has chosen/turned to</note> । **martyānām** <note>of mortals</note> ।
**kaḥ** <note>who</note> । **vipraḥ** <note>wise man</note> । **vipra-vāhasā** <note>O you who are borne by the wise</note> । **kaḥ** <note>who</note> । **yajñaiḥ** <note>with sacrifices</note> । **vājinī-vasū** <note>O you wealthy in horses or food</note> ॥ ७ ॥

## Commentary (Sayana)
O <term>Vajinivasu</term> <note>original: "vājinīvasū"; meaning those who possess wealth in the form of food or horses</note>, among the many mortals, who has turned to you today—that is, who serves you in every way? O <term>Vipravahasa</term> <note>original: "vipravāhasā"; meaning those who are to be carried/brought to the sacrifice by the wise</note>, which wise man has chosen you? Which sacrificer has turned to you with offerings? The poet asks these questions repeatedly because he is <note>original: "atyantavilaṃbam asahamānaḥ"</note> **unable to endure any further delay** in their arrival.

---

-> ॥ Now the Eighth [Verse] ॥ <-

## Hymn Text
O **Ashvins**, may your chariot come—the swiftest of all chariots. Overcoming many [obstacles], desiring us, may the **song of praise** [reach you] among mortals. ॥ ८ ॥

**Word-by-word Analysis:**
**ā** । **vām** <note>of you two</note> । **rathaḥ** <note>the chariot</note> । **rathānām** <note>of all chariots</note> । **yeṣṭhaḥ** <note>most swift/best at going</note> । **yātu** <note>may it come</note> । **aśvinā** <note>O Ashvins</note> ।
**puru** <note>many</note> । **cit** <note>even/indeed</note> । **asmat-yuḥ** <note>desiring us</note> । **tiraḥ** <note>crossing over/overcoming</note> । **āṅgūṣaḥ** <note>a hymn of praise</note> । **martyeṣu** <note>among mortals</note> । **ā** ॥ ८ ॥

---

## Commentary (Sayana)
O **Ashvins**, may your unique chariot, which is <term>Yeshtha</term> <note>original: "yeṣṭhaḥ"; meaning the swiftest or most excellent traveler</note> among the chariots of all other gods, come hither. What is its nature? It is <term>Tirah</term> <note>original: "tiraḥ"; meaning the destroyer or overcomer</note> of many who oppose us. It is <term>Asmayu</term> <note>original: "asmayuḥ"; meaning one who favors or desires us</note>. Among all the mortal sacrificers, it is <term>Angusha</term> <note>original: "āṅgūṣaḥ"; meaning worthy of praise</note>. The word "a" <note>original: "ākāraḥ"</note> is a filler. Alternatively, <term>Angusha</term> refers to the **hymn of praise** itself; the hymn, desiring to join us with strength, is prompted by our mortal priests. This chariot or praise overcomes <note>original: "tiraskaroti"</note> even the many forces of the enemy from all sides.

---

-> ॥ Now the Ninth [Verse] ॥ <-

## Hymn Text
May our **repeated praise** be most pleasant to you both, O you who **delight in sweetness**. Turning hither, O wise ones, fly [to us] with your steeds like **hawks**. ॥ ९ ॥

**Word-by-word Analysis:**
**śam** <note>pleasant/auspicious</note> । **ūm** <note>filler word</note> । **su** <note>well/very</note> । **vām** <note>to you two</note> । **madhu-yuvā** <note>O you two who are joined with sweetness</note> । **asmākam** <note>our</note> । **astu** <note>let it be</note> । **carkṛtiḥ** <note>repeated praise/commemoration</note> ।
**arvācīnā** <note>turned towards us</note> । **vi-cetasā** <note>O you two who are wise</note> । **vi-bhiḥ** <note>with birds/swift horses</note> । **śyenā-iva** <note>like two hawks</note> । **dīyatam** <note>fly/soar</note> ॥ ९ ॥

<vocab>
- **Vajinivasu**: Wealthy in horses or food; an epithet of the Ashvins emphasizing their power to provide.
- **Vipravahasa**: Borne by the prayers of the wise; indicates that the gods are moved to action by the intellectual and spiritual efforts of their devotees.
- **Ashvins**: The Twin Gods of the dawn, often depicted as divine physicians who travel in a three-wheeled chariot.
- **Yeshtha**: Going best or most swiftly; the superlative of 'going.'
- **Angusha**: A hymn of praise or a resonant song intended to attract the attention of the gods.
- **Asmayu**: Seeking us, well-disposed towards us; derived from the root for "us" combined with "desire."
- **Carkriti**: Commemoration or repeated praise; highlights the continuous nature of the ritual chant.
</vocab>

### || Rig Veda || [Book 4, Chapter 4, Section 15]

## Commentary (Sayana)
O **honey-loving ones** <note>original: "madhuyuvā"; meaning those who are young or possess the sweetness of Soma</note>, or you who possess sweetness, may the **repeated praise** <note>original: "carkṛtiḥ"; the act of doing again and again, i.e., the recitation of hymns</note> performed for your sake, or the repeated invitation for your arrival, be thoroughly **beneficial and pleasant** <note>original: "śamu"</note> to us. O you who are **turned toward us** <note>original: "arvācīnāvagasmadabhimukhāñcanau"</note>, O you of **distinguished wisdom**, come like **two hawks** <note>original: "śyeneva"</note> with your swift-moving wings or reins. Come to us!

---

-> ॥ Now the Tenth [Verse] ॥ <-

## Hymn Text
O **Ashvins**, whenever and wherever you may be, may you **hear this invocation**. Truly, **excellent riches** <note>original: "vasvīḥ"</note> and enjoyments provided by the offerings reach you; for these offerings are prepared well for you. ॥ १० ॥

**Word-by-word Analysis:**
**aśvinā** <note>O Ashvins</note> । **yat** <note>if/when</note> । **ha** <note>indeed</note> । **karhi** । **cit** <note>at any time/wherever</note> । **śuśrūyātam** <note>may you hear</note> । **imam** <note>this</note> । **havam** <note>invocation</note> ।
**vasvīḥ** <note>excellent (riches/offerings)</note> । **ū** <note>particle for emphasis/filling the meter</note> । **iti** । **su** <note>well</note> । **vām** <note>of you two</note> । **bhujaḥ** <note>enjoyments/wealth</note> । **pṛñcanti** <note>they mix/reach</note> । **su** <note>well</note> । **vām** <note>of you two</note> । **pṛcaḥ** <note>those that satisfy/reach</note> ॥ १० ॥

---

## Commentary (Sayana)
O Ashvins, in whatever place you may be situated at any time, may you **hear** <note>original: "śuśrūyātam"</note> this my call or invocation. The meaning is: having heard it, please come. For what purpose? It is said: **Excellent** <note>original: "vasvīḥ"</note> or praiseworthy enjoyments, which are the wealth of the sacrificial offerings, **thoroughly mix** with or reach you. The word <term>u</term> is a particle used to complete the meter. What kind of enjoyments? They are those that **desire to reach you** <note>original: "vām su pṛcaḥ"</note>. Alternatively, it means that the **worshippers** <note>original: "stotāro"</note> who satisfy the gods well are providing you with these excellent enjoyments/riches.

-> ॥ Thus ends the 14th Varga of the 4th Chapter of the 4th Book ॥ <-

---

The third hymn of this section, beginning with "Toward the most beloved," consists of nine verses. The Seer (Rishi) is **Avasyu**, the son of Atri. The meter is <term>Pankti</term> <note>a Vedic meter consisting of five segments of eight syllables each</note>. The deities are the **Ashvins**. This is confirmed by the index: "Avasyu's nine-verse hymn in Pankti meter." This hymn is utilized in the <term>Prataranuvaka</term> <note>the early morning recitation</note> during the ceremony for the Ashvins in the Pankti meter section. This is indicated in the ritual manuals (Asvalayana Shrauta Sutra 4.15).

Toward the **most beloved chariot**, which is bounteous and **carrier of wealth**, the singer-sage **Avasyu** honors you, O **Ashvins**, with a song of praise. O **Sweet Ones**, hear my invocation! ॥ १ ॥

**Word-by-word Analysis:**
**prati** <note>toward</note> । **priya-tamam** <note>most beloved</note> । **ratham** <note>chariot</note> । **vṛṣaṇam** <note>bounteous/showering (blessings)</note> । **vasu-vāhanam** <note>carrier of wealth</note> ।
**stotā** <note>the praiser</note> । **vām** <note>of you two</note> । **aśvinau** <note>O Ashvins</note> । **ṛṣiḥ** <note>the sage</note> । **stomena** <note>with a hymn of praise</note> । **prati** । **bhūṣati** <note>honors/adorns</note> । **mādhvī** <note>O you who possess sweetness</note> । **iti** । **mama** <note>my</note> । **śrutam** <note>hear</note> । **havam** <note>invocation</note> ॥ १ ॥

[Mandala 5, Adhyaya 6, Hymn 75] || Fourth Book || 529

## Commentary (Sayana) — Continued from previous page

The seer Avasyu honors the Ashvins with a hymn of praise. He adorns them. What kind of chariot does he praise? One that is **bountiful** <note>original: "vṛṣaṇam"; literally 'a bull' or 'showering,' referring to the chariot's ability to rain down rewards</note>, a showerer of fruits/rewards, and a **bearer of wealth** <note>original: "vasuvāhanam"</note>, one that carries riches. The meaning is that he praises the arrival of such a chariot. Therefore, O **sweet ones** <note>original: "mādhvī"; those who know the 'honey-wisdom' or Madhu-vidya</note>, you who are experts in the sweet science, **hear my invocation** <note>original: "mama havam śrutam"</note>; listen to my call.

---

## Hymn Text

-> ॥ Now the Second [Verse] ॥ <-

O **Ashvins**, come past all [other sacrificers]. May I, the seer, always **overcome** all [hostile] people. O **performers of wonders**, you with **golden paths**, most **blissful**, borne by the **rivers**, O **sweet ones**, hear my invocation. ॥ २ ॥

**Word-by-word Analysis:**
**ati** <note>past/beyond</note> । **ā** । **ayātam** <note>come</note> । **aśvinā** <note>O Ashvins</note> । **tiraḥ** <note>across/overcoming</note> । **viśvā** <note>all</note> । **aham** <note>I</note> । **sanā** <note>always</note> ।
**dasrā** <note>performers of wonders / destroyers of enemies</note> । **hiraṇya-vartanī** <note>having golden paths</note> । **su-sumṇā** <note>very blissful/kind</note> । **sindhu-vāhasā** <note>borne by the rivers/sea</note> । **mādhvī** <note>O sweet ones</note> । **mama** <note>my</note> । **śrutam** <note>hear</note> । **havam** <note>invocation</note> ॥ २ ॥

## Commentary (Sayana)

O **Ashvins**, **come past** <note>original: "atyāyātam"</note>; that is, come to me after having bypassed all other sacrificers. Do so in such a way that I, the seer, may always **set aside** <note>original: "tiraḥ-karomi"</note> or overcome all people who are opposed to us. Alternatively, regarding the word "across" <note>original: "tiraḥ"</note>, the **Nirukta** <note>Yaska's ancient Sanskrit treatise on etymology and semantics</note> explains it as "of that which is reached." In this sense, the meaning is: "May I perform all your sacred rites which have been attained." 

You are **eternal** <note>original: "sanā"</note>, **performers of wonders** <note>original: "dasrā"</note> who cause the destruction of enemies, and you have **golden paths** <note>original: "hiraṇya-vartanī"</note> meaning you possess golden chariots. You are **very blissful** <note>original: "suṣumṇā"</note> because you possess excellent wealth, and you are **borne by the rivers** <note>original: "sindhu-vāhasā"</note> because you cause the rivers to flow by sending down rain. Being such as you are, come hither!

---

## Hymn Text

-> ॥ Now the Third [Verse] ॥ <-

Bearing **treasures** for us, O **Ashvins**, may you two come. O **Rudras**, you with **golden paths**, **enjoying** [the sacrifice], O **possessors of food-wealth**, O **sweet ones**, hear my invocation. ॥ ३ ॥

**Word-by-word Analysis:**
**ā** । **naḥ** <note>to us</note> । **ratnāni** <note>treasures/jewels</note> । **bibhratau** <note>bearing</note> । **aśvinā** <note>O Ashvins</note> । **gacchatam** <note>come</note> । **yuvam** <note>you two</note> ।
**rudrā** <note>O Rudras/terrible ones</note> । **hiraṇya-vartanī** <note>having golden paths</note> । **juṣāṇā** <note>enjoying/accepting</note> । **vājinī-vasū** <note>possessors of food-wealth</note> । **mādhvī** <note>O sweet ones</note> । **mama** <note>my</note> । **śrutam** <note>hear</note> । **havam** <note>invocation</note> ॥ ३ ॥

## Commentary (Sayana)

O **Ashvins**, **bearing** or holding for us **treasures** <note>original: "ratnāni"</note>, which are delightful riches, may you two come to us. O **Rudras**, either as sons of the storm-god Rudra or as those who are worthy of praise; O **possessors of food-wealth** <note>original: "vājinī-vasū"</note>, you who have wealth in the form of food; you two who have **golden paths** <note>original: "hiraṇya-vartanī"</note> with your golden chariots, and who are **enjoying** <note>original: "juṣāṇā"</note> or partaking in the sacrifice—please come! The final phrase, "O sweet ones," and what follows, has already been explained in the previous verses.

### Vocabulary
- **Ashvins (Aśvinā):** The twin deities, divine physicians of the gods.
- **Golden-pathed (Hiraṇyavartanī):** Having a path or a chariot made of gold.
- **Sweet ones (Mādhvī):** Those who love or possess the sweetness of the Soma juice or 'honey-wisdom.'
- **Performers of wonders (Dasrā):** Skilled in wonderful deeds; often interpreted as destroyers of illness or enemies.
- **River-borne (Sindhuvāhasā):** Carried by the sea or rivers, often linked to their role in the water cycle.
- **Treasures (Ratnāni):** Precious things or delightful gifts.
- **Wealthy in food (Vājinīvasū):** Having wealth consisting of strength or nourishment.
- **Nirukta:** A reference to the ancient etymological dictionary used to interpret Vedic words.

## Hymn Text

-> ॥ Now the Fourth [Verse] ॥ <-

O you who **shower wealth** <note>original: "vṛṣanvasū"; deities who rain down riches upon their worshippers</note>, my **well-formed praise** <note>original: "suṣṭubhaḥ"</note> is placed upon your **chariot** as a **voice of prayer** <note>original: "vāṇīcī"</note>. Moreover, for you, the **exalted seeker** <note>original: "kakuho mṛgaḥ"</note> of radiant form prepares the **nourishing oblation**. ## Commentary (Sayana)

O **showering-wealthy ones** <note>original: "vṛṣanvasū"</note>, you who rain down riches or possess the power of the rain, O **Ashvins**; the **prayerful speech** <note>original: "vāṇīcī"</note> consisting of the praise of me, the good singer, is **placed** <note>original: "āhitā"</note> upon your **chariot** <note>original: "rathe"</note>. This means it has been composed by us [for your journey]. Furthermore, for **you** <note>original: "vāṃ"</note>, the **great** <note>original: "kakuho"</note> **seeker** <note>original: "mṛgaḥ"; here interpreted as the one who searches for the gods, i.e., the sacrificer</note> who possesses a beautiful **form** <note>original: "vapuṣo"</note>, **prepares** <note>original: "kṛṇoti"</note> the **food** <note>original: "pṛkṣo"</note> or sacrificial offering. Therefore, hear my invocation.

## Hymn Text

-> ॥ Now the Fifth [Verse] ॥ <-

With an **awakening mind**, O **lords of the chariot**, O **swift ones**, hear the call. O **Ashvins**, you go with your **steeds** <note>original: "vibhiḥ"; literally "birds," but referring here to horses as swift as birds</note> to the guileless **Chyavana**. O **sweet ones**, hear my invocation. ॥ ५ ॥

**Word-by-word Analysis:**
**bodhit** <note>awakening/perceiving</note> । **manasā** <note>with the mind</note> । **rathyā** <note>O masters of the chariot</note> । **iṣirā** <note>O swift/vigorous ones</note> । **havam** <note>the call</note> । **a-śrutā** <note>hear (imperative)</note> ।
**vi-bhiḥ** <note>with birds/steeds</note> । **cyavānam** <note>to the sage Chyavana</note> । **aśvinā** <note>O Ashvins</note> । **ni** । **yāthaḥ** <note>you two go</note> । **ahvayāviṇam** <note>the one without deceit</note> । **mādhvī** <note>O sweet ones</note> । **mama** <note>my</note> । **śrutam** <note>hear</note> । **havam** <note>invocation</note> ॥ ५ ॥

## Commentary (Sayana)

O **Ashvins**, you whose **minds are ever-wakeful** <note>original: "bodhinmanasā"</note>, lords of the chariot, **swift-moving** <note>original: "iṣirā"</note> or those who should be approached by all, you are the **listeners of the invocation** <note>original: "havanaśrutā"</note>. You **go toward** <note>original: "niyāthaḥ"</note> the **Sage Chyavana** <note>original: "cyavānam"</note>, who was **free from deceit** <note>original: "ahvayāviṇam"</note> or illusion, using your **horses** <note>original: "vibhiḥ"</note>. Just as you reached that sage [to help him], come down the path toward me. This is confirmed in another scripture: "You stripped the old covering from the aging Chyavana" <note>original: "pra cyavānājjujuruṣo vavriṃ"; quoting Rig Veda 5.74.5, referring to the Ashvins restoring the sage's youth</note>.

-> ॥ Thus ends the fifteenth Varga of the fourth Adhyaya of the fourth Mandala ॥ <-

O **sweet ones**, hear my invocation. ॥ ६ ॥

<meta>This page transitions from the conclusion of the previous hymn (ending Varga 16) into the beginning of Mandala 5, Sukta 76 of the Rig Veda. In the traditional study system used here, it is identified as the 17th Varga (section) of the 4th Adhyaya in the 4th Ashtaka. The focus remains on the Ashvins—the divine twin physicians of the gods—invoked at dawn alongside the ritual fire.</meta>

The Dawn has shone forth. Agni, the fire, has also risen with bright rays, appearing with his "cattle" <note>original: "pashuman"</note>—this means the offerings have been illuminated. Alternatively, "cattle" refers to his rays. With his bright rays, he has been placed <note>original: "adhāyi"</note> upon the altar. O **bestowers of wealth** <note>original: "vṛṣaṇvasū"</note>, O **miracle-workers** <note>original: "dasrau"</note>, your immortal and steady chariot has been yoked. This means: let it be joined with horses. In the Vedic language <note>original: "chandasi"</note>, the aorist tense is used here in the sense of a prayer or request. The phrase "O sweet ones" <note>original: "mādhvī"</note> and so on has already been explained.

-> ॥ Thus ends the sixteenth Varga of the fourth [Adhyaya] of the fourth [Ashtaka] ॥ <-

The fourth hymn, beginning with **"The fire shines forth"** <note>original: "ā bhātyagniḥ"</note>, consists of five verses. It was seen by the seer Bhauma Atri, is composed in the Trishtubh meter, and is dedicated to the **Ashvins**. The Index <note>original: "Anukramanika"</note> states: "The fire shines, five verses, Trishtubh." This hymn is used in the *Pravargya* ritual for the act of bringing forward the offering. This is indicated in the ritual manuals: "The fire shines, just these two" (Ashvalayana Shrauta Sutra 4.6). During the morning recitation <note>original: "prātaranuvāka"</note>, in the section for the Ashvins and the Trishtubh meter, and in the *Ashvina-Shastra* litany, these are the first two hymns. It is indicated: "The two hymns beginning with 'The fire shines forth'" (Ashvalayana 4.15). In the Horse Sacrifice <note>original: "Ashvamedha"</note>, during the additional recitation by the Hotar priest, this hymn is used as the concluding verse: "The fire shines forth; with the Lord of the Field" (Ashvalayana 9.11).

-> ॥ Here is the First Verse ॥ <-

## Hymn Text

The fire shines forth at the **front** of the dawns; the **divine voices** of the inspired poets have risen. O **charioteers**, O **Ashvins**, come hither now to the **swelling hot-offering**. ॥ १ ॥

**Agni** | **shines** | **the face/front** | **of the dawns** | **Up** | **of the inspired poets** | **divine** | **voices** | **have risen** ।
**Hither-facing** | **now** | **charioteers** | **here** | **come** | **swelling/overflowing** | **O Ashvins** | **the hot-offering/vessel** | **towards** ॥ १ ॥

---

## Commentary (Sayana)

**At the front of the dawns** <note>original: "uṣasāmanīkam"</note>: becoming the very face or vanguard. The word **face** <note>original: "anīka"</note> means the mouth or the beginning. The meaning is that Agni is awakened at the time of dawn. Such a fire shines forth; it blazes. Or, it means he illuminates the "face" of the dawns. Indeed, the ritual fires are kindled at the time of dawn. Furthermore, the **divine** <note>original: "devayā"</note> or god-seeking **voices** <note>original: "vācaḥ"</note>—the hymns—of the **inspired** <note>original: "viprāṇām"</note> and wise praisers have risen. They are standing up. Because of this, O **charioteers** <note>original: "rathyā"</note>, the masters of the chariot, O Ashvins, turn **toward us** <note>original: "arvāñcā"</note> and surely come here today, on this day of sacrifice. Toward what? Toward the **swelling** <note>original: "pīpivāṃsam"</note> or great **hot-offering** <note>original: "gharmam"</note>—the radiant sacrifice. Alternatively, "swelling" refers to the Soma juice that has been increased by the *Vasativari* waters and is flowing. Or, come toward the *Pravargya* vessel <note>term: Gharma (the heated clay pot or the milk offered in it during the Pravargya rite)</note> which is "swelling" with ghee and other offerings. This hymn is specifically applied in the *Pravargya* ritual.

<vocab>
अश्विनौ (Ashvinau) - The twin Vedic deities, often associated with healing and the transition from darkness to light.
अग्नि (Agni) - The Vedic deity of fire and the mediator between gods and humans.
उषा (Usha) - The goddess of dawn, whose arrival precedes the sun.
घर्म (Gharma) - A term for heat, the hot milk offering, or the vessel used in the Pravargya ritual.
प्रवर्ग्य (Pravargya) - A significant preliminary ritual to the Soma sacrifice involving the heating of milk.
विप्र (Vipra) - An inspired poet, sage, or "quiverer" who receives divine inspiration.
अनीक (Anika) - Literally "face," "point," or "front"; used here to describe Agni's appearance at dawn.
</vocab>

<meta>This page continues the translation of Rig Veda Mandala 5, Sukta 76, which is dedicated to the Ashvins—the celestial twin deities associated with healing and the transitions of dawn and dusk. ## Hymn Text

-> ॥ Now the Second [Verse] ॥ <-

Do not neglect the **prepared offering**, O you who are most swift to arrive; surely, O Ashvins, come near here as you are praised. Arrive at **daybreak** <note>original: "divābhipitve"</note> with protection; you who are the most swift to come to the one in need, be the most productive of happiness for the giver. ॥ 2 ॥

> Do not | prepared | [neglect] | most swift to arrive | near | surely | Ashvins | praised | here |
> by day | at the approach | with protection | most swift to arrive | toward | distress | for the giver | most productive of happiness ॥ 2 ॥

---

-> ॥ Now the Third [Verse] ॥ <-

And come at the **gathering of cattle**, in the morning of the day, at midday, and at the **rising of the sun**. By day and by night, come with the most peaceful protection; for now, O Ashvins, the drinking [of other gods] has not extended [to exclude you]. ॥ 3 ॥

> And | [hither] | come | at the gathering of cattle | in the morning | of the day | at midday | at the rising | of the sun |
> by day | by night | with protection | most peaceful | not | now | drinking | Ashvins | [hither] | has extended ॥ 3 ॥

---

## Commentary (Sayana)

The two **Ashvins** <note>original: "ashvinau"</note> should not neglect or harm the prepared **Gharma** <note>original: "gharmaṃ"</note> <term>Gharma: A sacrificial vessel or the heated milk offering within it</term>. Rather, they should come very near to the vessel. Surely, even now, in this sacrifice, the Ashvins—who are the swiftest of travelers—are praised. At the approach of day, which is the morning time, they arrive with their protection. They are most swift to come toward **distress** <note>original: "avartim"</note>. "Varti" means livelihood or life; its absence is "Avarti" (poverty or lack of food). They are the swiftest to reach such a state [to remedy it]. Having arrived, may they be the bestowers of happiness for the sacrificer who has given the offering.

---

The day is divided into equal parts: twofold, threefold, fivefold, or fifteenfold. Here, the **fivefold division** is used. Moreover, come! Arrive! When? At the **gathering of cattle** <note>original: "sangave"</note>. This is the time when the cows gather at the milking ground. After the late-night period, the cows graze on grass in the forest and then return for milking at the "Sangava" time. Likewise, come in the morning. Also at midday (the middle of the day). Also at the "rising of the sun," which refers to the time when the sun has fully ascended—meaning the afternoon. This also implies the evening time. Not only at these stated times, but rather by day and by night—always—arrive with protection that is most peaceful, or for the sake of the offering. Why should they come now? Because the drinking of the other gods, which was accepted earlier, does not extend so far as to exclude the Ashvins. <note>This implies the Ashvins have a unique or enduring place in the ritual drinking that is not superseded by others.</note>

<summary>This page contains verses 2 and 3 of Sukta 76, where the Ashvins are invoked to attend the sacrifice at all major divisions of the day, particularly during the Gharma ritual. Sayana explains the various times of day, including a specific period when cattle return from grazing.</summary>
<keywords>Ashvins, Gharma offering, Sangava, Vedic timekeeping, morning sacrifice, Sayana Bhashya, Rig Veda 5.76</keywords>

## Hymn Text

-> ॥ Now the Fourth [Verse] ॥ <-

Indeed, this is your **ancient dwelling**, your home; these are your houses, O Ashvins, this is your **residence**. From the high heaven, from the **mountain** <note>original: "parvatāt"</note>, or from the **watery clouds** <note>original: "abjo"</note>, come to us bringing nourishment and strength. ॥ 4 ॥

**Word-by-word Analysis —**
This | indeed | your | ancient | dwelling | home | these | houses | O Ashvins | this | residence |
[Hither] | to us | from heaven | from the great | mountain | [hither] | from the waters | come | nourishment | strength | bringing ॥ 4 ॥

## Commentary (Sayana)

O **Ashvins**, this ancient place is your **home** <note>original: "okaḥ"</note>, a dwelling fit for you, known as the **Northern Altar** <term>Uttaravedi: A specific elevated altar used in Vedic rituals</term>. Then, speaking with reference to the sacrificial ground for the Soma ritual, the text says: **"These are your houses"**—referring to the halls such as the **Ancient Beam** <term>Prachinvamsha: A hall where the sacrificer's family stays</term>. **"This residence"** refers to the house where the gods are worshipped. For **us**, come from **heaven**, or from the **great mountain**—meaning the clouds that possess mountains of water—or from that which is **born of water**, meaning the mid-air or atmosphere. Come to us! Do you come empty-handed? No. You come **bringing nourishment and strength**—meaning food that is the essence and means of power. ॥ 4 ॥

## Hymn Text

-> ॥ Now the Fifth [Verse] ॥ <-

May we come together with the **new protection** of the Ashvins, which brings happiness and provides **excellent guidance**. O **Immortal Ones**, bring us wealth, and also **heroic sons**, and all **auspicious fortunes**. ॥ 5 ॥

**Word-by-word Analysis —**
Together | of the Ashvins | with protection | new | bringing happiness | with excellent guidance | may we go |
[Hither] | to us | wealth | bring | [hither] | and | heroes | [hither] | all | immortal | fortunes ॥ 5 ॥

---

## Commentary (Sayana)

May we **come together** with the **new protection** of the Ashvins—protection that is freshly granted—and with that which **brings happiness** and **excellent guidance**, meaning a well-directed arrival. Or perhaps both terms describe the nature of their protection. May we be united with them through these qualities. **Bring to us wealth**. And **bring heroes**, meaning sons and followers. O **Immortal Ones** <note>original: "amṛtā"</note>—you who are beyond the laws of death—bring us **all fortunes**, meaning every state of being blessed or fortunate. ॥ 5 ॥

-> ॥ Thus ends the seventeenth section of the fourth chapter of the fourth book ॥ <-

## Critical Notes

**"Those who travel in the morning"** <note>original: "Prataryāvāṇā"</note> — This is the fifth hymn of this section, consisting of five verses, composed in the **Trishtubh meter** and dedicated to the **Ashvins**. This is how it is introduced in the Index. Its ritual use, along with the previous hymn, is mentioned regarding the **Morning Recitation** <term>Prataranuvaka: The first set of hymns chanted at daybreak</term> and the **Ashvina-shastra** <term>Ashvina-shastra: A specific recitation dedicated to the Ashvins during the Soma sacrifice</term>. In the **Atiratra** sacrifice, specifically for the **Maitravaruna** priest, this hymn is to be recited. As it is stated in the ritual manuals: "Those who travel in the morning... the Lord of the Field... the honey-sweet wave." (**Ashvalayana Shrauta Sutra 9.11**).

<vocab>
**Ashvinau**: The twin physicians of the gods, associated with the dawn.
**Abja**: Literally "water-born"; refers to the moisture-laden atmosphere or clouds.
**Iṣ and Ūrj**: A common Vedic pair meaning food/refreshment and vital strength.
**Mayobhu**: That which causes or creates happiness or "maya."
**Saubhagāni**: Good fortunes or blessings that make one "subhaga" (fortunate).
</vocab>

This hymn is dedicated to the Ashvins, the twin celestial physicians who herald the dawn. # Rig-Veda-Sanhita: Mandala 5, Hymn 77

### Page 535

-> ॥ Here is the first verse ॥ <-

Sacrifice in the early morning to the **early-comers** <note>original: "prātaryāvāṇā"</note>, the **foremost ones**; let them drink before the **greedy** <note>original: "gr̥dhrāt"</note>, the **niggardly enemy**. For in the morning, the **Ashvins** uphold the sacrifice; the **poets** <note>original: "kavayaḥ"</note>, the ancient sharers of wisdom, praise them. ॥ 1 ॥

> Early-comers | foremost | sacrifice [to them] | before | the greedy | the niggardly | let them [the Ashvins] drink |
> morning | indeed | the sacrifice | the Ashvins | uphold | [thus] | forth | praise | the poets | the first-sharers ॥ 1 ॥

---

## Commentary (Sayana)

O my **priests** <term>Ritvijah: The officiating priests of a Vedic sacrifice</term>, sacrifice to the **Ashvins**, who are the **early-comers**—those who go to the sacrifice at the very break of dawn. They are the **foremost**, meaning they arrive before other deities or are the most excellent. Why is this early timing necessary? The reason for this first sacrifice is stated: so they may **drink before** the **greedy**, the **niggardly** <note>original: "araruṣaḥ"</note>—referring to the demons and those who do not offer gifts—can reach the oblation. 

One might ask: "How can we sacrifice to them before they have even arrived?" To this, the text replies: The **Ashvins uphold** and take part in the **sacrifice in the morning**. The **poets**, the ancient learned sages, praise these two precisely at dawn. As the scripture says: **"Those who are learned are indeed the poets"** <note>original: "Aitareya Brahmana 2.38"</note>.

---

## Hymn Text

-> ॥ Now the second verse ॥ <-

Sacrifice in the morning! Impel the **Ashvins**; the path to the gods at **evening** is not **favored**. Even if **another** sacrifices besides us and delights them, the **earlier and earlier** sacrificer becomes the **most favored** <note>original: "vanīyān"</note> of the gods. ॥ 2 ॥

> morning | sacrifice | the Ashvins | impel | not | evening | is | the path to the gods | unfavored |
> and | another | than us | sacrifices | and | delights | earlier-earlier | the sacrificer | more favored ॥ 2 ॥

---

## Commentary (Sayana)

O my men, **sacrifice** to the **Ashvins**—worship and praise them—at the very break of **morning**. **Impel** them, meaning send forth the oblations to them. At **evening** time, the oblation that **goes to the gods** <note>original: "devayāḥ"</note> **is not** accepted. In other words, the gods do not receive it then. Such an offering becomes **unfavored**, or unfit for consumption. As the sacred tradition <term>Shruti</term> states: **"The forenoon belongs to the gods."** 

Furthermore, even if **another** person besides **us** sacrifices with the **Soma** <term>Soma: A sacred ritual drink</term> and **delights** the gods with offerings, among all seekers, the **earlier and earlier sacrificer**—the one who is most prompt in their worship—is the one most likely to be **favored** and honored by the gods.

<margin>The verse beginning with "Golden-skinned..." <note>original: "hiraṇyatvak"</note> is the consecrating verse used for the oblation in the animal sacrifice dedicated to the Ashvins. This is indicated in the ritual manuals: "The golden-skinned, honey-leafed, dripping with clarified butter..." <note>original: "Ashvalayana Shrauta Sutra 3.8"</note>.</margin>

<summary>This page contains the first two verses of Rig Veda 5.77, emphasizing the necessity of worshipping the Ashvins at dawn to ensure the sacrifice is accepted before rivals can interfere. Sayana’s commentary reinforces the theological preference for morning rituals over evening ones.</summary>

<keywords>Ashvins, morning sacrifice, Sayana, Aitareya Brahmana, ritual timing, priests, Soma, Veda translation</keywords>

### Page 536
### Adhyaya 4, Sukta 4, Varga 18

## Hymn Text

-> ॥ Here is the third verse ॥ <-

Your chariot, **golden-skinned** <note>original: "hiraṇyatvak"</note>, **honey-colored** <note>original: "madhuvarṇo"</note>, and **dripping with clarified butter** <note>original: "ghṛtasnuḥ"</note>, approaches us carrying **nourishment** <note>original: "pṛkṣo"</note>. O **Ashvins** <term>Ashvina: The twin celestial horsemen/physicians</term>, you move with the **speed of thought** <note>original: "manojavā"</note> and the **velocity of the wind** <note>original: "vātaramhā"</note>; with that chariot, you pass beyond all **difficulties** <note>original: "duritāni"</note>. ॥ 3 ॥

**Word-by-word Analysis:**
**Golden-skinned** | **honey-colored** | **dripping-clarified-butter** | **nourishment** | **carrying** | **hither** | **chariot** | **moves** | **of you two** |
**speed-of-thought** | **Ashvins** | **velocity-of-the-wind** | **by which** | **you go beyond** | **difficulties** | **all** ॥ 3 ॥

---

## Commentary (Sayana)

The chariot belonging to you two approaches, carrying **nourishment** <note>original: "pṛkṣo"</note>, which refers to food or the nectar of immortality. It comes facing toward us. What is this chariot like? It is **golden-skinned**, meaning its form is covered or enveloped in gold. It is **honey-colored**, possessing a beautiful and pleasing hue. It is **dripping with clarified butter**, which implies the flowing of water or sacred offerings. It moves with the **speed of thought** and has a **velocity like the wind**. O **Ashvins**, with such a chariot, you go beyond or overcome all **difficulties**, which refers to dangerous or impassable paths.

---

## Hymn Text

-> ॥ Now the fourth verse ॥ <-

He who performs many **pleasing works** <note>original: "caniṣṭhaṃ"</note> for the **Nasatyas** <term>Nasatyas: Another name for the Ashvins, meaning "the truthful ones" or "those who never fail"</term> and gives much **food** <note>original: "pitvo"</note> during the distribution of offerings; he shall protect his **offspring** <note>original: "tokam"</note> through his **sacrificial labors** <note>original: "śamībhiḥ"</note> and overcome the **godless** <note>original: "anūrdhvabhāsaḥ"</note> in their own dwelling. ॥ 4 ॥

**He | the most | for the Nasatyas | performs | most pleasing | food | gives | in the distribution |
he | offspring | his own | shall protect | through labors | those of non-rising light | the dwelling | indeed | shall overcome ॥ 4 ॥**

---

## Commentary (Sayana)

The **sacrificer** <term>Yajamana: The person for whom a sacrifice is performed</term> who, in the distribution of offerings during a sacrifice, performs very many and most pleasing works for the **Nasatyas** (the Ashvins). The word **pleasing** <note>original: "cana"</note> is a synonym for food. Thus, he performs rituals involving much food. He also **gives food** <note>original: "pitvo"</note>—here the sixth case is used in the sense of the objective case. Such a sacrificer will **protect his own son** or offspring through his **sacrificial labors** or ritual actions. He shall always **overcome** or strike down those of **non-rising light** <note>original: "anūrdhvabhāso"</note>, meaning those who lack the rising heat of the sacrificial fires. Alternatively, this refers to those who do not sacrifice and are thus devoid of Agni's light; he overcomes them in their own **dwelling** <note>original: "sadmit"</note>.

---

## Hymn Text

-> ॥ Now the fifth verse ॥ <-

May we attain the **blissful** <note>original: "mayobhuvā"</note> and **new** protection of the **Ashvins** through their excellent guidance. O **Immortal Ones**, bring us **wealth** <note>original: "rayiṃ"</note>, **heroic sons** <note>original: "vīrān"</note>, and all **auspicious things** <note>original: "saubhaṅgāni"</note>. ॥ 5 ॥

**Together with | of the two Ashvins | with protection | new | bliss-producing | with good guidance | may we go |
hither | to us | wealth | bring | hither | and | heroes | hither | all | O Immortals | auspicious things ॥ 5 ॥**

Sayana's commentary clarifies technical terms regarding sacrificial food and the nature of those who do not worship the gods.</summary>

<meta>This page marks the conclusion of the 18th Varga of the 4th Adhyaya (Chapter) and the beginning of Sukta 78 in the 5th Mandala. The text transitions into a new series of prayers addressed to the Ashvins, the celestial twins, composed by the seer Saptavadhri.</meta>

The fifth verse beginning with "With the Ashvins" is completed.
-> ॥ Thus ends the eighteenth Varga in the fourth Adhyaya of the fourth Ashtaka ॥ <-

The sixth hymn, beginning with "O Ashvins, come hither," consists of nine verses. Regarding this, the Index of Verses <term>Anukramanika: A traditional catalog of Vedic hymns listing the author, deity, and meter</term> states: "The Ashvins are the deities; there are nine verses; Saptavadhri is the seer; the meters begin with Ushnih; the fourth is Trishtubh; the last five are Anushtubh." 

Saptavadhri is the name of the Seer, a descendant of Atri. Of the verses, the first three are in the **Ushnih** meter, the fourth is **Trishtubh**, and the remaining five are **Anushtubh**. 

In the Morning Recitation <term>Prataranuvaka: The early morning litany of the Soma sacrifice</term> dedicated to the Ashvins, the first triplet of this hymn is assigned to the section in the Ushnih meter. This is indicated in the ritual manuals: "The two triplets 'Ashvins, our path' and 'Ashvins, come hither' are used" (Ashvalayana Shrauta Sutra 4.15). On the third day of the Ten-Night sacrifice, this triplet to the Ashvins is used in the **Prauga-shastra** <term>Prauga-shastra: A specific group of seven triplets recited by the Hotri priest</term>. It is indicated: "Ashvins, come hither; come to the juice pressed by the stones" (Ashvalayana Shrauta Sutra 7.10).

---

## Hymn Text

-> ॥ Here is the first verse ॥ <-

O **Ashvins** <term>Ashvin: The twin gods of the dawn and healing, often depicted as horsemen</term>, come hither; O **Nasatyas** <note>original: "nāsatyā", an epithet meaning "those who do not fail" or "the truthful ones"</note>, do not turn away.
Fly like **swans** <note>original: "haṃsā-iva"</note> to the pressed [Soma] juices. ॥ 1 ॥

**Word-by-word Analysis:**
**Ashvins** | **hither** | **here** | **come** | **Nasatyas** | **not** | **away** | **turn/desire** |
**swans-like** | **fly** | **to** | **pressed-juices** | **near** ॥ 1 ॥

## Commentary (Sayana)

O **Ashvins**, come hither to this sacrifice. O **Nasatyas**, **do not turn away**. The root *venati* refers to the act of desiring or longing. **The meaning is: do not be without desire [for us]. Or, do not be indifferent or lacking in will.** 
**Like two swans**, just as those birds approach clear water, in that same way **fly down toward the pressed Soma juices.** **Come near** them.

---

## Hymn Text

-> ॥ Now the second verse ॥ <-

O **Ashvins**, like two **deer** <note>original: "hariṇā-iva"</note>, or like two **Gaura antelopes** <note>original: "gaurā-iva"</note> seeking **pasture** <note>original: "yavasam"</note>,
fly like **swans** to the pressed juices. ॥ 2 ॥

**Word-by-word Analysis:**
**Ashvins** | **deer-like** | **Gaura-antelopes-like** | **after** | **pasture** |
**swans-like** | **fly** | **to** | **pressed-juices** | **near** ॥ 2 ॥

## Commentary (Sayana)

O **Ashvins, like two deer or like two Gaura antelopes.** Just as they **run after pasture** or grass, in that same way, **and like swans, come to the Soma.**

---
<note>
The imagery on this page highlights the swiftness and eagerness of the gods. By comparing the Ashvins to swans, deer, and antelopes, the poet emphasizes their natural and rapid attraction to the ritual offerings, just as animals are drawn to water or food.
</note>

<meta>This page continues the 78th hymn of the 5th book (Mandala) of the Rig Veda. The previous page introduced the seer Saptavadhri and the ritual uses of the first three verses. ## Hymn Text

->॥ Here is the third verse ॥<-
O **Ashvins** <term>Ashvin: The twin celestial healers of the Vedas, often associated with the dawn</term>, lords of swift strength, accept this sacrifice for our prosperity. Like two **swans** <note>original: "hamsau", referring to the Indian Bar-headed goose, a symbol of purity and discernment</note>, fly hither to the pressed juices. ॥ 3 ॥

->॥ Here is the fourth verse ॥<-
When the sage Archi, descending into the **fire-pit** <term>Rbisa: An underground pit or oven, sometimes used for warmth or as a trap</term>, called out to you both like a woman in distress—with the swiftness of a hawk, with your newest and most healing speed, come hither, O Ashvins. ॥ 4 ॥

---

## Commentary (Sayana)

**O Ashvins! Lords of swift strength—those who provide food for dwelling. Accept our sacrifice for the attainment of our desires. Like two swans, fly toward the pressed juices.** ॥ 3 ॥

O **lords of swift strength** <note>original: "vājinīvasū", meaning those whose wealth consists of food or speed</note>, you two are the dwelling-place of nourishment. Accept, or partake in, our sacrifice for the sake of obtaining what is desired.

---

**When Archi, our father, as he was descending into the fire-pit, called out to you both like a woman in distress—with the swiftness of a hawk, with your most healing speed, come hither, O Ashvins.** ॥ 4 ॥

The sage **Archi** <note>original: "Arci", identified here as the father of the seer</note>, when he was calling out to or praising you both, was like a **woman in distress** <note>original: "nādhamānā yoṣā", a woman seeking protection or a wife pleasing her husband</note>. Just as such a woman seeks her husband, he acted while being thrown into the **fire-pit** <term>Tushagni: A fire made from chaff or husks, often slow-burning</term>. As he was being released from that fire-pit, he called out. Come to protect him with the **swiftness of a hawk** <note>original: "syenasya javasa", comparing the speed of the gods' chariot to the fastest of birds</note>. The word *cit* here indicates a comparison. Alternatively, come with your **newest speed**—the first and constant speed of a hawk—and with a chariot that is most **healing** or brings the greatest happiness to us. ॥ 4 ॥

---

## Critical Notes

->॥ Thus ends the nineteenth Varga in the fourth Adhyaya of the fourth book ॥<-

Regarding this, those who know the ancient stories tell the legend of **Saptavadhri**:

His enemies <note>original: "bhrātṛvyāḥ", literally cousins or rivals</note> forcibly threw the Seer into a large chest. They carefully sealed it and kept it inside their house. They did this so that he could not be with his wife at night. Every morning, they would open the chest and subject the sage to hardship <note>original: "nirmathayanti", literally 'to churn' or 'to stir up', implying physical agitation or torment</note>.

Having stayed in that chest for a long time, the sage grew thin and miserable. He long pondered a way to escape. Having fixed his mind, he praised the **Nasatyas** <note>the Ashvins</note> with a focused heart. The Ashvins arrived, opened the chest, and quickly lifted the Seer out, restoring his youth and vigor. The sage then enjoyed the company of his wife, and later, out of fear of his enemies, he would return to the chest and stay there as before. It was during his time residing in that chest that he perceived these two Vedic verses.

<summary>This page contains the 3rd and 4th verses of Sukta 78, where the Ashvins are invoked to rescue the sage from a fire-pit, followed by the legendary backstory of the Seer Saptavadhri being imprisoned in a chest.</summary>
<keywords>Ashvins, Saptavadhri, Rbisa, fire-pit, Archi, Sayana's commentary, Vedic legend, Hamsa, Syena</keywords>

## Hymn Text
->५.७८.५<-
**Open wide, O Lord of the Forest** <note>original: "vanaspate", referring here to the wooden chest made from a tree</note>, **like the womb of a woman about to give birth. Hear my call, O Ashvins, and set Saptavadhri** <note>original: "sapravadhriṃ", the sage whose name literally means "one with seven eunuchs/restraints"</note> **free.** ॥ 5 ॥

**Open wide. O Lord of the Forest. The womb. Of a woman about to give birth. Like.**
**Hear. My. O Ashvins. Call. Saptavadhri. And. Set free.** ॥ 5 ॥

---

## Commentary (Sayana)
O **Vanaspati**, you who are a chest made from a tree, **open wide**. Move apart. Become open. **Like a woman about to give birth**—just as the **womb** <note>original: "yoniḥ"</note> or birth canal of a woman ready for labor opens, so may you also open. For that purpose, O **Ashvins**, **hear my call**, my invitation. Hear it, and **set me free**, the sage, and release me.

---

## Hymn Text
->॥ Here is the sixth verse ॥<-
**For the frightened, praying sage Saptavadhri, O Ashvins, you two—by your mystic powers—have caused the tree to open and shut.** ॥ 6 ॥

**For the frightened. For the praying. For the sage. For Saptavadhri.**
**By mystic powers. O Ashvins. You two. The tree. Together. And. Apart. And. You moved.** ॥ 6 ॥

---

## Commentary (Sayana)
For the **frightened** one, who fears being unable to escape, for the **one praying** and begging for release, for the **sage Saptavadhri**, O **Ashvins**, **you two** with your **mystic powers** <note>original: "māyābhiḥ", referring to divine or miraculous abilities</note> have **moved** the **tree**—the wooden chest—to **come together** and **separate** <note>original: "saṃ ca vi cācathaḥ"</note> so that I might exit.

---

## Hymn Text
->॥ Here is the seventh verse ॥<-
**Just as the wind stirs the lotus pond on every side, so may your embryo move and come forth, ten months old.** ॥ 7 ॥

**Just as. The wind. The lotus pond. Stirs. On every side.**
**So. Your. Embryo. May it move. Out. May it come. Ten-month-old.** ॥ 7 ॥

---

## Commentary (Sayana)
The triplet of verses beginning with this one is known as the **Secret Knowledge of Childbirth** <term>Garbhasravini Upanishad: A "secret" or sacred formula intended to cause the fetus to "glide out" easily during labor</term>. With this triplet, the sage Saptavadhri praised the Ashvins to ensure the safe delivery of his own pregnant wife. **Just as the wind stirs the lotus pond**, such as a lake...

<vocab>
Vanaspati — Literally "Lord of the Forest," used here as a metaphor for the wooden chest;
Ashvin — Twin celestial healers known for rescuing those in distress;
Saptavadhri — The name of the seer of this hymn;
Yoni — The womb or birth canal;
Garbhasravini Upanishad — A specialized ritual chant for easing labor;
Pushkarini — A pond or lake filled with lotuses.
</vocab>

## Hymn Introduction
**"To the great [Dawn] today"** <note>original: "mahe no adya"</note> is a hymn of ten verses, the seventh hymn of this section, authored by Satyasravas of the line of Atri <note>original: "ātreyasya satyaśravasa"</note>. It is composed in the **Pankti** metre <note>a Vedic metre consisting of five feet of eight syllables each</note> and is dedicated to **Ushas** (the Goddess of Dawn). The ancient Index <note>the "Anukramani", a catalog of Vedic hymns</note> states: **"The ten verses starting 'To the great' by Satyasravas are to Ushas in the Pankti metre."** In the **Morning Litany** <note>the "Prataranuvaka", recited before sunrise</note>, in the ritual of the Pankti metre, and in the **Ashvina-shastra** <note>the litany to the Ashvin deities</note>, this hymn is used. It is indicated in the ritual manuals: **"The Pankti hymn 'To the great [Dawn] today'..."** <note>Ashvalayana Shrauta Sutra 4.14.</note>.

-> ॥ Therein, the first verse ॥ <-

## Hymn Text
**Awaken us today, O Dawn, for great wealth, O you who are possessed of heavenly light. Just as you have awakened us for Satyasravas, son of Vayya, O noble one, you who are rich in horses and pleasing words.** ॥ 1 ॥

<note>This verse establishes the transition from the night-rituals of the Ashvins to the morning-rituals of the Dawn. The poet asks for the same divine favor previously shown to his patron or ancestor, Satyasravas.</note>

# Mandala 5. Anuvaka 6. Hymn 79. || Fourth Ashtaka || 541

## Hymn Text

**Awaken us today, O Dawn, for great wealth—O radiant one! Even as you have awakened us in the past, [favor] Satyasravas, the son of Vayya, O well-born one, who are praised with truths concerning horses.** ॥ 1 ॥

**Pada-patha:**
**For the great. Us. Today. Awaken. O Dawn. For wealth. O radiant one.**
**As. Indeed. Us. You awakened. For Satyasravas. The son of Vayya. O well-born one. Praised with truths concerning horses.** ॥ 1 ॥

---

## Commentary (Sayana)

Today, on this day of sacrifice, O Goddess Dawn <note>original: "ushas"</note>, you who are **radiant** <note>original: "divitmatī", possessing light</note>, awaken us—that is, illumine or make us known—for the sake of obtaining **great wealth** <note>original: "mahe rāye"</note>. The sense is: when light is present, one is able to acquire wealth through the performance of seasonal rites. **Even as** <note>original: "yathā cit"</note> you awakened us in the past, just as you have given light in days gone by, do so today as well. O **well-born one** <note>original: "sujāte", beautifully manifested</note>, O you who are **praised with truths concerning horses** <note>original: "ashvasūnṛte"</note>—she whose speech of praise is true and dear, regarding horses—O Goddess of such nature, let your grace be upon me, Satyasravas, the son of Vayya <note>original: "vāyye"</note>.

---

## Hymn Text

-> ॥ Now the second verse ॥ <-

**O Daughter of Heaven, you who dawned for Sunitha, the son of Shuchadratha—even so, dawn now, O mighty one, for Satyasravas, the son of Vayya, O well-born one, who are praised with truths concerning horses.** ॥ 2 ॥

**Pada-patha:**
**Who. For Sunitha. The son of Shuchadratha. Dawned. O Daughter. Of Heaven.**
**She. Dawn. O mighty one. For Satyasravas. The son of Vayya. O well-born one. Praised with truths concerning horses.** ॥ 2 ॥

---

## Commentary (Sayana)

O Daughter of Heaven, daughter of the Sun <note>original: "divo duhitar"</note>, O Dawn! You who **dawned** <note>original: "vyauccah", dispelled the darkness</note> in the past for **Sunitha** <note>original: "sunīthe"</note>, a king of that name who was the **son of Shuchadratha** <note>original: "shauchadrathe"</note>; may you, the same goddess, dawn now for me, Satyasravas, the son of Vayya, who am exceedingly **mighty** <note>original: "sahīyasi"</note>. Dispell the darkness. The root *ucch* is used in the sense of "shining away" or "dispelling." The rest of the verse is as previously explained.

---

## Hymn Text

-> ॥ Now the third verse ॥ <-

**May she, the bringer of wealth, dawn for us today, O Daughter of Heaven—she who dawned [in the past], O mighty one, for Satyasravas, the son of Vayya, O well-born one, who are praised with truths concerning horses.** ॥ 3 ॥

**Pada-patha:**
**She. For us. Today. The bringer of wealth. Dawn. O Daughter. Of Heaven.**
**Who. Dawned. O mighty one. For Satyasravas. The son of Vayya. O well-born one. Praised with truths concerning horses.** ॥ 3 ॥

---

## Commentary (Sayana)

O Daughter of Heaven, O Dawn! You are she, the famous one, the **bringer of wealth** <note>original: "ābhavadvasuḥ", she who brings riches near</note>. Dawn for us today on this day. Dispell the darkness. O **mighty one** <note>original: "sahīyasi"</note>, you **who** <note>original: "yo", here used for "yā" (feminine)</note>—the vowel 'u' in the text is a filler and has no separate meaning—you who dawned in the past, dawn also today.

-> || Now the fourth verse || <-

## Hymn Text

**Those bearers [of the sacrifice] who praise you with hymns, O luminous one; being well-favored, O bountiful one, they become glorious, generous, and bounteous—O well-born one, who are praised with truths concerning horses.** ॥ 4 ॥

---

**Word-by-word (Pada-patha):**
**Towards. Those. You. O luminous one. With hymns. They praise. The bearers.**
**With riches. O bountiful one. Well-favored. Possessing gifts. Very bounteous. O well-born one. Praised with truths concerning horses.** ॥ 4 ॥

## Commentary (Sayana)

O **luminous one** <note>original: "vibhāvari"</note>, you who are endowed with light. <note>The word "vibhāvari" is formed from the term for "radiance" (vibhā) with a Vedic suffix, or from the root "bhā" meaning to shine, in the sense of one who performs that action.</note> O Dawn <note>original: "ushas"</note>, towards you, those **bearers** <note>original: "vahnayaḥ"</note>—meaning the priests or singers who carry the sacrifice—who **praise** <note>original: "gṛṇanti"</note> you with **hymns** <note>original: "stotraiḥ"</note> of adoration; those singers, through your grace, O **bountiful one** <note>original: "maghoni"</note> who are possessed of wealth, become **well-favored** <note>original: "suśriyo"</note>. That is, they become people who are sought after because of their excellent beauty or fortune. They become **possessing gifts** <note>original: "dāmanvanto"</note>, and **very bounteous** <note>original: "surātayaḥ"</note>. The word "rāti" means a gift; thus, they become people of great giving.

---

-> || Now the fifth verse || <-

## Hymn Text

**Since indeed these groups of yours offer gratification for the sake of receiving wealth, they bestow upon us undiminished prosperity—those desiring ones, who give the oblation—O well-born one, who are praised with truths concerning horses.** ॥ 5 ॥

---

**Word-by-word (Pada-patha):**
**Since. Indeed. For. Your. Groups. These. They gratify. For the gift of wealth.**
**Around. Indeed. Desiring. They bestow. Giving. Prosperity. Undiminished. O well-born one. Praised with truths concerning horses.** ॥ 5 ॥

## Commentary (Sayana)

O **Dawn, since indeed** <note>original: "yacciddhi"</note>; here the word "hi" is a filler word to complete the meter. **Since** <note>original: "yat"</note> whoever **these** <note>original: "ime"</note> **groups** <note>original: "gaṇāḥ"</note> or assemblies standing before you, who belong to you, **offer gratification** <note>original: "chadayanti"</note> for the sake of **receiving wealth** <note>original: "maghattaye"</note>—which means either the giving of wealth or the state of possessing wealth—they all **bestow upon us** <note>original: "paridadhuḥ"</note>, or hold for us, [benefits] from all sides, being **desiring** <note>original: "vaṣṭayaḥ"</note> or longing for us. What are they doing? They are **giving** <note>original: "dadataḥ"</note>, or sacrificing, **undiminished** <note>original: "advayam"</note> **prosperity** <note>original: "rādho"</note> in the form of the sacrificial oblation. "Undiminished" means wealth that is not failing, or that which does not bring shame. The sense is: those who praise you while giving the oblation, they all hold the fruit of that praise for our sake. Or, the phrase "since indeed" <note>original: "yaccit"</note> should be interpreted as "even though." In that case, the next sentence should be understood as "even so." The rest of the meaning remains the same.

-> || Thus ends the twenty-first section (varga) of the fourth chapter of the fourth book || <-

---

-> || Now the sixth verse || <-

## Hymn Text

**O bountiful Dawn, grant to these patrons fame accompanied by heroes; they who, as wealthy masters, have granted us undiminished riches—O well-born one, who are praised with truths concerning horses.** ॥ 6 ॥

<vocab>
<term>vibhāvari (luminous)</term>: An epithet for the Dawn, emphasizing her role as the bringer of light.
<term>maghoni (bountiful)</term>: A feminine title for one who possesses and distributes great wealth (magha).
<term>vahnayaḥ (bearers)</term>: In the Vedas, this can refer to the flames of fire carrying the sacrifice, or the priests themselves who "bear" the weight of the ritual duties.
<term>advayam (undiminished/not dual)</term>: Sayana interprets this as wealth that is constant or "not shameful," implying it is honest and substantial.
</vocab>

<summary>This page describes how the Goddess of Dawn (Usha) inspires generosity and wealth among the priests and patrons who worship her, granting them fame and undiminished prosperity. The commentary by Sayana clarifies the ritual context where the Dawn's light enables the performance of sacrifices that lead to material and social rewards.</summary>

## Hymn Text

-> **[Word-by-word breakdown of Verse 6]** <-

Towards. Upon these. Bestow. Accompanied by heroes. Glory. O Dawn. Bountiful one. Upon the patrons. Who. To us. Riches. Without hesitation. Liberal givers. Have bestowed. O well-born one. Joyous in horses. ॥ 6 ॥

---

-> **|| Now the seventh verse ||** <-

Bring to them, O bountiful Dawn, shining wealth and great glory; those patrons who, without hesitation, have shared with us riches consisting of cattle—O well-born one, who are joyous in horses. ॥ 7 ॥

**[Word-by-word breakdown]**
To them. Shining wealth. Great. Glory. O Dawn. Bountiful one. Towards. Bring. Who. To us. Riches. Without hesitation. Consisting of cattle. Have shared. Patrons. O well-born one. Joyous in horses. ॥ 7 ॥

---

-> **|| Now the eighth verse ||** <-

And also bring to us, O Daughter of Heaven, nourishment rich in cattle, together with the rays of the sun and the bright, glowing flames—O well-born one, who are joyous in horses. ॥ 8 ॥

**[Word-by-word breakdown]**
And. To us. Rich in cattle. Nourishment. Towards. Bring. Daughter. Of Heaven. Together with. Of the sun. With rays. With bright. With glowing. With flames. O well-born one. Joyous in horses. ॥ 8 ॥

---

-> **|| Now the ninth verse ||** <-

Shine forth, O Daughter of Heaven; do not delay your work. Let not the Sun burn you with his heat as he would an enemy or a thief—O well-born one, who are joyous in horses. ॥ 9 ॥

---

## Commentary (Sayana)

**[Commentary on Verse 6]**
O Goddess **Dawn** <note>original: "uṣo devi"</note>, O **bountiful one** <note>original: "maghavati"</note>, please **bestow** <note>original: "dhāḥ"</note> or bring upon these **patrons** <note>original: "sūriṣu"</note>—the singers or those who offer praise—**glory accompanied by heroes** <note>original: "vīravad-yaśo"</note>, which means either food or fame that is accompanied by sons and other brave descendants. This is requested specifically for **those liberal givers** <note>original: "ye maghavāno"</note> and wise patrons who **have bestowed** <note>original: "arāsata"</note> upon us—the ones praising you—**riches** <note>original: "rādhāṃsi"</note> or wealth that is **unhesitating** <note>original: "ahrayā"</note>, meaning wealth that is not deficient or shameful.

**[Commentary on Verse 7]**
O **bountiful one** <note>original: "maghoni"</note>, O Dawn, **bring** <note>original: "ā vaha"</note> to those **sacrificers** <note>original: "tebhyaḥ yajamānebhyaḥ"</note> a **shining wealth** <note>original: "dyumnam"</note> in the form of gold and such, and **great glory** <note>original: "bṛhad yaśaḥ"</note>, meaning either great food or immense fame. These are the patrons who are wealthy and have **shared** <note>original: "bhajanta"</note> or given to us **riches** <note>original: "rādhāṃsi"</note> that are **consisting of cattle** <note>original: "gavyā"</note> and horses—essentially giving herds of cows and groups of horses. They are the **patrons** <note>original: "sūrayaḥ"</note> or givers.

**[Commentary on Verse 8]**
**And also** <note>original: "utāpi ca"</note> bring to us **nourishment rich in cattle** <note>original: "gomatiḥ iṣaḥ"</note>, meaning food accompanied by cows, O **Daughter of Heaven** <note>original: "divo duhitar"</note>, O Dawn. At what time? **Together with the rays of the sun** <note>original: "sūryasya raśmibhiḥ sākam"</note>, which are **glowing** <note>original: "śocadbhiḥ"</note> or illuminating, and with **bright** <note>original: "śukraiḥ"</note> or pure **flames** <note>original: "arcibhiḥ"</note>, which refers to the heat or light of the ritual fire. This implies bringing these gifts at the time of sunrise and at the time when the sacrificial fires are kindled.

<note>The vocabulary section explains key terms: "Uṣas" is the Goddess of Dawn; "Maghoni" refers to her as the bounteous one; "Rādhāṃsi" refers to wealth or gifts; "Sujāte" means well-born; "Aśvasūnṛte" is a title for the Dawn meaning she is joyous in horses or rich in the truth of the morning; and "Sūri" refers to the patron or wise man who sponsors the ritual.</note>

<summary>In these verses, the sage Satyasravas prays to the Dawn (Usha) to reward the wealthy patrons who support the Vedic sacrifice with glory, cattle, and horses. The imagery links the appearance of the dawn with the kindling of ritual fires and the movement of the sun's rays.</summary>

## Hymn Text
**[Word-by-word breakdown of Verse 9]**
Shine | forth | daughter | of heaven | not | for long | prolong | the work | not | indeed | you | a thief | like | an enemy | burns | the sun | with his ray | O well-born one | joyous in horses. ॥ 9 ॥

## Commentary (Sayana)
O Dawn, daughter of heaven, shine forth! Bring the light of morning. Do not cause a long delay for our sacred work <note>original: *apaḥ* - referring to the morning sacrificial rites</note>. Let not the Sun scorch you with his brilliant heat as a king or authority might punish an enemy or a thief. The meaning is: let the sun not rise so quickly that your beautiful light is consumed before we finish our duties.

---

## Hymn Text
->॥ Now the tenth verse ॥<-
<note>RV 5.79.10</note>
Whether it be this much, O Dawn, or whether it be more, you are worthy to give; you who, while shining for those who praise you, are never diminished, O well-born one, joyous in horses. ॥ 10 ॥

**[Word-by-word breakdown]**
This much | or | indeed | O Dawn | you | more | or | to give | are worthy | who | for those who praise | O luminous one | shining | not | are diminished | O well-born one | joyous in horses. ॥ 10 ॥

## Commentary (Sayana)
O Dawn, are you intending to give us only this much? The word *it* here emphasizes that we have only requested certain blessings in this hymn. Or, are you worthy to give even more—even that which we have not asked for? Give us all that is fit to be given. O Luminous One <note>original: *vibhāvari*</note>, you who shine forth to enable the worldly and Vedic activities of those who praise you, you are never diminished <note>original: *na pramīyase* - you do not perish or get angry</note>. Thus, you are truly worthy to grant these gifts. 
<note>Linguistic note: the verb "diminished" or "perish" is derived from the root *mīñ*, meaning to injure or destroy, used here in a specific grammatical form.</note>

## Commentary (Sayana)
<note>Introduction to Hymn 80</note>
The eighth hymn of this section <note>Mandala 5, Hymn 80</note>, beginning with "Traveling in light," consists of six verses. According to the Index of Verses, it is a six-verse piece by the Seer <term>Satyashravas</term>. Since the meter is not explicitly named, it is understood to be in the <term>Trishtubh</term> meter <note>a rhythm of 44 syllables</note>. As it addresses the morning, the deity is <term>Ushas</term> (the Dawn). This hymn is used in the morning recitation <note>the *Prataranuvaka* ritual</note> and the Ashvina Litany during the morning sacrifice. This is indicated by the liturgical manuals which quote the opening line: "Traveling in light, O Dawn, with strength."

---

## Hymn Text
->॥ Here is the first verse ॥<-
<note>RV 5.80.1</note>
The poets awaken with their hymns to meet the divine Dawn—she who travels in light, the vast one, true through the Cosmic Order, red-tinted, radiant, and bringing the sun. ॥ 1 ॥

**[Word-by-word breakdown]**
Traveling in light | the vast one | by the Cosmic Order | true to the Order | red-tinted | radiant | divine | Dawn | the sun | bringing | towards | the poets | with hymns | awaken. ॥ 1 ॥

### Vocabulary Breakdown
- **Ushas (Ushas):** The Goddess of Dawn, the deity addressed in these hymns.
- **Duhitar (Daughter):** Specifically the daughter of the Sky or Heaven.
- **Sura (Sura):** The Sun.
- **Satyashravas (Satyashravas):** The Rishi (the inspired seer) who composed or perceived this hymn.
- **Trishtubh (Trishtubh):** A standard Vedic poetic meter.
- **Rita (Rita):** The fundamental Cosmic Order or Truth that governs the universe.
- **Vibhavari (Vibhavari):** Luminous or shining; a common title for the Dawn.
- **Prataranuvaka (Prataranuvaka):** The formal morning litany recited at the start of a Vedic ritual.

## Commentary (Sayana)

<note>This is the conclusion of the commentary for Verse 1, describing the Goddess Ushas.</note>
...she who is shining, whose chariot is radiant, the great one, who remains constant to the <term>Ṛta</term> <note>Truth or Cosmic Order</note>, appearing in a reddish-gold form, the shining goddess Ushas who brings the light and follows the Sun. In this way, the wise <term>Vipras</term> <note>inspired poets or priests</note> celebrate the great majesty of the Dawn with their hymns of praise.

---

## Hymn Text

-> ॥ Now the second verse ॥ <-

This visible Dawn, awakening the people and making the paths easy to travel, moves forward. Great in her chariot, vast, and all-pervading, Ushas bestows light at the beginning of the days. ॥ 2 ॥

> **[Word-by-word breakdown]**
> This | people | visible | awakening | easy-to-traverse | paths | making | moves | in the beginning <note>original: *aye* - a variant of *agre*</note> | great-charioted | vast | all-pervading | Ushas | light | bestows | in the beginning | of days. ॥ 2 ॥

---

-> ॥ Now the third verse ॥ <-

Yoking her chariot with reddish rays, she who is unfailing creates wealth that is unceasing. Clearing the paths for a prosperous journey, the goddess, praised by many and possessing all boons, shines forth. ॥ 3 ॥

> **[Word-by-word breakdown]**
> This | with rays <note>literally "cows"</note> | reddish | yoking | unfailing | wealth | unceasing | has made <note>original: *cake* - a variation of *cakre*</note> | paths | clearing | for a prosperous journey | goddess | much-praised | all-desirable | shines | forth. ॥ 3 ॥

---

-> ॥ Now the fourth verse ॥ <-

This Dawn becomes white, doubling her splendor, revealing her form from the East. She follows the path of Truth <note>Ṛta</note> perfectly; like one who knows the way, she does not confuse the directions. ॥ 4 ॥

---

## Commentary (Sayana)

The visible Dawn is the one who awakens. Whom? The people—meaning those who were fast asleep. Making the paths easy to travel <note>original: *sugān*</note>, she moves in the beginning, in front of the Sun. What is the nature of this Dawn? She has a massive chariot <note>original: *bṛhad-rathā*</note>, she is vast, and she is all-pervading—either pervading the entire universe or satisfying everyone. Such a Dawn bestows the brilliance of light at the start of the days.

---

This Dawn yokes her chariot with reddish-colored "cows"—meaning her rays of light. She is unfailing or undiminished. She makes wealth "un-decaying" <note>original: *aprayu*</note> or unwavering. What else does she do? She clears or illuminates the paths. For what purpose? For a "good journey" <note>original: *suvitāya*</note>, meaning for easy and prosperous movement. The goddess, shining, praised by many, and desirable to all, radiates her light.

---

## Critical Notes

1. **Orthography/Typographical Variations:**
   - In several instances, the word for "in front/beginning" is printed as **aye** instead of the standard Vedic **agre** in the Samhita (line 2 of v.2), Padapatha, and Commentary.
   - Verse 3 Samhita contains **cake** instead of the expected **cakre** ("has made"), though the Padapatha and Commentary use the standard form.
   - Verse 3 commentary uses **asedhanti** ("not stopping/unfailing") for the original **asredhanti**.
2. **Layout:** The page is structured with section headings for each verse, followed by the Samhita (continuous text) and Padapatha (word-by-word breakdown), and finally the corresponding Bhashya (Sayana's traditional commentary).

## Hymn Text

This | all-white | becomes | vast | making-visible | her-body | in-the-front | 
of-the-Sacred-Law | the-path | follows | straightly | like-one-who-knows | indeed | the-directions | she-does-not-harm. ॥ 4 ॥

---

## Commentary (Sayana)

This Dawn becomes white, meaning she is exceptionally radiant. She is "vast" (*vibarhā*), having spread through the two realms of the upper and middle worlds. Afterwards, she reveals her own body (*tanvam*), making it manifest. Where? In the front, which is to say, in the eastern direction. Furthermore, she correctly follows the path of <term>Ṛta</term> <note>original: *ṛtasya*, referring here to the Sun or the Cosmic Order</note>. Moreover, she is like one who knows, making everything in the world known. The word "like" (*iva*) here is used in the sense of "truly." She does not harm the directions; she does not diminish them. On the contrary, she illuminates the directions. Alternatively, the sense is that because she understands perfectly how she must follow, she moves along the path of the Sacred Law.

---

## Hymn Text

-> ॥ Now the fifth verse ॥ <-

This radiant one, like a woman who knows her body, has stood up for us to see, like one who is upright after bathing. Warding off the hated darkness, the Dawn, daughter of Heaven, has come with her light. ॥ 5 ॥

## Commentary (Sayana)

This Dawn, like a pure-colored, stainless, and well-decorated woman (*śubhrā na*), making her limbs or body known (*tannvo vidānā*), has stood up for our sake, or before us, so that everyone may see her (*dṛśaye*). She rises in the eastern direction. She is like one who is upright after performing a bath (*snātī ūrdhveva*), as if rising up from her cleansing. What is she doing? Warding off the hateful darkness, the daughter of Heaven, Ushas, has come (*agāt*) with her brilliance or light. She arrives.

She impels them. Furthermore, she bestows or grants desirable wealth (*vāryāṇi*) to the giver of oblations (*dāśuṣe*), the sacrificer...

<meta>This page transitions from the conclusion of a previous hymn (likely dedicated to the Dawn) to the start of Mandala 5, Sukta 81. The metadata provided for the previous page mentions Mandala 4, but the current transcription explicitly identifies the start of Mandala 5, Sukta 81, dedicated to Savitr.</meta>

...like a young woman, eternally youthful, she mixes everything together, or again even today, just as before, the light of the sun—the radiant one—creates.
-> ॥ Here ends the twenty-third group of the fourth section ॥ <-

The hymn beginning with "They yoke the mind" (*yuñjate mana*) consists of five verses and is the ninth hymn of this section. The index (*Anukramaṇikā*) states: "The five verses beginning with *yuñjate* were seen by Shyavashva; it is dedicated to Savitr and is in the Jagati meter." The seer is a sage named Shyavashva, a descendant of Atri. The meter is <term>Jagati</term> <note>A Vedic meter consisting of four lines of twelve syllables each</note>. The deity is <term>Savitr</term> <note>The solar deity representing the impelling, creative power of the sun</note>. In the ritual of the <term>Prashtya-Abhiplava</term> six-day sacrifice, this is the hymn to Savitr used in the <term>Vaishvadeva Shastra</term> on the first day. This is indicated in the ritual manual: "The four verses beginning with *yuñjate mana iha*." (Asvalayana Shrauta Sutra 7.5). The first verse is also used in the praise-song (*Stotra*), as noted: "They yoke the mind and they yoke the thoughts..." (Asvalayana Shrauta Sutra 5.12).

---

## Hymn Text

-> ॥ Here is the first verse ॥ <-

<note>RV 5.81.1</note>
**The wise ones yoke the mind, and they yoke the thoughts—those wise ones of the Great Wise One, the Knower of Wisdom.**
**He alone, the Knower of the Sacred Ways, ordains the priestly offices; Great indeed is the praise of the divine Savitr.**

**[Word-by-word breakdown (Pada-patha)]**
They yoke | the mind | and | they yoke | the thoughts | the wise ones | of the wise | of the great | of the knower of wisdom |
separately | the priestly offices | he ordains | the knower of ways | he | alone | great | of the god | of Savitr | the complete praise. ॥ 1 ॥

---

## Commentary (Sayana)

**The wise ones** (*viprāḥ*), meaning the intelligent priests and the patron of the sacrifice, **yoke the mind** (*manaḥ yuñjate*). They harness their own minds; this means they form a firm intention in all their ritual acts to receive the favor of Savitr. **And also** (*uta*) **they yoke the thoughts** (*dhiyaḥ*), meaning they perform the ritual actions or attain the results. Under whose command is this done? It is said: **By the command of the Wise One** (*viprasya*), the intelligent, **the Great** (*bṛhataḥ*), the mighty, **the Knower of Wisdom** (*vipaścitaḥ*), the one who is worthy of praise or possesses perfect knowledge—the god Savitr. Indeed, the scripture says: "Savitr is the lord of all impulses." That same Savitr **ordains** (*vidadhe*) the **priestly offices** (*hotrāḥ*), the actions appropriate for the seven types of priests. He is the **knower of the ways** (*vayunavit*). The word *vayuna* is a name for "wisdom" or "knowledge." He alone is the knower of the specific wisdom required for each performance. He establishes these roles separately. Furthermore, the **complete praise** (*paristutiḥ*) of that **divine Savitr** is **great** (*mahī*), meaning it is vast and extremely abundant. It implies he is a worthy object of such great praise.

---

In the ritual of bringing forward the sacrificial cart (*Havirdhana*), when the pole is being tied, this verse "He puts on all forms" (*viśvā rūpāṇi*) is to be recited. This is indicated in the rule: "The Sage puts on all forms" (Asvalayana Shrauta Sutra 4.9).

---

## Hymn Text

-> ॥ Here is the second verse ॥ <-

<note>RV 5.81.2</note>
**The Sage puts on all forms; he has brought forth what is good for the two-footed and the four-footed.**
**Savitr, the Most Desirable, has illuminated the firmament; he shines following the departure of the Dawn.**

<vocab>
Savitr: The solar deity of inspiration.
Vipra: A wise man, sage, or inspired priest.
Jagati: A specific rhythmic meter in Vedic poetry.
Shyavashva: The name of the seer (Rishi) who revealed this hymn.
Hotra: The office or invocation of the priest.
Paristuti: A comprehensive hymn of praise.
Havirdhana: A cart or shed used for storing sacrificial offerings.
</vocab>
