<meta>This page continues the commentary on the 81st hymn of the 5th book (Mandala) of the Rig Veda, dedicated to the solar deity Savitr. The previous page concluded with the commentary on Verse 1. This page provides the word-for-word breakdown (Padapatha) and Sayana’s explanation for Verse 2, followed by the text and commentary for Verses 3 and 4.</meta>

548
|| Rig Veda || [Book 4, Chapter 4, Verse-group 24]

## Hymn Text & Padapatha (Verse 2)

**All | forms | towards | he clothes himself | the Sage | forth | he has sent | welfare | for the two-footed | for the four-footed.**
**Separately | the sky | he has beheld | Savitr | the adorable | following | the departure | of the Dawn | far and wide | he shines.**

---

## Commentary (Sayana) on Verse 2

The Sage—the wise Savitr—clothes himself in all forms; he binds or sustains them within himself. Furthermore, he has sent forth—meaning he permits or ordains—welfare, such as the ability to move and act. For whom? For the two-footed, meaning humans, and for the four-footed, such as cattle and horses. Furthermore, Savitr—the deity who impels all things—being adorable or worthy of choice, has beheld. He makes things known or illumines them. What does he illumine? The sky (<term>Naka</term>). The commentator notes that the word **Naka** refers to heaven because "there is no (<term>na</term>) pain (<term>aka</term>) there" <note>original: "na-asmin-arka-duhkham-asti-iti nakah"</note>. The meaning is that he illumines heaven for the sake of the person performing the sacrifice. That deity shines far and wide following the departure or the rising of the Dawn. Indeed, the Dawn rises just before the sun appears.

---

->॥ Here is the third verse ॥<-

## Hymn Text (Verse 3)

**Whose departure the other gods have followed, following the greatness of the god with strength.**
**He who has measured out the earthly regions, he is the bright one, the god Savitr, in his majesty.**

### Padapatha
Whose | departure | following | the others | indeed | have gone | the gods | of the god | the greatness | with strength | who | the earthly | has measured out | he | the bright one | the regions | the god | Savitr | with majesty.

---

## Commentary (Sayana) on Verse 3

Other gods indeed—even deities like Agni (Fire) and others—have followed the departure or movement of the divine, shining Savitr. They go toward or attain his greatness or importance. This is because if the Sun (Savitr) does not rise, rituals like the daily fire-offering (<term>Agnihotra</term>) cannot be completed, and thus those gods would lack their offerings and praises. They also become endowed with strength through him. That Savitr who has measured out or defined the earthly regions—the worlds of the earth and so on—by his own majesty, he is the god **Etasha**. The name <term>Etasha</term> refers to one who is of this color: white and shining <note>original: "etadvarnaḥ śubhraḥ"</note>. The word "shines" is understood to complete the sentence. The commentator notes that the grammatical form of the word "Etasha" contains a specific suffix used in Vedic Sanskrit, similar to other archaic forms found in the scriptures.

---

->॥ Here is the fourth verse ॥<-

## Hymn Text (Verse 4)

**And you go, O Savitr, to the three luminous realms; and with the rays of the Sun, you are joined.**
**And you encompass the Night from both sides; and you become Mitra, O God, by your laws.**

### Padapatha
And | you go | O Savitr | the three | luminous realms | and | of the Sun | with the rays | together | you are joined | and | the Night | from both sides | around | you go | and | Mitra | you become | O God | by laws.

---

## Commentary (Sayana) on Verse 4

O divine Savitr, you also go to the three luminous realms—the three shining heavens. It has been said elsewhere in the Vedas that there are "three heavens and three earths." Furthermore, you are joined with the rays of the Sun; you come into union with them.

Savitr (The Impeller deity), Ushas (The Dawn), Naka (Heaven/Sky, literally "place of no pain"), Etasha (The Bright/Shining one, often associated with the sun-horse), Rochana (Luminous realms of light), Dharman (Cosmic laws or ordinances), Mahitvana (By his greatness)
</vocab>

[Mandala 5, Anuvaka 6, Hymn 82] || Fourth Ashtaka || 549

This is the form of the phrase "rising together" <note>original: "ucca samavaya"</note>. Savitr is the sun as it exists before sunrise, whereas Surya is the sun that exists during its rising and setting. And also, you encompass the night on both sides—meaning you move around both flanks of it. And also, O God Savitr, by your laws (<term>dharma</term>)—those actions which sustain the world—you become Mitra. You are the deity named Mitra [the Friend]. Or, by granting light and other gifts, you are the friend of the entire world.

## Hymn Text
-> ॥ Here is the fifth verse ॥ <-

**And you alone are the master of creation; and you become Pushan, O God, by your movements.**
**And you rule over this entire world; Shyavashva has attained your hymn of praise, O Savitr.**

**Word-by-word Analysis (Padapatha)**
And | you are the master | of creation | you | alone | indeed | and | Pushan | you become | O God | by movements |
And | this | all | world | over | you rule | Shyavashva | your | O Savitr | hymn of praise | has attained.

---

## Commentary (Sayana)

O **Savitr, you alone** are the **master of creation** (<term>prasava</term>), which here means the act of granting permission for all deeds. Whether people perform worldly actions like walking or Vedic rituals like the Fire Offering (<term>Agnihotra</term>), you alone have the power to permit them all. **And also you become Pushan**, the Nourisher, **O God, by your movements** or paths. And also, **you rule over this entire world**, the collective of all beings. You are capable of sustaining them. Because you possess such great power, therefore, **O Savitr, the sage Shyavashva attains** or performs this **hymn of praise** (<term>stoma</term>) for **you**. The sage speaks of himself in the third person here.

-> ॥ Thus ends the twenty-fourth group in the fourth chapter of the fourth book ॥ <-

The tenth hymn, beginning with "**That [glory] of Savitr**," consists of nine verses and is the work of the sage Shyavashva. Regarding this, the Index (<term>Anukramani</term>) says: "**'That [glory] of Savitr' is a nine-verse hymn in Gayatri meter, though the first is Anustubh.**" Thus, the first verse is in the Anustubh meter and the remaining are in Gayatri. Since it states "to Savitr," the deity is Savitr. In the Agnishtoma sacrifice, the first triplet (<term>trca</term>) of the chant to the All-Gods (<term>Vaishvadeva-shastra</term>) serves as the opening (<term>pratipat</term>). The following verse, "**Today, O God...**" (RV 5.82.4), is the companion verse (<term>anuchara</term>). This is indicated in the liturgical manuals: "We choose that of Savitr" and "Today, O God Savitr" are the opening and companion verses of the Vaishvadeva chant (Asvalayana Shrauta Sutra 5.18).

## Hymn Text
-> ॥ The first verse thereof ॥ <-

**We choose that enjoyment of the divine Savitr.**
**The best, the most all-bestowing, and swift; we meditate on the portion of Bhaga.**

**Word-by-word Analysis (Padapatha)**
That | of Savitr | we choose | we | of the god | enjoyment |
The best | the most all-bestowing | swift | of the portion [Bhaga] | we meditate.

---

## Commentary (Sayana)

**We**, the chanters, **choose**—meaning we pray for—**that** well-known **enjoyment** (<term>bhojanam</term>), which refers to wealth that is to be enjoyed.

<meta>This page continues the commentary on the 82nd hymn of the 5th Mandala, dedicated to Savitr. ### || Rig Veda || [Book 4, Chapter 4, Group 25]

Whose is this wealth? It belongs to the god Savitr, the Impeller <note>original: "prerakasya"</note>. And having obtained it, it is the best, most praiseworthy, and most supportive—meaning it provides all enjoyments. It is a "striker" <note>original: "turam"</note>, meaning a destroyer of enemies, because with wealth one is able to overcome foes. We hold such wealth—meaning we enjoy it—through the grace of Savitr, who is also Bhaga, the Adorable One. Or, it means we choose this wealth and, because of our prayer, we shall obtain it.

---

-> || Here is the second verse || <-

## Hymn Text
**For his own glory is most supreme; no one at all can diminish the beloved sovereignty of this Savitr.**
**For his | indeed | own glory-most | of Savitr | any | at all | beloved | not | do they diminish | self-sovereignty.**

## Commentary (Sayana)
Of this Savitr, his own glory <note>original: "yashas"</note> is supreme and extraordinary. His **sovereignty** (<term>svarajyam</term>—meaning his self-luminous power and lordship) is beloved by everyone. No one at all—not even the demons <note>original: "asuradayah"</note>—can **diminish** or harm it.

---

-> || Here is the third verse || <-

## Hymn Text
**For he, Savitr the Dispenser, provides treasures to the giver; we seek that wonderful portion.**
**He | indeed | treasures | for the giver | provides | Savitr | the Dispenser | that | portion | wonderful | we seek.**

## Commentary (Sayana)
For he indeed is Savitr, the **Dispenser** (<term>Bhaga</term>—the one to be worshiped), the god who **provides** or grants **treasures** (<note>original: "ratnani"</note>—lovely riches) to the **giver** (<note>original: "dashushe"</note>—the one who offers oblations to me). We **seek** or pray to that god for that **wonderful** and desirable **portion** of wealth.

---

Regarding the verses beginning "Today for us" <note>original: "Adya no"</note>: one should offer an oblation with each of these two verses (the fourth and fifth) if one has seen an unpleasant dream. It is indicated in the *Grihya Sutra* (3.6) that "with the two verses 'Today for us, O God Savitr...'" one performs this rite.

---

-> || Here is the fourth verse || <-

## Hymn Text
**Today, O God Savitr, grant us prosperity accompanied by offspring; drive away the influence of bad dreams.**
**Today | for us | O God | Savitr | offspring-possessing | grant | prosperity | away | bad-dreaming | drive.**

## Commentary (Sayana)
**O God Savitr**, on this **today**—this day of sacrifice—**grant** or impel toward us **prosperity** consisting of wealth and **offspring** such as sons. As for **bad dreaming** (<term>duhsvapnyam</term>)—which refers to bad dreams or the poverty that causes great sorrow—**drive** it far **away**.

---

-> || Here is the fifth verse || <-

## Hymn Text
**O God Savitr, drive away all evils; send to us that which is auspicious.**
**All | O God | Savitr | evils | away | drive | what | auspicious | that | to us | toward | send.**

<meta>This page continues the commentary on the 82nd hymn of the 5th Mandala of the Rig Veda, dedicated to Savitr. # Mandala 5, Section 6, Hymn 82 | Fourth Book (Ashtaka) | Page 551

O God Savitr, drive away all misfortunes. Whatever is **good**—such as offspring, cattle, or homes—bring that to us; impel it toward us. For the scripture <note>original: "shruti"</note> says: "Offspring is indeed good, cattle are good, a home is good."

->॥ Here ends the twenty-fifth group (varga) of the fourth chapter in the fourth book. ॥<-

---

## Hymn Text

->॥ Now the Sixth Verse ॥<-

**May we be sinless before Aditi, under the impulse of God Savitr; may we hold all desirable things.**

**Word-for-Word Breakdown (Padapatha):**
**Sinless | before Aditi | of the God | of Savitr | in the impulse | all | desirable things | may we hold.**

---

## Commentary (Sayana)

We, the performers of the ritual, should be **sinless** (<term>anagasah</term>—without fault or offense) before **Aditi** (<term>Aditi</term>—here interpreted as the indivisible goddess, the Earth). This occurs in the **impulse** (<term>save</term>—the command or permission) of the god Savitr, the Impeller. For it is upon the Earth that sins and faults are committed. Being free from such sins, may we **hold** (<note>original: "dhimahi"</note>—possess or maintain) all **desirable things** (<note>original: "vamani"</note>—wealth and riches that are sought after).

In the Four-Month Sacrifices (<term>Caturmasya</term>), specifically during the ritual section for the All-Gods (<term>Vaishvadeva Parvan</term>), the verse beginning "Towards the Lord of All-Gods..." (Verse 7) serves as the invitatory prayer for the twelve-layered cake offered to Savitr. This is documented in the *Ashvalayana Shrauta Sutra* (2.16): "Towards the Lord of the All-Gods, the protector of the good, the desirable thing today, O Savitr." 

In the Preliminary Sacrifice (<term>Prayaniya</term>), this same verse is used as the invitatory prayer for Savitr, as noted in the Sutras (4.3): "Towards the Lord of the All-Gods... he who knows all these born beings." 

Furthermore, in the rituals concerning the remaining sacrificial offerings (<term>Devasavam Havishshesha</term>), this is also the invitatory prayer for Savitr, as indicated (4.11): "Towards the Lord of the All-Gods... not to be diminished is the power of the divine Savitr."

---

## Hymn Text

->॥ This is the Seventh Verse ॥<-

**Today, with well-spoken hymns, we choose Savitr, the Lord of All-Gods, the protector of the good, whose impulse is true.**

**Word-for-Word Breakdown (Padapatha):**
**Towards | All-Gods-Lord | Protector of the good | with well-spoken hymns | today | we choose | true-impulse | Savitr.**

---

## Commentary (Sayana)

**Lord of All-Gods**: This refers to the one under whose control all the gods reside. This is because Savitr is the soul of all, as the scripture <note>original: "shruti"</note> states: "They call him Indra, Mitra, Varuna, Agni," meaning other deities are merely manifestations of his divine power. 

**Protector of the good** (<term>satpatim</term>): The guardian and protector of those who perform the sacred rites. 

**Whose impulse is true** (<term>satyasavam</term>): The one whose permission or command is unfailing and truthful. 

On **today** (this current day of sacrifice), we **choose** (<note>original: "vrinimahe"</note>—to serve, share in, or worship) the god Savitr with **well-spoken hymns** (<term>suktaih</term>—beautifully composed prayers).

---

## Hymn Text

->॥ Now the Eighth Verse ॥<-

**He who goes before both these days without failing, the wise God Savitr.**

**Word-for-Word Breakdown (Padapatha):**
**He who | these (two) | both | days | before | goes | without failing | wise | God | Savitr.**

<meta>This page concludes the commentary on Hymn 82 (dedicated to Savitr, the solar impeller) and begins the technical introduction and first verse of Hymn 83 (dedicated to Parjanya, the god of rain and clouds). This transition marks the end of the 26th Varga and the beginning of the 27th Varga within the fourth chapter of the fourth book.</meta>

# Rig Veda | Book 4, Chapter 4, Group 27

The connection of the previous verse is as follows: we choose that God Savitr, who is **well-meditating** <note>original: "svādhīḥ," meaning one with excellent thoughts or well-performed actions</note> or **one who performs good deeds**, and who moves before these two—the day and the night—without being heedless or negligent.

In the **Introductory Sacrifice** <term>Prāyaṇīya</term>, the verse beginning "He who [makes] all these..." serves as the offering prayer <term>yājyā</term> for Savitr. This is indicated in the ritual manuals: "He who [makes] all these born beings, the well-protecting Earth, the harmless Heaven" <note>Ashvalayana Shrauta Sutra 4.3</note>. During the **Horse Sacrifice** <term>Ashvamedha</term>, after the horse is released, a special offering to Savitr must be performed at each pressing of the Soma. In that ritual, this verse serves as the invitatory prayer <term>anuvākyā</term> during the midday pressing. This is also indicated: "He who [makes] all these born beings, may the God Savitr come, the possessor of fine jewels" <note>Ashvalayana Shrauta Sutra 10.6</note>.

->॥ This is the ninth verse ॥<-

## Hymn Text

**He who makes all these born beings hear him by his glory, and who impels them, is Savitr.** ॥9॥

**Word-for-Word Breakdown (Pada-patha):**
**He | these | all | born beings | makes hear | by [his] glory | and | impels | Savitr.** ॥9॥

---

## Commentary (Sayana)

That God who makes **all these**—meaning all created living beings, the **mobile ones**—hear him through his **glory** <note>original: "shlokena," meaning fame or praise</note>. This means that everyone hears the praise offered to him. Alternatively, he makes all these beings hear him by the **sound of rumbling** <note>original: "garjana-shabdena"</note> as he prepares to bring rain. Furthermore, **Savitr** (the Impeller) **impels** <note>original: "pra-suvāti," drives or stimulates</note> them. We choose Him—this is the intended meaning.

->॥ Thus ends the twenty-sixth group (varga) of the fourth chapter in the fourth book. ॥<-

---

The eleventh hymn, beginning with the words "Speak toward" <note>original: "acchā vada"</note>, consists of ten verses and was seen by the seer **Atri**, the son of the Earth <note>original: "Bhauma Atri"</note>. The **Vedic Index** <term>Anukramaṇikā</term> states: **"Speak [toward] has ten verses, dedicated to Parjanya; the first three are in the Jagati meter, and the second to last is in the Anushtup meter."** Specifically, the ninth verse ("When, O Parjanya...") is in the **Anushtup** meter <note>8 syllables per line</note>, while the three verses starting with "Strike down the trees..." are in the **Jagati** meter <note>12 syllables per line</note>. The remaining six are in the **Trishtubh** meter <note>11 syllables per line</note>. The deity of this hymn is **Parjanya** <note>the god of rain clouds</note>.

With this hymn, one should worship the directions/quarters of the sky, verse by verse. This is indicated in the manuals: **"When the ritual is established, one should worship all the directions with the four verses beginning 'Speak toward the mighty one with these songs,' or with the entire hymn verse by verse."** <note>Ashvalayana Shrauta Sutra 2.13</note>.

->॥ Now the first verse ॥<-

## Hymn Text

**Speak toward the mighty one; with these songs praise Parjanya; worship him with reverence. The bellowing bull, the quick-giver, places the seed as a germ in the plants.** ॥1॥

**Word-for-Word Breakdown (Pada-patha):**
**Toward | speak | the mighty | with songs | these | praise | Parjanya | with reverence | [and] | worship.**
**Bellowing | the bull | the quick-giver | seed | places | in the plants | the germ.** ॥1॥

---

## Commentary (Sayana)

O singer, **speak toward**—address—the **mighty** or powerful **Parjanya**. Pray to him. The name **Parjanya** has been explained in various ways by the etymologist **Yaska**: **"Parjanya is the 'satisfier' <note>original: 'tarpa-yitā'</note>, derived from the root 'tṛp' (to satisfy) with its first and last sounds reversed; or he is the 'conqueror of others' <note>original: 'paro jetā'</note>."**

<meta>This page continues the commentary on the first verse of Hymn 83, dedicated to Parjanya, and provides the text and commentary for verses 2 and 3. The previous page established the beginning of this hymn, which is an invocation to the deity of rain and thunder.</meta>

## Commentary (Sayana - continued)
...or he is the producer, or the impeller of fluids <note>original: "vā janayitā vā prājayitā vā rasānāṃ." This is a citation from the **Nirukta** (10.10), an ancient text on etymology</note>. Celebrate him with these songs, which are words of praise. Worship him with **reverence** <note>original: "namasā," here interpreted as food or sacrificial offerings</note>, serving him from all sides. Praise that Parjanya, who is the **bull** <term>Vrishabha</term> <note>a metaphor for power and fertility</note>, the shedder of waters, the **quick-giver** <note>original: "jīradānuḥ," one who grants life-sustaining rain quickly</note>, who, making a thundering sound, places the **seed** <note>original: "retas," referring to water as the fertilizing principle</note> in the plants as if in a womb.

---

## Hymn Text (Verse 2)
-> ॥ Now the Second Verse ॥ <-

He smites the trees, and he smites the **demons** <term>Rakshasas</term>; the whole world fears his great weapon. Even the innocent man flees before the mighty one, when Parjanya, thundering, smites the **evildoers**. ॥ 2 ॥

**Word-for-Word Breakdown (Pada-patha):**
**Smites | trees | he smites | and | he smites | demons | the whole | fears | world | from the great weapon.**
**And | the innocent | flees | from the mighty one | when | Parjanya | thundering | smites | the evildoers.** ॥ 2 ॥

## Commentary (Sayana)
This mantra is clearly explained in the **Nirukta** <term>Yaska's etymological treatise</term>. That explanation is written here: Parjanya strikes down the trees and strikes down the demons. All living beings here are afraid of his great weapon, for his strike is indeed great. Even a person who has committed no offense flees in fear from this deity who possesses the power of rain, when Parjanya, while thundering, destroys those of evil deeds, the sinners <note>original: "nirukta 10.11"</note>.

---

## Hymn Text (Verse 3)
-> ॥ Now the Third Verse ॥ <-

Like a **charioteer** <term>Rathi</term> whipping his horses, he makes his messengers, the rain-clouds, appear. From afar, the roars of the **lion** arise when Parjanya makes the sky full of rain. ॥ 3 ॥

**Word-for-Word Breakdown (Pada-patha):**
**Like a charioteer | with a whip | horses | whipping | visible | messengers | he makes | the rainy ones | indeed.**
**From afar | of the lion | the thunders | upward | arise | when | Parjanya | makes | rainy | the sky.** ॥ 3 ॥

## Commentary (Sayana)
**Like a charioteer** means like the master of a chariot. Just as such a person, whipping his horses, makes his **messengers** <note>or soldiers</note> appear, so too does Parjanya. By whipping the **horses**—which are the clouds—and urging them forward, he makes visible his messengers, which are the clouds that bring rain, or perhaps the **storm-gods** <term>Maruts</term> who act as his heralds. The word **indeed** <note>original: "aha"</note> is a filler for the meter. This being so, the **thunders** <note>the roaring sounds</note> of the **lion** arise from a distance. Here, **lion** <note>original: "simha"</note> refers to the cloud, either because it "overpowers" <note>from the root *sah*</note> the drought or because it "sounds" <note>from the root *hins*</note>. These roars rise up when Parjanya makes the **sky** <note>original: "nabhas," the atmosphere</note> possessed of rain.

---

## Verse 4 Introduction
The fourth verse, beginning with "The winds blow forth," is the offering prayer <term>yājyā</term> for the cereal offering <term>charu</term> dedicated to Parjanya. This is indicated in the ritual rules: "The winds blow forth, the lightnings fly" and so on, in the section on the establishment of the sacred fires <note>original: "Ashvalayana Shrauta Sutra 2.15"</note>. That text is as follows:

## Hymn Text (Verse 4)

The winds blow forth, the lightnings fall; the plants spring up, and the sky swells. Refreshment is born for the whole world when Parjanya protects the earth with his **seed** <note>original: "retas," a metaphor for rain as a fertilizing fluid</note>. ॥ 4 ॥

**Word-for-Word Breakdown (Pada-patha):**
**Forth | the winds | blow | fall | lightnings | up | the plants | spring | swells | the sky.**
**Refreshment | for the whole | world | is born | when | Parjanya | the earth | with seed | protects.** ॥ 4 ॥

---

## Commentary (Sayana)

The winds blow forth for the sake of rain. Lightnings fall, moving and wandering in every direction. The plants spring up; they rise and grow. The sky—the atmosphere—swells and flows with water. **Refreshment** <note>original: "Ira," interpreted here as food or the earth itself</note> is born for the sake of the entire world, for the benefit of all living things; it becomes capable of sustaining life. When does this happen? It happens whenever the god Parjanya protects or approaches the earth with his "seed," which is the rain-water.

---

## Hymn Text (Verse 5)
-> ॥ Now the Fifth Verse ॥ <-

In whose law the earth bows low; in whose law the **hoofed creatures** <term>Shaphavat</term> leap with joy; in whose law the plants take all forms; O Parjanya, grant us great **refuge** <note>original: "sharma," meaning protection or happiness</note>. ॥ 5 ॥

**Word-for-Word Breakdown (Pada-patha):**
**In whose | law | the earth | bows low | in whose | law | the hoofed ones | leap |**
**In whose | law | the plants | of all forms | He | to us | O Parjanya | great | refuge | grant.** ॥ 5 ॥

---

## Commentary (Sayana)

In the law—which means the activity—of Parjanya, the earth bows low, meaning it humbles itself or settles beneath the weight of the rain. In his law, the **hoofed creatures** <note>original: "shaphavat," referring to cattle, horses, and other four-legged animals</note> are nourished, filled, or move about excitedly. In his law or activity, the plants become "all-formed," taking on many various shapes and colors as they bloom. O Parjanya, you who are great, grant to us **great happiness** <note>original: "mahi sharma," a plea for vast protection and comfort</note>.

-> ॥ Thus ends the twenty-seventh Varga of the fourth chapter of the fourth book ॥ <-

## Hymn Text (Verse 6)
-> ॥ Now the Sixth Verse ॥ <-

Come hither with this thundering, shedding waters, our **Mighty Father** <term>Asura Pita</term>. ॥ 6 ॥

**Word-for-Word Breakdown (Pada-patha):**
**From the sky | to us | rain | O Maruts | grant | forth | flow | of the shedding | stallion | the streams.**
**Hither | with this | thundering | come | waters | shedding | the Mighty | Father | our.** ॥ 6 ॥

## Commentary (Sayana)

O Maruts, grant us rain from the sky, from the midst of the atmosphere. Make the streams of the "shedding stallion"—the rain-cloud—flow forth. The shedder <unclear>...</unclear> <note>The text breaks here; Sayana is explaining the metaphor of the horse as a cloud that pours out its strength as rain.</note>

<meta>This page concludes the commentary for verse 6 and provides the full text and commentary for verses 7 and 8 of Hymn 83 in the 5th Mandala of the Rig Veda. The hymn continues its petition to Parjanya, the deity of rain and storms, using vivid pastoral metaphors of chariots, skin-bags, and buckets to describe the release of rain.</meta>

...the streams of water belonging to the pervasive, rain-giving cloud. O Parjanya, come toward us with this thundering cloud. What does he do? Pouring down the waters, that divine spirit, though he is the **dispenser of waters** <note>original: "udakānāṃ nirasitā," one who ejects or throws out water</note>, is also our father and protector.

-> || Now the Seventh Verse || <-

## Hymn Text
Roar out, thunder, deposit the **seed** <note>original: "garbha," literally 'embryo' or 'fetus,' referring here to the life-giving moisture for plants</note>; fly around with your water-bearing chariot. Draw well your loosened **skin-bag** <term>Dṛti</term> downward; let the heights and the hollows be made level. ॥ 7 ॥

**Word-for-Word Breakdown (Pada-patha):**
**Toward | roar | thunder | the embryo | in | place | with the water-bearing | around | fly | with the chariot.**
**The skin-bag | well | draw | loosened | downward | level | let them | become | the heights | the hollows.** ॥ 7 ॥

## Commentary (Sayana)
Roar toward the earth. Make a sound. The word is repeated for the sake of emphasis. **Thunder** <note>original: "stanaya"</note>; make a rumbling sound. Deposit the water, which stays within the plants like an embryo. For that purpose, fly all around with a chariot that possesses water. Draw the cloud—which, like a leather skin-bag, holds the water—downward and facing the earth for the sake of rain, whether it be tightly bound or **loosened** <note>original: "viṣitam," can mean either bound/contained or released/unbound</note>. When this is done, let the elevated regions and the low-lying valleys become **level** <note>original: "samā," equal</note>. This means let them all be equally filled with water.

---

-> || Now the Eighth Verse || <-

## Hymn Text
Draw up the great **bucket** <note>original: "kośa," a vessel or pail, used here as a metaphor for a massive rain-cloud</note> and pour it down; let the released rivers flow forward. Drench heaven and earth with **fatness** <term>Ghṛta</term>; let there be a good drinking-place for the **unslayable cows** <term>Aghnyā</term>. ॥ 8 ॥

**Word-for-Word Breakdown (Pada-patha):**
**The great | bucket | up | draw | down | pour | let them flow | the rivers | released | forward.**
**With fatness | heaven and earth | thoroughly | drench | a good drinking-place | let it | become | for the unslayable ones.** ॥ 8 ॥

## Commentary (Sayana)
O Parjanya, draw up the great, swollen bucket—the cloud—and make it rise. Having done so, pour it out; make it drip downward. Let the rivers, being released, flow toward the east; for generally, rivers flow eastward. Drench heaven and earth—both the sky and the ground—excessively with **fatness** <note>original: "ghṛtena," usually meaning clarified butter, but in the context of the sky, it refers to rain-water</note>. For the **unslayable cows** <note>original: "aghnyābhyaḥ," those that must not be killed</note>, let there be water that is easy and excellent to drink.

<meta>This page concludes the final two verses of the hymn to Parjanya (the rain god) and introduces the following hymn dedicated to Prithivi (the Earth goddess). It continues the theme of the life-giving and occasionally destructive power of the storm, ending with a prayer of gratitude and a request for the rain to cease once the earth is replenished.</meta>

## Hymn Text

-> || Now the Ninth Verse || <-

When you, O **Parjanya** <term>Parjanya: the Vedic deity of rain and thunder</term>, roaring and thundering, strike the **evil-doers** <note>original: "duṣkṛtaḥ"; while usually meaning 'sinners,' the commentator interprets these as the clouds that withhold rain</note>, then everything that exists upon the earth rejoices. ॥ 9 ॥

**Word-for-Word Breakdown (Pada-patha):**
**When | Parjanya | roaring | thundering | you strike | the evil-doers | toward | this | all | rejoices | what | soever | and | on the earth | above.** ॥ 9 ॥

---

## Commentary (Sayana)

O **Parjanya**, when you are **roaring**—making an intense sound—and **thundering**, and you **strike** or tear apart the **evil-doers**, by which we mean the clouds that withhold water, then **this all**—the entire world—**rejoices**. The term "all" is further specified: **whatsoever is upon the earth**, meaning all things both moving and unmoving established on the ground, this entire world rejoices. It is filled with joy. It is well known that rain is the cause of satisfaction for the whole world.

---

## Hymn Text

-> || Now the Tenth Verse || <-

You have sent the rain; now **hold it back well** <note>original: "ud-u ṣū gṛbhāya," literally 'to seize or take up,' meaning to stop the downpour</note>. You have made the **deserts** <term>Dhanva: waterless regions</term> crossable once more. You have given life to the plants for our food, and you have received **praise** <note>original: "manīṣām," literally 'wisdom' or 'thought,' here meaning a hymn of praise</note> from the people. ॥ 10 ॥

**Word-for-Word Breakdown (Pada-patha):**
**You have rained | the rain | up | [particle] | well | hold back | you have made | the deserts | across | to go | [particle] | you have generated | the plants | for food | [particle] | and | from the creatures | you have obtained | the praise.** ॥ 10 ॥

---

## Commentary (Sayana)

This verse is intended to stop the excessive rain. O **Parjanya**, you **have rained**. You have performed the act of raining. Now, **hold it back well**; that is, take it up or bring it to an end. You **have made** the **deserts**, which are regions without water, into places possessing water. For what purpose? **To go across**; so that they may be traversed. You **have generated the plants**. For what purpose? **For food**, meaning for wealth or for enjoyment. The word **kam** <note>original: "kam," a Vedic particle</note> is a filler for the poetic meter, similar to its use in other Vedic passages. And also, you **have obtained** the **praise**, the hymn of tribute, from the subjects or living beings.

-> || Thus ends the twenty-eighth section (Varga) of the fourth chapter (Adhyaya) of the fourth book (Ashtaka) || <-

---

## Sukta Introduction

The twelfth hymn, beginning with the words "**Strongly indeed**" <note>original: "Baḷitthā"</note>, consists of three verses. Its seer is Atri, the son of the Earth; its deity is **Prithivi** (the Earth); and its meter is **Anushtubh** <note>a meter consisting of four quarters of eight syllables each</note>. It is recorded in the index: "The three verses of 'Strongly indeed' are dedicated to the Earth in the Anushtubh meter." The ritual application of this hymn follows its character. The first verse is used as the invitatory prayer (*Anuvakya*) for the offerings to the Earth among the offerings to the gods. This is indicated in the ritual manuals: "**Strongly indeed, of the mountains, you who bear the weight of the trees**" (Asvalayana Shrauta Sutra 6.14). Furthermore, in the ritual of the Earth-stome (*Bhumi-stoma*), this is the lead hymn for the Marutvatiya litany (Asvalayana Shrauta Sutra 9.5).

<vocab>
**Parjanya (पर्जन्य):** The deity associated with the rain-cloud, thunder, and the vitalizing power of the storm.
**Dushkrita (दुष्कृत):** Literally "evil-doers." In this agricultural context, the commentator views the "wicked" as the clouds that refuse to release their water.
**Oshadhi (ओषधी):** Herbs or plants, specifically those that die after ripening.
**Manisha (मनीषा):** Inspired thought or wisdom, which in the context of a ritual refers to the hymn or prayer offered by the worshiper.
**Anushtubh (आनुष्टुभ):** One of the most common Vedic meters, often used for praise and narrative.
**Viniyoga (विनियोग):** The specific ritual context or "application" in which a particular verse must be recited.
</vocab>

# Mandala 5, Anuvaka 6, Hymn 84 | Fourth Ashtaka | Page 557

## Hymn Text

-> || This is the First Verse || <-

Truly, you bear the **cleaving** <note>original: "khidram"; refers to the gaps or the weight/pressure of the mountains</note> of the mountains, O **Earth** <term>Pṛthivī: The Goddess of the Earth, whose name literally means "The Wide One"</term>. By your greatness, O mighty one, you who are full of **slopes** <note>original: "pravatvatī"; can also mean "abounding in streams"</note>, you quicken the soil. ॥ 1 ॥

**Word-for-Word Breakdown (Pada-patha):**
> **Truly | thus | of the mountains | the cleaving | you bear | O Earth | forth | which | the ground | full of slopes | by greatness | you quicken | O mighty one.** ॥ 1 ॥

---

-> || Now the Second Verse || <-

The **hymns of praise** <term>Stomas: Vedic liturgical chants</term> stir you, O wandering one, with their **movements** <note>original: "aktubhiḥ"; typically "nights" or "rays," but here interpreted by the commentator as the "movements" or "gestures" of the chanting</note>. You cast forth the swelling **cloud** <note>original: "perum"; that which fills or nourishes</note> like a whinnying horse, O radiant one. ॥ 2 ॥

**Word-for-Word Breakdown (Pada-patha):**
> **Hymns | you | O wandering one | toward | they stir | with movements | forth | which | strength/cloud | like | whinnying | the filler/cloud | you cast | O radiant one.** ॥ 2 ॥

---

-> || Now the Third Verse || <-

With your might, you hold even the **trees** <term>Vanaspati: "Lords of the Forest," referring to large trees</term> firm upon the ground, when the lightnings of your **cloud** <note>original: "abhra"; the water-bearing cloud</note> and the rains of heaven pour down. ॥ 3 ॥

**Word-for-Word Breakdown (Pada-patha):**
> **Firm | even | which | trees | by the ground | you hold fast | by power | when | your | of the cloud | lightnings | from heaven | pour down | rains.** ॥ 3 ॥

## Commentary (Sayana)

**This Earth is of two forms: she is both the visible deity of the ground we see and the deity of the middle sphere <term>Antariksha: the atmosphere or mid-region between Earth and Heaven</term>. Here, she is addressed and described in that middle station. O Earth, you who possess the quality of being "wide," O deity of the middle realm: you truly bear the "cleaving"—the splitting or tearing—of the mountains, which here refers to the clouds. O mighty one, O you who abound in streams of water, you who gladden the visible earth with your greatness or with your great waters.**

---

**O wandering goddess, you who move in various ways, the singers of hymns stir you with their flowing chants. They praise you. Furthermore, you cast forth the nourishing cloud—which makes a sound like a whinnying horse—O radiant and swift-moving one.**

**The verse beginning "Firm even..." is the consecrating text <term>Yājyā: a sacrificial prayer</term> for Earth during the offerings of the gods. This same verse is the opening of the hymn in the Earth-stome ritual in the Niskevalya ceremony. The ritual rules for this have been cited previously.**

*   **Typography:** The Vedic 'ḷa' (ळ) is used where a 'd' (ड) appears between two vowels. The text includes full accentuation marks (svaras) to guide the chanting.

# Page 558 || Rig Veda || Book 4, Chapter 4, Section 30

O Earth, you who are **firm** <note>original: "dr̥ḷhā"</note>. Through the use of a grammatical substitution <note>original: "supāṃ suluk"; a Paninian rule for Vedic Case-ending variation</note>, the word takes the form of the third case. Together with the firm **ground** <term>Kṣmayā: The solid earth or soil</term>, you **hold** <note>original: "dadharṣi"</note> or support the **trees** <term>Vanaspati: Literally "Lords of the Forest"</term> with your might and strength. Alternatively, "firm" is used as a predicate adjective, meaning you hold the trees after having made them firm. **When** <note>original: "yadyasyāste"</note> the rains from your **lightning**-filled, shining cloud—here the sixth case is used in the sense of the fifth case—from the cloud that carries away the waters, from the sky, the atmosphere, or from the Sun, it rains. Or, it means when the masses of water from your cloud fall and rain down from the shining heavens.

-> ॥ Thus ends the twenty-ninth Varga of the fourth Adhyaya of the fourth Ashtaka ॥ <-

The thirteenth hymn, beginning with **"To the Sovereign"** <note>original: "Pra samrāja"</note>, consists of eight verses. It is attributed to the seer Atri Bhauma, composed in the Trishtubh meter, and dedicated to the god Varuna. The ritual application is determined by its characteristic marks as cited in the Index: **"To the Sovereign, eight verses to Varuna."**

-> ॥ Of these, the first verse ॥ <-

## Hymn Text
Sing a great, deep, and dear **prayer** to the **Sovereign** Varuna, the renowned, who has spread the **earth** for the **Sun** to rest upon, just as a **preparer of the sacrifice** spreads a skin. ॥ 1 ॥

**Word-for-Word Breakdown (Pada-patha):**
**Forth | to the Sovereign | great | sing | deep | prayer | dear | to Varuna | to the renowned | forth | who | spread | like a preparer of the sacrifice | a skin | for spreading | the earth | for the Sun.** ॥ 1 ॥

---

## Commentary (Sayana)
The Rishi addresses himself, saying: O Seer, you must **sing** <note>original: "prārca"; to chant or proclaim</note> a **prayer** <term>Brahma: Here referring to a hymn of praise</term> that is **great** (meaning abundant), **deep** (meaning profound or difficult to fathom and full of many meanings), and **dear** (pleasant) for **Varuna**. Varuna is the **Sovereign** <term>Samrāj: A supreme ruler or universal king</term> who shines perfectly, the Lord who is **renowned** and heard of everywhere, the one who wards off calamity and encompasses all people. **Who** (Varuna), like a **preparer of the sacrifice** <term>Śamitṛ: The person who prepares the sacrificial animal, often spreading the hide</term> who strikes and spreads a skin for a seat, **spread out** <note>original: "vijaghāna"</note> the **earth**. In this context, "earth" refers to the broad atmosphere. According to the sacred text, "the atmosphere is also called the Earth" <note>original: "tr̥tīyāsyāṃ pr̥thivyām"</note>. He spread it for the **Sun** as a place to be laid out. Indeed, once it is spread out, it becomes suitable for the activities of the world; therefore, he expanded the atmosphere for the world's functioning. As it is said in the Rig Veda (1.24.8): **"King Varuna has truly made a wide path..."**

---

-> ॥ Now the second verse ॥ <-

## Hymn Text
He has stretched the atmosphere through the **woods**, placed speed in horses, milk in **cows**, wisdom in hearts, fire in the **waters**, the sun in the sky, and **Soma** upon the mountain. ॥ 2 ॥

Varuna: God of the cosmic order and the waters; Samrāj: Supreme Sovereign; Brahman: Sacred hymn or prayer; Antariksha: The mid-region or atmosphere; Shamitṛ: Sacrificial preparer/immolator; Prithivī: The Earth (or broad space); Surya: The Sun.
</vocab>

## Hymn Text (Word-for-Word Analysis of 5.85.2)

In the forests | apart | the atmosphere | [He] spread | strength | in the horses | milk | in the cows | in hearts | will | Varuna | in the waters | fire | in heaven | the sun | [He] placed | Soma | on the mountain. ॥ 2 ॥

---

## Commentary (Sayana)

This Varuna spread the atmosphere in the forests, atop the trees. He expanded [it]. Likewise, the **Vajasaneyaka** <note>The Vajasaneyi Samhita of the White Yajur Veda</note> says: "In the forests indeed, over these treetops, the atmosphere is spread; therefore the scripture says: 'In the forests He spread the atmosphere apart.'" 

He spread **strength** <note>original: "vāja"</note> or power in the horses. He placed milk in the **cows** <term>Usriyā: A Vedic term for cows, literally "the ruddy ones" or those from whom enjoyments flow</term>. The etymology of *Usriya* is: "that from which enjoyments flow out." 

In the hearts—meaning in the minds—He placed **will** <term>Kratu: The mental determination or intention to perform an action</term>. For what a person meditates upon with the mind, that he performs through action. 

In the waters—referring to the clouds, the oceans, or the submarine fire—He spread fire everywhere; this is the connection. Furthermore, in the sky, in the celestial realm, He placed the Sun. He established it there. And He placed the Soma plant on the mountain.

---

## Hymn Text

-> ॥ Now the third verse ॥ <-

Varuna let loose the cask with its opening facing downward; it moistened the two worlds and the atmosphere. With that, the King of the whole universe wets the earth, just as rain wets the barley. ॥ 3 ॥

**With opening facing downward | Varuna | the cask | forth | let loose | the two worlds | the atmosphere | with that | of all | the universe | the King | barley | like | rain | apart | wets | the earth. ॥ 3 ॥**

---

## Commentary (Sayana)

**With its opening facing downward** <note>original: "nīcīnabāraṃ"</note> means having the exit-hole or mouth directed toward the ground. He let loose or created it. What? The **cask** <term>Kavandha: Literally a "headless trunk" or a "water-vessel," used here as a metaphor for a rain-cloud</term>. "Kavana" signifies water; that which holds water is a *kavandha* or cloud. He made it so. Alternatively, *kavandha* can mean the water itself; He made that water have a downward-facing path for exit. The meaning is: having split the cloud, He made the water flow downward. 

Toward what? It is said: toward the **two worlds** <term>Rodasī: A common Vedic term for Heaven and Earth</term> and the atmosphere. This was done for the benefit of the three worlds. With that water, Varuna, who is the King and Master of the entire universe and all living beings, wets the earth. He moistens it. 

The text uses a comparison: **just as rain wets the barley** <note>original: "yavaṃ na vr̥ṣṭiḥ"</note>. Just as a man who sows or a rain-shower spreads water everywhere so that the barley may sprout, so Varuna wets the earth everywhere. Alternatively, the connection is "the rain is Varuna himself," meaning he acts as the rain-cloud. In this interpretation, the word "man" should be understood: "as a man [wets] the barley." Regarding this, one should consult the **Nirukta** <note>Yaska's Nirukta 10.4; an ancient treatise on etymology and semantics</note> which explains: "Varuna [let loose] the cask with its opening facing downward," and so on.

---

## Hymn Text

-> ॥ Now the fourth verse ॥ <-

He wets the ground, the earth, and even the heavens, when Varuna wishes to milk [the clouds]. The mountains are clothed with clouds, and the mighty heroes slacken [their strength]. ॥ 4 ॥

<meta>This page continues the commentary for Rig Veda, Mandala 5, Hymn 85, dedicated to the deity Varuna. The previous page ended with the beginning of Verse 4, describing Varuna’s role in bringing rain. This page completes the explanation of Verse 4 and provides the text and commentary for Verse 5 and the beginning of Verse 6. In the traditional study system, this marks the transition into the 31st Varga (section) of the 4th Adhyaya (chapter) in the 4th Ashtaka (book).</meta>

## Hymn Text

### Verse 4 (Word-for-Word Analysis)
[He] wets | the earth | the ground | and | heaven | when | milked [water] | Varuna | rain | then | indeed | together | with a cloud | they clothe | the mountains | desiring strength | striving | heroes. ॥ 4 ॥

---

## Commentary (Sayana)

Varuna wets the ground and the earth—referring here to the wide atmosphere. As mentioned previously, the word "earth" <note>original: "pṛthivī"</note> can also be used to denote the atmosphere. He also wets the heavens, the celestial realm. This occurs when he desires the "milked" <note>original: "dugdham"</note> rain, which is the filling of water. Alternatively, "milked" refers to the water itself, which by extension signifies the effects of water, such as the growth of plants. When he desires, "May the plants and such grow," immediately they "clothe" or cover [the land]. Who? The mountains, meaning the clouds. With what? With mist or a cloud. Furthermore, the "heroes"—the Maruts <note>Storm deities who accompany Indra or Varuna</note> who specifically impel the rain—strive and set the clouds in motion, desiring strength.

-> ॥ Now the fifth verse ॥ <-

## Hymn Text

### Verse 5
I proclaim this, the great, mysterious power of the famous divine Varuna; 
Standing in the atmosphere, he measured out the earth with the sun, 
as if using a measuring rod. ॥ 5 ॥

### Verse 5 (Word-for-Word Analysis)
This | indeed | well | of the Asura | famous | great | mysterious power | of Varuna | forth | [I] proclaim | with a measure-like | standing | in the atmosphere | apart | who | measured | the earth | with the sun. ॥ 5 ॥

---

## Commentary (Sayana)

"Of the Asura" <term>Asura: In the early Rig Veda, this term refers to powerful divine beings or "lords," before later shifting to mean demons.</term> refers to that which relates to an Asura. This relationship is defined by the role of the killer and the killed; thus, it means "the killer of Asuras." Alternatively, "Sura" can mean a cloud, and since a cloud gives life, it relates to that. I proclaim the great **mysterious power** <term>Maya: In this context, the commentator glosses this as "prajñā" or extraordinary wisdom and creative power</term> of the well-known Varuna. What is this power? It is described thus: that Varuna, while standing in the atmosphere, measures out or defines the limits of the earth and the atmosphere using the sun, as if it were a staff or a measuring rod. This is his miraculous power.

-> ॥ This concludes the 30th section (Varga) of the 4th chapter of the 4th book ॥ <-

-> ॥ Now the sixth verse ॥ <-

## Hymn Text

### Verse 6
No one has dared to challenge this great, mysterious power of the wisest god, 
whereby the rushing rivers, though pouring their water into the one sea, 
do not fill it. ॥ 6 ॥

### Verse 6 (Word-for-Word Analysis)
This | indeed | now | of the wisest | mysterious power | great | of the god | no one | [has] challenged | the one | which | with water | not | [they] fill | the rushing | pouring in | the rivers | the sea. ॥ 6 ॥

---

## Commentary (Sayana)

Of the wisest <note>original: "kavitamasya"</note>—meaning the one of excellent wisdom—the shining or praiseworthy god Varuna... this all-enpassing [power]...

<vocab>
वरुण (Varuna) - A major Vedic deity, the guardian of cosmic order (Ṛta) and the lord of the waters.
माया (Maya) - Extraordinary wisdom or the divine power to create and organize the universe.
असुर (Asura) - A title for a powerful lord; here applied to Varuna as a master of cosmic forces.
सूर्य (Surya) - The Sun, used by Varuna as a tool to measure the dimensions of the world.
महीं (Mahīm) - Great or vast.
अवनयः (Avanayaḥ) - Moving waters or rivers.
</vocab>

<summary>This page explains Varuna's cosmic governance, specifically his ability to produce rain and his "Maya" (divine wisdom) used to measure the earth with the sun. It also introduces the paradox of the sea never being filled despite the constant inflow of rivers as a testament to his power.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the commentary on the 85th Hymn (Sukta) of the 5th Mandala, dedicated to Varuna. It concludes the explanation of Varuna’s cosmic power (Verse 6) and moves into prayers for the forgiveness of sins committed against friends, family, and strangers (Verses 7 and 8).</meta>

No one has ever challenged <note>original: "na-dadharsa"</note> this established, vast, and mysterious wisdom <note>original: "maya"</note>. No one can harm it. The word "nu" is used here for poetic completion. Even though the many shining <note>original: "enih"</note> rivers, which are always in motion and pouring forth their waters, flow into it, they do not fill up the single ocean. This is the great work of Varuna. 

It should not be argued that such a task—stretching from the expansion of the atmosphere to the filling of the ocean—is only suitable for the Supreme Lord <note>original: "Parameshwara"</note> and not for Varuna. This is because Varuna is simply a form or manifestation of that same Lord, as the scriptures <note>original: "Sruti"</note> state: "He is Brahma..."

---

## Hymn Text

-> || Now the Seventh Verse || <-

O Varuna, if we have committed an offense against a comrade, or a friend, or a lifelong brother; 
Whether against a neighbor who is always with us, or even a stranger—
O Varuna, whatever sin we have committed, please release us from it. ॥ 7 ॥

**A comrade. | O Varuna. | A friend. | Or. | A companion. | Or. | Always. | Indeed. | A brother. | Or. |**
**A neighbor. | Or. | Constant. | O Varuna. | A stranger. | Or. | Which. | Ever. | Sin. | We have committed. | Release. | That. ॥ 7 ॥**

## Commentary (Sayana)

O Varuna, regarding a **comrade** <note>original: "aryamyam"</note>. This word refers to a companion or the deity Aryaman himself. The root implies one who gives <note>original: "pradataram"</note>. Alternatively, it refers to a teacher or Guru <note>original: "aryama"</note> who instructs through the scriptures. Against him, or a **friend** <note>original: "mitryam"</note>—derived from a root meaning affection—meaning one who is devoted to us. Or a **companion** <note>original: "sakhayam"</note>, meaning one of equal reputation. Or a **lifelong brother**. Or a **constant neighbor** <note>original: "vesham"</note>, one who lives in a nearby house. Or even a **stranger** <note>original: "aranam"</note>, meaning someone who does not speak the same language, or one who does not give generously. Whatever **sin** <note>original: "agas"</note> or offense we **have committed** <note>original: "cakṛma"</note> against these people, **release** <note>original: "shishrathah"</note> us from it; destroy the consequences of that sin for us.

---

## Hymn Text

-> || Now the Eighth Verse || <-

If we have cheated like gamblers at play, whether it be true or whether we know it not; 
O God, cast all these sins away like loosened bonds, 
so that we may be dear to you, O Varuna. ॥ 8 ॥

**Gamblers. | If. | They have cheated. | Like. | In play. | Which. | Or. | Indeed. | Truth. | And. | Which. | Not. | We know. |**
**All. | Those. | Away. | Cast. | Like loosened [bonds]. | O God. | Then. | Of you. | May we be. | O Varuna. | Dear ones. ॥ 8 ॥**

## Commentary (Sayana)

**Gamblers** <note>original: "kitavasah"</note> refer to those who play with dice. A gambler <note>original: "kitava"</note> is so called because he says, "What do you have? <note>original: "kim tava asti"</note> I have won everything!" **Like in play**, just as in a game of dice, if people **have cheated** <note>original: "riripuh"</note>, meaning they smear us with sin or impose guilt upon us—as when enemies claim, "You committed this sin"—so too with us. <note>The particle 'na' here is used for comparison.</note> Or, if the sin is **truth**, meaning an actual offense committed without false accusation <unclear>...</unclear>

---

- <term>Varuna</term>: The Vedic deity responsible for upholding cosmic and moral law (Rta).
- <term>Aryaman</term>: A solar deity representing hospitality, manners, and the rules of society.
- <term>Mitra</term>: A deity often paired with Varuna, representing friendship, contracts, and morning light.
- <term>Maya</term>: In the Rig Veda, this refers to a divine, creative power or the mysterious wisdom used by gods to shape the universe.

## Commentary (Sayana)
...we have performed. Moreover, whatever sin <note>original: "papam"</note> we have committed unknowingly—not being aware of it—please release <note>original: "vishya"</note> all of those sins. Let them be released as easily as one might loosen a binding or as a fruit falls when its stem weakens. The verbal root "si" used here with a prefix specifically denotes "releasing" or "unbinding." O God, thereafter may we be dear to you. May we remain in your favor.

---

The fourteenth hymn of this section <note>Mandala 6, Sukta 60</note>, beginning with "Indra and Agni," consists of six verses. The seer is Bharadvaja <note>The OCR "acherasthama" likely refers to the lineage of the Rishi Bharadvaja</note>, the meter is Anustubh, and the deities addressed are Indra and Agni together. The sixth verse is in the Virat-Purva meter. This is because the rules define this meter as having two sections of ten syllables followed by three sections of eight syllables. Thus, the ancient Index <note>original: "Anukramani"</note> states: "Indra and Agni, six verses, the meter is Anustubh, ending in a Virat." The ritual application <note>original: "viniyoga"</note> is determined by the specific marks or signs within the verses.

-> ।। Here is the first verse ।। <-

## Hymn Text
O Indra and Agni, that mortal whom you both protect in battles, he breaks through even the strongest obstacles; he gains glorious wealth, just as the voices of the wise break through silence. ॥ 1 ॥

> **Padapatha:**
> **Indra-Agni. | Thus. | Whom. | You two protect. | Both. | In battles. | Mortal. |**
> **Strong/Firm. | Even. | He. | Forth. | Breaks. | Glorious wealth. | Voices-like. | Of the wise.** ॥ 1 ॥

## Commentary (Sayana)
O **Indra and Agni**, you two who are inseparable from one another: **that mortal whom you protect** or guard **in battles** <note>original: "vajeshu"</note> or wars, **that mortal** even against **strong** or firm things, **breaks** <note>original: "bhedati"</note> or pierces through. This refers to him capturing the **glorious** and shining **wealth** belonging to his enemies. This is compared to the **voices of the wise** <note>original: "rishi-varnih"</note>—just as the words of a sage overcome the arguments of an opponent. Alternatively, it may refer to Agni existing in three places, breaking through the speech of enemies.

---
-> ।। Now the second verse ।। <-

## Hymn Text
They who are difficult to overcome in armies, they who are invincible in battles, they who watch over the five tribes—O Indra and Agni, we invoke them. ॥ 2 ॥

> **Padapatha:**
> **Which. | In armies. | Difficult-to-overcome. | Which. | In battles. | Invincible. |**
> **Which. | Five. | Tribes/People. | Over. | Indra-Agni. | Thus. | Them. | We invoke.** ॥ 2 ॥

## Commentary (Sayana)
**Which** refers to the two deities, Indra and Agni. They are **difficult to overcome** <note>original: "dustara"</note> in **armies**, meaning they cannot be defeated by opposing forces. **Which** are also **invincible** <note>original: "avayya"</note> or worthy of being praised in **battles** or conflicts. **Which** look over the **five tribes** <note>original: "pancha charshanih"</note>. The word "charshanih" refers to human beings or the five primary tribes of people; the sense is that the deities "protect" them (which is an implied verb here). **Them**, those two beings of great power, **we invoke** or praise.

<vocab>
Indra-Agni: A dual deity representing the combined power of the king of gods and the sacrificial fire.
Mortal (Martya): A human being, contrasting with the immortal gods.
Vaja: Often translated as strength or battle, but also refers to the plunder or "booty" won in war.
Pancha Charshanih: The "Five Tribes," a common Vedic term for the totality of the Aryan people or all of humanity.
Anustubh: A common Vedic meter consisting of four quarters of eight syllables each.
Sayana: A 14th-century scholar whose commentary (bhashya) is the standard for understanding the Vedas.
</vocab>

<meta>This page continues the translation of Rig Veda, Mandala 6, Sukta 60 (addressed to Indra and Agni). ## Hymn Text

->|| The Third Verse ||<-

Theirs is this conquering power, the sharp thunderbolt of the generous ones. Held in their hands, it rushes forth for the sake of the cattle, as the slayers of the covering demon. ॥ 3 ॥

**Word-by-word Analysis:**
Theirs. Indeed. Conquering. Power. Sharp. Thunderbolt. Of the generous ones. Against [the enemy]. In the hands. Of the cattle. For the slayer of the covering demon <note>Vritra</note>. Towards. It rushes. ॥ 3 ॥

---

## Commentary (Sayana)

**Conquering** <note>original: "arvat"</note> means overpowering. Their **power** <note>original: "shavah"</note> or strength belongs to them alone. The **thunderbolt** <note>original: "didyut"</note> or *Vajra* of those two **generous ones** <note>original: "maghonoh"</note>—who are possessed of great food or wealth—is **sharp** <note>original: "tigmam"</note> and rests in their **hands** <note>original: "gabhastyoh"</note>. Such are these two gods. For the sake of obtaining **cattle** <note>original: "gavam"</note>—referring either to actual cows stolen by the *Panis* <note>a class of demons who hid the celestial cows</note> or to the waters—they approach with a **swift** <note>original: "dushna"</note> chariot, which moves with irresistible force. They go forth for the **slaying of the covering demon** <note>original: "vritraghna"</note>, either to strike the clouds that hold back rain or to kill the demon Vritra himself. They advance toward the enemy.

---

## Hymn Text

->|| The Fourth Verse ||<-

We invoke you both, Indra and Agni, in the rush of chariots; you two are the lords of swift-moving wealth, the all-knowing, the most highly praised with songs. ॥ 4 ॥

**Word-by-word Analysis:**
Those two. You two. In the rush. Of chariots. Indra and Agni. We invoke. Lords. Of the swift-moving. Wealth. All-knowing. Most highly praised with songs. ॥ 4 ॥

---

## Commentary (Sayana)

**O Gods**, we **invoke** <note>original: "havamahe"</note> or praise you two, who possess the qualities to be described. For what purpose? **In the rush of chariots**, meaning in battle, to urge the chariots forward. What is your nature? You are **Indra and Agni**, joined as a pair. You are the **lords** <note>original: "pati"</note> or masters of **swift-moving wealth** <note>original: "turasya radhasah"</note>, such as cattle and riches that are in constant motion. You are **all-knowing** <note>original: "vidvansa"</note> and the **most highly praised with songs** <note>original: "girvanastama"</note>, most worthy of being worshipped through our hymns. Such are you two whom we call upon.

---

## Hymn Text

->|| The Fifth Verse ||<-

Increasing day by day, undeceivable gods who protect the mortal; the worthy ones, I place them in front, just as one places the harness on the two shoulders of a horse. ॥ 5 ॥

**Word-by-word Analysis:**
Those two. Increasing. Along. The days. The mortal [man]. The gods. Undeceivable. Worthy. Indeed. In front. I place. Like the two shoulders. The gods. For the horse. ॥ 5 ॥

Note: The previous page translation provided in the prompt referenced Mandala 6, but the current manuscript text identifies itself as Mandala 5, following the numbering of the Atri clan. # Rig Veda: Volume 4, Chapter 4, Section 33

## Commentary by Sayana
[Conclusion of the commentary on Mandala 5, Hymn 86, Verse 5]

Those two <note>Indra and Agni</note> indeed grow day by day. This means they are always in a state of increased power. He provides an illustration for this growth: **like two mortals** <note>original: "martā-iva"</note>, meaning like two men who grow [in strength] every day. These two shining gods, who are **invincible** <note>original: "adabhā"</note> and highly **venerable** <note>original: "hantā-cit"</note>—the word "cit" here indicates worship—are placed before us. I place these two gods of great majesty in front for the sake of obtaining horses. **Like Amsha** <note>original: "amśāv-iva"</note>; Amsha is the name of a deity who resides among the twelve Adityas <note>solar deities</note>. He also represents the god Bhaga. Like the two Adityas, they are radiant.

---

## Hymn Text
-> ॥ The Sixth Verse ॥ <-

**Thus, for Indra and Agni, the offering has been poured, a strengthening power, like clarified butter purified by the stones. May those two maintain great fame among the wise patrons and wealth among those who sing their praise; may they maintain nourishment among those who sing their praise.** ॥ 6 ॥

-> Word-by-word Analysis <-

**Thus. For Indra and Agni. Has been poured. The offering. Strengthening. Clarified butter. Like. Purified. By the stones.**
**Those two. Among the wise patrons. Fame. Great. Wealth. Among those who sing praise. May they maintain. Nourishment. Among those who sing praise. May they maintain.** ॥ 6 ॥

---

## Commentary by Sayana
[Commentary on Mandala 5, Hymn 86, Verse 6]

**Thus** <note>original: "eva"</note> means in the manner now being performed, specifically with the accompaniment of these hymns of praise. For **Indra and Agni**, the **offering** <note>original: "havyam"</note> has been **poured** <note>original: "ahāvi"</note> or released. What is the nature of that offering? It is **strengthening** <note>original: "śūṣam"</note>, or power-giving. Like what? Like **clarified butter** <note>original: "ghṛtam"</note> or Soma-juice that is **purified** <note>original: "pūtam"</note> and pressed **by the stones** <note>original: "adribhiḥ"</note>. Just as that Soma is given to you, so too are the sacrificial cakes and other offerings. May those two gods **maintain** <note>original: "didhṛtam"</note> or bestow **great** <note>original: "bṛhat"</note>, abundant **fame** <note>original: "śravaḥ"</note>—meaning either food or glory—and **wealth** <note>original: "rayim"</note> among the **wise patrons** <note>original: "sūriṣu"</note>, meaning us. May they maintain **nourishment** <note>original: "iṣam"</note> among **those who sing praise** <note>original: "gṛṇatsu"</note>. The repetition of the final phrase is for the sake of emphasis and respect.

-> **॥ This concludes the thirty-second section of the fourth chapter of the fourth book ॥** <-

---

## Hymn Introduction
[Introduction to Mandala 5, Hymn 87]

The hymn beginning with **"Toward you, the great"** <note>original: "pra vo mahe"</note> consists of nine verses. It is the fifteenth hymn [of this section], composed by the sage **Evayamarut** of the Atri clan. Its deity is the **Maruts** <note>the storm gods</note> and its meter is **Atijagati** <note>a Vedic meter with 13 syllables per line</note>. As the Index states: **"Toward you" has nine verses, by Evayamarut, to the Maruts, in Atijagati meter.** In the ten-night sacrifice, on the sixth day during the third libation, the priest known as the *Achhavaka* recites this hymn. This is indicated in the ritual manuals: **"The Evayamarut hymn is spoken [followed] by the Vrishakapi hymn."** <note>referring to Ashvalayana Shrauta Sutra 9.4</note>.

---

## Hymn Text
-> ॥ The First Verse ॥ <-

**May your hymns go forth to the great Vishnu, who is accompanied by the Maruts; to the mountain-born Evayamarut. [Go forth] to the host, the sacrificial, the well-adorned, the powerful, the joyful-seeking, the noisy-vowed strength.** ॥ 1 ॥

-> Word-by-word Analysis <-

**Forth. Your. To the great. Hymns. May they go. To Vishnu. To the one with the Maruts. Mountain-born. Evayamarut.**
**Forth. To the host. To the sacrificial. To the well-adorned. To the powerful. To the joyful-seeking. To the noisy-vowed. To the strength.** ॥ 1 ॥

This hymn is dedicated to the Maruts, the storm deities, who are here addressed with the unique refrain "Evayamarut." ## Commentary by Sayana
**[Continued from the previous page – Rig Veda 5.87.1]**

May the **praises** <note>original: "matayaḥ"</note>—the hymns of praise produced in the voice and arising as if from mountains—**go forth** <note>original: "prayantu"</note>. For whom? For you <note>the commentator notes a grammatical shift in number here</note>. They go to the all-pervading **Vishnu**, or perhaps to Indra who is accompanied by the Maruts. Whose praises are these? It is said they belong to the sage named **Evayamarut** <note>The commentator suggests the name of the seer of this hymn is derived from the refrain</note>. There is an omission of the possessive case ending here. Alternatively, this sage is the one who "gives birth" to these mountain-born praises.

The second half of the verse praises the Maruts directly. Furthermore, let the praises go forth to the **Marut host** <note>original: "śardhāya"</note>, which represents their strength. All other words here are adjectives describing this strength. They go to the one who is pre-eminently **to be worshipped** <note>original: "prayajyu"</note> and to the one adorned with **beautiful ornaments** <note>original: "sukhādi"</note>. 

<term>Khadi: A specific type of ring or bracelet worn by the Maruts on their hands and feet, symbolizing their status and brilliance.</term> 

As the scripture says: "With rings on their hands" <note>Rig Veda 1.168.3</note> and "rings on their feet" <note>Rig Veda 5.54.11</note>. The praises also go to the powerful one who **desires hymns** <note>original: "bhandadiṣṭi"</note>, to the one whose sacred duty is the **shaking of the clouds** <note>original: "dhunivrata"</note>, and to the one who possesses the power of movement.

---

## Hymn Text

-> ॥ The Second Verse ॥ <-

Those who were born by the greatness [of Vishnu], and those who, of their own accord, speak forth through their wisdom—O Evayamarut! O Maruts, because of your active power, your strength is not to be defied; by your gift and your majesty, you are as unassailable as the mountains. ॥ 2 ॥

**[Word-by-word Analysis]**

Forth. Those. Born. By greatness. Those. And. Now. By themselves. Forth. By wisdom. They speak. Evayamarut.
By active power. That. Your. Maruts. Not. To be defied. Strength. By the gift. By majesty. That. Of them.
Unassailable. Like. Mountains. ॥ 2 ॥

---

## Commentary by Sayana

The poet speaks of those who were born or manifested along with the great Vishnu or Indra. **Evayamarut** <note>referring to the sage or the deity</note> praises those Maruts who were manifested quickly and by their own power, possessing the **wisdom** <note>original: "vidmanā"</note> regarding the approach to the sacrifice. 

<note>The commentator notes a grammatical variation where the plural "they speak" is used for a singular subject, a common feature of Vedic Sanskrit.</note>

Now, the poet addresses them directly: O Maruts, that famous **strength** <note>original: "śavas"</note> of yours, which is characterized by the **active power** <note>original: "kratu"</note> of moving the clouds and the world, is **not to be defied** <note>original: "nādhṛṣe"</note>. It cannot be overcome by anyone. It is also not to be surpassed by the actions or works of others, such as the demons. 

Furthermore, this strength of yours is accompanied by your great **majesty** <note>original: "mahnā"</note> and your willingness to give desired **gifts** <note>original: "dāna"</note>. You are truly powerful and **unassailable** <note>original: "adhṛṣṭāsaḥ"</note>. He provides an illustration: **like the mountains** <note>original: "adrayo na"</note>. Just as mountains cannot be shaken or moved, so too are you immovable and invincible.

<meta>This page continues the translation and commentary of Rig Veda, Mandala 5, Hymn 87 (though the OCR header lists it as Sukta 41, the content identifies it as 87). This hymn is unique for its rhythmic refrain "Evayamarut." It continues the praise of the Maruts, the storm deities, focusing on their celestial origin and their powerful movement.</meta>

## Hymn Text
-> ॥ The Third Verse ॥ <-

**Those who are heard from the great heaven with a song, seekers of grace, excellent in being, O Evayamarut! No impeller rules their assembly; they are like fires flashing with their own lightning, the drivers of the rushing waters.** ॥ ३ ॥

-> Word-by-Word Breakdown <-

**Forth | those | from heaven | great | are heard | with a song | seekers of grace | excellent in being | O Evayamarut!**
**Not | whose | impeller | in the common dwelling | rules | [intensive] | fires | like | self-lightning | forth | the rushing | of the sounding [rivers]** ॥ ३ ॥

---

## Commentary (Sayana)

Those Maruts, coming from the **great heaven** <note>original: "bṛhato divaḥ"</note>, are **heard** <note>original: "pra śṛṇvire"</note>; the sage Evayamarut has praised them with a song. What are these Maruts like? They are **radiant** or seekers of favor <note>original: "sumnukāno"</note> and **excellent in their nature** <note>original: "subhvaḥ"</note>. Of these Maruts, while they reside in their **common dwelling** <note>original: "sadhastha"</note> or their own abode, no **impeller** <note>original: "irī"</note> or driver **rules** <note>original: "īṣṭe"</note> over them to force them to move. The word **ā** here serves as a conjunction. They are **like fires** <note>original: "agnayo na"</note> in that they are **flashing by their own light** <note>original: "svavidyutaḥ"</note> like lightning, and they are the **movers** <note>original: "syandrāso"</note> of the **sounding** <note>original: "dhunīnām"</note> rivers by means of their rain ॥

---

## Hymn Text
-> ॥ The Fourth Verse ॥ <-

**He of the wide stride has stepped forth from the great, common seat, O Evayamarut. When he himself has yoked [his horses] from his own [abode] with the movers, they go forward with their men, vying with each other, of vast power, increasers of happiness.** ॥ ४ ॥

-> Word-by-Word Breakdown <-

**He | strode | from the great | out | wide-striding | from the common | seat | O Evayamarut!**
**When | yoked | by himself | from his own | [preposition] | with the movers | vying with each other | of vast power |**
**goes | increasers of happiness | with men [leaders]** ॥ ४ ॥

---

## Commentary (Sayana)

**He**, the host of Maruts, having **wide strides** <note>original: "urukramah"</note>, **strode out** <note>original: "niścakrame"</note> from the **great** and **common seat** <note>original: "samānasmāt sadasah"</note>, which refers to the mid-air or the atmosphere. The sage Evayamarut says that **when** <note>original: "yadā"</note> the host was **yoked** <note>original: "ayukta"</note> **by himself** <note>by his own will</note> from **his own** <note>original: "svāt"</note> place—the word **adhi** here simply reinforces the sense of "from"—he was joined with the **movers** <note>original: "kṣubhir"</note>, who are the horses or leaders that carry them, in order to answer the prayer for their arrival. 

Now the description shifts to the plural form. At that time, they are **vying with each other** <note>original: "vispardhaso"</note>; they have a competition among themselves, each thinking "I shall go first, I shall go first!" Alternatively, it means they are "without rivals," for no one can compete with them. They possess **distinguished power** <note>original: "vimanhaso"</note> and are **increasers of happiness** <note>original: "śevridhaḥ"</note> as they **go forth** <note>original: "jigāti"</note>. <note>The commentator notes that a singular verb is used here in place of a plural one by grammatical substitution.</note> ॥

<vocab>
<term>Marut: Storm deities in the Veda, known for their brilliance, collective strength, and association with Rudra.</term>
<term>Sumnukāna: Seeking or granting happiness/grace; radiant.</term>
<term>Evayamarut: A unique ritual exclamation or the name of the sage who saw this hymn; literally "The Marut who goes according to his will."</term>
<term>Sadhastha: A common gathering place or dwelling, often referring to the sacrificial ground or the atmospheric realm.</term>
<term>Urukrama: 'Wide-striding'; a title usually associated with Vishnu but here applied to the Marut host to show their pervasive power.</term>
<term>Shevridha: Those who increase 'Sheva' (happiness or auspiciousness).</term>
<term>Vispardhas: Either 'competing with one another' (showing speed and vigor) or 'having no rivals' (showing supreme power).</term>
</vocab>

<summary>These verses describe the Maruts as self-luminous beings who descend from the highest heaven and the atmosphere. They are depicted as a powerful, independent host that moves by its own will to bring rain and joy to the world.</summary>
<keywords>Maruts, Evayamarut, atmospheric gods, Vedic ritual, lightning, wide-stride, celestial assembly</keywords>

<meta>This page continues the translation of Rig Veda, Mandala 5, Hymn 87. It covers verses 5 and 6. The previous page established the identity of the Maruts as powerful storm deities and introduced the recurring refrain "Evayamarut," which serves as both a title for the sage-poet and a rhythmic call to the gods. This page concludes the 33rd section (Varga) of the fourth book (Ashtaka).</meta>

-> ॥ The Fifth Verse ॥ <-

## Hymn Text

**Like a sound, may your mighty, raining, brilliant, moving, and great [power] not cause [me] to tremble, O Evayamarut! Overcoming [enemies] with that sound, you fashion [all things], you who are self-radiant, with steady rays, golden, well-armed, and rushing onward.** ॥ ५ ॥

**Word-by-Word Breakdown**
**Sound | like | your | mighty | causes to tremble [not] | raining/showering | brilliant | moving | great | O Evayamarut!**
**By which | overcoming | they fashion | self-radiant | standing | rays | golden | well-armed | rushing.** ॥ ५ ॥

---

## Commentary (Sayana)

O **Maruts** <note>storm deities</note>, may **your** <note>original: "vaḥ"</note> **sound** <note>original: "svanaḥ"</note>, which is the noise generated by your great speed, **not cause to tremble** <note>original: "na rejayat"</note>—that is, let it not terrify—me, the sage Evayamarut. <note>The commentator notes a grammatical substitution where the second case ending is dropped</note>. This "sound" is further described: it is **mighty** <note>original: "amavān"</note> or powerful; it is **showering** <note>original: "vṛṣā"</note> because it brings the rain; it is **brilliant** <note>original: "tveṣaḥ"</note> and flashing; it is **moving** <note>original: "yayiḥ"</note> or wandering; and it is **great** <note>original: "taviṣaḥ"</note> or highly increased. **By which** sound, **overcoming** <note>original: "sahantaḥ"</note> your enemies, you **fashion** <note>original: "chuñjate"</note> or accomplish your works. <note>Sayana notes the use of the imperative mood for the present tense here</note>. 

What is your nature? You are **self-radiant** <note>original: "svaro-ciṣaḥ"</note>, meaning your rays of light are under your own control. You **possess steady rays** <note>original: "sthā-raśmānaḥ"</note> or firm boundaries; you are **golden** <note>original: "hiraṇyayā"</note>, adorned with gold ornaments; you are **well-armed** <note>original: "svāyudhāsaḥ"</note> with weapons ready at hand; and you are **rushing** <note>original: "iṣmiṇaḥ"</note>, meaning you either possess food or move with great speed.

-> ॥ This concludes the thirty-third section of the fourth chapter of the fourth book ॥ <-

-> ॥ The Sixth Verse ॥ <-

## Hymn Text

**Boundless is your greatness, O you of ever-increasing power! May your brilliant strength protect [me], O Evayamarut! For you truly stand within the ritual's binding for the sake of vision; protect us from the reviler, you who shine like fires.** ॥ ६ ॥

**Word-by-Word Breakdown**
**Boundless | your | greatness | of increased power | brilliant | strength | may protect | O Evayamarut!**
**Standers | indeed | in the binding | for the sake of vision | you are | those | us | protect | the reviler | shining | like | fires.** ॥ ६ ॥

---

## Commentary (Sayana)

O **Maruts**, **your** **greatness** <note>original: "mahimā"</note> is **boundless** <note>original: "apāraḥ"</note>, meaning it is without limit. O **you of increased power** <note>original: "vṛddha-śavasaḥ"</note>, whose strength is vast, may your **brilliant** and flashing **strength** <note>original: "śavaḥ"</note> **protect** <note>original: "avatu"</note> me, the sage Evayamarut. <note>Again, the commentator notes the dropping of the accusative case ending</note>. You **indeed** <note>original: "hi"</note> are **those who stand** <note>original: "sthātāraḥ"</note> by a fixed rule within the **binding** <note>original: "prasitau"</note>—referring to the powerful constraints of the regulated sacrifice—for the purpose of **vision** <note>original: "saṃdṛśi"</note> or being seen by the worshippers. **Protect** <note>original: "uruṣyata"</note> **us** from **the reviler** <note>original: "nidaḥ"</note>, the mocking enemy. You are **shining like fires** <note>original: "agnaya iva śuśukvāṃsaḥ"</note> as you perform this protection.
