<header>Mandala 6, Anuvaka 1, Sukta 15] || Fourth Ashtaka || 627</header>

## Hymn Text

-> म० ६. अ० १. सू० १५. <-

**Agni | the Invoker | the Master of the house | he | the King | all | knows | births | the Knower of all beings | of the gods | and | who | of mortals | the most skilled sacrificer | he | forth | let him sacrifice | the observer of Truth ॥ १३ ॥**

---

## Commentary (Sayana)

The **Invoker** <note>original: "hotā," the one who calls the gods to the ritual</note> who calls the gods, the **King** <note>original: "rājā," the shining one</note>, that Agni is the **Master of the house** <note>original: "gṛhapatiḥ"</note>, the sovereign of the households. Likewise, being the **Knower of all beings** <note>original: "jātavedāḥ," one possessing wisdom of all that is born</note>, he **knows** <note>original: "veda"</note> all creations and living things. Among the gods like Indra and also among **mortals** <note>original: "martyānām," human beings</note>, Agni is the **most skilled sacrificer** <note>original: "yajiṣṭhaḥ"</note>. He is the **observer of Truth** <note>original: "ṛtāvā," where Truth refers to the cosmic order or the sacrifice itself</note>. May that Agni **sacrifice** <note>original: "pra yajatām"</note>—may he perform the sacrifice for the gods excellently.

The verse beginning with "O Agni, whatever today..." <note>original: "agne yad adya," referring to verse 14</note> is the recitation for the **Maker of the Good Sacrifice** <note>term: "sviṣṭakṛt," a specific offering at the end of a ritual to correct any errors</note> during the New and Full Moon sacrifices. This is indicated in the ritual manuals: "With 'O Agni, whatever today... the Invoker of the people's sacrifice,' he performs the sacrifice without pausing for breath." <note>original: "anvānaṃ yajati," from the Ashvalayana Shrauta Sutra 1.6</note>.

---

## Hymn Text

-> ॥ This is the Fourteenth Verse in the Hymn ॥ <-

**O Agni, whatever today for the person of the sacrifice, O Invoker of pure brilliance, you truly desire, for you are the Sacrificer. You shall sacrifice in the Truth with your greatness; since you have become all-pervading, carry the oblations, O Youngest One, which are offered to you today ॥ १४ ॥**

**Agni | whatever | today | of the person | of the sacrifice | O Invoker | O one of pure brilliance | you desire | you | indeed | the Sacrificer |**
**in the Truth | you shall sacrifice | with greatness | when | you have become | all-pervading | the oblations | carry | O Youngest One | which | to you | today ॥ १४ ॥**

---

## Commentary (Sayana)

O **Invoker of the sacrifice** <note>original: "adhvarasya hotar"</note>, the one who completes the ritual, O **one of pure brilliance** <note>original: "pāvakaśoce," meaning your light purifies</note>—O Agni of such nature, whatever is to be done today at this time by the **person** <note>original: "viśaḥ," the human patron/sacrificer</note>, may you **desire** that <note>original: "veḥ," meaning to love or accept the task</note>. Indeed, because you are the **Sacrificer** <note>original: "yajvā"</note> for the gods, therefore you **sacrifice** <note>original: "yajāsi"</note> in the **Truth** <note>original: "ṛtā," the true ritual</note>. Sacrifice to the gods. Furthermore, since you have become **all-pervading** <note>original: "vibhūḥ"</note> by your own **greatness** <note>original: "mahinā"</note>, for this reason, O **Youngest One** <note>original: "yaviṣṭha," an epithet for Agni because he is freshly kindled each time</note>, carry those **oblations** <note>original: "havyā"</note> which we offer to you now today. Bring these offerings to your form known as the **Maker of the Good Sacrifice** <note>original: "sviṣṭakṛt"</note>.

---

## Hymn Text

-> ॥ Now the Fifteenth Verse ॥ <-

**Behold the well-placed food-offerings; indeed, let Heaven and Earth be established for the sacrifice. Come to us, O generous one, in the winning of strength; O Agni, may we cross over all difficulties, may we cross them, by your protection may we cross them ॥ १५ ॥**

**Towards | the food-offerings | well-placed | indeed | behold | down | you | may be established | Heaven and Earth | for the sacrifice |**
**towards | us | O generous one | in the winning of strength | O Agni | all | difficulties | may we cross | those | may we cross | by your | protection | may we cross ॥ १५ ॥**

---

## Commentary (Sayana)

O Agni, **behold** <note>original: "khyaḥ," look upon</note> the **food-offerings** <note>original: "prayāṃsi"</note> which are **well-placed** <note>original: "sudhitāni," well-arranged</note> upon the sacrificial altar...

<meta>This page concludes the commentary for Rig Veda, Mandala 5, Hymn 43, Verse 15, and provides the full text and explanation for Verses 16 and 17. # Rig Veda [Ashtaka 4, Adhyaya 5, Varga 20]

...beholding <note>original: "abhipasyasi"</note> every moment. Indeed, you are the filler of desires. May the sacrificer place you—who are such a person—to worship <note>original: "yajadhyai"</note> all the gods characterized by the two worlds of Heaven and Earth <note>original: "rodasī"</note>. This sacrificer has established you. O bountiful <note>term: "Maghavan," an epithet usually for Indra but here applied to Agni as the possessor of riches</note> Agni, protect <note>original: "ava"</note> us in the winning of spoils—whether in battle or in the sharing of food. And may we cross over <note>original: "tarema"</note> all difficulties and sorrows. The rest of the vow is as previously stated.

-> ॥ So ends the nineteenth varga of the fifth Adhyaya ॥ <-

During the "Leading Forward of the Fire" <note>term: "Agnipranayana," a ritual where the fire is moved to a new altar</note>, the verse "O Agni, with all..." is to be recited as the invitatory verse. This is indicated in the ritual manuals: "With the verse 'O Agni, with all the fair-flamed gods,' one should pause at the half-verse" <note>reference: Ashvalayana Shrauta Sutra 2.17</note>.

-> ॥ This is the sixteenth verse of the hymn ॥ <-

## Hymn Text
O Agni, with all the fair-flamed gods, you, the first among them, sit upon this woolly seat. For the sacrificer, lead this nested, ghee-blessed sacrifice successfully to the Stimulator. ॥ १६ ॥

---

## Word-by-Word Breakdown
O Agni | with all | O thou of beautiful flames | with the gods | woolly | the first | sit | the seat | nested | possessing clarified butter | for the Stimulator | the sacrifice | lead | for the sacrificer | successfully ॥ १६ ॥

---

## Commentary (Sayana)
O **thou of beautiful flames** <note>original: "svanīka," meaning one with beautiful fire-fronts</note>, together with **all** the gods, you who are **the first** (the most excellent) among the gods, **sit** <note>original: "sīda"</note> upon the **seat** <note>original: "yonim," the place of origin, here referring to the High Altar or Uttaravedi</note> which is **woolly** <note>original: "ūrṇāvantam," cushioned with tufts of wool</note>. What kind of seat? It is **nested** <note>original: "kulāyinam"</note>. A "kulāya" is a nest; this seat is like a nest because it is prepared with substances like fragrant resin <note>original: "guggulu"</note>. As the scripture says: "In the sacrifice, a sort of nest is made when there are items made of pine wood, enclosures, fragrant resins, wool tufts, and sweet-smelling grasses" <note>reference: Aitareya Brahmana 1.28</note>. It also **possesses clarified butter** <note>original: "ghṛtavantam"</note>, meaning it is anointed with ghee. Having sat thus upon the High Altar, **lead** <note>original: "naya"</note> or carry the **sacrifice** of this **sacrificer** with straightforwardness to the gods, for the sake of **the Stimulator** <note>term: "Savitre," the solar deity Savitar who impels the sacrifice</note>.

---

-> ॥ Now the seventeenth verse ॥ <-

## Hymn Text
This very Agni, the wise priests churn like the sage Atharvan did; him who was wandering in distress, they brought forth from the dark nights—him who is never confused. ॥ १७ ॥

---

## Word-by-Word Breakdown
This | [particle] | that | like Atharvan | Agni | they churn | the wise priests | whom | wandering in distress | [towards] | they brought | the unconfused | from the dark nights ॥ १७ ॥

---

## Commentary (Sayana)
The **wise priests** <note>original: "vedhasaḥ," the creators or performers of the ritual</note> **churn** <note>original: "manthanti," referring to kindling fire by friction</note> **this** visible and **well-known** Agni, just **as the sage Atharvan** <note>note: Atharvan is the legendary first priest to have discovered or "churned" fire</note> churned him in the past. They churn him from the two fire-sticks...

<vocab>
- svanīka: Having beautiful flames or a fair appearance (epithet of Agni).
- ūrṇāvantam: Soft or woolly; referring to the cushioned altar.
- yoni: Receptacle, place, or the fire-altar (specifically the Uttaravedi).
- kulāyinam: Nested; arranged like a nest (referring to the preparation of the ritual space).
- vedhasaḥ: Wise ones, creators, or priests performing the sacrifice.
- atharvavat: Like the sage Atharvan, who first kindled fire.
- mathnanti: They churn or kindle the fire (through friction of the fire-sticks).
- savitre: For Savitar, the stimulator/impeller.
</vocab>

<meta>This page continues the commentary on the Rig Veda, Mandala 6, Hymn 15. # Mandala 6, Anuvaka 1, Hymn 15 | Fourth Ashtaka | Page 629

...they generate. To the one moving crookedly <note>original: "ankuṃyantaṃ"</note>. *Anku* refers to a base or crooked movement. Desiring that for himself, fleeing here and there after departing from the gods—that wise <note>original: "amūram"</note> or non-deluded Agni, they brought from the dark ones <note>original: "śyāvyābhyaḥ"</note>. *Shyavi* is a name for the night. The gatherings of darkness existing there are the "dark ones." The connection is that they bring him, or cause him to come, from them.

---

## Hymn Text

-> ॥ Verse 18 ॥ <-

**Be born for the feast of the gods, in the sacrifice extended by all, for our welfare.**
**Bring the immortal gods, the augmenters of Truth, and cause the sacrifice to reach the gods. ॥ 18 ॥**

**Be born. For the feast of the gods. In the sacrifice extended by all. For welfare.**
**Bring. The gods. The immortal. The augmenters of Truth. The sacrifice. Among the gods. Cause to touch. ॥ 18 ॥**

## Commentary (Sayana)

O Agni, being churned <note>Refers to the ritual production of fire by rubbing sticks together</note> in the **sacrifice extended by all** <note>original: "sarvatātā"</note>, may you **be born** or manifested. For what purpose? **For the feast of the gods** <note>original: "devavītaye"</note>, meaning for the sake of the sacrificer who desires the gods. <note>Grammar note: The fourth case (dative) is used here in the sense of the sixth case (genitive)</note>. It is for the **welfare** or the non-destruction of such a sacrificer. And having been born, **bring** <note>original: "ā vakṣi"</note> the **immortal** gods who are free from death and are the **augmenters of Truth** <note>original: "ṛtāvṛdhaḥ"</note> or the strengtheners of the sacrifice. After that, **cause to touch** or reach our **sacrifice among** those **gods**.

---

## Hymn Text

-> ॥ Verse 19 ॥ <-

**We have indeed kindled you, O Lord of the House, among the people, O Agni, making you great with hymns.**
**May our domestic duties be prosperous, and sharpen us with your intense radiance. ॥ 19 ॥**

**We. Indeed. You. O Lord of the House. Among the people. O Agni. With hymns. Kindled. Great.**
**Prosperous. Our. Domestic duties. May they be. With intense. Our. With radiance. Completely. Sharpen. ॥ 19 ॥**

## Commentary (Sayana)

O **Lord of the House** <note>term: "Grihapati," an epithet for Agni as the protector of the domestic hearth and ritual</note>, O Agni who protects the sacrifices, among all **living beings**, **we indeed** have **made** you **great** through the act of **kindling**. For this reason, may **our domestic duties** <note>original: "gārhapatyāni"</note> or the roles of the householder be **prosperous** <note>original: "asthūri"</note>. A cart drawn by a single horse is called *sthuri*; the opposite of that is a cart equipped with many horses, called *asthuri*. By this term, "completeness" or "stability" is implied. May our household lives be complete with sons, cattle, and wealth. Furthermore, **sharpen us** <note>original: "sam śiśādhi"</note> or unite us with your **intense** or piercing **radiance**.

-> ॥ So ends the twentieth varga of the fifth Adhyaya of the fourth Ashtaka ॥ <-
-> ॥ So ends the first Anuvaka in the sixth Mandala ॥ <-

---

- **जनिष्ठा (janiṣṭhāḥ):** be born / manifested
- **देववीतये (devavītaye):** for the consumption/desire of the gods
- **सर्वताता (sarvatātā):** in the sacrifice extended by all
- **ऋतावृधः (ṛtāvṛdhaḥ):** augmenters of Truth/Sacrifice
- **पिस्पृशः (pispṛśaḥ):** cause to touch / reach
- **गृहपति (gṛhapati):** lord of the house / master of the hearth
- **अर्कैः (arkaiḥ):** with hymns/praises
- **गार्हपत्यानि (gārhapatyāni):** household duties / domestic fires

- **तिग्मेन (tigmena):** sharp / intense

<meta>This page transitions from the conclusion of the first section (Anuvaka) to the beginning of the second section of the sixth Mandala. It provides the structural overview and initial verses of Hymn 16, which is a long litany to Agni.</meta>

# ॥ Rig Veda ॥ [Book 4. Chapter 5. Class 21.]

In the second section <note>original: "anuvāke"</note> there are 9 hymns. Among them, the first hymn, beginning with **"You, O Agni, of sacrifices,"** consists of forty-eight verses. It was revealed to the seer Bharadvaja and is dedicated to Agni. The first and sixth verses are in the *Vardhamana Gayatri* meter <note>A variation of the Gayatri meter where the syllable count per line increases, specifically 6-7-8 syllables</note>, as they possess the defined characteristics of that form. The twenty-seventh verse is in the *Anushtubh* meter <note>A poetic structure of four lines with eight syllables each</note>. The two verses beginning **"To you, O Agni, the gods [bring] fire"** are also in *Anushtubh*. The verse preceding them, **"He who to the divine [gives]..."**, is in *Trishtubh* meter <note>A meter of four lines with eleven syllables each</note>. The remaining forty-two verses are in the standard *Gayatri* meter. This is summarized in the Index <note>original: "Anukramani"</note> as follows: **"The hymn 'You, Agni' has forty-eight verses; the first and sixth are Vardhamana, the twenty-seventh is Anushtubh, as are the two before the end, and the one preceding those is Trishtubh."**

Regarding the ritual application <note>original: "viniyoga"</note>: This hymn is recited in the *Gayatri* meter during the morning litany <note>original: "Prataranuvaka"</note> and the Ashvina-shastra of the Agnistoma sacrifice. However, the last three verses are to be excluded. It is directed: **"One should remove the last three from the hymn 'You, Agni, of sacrifices'"** (Asvalayana Shrauta Sutra 4.13). In the Vishvajit sacrifice, if the *Brihat Saman* is used as the *Agnishtoma Saman*, then the first six verses serve as the introductory and corresponding chants <note>original: "stotriya-anurūpāthāḥ"</note>. It is noted: **"The two sets for the 'You, Agni, of sacrifices' hymn are the introductory and corresponding verses"** (Asvalayana Shrauta Sutra 9.7).

---

## Hymn Text

-> ॥ The First Verse ॥ <-

**You, O Agni, are the priest of all sacrifices, established by the gods among the human race. ॥ 1 ॥**

**You. O Agni. Of sacrifices. The priest. Of all. Established. By the gods. In the human. Race. ॥ 1 ॥**

---

## Commentary (Sayana)

O Agni, **you** are the **priest** <note>original: "hotā," the invoker who performs the manual offering or calls the gods</note> of **all sacrifices**, which are distinguished into seven forms <note>Referring to the seven *Somasamsthas* or standard types of Soma rituals</note>. Or rather, you are the invoker of the gods related to the sacrifices. Why is this so? He explains: Because you have been **established** or placed as the priest **by the gods** among the **human race** <note>original: "mānuṣe jane"</note>, meaning among the descendants of Manu, the sacrificers. This is the meaning.

---

## Hymn Text

-> ॥ The Second Verse ॥ <-

**With your pleasant tongues, sacrifice for us in the rite to the great [gods]; bring the gods here and worship them. ॥ 2 ॥**

**He. Our. With pleasant. In the rite. With tongues. Sacrifice. The great. Hither. The gods. Bring. Worship. And. ॥ 2 ॥**

---

## Commentary (Sayana)

O Agni, may **you**, on **our** behalf, **sacrifice** to the **great** gods during the **rite** <note>original: "adhvare," the sacrifice</note> with your **pleasant tongues**—meaning your flames, which are either delightful or worthy of praise <note>original: "mandrābhiḥ"</note>. Satiate them with oblations. How should this be done? It is said: **Bring** the gods who are to be worshipped, such as Indra and others, and then **worship** them. This means you should give the oblations to them.

Regarding the "Path-making Agni" <note>original: "Agniḥ Pathikṛt"</note>, the preparatory verse <note>original: "anuvākyā"</note> is the one beginning **"You know [the way]..."** It is noted in the ritual manuals: **"For you, O wise one, know the path; we have come to the path of the gods"** (Asvalayana Shrauta Sutra 3.10).

<note>
**Technical Terms:**
- **Agni:** The god of fire and messenger between gods and humans.
- **Bharadvaja:** The ancestral seer of the sixth book of the Rig Veda.
- **Gayatri/Anushtubh/Trishtubh:** Specific poetic meters used in Vedic chanting.
- **Hotri:** The primary priest who recites the Rig Veda.
- **Yajna/Adhvara:** Terms for the Vedic sacrificial ritual.
- **Pathikrit:** "Path-maker," an epithet for Agni when he guides the soul or the ritual.
</note>

<keywords>Agni, Bharadvaja, Gayatri meter, Hotri priest, Vedic sacrifice, Sayana commentary, human race, ritual fire, path-maker</keywords>

->॥ This is the third [verse] ॥<-

## Hymn Text
For you, O Disposer, know the highways and the paths to the gods directly, O Agni, at the sacrifices, O Wise One. ॥ 3 ॥

**Word-by-Word Analysis**
You know | indeed | O Disposer | the highways | the paths | and | the gods | directly | O Agni | at the sacrifices | O Wise One <note>original: "su-krato"</note> ॥ 3 ॥

---

## Commentary (Sayana)
O **Disposer** <note>original: "vedho"</note>, the Arranger; O **Wise One** <note>original: "sukrato"</note>, you who perform beautiful deeds; O divine Agni, endowed with qualities such as giving; you **know** <note>original: "vettha"</note> **directly** and quickly the **highways** <note>original: "adhvanaḥ"</note>, meaning the great paths, **and the paths** <note>original: "pathaśca"</note>, meaning the smaller paths, leading to the gods **at the sacrifices** <note>original: "yajñeṣu"</note> such as the New and Full Moon rituals. **For** <note>original: "hi"</note> since this is so, the meaning is: therefore, you should lead the sacrificer <note>original: "yajamana"</note> who has strayed from the sacrificial path back to that path once again.

---
---

->॥ Now the fourth [verse] ॥<-

## Hymn Text
I praise you then in two ways; Bharata, with food-bringers, for prosperity, worshipped the worshipful one at the sacrifices. ॥ 4 ॥

**Word-by-Word Analysis**
You | I praise | then | in two ways | Bharata | with food-bringers <note>original: "vājibhiḥ"</note> | prosperity | he worshipped | at the sacrifices | the worshipful one ॥ 4 ॥

---

## Commentary (Sayana)
O Agni, **I praise you**. **Then**, King **Bharata** <note>the son of Dushyanta, a famous ancestral king</note>, along **with the food-bringers** <note>original: "vājibhiḥ"</note>—meaning the priests who possess the sacrificial food—praised you **in two ways** <note>original: "dvitā"</note>, seeking **prosperity** <note>original: "śunam"</note> or happiness, which is twofold: the attainment of what is desired and the removal of what is undesired. Having praised you, **he worshipped** <note>original: "īje"</note> **you**, the one **worthy of sacrifice** <note>original: "yajñiyam"</note>, **at the sacrifices** <note>the grammar uses the locative case "in the sacrifices" to mean "by means of sacrifices"</note>. The implication is that you granted him both kinds of happiness.

---
---

->॥ Now the fifth [verse] ॥<-

## Hymn Text
You [gave] these many desirable things to Divodasa who presses the juice, and to Bharadvaja who offers. ॥ 5 ॥

**Word-by-Word Analysis**
You | these | desirable things | many | to Divodasa | to the one pressing [Soma] | to Bharadvaja | to the one who offers ॥ 5 ॥

---

## Commentary (Sayana)
O Agni, **you** [granted] **these** visible, **many** <note>original: "puru"</note>, **desirable** <note>original: "vāryā"</note> riches—which are to be chosen and enjoyed—**to Divodasa who presses the juice**. This is an implied comparison: just as you gave wealth to the King named Divodasa when he performed the Soma-pressing <note>the ritual extraction of the sacred Soma plant juice</note>, so also [give wealth] **to the offering** <note>original: "dāśuṣe"</note> seer **Bharadvaja**, who has given the sacrificial oblations. This last part "give to him" is added to complete the sense.

->॥ Thus ends the twenty-first section of the fifth chapter of the fourth book ॥<-

->॥ Now the sixth [verse] ॥<-

## Hymn Text
You are the immortal messenger; bring here the divine people, hearing the wise man's beautiful praise. ॥ 6 ॥

**Word-by-Word Analysis**
You | the messenger | the immortal one | here | bring | the divine | people | hearing | of the wise man | the beautiful praise ॥ 6 ॥

<meta>This page continues the commentary on Rig Veda, Mandala 6, Hymn 16. It concludes the commentary for verse 6 and covers verses 7 through 9. This corresponds to the 22nd section (Varga) of the 5th Chapter (Adhyaya) in the 4th Book (Ashtaka) of the collection.</meta>

You who are immortal <note>original: "amartya"</note>, possessing the nature of deathlessness, having become a messenger, bring here the divine people—those related to the gods. Bring them to our sacrifice. While doing what? Hearing the beautiful praise <note>original: "suṣṭuti"</note> of the wise Bharadvaja <note>the seer of this hymn</note>.

---

-> ॥ Now the seventh [verse] ॥ <-

## Hymn Text
O Agni, mortals with focused minds praise you, the divine, at the sacrifices for the gratification of the gods. ॥ 7 ॥

**Word-by-Word Analysis**
You | O Agni | with focused minds <note>original: "su-ādhyaḥ"</note> | mortals <note>original: "martāsaḥ"</note> | for the gratification of the gods | at the sacrifices | the divine | they praise ॥ 7 ॥

## Commentary (Sayana)
O **Agni**, O shining one, **mortals**—meaning human beings—who possess **focused minds** <note>original: "svādhyaḥ"; those whose meditation is beautiful</note>, **praise** you or request from you **at the sacrifices** for the purpose of the **gratification of the gods** <note>original: "devavītaye"</note>. ॥ 7 ॥

---

-> ॥ Now the eighth [verse] ॥ <-

## Hymn Text
I worship your glorious appearance and also your wisdom, O giver of beautiful gifts; all those who possess desires enjoy [your favor]. ॥ 8 ॥

**Word-by-Word Analysis**
Your | indeed | I worship | glorious appearance | and | wisdom/action | O giver of beautiful gifts | all | they enjoy | those with desires ॥ 8 ॥

## Commentary (Sayana)
O **Agni**, **I worship** <note>original: "prayakṣi"</note>, meaning I honor with excellence, **your glorious appearance** <note>original: "saṃhṛśam"</note>, which is either your well-visible light or that which reveals everything. **And also** <note>original: "utāpi"</note> I worship the **wisdom** <note>original: "kratuṃ"</note>—meaning your ritual action or your great knowledge—of you, the **giver of beautiful gifts**. It is not only I, but **all** other sacrificers as well, who, being **desirous** <note>original: "kāminaḥ"</note> and possessing various goals by your grace, **enjoy** <note>original: "juṣanta"</note> and serve your appearance and your wisdom. ॥ 8 ॥

---

-> ॥ Now the ninth [verse] ॥ <-

## Hymn Text
You are the Invoker-priest established by Manu, the carrier [of offerings] through your mouth, most wise; O Agni, sacrifice to the divine people of the heavens. ॥ 9 ॥

**Word-by-Word Analysis**
You | the Invoker-priest | established by Manu | the carrier | through the mouth | most wise | O Agni | sacrifice | of heaven | the people ॥ 9 ॥

## Commentary (Sayana)
O **Agni**, **you** are the **Invoker-priest** <term>Hotar; the priest who recites the hymns of the Rig Veda</term> and are **established by Manu** <note>original: "manurhitaḥ"; Manu is the legendary first human and first sacrificer</note>. Through your **mouth** <note>original: "āsā"</note>—that is, through your flame which serves as your mouth—you are the **carrier** <note>original: "vahni"</note> of the ritual offerings. You are **most wise** <note>original: "viduṣṭaraḥ"</note>, knowing everything perfectly. For this reason, O Agni, **sacrifice** to the **people of heaven**—the divine subjects who belong to the celestial world. ॥ 9 ॥

---

## Ritual Notes
Regarding the New and Full Moon sacrifices <term>Darśapūrṇamāsa</term>, the three verses starting with "Come, O Agni, for the gratification" are used as the wood-kindling verses <term>Sāmidhenī; verses recited while wood is added to the fire</term>. This is indicated [in the manuals]: "**Come O Agni for gratification, being praised, worthy of praise, to be honored...**" <note>quoting Ashvalayana Shrauta Sutra 1.2</note>. 

Furthermore, if the Household fire <term>Gārhapatya</term> and the Offering fire <term>Āhavanīya</term> accidentally come into contact with each other, a cake <term>Purodāśa</term> offered on eight potsherds is given to Agni-Viti. The verse "Come O Agni for gratification" is used as the invitatory verse <term>Anuvākyā</term> for that rite. This is also indicated: "**Come O Agni for gratification, he who [brings] Agni for the gratification of the gods**" <note>quoting Ashvalayana Shrauta Sutra 3.13</note>.

<summary>This page translates verses 7-9 of Rig Veda 6.16, where Agni is praised as the messenger and priest established by Manu, and includes ritual instructions for using these verses in the New and Full Moon sacrifices.</summary>
<keywords>Agni, Manu, Hotar priest, Bharadvaja, Darshapurnamasa, Samidheni, Vedic ritual, Sayana's commentary</keywords>

# Mandala 6. Chapter 2. Hymn 16. || Fourth Book || 633

---

## Hymn Text

->|| This is the tenth verse in the hymn ||<-

**O Agni, come for the feast, being praised for the sake of giving oblations. Sit down as the invoker upon the sacrificial grass. ॥ 10 ॥**

**Agni | Come | For the feast <note>original: "vītaye"</note> | Being praised | For the giving of oblations | Down | Invoker <note>original: "hotā"</note> | Sit | Upon the sacrificial grass ॥ 10 ॥**

---

->|| Now the eleventh ||<-

**O Angiras, we strengthen you with fuel and with clarified butter. Shine greatly, O most youthful one. ॥ 11 ॥**

**That | You | With fuels | O Angiras | With clarified butter | We strengthen | Greatly | Shine | O most youthful one ॥ 11 ॥**

---

->|| Now the twelfth ||<-

**O God, lead us toward that broad and famous wealth, O Agni, which is great and endowed with heroic power. ॥ 12 ॥**

**He | Us | Broad | Famous | Toward | O God | Lead/Attain | Great | O Agni | Good-heroic-power ॥ 12 ॥**

---

->|| Here begins the first of the [next triplet], the thirteenth in the hymn ||<-

**O Agni, Atharvan churned you out from the lotus leaf, from the head of the entire universe, the priest of the sacrifice. ॥ 13 ॥**

**You | O Agni | From the lotus | From/Upon | Atharvan | Out | Churned | From the head | Of the all/universe | Priest <note>original: "vāghataḥ"</note> ॥ 13 ॥**

---

## Commentary (Sayana)

**[Verse 10]**
O **Agni**, please come. For what purpose? For the **feast** <note>original: "vītaye"</note>, meaning for the consumption of the oblations. Furthermore, for the **giving of oblations** <note>original: "havyadātaye"</note>, to give the offerings to the gods. You, being **praised** by us, should **sit down** <note>original: "niṣatsi"</note> as the **invoker** <note>the *Hotar* priest who calls the gods</note> upon the **sacred grass** <note>original: "barhiṣi"</note> that has been spread out.

->|| Thus ends the twenty-second section (Varga) of the fifth [Adhyaya] of the fourth [Ashtaka] ||<-

**[Verse 11]**
O **Angiras**—a name for Agni implying he possesses qualities like movement, or that he is in the form of embers, or that he is the son of the sage Angiras—we **strengthen** <note>original: "vardhayāmasi"</note> **you**, who possess the qualities mentioned before. We do this with **fuels** <note>original: "samidbhiḥ"</note>, the wooden logs used for kindling, and with **clarified butter** <note>original: "ghṛtena"</note> (ghee). Therefore, O **most youthful one** <note>original: "yaviṣṭhya"; Agni is called this because he is born anew every time the fire is lit</note>, **shine** very **greatly**.

**[Verse 12]**
O **God**, O shining Agni, you who possess the previously mentioned qualities, **bring us toward** <note>original: "achā vivāsasi"</note> wealth that is **broad** (extensive), **famous** (praiseworthy), **great**, and endowed with **excellent heroic power**. Regarding this, the *Vajasaneyaka* <note>a text of the White Yajurveda</note> states: "The phrase 'toward the god you lead' means 'bring us to that wealth'."

Regarding the ritual of **churning fire** <note>the *Agnimanthana* ritual where fire is created by friction</note>, the three verses starting with **"O Agni, from the lotus leaf..."** are to be recited. This is indicated in the *Ashvalayana Shrauta Sutra* (2.16): "Recite the three verses starting with *tvām agne puṣkarād adhi*, leaving half a verse remaining before pausing."

**[Verse 13]**
O **Agni**, the sage named **Atharva** **churned you out** <note>original: "nira-manthata"</note>—produced you by friction—from the **lotus leaf** <note>original: "puṣkarād adhi"</note> placed upon the two fire-sticks...

## Critical Notes
- The commentary for verse 12 cites the **Vajasaneyaka** <note>the White Yajurveda tradition</note> for interpreting the term "lead us toward."
- It also quotes the **Ashvalayana Shrauta Sutra** (2.16.) regarding the liturgical use of these verses during the ritual of churning fire (**Agnimanthana**).
- The text at the bottom "VOL. III. 7 Y" indicates the volume and signature of the printed book.

# Rig Veda || Book 4. Chapter 5. Section 24.

...produced [Agni] from that [lotus]. What kind of lotus? From the "head," meaning that which supports the head of the whole world; from the "priest" <note>original: "vāghataḥ"</note>, meaning the one who carries the sacrifice. Indeed, it is said in the sacred scriptures <note>the Brahmanas</note> that **"Prajapati <note>the Creator deity</note> spread the earth upon a lotus leaf."** Since the earth is the foundation of the entire world, the lotus leaf is considered the supporter of the whole world. Here, the word "lotus" refers specifically to the lotus leaf. This is clearly stated in the Taittiriya scripture: **"He says, 'from the lotus, O Agni,' because he found him [Agni] lying upon a lotus leaf."**

---

## Hymn Text

-> ॥ Now the fourteenth verse ॥ <-

**The sage Dadhyanc, the son of Atharvan, kindles you, the slayer of Vritra, the destroyer of forts. ॥ 14 ॥**

**Word-for-word breakdown:**
That | [particle] | You | Dadhyanc | Sage | Son | Kindles | Of Atharvan | Vritra-slayer | Fort-destroyer ॥ 14 ॥

---

## Commentary (Sayana)

O **Agni**, you who possess the qualities mentioned before—that very you is kindled by **Dadhyanc**, the **sage** of that name, who is the **son of Atharvan**. He illuminated you. Of what nature are you? You are the **slayer of Vritra** <note>original: "vṛtra-haṇam"</note>, the destroyer of enemies who cover or obstruct the light, and the **destroyer of forts** <note>original: "purandaram"</note>, the one who tears down the cities of the demons <note>the Asuras</note>.

---

## Hymn Text

-> ॥ Now the fifteenth verse ॥ <-

**The powerful Pathya kindled you, the greatest slayer of Dasyus, the winner of wealth in every battle. ॥ 15 ॥**

**Word-for-word breakdown:**
That | [particle] | You | Pathya | The powerful/bull | [intensifier] | Kindles | Dasyu-slayer-best | Wealth-winner | In battle after battle ॥ 15 ॥

---

## Commentary (Sayana)

**Pathya Vrishan** <note>literally "Pathya the Bull"</note> is the name of a certain sage. That very you, O Agni, he **kindled** or thoroughly ignited. What is your nature? You are the **greatest slayer of Dasyus** <note>original: "dasyuhantamam"</note>, the one who preeminently destroys the enemies who cause decay or destruction <note>the Dasyus were often portrayed as the enemies of the Vedic rituals</note>, and you are the **winner of wealth** <note>original: "dhanañjayam"</note> in every single **battle**.

-> **॥ This ends the twenty-third section of the fifth chapter of the fourth book ॥** <-

---

## Critical Notes

In the **Ukthya** sacrifice, during the **Third Savana** <note>the evening libation of Soma</note>, the two triplets beginning with "Come here..." <note>verse 16</note> are used as the ritual verses <note>Stotriya and Anurupa</note> for the **Maitravaruna** priest. This is noted in the **Ashvalayana Shrauta Sutra (6.1)**. In the occasional Ukthya sacrifices <note>Abhaplavika</note>, these two triplets are optional alternatives for the ritual verses, as noted in the Sutras: **"Come here, let me speak to you... Agni, the Bharata, has come." (A. 7.8)**. Furthermore, in the ritual of the re-establishment of the sacred fires <note>Punara-dheyiki</note>, this verse serves as the invitation for the final portion of the ghee offering, as noted: **"The two ghee offerings to Agni are 'Come here, let me speak to you...'" (A. 2.8)**.

---

## Hymn Text

-> ॥ This is the sixteenth verse of the hymn ॥ <-

**Come here, O Agni, so I may speak these other songs to you; you shall grow strong with these drops of Soma. ॥ 16 ॥**

**Word-for-word breakdown:**
Toward | Come | [particle] | Well | Let me speak | To you | O Agni | Thus | Other | Songs | With these | You shall grow | With the drops <note>the Soma drops</note> ॥ 16 ॥

# Mandala 6. Chapter 2. Hymn 16. || Fourth Ashtaka || 635

## Commentary (Sayana)
[Continuation of commentary on verse 16]

O **Agni, come**. Approach. "For **you**, the **songs**," meaning "Let me speak well of you," is the prayer. Hear these songs. The word "**u**" is used here as a metrical filler. The meaning is: "Hear [these], and not the other songs made by the demons <note>original: "asuraiḥ"</note>." Thus says the scripture: **"The 'other' songs are indeed of the demons."** <note>Aitareya Brahmana 3.49</note>. Moreover, having arrived, you **thrive** with these **Soma drops** <note>original: "indubhiḥ"</note>, the sacred juices of the sacrifice.

---

## Hymn Text
-> ॥ Now the seventeenth verse ॥ <-

**Wherever your mind and superior skill are placed, there you make your dwelling. ॥ 17 ॥**

**Word-for-word breakdown:**
Which | and | where | and | your | mind | skill | you place | superior | there | dwelling | you make ॥ 17 ॥

## Commentary (Sayana)
O **Agni, your mind**, which is your gracious inner heart, in **whatever** place or in **whichever** sacrificer <note>the *Yajamana* or person performing the ritual</note> it resides, **there** in that sacrificer, you **place** <note>original: "dadhase"</note> the **superior**, most excellent, and **strengthening** food or power. Furthermore, you **make** a **dwelling** <note>original: "sadaḥ"</note>, a place for yourself, within that sacrificer.

---

## Hymn Text
-> ॥ Now the eighteenth verse ॥ <-

**Indeed, O Dweller, may your light not be harmful to the eyes of the people; then you shall enjoy our worship. ॥ 18 ॥**

**Word-for-word breakdown:**
Not | indeed | your | fulfillment | eye-harming | may it be | of people | O Dweller | then | worship | you enjoy ॥ 18 ॥

## Commentary (Sayana)
O **Agni, your fulfillment**, your filling radiance, **may it not be eye-harming** <note>original: "akṣipat"</note>, meaning the destroyer or damager of eyes. Let it not be so. May it always grant us the ability to see. O **Dweller of the people** <note>original: "nemānāṃ vaso"</note>—the word "nema" can mean "few" or "some"—O you who dwell among those few who are your dedicated sacrificers. **Then**, for this reason, **enjoy** the **worship** <note>original: "duvaḥ"</note> or service performed by us, the sacrificers.

---

## Hymn Text
-> ॥ Now the nineteenth verse ॥ <-

**Agni has been reached, the supporter of oblations, the slayer of Vritra, the greatly conscious, the lord of the good, and the protector of Divodasa. ॥ 19 ॥**

**Word-for-word breakdown:**
Towards | Agni | has been reached | supporter | Vritra-slayer | greatly-conscious | of Divodasa | lord of the good ॥ 19 ॥

## Commentary (Sayana)
This **Agni has been reached**; he is approached by us with songs of praise. Of what nature is he? He is the **supporter** <note>original: "bhārataḥ"</note> who carries the offerings/oblations. He is the **slayer of Vritra**, the destroyer of the enemies of the King named **Divodasa**. He is **greatly conscious**, meaning the one who makes many people aware, or the one who knows all. This implies he is omniscient. He is the **lord of the good**, the protector of the virtuous sacrificers.

# 636 || Rig Veda || [Ashtaka 4, Adhyaya 5, Varga 25]

## Hymn Text

-> ॥ Now the twentieth verse ॥ <-

**He indeed, surpassing all earthly things, shall grant wealth through his greatness; winning, unopposed, and uninjured. ॥ 20 ॥**

**Word-for-word breakdown:**
He | indeed | all | surpassing | earthly | wealth | shall grant | through greatness | winning | unopposed | uninjured ॥ 20 ॥

---

## Commentary (Sayana)

Indeed, that **Agni** <note>The Fire God</note>, surpassing **all** <note>original: "viśvā"</note> things **pertaining to the earth**—meaning all created beings and objects on the earth—by his **greatness** <note>original: "mahitvā"</note> or his own majesty, may he **grant wealth** <note>original: "rayiṃ dāśat"</note> to us. Alternatively, the sense is: may he exceedingly grant all wealth existing on the earth. What is the nature of this Agni? Through his **greatness** of heat or splendor, he is **winning** <note>original: "vanvan"</note>, meaning he consumes firewood or destroys enemies. He is **unopposed** <note>original: "avāto"</note> by any other enemies and is **uninjured** <note>original: "astṛtaḥ"</note>, meaning he is harmed by no one.

-> ॥ Thus ends the twenty-fourth section of the fifth chapter of the fourth book. ॥ <-

---

## Hymn Text

-> ॥ Now the twenty-first verse ॥ <-

**Like the ancient ones, O Agni, with a newer, ever-extending splendor, you have spread the great light. ॥ 21 ॥**

**Word-for-word breakdown:**
He | like the ancient | with a newer | O Agni | with splendor | with extending | great | you have spread | with light ॥ 21 ॥

---

## Commentary (Sayana)

O **Agni**, you who possess the qualities mentioned before, **like the ancient** <note>original: "pratnavat"</note> fires of the past, with a **newer** or more recent splendor and with a **radiant** and perfectly **pervading** light, **you have spread** <note>original: "tatantha"</note> the **great** <note>original: "bṛhat"</note> mid-region <note>the *Antariksha*, the space between heaven and earth</note>.

---

## Hymn Text

-> ॥ Now the twenty-second verse ॥ <-

**O friends, for Agni, the subduer, perform the hymn and the sacrifice boldly; sing a song for the wise creator. ॥ 22 ॥**

**Word-for-word breakdown:**
Forward | your | friends | for Agni | hymn | sacrifice | and | boldly | perform | song | and | for the wise creator ॥ 22 ॥

---

## Commentary (Sayana)

O **friends** <note>original: "sakhāyaḥ"</note>—the priests of equal standing—**you** must **sing** <note>original: "gāya"</note> a **hymn** <note>original: "stomaṃ"</note> of praise for **Agni**, who is the **wise creator** <note>original: "vedhase"</note> and the subduer of enemies. Likewise, **offer** <note>original: "prārca"</note> the **sacrifice**, which is the means of worship consisting of the <term>oblation</term> <note>the *Havis*, or sacred food offered into the fire</note>.

---

## Hymn Text

-> ॥ Now the twenty-third verse ॥ <-

**For he is the one who sits through the human generations as the priest, the wise in action, the messenger and carrier of oblations. ॥ 23 ॥**

**Word-for-word breakdown:**
He | indeed | who | human | generations | sits | priest | wise in action | messenger | and | carrier of oblations ॥ 23 ॥

---

# 637 || Rig Veda || [Mandala 6, Hymn 16, Verses 24–26]

## Commentary (Sayana)

He, indeed, that **Agni** <note>The Fire God</note>, let him **sit** <note>original: "sīdat"</note>. Let him sit upon the sacred grass at our sacrifice. He is the **invoker** <note>original: "hotā"</note> who calls the gods to the ritual and he possesses **transcendent wisdom** <note>original: "kavikratuḥ"</note>. He oversees the **human ages** <note>original: "mānuṣā yugā"</note>, which refers to the specific times or cycles pertaining to men when sacrifices are performed. <note>The grammar uses the second case/accusative for "continuous duration of time."</note> For all this time, he acts as the **messenger** <note>original: "dūtaḥ"</note> of the gods. He is also the **carrier of oblations** <note>original: "havyavāhanaḥ"</note>, the one who bears the sacrificial offerings to the heavens.

---

## Hymn Text

-> ॥ Now the twenty-fourth verse ॥ <-

**O Beneficent One, worship here those two kings of pure vows, the Adityas, the host of Maruts, and Heaven and Earth. ॥ 24 ॥**

**Word-for-word breakdown:**
Those | two kings | of pure vows | the Adityas | the Marut | host | O Beneficent One | worship | here | Heaven and Earth ॥ 24 ॥

## Commentary (Sayana)

Those two famous, radiant **kings** <note>original: "rājānā"</note> of **pure vows** <note>original: "śucivratā"</note>—referring to the gods Mitra and Varuna—and the **Adityas** <note>original: "ādityān"</note> (the solar deities who are the sons of the goddess Aditi, such as Dhātṛ and others), the **host of Maruts** <note>original: "mārutaṃ gaṇam"</note> (the assembly of storm gods), and **Heaven and Earth** <note>original: "rodasī"</note>; O **Beneficent One** <note>original: "vaso"</note>, you who desire to dwell with us, **worship** <note>original: "yakṣi"</note> these gods here at this sacrifice.

---

## Hymn Text

-> ॥ Now the twenty-fifth verse ॥ <-

**O Agni, Son of Strength, your appearance is auspicious for the mortal who desires food, O immortal one. ॥ 25 ॥**

**Word-for-word breakdown:**
Auspicious | your | O Agni | appearance | desires | for the mortal | of strength | Son | of the immortal ॥ 25 ॥

## Commentary (Sayana)

O **Son of Strength** <note>original: "ūrjo napāt"</note>, an epithet for Agni who is churned from wood by force, O Agni! Your **appearance** <note>original: "saṃdṛṣṭiḥ"</note> or splendor is **auspicious** <note>original: "vasvī"</note>, meaning it is excellent and provides a home. For the **mortal** <note>original: "martyāya"</note> man—the one performing the sacrifice—that light **desires food** <note>original: "iṣayate"</note>, meaning it grants or provides nourishment to him. You are of the **immortal** <note>original: "amṛtasya"</note>, one who is free from death.

-> ॥ Thus ends the twenty-fifth section of the fifth chapter of the fourth book. ॥ <-

---

## Hymn Text

-> ॥ Now the twenty-sixth verse ॥ <-

**May the giver be most excellent today, O Agni, honoring you; possessing great wealth, may the mortal attain perfect praise. ॥ 26 ॥**

**Word-for-word breakdown:**
Through ritual | the giver | let him be | most excellent | today | you | honoring | possessing great wealth | the mortal | has attained | perfect praise ॥ 26 ॥

## Commentary (Sayana)

O Agni, **today** <note>original: "adya"</note>, at this moment, through the **ritual** <note>original: "ṛtvā"</note> consisting of service and devotion, may the **giver** <note>original: "dāḥ"</note>—the patron of the sacrifice who **honors** <note>original: "vanvan"</note> or serves you—be **most excellent** <note>original: "śreṣṭhaḥ"</note> or highly praiseworthy. May he also be **possessing great wealth** <note>original: "surekṇāḥ"</note>, endowed with beautiful riches. Furthermore, may that **mortal** <note>original: "martaḥ"</note> man **attain** <note>original: "ānaśa"</note> or reach **perfect praise** <note>original: "suvṛktim"</note>, which is a hymn directed toward you. This means: let him always be your singer of praise.

<summary>This page contains verses 24-26 of Rig Veda 6.16, focusing on Agni's role as a divine priest who summons other deities (Mitra, Varuna, Maruts) and grants prosperity and the gift of song to his worshippers.</summary>

# 638 || Rig Veda || [Ashtaka 4, Adhyaya 5, Varga 26]

## Hymn Text

-> ॥ Now the twenty-seventh verse ॥ <-

**Those people, O Agni, who are protected by you and who seek nourishment for their entire lives; they overcome the hostilities of the enemy and conquer the enmities of the foe. ॥ 27 ॥**

**Word-for-word breakdown:**
They | your | O Agni | protected-by-you | seeking-strength | all | life | crossing-over | of-the-enemy | enmities | conquering | of-the-enemy | enmities ॥ 27 ॥

---

## Commentary (Sayana)

O Agni, those people who belong to you—the singers who praise you—are **protected by you** <note>original: "tvotāḥ"</note>. Because they are protected, they **seek strength** <note>original: "iṣayantaḥ"</note>, desiring nourishment for themselves, and they obtain **their whole life** <note>original: "viśvam āyuḥ"</note>, which means they obtain all manner of food. Alternatively, it means they desire and attain a full **lifespan** <note>original: "āyuḥ"</note> characterized by the ideal length of a hundred years. Furthermore, they are **crossing over** <note>original: "tarantaḥ"</note> or bypassing the hostile armies of the enemy, and they are **conquering** <note>original: "vanvantaḥ"</note> or striking down those same enemy forces.

---

## Hymn Text

-> ॥ Now the twenty-eighth verse ॥ <-

**Agni, with his sharp flame, shall strike down every devouring demon. Agni wins wealth for us. ॥ 28 ॥**

**Word-for-word breakdown:**
Agni | with-sharp | flame | shall-strike | every | down | devourer | Agni | for-us | wins | wealth ॥ 28 ॥

---

## Commentary (Sayana)

This Agni, with his **sharp** <note>original: "tigmena"</note> or piercing **flame** <note>original: "śociṣā"</note> and brilliance, strikes down every **devourer** <note>original: "atriṇam"</note>, referring to the **Rakshasas** <note>monstrous beings or demons who disrupt rituals</note> and similar threats. Moreover, let Agni **win** <note>original: "vanate"</note> or grant **wealth** <note>original: "rayim"</note> to us.

---

## Hymn Text

-> ॥ Now the twenty-ninth verse ॥ <-

**O Jatavedas, O All-Seeing One, bring us wealth accompanied by brave sons. O Wise One, slay the demons. ॥ 29 ॥**

**Word-for-word breakdown:**
With-good-heroes | wealth | [towards] | bring | O Jatavedas | O All-Seeing-One | slay | the-demons | O Wise-Performer ॥ 29 ॥

---

## Commentary (Sayana)

O **Jatavedas** <note>An epithet of Agni meaning "Knower of All Births" or "Knower of Wealth"</note>, O **All-Seeing One** <note>original: "vicarṣaṇe"</note> who observes all things specially, bring us wealth that is **accompanied by brave sons** <note>original: "suvīram"</note>—that is, wealth joined with excellent sons and grandsons. Likewise, O **Wise One** <note>original: "sukrato"</note> of good deeds, **slay** <note>original: "jahi"</note> and destroy the **demons** <note>original: "rakṣāṃsi"</note>.

---

## Hymn Text

-> ॥ Now the thirtieth verse ॥ <-

**Protect us, O Jatavedas, from distress and from the malicious man. Guard us, O Sage of Prayer. ॥ 30 ॥**

**Word-for-word breakdown:**
You | us | protect | from-distress | O Jatavedas | from-the-malicious | guard | us | of-prayer | O Sage ॥ 30 ॥

<term>Agni</term> The Vedic god of fire and the medium of sacrifice.
<term>Jatavedas</term> A title for Agni, signifying his wisdom regarding all created things.
<term>Rayi</term> Wealth, often interpreted in the Vedas as cattle, sons, and food.
<term>Rakshas</term> Malevolent spirits or demons that obstruct the path of the righteous.
<term>Sukratu</term> One who possesses great wisdom or performs good sacrificial acts.
<term>Vicarsani</term> An epithet meaning all-seeing or all-pervading, applied to gods who watch over humanity.

# 639 || Rig Veda || [Ashtaka 4, Adhyaya 5, Varga 26]

O Knower of all created beings <note>original: "jātavedas"</note>, protect us from sin <note>original: "aṃhasaḥ"</note> or evil. Likewise, O Lord of Prayer <note>original: "brahmaṇaspate"</note>, O Poet <note>original: "kave"</note>, O Creator of Speech, O Agni! For Agni indeed produces sound. As it is remembered in traditional texts: "The mind strikes the bodily fire, which impels the breath; the breath, moving in the chest, produces a low sound." To such an Agni, protect us from the wicked enemy who wishes us harm.

->॥ Thus ends the twenty-sixth section of the fifth chapter of the fourth book ॥<-

---

## Hymn Text

->॥ Now the thirty-first verse ॥<-
O Agni, whatever mortal with evil intent offers us up for slaughter, protect us from that sin. ॥ 31 ॥
<note>RV 6.16.31</note>
**Who | us | O Agni | evil-intentioned | toward | mortal | for-slaughter | gives | from-that | us | protect | from-sin ॥ 31 ॥**

---

## Commentary (Sayana)

O Agni, whatever mortal man <note>original: "martaḥ"</note> with evil intentions <note>original: "durevaḥ"</note> offers us up for slaughter <note>original: "vadhāya"</note>—meaning he intends to strike us with his weapon—protect us from that man and from sin <note>original: "aṃhasaḥ"</note>.

---

## Hymn Text

->॥ Now the thirty-second verse ॥<-
O Divine One, with your tongue, completely obstruct that evildoer, that mortal who wishes to kill us. ॥ 32 ॥
<note>RV 6.16.32</note>
**That | that | O Divine | with-tongue | completely | obstruct | evildoer | mortal | who | us | wishes-to-kill ॥ 32 ॥**

---

## Commentary (Sayana)

O Divine, shining Agni, obstruct <note>original: "paribādhasva"</note>—meaning completely destroy—that specific evildoer mentioned, with your tongue <note>original: "jihvayā"</note>, which is your flame. This applies to any mortal man who wishes to kill <note>original: "jighāṃsati"</note> us.

---

## Hymn Text

->॥ Now the thirty-third verse ॥<-
O Overcoming One, grant to Bharadvaja widespread protection and Agni, excellent wealth. ॥ 33 ॥
<note>RV 6.16.33</note>
**For-Bharadvaja | widespread | protection | grant | O Overcoming-One | O Agni | excellent | wealth ॥ 33 ॥**

---

## Commentary (Sayana)

O Overcoming One <note>original: "sahantya"</note>, you who subdue enemies, O Agni, grant <note>original: "yaccha"</note> to me, the sage Bharadvaja, widespread <note>original: "saprathaḥ"</note>—meaning broad and extensive—protection <note>original: "śarma"</note>, which refers to happiness or a home. Likewise, give excellent <note>original: "vareṇyam"</note> wealth <note>original: "vasu"</note>.

In the Full Moon sacrifice <note>original: "paurṇamāsyām"</note>, the verse beginning with "Agni overcomes enemies" serves as the invitatory verse <note>original: "anuvākyā"</note> for the offering of clarified butter. It is indicated in the ritual manuals: "Agni struck down the enemies" is the invitatory verse for the previous butter offering. In the sacrifices involving offerings of cakes, animals, or Soma <note>original: "iṣṭi-paśu-someṣu"</note>, where no specific rule like "increase" or "nourish" is mandated, this same verse serves as the first invitatory for the butter offering. For the Agni-ritual during the Upasad ceremony <note>a preparatory rite in the Soma sacrifice</note>, this is the invitatory verse, and for the evening ritual, this same verse serves as the sacrificial chant <note>original: "yājyā"</note>.

# 640 || Rig Veda || [Ashtaka 4, Adhyaya 5, Varga 28]

It is also indicated in the ritual manuals: "Agni shall strike the enemies" <note>original: "agnir vṛtrāṇi jaṅghanat"</note> and "Like a fierce predator" <note>original: "uṣra iva śaryahā"</note>—these verses are used in a reversed order for the invitatory and offering prayers. Reference: Ashvalayana Shrauta Sutra 4. 8.

-> ॥ This is the thirty-fourth verse ॥ <-
## Hymn Text
**Agni shall strike the enemies, seeking wealth through praise; ignited, bright, and invoked with offerings. ॥ 34 ॥**

**Agni | the enemies | shall strike | seeking wealth | through praise | ignited | bright | invoked ॥ 34 ॥**

---

## Commentary (Sayana)
Being praised with a hymn <note>original: "vipanyayā"</note>, Agni—who is "seeking wealth" <note>original: "draviṇasyuḥ"</note>, meaning he desires to give wealth to his praisers or perhaps desires the sacrificial food for himself—shall "strike the enemies" <note>original: "vṛtrāṇi jaṅghanat"</note>. This refers to the destruction of obstructive forces like demons <note>original: "rakṣas"</note> or darkness. What is the nature of this Agni? He is "ignited" <note>original: "samiddhaḥ"</note> or perfectly kindled; therefore, he is "bright" <note>original: "śukraḥ"</note> or of a brilliant color, and he is "invoked" <note>original: "āhutaḥ"</note> by the sacrificial offerings.

---

-> ॥ Now the thirty-fifth verse ॥ <-
## Hymn Text
**In the womb of the mother, the father of the father, shining in the imperishable place; sitting in the seat of Truth. ॥ 35 ॥**

**In the womb | of the mother | of the father | the father | shining | in the imperishable | sitting | of Truth | the seat | [towards] ॥ 35 ॥**

---

## Commentary (Sayana)
In this verse, the words "mother" and "father" refer to the Earth and the Sky. As the scripture <note>original: "śruti"</note> says: "Sky is the father, Earth is the mother." In the "womb of the mother" <note>original: "māturgarbhe"</note>, which is the middle of the Earth, in the "imperishable" <note>original: "akṣare"</note> place—meaning the sacrificial altar <note>original: "vedi"</note> which is free from decay—Agni is "shining" <note>original: "vidyutānaḥ"</note> with particular brilliance. He is called the "father of the father" <note>original: "pituḥ pitā"</note> because he protects the Sky (the father) by providing it with nourishment through the smoke of the offerings. Being such, he sits in the "seat of Truth" <note>original: "ṛtasya yonim"</note>, which refers to the Northern Altar <note>term: "Uttaravedi" (the raised platform used for the main soma sacrifices)</term>. <note>Grammatical note: the second case ending is used here in place of the seventh case to indicate location.</note> The meaning is that while sitting on the Northern Altar, Agni "strikes the enemies," connecting this verse back to the previous one.

-> ॥ Thus ends the twenty-seventh section of the fifth chapter of the fourth book ॥ <-

---

-> ॥ Now the thirty-sixth verse ॥ <-
## Hymn Text
**O Knower of all beings, O Distinguished one, bring us sacred food with offspring; O Agni, that which shines in heaven. ॥ 36 ॥**

**Sacred-food | with-offspring | bring | O Knower-of-all-beings | O Distinguished-one | O Agni | which | shines | in heaven ॥ 36 ॥**

---

## Commentary (Sayana)
O "Knower of all beings" <note>original: "jātavedas"</note> (knower of everything born), O "Distinguished one" <note>original: "vicarṣaṇe"</note> (one who sees specifically), O Agni, bring to me "sacred food" <note>original: "brahma"</note>—meaning food or prayer—along with "offspring" <note>original: "prajāvat"</note> such as sons and grandsons. What kind of food? That which "shines in heaven" <note>original: "divi dīdayat"</note>, meaning the excellent food that is distributed among the gods and shines with splendor; bring that to us.

---

-> ॥ Now the thirty-seventh verse ॥ <-
## Hymn Text
**We offer our songs to you of lovely appearance, O Child of Strength, we who possess sacrificial food. ॥ 37 ॥**

**Towards | you | of-lovely-appearance | possessing-food | O Child-of-strength | O Agni | we-offer | songs ॥ 37 ॥**

- Agni: The deity of fire, central to the Vedic sacrifice.
- Vritra: Originally a specific demon, here used generally for "enemies" or "obstructions."
- Dravinasyu: One who seeks or possesses wealth; used for both the deity and the worshipper.
- Ritasya yoni: The "womb of Truth" or "seat of Cosmic Order," often identifying the sacrificial altar.
- Jatavedas: A common epithet for Agni, meaning "he who knows all things produced."
- Vicharshana: An epithet meaning "all-seeing" or "active among the people."

<meta>This page continues the commentary on Rig Veda Mandala 6, Hymn 16, specifically concluding the explanation for verse 37 and covering verses 38 through 40. # 641 || Rig Veda || [Ashtaka 4, Adhyaya 5, Varga 29]

## Commentary (Sayana)
[Continuation of commentary on verse 37]

O **Produced by Strength** <note>original: "sahaskṛta"</note>—O Agni, you who are brought forth through the forceful friction of the fire-sticks—we, **possessing food** <note>original: "prayaysvanto"</note> in the form of offerings, **unite our words** <note>original: "sampṛñmahe"</note> of praise toward you. This means we release or utter our hymns toward you, who are **beautiful to behold** <note>original: "ratnasandṛśaṃ"</note>, appearing as lovely as a jewel or worthy of being gazed upon.

---

-> ॥ This is the thirty-eighth verse ॥ <-

## Hymn Text
**We have come to your shelter, O Agni, who look like gold; as one seeks the shade to escape the burning heat. ॥ 38 ॥**

**Pada-patha:**
Toward | shade-like | heat (from) | we have come | shelter | your | we | O Agni | gold-looking ॥ 38 ॥

---

## Commentary (Sayana)
O Agni, who are **golden in appearance** <note>original: "hiraṇyasandṛśo"</note>—meaning your light is beneficial and lovely, or your brilliance shines like gold—we have **come to your shelter** <note>original: "śarma... upāganma"</note>, seeking refuge in you. From what? From your **burning glow** <note>original: "ghṛṇer"</note> or fierce heat. He provides an illustration: **Like a shadow** <note>original: "chāyām-iva"</note>. Just as those distressed by the scorching sun seek the cool shade, in the same way, we approach you for protection.

Regarding the ritual use in the morning *Upasad* <note>term: Upasad; a specific ceremony performed as part of the Soma sacrifice</note> dedicated to Agni: the verse **"He who like the fierce..."** (v. 39) is the offering prayer <note>term: yājyā; the verse recited at the moment the offering is poured into the fire</note>, while for the evening ritual, the verse **"Like the brilliant..."** is the invitatory prayer <note>term: anuvākyā; the verse used to invite the deity to the sacrifice</note>. This is indicated in the ritual manual: **"Agni shall strike the enemies... He who like the fierce archer."** (Ashvalayana Shrauta Sutra 4. 8).

---

-> ॥ This is the thirty-ninth verse ॥ <-

## Hymn Text
**You, who like a fierce archer striking with arrows, or like a bull with sharp horns, O Agni, have shattered the fortresses. ॥ 39 ॥**

**Pada-patha:**
Who | fierce-like | arrow-striker | sharp-horned | like | bull | O Agni | cities | have broken ॥ 39 ॥

---

## Commentary (Sayana)
This Agni, who is like a fierce warrior with uplifted strength, or like a bowman who is an **arrow-striker** <note>original: "śaryahā"</note>—one who slays enemies with arrows—and who is **like a bull with sharp horns** <note>original: "tigmaśṛṅgo na vaṃsagaḥ"</note> whose gait is desirable; O Agni, that same you have **shattered the cities** <note>original: "pura rurojitha"</note>. This refers to the three iron, silver, and golden cities of the demons <note>term: Asuras</note>. 

According to the scripture <note>term: Shruti</note>, **"Agni is indeed Rudra,"** and therefore the **burning of the Triple-City** <note>term: Tripura-dahana; the famous myth where the god Shiva/Rudra destroyed three demon fortresses with a single arrow</note> accomplished by Rudra is here praised as being performed by Agni himself. Alternatively, since Agni resided in the tip of the arrow that was the instrument for burning the Triple-City, it is said that Agni broke the fortresses. One should reflect on the Brahmana passage: **"The gods and demons were fighting in these worlds..."** (Aitareya Brahmana 1. 23).

When the fire is being produced by friction <note>term: Agnimanthana</note>, the verse **"Whom in the hand..."** (v. 40) is the invitatory prayer. It is indicated: **"One should pause at the half-verse 'Whom in the hand like a ring'..."** (Ashvalayana Shrauta Sutra 2. 16).

---

-> ॥ This is the fortieth verse ॥ <-

## Hymn Text
**Whom they bear in their hands like a decorative ring, or like a newborn babe; Agni, the leader of the people, the lord of the perfect sacrifice. ॥ 40 ॥**

**Pada-patha:**
Toward | whom | in hand | like | ring | infant | born | like | they bear | of the people | Agni | of good-sacrifice ॥ 40 ॥

---

## Commentary (Sayana)
That Agni, produced by friction, whom the priests **bear in their hands** <note>original: "ā bibhrati"</note> like a **newborn infant** <note>original: "śiśuṃ jātaṃ na"</note>—as one carefully carries a recently born son in one's arms—

<meta>This page concludes the commentary on verse 40 of the previous hymn and begins the commentary on Rig Veda Mandala 4, Hymn 15. The previous page discussed Agni's golden appearance and his role as a protector. This page transitions into the ritual of churning new fire and placing it into the consecrated sacrificial fire-pit.</meta>

# 642 || Rig Veda || [Ashtaka 4, Adhyaya 5, Varga 29]

## Commentary (Sayana)
[Continuation of commentary on verse 40]

...the *Adhvaryu* <note>term: Adhvaryu; the priest responsible for the physical ritual manual labor</note> priests hold him facing forward. The word **na** <note>original: "na"</note> appearing before the word is used for comparison. **Like a devourer** <note>original: "khādinaṃ na"</note>—meaning like a tiger or another beast of prey. The sense is that just as men are extremely alert and careful when holding such a beast, these priests are equally attentive. Alternatively, it refers to the present moment: O priests, serve this Agni, the devourer of oblations, whom you are now holding in your hands, the one who perfectly accomplishes the beautiful sacrifice for the people.

---

-> ॥ This concludes the twenty-eighth Varga of the fifth Adhyaya in the fourth Ashtaka ॥ <-

When the fire produced by churning is being cast into the *Ahavaniya* <note>term: Ahavaniya; the consecrated eastern fire where oblations to the gods are poured</note>, the triplet of verses starting with **"Toward the god, for the gods’ feast"** <note>original: "pra devaṃ devavītaye"</note> should be recited. This is indicated in the *Ashvalayana Shrauta Sutra* (2.16): **"Toward the god, for the gods' feast... with these two verses, the fire is ignited by fire."**

---

-> ॥ Here begins the forty-first verse of the hymn ॥ <-

## Hymn Text

**Carry forward the god, for the gods' feast, the best procurer of wealth; let him sit down in his own source. ॥ 41 ॥**

**Pada-patha:**
Toward | god | god-feast (for) | carry | wealth-finding-best | in | his-own | source | let sit ॥ 41 ॥

---

## Commentary (Sayana)

O Adhvaryu priests, **carry forward** <note>original: "prabharata"</note>—that is, cast into the Ahavaniya fire—the **god** <note>original: "devam"</note> who is shining and the **best procurer of wealth** <note>original: "vasuvittamam"</note>, the one who makes known and grants riches. For what purpose? **For the gods' feast** <note>original: "devavītaye"</note>; so that the gods may consume the offerings. 

The *Brahmana* <note>term: Brahmana; ancient prose texts that explain the meaning and ritual application of the Vedas</note> states: **"Toward the god, for the gods' feast, carry the best procurer of wealth—this is the appropriate form for what is being cast; what is appropriate in the sacrifice, that is successful. Let him sit down in his own source—this indeed is his own source, where Agni meets fire."** (Aitareya Brahmana 1.16). 

And let that fire **sit down** <note>original: "ā niṣīdatu"</note>—become established—**in his own source** <note>original: "sve yonau"</note>, which is his original place, the Ahavaniya fire-pit. The Brahmana confirms: **"This indeed is his own source, where Agni meets fire."** (Aitareya Brahmana 1.16).

---

-> ॥ Now the forty-second verse ॥ <-

## Hymn Text

**Sharpen the newborn [Agni] in the All-Knower, the dear guest, the lord of the house, in his pleasant [abode]. ॥ 42 ॥**

**Pada-patha:**
In | newborn | All-Knower (in) | dear | sharpen | guest | pleasant (in) | in | house-lord ॥ 42 ॥

---

## Commentary (Sayana)

O Adhvaryu priests, **sharpen** <note>original: "ā śiśīta"</note>—place or refine—the **newborn** <note>original: "jātam"</note> fire, which has just been produced, into the **All-Knower** <note>term: Jatavedas; a common name for Agni implying he knows all created beings</note>, the wise Ahavaniya fire. This includes a hidden comparison: like a **dear guest** <note>original: "atithim-iva priyam"</note>. Thus, place Agni, who is the **lord of the house** <note>original: "gṛhapatim"</note>, in the **pleasant** <note>original: "syone"</note> or comfortable Ahavaniya fire.

The word "sharpen" <note>original: "ā śiśīta"</note> is a complex Vedic form. It could come from the root *shi*, meaning to sleep, used here to mean "make him rest" or "establish him." Or it may be a form of the root *shyai* meaning "to go," thus "make him go toward" or "reach." Alternatively, it is from the root *sho* meaning "to sharpen" or "to refine," suggesting the priest should "refine" or "prepare" the fire as it is cast. The second **ā** <note>original: "ā"</note> in the verse is a filler for the poetic meter. One should consult the Brahmana (Aitareya 1.16) which explains: **"One is the newborn, the other is the All-Knower,"** referring to the churned fire being added to the existing ritual fire.

<summary>This page describes the ritual procedure for moving newly churned fire into the main sacrificial altar, comparing Agni to a precious guest and a lord being established in his home.</summary>
<keywords>Agni, Ahavaniya, ritual fire, Adhvaryu, Jatavedas, Aitareya Brahmana, Vedic ritual, fire churning</keywords>

# 643 || Rig Veda || [Ashtaka 4, Adhyaya 5, Varga 19]

-> || The Forty-Third Verse || <-

## Hymn Text

**O Agni, harness those horses of yours, O God, who are well-trained. They carry you fittingly to the sacrifice. ॥ 43 ॥**

**Word-by-word analysis (Padapatha):**
Agni | harness | indeed | which | your | horses | O God | well-trained | fittingly | they carry | to the sacrifice ॥ 43 ॥

---

## Commentary (Sayana)

O **shining God** <note>original: "deva"</note> Agni, **harness those horses**; join them to your own chariot. **Those which are yours**, the **well-trained** <note>original: "sādhavaḥ"</note>—meaning those who are efficient or well-behaved—**horses**, they **carry** you **fittingly** <note>original: "aram"</note>, which is to say, sufficiently. For what purpose? For the **sacrifice** <note>original: "manyave"</note>. Here, the word *Manyu* refers to the sacrifice <note>original: "yāga"</note> because it is where the gods are known or recognized as those who should be worshipped. Therefore, the sense is: harness those horses to the chariot for the sake of the sacrifice. The word **hi** <note>original: "hi"</note> serves as an emphasis (indeed).

---

-> || The Forty-Fourth Verse || <-

## Hymn Text

**Come towards us; bring the gods to the feast of offerings and for the drinking of Soma. ॥ 44 ॥**

**Word-by-word analysis (Padapatha):**
Towards | us | come | bring | toward | the offerings | for the feast | bring | the gods | for the drinking of Soma ॥ 44 ॥

---

## Commentary (Sayana)

O **Agni, come towards us** <note>original: "acchā"</note>—meaning facing our direction. Furthermore, **bring the gods** here, looking toward the **offerings** <note>original: "prayāṃsi"</note>, which are the foods characterized as oblations. For what purpose? **For the feast** <note>original: "vītaye"</note>, so that they may taste those oblations. Likewise, bring those gods for the **drinking of Soma** <note>original: "somapītaye"</note> as well.

---

-> || The Forty-Fifth Verse || <-

## Hymn Text

**Rise up, O Agni, sustainer of the sacrifice, shining brightly with unceasing light; O ageless one, blaze forth. ॥ 45 ॥**

**Word-by-word analysis (Padapatha):**
Up | Agni | sustainer | brightly | with unceasing | shining intensely | blaze | forth | shine | O ageless one ॥ 45 ॥

---

## Commentary (Sayana)

O **Bharata** <note>term: Bharata; a title for Agni meaning the 'sustainer' or 'bearer' of the oblations</note>, O Agni who bears the offerings, **blaze upwards** <note>original: "ucchocha"</note>. Shine even higher. He explains this further: O **ageless** <note>original: "ajara"</note> Agni, you who are free from decay, **shining intensely** <note>original: "davidyutat"</note>, you must **shine forth** with **bright** <note>original: "dyumat"</note> and **unceasing** <note>original: "ajasreṇa"</note> radiance. <note>Sayana notes a grammatical technicality here: "dyumat" is used as an adverbial instrumental despite its ending.</note> Shine with a light that is never interrupted. Alternatively, the meaning is: O Agni, first blaze upwards yourself, and then illuminate the entire world with your own light.

-> || This concludes the nineteenth Varga of the fifth Adhyaya in the fourth Ashtaka || <-

---

-> || The Forty-Sixth Verse || <-

## Hymn Text

**The mortal who, with an offering, would serve the god Agni, should praise him at the sacrifice. With hands outstretched and with reverence, he seeks the favor of the invoker, the true sacrificer between the two worlds. ॥ 46 ॥**

<summary>This page contains the ritual invocation of Agni, asking him to harness his horses to bring the gods to the sacrifice to consume oblations and Soma. It highlights Agni's role as "Bharata" (the sustainer) and his eternal, unceasing brilliance.</summary>

# 644 || Rig Veda || [Ashtaka 4, Adhyaya 5, Varga 20]

## Hymn Text (Verse 46 Word-by-word)

**Desiring | who | the God | mortal | should serve | Agni | should praise | in the sacrifice | possessing offerings | the Priest | the true-sacrificer | of the two worlds | with upturned hands | with reverence | indeed | should worship ॥ 46 ॥**

---

## Commentary (Sayana)

**Whatever mortal** <note>original: "martaḥ"</note>—that is, a human being—who is a **possessor of offerings** <note>original: "haviṣmān"</note>, a patron of the sacrifice, **should serve** or attend to any **God** with **food** <note>original: "vītī"</note> that is characterized as a beloved oblation, he **should praise** or laud **Agni** at that **sacrifice**. The meaning is that Agni is the one honored in all sacrifices. 

What kind of Agni? One who is the **Priest** <note>original: "hotāram"</note>, the invoker of the gods who dwell in the **two worlds** <note>original: "rodasyoḥ"</note>—heaven and earth—and who is the **true-sacrificer** <note>original: "satya-yajam"</note>, meaning one who worships with an oblation that is effective and unfailing. Furthermore, this patron, with **upturned hands** <note>original: "uttāna-hastaḥ"</note>—in the gesture of prayer with palms joined—**should worship** or serve such an Agni with **reverence** <note>original: "namasā"</note>, which may mean either a physical bow or the offering itself.

---

## Hymn Text

-> ॥ The Forty-Seventh Verse ॥ <-

**O Agni, we bring to you an oblation fashioned by the heart through this hymn. May these [offerings] become for you oxen, bulls, and cows. ॥ 47 ॥**

**Word-by-word analysis (Padapatha):**
Bring | to you | O Agni | with a hymn | oblation | by the heart | fashioned | we bring | they | for you | may they become | oxen | bulls | cows | and ॥ 47 ॥

---

## Commentary (Sayana)

The sage **Ashvalayana** <note>A famous teacher of Vedic ritual; this refers to his Grihya Sutra 1.1</note> considers that this verse praises the act of study itself. **O Agni, we bring** <note>original: "abharāmasi"</note> or offer **to you** an **oblation** <note>original: "haviḥ"</note> that exists in the form of a **hymn** <note>original: "ṛcā"</note>, which has been **fashioned** or refined **by the heart** <note>original: "hṛdā taṣṭam"</note>. In other words, we have made the sacred verse itself the sacrificial offering. 

The word **they** <note>original: "te"</note> refers back to the previously mentioned oblation in the form of the hymn. Although "hymn" is singular, the pronoun is plural to match the animals it represents. May that oblation in the form of a hymn **become for you**—that is, for your enjoyment—**oxen** <note>original: "ukṣāṇaḥ"</note> capable of sprinkling, **bulls** <note>original: "ṛṣabhāsaḥ"</note>, and **cows** <note>original: "vaśāḥ"</note>. The implication is: let this hymn be transformed into the form of bulls and cows so that it may be food for you to consume.

---

## Hymn Text

-> ॥ The Forty-Eighth Verse ॥ <-

**The gods kindle Agni, the foremost, the greatest slayer of Vritra; by whom wealth is recovered and the demons are crushed by his power. ॥ 48 ॥**

**Word-by-word analysis (Padapatha):**
Agni | the gods | the foremost | kindle | the greatest slayer of Vritra | by whom | wealth | brought back | crushed | demons | by the powerful one ॥ 48 ॥

---

## Commentary (Sayana)

**The gods** <note>original: "devāso"</note> **kindle** or illuminate **Agni**, who is the **foremost** <note>original: "agriyam"</note> or principal one, and the **greatest slayer of Vritra** <note>original: "vṛtrahantamam"</note>—the most excellent destroyer of obstacles or enemies. By **Agni**, the **wealth** <note>original: "vasūni"</note>—meaning riches or sacrificial foods—that had been carried away by the **Asuras** <note>demonic beings</note> is **brought back**...

<meta>The text ends here mid-sentence in Sayana's commentary for verse 48. The discussion of Agni's role in recovering stolen wealth and destroying the Rakshasas (demons) will likely continue on the next page.</meta>

<summary>This page concludes the 16th hymn of the sixth Mandala, focusing on the proper way for humans to worship Agni and the metaphysical transformation of a recited hymn into a physical sacrificial offering (cattle). It also introduces Agni's role as the primary deity used by the gods to destroy demons and recover lost wealth.</summary>

<keywords>Agni, Sayana commentary, Ashvalayana, Vritra, sacrifice, ritual gesture (uttana-hasta), hymn as oblation, cattle symbolism, Rig Veda Mandala 6</keywords>

# 645 || Rig Veda || [Ashtaka 4, Adhyaya 6, Varga 1]

## Commentary (Sayana)
...brought from the presence of the patron <note>original: "yajamānāt"</note>. The connection of the words is: they kindle that Agni—the powerful one by whom the demons <note>original: "rakṣāṃsi"</note>, who are the enemies of the sacrifice, were crushed or destroyed <note>original: "tṛlhā"</note>.

-> ॥ Thus ends the twentieth varga of the fifth chapter of the fourth book ॥ <-

By the illumination of the meaning of the Veda, removing the darkness of the heart, may **Vidyatirtha-Maheshvara** <note>The spiritual teacher of the commentator Sayana, often equated with the Supreme Lord</note> grant the four goals of human life <note>The puruṣārthas: righteousness, prosperity, pleasure, and liberation</note>.

**Thus concludes the fifth chapter of the fourth book (Ashtaka) in the "Light of the Veda’s Meaning," the commentary on the Rig Veda Samhita composed by Sayanacharya, the pillar of the empire of King Virabukka, the supreme lord of kings and promoter of the Vedic path.**

---

-> He whose breath is the Vedas, who from the Vedas created the entire world, <-
-> I bow to that Vidyatirtha-Maheshvara. <-

The sixth chapter of the fourth book begins. In the second section <note>original: "anuvāka"</note> of the sixth Mandala, the first hymn has been explained. This second hymn <note>Hymn 17</note>, beginning with "Drink the Soma," is seen by the seer **Bharadvaja** and is in the **Trishtubh** metre <note>A rhythmic meter of 44 syllables</note>. The final verse is a two-footed <note>original: "dvipadā"</note> Trishtubh. As stated in the Index <note>original: "Anukramaṇī"</note>: "The hymn 'Drink' <note>original: "pibā"</note> consists of fifteen verses addressed to Indra in the Trishtubh metre, ending with a two-footed verse."

In the **Abhijit** sacrifice, this hymn is part of the recitation for Indra associated with the Maruts <note>original: "marutvatīya-śastra"</note>. It is indicated: "Drink the Soma, praise him," for the midday session. In the **Dasharatra** rite (the ten-night sacrifice), on the eighth day, this hymn is used in the same recitation. It is indicated: "Drink the Soma, towards that which is his, Heaven and Earth." In the one-day **Suryastuta** sacrifice, performed by one desiring fame, this hymn is the designated recitation. It is indicated: "For one desiring fame in the Suryastuta, 'Drink the Soma' is used." Even in the **Mahavrata** rite, this hymn belongs to the Marutvatiya recitation. Likewise, it is indicated in the *Aitareya Aranyaka* (5.1): "Drink the Soma, towards that which, O fierce one, you pierced; with what beauty, of the same age, of the same dwelling." In the midday libation, the first three verses are the offering-prayers <note>original: "yājyās"</note> for the priests (the Hotri, Maitravaruna, and Brahmanachhamsin). It is indicated: "The three beginning with 'Drink the Soma, towards that which, O fierce one, you pierced' are the prayers; 'come down, O you who desire Soma,' they say."

-> ॥ Here is the first verse ॥ <-

---

## Hymn Text
Drink the Soma, O fierce Indra, for whom you broke open the great stall of cows while being praised. O bold one, you who hold the thunderbolt in your hand <note>original: "vajrahasta"</note>, you have struck down all the powers of the enemy <note>original: "vṛtram"</note> with your might. ॥ 1 ॥

<vocab>
- Sayanacharya: The 14th-century scholar who provided the most influential commentary on the Vedas.
- Bharadvaja: An ancient sage (Rishi) and the primary seer of the hymns in the sixth book of the Rig Veda.
- Trishtubh: A major Vedic meter consisting of four lines of eleven syllables each.
- Marutvatiya-shastra: A specific set of hymns recited for Indra in the company of the Maruts (storm gods) during the Soma sacrifice.
- Vritra: The primary antagonist in the Rig Veda, a serpent or dragon representing drought and obstruction, slain by Indra.
- Vajrahasta: A common epithet for Indra, meaning "holding the thunderbolt (Vajra) in his hand."
</vocab>
