# 646 || Rig Veda || [Book 4, Chapter 6, Verse 1]

## Hymn Text

<note>Rig Veda 4.16.1 Word-for-word breakdown (The full verse was on the previous page)</note>
Drink. The **Soma**. Towards. Which. O **fierce one**. You pierced. The **enclosure**. Belonging to **cows**. Great. Being **praised**. **Indra**.
Who. O **daring one**. You struck. **Wielder of the thunderbolt**. All. **Vritra**. The **enemy**. With **powers**. Towards. || 1 ||

---

## Commentary (Sayana)

O **fierce one of uplifted strength, Indra**, being **praised by the Angirases** <note>The Angirases are a legendary family of fire-priests</note>, for the sake of that Soma which you—for the purpose of drinking it—**pierced** <note>original: "tardaḥ"</note> or revealed the great wealth, the herd belonging to the cows that had been carried away by the Panis <note>The Panis were demon-merchants who stole the celestial cows</note>. The root *tard* means "to strike" but here signifies "to make visible." Drink that Soma. Perform the drinking. O **daring one**, the crusher of enemies, **wielder of the thunderbolt**, O **Indra**, you who, accompanied by **powers** <note>original: "śavobhiḥ"</note>, destroyed all of **Vritra, the coverer** <note>original: "vṛtram āvarakam"</note>, and the **enemy** <note>original: "amicayaṃ"</note>. <note>Sayana explains a grammatical substitution here: from the word "amica," the second person singular ending takes the "iyā" form.</note> The connection is: you who destroyed the enemy, drink the Soma.

---

## Hymn Text

-> || Now the Second [Verse] || <-
<note>Rig Veda 4.16.2</note>
**Drink this, you who possess the dregs, the deliverer, who has handsome jaws, the bull of prayers.
You, the breaker of cow-pens, the wielder of the thunderbolt, who stands upon your two bay horses; O Indra, reveal marvelous riches to us.** || 2 ||

**Word-for-word breakdown:**
He. This. Drink. Who. **Possessor of dregs**. **Deliverer**. Who. **Handsome-jawed**. **Bull**. Who. **Of prayers**.
Who. **Breaker of cow-pens**. **Wielder of the thunderbolt**. Who. **Standing on bay horses**. He. **Indra**. **Marvelous**. Towards. **Pierce [reveal]**. **Riches**. || 2 ||

---

## Commentary (Sayana)

O **Indra**, you are the **possessor of the dregs** <note>original: "ṛjīṣī"</note>. By the word *rijisha*, we mean the Soma from which the juice has already been extracted. You are the **deliverer** <note>original: "tarutraḥ"</note> who carries us across or protects us from enemies. You are **handsome-jawed** <note>original: "śipravān"</note>, possessing beautiful cheeks or a helmet. You are the **bull** <note>original: "vṛṣabhaḥ"</note>—the showerer of desires—for the **prayers** <note>original: "matīnām"</note> of the singers. <note>The word "mati" comes from the root *man*, meaning "to think," used here for those who perform the act of praise.</note> Such as you are, drink this Soma. O **Indra**, you are the **wielder of the thunderbolt**, the **breaker of cow-pens** <note>original: "gotrabhid"</note>—the cleaver of the clouds or the mountain enclosures—and you **stand upon your two bay horses** <note>original: "hariṣṭhā"</note>. O **Indra**, **reveal** <note>original: "abhitṛndhi"</note> or manifest for us **marvelous riches** or food.

---

## Hymn Text

-> || Now the Third [Verse] || <-
<note>Rig Veda 4.16.3</note>
**Even so drink, in the ancient manner; let the Soma exhilarate you. Listen to our prayer and grow strong by our songs.
Make the sun visible; satisfy our desires; slay the enemies; reveal the cows, O Indra.** || 3 ||

**Word-for-word breakdown:**
Even so. Drink. **In the ancient manner**. Let [it] exhilarate. You. Listen. **Prayer**. Grow strong. And. By **songs**.
Visible. **Sun**. Make. Satisfy. **Desires**. Slay. **Enemies**. Towards. **Cows**. **Indra**. **Pierce [reveal]**. || 3 ||

---

## Commentary (Sayana)

O **Indra**, just as you drank the ancient Somas **in the ancient manner** <note>original: "pratnathā"</note>, even so drink this Soma of ours...

<term>Indra</term>: The king of the gods in the Vedic pantheon, known for his strength and for drinking Soma.
<term>Soma</term>: A ritual beverage offered to the gods, believed to grant immortality and strength.
<term>Rijishi</term>: A title for Indra, meaning he who accepts even the "Rijisha" or the residue of the pressed Soma stalks.
<term>Tarutra</term>: A conqueror or one who helps someone cross over difficulties (from the root *tṛ*, "to cross").
<term>Vrishabha</term>: Literally "bull," but used here as a metaphor for a powerful male or a "bestower" of rain and blessings.
<term>Vajrabhrit</term>: "Bearer of the Vajra," Indra's lightning-bolt weapon.
<term>Vajan</term>: This term can refer to food, strength, or the spoils of victory (plunder).
<term>Pratnatha</term>: An adverbial form meaning "as in olden times" or "according to ancient custom."

<summary>This page contains the commentary on Rig Veda 4.16.1-3, where the sage Bharadvaja invokes Indra to drink Soma and grant riches. The text emphasizes Indra's mythological roles as the slayer of Vritra and the liberator of the celestial cows from the Panis.</summary>
<keywords>Indra, Soma, Vritra, Sayana, Vedic Sacrifice, Panis, Rig Veda 4.16, Bharadvaja</keywords>

# 647 || Rig Veda || [Mandala 6, Hymn 17]

## Commentary (Sayana)
[Continuation from previous page for Verse 3]

Drink. Perform the drinking. And that **Soma** <note>The sacred ritual drink of the Vedic people</note>, having been drunk by you, may it **exhilarate** <note>original: "mandatu"</note> or gladden you. **Hear** <note>original: "śrudhi"</note> the **prayer** <note>original: "brahmā"</note> or the hymn composed by us. And also, **increase** <note>original: "vardhasva"</note> through our **songs** <note>original: "gīrbhiḥ"</note> or words of praise; may you flourish. Furthermore, **make manifest** <note>original: "āviṣkṛṇuhi"</note> or reveal the **Sun** <note>original: "sūryam"</note>, the god who impels everything. The meaning is: "act in such a way that we may see the sun." **Swell** <note>original: "pīpihi"</note> our **nourishments** <note>original: "iṣo"</note> or foods; cause them to flow for us. **Slay** <note>original: "jahi"</note> or destroy our enemies, our rivals. O **Indra**, **reveal** <note>original: "abhitṛndhi"</note> or bring to light the cows that were carried away by the **Panis** <note>The Panis were mythical demons who hoarded the world's light and cattle in a dark cave</note>.

---

-> ॥ Now the Fourth [Verse] ॥ <-

## Hymn Text
These **exhilarating drinks** <note>original: "madāḥ"</note>, O **Indra**, possessor of **self-power** <note>original: "svadhāvaḥ"</note>, these [Somas] having been **drunk**, may they **strengthen** <note>original: "ukṣayanta"</note> you **greatly** <note>original: "bṛhat"</note>, the **radiant one** <note>original: "dyumantam"</note>. May the **gladdening** <note>original: "matsarāso"</note> [Somas] **exult** <note>original: "jahṛṣanta"</note> you, the **great** <note>original: "mahām"</note>, the **flawless** <note>original: "anūnam"</note>, the **mighty** <note>original: "tavasam"</note>, the **all-pervading** <note>original: "vibhūtim"</note>, the **subduer** <note>original: "prasāham"</note> [of enemies]. ॥ 4 ॥

**Word-for-word breakdown:**
These. You. **Exhilarating drinks**. **Greatly**. **Indra**. **Possessor of self-power**. These. **Drunk**. They **strengthen**. The **radiant one**.
The **great**. The **flawless**. The **mighty**. The **all-pervading**. The **gladdening [Somas]**. They **exult**. The **subduer**. ॥ 4 ॥

## Commentary (Sayana)
O **Indra**, you who possess **food** <note>Sayana glosses "svadhāvaḥ" as "possessor of food," though it literally refers to "self-power" or "inherent nature"</note>, these **exhilarating** <note>original: "madāḥ"</note> **Somas**, once **drunk**, let them **strengthen** <note>original: "ukṣayantu"</note> or sprinkle you, the **radiant one** <note>original: "dyumantam"</note>, **greatly** <note>original: "bṛhat"</note> or excessively. Moreover, O Indra, let the **exhilarating** <note>original: "matsarāso"</note> Somas **gladden** <note>original: "jahṛṣanta"</note> or greatly delight you. In what manner? You who are **great** <note>original: "mahām"</note> or abundant; **flawless** <note>original: "anūnam"</note> or devoid of any deficiency in qualities—meaning perfect in qualities; **mighty** <note>original: "tavasam"</note> or grown strong; **all-pervading** <note>original: "vibhūtim"</note> or powerful; and the **subduer** <note>original: "prasāham"</note> or conqueror of enemies.

---

-> ॥ Now the Fifth [Verse] ॥ <-

## Hymn Text
With **which [Somas]**, **rejoicing** <note>original: "mandasānaḥ"</note>, you **caused to dwell** <note>original: "avāsayaḥ"</note> the **Sun** <note>original: "sūryam"</note> and the **Dawn** <note>original: "uṣasam"</note>, while **tearing away** <note>original: "apardardat"</note> the **firm** <note>original: "dṛḷhāni"</note> [shadows]. O **Indra**, you **pushed away** <note>original: "nutthyāḥ"</note> the **great mountain** <note>original: "mahām adrim"</note> surrounding the **cows**, that which was **immovable** <note>original: "acyutam"</note>, away from its **own place** <note>original: "svāt sadasaḥ"</note>. ॥ 5 ॥

**Word-for-word breakdown:**
With **which**. The **Sun**. The **Dawn**. **Rejoicing**. You **caused to dwell**. **Away**. The **firm [things]**. **Tearing**.
The **great**. The **mountain**. **Around**. The **cows**. **Indra**. **Being**. You **pushed away**. The **immovable**. From the **place**. **Away from**. **Own**. ॥ 5 ॥

## Commentary (Sayana)
O **Indra**, with **those [Somas]**, you, **rejoicing** <note>original: "mandasānaḥ"</note> or being delighted, **caused to dwell** <note>original: "avāsayaḥ"</note> the **Sun** <note>original: "sūryam"</note>, the god who impels all, and the goddess **Dawn** <note>original: "uṣasam"</note> in their own places. Alternatively, you acted such that the Sun and Dawn might dispel the darknesses. Doing what? **Tearing away** <note>original: "apardardat"</note> or splitting apart the **firm** <note>original: "dṛḷhāni"</note> or dense darknesses. Furthermore, O Indra, you **pushed away** <note>original: "nutthyāḥ"</note> or moved the **great mountain** <note>original: "mahām adrim"</note> or rock that was **surrounding** <note>original: "pari santam"</note> the **cows** stolen by the Panis. What kind of mountain? One that was **immovable** <note>original: "acyutam"</note> or unshakable and indestructible—meaning steady—away from its **own place** <note>original: "svāt sadasaḥ"</note>.

-> ॥ Thus ends the first group (Varga) in the sixth [chapter] of the fourth [book] ॥ <-

# 648 || Rig Veda || [Book 1, Hymn 62, Section 22]

## Hymn Text

-> ॥ Now the sixth [verse] ॥ <-

By your **wisdom**, by your **deeds**, you placed the **cooked** [milk] in the **raw** [cows] by your **power**. You opened the **doors** for the **cows**; you, [accompanied by] the **Angirases**, released them from the **stronghold**. ॥ 6 ॥

**Word-by-word Analysis:**
**tava** (your); **kratvā** (by wisdom); **tava** (your); **daṃsanābhiḥ** (by deeds); **āmāsu** (in the raw [cows]); **pakvam** (the cooked [milk]); **śacyā** (by power); **ni dīdhaḥ** (you placed); **aurṇoḥ** (you opened); **duraḥ** (doors); **usriyābhyaḥ** (for the cows); **vi dṛḷhā** (the firm [obstacles]); **ut asṛjaḥ** (you released); **ūrvāt** (from the stronghold); **gāḥ** (the cows); **aṅgirasvān** (accompanied by the Angirases). ॥ 6 ॥

---

## Commentary (Sayana)

O **Indra**, by **your wisdom** <note>original: "tava kratvā"</note>—that is, by your intellect—and by **your deeds**—your heroic actions—you **placed** <note>original: "nidīdhaḥ"</note> the well-known **cooked** or matured milk within the **raw** <note>The ancient poets marvelled that white, "cooked" (warm/ready) milk came from the "raw" (living/unprocessed) body of the cow</note> or unbaked cows, using your **power**. Furthermore, O Indra, for the **cows** <note>original: "usriyābhyo"</note>—meaning, in order to let the cows out—you **opened** the **doors** which were **firm** <note>original: "dṛḷhā"</note>, or made solid by stones and other barriers. **Accompanied by the Angirases** <note>A group of semi-divine fire-priests who assisted Indra in his myths</note>, you **released** or led the **cows** out **from the stronghold** <note>original: "ūrvāt"</note>, which refers to the cattle-pen or the mountain cave where they were hidden.

---

## Hymn Text

-> ॥ Now the seventh [verse] ॥ <-

You **spread** the wide **earth**, O performer of **great deeds**; you, the **exalted one**, supported the **lofty sky**, O **Indra**. You **sustained** the two **worlds**, which have the **gods as sons**, the **ancient mothers**, the **mighty daughters** of the **sacred law**. ॥ 7 ॥

**Word-by-word Analysis:**
**paprathaḥ** (you spread); **kṣām** (the earth); **mahi daṃsaḥ** (great in deeds); **vi urvīm** (the wide); **upa stabhāyaḥ** (you supported); **dyām** (the sky); **ṛṣvaḥ** (exalted); **bṛhat** (lofty); **indra** (O Indra); **adhārayaḥ** (you sustained); **rodasī** (heaven and earth); **devaputre** (having the gods as sons); **pratne** (ancient); **mātarā** (the mothers); **yahvī** (the mighty daughters); **ṛtasya** (of the sacred law). ॥ 7 ॥

---

## Commentary (Sayana)

O **Indra**, with your **great deed**, you **spread** <note>The root *prā* means to fill or expand</note> and specifically filled the **wide earth** <note>original: "kṣām"</note>. O Indra, you being **exalted** or great, **supported** the **lofty sky** <note>original: "dyām"</note>. The meaning is that Indra acts in such a way that the sky, which stands without any visible support, does not fall. Furthermore, you **sustained** <note>original: "adhārayaḥ"</note> the **two worlds** <note>original: "rodasī"</note>, meaning Heaven and Earth, by nourishing them. What are these two worlds like? They have **the gods as their sons** <note>original: "devaputre"</note>; they are the **ancient mothers** or creators; they are the **mighty daughters** <note>original: "yahvī"</note> of the **sacred law** <note>original: "ṛtasya"</note>, which refers either to the cosmic waters or the sacrifice. Alternatively, they are the two mothers of the universe and the mighty daughters of the **Supreme Being** <note>original: "brahmaṇo"</note>; the word *yahuḥ* is a synonym for offspring.

---

## Hymn Text

-> ॥ Now the eighth [verse] ॥ <-

O **Indra**, all the **gods** placed the **battle** in you alone, the **mighty one**, when the **non-god** challenged the **gods**. They chose **Indra** in the **conquest of light**; [therefore] **worship** [him]. ॥ 8 ॥

<keywords>Indra, Angiras, cows (Usriya), Heaven and Earth (Rodasi), Sacred Law (Rta), Vedic cosmogony, Sayana's commentary</keywords>

# 649 || Rig Veda || [Book 6, Hymn 17, Verses 8–10]

## Hymn Text

Then all the **gods**, O **Indra**, placed you alone, the **mighty** one, in the **front** for the **battle**, when the **godless** [one] **defied** the gods in the **struggle for light**; they choose **Indra** with **hymns**. ॥ 8 ॥

**Word-by-word Analysis:**
**adha** (then); **tvā** (you); **viśve** (all); **puraḥ** (in front); **indra** (O Indra); **devāḥ** (gods); **ekam** (alone/singular); **tavasam** (mighty); **dadhire** (placed); **bharāya** (for the battle); **adevaḥ** (godless/demon); **yat** (when); **abhi** (towards); **ohiṣṭe** (defied/challenged); **devān** (the gods); **svaḥ-sātā** (in the wining of light/heaven); **vṛṇate** (they choose); **indram** (Indra); **arcaiḥ** (with songs of praise). ॥ 8 ॥

---

## Commentary (Sayana)

**Then** <note>original: "adha"</note>—at this time—**all the gods**, including Agni and others, O **Indra**, placed **you**, the **one** primary, **mighty** <note>original: "tavasam"</note> and powerful one, **in the front** <note>original: "pura dadhire"</note>—that is, they made you their leader—**for the battle**. This happened **when the godless** demon **Vritra** <note>The personification of drought and chaos who imprisoned the waters</note> **defied** or approached the gods for the sake of war. <note>The root "oh" implies movement or challenge.</note> Furthermore, during this **struggle for light** <note>original: "svarṣātā"</note>, which refers to the battle, the **Maruts** <note>Storm deities and Indra's loyal companions</note> **choose** or remained devoted to **Indra**. The meaning is that even when other gods fled in fear, the Maruts stood by Indra. Thus, they "placed him in the front."

---

## Hymn Text

->|| Now the ninth [verse] ||<-

Then even **Heaven** bowed **away** from your **thunderbolt**, in **two ways**, through **fear** of your own **wrath**, when **Indra** struck the **serpent** who was **surging forward**, [striking him] **down** into a **long sleep**. ॥ 9 ॥

**Word-by-word Analysis:**
**adha** (then); **dyauḥ** (Heaven); **cit** (even); **te** (your); **apa** (away); **sā** (that); **nu** (indeed); **vajrāt** (from the thunderbolt); **dvitā** (in two ways); **anamat** (bowed/bent); **bhiyasa** (through fear); **svasya** (from your own); **manyoḥ** (wrath/anger); **ahim** (the serpent); **yat** (when); **indraḥ** (Indra); **abhi-ohasānam** (surging forward/attacking); **ni** (down); **cit** (indeed); **viśvayuḥ** (throughout all life/time); **śayathe** (in a place of lying/death); **jaghāna** (struck/killed). ॥ 9 ॥

---

## Commentary (Sayana)

**That** famous **Heaven** <note>original: "dyauḥ"</note>, which serves as the refuge for the gods, even she, O Indra, **then**—at that moment—**bowed away** in **two ways** or in different directions from **your thunderbolt** and through **fear** of **your own wrath**. The word "nu" is a filler for the meter. **Indra**, the one who sustains **all life**, **struck** the **serpent Vritra** as he was **surging forward** or attacking. He struck him down into a **long sleep** <note>original: "śayathe"</note>—meaning into death. The word "cit" is also a filler. The connection is: when Indra killed Vritra, at that time even Heaven bowed.

---

## Hymn Text

->|| Now the tenth [verse] ||<-

Then **Tvashtri** fashioned for you, O **mighty** one, the **great thunderbolt**, **thousand-edged**, **hundred-pointed**, with which you, O **drinker of Soma-dregs**, **crushed** the **bellowing serpent**. ॥ 10 ॥

**Word-by-word Analysis:**
**adha** (then); **tvaṣṭā** (Tvashtri); **te** (for you); **mahaḥ** (great); **ugra** (O mighty one); **vajram** (thunderbolt); **sahasra-bhṛṣṭim** (thousand-edged); **vavṛtat** (fashioned/turned); **śata-aśrim** (hundred-pointed); **nikāmam** (according to desire); **aramanasam** (roaring/bellowing); **yena** (with which); **navantam** (bellowing/shouting); **ahim** (the serpent); **sam piṇak** (crushed); **ṛjīṣin** (possessor of Soma-dregs). ॥ 10 ॥

---

## Commentary (Sayana)

**Then**, O **mighty** Indra of immense power, **Tvashtri** <note>The divine architect and smith of the gods</note> **fashioned** or completed the **great thunderbolt** for you. Of what kind was it? It was **thousand-edged** <note>original: "sahasrabhṛṣṭim"</note> and **hundred-pointed**. O **drinker of Soma-dregs** <note>original: "ṛjīṣin"; a title for Indra referring to the residue of the pressed Soma plant</note>, with that thunderbolt you **crushed** the **serpent** who was **bellowing** <note>original: "navantam"</note> or shouting...

<vocab>
**Indra**: The king of the gods and deity of thunder and rain.
**All the Gods**: Refers to the collective pantheon (Visvedevas).
**For the battle**: The Sanskrit *bharāya* literally means "for the carrying" or "for the load," metaphorically referring to the burden of war.
**Vritra**: The "Enveloper," a dragon/serpent demon representing drought.
**Maruts**: Storm-gods who are the sons of Rudra and allies of Indra.
**Heaven**: *Dyauḥ*, personified as a goddess who trembles at Indra's power.
**Thunderbolt**: *Vajra*, the primary weapon of Indra, crafted from the bones of a sage or by Tvashtri.
**Tvashtri**: The celestial artisan who crafts the weapons and forms of all beings.
**Hundred-edged**: A description of the complexity and lethality of the Vajra.
**Indra as possessor of Soma dregs**: *Rijishin* refers to Indra's fondness for the Soma juice, even the remains of the pressing.
</vocab>

<summary>This page describes the mobilization of the gods behind Indra as their leader to face the demon Vritra. It details the creation of Indra's thousand-edged thunderbolt by the divine smith Tvashtri and the cosmic fear felt by Heaven during the battle.</summary>
<keywords>Indra, Vritra, Tvashtri, Vajra, Maruts, Battle of Heaven, Soma-dregs, Vedic Mythology</keywords>

# 650 || Rig Veda || [Book 4, Chapter 6, Section 2]

...him, who was unyielding, whose mind was intent on attacking enemies <note>original: "aramansam"</note>. You crushed <note>original: "sampiṇak"</note> that sounding serpent Vritra, the demon; the meaning is that you acted with your thunderbolt against him.

-> ॥ Thus ends the second section of the sixth chapter of the fourth book ॥ <-

## Hymn Text

-> ॥ The Eleventh Verse ॥ <-

**All the Maruts, being of one mind, strengthen you, O Indra. For you, Pushan and Vishnu cooked a hundred buffaloes. For him, the slayer of Vritra, the intoxicating Soma-stalk [juice] flowed into three lakes.** ॥ 11 ॥

---

### Word-by-word Analysis
**vardhān** (they strengthen); **yam** (whom); **viśve** (all); **marutaḥ** (the storm-gods); **sa-joṣāḥ** (harmonious/of one mind); **pacan** (cooking/they cooked); **śatam** (a hundred); **mahiṣān** (buffaloes); **indra** (O Indra); **tubhyam** (for you); **pūṣā** (the god Pushan); **viṣṇuḥ** (the god Vishnu); **trīṇi** (three); **sarāṃsi** (lakes/vessels); **dhāvan** (flowing/running); **vṛtra-hanam** (Vritra-slaying); **madiram** (intoxicating); **aṃśum** (the Soma-stalk/juice); **asmai** (for him). ॥ 11 ॥

---

### Commentary (Sayana)
O Indra, all the **Maruts** <note>The storm-god companions of Indra</note>, being **of one mind** and pleased together, **strengthen** you with songs of praise. For your sake, O Indra, the god named **Pushan** and the god named **Vishnu cooked a hundred**—meaning a great number—of **buffaloes** <note>original: "mahiṣān"</note>, which are male sacrificial animals. Furthermore, for you, the **Soma-juice** <note>original: "aṃśum"</note> is **flowing** into **three lakes**. These "lakes" refer to the three specific ritual vessels used in the sacrifice: the *Drona-kalasha*, the *Putabhrit*, and the *Ahavaniya*. The meaning is that these vessels are being filled with Soma. What kind of Soma? It is **intoxicating** and **Vritra-slaying**. In this context, the term "Vritra-slaying" <note>original: "vṛtrahaṇam"</note> is applied to the Soma itself, because once Indra has drunk the Soma, he becomes capable of slaying Vritra and his other enemies.

---

## Hymn Text

-> ॥ The Twelfth Verse ॥ <-

**You released the great flood of the rivers that was obstructed and surrounded; you let forth the waves of the waters. O Indra, you directed their paths downward; you sent the active waters flowing down to the ocean.** ॥ 12 ॥

---

### Word-by-word Analysis
**ā** (towards/completely); **kṣodaḥ** (the flood/agitated water); **mahi** (great); **vṛtam** (enclosed/covered); **nadīnām** (of the rivers); **pari-sthitam** (standing around/obstructed); **asṛjaḥ** (you released); **ūrmim** (the wave); **apām** (of the waters); **tāsām** (of them); **anu** (along/following); **pra-vataḥ** (downward slopes); **indra** (O Indra); **panthām** (the path); **pra** (forward); **ardayaḥ** (you caused to go); **nīcīḥ** (downward-facing); **apasaḥ** (the active ones/waters); **samudram** (to the ocean). ॥ 12 ॥

---

### Commentary (Sayana)
O Indra, you **released** <note>original: "asṛjaḥ"</note> the **great flood** of the **rivers** or streams, which had been **enclosed** or covered by the demon Vritra and was **obstructed** on all sides. You did this so that the rivers might be full and flow freely. You released the **wave** or the collective mass of the **waters**. <note>The repetition of "waters" in the verse is for the sake of emphasis or respect.</note> Furthermore, O Indra, you followed or prepared the **paths** for those rivers along the **downward slopes**. Additionally, you **sent** <note>original: "pra-ardayaḥ", from the root 'ard' meaning to move or lead</note> the **active** waters—the word **apasaḥ** here simply refers to the waters themselves—which were **flowing downward** with great speed, toward the **ocean**.

# 651 || Rig Veda || [Book 6, Chapter 2, Hymn 17]

-> || Now the Thirteenth Verse || <-

## Hymn Text
Thus, for our protection, may this new prayer bring you to us—you who have performed all those famous deeds, the great, the fierce, the ageless Indra, the giver of strength, the one with heroic followers, well-armed and wielding the auspicious thunderbolt. ॥ 13 ॥

**Word-by-word Analysis:**
**evā** (thus); **tā** (those); **viśvā** (all); **cakṛvāṃsam** (having performed); **indram** (Indra); **mahām** (great); **ugram** (fierce/powerful); **ajuryam** (ageless); **saho-dām** (giver of strength); **su-vīram** (having good heroes/followers); **tvā** (you); **svāyudham** (well-armed); **su-vajram** (having a good thunderbolt); **ā** (towards); **brahma** (prayer/hymn); **navyam** (new); **avase** (for protection); **vavṛttyāt** (may it turn/bring). ॥ 13 ॥

---

## Commentary (Sayana)
O **Indra**, may the **new**—meaning a prayer <note>original: "brahma"</note> recently composed by us and not performed by others before—bring **you** to us for **our protection**. May it turn you toward us. What kind of Indra? One who, in the **manner described**, has **performed** all those well-known and **all-encompassing** deeds; **Indra**, the Lord, the **great**, the **fierce** and powerful, the **ageless**, the **giver of strength** or power; one who has **good heroes**, meaning the Maruts <note>The storm-god companions of Indra</note> are his followers; the **well-armed** one; the one **endowed with the auspicious thunderbolt** <note>the *Vajra*, the primary weapon of Indra</note>.

---

-> || Now the Fourteenth Verse || <-

## Hymn Text
O Indra, grant to us, the luminous and wise, strength, power, food, and wealth. O Indra, grant to me, Bharadwaja, followers and wise singers; O Indra, be our protector in the days to come. ॥ 14 ॥

**Word-by-word Analysis:**
**saḥ** (that/you); **naḥ** (to us); **vājāya** (for strength/spoils); **śravase** (for fame/glory); **iṣe** (for food); **ca** (and); **rāye** (for wealth); **dhehi** (place/bestow); **dyumantaḥ** (luminous); **indra** (O Indra); **viprān** (the wise); **bharad-vāje** (to Bharadwaja); **nṛ-vataḥ** (with men/followers); **indra** (O Indra); **sūrīn** (wise singers/patrons); **divi** (in the day); **ca** (and); **sma** (indeed); **edhi** (be); **pārye** (in the future/to be reached); **naḥ** (our); **indra** (O Indra). ॥ 14 ॥

---

## Commentary (Sayana)
O **Indra**, **you**, grant to **us**, the **luminous** and **wise** singers, **strength**, **power**, **food**, and **wealth**. Furthermore, O **Indra**, grant to me, **Bharadwaja** <note>The seer/sage of this hymn family</note>, **followers**—meaning those who serve—and make our **wise** singers your praisers, specifically our sons and grandsons. O **Indra**, **be** indeed **our** protector in the **days** that are to be reached or are **approaching**.

In the ritual of the sixth day, during the third libation <note>term: *savana* — the pressing of Soma juice</note>, in the recitation of the *Brahmanacchamsi* priest, this is the third verse of the corresponding triplet. This is indicated in the Ashvalayana Shrauta Sutra (8.3): "May we obtain through this the god-given strength" are the opening and corresponding hymns.

---

-> || This is the Fifteenth Verse || <-

## Hymn Text
Through this, may we obtain god-given strength; may we rejoice for a hundred winters, blessed with heroic sons. ॥ 15 ॥

**Word-by-word Analysis:**
**ayā** (through this); **vājam** (strength/wealth); **deva-hitam** (god-given); **sanema** (may we obtain); **madema** (may we rejoice); **śata-himāḥ** (a hundred winters); **su-vīrāḥ** (with good heroes/sons). ॥ 15 ॥

<meta>This page concludes the commentary for the previous section (Mandala 6, Sukta 32) and introduces Sukta 33 of the same Mandala. 652 || Rig Veda || [Book 4, Chapter 6, Verse Group 4]

Through this praise, may we enjoy the food <note>original: "vāja"</note> given by the shining god Indra, which is beneficial to the gods. May we share in it. Furthermore, may we, accompanied by excellent sons <note>original: "su-vīrāḥ"</note>, rejoice and be happy.

-> || Thus ends the third verse-group of the sixth chapter of the fourth book || <-

---

The third hymn of this section, beginning with "Praise Him" <note>original: "tam u ṣṭuhi"</note>, consists of fifteen verses. The seer <term>Rishi: the inspired poet-sage who "saw" the hymn</term> is Bharadvaja, the meter is <term>Trishtubh: a Vedic meter of 44 syllables</term>, and the deity is Indra. The Index of Hymns confirms this: "Praise Him..." In the <term>Abhijit: a specific one-day sacrifice</term>, this hymn is used during the <term>Nishkevalya: a ritual recitation dedicated exclusively to Indra</term> at the midday offering. This is indicated in the ritual manuals: "Praise Him is for the midday" (Ashvalayana Shrauta Sutra 8.5). In the 'nest-named' one-day rite of Indra and Agni, it is also used for the Nishkevalya, as noted: "Stay, O Haris... Praise Him is for the midday" (Ashvalayana Shrauta Sutra 9.7). It is also used in the <term>Mahavrata: a 'Great Vow' rite celebrating the winter solstice</term> for the Nishkevalya, as stated in the Fifth Aranyaka: "Praise Him who has conquering power; You are pressed; To the one who knows the goal, Indra, Soma—these three" (Aitareya Aranyaka 5.8).

## Hymn Text

-> || Here is the First Verse || <-
Praise him who has conquering power, who strikes the enemy and is unassailable, the much-invoked Indra. With these songs of praise, increase the strength of the invincible, the fierce, the overwhelming one, the bull among the people. ॥ 1 ॥

**Word-by-word Analysis:**
**tam** (him); **ūṃ** (indeed - emphatic); **stuhi** (praise); **yaḥ** (who); **abhibhūti-ojāḥ** (having conquering power); **vanvan** (striking/conquering); **avātaḥ** (unassailed/unharmed); **puru-hūtaḥ** (invoked by many); **indraḥ** (Indra);
**aṣāḷham** (invincible); **ugram** (fierce/powerful); **sahamānam** (overwhelming); **ābhiḥ** (with these); **gīrbhiḥ** (with songs/words); **vardha** (increase/strengthen); **vṛṣabham** (the bull/showering leader); **carṣaṇīnām** (of the people). ॥ 1 ॥

---

## Commentary (Sayana)

The one who has **conquering power** <note>original: "abhibhūtyojā"</note> means one possessing overwhelming luster. **Striking** <note>original: "vanvan"</note> means harming or destroying enemies. **Unassailable** <note>original: "avātaḥ"</note> means one who is not harmed by enemies. This is a form of the root *van* with a negative prefix; or alternatively, from the root *vā*, meaning "not approached" [by enemies]. **Much-invoked** means called upon by many—this is the Indra who exists. O Bharadvaja, **praise him**! Praise that very Indra. Furthermore, **increase** or strengthen that Indra **with these** words of praise that are about to be spoken. What is he like? He is **invincible** (unconquered), **fierce** (powerful or elevated), **overwhelming** (subduing enemies), and the **bull** (the one who showers blessings) **of the people** (of all subjects).

---

## Hymn Text

-> || Now the Second Verse || <-
He is the warrior, the hero, the creator of battle-noise, the fighter, the great destroyer, the roaring one, the possessor of the Soma-remnants. Raising the great dust, the stirrer of human tribes, he alone became the conqueror. ॥ 2 ॥

**Word-by-word Analysis:**
**saḥ** (he); **yudhmaḥ** (warrior); **satvā** (hero/being); **khaja-kṛt** (maker of battle-noise); **samadvā** (warrior/fighter); **tuvi-mrakṣaḥ** (great destroyer); **nadanumān** (roaring/thundering); **ṛjīṣī** (possessor of Soma-residue);
**bṛhat-reṇuḥ** (raising great dust); **cyavanaḥ** (the stirrer/shaker); **mānuṣīṇām** (of human); **ekaḥ** (alone/one); **kṛṣṭīnām** (of tribes/people); **abhavat** (became); **sahāvā** (the conqueror/powerful). ॥ 2 ॥

---

## Commentary (Sayana)

**Raising the great dust** means he is the one who kicks up the great or massive **dust** <note>original: "reṇu"</note> or earth. This refers to his actions in battles. He alone <unclear>...</unclear>

653 || Rig Veda || [Book 4, Chapter 6, Verse Group 2, Hymn 18]

## Commentary (Sayana)
<note>Continued from the previous page for Rig Veda 6.18.2</note>

The chief, the powerful one, that Indra has become the shaker <note>original: "cyavano"</note>—the one who approaches—of the human subjects <note>original: "kṛṣṭīnām"</note> related to Manu <term>Manu: the ancestral father of humanity in Vedic thought</term> and the sacrificers. What is he like? He is a warrior <note>original: "yudhmaḥ"</note> and a giver <note>original: "satā"</note>. <note>This word "sata" is a form derived from the root "san," meaning to gain or give.</note> He is the maker of battles <note>original: "khajakṛt"</note>. <note>The word "khaja" is a traditional name for battle or conflict.</note> He possesses exhilaration <note>original: "samadvā"</note>; that is, he possesses the joy <note>original: "madaḥ"</note> shared with the sacrificers. He is the "many-softener" <note>original: "tuvimrakṣaḥ"</note>. <note>The root "mrakṣ" refers to the act of smearing or softening; here it means he softens or moistens many things through the shedding of rain.</note> He is noisy and possesses the Soma-residue <note>original: "ṛjīṣī"</note>. The word <term>Rijisha: the remains of the Soma stalks after they have been pressed twice</term> refers to the Soma that has been pressed for the first two sessions and is pressed once more for the third session. He is the one who possesses that.

---

## Hymn Text
->॥ Here is the Third Verse ॥<-

You indeed then subdued the Dasyus alone; you won the subjects for the Arya.
Is that heroic power of yours still real, Indra, or is it not? Tell us truly in due season. ॥ ३ ॥

**Word-for-Word Breakdown:**
You | indeed | now | that | subdued | Dasyus | alone | subjects | won | for the Arya |
Is | [interrogative] | now | heroic power | that | your | Indra | not | [interrogative] | is | that | in due season | [imperative] speak ॥ ३ ॥

---

## Commentary (Sayana)

O Indra, "that" <note>original: "tyat"</note> which was said of you, you are he. <note>The word "tyat" is a synonym for "tat" (that), used here with a grammatical shift in gender.</note> You quickly subdued the Dasyus <term>Dasyus: enemies of the Vedic people, described by Sayana as those who do not perform the sacred rituals</term>. You made them disciplined. The word "ha" is used for emphasis. Furthermore, you, the unique and chief one, won the subjects <note>original: "kṛṣṭīḥ"</note>—meaning sons, servants, and so on—for the Arya, the person who performs the sacred rites. You gave them to him.

While praising him in this way, the Rishi <note>the seer Bharadvaja</note> did not perceive Indra's presence. At that moment, doubting the existence of Indra's heroic strength, he speaks the second half of the verse. O Indra, that heroic power <note>original: "vīryam"</note> or capability of yours which was spoken of before, does it "now" truly exist? <note>The particles "svit" and "nu" are used together here to express doubt or inquiry.</note> Or does it not exist? Therefore, speak to us <note>original: "vi vocaḥ"</note> clearly and specifically "in due season" <note>original: "ṛtuthā"</note>, at the proper time of the rite.

---

## Hymn Text
->॥ Here is the Fourth Verse ॥<-

Truly I believe your power is real, you who are born of many, O mightiest one, of the swift the swiftest;
The most powerful of the powerful, the stronger of the strong, you have become the overcomer of the miser. ॥ ४ ॥

**Word-for-Word Breakdown:**
Real | indeed | for | your | born-of-many | I believe | power | O mightiest | of the swift | of the swift |
Powerful | of the powerful | of the strong | stronger | of the miser | overcomer | you have become ॥ ४ ॥

---

## Commentary (Sayana)

Having expressed doubt in the previous verse about whether Indra's strength exists or not, the Rishi now affirms that the strength truly exists. The word "hi" (for) is used in the sense of "because." Because of this reason, O mightiest <note>original: "sahiṣṭha"</note>, O most powerful Indra, I believe in the power of you who are "born of many" <note>original: "tuvijātasya"</note>—that is, manifested in many sacrifices...

<note>Commentary for 6.18.4 continues on the next page</note>

<vocab>
- **Indra:** The primary deity of the hymn, known for his strength and leadership.
- **Dasyu:** Described here as 'karma-hina' (lacking ritual action); the enemies of the Vedic way of life.
- **Kristi (Kristih):** Human subjects or people; often refers to the clans or families of the sacrificers.
- **Virya:** Heroic power, manly strength, or effective capability.
- **Rijisha:** The residue or pulp of the Soma plant after the juice has been extracted.
- **Savana:** The three daily sessions (morning, midday, and evening) of the Soma sacrifice.
</vocab>

654 || Rig Veda || [Book 4, Chapter 6, Verse Group 5]

## Commentary (Sayana)
I consider that your strength <note>original: "sahaḥ"</note>—the strength of you who have appeared and who strike those who harm us—is truly present. You are the striker of enemies, the powerful one. You are fierce, full of energy, and grown great; you are one who cannot be overcome or controlled by enemies. <note>The word used here is a form of the root "radh," which means to subjugate or bring under control.</note> You have become the striker of those rivals who ought to be subjugated. It is certainly so. What is this strength like? It is fierce, uplifted, and even more exceedingly grown. Because you strike enemies like Vritra and others, it means your strength is truly evident.

---

## Hymn Text
->॥ Here is the Fifth Verse ॥<-
Let that ancient friendship of ours be with you. With the <term>Angiras: a group of semi-divine ancestral sages</term> speaking the truth, you struck the demon <term>Vala: a cave-demon who stole the cows of the gods</term>. O Shaker of the unshakeable, O Beautiful one, you opened all the doors of his cities as he launched his weapons. ॥ 5 ॥

**Word-by-Word Breakdown**

Striker. Shaker of the unshakeable. Beautiful one. Launching weapons. You opened. The cities. Wide. The doors. His. All. ॥ 5 ॥

## Commentary (Sayana)
"Ancient" <note>original: "pratnam"</note> means from olden times; that is, continuing for a long time. That famous friendship of ours—characterized by the relationship between the singer and the one being praised—O Indra, let it be with you. The plural form "with you" <note>original: "yuṣme"</note> is used as a mark of respect. O shaker of those things that are otherwise immovable <note>original: "acyutacyut"</note>, O beautiful Indra <note>original: "dasma"</note>, you, along with the Angiras sages who were speaking the truth and praising you, struck the demon named Vala. Furthermore, you opened the cities <note>original: "puraḥ"</note> of this Vala; you caused them to go away, meaning you separated them from him. You opened all the doors of those cities.

The word "indeed" <note>original: "hi"</note> serves here to complete the meter of the verse. In the winning of offspr—

655 || Rig Veda || [Book 4, Chapter 6, Verse Group 2, Hymn 18]

## Commentary (Sayana)
[Continuation of Verse 6 commentary]

For the sake of obtaining <note>original: "sātā"</note> offspring and sons, that Indra is to be invoked. The wielder of the thunderbolt <term>Vajri: a title for Indra referring to his primary weapon, the Vajra</term>, in battles <note>original: "samatsu"</note>, becomes "vitantasāyya"—one who is to be made known or expanded upon specifically through hymns of praise. Alternatively, "vitantasāyya" means the destroyer of enemies. The root "tantasa" refers to the act of injuring or killing <note>original: "hiṃsā-karmā"</note>; this is the form of the one who performs that action.

---

->॥ Here is the Seventh Verse ॥<-

## Hymn Text
By his majesty, he has surpassed the generations of men; by his immortal name, he has moved forward. Through glory, through power, and through wealth, through heroic might—he is the foremost of leaders, dwelling with these qualities. ॥ 7 ॥

**Word-by-Word Breakdown**
He. By majesty. Generation. Of men. By immortal. Name. Surpasses. Forward. Moved.
He. By glory. He. By power. And. By wealth. He. By heroic might. Best of leaders. Dwelling together. ॥ 7 ॥

## Commentary (Sayana)
That Indra, with his immortal—meaning undecaying—name, which humbles his enemies, and with his majesty <note>original: "majmanā"</note>, which means strength (this is a known name for strength), has surpassed the birth or the assembly <note>original: "saṅgham"</note> of men. He has moved beyond them. That Indra dwells together with glory, which is fame. Furthermore, he dwells with power, which is strength. And also, as the best of leaders <note>original: "nṛtamaḥ"</note>, he dwells together with wealth and with heroic capacity.

---

->॥ Here is the Eighth Verse ॥<-

## Hymn Text
He who is never confused in battle, nor is he a man of falsehood; he of the wise name struck down Chumuri and Dhuni. Indra struck Pipru, Shambara, and Shushna, for the shattering and the prostration of their cities, even now. ॥ 8 ॥

**Word-by-Word Breakdown**
He. Who. Not. For confusion. Not. Falsehood. Person. Was. Of wise name. Chumuri. Dhuni. And.
Struck down. Pipru. Shambara. Shushna. Indra. Of the cities. For shattering. For prostration. Now. Even. ॥ 8 ॥

## Commentary (Sayana)
Indra never becomes confused <note>original: "muhe"</note> in the midst of battle. He is never a "person of falsehood"—that is, he is never a creator of things in vain or for no purpose; rather, he is "one of a wise name" <note>original: "sumantunāmā"</note>, which means he possesses a name synonymous with great wisdom or renown. For the shattering <note>original: "cyautnāya"</note> or destruction of the cities belonging to the enemies, and for the prostration or death of those enemies, Indra performs his work even now—"quickly" is the implied meaning. Likewise, he struck down <note>original: "vṛṇak"</note> the two demons named <term>Chumuri and Dhuni: two specific demons or 'asuras' mentioned in the Rig Veda as enemies of Indra's protégés</term>. The word "vṛṇakti" refers to the act of killing. Furthermore, he destroyed the three demons named <term>Pipru, Shambara, and Shushna: recurring antagonists in the Vedas who represent drought or obstruction</term>.

656 || Rig Veda || [Book 4, Chapter 6, Section 6]

## Hymn Text

-> ॥ Here is the Ninth Verse ॥ <-

Mount your chariot, O Indra, with rising energy, with power, and with most praiseworthy strength, for the slaying of the enemy <note>original: "vritra-hatyāya"</note>. Take the thunderbolt in your right hand, and destroy the illusions <note>original: "māyāḥ"</note> of the foe, O bounteous giver! ॥ 9 ॥

**Word-by-Word Analysis**
Up. Rising. With energy. With most praiseworthy strength. And. For the slaying of the enemy. Chariot. Indra. Mount. Take. Thunderbolt. In hand. Indeed. Right hand. And. Against. Completely. Destroy/Rejoice against. O bounteous giver. The illusions. ॥ 9 ॥

---

## Commentary (Sayana)

O **Indra**, being endowed **with rising energy** <note>original: "udavatā"</note>—where the root refers to movement—and **with power** <note>original: "tvakshasā"</note>, which means that which cuts the bodies of enemies, and **with most praiseworthy strength** <note>original: "panyasā"</note>, you should **mount your own chariot for the slaying of the enemy** <note>original: "vritra-hatyāya"</note>. **Similarly, take** <note>original: "ādhisva"</note> **the thunderbolt**, your own weapon, **in your right hand** <note>original: "dakshiṇā haste"</note>. Following that, O Indra, bounteous giver <note>original: "purudatra"</note> of much wealth, having approached the demonic illusions <note>original: "māyāḥ"</note>, **destroy them completely**. Here, the word for "rejoice" <note>original: "mandati"</note> is used in the sense of the act of killing <note>original: "vadha-karmā"</note>.

---

## Hymn Text

-> ॥ Here is the Tenth Verse ॥ <-

As fire consumes the dry forest, O Indra, your weapon shall burn the demon; you are like the fearsome lightning. With your deep-striking spear, he who is the breaker of enemies made a roar in battle and crushed the powers of evil. ॥ 10 ॥

**Word-by-Word Analysis**
Fire. Like. Dry. Forest. Indra. Weapon. Demon. Down. You burn. Lightning. Like. Fearsome. With a deep. With a spear. Who. Breaker of enemies. Made a sound. Difficulties/Sins. Crushed. And. ॥ 10 ॥

---

## Commentary (Sayana)

**Like fire** <note>original: "agnir na"</note>—here the word "na" is used for comparison. Just as fire burns a dry, sapless forest or a collection of trees, O Indra, your weapon <note>original: "hetiḥ"</note>, the thunderbolt, destroys enemies in the same way. The text explains this: **like the fearsome lightning** <note>original: "ashanir na bhīmā"</note>. Just as lightning is terrifying, you, who are similarly fearsome, **burn down the demon** <note>original: "rakshas"</note>. Burn him completely with the thunderbolt. That Indra, **with a deep**—meaning unassailable by enemies—and **great spear** <note>original: "rishtyā"</note> (the word "rishti" here is a name for something great), and as the **breaker of enemies** <note>original: "harojaḥ"</note>, **made a roar** <note>original: "adhvanayat"</note>, which is the characteristic sound of shouting in battle. Furthermore, he **crushes** <note>original: "dambhayat"</note> and breaks **difficulties** <note>original: "duritā"</note> or sins. The phrase "burn down the demon" from the earlier part of the verse connects here as well.

-> ॥ Thus ends the fifth group in the sixth chapter of the fourth book ॥ <-

## Hymn Text

-> ॥ Here is the Eleventh Verse ॥ <-

Come, O Indra, with thousands of earthly riches, O you of many splendors, with many foods. Come, O son of strength, he whom no godless man can ever hope to keep away, O you who are invoked by many! ॥ 11 ॥

## Hymn Text

<note>Conclusion of the Word-by-Word Analysis for RV 6.18.11</note>
Come. A thousand. By paths. O Indra. With wealth. O possessor of great fame. With many powers. Towards us.
Come. O Son. [of] Strength. Of whom. Now. Indeed. The godless one. Is able. O much-invoked one. To separate. ॥ 11 ॥

-> ॥ Now the Twelfth Verse ॥ <-

<note>RV 6.18.12 Samhita-patha</note>
The greatness of the **possessor of great fame**, the **ancient**, the **crusher of foes**, has **overflowed** beyond **heaven** and **earth**.
There is **no enemy** for him, **no equal** exists, **no support** [outside himself] for the **one of many wisdoms**, the **victorious**. ॥ 12 ॥

<note>RV 6.18.12 Word-by-Word Analysis</note>
Indeed. Of the possessor of great fame. Of the ancient. Of the crusher. Of heaven. Overflows. Greatness. Of the earth.
Not. Of him. Enemy. Not. Equal/Counterpart. Exists. Not. Standing-place/Support. Of the one of many wisdoms. Of the victorious. ॥ 12 ॥

-> ॥ Now the Thirteenth Verse ॥ <-

<note>RV 6.18.13 Samhita-patha</note>
That **deed** of yours has become **manifest today**, which [you did] for **Kutsa**, for **Ayu**, and for **Atithigva**.
You **crushed many thousands** down **to the earth**; you **brought Turvayana** to prominence by your **daring**. ॥ 13 ॥

<note>RV 6.18.13 Word-by-Word Analysis</note>
Indeed. That. Your. Today. Deed. Done. Has become. Kutsa. Which. Ayu. Atithigva. For him.
Many. Thousands. Down. You crushed. Toward. The earth. Up. Turvayana. By daring. You brought. ॥ 13 ॥

---

## Commentary (Sayana)

**[Verse 11]**
O **possessor of great fame** <note>original: "tuvidyumna"</note>, meaning one with much wealth, O **son of strength** <note>original: "sahasah sūno"</note>, Indra. His status as the "son of strength" is established in another scripture: *"I think of him as born from power"* <note>original: "ojasō jātamuta manya ēnaṃ"; RV 10.73.10</note>. Being joined **with wealth** <note>original: "rāyā"</note>, you, with **a thousand** <note>original: "sahasraṃ"</note>—meaning with many—**paths** <note>original: "pathibhiḥ"</note>—paths are vehicles because one travels by them—and with **many powers** <note>original: "tuvivājebhiḥ"</note>, please **come towards us** <note>original: "arvāṅ āyāhi"</note>. O **much-invoked** <note>original: "puruhūta"</note> Indra, no **godless one** <note>original: "adevaḥ"</note>—that is, any demon—**is able** <note>original: "nu cidīśe"</note> to **separate** <note>original: "yōtōḥ"</note> you from your strengths. Here, the phrase "nu cid" <note>original: "nūcid"</note> is used in the sense of a negation.

**[Verse 12]**
The **greatness** <note>original: "mahimā"</note> of the **possessor of great fame** <note>original: "tuvidyumnasya"</note>—referring either to great renown or great wealth—the **ancient** <note>original: "sthavirasya"</note> or fully grown, the **crusher** <note>original: "ghṛṣveḥ"</note> of enemies, namely Indra, has **overflowed** <note>original: "prararapshe"</note> beyond **heaven** <note>original: "divo"</note> and the **earth** <note>original: "pṛthivyāḥ"</note>. This means it has exceeded them. Because the word "virapshi" is listed among the names for "great," and names are generally derived from roots, the root "rapsh" here expresses the sense of exceeding or overflowing. For Indra, who is **victorious** <note>original: "sahyoḥ"</note> and an overcomer of enemies, and **possesses many wisdoms** <note>original: "purumāyasya"</note>, there **is no enemy** <note>original: "shatruh"</note> who can destroy him. There is **no equal** <note>original: "pratimānaṃ"</note> or representative for him. There is **no support** <note>original: "pratiṣṭhiḥ"</note> or external refuge for him; this means that he himself is the support of all things.

**[Verse 13]**
O Indra, **today** <note>original: "adya"</note>—even at this time—**that deed** <note>original: "kṛtaṃ karaṇaṃ"</note> or action **done** by you **has become manifest** <note>original: "prabhūt"</note>. It prevails and shines forth.

<meta>This page continues the commentary on Rig Veda, Mandala 4, Hymn 30. The previous page discussed Indra’s heroic deeds in supporting his allies. 658

## Rig Veda: Ashtaka 3, Adhyaya 6, Varga 6

## Commentary (Sayana)
What is that deed? It is explained as follows: You protected the sage named Kutsa from the demon Shushna and others; you protected the one named Ayu from his enemies; and you protected Atithigva <note>literally "one who goes towards guests," a title for King Divodasa</note>, also known as the son of Purukutsa, and Divodasa himself from the demon Shambara. The phrase "that [deed] is powerful" connects with the previous statement. Because the word "protected" <note>original: rarakṣitha</note> is heard in the second person, an appropriate action must be understood here. 

Furthermore, for this aforementioned Atithigva, you bestowed many, even thousands, of Shambara’s riches. The meaning is that Indra, having slain Shambara, gave his wealth to Divodasa. Likewise, O Indra, with your daring thunderbolt, having struck Shambara, you raised up <note>or rescued</note> Turvayana, who travels swiftly on the earth, for the sake of the earth. You caused him to emerge from distress.

In the ritual of the one-day sacrifice <note>original: ekāha</note>, specifically during the recitation for the Marutvatiya Shastra <note>a specific invocation to Indra and the Maruts</note>, this hymn beginning with "The gods followed you..." serves as the opening. This is indicated in the ritual manuals: **"The gods followed you, the slayer of the serpent; then, O God, they yielded to your great power."** (Ashvalayana Shrauta Sutra 9.5).

---

->॥ This is the fourteenth verse of the hymn ॥<-

## Hymn Text
The gods followed you, O **Slayer of the Serpent**, then, O **God**, all of them rejoiced in you, the **wisest of the wise**. When you granted **relief** <note>or wealth</note> to the **oppressed**, to the **heavenly one**, and to the **person** himself, as you were being **praised**. ॥ 14 ॥

**Word-by-Word Analysis:**
Followed. You. For the slayer of the serpent. Then. O God. The gods. Rejoiced. All. The wisest. Of the wise.
You made/granted. When. Relief/Wealth. To the oppressed. To the heavenly one. To the person. To the body/self. Being praised. ॥ 14 ॥

---

## Commentary (Sayana)
O **God**, O shining Indra, at **that time**, **all** the **gods** (meaning the praisers) **rejoiced** and praised **you** for the **slaying of the serpent** <note>Vritra</note>. This implies the granting of rain. What kind of person are you? You are the **wisest of the wise**, the most intelligent among the sagacious. **And when**, at the time you were **being praised** by the singers, you **granted** **relief** (meaning wealth) to the **oppressed** person (one afflicted by poverty and other trials), to the **heavenly** singer, and to the **person** (the children/descendants of the praisers). 

Alternatively: O Lord Indra, at that time all the gods—the residents of heaven—rejoiced in you. The "serpent" refers to Vritra himself. For his slaying, they praised you, the wisest of poets. And during that praise, for the sake of the inhabitant of heaven who was **oppressed** by the demons, you **granted relief** for his person, for his beauty, and for your own glory through the slaying of Vritra.

---

->॥ Now the fifteenth verse ॥<-

## Hymn Text
The Heaven and the Earth followed that strength of yours; the immortal gods yielded to it, O Indra. Being a doer of deeds, perform that which is yet undone; generate a newer song of praise through the sacrifices. ॥ 15 ॥

<vocab>
- Slayer of the Serpent (ahighne): A title for Indra referring to his victory over Vritra, the demon of drought.
- Wisest of the wise (kavitamam kavīnām): A superlative title emphasizing Indra's supreme intelligence and poetic vision.
- Relief (varivaḥ): Can mean physical space, wealth, or spiritual comfort; essentially "room to breathe" given to the suffering.
- Oppressed (bādhitāya): Refers to those restricted or harmed by enemies or natural disasters like drought.
- Doer of deeds (kṛtnaḥ): An epithet for Indra as an active, creative force in the universe.
</vocab>

<summary>This page describes Indra’s role as the protector of sages like Kutsa and Divodasa, his slaying of the dragon Vritra to release the waters, and the subsequent celebration by the gods. It emphasizes Indra's supreme wisdom and his role in providing relief to the suffering through his heroic actions.</summary>
<keywords>Indra, Vritra, Divodasa, Shambara, Atithigva, Kavi, serpent-slayer, Vedic sacrifice, wealth, protection</keywords>

## Hymn Text (6.18.15 Word-for-word Recitation)

Following | Heaven and Earth | indeed | that | your | power | immortals | yield | Indra | gods |
accomplish | O Doer | unaccomplished | which | your | is | hymn | newer | generate | through sacrifices || 15 ||

---

## Commentary (Sayana on 6.18.15)

O Indra, Heaven and Earth <note>original: dyāvāpṛthivī</note> yield to that well-known power of yours. The immortal gods—those whose nature is to never die—follow your strength. O Doer of many deeds <note>original: kṛtno</note>, whatever work of yours remains unaccomplished, perform it! Do it now. Furthermore, through sacrifices, generate a newer <note>original: navīyo; more modern or fresh</note> hymn of praise in the ritual gatherings.

-> ॥ This concludes the sixth section <note>varga</note> of the sixth chapter <note>adhyaya</note> of the fourth book <note>ashtaka</note> ॥ <-

---

## Hymn Text (6.19.1-2 Introduction)

The fourth hymn, beginning with "Great is Indra," consists of thirteen verses. The Seer <note>Rishi</note> is Bharadvaja; the meter is Trishtubh <note>a rhythmic cycle of 44 syllables</note>; and the deity is Indra. The ritual tradition states: "Great is Indra, etc." In the Midday Libation <note>the second of three daily Soma offerings</note>, when there is an excess of Soma, this hymn is used as a recitation. This is indicated in the ritual manuals: **"Great is Indra, the filler of men... O Vishnu, now truly..."** (Ashvalayana Shrauta Sutra 6.7). Additionally, during the second *Chandoma* day of the integrated sacrifice, this is the hymn for the Marutvatiya ritual <note>dedicated to Indra as lord of the Maruts, the storm-gods</note>. As stated: **"Great is Indra, the filler of men, is the Marutvatiya hymn"** (Ashvalayana Shrauta Sutra 8.7).

-> ॥ Here begins the first verse ॥ <-

Great is Indra, like a leader filling the needs of people, and twice-mighty, unassailable in his strengths.
Turning toward us, he has grown for heroic deeds; he is vast, broad, and well-served by the performers of the rite. || 1 ||

### Word-for-word Recitation (6.19.1)

Great | Indra | like-a-leader | fully | fulfilling-people | and | twice-mighty | unassailable | with-strengths |
toward-us | he-has-grown | for-heroic-deeds | vast | broad | well-served | by-the-performers | he-became || 1 ||

---

## Commentary (Sayana on 6.19.1)

<term>nṛvat</term> Just as a leading king fulfills the desires of his servants and others, in the same way, <term>carṣaṇiprāḥ</term> the one who fulfills the desires of the people—the singers of praise—may the great Indra come here. (The word "come" is implied by the prefix *ā*). Furthermore, <term>dvibarhā</term> he who is powerful in both worlds <note>Heaven and Earth</note>, and <term>aminaḥ</term> who is unassailable by the strengths of his enemies, this Indra <term>asmadryag</term> turns his face toward us. In this way, <term>vāvṛdhe</term> he grows or increases <term>vīryāya</term> for the purpose of performing heroic deeds. <term>uruḥ</term> Wide in body and <term>pṛthuḥ</term> famous for his qualities, he <term>sukṛto bhūt</term> becomes well-attended by the <term>kartṛbhiḥ</term> sacrificers who perform the ritual correctly.

---

## Hymn Text (6.19.2)

-> ॥ Now the second verse ॥ <-

May the prayer place Indra alone for the sake of gain—the greatest, lofty, ageless, and young;
Increasing with unyielding power, he who immediately grows by the help of our prayers. || 2 ||

<vocab>Indra (the king of gods), charshanipra (fulfilling the wishes of men or priests), dvibarha (powerful in both the celestial and earthly worlds), sati (gain or wealth), Bharadvaja (the sage who "saw" this hymn), Traishtubha (the poetic meter of 11 syllables per line), Marutvatiya (an invocation relating to Indra and the storm-gods)</vocab>

६६०     || Rig Veda ||     [Adhyaya 4. Sukta 6. Varga 7.]

Indra | indeed | sacred thought | for the sake of gain | should hold | great | noble | unaging | young |

## Commentary (Sayana)
May our sacred thought <note>original: dhiṣaṇā</note>—our prayer of praise—hold Indra fast for the sake of receiving gifts <note>original: sātaye</note>. What is Indra like? He is great, noble <note>original: ṛṣvam</note>, unaging, and eternally young. He has grown mighty through strength <note>original: śavasā</note> that cannot be overcome by enemies. He is the one who, as soon as he was born, grew instantly and "not partially" <note>original: asāmi</note>, meaning he grew exceedingly and completely.

->॥ Now the third verse ॥<-

## Hymn Text
May you make your two arms broad and capable of great deeds; measure out for us abundance and food.
O Indra, domestic friend, like a cowherd with his herds, turn us toward you in the battle || 3 ||

**Word-for-word Recitation:**
Broad | indeed | doers of deeds | many-giving | the two arms | towards us | together | measure | food and fame |
like herds | of cattle | cowherd | domestic friend | us | Indra | towards | hither | turn | in battle || 3 ||

## Commentary (Sayana)
O Indra, you possess two arms <note>original: gabhastī</note> that are broad, the performers of great deeds, and the givers of many gifts. Prepare <note>original: saṃmimīhi</note> these arms to be directed toward us to grant us food and fame. Furthermore, O Indra, you who are a domestic friend <note>original: damūnāḥ</note> with a controlled mind, turn us toward yourself in the struggle of battle. The poet provides an example here: just as a cowherd <note>original: paśupāḥ</note>, the protector of cattle, turns his herds <note>original: yūtheva</note> in the right direction, so may you guide us.

## Hymn Text
We who desire food now surely call upon that Indra, the driver away of enemies, along with his powerful helpers;
just as the ancient singers were, may we be beyond reproach, blameless, and unhurt || 4 ||

**Word-for-word Recitation:**
That | your | Indra | driver away | of him | with powers | here | now | desiring food | we call |
just | as | ancient | singers | were | beyond reproach | blameless | unhurt || 4 ||

## Commentary (Sayana)
Now, today, in this sacrifice, we who are singers desiring food <note>original: vājayantaḥ</note> call upon you, the famous Indra. We call upon you along with your helpers, the Maruts <note>the storm gods</note>, who are powerful and capable. You are the driver away <note>original: catinam</note>—the destroyer—of enemies. We praise you so that, by your grace, we may become like the ancient singers <note>original: jaritāraḥ</note> of old. Those ancestors were beyond reproach <note>original: anedyāḥ</note>, blameless and free from sin <note>original: anavadyāḥ</note>, and remained unhurt <note>original: ariṣṭāḥ</note> by any violence. We pray to be just like them.

M. 6. A. 2. S. 19. || Fourth Ashtaka || 661

## Hymn Text

-> ॥ Now the fifth verse ॥ <-

The upholder of laws, the giver of wealth, strengthened by Soma; he is the wearer of beautiful excellence, possessing much food. In him, the paths of wealth have come together, just as rivers flow together into the sea. || 5 ||

**Word-for-word Recitation:**
Upholder of laws | giver of wealth | strengthened by Soma | he | indeed | of the beautiful | wearer | possessing much food | 
together | have come | paths | of wealth | in him | in the sea | like | rivers | approaching || 5 ||

---

## Commentary (Sayana)

He indeed, that Indra, is the **upholder of laws** <note>original: dhṛtavrato</note>, meaning he whose actions are fixed and ordained. He is the **giver of wealth** <note>original: dhanadāḥ</note>. In response to the question of what kind of wealth he gives, the text provides adjectives even for the secondary mention of wealth: **of the beautiful and excellent** <note>original: vāmasya vasuna</note>. This refers to desirable, excellent wealth. Alternatively, it means he is the master of wealth. He is **strengthened by Soma** <note>original: somavṛddhaḥ</note>, meaning he is nourished and increased by the sacred drink. He is **possessing much food** <note>original: purukṣu</note>. In this very Indra, the **paths** <note>original: pathyāḥ</note>—which are beneficial to the singers—of **wealth** <note>original: rāyo</note> **have come together** <note>original: saṃjagmire</note> or united. An illustration is provided: just as **rivers** <note>original: sindhavo</note> flow **into the sea** <note>original: samudre na</note>, approaching it, so too does all wealth converge in him.

-> ॥ Thus ends the seventh varga in the sixth chapter of the fourth book ॥ <-

---

## Hymn Text

-> ॥ Now the sixth verse ॥ <-

Bring to us the most powerful strength, O Hero; bring most vigorous, fierce, and invincible power. O Lord of Bay Horses, grant us all the virile splendors intended for mankind, so that we may rejoice. || 6 ||

**Word-for-word Recitation:**
Most powerful | to us | hither | bring | O Hero | strength | most vigorous | power | O Overcomer | fierce |
all | splendors | virile | of men | to us | grant | O Lord of Bay Horses | to make us rejoice || 6 ||

---

## Commentary (Sayana)

O **Heroic** <note>original: śūra</note> and courageous Indra, **bring** <note>original: ā bhar</note> to **us** <note>original: naḥ</note> the **most powerful** <note>original: śaviṣṭhaṃ</note> **strength** <note>original: śavo</note> or might. O **Overcomer** <note>original: abhibhūte</note> who subdues enemies, bring us the **most vigorous** <note>original: ojiṣṭham</note> and **fierce** <note>original: ugram</note> or unbearable **power** <note>original: ojo</note> and brilliance. O **Lord of Bay Horses** <note>original: harivo</note>, **grant** <note>original: dāḥ</note> to us **all** <note>original: viśvā</note> those **virile** <note>original: vṛṣṇyā</note> or outpouring and **shining** <note>original: dyumnā</note> riches that are designed for the enjoyment **of men** <note>original: mānuṣāṇām</note>, in order **to make us rejoice** <note>original: mādayadhyai</note>.

---

## Hymn Text

-> ॥ Now the seventh verse ॥ <-

That exhilaration of yours which conquers armies, O unyielding one, bring that to us, swelling with power; by which, in the winning of children and descendants, we may think of ourselves as victors, protected by you. || 7 ||

## Hymn Text (Word-for-word analysis of Verse 7)

That | your | exhilaration | overcomer of hostile armies | uninjured | Indra | that | to us | bring | greatly increased |
by which | of offspring | of descendants | in the gain | we may think [of you] | having conquered | protected by you || 7 ||

---

## Commentary (Sayana) on Verse 7

The **overcomer of hostile armies** <note>original: pṛtanāṣāṭ</note> means the one who defeats enemy forces. The **uninjured** <note>original: amṛdhraḥ</note> refers to that **exhilaration** <note>original: madaḥ</note> or joy which is to be given by you, O Indra. Bring that **greatly increased** <note>original: śūśuvāṃsam</note> or expanded exhilaration to us. **Protected by you** <note>original: tvotāḥ</note> and **having conquered** <note>original: jigīvāṃsaḥ</note> or being victorious, we—when there is a **gain** <note>original: sātau</note> or acquisition of **offspring** <note>original: tokasya</note> (sons) and **descendants** <note>original: tanayasya</note> (grandsons)—may **think [of you]** <note>original: maṃsīmahi</note>, meaning we shall praise you with that joy. The instruction "bring that" links back to the previous sentence.

---

-> ॥ Now the eighth verse ॥ <-

## Hymn Text (Verse 8)

Bring to us, O Indra, the showering vigor, the winner of wealth, greatly increased, and very capable; with which we may strike the enemies in battles—through your protections—both kin and non-kin. || 8 ||

**Word-for-word Recitation:**
Bring | to us | bring | showering | vigor | Indra | wealth-winning | greatly increased | very capable |
by which | we may strike | in battles | enemies | your | by protections | and | kin | non-kin || 8 ||

---

## Commentary (Sayana) on Verse 8

O Indra, **bring** <note>original: ābhara</note> or fetch for us the **showering** <note>original: vṛṣaṇam</note> (the one who pours down benefits) **vigor** <note>original: śuṣmam</note>, which is the strength characterized by an army. What kind of vigor? It is **wealth-winning** <note>original: dhanaspṛtam</note> (the protector of wealth), **greatly increased** <note>original: śūśuvāṃsam</note>, and **very capable** <note>original: sudakṣam</note> or possessing excellent strength. O Indra, by **your protections** <note>original: tavotibhiḥ</note> or your acts of guarding, in **battles** <note>original: pṛtanāsu</note>—<note>pṛtanā is a traditional name for battle</note>—let us **strike** <note>original: vaṃsā/hanāma</note> the **enemies** <note>original: śatrūn</note>. The word **and** <note>original: uta</note> is placed here out of its usual order; it connects **kin** <note>original: jāmīn</note> (relatives) and **non-kin** <note>original: ajāmīn</note> (strangers or enemies). The meaning is: bring that vigor by which we may strike both types of foes.

---

-> ॥ Now the ninth verse ॥ <-

## Hymn Text (Verse 9)

May your showering vigor come from behind, from above, from below, and from the front; may it come together from all sides, turned toward us; O Indra, grant us glory that is full of light. || 9 ||

**Word-for-word Recitation:**
Come | your | vigor | showerer | let it come | from behind | from | above | below | from | front |
from | all sides | toward | together | let it come | turned toward us | Indra | glory | full of light | grant | to us || 9 ||

---

## Commentary (Sayana) on Verse 9

O Indra, let your **showering** <note>original: vṛṣabhaḥ</note> **vigor** <note>original: śuṣmaḥ</note> be **turned toward us** <note>original: arvāṅ</note> and **come** <note>original: aitu</note> from the **behind** <note>original: paścāt</note> or the western direction. Let it come from **above** <note>original: uttarāt</note> or the northern direction. Let it come from **below** <note>original: adharāt</note> or the southern direction. And let it come from the **front** <note>original: purastāt</note> or the eastern direction. From **all sides** <note>original: viśvataḥ</note>, meaning from every quarter, let it **come together** <note>original: sametu</note> toward us. O Indra, **grant** <note>original: dhehi</note> or provide **to us** <note>original: asme</note> the **glory** <note>original: dyumnam</note> or wealth that is **full of light** <note>original: svarvat</note> or accompanied by happiness.

## Hymn Text
O Indra, with your heroic <note>original: nṛvatta</note> and most manly protections <note>original: ūtī</note>, let us obtain great and desirable wealth through your glorious aids. For you, O King, are the master of both kinds of wealth <note>original: ubhayasya vasva</note>; therefore, bestow upon us a treasure that is great, massive, and extensive. || 10 ||

**Word-for-word Recitation:**
Heroic | your | Indra | most manly | protection | let us obtain | desirable wealth | with glorious aids |
Master | indeed | of wealth | of both kinds | King | bestow | treasure | great | massive | extensive || 10 ||

---

## Commentary (Sayana)
**Heroic** <note>original: nṛvat</note> means accompanied by men or attendants. **With glorious aids** <note>original: omantebhiḥ</note> refers to those accompanied by fame or glory that is to be woven <note>original: otavyaiḥ</note>. O Indra, from **your** <note>original: te</note> **most manly protections** <note>original: nṛtamābhirūtī</note>, let us **obtain** <note>original: vamsīmahi</note> or enjoy **desirable wealth** <note>original: vāmaṃ</note>. **Indeed** <note>original: hi</note>, for this reason, O **King** <note>original: rājan</note>—resplendent Indra—you **rule** <note>original: īkṣe</note> over **both kinds** <note>original: ubhayasya</note> of **wealth** <note>original: vasvo</note>, namely earthly and heavenly. Therefore, **bestow** <note>original: dhāḥ</note>—place within us—a **treasure** <note>original: ratnaṃ</note> that is **great** <note>original: mahi</note>, **massive** <note>original: sthūraṃ</note> or abundant, and **extensive** <note>original: bṛhantaṃ</note> or magnified by virtues. Here, the word for treasure <note>original: ratna-śabdaḥ</note> is used in the masculine gender.

-> || Now the eleventh [verse] || <-

## Hymn Text
Let us invoke him here for new protection—that Indra who is accompanied by the Maruts <note>original: marutvantaṃ</note>, the showerer of benefits <note>original: vṛṣabhaṃ</note>, the ever-growing, the one whose enemies are praiseworthy <note>original: arkavāriṃ</note>, the divine ruler, the vanquisher of all, the fierce, and the bestower of strength. || 11 ||

**Word-for-word Recitation:**
Accompanied by the Maruts | the showerer | the growing | whose enemies are praiseworthy | divine | the ruler | Indra |
The vanquisher of all | for protection | for new | fierce | bestower of strength | here | him | let us invoke || 11 ||

---

## Commentary (Sayana)
**Here** <note>original: iha</note> in this sacrifice, for **new** <note>original: nūtanāya</note> or fresh **protection** <note>original: avase</note>, **let us invoke** <note>original: huvema</note>—meaning we praise or call upon—**that** <note>original: taṃ</note> famous Indra. What is he like? He is **accompanied by the Maruts** <note>original: marutvantaṃ</note> (the storm-gods); he is a **showerer** <note>original: vṛṣabhaṃ</note> who rains down the fulfillment of desires; he is **ever-growing** <note>original: vavṛdhānaṃ</note> or highly increased; he is **one whose enemies are praiseworthy** <note>original: arkavāri</note> (meaning his enemies are not insignificant or are easily handled); he is **divine** <note>original: divyaṃ</note> or shining; he is the **ruler** <note>original: śāsaṃ</note> or commander; he is the **vanquisher of all** <note>original: viśvasahaṃ</note> who overcomes the entire world; he is **fierce** <note>original: ugraṃ</note> or powerful; and he is the **bestower of strength** <note>original: sahodāṃ</note>.

-> || Now the twelfth [verse] || <-

## Hymn Text
O wielder of the thunderbolt, among those men in whose midst I am, make the one who thinks himself great submit to these [our] people. For indeed, we call upon you on this earth in the battle of heroes, for offspring, for cattle, and for water. || 12 ||

**Word-for-word Recitation:**
Person | O wielder of the thunderbolt | great | even | thinking himself | to these | to men | make submit | among whom | I am |
And | indeed | you | on the earth | in the battle of heroes | we call | for offspring | for cattle | for water || 12 ||

---

## Commentary (Sayana)
**Among whom** <note>original: yeṣu</note>—among those men in whose midst **I am** <note>original: ahamasmi</note> one—O **wielder of the thunderbolt** <note>original: vajrin</note> Indra, you [make submit] for these...

<vocab>
<term>Indra</term>: The king of the gods and the primary deity of the Rig Veda, often associated with storms, war, and the thunderbolt.
<term>Maruts</term>: A group of storm deities who are the constant companions and warriors of Indra.
<term>Vajrin</term>: An epithet of Indra meaning "the wielder of the Vajra" (the thunderbolt weapon).
<term>Ratna</term>: Usually translated as "jewel" or "treasure," but in the Vedic context, it refers more broadly to anything precious or delightful.
<term>Vṛṣabha</term>: Literally "bull," used here as a metaphor for Indra as a potent "showerer" of blessings and rain.
</vocab>

<note>Concluding commentary on verse 12</note>
Subdue <note>original: randhaya</note> or bring under control the person who considers himself to be very great <note>original: mahi</note>—meaning one who is full of self-importance—for the sake of men <note>original: nṛbhyaḥ</note>. The word *cit* is a particle used here to complete the meter. Now <note>original: adha</note>, upon this earth <note>original: pṛthivyām</note>, when battle <note>original: śūrasātī</note> has commenced, we call upon <note>original: hvāmahe</note> you, O Indra, you who reside in the heavenly world, for the sake of our sons <note>original: tanaye</note>, our cattle <note>original: goṣu</note>, and for water <note>original: apsu</note>.
