## Hymn Text

-> ॥ Now the thirteenth [verse] ॥ <-

O much-invoked Indra <note>original: puruhūta</note>, through these friendships <note>original: sakhyaiḥ</note> with you, may we indeed be superior to every other power. Destroying both kinds of enemies <note>original: vṛtrāṇi</note>, O Hero, and protected by you <note>original: tvotāḥ</note>, may we rejoice in great wealth. || 13 ||

**Word-for-word Recitation:**
We | your | through these | O much-invoked | friendships | than power-power | superior | indeed | may we be |
Destroying | enemies | of both kinds | O Hero | with wealth | may we rejoice | with great | protected by you || 13 ||

## Commentary (Sayana)

O **much-invoked** <note>original: puruhūta</note> Indra, you who are called upon by many, through **these** <note>original: ebhiḥ</note> well-known **friendships** <note>original: sakhyaiḥ</note>—which consist of the acts of a friend such as the chanting of hymns—and while **destroying** <note>original: ghnantaḥ</note> **both kinds** <note>original: ubhayāni</note> of **enemies** <note>original: vṛtrāṇi</note> (both those who are kin and those who are strangers), may we **indeed be** <note>original: syāma</note> **superior** <note>original: uttare</note> to **every power** <note>original: śacoḥ śacoḥ</note>. That is, may we be more powerful than all others. O **Hero** <note>original: śūra</note>, O valiant Indra, being **protected by you** <note>original: tvotāḥ</note>, may we **rejoice** <note>original: madema</note> or be delighted with **great** <note>original: bṛhatā</note> **wealth** <note>original: rāyā</note>.

-> ॥ Thus ends the eighth Varga of the sixth section of the fourth [Ashtaka] ॥ <-

---

## Hymn Text (Sukta 49)

The fifth hymn, beginning with **"Like the sky, he who Indra"** <note>original: dyauḥ na ya indra</note>, consists of thirteen verses. Its Seer <note>original: rishi</note> is Bharadvaja, the deity is Indra, and the meter is Trishtubh. The seventh verse, beginning "He who of Pipru" <note>original: vi piproḥ</note>, is in the Virat meter as it consists of four lines of ten syllables each. The Index <note>original: Anukramani</note> states: "The hymn 'Like the sky' contains a Virat verse regarding Pipru." 

Regarding the ritual application: In the *Prishthya Shadaha* <note>a six-day sacrificial cycle</note>, on the sixth day during the third libation, if the *Ukthya* hymns are being chanted as couplets, or if the ceremony concludes with the *Agnishtoma* rite, then the *Achhavaka* priest should recite this hymn in his own recitation <note>original: svashastra</note> after the introductory verses of the midday libation. This is indicated in the *Ashvalayana Shrauta Sutra* (8.4): "The Achhavaka recites 'Like the sky, he who Indra'." Furthermore, this same hymn is used as the *Nishkevalya-Nivid* recitation during the one-day sacrifice called *Indra-Vishnu-Utkranti*. As stated in the Sutra (9.7): "The midday recitation is 'Like the sky, he who Indra'."

-> ॥ Therein, the first [verse] ॥ <-

O Indra, you who like the sky encompass the earth, you who stand over the people in battles as their lord with power; bestow upon us, O Son of Strength, that wealth which brings thousands, which wins fertile lands, and which overcomes the enemy. || 1 ||

**Word-for-word Recitation:**
Sky | like | who | Indra | encompass | earth | lord | stood | wealth/power | with strength | in battles | people |
That | to us | thousand-bringing | fertile land-winning | bestow | O Son | of strength | Vritra-overcoming || 1 ||

<vocab>
- **Much-invoked (Puruhuta):** A common title for Indra, emphasizing that many worshippers call upon him simultaneously.
- **Enemies/Obstacles (Vritrani):** While "Vritra" is the name of a specific demon, the plural form often refers generally to all foes or barriers to success.
- **Hero/Valiant (Shura):** A warrior title for Indra.
- **With wealth (Raya):** Often implying not just currency, but cattle, progeny, and spiritual abundance.
- **Bharadvaja:** One of the seven great Sages (Rishis), traditionally credited with the composition of the sixth book of the Rig Veda.
- **Trishtubh (Traishtubha):** The most common Vedic meter, consisting of lines of eleven syllables.
- **Midday libation (Madhyandina Savana):** The second of the three daily offerings of Soma juice.
- **Son of Strength (Suno Sahasah):** A poetic title suggesting that the deity is the physical manifestation or "offspring" of power.
- **Overcoming Vritra/Enemies (Vritraturam):** Specifically meaning one who strikes down or triumphs over opposition.
</vocab>

[Mandala 6, Hymn 20, Verse 20] || Fourth Ashtaka || 665

## Commentary (Sayana)
[Continued from previous page]

The wealth <note>original: rayiḥ</note> in the form of a son <note>original: putrarūpaṃ dhanam</note>, which through might <note>original: śavasā</note> or strength, overcomes <note>original: abhitasthau</note>—meaning attacks or conquers—the enemies <note>original: aryaḥ</note> or hostile people in battles <note>original: pṛtsu</note>. On this point, an illustration is given: **like the sky** <note>original: dyauḥ na</note>. Just as the shining sun <note>original: dyotamānaḥ sūryaḥ</note> overcomes all earthly beings, so too does he. O **Son of Strength** <note>original: sahasaḥ sūno</note>—O Indra, son of power—give <note>original: daddi / dehi</note> that son to us. Of what kind? One who **brings a thousand** <note>original: sahasrabharaṃ</note>—meaning the possessor of a thousand-fold wealth; a **winner of fertile lands** <note>original: urvarāsām</note>—meaning the distributor of lands rich with crops; and a **conqueror of enemies** <note>original: vṛcaturaṃ</note>—meaning one who crosses over or defeats foes.

---

## Hymn Text
->।। Now the Second [Verse] ।।<-

O Indra, like the sun in the sky, all divine power was placed in you by the gods. When you, O Soma-drinker, along with Vishnu, slew the serpent Vritra who had encompassed the waters. || 2 ||

->Word-for-word Recitation<-

Of the sky | Like | In you | Following | O Indra | Together | Divine power | By the gods | Was placed | All | The serpent | When | Vritra | Waters | Encompassing | You slew | O Soma-drinker | With Vishnu | Associated || 2 ||

## Commentary (Sayana)

O Indra, like that of the sun <note>original: divo / sūryasya</note> in the sky, **all** <note>original: viśvam</note> the pervasive **divine power** <note>original: asuryam</note>—meaning lordship or strength—was **placed** <note>original: dhāyi / vyadhāyi</note> or established in **you** <note>original: tubhyam</note> **by the gods** <note>original: devebhiḥ</note>—here referring to the praisers. The sense is that a deity becomes powerful when being praised through hymns. O **Soma-drinker** <note>original: ṛjīṣin</note>—you who consume the Soma residue—you, **associated** <note>original: sacānaḥ</note> or coming together **with Vishnu**. <note>The word *sacānaḥ* is derived from the verbal root *ṣac*, meaning to associate.</note> This relates to the previous statement: that strength was established when you **slew** <note>original: han / avadhīḥ</note> the demon **Vritra**, the **serpent** <note>original: ahim</note> who had come and **encompassed** <note>original: vavrivāṃsam</note> or blocked the **waters** <note>original: apaḥ</note>.

---

## Hymn Text
->।। Now the Third [Verse] ।।<-

Overcoming, most mighty, more powerful than the powerful, receiving hymns, Indra of increased greatness became the king of the sweet Soma when he obtained the destroyer of all cities. || 3 ||

->Word-for-word Recitation<-

Overcoming | Most mighty | Than the powerful | More powerful | Receiver of hymns | Indra | Of increased greatness | King | Became | Of the sweet | Of the Soma | Of all | When | Of cities | The destroyer | He obtained || 3 ||

## Commentary (Sayana)

When Indra **obtained** <note>original: āvat / prāpat</note> the **destroyer** <note>original: dartṛm / dārakaṃ</note>—referring to the thunderbolt <term>Vajra: Indra's primary weapon used to shatter obstacles</term>—of **all** <note>original: viśvāsām</note> the **cities** <note>original: purām</note>, then he **became the king** <note>original: rājā abhavat</note> or master of the **sweet** <note>original: madhunaḥ</note> and **Soma-filled** <note>original: somyasya</note> nectar. What is his nature? He is **overcoming** <note>original: tūrvan</note>—meaning he strikes those who would strike him; **most mighty** <note>original: ojīyān</note>—exceedingly vigorous; **more powerful** <note>original: tavīyān</note> than even the **powerful** <note>original: tavasaḥ</note>; and **one for whom hymns are made** <note>original: kṛtabrahmā</note>—meaning the one for whom the hymn <note>original: brahma / stotraṃ</note> is performed by the praisers. Alternatively, it means the one by whom food <note>original: brahma / annam</note> is given to the praisers. He is **of increased greatness** <note>original: vṛddhamahāḥ</note>—of expanded splendor. Such an Indra became the king.

[Rig Veda || Mandala 1, Hymn 63 || Page 666]

## Hymn Text

-> ।। Now the Fourth [Verse] ।। <-

By the hundreds, the Panis <note>greedy demons who withhold cattle or light</note> fled away, O Indra, from the sage Dashoni in the battle for light <note>original: arkasāti</note>. With your deadly strikes, you left nothing remaining of the deceptive magic <note>original: māyā</note> of the devouring Shushna <note>the drought-demon</note>, nor did you leave any of his food behind. || 4 ||

**Word-for-word Recitation:**
By hundreds | Fled away | The Panis | O Indra | Sing/Praise | For Dashoni | For the Sage | In the battle for light | With weapons | Of Shushna | Of the devouring one | Deceptive powers | Of food | Not | Left remaining | Anything | At all | Forth. || 4 ||

---

## Commentary (Sayana)

In this "battle for light" <note>original: arkasātau</note>—the term *arkasāti* refers to a battle because "arka" or food/light is obtained therein. In that battle, for the sake of the wise <note>original: kavaye</note> and meditative Dashoni <note>a name for the Rishi Kutsa, who offers many oblations</note>—the fourth case ending is used here in the sense of the fifth <note>a grammatical note indicating "from" or "because of" the sage</note>.

O Indra, because of your help, the Asuras <note>demons</note> named the Panis fled away <note>original: apadrun / apādravan</note> along with their forces numbering in the hundreds. Furthermore, Indra did not leave behind <note>original: na prarirecīt</note> any of the deceptive tricks or magic <note>original: māyā</note> of the enemy Shushna, who is described as "all-consuming" <note>original: ābhuṣasya</note> because his strength is complete. Indra destroyed them with his weapons, which are the means of killing. He also did not leave any of the demon's food <note>original: pitvo / pituḥ</note> remaining; he took away all of his sustenance entirely.

---

## Hymn Text

-> ।। Now the Fifth [Verse] ।। <-

The great malice was cast aside and life was made secure for all when Shushna fell at the strike of the thunderbolt. For Kutsa, who acted as his charioteer, Indra made a wide space on the same chariot during the winning of the sun. || 5 ||

**Word-for-word Recitation:**
The great | Malice / Enemy | Aside | All-life | Was placed | Of the thunderbolt | When | In the falling | Fell | Shushna | Wide | He | On the same chariot | For the charioteer | Made | Indra | For Kutsa | Of the sun | In the winning. || 5 ||

---

## Commentary (Sayana)

When <note>original: yat</note> that demon Shushna fell <note>original: pādi</note> or was destroyed during the descent or strike of the thunderbolt <note>original: vajrasya patane</note>, then the all-pervading strength <note>original: viśvāyu</note> belonging to that great, treacherous Shushna was cast aside <note>original: apadhāyi</note>, meaning it was neutralized or pushed away.

That Indra then made <note>original: kaḥ / akarot</note> a wide <note>original: uru</note> or extensive space for the sake of Kutsa, who had become his charioteer <note>original: sārathi</note>, placing him on the same chariot <note>original: saratham</note> during the "winning of the sun" <note>original: sūryasya sātau</note> or the attainment of the solar light. 

As it has been said in other traditions: "Indra, desiring to kill the demon Shushna for Kutsa's sake, made Kutsa his own charioteer. Having slain his enemy Shushna, he then provided abundant protection for Kutsa." This verse describes that event.

-> ।। Thus ends the ninth section <note>varga</note> of the sixth lesson <note>anuvaka</note> of the fourth book <note>ashtaka</note> ।। <-

<vocab>
- **Shushna:** A demon associated with drought and scorching heat, often depicted as a "hisser" or "devourer."
- **Panis:** A class of atmospheric demons or stingy merchants in Vedic myth who steal and hide the cows (representing rays of light or wealth).
- **Indra:** The primary king of the gods in the Rig Veda, the god of thunder, rain, and war.
- **Kutsa:** A prominent Vedic sage and hero who is a close friend and protégé of Indra.
- **Vajra:** The "Thunderbolt," the divine and indestructible weapon forged for Indra by the craftsman Tvashtri.
- **Arkasati:** A compound term meaning the "attainment of light" or "winning of food," frequently used to describe the spoils of a righteous war.
- **Sarathi:** A charioteer; in this context, the human sage Kutsa is honored by driving Indra's own chariot.
- **Maya:** Creative or deceptive power; often used to describe the magical illusions used by demons to confuse their enemies.
</vocab>

## Hymn Text

-> || Now the Sixth [Verse] || <-

Just as the hawk [brought] the intoxicating Soma juice to him [Indra], he crushed the head of the slave Namuchi <note>a prominent demon in Vedic mythology</note>. He protected Nami, the son of Sayya, while he was sleeping, and provided him with abundance, food, and well-being. || 6 ||

**Word-for-word Recitation:**
Forth | The hawk | As if | Intoxicating | Soma-stalk | To him | The head | Of the slave | Of Namuchi | Crushing |
Forth | Protected | Nami | The son of Sayya | Sleeping | For abundance | With wealth | Fully | With food | Fully | Well-being || 6 ||

---

## Commentary (Sayana)

The word **hawk** <note>original: śyenaḥ</note> refers to the well-known bird of prey. The word **as if** <note>original: na</note> is used here in the sense of a conjunction or comparison. For this Indra, the hawk brought the **intoxicating** <note>original: madiraṃ</note> or exhilarating **Soma-stalk** <note>original: aṃśuṃ</note>. The prefix **Forth** <note>original: pra</note> stands in for the sense of "bringing toward" <note>original: āharat</note>. Since we only see the prefix, the full verb must be inferred from the context. 

Furthermore, this Indra, while **crushing** <note>original: mathāyan</note> or churning the **head** of the **slave** <note>original: dāsasya</note>—the demon named **Namuchi** who causes the destruction of living beings—**protected** <note>original: prāvat</note> the sage named **Nami**, the son of **Sayya**, while he was **sleeping**. Indra **joined** <note>original: sampṛṇak</note> that sage with **well-being** <note>original: svasti</note> meaning without any harm, with **wealth** consisting of cattle and other riches, and with **food**.

---

## Hymn Text

-> || Now the Seventh [Verse] || <-

O Wielder of the Thunderbolt, you shattered the strong fortresses of Pipru, who possesses serpent-like delusions, with your power. O Bountiful Giver, you granted that invincible wealth, a gift of offerings, to the sacrificer Rijishvan. || 7 ||

**Word-for-word Recitation:**
Asunder | Of Pipru | Of the serpent-illusioned | Strong | Fortresses | O Wielder of the Thunderbolt | With power | [Particle] | Shattered |
O Bountiful Giver | That | Wealth | Invincible | To Rijishvan | The gift | To the giver | You gave || 7 ||

---

## Commentary (Sayana)

O **Wielder of the Thunderbolt** <note>original: vajrin</note>, O Indra, you **shattered** <note>original: vidardaḥ</note> or tore apart the **strong** and firm **fortresses**—the ramparts and castles—belonging to the demon named **Pipru**, who is described as **serpent-illusioned** <note>original: ahimāyasya</note> because his deceptive powers are like those of a serpent. You did this with your **power** or strength. 

The word **as if** <note>original: na</note> here is merely a filler for the poetic meter. We see this confirmed in other verses such as "You crushed the forts of Pipru for the sake of the hero" <note>original: Rig Veda 1.51.5</note> and "Protect us with a hundred iron forts" <note>original: Rig Veda 1.3.7</note>. 

Moreover, O **Bountiful Giver** <note>original: sudāman</note>, you **gave** <note>original: dāḥ</note> that **wealth** <note>original: rekṇaḥ</note> which is **invincible** and cannot be obstructed by anyone, as a **gift** consisting of sacrificial offerings, to the royal sage named **Rijishvan** who has **given** his oblations to you.

## Hymn Text

## Commentary (Sayana)

**Of desirable bliss** <note>original: svabhiṣṭisumnaḥ</note> refers to Indra, by whom happiness or bliss (*sumna*) that is well-sought and approachable is given. That Indra [subdued] **Vetasu of ten wiles**—the word "ten-wiles" <note>original: daśamāyam</note> signifies one with many illusions—and the demon named **Dashoni**, and the one named **Tutuji**. And furthermore, **Tugra** and the demon named **Ibha**. [He delivered them] **to come** or to be accessed by the king named **Dyotana**. He **constantly delivered** <note>original: śaśvadupasṛja</note> them; that is, he brought them under control. An illustration is given: **like a mother** <note>original: mātuḥ na</note>. Just as a son is brought under the control of a mother, similarly, Indra brought these enemies under the king's control. The term **sīm** is a grammatical particle used to fill out the meter of the verse.

## Hymn Text

-> || Now the Ninth || <-

He conquers his rivals, unrivaled, bearing the Vritra-slaying thunderbolt in his hand;
He stands upon his two bay horses as a warrior on his chariot floor; the speech-yoked steeds carry the mighty Indra. || 9 ||

-> He | [particle] | rivals | conquers | unrivaled | bearing | thunderbolt | Vritra-slaying | in hand | <-
-> standing | two bay horses | upon | warrior-like | chariot-floor | speech-yoked | carry | Indra | mighty || 9 ||

## Commentary (Sayana)

**In his hand** <note>original: gabhastau</note>, **bearing** or holding his own weapon, the **thunderbolt** <note>original: vajra</note>, which is the **slayer of Vritra** <note>original: vṛtrahaṇam</note> (meaning the killer of enemies). Being **unrivaled** <note>original: apratītaḥ</note>, meaning unopposed by any enemy, that Indra **conquers** <note>original: vanate</note> or kills these rivals—referring to enemies like Vritra. He **stands upon** or mounts his **two bay horses** <note>original: harī</note>. An illustration is provided: **as a warrior on his chariot floor** <note>original: asteva gartam</note>. Just as a heroic archer or thrower stands upon the floor of a chariot, so does Indra. Furthermore, those two horses, which are **speech-yoked** <note>original: vachoyuja</note>—meaning they are yoked by a mere word, or alternatively, by the hymns of the praisers—**carry** the **mighty** or great Indra.

## Commentary (Sayana)

O **Indra**, **through your protection** <note>original: avasa</note>, may we—the praisers—**enjoy** <note>original: sanema</note> or obtain the **newer** <note>original: navyaḥ</note> or more excellent wealth given by you. The **Purus** <note>original: pūravo</note>, meaning human worshippers, **praise** <note>original: prastuvante</note> you through **sacrifices** joined **with this** hymn. **When** <note>original: yat</note>, for the sake of **showing favor** or granting wealth to the king **Purukutsa**, you **destroyed** the **seven autumnal forts** belonging to the **slaves** <note>original: dāsīḥ</note>—the enemies who destroy righteous works—

<term>Indra</term>: The king of the gods and deity of rain and war.
<term>Vajra</term>: Indra's primary weapon, often translated as thunderbolt or diamond-club.
<term>Puru</term>: An ancient Vedic tribe/clan often associated with the Sarasvati river.
<term>Purukutsa</term>: A famous king of the Ikshvaku dynasty assisted by Indra.
<term>Autumnal Forts (Sharadih Purah)</term>: Historically debated structures, possibly fortifications used during the flooding season or celestial metaphors.
</vocab>

# [Mandala 6, Chapter 2, Section 20] || The Fourth Ashtaka || 669

## Commentary (Sayana) - Continued from previous page
...the enemies. Striking and killing the progeny of the enemies, and providing wealth to the king named **Purukutsa** <note>original: purukutsāyai-tannāmakāya rājñe</note>. O Indra, you tore apart with your thunderbolt <note>original: śarmaṇā vajreṇa</note> the **seven** <note>original: sapta</note> cities belonging to the demon named **Sharat** <note>original: śāradīḥ</note>. For this reason, those who offer hymns praise you.

---

## Hymn Text - Verse 11
-> || Now the Eleventh || <-

O Indra, you were the ancient enhancer, seeking wide space for Ushanas, the son of Kavi;
Having struck down Navavastva, you gave back his own grandson—who was to be restored—to the great father. || 11 ||

**Word-by-word breakdown:**
You | enhancer | O Indra | ancient | were | seeking wide space | for Ushanas | son of Kavi |
away | Navavastva | to be restored | to the great | father | you gave | his own | grandson/son || 11 ||

## Commentary (Sayana)
O Indra, you are **ancient** <note>original: pūrvyaḥ</note>, meaning existing from of old. **Desiring wealth** <note>original: varivasyan</note> for **Ushanas** <note>original: uśane</note>, the son of the sage Kavi and a descendant of Bhrigu, you became an **enhancer** <note>original: vṛdho bhūḥ</note>, one who increases the prosperity of those who praise you. After striking down the demon named **Navavastva**, you **restored** <note>original: parādadātha</note> to the **great father** <note>original: mahe pitre</note>—the protector Ushanas—his **own grandson** <note>original: svaṃ napātaṃ</note> (or son) who had been captured by enemies in battle and was **to be given back** <note>original: anudeyam</note>. You killed his enemy and gave him back completely.

---

## Hymn Text - Verse 12
-> || Now the Twelfth || <-

O Indra, you are the Shaker; you sent the waters, which were possessed by the Shaker, flowing like rivers;
When, O Hero, you crossed over the sea, you safely brought Turvasha and Yadu across to the other side. || 12 ||

**Word-by-word breakdown:**
You | Shaker | O Indra | possessed by the Shaker | you sent | waters | rivers | like | flowing |
forth | when | sea | beyond | O Hero | you cross | to the other side | Turvasha | Yadu | safely || 12 ||

## Commentary (Sayana)
O Indra, you are the **Shaker** <note>original: dhuniḥ</note>, the one who makes enemies tremble. You **sent** <note>original: ṛṇoḥ</note> the **waters** <note>original: apaḥ</note>—which were held back by the demon named Dhuni—**flowing** <note>original: sravantīḥ</note> like **rivers** <note>original: sīrā na</note>. The meaning is that by killing the demon Dhuni, you released the waters he had obstructed. O **Hero** <note>original: śūra</note>, brave Indra, **whenever** <note>original: yat-yadā</note> you **crossed beyond the sea** <note>original: samudram-ati praparṣi</note>, you **brought across** <note>original: pāraya</note> both **Turvasha and Yadu** <note>historical: Turvasha and Yadu are two famous tribal groups or kings frequently mentioned as being protected by Indra</note> who were standing on the far shore. You enabled them to cross the sea safely.

## Hymn Text - Verse 13
-> || Now the Thirteenth || <-

You, O Indra, in every battle, have put to sleep the demons Dhuni and Chumuri;
For you, Dabhiti, kindling the sacrificial fire and preparing the oblation, shone with Soma-pressings and hymns. || 13 ||

<term>Indra: The king of the gods and deity of storms and battle</term>
<term>Kavya Ushanas: A legendary sage and priest of the Asuras who also had a close, sometimes complex relationship with Indra</term>

# 670 || Rig Veda || [Book 4. Chapter 6. Section 11.]

## Hymn Text (6.30.13 Word-by-word)
Your | indeed | that | Indra | all | in battle | are sleeping | Dhuni and Chumuri | which | indeed | you sent to sleep |
shined | indeed | for you | with Soma juices | pressing | Dabhiti | bringing sacrificial wood | having cooked offerings | with songs || 13 ||

---

## Commentary (Sayana)
O **Indra**, in the **battle** <note>original: ājau</note>, **all** this pervasive **action is yours** <note>original: tava ha... viśvaṃ... karma bhavati</note>. What kind of action? It is said: **those two, Dhuni and Chumuri.** These are the names of two <term>Asuras</term> <note>powerful beings often depicted as rivals to the gods</note>. **You sent them to sleep** <note>original: siṣvap</note>; those two demons now **lie asleep** <note>original: sastaḥ</note> in battle, meaning they are dead. 

<note>The commentator notes that a present tense verb is used here for a past event, and the second 'ha' is used to fill the meter.</note> 

Following that, O **Indra**, for **your** sake, the **royal sage named Dabhiti** <note>original: dabhītir-nāma rājarṣiḥ</note>—who **presses** <note>original: sunvan</note> the Soma, who **prepares cooked offerings** <note>original: pakthī</note>, and who **carries the sacrificial wood** <note>original: idhmabhṛtiḥ</note>—truly **shines** <note>original: dīdayat-it</note> with Soma juices and **songs** <note>original: arkaiḥ</note> accompanied by food oblations. The meaning is that you struck down Dhuni and Chumuri for him. As seen in other scriptures: "You cast down the <term>Dasyu</term> <note>an enemy or non-believer</note>, Chumuri and Dhuni."

->|| This concludes the tenth group (Varga) in the sixth chapter of the fourth book ||<-

**"These [prayers] indeed..."** <note>Refers to the start of Sukta 31</note>. This sixth hymn, consisting of twelve verses, is seen by the sage **Bharadvaja**. It is written in the **Trishtubh** meter and is dedicated to **Indra**. The ninth and eleventh verses are dedicated to the **All-Gods** <note>original: vaiśvadevyau</note>. As the Index <note>Anukramani</note> states: "These twelve; the ninth and eleventh are for the All-Gods." 

In the one-day sacrifice called **Upahavya**, this hymn is designated for the <term>Marutvatiya</term> <note>an offering to Indra as leader of the Maruts, the storm gods</note> section. This is indicated in the ritual manuals: "‘These to you, who alone...’ is for the midday [libation]" <note>original: Āśvalāyana Śrauta Sūtra 9. 7</note>. It is also used in the one-day sacrifice named **Indra-Vishnu-Utkranti** for the Marutvatiya section. Furthermore, it is used in the **Third Chandoma** day.

->|| Here is the first verse ||<-

## Hymn Text (6.31.1)
These [prayers] indeed, O Hero, call to you, the one worthy of being called, from the singer who desires much;
The ageless, ever-new one seated in the chariot; wealth, the cause of prosperity, approaches you through praise. || 1 ||

**Word-by-word:**
These | indeed | you | of the one who desires much | of the singer | worthy of being called | O Hero | worthy of being called | they call |
prayers | seated in the chariot | ageless | ever-new | wealth | cause of prosperity | approaches | through praise || 1 ||

---

## Commentary (Sayana)
Of the one who **desires much** <note>original: purutamasya</note>—meaning one who yearns for abundant rewards. Of the **singer** <note>original: kāroḥ</note>, the sage Bharadvaja. **These prayers** <note>original: imā dhiyaḥ</note>, which are praiseworthy, call to **you, the Hero** Indra, who are **worthy of being called** <note>original: havyaṃ</note>. 

What is Indra like? He is **seated in a chariot** <note>original: rathesthām</note>, **ageless** <note>original: ajaram</note>, and **ever-new** <note>original: navīyaḥ</note> <note>meaning he remains fresh and powerful despite being ancient</note>. Furthermore, **wealth** <note>original: rayiḥ</note>—characterized by the oblations offered—which is the **source of the world's prosperity** <note>original: vibhūtiḥ</note>, **approaches you** <note>original: īyate</note> through the most excellent **praises** <note>original: vacasyā</note>.

<summary>This page describes Indra's victory over the demons Dhuni and Chumuri on behalf of the sage Dabhiti and begins a new hymn (Sukta 31) where the sage Bharadvaja invokes Indra as an ageless, chariot-seated warrior who brings prosperity.</summary>

# 671 || Rig Veda || [Book 4. Chapter 6. Section 11.]

## Hymn Text

-> ॥ Verse 2 ॥ <-

I praise that very **Indra**, who is known [by all], who is **borne by songs**, and who **prospers through sacrifices**. The **greatness** of him, who possesses **vast wisdom**, exceeds the heaven and the earth in its magnitude. || 2 ||

-> **Word-by-word Breakdown** <-

That | indeed | I praise | Indra | who | known | borne by songs | by songs | prospering through sacrifice |
whose | heaven | reaches | with greatness | of the earth | of many-wonders | exceeded | greatness || 2 ||

---

## Commentary (Sayana)

That Indra who is **all-knowing** <note>original: vidānaḥ</note>—or understood by all—who is **borne by songs** <note>original: girvāhasam</note> (meaning he is to be carried or reached through hymns), who is **prospered by sacrifices** <note>original: yajñavṛdham</note> (meaning he is increased by the offerings); I praise <note>original: stuṣe</note> that very Indra. 

The connection is this: I praise him whose **majesty** <note>original: mahitvam</note>—the greatness of that Indra who possesses **great wisdom** <note>original: purumāyasya</note> or many words—exceeds <note>original: ririce</note> the **heaven** <note>original: divam</note> (here the second case is used in the sense of the "from" or fifth case) and the **earth** <note>original: pṛthivyāḥ</note> by his own **magnitude** <note>original: mahvā</note>.

---

## Hymn Text

-> ॥ Verse 3 ॥ <-

He indeed turned the spreading, **featureless darkness** into something **full of light** by means of the **Sun**. O **Powerful One**, when do **mortals**, desiring to worship, not neglect the **abode of the immortal**? || 3 ||

-> **Word-by-word Breakdown** <-

He | indeed | darkness | featureless | spreading | by the sun | full of light | made |
when | your | mortals | of the immortal | abode | desiring to worship | not | neglect | O Powerful One || 3 ||

## Commentary (Sayana)

**He indeed** <note>original: sa it</note>, that same Indra, made the **featureless** <note>original: avayunam</note> (meaning without knowledge or the destroyer of knowledge) **darkness** <note>original: tamaḥ</note> that was **spreading** <note>original: tatantvat</note> throughout the sky, into something **possessing light** <note>original: vayunavat</note> or clarity, by using the **Sun** <note>original: sūryeṇa</note> (the deity placed in the heavens). 

The second half of the verse addresses Indra directly. O **Powerful One** <note>original: svadhāvaḥ</note> (meaning one possessed of strength), when—meaning at all times—do **mortals** <note>original: martāḥ</note> (human beings) who **desire to worship** <note>original: iyakṣantaḥ</note> you, not **neglect** <note>original: na minanti</note> (not harm or ignore) your **abode** <note>original: dhāma</note> called heaven? This refers to the gods residing there. The sense is that they never neglect the living beings or the divine path.

# 672 || Rig Veda || [Book 4. Chapter 6. Section 12.]

## Commentary (Sayana) — Verse 4 (Continued)

That **Indra** who performed those well-known deeds, such as the **slaying of Vritra** <note>original: vṛtravadhādīni</note>—where indeed does he reside today? In what place or among what people does he dwell? Because of Indra's vast manifestations and greatness, it is impossible to determine his exact location. Now follows a direct praise: O Indra, what kind of sacrifice <note>original: yajña</note> brings happiness and peace to your mind? What kind of prayer <note>original: arka</note> is capable of "choosing" you <note>meaning, inviting your presence</note>? And who is the invoker <note>original: hotā</note> that is most capable of calling upon you?

---

## Hymn Text — Verse 5

-> ॥ The Fifth Verse ॥ <-

Just as now, O **Doer of many deeds**, your friends who were born in ancient times and the elders of old were active [in your service]. Those of the middle age, and those of recent times—O **Much-invoked**, heed the prayer of the most recent [worshipper]. || 5 ||

**Word-by-word Breakdown:**

Now | indeed | your | active | born in olden times | ancient ones | were | doer of many deeds | friends | 
who | those of the middle age | and | those of recent times | and | of the most recent | O Much-invoked | heed/notice || 5 ||

## Commentary (Sayana)

The "ancient ones" <note>original: purājāḥ</note> who were born in former times, the elders <note>original: pratnāsaḥ</note> like the **Angirases** <note>a legendary family of fire-priests and sages</note> and others, were active just like the worshippers of today. The word *hi* here is used to make a comparison. O Indra, **doer of many deeds** <note>original: purukṛt</note>, these "friends" <note>original: sakhāyaḥ</note>—meaning your praisers—existed then. Those who belong to the middle period <note>original: madhyamāso</note> and those who are "new" or of the present day <note>original: nūtanāso</note> were all your praisers. Therefore, O **Much-invoked** <note>original: puruhūta</note> Indra, you who are called upon by many, please **heed** <note>original: bodhi</note> or take notice of the hymn of even the most recent <note>original: avamasya</note> worshipper—meaning me.

-> ॥ This concludes the eleventh section of the sixth chapter of the fourth book ॥ <-

---

## Hymn Text — Verse 6

-> ॥ The Sixth Verse ॥ <-

Asking of him, the later ones have followed your ancient, famous deeds, O Indra. We worship you, O Hero, **Borne by Prayers**, as far as we know you, the Great one. || 6 ||

**Word-by-word Breakdown:**

Him | asking | later ones | supreme | ancient | your | Indra | by what is heard | followed |
we worship | Hero | borne by prayers | as much | indeed | we know | that | you | Great one || 6 ||

## Commentary (Sayana)

O Hero, O Brave one, <term>Brahmavāhas</term> <note>original: brahma-vāhas; one who is "carried" or reached by the power of sacred prayers/mantras</note>, the "later ones" <note>original: avarāso</note>, meaning modern men, are asking about you and worshipping you, who possess such liberated qualities. <note>The sage notes that the word "asking" here functions as a synonym for "worshipping."</note> They have followed after your supreme <note>original: parāṇi</note>, ancient <note>original: pratnā</note> deeds, which are famous and "worthy of being heard" <note>original: śrutyā</note>.

<summary>This page records Indra's transition from a legendary hero of the past to a living presence for modern worshippers. It emphasizes that while the great sages of old (like the Angirases) praised him, he should also heed the prayers of current, "more recent" devotees.</summary>

# 673 || Rig Veda || [Book 6. Hymn 2. Verse 21.]

## Commentary (Sayana) — Verse 6 (Continued)

...the act of guiding or binding. That is, binding [the deity] with words in the form of praise. In that same way, we also worship you <note>original: arcāmasi</note>, who are great and abundant. We praise you. The connection here is: whatever deeds [of yours] we know and understand, we praise you through those specific deeds.

## Hymn Text

-> ॥ The Seventh Verse ॥ <-

The demonic force has spread itself against you; O Great One, as you manifest, stand firm against it. With your ancient, allied, and constant companion, the **Thunderbolt**, O Bold One, drive those forces away. || 7 ||

> **Word-by-word Breakdown:**
> Against | you | force | of the demon | spread | manifested | Great One | against | that | well | stand | 
> your | ancient | allied | companion | with the thunderbolt | O Bold One | away | those | drive || 7 ||

## Commentary (Sayana)

O **Indra**, the force <note>original: pājaḥ</note>, which refers to the strength of the army belonging to the **Rakshasas** <note>demonic beings</note>, has spread itself against you. It stands in opposition. Therefore, as you are being "born" or manifesting <note>original: jajñānam</note> in your great form, stand firm and ready against that force. Having stood your ground, O Bold One <note>original: dhṛṣṇo</note>—you who overpowers enemies—drive away <note>original: apanudasva</note> that demonic strength with your **Thunderbolt** <note>original: vajreṇa</note>. This means you should destroy them. What kind of weapon is it? It is ancient <note>original: pratnena</note>, it is "allied" or fit for the task <note>original: yujyena</note>, and it is your eternal companion <note>original: sakhyā</note>.

---

## Hymn Text

-> ॥ The Eighth Verse ॥ <-

O Hero, sustainer of the singers, O Indra, listen quickly to this new worshipper who desires to compose a prayer. For you have always been the kinsman of our ancestors in days of old, and you are easily invoked at the sacrifice. || 8 ||

> **Word-by-word Breakdown:**
> He | indeed | listen | Indra | of the new | desiring to pray | Hero | sustainer of singers | 
> You | for | kinsman | in ancient days | of the ancestors | always | have been | easily invoked | in the sacrifice || 8 ||

## Commentary (Sayana)

O **Sustainer of Singers** <note>original: kārudhāyaḥ; those who support the poets</note>, O Hero Indra, you who are so famous—listen quickly <note>original: kṣipram śrudhi</note> to my prayer. I am a "new" worshipper <note>original: nūtanasya</note>, one living in the present time who desires to fashion a hymn <note>original: brahmaṇyataḥ</note>. Why should you listen? Because, O Indra, when the sacrifice or the desire for worship arises <note>original: eṣṭau</note>, you are the one who is "well-invoked" <note>original: suhavaḥ</note>. In ancient times <note>original: pradivi</note>, you were the kinsman and friend <note>original: āpiḥ</note> of our ancestors, such as the **Angirases** <note>a semi-divine family of fire-priests</note>, and you have been so for a very long time. For this reason, listen to my current praise.

# ६१५ || Rig Veda || [Book 4. Chapter 6. Verse 12.]

<note>This fragment concludes the commentary on Verse 11 from the previous page.</note>

The gods are those "whose tongue is Fire" <note>Sanskrit: *agnijihvāḥ*; meaning Agni acts as the mouth of the gods to receive offerings</note>. They are those whose place is held by the Fire-tongue. They touch the butter and the sacrifice. These are the gods who, for the sake of destroying enemies, made Manu—the royal seer—superior to the *Dasyus* <note>enemies or non-believers</note>. The prayer concludes: "O Indra, come along with them" <note>referring to the connection with the previous verse</note>.

## Hymn Text

-> ॥ The Twelfth Verse ॥ <-

**Become our leader in easy paths and in difficult ones, O path-maker, the all-knowing.**
**With those tireless, wide-striding, and swiftest horses, O Indra, bring us strength.** || 12 ||

**He. Our. Become. Leader. In easy paths. And. In difficult paths. Path-maker. All-knowing.**
**Those. Tireless. Great. Swiftest. With them. To us. Indra. Toward. Bring. Strength.** || 12 ||

## Commentary (Sayana)

O Indra, you are the **path-maker** <note>*pathikṛt*: the creator of ways</note> and the **all-knowing** <note>*vidvānaḥ*: one who knows everything</note>. May you **become** <note>*bodhi*: a poetic Vedic form of the command 'be' or 'become'</note> our **leader** <note>*puraetā*: one who goes before</note> both in **easy paths**—those that are pleasant to travel—and also in **difficult paths**—those that are hard to traverse.

Furthermore, O Indra, your horses are **tireless** <note>*ashramāsaḥ*: free from exhaustion</note>, **great** <note>*uravo*</note>, and **swiftest** <note>*vahiṣṭhā*: the best at carrying or pulling</note>. **With those** horses, **bring** <note>*abhivakṣi*</note> **strength** <note>*vājam*: often referring to food or the spoils of victory</note> to us.

-> ॥ This ends the twelfth section of the sixth chapter of the fourth book ॥ <-

---

## Introduction to Hymn 22

The seventh hymn, beginning with "He who alone," consists of eleven verses. The seer <note>author/poet</note> is Bharadvaja, the meter is *Trishtubh*, and the deity is Indra. As stated in the Index <note>*Anukramani*</note>: "He who alone, eleven verses." 

In the ritual context: During the first day of the *Abhillavika* sacrifice and the first day of the "Ten Nights" <note>*Dasharatra*</note> ceremony, at the midday libation <note>*madhyandina-savana*</note>, in the recitation by the *Brahmanachamsi* priest, three "obtained hymns" <note>*sampata-suktas*</note> are used in place of the *Ahina* hymn. This is the second of those three hymns. This is indicated in the ritual manual <note>Ashvalayana Shrauta Sutra 7.5</note>: "He who alone, the destroyer with prominent horns." 

This hymn is also designated for the *Nishkevalya* litany in the one-day sacrifice called *Upahavya*. This is noted in the manual <note>Ashvalayana Shrauta Sutra 9.7</note>: "He who alone, at midday."

---

## Hymn Text

-> ॥ The First Verse ॥ <-

**That Indra alone, who is to be invoked by the peoples, I worship with these songs.**
**He who rules as the mighty bull, possessing power, the truthful, the courageous, the one of many wonders, the powerful.** || 1 ||

**He. One. Indeed. To be invoked. Of the peoples. Indra. Him. With songs. Toward. I worship. With these.**
**Who. Rules. Bull. Possessing power. Truthful. Courageous. Of many wonders. Powerful.** || 1 ||

## Commentary (Sayana)

**Indra** is the one who, among **the peoples** <note>*charshanīnam*: men or subjects</note>, is the **only one** to be **invoked** <note>*havyaḥ*: to be called upon</note> during times of trouble. I **worship** that Indra with **these songs** of praise...

<vocab>
Indra: The king of the gods and deity of rain and war.
Peoples (Charshani): Referring to the human subjects or the five tribes of men.
To be invoked (Havya): Worthy of being called to the sacrifice.
Leader (Puraeta): One who leads from the front.
Path-maker (Pathikrit): An epithet for a deity who clears obstacles.
Strength/Food (Vaja): A multi-layered term for vitality, wealth, and sustenance.
Bull (Vrishabha): A common metaphor for great strength and virility.
Power (Vrishnyavan): Possessing manly or reproductive strength.
Sampata hymns: Specifically chosen hymns used in complex Vedic rituals.
Midday libation (Madhyandina-savana): The second of the three daily ritual offerings of Soma.
</vocab>

<keywords>Indra, Bharadvaja, Path-maker, Vedic Rituals, Midday Libation, Strength, Leadership</keywords>

# ६७६ || Rig Veda || [Book 4. Chapter 6. Verse 13.]

## Commentary (Sayana)
<note>This section concludes the explanation of Verse 1 from the previous page.</note>

I worship that Indra with words of praise. I glorify him. It is that Indra who **masters** <note>Sanskrit: *patyate*; meaning he approaches or rules over</note> those who sing his hymns. Or, it means he masters and rules the worlds. What is his nature? He is the **bull** <note>a common metaphor for a virile, powerful leader</note> who showers down the fulfillment of desires. He is powerful, truthful, and consistent in his actions. He is the destroyer of enemies, or the giver of what is desired <note>the commentator notes that the word *satvā* can be derived from roots meaning either to destroy or to give</note>. He possesses **great wisdom** <note>literally "many illusions" or "extraordinary powers" (*purumāyo*)</note>, is mighty, and is the overcomer of all. I glorify that Indra—this is the connection of the words.

---

## Hymn Text
-> ॥ The Second Verse ॥ <-

**Him indeed our ancient fathers, the nine-fold ones, the seven sages, seeking strength,**
**[praised] him who humbles the attacker, the conqueror, who dwells in the mountains, of unerring speech, the most powerful.** || 2 ||

**Pada-patha:**
**Him. Indeed. Our. Ancient. Fathers. Nine-fold ones. Seven. Sages. Toward. Seeking strength.**
**Humber of the attacker. Conqueror. Dwelling in the mountains. Of unerring speech. With prayers. Most powerful.** || 2 ||

## Commentary (Sayana)

Our **ancient fathers** <note>the *Pitaras* or ancestors</note> were the **Angirases**. Among them were the **nine-fold ones** <note>Sanskrit: *Navagvas*; a group of mythical ancestors who performed a sacrifice lasting nine months</note> and the **seven sages** <note>the *Sapta Rishis*, the legendary seven wise men of Vedic tradition</note> who were filled with wisdom. These ancestors were **seeking strength** <note>or "providing food" in the form of sacrificial offerings to Indra</note>. They sought to make Indra powerful through their rituals. These fathers of ours praised that very Indra with their **prayers** <note>sacred thoughts or hymns</note>. 

What is Indra like? He is the **humbler of the attacker** <note>he who destroys enemies who approach him</note>. He is the **conqueror** <note>literally "the crosser" (*taturim*) who overcomes all difficulties</note>. He **dwells in the mountains** <note>or remains firm like a mountain</note>. He is of **unerring speech**—meaning his word and his commands are never betrayed or transgressed. Finally, he is the **most powerful** among all.

---

## Hymn Text
-> ॥ The Third Verse ॥ <-

**We beg of that Indra for wealth, rich in heroes, with many attendants, and abundant food,**
**which is continuous, ageless, and full of light; O Lord of the Bay Horses, bring it to us so we may rejoice.** || 3 ||

**Pada-patha:**
**Him. We beg. Indra’s. Wealth. Rich in heroes. Accompanied by men. Possessing much food.**
**Which. Continuous. Ageless. Full of light. That. Toward. Bring. O Lord of the Bay Horses. So that we may rejoice.** || 3 ||

## Commentary (Sayana)

We **beg** <note>request</note> of that Indra for this **wealth** <note>the word *rayi* implies overall prosperity</note>. This wealth is **rich in heroes**, meaning it includes many sons and grandsons. It is **accompanied by men**, meaning it comes with many servants and attendants. It is **possessing much food** <note>or "possessing many cattle"</note>. 

This wealth is **continuous** <note>uninterrupted</note>, **ageless** <note>free from decay or loss</note>, and **full of light** <note>full of happiness or heavenly qualities</note>. Therefore, O **Lord of the Bay Horses** <note>Sanskrit: *Harivan*; an epithet of Indra whose chariot is pulled by two tawny/bay horses</note>, bring that wealth to us so that we may be filled with joy.

<vocab>
Indra: The king of the Vedic gods, associated with storms, war, and strength.
Pitaras: The "Fathers" or ancestral spirits, often viewed as semi-divine beings who established the first sacrifices.
Navagvas: A specific group of the Angiras ancestors known for their nine-month ritual.
Vipras: Inspired poets or sages who possess sacred knowledge.
Rayi: A broad term for wealth, including cattle, children, and spiritual prosperity.
</vocab>

<summary>This page describes Indra as a powerful, wise ruler and records how the ancient ancestors (the Angirases and Navagvas) worshipped him. It concludes with a prayer for enduring, heroic wealth and prosperity that brings happiness to the community.</summary>
<keywords>Indra, ancestors, Navagvas, Seven Sages, Angirases, wealth, Harivan, Vedic sacrifice, Sayana, Rig Veda</keywords>

# ६७७ || Rig Veda || [Book 4. Chapter 6. Verse 13.]

## Hymn Text

-> ॥ The Fourth Verse ॥ <-

**Indra, tell us if in the past your singers attained happiness. What is your allotted portion? What is your food, O slayer of Asuras, you who are difficult to withstand, much-invoked, and possessor of great wealth?** || 4 ||

**Word-by-word Analysis (Padapatha):**
**That. To us. Speak out. If. Your. In the past. Indeed. Singers. Attained. Happiness. Indra.**
**What. Your. Portion. What. Food. Difficult to withstand. Distresser of enemies. Much-invoked. Possessor of much wealth. Slayer of the Asuras.** || 4 ||

---

## Commentary (Sayana)

O Indra, if in former times your **singers** <note>Sanskrit: *jaritāraḥ*; those who chant the hymns of praise</note> attained happiness, then declare that happiness to us. O **difficult to withstand** <note>Sanskrit: *dudha*; meaning one who is hard to hold back or resist</note>, O **distresser of enemies** <note>Sanskrit: *khidvaḥ*</note>, O much-invoked one, O possessor of great wealth! For you, who are the **slayer of the Asuras** <note>The *Asuras* were the powerful celestial rivals of the Devas (gods) in Vedic mythology</note>, what **portion** <note>Sanskrit: *bhāga*; the specific share of the sacrificial offering</note> has been prepared in the sacrifices? What **food** <note>Sanskrit: *vayaḥ*; specifically the sacrificial nourishment or oblation known as *havis*</note> has been prepared? 

The meaning is this: if certain ancient people in the past received happiness from you, then I will consider that I too shall obtain that happiness. Therefore, I must endure any delay in the arrival of that happiness with the understanding that it will eventually come.

---

## Hymn Text

-> ॥ The Fifth Verse ॥ <-

**The prayer of the worshiper, reaching out and praising, approaches that Indra who holds the thunderbolt in his hand and stands in his chariot—he who is the grasper of much, the doer of many deeds, the giver of strength, the nourishing one who leads us to the path.** || 5 ||

**Word-by-word Analysis (Padapatha):**
**Him. Asking/Praising. Thunderbolt-handed. Standing in the chariot. Indra. Trembling with devotion. Speaking [praise]. Whose. Now. Song/Prayer.**
**Grasper of much. Performer of many deeds. Giver of strength. Path. For the sake of food/desire. Approaches. The strong/nourishing one. Toward.** || 5 ||

---

## Commentary (Sayana)

In the previous verses, Indra was somewhat reproached by the seer, but now Indra has granted the seer his desires. Therefore, the sage, his wishes now fulfilled, says:

The **prayer** <note>Sanskrit: *gīḥ*; the hymn or song of praise</note> of the sacrificer, which is **trembling with devotion** <note>Sanskrit: *vepī*; characterized by the performance of rituals like the Yajna</note> and is a **speaker of qualities** <note>Sanskrit: *vakkari*; one that enumerates the divine attributes</note>, reaches toward that Indra. How is Indra described? He is **holding the thunderbolt** (*vajra*) in his hand and is **standing in his chariot**. He is the **grasper of much** <note>Sanskrit: *tuviyābham*; he who takes hold of many offerings or enemies</note>, the **performer of many deeds**, and the **giver of strength**. 

That sacrificer approaches the **path** <note>Sanskrit: *gātum*; meaning the way to happiness or success</note> for the sake of obtaining food or the fulfillment of desires. Furthermore, he approaches the **nourishing** <note>Sanskrit: *tumram*; also interpreted as one who causes the enemy to faint or wither</note> Indra who is turned toward his wishes.

-> ॥ Thus ends the thirteenth section of the sixth chapter of the fourth book ॥ <-

# ६७८ || Rig Veda || [Book 4. Chapter 6. Verse 14.]

->॥ The Sixth Verse ॥<-

## Hymn Text

**With this power, O self-powerful one, with your mountain-like thunderbolt that moves as swift as thought, you shattered that well-known [demon] who was growing by his own delusive craft. O loud-shouting Indra, possessor of beautiful might, you shattered even the immovable, strengthened, and firm fortresses with your striking power.** || 6 ||

**Word-by-word Analysis (Padapatha):**
**With this. Indeed. That one. By delusive power. Growing. Moving swift as thought. Self-powerful. With the mountain-like weapon.**
**Unshakable. Even. Strengthened. Possessing beautiful might. You shattered. Completely. Firm. By striking power. O loud-shouter.** || 6 ||

---

## Commentary (Sayana)

O **self-powerful** <note>Sanskrit: *svatavaḥ*; meaning one whose strength is inherent and belonging to himself</note> Indra, with this **mountain-like** <note>Sanskrit: *parvatena*; referring to the thunderbolt which is described as having many joints or 'mountain-like' knots. Sayana quotes another verse (RV 1.80.6) to confirm the Vajra has a hundred joints</note> weapon of yours, the **thunderbolt** <note>original: *vajra*</note> that moves as fast as the mind, you **shattered** <note>Sanskrit: *vyarujaḥ*</note> that famous Vritra who was increasing by **his delusive power** <note>Sanskrit: *māyā*</note>. Likewise, O possessor of **beautiful might** <note>Sanskrit: *svojaḥ*</note> and O **loud-shouter** <note>Sanskrit: *virapśin*; an epithet for the great Indra</note>, you have broken with your striking thunderbolt the **firm** <note>Sanskrit: *dṛḷhā*</note> fortresses, even those that were **unshakable** <note>Sanskrit: *acyutā*</note> and **strengthened** <note>Sanskrit: *vīḷitā*</note> against destruction.

---

->॥ The Seventh Verse ॥<-

## Hymn Text

**To you, the most powerful and ancient one, I offer this newer hymn of praise to be celebrated as in the days of old. May that immeasurable Indra, who is well-conveyed, carry us across all difficult paths.** || 7 ||

**Word-by-word Analysis (Padapatha):**
**That. For you. With a hymn of praise. Newer. Most powerful. Ancient. Like the ancients. To be celebrated/extended.**
**He. Us. May he carry. Immeasurable. Well-conveyed. Indra. All. Across. Difficulties.** || 7 ||

---

## Commentary (Sayana)

With a **newer** <note>original: *navyasya*; meaning a fresh or more recent composition</note> **hymn of praise** <note>Sanskrit: *dhiyā*</note>, I have set out **to extol** <note>Sanskrit: *paritansayadhyai*; to spread or extend the glory of</note> you, O Indra, who are the most powerful and **ancient** <note>Sanskrit: *pratnam*</note>, just as the **ancient seers** <note>Sanskrit: *pratnavat*</note> used to do. May that **immeasurable** <note>Sanskrit: *animānaḥ*; one whose limits cannot be measured</note> Indra, who is **well-conveyed** <note>Sanskrit: *suvahnā*; meaning he possesses an excellent chariot and horses</note>, **carry us across** <note>Sanskrit: *ati vakṣat*</note> all **difficulties** <note>original: *durgaḥāṇi*; meaning places or situations that are hard to cross</note>.

---

->॥ The Eighth Verse ॥<-

## Hymn Text

**For the person who offers, light up the earthly, heavenly, and intermediate regions. O Showerer of benefits, burn the haters of the sacred word from all sides with your glow; consume the earth and the waters.** || 8 ||

**Word-by-word Analysis (Padapatha):**
**Completely. For the person. For the one who milks the offering. Earthly. Heavenly. You light up. Mid-air.**
**Burn. O Showerer. From all sides. With a glow. Those. Haters of the sacred word. Make them blaze. The earth. The waters. And.** || 8 ||

---

## Commentary (Sayana)

O Indra, for the sake of the **person who offers** <note>Sanskrit: *janāya duhvane*; literally 'for the man who milks', referring to the sacrificer who draws out the essence of the offering</note>, illuminate the **earthly** regions, the **heavenly** regions, and the **intermediate** air. O **Showerer of benefits** <note>Sanskrit: *vṛṣan*; an epithet comparing Indra’s power to a bull's</note>, burn those who are **haters of the sacred word** <note>Sanskrit: *brahmadviṣe*; those who hate prayers, priests, or the Vedas</note> from every side with your **glow** <note>Sanskrit: *śociṣā*</note>. Cause the **earth** <note>Sanskrit: *kṣām*</note> and the **waters** <note>Sanskrit: *apaḥ*</note> [of the enemy] to be consumed.

<summary>In these verses, the sage glorifies Indra's destruction of Vritra and his fortresses using the thunderbolt, while requesting protection across life's difficulties and the destruction of those who hate sacred rituals.</summary>
<keywords>Indra, Vritra, Vajra, Thunderbolt, Māyā, Brahmadviṣ, Sayana, Rig Veda, Ancient Seers, Protection</keywords>

# ६७९ || Rig Veda || [Book 6. Chapter 2. Hymn 22.]

## Commentary (Sayana) — Continued (Verse 8)

O **Indra**, for the **malicious one** <note>Sanskrit: *druhvaṇe*; referring to a person or demon who seeks to harm virtuous people</note>—here the dative case is used in the sense of the genitive—**illuminate** the **earthly** places, the **heavenly** places, and those residing in the **mid-region** <note>original: *antarikṣa*</note>. Set them all ablaze. O **Showerer** <note>Sanskrit: *vṛṣan*; an epithet for Indra as the pourer of rewards and rain</note> of desires, O Indra, **burn** **those** demons and enemies who exist **everywhere** with your **flame** <note>Sanskrit: *śociṣā*</note>. Consume them. Furthermore, to burn the **hater of sacred prayer** <note>Sanskrit: *brahmadviṣe*; one who hates the Vedas or the Brahmanas</note>, make the **earth** and the **mid-region** <note>Sanskrit: *ap* is used here as a name for the atmosphere/mid-region</note> **glow with heat**.

---

## Hymn Text

-> ॥ The Ninth Verse ॥ <-

**You are the King of the heavenly people and the King of the earthly world, possessing a terrifying appearance. O Indra, place the thunderbolt in your right hand; O un-aging one, you destroy all delusive powers.** || 9 ||

-> ॥ Word-by-word Analysis ॥ <-

**You are. Of the people. Of the heavenly. King. Of the earthly. Of the world. Of terrifying appearance. Place. The thunderbolt. In the right. O Indra. In the hand. All. O un-aging one. You destroy. Away. The delusive powers.** || 9 ||

---

## Commentary (Sayana)

O Indra of **terrifying appearance** <note>Sanskrit: *tveṣasaṃhṛk*; one whose sight is brilliant or formidable</note>, you **are** the **King** or lord of the **heavenly people**. You are also the **King** of the **earthly** and **moving** world. **Place** the **thunderbolt** <note>original: *vajra*</note> **in your right hand**. With that **thunderbolt** held in place, **you destroy** <note>Sayana notes the root *day* can mean to give, to hurt, to move, or to protect; here it means to strike or destroy</note> **all** the **delusive powers** <note>original: *māyāḥ*; the magical or deceptive powers of the Asuras/demons</note>. O **un-aging one** <note>Sanskrit: *ajurya*; one who cannot be made to decay</note>, this refers to you, Indra.

---

## Hymn Text

-> ॥ The Tenth Verse ॥ <-

**O Indra, bring to us great and uninjured prosperity for the sake of overcoming our enemies—that prosperity by which, O wielder of the thunderbolt, you make the Dasa and the Arya people, and the human tribes, subject to us, and by which you strike the enemies with swift destruction.** || 10 ||

-> ॥ Word-by-word Analysis ॥ <-

**Bring. Joined together. O Indra. To us. Prosperity. For overcoming enemies. Great. Uninjured. By which. The Dasa [peoples]. The Arya [peoples]. The enemies. You make. O wielder of the thunderbolt. Swift-striking. Human tribes.** || 10 ||

---

## Commentary (Sayana)

O **Indra**, **bring** to **us** a **joined** and continuous **prosperity** <note>Sanskrit: *svasti*; well-being or auspiciousness</note> characterized by security, which is **great** and **uninjured** <note>Sanskrit: *amṛdhrām*; not harmed by others</note>, for the purpose of **overcoming enemies**. O **wielder of the thunderbolt** <note>original: *vajrin*</note>, bring that prosperity **by which** you **make** the **Dasa** <note>Sanskrit: *dāsāni*; those who do not perform sacred rites</note> and the **Arya** <note>Sanskrit: *āryāṇi*; those who perform sacred rites</note>—both being classes of **human tribes** <note>Sanskrit: *nāhuṣāṇi*; related to Nahusha, a word for 'man'</note>—subject to your will. With that, you made the **enemies** <note>original: *vṛtrā*</note> **swiftly destroyed** <note>Sanskrit: *sutukā*; accompanied by good or effective striking</note>.

<summary>This page concludes Indra's invocation to burn the haters of prayer and describes him as the sovereign of both heaven and earth who wields the thunderbolt. It emphasizes his power to dispel demonic illusions (Maya) and his role in establishing prosperity (Svasti) over both the Dasa and Arya tribes.</summary>

# ६९० || Rig Veda || [Book 4. Chapter 6. Varga 15.]

## Hymn Text

-> ॥ The Eleventh Verse ॥ <-

**O Many-invoked Ordainer, worshipped with sacrifice, come to us with your teams of steeds that bring all desirable things. Neither a non-god nor a god can obstruct them; come quickly with these, turning toward our exhilaration.** || 11 ||

-> ॥ Word-by-word Analysis ॥ <-

**He. To us. With teams of steeds. O Many-invoked. O Ordainer. With those providing all boons. Come. O One worshipped with sacrifice. Not. Which. A non-god. Obstructs. Not. A god. With these. Come. Quickly. Facing the exhilaration.** || 11 ||

---

## Commentary (Sayana)

O **Many-invoked** <note>Sanskrit: *puruhūta*; one called upon by many worshippers</note>, O **Ordainer** <note>Sanskrit: *vedhas*; the creator or arranger of the sacrifice</note>, O **One worshipped with sacrifice** <note>Sanskrit: *prayajyo*; Indra, who is to be worshipped with excellent offerings</note>, may you **come** to **us** with your **teams of steeds** <note>Sanskrit: *niyudbhiḥ*; refers to the specific horses or "teams" that draw Indra's chariot</note> which are **providing all boons** <note>Sanskrit: *viśvavārābhiḥ*; things to be chosen or desired by everyone</note>. Neither an **non-god** <note>Sanskrit: *adevas*; an Asura or demon</note> can **obstruct** or stop **which** teams of steeds, **nor** can a **god** stop them. With **these** teams of steeds, **come** toward us quickly, **facing the exhilaration** <note>Sanskrit: *madyadrik*; turned toward the intoxicating joy of the Soma libation</note>. The repetition of the word for "coming" in the commentary is a Vedic grammatical variation.

-> ॥ Thus ends the fourteenth section of the sixth chapter of the fourth book ॥ <-

---

The eighth hymn, beginning with **"When indeed the Soma is pressed,"** consists of ten verses. The Seer is Bharadvaja, the meter is Trishtubh, and the deity is Indra. This is noted in the Index <note>the *Anukramani*</note>. In the *Vishuvat* rite, this hymn is used for the *Nishkevalya* Shastra. This is indicated in the ritual manuals: "When indeed the Soma is pressed, you... these ancient..." <note>quoting Ashvalayana Shrauta Sutra 9.7.1</note>. Also, in the *Mahavrata* rite, this is the first of three hymns for the *Nishkevalya* Shastra, as indicated in the Fifth Aranyaka: "The three hymns beginning 'When indeed the Soma is pressed', 'Indra, who is the crusher', and 'O Indra, the Soma'..." <note>quoting Aitareya Aranyaka 5.4.1</note>.

---

## Hymn Text

-> ॥ The First Verse ॥ <-

**When indeed the Soma is pressed, O Indra, when the hymn is being uttered, when the prayer and the recitation are performed—then, O Lord of Wealth, holding the thunderbolt in your arms, you come with your two harnessed bay horses.** || 1 ||

-> ॥ Word-by-word Analysis ॥ <-

**When pressed. Indeed. You. O Crusher of enemies. O Indra. In the Soma. In the hymn. In the prayer. Being recited. In the Shastra. When. Or. With the two harnessed. O Lord of Wealth. With the two bay horses. Bearing. The thunderbolt. In the two arms. O Indra. You go.** || 1 ||

---

## Commentary (Sayana)

**When indeed the Soma is pressed**: Only when the libation is prepared, and while the **prayer** <note>Sanskrit: *brahmaṇi*; the great or expansive prayer</note>, the **hymn** <note>Sanskrit: *stome*; the song of praise</note>, and the **recitation** <note>Sanskrit: *ukthe*; the Shastra or recited portion</note> are **being performed**, do you arrive. O **Indra**, you are the **crusher of enemies** <note>Sanskrit: *nimidhnaḥ*; one who strikes down or subdues</note>, harnessing your horses. O **Lord of Wealth** <note>Sanskrit: *maghavan*; a common title for Indra implying his generosity and power</note>, **bearing** your own weapon, the **thunderbolt**, in your **arms**, and with the **two bay horses** that are **harnessed** to your chariot, **you come**. The connection is that you arrive specifically when the Soma has been pressed.

<summary>This page concludes Hymn 22 with a plea for Indra to arrive with his unstoppable steeds and begins Hymn 23, describing Indra's arrival at the sacrifice with his thunderbolt and bay horses while hymns are being recited.</summary>
<keywords>Indra, Soma, Bharadvaja, Niyuts (steeds), Maghavan, Thunderbolt (Vajra), Trishtubh meter, Sayana's commentary, Vedic ritual</keywords>

<meta>This page continues the 23rd Hymn (Sukta) of the 6th Mandala of the Rig Veda. The previous page introduced the first verse of this hymn. This page contains verses 2 and 3, along with their word-by-word analysis (Padapatha) and the commentary by the scholar Sayana.</meta>

# Mand. 6. Anuv. 2. Suk. 23. ]  || Fourth Ashtaka ||  641

-> ॥ Now the Second Verse ॥ <-

## Hymn Text

Whether in the heavenly world, in the far-reaching battle for the acquisition of men, O Indra, slayer of Vritra, you protect the Soma-presser; or whether, for the sake of the capable but fearful man, you—remaining fearless yourself—subdue the arrogant Dasyus <note>Sanskrit: *dasyūn*; refers to enemies of the Vedic rituals or chaotic forces</note>. || 2 ||

**Word-by-word Analysis:**
Whether. Or. In the sky. In the far-reaching. The Soma-presser. O Indra. In the slaying of Vritra. You protect. In the acquisition of men.
Whether. Or. Of the capable. Of the fearful. Fearless. You subdued. The arrogant. O Indra. The Dasyus. || 2 ||

---

## Commentary (Sayana)

O **Indra**, when the **far-reaching** <note>original: *pārye*; meaning a goal to be reached or a decisive moment</note> **slaying of Vritra**—which is a **battle** to be shared by many warriors—occurs **in the sky**, you **protect** the **Soma-presser**, the master of the sacrifice who extracts the juice. Or, "Whether" <note>original: *vā*; used here in a conjunctive sense</note>. You, O Indra, being **fearless** yourself, **subdue** or bring under control the **arrogant** and destructive **Dasyus** <note>Sanskrit: *dasyūn*; those who diminish or destroy the righteous</note> for the sake of the **capable** man who is nonetheless **fearful** of his enemies. All of this action is connected to the previous verse: it happens when the Soma is pressed. As it has been said:

> Whether you bear the unborn with your two bay horses, O slayer of Vritra; and whether you protect the men in battle who are pressing the Soma; and whether you fulfill the work of the very capable sacrificer and subdue his enemies for him while he fears—all this occurs when the Soma is pressed and the hymns of praise and recitation have begun. Thus, these two verses share a single purpose.

-> ॥ Now the Third Verse ॥ <-

## Hymn Text

May Indra be the **drinker** of the **pressed Soma**; may he be the **mighty leader** of the **singer** with his **protection**. He is the **maker of a place** for the **heroic presser**, and the **giver of wealth** even to the **singing praiser**. || 3 ||

**Word-by-word Analysis:**
The drinker. The pressed. Indra. May he be. The Soma. The leader. Mighty. The singer. With protection.
The maker. For the hero. For the presser. Indeed. A place. The giver. Wealth. To the one who praises. To the singer. Even. || 3 ||

---

## Commentary (Sayana)

May **Indra be the drinker** of the **Soma** that has been **pressed**. <note>Sayana notes a grammatical rule: because the word "drinker" (pātā) ends in a specific suffix, the usual rule for the genitive case is modified here</note>. What kind of leader? He is the **mighty leader** who, through the path of **protection**, guides the **singer** or the one who recites the hymns. He is the **maker**—meaning the giver—of a **place** or station for the **heroic** man who is capable in the work of sacrifice and for the **presser** who performs the Soma extraction. The word "Indeed" <note>original: *u*; a particle used here to fill the meter of the verse</note>. He is the **giver** of **wealth** <note>Sanskrit: *vasu*; material riches or spiritual abundance</note> to the **singing praiser**—the word "even" <note>original: *cit*; used here as "and"</note> links the two—the one who offers the song of praise. The term **singer** <note>Sanskrit: *kīri*; a name for a praiser or priest</note> refers to the one performing the recitation.

<vocab>
<term>Indra</term>: The king of the gods and the primary recipient of the Soma offering.
<term>Vritra-slaying</term>: A central myth where Indra defeats the dragon of drought; here used as a metaphor for victory in battle.
<term>Soma</term>: The sacred, pressed juice of a plant used in Vedic rituals to invigorate the gods.
<term>Jaritri (Praiser)</term>: The singer or priest who recites the hymns during the sacrifice.
<term>Vasu (Wealth)</term>: Desirable goods, often including cattle, horses, and prosperity.
<term>Sushvi (Presser)</term>: The one who has physically extracted the Soma juice for the ritual.
<term>Purusati (Battle)</term>: Literally the "acquisition of men," referring to a conflict or competition where warriors are gathered.
</vocab>

<keywords>Indra, Soma sacrifice, Vritra-slaying, protection, Dasyus, wealth, singer, ritual pressing</keywords>

# ## 642 || Rig Veda || Book 4, Chapter 6, Section 16

-> ॥ Now the Fourth Verse ॥ <-

## Hymn Text

He who goes to the three ritual libations with his two bay horses, the bearer of the thunderbolt, the drinker of Soma, the giver of cattle. The maker of the heroic man, beneficial to people and surrounded by many sons; the hearer of the call of the one who praises, he who is carried by hymns of praise. ॥ 4 ॥

**Word-by-word Analysis:**
**The attainer. To these many. Ritual libations. With two bay horses. The bearer. The thunderbolt. The drinker. Soma. The giver. Cattle.**
**The maker. Heroic man. Beneficial to people. Surrounded by heroes. The hearer. The call. Of the one praising. Carried by hymns.** ॥ 4 ॥

---

## Commentary (Sayana)

May **Indra** be the **attainer** <note>original: *gantā*; one who goes or reaches a destination</note>, one who is inclined to go toward the **three ritual libations** <note>original: *savanāni*; the morning, midday, and evening pressings of the Soma juice</note> situated in the heart of the sacrifice, by means of **his two bay horses**. What is his nature? He is the **bearer** or holder of the **thunderbolt** <note>original: *vajra*; Indra’s primary weapon</note>, his own weapon. He is the **drinker** of the **pressed Soma**. He is the **giver** of **cattle**. He is the **maker** <note>original: *kartā*; one who grants or creates a status</note> or granter of a **heroic** son to the sacrificer—a son who is **beneficial to people** and **surrounded by many sons** <note>original: *sarvavīram*; literally "having all heroes," interpreted as having many sons or brave followers</note>. He is the **hearer** or one who causes others to hear the **call** or hymn of the **one who praises** him. He is **carried by hymns** <note>original: *stomavāhāḥ*; one who is borne or brought to the sacrifice by the power of the chants</note>.

-> ॥ Now the Fifth Verse ॥ <-

## Hymn Text

To this Indra, we offer that which he desires; we approach him who from of old has performed supportive works for us. When the Soma is pressed, we praise him, reciting the required hymns, so that our sacred prayer for Indra may be strengthening to him. ॥ 5 ॥

**Word-by-word Analysis:**
**To him. We. Which. He desires. That. We approach. To Indra. Who. For us. From of old. Supportive works. He performed. "Performed" is the meaning of "did."**
**Pressed. In the Soma. We praise. Reciting. Hymns. For Indra. Sacred prayer. Strengthening. So that. It may be.** ॥ 5 ॥

---

## Commentary (Sayana)

He who is **from of old** <note>original: *pradivaḥ*; ancient or eternal</note>, that **Indra** who **performs** for **us** the **supportive works** <note>original: *apaḥ*; literally "waters," but here interpreted as actions of nourishment or ritual deeds</note>, this Indra **desires** <note>original: *vavāna*; from the root meaning to love or desire</note> certain **hymns of praise**. We **approach** <note>original: *viviṣmaḥ*; literally "we pervade," meaning we perform or attend to</note> that Indra with these offerings. When the **Soma** is **pressed**, we **praise** him; we perform the hymns for Indra. **Reciting** the **required hymns** <note>original: *ukthā*; specifically the Shastra or recited portions of the ritual</note>—the grammatical ending for the plural is dropped here—we act so that the **sacred prayer** <note>original: *brahma*; here referring to the food of the sacrifice or the hymn itself</note>, which has the character of an offering, **may be** **strengthening** to **Indra**. ॥ 5 ॥

-> ॥ Thus ends the fifteenth section (Varga) of the sixth chapter of the fourth book. ॥ <-

-> ॥ Now the Sixth Verse ॥ <-

## Hymn Text

For you, O Indra, have made these sacred prayers into strengthening things; therefore we approach you with our inspired thoughts. When the Soma is pressed, O drinker of the pressed juice, may we perform with our sacrifices those ritual acts which are most pleasing and nourishing. ॥ 6 ॥

**Word-by-word Analysis:**
**Sacred prayers. Indeed. You have made. Strengthening things. So many. Yours. O Indra. With inspired thoughts. We approach.**
**Pressed. In the Soma. Drinker of the pressed juice. Most pleasing. Things to be accomplished. May we perform. Nourishing acts. With sacrifices.** ॥ 6 ॥

<vocab>
Indra: The King of the Gods and the primary deity of this hymn.
Soma: A sacred ritual drink offered to the gods.
Vajra: The thunderbolt, the weapon of Indra.
Savana: The three daily periods of Soma ritual (morning, midday, evening).
Brahma: In this context, it refers to the prayer, hymn, or the strengthening power of the ritual.
Yajna: Sacrifice or ritual worship.
Varga: A small subsection or "verse-group" within the chapters of the Rig Veda.
</vocab>

# ## 683 || Rig Veda || Book 4, Chapter 2, Sukta 23

## Commentary (Sayana)
<note>This section concludes the explanation for verse 6.</note>
O Indra, because you have **created** <note>original: *cakṛṣe*</note> the **prayers** <note>original: *brahmāṇi*; sacred hymns</note> which are themselves **increasing** <note>original: *vardhanāni*; that which causes growth or prosperity</note>, we therefore **reach** <note>original: *viviṣmaḥ*; encompass or pervade</note> those many prayers for you with our **intellects** <note>original: *matibhiḥ*</note>. The meaning is that you have designed such prayers so that they may become the means of my own growth. Furthermore, O **drinker of the pressed Soma** <note>original: *sutapā*</note>, may we **perform** <note>original: *kriyāsma*</note> the **most blissful** <note>original: *śaṃtamāni*</note>, **delightful** <note>original: *rāndyā*</note> prayers that are **carriers** <note>original: *vakṣaṇāni*; that which brings the god to the sacrifice</note> of the ritual and are accompanied by oblations.

---

-> ॥ Now the Seventh Verse ॥ <-

## Hymn Text
O Indra, delighting in us, notice our **sacrificial cake**; drink the **Soma** juice refined with milk. Sit upon this **sacrificial grass** of the worshiper, and make a **wide space** for the one who seeks you. ॥ 7 ॥

**Padapatha:**
**He. Our. Notice. Sacrificial cake. Delighting. Drink. Indeed. Soma. Refined with milk. Indra. Upon. This. Sacrificial grass. Of the worshiper. Sit. Wide. Make. For the one seeking you. [Particle]. Space.** ॥ 7 ॥

## Commentary (Sayana)
O Indra, **delighting** <note>original: *raraṇaḥ*</note> in the ritual, may you **notice** <note>original: *bodhi*; become aware of</note> **our** **sacrificial cake** <note>original: *puroḍāśam*; a baked grain offering</note> which is the primary oblation. Furthermore, **drink** <note>original: *piba*</note> **quickly** <note>original: *tu*</note> the **Soma** juice which is **refined with milk** <note>original: *go-ṛjīkam*; literally "refined by products of the cow," such as milk or curds</note> and prepared for the ritual. For that purpose, **sit upon** <note>original: *āsīda*</note> this **sacrificial grass** <note>original: *barhis*; the sacred grass spread on the altar</note> belonging to the **worshiper** <note>original: *yajamānasya*</note>. After that, **make** <note>original: *kṛdhi*</note> the **space** <note>original: *lokam*; place or realm</note> **wide** <note>original: *urum*; expansive</note> for the worshiper **who seeks you** <note>original: *tvāyataḥ*</note>. <note>The word "u" is a metrical filler.</note> ॥ 7 ॥

---

-> ॥ Now the Eighth Verse ॥ <-

## Hymn Text
O mighty one, rejoice according to your pleasure; may these **sacrifices** reach you. May these **invocations**, O **one called by many**, reach us; may this **prayer** be directed toward you for our protection. ॥ 8 ॥

**Padapatha:**
**He. Rejoice. Indeed. According to. Pleasure. Mighty. [Particle]. You. Sacrifices. These. Reach. [Particle]. These. Invocations. Called by many. To us. Toward. You. This. Prayer. For protection. Indra. Directed.** ॥ 8 ॥

## Commentary (Sayana)
O Indra, you of **mighty** <note>original: *ugra*</note> and uplifted strength, **rejoice** <note>original: *mandasva*</note> in a way that is **according to your pleasure** <note>original: *anu joṣam*</note> or desire. <note>The word "hi" is a verse-filler; its presence causes a specific grammatical accentuation in the verb "rejoice."</note> May **these sacrifices** <note>original: *yagnāso*; referring here to the Soma libations</note> **reach** <note>original: *pra-aśnuvantu*</note> **you**. O **one called by many** <note>original: *puruhūta*; an epithet of Indra</note>, may **these invocations** <note>original: *havāsaḥ*; calls or hymns of praise</note> belonging **to us** reach you. May **this prayer** <note>original: *iyaṃ dhīḥ*; this act of meditation or praise</note> be **directed** <note>original: *yamyāḥ*; focused or brought toward</note> **toward you** for our **protection** <note>original: *avase*</note>. ॥ 8 ॥

<summary>This page contains verses 7 and 8 of Rig Veda 6.23, where the worshiper invites Indra to accept the sacrificial cake and Soma juice, asking for divine favor and protection. Sāyana's commentary explains the ritual context, such as the preparation of Soma with milk and the spreading of sacred grass.</summary>
