# ## 694 || Rig Veda || Book 4, Chapter 6, Section 17

## Hymn Text

-> ॥ Now the Ninth Verse ॥ <-

**O friends, fill that bountiful Indra with Soma juices when they are pressed, just as is required. May there be many means for our nourishment; for Indra does not neglect the vigorous worshiper who seeks his protection.** ॥ 9 ॥

**Padapatha:**
**That. Your. Friends. Completely. Just as. In the pressed [juices]. With Somas. Him. Fill. The bountiful. Indra.**
**Many. For him. May it be. Our. For nourishment. Not. The vigorous. Indra. For protection. Neglects.** ॥ 9 ॥

---

## Commentary (Sayana)

O **friends** <note>original: *sakhāyaḥ*; here referring to the chanters or priests</note>, you who are the praisers, fill this **bountiful** <note>original: *bhojam*; the giver of rewards</note> Indra with **Soma juices** <note>original: *somebhiḥ*</note> according to his desire when they have been **pressed** <note>original: *suteṣu*</note>. Let there be **many** <note>original: *kuvit*; a term meaning manifold or much</note> resources or offerings for that Indra. For what purpose? For **our nourishment** <note>original: *bharāya*; for supporting or sustaining us</note>. Indra does **not neglect** <note>original: *na mṛdhāti*; does not ignore or harm</note> the **vigorous** <note>original: *suṣmim*; the diligent sacrificer who is intent on the pressing of the juice</note> worshiper who seeks **protection** <note>original: *avase*; for the sake of satisfaction or guarding</note>.

---

## Hymn Text

-> ॥ Now the Tenth Verse ॥ <-

**Thus indeed was Indra praised when the Soma was pressed among the Bharadvajas, that he, the lord of the wealthy, might be a guide for the singer and the giver of wealth that is desired by all.** ॥ 10 ॥

**Padapatha:**
**Thus. Indeed. Indra. In the pressed. Was praised. Soma. Among the Bharadvajas. Ruling. Indeed. Of the wealthy.**
**May he be. Just as. For the singer. And. The guide. Indra. Of wealth. Desired by all. The giver.** ॥ 10 ॥

---

## Commentary (Sayana)

Indra, who is the **ruler** <note>original: *kṣayan*; the lord or master</note> of the **wealthy** <note>original: *maghonaḥ*; the sacrificers who possess oblations</note>, was **thus praised** <note>original: *evam astāvi*</note> among the **Bharadvajas** <note>original: *bharadvājeṣu*; the clan of the seer Bharadvaja</note> when the Soma was **pressed** <note>original: *sute*</note>. The connection of the prayer is: may Indra be a **guide** <note>original: *sūriḥ*; one who impels others toward the right path</note> for the **singer** <note>original: *jaritre*</note>, and furthermore, may he be the **giver** <note>original: *dātā*</note> of **wealth** <note>original: *rāyaḥ*</note> that is **desired by all** <note>original: *viśvavārasya*</note>. The two instances of the word "it" <note>original: *it*; a particle</note> are used for poetic completion of the meter.

-> **॥ This concludes the sixteenth group of the sixth chapter of the fourth book ॥** <-
-> **॥ This concludes the second lesson of the sixth mandala ॥** <-

In the third **lesson** <note>original: *anuvāka*</note>, there are twenty hymns. Among them, the first hymn beginning with **"The bull-like, the intoxicating"** <note>original: *vṛṣā mada*</note> consists of ten verses; its **seer** <note>original: *ṛṣi*</note> is Bharadvaja, its meter is **Trishtubh** <note>original: *traiṣṭubha*; a meter of 44 syllables</note>, and its deity is Indra. This is indicated in the **index** <note>original: *anukrānta*</note> by the word "Vṛṣā." In the **solstice festival** <note>original: *viṣuvati*</note>, this hymn is used for the **Pure Cup** <note>term: *niṣkevalya*; a specific libation and chant dedicated exclusively to Indra</note> ceremony. This is also stated in the Ashvalayana Shrauta Sutra (8.6): "The bull-like, the intoxicating, for the most great..."

<meta>This page continues from the previous translation of Book 6, Hymn 23, transitioning into Hymn 24 of the same Book. This section belongs to the third "Lesson" (Anuvaka) of the sixth Mandala, as organized in the traditional eight-part (Ashtaka) system of the Rig Veda.</meta>

# ## 685 || Rig Veda || Book 6, Chapter 3, Hymn 24

-> ॥ Here is the first verse ॥ <-

## Hymn Text

**O Indra, the exhilaration of the Soma is a showerer of boons; the hymn and the recitations together are powerful. You are the drinker of the pressed juice, the consumer of the Soma-residue. The Lord of Wealth is to be worshiped by men with hymns—the heavenly king of songs, whose protection never fails.** ॥ 1 ॥

**Padapatha (Word-by-word analysis):**
**Showerer. Exhilaration. Indra. Hymn. Recitations. Together. In the Somas. Drinker of the pressed [juice]. Consumer of the Soma-residue.**
**Worthy of worship. Lord of Wealth. By men. With hymns. Dweller in heaven. King. Of songs. Undiminished protection.** ॥ 1 ॥

---

## Commentary (Sayanacharya)

In the sacrifices involving **Soma** <note>original: *someṣu*; the sacred ritual drink</note>, the intoxication produced in Indra by drinking the juice is the **showerer** <note>original: *vṛṣā*; literally "the bull," metaphorically the one who rains down or showers boons</note> of the sacrificer's desires. Alternatively, he is the one who causes the rain that delights all people. The **hymn** <note>original: *ślokaḥ*; the sound of praise</note> along with the "Ukthya" recitation <note>original: *ukthā*; a specific rhythmic chant</note> is also a showerer of rewards. Indra is the **drinker of the pressed juice** <note>original: *sutapā*</note> and the **consumer of the residue** <note>original: *ṛjīṣī*; one who accepts even the *ṛjīṣa*, the stalks left after the juice is pressed</note>. This **Lord of Wealth** <note>original: *maghavā*</note> is **worthy of worship** <note>original: *archyo*</note> by **men** <note>original: *nṛbhyaḥ*; here meaning the leaders of the hymns</note> through their songs. Indra, the **heavenly dweller** <note>original: *dyukṣo*</note> and **Lord** <note>original: *rājā*</note> of the **songs** <note>original: *girāṃ*</note> of praise, possesses **undiminished protection** <note>original: *akṣitotiḥ*; his guarding power never decays</note>.

---

-> ॥ Now the second verse ॥ <-

## Hymn Text

**The conqueror, the hero, friendly to men, the wise one, the hearer of the call of the singer, he of wide protection. The source of wealth, the praised of men, the sustainer of poets—the powerful one, when praised in the assembly, grants us strength.** ॥ 2 ॥

**Padapatha (Word-by-word analysis):**
**Conqueror. Hero. Friendly to men. Possessor of distinct knowledge. Hearer. Call. Of the singer. Wide protection.**
**Source of wealth. Praise. Of men. Sustainer of poets. Powerful. Praised. In the assembly. He gives. Strength (or food).** ॥ 2 ॥

---

## Commentary (Sayanacharya)

The **powerful** <note>original: *vājī*; one possessing food or strength</note> Indra, being **praised** <note>original: *stutaḥ*</note> by us in the **assembly** <note>original: *vidathe*; the sacrificial gathering</note>, **grants strength** <note>original: *dāti vājam*; gives us food or vital force</note>. What kind of Indra? He is the **conqueror** <note>original: *taturiḥ*; the destroyer of enemies</note>, the **hero** <note>original: *vīro*; the valiant one</note>, the one **friendly to men** <note>original: *naryo*</note>, the **wise one** <note>original: *vicetā*; having discriminating knowledge</note>, and the **hearer** <note>original: *śrotā*</note> of our **call** <note>original: *havam*; our hymn</note>. He provides **wide protection** <note>original: *urvyūtiḥ*; vast or extended safety</note> for the **singer** <note>original: *gṛṇataḥ*; the one praising him</note>. He is the **source of wealth** <note>original: *vasuḥ*; one who enables people to dwell comfortably</note>, the **praise of men** <note>original: *nṛṇāṃ śaṃsaḥ*; the one to be celebrated by human beings</note>, and the **sustainer of poets** <note>original: *kārudhāyāḥ*; the supporter of the singers and makers of hymns</note>. The connection is that an Indra of such qualities grants us strength.

---

-> ॥ Now the third verse ॥ <-

## Hymn Text

**O hero, you are great like the axle between two wheels; you exceed both heaven and earth in majesty. O much-invoked Indra, your many protections have spread out like the branches of a tree.** ॥ 3 ॥

**Padapatha (Word-by-word analysis):**
**Axle. Like. Of two wheels. Hero. Great. Forward. Your. In majesty. He exceeded. Of heaven and earth.**
**Of a tree. Indeed. Your. Much-invoked. Branches. Out. Protections. They have grown. Indra. Many.** ॥ 3 ॥

<margin>
VOLUME III. &nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp; 8 M
</margin>

<vocab>
**Showerer of boons / powerful** <note>original: *vṛṣā*</note>
**One who receives the soma-residue (ṛjīṣa)** <note>original: *ṛjīṣin*</note>

# ## 686 || Rig Veda || [Ashtaka 4, Adhyaya 6, Varga 17]

O Heroic, Powerful Indra! O Great One! Your **greatness** <note>original: mahimā</note> exceeds the two worlds of **Heaven and Earth** <note>original: rodasyor-dyāvāpṛthivyoḥ</note>. That is to say, you are greater than both. An illustration is given here: **Like the axle of two wheels** <note>original: cakrayora-akṣo na</note>. Just as the axle belonging to a chariot extends outward beyond the two wheels, so do you exceed the worlds. O **Indra, invoked by many** <note>original: puruhūta</note>, your ancient and numerous **protections** <note>original: ūtayo</note> grow forth abundantly. They grow specifically in various ways. An illustration for this: **Like those of a tree** <note>original: vṛkṣasya nu</note>. Just as the branches of a tree grow out, so do your protections.

---

-> ॥ Here is the Fourth Verse ॥ <-

## Hymn Text
**O Much-performing Indra, the powers of you, the wise one, are all-pervading like the paths of cows. Like the tethering-ropes of calves, O Indra, your powers are binding [to enemies], O Bountiful Giver, while you remain unbound yourself.** ॥ 4 ॥

**Padapatha (Word-by-word analysis):**
**Of the powerful one. Your. O Much-performing one. Powers. Like of cows. Paths. All-pervading.**
**Of calves. Like. Tethering-ropes. Your. Indra. Having bonds. Unbound. O Bountiful Giver.** ॥ 4 ॥

## Commentary (Sayanacharya)
O **Much-performing Indra** <note>original: puruśāka; one who performs many deeds</note>, the **powers** <note>original: śākāḥ; also meaning actions</note> of you, the **wise one** <note>original: śacīvataḥ</note>, move everywhere. Here is an illustration: **Like the paths of cows** <note>original: gavām-iva sutayaḥ</note>. Just as the paths of milch-cows are all-pervading and go everywhere, so are your deeds. Furthermore, **like the tethering-ropes of calves** <note>original: vatsānām na tantayaḥ</note>. A **tethering-rope** <term>tanti: a long rope to which many smaller cords are attached for tying several calves at once</term> is a long, stretched rope. Just as these ropes are the binders of many calves, O **Bountiful Giver** <note>original: sudāman</note> Indra, your powers are **possessors of bonds** <note>original: dāmanvantaḥ</note>—meaning they bind your many enemies—while you yourself are **unbound** <note>original: adamānaḥ</note>, not tied down by others.

---

-> ॥ Here is the Fifth Verse ॥ <-

## Hymn Text
**Indra performs one deed today and another different deed tomorrow. He repeatedly performs both the inauspicious and the auspicious. Mitra, Varuna, Pushan, and Aryaman are our [protectors] here; he is the encompasser of our will.** ॥ 5 ॥

**Padapatha (Word-by-word analysis):**
**Another. Today. Deed. Another. Indeed. Tomorrow. The inauspicious (non-being). And. The auspicious (being). Repeatedly. Performer. Indra.**
**Mitra. Our. Here. Varuna. And. Pushan. Aryaman. Of will. Encompasser. Is.** ॥ 5 ॥

## Commentary (Sayanacharya)
This Indra performs **one deed** <note>original: karvaram; a name for action</note> **today**, on this day. He performs **another** <note>original: anyad-u</note> different deed **tomorrow**, on the following day. This is further explained: **the inauspicious** <note>original: asat; literally "non-being" or "unreal"</note>, such as the striking of the thunderbolt, and **the auspicious** <note>original: sat; literally "being" or "real"</note>, such as the bringing of rain and other good works. Alternatively, the "inauspicious" refers to deeds like the slaying of the three-headed Vishvarupa, while the "auspicious" refers to the slaying of the demon Vritra who oppressed the world. This Indra is the **repeated performer** <note>original: ācakriḥ</note> of such deeds again and again. In this way, performing mutually distinct...

<vocab>
- **Śacīvat** (śacīvat): Possessed of power or wisdom.
- **Puruśāka** (puruśāka): Much-performing; one who does many powerful deeds.
- **Karvaram** (karvaram): A deed or religious action.
- **Sudāman** (sudāman): A bountiful or excellent giver.
- **Tanti** (tanti): A long tethering rope used to secure multiple animals.
- **Adamānaḥ** (adamānaḥ): Unbound, untamed, or not subject to others' control.
- **Ācakriḥ** (ācakriḥ): A frequent or repetitive doer/performer.
</vocab>

# ## 687 || Rig Veda || [Ashtaka 4, Adhyaya 6, Varga 17-18]

## Commentary (Sayanacharya)
[Continuation of commentary for Mandala 6, Sukta 24, Verse 5]

Indra, by his own greatness, repeats his deeds again and again, performing unique and extraordinary actions every single day. Such an Indra is the **attainer** <note>original: paryaitā; one who causes one to reach or obtain</note> of the fruit we desire in this sacrifice, such as **Heaven** <note>original: svargādeḥ</note>. <note>Grammatical note: The word "asleḥ" is a form in the lit (perfect) tense.</note> May Mitra (the deity presiding over the day), Varuna (the deity presiding over the night/sovereignty), Pushan (the nourisher), and Aryaman (the impeller/Savita)—all being regulated by the **Moon** <note>original: candreṇa; likely referring to the lunar cycles or Soma</note>—be the ones who lead us to the fulfillment of our desires. Alternatively, Mitra and the others are mentioned here in their own right. May Mitra and the others, and Indra, each individually be the attainers of our desires. As stated in the **Brihaddevata** <note>term: Brihaddevata; an ancient catalog of the deities of the Rig Veda hymns</note>: <term>protye’nyad-iti</term> "These two verses are remembered as being dedicated to the **Universal Gods** <note>term: Vishvedevas; a group of various deities invoked together</note>."

-> ॥ This concludes the seventeenth Varga of the sixth Adhyaya of the fourth Ashtaka ॥ <-

---

## Hymn Text
-> ॥ Here is the Sixth Verse ॥ <-

<note>RV 6.24.6</note>
**O Indra, like waters flowing from the summit of a mountain, the worshippers have directed their prayers to you through hymns and sacrifices. Like horses reaching the prize in a race, the singers, desiring strength, have reached you with these beautiful praises, O you who are carried by songs!** ॥ 6 ॥

**Pada-patha (Word-by-word analysis):**
**Away. You. Waters. Like. Of a mountain. From the back/summit. With hymns. Indra. They led. With sacrifices.**
**Him. You. With these. With beautiful praises. Desiring strength/food. The prize/race. Like. They went. O carrier of songs. Horses.** ॥ 6 ॥

## Commentary (Sayanacharya)
O Indra, the worshippers have brought forth their desires from you through **Ukthas** <note>term: Ukthas; specific recited verses or "shastras"</note> and **sacrifices** <note>original: yajñaiḥ</note> consisting of oblations. They cause these desires to be attained in various ways. An illustration is provided: **Like waters from the back of a mountain** <note>original: parvatasyādreḥ pṛṣṭhād-āpo na</note>; just as water flows down from the heights, so do these prayers flow. Furthermore, O **carrier of songs** <note>original: girvāhaḥ; Indra, who is "carried" or pleased by songs of praise</note>, the singers of the **Bharadvaja** <note>term: Bharadvaja; the family of seers to whom this book of the Rig Veda is attributed</note> clan, making you strong or desiring food for themselves, have reached you—the famous one—with these aforementioned beautiful praises. An illustration for their swift approach: **Like horses reaching the race** <note>original: ājiṃ na; refers to a battle-line or a prize-competition</note>; just as swift horses quickly reach the goal, so do these songs reach you.

---

## Hymn Text
-> ॥ Here is the Seventh Verse ॥ <-

<note>RV 6.24.7</note>
**Neither the passing years, nor the months, nor the days make Indra grow old or diminish him. May his body, which is already vast, grow even further, being celebrated by songs and recited hymns.** ॥ 7 ॥

**Pada-patha (Word-by-word analysis):**
**Not. Whom. They age. The autumns/years. Not. The months. Not. The heavens/days. Indra. They cause to diminish.**
**Of the one who is already great. Even. Let it grow. His. Body. With songs of praise. With recited hymns. And. Being celebrated.** ॥ 7 ॥

## Commentary (Sayanacharya)
The **autumns** <note>original: śaradaḥ; used metaphorically for years</note> do not age this Indra, they do not cause him to decay or waste away. Likewise, the months do not diminish him. Similarly, the **heavens** <note>original: dyāvaḥ; here meaning the passing days</note> do not make Indra small or cause him to waste away... <note>The text breaks off here and continues on the next page.</note>

<summary>This page describes Indra as an eternal being unaffected by time (years, months, or days) and illustrates how the prayers of the Bharadvaja clan reach him as swiftly as racing horses or falling water.</summary>

# ## 688 || Rig Veda || [Book 4, Chapter 6, Section 18]

The body of Indra—who is already ancient and greatly powerful—should be further strengthened by our **hymns** <note>original: stomebhiḥ; songs of praise</note> and **recitations** <note>original: ukthaiḥ; poetic verses recited during the sacrifice</note> as he is being praised. May his form become truly vast.

---

-> ॥ Here is the Eighth Verse ॥ <-

## Hymn Text
He does not bow to the strong, nor to the firm, nor to the arrogant who is incited by the **Dasyus** <note>term: Dasyu; enemies of the Vedic people who do not perform the sacred rituals</note>, even while being praised. To Indra, even the high mountains are like level plains; even in the deep, there becomes a **ford** <note>original: gādham; a shallow place or firm standing ground</note> for him. ॥ 8 ॥

**Word-by-word Breakdown:**
Not. To the strong. He bows. Not. To the firm. Not. To the arrogant. To the one incited by the Dasyus. Being praised.
Plains/Fields. Of Indra. The mountains. Even. High. In the deep. Even. There becomes. A ford. For him. ॥ 8 ॥

## Commentary (Sayana)
Indra, when being praised by us, does not bow to a worshipper who relies only on his own "strong limbs." He does not submit to one who is merely stubborn or unyielding in battle. Nor does he yield to a patron of the sacrifice who is enthusiastic but driven by the impulses of the **Dasyus**—those who have abandoned sacred works. The meaning is that even if praisers possess many qualities, Indra does not come under the control of those who side with the enemies of the ritual. Furthermore, even the great and high mountains become like **easy paths** <note>original: sugamanāḥ; places easy to traverse</note> for Indra, to be cast aside at will. Even in a deep, bottomless place, a firm standing ground or subject of focus appears for Indra.

---

-> ॥ Here is the Ninth Verse ॥ <-

## Hymn Text
With a deep and wide mind, O **Mighty One** <note>term: Amatrin; an epithet meaning one who possesses 'amatra' or strength</note>, grant us food and **treasures** <note>original: vājān; often referring to the spoils of war or vital strength</note>, O drinker of the pressed Soma. Stand firm and upright for our protection, without failing us, at the **breaking of the dawn** <note>original: aktoḥ vyuṣṭau</note> and during the **night's transition** <note>original: paritakmyāyām</note>. ॥ 9 ॥

**Word-by-word Breakdown:**
With the deep. To us. With the wide. O Mighty One. Forward. Foods. Grant. O drinker of the pressed Soma. Treasures/Strengths.
Stand. Indeed. Well. Upright. For protection. Not harming/failing. Of the night. In the dawning. In the night's wandering. ॥ 9 ॥

## Commentary (Sayana)
O Mighty One! (The word *amatra* means strength; therefore, you who possess it). O **drinker of the pressed Soma** <note>term: Sutapāvan; a title for Indra as the consumer of the sacred Soma juice</note>, Indra! With a mind that is deep—unfathomable to others—and wide, grant to us **foods** <note>original: iṣaḥ</note> and **strengths** <note>original: vājān</note>. Moreover, at the dawning of the night (at daybreak) and during the wandering period of the night, O Indra, for our protection, stand well-prepared and upright, without harming or failing us.

---

-> ॥ Here is the Tenth Verse ॥ <-

## Hymn Text
Stay with us for our protection in the **face-to-face encounter** <note>original: abhīke; refers to the presence of the deity or the heat of battle</note>. Protect that singer, O Indra, from harm from this side or that. Protect him from harm at home and in the forest. May we rejoice for **a hundred winters** <note>note: a traditional Vedic idiom for a long life of a hundred years</note>, blessed with heroic sons. ॥ 10 ॥

---

<summary>This page describes Indra’s refusal to submit to the arrogant or those who do not follow the sacred law, emphasizing his power to turn obstacles like mountains and deep waters into easy paths. The verses conclude with a prayer for protection throughout the day and night and a wish for a long, prosperous life.</summary>

# ## 689 || Rig Veda || [Book 6, Chapter 3, Section 25]

## Hymn Text
<note>RV 6.24.10 Padapatha — word-by-word breakdown</note>
Accompany. This leader. For protection. In the encounter. From here. Or. Him. Indra. Protect. From the injurer. At home. And. Him. In the forest. Protect. From the injurer. May we rejoice. For a hundred winters. Possessing good sons. ॥ 10 ॥

---

## Commentary (Sayana)
<note>Commentary on RV 6.24.10</note>
O Indra, favor this leader of rituals and songs of praise in the encounter <note>original: abhīke; meaning the battle or meeting</note> for the sake of protection. Serve him. Protect that singer from the enemy who is near <note>original: itah; from here</note> or from the one who is far away and high above. The word "or" <note>original: vā</note> implies a combination of both the stated and the intended enemies. O Indra, protect that praiser. Protect him. Likewise, protect him from the enemy at home <note>original: amā; a name for the home</note> and in the forest <note>original: araṇye; in the wilderness</note>. Guard him. After that, may we, possessing excellent sons, rejoice <note>original: madema; feel great joy</note> for a hundred winters <note>original: śatahimāḥ; meaning a full lifespan of a hundred years</note>. ॥

->॥ This concludes the eighteenth section of the sixth chapter of the fourth book ॥<-

---

<note>Introduction to Sukta 25</note>
The second hymn, beginning with "Whatever protection of yours" <note>original: yā ta ūtiḥ</note>, consists of nine verses. It was seen by the **Rishi** <note>term: Rishi; the inspired seer who "saw" or composed the hymn</note> Bharadvaja, is in the **Trishtubh** meter <note>term: Trishtubh; a poetic meter of 11 syllables per line</note>, and is dedicated to Indra. It is described in the index as: "Whatever your nine." In the six-day ritual cycles of **Prishthya** and **Abhiplava**, this hymn is used for the recitation of the **Nishkevalya** <note>term: Nishkevalya; a specific midday chant dedicated solely to Indra</note> during the second day. This is indicated in the **Ashvalayana Shrauta Sutra** (7.6): "The verse 'Whatever protection of yours is lowest' belongs to the midday."

## Hymn Text
->॥ Here is the first verse ॥<-
<note>RV 6.25.1</note>
Whatever protection of yours is lowest, whatever is highest, whatever is middle, O mighty Indra; with those, favor us well in the slaying of **Vritra** <note>note: Vritra was the dragon/demon of drought; "Vritra-hatya" refers to the battle to release the waters</note>. And with these spoils of war, O exalted one, make us great. ॥ 1 ॥

<note>Padapatha — word-by-word breakdown</note>
Whatever. Your. Protection. Lowest. Whatever. Highest. Whatever. Middle. Indra. Powerful one. Is.
With those. Indeed. Well. In the slaying of Vritra. Protect. Us. With these. And. Foods/Spoils. Great. Us. Exalted one. ॥ 1 ॥

---

## Commentary (Sayana)
<note>Commentary on RV 6.25.1</note>
O powerful Indra, whatever protection—your act of guarding—is lowest, whatever is highest or most excellent, and whatever is middle: with those protections, protect <note>original: avīḥ; preserve or favor</note> us perfectly in the slaying of Vritra, which is to say, in battle. Furthermore, O fierce and exalted Indra, you who are great, join us with these **Vajas** <note>term: Vaja; often meaning "spoils of war" or "nourishing food"</note> which are the means of our sustenance. ॥

---

## Hymn Text
->॥ Now the second verse ॥<-
<note>RV 6.25.2</note>
With these protections, Indra, harming the contending rivals, distress the fury of the enemy. With these, subdue all the attacking, dispersing **Dasa** <note>term: Dasa; groups often described as the enemies of the Arya</note> tribes for the sake of the **Arya** <note>term: Arya; the noble performers of the Vedic rituals</note>. ॥ 2 ॥

<note>Padapatha — word-by-word breakdown</note>
With these. Rivals. Contending. Harming. Of the enemy. Distress. The fury. Indra.
With these. All. Attacking. Dispersing. For the Arya. The tribes. Down. Strike. The Dasa ones. ॥ 2 ॥

<vocab>
- Indra: The primary king of the gods, associated with storms and war.
- Shushmin: A title meaning "The Mighty" or "The Powerful."
- Bharadvaja: The ancestral seer of the Bharadvaja family, credited with this book of the Rig Veda.
- Trishtubh: One of the most common Vedic meters, consisting of four lines of 11 syllables.
- Vritra-hatya: Literally "the killing of Vritra"; a metaphor for overcoming obstacles or winning battles.
- Uti: Divine assistance, protection, or aid.
- Shatahimah: A prayer for longevity, literally "lasting a hundred winters."
</vocab>

## 690 || Rig Veda || [Ashtaka 4, Adhyaya 4, Varga 19]

## Commentary (Sayana) — Continued
<note>This concludes the commentary on verse 2</note>
O Indra, with these our praises, protect our armies while harming the clashing <note>original: mithatīḥ</note> enemy armies. Do not let them be injured; this is the meaning of protection. Destroy the anger <note>original: manyu</note> of the enemy that is present in battles and similar struggles. Furthermore, with these very same praises, cause all the attacking <note>original: abhiyujo</note>, scattered <note>original: viṣūcīḥ</note>, and ritual-destroying <note>term: Dasa; here interpreted by Sayana as "karmāṇāmupakṣapayitrīr," or those who cause the decay of sacred acts</note> people to submit to the **Arya** <note>term: Arya; here defined as the "yajamāna," the noble patron who performs the sacrifices and rituals</note>. Destroy them.

---

->॥ The Third Verse ॥<-

## Hymn Text
Whether they are kinsmen <note>original: jāmayaḥ</note> or whether they are strangers <note>original: ajāmayaḥ</note>, those who come toward us as attackers and wish us harm: O Indra, shatter their failing strength and destroy their manly powers <note>original: vṛṣṇyāni</note>. Turn them back. ॥ 3 ॥

**Padapatha:**
Indra. Kinsmen. And. Those who. Strangers. Coming toward. Attackers. Have joined battle.
You. Of them. Failing. Strengths. Shatter. Manly powers. Make. Turning away. ॥ 3 ॥

## Commentary (Sayana)
O Indra, there are enemies who are relatives <note>original: jñātirūpāḥ</note> or near to us, and there are also enemies who are strangers living in distant lands. When these attackers face us with harmful intent, we pray that you make the strength belonging to both types of these enemies weak and failing. Likewise, destroy their manly powers and valor. Furthermore, make both types of these enemies turn their backs <note>original: parāṅmukhān</note> and flee.

---

->॥ The Fourth Verse ॥<-

## Hymn Text
The hero, with physical brilliance, conquers even a hero with his body when they contend in struggle. When they cry out <note>original: vi krandasi</note> for the sake of children, for cattle, for progeny, or for water in the fertile fields. ॥ 4 ॥

**Padapatha:**
The hero. Or. A hero. Conquers. With bodies. With physical brilliance. In struggle. When. They two perform.
For a son. Or. For cattle. For a grandson. When. For water. Apart. The two crying ones (Heaven and Earth). In fertile fields. They two speak. ॥ 4 ॥

## Commentary (Sayana)
O Indra, a warrior favored by you conquers—that is, kills—even a hero with his own limbs and body. The word "or" <note>original: vā</note> is used here in the sense of "even." Alternatively, the word "or" suggests another possibility: that even one who is not a natural hero can conquer a hero if he is favored by you. When does he conquer? He explains this next: When two opposing sides, shining with physical strength, engage in battle <note>original: taruṣi</note> with one another. And when they contend for the sake of sons, or for the sake of cattle, or for the sake of grandsons, or for water—

<vocab>
Indra (King of the gods), Kinsmen (jāmayaḥ), Strangers (ajāmayaḥ), Hero/Warrior (śūra), Manly powers (vṛṣṇyāni), Battle/struggle (taruṣi), The two crying worlds/Heaven and Earth (krandasī), Fertile fields (urvarāsu)
</vocab>

[Mantra 6. Section 3. Hymn 25.] || Fourth Book || 691

<note>This is the conclusion of the commentary for verse 4, which discussed the various types of land or conditions over which battles are fought.</note>
...in the causes [of battle], on the fertile fields, or on all kinds of primary lands, when the two armies <note>original: krandasī; literally 'the two crying out,' usually referring to Heaven and Earth, but here interpreted as opposing forces</note> shouting and crying out, speak against each other or dispute. O Indra, the meaning is that the gain of sons and similar blessings, as well as victory, belongs to the one favored by you.

## Hymn Text

-> ॥ The Fifth Verse ॥ <-

No hero, no swift attacker, no daring one has ever fought you; no warrior, even when filled with wrath, has ever fought you, O Indra. None among these is your equal. You overpower all born beings. ॥ 5 ॥

**Word-by-word Analysis:**
Not. Indeed. You. Hero. Not. Swift. Not. Daring. Not. You. Warrior. Thinking [himself angry]. Fought.
Indra. None. You. Against [equal to]. Is. Of these. All. Born beings. Overpower. Are. Them. ॥ 5 ॥

## Commentary (Sayana)

O Indra, no hero—a person of great prowess—has ever fought with you; that is, they do not fight. Likewise, no swift one <note>original: turaḥ</note>—one who injures other enemies—fights with you. No daring assailant <note>original: dhṛṣṇuḥ</note> fights you. No warrior <note>original: yodhaḥ</note> or soldier, even when becoming enraged <note>original: manyamānaḥ</note> in battle, fights with you. O Indra, among all these heroes and others, there is none <note>original: nakiḥ</note> who is your counterpart or rival <note>original: pratyasti</note>; there is no equal to you. You overpower <note>original: abhyasi</note> all born beings <note>original: viśvā jātāni</note>, meaning you overcome all those heroes and creatures.

-> ॥ Thus ends the nineteenth section of the fourth chapter of the fourth book ॥ <-

---

## Hymn Text

-> ॥ The Sixth Verse ॥ <-

He rules over the wealth of both sides when the wise priests invoke him in the assembly; whether in a great enclosure or in a dwelling full of men, when the two spacious ones are spread out in conflict. ॥ 6 ॥

**Word-by-word Analysis:**
He. Rules. Of both. Wealth. Of two. When. Priests. In the assembly/battle. Invoke.
In an enclosure. Or. Great. Full of men. In a dwelling. Or. The two spacious ones. When. They are spread out. ॥ 6 ॥

## Commentary (Sayana)

Between the two <note>original: ayoḥ; referring to the two parties or sides</note>, that person <note>the one who praises Indra</note> rules over <note>original: patyate</note> or possesses the wealth <note>term: nṛmṇam; Sayana glosses this as 'dhana' or wealth, though it literally means 'manly strength'</note>. The poet describes between whom and where this person rules: when <note>original: yadi</note> for a particular person—the particle *yadi* here is used in the sense of 'for whom'—the priests <note>original: vedhasaḥ</note>, who are the performers of the sacred rites, invoke <note>original: havante</note> or praise Indra in the assembly or sacrifice <note>original: samithe</note>, that person becomes the master of wealth. This applies whether in a great <note>original: mahaḥ</note> enclosure <note>original: vṛce; interpreted here as a restriction or a penned-in area for cattle</note> or in a dwelling <note>original: kṣaye</note> filled with servants and men <note>original: nṛvati</note>. When the two <note>referring to two people or two armies</note> who are spacious or expansive <note>original: vyacasvantā</note> are spread out <note>original: vitantasete</note> or separated from each other in conflict. 

<note>Sayana provides a grammatical note: The word 'vitantasete' comes from the root 'tas,' meaning 'to exhaust or decay,' preceded by the prefix 'vi'. Alternatively, it is a form from the root 'tantas' found in the Kandvadi group of verbs.</note>

<vocab>
**Indra**: The king of the gods and patron of warriors.
**Shura**: A hero or valiant person.
**Yodha**: A combatant or soldier.
**Nrumnam**: Strength or wealth; that which belongs to a 'man' (nṛ).
**Vedhas**: A wise person or a priest who arranges the sacrifice.
**Samitha**: A coming together, which can mean an assembly for a sacrifice or a battle.
**Vrica**: An enclosure or an obstacle.
**Kshaya**: A place of residence or a home.
</vocab>

[Rig Veda] || [Book 4, Chapter 6, Class 20] || 692

->॥ The Seventh Verse ॥<-

## Hymn Text
And then your subjects, whenever they tremble [with fear], O Indra, be their **protector** and also their **defender**. Those who are our best leaders, the noble ones who have placed you, O Indra, before us as our patrons—[be their protector]. ॥ 7 ॥

**Word-by-word Analysis:**
And then. Indeed. Your. Subjects [people]. When. Tremble. Indra. Protector. And. Be. Defender.
Ours. Who. Best of men [leaders]. Noble. Indra. Wise ones [patrons/priests]. Placed. Forward. Us. ॥ 7 ॥

---

## Commentary (Sayana)
**And then** <note>original: adha sma</note> even also, O Indra, **your subjects**—meaning your men or people—**whenever they tremble** <note>original: yad ejān</note>, that is, whenever they might shake or quiver out of fear, may you become their **protector** <note>original: chātā; interpreted as pālakaḥ</note>. **And also** <note>original: utāpi ca</note> be their **defender** <note>original: varūtā; meaning one who covers or supports</note>. **Ours**, meaning those belonging to us, the **best of men** or the highest leaders, those men who, O Indra, [are] the **noble ones** <note>original: aryaḥ</note>—meaning those who cause us to reach you—be their protector. O Indra, the **wise ones** <note>original: sūrayo</note> who are the chanters of praise and have **placed us forward**, meaning they have prioritized us; be their protector as well.

In the **Sakamedha** <note>a specific seasonal ritual within the Four-Month sacrifices</note>, this verse serves as the offering prayer <note>term: yājyā; the verse recited as the oblation is poured</note> for the Great Indra and Agni, or specifically for Indra the slayer of Vritra. This is indicated in the ritual manuals: "Power has been granted to you for your great lordship... [by] Vishvakarman, growing by the oblation." (Ashvalayana Shrauta Sutra 2.18). Likewise, in the one-day sacrifice called **Anukri**, during the **Nishkevalya** <note>a specific midday libation to Indra</note> portion, this very verse begins the hymn. This is also indicated: "Power has been granted to you for your great lordship... and 'How may I serve you, O Wise One?'—these are the two verses." (Ashvalayana Shrauta Sutra 9.5).

->॥ This is the Eighth Verse of the Hymn ॥<-

## Hymn Text
Power has been granted to you for your great lordship; all things were truly granted to you in the slaying of Vritra. Strength and might were granted [to you], O Indra, worthy of sacrifice, by all the gods in the conquest of enemies. ॥ 8 ॥

**Word-by-word Analysis:**
Granted. To you. Was given. For the Great. Power [lordship]. Truly. To you. All. After. In the slaying of Vritra.
After. Sovereignty. After. Might. O Worthy of Sacrifice. Indra. By the gods. After. To you. In the conquest of men. ॥ 8 ॥

---

## Commentary (Sayana)
O Indra, **for your great power**, meaning for the sake of your sovereign lordship, it was **granted** <note>original: anudāyi; literally 'was given following/according to'</note> to you. In the **slaying of Vritra**, for the purpose of killing that demon, **all** things were **truly** <note>original: satrā; meaning 'in truth'</note> granted to you. He explains what was granted and by whom: that **sovereignty** or strength by which he supports the universe was granted; that **might** or strength characterized by those qualities by which he overcomes enemies was granted. O **Worthy of Sacrifice** <note>original: yajatra</note> Indra, in the **conquest of men** <note>original: nṛṣahye; referring to battle</note>, all this was granted to you **by the gods**, meaning by all the divine beings together.

<vocab>
- **Indra**: The king of the gods and the primary deity of this hymn.
- **Chātā**: A protector or one who dispels fear.
- **Varūtā**: A defender or one who provides shelter.
- **Sūrayaḥ**: The patrons or wise priests who organize the sacrifice.
- **Vṛtra-hatye**: The mythic battle where Indra slays Vritra, the demon of drought/obstruction.
- **Nṛṣahye**: A term for battle, literally "the overcoming of men."
- **Yajatra**: An epithet for a deity worthy of receiving sacrificial offerings.
- **Sakamedha**: The third of the four-month (Chaturmasya) sacrifices, dedicated to various gods including Indra.
- **Nishkevalya**: A specific chant or cup of Soma offered exclusively to Indra at the midday pressing.
</vocab>

The commentary explains that Indra's supreme power and strength were collectively bestowed upon him by all the gods specifically for the task of slaying the demon Vritra.</summary>

## Hymn Text
->॥ The Ninth Verse ॥<-

Thus, O Indra, drive together our rivals in battles; subdue the godless, deceptive [armies]. May we, the **Bharadvajas**, praising you, surely find a dwelling place with your protection and sustenance. ॥ 9 ॥

---

## Commentary (Sayana)
**Word-by-word Analysis:**
Thus. Our. Rivals. Together. Drive. In battles. Indra. Subdue. Deceptive. Godless.
May we find. Of a dwelling. With protection/sustenance. Praising. The Bharadvajas. And. Your. Indra. Surely. ॥ 9 ॥

**Interpretation:**
O **Indra**, you who are praised in **this manner** <note>original: evam</note>, **drive together** <note>original: samaja; drive or impel for the sake of killing</note> **our rivals** <note>original: spṛdhaḥ; enemy armies</note> **in battles** <note>original: samatsu</note>. Furthermore, **subdue** <note>original: rarandhi; bring under our control</note> the **deceptive** <note>original: mithitīḥ; those who cause harm</note> and **godless** <note>original: adevīḥ; demonic or ungodly</note> armies. **And also** <note>original: utāpi ca</note>, O Indra, may **we**, the **Bharadvajas** <note>the family of the seer Bharadvaja</note> who are **praising** you, **surely** <note>original: nūnam</note> **find** or obtain a **dwelling place** <note>original: vastoḥ vāsam; a place to reside</note> along **with protection** <note>original: avasā; specifically implying food or sustenance that protects</note>.

->॥ Thus ends the twentieth Class (Varga) of the sixth Chapter of the fourth Book ॥<-

---

The third hymn [of this section], beginning "Hear us, O Indra" <note>original: śrudhī na indra</note>, consists of eight verses. The seer is **Bharadvaja**, the meter is **Trishtubh**, and the deity is **Indra**. As stated in the Index: "Hear us, eight [verses]" <note>original: śrudhī no'ṣṭāviti</note>. Its application is according to its characteristics <note>original: laiṅgikaḥ; used in rituals where the text's meaning fits the action</note>.

## Hymn Text
->॥ The First Verse [of Sukta 27] ॥<-

Hear us, O Indra! We call upon you for the acquisition of great wealth, you who are showered [with Soma]. When the people meet together in the contest for heroes, grant us formidable protection on the decisive day. ॥ 1 ॥

---

## Commentary (Sayana)
**Word-by-word Analysis:**
Hear. Our. Indra. We call. You. Of great. Of wealth/food. In the acquisition. Showered [with Soma].
Together. When. People. Met. In the contest for heroes. Formidable. Our. Protection. On the decisive. Day. Grant. ॥ 1 ॥

**Interpretation:**
O **Indra**, we, the chanters, **shower you** <note>original: vavṛṣāṇaḥ; literally "raining" or saturating the deity with Soma offerings</note> with Soma-juice and **call upon you** <note>original: hvayāmasi</note> for the **acquisition** <note>original: sātau</note> of **great wealth** or food <note>original: maho mahato vājasya</note>. O Indra, **hear** <note>original: śrudhi</note> this call of **ours**. **Whenever** <note>original: yad</note> **people** <note>original: viśo janāḥ</note> **meet together** <note>original: sam ayanta</note> in the **contest for heroes** <note>original: śūrasātā; a synonym for battle where heroes are "won" or proved</note>, then on that **decisive day** <note>original: pārye'hani; the "final" or "crossing" day of battle</note>, **grant** <note>term: adāḥ; give or provide</note> **us formidable** <note>original: ugram; powerful/elevated</note> **protection**.

---

## Hymn Text
->॥ The Second Verse ॥<-

The seeker of spoils calls to you, the son of the seeker of spoils, for the acquisition of great and desirable wealth. In the midst of enemies, O Indra, the fist-fighter, fighting for cattle, looks to you—the protector of the good and the overcomer [of foes]. ॥ 2 ॥

- Indra: The king of the gods, associated with storms and war.

## Hymn Text

**You, the vigorous one, the son of the vigorous, invokes in the capture of great, desirable wealth.**
**You, O Indra, the protector of the good, the rescuer; the fist-striker, fighting for cattle, beholds you. ॥ 2 ॥**

---

## Commentary (Sayana)

The **vigorous one** <note>original: vājī; one who possesses sacrificial food</note>, who is the **son of the vigorous** <note>original: vājineyaḥ; the son of Vajini, referring here to the seer Bharadvaja</note>, O Indra, **invokes** <note>original: havate; praises or calls upon</note> you for the purpose of the **attainment** <note>original: sātau</note> of **great** <note>original: mahaḥ</note> and **desirable wealth** <note>original: gadhyasya; wealth that is sought after or to be obtained by all</note>. Furthermore, O Indra, the **protector of the good** <note>original: sat-patim; the guardian of virtuous people</note> and the **rescuer** <note>original: tarutram; one who helps cross over or saves from wicked people</note>, Bharadvaja invokes you during **troubles** <note>original: vṛtreṣu; refers to obstacles or enemy attacks</note>. The **fist-striker** <note>original: muṣṭihā; one who kills enemies with the strength of his fists</note>, **fighting** <note>original: yudhyan</note> with enemies for the sake of **cattle** <note>original: goṣu</note>, **beholds** <note>original: caṣṭe; looks toward or meditates upon</note> you, O Indra, as his protector.

---

## Hymn Text

->॥ The Third Verse ॥<-

**You impelled the seer at the winning of the hymn; you struck down Shushna for the sake of the giver Kutsa.**
**You struck off the head of the invulnerable one, intending to perform a praiseworthy deed for Atithigva. ॥ 3 ॥**

**You. The seer. Impelled. At the winning of the hymn. You. For Kutsa. Shushna. The giver. Struck.**
**You. The head. Of the invulnerable one. Away. Struck. For Atithigva. Praiseworthy. Intending to perform. ॥ 3 ॥**

---

## Commentary (Sayana)

O Indra, you **impelled** <note>original: codayah; inspired or urged</note> the **seer** <note>original: kavim; referring to the sage Bhargava</note> for the purpose of **obtaining food** <note>original: arkasātau; literally "at the winning of the light/hymn," interpreted here as food resulting from worship</note>. Additionally, O Indra, you **struck down** <note>original: vak; a form meaning to cut or destroy</note> the demon **Shushna** <note>a drought-demon representing dehydration</note> for the sake of **Kutsa** <note>a favorite protégé of Indra</note>, who had **given offerings** <note>original: dāśuṣe</note>. 

Similarly, intending to **perform** <note>original: kariṣyan</note> a **praiseworthy** <note>original: śasyam; worthy of being sung</note> deed or to grant happiness to **Atithigva** <note>another name for King Divodasa, known for his hospitality to guests</note>, you **struck off** <note>original: parāhan; killed or struck away</note> the **head** <note>original: śiraḥ</note> of **Shambara** <note>a powerful mountain-dwelling demon</note>, who considered **himself invulnerable** <note>original: amarmaṇaḥ; one who believes they have no vital points or 'marma' that can be pierced</note>.

---

## Hymn Text

->॥ The Fourth Verse ॥<-

**You brought forward the chariot, the great instrument of war; you protected the fighting Vrishabha, Dashadyu.**
**You, along with Vetasu, struck down Tugra; O Indra, you strengthened Tuji as he sang praises. ॥ 4 ॥**

**You. The chariot. Forward. Brought. The warrior/instrument. Great. Protected. Fighting. Vrishabha. Dashadyu.**
**You. Tugra. In the fight with Vetasu. Together. Struck. You. Tuji. Praising. Indra. Strengthened. ॥ 4 ॥**

---

## Commentary (Sayana)

O Indra, you **brought forward** <note>original: prabharaḥ; provided or presented</note> the **great** <note>original: ṛṣvam</note> **chariot** <note>original: ratham</note>, which is a **means of war** <note>original: yodham</note>, for the king named **Vrishabha**. Furthermore, you **protected** <note>original: āvaḥ; guarded or saved</note> the king named **Vrishabha Dashadyu** <note>interpreted as "one whose battle lasted ten days"</note> while he was **fighting** <note>original: yudhyantam</note> with his enemies. Additionally, for the sake of the king named **Vetasu**, you **struck down** <note>original: ahan</note> **Tugra** <note>an enemy of Vetasu</note>. O Indra, you **strengthened** <note>original: tūtoḥ; increased the power of or incited</note> **Tuji** as he was **singing** <note>original: gṛṇantam</note> your praises.

## Commentary (Sayana)
Being a companion, you **slew the demon Tugra.** You have killed him. There is a certain demon named Vetasu. Here, Tugra is said to be different from him. Alternatively, the word "Vetasu" <note>original: vetasave</note> is in the dative case used in the sense of the instrumental; meaning, you have slain Tugra along with the demon Vetasu. This is also heard in another sacred verse:
> "Like a father, I subdued the Vetasus for the sake of victory, and Tugra and Smadibha for Kutsa." (Rig Veda 10.49.4)
O Indra, you have **strengthened** <note>original: tūtoḥ; increased or nourished</note> the King named **Tuji** who was **praising** <note>original: gṛṇantam</note> you.

---

-> ॥ Now the Fifth Verse ॥ <-

## Hymn Text
**O Indra, you performed that praiseworthy deed by your power; O Hero, you break through the hundreds and thousands.
You slew the servant Shambara as he came down from the mountain; you protected Divodasa with your wonderful aids. ॥ 5 ॥**

**Word-for-Word Analysis (Pada-patha):**
You. That. Praiseworthy. Indra. By power. Did. Who. Through. Hundreds. Thousands. Hero. You break.
Down. From the mountain. The servant. Shambara. Slaying. Forward. You protected. Divodasa. With wonderful. Aids. ॥ 5 ॥

## Commentary (Sayana)
O Indra, you who are **by power** <note>original: barhaṇā</note> a destroyer of enemies, you **performed** <note>original: kaḥ; did</note> **that** praiseworthy <note>original: ukthyam</note> deed. What is that deed? It is explained: O **Hero** <note>original: śūra</note> Indra, you **break through** <note>original: pradarṣi; tore apart or destroyed</note> the **hundreds** and **thousands** of soldiers who followed Shambara. As it is said in another Vedic text:
> "O priests, he who [destroyed] the hundred [cities] of Shambara." (Rig Veda 2.14.6)
Likewise, you **slew** <note>original: avahan</note> the **demon Shambara**, the **servant** <note>original: dāsam; one who destroys or neglects sacrificial rites</note>, as he emerged **from the mountain**. This is also heard elsewhere:
> "He who discovered Shambara dwelling in the mountains." (Rig Veda 2.12.11)
Furthermore, you **protected** <note>original: prāvaḥ; guarded excellently</note> King **Divodasa** with your **wonderful** <note>original: citrābhiḥ; varied or marvelous</note> **aids** <note>original: ūtibhiḥ; protections</note>.

-> ॥ Thus ends the twenty-first section of the sixth chapter of the fourth book ॥ <-

-> ॥ Now the Sixth Verse ॥ <-

## Hymn Text
**O Indra, rejoicing in the Soma-drinks offered with faith, you sent Chumuri to sleep for the sake of Dabhiti.
With your might, you slew sixty thousand together with Raji, for the sake of Pithinasa. ॥ 6 ॥**

**Word-for-Word Analysis (Pada-patha):**
You. With faith. Rejoicing. With Soma-drinks. For Dabhiti. Chumuri. Indra. You sent to sleep.
You. Raji. For Pithinasa. Slaying. Sixty. Thousands. With might. Together. Slew. ॥ 6 ॥

## Commentary (Sayana)
O Indra, you are **rejoicing** <note>original: mandasāno; being delighted</note> through **faith** <note>original: śraddhābhiḥ</note>, which refers to actions performed with great respect and devotion. A deed joined with faith becomes powerful. As it is heard in the scriptures:
> "Whatever one performs with knowledge, with faith, and with the secret teachings, that alone becomes more potent." (Chandogya Upanishad 1.1.10)

**Indra**: The king of the gods and deity of storms and battle.
**Shambara**: A mountain-dwelling demon or chieftain frequently mentioned as an enemy of Indra.
**Divodasa**: A famous king and patron of the Bharadvaja clan, protected by Indra.
**Dabhiti**: A devotee or king for whom Indra subdued enemies.
**Chumuri**: An enemy or demon defeated by Indra.

## Commentary (Sayana - continued from previous page)
Exhilarated by the Soma-juices, you cast into sleep <note>original: siṣvapaḥ; caused to sleep, meaning killed</note> the demon named **Chumuri** for the sake of the royal sage named **Dabhiti**. Furthermore, O Indra, while you were granting <note>original: daśyan</note> either a girl named **Rajim** or a kingdom to **Pithinasa**, you slew <note>original: āhanaḥ</note> **sixty thousand** <note>original: ṣaṣṭiṃ sahasrā</note> warriors at once <note>original: sacā</note> by your wisdom.

## Hymn Text
**O Indra, most powerful one, may I—along with the wise singers—attain that great happiness and power of yours. O companion of heroes, may we attain that which the heroes praise, that which was given to Nahusha in his triple-shelter. ॥ 7 ॥**

### Pada Patha
I . Even . That . By the wise singers . May [I] attain . Your . Greater . Indra . Happiness . Power .
By that . Which . They praise . O companion of heroes . Heroes . By the triple-shelter . By Nahusha . O most powerful one . ॥ 7 ॥

## Commentary (Sayana)
O **companion of heroes** <note>original: sadhavīra; one who is with heroic men</note>, O **most powerful** <note>original: śaviṣṭha</note> Indra, the heroes (the singers) praise the happiness <note>original: sumnam</note> and power <note>original: ojas</note> given by you. This happiness is associated with **Nahusha**, the "binder of enemies," and his **triple-shelter** <note>original: trivarūthena; that which covers or protects the three worlds</note>. O Indra, may I—the seer Bharadvaja—along with my **wise singers** <note>original: sūribhiḥ</note>, also attain <note>original: ānaśyām</note> that exceedingly praiseworthy happiness and power granted by you.

-> ॥ Now the Eighth Verse ॥ <-

## Hymn Text
**O Mighty Indra, may we be your dearest friends during this, your invocation. May Kshatrashri, the son of Pratardana, be the most excellent for the destruction of enemies and the winning of wealth. ॥ 8 ॥**

### Pada Patha
We . Your . In this . Indra . In your invocation . Friends . May we be . O Mighty one . Dearest .
The son of Pratardana . Kshatrashri . Let [him] be . Most excellent . In the destruction . Of the enemies (Vritras) . In the winning . Of wealth . ॥ 8 ॥

## Commentary (Sayana)
O **Mighty** <note>original: mahina; worshipful</note> Indra, may we, your singers, be **dearest** <note>original: preṣṭhāḥ</note> to you and remain your **friends** <note>original: sakhāyaḥ</note> during this invocation—this hymn composed for your sake. May **Kshatrashri** <note>the name means 'the glory of the dominion'</note>, the son of King **Pratardana** and my royal patron, be the **most excellent** <note>original: śreṣṭhaḥ</note> of all. For what purpose? The connection is: let him be the best for the **destruction** <note>original: ghane</note> of enemies <note>original: vṛtrāṇām</note> and for the **winning** <note>original: sanaye</note> of riches and possessions.

-> ॥ Thus ends the twenty-second Varga of the sixth Adhyaya in the fourth Ashtaka ॥ <-

---

## Critical Notes
The fourth hymn (Sukta 27), beginning with "**Kim ay mad**" <note>original: kim ay mada</note>, consists of eight verses and was **seen by the seer Bharadvaja**. The index <note>Anukramani</note> states: "The end of this..."

<vocab>
**Indra** (इन्द्र): The King of the gods and the primary deity of this hymn, celebrated for his strength and generosity.
**Bharadvaja** (भरद्वाज): The Vedic Rishi (seer) to whom the hymns of the 6th book (Mandala) are revealed.
**Sumna** (सुम्न): Divine benevolence, favor, or the resulting happiness/peace.
**Ojas** (ओजस्): Spiritual or physical vital energy; the "brilliance" of a warrior-god.
**Nahusha** (नहुष): A legendary figure; Sayana interprets the name here as "one who binds or checks enemies."
**Pratardana** (प्रतर्दन): A historical/mythological king of Kashi known for his righteousness and valor.
**Kshatrashri** (क्षत्रश्री): The son of Pratardana; he is the "Yajamana" or patron who sponsored the ritual where this hymn was sung.
**Sadhavira** (सधवीर): A title for Indra, meaning one who is always accompanied by heroic followers (Maruts or human warriors).
</vocab>

<meta>This page begins Sukta 27 of the 6th Mandala. It follows the previous page’s themes of the Rishi Bharadvaja seeking Indra’s favor, moving from general petitions to a specific interaction where the Rishi first challenges and then praises the god’s responsiveness.</meta>

<note>This hymn contains a Praise of Gifts (Dānastuti) for King Abhyavartin, son of Cayamana. The Seer (Rishi) is Bharadvaja. The Meter is Trishtubh (a rhythmic cycle of 44 syllables). Regarding the divinity: for the first eight verses the deity is Indra; however, because the final verse is a praise of a gift, the "Gift" itself is considered the deity according to the rule that the subject of the verse is its deity. Its ritual application is determined by the internal meaning of the text.</note>

---

-> || Here is the First Verse || <-

## Hymn Text
What has Indra done in the **exhilaration** <note>original: made</note> of this Soma? What indeed has he done in the **drinking** <note>original: pītau</note> of this? What has he done in the **friendship** <note>original: sakhye</note> of this? Or what did the **singers** <note>original: raṇāḥ</note> who are in the **dwelling-place** <note>original: niṣadi</note> formerly obtain from you, and what have the **modern ones** <note>original: nūtanāsaḥ</note> obtained? ॥ 1 ॥

### Word-for-Word Analysis (Pada Patha)
What | of this | in exhilaration | what | indeed | of this | in drinking | Indra | what | of this | in friendship | has he done | singers | or | who | in the dwelling | what | from you | of this | formerly | have they obtained | what | indeed | the modern ones || 1 ||

## Commentary (Sayana)
The Seer Bharadvaja, being unable to tolerate a delay in receiving the rewards of his ritual, **challenges Indra** <note>original: ākṣipati; literally "throws a reproach at" or "questions"</note> with this verse. In the **exhilaration** <note>original: made</note> produced by this Soma, what has Indra **done**? What act has he performed? Furthermore, during the **drinking** of this Soma, what did he do? In the **friendship** of this Soma, what did he do? <note>The sense is that Indra is expected to act or provide a blessing because he has shared in the Soma and friendship of the worshiper.</note> The phrase "friendship" implies that before the actual drinking, Indra dwells together with the Soma and the worshiper.

Regarding the **dwelling-place** <note>original: niṣadi; the place where one sits</note> or house of this Soma, what did the **singers** <note>original: raṇāḥ; those who rejoice in song</note> of the **past** <note>original: purā</note> obtain <note>original: vividre</note> from you, O Indra? And what have the **modern** singers of the present day obtained? <note>The Rishi is asking for tangible proof of Indra's favor, comparing his current situation to the legendary rewards given to ancient ancestors.</note>

---

-> || Now the Second Verse || <-

## Hymn Text
**Good** <note>original: sat; meaning beneficial, real, or auspicious</note> has Indra done in the **exhilaration** of this [Soma]; **good** indeed has he done in the **drinking** of this; **good** has he done in the **friendship** of this. The **singers** who are in the **dwelling-place** formerly obtained **good** from you, and the **modern ones** have indeed obtained **good**. ॥ 2 ॥

### Word-for-Word Analysis (Pada Patha)
Good | of this | in exhilaration | good | indeed | of this | in drinking | Indra | good | of this | in friendship | has he done | singers | or | who | in the dwelling | good | from you | of this | formerly | have they obtained | good | indeed | the modern ones || 2 ||

## Commentary (Sayana)
When he was reproached in this manner, Indra bestowed the desired wealth upon the Seer. Thereafter, the Seer, having had his desires fulfilled by Indra's presence, now **retracts** <note>original: nirākaroti; cancels or resolves</note> the questioning words he spoke previously. Indra **performed a good** <note>original: sat; a beneficial or auspicious act</note> deed in the **exhilaration** of this Soma. He performed a **good** deed in the **drinking** of this Soma. He performed a **good** deed in the **friendship** of this. Those **singers** who are in the **dwelling**—meaning the **sacrificial hall** <note>original: yajñagṛhe</note>—formerly obtained **good** from you, O Indra. And the **modern** singers of today have indeed obtained only **good** <note>meaning their prayers have been answered with wealth and success</note>.

---

<vocab>
- भरद्वाज (Bharadvāja): The principal Seer of the 6th book of the Rig Veda.
- त्रिष्टुप् (Triṣṭup): A powerful 11-syllable Vedic meter associated with Indra.
- दानस्तुति (Dānastuti): A "praise of liberality," usually thanking a king for gifts given during a sacrifice.
- सोम (Soma): The sacred plant and juice offered to the gods to inspire them.
- मदे (Made): The state of divine inspiration or intoxication resulting from Soma.
- सख्ये (Sakhye): The bond of friendship/alliance between the god and the human worshiper.
- निषदि (Niṣadi): Literally "sitting down," referring here to the assembly in the ritual tent or hall.
- रणा (Raṇā): Singers or praisers who take delight in the ritual.
- सत् (Sat): A multifaceted term meaning "good," "true," "existing," or "beneficial."
</vocab>

# Rig Veda — Ashtaka 4, Adhyaya 6, Varga 23

<page-num>699</page-num>

-> ॥ Now the Third Verse ॥ <-

## Hymn Text

O **Bountiful Lord** <note>original: Maghavan</note>, we truly do not know the limit of your total **greatness** <note>original: mahimanaḥ</note>, nor of your **generosity** <note>original: maghavattvasya</note>. O Indra, no one has ever seen the full extent of your **power** <note>original: indriyam</note> or your **ever-new wealth** <note>original: rādhaso rādhasaḥ nūtanasya</note>. ॥ 3 ॥

**Word-for-Word Analysis (Padapatha):**
Not | indeed | your | greatness | of the whole | not | O Bountiful One | of the state of being bountiful | we know |
not | of wealth | of wealth | of the new | O Indra | no one | has seen | the power | your ॥ 3 ॥

---

## Commentary (Sayana)

O **Maghavan** <note>A title for Indra meaning "Possessor of Riches"</note>, we do not know the **greatness** of your entire, complete majesty. The word **nu** serves here as a rhythmic filler. Likewise, we do not know the extent of your **maghavattvasya**—your quality of being the ultimate wealthy patron. We also cannot grasp all your **ever-new wealth**, which is worthy of praise. <note>Sayana notes that although the text uses the possessive case here, it should be understood as the object of the verb "to know."</note> O Indra, your **power** <note>original: indriyam; specifically his vital force or virility</note> has been seen by no one; it remains beyond human perception.

---

-> ॥ Now the Fourth Verse ॥ <-

## Hymn Text

That **power** <note>original: indriyam</note> of yours was made known by which you slew the **progeny** <note>original: śeṣaḥ</note> of **Varashikha**; when, O Indra, from the **might** <note>original: śuṣmāt</note> and the very **clash** <note>original: svanāt</note> of your hurled **thunderbolt** <note>original: vajrasya</note>, the strongest [among them] was shattered. ॥ 4 ॥

**Word-for-Word Analysis (Padapatha):**
This | that | your | power | was known | by which | you slew | of Varashikha | the progeny |
of the thunderbolt | which | your | of the hurled | from the might | from the sound | even | O Indra | the highest | shattered ॥ 4 ॥

---

## Commentary (Sayana)

O Indra, through that heroic power of yours, you **slew** the **progeny**—which means the sons—of a certain demon named **Varashikha**. <note>The term 'Shesha' is identified here as a synonym for offspring or children.</note> This specific heroic deed was known and recognized by us. O Indra, because of the **might** or strength of your **thunderbolt** as it was hurled, and even from its mere **sound** <note>original: svanāt</note>, the most excellent and powerful among Varashikha’s sons was utterly broken and destroyed.

---

-> ॥ Now the Fifth Verse ॥ <-

## Hymn Text

Indra slew the **progeny** <note>original: śeṣaḥ</note> of **Varashikha**, acting in favor of **Abhyavartin**, the son of **Cayamana**. When he struck the **Vrichivans** at **Hariyupiya**, the vanguard fled in fear while the rear was shattered. ॥ 5 ॥

**Word-for-Word Analysis (Padapatha):**
He slew | Indra | of Varashikha | the progeny | for Abhyavartin | for the son of Cayamana | showing favor |
the Vrichivans | when | at Hariyupiya | striking | the former | half | through fear | the other | shattered ॥ 5 ॥

<summary>These verses praise Indra's immeasurable power and recount his destruction of the demon Varashikha's sons at Hariyupiya to aid King Abhyavartin. The text highlights that even the mere sound of Indra's thunderbolt was enough to shatter his enemies.</summary>

## Commentary (Sayana)
[Continuation of the commentary on Verse 5]

The commentator explains the previously stated meaning with this verse: This Indra, while **showing favor** <note>original: śikṣan</note>—meaning granting desired wealth—to King **Abhyavartin** <note>the son of King Chayamana</note>, killed the remaining sons of the **Asura** <note>a powerful, often oppositional celestial being</note> named **Varashikha**. How he killed the sons of Varashikha is now described. Whenever Indra was at **Hariyupiya** <note>original: hariyūpīyāyām; either a specific river or a city</note>, he killed the **Vrichivantas** <note>original: vṛcīvantaḥ; the descendants of Vrichivan, a forefather of the Varashikha clan</note> who were stationed on the eastern side <note>original: pūrve-ardhe</note>. At that time, the eldest and best son of Varashikha, who was stationed on the western side, was **shattered** <note>original: darta; torn apart or destroyed</note> by sheer **terror** <note>original: bhiyasā</note>.

-> ॥ This concludes the twenty-third section <note>original: varga</note> of the sixth chapter of the fourth book ॥ <-

---

## Hymn Text
-> ॥ Now the Sixth Verse ॥ <-

**One hundred and thirty armored men, O Indra, came together at the Yavyavati river, O Invoked-by-Many, seeking glory. The Vrichivantas, falling upon your weapon and breaking the sacrificial vessels, went to their own destruction.** ॥ 6 ॥

**Word-for-Word Analysis (Pada-patha):**
Thirty | hundred | armored ones | O Indra | together | at the Yavyavati | O One-Invoked-by-Many | by desire for glory | 
The Vrichivantas | upon the weapon | falling | vessels | breaking | down | to [pointless] ends | they went ॥ 6 ॥

## Commentary (Sayana)
The commentator now elaborates on the meaning just stated. O **Invoked-by-Many** <note>original: puruhūta; an epithet for Indra whom many call upon</note> Indra, out of **desire for glory** <note>original: śravasyā; desiring "shravas," which can mean food or fame</note>—meaning they desired to conquer you in battle to obtain food or renown—they came **falling upon** <note>original: patyamānā</note> or attacking your **weapon** <note>original: śarave; intending to strike you</note>. These **armored ones** <note>original: varmiṇaḥ; wearing coats of mail</note>, numbering **one hundred and thirty** <note>original: triṃśacchataṃ; thirty more than a hundred</note>, were the **Vrichivantas**, the sons of Varashikha. They came all together to the previously mentioned **Yavyavati** <note>another name for the Hariyupiya river</note>. There, **breaking the vessels** <note>original: pātrā bhindānā; smashing the tools used in sacrifices</note>, they **went to pointless ends** <note>original: nyarthānyāyan</note>. This means they met their total destruction.

## Hymn Text
-> ॥ Now the Seventh Verse ॥ <-

**He whose two shining, grass-seeking horses move between heaven and earth, repeatedly licking [the ground]; He gave the Turvasha tribe over to Srinjaya, showing favor to Daivavata against the Vrichivantas.** ॥ 7 ॥

**Word-for-Word Analysis (Pada-patha):**
Whose | two horses | shining | seeking-good-grass | between | indeed | well | they move | repeatedly-licking | 
He | to Srinjaya | the Turvasha | away | gave | the Vrichivantas | to [Abhyavartin] the son of Devavata | showing favor ॥ 7 ॥

## Commentary (Sayana)
The two **shining** <note>original: aruṣā-aruṣau</note> ones, **seeking good grass** <note>original: suyavasyū</note>, and **repeatedly licking** <note>original: rerihāṇā</note>—meaning they taste the grass over and over, or perhaps perform a specific movement—these are the two **horses** <note>original: gāvā; though the word often means "cows," in this context it refers to Indra's steeds</note> belonging to Indra. They move-

<vocab>
- **Vrichivantas** (vṛcīvantaḥ): A specific clan or tribe, sons of the Asura Varashikha, who were enemies of Indra's devotee.
- **Hariyupiya/Yavyavati** (hariyūpīyā/yavyāvatī): The location of the battle; modern scholars often debate if this refers to a river or an ancient city (like Harappa).
- **Puruhuta** (puruhūta): A common title for Indra meaning "The One Many Call Upon."
- **Srinjaya** (sṛñjayāya): A king or patron protected by Indra.
- **Turvasha** (turvaśam): An ancient tribe or king often mentioned as being defeated or moved by Indra.
- **Varminah** (varmiṇaḥ): Soldiers wearing protective armor/mail.
</vocab>

# Rig Veda — Book 4, Chapter 6, Section 24

<page-num>700</page-num>
<header>॥ Rig Veda ॥ [Ashtaka 4, Adhyaya 6, Varga 25]</header>

## Commentary (Sayana)
[Conclusion of the commentary on Verse 7]

...moving <note>original: carato</note> in the atmosphere between heaven and earth. The particles **u** and **su** <note>original: u su itīmau pūraṇau</note> are used here as rhythmic fillers to complete the verse. That Indra handed over King **Turvasha** to the king named **Sanjaya**. What was he doing at that time? He was subduing <note>original: śikṣan</note> the **Vrichivantas**, the descendants of **Varashikha**, for the sake of King **Abhyavartin**, who was born in the lineage of **Devavata**. Alternatively, it means Indra was bestowing the wealth of those enemies upon the king.

---

## Hymn Text

-> ॥ Now the Eighth Verse ॥ <-

**O Agni, the wealthy sovereign Abhyavartin, the son of Chayamana, gives to me twenty pairs of cows along with chariots and female attendants. This sacrificial gift of the descendants of Prthu is impossible for anyone to destroy.** ॥ 8 ॥

**Word-for-Word Analysis (Pada-patha):**
Twofold | O Agni | possessing chariots | twenty | cows | with women | the wealthy one | to me | the sovereign | Abhyavartin | son of Chayamana | gives | indestructible | this | gift | of the descendants of Prthu ॥ 8 ॥

---

## Commentary (Sayana)

Now the seer **Bharadvaja** proclaims to **Agni** the various forms of wealth given to him by King **Abhyavartin**. O Agni, the wealthy or most liberal sovereign <note>one who has performed the Rajasuya sacrifice</note> Abhyavartin, the son of **Chayamana**, gives to me twenty cows that are in pairs <note>original: mithunabhūtan; likely meaning a bull and a cow together for breeding</note>, along with chariots and female attendants. This gift belongs to King Abhyavartin, who is a descendant of **Prthu** <note>The text uses the plural "of the Parthyavanas" as a mark of respect for the king</note>. This **sacrificial gift** <note>original: dakṣiṇā</note> is "indestructible" <note>original: dūrṇāśā</note>, meaning it is so vast or significant that it cannot be diminished by anyone.

-> ॥ This concludes the twenty-fourth section <note>varga</note> of the sixth chapter of the fourth book ॥ <-

# Rig Veda — Book 4, Chapter 6, Section 25

The fifth hymn of this section, beginning with "May the cows come," consists of eight verses. The **Index of the Veda** <note>original: anukramaṇikā</note> describes it as follows: "The hymn 'May the cows come' <note>ā gāvo</note> is dedicated to cows; the second verse or the final quarter-verse may alternatively address **Indra**. The meters are as follows: the first three verses are in **Jagati** <note>a 48-syllable meter</note>, the last is in **Anustubh** <note>a 32-syllable meter</note>, and the remaining four are in **Trishtubh** <note>a 44-syllable meter</note>." 

The seer is **Bharadvaja**. The deity of the entire hymn is the **Cow** <note>original: gauḥ</note>, though for the second verse and the final part of the last verse, Indra is an alternative deity. This hymn is used during the ritual of "standing near the cows" <note>gavāmupasthāna</note>. This is confirmed by the ritual manuals which state: "One should recite the hymn beginning with 'May the cows come'."

---

## Hymn Text

-> ॥ There, the First Verse ॥ <-

**May the cows come and bring us good fortune; let them rest in the cow-pen and be happy among us. May they be prolific here and of many colors, yielding milk for Indra at many dawns.** ॥ 1 ॥

**Word-for-Word Analysis (Pada-patha):**
Hither | the cows | have come | and | fortune | have made | let them sit | in the cow-pen | let them rejoice | among us | possessing offspring | many-colored | here | let them be | for Indra | many | dawns | yielding milk ॥ 1 ॥

<vocab>
- **Bharadvaja**: The ancient sage and seer of this family book of the Rig Veda.
- **Agni**: The deity of fire, often the witness to royal gifts.
- **Abhyavartin**: A historical patron king who rewarded the priests.
- **Dakshina**: The honorarium or gift given to a priest after a ritual.
- **Gavah**: Cows, regarded as the primary source of wealth and sacredness.
- **Anukramanika**: An ancient systematic index providing the metadata for each hymn.
- **Jagata / Trishtubh / Anustubh**: Different poetic meters used in Vedic Sanskrit.
</vocab>

<keywords>Abhyavartin, Chayamana, Bharadvaja, dakshina, cows, Vedic meters, prosperity, livestock, Agni</keywords>

--- Page 769 ---
<meta>This page follows the transition from the narrative of King Abhyavartin's generosity to a hymn focused on the sanctity and protection of cows. The previous page concluded the commentary on Verse 1 of the 28th Hymn, which describes cows arriving at the homestead.</meta>

## Commentary (Sayana)
The cows have arrived <note>original: gāva āgman</note>. May they come to our home. And also, may they bring <note>original: akran</note> auspicious <note>original: bhadram</note> and pleasant fortune. Thus, may they sit in our stall <note>original: goṣṭhe</note>, the designated place for cows. Let them settle down. After that, may they rejoice <note>original: raṇayantu</note> among us. Furthermore, in this stall, may there be cows of many colors <note>original: purūrūpā</note>, accompanied by their offspring <note>original: prajāvatīḥ</note>, numerous <note>original: pūrvīr</note>, and may they be milking <note>original: duhānā</note> for the sake of <term>Indra</term> <note>the king of the gods</note> toward the times of dawn <note>original: uṣasaḥ</note>.

---

-> ॥ Now the second verse ॥ <-

## Hymn Text
Indra helps the one who sacrifices and the one who satisfies [the gods]; he gives and does not steal what belongs [to the worshiper]. Increasing his wealth more and more, he places the god-seeking man in an unbroken pasture. ॥ 2 ॥

**Word-for-Word Analysis (Pada-patha):**
Indra | to the sacrificer | to the one who satisfies | and | helps | near | indeed | gives | not | his own | steals | 
more and more | wealth | indeed | of him | increasing | in an unbroken | pasture | down | places | the god-seeking one ॥ 2 ॥

## Commentary (Sayana)
Indra helps <note>original: śikṣati</note> the sacrificer <note>original: yajvane</note>—one whose nature is to perform sacrifice—and the one who satisfies <note>original: pṛṇate</note>—the one who pleases the gods with hymns of praise. He bestows the desired wealth. This giving is not merely a one-time event, but constant, as the text says: "He gives indeed" <note>original: uped dadāti</note>. He approaches and always gives. He does not steal <note>original: muṣāyati</note> the personal property belonging to the sacrificer or the singer of praises; he never takes it away. 

Furthermore, for this person—who is both a sacrificer and a praiser—Indra increases <note>original: vardhayan</note> the wealth he himself has bestowed, over and over again. He places <note>original: nidadhāti</note> that god-seeking man <note>original: devayum</note>—one who desires the god Indra—in an unbroken <note>original: abhinne</note> wasteland or pasture <note>original: khilye</note>. A <term>khilya</term> <note>original: khilam</note> is a place that is unobstructed or unploughed. This term <note>khilya</note> refers to a place that cannot be reached or seized by others; Indra establishes the worshiper there, meaning he ensures they have a secure place to live.

The verses beginning "Those belonging to the gods..." <note>original: daivīnāṃ</note> and "They are not lost..." <note>original: na tā naśanti</note> are used as the offering and invitatory verses <note>original: yājyā-puronuvākye</note> for the Cow-Deity, as noted in the Ashvalayana Shrauta Sutra (6.14). Also, in the "Cow-Praise" ritual <note>original: go-stome</note>, these serve as the opening verses for the <term>Marutvatiya</term> <note>prayers to Indra with the storm-gods</note> and the <term>Nishkevalya</term> <note>prayers exclusive to Indra</note> litanies. This is indicated by the citation: "The racer does not reach them... they are not lost, the thief does not harm them" (Ashvalayana Shrauta Sutra 9.5).

---

-> ॥ And he speaks this third verse of the hymn ॥ <-

## Hymn Text

[He <note>referring to a thief or predator mentioned in the previous verse</note>] should not deceive or harm our cows. Likewise, let not the weapon <note>original: vyathiḥ</note> of the enemy <note>original: amitrasya</note> or foe overpower <note>original: nādadharṣati</note> or attack these cows. ->॥ Now the Fourth Verse ॥<-

## Hymn Text

The dust-stirring war-horse does not reach them, nor do they go to the place of slaughter. These cows of the mortal who performs sacrifice wander across his wide-reaching and fearless pasture. ॥ 4 ॥

**Word-for-Word Analysis (Pada-patha):**
Not | them | the war-horse | the stirrer of dust | reaches | not | the place of preparation/slaughter | near | they go | them | toward | wide-striding | fearless | of him | those | according to | cows | of the mortal | specifically | wander | of the sacrificer ॥ 4 ॥

---

## Commentary (Sayana)

**The stirrer of dust** <note>original: reṇukakāṭo</note> refers to the excessive rising of earthly dust. **The war-horse** <note>original: arvā</note>, a horse that has arrived for the purpose of battle, **does not reach these cows**. That is, he cannot capture them. Likewise, **those cows do not go to the place of preparation** <note>original: saṃskṛtatram</note>—meaning they should not go to the place of butchering or slaughter. Furthermore, **those cows wander** <note>original: vi caranti</note> or travel specifically **according to** the **wide-reaching** <note>original: urugāyam</note> and **fearless** <note>original: abhayam</note> region belonging to **that mortal** man, the **sacrificer** <note>original: yajvano</note>. Let them move about freely.

->॥ Now the Fifth Verse ॥<-

## Hymn Text

To me, the cows are <term>Bhaga</term> <note>the god of fortune and wealth</note>; the cows are Indra; the cows provide the first draught of <term>Soma</term> <note>the sacred ritual drink</note>. O people! These cows are Indra himself. With my heart and mind, I indeed desire Indra. ॥ 5 ॥

**Word-for-Word Analysis (Pada-patha):**
Cows | Bhaga | cows | Indra | to me | provide | cows | of Soma | of the first | the portion | these | which | cows | he | O people | Indra | I desire | indeed | with heart | with mind | even | Indra ॥ 5 ॥

---

## Commentary (Sayana)

May the **cows** alone be **Bhaga**—which is to say, wealth—for me. And may **Indra grant me cows**. May the **cows be the portion** <note>original: bhakṣo</note> or the consumption **of the first** and best of offerings, the **Soma**. This is because the pressed Soma juice is mixed <note>original: saṃśrayaṇāt</note> with products of the cow, such as clarified butter <note>ghee</note>. O **people** <note>original: janāso</note>, **these cows** that exist in this way are **him**—meaning they are Indra. The cows themselves are Indra because he is nourished and satisfied by the offerings of curds and butter derived from them. **I indeed desire** <note>original: icchāmītt</note> or long for such an Indra with a **mind** and **heart** joined with faith. The meaning is: I wish to worship such an Indra specifically through the cows, who are the means of the sacrifice.
