## Hymn Text
O cows, you fatten even the lean, and make even the unlovely fair-appearing. You make the home auspicious, O you of auspicious voices; your great strength is celebrated in our assemblies. ॥ 6 ॥

**Word-for-Word Analysis (Pada-patha):**
You | cows | fatten | the lean | indeed | the unlovely | indeed | you make | fair-appearing | auspicious | the home | you make | auspicious-voiced | great | your | strength or food | is spoken of | in the assemblies ॥ 6 ॥

---

## Commentary (Sayana)
O cows, you **fatten** <note>original: medayatha</note>. This means you provide nourishment or causing to thrive. Likewise, even for one who is **lean** <note>original: kṛśaṃ</note> or emaciated, and even for one who is **unlovely** <note>original: aśrīraṃ</note> or inauspicious, you **make them fair-appearing** <note>original: supratīkam</note>, having beautiful forms or limbs. O **auspicious-voiced** ones <note>original: bhadravācaḥ</note>—you who are endowed with pleasant sounds <note>referring to the lowing of the cattle</note>—make our home **auspicious** <note>original: bhadraṃ</note>. That is, make the household thrive by being filled with cattle. In the **assemblies** <note>original: sabhāsu</note>, which are the sacrificial gatherings, O cows, your **great** <note>original: bṛhat</note> or immense **strength** <note>original: vayaḥ</note>—meaning the food or offerings derived from you—is spoken of. This means it is offered by all participants.

---

->॥ Now the Seventh Verse ॥<-

## Hymn Text
May you have many offspring, grazing upon good pasture, drinking pure waters at fertile drinking places. May the thief never master you, nor the wicked seeker of evil; may the weapon of Rudra avoid you. ॥ 7 ॥

**Word-for-Word Analysis (Pada-patha):**
Having offspring | good pasture | grazing | pure | waters | at a good drinking place | drinking | not | you | the thief | let him master | not | the evil-seeker | around | you | the weapon | of Rudra | let it avoid ॥ 7 ॥

---

## Commentary (Sayana)
O cows, may you be **having many offspring** <note>original: prajāvatīḥ</note>—it is implied that you should be accompanied by many calves. May you be **grazing** <note>original: riśantīḥ</note>—meaning consuming for the sake of nourishment—upon **good pasture** <note>original: suyavasaṃ</note> or excellent grass. May you be **drinking** <note>original: pibantīḥ</note> the **pure** <note>original: śuddhāḥ</note> and clear **waters** <note>original: apaḥ</note> at a **good drinking place** <note>original: supra pāṇe</note> such as a pond or lake where drinking is easy and pleasant. Let no **thief** <note>original: stenaḥ</note> or robber **master you** <note>original: mā īśata</note>. May he never become your owner. Likewise, let no **evil-seeker** <note>original: aghaśamsaḥ</note>, such as a tiger or a human enemy, master you. Furthermore, may the **weapon** <note>original: hetiḥ</note> or missile of <term>Rudra</term> <note>the god of storms and destruction, here identified as the Supreme Lord in the form of Time</note> **avoid you** <note>original: parivṛjyāḥ</note>. May it bypass or spare you.

## Commentary (Sayana)

<note>Sayana concludes the commentary on the final verse of the Hymn to the Cows, Rig Veda 6.28.8</note>

May this **filling and nourishing** <note>original: upaparcanam-āpyāyanam</note> be united with these cows. Let it be joined. O Indra, because of your **heroic power** <note>original: vīrye</note>, may this filling and nourishing be in the **seeding of the bull** <note>original: ṛṣabhasya retasi</note> who provides the cows with offspring. The meaning is this: when the cows are nourished, Indra himself becomes nourished through the medium of the oblations—such as milk and ghee—that come from them. The repetition of the word "toward" <note>original: upa</note> is meant to complete the meter of the verse.

<meta>This page continues the commentary on the 29th hymn (Sukta) of the 6th book (Mandala) of the Rig Veda. ## Commentary (Sayana)
<note>This concludes the explanation of the first verse of hymn 6.29, focusing on the worshipper's intent and Indra's nature.</note>

...His intellect is of such a nature. Desiring that intellect, or longing for it. <note>The commentator explains a technical grammatical point: "Kriyāgrahaṇam" implies that even when an action is the object, it can take the dative case of purpose.</note> The word "cakānāḥ" is a Vedic form of the root meaning "to desire." 

Alternatively, the phrase "maho" refers to a "great deed" being performed; "sumataye" means "for the sake of a beautiful hymn of praise," and "cakānāḥ" means "sounding" or "uttering." <note>original: "kai gai śabde"—referring to the linguistic roots for sound.</note> Because <note>original: hi</note> Indra, who holds the thunderbolt in his hand <note>original: vajrahasto</note>, is the giver of great wealth, you should worship him—the foremost, the beautiful, and the great—for the sake of protection <note>original: avase</note>. Honor him with sacrificial offerings.

---

->॥ The Second Verse ॥<-

## Hymn Text
In whose hand the manly ones have sprinkled [wealth], who stays in the golden chariot, the chariot-rider; in his sturdy arms the reins [are held], as the showering horses are yoked upon the path. ॥ 2 ॥

**Word-for-Word Analysis (Padapatha):**
Toward (ā). In whom (yasmin). In the hand (haste). Manly/Heroic (naryaḥ). They have sprinkled (mimikṣuḥ). Toward (ā). In the chariot (rathe). Golden (hiraṇaye). Chariot-rider (rathe-sthāḥ).
Toward (ā). Reins (raśmayaḥ). Of the two arms (gabhastyoḥ). Of the two sturdy/broad ones (sthūrayoḥ). Toward (ā). On the path (adhvan). Horses (aśvāsaḥ). Showerers/Strong (vṛṣaṇaḥ). Being yoked (yujānāḥ). ॥ 2 ॥

---

## Commentary (Sayana)
In whom—that is, in Indra—the "manly" <note>original: naryā</note> riches, which are beneficial to men, are "sprinkled" or filled. <note>The commentator notes a grammatical shift where an active verb form is used for a passive meaning.</note> 

If one asks "where exactly in Indra?", the text says "in his hand"—meaning in his arm. Alternatively, the word "manly" could be an adjective describing Indra himself. In that case, "in the hand" means "in the slayer" <note>Indra as the destroyer of enemies</note>. As the ancient etymologist Yaska states: "The word for hand (*hasta*) comes from the root *han* (to slay), because it reaches out to strike." <note>Nirukta 1.7</note>. 

Or, the meaning could be that riches existing in Indra "sprinkle" or fill the singers with abundance. Furthermore, Indra, who is by nature a "chariot-rider" <note>original: ratheṣṭhā</note>, remains in a golden chariot. Or, it means that while Indra stays in the golden chariot, the riches contained within that chariot "sprinkle" or rain down upon the worshippers. 

In whose "sturdy" <note>original: sthūrayoḥ</note> or broad "arms" <note>original: gabhastyoḥ—a synonym for arms</note> the reins are "sprinkled" or firmly held. And whose "showering" <note>original: vṛṣaṇaḥ—meaning potent or strong</note> horses, being yoked to the chariot, "sprinkle" or cover the path. This simply means they arrive or travel swiftly. We praise that Indra—this concluding thought is implied.

---

## Hymn Text
For the sake of glory, they have sprinkled your feet with worship, O bold one, wielder of the thunderbolt, powerful with strength, giver of rewards. Wearing a fragrant garment for the sake of being seen, you have become like the sun, O agile dancer. ॥ 3 ॥

**Word-for-Word Analysis (Padapatha):**
For glory (śriye). Your (te). Two feet (pādau). Worship/Service (duvaḥ). Toward (ā). They have sprinkled (mimikṣuḥ). Bold (dhṛṣṇuḥ). Wielder of the thunderbolt (vajrī). With strength (śavasā). Giver of rewards (dakṣiṇā-vān).
Wearing (vasānaḥ). Garment/Armor (atkam). Fragrant (surabhim). For seeing (dṛśe). For whom (kam). The Sun/Heaven (svaḥ). Like (na). Dancer (nṛta). Agile/Impelling (iṣiraḥ). You have become (babhūtha). ॥ 3 ॥

## Commentary (Sayana)
<note>Continued from the previous page for Rig Veda 4.17.3</note>

O Indra, for the sake of prosperity <note>original: "śriyai," meaning wealth or sovereignty</note>, they sprinkle or offer service <note>original: "duvaḥ," meaning worship or attendance</note> at your two feet. The sage Bharadwaja offers this service. Although the text uses the plural, it refers to the singular act of the sage; or alternatively, it means that they (the worshippers) perform the service to honor your feet for the sake of prosperity. You are the one who, through your power <note>original: "śavasā"</note>, are bold and a subduer of enemies. You are the wielder of the thunderbolt and the possesser of sacrificial rewards <note>original: "dakṣiṇāvān"</note>. These rewards are the wealth to be given to those who chant your praises. O Leader Indra, you clothe yourself in your own fragrant, praiseworthy, and ever-moving form so that all may see you. Like the sun <note>original: "svarṇaṃ sūrya iva"</note>, you have become desirable or one who is to be approached. The word "kam" serves here as a rhythmic filler.

---

-> ॥ Now the Fourth Verse ॥ <-

## Hymn Text
<note>RV 4.17.4</note>

That Soma has become most well-mixed and pressed; in this [sacrifice], the cooked offering is prepared and the parched grains are ready. Men who compose prayers, chanting the hymns of praise, being most dear to the gods, praise Indra. ॥ 4 ॥

**Word-for-Word Analysis (Padapatha):**
That (saḥ). Soma (somaḥ). Most well-mixed (āmiśla-tamaḥ). Pressed (sutaḥ). Has become (bhūt). In which (yasmin). Cooked offering (paktiḥ). Is cooked (pacyate). They are (santi). Parched grains (dhānāḥ).
Indra (indram). Men/Leaders (naraḥ). Praising (stuvantaḥ). Makers of prayer (brahma-kārāḥ). Hymns (ukthā). Chanting (śaṃsantaḥ). Most favored by the gods (deva-vātatamāḥ). ॥ 4 ॥

---

## Commentary (Sayana)

The Soma that will be described becomes **most well-mixed** <note>original: "āmiślatama," meaning perfectly blended</note> once it is pressed; it is prepared specifically to be united with Indra. When this Soma is pressed, the **cooked offering** <note>original: "paktiḥ," referring to the Purodasha or sacrificial cake</note> is prepared. The **parched grains** <note>original: "dhānāḥ," which are roasted barley</note> are also present, having been refined for the sake of the oblation. When the Soma is pressed, the "men"—referring to the leaders or the officiating priests who are the **makers of prayer** <note>original: "brahmakāra," those who prepare the sacred food and the hymns</note>—praise Indra with songs and chant the *uktha* <note>original: "ukthāni," specifically the recited hymns or Shastras</note>. They are **most favored by the gods** <note>original: "devavātatama," meaning they have reached or are most beloved by the divine</note>. The meaning is that the Soma has become fully mingled with Indra's presence.

---

-> ॥ Now the Fifth Verse ॥ <-

## Hymn Text
<note>RV 4.17.5</note>

The end of your strength, which is to be established, is not found; by your greatness, you have pushed apart heaven and earth. The wise patron, hurrying and seeking favor through worship, fills those [realms] like a shepherd with his flocks in the waters. ॥ 5 ॥

**Word-for-Word Analysis (Padapatha):**
Not (na). Your (te). End (antaḥ). Of strength (śavasaḥ). To be placed/known (dhāyi). Of this (asya). Apart (vi). Indeed (tu). Pushed (babandhe). Heaven and Earth (rodasī). By greatness (mahitvā).
Fully (ā). Those (tā). The wise patron (sūriḥ). Fills (pṛṇati). Hurrying (tūtujānaḥ). Like flocks (yūthā-iva). In the waters (apsu). Worshiping together (sam-ījānaḥ). With protection (ūtī). ॥ 5 ॥

---

## Commentary (Sayana)

O Indra, the end or the limit of **your strength** <note>original: "śavasaḥ"</note>, which possesses the qualities just described, is "not placed" <note>original: "na dhāyi"</note>. Here, the root *dha* (to place) should be understood in a unique sense—it was not "placed down" or "known" by us. This power of yours, through its **greatness** <note>original: "mahitvā"</note>, quickly pushed apart **heaven and earth** <note>original: "rodasī"</note>. Because—

<vocab>
Indra: The King of the gods and deity of rain and thunder.
Soma: A sacred ritual drink prepared from a plant, offered to the gods.
Pakti (Cooked offering): Usually refers to the Purodasha, a cake made of ground grain offered in the fire.
Dhana (Parched grains): Barley grains that have been roasted, a common Vedic offering.
Brahmakara (Maker of prayer): A priest who composes or prepares the sacred hymns and ritual food.
Shavas (Strength): The divine might of Indra.
Rodasi (Heaven and Earth): A dual term referring to the two worlds as a pair.
Suri (Wise patron): The leader or sacrificer who sponsors the ritual.

[Mandala 6, Adhyaya 7, Sukta 30]     ॥ Fourth Ashtaka ॥     707

## Commentary (Sayana)
...meaning that Heaven and Earth are afraid. The <term>Sūri</term> <note>the wise patron or the one who chants the praises</note>, being swift and diligent, satisfies Indra with <term>ūtī</term> <note>literally "protection," here referring to the satisfying oblation of the sacrifice</note> while worshipping him properly. He fills Indra [with strength]. An analogy is provided: just as a cowherd satisfies his herds of cattle by leading them to water to drink, so too does the worshipper satisfy the deity.

## Hymn Text
->॥ Now the Sixth Verse ॥<-

**Thus indeed, let the great Indra be easy to invoke; whether he comes to us or stays away, he of the golden jaw is a warrior. For he was born with incomparable strength; he shall slay many <term>Vṛtras</term> <note>obstacles or demonic forces</note> and strike down the <term>Dasyus</term> <note>those who oppose the sacred laws</note>.** ॥ 6 ॥

**Word-for-Word Analysis (Pada-patha):**
Thus (eva). Indeed (it). Indra (indram). Easy to invoke (su-havam). Great (ṛṣvaḥ). Let him be (astu). With coming (ūtī). Without coming (anūtī). Golden-jawed (hiri-śipraḥ). A warrior (satvā).
Thus (eva). For (hi). Born (jātaḥ). Of incomparable strength (asamāti-ojāḥ). Many (puru). And (ca). Obstacles/enemies (vṛtrā). He slays (hanati). Down (ni). The enemies/Dasyus (dasyūn). ॥ 6 ॥

## Commentary (Sayana)
In the manner previously described, let the great Indra be <term>suhavaḥ</term>, meaning easy to be invoked or called upon for help. The word *it* serves as a rhythmic filler. <term>Hiriśipraḥ</term>: the word <term>śipra</term> can refer to either the jaws or the nose; thus, he has golden-colored jaws. Whether by his arrival (<term>ūtī</term>) or even by his non-arrival (<term>anūtī</term>), he remains a <term>satvā</term>, one who causes wealth to reach us. This implies that whether he is personally present at the sacrifice or not, he bestows wealth upon his praisers. For he was born in this way, possessing <term>asamātyojāḥ</term>—strength or vital power (<term>ojas</term>) that is unequal, incomparable, and superior to all. Being so, may he destroy many <term>Vṛtras</term>, referring to the "coverers" or "obstructers" such as the Rakshasas and other demons. Likewise, may he strike down the <term>Dasyus</term>, those enemies who seek to diminish or destroy the righteous.

->॥ This concludes the first Varga in the seventh Adhyaya of the fourth Ashtaka ॥<-

The seventh hymn, beginning with the words "Truly he increased," consists of five verses. Its seer is <term>Bharadvāja</term>, its meter is <term>Trisṭubh</term>, and it is dedicated to Indra. This is confirmed by the Index of hymns. In the <term>Agniṣṭoma</term> sacrifice, during the midday libation <note>original: "mādhyaṃdina-savana"</note>, this hymn is to be recited as part of the <term>Acchāvāka</term> priest's ritual chant. This is indicated in the <term>Āśvalāyana-Śrauta-Sūtra</term> (5.16): "The hymn *ud vinvasya* is omitted; [recite] *bhūya it*." Similarly, in the <term>Mahāvrata</term> rite, this hymn is used in the <term>Niṣkevalya</term> chant. This is noted in the <term>Aitareya Āraṇyaka</term> (5.6): "Truly he increased for heroic power..."

---

## Hymn Text
->॥ Therein, the First Verse ॥<-

**Truly he has increased for heroic power; alone and unaging, he bestows wealth. Indra has surpassed both Heaven and Earth; even one half of him is a match for both worlds.** ॥ 1 ॥

**Word-for-Word Analysis (Pada-patha):**
More/Greatly (bhūyaḥ). Indeed (it). He increased (vavṛdhe). For heroic power (vīryāya). Alone (ekaḥ). Unaging (ajuryaḥ). He bestows (dayate). Wealth (vasūni).
He surpassed (pra-rarice). Than heaven (divaḥ). Indra (indraḥ). Than earth (pṛthivyāḥ). A half (ardham). Indeed (it). Of him (asya). Against (prati). Worlds (rodasī). Both (ubhe). ॥ 1 ॥

[Rig Veda] — [Ashtaka 4, Adhyaya 1, Varga 2] — 708

## Commentary (Sayana) — Continued from previous page
This Indra has grown even more significantly; he has become greatly enlarged. For what purpose? For **heroic power**, to perform heroic deeds such as the slaying of the demon Vritra <note>original: Vṛtra-vadha</note>. He is the one chief, unaging, and impossible to decay; this Indra bestows **riches** and wealth upon the singers. Likewise, this Indra exceeds the heavens and the earth. Furthermore, both **Heaven and Earth** <note>original: Rodasī</note> are like half of him; this means that the two parts—Heaven and Earth—are represented by only half of Indra's vast form.

---

-> ॥ Now the Second Verse ॥ <-

## Hymn Text
**Now I acknowledge his great divine power, which he sustains and no one can diminish. Day by day, the Sun has become visible; with good wisdom, he established the dwellings extensively.** ॥ 2 ॥

**Word-for-Word Analysis (Pada-patha):**
Now (adha). I acknowledge (manye). Great (bṛhat). Divine power (asuryam). His (asya). Which (yāni). He sustains (dadhāra). No one (nakiḥ). Forth (ā). Diminishes (mināti).
Day by day (dive-dive). The Sun (sūryaḥ). Visible (darśataḥ). Has become (bhūt). Apart (vi). Dwellings (sadmāni). Extensively (urviyā). Of good wisdom (su-kratuḥ). Established (dhāt). ॥ 2 ॥

## Commentary (Sayana)
Now I acknowledge—that is, I **praise—the great, vast divine power of this Indra, which is the strength skilled in slaying the Asuras** <note>original: Asurya</note>. The word "acknowledge" <note>manyati</note> is used here in the sense of offering praise. And those deeds which Indra **sustains** or maintains, **no one can diminish** or destroy them. What are these deeds? It is explained: **Day by day**, every single day, the **Sun**, which had been enveloped by the demon Vritra, **has become visible** or worthy of being seen. By slaying the obscuring demon, Indra caused the Sun to shine—this is one deed. That Indra, being **of good wisdom** or possessor of noble actions, **established** or created the **dwellings**—meaning the worlds—**extensively** and wide. This is his other deed. The meaning is that he has performed these and many other such great acts.

---

-> ॥ Now the Third Verse ॥ <-

## Hymn Text
**Even today, and even of old, that work for the rivers exists, when you carved a path for them, O Indra. The mountains sat down like [restrained guests]; the worlds were made firm by you, O wise one.** ॥ 3 ॥

**Word-for-Word Analysis (Pada-patha):**
Today (adya). Even (cit). Now (nu). Even (cit). That (tat). Work (apaḥ). Of the rivers (nadīnām). When (yat). For these (ābhyaḥ). You carved (aradaḥ). A path (gātum). Indra (indra).
Down (ni). Mountains (parvatāḥ). Settled/Sat (seduḥ). Like (na). Those who sit in the home (ahva-sadaḥ). By you (tvayā). Made firm (dṛḷhāni). O wise one (su-krato). Worlds/Spheres (rajāṃsi). ॥ 3 ॥

## Commentary (Sayana)
O Indra, **even today** and **even of old**, your **work** regarding the **rivers** remains active. For **these** rivers, you **carved** out a **path** or a way for them to flow; this deed of yours proceeds forever without being exhausted. Furthermore, by your command, the **mountains** **sat down** or became stationary.

<vocab>
- **Indra**: The king of the gods in the Rig Veda, associated with storms, war, and the release of waters.
- **Asuryam**: Divine power; in early Vedic Sanskrit, this refers to the potent, life-giving power of the gods (Asuras), before the term "Asura" shifted to mean "demon."
- **Sukratu**: One of good wisdom or right action; an epithet describing Indra’s skillful governance of the universe.
- **Rajansi**: The worlds or celestial spheres; often referring to the layers of the atmosphere or space.
- **Dadhara**: Sustained, supported, or maintained; referring to Indra’s role as the upholder of cosmic order.
- **Gatum**: A path, way, or course; specifically used here for the channels Indra carved for the flowing rivers.
</vocab>

[Rig Veda] — [Ashtaka 4, Adhyaya 7, Varga 2] — 709

## Commentary (Sayana) — Continued from previous page
...they became still. Having abandoned their flight, they sat down motionlessly in a certain place. **Like those sitting for food** <note>original: annasado na</note>. This refers to men who sit still for the sake of food that is to be eaten. Just as they remain motionless for a meal, so it is here. For this reason, O **Indra of good deeds** <note>original: su-kratu</note>, all the worlds were made firm and established by you.

---

## Hymn Text
->|| Now the Fourth Verse ||<-

**Truly, there is no other like you, Indra; neither god nor mortal is greater. You slew the serpent who lay encompassing [the waters]; you released the waters toward the ocean.** ॥ 4 ॥

**Word-for-Word Analysis (Pada-patha):**
Truly (satyam). Indeed (it). That (tat). Not (na). Like you (tvā-vān). Other (anyaḥ). Is (asti). Indra (indra). God (devaḥ). Not (na). Mortal (martyaḥ). Greater (jyāyān).
He slew (ahan). The serpent (ahim). Lying around (pari-śayānam). The flood (arṇaḥ). Down (ava). He released (asṛjaḥ). The waters (apaḥ). Towards (achā). The ocean (samudram). ॥ 4 ॥

## Commentary (Sayana)
O **Indra**, that which is about to be said is **truly** the truth and not a falsehood. There is **no other god** who is **like you**. Likewise, there is **no mortal** man who is your equal. Indeed, there is no god or man who is **greater** or superior to you. This point is established as absolute truth. Furthermore, you **slew the serpent**—the cloud <note>original: megha</note>—which was **lying around** and encompassing the **flood** of water. Having struck it, you **released the waters** in a downward direction **towards the ocean**, which refers to either the atmosphere or the literal sea.

---

## Hymn Text
->|| Now the Fifth Verse ||<-

**O Indra, you forced open the gates of the waters that were spreading in all directions; you broke the firm [stronghold] of the mountain. You became the king of the world and of the tribes, producing the Sun, the Heaven, and the Dawn all together.** ॥ 5 ॥

**Word-for-Word Analysis (Pada-patha):**
You (tvam). Waters (apaḥ). Wide (vi). Gates (duraḥ). Spreading in all directions (viṣūcīḥ). Indra (indra). Firm (dṛḷham). Broke (arujaḥ). Of the mountain (parvatasya).
King (rājā). You became (abhavaḥ). Of the world (jagataḥ). Of the tribes (carṣaṇīnām). Together (sākam). The Sun (sūryam). Generating (janayan). The Heaven (dyām). The Dawn (uṣasam). ॥ 5 ॥

## Commentary (Sayana)
O **Indra**, you **opened the gates** <note>original: duraḥ</note> that were obstructed by the demon Vritra so that the **waters**, which were **spreading in all directions**, could flow everywhere. You **broke** the **firm** or solid part of the **mountain** <note>original: parvata</note>—here meaning the cloud which possesses "knots" or sections <note>original: parvavan</note>—which was binding the waters. Moreover, you **became the king** or the sovereign lord **of the world** and of the **tribes** or people. While doing what? **Generating** or manifesting the **Sun**, the **Heaven** (the sky), and the **Dawn**—these three which were previously covered by darkness—**all together** or simultaneously. You brought them into the light.

->|| Thus ends the second Varga of the seventh Adhyaya of the fourth Ashtaka ||<-

The eighth Sukta (Sukta 32), beginning with "He who alone" <note>original: abhūreka</note>, contains five verses. The seer is Bharadvaja or Suhotra. The penultimate verse is in the Shakvari meter.

<meta>This page continues the Rig Veda commentary by Sayana. It marks the beginning of the 3rd Varga (section) of the 7th Adhyaya (chapter) in the 4th Ashtaka (book). It transitions from the conclusion of Sukta 30 to the start of Sukta 31 of Mandala 6.</meta>

# Rig Veda #
### [Book 4, Chapter 7, Section 3] ###

The remaining four verses are in the <term>Trishtubh</term> <note>a meter consisting of four lines of eleven syllables each</note> meter. The deity is Indra. The index states: "The hymn beginning with 'You alone have become' consists of Trishtubh verses, but the fourth is in the <term>Shakvari</term> <note>a longer meter of 56 syllables</note> meter." For the <term>Mahavrata</term> <note>a significant rite in the Agnicayana or Soma sacrifice</note>, these eight hymns starting from this one are to be recited during the <term>Nishkevalya Shastra</term> <note>a specific invocation to Indra</note>. This is confirmed by the fifth book of the *Aitareya Aranyaka* (5.1.3): "The eight hymns beginning with 'You alone, O Lord of wealth, have become...'" Likewise, on the sixth day of the <term>Prishthya</term> <note>a six-day sacrifice</note> ceremony, this hymn is used as the <term>Nivid-dhana</term> <note>a hymn containing a specific formula or invitation to the gods</note> for the <term>Nishkevalya</term> recitation. It is indicated in the *Ashvalayana Shrauta Sutra* (8.1): "The Nishkevalya consists of 'Indra, come to us,' 'Now surely of this,' and 'You alone have become...'" Furthermore, in the <term>Vishvajit</term> sacrifice during the midday libation, this is to be recited by the <term>Achhavaka</term> priest as the <term>Samasukta</term> <note>a hymn corresponding to a chant</note>. This is noted in the *Ashvalayana Shrauta Sutra* (8.7): "The Samasuktas are 'You alone, O Lord of wealth...'"

---

## Hymn Text

-> ॥ Here is the First Verse ॥ <-
<note>Rig Veda 6.31.1</note>
**You alone, O Lord of wealth, have become the master of riches; you, O Indra, hold the peoples within your hands. Concerning offspring, waters, and descendants, and in the presence of the sun, the people of diverse speech have spoken their praises.** ॥ 1 ॥

**Word-for-Word Analysis (Pada-patha):**
You have become (abhūḥ). Alone (ekaḥ). O Lord of wealth (rayi-pate). Of riches (rayīṇām). [In your] (ā). Hands (hastayoḥ). You hold (adhi-thāḥ). Indra (indra). The peoples (kṛṣṭīḥ).
Concerning (vi). Offspring (toke). In the waters (apsu). In the descendant (tanaye). And (ca). In the sun (sūre). They have spoken (avocanta). The people (carṣaṇayaḥ). Of diverse speech (vi-vācaḥ). ॥ 1 ॥

---

## Commentary (Sayana)

O **Lord of wealth** <note>original: rayipate</note>, protector of riches, you, **Indra**, being the **one** supreme being, **have become** <note>original: abhūḥ</note>—that is, you are—the master **of riches** <note>original: rayīṇām</note>. Alternatively, the connection is: "of riches, O Lord of riches." The repetition of the word "wealth" is for emphasis, similar to the phrase: **"O Indra, you alone are the Lord of Cattle among cattle"** <note>original: gavām asi gopati-reka indra; Rig Veda 7.98.6</note>. In that context, it should be understood that you are the one primary master. Furthermore, O **Indra**, you **hold** <note>original: adhithāḥ</note> the **peoples** <note>original: kṛṣṭīḥ</note>—your subjects—within your own two **hands** <note>original: hastayoḥ</note>. This means the entire world exists under your command. Moreover, **men** <note>original: carṣaṇayaḥ</note>, possessing **diverse voices** <note>original: vivācaḥ</note> or distinct hymns of praise, **have spoken** <note>original: avocanta</note> various prayers when motivated by the need for **offspring** <note>original: toke</note> (meaning a son), **waters** <note>original: apsu</note>, the **sun** <note>original: sūre</note> (which stimulates enemies), and **descendants** <note>original: tanaye</note> (meaning grandsons). They speak in various ways.

---

## Hymn Text

-> ॥ Now the Second Verse ॥ <-
<note>Rig Veda 6.31.2</note>
**Through fear of you, O Indra, all the earthly regions—even those that are unshakeable—are made to tremble. Heaven and Earth, the mountains, the forests—everything firm is afraid at your onset.** ॥ 2 ॥

**Word-for-Word Analysis (Pada-patha):**
From you (tvat). Through fear (bhiyā). Indra (indra). Earthly (pārthivāni). All (viśvā). Unshakeable (acyutā). Even (cit). They are made to tremble (cyavayante). Regions (rajāṃsi).
Heaven and Earth (dyāvākṣāmā). Mountains (parvatāsaḥ). Forests (vanāni). Everything (viśvam). Firm (dṛḷham). Is afraid (bhayate). At the onset (ajman). Toward (ā). Of you (te). ॥ 2 ॥

---

## Commentary (Sayana)

O **Indra**, **through fear** <note>original: bhiyā</note> **of you** <note>original: tvattaḥ</note>, **all** the pervasive **earthly** <note>original: pārthivāni</note> realms—a name for both the Earth and the Mid-air—and the **waters** <note>original: rajāṃsi</note> that exist there, which are **even unshakeable** <note>original: acyutā cit</note> or impossible to displace, [are nonetheless moved] <unclear>...</unclear>

**Word-by-word Breakdown:**

## Commentary (Sayana)

O **Indra**, you, together with **Kutsa** <note>a legendary hero and protégé of Indra</note>, fought against **Shushna** <note>original: "śuṣṇa"; a demon of drought whose name implies "the drier"</note>, who was powerful and impossible to wither. For the sake of aiding Kutsa, you engaged in battle with that demon. Likewise, in the **battle for cows** <note>original: "gaviṣṭau"; literally "the search for cows," a common Vedic term for war</note>—so called because "cows" (arrows or rays) go forth or are sought there—you **struck** <note>original: "darśaḥ"; meaning you destroyed or bit into</note> the demon named **Kuyava** <note>meaning "of bad harvests"</note>. Furthermore, in the **onset** <note>original: "prapitve"; the clashing or falling together of armies</note> of the battle, you **stole** the **wheel of the Sun** which is a part of his chariot. From that time on, the Sun’s chariot became one-wheeled. This is traditionally taught: <note>original: "sapta yuñjanti ratham ekacakram"; Rig Veda 1.164.2</note> "Seven yoke the one-wheeled chariot." The legend says that when the Sage Etasha was in battle with the Sun, Indra arrived to assist him and seized the Sun’s wheel. Another Vedic text says: <note>original: "sūraścakraṃ pra vṛhajjāta ojasā"; Rig Veda 1.130.9</note> "He seized the Sun’s wheel with his innate might." Additionally, you **drove away** <note>original: "aviveḥ"</note> the **evils** <note>original: "rapāṃsi"; referring to sinful beings like the Rakshasas</note> from this world. This means you struck them down.

to Bharadvaja | to the one praising | riches || 4 ||

...the fortresses <note>original: "purah"</note>, which were unassailable and had never been reached by anyone else. You struck them down; you destroyed them. ## Hymn Text

## Commentary (Sayana)

O **Indra of true warriors** <note>original: "satyasatvan"; one whose soldiers or followers are steadfast and true</note>. O **possessor of much wealth** <note>original: "tuvinṛmṇa"; one who holds abundant riches or power</note>. O Indra of such qualities, **mount your formidable** <note>original: "bhīmaṃ"; terrifying to enemies</note> **chariot** for the sake of the **great battle** <note>original: "mahate raṇāya"</note>. O **traveler of great paths** <note>original: "prapathin"; one who knows the best or most excellent ways</note>, come **toward me** <note>original: "madrik"</note> on that chariot along with your **protection** <note>original: "avasā"</note>. Furthermore, O **famous Indra** <note>original: "śruta"</note>, **make us heard**—that is, make us famous—among all the **tribes** <note>original: "carṣaṇibhyaḥ"; the various peoples or communities</note>. ---

The ninth hymn of this section <note>Sukta 33 in the standard numbering</note>, beginning with the word **Apurvya** ("unprecedented"), consists of five verses. It is composed in the **Trishtubh** meter and is dedicated to **Indra**. This hymn is designated to be recited during the *Nishkevalya* Shastra <note>a specific chant for Indra</note> on the second *Chandomika* day of the Vedic sacrifice. It is indicated in the ritual manuals: *Apurvya purutamani tam su te kirttim* (Ashvalayana Shrauta Sutra 7.9). This hymn is also prescribed for the *Mahavrata* rite <note>an important end-of-year festival</note>.

->॥ Now the First Verse ॥<-

## Hymn Text

I fashion unprecedented, numerous, and most blissful songs of praise with my mouth for this great, heroic, powerful, and swift Indra, the wielder of the thunderbolt, the ancient and mighty one. || 1 ||

**Word-by-word Breakdown:**
Unprecedented | most numerous | for him | for the great | for the hero | for the powerful | for the swift | 
for the mighty | for the wielder of the thunderbolt | most blissful | words | with the mouth | for the ancient | I fashion || 1 ||

---

## Commentary (Sayana)

**Unprecedented** <note>original: "apūrvyā"; meaning new, never performed by previous poets</note>, **most numerous** <note>original: "purutamāni"</note>, and **most blissful** <note>original: "śaṃtamāni"; bringing the greatest peace or happiness</note> **words** <note>original: "vacāṃsi"</note>—which are sentences in the form of praise—**I fashion** <note>original: "takṣaṃ"; literally "I carve" or "I craft," as a carpenter crafts wood</note> with my mouth for this Indra.

<vocab>
<term>Satyasatvan</term> (having true followers/warriors): Refers to Indra as a leader of a loyal and effective divine army.
<term>Tuvinrimna</term> (possessing much wealth/power): A common epithet emphasizing Indra's ability to bestow material rewards on his worshippers.
<term>Rana</term> (battle/war): In the Vedic context, often refers to the cosmic struggle to release water or light.
<term>Madrik</term> (towards me): A personal plea for the deity's direct attention.
<term>Charshani</term> (people/tribes): Refers to the settled human communities that offer sacrifices.
<term>Apurvya</term> (unprecedented/new): Highlights the poet's creativity; the gods are said to enjoy "new" songs more than old ones.
<term>Vajrin</term> (wielder of the thunderbolt): Indra's primary attribute, the *Vajra*, used to slay demons.
<term>Taksham</term> (I fashion/create): The Vedic poets viewed the composition of hymns as a skilled craft, similar to woodworking or chariot-building.
</vocab>

<summary>This page concludes the praises for Indra's past victories over the demon Shambara and begins a new hymn (Sukta 33) where the poet Bharadvaja crafts "unprecedented" songs to invoke Indra's protection and fame.</summary>
<keywords>Indra, Bharadvaja, Divodasa, Shambara, Vedic sacrifice, hymn-crafting, Trishtubh meter, protection, fame</keywords>

<meta>This page continues the commentary on the first verse of Hymn 32, which focuses on the poet's creative act of composing hymns for Indra. It then presents verses 2 and 3 of the same hymn, describing Indra's cosmic deeds: the illumination of the world, the liberation of the "cows" (often symbolizing rays of light or wisdom) from the mountain-prison, and the destruction of the fortresses belonging to the demons with the help of the Angiras priests.</meta>

[Rig Veda]      || Mandala 6, Adhyaya 3, Hymn 32 ||      713

[Completion of commentary on Verse 1]
...**I fashion** <note>original: "atakṣaṃ"</note>; I create. For what kind of person? For the **great** <note>original: "mahe"</note>, for the mighty hero who is the slayer of various enemies, the powerful, the swift, the one uniquely worthy of praise, the wielder of the thunderbolt, and the ancient, exalted one.

---

## Hymn Text

->॥ Now the Second Verse ॥<-

He illuminated the **two Mothers** with the sun for the sake of the **Seers**; shattering the mountain as he shouted. Desiring them with wise meditations and songs of praise, he released the confinement of the **cows**. || 2 ||

**[Word-by-word Breakdown]**
He | the two Mothers | with the sun | of the Seers | illuminated | shattering | the mountain | shouting | 
with wise meditations | with chanters | desiring | upward | of the cows | released | the bond || 2 ||

---

## Commentary (Sayana)

That **Indra** illuminated—made manifest—the **two Mothers** <note>original: "mātarau"</note>, namely Heaven and Earth, with the **sun** <note>original: "sūryeṇa"</note> for the sake of the **Seers** <note>original: "kavīnām"</note>, the Angirases who possess transcendent vision. What was he doing? He was **shattering** <note>original: "rujan"</note> the **mountain** <note>original: "adrim"</note>—the rock-fortress where the cows were forcibly hidden from sight. Alternatively, the phrase "of the Seers" refers to the Angirases in the sense of the third case (instrumental): "by the Seers." In this connection, he is the one **being praised** <note>original: "gṛṇānaḥ"</note> by the Angirases. Furthermore, being **repeatedly desired** <note>original: "vāvaśānaḥ"</note> by the Angirases, who are **chanters** <note>original: "ṛkvabhiḥ"</note> possessing **excellent meditations** <note>original: "svādhībhiḥ"</note>, he **released** <note>original: "udasṛjat"</note> or untied the **bond** <note>original: "nidānam"</note>— the confinement—of the **cows** <note>original: "usriyāṇām"</note> who had been stolen by the Panis, the servants of the demon Vala.

---

## Hymn Text

->॥ Now the Third Verse ॥<-

With the **bearers** and the **chanters**, he constantly conquered for the sake of the **cows** alongside those who **kneel in prayer**; he of many deeds has won. A **destroyer of fortresses**, seeking friendship with his **friends**, he, being a **Seer** himself, shattered the firm strongholds with the **Seers**. || 3 ||

**[Word-by-word Breakdown]**
He | with the bearers | with the chanters | among the cows | constantly | with those who kneel | the doer of many deeds | conquered | 
the fortresses | the destroyer of fortresses | with friends | seeking friendship | the firm [forts] | shattered | with the Seers | a Seer | being || 3 ||

---

## Commentary (Sayana)

That Indra, the **doer of many deeds** <note>original: "purukṛtvā"</note>, conquered the demons for the sake of the **cows** <note>original: "goṣu"</note>. He did this in the company of the **bearers** <note>original: "vahnibhiḥ"</note>, those who carry the oblations, the **chanters** <note>original: "ṛkvabhiḥ"</note> or praisers, and the Angirases who are **always kneeling** <note>original: "śasvat-mita-jñubhiḥ"</note> with bent knees in devotion. Having conquered them, Indra, the **destroyer of fortresses** <note>original: "purohā"</note>, **shattered** <note>original: "ruroja"</note> the **firm** <note>original: "dṛḷhāḥ"</note> strongholds belonging to the Asuras. He did this alongside his **friends** <note>original: "sakhibhiḥ"</note>, the **Seers** <note>original: "kavibhiḥ"</note>—the Angirases of transcendent wisdom—because he was **seeking friendship** <note>original: "sakhīyan"</note> for himself and was **himself a Seer** <note>original: "kaviḥ san"</note> possessing that same transcendent wisdom.

---

## Hymn Text

->॥ Now the Fourth Verse ॥<-

O Showerer of boons, come toward the singer with fresh means, with great strengths and with great powers; with many heroes, O Lord of the people, O you who delight in songs, proceed for our welfare. || 4 ||

> He | with fresh [means] | the singer | toward | great | with strengths | with great | and | with powers | 
> with many heroes | O Showerer | of the people | [towards] | O you who delight in songs | for welfare | forward | go || 4 ||

---

## Commentary (Sayana)

**O Showerer** <note>original: "vṛṣabha"</note>, you who rain down the fulfillment of desires; **O you who delight in songs** <note>original: "gīrvaṇas"</note>, O Indra, who are to be honored by the speech of praise: may you **proceed** <note>original: "pra yāhi"</note>—that is, come—**toward** <note>original: "acchā"</note> the **singer** <note>original: "jaritāram"</note>, the one who praises you among the **people** <note>original: "kṣitīnām"</note> (humanity). Come along with **great** <note>original: "maho"</note> and mighty **strengths** <note>original: "vājebhir"</note> and with great **powers** <note>original: "śuṣmair"</note> (forces). Come with **fresh** <note>original: "nīvyābhir"</note>—meaning newer or more recent—**many-heroed** <note>original: "puruvīrābhir"</note> mares <note>note: Sayana interprets "nīvyābhir puruvīrābhir" as mares that produce many heroic offspring or are exceptionally powerful</note>. For what purpose? **For welfare** <note>original: "suvitāya"</note>, which means for the sake of beautiful happiness or the attainment of bliss. ||

---

## Hymn Text

->॥ Now the Fifth Verse ॥<-

With impetuous force, moved by his horses, Indra, the conqueror of the swift, released the waters from the south. Thus being released, they entered their unassailable goal day by day, never to return. || 5 ||

> He | with impetuous [force] | with strength | moved | by horses | the waters | Indra | from the south | conqueror of the swift | 
> thus | being released | without turning back | the goal | day by day | they entered | the unassailable || 5 ||

---

## Commentary (Sayana)

**The conqueror of the swift** <note>original: "turāṣāṭ"</note>, the one who endures and overcomes violent enemies: **that Indra**, being **moved** <note>original: "taktaḥ"</note> or joined **with impetuous** <note>original: "sargeṇa"</note> and all-endeavoring **strength** <note>original: "śavasā"</note> and by **horses** <note>original: "atyair"</note>—which are either constantly moving steeds or rays of brilliance—is said to release the **waters** <note>original: "apaḥ"</note> **from the south** <note>original: "dakṣiṇataḥ"</note>, referring to the time of the southern solstice <note>term: Dakshinayana; the southern path of the sun often associated with the rainy season in Vedic interpretation</note>. **Thus** <note>original: "itthā"</note>, in this manner, these **being released** <note>original: "sṛjānāḥ"</note> waters **entered** <note>original: "viviśuḥ"</note> or pervaded the **goal** <note>original: "artham"</note>, which is the **unassailable** <note>original: "apramṛṣyam"</note> ocean that cannot be shaken by others. They do so **day by day** <note>original: "dive-dive"</note> in such a way that there is **no turning back** <note>original: "anapāvṛt"</note>, meaning they do not return. The word "goal" <note>original: "artham"</note> here is a form ending in the suffix *tyan* <note>note: a grammatical technicality regarding the Vedic formation of the word</note>. ||

---

->॥ Thus ends the fourth section (Varga) of the seventh Chapter (Adhyaya) of the fourth Book (Ashtaka). ॥<-

**"He who is most mighty"** <note>original: "ya ojiṣṭha iti"</note>: Thus begins the tenth hymn, consisting of five verses. Its seer is Shunahotra, its meter is Trishtubh, and its deity is Indra. It is indexed as follows: **"He who is most mighty, by Shunahotra..."** <note>original: "ya ojiṣṭhaḥ śunahotras tv iti"</note>. Its application <note>term: viniyoga; the ritual use of the hymn</note> is mentioned in the "Solely-Appropriated" <note>original: "niṣkevalya"</note> libation of the Mahavrata ceremony.

<vocab>Bull/Showerer (vṛṣabha): a title for Indra denoting his power to grant boons like rain; Delighter in Songs (gīrvaṇaḥ): one who is nourished or pleased by hymns; Indra: the king of the gods; Conqueror of the Swift (turāṣāṭ): an epithet of Indra as the subduer of fast-attacking foes; Singer (jaritāram): the poet or priest chanting the hymn; Strengths/Victuals (vājebhiḥ): can mean food, sacrificial offerings, or strength; Welfare (suvitāya): a good path or prosperity; Strength (śavasā): heroic power; From the south (dakṣiṇataḥ): referring to the southern direction or the winter solstice; Being released (sṛjānāḥ): the act of letting flow; They entered (viviśuḥ): to permeate or reach; Shunahotra: the name of the sage/seer of the next hymn.</vocab>

<summary>This page concludes the 32nd hymn of Mandala 4, describing Indra as a provider of welfare who releases the celestial and terrestrial waters during the southern transit of the sun. It also introduces the following hymn by the seer Shunahotra, noting its ritual significance in the Mahavrata ceremony.</summary>

# Mandala 6. Chapter 3. Hymn 33. || Fourth Book || 715

## Hymn Text

->|| Here is the First Verse ||<-

O Indra, grant us that most vigorous joy, O Bountiful One, the giver of good things, the liberal one; that which, possessing fine horses, might win a group of noble steeds, and might utterly subdue the enemies and the foes in battles. || 1 ||

**Word-by-Word Breakdown:**
Which | most vigorous | O Indra | that | well | to us | grant | joy <note>Interpretive note: Referring here to a son or a state of being</note> | O Bountiful One | giver of good things | liberal | possessing fine horses | which | might win | with good horses | enemies | in battles | might subdue | foes || 1 ||

---

## Commentary (Sayana)

**O Bountiful One** <note>original: "vṛṣan"</note>, O Indra, you who rain down the fulfillment of desires: grant to us **that** <note>original: "tam"</note> son who is **most vigorous** <note>original: "ojiṣṭha"</note>, most endowed with vitality, and most powerful. He is your **joy** <note>original: "madaḥ"</note>, meaning the one who gladdens you; in other words, the singer who offers praise. He is the **giver of good things** <note>original: "svabhiṣṭiḥ"</note>, one who is worthy of being sought out, and **liberal** <note>original: "dāsvān"</note>, meaning he possesses the quality of giving oblations. **Grant** <note>original: "dāḥ"</note>—that is, bestow—**well** <note>original: "su"</note> upon us such a son endowed with these qualities. The connection of the verse is: grant that son who, **possessing fine horses** <note>original: "su-aśvaḥ"</note>, might **win** <note>original: "vanavat"</note> or acquire a **group of noble steeds** <note>original: "sauvaśvyam"</note> in the midst of **battles** <note>original: "samatsu"</note> (warfare); and who might **utterly subdue** <note>original: "sāsahat"</note> the **enemies** <note>original: "vṛtrā"</note>—those who obstruct—and the **foes** <note>original: "amitrān"</note>. ||

---

## Hymn Text

->|| Now the Second Verse ||<-

For you indeed, O Indra, do people with diverse voices call for protection in the battle for heroes; with the wise sages you have laid low the Panis; and the one protected by you surely becomes the winner of strength-wealth with his horse. || 2 ||

**Word-by-Word Breakdown:**
You | indeed | O Indra | for protection | diverse-voiced | call | people | in the battle for heroes | you | with the wise | [intensifier] | the Panis | have laid low | protected by you | surely | the winner | strength-wealth | the horse-rider || 2 ||

---

## Commentary (Sayana)

**O Indra**, **indeed** <note>original: "hi"</note> it is **you** whom **people** <note>original: "carṣaṇayaḥ"</note> (human beings) who are **diverse-voiced** <note>original: "vivācaḥ"</note>—meaning those whose speech takes the form of various hymns of praise—**call** <note>original: "havante"</note> or invite for the sake of **protection** <note>original: "avase"</note> in the **battle for heroes** <note>original: "śūrasātau"</note>, the combat where heroes find their portion. Furthermore, **you**—along with the **wise** <note>original: "viprebhiḥ"</note>, the sagely Angirasas—**have laid low** <note>original: "vyaśāyaḥ"</note>, meaning you specifically struck down and killed, the **Panis** <note>term: Pani (the miserly demons who were the followers of Vala and stole the celestial cows)</note>. Therefore, the person who is **protected by you** <note>original: "tvota it"</note> becomes the **winner** <note>original: "sanitā"</note> or the possessor of **strength-wealth** <note>term: Vaja (a multifaceted word meaning strength, food, or the spoils of war)</note>, and he becomes an **approacher** <note>original: "arvā"</note> of that wealth. ||

---

## Hymn Text

->|| Now the Third Verse ||<-

O Hero, you struck down both of those enemies—the non-Aryan foes and the Aryan ones; like woods cut down, you struck them with well-placed hymns; reveal yourself in the battles, O most manly of men. || 3 ||

**Word-by-Word Breakdown:**
You | those | O Indra | both | foes | enemies | the Aryans | and | O Hero | you struck | like woods | with well-placed | with hymns | [reveal] | in battles | you reveal | of men | most manly || 3 ||

<vocab>
इन्द्र (Indra): The king of gods and god of storms and war.
वृषन् (Vrsan/Bountiful): A title for Indra meaning "the bull" or "the showerer of blessings."
वृत्र (Vrtra/Obstacle-Enemies): Originally the dragon-demon of drought, here referring to any obstructing enemies.
पणि (Pani/Miserly spirits): Mythological figures known for their greed; often used to describe those who do not sacrifice.
शूरसातौ (Battle for heroes): A technical term for a conflict where warriors win their glory or loot.
वाज (Vaja): A term signifying vital energy, speed, or the tangible rewards of victory like grain and cattle.
</vocab>

<meta>This page continues the commentary for Rig Veda, Mandala 4, Hymn (Sukta) 20. The previous page concluded the discussion on the third verse, specifically focusing on Indra's role as a conqueror of both 'Arya' and 'Dasa' enemies. This page completes that thought and provides the text and commentary for Verse 4 and the beginning of Verse 5. Note: While the previous page's metadata mentioned Mandala 6, the current source text clearly identifies this as Mandala 4, Sukta 20, which is part of the fourth book of the Rig Veda.</meta>

## Commentary (Sayana) - Continued from previous page
O Indra, you, desiring to strike both kinds of enemies, slew them. You harmed them. Who are these "both kinds"? They are the **Dasas** <note>original: "dāsa"</note>, the destroyers and enemies of the sacred rites, such as the demon Vala and others. Also, the **Aryas** <note>original: "āryā"</note>, who are excellent through their performance of rituals, and the **Vritras** <note>original: "vṛtrāṇi"</note>, the "concealers" like Vishvarupa and others—both these types, O Hero, you have struck down. Among men, the leaders, O Indra, you are the most excellent leader. In battles, you tear apart the enemies with your **well-placed** <note>original: "sudhitebhiḥ"</note> and personal weapons. You also split open other enemies. An illustration is provided: **like forests** <note>original: "vaneva"</note>. Just as a woodcutter cuts down groups of trees in the forests with an axe or similar tool, so do you act.

---

## Hymn Text
->|| Here is the Fourth Verse ||<-
O Indra, with your protections accompanied by songs of praise, be our friend, our protector for our prosperity, and present through our whole life. When we, fighting in the battle where the armies are divided, call upon you, O Hero, let it be for the winning of the light. || 4 ||

**Padapatha:**
He | You | Our | Indra | With songs of praise | With protection | Friend | Through all life | Protector | For prosperity | Be | In the winning of light | When | We call | You | Fighting | In the division of armies | In battles | Hero || 4 ||

## Commentary (Sayana)
O Indra, may you, being such as you are, **with protections accompanied by songs of praise** <note>original: "arkavābhirūtī"</note>, be the **protector** <note>original: "avitā"</note> for our **prosperity** <note>original: "vṛdhe"</note> or growth. Likewise, you who are **present through all life** <note>original: "viśvāyuḥ"</note>—meaning you who go everywhere—be our **friend** <note>original: "sakhā"</note>. Regarding the term **the division of armies** <note>original: "nemadhitā"</note>: the word *nema* means "half." It has been said in the ancient texts: <quote>The word 'nema' refers to a half</quote>. Thus, these are battles in which men are placed in two opposing halves. In such **battles** <note>original: "pṛtsu"</note>, as we are **fighting** <note>original: "yudhyantaḥ"</note>, and **when** <note>original: "yat"</note> we **call** <note>original: "hvayāmasi"</note> upon you, O Hero, for the purpose of **winning the light** <note>original: "svarṣātā"</note>—that is, for the sharing of wealth that is as desirable as the sun—at that time, be our protector and friend.

---

## Hymn Text
->|| Here is the Fifth Verse ||<-
Indra, truly be ours now and be ours in the future; be the granter of happiness and be with us in our approach. Thus praising you, may we remain under the protection of the Mighty One in the ultimate heaven, possessing many cattle. || 5 ||

**Padapatha:**
Truly | Our | Indra | For the future | And | May you be | Be | Granter of happiness | And | Our | In the approach | Thus | Praising | Of the Mighty One | In the protection | In heaven | May we be | In the end | Possessing many cattle || 5 ||

## Commentary (Sayana)
O Indra, you should **truly** <note>original: "nūnam"</note> be **ours** <note>original: "naḥ"</note> today. That is, belong to us. And **for the future** <note>original: "aparāya ca"</note>, at another time as well, be ours. Moreover, when we **approach** <note>original: "abhiṣṭau"</note> you, be a **granter of happiness** <note>original: "mṛḷīkaḥ"</note> to us. **Thus** <note>original: "itthā"</note>, in this manner, we who are **praising** <note>original: "gṛṇantaḥ"</note> you...

<vocab>
- **Indra**: The king of the gods and deity of rain and battle.
- **Arkavābhiḥ**: Accompanied by hymns or songs of praise.
- **Ūtī**: Derived from *ūti*, meaning protection or help.
- **Sakhā**: A friend or companion.
- **Vṛdhe**: For the sake of increase, growth, or prosperity.
- **Svarṣātā**: The winning or acquisition of *Svar* (heaven or light).
- **Nemadhitā**: A technical term for battle, literally "the placing of halves" (two sides).
- **Pṛtsu**: In clashes or battles.
- **Mṛḷīkaḥ**: Merciful or one who bestows bliss/happiness.
- **Sharman**: A house, shelter, or state of protection.
</vocab>

**The hymn beginning with "Together toward you"** <note>original: "saṃ ca tve jagmura"</note> is the eleventh hymn of this section, consisting of five verses, seen by the seer Sunahotra. This is recorded in the Index <note>Anukramani</note>. In the ritual of the third "Chandomika" day, these first two hymns are used. This is indicated in the scriptures: "The hymns beginning with 'Together toward you'..." (Ashvalayana Shrauta Sutra 9.7). This hymn is also used in the **Nishkevalya** <term>Nishkevalya: A specific series of recitations dedicated exclusively to Indra</term> portion of the **Mahavrata** <term>Mahavrata: A major "Great Vow" soma sacrifice</term> ceremony.

## Hymn Text

Together toward you, O Indra, many songs have gone; and from you, O All-pervading One, wise thoughts emerge. In the past and certainly now, the praises of the Rishis have vied for Indra's attention, as have the recited hymns and songs of praise. ॥ 1 ॥

---

## Commentary (Sayana)

**Together | and | in you | [they] have gone | songs | Indra | many | away | and | from you | go | all-pervading | wise thoughts |**
**formerly | now | and | praises | of the Rishis | vied | for Indra | [the] more | recited hymns and songs ॥ 1 ॥**

O Indra, **in you** <note>original: "tve"</note>, **many songs** <note>original: "pūrvīr-giraḥ"</note> and praises have **come together** or united. From **you** <note>original: "tvat"</note>, the **all-pervading** and extensive **wise thoughts** of the chanters **emerge** in various ways. The rest of the verse is spoken in the third person. In **former times** and **now** (this very day), the **praises** of the **Rishis**—those like Bharadvaja who can see truths beyond the reach of the senses—have **vied** <note>original: "paspṛdhre"</note> for Indra's favor. This means they were filled with a spirit of "me first, me first" in their haste to be the one to praise Indra. Likewise, the **recited hymns** <term>Uktha: The recited portion of the liturgy, as opposed to the sung portion</term> and the **songs of praise** <note>original: "arkā"</note> which serve as instruments of worship, have also **vied** with one another.

-> ॥ Here is the second verse ॥ <-

## Hymn Text

He who is called by many, exalted by many, the great one, the only one highly extolled through sacrifices—like a chariot joined for great strength, may Indra be celebrated by us. ॥ 2 ॥

---

## Commentary (Sayana)

**called by many | who | exalted by many | great | one | highly extolled | is | through sacrifices |**
**chariot | like | for great | strength | joined | by us | Indra | to be celebrated | became ॥ 2 ॥**

Indra is **called by many** <note>original: "puruhūto"</note> and **exalted by many** <note>original: "purugūrto"</note>. He is the **great** one and the **only** principal deity possessing these qualities. He is **highly extolled** in many ways through **sacrifices** performed by worshippers, or through the hymns that serve as the means of sacrifice. That Indra, **like a chariot** <note>original: "ratho na"</note> which is **joined** (yoked) for the sake of **great strength**...

For that purpose, being joined with our praises, may he be delighted by us, his praisers. May he always be worthy of praise.

-> ॥ Now the Third Verse ॥ <-

## Hymn Text

**Neither do prayers harm him, nor do hymns; reaching Indra, they increase his power.**
**Whether a hundred or a thousand praisers chant to the lover of song, that is a source of bliss for him. ॥ 3 ॥**

Neither | whom | harm | prayers | nor | voices | Indra | reaching | indeed | toward | increasing |
If | praisers | a hundred | if | a thousand | chant | lover of song | bliss | that | for him ॥ 3 ॥

---

## Commentary (Sayana)

Prayers <note>original: "dhītayaḥ," meaning actions or services</note> do not harm or disturb this Indra. Nor do voices <note>original: "vāṇīḥ," meaning hymns of praise</note> disturb him. In human life, a man who is unable to give what is asked of him is often distressed or annoyed by the services and praises of others <note>because he feels the burden of the debt</note>. However, because Indra possesses vast wealth and is a great giver, the services and songs directed toward him never become a cause of distress for him. This is the meaning.

What happens then? The text says: Reaching that Indra, these prayers increase him <note>strengthen his power</note>. Furthermore, if a hundred praisers chant to that Indra—who is the lover of song <note>original: "girvaṇasam," one who enjoys being praised</note>—or even if a thousand praisers chant, all those songs of praise become a source of "Sham" <note>peace, comfort, or bliss</note> for this Indra.

---

-> ॥ Now the Fourth Verse ॥ <-

## Hymn Text

**In the heavens, like light, with the measure of the month, the Soma has been poured into Indra.**
**As water rushes toward people in a desert, so the invocations have increased along with the sacrifices. ॥ 4 ॥**

For him | this | in heaven | like light | with the measure | desiring to sprinkle | in Indra | down | was fixed | Soma |
People | like | in a desert | toward | together | when | waters | together | have increased | invocations | with sacrifices ॥ 4 ॥

---

## Commentary (Sayana)

On this day <note>referring to the day of the Soma sacrifice</note>, by means of the hymn which is the instrument of worship <note>original: "arcā," like light or a prayer</note>, and with the "measure" <note>original: "māsā"</note>—that is, with the ritual formulas such as "For you, Indra, the Vritra-slayer..."—the Soma is prepared. This Soma, which is "desiring to sprinkle" <note>original: "mimikṣaḥ"</note> and is mixed with the ritual waters <term>Vasativari: special waters collected the night before a Soma sacrifice</term>, has been fixed or dedicated to this Indra. 

Alternatively, the poet says: "I will speak this praise for Indra." In the heavens, like the sun <note>original: "arkaḥ"</note>, or like the moon <note>original: "māsaḥ," the one who measures or divides time</note>, Indra exists as the pourer of the waters of rain. Into this Indra, the pressed Soma is directed. Furthermore, just as waters rush toward people in a desert <note>original: "dhanvan"</note>, so the invocations <note>original: "havanāni," the calls to the gods</note> have grown and increased toward Indra, along with the offerings of cakes <term>Purodasha: a sacrificial hearth-cake made of ground rice or barley</term> and other sacrifices.

इन्द्र (Indra), धीतयः (dhītayaḥ - prayers/works), वाणीः (vāṇīḥ - hymns/voices), गिर्वणसम् (girvaṇasam - lover of praise), सोमः (somaḥ), मिमिक्षः (mimikṣaḥ - desiring to sprinkle/mix), हवनानि (havanāni - invocations)
</vocab>

...they increased [him]. They strengthened him. Here is an illustration: As in a desert <note>original: 'dhanvan'</note> or an arid region <note>original: 'marudeśe'</note>, waters flowing <note>original: 'saṃyat'</note> toward a person or living creature sustain them. ## Hymn Text
**For this Indra, this great hymn of praise, this prayer, has been spoken by the wise ones with their thoughts. May Indra, who is present in all lives, be our protector and the one who increases our strength in the great, unendurable battle against the covering foe.** ॥ 5 ॥

**Pada-patha:**
For him | this | great | hymn of praise | for him | for Indra | prayer | with thoughts | has been spoken |
unendurable | as/so | in the great | battle | Indra | present in all lives | protector | increaser | and ॥ 5 ॥

## Commentary (Sayana)
For this Indra, this great <note>original: "mahi"</note> hymn of praise <note>original: "āṅgūṣam"</note> or prayer has been spoken <note>original: "avāci"</note> by the wise ones <note>the praisers</note> through their thoughts. The repetition of "for this Indra" and "the prayer" is for the sake of showing deep respect. He, Indra, who is "all-living" <note>original: "viśvāyuḥ," meaning he who goes everywhere or is the life of all</note>, may he become our protector <note>original: "avitā"</note> and the one who increases our strength <note>original: "vṛdhaḥ"</note> in the great and mighty battle <note>original: "vṛtratūrye"</note>. The syntax suggests: "It has been spoken so that he might be our protector."

The twelfth hymn <note>Sukta 36</note> beginning with "When will they be" <note>original: "kadā bhuvan"</note> consists of five verses. Its seer <note>Rishi</note> is Nara. The meter is Trishtubh and it is dedicated to Indra. As stated in the Index <note>Anukramani</note>: "When, O Nara..." Its ritual application <note>viniyoga</note> is mentioned in the third *Chandoma* and in the *Mahavrata* ceremony during the *Nishkevalya* Shastra recitation.

-> ॥ Therein, the First Verse ॥ <-

## Hymn Text
**When will our prayers find their home in your chariot? When will you grant the thousandfold nourishment to the praiser? When will you clothe this hymn with wealth? When will you make our sacrificial acts rich with the jewels of food?** ॥ 1 ॥

**Pada-patha:**
When | will be | chariot-dwelling | prayers | when | to the praiser | thousandfold-nourishment | you give |
when | hymn | clothe | of this [praiser] | with wealth | when | sacrificial acts | you make | food-jeweled ॥ 1 ॥

---

## Commentary (Sayana)
O Indra, at what time <note>original: "kadā"</note> will our prayers <note>original: "brahma"</note> become "chariot-dwellers" <note>original: "rathakṣayāṇi"</note>? This means: when will they reach you as you are seated in your chariot? At what time will you grant <note>original: "dāḥ"</note> to me, the praiser, "thousandfold nourishment" <note>original: "sahasrapoṣam"</note>, such as a herd of cows or a son that sustains a thousand people? And when will you clothe <note>original: "vāsayaḥ"</note> or fill the hymn <note>original: "stomam"</note> of this, your praiser, with wealth <note>original: "rāyā"</note>? When will you make our sacrificial acts <note>original: "dhiyaḥ"</note>, such as the fire-offering <note>Agnihotra</note>, delightful with "jewels of food" <note>original: "vājaratnāḥ"</note>? In this way, the praiser, unable to endure the delay of the reward, questions Indra with this verse.

</vocab>

-> ॥ Now the Second [Verse] ॥ <-

## Hymn Text
**When, O Indra, will that time be when, with our men, you cause us to encounter their men, and with our heroes, their heroes? Win the battles! Gain the three-layered cows! O Indra, place within us a sun-like glory.** ॥ 2 ॥

**Word-by-word analysis:**
When | indeed | that | O Indra | which | with men [our men] | men [enemy men] | with heroes [our sons] | heroes [enemy sons] | you cause to encounter | win | the battles |
three-layered | the cows | further | you may win | among the cows | O Indra | glory | sun-like | place | in us ॥ 2 ॥

---

## Commentary (Sayana)
Unable to endure the delay of the reward, the Seer <note>the Rishi or poet-sage</note> asks Indra through this verse: "O Indra, when indeed shall that happen? When, through our men <note>original: 'nṛbhiḥ,' our male warriors</note>, will you cause us to encounter their men <note>the enemy warriors</note>? And when, through our heroes <note>original: 'vīraiḥ,' our sons and brave ones</note>, will you cause us to encounter their heroes <note>the enemy's sons</note>?" 

The verb "cause to encounter" <note>original: 'nīḷayāse,' from the root 'nīḷ,' meaning to join or bring together</note> refers to the act of clashing in battle. The poet is speculating: "When will such a meeting in battle occur?" Furthermore, he asks: "For our sake, when will you win the battles <note>original: 'ājīn'</note>? And when, among the enemies who possess cattle, will you win for us the 'three-layered' cows <note>original: 'tri-dhātu,' referring to cows that provide the three ritual substances: milk, curd, and clarified butter/ghee</note>? O Indra, when will you place within us <note>original: 'asme'</note> glory <note>original: 'dyumnam,' meaning wealth or splendor</note> that is sun-like <note>original: 'svarvat,' pervasive like the light of the heavens</note>?"

---

-> ॥ Now the Third [Verse] ॥ <-

## Hymn Text
**When, O Indra, will that be, when for the singer, O most powerful one, you will provide food of every form? When will you join our prayers and praises [to yourself] like teams of horses? When will you come to our cattle-bestowing invocations?** ॥ 3 ॥

**Word-by-word analysis:**
When | indeed | that | O Indra | which | for the singer | of every form | food | you make | O most powerful one |
When | the prayers | and | the praises | you join [to yourself] | When | cattle-bestowing | the invocations | you may go to ॥ 3 ॥

---

## Commentary (Sayana)
Several more questions are posed in this verse. "O Indra, when indeed shall that happen? O most powerful <note>original: 'śaviṣṭha'</note> Indra, when will you provide for the singer <note>the one performing the praise</note> food <note>original: 'brahma,' interpreted here by Sayana as 'annam' or food</note> of every form? This is the poet's inquiry. And when will you join our ritual acts <note>original: 'dhiyaḥ'</note> and our praises <note>original: 'niyutaḥ'</note> to yourself?" 

The particle "and" <note>original: 'na' is used here in a cumulative sense</note> connects the thoughts. "When will you come to the invocations <note>original: 'havanāni,' the songs of praise</note> that are cattle-bestowing <note>original: 'go-maghāni,' meaning those that result in the gift of cows</note>?" The term for bestowing <note>original: 'magha'</note> here implies the act of giving a great gift.

---

-> ॥ Now the Fourth [Verse] ॥ <-

## Hymn Text
**O bestower of cattle, place for the singer nourishing foods, shining with horses and renowned for strength...** ॥ 4 ॥

<vocab>
**Indra:** The chief warrior deity of the Vedas, often invoked for strength and rain.
**Singer (Jaritr):** The poet or priest who chants the hymns during the ritual.
**Cattle-bestowing (Gomagha):** A descriptor for a gift or a ritual that results in gaining wealth in the form of cows.
**Glory (Dyumna):** A term that encompasses physical wealth, fame, and spiritual radiance.
**Most powerful (Shavishtha):** A superlative title specifically used for Indra's supreme might.
**To encounter (Nīḷayāse):** To bring two opposing sides together, specifically in the context of a battlefield.
**Battles (Ājīn):** Contests or struggles, often where livestock was the prize.
**Three-layered (Tridhātu):** A ritual term referring to the three dairy products essential for Vedic sacrifice.
</vocab>

## Hymn Text

**O Indra, bestow upon the singer riches in cattle, the joy of horses, and the renown of strength. Grant us abundance, we who are the sons of Bharadvaja. Make the milk-giving cow prosper, and let our provisions be brilliantly radiant.** ॥ 4 ॥

---

## Commentary (Sayana)

O Indra, you are he who should bestow upon the singer <note>original: 'jaritre,' the one performing the praise</note> these provisions <note>original: 'pṛkṣa'</note> which are the givers of cattle <note>original: 'gomaghā'</note>, which bring delight through horses <note>original: 'aśvacandrāḥ'</note>, and are famous for their strength or power <note>original: 'vājaśravasaḥ'</note>. Grant these unto us, the descendants of Bharadvaja. Furthermore, O Indra, make the cow <note>original: 'dhenu'</note>, who is a good milker, prosper or swell with milk. Also, may these provisions and the cow be endowed with beautiful light; may you make them shine. The meaning is: let them be possessed of a beautiful luster.

---

-> ॥ Now the Fifth [Verse] ॥ <-

## Hymn Text

**O Hero, O Powerful One, dispose of our adversary in some other way when you are praised for breaking open the doors. May I never be separated from the cow that yields pure milk. O Wise One, satisfy the descendants of Angiras with food.** ॥ 5 ॥

**[Word-by-word analysis]**
Him | towards | now | the adversary | in another way | even | O Hero | since | O Powerful One | wide | the doors [of the enemy] | you are praised |
not | down | may I go away | from the pure-milking | cow | O descendant of Angiras | with food/prayer | O Wise One | satisfy ॥ 5 ॥

---

## Commentary (Sayana)

O Indra, "now" <note>today</note> dispose of our "adversary" <note>original: 'vṛjanam,' interpreted here as an obstacle or enemy</note> "in some other way" <note>in a manner different from how living beings are treated</note>. The meaning is: make him reach that different state called death. The word "ā" serves to complete the sense. O Powerful One <note>original: 'śakra,' he who is capable in all deeds</note>, O Hero endowed with valor, you are the one who "breaks the doors" <note>original: 'vi duro,' the one who specifically tears apart the doors or defenses of the enemies</note>. Because you are praised by us for this reason, may I "not be separated" <note>original: 'mā niraraṃ,' may I not go away</note> from the "cow" belonging to Indra who milks "pure" <note>clear</note> things. This "cow" refers to the voice or the hymn of praise. Alternatively, it means: let me not be separated from the cow given by you, which milks pure milk. 

<note>The word 'araṃ' is a form of the verbal root meaning 'to go.'</note> 

The meaning is: let that [blessing] always dwell among us. O Wise One <note>original: 'vipra,' the sage-like Indra</note>, "satisfy" <note>delight</note> us, who are born of the clan of Angiras, with "food" <note>original: 'brahmaṇā,' which Sayana here glosses as 'anna' or food</note>.

-> ॥ Thus ends the seventh section of the seventh chapter of the fourth book ॥ <-

---

The thirteenth hymn, beginning with "In the company of exhilarations," consists of five verses. The Seer is Nara, the meter is Trishtubh, and the deity is Indra. This is as stated in the index. In the ritual of the Fifth Day of the Prishthya ceremony, this hymn is to be recited during the Nishkevalya Shastra. It is also indicated in the ritual manuals: "This prayer of mine, Indra, for exhilaration," and "In the company of exhilarations" are the Nishkevalya hymns (Ashvalayana Shrauta Sutra 7.12). In the Vishvajit sacrifice, during the midday libation, this is to be recited as the "Sama-hymn" by the Prashastri priest. It is indicated as: "In the company of exhilarations, he who was born..."

<vocab>
Indra: King of the gods, the primary deity of the Rig Veda, often associated with thunder and strength.
Gomagha: A term for wealth consisting specifically of cattle.
Bharadvaja: A famous sage (Rishi) and the traditional author of the sixth book (Mandala) of the Rig Veda.
Vrijana: A complex Vedic term; here Sayana interprets it as an enemy or an enclosure to be breached.
Angirasa: A member of the Angiras family, one of the most ancient clans of fire-priests.
Brahman: In this context, interpreted as either a sacred prayer or the sacrificial food that sustains.
</vocab>

# Rig Veda # [Book 4, Chapter 7, Section 8]

The Sama-hymns beginning with "Thus he was alone" <note>original: 'evābhūreka iti sāmasūktāni'</note>. (Aitareya Aranyaka 8. 7). The liturgical application <note>original: 'viniyoga'</note> is also stated in the *Nishkevalya* litany during the *Mahavrata* <note>a major Soma sacrifice performed at the winter solstice</note> ceremony.

---

## Hymn Text

-> ॥ The First Verse ॥ <-

**Truly, your exhilarations are beneficial to all people; truly, those riches of yours which are earthly [belonging to the three worlds]. Truly, you were the distributor of foods, because you maintain divine power among the gods.** ॥ 1 ॥

**Word-by-word analysis:**
Truly | exhilarations | your | beneficial to all people | truly | riches | then | which | earthly | 
truly | of foods | were | distributor | because | among the gods | you maintain | divine power ॥ 1 ॥

---

## Commentary (Sayana)

O **Indra**, your <note>belonging to you</note> **exhilarations** <note>original: 'madāsaḥ', the joy or intoxication produced by drinking Soma</note> are **truly** <note>original: 'sacā'; this is a name for 'truth' or 'truly'</note> **beneficial to all people** <note>original: 'viśvajanyāḥ', helping all people</note>. Alternatively, *sacā* is a name for 'great'; thus, it should be joined as "your great exhilarations." Furthermore, those **riches** <note>original: 'rāyaḥ', groups of wealth</note> of yours which exist in the three worlds characterized by the **earth** <note>original: 'pārthivāsaḥ'</note>—these also are **truly** beneficial to all people. Moreover, you **were** the **distributor** <note>original: 'vibhaktā', the giver</note> or are the distributor of **foods** <note>original: 'vājānām'</note> **truly**. Or, it should be joined as "of great foods." Since <note>original: 'yat'</note> you **maintain** or hold **divine power** <note>original: 'asuryam', might or spiritual strength</note> among the **gods**, for that reason you act in this way.

---

## Hymn Text

-> ॥ Now the Second [Verse] ॥ <-

**The people have followed and worshipped his strength; they have truly placed [him] for heroic deeds. For the one who seizes the continuous [enemies], the destroyer, and the swift one, they perform the ritual even in the slaying of Vritra.** ॥ 2 ॥

**Word-by-word analysis:**
After | forth | worshipped | people | strength | his | truly | placed | after | for heroic deeds | 
the seizer of the continuous | the destroyer | the swift | and | ritual | they perform | even | in the slaying of Vritra ॥ 2 ॥

---

## Commentary (Sayana)

The **people** <note>the sacrificer</note> **worship** <note>original: 'anu pra yeje', they worship continuously and excellently</note> the **strength** <note>original: 'ojas', power</note> of this Indra. Furthermore, the sacrificers have **truly** <note>original: 'sacā'</note> placed him in front <note>original: 'purodadhire'</note> to perform **heroic deeds** <note>original: 'vīryāya'</note>. Alternatively, one should join it as "the great Indra." Moreover, they **perform** <note>original: 'vṛñjanti', they accomplish</note> the **ritual** <note>original: 'kratum', the act of service</note> for that Indra, who is the **seizer of the continuous** <note>original: 'syūmagṛbhe', one who seizes enemies that exist in an uninterrupted line</note>, the **destroyer** <note>original: 'dudhaye', from a root meaning to harm or kill</note> of those enemies, and the **swift** <note>original: 'arvate', one who goes toward the enemies</note>. For what purpose? For the **slaying of Vritra** <note>original: 'vṛtrahatye', for the purpose of killing the obstructing enemy</note>.

<note>
This page explores the dual nature of Indra: his role as a provider of earthly wealth and food (vāja), and his martial role as the slayer of Vritra (the demon of drought/obstruction). Sayana uses the word 'sacā' to emphasize the truth or greatness of these attributes.
</note>
