# Rig Veda # [Mandala 6, Anuvaka 3, Hymn 36]

<page-num>723</page-num>

-> ॥ The Third Verse ॥ <-

## Hymn Text
**Together with him, the helpful powers, the heroic deeds, the manly strengths, and the harnessed teams attend to Indra. Like rivers to the ocean, the hymns, mighty in praise, enter into him of wide-reaching scope.** ॥ 3 ॥

---

**Word-by-word analysis:**
Him | together | helpful-powers | heroic-deeds | manly-strengths | harnessed-teams | attend | Indra | ocean | like | rivers | mighty-in-praise | wide-reaching | hymns | into | enter ॥ 3 ॥

## Commentary (Sayana)
The **helpful powers** <note>original: 'ūtayaḥ'</note>, interpreted here as the **Maruts** <note>the storm-gods and companions of Indra</note>, moving together and united, **attend** <note>original: 'saścuḥ'</note> or serve that Indra. Alternatively, the "helpful powers" may refer to satisfying foods that, being present together, serve him. Likewise, his **heroic deeds** <note>virile powers</note>, his **manly strengths**, and the **harnessed teams** <note>original: 'niyutaḥ', specifically the mares yoked to his chariot</note> all serve Indra. Furthermore, the **hymns** <note>original: 'giraḥ'</note> or praises, which are **mighty in praise** <note>original: 'uktha-śuṣmāḥ'; those whose strength lies in the *uktha* or recited verse</note>, **enter into** that Indra of **wide-reaching scope** <note>one who is vastly pervasive</note>. An illustration is provided: **like rivers to the ocean**. Just as flowing rivers enter the ocean and, once entered, are no longer seen as separate entities, in the same way, all praises become one with Indra.

-> ॥ The Fourth Verse ॥ <-

## Hymn Text
**O Indra, being praised, release for us the source of wealth, of many-delighting riches. You have become the peerless lord of people, the sole king of the entire world.** ॥ 4 ॥

---

**Word-by-word analysis:**
He (You) | of wealth | source | near | release | being-praised | many-delighting | you | Indra | of riches | lord | have become | peerless | of people | sole | of the entire | world | king ॥ 4 ॥

## Commentary (Sayana)
O **Indra**, being **praised** by us, **release** or bestow the **source** <note>original: 'khām'; literally a fountain or opening</note> of **wealth**. This word is often used for rivers; here it refers to the "stream" of riches connected to that source. Join us with this stream. What kind of wealth? It is **many-delighting** <note>original: 'puruścandrasya', giving joy to many</note> and it is **of riches** <note>original: 'vasvaḥ'</note> that provide habitation. Furthermore, you have become the **peerless** <note>incomparable and supreme</note> **lord** or sovereign of all **people** <note>all living beings</note>. Likewise, you have become the **sole** and extraordinary **king** or master of the **entire world** <note>the whole collection of created beings</note>.

-> ॥ The Fifth Verse ॥ <-

## Hymn Text
**So listen to us, you who are worthy of being heard, you who desire service, like the heaven with its vastness, the lord of wealth... so that you may be ours, delighting in power, throughout every age, perceived through your vitality.** ॥ 5 ॥

<vocab>
<term>Indra</term>: The king of the gods, associated with storms, war, and the power of the senses.
<term>Maruts</term>: A group of storm-deities who act as Indra's military retinue.
<term>Uktha</term>: A specific type of recited Vedic hymn or "shastra."
<term>Pada-patha</term>: The "word-by-word" recitation of the Veda where each word is isolated.
<term>Sayana</term>: The influential 14th-century scholar whose commentary (Bhashya) is standard for understanding the Vedas.
</vocab>

<summary>This page describes Indra as the central point where all powers, steeds, and hymns converge, comparing the merging of prayers into his vast nature to rivers flowing into the sea. It also petitions Indra as the peerless king of the world to "open the fountain" of wealth for his worshippers.</summary>
<keywords>Indra, Maruts, ocean analogy, king of the world, fountain of wealth, Vedic sacrifice, Sayana commentary</keywords>

# Rig Veda # [Book 4, Chapter 1, Group 9]

<page-num>724</page-num>

## Hymn Text
**Hearken then, with your power of hearing, you who desire our service; as the sun overcomes the earth, so do you overcome the many riches of the enemy. May you be ours through your strength, being celebrated; known in age after age by the food of our oblation.** ॥ 5 ॥

---

## Commentary (Sayana)
O **Indra**, **hearken** <note>original: 'shrudhi'</note> quickly to the **hearing** <note>original: 'shrutya'</note>, which refers to the hymns of praise that deserve to be heard. You are **desiring our service** <note>original: 'duvoyuh'</note>, wishing for our worship. You **overcome** <note>original: 'abhibhavasi'</note> the **riches** <note>original: 'rayah'</note> belonging to the **enemy** <note>original: 'aryah'</note>—which are **many** <note>original: 'bhuma'</note>—just as the **sun** <note>original: 'dyauh na'</note> overcomes the world with its light. This is the connection. Furthermore, being joined with your own **strength** <note>original: 'shavasa'</note> and being **celebrated** <note>original: 'chakanah'</note> by those to be praised, you are **well-known** <note>original: 'chekitanah'</note> in **age after age** <note>original: 'yuge yuge'</note> through the **food** <note>original: 'vayasa'</note> characterized by the sacrificial oblation. **As** <note>original: 'yatha'</note> or in whatever manner you are ours uniquely, so may you **be** <note>original: 'asah'</note>.

-> ॥ Thus ends the eighth group of the seventh [hymn] of the fourth [book] ॥ <-

---

## Hymn Text (Sukta 48)
**"Hither with the chariot"** <note>original: 'Arvayatham'</note> is the beginning of the fourteenth hymn, consisting of five verses. The Seer is **Bharadvaja** <note>a famous sage of the Rig Veda</note>; the meter is **Trishtubh** <note>a poetic meter of 11 syllables per line</note>, and the deity is **Indra**. This is stated in the Index <note>original: 'Anukramani'</note>. Its ritual **application** <note>original: 'viniyoga'</note> is mentioned in the *Nishkevalya* Shastra of the *Mahavrata* ceremony.

-> ॥ Here is the first verse ॥ <-

**Hither, toward us, may your harnessed bay horses bring the chariot that contains all desirable things, for your protection, O Indra. For the singer calls you, O possessor of heaven; may we today be prosperous, celebrating together with you.** ॥ 1 ॥

**Word-by-word Analysis:**
Hither | chariot | containing-all-desirable-things | your | protection | Indra | harnessed | bay-horses | let-them-bring | singer | even | indeed | you | they-call | possessor-of-heaven | may-we-be-prosperous | celebrating-together | your | today ॥ 1 ॥

---

## Commentary (Sayana)
O **Indra** of **terrible and exalted strength** <note>original: 'ugrodhurnabala'</note>, let your **bay horses** <note>original: 'harayah'</note>, which are **harnessed** <note>original: 'yuktasoh'</note> to the chariot, **bring** <note>original: 'vahantu'</note> that **chariot** <note>original: 'ratham'</note> **hither** <note>original: 'arvak'</note>, toward us. This chariot is **containing all desirable things** <note>original: 'vishvavaram'</note>, meaning it is sought after by all. **For** <note>original: 'hi'</note> as the **possessor of heaven** <note>original: 'svarvan'</note>—possessing a multitude of excellent qualities—the **singer** <note>original: 'kirishchid'</note>, namely the Rishi Bharadvaja, **calls** <note>original: 'havante'</note> you. Therefore, let them bring the chariot toward him. And **today** <note>original: 'adya'</note>, at this time, **celebrating together** <note>original: 'sadhamadah'</note> with you, **may we be prosperous** <note>original: 'dhimahi'</note>, meaning may we become enriched.

**In the third round of the sacrifice, for the Acchavaka priest, the verse "Into the wooden vessel" is the offering-prayer. This is indicated in the ritual manual: "The bay horses have come to the work in the wooden vessel" is the prayer (Ashvalayana Shrauta Sutra 6.4).**

---

## Hymn Text
-> ॥ Here is the second verse ॥ <-
**Into the wooden vessel, the bay-colored [Soma drops], performing their work, have gone; being purified, they have become straight-moving. May Indra, our ancient one, drink of this; he is the lord of the exhilarating Soma-juice.** ॥ 2 ॥

<vocab>
- <term>Indra</term>: The king of the gods and the primary recipient of the Soma sacrifice.
- <term>Bharadvaja</term>: One of the seven great Rishis (sages), to whom the sixth book of the Rig Veda is attributed.
- <term>Bay horses</term> (Harayah): The golden or reddish-brown horses that draw Indra's chariot.
- <term>Vishvavaram</term>: Literally "all-choosing," referring to something that contains everything one could desire.
- <term>Dhimahi</term>: Usually "we meditate," but here the commentator interprets it as "may we be prosperous" or "full."
- <term>Celebrating together</term> (Sadhamadah): Refers to the communal joy of the sacrifice, often involving the drinking of Soma.
- <term>Wooden vessel</term> (Drona): The large wooden vat used to collect and hold the Soma juice after it is pressed and filtered.
</vocab>

<summary>This page concludes the 47th hymn with a plea for Indra's attention and introduces the 48th hymn, where the Rishi Bharadvaja invites Indra to the sacrifice, describing the arrival of his horses and the preparation of the Soma juice in the wooden vessel.</summary>
<keywords>Indra, Bharadvaja, Soma sacrifice, bay horses, Drona vessel, prosperity, Rig Veda 6.48, ritual commentary</keywords>

## Hymn Text

<note>Rig Veda 6.37.2 (Word-by-word analysis/Pada-patha and end of commentary)</note>

**Forth** <note>original: 'pro'</note> | **indeed** <note>original: 'iti'</note> | **in the wooden vessel** <note>original: 'drone'</note> | **the golden ones** <note>original: 'harayah'</note> | **to the work** <note>original: 'karma'</note> | **they have gone** <note>original: 'agman'</note> | **being purified** <note>original: 'punanasah'</note> | **moving straight** <note>original: 'rijyantah'</note> | **they have been** <note>original: 'abhuvan'</note> | **Indra** <note>original: 'indrah'</note> | **our** <note>original: 'nah'</note> | **of this** <note>original: 'asya'</note> | **the ancient** <note>original: 'purvyah'</note> | **may he drink** <note>original: 'papiyat'</note> | **heaven-dwelling** <note>original: 'dyukshah'</note> | **of the exhilarating** <note>original: 'madasya'</note> | **of the Soma** <note>original: 'somyasya'</note> | **king** <note>original: 'raja'</note> ॥ २ ॥

---

## Commentary (Sayana)

The **golden-colored** <note>original: 'harayah'</note> Soma juices **have gone forth** <note>original: 'pro agman'</note> to our **work** <note>original: 'karma'</note>, which is the sacrifice. They proceed intensely and reach it. Having reached it, and **being purified** <note>original: 'punanasah'</note> or filtered, **they have been** <note>original: 'abhuvan'</note> **moving straight** <note>original: 'rijyantah'</note> into the **wooden vessel** <note>original: 'drone'</note> <note>term: Drona-kalasha; a large wooden trough or vat used to hold the pressed Soma juice during the ritual</note>. The **ancient** <note>original: 'purvyah'</note> Indra—who is **heaven-dwelling** <note>original: 'dyukshah'</note>, meaning either an inhabitant of the bright sky or the very source of light—is the **king** <note>original: 'raja'</note> or lord of the **exhilarating** <note>original: 'madasya'</note> **Soma juice** <note>original: 'somyasya'</note>. May such an Indra **drink** <note>original: 'papiyat'</note> of this Soma.

---

## Hymn Text

-> ॥ Now the Third [Verse] ॥ <-
<note>Rig Veda 6.37.3</note>

**Approaching from all sides, may the horses harnessed to the chariot, moving straight, bring the powerful Indra in his fine-wheeled chariot toward our praiseworthy oblation; let not the nectar of the wind now be exhausted.** ॥ ३ ॥

**Word-by-word analysis:**
**Approaching** <note>original: 'asasanasah'</note> | **the powerful** <note>original: 'shavasanam'</note> | **towards** <note>original: 'achha'</note> | **Indra** <note>original: 'indram'</note> | **in the fine-wheeled [chariot]** <note>original: 'suchakre'</note> | **harnessed to the chariot** <note>original: 'rathyasah'</note> | **horses** <note>original: 'ashvah'</note> | **toward** <note>original: 'abhi'</note> | **the oblation** <note>original: 'shravah'</note> | **moving straight** <note>original: 'rijyantah'</note> | **may they bring** <note>original: 'vaheyuh'</note> | **now** <note>original: 'nu'</note> | **indeed** <note>original: 'chit'</note> | **now** <note>original: 'nu'</note> | **of the wind** <note>original: 'vayoh'</note> | **the nectar** <note>original: 'amritam'</note> | **apart** <note>original: 'vi'</note> | **may it be exhausted** <note>original: 'dasyet'</note> ॥ ३ ॥

---

## Commentary (Sayana)

May the **horses** <note>original: 'ashvah'</note> **harnessed to the chariot** <note>original: 'rathyasah'</note>, **approaching** <note>original: 'asasanasah'</note> from all sides and **moving straight** <note>original: 'rijyantah'</note>, **bring** <note>original: 'vaheyuh'</note> **towards** <note>original: 'achha'</note> us the **powerful** <note>original: 'shavasanam'</note> Indra—who acts with great strength—seated in his **fine-wheeled** <note>original: 'suchakre'</note> chariot, to receive our praiseworthy **oblation** <note>original: 'shravah'</note>. The particle **'nu chit'** <note>original: 'nu chit'</note> is used here in the sense of a prohibition or negation. May the **nectar** <note>original: 'amritam'</note>—the oblation of Soma which is the cause of immortality—**not be exhausted** <note>original: 'nu... nu chit vi dasyet'</note> now on account of the **wind** <note>original: 'vayoh'</note>. The logic here is that the Soma collected in the sacrificial vessel is susceptible to being dried up by the wind; therefore, the horses should bring Indra quickly so he may drink it before it diminishes.

---

## Hymn Text

-> ॥ Now the Fourth [Verse] ॥ <-
<note>Rig Veda 6.37.4</note>

**Indra, the most excellent and most active among the wealthy patrons, sends the sacrificial gift of this worshiper. O wielder of the thunderbolt, you by whom we bypass sin; O bold one, you distribute wealth to the wise.** ॥ ४ ॥

**Word-by-word analysis:**
**The most excellent** <note>original: 'varishthah'</note> | **of this** <note>original: 'asya'</note> | **the sacrificial gift** <note>original: 'dakshinam'</note> | **sends** <note>original: 'iyarti'</note> | **Indra** <note>original: 'indrah'</note> | **of the wealthy patrons** <note>original: 'maghonam'</note> | **the most active** <note>original: 'tuvikurmitamah'</note> | **by which** <note>original: 'yaya'</note> | **O wielder of the thunderbolt** <note>original: 'vajrivah'</note> | **you bypass** <note>original: 'pariyasi'</note> | **sin** <note>original: 'amhas'</note> | **wealth** <note>original: 'magha'</note> | **and** <note>original: 'cha'</note> | **O bold one** <note>original: 'dhrishno'</note> | **you distribute** <note>original: 'dayase'</note> | **to** <note>original: 'vi'</note> | **the wise** <note>original: 'surin'</note> ॥ ४ ॥

---

## Commentary (Sayana)

Indra is the **most excellent** <note>original: 'varishthah'</note> (the greatest) and the **most active** <note>original: 'tuvikurmitamah'</note> (one who performs many types of deeds). Among the **wealthy patrons** <note>original: 'maghonam'</note>—those who possess wealth in the form of sacrificial oblations—he **sends** <note>original: 'iyarti'</note> or impels **this** <note>original: 'asya'</note> worshiper's **sacrificial gift** <note>original: 'dakshinam'</note> to be given during the ritual. Alternatively, the term "wealthy patrons" and "of this" refer to the same person, with a variation in grammatical number. Of the wealthy [patron]... <note>The text continues on the following page</note>

## Hymn Text
Indra is the giver of ancient **strength**; may Indra, whose power is great, increase through our **songs**. May Indra be the best slayer of the **coverer** <note>The demon Vritra</note>, for he is a warrior; being the wise guide, he quickly fulfills the desires of his people. || 5 ||

**Padapatha:**

## Commentary (Sayana)
May this Indra be the giver of **ancient** <note>original: 'sthavirasya'</note> strength—meaning either food or physical power. May that Indra, being one of **augmented splendor** <note>original: 'vriddhamamhah'</note>, increase through our songs of praise. May that Indra, the warrior who destroys enemies, be the **best slayer** <note>original: 'hanishthah'</note> of Vritra, the enemy who covers and obstructs the world. Furthermore, may that Indra, as the **wise guide** <note>original: 'surih'</note> or the one who impels, **hastening** <note>original: 'tutujanah'</note> to help, fulfill those desires for wealth for us.

The fifteenth hymn, beginning with "May he drink" <note>original: 'apad it'</note>, consists of five verses. The **seer** <note>Rishi</note> is Bharadvaja, the **meter** is Trishtubh, and the **deity** is Indra. This is stated in the index of verses. Its **ritual application** <note>viniyoga</note> is mentioned in the Niskevalya litany of the Mahavrata ceremony.

## Hymn Text
May he indeed drink; may the most wonderful one protect us; may he support our great, brilliant **invocation of Indra**. In the path of the divine people, the generous one accepts the most **praiseworthy prayer** and the gift of the worshiper. || 1 ||

**Padapatha:**
May he drink | indeed | [particle] | indeed | us | the most wonderful | the great | may he support | brilliant | invocation of Indra |
the most praiseworthy | prayer | of the divine | in the path | of the person | the gift | he accepts | the generous one || 1 ||

## Commentary (Sayana)
May that Indra, who is the **most wonderful** <note>original: 'cicattamah'</note> or the most venerable, **drink** <note>original: 'apat'</note> from this sacrificial vessel. Or, the meaning could be: from this enemy, may he **protect** <note>original: 'pat'</note> us. The particles 'ut' and 'u' are used for poetic completion. Likewise, may that Indra **support** <note>original: 'bharshat'</note>—meaning maintain or carry—our great and **brilliant** <note>original: 'dyumatim'</note> invocation. In the **path** <note>original: 'yaman'</note> of the divine...

<vocab>
- **Indra**: The king of gods and primary deity of this hymn.
- **Vritra**: The "Coverer" or "Obstructor," a chaos-demon slain by Indra to release the waters.
- **Bharadvaja**: A famous sage and the traditional author of the sixth book of the Rig Veda.
- **Trishtubh**: A Vedic meter consisting of four lines of eleven syllables each.
- **Vaja**: A versatile term meaning strength, food, or the spoils of victory.
- **Dakshina**: Traditionally a gift given to priests, here referring to the divine rewards granted by Indra.
- **Viniyoga**: The specific point in a ritual where a verse is recited.
- **Magha**: Riches or bounties, often referring to the gifts Indra bestows.
</vocab>

# Mandala 6, Anuvaka 3, Hymn 38. ] || Fourth Book || 727

The **highly praiseworthy** <note>original: 'panyasim'</note>, most excellent **prayer** <note>original: 'dhitim'</note> in the form of service being performed in the sacrifice, and the **oblation** <note>original: 'havis'</note> to be given, are accepted by the **generous** <note>original: 'sudanu'</note> Indra. May he partake in them.

---

## Hymn Text
-> || Now, the Second Verse || <-
From afar, even, the ears of this Indra are present [to hear]. The praiser, speaking aloud, makes a sound from the **shout** <note>The loud praise or ritual sound; original: 'ghoshat'</note> of Indra. May this **invocation of the gods** <note>original: 'devahutih'</note>, being recited, turn this Indra toward me. || 2 ||

### Word-for-Word Analysis
From afar | even | [particle] | are present | of this | ears | from the shout | of Indra | makes sound | speaking |
[particle] | this | him | invocation of the gods | may he turn | toward me | Indra | this | being recited || 2 ||

## Commentary (Sayana)
The two ears of this Indra **come from a distant place** <note>original: 'duraccit'</note> for the purpose of hearing the hymn of praise. Because of the **shout** <note>original: 'ghoshat'</note>—the hymn of praise that is to be proclaimed—the praiser who is speaking/praising **makes a sound** <note>original: 'tanyati'</note>; or rather, he spreads the sound everywhere. May this **invocation of the gods** <note>original: 'devahutih'</note>—this praise in the form of a call to the god Indra—being itself **urged forward** <note>original: 'ricyamana'</note>, turn this Indra **toward me** <note>original: 'madryak'</note>. May it cause him to return. The word "this" <note>original: 'iyam'</note> is repeated for emphasis or to complete the meter.

---

## Hymn Text
-> || Now, the Third Verse || <-
I praise that Indra for you with the **highest prayer** <note>original: 'dhiya paramaya'</note>, that Indra who was **born of old** <note>original: 'purajam'</note> and is **ageless** <note>original: 'ajaram'</note>, along with songs of praise. In him, the **sacred word** <note>original: 'brahma'</note> and the **songs** <note>original: 'girah'</note> are placed; may the great **hymn of praise** <note>original: 'stoma'</note> further increase Indra. || 3 ||

### Word-for-Word Analysis
That | for you | with prayer | with the highest | born of old | ageless | Indra | [prefix] | I praise | with songs |
Sacred word | and | songs | are placed | [prefix] | in him | great | and | hymn of praise | [prefix] | increases | in Indra || 3 ||

## Commentary (Sayana)
O [priests], I praise that famous Indra for you. <note>The commentator notes a grammatical variation where "you" is plural but refers to the singular Indra, or implies the priests addressing the audience</note>. With the most excellent **prayer** <note>original: 'dhiya'</note> or hymn, and with **songs** <note>original: 'arkaih'</note> which are means of worship, along with the oblations, I celebrate him. Of what kind is he? He is **born in the ancient time** <note>original: 'purajam'</note>, meaning he is eternal, and **ageless** <note>original: 'ajaram'</note>, meaning free from decay and constant. For this reason, in this Indra, the **sacred prayers** <note>original: 'brahmani'</note>—which are the foods characterized as oblations—and the **songs** <note>original: 'girah'</note> of praise are placed. They are united and joined with him. Also, the great, flourishing **hymn of praise** <note>original: 'stoma'</note> increases him further.

---

## Hymn Text
-> || Now, the Fourth Verse || <-
May the **sacrifice** <note>original: 'yajna'</note> and the **Soma** juice increase Indra; may the **sacred word** <note>original: 'brahma'</note>, the **songs** <note>original: 'girah'</note>, the **hymns** <note>original: 'uktha'</note>, and the **thoughts** <note>original: 'manma'</note> increase him. May the **dawns** <note>original: 'ushasah'</note> increase him at the time of their coming, and may the months, the autumns, and the days increase Indra. || 4 ||

# Rig Veda || [Ashtaka 4. Adhyaya 7. Varga 11.] || 728

## Hymn Text

<note>Rig Veda 6.62.4 Word-for-Word Analysis (continued from previous page)</note>
May increase | whom | sacrifice | and | Soma | Indra | may increase | prayer-offering | songs | hymns of praise | and | thought | 
strengthen | I | him | of the dawn | at the coming | of the night | may increase | months | autumns | heavens [days] | Indra || 4 ||

---

## Commentary (Sayana)

Whom—Indra—the **sacrifice** <note>original: 'yajna'</note> or the act of worship strengthens. And also, the **Soma** <note>The sacred ritual drink</note> which is the means of that sacrifice, strengthens that same Indra. Likewise, the **prayer-offering** <note>original: 'brahma'</note> in the form of food offerings like the sacrificial cakes <note>original: 'purodasha'</note>, strengthens Indra. The **songs** <note>original: 'girah'</note> of praise, the **thoughts** <note>original: 'manma'</note> to be meditated upon, and the **hymns of praise** <note>original: 'uktha'</note> also strengthen him. Strengthen him! I [the priest] strengthen him at the **coming of the dawn** <note>original: 'ushasasam yaman'</note> and at the end of the night. The **months**, the **autumns** <note>Representing the passing years</note>, and the **heavens** <note>interpreted here as the passing days</note> also strengthen this Indra.

---

## Hymn Text

-> ॥ Now, the Fifth Verse ॥ <-

<note>Rig Veda 6.62.5</note>
**Thus, him who is born for power, who is fully grown for the sake of granting wealth and for his renowned fame; the great, the fierce, for our protection, O wise one, now let us worship him in the battles for the conquest of enemies.** || 5 ||

**Word-for-Word Analysis**
Thus | born | for power | fully | growing | for wealth | and | for the renowned | great | fierce | for protection | O wise one | now | [particle] | let us worship | in the battles for the conquest of enemies || 5 ||

## Commentary (Sayana)

O **wise one** <note>original: 'vipra'; an inspired poet or priest</note>! Indra is **thus born** <note>manifesting his power</note> for the sake of **subduing enemies** <note>original: 'sahase'</note>. He is **fully growing** <note>attaining great strength</note> for the sake of granting **abundant wealth** <note>original: 'radhase'</note>. You, who are **great** and **fierce** with elevated strength—him we surely **worship** <note>original: 'avivasema'; serve or attend to</note> today for the sake of **renowned wealth** <note>original: 'shrutaya radhase'</note> and for our **protection** <note>original: 'avase'</note> during **battles against the foe** <note>original: 'vritra-turyeshu'; literally the overcoming of Vritra or enemies</note>.

-> ॥ Thus ends the tenth Varga of the seventh Adhyaya of the fourth Ashtaka ॥ <-

## Critical Notes

The sixteenth hymn, beginning with "Of the gladdening sage," consists of five verses. The **Seer** <note>The inspired composer</note> is Bharadvaja; the meter is **Trishtubh** <note>a meter of 44 syllables</note>; it is dedicated to the **Ashvins** <note>The twin gods of the dawn and healing</note>. The beginning is as cited in the Index. The ritual application has been previously mentioned.

**Of the gladdening, wise, divine carrier of the sacrifice, of the inspired speaker of sweet words; O Divine Ashvins, bestow upon the singer who possesses wealth of cattle, that which belongs to the Grandson of the Waters.** || 1 ||

Of the **gladdening** <note>original: 'mandrasya'; causing delight or intoxication</note>, of the **wise** <note>original: 'kaveh'; the far-seeing seer</note>, of the **divine** <note>dwelling in the heavens</note>, of the **carrier** <note>original: 'vahneh'; the one who carries the sacrifice to the gods</note>, of the one who has **inspired thoughts**... <note>The text notes that the wise and meditated-upon praisers belong to him</note>. Of that...

<vocab>
- **Indra**: The king of the gods, associated with storms and strength.
- **Ashvins**: The twin horsemen, healers of the gods and heralds of the dawn.
- **Soma**: A ritual drink made from a plant, considered the food of the gods.
- **Vritra-turyeshu**: Specifically refers to battles against 'Vritra' (the cosmic serpent/inhibitor) but often symbolizes any struggle against enemies.
- **Grandson of the Waters**: <term>Apam Napat</term>; a deity associated with fire born from water (lightning or ritual fire).
</vocab>

# Mandala 6. Adhyaya 3. Sukta 39. || Fourth Ashtaka || 729

<note>This section concludes the commentary on the first verse of the hymn.</note>

...of the word <note>original: 'vacanasya'</note>, meaning that which is to be spoken of or worthy of praise. Of him, the one who is famous everywhere, the one to be served <note>original: 'sacanasya'</note>—of such a one is the sweet <note>original: 'madhvo'</note> honey-like Soma. <note>Grammatical note: The author observes that a rule of grammar is applied here where the sixth case (genitive) is used in place of the fourth case (dative) to indicate the recipient of an action.</note> O Indra, may you drink <note>original: 'apah'</note> this Soma of ours. Furthermore, O shining god Indra, for the one who praises you <note>original: 'grunate'</note>—<note>The dative case is used here in the sense of the instrumental 'by the one praising'</note>—by me who praises you, grant us food <note>original: 'ishah'</note> that is "cow-foremost" <note>original: 'go-agrah'</note>, meaning wealth or nourishment where cattle are the most prominent part. Join us with such abundance.

## Hymn Text

->॥ Now, the Second Verse ॥<-

**This [Indra], desiring [the cows], encompassed the mountain-stronghold; with those of true thoughts, he joined with the followers of the Cosmic Order. He shattered the unbroken ridge of Vala; with his words, Indra fought against the Panis.** ॥ 2 ॥

**This. | Desiring. | Around. | The mountain. | The cows. | With true thoughts. | Linked with the Cosmic Order. | Joining. |
He shattered. | The unbroken. | Apart. | Of Vala. | The ridge. | The Panis. | With words. | Against. | He fought. | Indra.** ॥ 2 ॥

## Commentary (Sayana)

This Indra, desiring <note>original: 'ushanah'</note> the cows <note>original: 'usrah'</note> that were located near the mountain—that is, the mass of rocks created by the demon Vala to hide the cattle—joined <note>original: 'yujanah'</note> with the Angirases <note>The ancestral fire-priests</note> who perform truthful rituals <note>original: 'rtadhitibhih'</note>. Being joined with the praise-song <note>original: 'rtayuk'</note> produced by them, he shattered <note>original: 'virujat'</note> the high ridge <note>original: 'sanum'</note> of the demon Vala, which was a mountain height that had never been broken by anyone else. Furthermore, Indra fought against <note>original: 'abhiyodhat'</note> the Panis <note>A group of demons or 'niggards' who stole the cows of the gods</note>, who were the followers of Vala, using words as his weapons—either through his thunderous roars or the power of the priests' hymns.

## Hymn Text

->॥ Now, the Third Verse ॥<-

**This Soma-drop, this Indra, illumined the darkness, the nights, the days, and the autumns. The gods established him as the banner of the days; in his pure birth, he created the Dawn.** ॥ 3 ॥

**This. | He illumined. | The flashes/darkness. | Apart. | The nights. | At night. | By day. | The autumns. | The Soma-drop. | Indra. |
This. | The banner. | They established. | Now. | Indeed. | Of the days. | In the pure birth. | The Dawn. | He created.** ॥ 3 ॥

## Commentary (Sayana)

O Indra, this Soma-drop <note>original: 'indu'</note>, which is regulated and drunk by you, has illumined <note>original: 'vyadyotayat'</note> the nights <note>original: 'aktun'</note> which were previously unlit. Here, the word "nights" also implies the cycles of time associated with them, such as the fortnights and months. He also illumined the evenings <note>original: 'dosha'</note>, the days <note>original: 'vastoh'</note>, and the autumns <note>original: 'sharadah'</note> or years. 

Why is this so? The text explains: Long ago, the gods established <note>original: 'adadhuh'</note> this Soma—existing in the form of the Moon in the sky—as the "banner" <note>original: 'ketum'</note> or the indicator of the days. Because he makes the days known through the lunar cycles, he is their signal. In his pure birth <note>original: 'shuci-janman'</note>, he also created the Dawn. Therefore, through him...

# || Rig Veda || [Adhyaya 7, Varga 11]

All the fortnights and months are made manifest, because the divisions of lunar days <term>tithi<gloss>lunar days based on the moon's phases</gloss></term> are dependent on the movement of the moon. Furthermore, this Soma has made the times of dawn <note>original: 'uṣasaḥ'</note>—the hours of daybreak—bright with its own "pure-born" light and white radiance. It continues to do so.

## Hymn Text

->॥ Now, the Fourth Verse ॥<-

**This [Indra], being radiant, illumined the unlit [realms]; he caused the many ancient dawns to shine by the Cosmic Law. He moves with horses yoked to the Truth, with the light-finding nave [of his chariot], fulfilling the needs of the people.** ॥ 4 ॥

**Pada-patha <note>The word-by-word breakdown used for linguistic analysis</note>:**
This. | Illumined. | The unlit. | Shining. | This. | Caused to shine. | Apart. | By the Cosmic Law <note>original: 'ṛtena'</note>. | The many. | 
This. | Moves. | With those yoked to the Truth. | With horses. | By the light-finder. | By the nave. | Fulfilling the needs of the people. ॥ 4 ॥

## Commentary (Sayana)

This Indra, being "shining" <note>original: 'rucano'</note>—that is, glowing in the form of the Sun—illumined <note>original: 'arocayat'</note> all the worlds that were "unlit" <note>original: 'arucaḥ'</note> and soiled by darkness. He makes them bright. Likewise, this Indra caused the "many" <note>original: 'pūrvīḥ'</note> dawns to "shine" <note>original: 'vivāsayat'</note> by means of "Truth" <note>original: 'ṛtena'</note>—meaning by his light, which is true and pervasive. This means he removes the darkness residing there. 

Furthermore, with "horses yoked to the Truth" <note>original: 'ṛtayugbhir'</note>—meaning horses joined to the sacred hymn—and with a chariot that has a "nave" <note>original: 'nābhinā'</note> to which they are harnessed, which is a "finder of heaven" <note>original: 'svarvidā'</note>—meaning it secures wealth that is excellent to attain—this very Indra "moves" <note>original: 'īyate'</note> or goes forth. He does so while being a "filler of the people" <note>original: 'carṣaṇiprāḥ'</note>, meaning one who fulfills the desires of human beings.

---

## Hymn Text

->॥ Now, the Fifth Verse ॥<-

**Now, O ancient King, being praised, quickly pour out many nourishments for the singer who deserves the gift of wealth. Bestow waters, herbs, forests without poison, cattle, horses, and men for the worshiper to behold.** ॥ 5 ॥

**Pada-patha:**
Now. | Being praised. | To the one praising. | O ancient. | O King. | Nourishments. | Pour out. | For the giving of wealth. | Many. | 
Waters. | Herbs. | Free from poison. | Forests. | Cattle. | Horses. | For the beholding of men. | Bestow. ॥ 5 ॥

---

## Commentary (Sayana)

O "Ancient" <note>original: 'pratna'</note>—meaning existing from of old—O "King" <note>original: 'rājan'</note>—the shining Indra—you who are "being praised" <note>original: 'gṛṇānaḥ'</note> by us, "quickly" <note>original: 'nu'</note> "pour out" <note>original: 'pinva'</note>—meaning bestow or provide—"many" <note>original: 'pūrvīḥ'</note> "nourishments" <note>original: 'iṣaḥ'</note>—meaning foods—for the "singer" <note>original: 'gṛṇate'</note>—the one praising you—for the sake of "giving wealth" <note>original: 'vasudeyāya'</note>—meaning for the person to whom wealth should be granted by you. 

Furthermore, for the "beholder of men" <note>original: 'nṛcase'</note>—referring to the worshiper who offers the hymn—bestow <note>original: 'rirīhi'</note> "waters" <note>original: 'apaḥ'</note> in the form of rain, "herbs" <note>original: 'oṣadhīḥ'</note> like rice and barley, and "forests" <note>original: 'vanāni'</note> consisting of fruit-bearing trees like mango and jackfruit, which are "without poison" <note>original: 'aviṣā'</note>—meaning non-toxic or protective. Also grant "cattle" <note>original: 'gāḥ'</note>, "horses" <note>original: 'arvataḥ'</note>, and "men" <note>original: 'nṝn'</note> to serve as workers.

[Mandala 6, Anuvaka 3, Hymn 40]     || The Fourth Book <note>original: 'Ashtaka'</note> ||     731

The application <term>viniyoga<gloss>the specific ritual use of a verse</gloss></term> of the previous hymn has concluded. In the first "Night Cycle" <note>original: 'Ratri-paryaya', a specific stage of the Atiratra sacrifice</note>, this is the primary offering-verse for the assistant priest <term>Achhavaka<gloss>one of the four Hotri-priests responsible for certain recitations</gloss></term>. It is indicated in the ritual manuals: "Indra, drink! For you it is pressed for exhilaration" (Asvalayana Shrauta Sutra 6.14).

-> ॥ This is the first verse of that sequence ॥ <-

## Hymn Text

**Indra, drink! For you the [Soma] is pressed for exhilaration; unyoke your two bay horses <note>original: 'Hari', Indra's iconic golden-brown steeds</note>, those two companions. And sit down before our assembly and sing along; then grant strength <note>original: 'vayaḥ', often glossed as food or vital power</note> to the sacrifice and the one who praises you.** ॥ 1 ॥

**Word-by-word Breakdown <note>Pada-patha</note>:**
Indra. | Drink. | For you. | Pressed. | For exhilaration. | Unyoke. | [Those]. | The two bay horses. | Apart. | Release. | The two companions. | 
And. | Forth. | Sing. | In the assembly. | Having sat down. | Then. | For the sacrifice. | To the one praising. | Strength. | Grant. ॥ 1 ॥

---

## Commentary (Sayana)

O **Indra**, **drink** **that** Soma **which** has been **pressed** <note>original: 'suto'</note> **for you** for the sake of **exhilaration** <note>original: 'madāya'</note>. Since the Soma is to be drunk by you, for that reason, **unyoke** <note>original: 'avasya'</note>—meaning bring to a halt—the **two bay horses** <note>original: 'harī'</note> who are of equal fame or are your friends <note>original: 'sakhāyā'</note>. After that, **release** them from the chariot. **And also** <note>original: 'utāpi ca'</note>, having **sat down** <note>original: 'niṣadya'</note> facing **the assembly** <note>original: 'gaṇe'</note> of our singers, **sing along** <note>original: 'pragāya'</note>—that is, celebrate the hymn we have composed. Then, after that, **grant** <note>original: 'dhāḥ'</note> **strength** <note>original: 'vayaḥ'</note>, meaning food, **to the sacrifice**—meaning the sacrificer—and to the one **praising** <note>original: 'gṛṇate'</note> you.

In the second "Night Cycle," this is the offering-verse for the assistant priest: "Drink of this." It is indicated: "Drink of this is the offering-verse" (Asvalayana Shrauta Sutra 6.4).

-> ॥ This is the second verse in the hymn ॥ <-

## Hymn Text

**Drink of this, of which you drank upon being born, O Indra, for exhilaration and for heroic action, O mighty one <note>original: 'virapśin'</note>. The cows, the men, the waters, and the stone have prepared this drop for you, for your drinking.** ॥ 2 ॥

**Word-by-word Breakdown:**
Of this. | Drink. | Of which. | Being born. | Indra. | For exhilaration. | For action. | You drank. | O Mighty One. | 
That. | Indeed. | For you. | The cows. | The men. | The waters. | The stone. | The drop. | Together. | Have prepared <note>original: 'sam-ahan', literally 'brought together'</note>. | For drinking. | Together. | For him [Indra]. ॥ 2 ॥

---

## Commentary (Sayana)

O **Indra**, **drink of this**—this Soma. O **Mighty One** <note>original: 'virapśin'</note>, O great one, you who **being born** <note>original: 'jajñāno'</note>—at the very moment of birth—**drank** <note>original: 'apibaḥ'</note> **of which** Soma previously. For what purpose? For **exhilaration** <note>original: 'madāya'</note>—joy—and for **action** <note>original: 'kratve'</note>, meaning to perform heroic deeds such as the slaying of the demon Vritra. **That indeed** <note>original: 'tamu'</note>, that very same **drop** <note>original: 'indu'</note> of Soma, **the cows** (the milk and curds mixed in), **the men** (the officiating priests), **the waters** (the ritual 'Vasativari' waters), and **the stone** (the pressing stone)—all these **have prepared** <note>original: 'samahan'</note> or brought together for **your**—Indra's—**drinking**. <note>Sayana notes that 'samahan' is a form of the root 'hi' meaning 'to go' or 'to bring near'.</note>

## Commentary (Sayana)

...separately. This is used in the same sense as the word "distinctly." You exist in a separate or different place. Or, in your own <note>original: 'sve'</note> home or house. Or, what is the use of this specific detail? In whatever place you are, coming from that place, O you who are praised by songs <note>original: 'girvaṇaḥ'</note> and who possess horses <term>niyutvān<gloss>one who is accompanied by the Niyut horses, specifically associated with Indra and Vayu</gloss></term>, and who are in harmony with the Maruts <note>the storm-deities who accompany Indra</note>, protect our sacrifice <note>yajña</note> for our protection. Protect. Or, protect our Soma—the means of sacrifice—for our satisfaction. Drink it.

->॥ Thus ends the twelfth section <note>varga</note> of the seventh chapter <note>adhyāya</note> in the fourth book <note>aṣṭaka</note> ॥<-

---

The hymn beginning with "Ahelamana" consists of five verses. It is the eighteenth hymn <note>of this section</note>, seen by the seer Bharadvāja, composed in the Trishtubh meter, and dedicated to Indra. It is recorded in the tradition as: "Ahelamana..." ॥ Its ritual application has been explained previously. ॥

## Hymn Text

->॥ Here is the first verse ॥<-

**Without being angry, come to the sacrifice; for you, the pressed Soma drops are purified. Like cows [returning to their stall], O wielder of the thunderbolt, they reach their own home; come, O Indra, you who are the first among those worthy of sacrifice.** ॥ 1 ॥

**Word-by-word Breakdown <note>Pada-patha</note>:**
Without anger. | Unto. | Come. | The sacrifice. | For you. | Are purified. | Drops. | Pressed. |
Cows. | Like. | O wielder of the thunderbolt. | Own. | Home. | Towards. | Indra. | Hither. | Come. | First. | Of those worthy of sacrifice. ॥ 1 ॥

---

## Commentary (Sayana)

O Indra, **without being angry** <note>original: 'aheḷamānaḥ'</note>, come to our sacrifice. Approach it. Because for your sake, the **pressed** <note>original: 'sutāsaḥ'</note> **drops** <note>original: 'indavaḥ'</note> of Soma **are purified** <note>original: 'pavante'</note> or cleansed by the wool filter <note>daśā-pavitra</note>. O **wielder of the thunderbolt** <note>original: 'vajrin'</note>, just as **cows** <note>original: 'gāvaḥ'</note> [return to] their own stall, [the Soma drops] reach their **own home** <note>original: 'svam okaḥ'</note> or place, which is characterized by the sacrificial vessels <note>such as the drona-kalasha</note>, directly. Therefore, O Indra, you who are the **first** or chief among the gods **worthy of sacrifice** <note>original: 'yajñiyānām'</note>, come here. Approach. ॥

---

## Hymn Text

->॥ Now the second verse ॥<-

**That tongue of yours which is well-fashioned, which is the most excellent, with which you constantly drink the surge of the sweet [Soma]—with that, protect us. The priest <term>Adhvaryu<gloss>the priest responsible for the physical ritual and the Soma preparation</gloss></term> has stood before you; O Indra, let your thunderbolt, which seeks the light, be ready.** ॥ 2 ॥

**Word-by-word Breakdown <note>Pada-patha</note>:**
Which. | Your. | Tongue. | Well-fashioned. | Which. | Most excellent. | With which. | Constantly. | You drink. | Of the sweet. | The surge. |
With that. | Protect. | Forth. | Your. | Priest. | Has stood. | Together. | Your. | Thunderbolt. | Let it be. | Indra. | Seeking the light. ॥ 2 ॥

---

## Commentary (Sayana)

O Indra, **that tongue** <note>original: 'kākut'</note> of **yours** which is **well-fashioned** or beautifully made by the Creator. And which is the **most excellent** <note>original: 'variṣṭhā'</note> or most widely extended. And with **which** you **constantly** or many times **drink** the **surge** or juice of the **sweet** Soma...

<vocab>
गिर्वणः (Girvaṇas — one who is pleased by songs of praise), नियुत्वान् (Niyutvān — possessing horses, specifically the Niyut team), सजोषाः (Sajoṣāḥ — being in harmony or associated with others), अहेळमान (Aheḷamāna — not being angry or being well-disposed), इंदवः (Indavaḥ — drops of Soma juice), सुतासः (Sutāsaḥ — the extracted or pressed juice), वज्रिन् (Vajrin — the wielder of the thunderbolt, Indra), काकुत् (Kākut — the tongue or the palate), वरिष्ठा (Variṣṭhā — the most excellent or widest), अध्वर्यु (Adhvaryu — the ritual priest), गव्युः (Gavyuḥ — one who desires cattle or, figuratively, one who seeks the light of heaven).
</vocab>

<header>॥ Rig Veda ॥ [Book 4, Chapter 1, Section 13]</header>

With that tongue <note>referring to the flame of Agni or the speech of the priest</note>, protect our Soma. Drink it. For that purpose, the priest <term>Adhvaryu<gloss>the officiating priest who performs the physical ritual manual labor</gloss></term>, who is the leader of the melodic chant, having taken up the Soma, has set out. He has gone from the cart-shed <note>original: 'havirdhāna'</note> toward the area of the high altar <note>original: 'uttaravedi'</note>. Furthermore, O Indra, desiring the cattle belonging to the enemy <note>original: 'gavyuḥ'</note>, may your thunderbolt <term>Vajra<gloss>the primary weapon of Indra, associated with lightning</gloss></term> be turned toward them. May it be joined with the enemies; that is, may it strike them.

---

->॥ Now the Third Verse ॥<-

## Hymn Text
**This flowing drop, the bull who bestows desires, multiform in appearance—this Soma has been prepared for the showerer of blessings, Indra.**
**Drink this, O Lord of the Bay Horses, O Steadfast One, O Fierce One; you are the master of this Soma throughout the passing days, for this is your food.** ॥ 3 ॥

**Word-by-word Breakdown:**
This. | Flowing drop. | Bull/Bestower. | Multiform. | For Indra. | For the showerer of blessings. | Prepared/Consecrated. | Soma. |
This. | Drink. | O Possessor of Bay Horses. | O Steadfast One. | O Fierce One. | Of which. | You rule/master. | Throughout the days. | Which. | Your. | Food. ॥ 3 ॥

## Commentary (Sayana)
The word <term>drapsa<gloss>flowing drop</gloss></term> refers to that which has the nature of flowing. He is a <term>vṛṣabha<gloss>bull</gloss></term> because he showers or fulfills desires. He is <term>viśvarūpa<gloss>multiform</gloss></term> because he is endowed with many various forms. This Soma, of such a nature, has been <term>samakāri<gloss>prepared</gloss></term>—meaning consecrated through the pressing and purifying rites—for the sake of being drunk by <term>Indra</term>, who is the <term>vṛṣṇe<gloss>the showerer</gloss></term> or bestower of rewards. 

O <term>Harivaḥ</term>, you who possess the two Bay Horses <note>original: 'hari'</note>! O <term>Sthātar</term>, the one who stands as the ruler over all! O <term>Ugra</term>, Indra of formidable strength! Drink this Soma of such quality. You alone are the lord and master <term>veśiṣe</term> of this Soma <term>pradivi</term>—this is a singular usage for a category, meaning throughout the many passing days or the duration of time. The connection is: drink this which is <term>annam</term>, the food prepared and intended for you.

---

->॥ Now the Fourth Verse ॥<-

## Hymn Text
**This Soma is pressed; it is more excellent than the unpressed offering, O Indra. It is better for you who are the Knower, and for your delightful joy.**
**O Conqueror, come to this sacrifice; through this, fill yourself with all your many powers.** ॥ 4 ॥

**Word-by-word Breakdown:**
Pressed. | Soma. | Than the unpressed. | Indra. | Better. | This. | More excellent. | For the Knower. | For joy. |
This. | O Conqueror. | Near. | Come. | Sacrifice. | By that. | All. | Powers/Strengths. | Fill. ॥ 4 ॥

## Commentary (Sayana)
O <term>Indra</term>, this <term>suta<gloss>pressed</gloss></term> Soma is <term>vasyān</term>, meaning more excellent or possessing more wealth, than the Soma of others that remains <term>asṛtāt</term>, or unpressed/unprepared. Likewise, for you who are <term>cikituṣe</term>—the wise one who recognizes the quality of the offering—this is <term>śreyān</term>, the best for your <term>raṇāya</term>, your beautiful and delightful enjoyment. The meaning is that it will cause you to rejoice exceedingly. 

O <term>titirvaḥ</term>, Indra, the one who overcomes or crosses over enemies! Come near to this sacrifice, which is the means of worship. And having approached the Soma, <term>āpṛṇasva</term>, fill up <term>viśvās taviṣīḥ</term>, all your various strengths and powers.

<note>Translator's note: The vocabulary section below summarizes the key terms used in Sāyaṇa's analysis of the attributes of both the offering (Soma) and the deity (Indra).</note>

*   **Drapsa**: Flowing drop or spark.
*   **Vṛṣabha**: Bull (metaphor for the bestower of abundance).
*   **Viśvarūpa**: Possessing all forms.
*   **Soma**: The sacred ritual drink.
*   **Indra**: The king of the gods.
*   **Harivaḥ**: Master of the Bay Horses (Indra's horses).
*   **Titirvaḥ**: The overcomer or vanquisher of foes.
*   **Taviṣīḥ**: Vital strengths or heroic powers.

<header>Mandala 6, Chapter 3, Hymn 42] ॥ Fourth Ashtaka ॥ 735</header>

-> ॥ Now the Fifth Verse ॥ <-

## Hymn Text
We call upon you, O Indra; come toward us. The Soma is sufficient for your body. O performer of a hundred deeds <term>Shatakratu<gloss>an epithet of Indra meaning one who possesses a hundred powers or has performed a hundred sacrifices</gloss></term>, delight yourself in the pressed juices. Protect us in battles and protect us among the clans. ॥ 5 ॥

**Word-by-word Analysis:**
We call | you | toward [us] | O Indra | come | hither-facing | sufficient | for you | Soma | for the body | becomes | O performer of a hundred deeds | delight yourself | in the pressed [juices] | [thoroughly] | us | protect | in battles | [thoroughly] | among the clans. ॥ 5 ॥

---

## Commentary (Sāyaṇa)
O Indra, we **call upon** <note>original: 'hvayāmasi'</note> you. Therefore, being turned toward us, **come hither**. Our **Soma is sufficient for your body**; let it be enough. The meaning is: may it satisfy your body according to your desire. O **Shatakratu** <note>meaning "of many-fold actions"</note>, O Indra, you should **delight yourself** <note>root 'mad' implies satisfaction and joy</note> in our **pressed** Soma juices. Thereafter, **protect us thoroughly in battles** <note>original: 'pṛtanāsu'</note>—that is, guard us excellently in war. Not only in battles, but also protect us **among the clans** <note>original: 'vikṣu'</note>, meaning among all the people.

-> ॥ Thus ends the thirteenth section (varga) of the seventh lesson of the fourth book ॥ <-

---

The nineteenth hymn, beginning with "Toward him" <note>original: 'Pratyasmā'</note>, consists of four verses. It was seen by the seer <term>Rishi<gloss>a semi-divine poet-seer who "heard" or "saw" the eternal hymns</gloss></term> Bharadvāja and is addressed to Indra. The fourth verse is in the <term>Brihati<gloss>a Vedic meter of 36 syllables</gloss></term> meter, while the rest are in the <term>Anustup<gloss>a common Vedic meter of 32 syllables</gloss></term> meter. This is confirmed by the Index <note>original: 'Anukramani'</note>, which states: "Toward him, a group of four verses, Anustup with a Brihati at the end." This hymn is to be recited during the morning libation <note>original: 'prātaḥsavana'</note> by the <term>Acchāvāka<gloss>one of the secondary priests involved in the Soma sacrifice</gloss></term> while the Soma is being brought forward. This is indicated in the ritual manuals: "Having recited for the one being brought up with 'Toward him'..." <note>Aitareya Brahmana 5.7</note>.

-> ॥ Therein the First Verse ॥ <-

## Hymn Text
Bring [the Soma] to him who desires to drink, to the one who knows all things. To the one who comes timely, the one who is ever-going [to the sacrifice], to the leader who is never left behind. ॥ 1 ॥

**Word-by-word Analysis:**
Toward | him | who desires to drink | all things | to the knower | bring | who comes timely | to the one who goes [to the sacrifice] | who is not left behind | to the leader. ॥ 1 ॥

---

## Commentary (Sāyaṇa)
O priest <term>Adhvaryu<gloss>the officiating priest who performs the manual ritual acts</gloss></term>, **bring** toward this Indra, offer the Soma. To what kind of Indra? To him who **desires to drink** <note>original: 'pipīṣate'</note>, to him who **knows** all things that should be known, to the one who **comes timely** <note>original: 'araṃgamāya'</note> or with sufficient speed, to the one who is **ever-going** to the sacrifices, and to the one who is **never left behind** <note>original: 'apaścād-daghvane'</note>. The word 'dagh' implies motion; he is the one who goes in front of everyone and is never at the rear. To the **leader** <note>original: 'nare'</note> of the sacrifices.

७३६

<header>॥ Rig Veda ॥ [Book 6. Chapter 1. Section 14.]</header>

Regarding the third <term>Svarasaman<gloss>a specific type of day in the year-long Soma sacrifice</gloss></term>, during the <term>Nishkevalya<gloss>a midday libation dedicated exclusively to Indra</gloss></term>, the triplet beginning with "Toward him" <note>original: 'em enam'</note> is used as the hymn of praise. This is indicated in the ritual manuals: "The verse 'Toward him, go forth' or all of them..." <note>Ashvalayana Shrauta Sutra 8. 5.</note> ॥

## Hymn Text

->॥ Here is the first [actually second] verse in the hymn ॥<-

Go toward this Indra, the greatest drinker of Soma, with Soma offerings, with the vessel-holding [priests], [he who is] the possessor of the residue, with the pressed drops of Soma. ॥ २ ॥

**Word-by-word Analysis:**
Toward | [particle] | him | toward | go | with Somas | the greatest drinker of Soma |
with the vessels | possessor of the residue | Indra | with the pressed [juices] | with the drops. ॥ २ ॥

---

## Commentary (Sāyaṇa)

O **Adhvaryu priests**, go toward <note>original: 'pratyetana'</note> **this Indra** who is the **greatest drinker of Soma**, using the **Somas** as the means of worship. The particle **im** <note>original: 'īm'</note> is used for rhythmic or ornamental purposes and does not change the meaning. What kind of Indra is he? He is **the possessor of the vessels** <note>original: 'amavadbhir'</note>—referring to the Soma cups like the *Grahas* and *Chamasas*. He is also **the possessor of the residue** <note>original: 'ṛjīṣiṇam'</note>. The word *Rijisha* can mean the strength that overcomes enemies. Thus, he possesses that strength. Alternatively, the word **possessor of the residue** should be connected to the later words: he possesses the **Soma residue** <note>original: 'ṛjīṣam'</note> through the **pressed drops of Soma**. The *Rijisha* is the Soma plant after its essence has been extracted. Or, it could mean he is associated with the **immeasurable** <note>original: 'amāvair'</note> pressed Somas. <note>The root 'ṛj' means to go; Sāyaṇa explains the grammatical derivation of 'ṛjīṣa' as a means of movement or attainment.</note> The word implies he is "connected" to the sacrifice. The construction is: go toward such an Indra. Others say: go toward **this Indra** who is made strong by the pressed **Somas** contained in the cups and vessels. ॥

---

## Hymn Text

->॥ Now the Third Verse ॥<-

If you honor him with the pressed drops, with the Somas, the wise one knows every [desire]; the bold one approaches [and grants] it. ॥ ३ ॥

**Word-by-word Analysis:**
If | with the pressed [juices] | with the drops | with the Somas | toward | you honor |
he knows | of everything | the wise one | the bold | him | [particle] | toward | approaches. ॥ ३ ॥

---

## Commentary (Sāyaṇa)

O **Adhvaryu priests, if you honor** <note>original: 'pratibhūṣatha'</note> Indra—meaning if you go toward him—with the **pressed, shining, or flowing drops of Soma**, then at that time the **wise one** <note>original: 'medhiro'</note>—meaning the intelligent one or the one who possesses the sacrifice <note>original: 'medha'</note>—that Indra **knows** <note>original: 'veda'</note> **every** desire of yours. Having known it, being the **bold** <note>original: 'dhṛṣat'</note> subduer of enemies, **he approaches and fulfills** <note>original: 'ā īṣate'</note> that very desire. ॥

## Hymn Text

->|| Now the fourth [verse] ||<-

For him, for him alone, O **Adhvaryu**, bring forth this pressed food [Soma juice]. May he, many times, protect us from the assault of the conquering, powerful enemy. ॥ ४ ॥

**Word-by-word Analysis:**
For us | for him | indeed | of the food [Soma] | O **Adhvaryu** | bring forth | the pressed [juice] |
many times | of all | conquering | powerful | from the assault | may he protect. ॥ ४ ॥

---

## Commentary (Sāyaṇa)

For him, for him alone—meaning for this **Indra** and no other—O **Adhvaryu** <term>Adhvaryu<gloss>the priest responsible for the physical ritual acts, like pouring the Soma</gloss></term>, you must bring forth <note>original: 'pra-bhara'</note>, or offer, the pressed juice of the **food** in the form of **Soma**. And may that Indra protect us many times <note>original: 'kuvit'</note> from the **assault** or the injury caused by every **conquering** and **powerful** enemy who exerts himself against us. ॥

->|| Thus ends the fourteenth section (Varga) of the seventh [Chapter] of the fourth [Ashtaka] ||<-

The twentieth hymn, beginning with "Whose famous [Soma]," consists of four verses. Its seer is **Bharadvaja**, its meter is <term>Ushnih<gloss>a Vedic meter consisting of 28 syllables</gloss></term>, and its deity is **Indra**. It is indexed accordingly: "The hymn beginning with *Whose* is in the Ushnih meter." In the <term>Mahavrata<gloss>a 'Great Vow' ritual performed at the end of the year</gloss></term> ceremony, specifically during the <term>Nishkevalya<gloss>a midday ritual dedicated exclusively to Indra</gloss></term> libation, this hymn is used within the collection of Ushnih triplets. This is indicated in the fifth book of the <term>Aitareya Aranyaka<gloss>a 'forest book' attached to the Rig Veda detailing secret rituals</gloss></term>: "The three triplets beginning with 'Whose famous Shambara' are in the Gayatri meter" <note>The commentator notes a ritual instruction from Aitareya Aranyaka 5.1.1; there is a minor technical discussion regarding the meter here</note>. ॥

---

## Hymn Text

->|| Here is the first [verse] ||<-

Indra, in whose exhilaration you subdued the famous **Shambara** for the sake of **Divodasa**; this is that pressed Soma, O Indra, drink it. ॥ १ ॥

**Word-by-word Analysis:**
Of whom | that famous | **Shambara** | in exhilaration | for **Divodasa** | you subdued |
this | that | Soma | Indra | for you | pressed | drink. ॥ १ ॥

---

## Commentary (Sāyaṇa)

O **Indra**, in the **exhilaration** <note>original: 'made'</note> or joy produced by drinking this Soma, you **subdued** or destroyed the demon **Shambara** for the sake of King **Divodasa**. Or rather, as the grammarian **Yaska** says: "The root *radhyati* means to bring under control" <note>original: 'radhyatir vaśagamane'</note>. The word "that" <note>original: 'tyat'</note> is used as an adverb to mean "famously" or "as is well known." O Indra, this is that very Soma which has been **pressed** for your sake. Therefore, drink it. ॥

---

## Hymn Text

->|| Now the second [verse] ||<-

Whose strong pressed [juice] and intoxicating [exhilaration] you preserve... this is that pressed Soma, O Indra, drink it. ॥ २ ॥

---

<vocab>
- इन्द्र (Indra): The King of the Gods and the primary deity of the Soma sacrifice.
- सोम (Soma): A sacred plant and the ritual drink pressed from it, offered to the gods.
- शम्बर (Shambara): A drought-demon or chieftain defeated by Indra in Vedic mythology.
- दिवोदास (Divodasa): A famous king of the Bharata clan and a patron of the Rishi Bharadvaja.
- अध्वर्यु (Adhvaryu): The "working" priest who handles the physical materials of the sacrifice.
- भरद्वाज (Bharadvaja): The historical seer (Rishi) of the sixth book of the Rig Veda.
</vocab>

# Rig Veda: Mandala 6, Sukta 47

## Hymn Text

<note>RV 6.47.2 (Word-by-word Analysis)</note>
> Whose | sharp | pressed | exhilaration | middle | end | and | you protect |
> This | he | Soma | O Indra | for you | pressed | drink. ॥ २ ॥

---

## Commentary (Sayana)

O **Indra**, you protect <note>original: 'rakshase'</note> the **sharp-pressed** <note>original: 'tivra-sutam'</note> part of this Soma. "Sharp-pressed" refers to the juice whose extraction is intense, belonging to the morning libation. You also protect that **exhilaration** <note>original: 'madam'</note>—the intoxicating Soma juice—of the **middle** <note>original: 'madhyam'</note> session (the midday libation) and the **end** <note>original: 'antam'</note> session, which belongs to the **third libation** <term>Tritya-savana<gloss>the final of the three daily Soma offerings, held in the evening</gloss></term>. This Soma here is pressed for your sake; **drink it**.

---

## Hymn Text

-> ॥ Now the third [verse] ॥ <-
<note>RV 6.47.3</note>
Whose cows from within the rock, in your exhilaration, you released, though they were firmly held.
This is that Soma, O Indra, pressed for you; drink it! ॥ ३ ॥

<note>RV 6.47.3 (Word-by-word Analysis)</note>
> Whose | cows | within | of the rock | by exhilarations | firm | you released |
> This | he | Soma | O Indra | for you | pressed | drink. ॥ ३ ॥

---

## Commentary (Sayana)

When the exhilarating juice of **whose** Soma was drunk, you **released** <note>original: 'avasrijah'</note> the **cows** that were stolen by the **Panis** <term>Panis<gloss>a class of demons or tight-fisted merchants who hid the cows of the gods</gloss></term>. These cows were located **within the rock** <note>original: 'ashmanah'</note>, inside the mountain where they were placed by the demon **Vala**, and they were **firmly held** with strong enclosures. You released them from Vala’s bonds. **"This is that Soma..."** and so on is the same as before.

## Hymn Text

-> ॥ Now the fourth [verse] ॥ <-
<note>RV 6.47.4</note>
Rejoicing in whose juice, you have assumed your bountiful strength.
This is that Soma, O Indra, pressed for you; drink it! ॥ ४ ॥

<note>RV 6.47.4 (Word-by-word Analysis)</note>
> Whose | rejoicing | of the food (Soma) | bountiful | you have held | strength |
> This | he | Soma | O Indra | for you | pressed | drink. ॥ ४ ॥

## Commentary (Sayana)

O **Indra**, by the drinking of **whose food** <note>original: 'andhasah'</note>—meaning the food characterized as Soma—you become **rejoicing** <note>original: 'mandano'</note>, delighted and glad, and you **hold** or maintain your **bountiful** and extraordinary **strength** <note>original: 'shavas'</note>. The meaning is that through this Soma, your "Indra-hood" (your power as a lord) was produced. **This Soma here is pressed; drink it.**

-> ॥ Thus ends the fifteenth section (Varga) of the seventh [Chapter] of the fourth [Ashtaka] ॥ <-
-> ॥ Thus ends the third subdivision (Anuvaka) of the sixth Circle (Mandala) ॥ <-

**In the fourth subdivision (Anuvaka), there are six hymns. Among them, the first hymn, beginning with "Who is the giver of wealth" [RV 6.48], consists of twenty-four verses. Its seer is Shamyu, the son of Brihaspati; its deity is Indra. The first six verses are in the Anushtubh meter; the seventh, eighth, and ninth are in the Virat...**

## Hymn Text

-> ॥ Here is the first verse ॥ <-

## Commentary (Sayana)

O **wealthy** <note>original: 'rayivo'</note> Indra, **which** Soma is **most wealthy** <note>original: 'rayitamo'</note>—meaning exceedingly full of riches—and **which** is **most glorious** <note>original: 'dyumnavattamo'</note> with shining **splendors** <note>original: 'dyumnaiḥ'</note> or fame; O **Lord of the Oblation** <note>original: 'svadhapate'</note>—O Indra, protector of the food in the form of Soma—**that Soma**, being **pressed** <note>original: 'abhiṣutaḥ'</note>, **is** <note>original: 'asti'</note> the **exhilaration** <note>original: 'mado'</note> that gladdens **you** <note>original: 'te'</note>.

## Hymn Text

-> ॥ Now the second [verse] ॥ <-

Which is helpful, O powerful one, the giver of wealth for the prayers;
That Soma is pressed; it is for you, O Lord of the Oblation, an exhilaration. ॥ २ ॥

**Word-by-word Analysis:**

Soma | pressed | it | O Indra | for you | is | O Lord of the Oblation | exhilaration. ॥ २ ॥

## Commentary (Sayana)

O **powerful one** <note>original: 'tuvi-shagma'</note> who brings much happiness, O Indra! **Which** Soma is **helpful** <note>original: 'shagmah'</note> or bestowing of joy, and is the **giver** <note>original: 'dāmā'</note> of **wealth** <note>original: 'rāyo'</note> for the **prayers** <note>original: 'matīnām'</note> of the chanters; O **Lord of the Oblation** <note>original: 'svadhapate'</note>, **that Soma**, having been **pressed**, is the exhilarator for **you**.

## Hymn Text

-> ॥ Now the third [verse] ॥ <-

**Word-by-word Analysis:**
By which | grown | and | with strength | swift | and | with your own | with protections |
Soma | pressed | it | O Indra | for you | is | O Lord of the Oblation | exhilaration. ॥ ३ ॥

## Commentary (Sayana)

These two instances of the word **na** <note>original: 'na-shabdau'</note> are used in the sense of a conjunction <note>original: 'samuccayārthau'</note> meaning "and." **By which** Soma, when drunk, you have become **grown** <note>original: 'vṛddho'</note> or greatly increased, **and** with your **own**—

Regarding the fourth day of the <term>Prishthya Shadaha<gloss>a specific six-day cycle within a Vedic sacrifice</gloss></term>, during the <term>Prauga Shastra<gloss>a series of recitations performed by the Hotri priest during the morning libation</gloss></term>, the triplet of verses dedicated to Indra beginning with **"That [Indra] of yours"** <note>original: 'tyamu vaḥ'</note> is prescribed. ## Hymn Text

-> ॥ Here is the fourth verse of the hymn ॥ <-

I praise that [Indra] of yours, the one who does not strike [devotees], the Lord of strength;
Indra, the conqueror of all, the Leader, the most liberal bestower, the observer of all people. ॥ ४ ॥

**Word-by-word Analysis:**
That | indeed | for you | non-striker | I praise | of strength | the Lord |
Indra | all-conquering | the Leader | most liberal | observer of all people. ॥ ४ ॥

---

## Commentary (Sayana)

O priests and sacrificers, **for you** <note>original: 'vaḥ'</note>—meaning for your sake—**I praise** <note>original: 'gṛṇīṣe'</note> or laud **that very** <note>original: 'tyamu'</note> Indra. Alternatively, the word **praise** <note>original: 'gṛṇīṣe'</note> is interpreted as "You all praise" <note>original: 'gṛṇīta'</note>; this is a change of grammatical person common in Vedic Sanskrit. What kind of Indra? One who is **non-striking** <note>original: 'aprahaṇam'</note>—meaning he does not strike down his devotees but instead favors them; he is the **Lord of strength** <note>original: 'śavaso patiṃ'</note> or its protector; the **conqueror of all** <note>original: 'viśvāsāhaṃ'</note> who overcomes every enemy; the **Leader** <note>original: 'naraṃ'</note>; the **most liberal bestower** <note>original: 'maṃhiṣṭhaṃ'</note> or greatest giver; and the **observer of all people** <note>original: 'viśvacharṣaṇim'</note>, the witness of everything.

## Hymn Text

-> ॥ Now the fifth verse ॥ <-

Whom songs [of praise] indeed increase, the Lord of swift wealth;
His strength, indeed, the two divine Goddesses, Heaven and Earth, quickly serve. ॥ ५ ॥

**Word-by-word Analysis:**
Whom | they increase | indeed | songs | the Lord | of the swift | wealth |
Him | indeed | now | his | Heaven and Earth | the two Goddesses | strength | they serve. ॥ ५ ॥

---

## Commentary (Sayana)

The **songs** <note>original: 'giraḥ'</note> or praises related to Indra **increase** <note>original: 'vardhayanti'</note> **that very** <note>original: 'yamit'</note> strength of his. Of what kind is he? The **Lord** <note>original: 'patiṃ'</note> or master. Of what? **Of the wealth** <note>original: 'rādhasaḥ'</note> **of the swift** <note>original: 'turasya'</note>—meaning the wealth of the enemy who strikes. This implies he is the one who seizes the enemies' riches. **The two divine Goddesses** <note>original: 'devī'</note>, whose nature is to shine, namely **Heaven and Earth** <note>original: 'rodasī'</note>, **now** <note>original: 'nu'</note>—meaning quickly—**serve** <note>original: 'saparyataḥ'</note> or attend to **that very** <note>original: 'tamit'</note> **strength** <note>original: 'śuṣmaṃ'</note> or overwhelming power of this Indra.

-> ॥ Thus ends the sixteenth Varga in the seventh Chapter of the fourth [Ashtaka] ॥ <-

## Hymn Text

<note>RV 6.44.6 Word-for-word Analysis (Pada-patha)</note>
That | for you | of the hymn | greatness | for Indra | to be spread out | a wise man | like | whose | protections | [prefix] | when | he grows | dwelling together. ॥ ६ ॥

## Commentary (Sayana)

O praisers, I spread out <note>original: 'upastṛṇīṣaṇi'</note>—meaning it should be spread out or extended by approaching—that greatness or majesty <note>original: 'barhaṇā'</note> of your <note>original: 'vaḥ'</note> hymn <note>original: 'ukthasya'</note> for the sake of Indra. The meaning is: extend the praise so that Indra may know the majesty of the hymn. The <term>protections<gloss>uti; divine aid or assistance</gloss></term> of this Indra are like a <term>Vipra<gloss>a wise, inspired poet or sage</gloss></term>; they are skilled in all works. Alternatively, the word "like" <note>original: 'na'</note> is a filler; it should be joined as "of the wise Indra." To that Indra, when <note>original: 'yat'</note> in him the protections dwelling together <note>original: 'sakhitaḥ'</note> or united appear <note>original: 'vi rohati'</note>, [this praise is offered].

## Hymn Text

<note>RV 6.44.7</note>
The most recent friend found the skilled [sacrificer]; drinking [the Soma], he gathered better wealth for the gods.
Having gained [offerings], with his powerful, shaking [forces], he became a protector to his friends out of a desire to guard them. ॥ ७ ॥

<note>RV 6.44.7 Word-for-word Analysis (Pada-patha)</note>
He found | the skilled | friend | most recent | drinking | for the gods | better [wealth] | he gathered |
having gained | with powerful | shaking [forces] | desiring to protect | a protector | he became | for friends. ॥ ७ ॥

---

## Commentary (Sayana)

That Indra found <note>original: 'avidat'</note> or knows the <term>sacrificer<gloss>the person performing the ritual</gloss></term> who is skilled <note>original: 'dakṣam'</note> or capable in rituals. Of what sort is he? He is a friend <note>original: 'mitraḥ'</note>, most recent <note>original: 'navīyān'</note>—meaning very new, most auspicious, or most worthy of praise. And he, drinking <note>original: 'papānaḥ'</note> the Soma, gathers <note>original: 'acait'</note>—meaning accumulates or provides—excellent wealth for the gods or the praisers. Furthermore, having gained <note>original: 'sasavān'</note>—where 'sasa' is a name for food—meaning being endowed with food in the form of oblations, that Indra, joined with powerful <note>original: 'staulābhiḥ'</note> and shaking <note>original: 'dhautarībhiḥ'</note> mares, hands, or the <term>Maruts<gloss>storm deities</gloss></term>, became a protector <note>original: 'pāyuḥ'</note> for his friends <note>original: 'sakhibhyaḥ'</note>, the praisers, coming with a desire to protect them. Alternatively, the word 'sasavān' is a form of the root meaning 'to win' or 'to enjoy'; the connection is that he enjoys [the offerings] with those powerful, shaking forces.

<meta>This page continues the commentary on the 47th hymn (Sūkta) of the sixth Mandala of the Rig Veda. The previous page (741) began the explanation of verse 8, discussing the ritual path and the role of the creator or ordainer in the Soma sacrifice.</meta>

The creator <note>original: 'vedhā'</note> and ordainer of the sacrifice, who is the witness of everything—the Soma—was drunk <note>original: 'apāyi'</note> on the path of Truth <note>original: 'ṛtasya'</note>. That is, it was drunk by the god Indra. Alternatively, the "creator" refers to Indra himself, who was "drunk" in the sense of being exhilarated by the drink; may he drink the Soma. <note>The commentator notes a grammatical variation here: 'vyatyayena karttari cviṇ'.</note> For the sake of Indra's glory, the gods and the chanting priests performed their ritual works <note>original: 'mānāṃsi śriye... akran'</note>. Indra, holding <note>original: 'dadhāno'</note> a great <note>original: 'maho'</note> and personal body <note>original: 'vapuḥ'</note> that strikes fear into his enemies, is to be honored and shared with through songs of praise. For the sake of vision <note>original: 'dṛśaye'</note>, may he reveal <note>original: 'vyāvaḥ'</note> or manifest his favorable radiance. Or, the word "lovely" <note>original: 'venyaḥ'</note> is derived from the root meaning "to desire" and "body" <note>original: 'vapuḥ'</note> refers to form; thus, being praised by words, may the lovely Indra reveal his brilliant form for all to see.

->॥ Now the Ninth Verse ॥<-

## Hymn Text
O Indra, place in us the most brilliant strength; repel the many hostilities of the people.
Make our life-force more extensive through your powers; assist us in the acquisition of wealth. ॥ ९ ॥

**Word-for-word Analysis (Pada-patha):**
The most brilliant | strength | place | in us | [end of phrase] | repel | of the people | the many | hostilities |
more extensive | life-force | make | through [your] powers | of wealth | in the acquisition | us | assist. ॥ ९ ॥

---

## Commentary (Sayana)
O Indra, **place** <note>original: 'dhehi'</note>—meaning establish or hold—the **most brilliant** <note>original: 'dyumattamaṃ'</note> and most radiant **strength** <note>original: 'dakṣaṃ'</note> **in us** <note>original: 'asme'</note>. **Repel** <note>original: 'sedha'</note> or ward off the **many** <note>original: 'pūrvīḥ'</note> **hostilities** <note>original: 'arātīḥ'</note> and enemy armies of the people who oppose us. Furthermore, **make** <note>original: 'kṛṇuhi'</note> our **life-force** <note>original: 'vayaḥ'</note> or food **more extensive** <note>original: 'varṣīyaḥ'</note> and greatly increased through your own **powers** <note>original: 'śacībhiḥ'</note> or wisdom. Likewise, **assist us** <note>original: 'asmān aviddhi'</note> and lead us **in the acquisition** <note>original: 'sātau'</note> or the sharing of **wealth**. Alternatively, it means: look upon us for the purpose of sharing wealth.

->॥ Now the Tenth Verse ॥<-

## Hymn Text
O Indra, O Bountiful One, we have become yours alone, [we who are] for the Giver; O Lord of Bay Horses, do not be indifferent to us.
No kinsman is seen among mortals; why then, dear friend, do they call you the "Impeller of the Destitute"? ॥ १० ॥

**Word-for-word Analysis (Pada-patha):**
O Indra | for you | indeed | O Bountiful One | we have become | we | for the Giver | O Lord of Bay Horses | not | [prefix] | be indifferent |
No one | kinsman | to be seen | among mortals | what | indeed | Impeller of the Destitute | you | they call. ॥ १० ॥

---

## Commentary (Sayana)
O **Bountiful One** <note>original: 'maghavan'</note>, O wealthy Indra, **we have become** <note>original: 'abhūma'</note> yours alone—dedicated to **you** <note>original: 'tubhyam'</note> who are the **Giver** <note>original: 'dātre'</note> of all desires. Alternatively, we have become those who exist for your sake, occupied in the giving of oblations to the Giver. O **Lord of Bay Horses** <note>original: 'harivo'</note>, for this reason, **do not be indifferent** <note>original: 'mā vivenaḥ'</note>. Do not be without desire for us; rather, always desire and favor us.

<meta>This page continues the commentary on the 44th hymn (Sūkta) of the sixth Mandala of the Rig Veda. The previous page concluded the explanation of the 10th verse, discussing the unique relationship between the worshiper and Indra.</meta>

The word "Venati" <note>original: 'venatiḥ'</note> refers to the act of desiring or shining. Among mortals <note>original: 'martyatrā'</note>, that is, in the midst of human beings, no other friend or kinsman like you is seen <note>original: 'nakirdṛśe'</note>. What is the significance of this specific description? It means: "O Indra, the people of old <note>original: 'purājāḥ'</note> describe you as the one who impels or encourages <note>original: 'radhracodanaṃ'</note> the worshiper who possesses abundant wealth."

->॥ This concludes the seventeenth section (Varga) of the seventh chapter of the fourth book (Ashtaka) ॥<-

## Hymn Text

->॥ Now the Eleventh Verse ॥<-

**O Showerer, do not give us over to the consumer; O Wealthy One, may we not suffer in your friendship.**
**Many are your restraints, O Indra, among the people; strike those who do not offer Soma, and uproot those who give no gifts. ॥ ११ ॥**

**Do not | to the consumer | O Showerer | us | give | do not | your | O Wealthy One | in friendship | may we suffer |**
**Many | your | O Indra | restraints | among people | strike | those who do not press Soma | [intensifier] | uproot | those who do not give gifts ॥ ११ ॥**

## Commentary (Sayana)

O <term>Vṛṣabha</term> <note>literally "the Bull," but interpreted here as the "Showerer of Desires"</note>, O Indra, do not give us over <note>original: 'mā rarīthāḥ'</note> to the <term>Jasvane</term> <note>the "consumer" or "exhauster," referring to demons or Rakshasas who waste away one's life</note>. Being in your friendship <note>original: 'sakhye'</note>, you who are <term>Revata</term> <note>possessing great wealth</note>, may we not be harmed or suffer. O Indra, your "many restraints" <note>original: 'pūrvīḥ niṣidhaḥ'</note>—which can be understood as prohibitions or even as ropes/nets to catch enemies—are placed among the people who are our foes. For this reason, strike <note>original: 'jahi'</note> those who do not perform the Soma sacrifice <note>original: 'asuṣvīn'</note>, and utterly uproot <note>original: 'pravṛha'</note> those who do not provide oblations <note>original: 'apṛṇataḥ'</note>. The root *pṛṇ* denotes the act of giving.

---

## Hymn Text

->॥ Now the Twelfth Verse ॥<-

**Like a thundering rain-cloud, Indra raises up wealth consisting of horses and cattle.**
**From of old, you are the sustainer of the poet; let not the miserly, non-givers harm you, the Bountiful One. ॥ १२ ॥**

**Up | like a thundering cloud | thundering | raises | Indra | wealth | consisting of horses | consisting of cattle |**
**You | are | from of old | sustainer of the poet | not | you | the non-givers | [intensifier] | harm | the Bountiful One ॥ १२ ॥**

## Commentary (Sayana)

Just as the rain-god <term>Parjanya</term> <note>the deity of rain and thunder</note>, thundering and roaring, causes the clouds to rise, so does Indra raise up <note>original: 'udiyarti'</note> wealth <note>original: 'rādhāṃsi'</note> consisting of two groups: horses and cattle, in order to give them to those who praise him. The second half of the verse is addressed directly to the deity. O Indra, you are from ancient times <note>original: 'pradivaḥ'</note> the sustainer or supporter of poets and singers <note>original: 'kārudhāyāḥ'</note>. May the miserly ones <note>original: 'adāmānaḥ'</note>, who do not offer oblations, not harm or overpower you, who are the <term>Maghavan</term> <note>the Bountiful or Wealthy Lord</note>. Alternatively, there is a shift in grammatical case here, and the meaning is: let them not harm you, the wealthy one.
