The previous page discussed the eleventh verse, where the worshiper prays to Indra for protection and for the removal of those who do not offer gifts. This page moves into the final verses of the first section (Varga) of this chapter, focusing on the ritual offering of Soma and Indra’s victory over his enemies.</meta>

744 | ॥ Rig Veda ॥ | [Book 4. Chapter 1. Section 18.]
:--- | :---: | ---:

-> ॥ Now the Thirteenth Verse ॥ <-

## Hymn Text

**O heroic Adhvaryu, bring forth the pressed juices for the great Indra, for he is indeed their King; He who has increased by the songs, both ancient and new, of the chanting Rishis. ॥ १३ ॥**

**Pada-patha:**
O Adhvaryu | Hero | [bring] forth | for the great | of the pressed [juices] | for Indra | bring | he | indeed | of this [Soma] | King |
Who | by ancient | and also | by new | by songs | has increased | of the chanting | of the Rishis ॥ १३ ॥

---

## Commentary (Sayana)

O Hero, <term>Adhvaryu</term> <note>the priest who manages the physical ritual and "impels" the offerings</note>, bring forth the pressed <term>Soma</term> juices for this great Indra. 

**Grammatical note: Genitive case used for the Accusative** <note>original: 'karmani ṣaṣṭhī'; the text uses "of the juices" to mean "the juices" themselves</note>.

Bring them, offer them, make them reach him. For indeed, Indra is the King and Master of this Soma. Who is this Indra? He is the one who increases and grows powerful through two kinds of hymns: those composed in ancient times and those being composed now by the chanting <term>Rishis</term> <note>inspired seers or poets</note>. Since Indra is the master of the Soma, it is implied that the Soma must be offered specifically to him.

In the ritual application, during the first night-cycle <note>original: 'rātri-paryāya'</note>, this verse serves as the recitation formula for the <term>Maitrāvaruṇa</term> priest. This is indicated in the ritual manuals: "In the exhilaration of this, the wise one of many forms" is the recitation. <note>Reference to Ashvalayana Shrauta Sutra 6. 4.</note>

---

-> ॥ This is the Fourteenth Verse of the Hymn ॥ <-

## Hymn Text

**In the exhilaration of this juice, the wise Indra, unassailable, struck down the many obstructing foes. Therefore, pour that sweet Soma for this heroic, strong-jawed one, so that he may drink. ॥ १४ ॥**

**Pada-patha:**
Of this | in exhilaration | many | years [or forms] | knowing | Indra | the Vritras | unassailable | struck |
That | [intensifier] | forth | pour | possessing sweetness | for this | Soma | for the hero | for the strong-jawed | for the sake of drinking ॥ १४ ॥

---

## Commentary (Sayana)

When Indra is in a state of joy or exhilaration <note>original: 'made'</note> from drinking this Soma, he—the wise and knowing one—struck down the many <term>Vritras</term> <note>the "envelopers" or enemies who obstruct the light and waters</note>. He did this while being himself unassailable <note>original: 'apratī'</note> and unopposed by others. 

Alternatively, the word "years" <note>original: 'varṣāṃsi'</note> can be interpreted as "forms." Thus: Indra, knowing the many forms or disguises created by the illusions <note>original: 'māyā'</note> of the demons, struck down the obstructing Rakshasas and others who had never been countered by anyone else before.

O Adhvaryu, pour <note>original: 'pra hoṣi'</note> that very same sweet, honey-like Soma for this hero, Indra, who is the "Vanquisher of Enemies" and the "Strong-jawed one" <note>original: 'śipriṇe', referring to Indra's beautiful or powerful jaws/cheeks</note>, so that he may drink.

In the ritual application, during the second night-cycle, this is the recitation formula for the Maitrāvaruṇa priest. It is noted: "May Indra be the drinker of the pressed juice, the slayer of Vritra." <note>Reference to Ashvalayana Shrauta Sutra 6. 4.</note>

<summary>These verses describe the ritual invitation to the Adhvaryu priest to offer Soma to Indra, highlighting Indra's role as the King of the sacrifice who destroys enemies when empowered by the sacred drink and the hymns of the Rishis.</summary>
<keywords>Adhvaryu, Indra, Soma, Vritra, Rishi, ritual recitation, Maitravaruna priest, Soma sacrifice, divine exhilaration</keywords>

[Mandala 6. Chapter 4. Hymn 44.] || Fourth Book || 745

## Hymn Text

-> ॥ This is the Fifteenth Verse ॥ <-

**May Indra be the drinker of the pressed Soma, the slayer of Vritra with his thunderbolt, while rejoicing. May he come toward our sacrifice even from a great distance—he who is the dwelling-place of all, the protector of prayers, and the nourisher of the ritual performers. ॥ १५ ॥**

**Pada-patha:**
Drinker | [of the] pressed [juice] | Indra | may he be | Soma | slayer | Vritra | with the thunderbolt | rejoicing |
Comer | [to the] sacrifice | from a distance | even | toward | the dwelling-place | of prayers | protector | of the performers-sustainer ॥ १५ ॥

---

## Commentary (Sayana)

May this Indra be the **drinker of the pressed Soma**. May he be an excellent drinker. <note>The commentator notes the use of the grammatical suffix 'tr̥n' to denote a 'skilful agent'</note>. Therefore, according to the rule <note>original: "na lokāvyaya..."</note>, the accusative case is used instead of the genitive for the object of the action. This same rule should be observed in words like **slayer** and others that follow. Exhilarated and **rejoicing** by that Soma, may he be the **slayer**—the destroyer—of the enemy **Vritra**, who is the "Coverer," using his **thunderbolt weapon**. 

For both of these purposes—drinking and slaying—may he be the **comer toward our sacrifice**, arriving even **from a great distance**. The meaning is: even if he is in a far-off land, may he come quickly to our sacrifice to drink the Soma. What is the nature of Indra? He is the **dwelling-place**, the one who provides a home for all; the **protector** of the **prayers** <note>or "meditations" and "actions"</note> of those who chant; and the **nourisher of the performers**, the <term>Yajamanas</term> <note>the patrons or hosts who institute the sacrifice</note> who perform the sacred work.

-> ॥ This ends the eighteenth section of the seventh chapter of the fourth book ॥ <-

In the third cycle of the night <note>original: 'tṛtīye rātri-paryāye'</note>, this verse serves as the consecrating prayer <note>original: 'yājyā'</note> for the <term>Prashastr̥</term> priest during the recitation. This is indicated in the ritual manuals: "This vessel is the drink of Indra" is the consecrating prayer <note>original: 'Āśv. 6. 4.'</note>.

---

## Hymn Text

-> ॥ This is the Sixteenth Verse of the Hymn ॥ <-

**This vessel, the drink of Indra, the dear immortal juice of Indra, has been drunk. May it exhilarate the God for benevolence, and may he drive away hatred and sin from us. ॥ १६ ॥**

**Pada-patha:**
This | that | vessel | Indra's-drink | of Indra | dear | immortal | has been drunk |
May it exhilarate | so that | for benevolence | the God | away | from us | hatred | may he drive | away | sin ॥ १६ ॥

---

## Commentary (Sayana)

The **vessel** <note>meaning the juice to be drunk</note> which is the **drink of Indra**, suitable for his consumption, and which is the **dear**, agreeable, **immortal** <term>Soma</term>—**this has been drunk**. May Indra drink it. <note>The commentator notes a grammatical variation where a passive verb form is used in an active sense: "apāyi" (was drunk) for "pibatu" (let him drink)</note>. Or, let this immortal juice be drunk by Indra. 

**So that**—in which manner—the Soma, once drunk, **may exhilarate** the **God** Indra **for benevolence** <note>original: 'saumanasāya', meaning 'gladness of heart' or 'goodwill'</note>, in that manner let it be drunk. Having drunk the Soma, may Indra **drive away** and separate **hatred** <note>meaning enemies</note> from us, and also separate and drive away **sin** <note>original: 'amhas'</note> from us.

---

[Rig Veda] || [Book 4. Chapter 1. Section 19.] || 746

## Hymn Text

-> ॥ This is the Seventeenth Verse ॥ <-

**O Bounteous Hero, rejoicing in this [Soma], slay the enemies—both the kinsman and the stranger, O Indra. Those with armies, who point their weapons toward us—strike them down so they turn away, O Indra, and destroy them. ॥ १७ ॥**

**Word-by-word breakdown:**
By this | rejoicing | slay | O Hero | enemies | kinsman | non-kinsman | O Bounteous one | enemies |
Toward-armies | toward | pointing-repeatedly | retreating | O Indra | [intensity] | strike | slay | and ॥ १७ ॥

---

-> ॥ This is the Eighteenth Verse ॥ <-

**O Bounteous Indra, in these battles of ours, bestow upon us great and easily-attained wealth. In the winning of waters, of offspring, and of descendants, O Indra, make us, the singers of praise, prosperous. ॥ १८ ॥**

**Word-by-word breakdown:**
In these | [filler] | our | O Bounteous one | O Indra | in battles | for us | great | wealth | easy-to-go | make |
Of waters | of offspring | of descendants | in the winning | O Indra | singers/wise ones | make | [filler] | our | prosperous/halving ॥ १८ ॥

---

-> ॥ This is the Nineteenth Verse ॥ <-

**May the powerful bay horses, yoked to the powerful chariot with powerful reins, bring you toward us, O Wielder of the Thunderbolt, for the powerful exhilaration [of Soma]. ॥ १९ ॥**

**Word-by-word breakdown:**
Toward | you | bay horses | powerful | being yoked | powerful-chariots | powerful-reins | horses |
Toward-us-turning | powerful | thunderbolt-wielder | for the powerful | exhilaration | well-yoked | may they carry ॥ १९ ॥

---

## Commentary (Sayana)

**Commentary on Verse 17:**
O **Bounteous** <note>original: "Maghavan"; the Lord of Wealth</note> and **Heroic** Indra, being **rejoicing** or exhilarated by **this** present Soma, **slay**—or destroy—the **enemies** who act against us. These enemies are of two types: the **kinsman** <note>original: "jāmi"; a relative or family member</note> and the **stranger** <note>original: "ajāmi"; one who is not a relative</note>. Furthermore, there are those **with armies** who have come against us; O Indra, **strike** those enemies who are **repeatedly pointing** or hurling their weapons at us so that they become **retreating** <note>original: "parācaḥ"; turning their backs</note>. After that, **slay them** as well.

**Commentary on Verse 18:**
O **Bounteous** Indra, **in these** our **battles** or struggles between armies, **bestow** <note>original: "kaḥ"; from the root 'kṛ' meaning to do or make</note> upon **us great** and **easily-attained wealth**. <note>The word "sma" in the text is a particle used to fill the meter</note>. Moreover, O Indra, for the sake of **winning**—or conquering—the **waters** <note>referring to either rains or the spoils of the river-lands</note>, as well as for the sake of obtaining **offspring** <note>original: "toka"; a son</note> and **descendants** <note>original: "tanaya"; a grandson</note>, make **us**, the **singers** of your praise, **prosperous**. Alternatively, the word **prosperous** <note>original: "ardham"</note> can mean "those who cut the enemies into halves" <note>original: "ardhakāriṇaḥ"</note>.

**Commentary on Verse 19:**
<note>This verse is notable for its repetitive use of the word "Vṛṣan" (powerful/bull/showerer), creating a rhythmic and potent invocation.</note>
May the **bay horses**—which are **powerful** <note>original: "vṛṣaṇo"</note>, yoked to **powerful chariots**, and controlled by **powerful reins**—carry you toward us. These horses are **well-yoked** and **fast**. O **Wielder of the Thunderbolt**, may these **powerful** steeds bring you **toward us** for the **powerful exhilaration** <note>original: "vṛṣṇe madāya"</note> provided by the Soma juice.

<summary>In these concluding verses of the hymn, the poet appeals to Indra to destroy all enemies, whether related or foreign, and to grant prosperity in the form of water, wealth, and lineage. The final verse uses a rhythmic repetition of "power" (vṛṣan) to invoke Indra's arrival at the sacrifice.</summary>
<keywords>Indra, Soma, Maghavan, battle, offspring, bay horses, Vrishan, prosperity, protection</keywords>

## Commentary (Sayana)
[Continuation of commentary for verse 19]

O **Indra**, may your **bay horses**, being **powerful** <note>original: *vṛṣṇaḥ*, referring to those who shower boons or are virile</note>, bring you here to drink this Soma for **exhilaration**. What kind of horses? They are **showering** ones, who fulfill desires; they are **yoked** to the chariot of their own accord; they have **powerful chariots** <note>original: *vṛṣarathāsaḥ*, those whose chariots shower boons</note>. They have **powerful reins** <note>original: *vṛṣaraśmayaḥ*</note>, meaning their reins are showerers [of speed or control]. They are **runners**, traveling constantly toward us; they are **powerful**, eternally youthful; O **Wielder of the Thunderbolt** <note>original: *vajrabāho*, one who carries the thunderbolt weapon in his arms</note>, they are well-yoked.

## Hymn Text

->॥ Now the Twentieth Verse ॥<-

**O Powerful One, your powerful horses have mounted the wooden vessel like waves sprinkling water, rejoicing in exhilaration. O Indra, for you—the powerful and virile—they bring the Soma pressed by the powerful stones. ॥ २० ॥**

**Word-by-word breakdown:**
Toward | your | O Powerful One | powerful ones | wooden vessel | have stood | water-sprinkling | like | waves | rejoicing |
O Indra | [forth] | for you | by powerful [stones] | of the pressed [Somas] | for the powerful | they bring | for the bull | Soma ॥ २० ॥

---

## Commentary (Sayana)

O **Powerful One**, O Indra who showers desires: your **powerful** <note>the youthful and vigorous</note> horses, like the **waves of the ocean** sprinkling water <note>original: *ghṛtapruṣo normayo*; Sayana interprets *ghṛta* here as water</note>, being **rejoicing** and exhilarated, have **mounted** <note>original: *asthuḥ*, meaning they have taken their place upon</note> your **wooden** chariot <note>original: *droṇam*, literally a vessel made of timber, here interpreted as the chariot</note>. The intent is: "therefore, please arrive." For what reason? He says: O **Indra**, for **you**, who are the eternally youthful **Bull** <note>the showerer of all benefits</note>, the priests **bring** <note>lead forth for the oblation</note> the **Soma**—which is your own limb/form—from among the **pressed Somas** prepared by the **powerful** stones that shower desires. Therefore, the meaning is: "please come."

->॥ Thus ends the nineteenth section of the seventh lesson of the fourth book. ॥<-

## Hymn Text

->॥ Now the Twenty-First Verse ॥<-

**You are the Bull of heaven, the Bull of the earth; you are the Bull of the rivers, the Bull of all that moves. For you, the Powerful One, O Bull, the Soma juice has swelled—sweet, honey-flavored, to be drunk at will. ॥ २१ ॥**

**Word-by-word breakdown:**
Powerful | you are | of heaven | bull | of earth | powerful | of rivers | bull | of those that move |
For the powerful | your | Soma-drop | O Bull | has swelled | sweet | juice | honey-drink | for choice/at will ॥ २१ ॥

---

## Commentary (Sayana)

O **Indra**, you **are the Bull** <note>the one who sprinkles or fertilizes</note> **of heaven**, through your oblations. You are the **Bull of the earth**, the showerer of desires upon the ground. You are the **Bull of the rivers**, the flowing ones, filling them with rain. Likewise, you are the **Bull** of **all that moves** <note>original: *striyānām*, interpreted here as the collective of all living beings, both stationary and mobile</note>, the showerer of—

[Continuation of commentary for verse 21]

...you are the showerer of those who measure or are honored. Or rather, the waters have become gathered together by the woman; you are the showerer of them. O **Bull** <note>original: *vṛṣabha*, the masculine pourer of desires</note>, O **Indu** (Soma), who showers fulfillments, the sweet, delicious, and praiseworthy juice—which is flavorful and like honey—has swelled and increased for you, the excellent and best pourer. ## Hymn Text

-> ॥ Now the Twenty-Second Verse ॥ <-

**This radiant god, being born with strength, checked the Pani while allied with Indra. This Indu stole the weapons of his own guardian and the illusions of the malevolent one. ॥ २२ ॥**

<note>Word-by-word breakdown (Padapatha):</note>
This | god | with strength | being born | with Indra | as an ally | the Pani | checked | 
this | of his own | guardian | weapons | Indu | stole | of the malevolent | illusions ॥ २२ ॥

## Commentary (Sayana)

This **Indu** (Soma), the shining god, appearing as he is being born in alliance with his friend **Indra**, checked the **Pani** <note>The Panis were a class of demons or "niggards" who stole and hid the celestial cows</note>—specifically the demon named **Vala** who seizes the cows. Alternatively, he is called **Pani** because he is the master of the Panis. He checked or obstructed that demon with strength and force. Furthermore, he stole the weapons (such as the thunderbolt) of the malevolent Vala, who was the "father" or guardian of his own wealth (the stolen cows). He also took away Vala's **illusions** <note>original: *māyāḥ*, the deceptive or magical powers of the demons</note>. O Indra, Soma performed all this through the strength of your friendship; therefore, who can possibly describe your greatness? Thus, this is a praise of Indra’s influence on Soma.

## Hymn Text

-> ॥ Now the Twenty-Third Verse ॥ <-

**He made the Dawns have a good husband; he placed the light within the Sun. This one, in three-fold form, found the hidden nectar in the heavens, in the shining realms, among the gathered gods. ॥ २३ ॥**

<note>Word-by-word breakdown (Padapatha):</note>
This | made | the Dawns | having a good husband | this | in the Sun | placed | light | within | 
this | three-fold | in heaven | in the shining [realms] | in the gathered [places] | found | nectar | hidden ॥ २३ ॥

## Commentary (Sayana)

This Soma made the **Dawns** <note>original: *uṣasaḥ*, the personified goddesses of daybreak</note> have a "good husband," meaning he made the Sun their protector and lord. This very Soma placed the light and brilliance within the orb of the Sun. This Soma—existing in three ways through the three ritual pressings <term>savana</term> <note>the morning, midday, and evening offerings</note>—found the **nectar** <note>original: *amṛtam*, the source of immortality</note> which was deeply hidden and invisible in the heavens, within the shining realms, and among the gods gathered in the third station. O Indra, it is through your help that Soma has performed these great deeds. This is a praise of Indra—

...is to be understood. This very Indra is referred to by the word "this." This Indra made the dawns to have "good lords" <note>original: *shobhanapatika*, likely meaning the sun or the gods who govern them</note>. He alone placed that light in the sun. In the heavens, among the shining gods existing in the three realms, this Indra alone found the nectar <note>original: *amṛtam*, the drink of immortality</note> which was hidden in three ways—manifested through the three daily libations—and covered within the ritual vessels. He obtained it.

-> ॥ Now the Twenty-Fourth Verse ॥ <-

## Hymn Text

**This one propped apart Heaven and Earth; this one yoked the seven-rayed chariot. This Soma, by his wisdom, held the "cooked" milk within the cows, like a fountain with a ten-fold mechanism. ॥ २४ ॥**

**This | Heaven and Earth | apart | propped | this | chariot | yoked | seven-rayed |**
**this | in the cows | by wisdom | the "cooked" | within | Soma | held | ten-fold mechanism | fountain ॥ २४ ॥**

---

## Commentary (Sayana)

This **Soma** <note>or Indra, as the commentary explores both identities</note> **propped apart Heaven and Earth**; he established them firmly in their various places. Furthermore, this Soma **yoked the seven-rayed chariot** of the Sun—the chariot endowed with seven rays or horses, and possessing seven wheels. Likewise, this Soma, through **wisdom** <note>original: *shachya*, referring to his conscious power or intention</note>, **held the "cooked"** or ripened milk produced **within the cows**. He holds this milk which is like a **fountain** <note>original: *utsam*, a source that flows upward</note>—this "fountain" is described as having a **ten-fold mechanism**. This means it is equipped with ten means or "engines" such as the eyes, ears, and other senses that cause the life-force to emerge. This term is explained by another verse from the supplementary texts:

> The eye, the ear, the mind, the speech, the exhaling and inhaling breaths, the body, this physical frame, and the two downward-voiding breaths—these I consider the "fountain with the ten-fold mechanism."

Alternatively, the verse may refer to Indra: This Indra propped apart Heaven and Earth, making them stay in their respective places. He alone yoked the seven-rayed chariot of the sun. He alone, through his own ritual action, holds the "cooked" milk within the cows. For the sake of such an Indra, Soma **held** or contained the flowing juice in a **fountain** that is **yoked by ten**, meaning it is governed by the ten ritual cups <note>original: *graha*</note> dedicated to deities like Indra and Vayu. In the morning libation <note>original: *pratahsavana*</note>, ten such cups are taken. As the Brahmanas <note>Sacred prose explanations of the rituals</note> state:

> Nine cups are taken in the morning; they praise with nine during the *Bahishpavamana* chant; when the chant is finished, they take the tenth cup. <note>Aitareya Brahmana 3.1</note>

Elsewhere it is traditionally taught:

> The Adhvaryu priest takes these ten great cups during the morning libation.

The adjective "ten-fold mechanism" is used with this ritual context in mind.

The first verse is in the *Atinicrit* meter. It is called *Atinicrit* because it consists of three lines of seven syllables and a middle line of six...

# 750 || Rig Veda || Book 4, Lesson 7, Group 21 <note>These numbers refer to the internal structural divisions of the manuscript: Adhyaya, Anuvaka, and Varga.</note>

## Commentary of Sayana
Based on the defining characteristics, the thirty-third verse is in the **Anushtubh** meter, while the remaining verses are in the **Gayatri** meter. In the final triplet (the last three verses), specifically the verse beginning "Brbu among the Panis," a carpenter named **Brbu** is praised. Therefore, that triplet is dedicated to him as the deity. The remaining thirty verses are dedicated to **Indra**. 

This is confirmed by the Index of Hymns: "The one who brought... thirty-three verses... the others are in Gayatri, the last is Anushtubh; in the final triplet, Brbu the carpenter is the deity." In the **Mahavrata** rite <note>A major Vedic ritual performed during the winter solstice</note>, specifically during the **Nishkevalya** litany, this entire hymn is used except for the final triplet. As the **Fifth Aranyaka** states: "He removes the three final verses of 'The one who brought from a distance'" <note>original Sanskrit: *Ai. Aa. 5.1.1*, referring to the Aitareya Aranyaka</note>.

---

## Hymn Text
->|| Here is the First Verse ||<-

**The one who brought Turvasha and Yadu from a distance with good guidance—that Indra is our young friend. ॥ १ ॥**

**The one | brought | from a distance | with good guidance | Turvasha | Yadu | Indra | that | our | young | friend ॥ १ ॥**

---

## Commentary of Sayana
That Indra brought **Turvasha and Yadu**—two kings of those names who had been cast away into a distant land by their enemies—back from that distant land with **good guidance** <note>original: *suniti*, meaning excellent leadership or a safe path</note>. May that **young** or ever-youthful Indra be **our friend**.

---

## Hymn Text
->|| Now the Second Verse ||<-

**Bestowing strength even upon the non-singer with a swift horse, Indra is the winner of the deposited wealth. ॥ २ ॥**

**On the non-singer | even | strength | bestowing | with a swift | even | horse | Indra | winner | deposited | wealth ॥ २ ॥**

---

## Commentary of Sayana
**Even upon the non-singer**: A "singer" (*vipra*) is a wise priest or praiser. Indra bestows **strength** <note>original: *vayah*, which can refer to food or vital energy</note> even upon a man who is the opposite of that (one who does not offer songs). If he does this for the non-singer, it goes without saying that he provides for his praisers. That Indra, with an **even swift horse**—one that moves as fast as a blink—is the **winner** or habitual conqueror of **wealth** that has been **deposited** or hidden away among enemies. <note>The commentator notes a grammatical rule: the suffix *-trn* on the word for "winner" (jeta) denotes a habitual or natural quality.</note>

---

## Hymn Text
->|| Now the Third Verse ||<-

**Great are his leadings, and his praises are many; his protections never diminish. ॥ ३ ॥**

**Great | his | leadings | many | and | praises | not | his | diminish | protections ॥ ३ ॥**

---

## Commentary of Sayana
The **leadings** of this Indra—his excellent ways of guiding or bringing us to our goals—are **great** and mighty. Furthermore, the **praises** or hymns performed by the singers are **many**. Likewise, the **protections** or aids of this Indra **never diminish**; they never fail or decrease, but rather they are always increasing.

---

## Hymn Text
->|| Now the Fourth Verse ||<-

**O friends, sing and chant to the one who is carried by prayer; for he is our great wisdom. ॥ ४ ॥**

**Friends | to the one carried by prayer | sing | forth | and | chant | he | for | our | wisdom | great ॥ ४ ॥**

<note>The following technical vocabulary is provided at the bottom of the page for reference:</note>
**Indra**: The primary deity of the hymn.
**Brbu**: A carpenter and patron praised in the final triplet of the hymn.
**Turvasha & Yadu**: Names of kings or tribes rescued by Indra.
**Suniti**: Good guidance or leadership.
**Pranitayah**: Guidance or ways of bringing/leading.
**Brahmavahase**: One to whom prayers are offered (literally "carried by prayer").
**Paravatah**: From a distant place.

# 751 || Rig Veda || Book 6, Lesson 4, Hymn 45. || The Fourth Octad || 751

## Commentary (Sayana)
<note>This paragraph completes the commentary for verse 4 from the previous page.</note>
O friends, you praisers <term>stotāraḥ</term> who are of equal fame: worship Indra, who is **carried by prayers** <note>original: *brahmavāhase*; one who is reached or conveyed by sacred mantras</note>. Recite the sacrificial litanies and sing the songs of praise. For he, indeed, is our great **foresight** <note>original: *pramatiḥ*; literally "excellent mind"</note>, meaning he is the giver of such superior intellect to us.

---

## Hymn Text
->॥ Here is the Fifth Verse ॥<-

**You alone, O Slayer of Vrtra, are the protector of one or of two; and even of such as we are. ॥ ५ ॥**

**Padapatha:**
You | one | O Slayer of Vrtra | protector | of two | are | and | of such | as | we ॥ ५ ॥

## Commentary (Sayana)
O **Slayer of Vrtra** <note>original: *vṛtrahan*; an epithet of Indra as the destroyer of the demon Vrtra or, more broadly, a "destroyer of enemies"</note>, O Indra! You are the protector and defender of a single worshiper or of two worshipers. This means you are the guardian of all who praise you. Moreover, you are the protector even of such people as we are—those who, being protected by you, have become possessed of many sons and grandsons. The sense is that you alone, and no other, are the guardian of such people.

---
->॥ This concludes the twenty-first group of the seventh lesson of the fourth book ॥<-
---

## Hymn Text
->॥ Here is the Sixth Verse ॥<-

**You lead us truly beyond our enemies; you make us reciters of hymns. You are called "rich in heroes" by men. ॥ ६ ॥**

**Padapatha:**
You lead | truly | [filler particle] | beyond | enemies | you make | reciters of hymns | by men | rich in heroes | you are called ॥ ६ ॥

## Commentary (Sayana)
O Indra, you alone lead us across and beyond our **enemies** <note>original: *dviṣaḥ*; those who beset or hate us</note>. You rescue us. The word "u" in the text is a functional filler. Furthermore, you make us **reciters of hymns** <note>original: *uktha-śaṃsinaḥ*; those who chant the sacrificial portions called Ukthas</note>, meaning you make us prosperous. Because you are praised by the men who lead the songs as being **rich in heroes** <note>original: *su-vīraḥ*; literally "possessing good heroes," referring here to the gift of brave sons and grandsons given to the worshipers</note>, please grant those same blessings to us.

---

## Hymn Text
->॥ Here is the Seventh Verse ॥<-

**The expansive one, the one carried by prayers, our friend, the one worthy of praise—I call him with songs as if for the milking of a cow. ॥ ७ ॥**

**Padapatha:**
The expansive | carried by prayers | with songs | the friend | worthy of praise | a cow | like | for milking | I call ॥ ७ ॥

## Commentary (Sayana)
I call upon the **expansive one** <note>original: *brahmāṇam*; the great or vast one</note>, the one who is **carried by prayers** <note>original: *brahmavāhasam*; borne by mantras in the form of praise</note>, our friend, and the one **worthy of praise** <note>original: *ṛgmiyam*; one who deserves the Rg-verses</note>. I call this friend with songs of praise for the purpose of **milking** <note>original: *dohase*; to draw out or fulfill</note>, just as one calls a cow to be milked. I invoke him to milk—that is, to fulfill—all our desires.

<summary>This page contains verses 5-7 of Rig Veda 6.45, where Indra is invoked as a personal protector of his worshipers and a source of prosperity, described through the metaphor of a cow providing milk.</summary>
<keywords>Indra, Slayer of Vrtra, Sayana, Vedic hymns, protection, offspring, prayer as a cow, sacrificial liturgy</keywords>

# 752 || Rig Veda || Book 4, Lesson 7, Group 23. || 752

## Hymn Text

-> ॥ Here is the Eighth Verse ॥ <-

**In whose two hands all riches are doubly placed—the riches of the Hero, the overcomer of armies. ॥ ८ ॥**

**Word-by-word Analysis:**
In whose | all | in the two hands | were placed | riches | down | in two ways | of the hero | of the overcomer of armies ॥ ८ ॥

---

## Commentary (Sayana)

Of the **hero** <term>vīrasya</term>, the powerful one, the **overcomer of armies** <term>pṛtanāsahaḥ</term>. The word *pṛtanāḥ* refers to the armies of the enemy. The sages "speak forth" <note>original: *nyucuḥ*; literally "they say down" or "declare"</note> that in the **two hands**—the arms of this Indra—all **riches** <term>vasūni</term> are situated **doubly** <note>original: *dvitā*; in two forms, namely divine and earthly</note>. The connection to the previous verses remains: we "invoke" that Indra.

---

## Hymn Text

-> ॥ Here is the Ninth Verse ॥ <-

**Shatter even the firm strongholds of the people, O Wielder of the thunderbolt, Lord of might; tear out the illusions, O you who never yield. ॥ ९ ॥**

**Word-by-word Analysis:**
Shatter | the firm [things] | even | O Wielder of the stone | of the people | O Lord of might | tear out | the illusions | O you who never yield ॥ ९ ॥

---

## Commentary (Sayana)

O **Wielder of the thunderbolt** <term>adrivaḥ</term>—the *adri* is the bolt <term>vajra</term> because one strikes with it—O Indra, **Lord of might** <term>śacīpate</term>, **shatter** <note>original: *vivṛha*; literally "uproot" or "break apart"</note> the **firm** and stable strongholds or forces **of the people** (the enemies). O **you who never yield** <note>original: *anānuta*; meaning one who is never humbled, the most exalted Indra</note>, **tear out** and destroy the **illusions** <term>māyāḥ</term> or deceptive powers created by the enemies.

---

## Hymn Text

-> ॥ Here is the Tenth Verse ॥ <-

**Indeed, we call upon you, O Truthful one, Drinker of Soma, O Indra, Lord of booty, we who are desiring food. ॥ १० ॥**

**Word-by-word Analysis:**
Him | indeed | you | O Truthful one | O Drinker of Soma | O Indra | of booty | O Lord | we call | desiring food ॥ १० ॥

---

## Commentary (Sayana)

O **Truthful one** <term>satya</term>, you whose nature is unfailing; O **Drinker of Soma** <term>somapāḥ</term>; O **Lord of booty** <term>vājānāṃ pate</term>, the protector of sustenance; O **Indra**, we, **desiring food** <term>śravasyavaḥ</term> (wishing for food/sustenance for ourselves), **call upon** <note>original: *ahūmahi*; we invoke or praise</note> **you indeed**, a lord of such qualities.

-> ॥ This concludes the twenty-second group of the seventh lesson of the fourth book ॥ <-

---

## Hymn Text

-> ॥ Here is the Eleventh Verse ॥ <-

**You are the one who was invoked in the past, or who is now invoked when wealth is at stake; O you who are worthy of being called, hear our call. ॥ ११ ॥**

**Word-by-word Analysis:**
Him | indeed | you | who | in the past | were | who | or | now | placed | wealth | worthy of being called | he | hear | the call ॥ ११ ॥

---

## Commentary (Sayana)

O **Indra**, it is **you indeed** whom we praise (this last part is understood). You **who in the past**, in ancient times, were **worthy of being called**... <note>The commentary ends mid-sentence on this page.</note>

<note>The following text completes the commentary for verse 11 from the previous page.</note>

...you have become one to be invoked for the sake of obtaining wealth. Or, when wealth has been placed—that is, stationed—among enemies, you have truly become, even today, one to be called upon. You, therefore, hear our **invocation** <note>original: *havam*; a call or prayer</note>, our hymn of praise. Hear it.

-> ॥ Here is the Twelfth Verse ॥ <-

## Hymn Text
**With our prayers and with your swift horses, may we, possessing horses, [win] glorious riches, O Indra. Through you, may we conquer the deposited wealth. ॥ १२ ॥**

**Word-by-word Analysis:**
By prayers | By horses | [Having] horses | Riches/Food | Indra | Glorious/Praiseworthy | By you | May we conquer | Deposited | Wealth ॥ १२ ॥

## Commentary (Sayana)
O Indra, by **prayers** <term>dhībhiḥ</term>—meaning by hymns of praise directed toward you—we, being favored by you, [conquer] the **horses** <term>arvataḥ</term> belonging to the enemy by using your own **horses** <term>arvadbhiḥ</term>. May we win **riches** <term>vājān</term>—meaning food or wealth—that are **glorious** <term>śravāyyān</term> (praiseworthy), and the **wealth** <term>dhanam</term> that has been **deposited** <term>hitam</term> (placed) among the enemies. Through your grace, may we be victorious.

---

-> ॥ Here is the Thirteenth Verse ॥ <-

## Hymn Text
**You became, O Hero, lover of praise, the Great One, O Indra, when wealth was at stake; in the battle, you were the conqueror. ॥ १३ ॥**

**Word-by-word Analysis:**
You became | Indeed | Hero | Lover of praise | Great | Indra | In wealth | Placed/At stake | In battle | Winner/Conqueror ॥ १३ ॥

## Commentary (Sayana)
O **Hero** <term>vīra</term>, the one who drives away enemies in various ways, O **Lover of praise** <term>girvaṇaḥ</term> (Indra, who is won over by songs), when **wealth** <term>dhane</term> **deposited** <term>hite</term> among enemies was the cause of conflict, you became the **Great One** <note>original: *mahān*; magnified or increased in power</note>. In the **battle** <term>bhare</term>, you became the **conqueror** <term>vitanatamsayyaḥ</term> of the enemies. <note>The teacher explains a technical point here: the root *tamas* is used here in the sense of "to conquer," and the word is formed with a specific grammatical suffix denoting the "doer" of the action.</note>

---

-> ॥ Here is the Fourteenth Verse ॥ <-

## Hymn Text
**Whatever speed of yours, O slayer of enemies, is most swift, with that [speed], impel our chariot. ॥ १४ ॥**

**Word-by-word Analysis:**
Which | Your | Speed | Slayer of enemies | Most swift | Is | With that | Our | Impel/Speed | Chariot ॥ १४ ॥

## Commentary (Sayana)
O **Slayer of enemies** <term>amitrahant</term>, the killer of those who are not friends, O Indra, whatever **speed** <term>jūtiḥ</term> (movement) of yours is **most swift** <term>makṣujavastamā</term> (exceedingly fast), with that movement, **impel** <term>hinvahi</term>—that is, drive or inspire—our **chariot** <term>ratham</term>. Make it move quickly for the sake of conquering the enemy.

O victorious Indra, you who are the most excellent charioteer and a great warrior: with our chariot—which is the attacker and Vanquisher of enemies—conquer the **wealth** <note>original: *dhanaṃ*; riches or booty</note> that has been deposited among the enemy. Be victorious for our sake.

## Hymn Text
**Praise him alone, who is the unique overseer of the people; he was born as the Lord, the one of powerful deeds. ॥ १६ ॥**

# 755 || Rig Veda || Book 6, Hymn 45 || 755

<note>The following text completes the commentary for verse 19 from the previous page.</note>

...who is like a friend, the **inciter of the singers** <note>original: *kīricodanam*</note>, meaning the stimulator of those who praise him; the **most excellent carrier of prayers** <note>original: *brahmavāhastamam*</note>, meaning one who is to be reached or carried by sacred mantras in an exceeding manner—that kind of Indra, I **invoke** <note>original: *huve*</note>; I call upon him.

---

## Hymn Text

-> ॥ Here is the Twentieth Verse ॥ <-
**He indeed alone masters all earthly riches; he is the most delighted by songs of praise and is unrestrained in his path. ॥ २० ॥**

**Word-by-word Analysis:**
He | Indeed | All | Earthly | Alone | Riches | Masters | Most delighted by songs | Unrestrained ॥ २० ॥

## Commentary (Sayana)
He indeed, that Indra, **alone masters** <term>eka eva patyate</term>—meaning he rules over and no one else—**all** the **earthly riches** <term>viśvāni pārthivā vasūni</term>, which are the types of wealth found upon the earth. The word "masters" <note>original: *patyati*</note> denotes the action of lordship or sovereignty. What kind of Indra is he? He is **most delighted by songs** <term>girvaṇastamaḥ</term>, meaning he is to be worshipped or enjoyed exceedingly through songs of praise; and he is **unrestrained** <term>adriguḥ</term> <note>original: *dhṛtagamanaḥ*</note>, meaning his movement is steady and his progress is unimpeded.

-> ॥ This ends the twenty-fourth section (varga) of the seventh chapter of the fourth [Ashtaka] ॥ <-

---

## Hymn Text

-> ॥ Here is the Twenty-First Verse ॥ <-
**O Lord of cows, fulfill our desire boldly with teams of steeds, with wealth of cattle, with horses, and with food. ॥ २१ ॥**

**Word-by-word Analysis:**
He | Our | With teams of steeds | [Particle of completion] | Fulfill | Desire | With foods | With horses | With cattle | O Lord of cows | Boldly ॥ २१ ॥

## Commentary (Sayana)
O **Lord of cows** <term>gopate</term> (protector of cattle), may **you** **fulfill** <term>ā pṛṇa</term>—meaning satisfy or fill up—**our desire** with **teams of steeds** <term>niyudbhiḥ</term> (specifically female horses) in a **bold** <term>dhṛṣat</term> manner, such that it is capable of destroying our poverty. Alternatively, the word "boldly" is an adjective for you; meaning you are the subduer of enemies. Likewise, fulfill our desire with **foods** <term>vājebhiḥ</term> accompanied by many **horses** <term>aśvibhiḥ</term> and many **cattle** <term>gomadbhiḥ</term>.

---

## Hymn Text

-> ॥ Here is the Twenty-Second Verse ॥ <-
**Sing that praise together for the much-invoked warrior when the Soma is pressed; it is as pleasant to the powerful one as fodder is to a cow. ॥ २२ ॥**

**Word-by-word Analysis:**
That | For you (all) | Sing | When pressed | Together | For the much-invoked | For the warrior | Pleasant | Which | For a cow | As/Like | For the powerful one ॥ २२ ॥

## Commentary (Sayana)
O praisers, **you** all, when the Soma has been **pressed** <term>sute</term>, come **together** <term>sacā</term> and **sing** <term>gāya</term>—meaning chant—**that** hymn to Indra, who is **much-invoked** <term>puruhūtāya</term> (called by many worshippers) and who is a **warrior** <term>satvane</term>, meaning either the subduer of enemies or the bestower of wealth. Sing that hymn which is **pleasant** <term>śam</term> (comforting or beneficial) to the **powerful** <term>śākine</term> Indra, **as** if **for a cow**. The meaning is: just as fresh grass is pleasing to a cow, so is this hymn pleasing to the mighty Indra.

The text uses the metaphor of cattle and fodder to describe the mutually nourishing relationship between the deity and the songs of the priests.</summary>

# 756 || Rig Veda || Book 6, Hymn 45 || 756

## Hymn Text

-> ॥ Here is the Twenty-third Verse ॥ <-

**The Wealthy One indeed does not withhold the gift of food consisting of cattle, if he should hear our prayers. ॥ २३ ॥**

**Word-by-word Analysis:**
Not | Indeed | The Wealthy One | Down | Withhold | Gift | Of food | Consisting of cattle | If | These | Hear | Prayers ॥ २३ ॥

---

## Commentary (Sayana)

The **Wealthy One** <term>vasuḥ</term>—meaning the one who causes others to dwell, Indra—does **not indeed** <note>original: *na gha*</note> **withhold** <term>ni yamate</term> or stop the **gift** <term>dānam</term> of **food** or **strength** <term>vājasya</term> that is **consisting of many cattle** <term>gomataḥ</term>. **If** <term>yat</term> he **hears** <term>upa śravat</term> **these** <term>sīm</term> **prayers** <term>giraḥ</term> or songs of praise of ours. The meaning is that whenever there is a song of praise, he always bestows gifts.

---

## Hymn Text

-> ॥ Here is the Twenty-fourth Verse ॥ <-

**Surely, the Slayer of Dasyus will go to the cattle-pen of Kuvitsa; by his mighty deeds, he will reveal the cows for us. ॥ २४ ॥**

**Word-by-word Analysis:**
Surely | Of Kuvitsa | Forth | Indeed | Cattle-pen | Consisting of cattle | Slayer of Dasyus | Will go | By mighty deeds | Open/Reveal | For us | Covered ॥ २४ ॥

---

## Commentary (Sayana)

**Of Kuvitsa** <note>original: *kuvitsasya*</note>: "Kuvit" means many or frequently, and "sa" means to destroy or hurt; thus, Kuvitsa is the name of a certain individual who causes much harm. Indra, the **Slayer of Dasyus** <term>dasyuhā</term>—referring to the killer of those who consume or destroy—**will go forth** <term>pra gamat</term> to that **cattle-pen** <term>vrajam</term> belonging to him which is **full of many cows** <term>gomantam</term>. Because <note>original: *hi*</note> this is so, therefore by his own **mighty deeds** or **powers of wisdom** <term>śacībhiḥ</term>, he **uncovered** <term>apa varat</term> or revealed those cows that were hidden away for our sake.

---

## Hymn Text

-> ॥ Here is the Twenty-fifth Verse ॥ <-

**O Lord of a Hundred Powers, these prayers of ours reach out to you, just as mother cows reach for their calf. ॥ २५ ॥**

**Word-by-word Analysis:**
These | Indeed | You | O Lord of a Hundred Powers | Towards | Forth | Reach out | Prayers | Indra | Calf | Like | Mothers ॥ २५ ॥

---

## Commentary (Sayana)

O **Lord of a Hundred Powers** <term>śatakrato</term>—meaning you of many-fold actions or many-fold wisdom—O Indra, **these** <term>imāḥ</term> **prayers** <term>giraḥ</term> or praises of ours **reach out** <term>pra nonuvuḥ</term> to you; they go toward you repeatedly. The root here denotes the act of moving. An illustration is provided: **Like mother cows to their calf** <term>vatsam na mātaraḥ</term>. Just as **mother** cows <term>mātaraḥ</term> quickly approach their **calf** <term>vatsam</term> waiting at home, so do these prayers approach you. Alternatively, our voices **resound** <term>abhi nonuvuḥ</term> around you; they praise you. Just as cows make a lowing sound <note>the "hambha" sound</note> when looking toward their calf, so do these songs cry out to you.

-> ॥ This ends the twenty-fifth section (varga) of the seventh chapter of the fourth [Ashtaka] ॥ <-

<summary>This page concludes a section of Hymn 45, focusing on Indra's willingness to reward his worshippers with cattle and food when he hears their prayers. It describes Indra as a "Slayer of Dasyus" who recovers stolen or hidden livestock and highlights the affectionate, natural connection between the worshipper's prayer and the deity.</summary>

<keywords>Indra, cattle, Dasyu, Shatakratu, prayers, mother and calf analogy, Sayana, Rig Veda commentary</keywords>

# 759 || Book 6, Chapter 4, Hymn 45 || 759

## Hymn Text

->॥ Here is the Twenty-sixth Verse ॥<-

**Your friendship, O Hero, is indestructible for the one who desires cattle; you are as a cow to him. For the one who desires a horse, become a horse. ॥ २६ ॥**

**दुः॒ऽनशं॑ । स॒ख्यं । तव॑ । गौः । अ॒सि॒ । वी॒र॒ । गव्य॑ते । अश्वः॑ । अ॒श्व॒ऽय॒ते । भ॒व॒ ॥ २६ ॥**
**Word-by-word Analysis:** Indestructible | friendship | your | cow | you are | O Hero | for the one desiring cows | horse | for the one desiring horses | be.

---

->॥ Here is the Twenty-seventh Verse ॥<-

**So delight yourself with the juice <note>Soma</note> for the sake of great wealth with your mighty body; do not subject the singer of your praises to the slanderer. ॥ २७ ॥**

**सः । मं॒द॒स्व॒ । हि । अंध॑सः । राध॑से । त॒न्वा॑ । म॒हे । न । स्तो॒तारं॑ । नि॒दे । कः॒ ॥ २७ ॥**
**Word-by-word Analysis:** He [You] | delight | indeed | with the juice | for wealth | with the body | for the great [wealth] | not | the singer | to the slanderer | make.

---

->॥ Here is the Twenty-eighth Verse ॥<-

**These songs of ours, O lover of hymns, reach you at every pressing of the juice, just as milch-cows reach their calf. ॥ २८ ॥**

**इ॒माः । ऊं॒ इति॑ । त्वा॒ । सु॒तेऽसु॑ते । नक्षंते । गि॒र्व॒णः॒ । गिरः॑ । व॒त्सं । गावः॑ । न । धे॒नवः॑ ॥ २८ ॥**
**Word-by-word Analysis:** These | [emphasis] | you | at every pressing | reach | O lover of hymns | songs | calf | cows | like | milch-cows.

---

->॥ Here is the Twenty-ninth Verse ॥<-

**[May the praise] of many singers reach you, the greatest subduer of many enemies, in the assembly of speech, [from those] making you strong with offerings of food. ॥ २९ ॥**

**पु॒हु॒ऽत॒मं । पु॒रू॒णां । स्तो॒तॄणां॑ । वि॒ऽवाचि॑ । वाजे॑भिः । वा॒ज॒ऽय॒तां ॥ २९ ॥**
**Word-by-word Analysis:** The greatest subduer | of many | of singers | in the assembly of speech | with strengths/offerings | making him strong.

---

## Commentary (Sayana)

**26.** O Indra, **your friendship** <term>sakhyam</term> is **indestructible** <note>original: *dūṇāśam* or *durṇāśam*</note>, meaning it is impossible to destroy; it is exceedingly firm. Therefore, O **Hero** <term>vīra</term>—meaning the one who displays power, Indra—**you are a cow** <term>gaurasi</term> to the one who **desires cattle for himself** <term>gavyate</term>. That is, you become the giver of cows. This is a figure of speech where the cause (the giver) is called by the name of the effect (the gift). Similarly, **become a horse** <term>aśvo bhava</term> for the one who **desires horses for himself** <term>aśvayate</term>. You are the bestower of horses.

**27.** O Indra, being such as you are, **delight yourself** <term>mandasva</term> or be joyful with your own **body** <term>tanvā</term> through the drinking of the **Soma juice** <term>andhasaḥ</term>. For what purpose? **For the sake of great wealth** <term>mahe rādhase</term>. The word "indeed" <note>original: *hi*</note> is a filler here. Furthermore, do **not subject** <term>na kaḥ</term>—meaning do not place—your **singer** <term>stotāram</term> under the control of a **slanderer** <term>nide</term> or a blamer.

**28.** O **lover of hymns** <term>girvaṇaḥ</term>—meaning Indra, who is to be addressed by songs of praise—when the **Soma is pressed again and again** <term>sute sute</term>, **these** <term>imāḥ</term> **songs** <term>giraḥ</term> or praises of ours **reach** <term>nakṣante</term> or pervade you. Just as **milch-cows** <term>dhenavaḥ</term> or cows that give milk **reach their calf** <term>vatsam gāvo na</term> with speed, so do our praises reach you.

**29.** O Indra, let the praise of us **many singers** <term>purūṇām stotṝṇām</term> reach you, who are the **greatest subduer** <term>purutamam</term> or the one who causes many enemies to faint or grow weary. The phrase "let it reach" is supplied to complete the sense. Of what kind of singers? Those in the **assembly of speech** <term>vivāci</term>—referring to the sacrifice where various voices consisting of hymns and recitations are heard—and those **making you strong** <term>vājayatām</term> or powerful with **offerings** <term>vājebhiḥ</term> characterized by sacrificial food <note>original: *havis*</note>.

</margin>

<summary>This page contains verses 26-29 of Hymn 45, where Indra is praised as a firm friend who provides cattle and horses to his devotees. The commentary by Sayana explains metaphors comparing Indra to the gifts he bestows and likens the devotee's prayers to cows rushing to their calf.</summary>
<keywords>Indra, Soma, friendship, cattle, horses, Sayana, Vedic sacrifice, hymns of praise</keywords>

# 758 || Book 6, Chapter 4, Hymn 45 || 758

->॥ Here is the Thirtieth Verse ॥<-

## Hymn Text
O Indra, may our hymn of praise be most effective in reaching you and be most intimate to you. Impel us toward great wealth. ॥ ३० ॥

**अ॒स्माक॑म् । इन्द्र॒ । भू॒तु॒ । ते॒ । स्तोमः॑ । वाहि॑ष्ठः । अन्त॑मः । अ॒स्मान् । रा॒ये । म॒हे । हि॒नु॒ ॥ ३० ॥**

**Word-by-word Analysis:** Our | O Indra | let it be | your | hymn | most effective [at reaching] | most intimate | us | for wealth | great | impel.

---

## Commentary (Sayana)
O Indra, may our **stoma**, our hymn of praise, be **vahishtha**, the best bearer or most effective at reaching you, and may it be **antama**, the closest to you. And you, **hinu**, impel or urge us toward **mahe raye**, great wealth.

---

->॥ Here is the Thirty-first Verse ॥<-

## Hymn Text
Bribu has stood at the highest summit of the Panis <note>the Panis were a group of wealthy, often stingy merchants or mountain-dwelling demons</note>, like a vast forest on the high banks of the Ganges. ॥ ३१ ॥

**अधि॑ । बृ॒बुः । प॒णीना॑म् । वषि॑ष्ठे । मू॒र्धन् । अस्था॑त् । उ॒रुः । कक्षो॒ न । गां॒ग्यः ॥ ३१ ॥**

**Word-by-word Analysis:** Above | Bribu | of the Panis | in the highest | head [summit] | has stood | vast | forest [shrubbery] | like | related to the Ganges.

---

## Commentary (Sayana)
**Bribu** is the name of a carpenter <note>original: "takṣā"</note> among the Panis. The sage Bharadwaja, having received wealth from him, praised his generosity with this triplet of verses. This act is remembered by Manu in the Law Books:
> "Bharadwaja, suffering from hunger with his son in a desolate forest, accepted many cows from Bribu, the carpenter of great fame." <note>original: "भरद्वाजः क्षुधार्त्तस्तु... म० १०. १०७"</note>

**Paninam** refers to the merchants of that name, or perhaps demons. Their carpenter, Bribu, **adhi asthat**, has stood upon the **varshishthe murdhan**, the highest head or a very elevated place. He is like a **gangyah kakshah**, a forest or thicket growing on the high banks of the Ganges, which is **uruh**, vast and extensive. The meaning is that although Bribu was of low birth <note>as a carpenter/Pani</note>, he became superior to all because of his great generosity.

---

->॥ Here is the Thirty-second Verse ॥<-

## Hymn Text
Whose auspicious gift, numbered in the thousands and moving swiftly like the wind, is bestowed immediately upon the one asking. ॥ ३२ ॥

**यस्य॑ । वा॒योःऽइ॑व । द्रु॒वत् । भ॒द्रा । रा॒तिः । स॒ह॒स्रिणी॑ । स॒द्यः । दा॒नाय॑ । मं॑हते ॥ ३२ ॥**

**Word-by-word Analysis:** Whose | wind-like | swiftly | auspicious | gift | consisting of thousands | immediately | for the sake of giving [to the seeker] | bestows.

---

## Commentary (Sayana)
**Vayoriva druvat**: Moving as swiftly as the wind, the **bhadra**, or auspicious, and **sahasrini**, thousand-fold, **ratih**, gift of Bribu, **manhate**, bestows the required wealth **sadyah**, immediately at the very time of praise, to me who is **danaya**, desiring a gift. This description of Bribu connects to the following verse.

---

->॥ Here is the Thirty-third Verse ॥<-

## Hymn Text
Therefore, all our noble poets always loudly praise Bribu, the best giver of thousands, the wise leader who wins thousands. ॥ ३३ ॥

**तत् । सु । नः॒ । वि॒श्वे॑ । अ॒र्यः । आ । सदा॑ । गृ॒ण॒न्ति॒ । का॒रवः॑ ।**
**बृ॒बुम् । स॒ह॒स्र॒ऽदा॒तम॑म् । सू॒रिम् । स॒ह॒स्र॒ऽसा॒तम॑म् ॥ ३३ ॥**

**Word-by-word Analysis:** Therefore | well | our | all | noble | [prefix] | always | praise | poets | Bribu | greatest giver of thousands | wise leader | greatest winner of thousands.

<summary>This page concludes Varga 26 of Mandala 6, moving from a prayer to Indra for wealth to the specific praise of Bribu, a historical or legendary donor who broke social norms through his immense generosity to the sage Bharadwaja.</summary>

<meta>This page concludes the commentary on the previous section regarding the generous donor Bribu and introduces Hymn 46 of the sixth book. # 759 || Book 6, Chapter 4, Hymn 46 || 759

## Commentary (Sayana)
[Continuation from the previous page regarding the donor Bribu]

All our singers <note>original: "kāravaḥ"</note>, who are the initiators of praises, laud that Bribu well. They praise him completely. What kind of man is he? He is one who gives wealth in the thousands most excessively <note>original: "sahasradātamam"</note>; he is the wise one <note>original: "sūrim"</note>, or rather the impeller; he is the most excellent possessor of thousands of hymns or wealth.

->॥ This ends the twenty-sixth varga in the seventh lesson of the fourth book. ॥<-

**You indeed [we call]** <note>original: "tvām id dhi"</note>: This third hymn, consisting of fourteen verses, is revealed to Shamyu, the son of Brihaspati <note>original: "Bārhaspatya"</note>. Its deity is Indra. The odd-numbered verses (first, third, etc.) are in the **Brihati** meter, while the even-numbered verses (second, fourth, etc.) are in the **Satobrihati** meter. This alternating pattern is known as a **Pragatha**. Thus, the Index <note>original: "Anukramani"</note> states: "The hymn beginning *tvām id dhi* consists of fourteen verses and is a Pragatha." 

The ritual application of the hymn is determined by its characteristic marks. If the **Jyotishtoma** sacrifice <note>a foundational seven-day Soma ritual</note> follows the **Brihat-Prishtha** chant, then the first Pragatha is to be used for the **Nishkevalya** shastra <note>a specific recitation for Indra at the midday pressing</note>. This is indicated in the ritual manuals: "If it is indeed the Brihat, we call upon you (*tvām id dhi havāmahe*)" <note>original: "Ashvalayana Shrauta Sutra 5.15"</note>. Even in the **Mahavrata** rite <note>a "Great Vow" ritual involving music and dance</note>, this Pragatha is to be recited during the Nishkevalya. The **Fifth Aranyaka** <note>Aitareya Aranyaka 5.1</note> similarly indicates: "The verses *tvām id dhi havāmahe* and *tvam hyehi cherave* are the corresponding strophes for the Brihat chant."

---

## Hymn Text

->॥ Here is the First Verse ॥<-

**You indeed we call upon, O singers, for the acquisition of strength [wealth].**
**You, O Indra, lord of the virtuous, men call upon in the midst of enemies; you they call in the race-courses of the horse.** ॥ १ ॥

**त्वाम् । इत् । हि । हवा॑महे । सा॒ता । वाज॑स्य । का॒रव॑: ।**
**त्वां । वृ॒त्रऽसु । इन्द्र॑ । सत्ऽप॑तिं । नर॑: । त्वां । काष्ठा॑सु । अर्व॑तः ॥ १ ॥**

---

## Commentary (Sayana)

**Singers** <note>original: "kāravaḥ"</note>: We who are the praisers, when there is an occasion for the **acquisition** <note>original: "sātā"</note> or the enjoyment of **strength** <note>original: "vājasya"</note>—meaning food or wealth—**call upon you indeed**, O **Indra**. We summon you with our songs of praise. 

O Indra, you are the **Lord of the Virtuous** <note>original: "Satpatim"</note>, the supreme protector of the good. Other **men** <note>original: "naraḥ"</note> also **call upon** you when **enemies** <note>original: "vṛtreṣu"</note>—those who obstruct or cover—are present, in order to conquer them. Furthermore, in the **courses** <note>original: "kāṣṭhāsu"</note> or battlefields belonging to the **horse** <note>original: "arvataḥ"</note>, where the horse gallops and stands, those desiring victory in war call only upon you. Therefore, the meaning is that we, too, call only upon you.

---

## Hymn Text

->॥ Here is the Second Verse ॥<-

**O wonderful one, wielder of the thunderbolt, being praised by us as great, O bold one, O possessor of the pressing stones,**
**bestow upon us cattle, horses, and chariots, O Indra, like wealth for a winner.** ॥ २ ॥

**स । त्वम् । नः॒ । चि॒त्र॒ । व॒ज्र॒ऽह॒स्त॒ । धृ॒ष्णु॒या । महः॑ । स्त॒वा॒नः । अद्रि॑ऽवः ।**
**गाम् । अश््व॑म् । र॒थ्य॑म् । इन्द्र॑ । सम् । कि॒र॒ । स॒चा । वाज॑म् । न । जि॒ग्युषे॑ ॥ २ ॥**

<vocab>
- कारवः (kāravaḥ): singers, poets, or makers of praise
- साता (sātā): in the obtaining, gaining, or distribution
- वाजस्य (vājasya): of food, strength, prize, or booty
- सत्पतिं (satpatiṃ): lord of the good, protector of the true/virtuous
- वृत्रेषु (vṛtreṣu): among enemies, among those who obstruct (often refers to the demon Vritra or his followers)
- काष्ठासु (kāṣṭhāsu): in the race-courses, goals, or boundaries of battle
- अर्वतः (arvataḥ): of the horse or the swift steed
- वज्रहस्त (vajrahasta): holding the thunderbolt (the Vajra) in hand
- सं किर (saṃ kira): pour out, bestow, scatter (as in a shower of gifts)
</vocab>

<summary>This page concludes the praise of the donor Bribu and introduces Hymn 46, a prayer to Indra for wealth and victory. Sayana explains that Indra is invoked by singers for food and by warriors in battle or horse races.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the commentary on the first hymn of the eighth book (Mandala 8) of the Rig Veda. The previous page discussed the initial calls to Indra and the generous nature of the deity. Here, Sayanacharya explains the concluding portion of the second verse and moves into the third and fourth verses, which form part of a specialized poetic couplet called a Pragatha.</meta>

# 760 || Rig Veda || Book 6, Chapter 1, Varga 27

## Hymn Text

He; You; to us; Wonderful one; **Thunderbolt-handed**; with boldness; Great; being praised; **Lord of the bolt**;
Cattle; related to horses; related to chariots; O Indra; together; bestow; alongside; **strength**; as if; for the victor. ॥ 2 ॥

---

## Commentary (Sayana)

O **Wonderful one** <note>original: "citra"</note>, meaning one who is worthy of being looked upon; O **Thunderbolt-handed** <note>original: "vajrahasta"</note>, one who holds the thunderbolt in his arm; O **Lord of the bolt** <note>original: "adrivo"</note>, possessor of the <term>Vajra (the lightning-bolt weapon of Indra)</term>. Alternatively, the word *Adri* refers to the lightning-bolt because it "tears asunder" <note>original: "adrivasya-attane"</note>; thus, "one who possesses that." Being such a one, through **boldness** <note>original: "dhṛṣṇuyā"</note>, meaning you are the over-whelmer of enemies; O **Great** one, such as you are, **being praised** <note>original: "stavāno"</note> by us, **bestow** <note>original: "saṃkira"</note> or give completely **cattle**, **chariot-mounts**, and **horses**. Just as you provide **strength** <note>original: "vājaṃ na"</note> or abundant food to a **victor** <note>original: "jigyuṣe"</note> for his enjoyment, so too bestow these upon us **alongside** <note>original: "sacā"</note> great abundance.

In the **Mahavrata** <note>a major sacrificial rite performed at the end of the year</note>, specifically during the **Nishkevalya** <note>a recitation dedicated solely to Indra at the midday pressing</note>, the remainder of this hymn beginning with "He who is the slayer..." <note>original: "yaḥ sacāhā"</note> is to be recited. This is indicated in the ritual texts: **"The remainder, 'He who is the all-seeing slayer,' is used in the hymn 'Let this be yours, O desired one.'"** <note>Aitareya Aranyaka 5. 10</note>. Furthermore, on the twenty-fourth day of the Soma sacrifice, during the midday pressing, the couplet <note>original: "pragātha"</note> beginning with "He who is the slayer" is an optional "corresponding" verse. This is noted: **"He who is the slayer, the all-seeing, from the sweet... until the solstice."** <note>Ashvalayana Shrauta Sutra 7. 4</note>.

---

-> ॥ The first verse of the couplet; the third in the hymn ॥ <-

He who is the **Slayer** together, the **All-seeing**, that **Indra** we invoke.
O **Thousand-fold virile**, O **Possessor of much wealth**, O **Lord of the good**, be for our **increase** in **battles**. ॥ 3 ॥

He; **Slayer-together**; **All-seeing**; Indra; him; **we invoke**; we;
**Thousand-testicled**; **Much-wealthy**; **Lord of the good**; become; **in battles**; our; **for increase**. ॥ 3 ॥

---

## Commentary (Sayana)

That Indra who is the **Slayer-together** <note>original: "sacāhā"</note>, the killer of great enemies, and the **All-seeing** <note>original: "vicarṣaṇiḥ"</note>, the special observer of all—him, Indra, **we invoke** <note>original: "hūmahe"</note> with words of praise. The second half of the verse is a direct address. O **Thousand-fold virile** <note>original: "sahasramuṣka"</note>, meaning "of a thousand organs." The <term>Kaushitaki Brahmana (an ancient commentary on rituals)</term> records that Indra, out of a desire for enjoyment, created organs in every joint of his body while being with whatever woman he encountered. This address refers to that legend. O **Possessor of much wealth** <note>original: "tuvinṛmṇa"</note>, and **Lord of the good** <note>original: "satpate"</note>, protector of the righteous; O Indra, **in battles** <note>original: "samatsu"</note> or wars, **be** for **our increase** or prosperity.

---

-> ॥ Now the fourth verse ॥ <-

You **subdue** the people like a **bull** with your **fury**, O bold one, in the **struggle** for the **spoils**.
Be our **awakener**, our **helper**, in the **great contest for wealth**, in our **bodies**, in the **waters**, and in the **sun**. ॥ 4 ॥

You subdue; the people; **like a bull**; with fury; O bold one; in the struggle; for the spoils;
Of us; **be mindful**; helper; **in the great contest for wealth**; in our bodies; in the waters; in the sun. ॥ 4 ॥

---

# 761 || Rig Veda || Book 6, Sukta 46, Verses 4–6

## Commentary (Sayana)
O **Ricishama** <note>original: "ṛcīṣama"; one who is equal to the hymns or whose form is established by them</note>, O Indra, you who are the crusher <note>original: "ghṛṣo"</note> of enemies: in the reward-giving battle <note>original: "mīḷhe"</note>, you strike down the enemies of our people with a bull-like, powerful anger. Strike them down! Likewise, in the battle for great wealth, be our protector <note>original: "avitā"</note>. Be mindful of us; that is to say, recognize yourself as our protector or become our guardian. For what purpose? For the sake of our children <note>original: "tanayeṣu"</note> and our bodies, and for the sake of the sun—that is, the attainment and sight of the sun’s light.

In the **Chaturvinshika** <note>a rite performed on the twenty-fourth day of a sacrificial session</note>, during the midday pressing, the priest known as the <term>Brahmanacchamsin</term> may use the <term>Pragatha</term> (a specific poetic couplet) beginning with **"Indra, bring us the pre-eminent"** as an alternative matching chant. This is indicated in the ritual texts: *"Indra, bring us the pre-eminent, a thousand, a hundred"* (Ashvalayana Shrauta Sutra 7.4).

O **Wonderful one** <note>original: "citra"</note>, one who is worthy of being looked upon; O <term>Vajra-hasta</term> (One with the thunderbolt in his arm); O one with beautiful jaws <note>original: "suśipra"</note>; O Indra, the connection is this: bring that food with which you have filled <note>original: "āprāḥ"</note> these two visible worlds, Heaven and Earth <note>original: "rodasī"</note>.

# 762 || Rig Veda || Book 6, Sukta 46, Verses 7–8

## Commentary (Sayana)
[Continuation of Verse 6 commentary]

...all the **pishtana** <note>original: "piṣṭanā"; refers to the Rakshasas (demons)</note>. They are called *pishtana* because they make noise while remaining hidden or unmanifest. Through the grammatical rule of <term>Prishodaradi</term> <note>a group of words in Sanskrit grammar that undergo irregular phonetic changes</note>, this term is formed. Make them well-shattered, agitated, and obstructed. O **Vasu** <note>original: "vaso"; a title for Indra as the 'Dweller' or 'Lord of Wealth'</note>, O Indra, make our enemies—those who belong to us as foes—easily conquerable, such that they are capable of being overcome with ease.

---

-> ॥ The Seventh Verse ॥ <-

## Hymn Text

If, O Indra, there is strength and wealth among the descendants of Nahusha, or among the people;
Whatever glory belongs to the **Five Tribes**, bring all that to us, along with all manly powers. ॥ 7 ॥

**Word-by-word Breakdown (Pada-patha):**
Whatever; Indra; among the descendants of Nahusha; [bring] near; strength; wealth; and; among the people;
Whatever; or; of the **Five Tribes**; glory; [bring] near; bear/bring; together; all; manly powers. ॥ 7 ॥

## Commentary (Sayana)

O Indra, whatever strength (*ojas*) and wealth (*nrimnam*) exists among the **descendants of Nahusha** <note>original: "nāhuṣīṣu"; Nahusha was a legendary king; here it refers to human populations associated with him</note> and among the **people** <note>original: "kṛṣṭiṣu"; refers to subjects or human communities</note>. The word "and" acts as a conjunction. Or, whatever belongs to the **Five Tribes** <note>original: "pañca kṣitīnām"; classically interpreted as the four castes (Varnas) plus the Nishadas (indigenous forest dwellers), representing all of humanity</note>—namely, their **glory** <note>original: "dyumnam"; interpreted here as "shining food"</note>—bring all of that to us. Deliver it. Likewise, bring to us **together** (*sacha*) all great and **manly powers** (*paunsya*).

---

-> ॥ The Eighth Verse ॥ <-

## Hymn Text

Or whatever heroic power exists in **Trukshu**, O Maghavan, or what is in the **Druhyu** people,
Or whatever manly strength is in the **Puru**, bestow all that upon us in the battle where men are overcome, so that we may destroy our enemies in the wars. ॥ 8 ॥

**Word-by-word Breakdown (Pada-patha):**
Whatever; or; in Trukshu; O Maghavan; in Druhyu; [bring] near; in the people; whatever; in Puru; whatever; and; manly strength;
To us; that; bestow; completely; in the conquering of men; enemies; in battles; for the sake of overcoming/injuring. ॥ 8 ॥

## Commentary (Sayana)

O **Maghavan** <note>original: "maghavan"; the Bountiful One</note>, wealthy Indra, whatever strength exists in the king named **Trukshu**, and whatever strength exists among the people known as the **Druhyu**, and whatever **manly strength** (*vri-shanyam*) exists in the king named **Puru**—bestow all that completely upon us, your praisers. When? During the **conquering of men** <note>original: "nṛsahye"; a battle where warriors must be withstood or overcome</note>, when war has commenced. For what purpose? To **overcome** <note>original: "turvaṇe"; to injure or strike down</note> the enemies and foes in the **battles** (*pritsu*).

---

## Critical Notes
During the **Chaturvinshika** <note>the twenty-fourth day of a sacrificial session</note>, during the <term>Nishkevalya</term> <note>a specific midday recitation for Indra</note>, the <term>Vairupa Samapragatha</term> beginning with "Indra, even for the three-metal..." <note>original: "indra chidhatu"</note> should be recited. This is indicated in the ritual manuals: *"Indra, even for the three-metal refuge... Indra in the swift attacks..."* (Ashvalayana Shrauta Sutra 9.3.1).

Mandala 6, Chapter 4, Hymn 46. ] || Fourth Book || 763

## Hymn Text

-> ॥ The ninth verse of the hymn ॥ <-

O Indra, grant us a three-fold shelter, triple-defending, and full of well-being. Bestow such a dwelling upon the wealthy patrons and upon me, and drive away the missile from them. ॥ 9 ॥

**Word-by-word Breakdown:**
Indra; three-fold <note>original: "tri-dhātu"; consisting of three layers or elements</note>; shelter; triple-defending <note>original: "tri-varūtham"; providing protection against three things</note>; possessing well-being;
dwelling/roof; grant; to the wealthy patrons; and; to me; and; drive away; the missile; from them. ॥ 9 ॥

---

## Commentary (Sayana)

O **Indra**, grant a **three-fold** <note>original: "tridhātu"</note>—meaning of three types or three-storied—**triple-defending** <note>original: "trivarūtha"</note>—meaning that which wards off the three: cold, heat, and rain—and **full of well-being**—meaning free from destruction—**shelter** or house. Grant this **dwelling** <note>original: "chardiḥ"; specifically a roofed protection</note>, distinguished by these qualities, to the **wealthy patrons** <note>original: "maghavadbhyaḥ"; "Magha" refers to wealth in the form of sacrificial offerings, so these are the patrons of the sacrifice</note> and to **me**, Bharadvaja <note>the sage/seer of this hymn</note>. Furthermore, **drive away** or separate from them the **missile** <note>original: "didyu"; a shining weapon or lightning-bolt</note> that is shining and propelled by the enemy.

---

## Hymn Text

-> ॥ The tenth verse ॥ <-

Those who, with a mind desiring cattle, have overpowered the enemy and strike them down boldly; then, O wealthy Indra, lover of songs, be our nearest protector of our bodies. ॥ 10 ॥

**Word-by-word Breakdown:**
Those who; desiring cattle; with a mind; the enemy; have overpowered/harmed; strike down; boldly;
Then; indeed; our; O wealthy one; Indra; O lover of songs; protector of the body; nearest; be. ॥ 10 ॥

---

## Commentary (Sayana)

**Those** people who, possessed of a **mind desiring the cattle** of the enemies, **overpowered** <note>original: "ādabhuḥ"; from the root 'dabh', meaning to harm or deceive</note> the enemy who seeks to destroy them. And those who, being **bold** <note>original: "dhṛṣṇuyā"</note>, strike us down with great force—O **Maghavan** <note>original: "maghavan"; possessor of wealth</note>, O **Indra**, O **lover of songs** <note>original: "girvaṇaḥ"; one who is to be served or gratified by words/praise</note>, **at this time** <note>original: "adha sma"</note>, from those enemies, be the **protector of our bodies** <note>original: "tanūpāḥ"</note> and be the **nearest** <note>original: "antamaḥ"; most intimate or closest</note> to us.

-> ॥ Thus ends the twenty-eighth section (Varga) of the seventh chapter (Adhyaya) of the fourth book (Ashtaka) ॥ <-

---

## Hymn Text

-> ॥ The eleventh verse ॥ <-

Now, O Indra, be there for our prosperity; protect the leader in the fight, when the birds and the sharp-headed missiles fly through the atmosphere. ॥ 11 ॥

**Word-by-word Breakdown:**
Now; indeed; our; for prosperity/growth; be; Indra; the leader; protect; in the fight;
When; in the atmosphere; fly; birds; missiles; sharp-headed <note>original: "tigma-mūrdhānaḥ"</note>. ॥ 11 ॥

## Commentary (Sayana) — Continued from previous page
O Indra, **then** <note>original: "adha sma"</note>—at that time—be there for **our growth** <note>original: "vṛdhe"</note> and prosperity. Furthermore, protect our leader <note>original: "nayaḥ"</note> who leads us in **battle** <note>original: "yudhi"</note>—save him. When is "then"? He answers: when **winged** <note>original: "parṇinaḥ"</note>, sharp-pointed <note>original: "tigmamūrddhānaḥ"</note>, and shining **missiles** <note>original: "didyavo"</note> or arrows fall in the **sky** <note>original: "antarīkṣe"</note>, having been launched by enemies; at that time, the connection is that you should be there for our prosperity.

---

-> ॥ The Twelfth Verse ॥ <-

## Hymn Text
Where the heroes spread out their bodies, risking the dear shelter of the ancestors; then, O Indra, grant a hidden protection for the body and for the offspring, and drive away the haters. ॥ 12 ॥

### Word-by-word Breakdown
**Where** <note>original: "yatra"</note>; **heroes** <note>original: "śūrāḥ"</note>; **bodies** <note>original: "tanvaḥ"</note>; **they spread out** <note>original: "vi-tanvate"</note>; **dear** <note>original: "priyā"</note>; **shelter** <note>original: "śarmma"</note>; **of the ancestors** <note>original: "pitṝṇām"</note>;
**then** <note>original: "adha"</note>; **indeed** <note>original: "sma"</note>; **grant** <note>original: "yaccha"</note>; **for the body** <note>original: "tanve"</note>; **for the offspring** <note>original: "tane"</note>; **and** <note>original: "ca"</note>; **protection/armor** <note>original: "chardih"</note>; **unperceived/hidden** <note>original: "acittam"</note>; **drive away** <note>original: "yāvaya"</note>; **hatred/enemies** <note>original: "dveṣaḥ"</note>. ॥ 12 ॥

### Commentary (Sayana)
**Where**—at which time—the **heroes**—the brave warriors—**spread out** their own **bodies**—meaning they expose their bodies before the enemies for the sake of their master's victory. Similarly, at this time, they spread out before the enemies the **dear** and pleasant **shelters**—the homes or lands—belonging to their **ancestors**—their fathers—meaning the properties earned by them. They "spread them out" in the sense that they are risking or abandoning them in the face of war. **Then**—at this time—**grant** or provide for our **body** and for our **offspring** <note>original: "tane"; meaning the son or descendants</note> a **protection** <note>original: "chardiḥ"</note>—an armor <term>kavacha (armor)</term> that wards off weapons—which is **unperceived** <note>original: "acittam"</note> by the enemy. Grant it in such a way that the enemy does not notice it; the meaning is to provide it before the enemy can recognize the defense. Furthermore, **drive away** the **hatred**—meaning separate us from the hating enemies.

---

-> ॥ The Thirteenth Verse ॥ <-

## Hymn Text
When, O Indra, you urge the horses in the charge for great wealth, on the uneven path and the crooked way, like hawks desiring food ... ॥ 13 ॥

### Word-by-word Breakdown
**When** <note>original: "yat"</note>; **Indra**; **in the charge** <note>original: "sarge"</note>; **horses** <note>original: "arvataḥ"</note>; **you urge** <note>original: "codayāse"</note>; **in the great wealth** <note>original: "mahā-dhane"</note>;
**on the uneven** <note>original: "asamane"</note>; **path** <note>original: "adhvani"</note>; **on the crooked** <note>original: "vṛjine"</note>; **way** <note>original: "pathi"</note>; **like hawks** <note>original: "śyenān-iva"</note>; **desiring fame/food** <note>original: "śravasyataḥ"</note>. ॥ 13 ॥

### Commentary (Sayana)
O **Indra**, for the sake of **great wealth**—meaning the great plunder to be won in the great battle—when there is a **charge** <note>original: "sarga"; a concentrated effort or military onset</note>, you **urge** or impel our **horses** on an **uneven** or difficult path. On the **crooked** <note>original: "vṛjine"</note> path—referring here to the way through the mid-air—our horses go like **hawks**. Just as hawks seeking meat go swiftly through the air, so too our horses—desiring **fame**—meaning food in the form of spoils for themselves—[the text continues onto the next page]
