<meta>This page concludes the commentary on Verse 13 of Rig Veda 6.47 and provides the full text, word-by-word breakdown (Padapatha), and Sayana’s explanation for Verse 14. It then transitions into the introductory technical details (Anukramani) for the next hymn, Sukta 48.</meta>

...the horses. When you cause them to move swiftly, at that time, grant protection to our bodies and to our offspring <note>original: "tanve tanayāya ca chardiḥ"</note>—this is how it connects to the previous verse.

->॥ The Fourteenth Verse ॥<-

## Hymn Text

Like a **river** rushing down a **slope**, moving very **swiftly**, when the **sound** of the shout follows the fear; those horses that turn back again and again like **birds** toward **meat**, caught by the **arms** to win the **prize**. ॥ 14 ॥

---

### Padapatha

**Like** a **river**; on a **slope**; **swiftly**; **going**; **if/when**; the **shout/sound**; **along/following**; the **sound/cry**;
**towards**; **which**; **birds**; **like**; **they turn back**; toward the **meat/prey**; **grasped**; by the **arms**; in the **cattle/prize** ॥ 14 ॥

---

## Commentary (Sayana)

This verse is intended to emphasize the same meaning previously stated. O Indra, when you **impel** or urge the horses that are **going** <note>original: "yato"</note> as **swiftly** as a **river** <note>original: "sindhuḥ"</note> flowing down a **slope** <note>original: "pravaṇe"</note> or low-lying land. When does this happen? **Following the shout** <note>original: "krośamanu"</note>. The word *krośa* here refers to fear; it means when there is a **sound** or a cry of distress in the circle of battle. What are these horses like? They are **grasped by the arms** <note>original: "bāhvor-gṛbhītāḥ"</note>, meaning they are controlled or held at the base of the arms and bound with a whip. These are the horses that **turn back again and again** <note>original: "vavṛtati"</note> when **wealth** in the form of **cattle** <note>original: "gavi"</note> is to be won. This is compared to how **birds** <note>original: "vayo na"</note>, such as hawks, circle back repeatedly when there is **meat** <note>original: "āmiṣi"</note> to be seized. The connection is: when you urge such horses during the cry of fear in battle, at that time, grant us protection. Although the priest himself is not involved in the fighting with horses, he prays for the victory of the King's men in his capacity as the royal priest <note>original: "rājapurohitatvena"</note>, so there is no contradiction in this prayer.

->॥ Thus ends the twenty-ninth section [varga] of the seventh chapter [adhyāya] of the fourth book [aṣṭaka] ॥<-

---

The fourth hymn, beginning with the word **"Sweet"** <note>original: "svāduḥ"</note>, consists of thirty-one verses and was seen by **Garga**, the son of Bharadvaja. The meter of the first verse is **Trishtup** <note>a meter of 44 syllables</note>; the verse beginning "ten horses" is **Anushtubh** <note>32 syllables</note>; "ten chariots" is **Gayatri** <note>24 syllables</note>; "great wealth" is a **Dvipada** <note>two-lined</note> verse; "yoking the two green steeds" is **Brihati** <note>36 syllables</note>; "of heaven and earth" is **Jagati** <note>48 syllables</note>; and the remaining verses are **Trishtup**. Regarding the deities: the first five verses are dedicated to **Soma**. In the first half-verse of the sixth, the **Gods** <note>Vishvedevas</note> are the deity; in the second half, the **Earth**; in the third, **Brihaspati**; and in the fourth, **Indra**. The four verses beginning with "Prastoka" are in praise of the **liberality** <note>term: Danastuti - a hymn praising a patron's gifts</note> of King Prastoka, the son of Srinjaya, and thus he is the deity there. The three verses starting "O Lord of the Forest" are dedicated to the **Chariot**. The three verses starting "Send forth your voice" are dedicated to the **Drum** <note>Dundubhi</note>. The half-verse "With horses' wings" is dedicated to **Indra**. The remaining verses are also dedicated to Indra. This is as stated in the Index: "The hymn 'Svadu' has thirty-one verses by Garga; the first five are for Soma; the half-verse 'Gavyuti' has deities as mentioned in the text; the praise of the gift of Prastoka, son of Srinjaya, is in Trishtup, Anushtubh, Gayatri, and Dvipada; the next two triplets are for the Chariot and Drum; the last half-verse is for Indra; 'Yujano' is Brihati; 'Divas-prithivya' is Jagati."

<vocab>
<term>Sindhu</term>: A river or the Indus river; here used as a metaphor for speed.
<term>Indra</term>: The king of the gods and patron of warriors.
<term>Soma</term>: The sacred ritual drink and the deity representing it.
<term>Bharadvaja/Garga</term>: Names of the sages (Rishis) to whom these hymns were revealed.
<term>Trishtup/Gayatri/etc.</term>: Specific poetic meters used in Vedic Sanskrit, defined by syllable counts.
<term>Danastuti</term>: A specific genre of Vedic verses that praise the generosity of a king or patron.
<term>Ratha</term>: The war chariot, personified here as a deity.
<term>Dundubhi</term>: The war drum, also personified as a deity to invoke power.
</vocab>

# The Rig Veda
## [Book 4, Chapter 7, Section 30]

The four verses beginning with "Truly this is sweet" are to be recited at the start of the *Agni-Maruta* litany <note>A specific ritual chant dedicated to Agni and the Storm Gods</note>. This is indicated in the ritual manuals: "The four verses 'Truly this is sweet' are in the middle, along with the invocation." <note>Reference to Ashvalayana Shrauta Sutra 5.20, a manual for Vedic sacrificial rites.</note>

-> ॥ Here is the First Verse ॥ <-

## Hymn Text

Truly this is sweet; it is full of honey. This is sharp; truly this is full of flavor. No one indeed can withstand Indra in battles once he has drunk of this essence. ॥ 1 ॥

**Word-by-Word Breakdown:**
Sweet; truly; this; honey-possessing; and; this; sharp; truly; this; flavor-possessing; and; this;
And so; now; of him/this; having drunk; Indra; not; anyone; at all; withstands/overcomes; in battles. ॥ 1 ॥

---

## Commentary (Sayana)

This pressed Soma <note>The sacred, energizing juice offered in Vedic rituals</note> is truly sweet, meaning it is pleasant to the taste. Furthermore, this Soma is "honey-like" <note>original: "madhumān"</note>, meaning it possesses a natural sweetness. Likewise, this Soma is "sharp" <note>original: "tīvraḥ"</note>, for it is indeed potent in producing a state of exhilaration. And this Soma is "flavorful" <note>original: "rasavān"</note>, meaning it is full of nourishing essence. 

By these four descriptive phrases, the supreme quality of the Soma's sweetness is established. Furthermore, regarding "this" <note>the commentator notes that the grammatical genitive 'asya' is used here to mean 'this'</note> Soma: no one at all <note>original: "na kaścana"</note> can withstand or overcome Indra in "battles" <note>original: "āhaveṣu"</note> once he has drunk this. The word **nu** in the text serves simply to complete the rhythmic meter of the line.

---

## Hymn Text

-> ॥ Now the Second Verse ॥ <-

This was sweet and most exhilarating here, in the drinking of which Indra rejoiced during the slaying of Vritra; he who destroyed the many strengths of Shambara and the ninety and nine ramparts. ॥ 2 ॥

**Word-by-Word Breakdown:**
This; sweet; here; most exhilarating; was; of which; Indra; in the slaying of Vritra; rejoiced;
Many; who; strengths/deeds; of Shambara; [destroyed]; ninety; nine; and; ramparts/fortresses; destroyed. ॥ 2 ॥

---

## Commentary (Sayana)

In this sacrifice, this Soma, having been tasted and drunk, was "most exhilarating" <note>original: "madiṣṭhaḥ"</note>, meaning it caused the highest degree of inspiration. Through the drinking of this Soma, Indra became "intoxicated" <note>original: "mamāda"</note>—or filled with divine fervor—at the time of the "slaying of Vritra" <note>Vritra is the serpent-demon of drought, the primary adversary of Indra</note>. 

This Soma <note>acting through Indra</note> destroyed the "many" <note>original: "purūṇi"</note> "strengths" <note>original: "cyautnā"</note> or powerful deeds of the demon Shambara. Likewise, it destroyed the "ramparts" <note>original: "dehyah"</note>—referring to the fortified cities of the demons or perhaps their physical bodies—numbering ninety and nine. The phrase "This Soma" from the first part of the verse connects to this act of destruction.

<summary>This page contains the first two verses of Rig Veda 6.47 and Sayana's commentary, focusing on the sweetness and intoxicating power of the Soma drink that empowers Indra to defeat the demons Vritra and Shambara.</summary>
<keywords>Soma, Indra, Vritra-slaying, Shambara, Vedic ritual, Agni-Maruta, Sayana, Sanskrit commentary</keywords>

# Book 6, Chapter 4, Hymn 47 | The Fourth Volume (Ashtaka) | 761

-> || Now the Third Verse || <-

## Hymn Text
This [Soma], being drunk, rouses my speech; this [Soma] has awakened my eager wisdom. This wise one measured out the six wide realms, from which no living being is ever distant. ॥ 3 ॥

---

This; my; drunk; up; rouses; speech; this; wisdom; eager; awakened;
This; six; wide [realms]; measured; wise; not; from which; living being; any; at all; far. ॥ 3 ॥

## Commentary (Sayana)
When this Soma is drunk, it "rouses" <note>original: "udiyartti"</note> or elevates my speech. This very same Soma "awakened" <note>original: "udajīgaḥ"</note> or manifested my "eager" <note>original: "uśatīm"</note>—meaning lovely or desired—wisdom. 

<note>Grammatical note: The word 'ajīgaḥ' is a specific form derived from the root 'gri', meaning to swallow or utter, here used in a causative sense to mean 'to make manifest.'</note>

Furthermore, this "wise" <note>original: "dhīraḥ"</note> or intelligent Soma "measured out" <note>original: "amimīta"</note> or created the "six wide realms" <note>original: "ṣaḷurvīḥ"</note>. These six are traditionally identified as: Heaven, Earth, Day, Night, the Waters, and the Plants. He created these such that no "living being" <note>original: "bhuvanaṃ"</note> or collection of creatures is "far" <note>original: "āre"</note> or removed from them; rather, all living things exist within these six realms.

-> || Now the Fourth Verse || <-

## Hymn Text
This is he who produced the width of the earth; this is he who produced the height of the sky. This Soma held the nectar in the three flowing places; he sustained the wide intermediate space. ॥ 4 ॥

---

This; he; who; width; of the earth; height; of the sky; made; this; he;
This; nectar; in the three; flowing [places]; Soma; held; wide; intermediate space. ॥ 4 ॥

## Commentary (Sayana)
Indeed, this is that Soma who "made" <note>original: "akṛṇot"</note> the "width" <note>original: "varimāṇam"</note> or the vast expansion of the earth. Likewise, this Soma made the "height" <note>original: "varṣmāṇam"</note>—the elevated and firm nature—of the sky. 

Furthermore, this Soma "held" <note>original: "dadhāra"</note> or preserved the "nectar" <note>original: "pīyūṣam"</note>, the essential fluid, within the "three flowing places" <note>original: "tisṛṣu pravatsu"</note>, which refer to the plants, the waters, and the cows <note>specifically their milk</note>. He also sustains the "wide intermediate space" <note>original: "uru antarikṣam"</note>, the atmosphere between heaven and earth. As another sacred verse states: 

> "O Soma, you generated all these plants; you generated the waters; you generated the cows. You have extended the wide intermediate space." <note>original: Rig Veda 1.91.22</note>

-> || Now the Fifth Verse || <-

## Hymn Text
This [Soma] found the variegated [dawn] with her bright head, in the presence of the dawns appearing as lights. This great Bull, accompanied by the Maruts, stayed the sky with a great pillar. ॥ 5 ॥

<note>The commentary for verse 5 continues on the following page.</note>

<keywords>Soma, Six Wide Realms (Shalurvi), creation of Earth and Sky, nectar (Piyusha), intermediate space (Antariksha), Sayana's commentary, Vedic cosmology</keywords>

# Rig Veda || [Book 3, Chapter 7, Varga 31]

## Hymn Text (Word-by-word Analysis for Verse 5)
This | found | all-visible | flood | of those dwelling in bright places | of the Dawns | in the presence.
This | Great | with great | support | up | heaven | supported | the Bull | accompanied by the Maruts ॥ 5 ॥

## Commentary (Sayana)
This Soma indeed found the "all-visible flood" <note>original: "viśvadarśatam arṇaḥ"</note>—meaning the solar light which stimulates all and is wonderful to behold. At what time? "In the presence of the Dawns" <note>original: "uṣasām anīke"</note>, meaning at the time of daybreak, for those Dawns whose "dwelling is the bright, pure atmosphere" <note>original: "śukrasadmanām"</note>. Furthermore, this great, highly-augmented Soma "supported the heavens" <note>original: "dyām udastambhāt"</note>—held the celestial realm aloft—using a "mighty support" <note>original: "mahatā skambhanena"</note>, which refers to the intermediary atmosphere. He did this so that the heavens would not fall, using the atmosphere as a foundation. What is the nature of this Soma? He is the "Bull" <note>original: "vṛṣabhaḥ"</note>, the generator of rain, for rain is produced through the <term>Soma</term> offerings. He is also "accompanied by the Maruts" <note>original: "marutvān"</note>, the storm-gods who are his constant companions.

---
-> ॥ This concludes the thirtieth Varga of the seventh chapter of the fourth volume ॥ <-
---

## Hymn Text
-> ॥ Now the Sixth Verse ॥ <-
Boldly drink the Soma from the jar, O Indra, slayer of Vritra, hero in the battle for riches. At the midday offering, pour it in; O repository of wealth, bestow wealth upon us. ॥ 6 ॥

**Word-by-word Analysis:**
Boldly | drink | in the jar | Soma | Indra | slayer of Vritra | hero | in the battle | for riches.
At the midday | offering | pour in | repository of wealth | wealth | in us | bestow. ॥ 6 ॥

## Commentary (Sayana)
O "Hero" <note>original: "śūra"</note> or powerful Indra, you who are the "slayer of Vritra" <note>original: "vṛtrahā"</note>—the destroyer of enemies who encompass and obstruct—when the "battle for riches" <note>original: "vasūnām samare"</note> or the struggle for wealth occurs, drink the Soma residing in the "jar" <note>original: "kalaśe"</note> (specifically the large <term>Drona-kalasha</term> vessel) in a "bold" <note>original: "dhṛṣat"</note> or confident manner. Furthermore, "pour it in" <note>original: "ā vṛṣasva"</note> during the "midday offering" <note>original: "mādhyandine savane"</note>. This means fill your belly with Soma, for the midday libation is specifically dedicated to Indra. Moreover, you who are the "repository of wealth" <note>original: "rayisthāno"</note> or the dwelling place of all riches, "bestow wealth" <note>original: "rayim dhehi"</note> or establish prosperity within us.

## Hymn Text
-> ॥ Now the Seventh Verse ॥ <-
O Indra, look upon us like a leader going before; lead us forward to even better fortune. Be a good guide across, ferry us over; be a good leader and a leader to desirable things. ॥ 7 ॥

**Word-by-word Analysis:**
Indra | forward | us | like a leader | look | forward | us | lead | further | better fortune | toward.
Be | a good crosser | ferry over | us | be | a good leader | and | a leader to desirable things. ॥ 7 ॥

## Commentary (Sayana)
O Indra, "look upon us" <note>original: "naḥ pra paśya"</note> or gaze toward us favorably, just like a "leader" <note>original: "pura-etā"</note> who goes in front. View us with excellence. Just as...

# Rig Veda || Book 6, Hymn 47, Verse 8

[Continuing from the previous page's commentary on Verse 7]
Just as a protector of the path <note>original: "mārgarakṣakaḥ"</note>, going ahead himself, watches over the travelers who need protection, in that same way, you should watch over us. Likewise, lead us toward the most excellent wealth <note>original: "vasyo vasīyaḥ"</note>, and lead us forward more effectively. Make us reach it. Also, be a "good traverser" <note>original: "supāraḥ"</note>, one who helps us cross over our difficulties. Lead us, your singers, across; make us overcome our enemies. Be a "leader of good conduct" <note>original: "sunītiḥ"</note> for us. Furthermore, be a "leader of desirable things" <note>original: "vāmanītiḥ"</note>—a bringer of wealth that is to be longed for. Or, in other words, be the one who brings the best for our sake.

In the ritual involving the sacrifice of an animal to Indra, the verse beginning with "To a wide realm" <note>original: "uruṃ naḥ"</note> is used as the <term>Yajya</term> <note>the verse recited during the actual offering</note> for the <term>Vapa</term> <note>original: "vapā"; the omentum or fatty part of the sacrificial animal</note>. This is indicated in the liturgical texts: "Knowing [the way], lead us to a wide realm... (Ashvalayana Shrauta Sutra 3.7)." This verse is also to be whispered as a prayer <note>original: "japya"</note> when the <term>Hotar</term> priests are moving toward the <term>Sadas</term> <note>the assembly tent</note>. This is also indicated: "Whispering 'Knowing [the way], lead us to a wide realm...' (Ashvalayana Shrauta Sutra 5.3)." Furthermore, on the twenty-fourth day of the multi-day rituals and in other groups of sacrificial days, this verse serves as the "starting verse" <note>original: "ārambhaṇīyā"</note> for the <term>Achhavaka</term> priest during the midday libation. This is indicated: "The verse 'Knowing [the way], lead us to a wide realm' is the starting verse... (Ashvalayana Shrauta Sutra 7.4)."

---

## Hymn Text

-> ॥ This is the eighth verse of the hymn ॥ <-

**Knowing the way, lead us to a wide realm, to light that is like heaven, to safety, and to well-being. O Indra, may we rest within your two tall, mighty arms, which are our refuge and protection. ॥ 8 ॥**

**Wide. / To us. / Realm. / Toward. / Lead [thou]. / Knowing. / Like-heaven. / Light. / Fearlessness. / Well-being. /
Tall. / Your. / O Indra. / Of the mighty. / Two arms. / Near. / May we stand. / Refuge. / Great. ॥ 8 ॥**

---

## Commentary (Sayana)

O Indra, you who are "knowing" <note>original: "vidvān"</note>—meaning you understand the way—lead us toward the "wide realm" <note>original: "uruṃ lokaṃ"</note>, the place known as heaven. Likewise, lead us toward the "light" <note>original: "jyotiḥ"</note> that is "like heaven" <note>original: "svarvat"</note>—meaning full of happiness—and "fearless" <note>original: "abhayaṃ"</note>, along with "well-being" <note>original: "svasti"</note> or safety. O Indra, may we "stand near" <note>original: "upastheyāma"</note>—meaning may we serve and stay within—your two "great" <note>original: "bṛhantā"</note> and "tall" <note>original: "ṛṣvā"</note> or beautiful "arms" <note>original: "bāhū"</note>, which belong to you, the "mighty" <note>original: "sthavirasya"</note> or aged/powerful one. May those arms be our "refuge" <note>original: "śaraṇā"</note> or protectors.

---

## Hymn Text

-> ॥ Now the Ninth Verse ॥ <-

**O Indra, place us on the best chariot-seat, O you who possess hundreds and horses. May I take hold of the most nourishing food; O generous one, let not the enemy’s wealth surpass us. ॥ 9 ॥**

**On the best. / Us. / O Indra. / Chariot-seat. / Place [thou]. / In the strongest. / O possessor of hundreds. / In the [two] horse-possessing. / [Toward]. /
Food. / [Toward]. / May I take. / Most increasing. / Not. / Us. / Let surpass. / O generous one. / Wealth. / Of the enemy. ॥ 9 ॥**

<vocab>
Indra: The king of the gods and deity of storms/war.
Loka: A world, realm, or field of existence.
Jyotih: Light, specifically spiritual or celestial light.
Abhayam: Literally "without fear"; state of security.
Svasti: Well-being, auspiciousness, or "it is well."
Bahu: Arms, representing the deity's power and protective reach.
Maghavan: "The Generous One," a common title for Indra.
Vapa: An anatomical offering (omentum) used in Vedic animal sacrifices.
Yajya: A specific type of sacrificial verse used for making an offering into the fire.
</vocab>

## Commentary (Sayana) — Continued
<note>This concludes the commentary on Verse 9</note>
O **Indra**, who are **most excellent and most wide-reaching** <note>original: "variṣṭha urutame"</note>, **place us** <note>original: "no'smān dhāḥ"</note> in your own **chariot-seat** <note>original: "vandhure"</note>. Furthermore, O **possessor of hundred-fold wealth** <note>original: "śatāvan"</note>, place us with your **two best-drawing horses** <note>original: "vahiṣṭhayoḥ"</note>. And among those foods, **bring** <note>original: "āvaksi"</note> to us the **most abundant** <note>original: "varṣiṣṭhaṃ"</note> and strengthening nourishment. O **bountiful** <note>original: "maghavan"</note> Indra, let no **other** <note>original: "aryo"; here referring to a rival or enemy</note> lord of wealth **destroy** <note>original: "mā tārīt"</note> our **riches**.

---

## Hymn Text
-> ॥ Verse 10 ॥ <-

**O Indra, be gracious to me; desire for me the means of life. Quicken my prayer like the edge of a blade made of iron. Whatever I, longing for you, speak at this time—be it right or wrong—accept that with pleasure. Make me attended by the protecting gods.** ॥ 10 ॥

**Indra. Be gracious. For me. Means of life. Desire. Quicken. Prayer/Intellect. Of iron. Like. Edge.**
**Whatever. Anything. And. I. Longing for you. This. Speak. That. Accept with pleasure. Make. Me. Attended by gods.** ॥ 10 ॥

## Commentary (Sayana)
O **Indra, be gracious** <note>original: "mṛḷa"</note>; that is, make us happy. **Desire** to give **to me** the **means of life** <note>original: "jīvātuṃ"</note>, which is like a medicine for living. Likewise, **quicken** <note>original: "codaya"</note> my **intellect** <note>original: "dhiyaṃ"</note>; impel it toward the subject of praise or ritual action; sharpen it. **Like the edge of iron** <note>original: "ayaso na dhārām"</note> means just as the edge of an iron sword or tool is made sharp and fine, in the same way, quicken my intellect to perceive subtle things. Furthermore, **whatever I speak now**—whether it is correct or incorrect—as one who is **longing for you** <note>original: "tvāyuḥ"</note>, **accept that with pleasure**. And **make me** one who is **attended by the gods** <note>original: "devavantaṃ"</note>, meaning one who is accompanied by the protecting deities.

-> ॥ This ends the twenty-first section (Varga) of the seventh Adhyaya of the fourth Ashtaka ॥ <-

---

## Ritual Notes
**In the sacrifice for one desiring long life <term>Ayushkameshti</term>, the verse "Indra the protector..." is the invitatory verse <term>Anuvakya</term>. This is indicated in the liturgical texts: "Indra the protector, Indra the helper... let him not [fail] you in this trial, O powerful one" (Ashvalayana Shrauta Sutra 2.10.1).**

---

## Hymn Text
-> ॥ Verse 11 ॥ <-

**The protector Indra, the helper Indra, the hero Indra, who is easily invoked at every call—I now invoke the powerful Indra, who is called by many. May the bountiful Indra grant us well-being.** ॥ 11 ॥

**Protector. Indra. Helper. Indra. At every call. Easily invoked. Hero. Indra.**
**I invoke. Now. Powerful. Called by many. Indra. Well-being. For us. Bountiful. Grant. Indra.** ॥ 11 ॥

## Commentary (Sayana)
I invoke **Indra, the protector** <note>original: "trātāraṃ"</note>, the one who guards us from enemies. Likewise, I invoke **Indra, the helper** <note>original: "avitāraṃ"</note>, the one who satisfies us with our heart's desires. He is **easily invoked** <note>original: "suhavaṃ"</note>—meaning he can be called upon with ease—**at every call** <note>original: "have have"</note> or in all our daily invocations. He is the **hero** <note>original: "śūraṃ"</note>, the one possessing great valor...

<summary>In these verses, the poet prays to Indra for longevity, a sharp intellect likened to an iron blade, and divine protection. The text also specifies the ritual use of these verses in sacrifices intended to secure a long and healthy life.</summary>
<keywords>Indra, prayer for intellect, iron blade metaphor, protection, long life ritual, Ayushkameshti, Sayana commentary</keywords>

<meta>This page continues the translation of the Rig Veda, Mandala 6, Hymn 47. The text includes the conclusion of the commentary on Verse 11, followed by the full text and commentary for Verses 12 and 13, and the opening mantra of Verse 14. This section focuses on a prayer for protection, wealth, and the removal of enemies through the grace of Indra.</meta>

I call upon **Indra** <note>original: "indraṃ hvayāmi"</note>, who is **capable** <note>original: "śakraṃ"</note> in all tasks and is **invoked by many** <note>original: "puruhūtaṃ"</note> for the sake of protection. May that **bountiful** <note>original: "maghavā"</note> and wealthy Indra, being thus called, **grant** <note>original: "dhātu"</note> us **welfare** <note>original: "svasti"</note>, which is the state of non-destruction. Or rather, may he ordain it for us.

---

->|| Verse 12 ||<-

## Hymn Text
**May Indra, the good protector and possessor of wealth, be very gracious to us with his protections—he who is all-knowing. May he drive away hatred and create fearlessness. May we be the masters of excellent heroic strength.** ॥ 12 ॥

**Pada-patha:**
| Word | Analysis |
| :--- | :--- |
| **Indraḥ** | The god Indra |
| **Su-trāmā** | The good protector |
| **Sva-vān** | Possessor of wealth/self-reliant |
| **Avaḥ-bhiḥ** | By means of protections |
| **Su-mṛḷīkaḥ** | Very gracious/bestower of happiness |
| **Bhavatu** | Let him be |
| **Viśva-vedāḥ** | All-knowing or possessing all |
| **Bādhatām** | Let him drive away/destroy |
| **Dveṣaḥ** | Hatred or enemies |
| **Abhayam** | Fearlessness |
| **Kṛṇotu** | Let him make/create |
| **Su-vīryasya** | Of excellent heroic power |
| **Patayaḥ** | Masters/lords |
| **Syāma** | May we be |

---

## Commentary (Sayana)
May that Indra, who is a **good protector** <note>original: "sutrāmā"</note> and **wealthy** <note>original: "svavān"</note>, be **very gracious** <note>original: "sumṛḷīkaḥ"</note>, or one who brings great happiness, through his **protections** <note>original: "avobhiḥ"</note>. Similarly, may that Indra, who is **all-knowing** <note>original: "viśvavedāḥ"</note>—meaning either he who possesses all wealth or he who knows all things—**drive away** <note>original: "bādhatām"</note> or destroy our **hatred** <note>original: "dveṣaḥ"</note>, meaning our hating enemies. Let him **make** <note>original: "kṛṇotu"</note> for us **fearlessness** <note>original: "abhayam"</note>. And through his grace, may we **become** <note>original: "syāma"</note> the **masters** <note>original: "patayaḥ"</note> of **excellent heroic strength** <note>original: "suvīryasya"</note>.

---

->|| Verse 13 ||<-

## Hymn Text
**May we abide in the good favor of that worshipful one, and also in his auspicious benevolence. May Indra, the good protector and possessor of wealth, drive hatred far away from us, even that which is hidden.** ॥ 13 ॥

**Pada-patha:**
**Of him. We. In good favor. Of the worshipful one. Also. In auspicious. In benevolence. May we be.**
**He. The good protector. Possessor of wealth. Indra. In us. From afar. Even. Hatred. Hidden. May he drive away.** ॥ 13 ॥

---

## Commentary (Sayana)
May we **be** <note>original: "syāma"</note> the objects of the **good favor** <note>original: "sumatau"</note>—that is, the beautiful and graceful intellect—of that **worshipful** <note>original: "yajñiyasya"</note> Indra who is worthy of sacrifice. Likewise, may we abide in his **auspicious** <note>original: "bhadre"</note> **benevolence** <note>original: "saumanase"</note>, which is the state of having a well-disposed mind. The meaning is: let Indra direct his graceful intellect and benevolence toward us. Furthermore, may that Indra, the **good protector** <note>original: "sutrāmā"</note> and **wealthy one** <note>original: "svavān"</note>, **drive away** <note>original: "yuyotu"</note> or separate **hatred** <note>original: "dveṣaḥ"</note>—meaning our enemies—**from us** <note>original: "asme"</note> to a **distant place** <note>original: "ārāt cit"</note>. The word **hidden** <note>term: "sanutaḥ"; Sayana identifies this as a synonym for "concealed" or "invisible"</note> refers to those enemies who are out of sight.

---

->|| Verse 14 ||<-

## Hymn Text
**O Indra, down towards you our songs and prayers hasten like water-currents down a slope, or like harnessed horses. Like wide-reaching wealth, you enjoy many offerings; O wielder of the thunderbolt, you unite the waters and the kine with the sun.** <note>The Sanskrit "Indun" can refer to Soma drops, the moon, or sparking points of light; in this context, it suggests Indra's role in releasing the celestial waters and light.</note> ॥ 14 ॥

<summary>This page contains prayers to Indra asking for his protection, wealth, and the removal of enemies, emphasizing his role as a "good protector" (Sutraman) and "all-knowing" benefactor. It includes the full grammatical breakdown and traditional commentary for these verses.</summary>

<meta>This page concludes the 32nd section (Varga) of the 7th Chapter (Adhyaya) within the 4th Book (Ashtaka) of the Rig Veda. It contains the final verses of Hymn 32, focusing on the relationship between the worshiper’s prayers and the god Indra, and Indra's absolute sovereignty over human status.</meta>

## Hymn Text

-> **Verse 14 (Word-by-Word Analysis)** <-

**Down | to you | [particle] | Indra | a slope | like | a wave | words | prayers | released | they flow | vast | like | wealth | pressings | many | waters | cows | O Wielder of the Bolt | you join | together | Soma-drops** ॥ 14 ॥

<note>original: "ava te iti indra pravataḥ na ūrmiḥ giraḥ brahmāṇi ni-sṛtaḥ dhanvante urū na rādhaḥ savanā purūṇi apaḥ gāḥ vajrin yuvase saṃ indūn"</note>

---

## Commentary (Sayana)

O **Indra**, the **words** <note>original: "giraḥ"</note> of the singer, which consist of recited hymns, and the **prayers** <note>original: "brahmāṇi"</note> in the form of chants, flow down toward you. That is, they reach you. In this context, an example is given: like a **wave** <note>original: "ūrmiḥ"</note> or a mass of water flows toward **sloping regions** <note>original: "pravataḥ"</note>. Just as water moves quickly from a high place to a lower place, so do these prayers.

The word "na" here is used for comparison. Furthermore, **vast wealth** <note>original: "urūṇi rādhaḥ"</note> in the form of sacrificial offerings, and **many ritual pressings** <note>original: "purūṇi savanā"</note>—the many extracted Soma juices—all go toward you alone. O **Wielder of the Bolt** <note>original: "vajrin"</note>, you **mix together** <note>original: "saṃ yuvase"</note> the **waters** <note>original: "apaḥ"</note> known as <term>Vasatīvarī (ritual water used in the Soma sacrifice)</term>, the **cows** <note>original: "gāḥ"</note> (referring to cow-products like ghee and curds), and the **Soma-drops** <note>original: "indūn"</note> for the sake of the sacrifice. This means that to worship you, the priests prepare the Soma by pressing it with ritual waters and refining it with milk and other substances.

---

-> **॥ Now the Fifteenth Verse ॥** <-

## Hymn Text

-> **Verse 15 (Continuous Recitation)** <-

**Who shall praise him? Who shall satisfy him? Who shall sacrifice, when the Bountiful Lord always knows his own power? Like one moving his feet, one after the other, he makes the first last and the last first by his powers.** ॥ 15 ॥

-> **Verse 15 (Word-by-Word Analysis)** <-

**Who | him | shall praise | who | shall satisfy | who | shall sacrifice | since | this | indeed | the Bountiful Lord | always | knows | feet | like | moving | one | another | he makes | the first | the last | by his powers** ॥ 15 ॥

---

## Commentary (Sayana)

Which singer can truly **praise** <note>original: "stavat"</note> this Indra? Who can **satisfy** <note>original: "pṛṇāt"</note> him? And who can **sacrifice** <note>original: "yajāte"</note> to him with offerings? Since this **Bountiful Lord** <note>original: "maghavā"</note>, the wealthy Indra, **always knows** <note>original: "viśvahāvet"</note> himself—meaning he knows his own essence and is all-knowing—no one is truly capable of praising, satisfying, or worshipping him perfectly.

Furthermore, the text explains why he is beyond the reach of ordinary praise: because Indra, by his own **wisdoms or powers** <note>original: "śacībhiḥ"</note>, makes the one who was **first** <note>original: "pūrvam"</note> (the primary or chief worshiper) into the **last** <note>original: "aparam"</note> (secondary), and the one who was last into the first, by alternating them. He can demote the chief singer and promote the lowly one.

An analogy is provided: **Like moving feet** <note>original: "praharan pādāviva"</note>. Just as a person walking on a path, by thrusting his feet forward, makes the leading foot the rear one and the rear foot the leading one, so does Indra shift the status of men. For this reason, Indra’s true nature is beyond the scope of mere praise. This group of five verses (starting from this one) establishes the absolute independence and sovereignty of Indra.

-> **॥ Thus ends the thirty-second section of the seventh chapter of the fourth book ॥** <-

<vocab>
**Indra (इन्द्र):** The king of the gods and the primary deity of this hymn.
**Vajrin (वज्रिन्):** "The Thunderbolt-Wielder," a common title for Indra referring to his primary weapon.
**Maghavan (मघवा):** "The Bountiful" or "The Generous," emphasizing Indra’s role as the distributor of wealth.
**Brahmāṇi (ब्रह्माणि):** Sacred prayers or songs of praise.
**Savanā (सवना):** The ritual extraction and offering of the Soma juice, usually performed three times a day.
**Śacībhiḥ (शचीभिः):** Through his "powers" or "acts of skill"; often personified as the goddess Shachi.
</vocab>

<meta>This page continues from the previous page of Mandala 6, Hymn 47 of the Rig Veda. It contains verses 16, 17, and 18. The previous page discussed Indra’s acceptance of sacrificial offerings (Soma) and his relationship with the worshipers’ prayers. ## Hymn Text

-> **Verse 16** <-

The Hero is heard of, taming every fierce enemy, leading one person after another to prominence. Hating the arrogant who prosper without sacrifice, the King of both earthly and heavenly wealth, Indra, repeatedly calls to the people for their protection.

**Word-by-word analysis:**
He is heard | the Hero | every fierce one | taming | one after another | leading forward | hater of the [unpious] prosperous | of both [worlds] | King | repeatedly calls | the people | Indra | the sons of Manu (mankind) ॥ 16 ॥

---

## Commentary (Sayana)

It is **heard** <note>original: "śṛṇve"</note>—meaning it is widely renowned—that this Indra is a powerful hero. What does he do? He acts by **taming** <note>original: "damāyan"</note> or subduing **every fierce** <note>original: "ugram-ugram"</note> and arrogant enemy. He is **leading forward** <note>original: "atine nīyamānaḥ"</note> or repeatedly bringing to the front **one person after another** <note>original: "anyam-anyam"</note>—moving his praise-singers from one state of success to another. 

Furthermore, he is the **hater of the arrogant** <note>original: "edhamāna-dviṭ"</note>, specifically those who grow wealthy but do not offer the Soma sacrifice. He is the **King** <note>original: "rājā"</note> or lord of **both** <note>original: "ubhayasya"</note> types of wealth: the heavenly and the earthly. This Indra **repeatedly calls** <note>original: "coṣkūyate"</note> to the **people** <note>original: "viśaḥ"</note>, his own attendants and **mankind** <note>original: "manuṣyān"</note>, for the purpose of protecting them.

---

## Hymn Text

-> **Verse 17** <-

He discards the friendships of those who came before and moves with those who come later. Shifting his favor, Indra, unassailable and casting off the unpious, passes through many years.

**Word-by-word analysis:**
Away | of the former ones | friendships | he discards | moving quickly | with the later ones | he goes | the unassailable | casting off | many | Indra | autumns (years) | he passes through ॥ 17 ॥

---

## Commentary (Sayana)

This Indra **discards** <note>original: "parā-vṛṇakti"</note> or lets go of the **friendships** <note>original: "sakhyā"</note> of the **former ones** <note>original: "pūrveṣām"</note>, referring to men who used to perform excellent deeds but perhaps no longer do. Instead, **moving quickly** <note>original: "vitarturāṇaḥ"</note>—meaning he acts with speed or punishes the former—he **goes** <note>original: "eti"</note> with or attains friendship with **the later ones** <note>original: "aparebhiḥ"</note>, those who are currently performing the sacred rites. 

Likewise, being **unassailable** <note>original: "ananubhūtiḥ"</note> and **casting off** <note>original: "avadhunvānaḥ"</note> or abandoning the people who do not serve him, Indra **passes through** <note>original: "tartarīti"</note> or exceeds **many** <note>original: "pūrvīḥ"</note> **autumns** <note>original: "śaradaḥ"</note>, which refers to years. The meaning is that he stays for a very long time in friendship with those who continue to praise him.

---

## Hymn Text

-> **Verse 18** <-

Indra has assumed every form as his own reflection; that form of his is for the purpose of making him known. Through his creative powers, Indra moves in many forms, for his bay horses are yoked, ten times a hundred.

**Word-by-word analysis:**
Form by form | a reflection | he became | that | his | form | for making [him] known | Indra | through creative powers | many-formed | moves | yoked | indeed | his | bay horses | hundreds | ten ॥ 18 ॥

<note>This famous verse is often cited in later Indian philosophy to explain how the supreme divinity appears as the many forms of the world.</note>

<term>Māyā (Creative Power)</term> — In this early Vedic context, Maya refers to the divine power of a god to transform, create, or assume different appearances, rather than the later philosophical concept of "illusion."

<term>Hari (Bay Horses)</term> — The golden-colored horses that pull Indra's chariot, symbolizing the rays of the sun or the power of his movement.

<summary>These verses describe Indra's supreme role as a ruler who humbles the proud and shifts his favor to those who remain faithful in worship. The final verse introduces the profound concept of Indra manifesting in all forms through his "Maya" or divine power, symbolized by his thousand horses.</summary>

<meta>This page concludes the commentary on Verse 18 of Mandala 6, Hymn 47, and introduces Verse 19. It continues the philosophical exploration of Indra’s nature, moving from his ability to take multiple forms to a Vedantic interpretation of Indra as the Supreme Soul. It then presents the text and initial commentary for Verse 19, where Indra is identified with the divine craftsman Tvashta.</meta>

<page-num>774</page-num>
<header>॥ Rig Veda ॥ [Book 4, Chapter 7, Class 33] <note>Refers to the Ashtaka system: Ashtaka 4, Adhyaya 7, Varga 33.</note></header>

## Commentary (Sayana)
**[Continuation of commentary on Rig Veda 6.47.18]**

This Indra, being the representative of all forms, has become every form—the various forms of deities such as Agni and others. He attains these forms. <note>The verbal root *bhū* signifies "attainment."</note> The meaning is that Indra, through his own divine greatness, becomes the forms of those various deities. Furthermore, his attainment of the forms of Agni and other deities serves for **clear perception** <note>original: "praticakṣaṇāya"</note>; it is so that he may be seen in distinct, unconfused forms, such as "This is Agni," "This is Vishnu," or "This is Rudra." 

Moreover, this Indra, through his **powers of wisdom** <note>original: "māyābhiḥ"; the commentator notes this is a synonym for knowledge or "jñāna"</note> and his own inner resolves, takes on **many forms** <note>original: "pururūpaḥ"</note>—having many types of bodies—and **approaches** <note>original: "īyate"</note> or goes to many worshipers. One might ask: "Since he has only two horses and one chariot, how can he go to many people simultaneously?" To this, the text says: The **bay horses** <note>original: "harayaḥ"</note> yoked to the chariot of this Indra are **ten hundred and a thousand** <note>original: "daśa śata sahasra"</note>—meaning they are infinite in number. Because of this, he assumes many bodies and goes to worshipers in different places at the same time.

Others, following the meaning of the root *id* as "supreme sovereignty," interpret that Indra is the **Supreme Soul** <note>original: "Paramātmā"</note>. Like space, he is all-pervading and consists of eternal bliss. It is he alone who, when limited by the "adjuncts" of the inner mind and body, is designated as the **individual soul** <note>original: "jīvātmā"</note>. Through his beginningless powers of illusion <note>original: "māyā-śaktibhiḥ"</note>, he manifests as the world, starting with the element of space. The functions of the sense organs, which perceive objects like sound, are also connected to him. All of this exists for the purpose of perceiving the true nature of that Supreme Soul. 

This meaning is established by the verse: **Every form** <note>original: "rūpaṃ rūpam"</note>—that which is formed, such as the body—is reached by the Supreme Soul, who is the nature of consciousness and all-pervading. He becomes the **counterpart** <note>original: "pratirūpaḥ"</note>, existing as a reflection in all bodies. That reflected form serves for the **clear perception** <note>original: "praticakṣaṇāya"</note> or the viewing of the nature of the Supreme Soul. That Lord Indra, through his powers of illusion, is endowed with many forms like space and the other elements, and thus **moves** <note>original: "īyate"</note> or acts. This also serves for the perception of the Supreme Soul. His **ten hundred and thousand bay horses** are the functions of the sense organs, which are ready to grasp external objects. That, too, serves for the realization of his true form. Thus, this verse explains how both the gross and subtle bodies, as well as the vast universe of elements, serve as the means for knowing the ultimate Truth.

---

-> ॥ **Verse Nineteen** ॥ <-

## Hymn Text

Yoking the two bay horses to the chariot, the Radiant Shaper <note>original: "tvaṣṭā"</note> shines greatly here. Who always remains on the side of the hater, even while the wise patrons are seated [at the sacrifice]? ॥ 19 ॥

**[Word-for-word analysis]**
Yoking | the two bay horses | in the chariot | greatly | the Shaper | here | shines | Who | always | of the hater | side | stays | and | among the seated | wise ones ॥ 19 ॥

---

## Commentary (Sayana)

**Yoking** <note>original: "yujānaḥ"</note> or harnessing the **two bay horses** <note>original: "haritā"</note> to his chariot, the **Shaper** <note>original: "tvaṣṭā"</note>—the radiant Indra—shines **greatly** <note>original: "bhūri"</note> here in the three worlds...

<vocab>
**Indra**: The king of the gods, here identified with the Supreme Soul.
**Maya**: Creative power, wisdom, or the illusion that makes the One appear as many.
**Supreme Soul (Paramatman)**: The ultimate, all-pervading reality in Vedic philosophy.
**Individual Soul (Jivatman)**: The divine spark within living beings, perceived as separate due to bodily limitations.
**Bay Horses (Haris)**: Indra's traditional steeds, interpreted here as the infinite faculties of perception.
**The Shaper (Tvashta)**: A divine craftsman deity, used here as an epithet for Indra as the creator of forms.
</vocab>

Verse 19 begins by describing Indra as the "Shaper" (Tvashta) who manifests brilliantly in the world.</summary>

It marks the conclusion of the 33rd Varga (sub-section) of the 7th Adhyaya (chapter) in the 4th Ashtaka (book).</meta>

<page-num>775</page-num>
<header>Mandala 6, Adhyaya 4, Sukta 47] || Fourth Ashtaka ||</header>

## Commentary (Sayana)
<note>Continued from the previous page regarding Rig Veda 6.47.19</note>

Indra shines and is radiant in **many** <note>original: "bhūriṣu"</note> or numerous regions. Moreover, while there are many praisers like us sitting here, who else but Indra exists as the **destroyer** <note>original: "pācakaḥ"</note> or the obstructer of the side of the hating enemy? The meaning is that Indra alone always strikes down the enemies. Alternatively, the word "side" <note>original: "pakṣaḥ"</note> ending in 's' can mean "proximity." Who else but Indra sits in the **vicinity** of the hating enemy? The sense is that Indra alone, being fearless, is capable of standing near the enemy.

---

## Hymn Text
-> ॥ Verse 20 ॥ <-

We have come, O Gods, to a region **without pasture**; though the earth is wide, it has become **distressing** and narrow. O **Brihaspati**, provide the wisdom for our **search for cattle**; O **Indra**, [show] the path to the **singer** who is in this state. ॥ 20 ॥

**Word-for-Word Breakdown (Pada Patha):**
**Without pasture** <note>original: "agavyūti"</note> . The region . To . We have come . O Gods . Wide . Being . The Earth . Narrow/Distressing . Has become .
O **Brihaspati** <note>Lord of Prayer</note> . [Forward] . Provide wisdom/Act . In the **search for cattle** <note>original: "go-iṣṭau"</note> . In this way . For him who is [in this state] . For the **singer** <note>original: "jaritre"</note> . O **Indra** . The path ॥ 20 ॥

---

## Commentary (Sayana)
Regarding this verse, it is said: In a desolate forest, the seer Garga, having lost his way, praised the Gods, the Earth, Brihaspati, and Indra with this verse for his own protection. In the first part of the verse <note>original: "pāde"</note>, he addresses the Gods; in the second part, the Earth; in the third, Brihaspati; and in the final part, Indra is praised.

O Gods, we have come to a region that is **without pasture** <note>original: "agavyūti"</note>, meaning it is beyond the range of cattle and devoid of their movement. Therefore, the implied meaning is: "Protect me." Even the Earth, though normally **wide** <note>original: "urvī"</note> and vast, has become **distressing** <note>original: "aṃhūraṇā"</note>. The word <term>aṃhavaḥ</term> refers to the "assailants" or the Dasyus <note>hostile tribes or demons</note>; it has become a place where they find delight <note>original: "ramaṇā"</note>. Therefore, may the Earth also protect us. 

O <term>Brihaspati</term>, provide the wisdom or the means for the **search for cattle** <note>original: "gaviṣṭau"</note>. In this manner, O <term>Indra</term>, make known the path to me, the **singer** <note>original: "jaritre"</note> and praiser, who is currently experiencing this suffering.

-> ॥ Thus ends the thirty-third Varga of the seventh Adhyaya of the fourth Ashtaka ॥ <-

---

## Hymn Text
-> ॥ Verse 21 ॥ <-

Day by day, appearing from his dwelling, he has driven away the uniform **black** nights; the **Bull** [Indra], providing garments of light, slew **Varchin** and the Dasa **Shambara** in the **enclosure**. ॥ 21 ॥

**Word-for-Word Breakdown (Pada Patha):**
Day by day . Uniform . The other . Half/Side . The **black** [nights] . He drove away . [Away] . From the dwelling . Born .
He slew . The **Dasa** <note>enemy/demon</note> . The **Bull** [mighty one] . Providing garments . [Up/Out] . In the **enclosure** <note>original: "vraje"</note> . **Varchin** . **Shambara** . And ॥ 21 ॥

---

## Commentary (Sayana)
This very Indra, **born from his dwelling** <note>original: "sadmanaḥ jāḥ"</note>—that is, manifesting himself as the Sun from a specific region in the atmosphere—drives away the **black** colored nights, which are uniform in appearance, day by day...

<vocab>
- agavyūti: a region without pasture; a wilderness or barren land.
- bṛhaspati: "Lord of Prayer," a deity often associated with wisdom and the priesthood of the gods.
- indra: the king of the gods, associated with storms, war, and the pathfinder.
- gaviṣṭi: literally "search for cows," often used to mean a battle or a quest for wealth/light.
- jaritṛ: a singer or priest who chants the Vedic hymns.
- aṃhūraṇā: a state of distress or a "narrowing" of the way, often caused by enemies.
- śambara: a famous Dasa (demon or enemy chief) defeated by Indra.
- varcina: a Dasa chieftain or demon associated with Shambara.
- varga: a structural division of the Rig Veda text used for memorization.
</vocab>

<header>|| Rig Veda || [Book 4, Chapter 7, Section 34]</header>

[Indra] drove them away <note>original: "samapāsedhat"</note>. He turns them back. For what purpose? To illuminate the other half, the other part of the day. Indeed, of a day consisting of both day and night, the night is one part. Furthermore, that Indra, the showerer of benefits <note>original: "vṛṣabhaḥ"</note>, [destroyed] the two Dasa-demons—the destroyers of sacrificial rites—who were seeking to dwell in wealth. He slew Varchin and Shambara, the demons of those names, at **Udavraja** <note>original: "udavraje"</note>. Udavraja is a specific region where "waters go" <note>original: "udakāni vrajanti"</note>. On that day, he killed them.

-> ॥ Now the Twenty-Second Verse ॥ <-

## Hymn Text
Now, O Indra, Prastoka has given ten jars [of gold] and ten spirited horses for your worshiper. We have received from **Divodasa**, the son of **Atithigva**, the riches of **Shambara** as wealth. ॥ 22 ॥

**Word-for-Word Breakdown:**
Prastoka . Indeed . Now . For the wealth/worshiper . For your . O Indra . Ten . Jars/Containers . Ten . Spirited horses . He gave .
From Divodasa . Of Atithigva . The wealth . Belonging to Shambara . Riches . We have received . ॥ 22 ॥

## Commentary (Sayana)
In these four verses starting from here, there is a <term>praise of liberality (Danastuti)</term> regarding the gifts of King <term>Prastoka, the son of Srinjaya</term>. He is also known by the names <term>Divodasa, Ashwattha, and Atithigva</term>. O Indra, for the sake of your worshiper <note>original: "te rādhasaḥ"</note>, who is your praiser—here the possessive case is used in the sense of the dative "for"—Prastoka the King has quickly given to me, <term>Garga</term>, who praises you, ten jars filled with gold and ten spirited horses. He bestowed them. The word "Indeed" <note>original: "it"</note> is a filler. And we have received this wealth from that Divodasa—that is, from Prastoka. What kind of wealth? It is the wealth of Atithigva, belonging to that same Prastoka, which was "of Shambara," meaning it came from the demon Shambara. The sense is that you [Indra] killed Shambara and gave his wealth to him [the King].

---

-> ॥ Now the Twenty-Third Verse ॥ <-

## Hymn Text
Ten horses, ten jars, ten garments for luxurious enjoyment, and ten lumps of gold—all these I have received from **Divodasa**. ॥ 23 ॥

**Word-for-Word Breakdown:**
Ten . Horses . Ten . Jars/Containers . Ten . Garments . For enjoyment .
Ten . [Thus] . Lumps of gold . From Divodasa . I have obtained/enjoyed . ॥ 23 ॥

## Commentary (Sayana)
Ten horses, ten jars filled with gold, and garments for "luxurious enjoyment" <note>original: "adhibhojanā"</note>. "Enjoyment" is a name for wealth; thus, garments whose value is great wealth. I have obtained ten such garments and ten <note>original: "daśo"</note> lumps of gold—that is, ingots of gold. All these I have obtained from Divodasa, who is Prastoka. I have enjoyed or received them.

<vocab>
- <term>Prastoka</term>: A king, the son of Srinjaya, noted for his generosity to the Rishi Garga.
- <term>Divodasa</term>: A celebrated king in the Rig Veda, a patron of the Bharadvaja family; here identified with Prastoka.
- <term>Atithigva</term>: Literally "one who presents cows to guests"; an epithet of Divodasa.
- <term>Shambara</term>: A mountain-dwelling demon (Asura) defeated by Indra; his captured wealth is often mentioned as being gifted to Indra’s human allies.
- <term>Danastuti</term>: A "praise of giving," a specific genre of Vedic verses where a priest thanks and praises a king for his generous donations.
- <term>Garga</term>: The seer (Rishi) of this hymn, a member of the Bharadvaja family.
- <term>Kosha</term>: Literally a "pail" or "container," here interpreted by Sayana as containers filled with gold coins or dust.
- <term>Hiranyapinda</term>: Lumps or ingots of gold.
- <term>Vajina</term>: Spirited or swift horses.
</vocab>

<summary>This page features a "praise of gifts" (Danastuti) where the sage Garga lists the immense wealth—including gold, horses, and fine clothing—received from King Prastoka (Divodasa) following Indra's victory over the demon Shambara. It highlights the historical relationship between Vedic seers and their royal patrons.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the commentary on the Rig Veda, Mandala 6, Hymn 47. The previous page introduced the "praise of liberality" (Danastuti), where the Rishi Garga celebrates the gifts received from King Prastoka (also known as Divodasa). This page details specific gifts—chariots, cows, and wealth—and begins a new section of verses dedicated to the ritual blessing of a war-chariot.</meta>

[Mandala 6. Adhyaya 4. Sukta 47.] || Fourth Ashtaka || 999

-> ॥ Now the Twenty-Fourth Verse ॥ <-

## Hymn Text
Ashvattha gave ten chariots with side-horses and a hundred cows to the descendants of Atharvan, and to Payu. ॥ 24 ॥

**Word-for-Word Breakdown:**
Ten | Chariots | Having side-horses | A hundred | Cows | To the Atharvans | Ashvattha | To Payu | He gave ॥ 24 ॥

---

## Commentary (Sayana)
He gave ten <note>original: "daśa"</note>—the number ten—chariots **having side-horses** <note>original: "praṣṭimataḥ"</note>. The term "side-horse" refers to a swift support; thus, "side-horses" are those horses that carry or pull in that manner. He gave chariots equipped with them, along with a hundred <note>original: "śatam"</note> cows, to the **Atharvans** <note>original: "atharvabhyo"</note>—the Rishis of the Atharvan clan—and specifically to **Payu** <note>original: "pāyave"</note>, the son of Bharadvaja, who bears this name and represents our voice. **Ashvattha** <note>original: "aśvattho"</note>—the one "possessing horses," also known as **Prastoka** <note>original: "prastauko"</note>—is the one who gave <note>original: "adāt"</note> or bestowed these gifts.

---

-> ॥ Now the Twenty-Fifth Verse ॥ <-

## Hymn Text
The son of Srinjaya, while bestowing great wealth that is beneficial to all people, has honored the Bharadvajas. ॥ 25 ॥

**Word-for-Word Breakdown:**
Great | Wealth | Beneficial to all people | Bestowing | The Bharadvajas | The son of Srinjaya | Honored/Worshipped ॥ 25 ॥

---

## Commentary (Sayana)
**The son of Srinjaya** <note>original: "sāñjayaḥ"</note>, namely Prastoka, **honored** <note>original: "abhyayaṣṭa"</note> or worshipped us, the **Bharadvajas** <note>original: "bharadvājān"</note> (the sons of Bharadvaja), who are **bestowing** <note>original: "dadhānān"</note> or holding great <note>original: "mahi"</note> **wealth** <note>original: "rādho"</note> that is **beneficial to all people** <note>original: "viśvajanyam"</note> or good for all mankind.

-> ॥ Thus ends the thirty-fourth varga of the seventh chapter of the fourth Ashtaka ॥ <-

The verse beginning with "Lord of the Forest" is designated for use when mounting a chariot <note>original: "rathārohaṇe viniyuktā"</note>. It is also indicated in the Grihya Sutras <note>original: "Gṛ. Sū. 2. 6."</note> that with the two verses starting "O Lord of the Forest, be firm-limbed," other wooden objects are also addressed.

---

-> ॥ This is the Twenty-Sixth Verse ॥ <-

## Hymn Text
O Lord of the Forest, may you be firm-limbed, our friend, a promoter, and full of heroes. You are bound together with cow-hides; be strong! May your rider win the spoils of victory. ॥ 26 ॥

**Word-for-Word Breakdown:**
O Lord of the Forest | Firm-limbed | Indeed | May you be | Our friend | A promoter | Full of heroes |
With cow-hides | Bound together | You are | Be strong | The rider | Your | May win | Things to be conquered ॥ 26 ॥

---

## Commentary (Sayana)
O **Lord of the Forest** <note>original: "vanaspate"</note>—referring to the chariot, which is a product of the forest trees—may you be **firm-limbed** <note>original: "vīḍvaṅgo"</note>, meaning having strong parts. May you be **our friend** <note>original: "asmatsakhā"</note>, one of whom we are friends. Be a **promoter** <note>original: "prataraṇaḥ"</note>, one who causes us to prosper, and be **full of heroes** <note>original: "suvīraḥ"</note>, equipped with excellent warriors, brave soldiers, or sons. Furthermore, you **are bound together** <note>original: "saṃnaddho'si"</note>, or well-fastened, **with cow-hides** <note>original: "gobhir"</note> (products of the cow such as leather straps). Being such, **be strong** <note>original: "vīḷayasva"</note>, or make us firm. May your **rider** <note>original: "āsthātā"</note>, the warrior stationed upon you, **win** <note>original: "jayatu"</note> the **spoils of victory** <note>original: "jetvāni"</note>, namely the enemy armies that are to be conquered.

<margin>VOL. III. 9 M</margin>

<vocab>
- <term>praṣṭimataḥ</term> (having side-horses): Refers to a chariot with extra horses harnessed to the sides for speed and stability.
- <term>atharvabhyaḥ</term> (to the Atharvans): Members of a priestly family descended from the sage Atharvan.
- <term>aśvatthaḥ</term> (Ashvattha): A proper name for King Prastoka, likely meaning "one who possesses many horses."
- <term>prastokaḥ</term> (Prastoka): A king and patron of the Bharadvaja family.
- <term>sārñjayaḥ</term> (descendant of Srinjaya): A patronymic for Prastoka.
- <term>bharadvāja</term> (Bharadvaja): The famous family of seers (Rishis) to whom this hymn is revealed.
- <term>vanaspati</term> (Lord of the forest): Literally "tree," but here used as a ritual title for the wooden war-chariot.
- <term>vīḍvaṅga</term> (firm-limbed): Having a strong or sturdy frame.
- <term>gobhiḥ</term> (with cow-hides): Referring to the leather straps and reinforcements used to hold the wooden chariot together.
- <term>jetvāni</term> (spoils of victory): Literally "things to be won," referring to enemy property or territory.
</vocab>

<summary>This page concludes the praise of King Prastoka's generosity to the Bharadvaja clan and introduces a ritual blessing for a war-chariot, personifying it as a "Lord of the Forest" bound with leather.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the translation of the Rig Veda, Mandala 6, Hymn 47. While the previous verses focused on the king's generosity, verses 27 and 28 shift to the "blessing of the chariot." These verses are part of a ritual for consecrating a war-chariot, imbuing a physical object of wood and leather with divine power and cosmic significance.</meta>

॥ Rig Veda ॥ [Book 4. Chapter 7. Varga 35.]

-> ॥ Now the Twenty-Seventh Verse ॥ <-

## Hymn Text
Raised from heaven and earth, brought as strength from the lords of the forest, the force of the waters surrounded by cow-hides—worship the chariot, which is Indra’s thunderbolt, with an oblation. ॥ 27 ॥

### Word-for-Word Breakdown
From heaven | From earth | From around | Power | Raised/Extracted | From the lords of the forest | From around | Brought | Strength | Of the waters | The force | Around | By cows | Surrounded | Of Indra | The thunderbolt | With an oblation | The chariot | Worship ॥ 27 ॥

---

## Commentary (Sayana)
The power or strength <note>original: "ojas"</note> that is the essence extracted <note>original: "uddhṛtam"</note> from the heavenly world <note>original: "dyulokāt"</note> and from the earth <note>original: "bhūmeḥ"</note> is the form of this chariot. Because the chariot is made of wood, it is a transformation of the "lords of the forest" <note>original: "vanaspati-vikāratvāt"</note>. Trees are the essence of the earth, and they are nourished and grown by the waters related to the heavens. Therefore, it is logical that the chariot contains the essence of both worlds. 

The word "from around" <note>original: "pari"</note> here functions as a preposition. Furthermore, the strength <note>original: "sahaḥ"</note> brought from the trees <note>original: "vanaspatibhyaḥ"</note> is the impeller or the speed <note>original: "ojmānam"</note> of the waters. It possesses a speed like the current of water. It is "surrounded by cows" <note>original: "gobhirāvṛtam"</note>, meaning it is wrapped or covered all around with leather, which is a product of the cow. 

It is "Indra’s thunderbolt" <note>original: "indrasya vajram"</note>—or rather, a part of the thunderbolt. For it is heard in the sacred tradition: "Indra raised the thunderbolt against the demon Vritra, and it split into three parts: one third became the thunderbolt, one third became the chariot, and one third became the sacrificial post." O priest <note>original: "adhvaryo"</note>, worship the chariot characterized by these qualities with an oblation <note>original: "haviṣā"</note> such as the rice-cake <note>original: "puroḍāśa"</note>. Based on the context, it should be understood that this verse and the next are the invitatory and offering verses for the chariot-deity oblation.

-> ॥ Now the Twenty-Eighth Verse ॥ <-

## Hymn Text
The thunderbolt of Indra, the face of the Maruts' host, the womb of Mitra, the navel of Varuna. O divine chariot, enjoying this our offering of oblation, receive our sacrifices. ॥ 28 ॥

### Word-for-Word Breakdown
Of Indra | The thunderbolt | Of the Maruts | The host/face | Of Mitra | The womb/inner part | Of Varuna | The navel | That [chariot] | This | Our | Gift of oblation | Enjoying | Divine | Chariot | In return | The sacrifices | Receive ॥ 28 ॥

---

## Commentary (Sayana)
The chariot which was called a part of "Indra’s thunderbolt" <note>original: "indrasya vajraḥ"</note> in the previous verse is also the "face" or the front <note>original: "anīkam"</note> of the host of gods known as the Maruts <note>the storm gods</note>, as it is swift-moving like them. 

It is the "womb of Mitra" <note>original: "mitrasya garbho"</note>. Mitra is the god who presides over the day; the chariot is "in his womb" or within him, because the chariot travels during the day. It is the "navel of Varuna" <note>original: "varuṇasya nābhiḥ"</note>. Varuna is the god who presides over the night. Just as the navel remains still in the center of the body, the chariot remains stationary somewhere at night. 

O "divine" <note>original: "deva"</note>—O shining—Chariot, you who possess these qualities, "enjoying" or serving this "gift of oblation" <note>original: "havyadātim"</note>—this sacrificial act of ours consisting of the giving of offerings—"receive" <note>original: "pratigṛbhāya"</note> our sacrificial offerings.

<summary>These verses ritualistically transform a physical chariot into a divine entity, identifying it as a portion of Indra's thunderbolt and linking its movements to the cycles of day (Mitra) and night (Varuna).</summary>
<keywords>Rig Veda, Chariot (Ratha), Indra's Thunderbolt (Vajra), Mitra, Varuna, Maruts, Ritual Consecration, Sayana's Commentary</keywords>

<meta>This page continues the translation of the Rig Veda, Mandala 6, Hymn 47. While the previous verses focused on the consecration of the war-chariot, this page shifts the focus to the ritual empowerment of the war drum (Dundubhi) used to inspire troops and terrify enemies in battle.</meta>

Mandala 6. Anuvaka 4. Sukta 47. | Fourth Ashtaka | 779

With the following triplet of verses, the war drum is to be touched or addressed during battle. As it is stated in the ritual manuals: "One should touch the war drum while reciting the triplet beginning with 'Fill the earth and heaven with sound...'" <note>Grihya Sutra 3.11.1</note>.

---

## Hymn Text

-> ॥ This is the Twenty-Ninth Verse ॥ <-

Fill the earth and the heaven with your sound; let all that is stationed in many places, the living and the moving world, know of you. O War Drum, in harmony with Indra and the gods, drive our enemies away to a distance further than the furthest. ॥ 29 ॥

**Word-for-Word Breakdown:**
Fill with sound | The earth | And | The heaven | In many places | Of you | Let them know | Specially situated | The moving world | He | O War Drum | In harmony | With Indra | With the gods | From a distance | Further than far | Away | Drive | The enemies ॥ 29 ॥

---

## Commentary (Sayana)

O War Drum <note>original: "dundubhe"</note>, fill the earth and also the heaven with sound. Inspire them with your own roar of victory. The meaning is: produce such a sound that both worlds are filled with your noise. Furthermore, let the world that is "specially situated" <note>original: "visthitam"</note>—referring to both the stationary and the moving classes of living beings—know <note>original: "manutām"</note> or recognize your sound in many ways <note>original: "purutrā"</note>. O War Drum, being in union <note>original: "sajūḥ"</note> with Indra and the other gods, drive away <note>original: "apasedha"</note> our enemies to a distance even further than the far distance. Here, the etymological text <note>Nirukta 9.12</note> states: "The word *Dundubhi* is an imitation of the sound it makes, or it comes from 'drum' (tree) because it is made of wood that is struck, or it comes from the root *dundubhyati* meaning the action of making sound."

---

## Hymn Text

-> ॥ Now the Thirtieth Verse ॥ <-

Make [the enemy] wail; grant us strength and vigor; thunder loudly, driving away all difficulties. O War Drum, drive the misfortunes away from here. You are the fist of Indra; make us firm. ॥ 30 ॥

**Word-for-Word Breakdown:**
Make wail | Strength | Vigor | To us | Grant | Loudly | Thunder | Difficulties | Driving away | Away | Drive | O War Drum | Misfortunes | From here | Of Indra | The fist | You are | Strengthen/Make firm ॥ 30 ॥

---

## Commentary (Sayana)

O War Drum, make them wail <note>original: "ākrandaya"</note>; cause our enemies to cry out in distress. Grant <note>original: "ā dhāḥ"</note> to us strength <note>original: "balam"</note> in the form of our army and vigor <note>original: "ojaḥ"</note> in the form of physical power. Likewise, destroying <note>original: "bādhamānaḥ"</note> the "difficult paths" <note>original: "duritā"</note>—meaning hardships or sins—thunder loudly <note>original: "niḥstanihi"</note>. The root *stan* means the action of making sound. O War Drum, drive away <note>original: "apaprotha"</note> from this place the "misfortunes" <note>original: "ducchunāḥ"</note>—referring to the enemy armies whose happiness <note>original: "shunam"</note> is the cause of our misery <note>original: "duḥkha"</note>. You are the "fist of Indra" <note>original: "indrasya muṣṭiḥ"</note>; like a fist, you are the striker of enemies. Therefore, make us firm <note>original: "vīḷayasva"</note> or strengthen us.

<vocab>
**Dundubhi**: A large ancient Indian war drum.
**Indra**: The king of the gods and patron of warriors.
**Nirukta**: An ancient treatise on etymology and the meaning of Vedic words.
**Ducchunā**: Literally "bad-happiness," interpreted here as misfortunes or enemy forces that bring grief.
</vocab>

<summary>This page contains verses 29 and 30 of Hymn 47, which are ritual invocations of the war drum (Dundubhi), asking it to terrify enemies and provide divine strength to the army. The commentary by Sayana provides etymological origins for the drum's name and explains its metaphorical role as "Indra's fist."</summary>
<keywords>war drum, Dundubhi, Indra, battle ritual, Vedic weaponry, Sayana, Nirukta, protection, strength</keywords>

## Rig Veda | [Book 4. Chapter 8. Section 1.]

## Hymn Text

-> ॥ The Thirty-First Verse ॥ <-

Drive those [cattle of the enemy] toward us; bring back these [cattle] of ours. The war drum, acting as a signal-bearer, sounds loudly and repeatedly. Our men, whose horses are as swift as wings, move forward. O Indra, let our warriors in chariots be victorious. ॥ 31 ॥

**Word-for-Word Breakdown:**
Toward | Those | Drive | Back | Bring | These | Signal-possessing | War Drum | Sounds repeatedly | Together | Wing-horsed | Move | Our | Men | Our | Indra | Charioteers | Let them conquer ॥ 31 ॥

---

## Commentary (Sayana)

The first half of this verse is dedicated to the deity of the War Drum <note>original: "dundubhi-devata"</note>, while the second half is dedicated to Indra. Alternatively, both halves may be considered dedicated to Indra. 

O Indra, **drive** <note>original: "aja"</note> **those** <note>original: "amūḥ"</note> cattle that are currently held among the enemies toward us. **Bring back** <note>original: "pratyāvartaya"</note> **these** <note>original: "imāḥ"</note> cattle belonging to us which the enemies desire to seize. Furthermore, this **war drum** <note>original: "dundubhi"</note>, **possessing signals** <note>original: "ketumat"</note> or awareness—meaning it is used so that everyone may be alerted—**sounds loudly** <note>original: "vāvadīti"</note>; it makes a great noise. **Our men** <note>original: "naraḥ"</note>, who are **wing-horsed** <note>original: "aśvaparṇāḥ"</note>—meaning horse-riders or those whose horses move as swiftly as if they had wings—**move forward** <note>original: "saṃcaranti"</note> together to fight the enemy. Such being the case, O **Indra**, let **our warriors on chariots** <note>original: "rathinaḥ"</note> **conquer** <note>original: "jayantu"</note> or defeat the enemies.

-> ॥ Thus ends the twenty-fifth varga in the seventh chapter of the fourth book ॥ <-

---

By the light of the meaning of the Veda, dispelling the internal darkness of the heart, may Vidya-tirtha-maheshvara <note>The spiritual teacher or the divine form of Lord Shiva worshipped by the commentators</note> grant the four goals of human life <note>The Purusharthas: Dharma (duty), Artha (prosperity), Kama (desire), and Moksha (liberation)</note>.

**Thus ends the seventh chapter in the commentary on the Rig-Veda-Sanhita, entitled "The Illumination of the Vedic Meaning" (Madhaviya Vedartha Prakasha), composed by Sayanacharya, the minister of the empire of King Vira Bukka, the supreme lord of kings and upholder of the Vedic path.**

---

I salute Vidya-tirtha-maheshvara, whose breath is the Vedas and who created the entire universe from the Vedas.

**Now the eighth chapter begins.** Four hymns in the fourth section <note>original: "anuvāka"</note> of the sixth book <note>original: "maṇḍala"</note> have been explained. The fifth hymn, beginning with the words "**Yajñāyajñā**" <note>original: "yajñāyajñeti"</note>, consists of twenty-two verses and is attributed to the Seer Shamyu <note>original: "śaṃyu"</note>, the son of Brihaspati. The ancient index <note>Anukramani</note> describes it as: "Yajñāyajñā, having two additional verses, Shamyu, the hymn for the Prishni <note>the dappled cow/cloud goddess</note> holding grass in hand, in the Pragatha and Brihati meters..."

# Mandala 6. Chapter 4. Hymn 48. || Fourth Book || 741

## Commentary (Sayanacharya)

The introductory analysis <note>original: "Anukramani"</note> defines the complex structure of this hymn. The meters used are varied: the Great Satobrhati <note>original: "Mahasatobrhati"</note> and two Great Barhata-Barhata verse-pairs <note>original: "Mahabarhatabarhata-pragathas"</note> are dedicated to Agni. The "Hump-backed" <note>term: "Kakubh" - a meter with a longer middle line</note> verse-pair, the "Forward-Ushnih" <note>term: "Puroushnih"</note>, the Brhati, and the Atijagati meters are dedicated to the Maruts. Regarding the final three verses, their deities are as indicated by their characteristic marks. The Kakubh verse-pair, the Puroushnih, and the Brhati meters are dedicated to Pushan. The Brhati, the Great Brhati, the "Barley-waisted" <note>term: "Yavamadhya" - a meter that is wider in the middle</note> meter, and the final Anushtubh are dedicated to the Maruts, or alternatively to Heaven and Earth, or to Prishni.

The verse beginning with "At every sacrifice" <note>original: "yajñā-yajñā vaḥ"</note> is in the Brhati meter, as it possesses the required characteristics of having feet of eight, twelve, and eight syllables. The second verse is in the Satobrhati meter, following the rule that odd-numbered feet are twelve syllables and even-numbered are eight. The third and fourth verses are Brhati and Satobrhati respectively. The fifth is Brhati, and the sixth is the Great Satobrhati <note>original: "Mahasatobrhati"</note>. This specific meter consists of three feet of eight syllables and two feet of twelve syllables. The seventh is the Great Brhati, which has four feet of eight syllables and one foot of twelve. The eighth is also a Great Satobrhati, composed of three feet of eight syllables and two of twelve. The ninth is Brhati and the tenth is Satobrhati. These first ten verses are dedicated to the deity **Agni**.

The eleventh verse is in the Kakubh meter. If the middle foot is twelve syllables and is flanked by two feet of eight syllables, it is called Kakubh. The twelfth is Satobrhati, and the thirteenth is Puroushnih. The Puroushnih meter has a first foot of twelve syllables and the second and third of eight syllables. The fourteenth is Brhati, and the fifteenth is Atijagati, consisting of fifty-two syllables. These five verses (11–15) are dedicated to the **Maruts**. For the three verses starting with the thirteenth, the deities may also be Indra and others as indicated by the text.

The sixteenth is Kakubh, the seventeenth is Satobrhati, the eighteenth is Puroushnih, and the nineteenth is Brhati. For these four (16–19), the deity is **Pushan**. The twentieth is Brhati, and the twenty-first is a Barley-waisted Great Brhati. This meter has two initial feet of eight syllables, a third of twelve, and fourth and fifth feet of eight syllables. These two verses (20–21) constitute a hymn to **Prishni**, the mother of the Maruts. The twenty-second is in the Anushtubh meter, dedicated to either Prishni or Heaven and Earth. The ritual application <note>original: "viniyoga"</note> of this hymn follows the characteristics of its verses. In the "Agni-Marut" litany, the verse "At every sacrifice" serves as the opening verse-pair <note>original: "stotriya-pragatha"</note>. This is indicated in the ritual manuals <note>original: "Ashvalayana Shrauta Sutra 5.20"</note>: "The two verse-pairs 'At every sacrifice for Agni' and 'The god who is the giver of wealth' are the opening and corresponding pairs."

---

## Hymn Text

-> ॥ Here follows the first verse ॥ <-

At **every sacrifice** for your **Agni**, with **speech upon speech** for his **strength**,
We shall loudly **praise** the **immortal** **Knower of Beings**, like a **dear friend**. ॥ 1 ॥

-> [Word-by-Word Analysis] <-

At-every-sacrifice | for-you | for-Agni | with-speech-upon-speech | and | for-strength |
Loudly-praise | we | the-immortal | the-knower-of-beings | the-dear | friend | like | I-shall-praise ॥ 1 ॥

---

## Commentary (Sayanacharya)

O reciters of praise! For you, at **every sacrifice** <note>original: "yajñā-yajñā"</note>—meaning in all ritual acts—perform a hymn of praise with **speech upon speech** <note>original: "girā-girā"</note>—consisting of words of adoration—for **Agni**, who is **strengthened** <note>original: "dakṣase"</note> or fully grown. The word "and" <note>original: "ca"</note> in the text indicates a change in the sequence...

<vocab>
**Yajña**: Sacrifice or ritual offering.
**Agni**: The sacred fire and the messenger god who carries offerings to heaven.
**Maruts**: The storm deities, brothers who accompany Indra and are sons of Prishni.
**Pushan**: A solar deity associated with journeys, nourishment, and the protection of cattle.
**Prishni**: The cow-goddess representing the dappled clouds and the mother of the Maruts.
**Bṛhatī**: A common Vedic meter usually totaling 36 syllables.
**Pragātha**: A style of singing where two verses are expanded into three for chanting.
**Jātavedas**: A common title for Agni, meaning "he who knows all created beings" or "he from whom wealth is born."
</vocab>
