# Rig Veda [Book 4, Chapter 5, Section 53.] || Fourth Book || Page 819

## Hymn Text

<note>RV 6.52.17 (continued from previous page)</note>
The sacred grass is spread <note>original: "stṛṇīre"</note>; while the **fire** is **kindled** <note>original: "samidhane agnau"</note>, I worship with a **sublime hymn** and **profound reverence**. O **worshipful Universal Gods**, today in **this** our **sacrifice** <note>original: "vidathe"</note>, **rejoice** in the **oblation**. ॥ 17 ॥

**Word-for-word breakdown (Pada-patha):**
Spread; on the sacred grass; kindled; in the fire; with a sublime hymn; with great; reverence; I worship; in this; our; today; in the sacrifice; O worshipful ones; Universal; Gods; in the oblation; rejoice. ॥ 17 ॥

---

## Commentary (Sayana)

O **Universal Gods** <note>original: "viśve devāḥ"</note>, while the sacred grass <term>Barhis: The ritual bed of darbha grass where gods are invited to sit</term> is spread upon the altar and while the fire is kindled, I **worship** <note>original: "vivāse"</note> or serve you with this hymn and with **great reverence** <note>original: "mahā namasā"</note>. O **worshipful ones** <note>original: "yajatrā"</note>, on **this day**, in **this** our **sacrifice**, **rejoice**—meaning be satisfied—**with the oblation** <note>original: "haviṣi"</note> we have offered. <note>Sayana notes that "haviṣi" (in the oblation) is a locative case used here with the meaning of the instrumental case (by means of the oblation).</note>

-> ॥ Thus ends the sixteenth section (varga) of the eighth chapter of the fourth book. ॥ <-

---

## Hymn Text

<note>Introduction to Sukta 53</note>
The fourth hymn of ten verses beginning with **"Vayam u tva"** is authored by the seer Bharadvaja and is dedicated to the deity **Pushan**. The verse beginning with "Yaṃ pūṣann" is in the Anushtubh meter, while the remaining verses are in the Gayatri meter. As stated in the Index <note>original: "Anukramani"</note>: "The ten verses to Pushan beginning with 'Vayam'; the verse 'Yaṃ pūṣann' is Anushtubh." This hymn is to be recited by those **seeking wealth** or those **going on a journey**. This is indicated in the Grihya Sutra (3.7): "One about to set out on a journey for business should recite 'Vayam u tva pathaspate'."

-> ॥ Here follows the first verse ॥ <-

<note>RV 6.53.1</note>
We yoke **thee**, O **Lord of the Path**, like a **chariot** for the **winning of wealth**; for our **sacred work**, O **Pushan**, we have joined with thee. ॥ 1 ॥

**Word-for-word breakdown (Pada-patha):**
We; indeed; thee; of the path; O Lord; a chariot; like; for the winning of wealth; for sacred work; O Pushan; we have joined. ॥ 1 ॥

---

## Commentary (Sayana)

O **Lord of the Path** <note>original: "pathaspate"</note>, protector of the road, O **Pushan**, for our **sacred work** <note>original: "dhiye"</note> and for the **winning of food** or wealth, we **join with thee** <note>original: "ayujmahi"</note>—meaning we turn thee toward us—just as one **yokes a chariot** <note>original: "rathaṃ na"</note> for a journey. The word **"u"** is a particle used here to fill the meter.

---

## Hymn Text

-> ॥ Now follows the second verse ॥ <-

<note>RV 6.53.2</note>
Lead **us** toward **heroic wealth** beneficial to men, to a **hero** who bestows **generous gifts**, to a **kindly master of the house**. ॥ 2 ॥

**Word-for-word breakdown (Pada-patha):**
Toward; us; beneficial to men; wealth; a hero; one who bestows generous gifts; kindly; the master of the house; lead. ॥ 2 ॥

---

## Commentary (Sayana)

O Pushan, **lead us** <note>original: "naya"</note> to obtain **wealth** <note>original: "vasu"</note> that is **beneficial to men** <note>original: "naryaṃ"</note>. Lead us to a **hero** <note>original: "vīraṃ"</note> who drives away poverty, and to one who **bestows generous gifts** <note>original: "prayatadakṣiṇam"</note>—meaning one who has given wealth to others before, or one whose sacrificial gift is pure. Lead us to such a **kindly** or desirable **master of the house** <note>original: "gṛhapatiṃ"</note>.

---

## Hymn Text

-> ॥ Now follows the third verse ॥ <-

<note>RV 6.53.3</note>
O **glowing** Pushan, urge even the **non-giver** to be **generous**; soften the **mind** of the **miserly one**. ॥ 3 ॥

**Word-for-word breakdown (Pada-patha):**
The non-giver; even; O glowing one; O Pushan; to giving; urge; of the miser; thoroughly; know; soft; the mind. ॥ 3 ॥

---

<vocab>
- Universal Gods (Viśve Devāḥ): A collective group of deities invoked together in Vedic rituals.
- Pushan (Pūṣan): A solar deity associated with journeys, the protection of cattle, and the discovery of lost things.
- Lord of the paths (Pathaspati): An epithet of Pushan as the guide for travelers and souls.
- Winning of wealth/food (Vājasāti): A common Vedic prayer goal, referring to both physical sustenance and prosperity.
- Pani (Paṇi): A class of mythological or historical beings characterized by their stinginess and hoarding of wealth/cattle.
- Glowing (Āghṛṇi): An epithet for Pushan, meaning radiant or shining with heat.
- Sacrificial fee/gift (Dakṣiṇā): The gift given to priests or the needy during a ritual, essential for its completion.
</vocab>

# Rig Veda || [Book 4, Chapter 8, Section 18.]

## Commentary (Sayana)

<note>This is the conclusion of the commentary for verse 3</note>
O **glowing** <note>original: "āghṛṇe"</note> **Pushan**, inspire even the man who is **unwilling to give** <note>original: "aditsantaṃ"</note> to bestow gifts upon us. Impel him! Soften the mind and the heart of the **Pani** <term>Pani: A class of miserly individuals, often described as merchants or demons who hoard wealth and cattle</term>, even if he is a **usurer** <note>original: "vārdhuṣikasya"</note> or a **greedy person**. Make him soft for the purpose of giving.

---

## Hymn Text

-> ॥ Verse 4 ॥ <-

Clear the **paths** for the **winning of wealth**; strike down the **obstructors**. O **powerful one**, may our **prayers** be **successful**. ॥ 4 ॥

**Word-for-word breakdown (Pada-patha):**
Apart; the paths; for the winning of wealth; clear; apart; the obstructors; strike down; may they be successful; O powerful one; our; prayers. ॥ 4 ॥

## Commentary (Sayana)

O **Pushan**, you who possess **manifest power** <note>original: "ugrodgīrṇabala"</note>, clear the **paths** <note>original: "patho"</note> for the **attainment of food** <note>original: "vajasataye"</note>. Make them purified. The meaning is: "Separate and reveal those paths by which we may travel to obtain wealth." Strike down the **obstructors** <note>original: "mṛdho"</note>, such as thieves and others. Repel them. Furthermore, may our **prayers** <note>original: "dhiyaḥ"</note>—that is, the ritual actions we perform to obtain food—be **successful** <note>original: "sādhantām"</note>. May they be accomplished and bear fruit.

---

## Hymn Text

-> ॥ Verse 5 ॥ <-

O **wise one**, pierce through the **hearts** of the **Panis** with your **goad**. Then make them **subject** to us. ॥ 5 ॥

**Word-for-word breakdown (Pada-patha):**
Around; pierce; of the Panis; with the goad; the hearts; O wise one; then; them; to us; make subject. ॥ 5 ॥

## Commentary (Sayana)

O **wise** <note>original: "kave"</note> **Pushan**, with your **goad** <note>original: "ārayā"</note>—which refers to a pointed iron staff or a cattle-prod—**pierce through** the hearts of the **Panis**, the greedy merchants. Pierce them all around. The meaning is: "Remove their hardness of heart." Thereafter, make these **Panis subject** <note>original: "randhaya"</note> to us; bring them under our control.

-> ॥ Thus ends the seventeenth section (varga) of the eighth chapter of the fourth book. ॥ <-

---

## Hymn Text

-> ॥ Verse 6 ॥ <-

O **Pushan**, prick with the **goad**; seek that which is **dear** in the **Pani's heart**. Then make him **subject** to us. ॥ 6 ॥

**Word-for-word breakdown (Pada-patha):**
Apart; O Pushan; with the goad; prick; of the Pani; seek; in the heart; what is dear; then; him; to us; make subject. ॥ 6 ॥

## Commentary (Sayana)

O **Pushan**, with your **prod** <note>original: "pratodena"</note>, prick the heart of the **Pani** or merchant. Pierce it thoroughly. Seek that which is **dear** to us—meaning wealth—within the heart of that Pani. Create in him the desire that "this must be given." After that, make him **subject** to us; bring him under our power.

---

## Hymn Text

-> ॥ Verse 7 ॥ <-

O **wise one**, tear and make **shredded** the **hearts** of the **Panis**. Then make them **subject** to us. ॥ 7 ॥

**Word-for-word breakdown (Pada-patha):**
Tear; shredded; make; of the Panis; the hearts; O wise one; then; them; to us; make subject. ॥ 7 ॥

<vocab>

- **Pani** (Paṇi): A class of stingy or greedy people/demons, often associated with withholding wealth or cows.
- **Vajasati** (Vājasāti): Winning of wealth, food, or strength.
- **Hridaya** (Hṛdaya): Heart.

# Rig Veda || Fourth Book || 821

<note>This section concludes the commentary for verse 7 of Hymn 53</note>
O wise poet, **Pushan**, scratch the hearts of the **Panis** <term>Panis: A class of wealthy, miserly individuals in the Rig Veda who hoard cows and wealth, refusing to offer sacrifices or give to others</term>. Scratch them. Having scratched them, make them **scattered** <note>original: "kikirā"</note> and loosened. The meaning is: make them soft [towards us]. ... [This refers to] another ritual vow.

---

-> ॥ Verse 8 ॥ <-

## Hymn Text
O **Pushan**, O **glowing one**, with that **goad** <note>original: "ārām"</note> which you carry, which **impels prayer**, with that, scratch the **heart** of every [miser] and make it **soft**. ॥ 8 ॥

**Word-for-word breakdown:**
Which; O Pushan; impelling prayer; goad; you carry; O glowing one; with that; of everyone; heart; scratch; scattered/soft; make. ॥ 8 ॥

## Commentary (Sayana)
O **glowing one** <note>original: "āghṛṇa"</note>, you who are possessed of manifest light, O **Pushan**, you carry in your hand a **goad** <note>original: "ārām"</note> that is the **impeller of prayer** <note>original: "brahmacodanīm"</note>, or the stimulator of food. With that instrument, **scratch** <note>original: "ālikha"</note> the **heart** of every greedy person. Make them **scattered** <note>original: "kikirā"</note>, that is, make them loose and soft [in their resolve to hoard wealth].

---

-> ॥ Verse 9 ॥ <-

## Hymn Text
O **glowing one**, that **goad** of yours which is **braided with cow-hair** and is the **procurer of cattle**—of that, we seek your **favor**. ॥ 9 ॥

**Word-for-word breakdown:**
Which; your; goad; braided with cow-hair; O glowing one; procurer of cattle; of that; your; favor; we seek. ॥ 9 ॥

## Commentary (Sayana)
O **glowing one**, O **Pushan**, that **goad** <note>original: "aṣṭrā"</note> of yours is **braided with cow-hair** <note>original: "goopaśā"</note>. The word *opaśa* refers to that which is bound or decorated; thus, it is a goad whose ornaments are made of cow-hair. Because of this, it is the **procurer of cattle**. We **seek** <note>original: "īmahe"</note> or pray for the **favor** <note>original: "sumnam"</note> or happiness associated with that [instrument] of yours.

---

-> ॥ Verse 10 ॥ <-

## Hymn Text
And also, make our **prayer** one that **wins cattle**, **wins horses**, **wins food**, and is **full of heroes**, for our **enjoyment**. ॥ 10 ॥

**Word-for-word breakdown:**
And; our; winning cattle; prayer; winning horses; winning food; and; full of heroes; make; for enjoyment. ॥ 10 ॥

## Commentary (Sayana)
Furthermore, O **Pushan**, make **our prayer** <note>original: "dhiyaṃ"</note>—which can mean either our intellect or our ritual action—such that it is a **winner of cattle**, a **winner of horses**, and a **winner of food**. Also, make it **full of heroes** <note>original: "nṛvat"</note>, meaning it grants us the companionship of heroic men or sons. Make this so for our **enjoyment** <note>original: "vītaye"</note>, which is to say, for our consumption and use.

---

-> ॥ Thus ends the eighteenth section of the eighth chapter of the fourth book ॥ <-

The fifth hymn, beginning with "Sam Pushan," consists of ten verses. It was seen by the seer **Bharadvaja**, is dedicated to the deity **Pushan**, and is composed in the **Gayatri** meter. It is introduced with the phrase "Sam Pushan." This hymn is to be recited by a person seeking **lost property**. This is indicated in the Grihya Sutras: "One who desires to find what is lost, or one who has lost his way, should recite 'Sam Pushan viduṣā...'" <note>original: "Gṛhya Sūtra 3. 7. 1"</note>

# Rig Veda || Book 4 || 922

<header>९२२ ॥ Rig Veda ॥ [Book 4, Adhyaya 8, Varga 19]</header>

## Hymn 54: To Pushan

-> ॥ Verse 1 ॥ <-

### Hymn Text

O **Pushan**, lead us together with a **knowing one** who **instructs** [us] **straightaway**, and who shall say, "It is **exactly here**." ॥ 1 ॥

**Word-for-word breakdown:**
Together; O Pushan; with a knowing one; lead; who; straightaway; instructs; who; indeed; this/here; [quote marker]; says. ॥ 1 ॥

---

-> ॥ Verse 2 ॥ <-

### Hymn Text

May we go with **Pushan**, who **oversees** the **houses**, and who shall also say, "**These** [animals] are the **very ones**." ॥ 2 ॥

**Word-for-word breakdown:**
Together; and; with Pushan; may we go; who; the houses; oversees; these; indeed; [quote marker]; and; says. ॥ 2 ॥

---

-> ॥ Verse 3 ॥ <-

### Hymn Text

The **wheel** of **Pushan** is not **damaged**, nor does the **vessel** fall down; nor does his **rim** waver. ॥ 3 ॥

**Word-for-word breakdown:**
Of Pushan; the wheel; not; is damaged; not; the vessel; down; falls; nor; his; wavers; the rim. ॥ 3 ॥

---

-> ॥ Verse 4 ॥ <-

### Hymn Text

He who has **served** him with an **oblation**—**Pushan** does not **neglect** him; he is the **first** to find **wealth**. ॥ 4 ॥

**Word-for-word breakdown:**
Who; him; with an oblation; served; not; him; Pushan; also; neglects; first; finds; wealth. ॥ 4 ॥

---

## Commentary (Sayana)

**1.** O **Pushan**, O **nourishing god** <note>original: "poṣaka deva"</note>, lead us together with—that is, make us meet—that person who is **knowing** <note>original: "viduṣā"</note>, who knows [the way]. Who is this knower? The one who **instructs** <note>original: "anuśāsati"</note> us **straightaway** <note>original: "añjasā"</note> or by the straight path, pointing out the means to recover lost property. And who says, "**This** is your lost **wealth**," showing where the lost property is. The word "knower" is connected to this action.

**2.** May we, favored by **Pushan**, meet with that person who **oversees** <note>original: "abhiśāsati"</note> or points out the **houses** in which our lost **cattle** <note>original: "paśavaḥ"</note> are staying. This person should be one who says, "**These** are your lost cattle, and they are staying right here."

**3.** The **wheel** <note>original: "cakram"</note> of **Pushan**, the nourisher, which is his weapon, is not **damaged**; it is not destroyed. The **vessel** <note>original: "kośaḥ"</note> or the hub of this wheel does not fall down or fail. Furthermore, the **rim** <note>original: "paviḥ"</note> or the edge of the wheel does not **waver** <note>original: "vyathate"</note>, meaning it does not become **blunt** <note>original: "kuṃṭhībhavati"</note> or ineffective. The underlying intent is: "By using that wheel-weapon, may you kill the thieves and reveal our wealth."

**4.** Whosoever, the sacrificer, has **served** <note>original: "avidhat"</note> or worshiped this **Pushan** with an **oblation** <note>original: "haviṣā"</note> such as a **cooked rice offering** <term>Charu: A dish of grain, usually rice or barley, boiled with milk or water for gods</term> or a **sacrificial cake** <term>Purodasha: A cake made of ground ghee-moistened rice or barley offered in fire</term>, **Pushan** does not **neglect** <note>original: "mṛṣyate"</note> him. The word "also" <note>original: "api"</note> here implies "even slightly"—he does not harm him even in the slightest. Consequently, that sacrificer, being **first** or foremost, **finds** or obtains **wealth**.

<summary>This page contains the first four verses of Hymn 54 addressed to Pushan, focusing on his ability to guide people to lost property and cattle, and the invincibility of his divine wheel. Sayana’s commentary explains these verses as prayers for the recovery of stolen goods and the protection of the sacrificer.</summary>
<keywords>Pushan, lost wealth, cattle, divine wheel, Sayana, guide, oblation, protector, thieves</keywords>

# Rig Veda || Book 4 || 823

<header>Mandal 6, Anuvaka 5, Sukta 54.] || Fourth Ashtaka ||</header>

->॥ Verse 5 ॥<-

## Hymn Text
May **Pushan** follow our **cattle**; may **Pushan** protect our **horses**; may **Pushan** grant us **sustenance**. ॥ 5 ॥

**Word-for-word breakdown:**
Pushan; cattle; after; let [him] go; our; Pushan; let [him] protect; horses; Pushan; food/wealth; let [him] grant; to us. ॥ 5 ॥

---

## Commentary (Sayana)
**Pushan**, the **nourishing god** <note>original: "poṣako devo"</note>, should follow after our cattle for the sake of their protection. And may that **Pushan** protect our **horses** <note>original: "arvato'śvān"</note> from thieves. Likewise, may **Pushan** grant—that is, provide—**food** <note>original: "vājaṃ"</note> to us.

->॥ This concludes the nineteenth Varga of the eighth Adhyaya in the fourth Ashtaka. ॥<-

---

->॥ Verse 6 ॥<-

## Hymn Text
O **Pushan**, go forth after the **cattle** of the **sacrificer** who **presses [Soma]**, and also of us who are **praising** [you]. ॥ 6 ॥

**Word-for-word breakdown:**
O Pushan; after; forth; cattle; go; of the sacrificer; who presses [Soma]; of us; who praise; also. ॥ 6 ॥

---

## Commentary (Sayana)
O **Pushan**, follow after the cattle—the **livestock** <note>original: "paśūn"</note>—of the **sacrificer** <note>original: "yajamānasya"</note> who is performing the **Soma libation** <note>original: "somābhiṣavaṃ kurvato"</note>. Go after them for the sake of protection. And also <note>original: "uta api ca"</note> follow the cattle of us who are performing **hymns of praise** <note>original: "stotram"</note> regarding you.

---

->॥ Verse 7 ॥<-

## Hymn Text
Let **none** be **lost**; let **none** be **injured**; let **none** be **broken** in a **pit**. Then come [back] with them **unharmed**. ॥ 7 ॥

**Word-for-word breakdown:**
Let none; be lost; let none; be injured; let none; [particle for 'together']; be broken; in a pit; then; with the unharmed [cows]; come. ॥ 7 ॥

---

## Commentary (Sayana)
O **Pushan**, let our **cattle-wealth** <note>original: "godhanaṃ"</note> not be lost. The words *mākiḥ* and *mākīm* are used here as particles of prohibition <note>equivalent to "let not"</note>. Let them not be **injured** <note>original: "riṣat"</note>—that is, let them not be harmed by **tigers** and other predators. And let them not be **broken** <note>original: "saṃśārī"</note> by falling into a **pit** <note>original: "kevaṭe kūpe"</note> or a well. Let there be no harm even by such an accident. This being so, come back at **eventide** <note>original: "sāyaṃkāla"</note> together with the **uninjured** <note>original: "ariṣṭābhiḥ"</note> cows.

---

->॥ Verse 8 ॥<-

## Hymn Text
We **pray** for **wealth** from **Pushan**, who **hears** [us], the **impeller**, who **possesses undiminished wealth**, and who is the **lord** of all. ॥ 8 ॥

**Word-for-word breakdown:**
Who hears; Pushan; we; the impeller; of undiminished wealth; the lord; of wealth; we pray. ॥ 8 ॥

---

## Commentary (Sayana)
We **pray for** <note>original: "īmahe" meaning "we ask for"</note> **riches** <note>original: "rayo dhanāni"</note> from the god **Pushan**, who is characterized thus: he **hears** our hymns; he is the **impeller** <note>original: "īryam"</note>, meaning the one who drives away **poverty**; he **possesses undiminished wealth** <note>original: "anaṣṭavedasam"</note>, meaning his riches never perish; and he is the **ruler** <note>original: "īśānam"</note> or lord of everything.

<summary>In these concluding verses of Hymn 54, Pushan is invoked as a divine herdsman who protects cattle and horses from theft, predators, and accidents (like falling into pits), ensuring the wealth of the sacrificer remains undiminished.</summary>

# Rig Veda || Page 924

<header>|| Rig Veda || [Book 4. Chapter 8. Section 21.]</header>

In the Four-Month sacrifices <note>The *Caturmasya*, a series of seasonal Vedic sacrifices performed every four months.</note>, during the ritual for the All-Gods (*Vaishvadeva*), when offering the oblation to Pushan, the verse **O Pushan, in your service** is used as the invitatory prayer <note>original: "anuvākyā"</note>. This is indicated in the ritual manuals: **"Fair today, O Savitar, fair tomorrow; O Pushan, in your service we..."** (Asvalayana Shrauta Sutra 2. 16).

---

## Hymn Text

-> ॥ This is the ninth verse of the hymn ॥ <-

O **Pushan**, in your **service** <note>original: "vrate"; refers to the sacred law or ritual activities dedicated to the god.</note> may we **never suffer harm** <note>original: "na riṣyema"</note> at any time. We are your **praisers** here. ॥ 9 ॥

**Word-for-word breakdown:**
O Pushan; your; in service/rite; we; not; may suffer harm; at any time; ever; praisers; your; here; we are. ॥ 9 ॥

## Commentary (Sayana)

O **Pushan**, the Nourisher: while we are abiding in your **service**—that is, in your ritual actions—may **we**, at **any time** whatsoever, **never suffer harm**. That is, may we not be injured. Being thus protected, **we** are your **praisers** here in this sacrifice; we exist as those who sing your glory.

---

## Hymn Text

-> ॥ Now the tenth verse ॥ <-

May **Pushan** place his **right hand** around us from **beyond**; let him **drive back** to us what was **lost**. ॥ 10 ॥

**Word-for-word breakdown:**
Around; Pushan; from beyond; hand; let [him] place; the right; again; to us; the lost; [let him] drive/bring back. ॥ 10 ॥

## Commentary (Sayana)

May **Pushan**, the nourishing god, place his **right hand** around us from **beyond**—meaning from a distant place, or to prevent cattle from wandering into dangerous areas inhabited by thieves and tigers. Let his hand be a "covering" or a "preventer" of danger. Furthermore, let him **drive back** to **us** our **lost** property, such as cattle. Let it come back; let him cause it to return.

-> ॥ This concludes the twentieth Varga of the eighth Adhyaya in the fourth Ashtaka. ॥ <-

---

## Sukta Introduction

The sixth hymn of this section, beginning with "Come hither," consists of six verses. The Seer is **Bharadvaja**, the meter is **Gayatri**, and the deity is **Pushan**. It is cataloged in the Index as: **"Come hither, six [verses]"**. Its ritual application has already been described.

---

## Hymn Text

-> ॥ The first verse of the hymn ॥ <-

Come hither, **Son of Deliverance**, O **Glowing One**; let us **journey together**. Be the **charioteer** of our **Order** <note>original: "ṛtasya"; refers to the cosmic truth or the sacrifice itself.</note>. ॥ 1 ॥

**Word-for-word breakdown:**
Hither; come; to you [two]; of deliverance; son; O glowing one; together; let us journey; charioteer; of truth/sacrifice; our; be. ॥ 1 ॥

## Commentary (Sayana)

O **Son of Deliverance** <note>original: "vimuco napāt"</note>. This refers to the Lord of Procreation (*Prajapati*), who "delivers" or releases all creatures from himself at the time of creation. O **Pushan**, son of that Prajapati, O **Glowing One** whose radiance has arrived: come to **you** <note>Sayana notes a grammatical peculiarity here, suggesting "you" refers to the singer reaching the god</note>. The word **vam** refers to the singer who goes toward and attains praise. O you who go to the singer, come to me! Let us **journey together**; let us meet and go together.

<vocab>
- **Pushan** (Pūṣan): A solar deity associated with nourishment, the finding of lost things, and the safe passage of souls and cattle.
- **Vrata** (Vrata): A sacred vow, rite, or the established order of a deity's activity.
- **Son of Deliverance** (Vimuco Napāt): A unique title for Pushan; it suggests his role in "untying" the bonds of the path or "releasing" life.
- **Rta** (Ṛta): The fundamental Law of the universe, often manifested in the physical world as the regular path of the sun and stars, and in the social world as the correct performance of sacrifice.
</vocab>

[Mandal 6. Chapter 5. Hymn 55.] || Fourth Volume || 925

May you, being such a one, be the charioteer <note>original: "rathī"; here meaning the leader or driver</note> and the swift guide of our immortal sacrifice. This being so, the oblation that is to be offered is also obtained by you; this is the intended meaning.

---

-> ॥ Now the Second Verse ॥ <-

## Hymn Text
We seek **Pushan**, the **best of charioteers**, the one with **braided hair**, the **lord** of **great bounty**, and our **friend** for the sake of **wealth**. ॥ 2 ॥

**Word-for-word breakdown:**
The best of charioteers; the one with braided hair; the lord; of bounty; great; of wealth; friend; we seek. ॥ 2 ॥

## Commentary (Sayana)
The word **best of charioteers** <note>original: "rathītamam"</note> means one who is an exceptional driver or, alternatively, an exceedingly swift leader. **The one with braided hair** <note>original: "kapardinam"</note> refers to one who possesses a *kaparda*, or a braided tuft of hair. He is the **lord** or master of **great bounty** <note>original: "maho rādhasaḥ"</note>—wealth that is obtained through him. We **seek** or pray to such a **Pushan**, who is our **friend** and ally, for the sake of **wealth** and riches.

---

-> ॥ Now the Third Verse ॥ <-

## Hymn Text
You are a **stream** of **wealth**, O **Radiant One**; you are a **heap** of **treasure**, O **goat-horsed** god; you are the **friend** of every **wise** worshiper. ॥ 3 ॥

**Word-for-word breakdown:**
Of wealth; a stream; you are; O Radiant One; of treasure; a heap; O goat-horsed; of the wise; of the wise; friend. ॥ 3 ॥

## Commentary (Sayana)
O **Radiant One** <note>original: "āghṛṇe"; meaning one who possesses arrived or inherent light</note>, O **Pushan**, you **are a stream** of **wealth**. That is, you are like a flowing current, meaning you grant abundant wealth to your praisers without interruption. O **goat-horsed** god <note>original: "ajāśva"</note>, you for whom goats—rather than horses—perform the duty of pulling the chariot: you are also a **heap** or a collection of **treasure**. This means that all gathered wealth resides within you. Furthermore, you are the **friend** and ally of every **wise** <note>original: "dhīvataḥ"</note> person who offers prayers and hymns.

---

-> ॥ Now the Fourth Verse ॥ <-

## Hymn Text
Let us **now praise Pushan**, the **goat-horsed** god, the **strong and vigorous** one, who is called the **paramour** of his **sister**. ॥ 4 ॥

**Word-for-word breakdown:**
Pushan; now; goat-horsed; near; let [us] praise; the vigorous; of the sister; who; paramour; is called. ॥ 4 ॥

## Commentary (Sayana)
Let us **now**, on this day, **praise** <note>original: "upastoṣāma"</note> the god **Pushan**, the Nourisher, who has **goats** as his vehicle and is **strong** or full of food <note>original: "vājinam"</note>. The connection is to that **Pushan** who **is called** the **paramour** <note>original: "jāraḥ"</note> or secret lover of his **sister**, the Dawn <note>original: "uṣasaḥ"</note>.

---

-> ॥ Now the Fifth Verse ॥ <-

## Hymn Text
May the **suitor** of the **mother**, the **blameless** one, the **paramour** of the **sister**, the **brother** of **Indra**, and **my friend**, hear us. ॥ 5 ॥

**Word-for-word breakdown:**
Of the mother; the suitor; the blameless; of the sister; the paramour; let [him] hear; us; the brother; of Indra; the friend; mine. ॥ 5 ॥

426 || Rig Veda || [Section 4, Chapter 8, Verse 22]

I have spoken to Pushan, the suitor and husband of the bowing Night, his mother. I praise him. May Pushan, the lover of his sister Dawn <note>original: "uṣaso jāraśca"</note>, hear our hymns. May Pushan, who was born alongside his brother Indra, be a companion and a friend to me, the singer of praises.

---

## Hymn Text

-> ॥ Now the Sixth Verse ॥ <-

**May the goat-horsed ones, carrying him, bring the divine Pushan—who is the refuge of the people—in his chariot. ॥ 6 ॥**

> **आ । अ॒जाश्वः॑ । पू॒षण॑म् । र॒थे । नि॒ऽमृभ्रः॑ । ते । जन॒ऽश्रिय॑म् । दे॒वम् । व॒ह॒न्तु॒ । बिभ्र॑तः ॥ ६ ॥**

## Commentary (Sayana)

The **goat-horsed ones** <note>original: "ajāsaḥ... ajāśchāgā"</note> refer to the goats that are famously the steeds of Pushan. The **fasteners** <note>original: "nimṛmbhā"</note> are those who bind or yoke the goats to the vehicle. May they, bearing him in his **chariot**, bring that **divine** Pushan who is the **refuge of the people**. The term **refuge of the people** <note>original: "janaśriyam"</note> describes one whom the assembly of worshipers resorts to or approaches. May they lead him here.

-> ॥ Thus ends the twenty-first section of the eighth chapter of the fourth volume ॥ <-

---

## Hymn Text

The seventh hymn of this section, beginning with "He who points to him," consists of six verses. The seer is Bharadvaja and the deity is Pushan. The meter of the final verse is *Anushtubh*, while the first five are in the *Gayatri* meter. This has been noted in the index. The ritual application has already been mentioned.

-> ॥ There, the First Verse ॥ <-

**Whoever points to him, saying "Pushan is the eater of porridge," by that man no other god needs to be praised. ॥ 1 ॥**

> **यः । ए॒नम् । आ॒ऽदि॒देश॑ति । क॒र॒म्भऽअ॑त् । इति॑ । पू॒षण॑म् । न । तेन॑ । दे॒वः । आ॒ऽदिशे॑ ॥ १ ॥**

## Commentary (Sayana)

Whatever worshiper points to this Pushan, the nourisher, and praises him by saying he is the **eater of porridge** <note>original: "karambhāt"; referring to a ritual meal of parched barley flour mixed with clarified butter</note>, that man does not need to point to or praise any other deity. This means that because one obtains all desired wealth from Pushan alone, the worshiper does not need to pray to another god.

---

## Hymn Text

-> ॥ Now the Second Verse ॥ <-

**And indeed, that best of charioteers, the protector of the righteous, Indra, slays the enemies with his companion as an ally. ॥ 2 ॥**

> **उ॒त । घ॒ । सः । र॒थिऽत॑मः । सख्या॑ । सत्ऽप॑तिः । यु॒जा । इन्द्रः॑ । वृ॒त्राणि॑ । जि॒घ्न॒ते ॥ २ ॥**

## Commentary (Sayana)

And also, that <term>Indra</term> (the King of the Gods), who is famous for being the slayer of foes, who is the **best of charioteers** <note>original: "rathītamaḥ"; an exceptionally great warrior</note> and the **protector of the righteous**, slays the **enemies** <note>original: "vṛtrāṇi"; can refer to the demon Vritra or obstacles in general</note> when joined with his **companion** Pushan acting as his **ally**. The meaning is that Pushan serves as a helper even to Indra himself.

## Hymn Text
**And that golden wheel of the sun, in the speckled cloud, the best of charioteers drove down. ॥ 3 ॥**

## Commentary (Sayana)
And also (*uta*) the **impeller** (*sūraḥ*), the **best of charioteers** (*rathītamaḥ*)—or the most excellent leader—Pushan, in the **speckled** (*paruṣe*)—meaning the knotty, mountainous, or shining—**cow** (*gavi*). <note>The word "cow" (go) is a common Vedic metaphor for the sun or the rays of light, because it "moves" (gacchati).</note> In that sun, he **drove down** (*nyairayat*), or continuously impelled, that **golden** (*hiraṇyayam*) **wheel** (*cakram*) belonging to his chariot.

## Hymn Text
**O much-praised, wonderful, wise one, whatever we say to you today, fulfill that desire for us. ॥ 4 ॥**

## Commentary (Sayana)
O **much-praised** (*puruṣṭuta*), you who are praised by many sacrificers; O **wonderful** (*dasma*), meaning beautiful to behold; O **wise one** (*maṃtumaḥ*), O knowledgeable Pushan; **whatever we may speak** (*yad... bravāma*) or praise you with **today, at this time** (*adyedānīm*), for the sake of a specific goal, **fulfill** (*sādhaya*) or produce **for us** (*naḥ*) that **thought-of wealth** (*manma*).

-> ॥ Now the Fifth Verse ॥ <-

## Hymn Text
**Lead this group of ours, who seek cattle, toward gain. O Pushan, you are heard of from afar. ॥ 5 ॥**

## Commentary (Sayana)
O **Pushan**, **for our gain** (*naḥ sātaye*) or profit, **lead** (*sīṣadhaḥ*) or bring to success **this group** (*imaṃ ca gaṇam*) of men who are **seekers of cattle** (*gaveṣaṇam*). ## Hymn Text
**We beg for your blessing, which keeps evil far away and brings wealth near, for total well-being today and total well-being tomorrow. ॥ 6 ॥**

## Commentary (Sayana)
O **Pushan**, **we beg** (*āmīmahe*) for **your** (*te*) **blessing** (*svastim*), the auspicious protection to be given by you, which **keeps evil far away** (*āreaghām*). <note>original: "āre-aghām"</note> This means a state where sin or suffering (*agham*) is at a distance (*āre*). It is **accompanied by wealth** (*upāvasam*), meaning wealth has come near it. Such a blessing we ask for today, at this time... <note>The text of the commentary breaks off here at the end of the page.</note>

<meta>This page concludes the commentary for the 22nd Varga (section) of the 8th Adhyaya (chapter) in the 4th Ashtaka (volume) and begins the 23rd Varga. It introduces the 57th Hymn of the Sixth Mandala, focusing on the shared worship of the gods Indra and Pushan.</meta>

For the **whole of the sacrifice** (*sarvatātaye*). A **Sarvatāti** is a sacrifice that is "stretched out" or performed by all the officiating priests. For that purpose. Alternatively, it means for the expansion of all enjoyments. For today and for the next day, we pray for this "whole-giving" sacrifice. We seek protection.

The eighth hymn of this chapter, beginning with "O Indra and Pushan," consists of six verses. The seer (composer) is Bharadvaja, the meter is Gayatri, and the deities are Indra and Pushan addressed together. As noted in the index: "Indra and Pushan, and Indra." The ritual application has already been described.

## Hymn Text

->॥ The First Verse ॥<-

O Indra and Pushan, we call upon you today for friendship, for well-being, and for the winning of wealth. ॥ 1 ॥
<note>RV 6.57.1</note>

**Indra | indeed | Pushan | we | for friendship | for well-being | we call | for the winning of wealth ॥ 1 ॥**

## Commentary (Sayana)

Because they are joined together in a pair, the names Indra and Pushan both take the dual form. O gods, Indra and Pushan, **now** (*nu*)—meaning today—we **call upon** (*huvema*) or praise you for **well-being** (*svastaye*), for **good friendship** (*sakhāya*), and for the **attainment of wealth** (*vāja-sātaye*)—where "vāja" refers to food or strength.

---

## Hymn Text

->॥ The Second Verse ॥<-

One approaches the Soma, pressed between the two boards, to drink it; the other desires the groat-cake. ॥ 2 ॥
<note>RV 6.57.2</note>

**Soma | the other | near | approached | for drinking | from the two boards | pressed | the groat-cake | the other | desires ॥ 2 ॥**

## Commentary (Sayana)

One of these two, namely Indra, **approaches** (*upāsadat*) to **drink** (*pātave*) the **Soma** which has been **pressed** (*sutam*) between the two **pressing-boards** (*camvoḥ*). <note>The "camvoḥ" are the ritual boards used to squeeze the juice from the Soma plant.</note> The other, Pushan, **desires** (*icchati*) the **groat-cake** (*karambhaṃ*), an offering made of parched barley-meal mixed with clarified butter.

---

## Hymn Text

->॥ The Third Verse ॥<-

Goats are the steeds of one; well-nourished bay horses are the steeds of the other. With these, they slay the enemies. ॥ 3 ॥
<note>RV 6.57.3</note>

**Goats | of the one | carriers | bay horses | of the other | well-nourished | with those two | enemies | they slay ॥ 3 ॥**

## Commentary (Sayana)

Of these two, Indra and Pushan, for **one** (*anyasya*)—Pushan—the **goats** (*ajāḥ*) are the **carriers** (*vahnayaḥ*) or the horses that pull his chariot. For the **other** (*anyasya*)—Indra—the **bay horses** (*harī*), which are **well-nourished** (*saṃbhṛtā*) and strong, are the carriers. With these two types of steeds, Indra **slays** (*jighnate*) his **enemies** (*vṛtrāṇi*).

## Hymn Text
**When Indra, the most powerful pourer of rain, led the great waters, there Pushan was his companion. ॥ 4 ॥**
<note>RV 6.57.4</note>

**When | Indra | led | the obstructed | the great | waters | the most powerful pourer | there | Pushan | was | together [with him] ॥ 4 ॥**

---

## Commentary (Sayana)
When the most powerful pourer <note>original: "vṛṣantamaḥ" — meaning Indra who causes excessive rain</note>, Indra, led or brought the mighty, deep waters—the rain-waters—to this world, then the god Pushan, the nourisher, was "together" <note>original: "sacā"</note> with him. That is to say, he becomes the helper of Indra.

-> ॥ The Fifth Verse ॥ <-

## Hymn Text
**We take hold of that good favor of Pushan and of Indra, just as one grasps a sturdy branch of a tree. ॥ 5 ॥**
<note>RV 6.57.5</note>

**That | of Pushan | the good favor | we | of a tree | [prefix] | like a branch | of Indra | and | [prefix] | we take hold of ॥ 5 ॥**

---

## Commentary (Sayana)
We take hold of—meaning we depend upon or seek shelter in—that well-known and auspicious favor <note>original: "sumati" — a benevolent state of mind or grace</note> of the nourishing god Pushan and of Indra. We do this just as one might grasp a prominent and strong branch of a tree <note>original: "mahīruha" — literally, that which grows from the earth</note> for support.

---

-> ॥ The Sixth Verse ॥ <-

## Hymn Text
**We rouse Pushan and Indra for great well-being, just as a charioteer pulls the reins. ॥ 6 ॥**
<note>RV 6.57.6</note>

**Up | Pushan | we rouse | like the reins | a charioteer | for the great | Indra | for well-being ॥ 6 ॥**

---

## Commentary (Sayana)
We urge or rouse <note>original: "udyuvāmahe"</note> the nourishing god Pushan and Indra for the sake of great well-being or protection. The act of "rousing" here implies drawing their attention. An illustration is provided: just as a charioteer <note>original: "sūta"</note> pulls or directs the reins <note>original: "abhīśūn"</note> that are tied to the horses, so do we direct our prayers to them.

## Sukta 58 Introduction
The ninth hymn of this chapter, beginning with "The bright one to you..." <note>original: "śukraṃ te"</note>, consists of four verses. The seer is Bharadvaja, and the hymn is dedicated to the god Pushan <note>term: Paushna (pertaining to Pushan)</note>. The second verse is in the <term>Jagati</term> meter <note>a Sanskrit poetic meter with 48 syllables</note>, and the remaining three verses are in the <term>Trishtubh</term> meter <note>a meter with 44 syllables</note>. This is confirmed by the index: "The four verses of 'The Bright One,' the second is Jagati." 

Regarding the ritual application: during the "Sacrifice to All Gods" <note>term: Vaishvadeva-parvan</note>, this hymn serves as the offering prayer <note>term: Yajya</note> for the oblation to Pushan. This is indicated in the ritual manuals: "The bright one is your other [aspect], the worshipful is your other... here, here for you, O self-strong ones" <note>Ashvalayana Shrauta Sutra 2.16</note>. Furthermore, this same verse is used as the offering prayer for the fat of the animal sacrificed to Pushan during the Eleven-Victim ceremony. This is indicated by: "The bright one is your other aspect... Pushan was born at the beginning of the paths" <note>Ashvalayana Shrauta Sutra 3.7</note>. It is also used in the six-day ritual <note>term: Abhiplava</note>, as noted: "The bright one is your other aspect... I saw the herdsman who never rests" <note>Ashvalayana Shrauta Sutra 4.6</note>.

<summary>This page concludes the 57th hymn, emphasizing the alliance between Indra and Pushan through metaphors of tree branches and charioteers, and introduces the 58th hymn dedicated to Pushan's dual nature.</summary>

<meta>This page continues from the commentary on Sukta 57. It begins the treatment of Rig Veda, Mandala 6, Sukta 58, which is a hymn dedicated to Pushan, the solar deity who guards paths and livestock. The focus here is on his dual nature and his role as a universal protector.</meta>

# Rig Veda — Book 4, Chapter 8, Section 24
**Page 830**

## Hymn Text

-> ॥ This is the First Verse ॥ <-

**One of your forms is bright, the other is worthy of sacrifice; you are like the heaven with day and night of varying forms. You protect all creative powers, O self-dependent one; O Pushan, may your auspicious gift be here for us. ॥ 1 ॥**
<note>RV 6.58.1</note>

---

**Padapatha:**
Bright | your | one | worthy of sacrifice | your | other | diverse-forms | [particle] | diverse-forms | day and night | [particle] |
like heaven | you are |
all | indeed | creative powers | you protect | O self-dependent one | auspicious | your | O Pushan | here | gift | let it be ॥ 1 ॥

## Commentary (Sayana)

O **Pushan**, one of **your** forms is **bright** <note>original: "śukra" — clear or white-colored</note>, which is the day characterized by light. Likewise, **your** other related form is **worthy of sacrifice** <note>original: "yajata" — used here in the sense of 'joining' or 'bringing together'</note>. The root *yaj* here refers to the act of joining; it is that which is to be joined with light but is inherently dark—this is the form called night. In this way, the **day and night**, which possess **diverse forms** <note>original: "viṣurūpe" — many-colored, specifically white and black</note>, are produced by your greatness.

Alternatively: O Pushan, your one form is bright and stainless, the producer of the day. Your other form is only "worthy of sacrifice" but does not emit light—this is the producer of the night. Therefore, the day and the night become "diverse forms" or uneven forms. If one asks how the sun is the creator of both day and night, the text says: **you are like heaven**. Just as the heaven <note>original: "dyu" — here referring to the Sun in the sky</note> is the illuminator, so too are you the illuminator. Why? He says: O **self-dependent one** <note>original: "svadhāvaḥ" — one possessing food or inherent power</note>, Pushan, because you **protect all creative powers** <note>original: "māyāḥ" — here interpreted as "prajñā" or wisdom/intelligence</note>, you are indeed like the Sun. May the **auspicious** or happy **gift** <note>original: "rāti" — a donation or favor</note> of such a being as you **be here** among us.

**The sage Yaska says:**
> One of yours is bright/red, the other is sacrificial; one is the sacrificial form, the other is non-sacrificial; the day and night are of uneven forms through your action, and you are like the Sun. You protect all wisdom, being the possessor of nourishment. <note>Nirukta 12.19</note>

---

## Hymn Text

-> ॥ This is the Second Verse ॥ <-

**He whose horses are goats, the protector of livestock, whose home is food, who stimulates the mind, and who is fixed in the whole world; Pushan, wielding the loose goad, the god moves about looking upon all beings. ॥ 2 ॥**
<note>RV 6.58.2</note>

Goat-horsed | protector of livestock | food-homed | mind-stimulating | in the world | in the whole | fixed |

## Commentary (Sayana)

**He whose horses are goats** <note>original: "ajāśvaḥ" — one whose vehicle is drawn by goats</note>; the **protector of livestock** <note>original: "paśupaḥ" — the guardian of animals</note>; and **one whose home is food** <note>original: "vājapastyaḥ" — one who has "vāja" (food/strength) in his "pastya" (house)</note>. He is **mind-stimulating** <note>original: "dhiyañjinvaḥ"</note>; "dhiyaḥ" refers to the praisers or the ritual acts. He is the one who pleases [continued on next page]

# Mandala 6, Chapter 5, Hymn 58 | Fourth Ashtaka | Page 931

...[The deity Pushan] is placed in every world by Prajapati <note>The Creator/Lord of Progeny</note> as a nourisher. Therefore, the nourishing god Pushan, holding the loosely-held whip in his own hand and raising it, travels through the sky, observing all the worlds—or all created beings—and illuminating them through his solar form.

Regarding the animal sacrifice dedicated to Pushan: for the offering of the omentum and the sacrificial cake, the two verses beginning with "O Pushan, those [boats] of yours..." are the two preparatory chants. This is indicated in the scriptures: "O Pushan, those boats of yours that move within the ocean" and "Pushan knows all these regions." <note>original: Āśvalāyana Śrauta Sūtra 9.3</note>

-> ॥ Of those two, the first is the third verse of the hymn ॥ <-

## Hymn Text

O Pushan, those golden boats of yours that move within the ocean, in the atmosphere—with them you go on a mission for the Sun, driven by love, seeking glory. ॥ 3 ॥

**Word-for-Word Analysis:**
Those | your | O Pushan | boats | within | the ocean | golden | in the atmosphere | move | with those | you go | on a mission | of the Sun | by love/desire | made | glory | desiring ॥ 3 ॥

---

## Commentary (Sayana)

O **Pushan**, those **golden** <note>original: "hiraṇyayīḥ" — golden or pleasingly bright</note> **boats** belonging to you which **move** <note>original: "caranti" — travel</note> **within the ocean** <note>the water-filled sky</note> or the atmosphere, **with those** boats you **go on a mission for the Sun**. You act as his messenger. 

<note>Sayana provides a mythological backstory here:</note> Once, when the Sun set out with the other gods to slay the demons, his wife felt a deep longing for her husband. The Sun sent Pushan as a messenger to her; it is for this reason that Pushan is praised here. Furthermore, you, **desiring glory** <note>original: "śravaḥ" — specifically food in the form of a sacrificial oblation</note>, are **made** to be controlled **by the desire** of the chanters regarding the safety of their paths and other needs.

-> ॥ Now the fourth verse ॥ <-

## Hymn Text

Pushan is the good kinsman of Heaven and Earth, the Lord of Nourishment, the Bountiful One of wonderful radiance, whom the gods gave to Surya, him who is moved by love, the powerful and swift-moving one. ॥ 4 ॥

**Word-for-Word Analysis:**
Pushan | good-kinsman | of Heaven | and | of Earth | of nourishment | lord | the Bountiful | of wonderful-radiance | whom | the gods | gave | to Surya | by love | made | powerful | the swift-moving ॥ 4 ॥

---

## Commentary (Sayana)

**Pushan**, the nourishing deity, is the **good kinsman** <note>original: "subandhuḥ" — a helpful or beautiful relative</note> **of Heaven and** also of the **Earth**. Likewise, he is the **Lord of Nourishment** <note>original: "iḷaspatiḥ" — "ila" refers to food or the earth</note> and the **Bountiful** <note>original: "maghavā"</note>. "Magha" is a name for wealth; thus, he is the one who possesses it. Alternatively, the word "magha" is derived from the root meaning "to give," signifying he is a giver. He is **of wonderful radiance** <note>original: "dasmavarcāḥ"</note>. "Varcas" refers to form or appearance; he has a "dasma" or wonderful, visible appearance. This Pushan, whom all the gods gave to Surya <note>Surya here refers to the daughter of the Sun, the solar bride. The commentary continues onto the next page</note>

<term>Pushan (Pūṣan)</term> — A solar deity who acts as a protector of travelers, a guide for the soul, and a bringer of nourishment.
<term>Golden Boats (Hiraṇyayīḥ nāvaḥ)</term> — A metaphor for the clouds or solar rays that move through the "ocean" of the sky.
<term>Maghava (Maghavā)</term> — An epithet usually reserved for Indra, meaning "The Bountiful" or "The Generous Giver of Riches."
<term>Surya (Sūryā)</term> — Distinct from the male Sun god (Sūrya), Sūryā is the daughter of the Sun, whose marriage to the Ashvins or her association with Pushan is a recurring Vedic theme.

<summary>This page describes Pushan as a celestial messenger who travels in "golden boats" across the sky. It highlights his role as a bridge between heaven and earth and his mythological connection to the family of the Sun.</summary>

<meta>This page concludes the commentary on the final verse of Hymn 58 (dedicated to the god Pushan) and begins Hymn 59 (dedicated to the dual deity Indra-Agni) in the Sixth Mandala of the Rig Veda. # Rig Veda | Book 6 | Hymn 59 | Page 932
### [Ashtaka 4, Adhyaya 8, Varga 25]

...[The gods] gave [Pushan] to the wife of the Sun, or rather to the daughter of the Sun named Surya, for her choice of the Ashvins as husbands. Indeed, it is heard in the scriptures: "The son Pushan chose his parents" <note>Rig Veda 10.85.14</note>. What is this Pushan like? He is "made" or influenced by the singers through their desires for cattle and other wealth; he is "tavas," meaning powerful or fully grown; and "svancha," meaning one who moves beautifully. The connection is: that Pushan, whom they gave, is a "good kinsman" <note>original: subandhu</note>.

->॥ Thus ends the twenty-fourth Varga of the eighth Adhyaya in the fourth Ashtaka ॥<-

---

The tenth hymn, beginning with **"Pra nu vocha,"** consists of ten verses. Its seer is the sage Bharadvaja, and its deities are Indra and Agni <note>the gods of storm/kingship and sacrificial fire, addressed here as a single pair</note>. The last four verses, starting from the seventh, are in the Anushtubh meter <note>a rhythm of 32 syllables</note>, while the remaining six are in the Brihati meter <note>a rhythm of 36 syllables</note>. As the Index of Hymns states: **"The ten verses to Indra-Agni beginning 'Pra nu' are in Brihati, with four Anushtubhs at the end."** The ritual application has been previously explained.

---

## Hymn Text

->॥ Here is the First Verse ॥<-

I proclaim now, during the Soma pressings, those heroic deeds of yours, which you both performed. Your enemies, the attackers of the gods, were slain; O Indra and Agni, you both live! ॥ 1 ॥

**Word-for-Word Analysis:**
Proclaim | now | I speak | during the [Soma] pressings | of you two | heroic deeds | which | you both performed | slain | your | fathers/harmers | enemies of the gods | O Indra and Agni | you live | you both ॥ 1 ॥

## Commentary (Sayana)

O **Indra and Agni**, those **heroic deeds**—the acts of a hero—**which you both performed**, I **proclaim** or declare **now** quickly, **during the Soma pressings** in our sacrifice. He then demonstrates that very heroism: O Indra and Agni, the **enemies of the gods**—those for whom the gods are the "shatravah" or destroyers—were the Asuras <note>demonic entities</note>. They were "pitarah," meaning harmers. <term>The root 'piy' means the act of harming</term>; this word is a form of that root. Such Asuras **were slain** by you two. But **you both live**; you remain possessed of life. In other words, you were not harmed by the Asuras.

---

## Hymn Text

->॥ Now the Second Verse ॥<-

Truly, O Indra and Agni, your greatness is most praiseworthy. You are brothers, born of the same father, twins, whose mothers are here and there. ॥ 2 ॥

**Word-for-Word Analysis:**
Truly | thus | greatness | of you two | O Indra and Agni | most praiseworthy | [is] | the same | of you two | the father/creator | brothers | you both | twins | here-and-there-mothers ॥ 2 ॥

## Commentary (Sayana)

O **Indra and Agni**, the **greatness** or majesty **of you two** is **truly** <note>original: "bat"</note> real in this manner. This means that all the greatness regarding your birth that is being described is factually true. It is **most praiseworthy**...

<vocab>
- Indra-Agni: A "dual deity" representing the combined power of the atmosphere and the sacrificial fire.
- Bharadvaja: A famous Vedic seer (Rishi) of the Sixth Book.
- Virya: Heroic power or specific miraculous deeds performed by gods.
- Asura: In this context, the opponents of the Vedic gods; often translated as "demons."
- Mahima: Divine majesty or the expansive power of a deity.
- Brihati: A specific poetic meter common in Vedic Sanskrit.
- Anushtubh: The most common meter in later Sanskrit, often used for storytelling.
</vocab>

# Rig Veda | Book 6 | Hymn 59 | Page 833
### [Ashtaka 4, Adhyaya 8, Varga 25]

## Commentary (Sayana)
Prajapati <note>the Lord of Progeny</note>, the most praised, is the same single progenitor (father) of you both. Therefore, you are both brothers. Moreover, you are twins <note>original: yamau</note>, born together, having the same mother here and there—that is, you have the same mother everywhere. For Aditi is their mother; she indeed is the wide-spreading Earth. Thus it is heard in the scriptures: "having the same mother in both places."

---

## Hymn Text
-> ॥ Now the Third Verse ॥ <-

Abiding together at the pressed Soma, like two swift horses at their feed; O Indra and Agni, we now call upon you two, the divine wielders of the thunderbolt, for protection. ॥ 3 ॥

**Word-for-Word Analysis:**
Abiding together | At the pressed [Soma] | Together | Two horses | Like [those] moving | At the feeding | Indra | Now | Agni | For protection | Here | Wielders of the thunderbolt | We | Divine | Call upon. ॥ 3 ॥

---

## Commentary (Sayana)
O **Indra and Agni**, at the **pressed Soma** <note>original: sute</note>, may you both be **united** and joined together. The word *okivāṃsā* <term>okivāṃsau: derived from the root 'uc', meaning to be gathered or together</term> expresses this state of being joined. An illustration is given: like two swift-moving **horses** at their **feeding** <note>original: adane</note>, i.e., at the grass to be eaten. **Now** <note>original: nu</note>, today, we **call upon** <note>original: havāmahe</note> such a pair of Indra and Agni **in this sacrifice** for the sake of **protection** <note>original: avasā</note>. Because of their mutual connection in this hymn, the dual grammatical ending is used for both the names Indra and Agni. What are Indra and Agni like? They are the **wielders of the thunderbolt** <note>original: vajriṇā</note>, equipped with that weapon, and **divine** <note>original: devā</note>, possessed of qualities like generosity.

---

## Hymn Text
-> ॥ Now the Fourth Verse ॥ <-

O Indra and Agni, increasers of Truth, the one who speaks flattering words among the Soma-pressings while [pretending to] praise you—O gods of far-reaching shouts, you do not consume [his offering] at all. ॥ 4 ॥

**Word-for-Word Analysis:**
Who | Indra-Agni | At the pressed [Somas] | Of you two | Praises | Truth-increasers | Flattering-speech | Speaking | Far-reaching-shouts | Not | Divine [ones] | Consume | Even. ॥ 4 ॥

---

## Commentary (Sayana)
O **increasers of truth** <note>original: ṛtāvṛdhā</note>—meaning the increasers of either the eternal Truth or of the sacrifice—O **Indra and Agni**, among the **pressed Somas**, should a singer **praise** you poorly or falsely, while **speaking flattering words** <note>original: joṣavākaṃ</note>—that is, words intended to please but which are themselves unpleasant or insincere—O **gods with far-reaching shouts** <note>original: pañjahoshiṇā</note> (meaning your fame or the sound of your praise is well-known and widespread), you two **do not consume** his Soma. The word **'chana'** is used simply to complete the poetic meter. Regarding this, the *Nirukta* <note>a foundational text on Vedic etymology by Yaska</note> states: "The word *joṣavākam* has an unknown specific name, but it refers to something that is intended to be pleasing." [It refers to the one who addresses] Indra and Agni...

<keywords>Indra, Agni, Aditi, Prajapati, Soma sacrifice, Truth (Rita), Nirukta, flattery, divine twins</keywords>

<meta>This page continues the translation of Rig Veda, Mandala 6, Sukta 59, following the commentary on the nature of Indra and Agni as brothers and twins. It transitions from the end of Varga 25 into the beginning of Varga 26 of the 8th Adhyaya.</meta>

When the Soma is pressed, one praises you both; you who increase the Cosmic Order <note>original: rtasya vardhayitārau</note>, you do not partake of the offering of that person who speaks with a liking for false words <note>original: joṣavākaṃ</note> or who is a babbler. You two gods, who are the recipients of earned offerings, do not eat of his [sacrifice]. (Nirukta 5.22).

---

## Hymn Text

-> ॥ Now the Fifth Verse ॥ <-

**O Indra and Agni, what mortal understands this work of yours? Harnessing horses that go in different directions, one [of you] moves in a common chariot.** ॥ 5 ॥

### Word-for-Word Analysis
O Indra and Agni | [Thus] | Who | Of this [work] | Of you two | O Gods | Mortal | Understands | Going in different directions | Horses | Harnessing | Moves | One | In a common | [Into] | Chariot. ॥ 5 ॥

## Commentary (Sayana)

O **shining ones** <note>original: devau</note>, Indra and Agni, what **mortal** <note>original: martyaḥ</note> man **understands** <note>original: ciketat</note> or knows this work of **yours** <note>original: vām</note>? The meaning is: no one at all. And what is that work? **One** of you, Indra, existing in the form of the Sun, **moves** <note>original: īyate</note>—approaching the entire world—**harnessing** <note>original: yuyujānaḥ</note> **horses** that go in **different directions** <note>original: viṣūcaḥ</note> (traveling to various ends) within **one chariot** that is **common** <note>original: samāne</note> to both of you for the sake of your joint purpose.

Alternatively, the "common chariot" of one form refers to the Year <note>original: saṃvatsara</note>, in which Indra, as the Sun, moves while harnessing horses that are various in form and all-pervading. The sense is: who could truly understand this work of yours as it really is?

-> **॥ Thus ends the twenty-fifth Varga of the eighth Adhyaya in the fourth Ashtaka ॥** <-

---

## Hymn Text

-> ॥ Now the Sixth Verse ॥ <-

**O Indra and Agni, this footless one has come before those with feet. Leaving the head, speaking loudly with her tongue, she moved; she has stepped over thirty steps.** ॥ 6 ॥

### Word-for-Word Analysis
O Indra and Agni | [Thus] | Footless | This [Dawn] | First | [Towards] | Has come | From those with feet | Leaving | The head | With the tongue | Speaking loudly | Moving | Thirty | Steps | [Down] | Has stepped. ॥ 6 ॥

## Commentary (Sayana)

O **Indra and Agni**, **this** <note>refers to the goddess Dawn, Usha</note> who is **footless** <note>original: apāt; meaning she moves through the air without physical feet</note> **has come** as the **first** <note>original: pūrvā</note> or earliest preceding light, coming **from those who have feet** <note>original: padvatībhyaḥ</note>, meaning the creatures who are currently sleeping. Furthermore, she is the **mover of the head** <note>original: śiro hitvī</note> of living beings; or, alternatively, it means she herself moves without a head <note>perhaps referring to the diffuse light of dawn</note>. **Moving** along, she is **speaking loudly** <note>original: vāvadat</note> or making much sound through the **tongue** (the faculty of speech) of the living beings who wake up. Thus, the moving Dawn **stepped over** <note>original: nyakramīt</note> **thirty steps**, which are the thirty segments of time <term>muhurtas: a unit of time lasting about 48 minutes; thirty make a full day and night</term>. She traverses these in a single day. This too is your divine work. The connection to the previous verse is: "who can understand this?"

<summary>This page discusses the mysterious and incomprehensible nature of Indra and Agni's cosmic deeds, specifically identifying Indra's solar role and the arrival of Dawn (Usha) as she marks the thirty divisions of the day.</summary>
<keywords>Indra, Agni, Sun, Dawn, Usha, Time-cycle, Muhurta, Chariot, Rig Veda commentary, Sayana</keywords>

<meta>This page continues the translation of Rig Veda, Mandala 6, Sukta 59, following the commentary on the nature of Indra and Agni. It provides the final three verses of the hymn (7, 8, and 9), focusing on a prayer for victory in battle and the granting of prosperity.</meta>

->॥ Now the Seventh Verse ॥<-

## Hymn Text
O **Indra and Agni**, truly the **warriors** stretch their **bows** in their **arms**. In this **great contest for wealth**, in the **raids for cattle**, do not let [the enemy] cast us aside. ॥ 7 ॥

**Word-for-Word Analysis**
**Indra and Agni** | [Thus] | Truly | **Stretch** | **Warriors** | **Bows** | **In their arms** | **Not** | **Us** | **In this** | **In the great contest for wealth** | **Away** | **Overcome/Cast aside** | **In the searches for cattle**. ॥ 7 ॥

---

## Commentary (Sayana)
O Indra and Agni, the **warriors** <note>original: naraḥ</note>, meaning human combatants, **stretch** <note>original: ātanvate</note> the **bows** <note>original: dhanvāni</note> in their **arms**; they are indeed making the bowstrings taut. In this **great contest for wealth** <note>original: mahādhane</note>, a battle characterized by the great riches to be won, and in the **searches for cattle** <note>original: gaviṣṭiṣu</note>, do **not cast us aside** <note>original: mā parāvṛktaṃ</note>. That is to say, do not abandon us.

---

->॥ Now the Eighth Verse ॥<-

## Hymn Text
O **Indra and Agni**, the **wicked hostilities** of the **enemy** **burn** me. Drive **away** the **hatreds**; **separate** them from the **sun**. ॥ 8 ॥

**Word-for-Word Analysis**
**Indra and Agni** | [Thus] | **Burn** | **Me** | **Wicked** | **Of the enemy** | **Hostilities** | **Away** | **Hatreds** | [Make] | **Separate** | **From the sun** | **From**. ॥ 8 ॥

---

## Commentary (Sayana)
O Indra and Agni, may the **wicked** <note>original: aghāḥ</note> or harmful **hostilities** <note>original: arātayaḥ</note> of the **enemy** <note>original: aryaḥ</note> who approaches us not **burn** <note>original: tapanti</note> me; they distress me. Drive them **away** <note>original: apākuruatam</note>. Likewise, **separate** <note>original: yuyutam</note> the **hatreds** <note>original: dveṣāṃsi</note>—meaning the hating enemies—**from the sun** <note>original: sūryād adhi</note>. The word "from" <note>original: adhi</note> here signifies the source of separation. Make it so that they **do not see the sun**; the meaning is: kill them.

---

->॥ Now the Ninth Verse ॥<-

## Hymn Text
O **Indra and Agni**, whatever **treasures** of **yours** are **heavenly** or **earthly**, **bestow** upon **us** **here** **wealth** that **nourishes** throughout a **full lifetime**. ॥ 9 ॥

**Word-for-Word Analysis**
**Indra and Agni** | [Thus] | **Of you two** | **Also** | **Wealth** | **Heavenly** | **Earthly** | **Bring/Give** | **To us** | **Here** | **Bestow** | **Wealth** | **Lifetime-nourishing**. ॥ 9 ॥

---

## Commentary (Sayana)
O Indra and Agni, whatever **heavenly** <note>original: divyāni</note> treasures—those existing in the sky—or **earthly** <note>original: pārthivā</note> treasures—those existing on the earth—belonging to the two worlds exist, they belong to **you two** <note>original: yuvoḥ</note> alone. For this reason, **bestow** <note>original: pra yacchatam</note> **wealth** <note>original: rayim</note> upon **us** in **this** sacrifice. What kind of wealth? **Nourishment for a full lifetime** <note>original: viśvāyupoṣam</note>.

The term *Ayavaḥ* refers to humans. It signifies that which is sufficient for the nourishment of all humans. Alternatively, it refers to that which is capable of nourishing the entirety of one's life. <note>original: chāndaso varṇalopaḥ — a technical grammatical note stating that a letter has been dropped in the Vedic or 'Chandas' usage</note>.

->॥ Now the Tenth Verse ॥<-

## Hymn Text

O **Indra and Agni**, **borne by hymns**, who **hear the call**, come with **all songs** for the **drinking** of **this Soma**. ॥ 10 ॥

**Pada-patha:**
**Indra and Agni** | [Thus] | **Borne by hymns** | **With praises** | **Hearing the call** | **With all** | **With songs** | **Come** | **Of this** | **Soma** | **For drinking**. ॥ 10 ॥

## Commentary (Sayana)

O **borne by hymns** <note>original: ukthavāhasā</note>, meaning you who are to be carried or reached by songs of praise; O **listeners of the call** <note>original: havanaśrutā</note>, you who hear the invitation to the sacrifice; being such, O **Indra and Agni**, **come** <note>original: āgataṃ / āgacchataṃ</note> by means of the **praises** <note>original: stomebhiḥ</note> and **all songs** <note>original: viśvābhir gīrbhiḥ</note>, which consist of the recited verses of the ritual. For what purpose? **For the drinking** <note>original: pītaye</note> **of this** <note>original: asya</note> our **Soma** juice.

->॥ Thus ends the twenty-sixth section (Varga) of the eighth chapter (Adhyaya) of the fourth book (Ashtaka) ॥<-

The eleventh hymn, beginning with "He destroys the covering enemy" <note>original: aya-vṛcam</note>, consists of fifteen verses. The seer is Bharadvaja, and the deities are Indra and Agni. The first three verses are in the *Trishtubh* meter; from the fourth onwards, nine verses are in the *Gayatri* meter; the thirteenth is *Trishtubh*, the fourteenth is *Brihati*, and the fifteenth is *Anustubh*. This is as stated in the Index: "The hymn beginning *ayavṛca* is mostly Gayatri, but starts with three Trishtubhs, and ends with Trishtubh, Brihati, and Anustubh." The general application of the hymn has been mentioned. In the Varunapraghasa rituals <note>a seasonal sacrifice</note>, this verse serves as the offering prayer (Yajya) for the oblation to Indra and Agni. It is indicated in the ritual manuals: <term>Indra and Agni, come with your protection; he destroys the covering enemy and gains strength</term> <note>Ashvalayana Shrauta Sutra 2.17</note>.

->॥ This is the First Verse ॥<-

## Hymn Text

He **destroys** the **covering enemy** and **wins strength**, who **worships** the **victorious** **Indra and Agni**, the **lords** of **abundant wealth**, the **most powerful** ones who **increase strength** with their **power**. ॥ 1 ॥

**Pada-patha:**
**Destroys** | **Covering [enemy]** | **And** | **Wins** | **Strength/Food** | **Indra** | **Who** | **Agni** | [Thus] | **Victorious** | [Thus] | **Worships** | **Ruling/Lords** | **Of wealth** | **Abundant** | **Most powerful** | **With power** | **Increasing strength**. ॥ 1 ॥

---

## Commentary (Sayana)

That person **destroys** <note>original: ayat / hinasti</note> the **covering enemy** <note>original: vṛcam / āvarakaṃ śatruṃ</note>. **And** <note>original: uta</note> also he **wins** <note>original: sanoti / labhate</note> **strength** <note>original: vājam</note>, meaning food or power. Who is this person? The one who **worships** <note>original: saparyāt / paricaret</note> the **victorious** <note>original: sahurī / śatrūṇām abhibhavatārau</note> **Indra and Agni**, who overpower their foes. <note>Note: Due to their dual nature, the dual grammatical form is used throughout here as before.</note> What kind of Indra and Agni? They are the **lords** <note>original: irajyantā / īśānau</note> of **abundant** <note>original: bhūreḥ</note> **wealth** <note>original: vasavyasya / vasusamūhasya</note>.

<vocab>
इंद्राग्नी (Indra-Agni): The dual deity of thunder/war and fire, उक्थवाहसा (Ukthavahasa): Borne by hymns, सोम (Soma): The sacred sacrificial drink, पीतये (Pitaye): For the purpose of drinking, भरद्वाज (Bharadvaja): The sage/seer of this family of hymns, सहुरी (Sahuri): Victorious or conquering, वाजम् (Vaja): Strength, food, or the prize of battle, वसव्यस्य (Vasavyasya): Pertaining to riches or treasure.

[Ma. 6. Su. 5. Hy. 60.] || Fourth Ashtaka || 837

## Commentary (Sayana)

The word "lordship" <note>original: irajyati</note> refers to the exercise of power. With "might" <note>original: sahasā</note>, meaning with strength that overcomes a thousand enemies; "desiring the prize" <note>original: vājayantau</note>, meaning they desire the food characterized by the sacrificial oblation for themselves. Or, it means they desire the food that is to be given to the singers of praises.

-> || Now the Second [Verse] || <-

## Hymn Text

O Indra, now you two fought for those—the cows, the waters, the sun, and the dawns that were carried away. O Indra, [you recovered] the directions, the sun, and the wonderful dawns; O Agni, you who are accompanied by your teams of horses, join with the waters and the cows. || 2 ||

**Word-for-word analysis:**
**Those | You two fought | For | The cows | O Indra | Now | The waters | The sun | The dawns | O Agni | Carried away |**
**The directions | The sun | The dawns | O Indra | Wonderful | The waters | The cows | O Agni | You join | Accompanied by teams of horses** || 2 ||

---

-> || This is the Third [Verse] || <-

## Hymn Text

O slayers of the enemy, with your enemy-slaying strengths, O Indra, come hither; with our offerings of reverence, O Agni. O Indra and Agni, may you both be with us with wealth and with the most excellent songs of praise. || 3 ||

**Word-for-word analysis:**
**Hither | Slayers of the enemy | With enemy-slaying | Strengths | O Indra | Come | With offerings of reverence | O Agni | Towards us |**
**You two | With wealth | With songs of praise | O Indra | O Agni | In us | Be | With the most excellent** || 3 ||

---

## Commentary (Sayana)

O Indra and Agni, **those** <note>original: tā</note> two of you **fought** <note>original: yodhiṣṭam</note> for the **cows**, the **waters**, the **sun**, and the **dawns** which were **carried away** <note>original: ūḷhāḥ</note>, meaning stolen by the Panis <note>The Panis were a class of demons who hid the cosmic treasures in a cave</note>. You engaged in battle with those demons. The word **now** <note>original: nūnam</note> is used merely to fill the meter of the verse. O Indra, you **join** <note>original: yuvase</note>—meaning you have connected this world with—the **directions** (East and so on), the **sun**, the **dawns**, the **wonderful** and desirable **waters**, and the **cows** that were stolen by the Panis. Alternatively, it means that by slaying the demons, you removed the obstruction covering the directions and other elements, making them distinct. O Agni, being **accompanied by your teams of horses** <note>original: niyutvān</note>, you also performed the same action.

**This third verse is the invitation-verse <term>anuvākyā</term> for the offering of the marrow <term>vapā</term> of the animal sacrificed to Indra and Agni. This is indicated in the liturgical manual: "O slayers of the enemy, with enemy-slaying strengths, bring [wealth] and teach us, O you with lightning in your hands..." (Ashvalayana Shrauta Sutra 3.9).**

O **slayers of the enemy** <note>original: vṛtrahaṇā</note>, killers of the demon Vritra; O Indra and Agni, **come hither** towards us with your **strengths** that are capable of **slaying the enemy**, and with the **offerings of reverence** <note>original: namobhiḥ</note> consisting of food to be given to us. O Indra and Agni, **you two** should **be** present **among us** with **wealth** <note>original: rādhobhiḥ</note> that is **most excellent** and with **songs of praise** <note>original: arkavebhiḥ</note> that are great and beyond reproach.

On the twenty-fourth day of the ritual <note>original: cāturviṃśike 'hani</note>, during the morning libation <term>prātaḥsavana</term>, in the recitation of the Acchavaka priest, there is a triplet of verses beginning with "I invoke those two"...

---

## Critical Notes

- This page completes the explanation of the first verse of the 60th hymn and provides the full text and commentary for verses 2 and 3.
- The imagery centers on the myth of the Panis, where Indra and Agni recover the light (Sun/Dawns) and the means of sustenance (Cows/Waters) from the demons.
- The technical term **niyutvān** refers to Agni (or Vayu) being drawn by specific teams of horses called Niyuts.
- The ritual application <term>viniyoga</term> links these verses to the **Aindragna Pashu**, a specific animal sacrifice dedicated to the dual deity Indra-Agni.

# Rig Veda # [Book 4, Chapter 8, Section 28]

...three verses. This is also indicated in the ritual manuals: "Those I call, of whom this..." and "This thought of yours, O beautiful ones..." <note>original: "tā huve yayoridam" and "iyaṃ vāmasya manmanaḥ" from the Ashvalayana Shrauta Sutra 7.2</note>.

In the six-day sacrificial sessions known as the *Prishthya* and *Abhiplava* <term>Prishthya/Abhiplava: specific sequences of a six-day Soma sacrifice</term>, when the number of chants is increased, the nine verses beginning with "Those I call" are used as insertions <note>original: āvapa, meaning verses added to fill out a ritual requirement</note>. It is stated: "The nine beginning with 'Those I call' and the eleven beginning with 'This thought of yours'" <note>Ashvalayana Shrauta Sutra 7.5</note>.

---

## Hymn Text

-> ॥ The fourth verse of the hymn ॥ <-

I call upon those two whose entire former deed here is celebrated; Indra and Agni do not neglect [their worshippers]. || 4 ||

**Word-for-word analysis:**
**Those | I call | Of whom both | This | Is celebrated | Entire | Formerly | Done | Indra-Agni | Thus | Not | They neglect/harm** || 4 ||

## Commentary (Sayana)

I call <note>original: huve</note> upon those two, such as they are, Indra and Agni. I summon them. Of those two, Indra and Agni, their heroic power—which was performed <note>original: kṛtam</note> in former times <note>original: purā</note> and which is the "entirety" of what has been proclaimed in the preceding verses—is celebrated <note>original: papne</note>. This means it is praised by the seers. The connection is: "I call upon those two." And those two, Indra and Agni, do not neglect <note>original: na mardhataḥ</note>; they do not harm the praisers. Therefore, the underlying sense is: "May they protect us as well when they are summoned." The word *mardhati* denotes the act of violence or harming.

---

## Hymn Text

-> ॥ Now the fifth [verse] ॥ <-

We invoke the fierce Indra and Agni, the strikers of enemies; may they be gracious to us in such a [battle]. || 5 ||

**Word-for-word analysis:**
**Fierce | With the striker | Enemies | Indra-Agni | We invoke | Those two | Us | May they be gracious | In such** || 5 ||

## Commentary (Sayana)

We invoke <note>original: havāmahe</note> Indra and Agni, who are fierce <note>original: ugrā</note>—meaning they possess immense and rising power—and who are the strikers <note>original: vighninā</note> of enemies <note>original: mṛdhaḥ</note>, meaning they specifically kill their foes. And may those two, Indra and Agni, in such a battle as this <note>original: īdṛśe</note>, be gracious to us. May they make us happy. Alternatively, the root *mṛl* denotes the act of compassion; thus, may they show compassion toward us.

-> ॥ This concludes the twenty-seventh section (Varga) of the eighth chapter of the fourth book ॥ <-

---

## Hymn Text

-> ॥ Now the sixth [verse] ॥ <-

Slay the obstacles of the Aryas, slay those of the Dasas, O lords of the good; drive away all haters. || 6 ||

**Word-for-word analysis:**
**They two slay | Obstacles/enemies | Relating to the Aryas | They two slay | Relating to the Dasas | Lords of the good | They two slay | All | Away | Haters** || 6 ||

## Commentary (Sayana)

Those two, Indra and Agni, slay <note>original: hataḥ</note> the "Vritras" <term>Vritras: here meaning obstacles or clusters of calamities</term> that are directed against the Aryas <note>original: āryaiḥ</note>, who are the performers of the sacrificial rites. Likewise, Indra and Agni, the protectors of the good <note>original: sat-patī</note>, slay the calamities relating to the Dasas. The Dasas <note>original: dāsāḥ</note> are the enemies who are devoid of ritual performance. They slay the troubles caused by them. Furthermore, they strike down all haters <note>original: dviṣaḥ</note>, meaning the hostile populations. They destroy them. Therefore, the sense is: "May they do the same for us."

# [Mandala 6, Anuvaka 5, Hymn 60] # [space] || The Fourth Ashtaka || [space] 739

On the *Chaturvimshika* day <term>Chaturvimshika: the twenty-fourth day of a sacrificial session</term>, during the morning pressing <term>Pratashsavana: the first of three daily ritual offerings of the Soma juice</term>, a triplet of verses beginning with "Indra and Agni, you two..." serves as the hymn for the *Acchavaka* priest <term>Acchavaka: one of the secondary priests who recites specific invitations to the gods</term> during the six-day ritual sequence. This is also indicated in the ritual manuals: "Indra and Agni, you two; these are indeed for the ritual of the sacrifice," regarding the *Acchavaka* <note>original reference: Ashvalayana Shrauta Sutra 7.2</note>.

->|| The first verse of the triplet (the seventh of the hymn) ||<-

## Hymn Text
O Indra and Agni, toward you both these hymns of praise have sounded out. Drink the pressed juice, you who cause happiness. || 7 ||

**Word-for-word analysis:**
**Indra-Agni | Thus | You two | These | Toward | Hymns of praise | Have sounded out | Drink | Causing happiness | Pressed [Soma]** || 7 ||

## Commentary (Sayana)
O **Indra and Agni**, **these hymns of praise** <note>original: stomaḥ</note>—meaning the chanters—**have sounded out toward** <note>original: abhyanūṣata</note> you; that is, they are praising you. O Indra and Agni, you who **cause happiness** <note>original: śambhuvā</note>, who bring joy into being, **drink** <note>original: pibataṃ</note> this **pressed** <note>original: sutam</note> Soma juice belonging to us.

---

->|| Now the eighth verse ||<-

## Hymn Text
O leaders, those teams of horses of yours which are much-desired by many, which exist for the giver [of offerings], O Indra and Agni, come with those! || 8 ||

**Word-for-word analysis:**
**Which | Yours | Are | Desired by many | Teams of horses | For the giver | O leaders | Indra-Agni | Thus | With those | Come** || 8 ||

## Commentary (Sayana)
O **leaders** <note>original: narā</note>, O guides Indra and Agni, those **teams of horses** <note>original: niyutaḥ</note> which **are yours** <note>original: vāṃ</note>, which are **desired by many** <note>original: puruspṛhaḥ</note> (sought after by many people), and which have appeared for the sake of the **giver** <note>original: dāśuṣe</note> (the patron of the sacrifice who gives oblations)—O **Indra and Agni**, **with those** teams, **come** <note>original: ā gataṃ</note> to us.

---

->|| Now the ninth verse ||<-

## Hymn Text
O leaders, come with those [teams] to this pressed ritual offering, O Indra and Agni, for the drinking of the Soma. || 9 ||

**Word-for-word analysis:**
**With those | Come | O leaders | To | This | Ritual offering | Pressed | Indra-Agni | Thus | For the drinking of the Soma** || 9 ||

## Commentary (Sayana)
O **leaders** <note>original: narā</note>, you guides Indra and Agni. The "ritual offering" <note>original: savanaḥ</note> refers to the Soma, so called because it is being pressed. Come **to this ritual offering**, toward this **pressed** <note>original: sutam</note> Soma. Or alternatively, come toward this morning pressing and the Soma pressed within it, **with those** horses, **come**. For what purpose? **For the drinking of the Soma** <note>original: somapītaye</note>, in order to consume that juice.

---

->|| Now the tenth verse ||<-

## Hymn Text
Praise him who, with his flame, embraces all the woods and makes them black with his tongue. || 10 ||

**Word-for-word analysis:**
**Him | Praise | Who | With flame | Woods | All | Embraces | Black | Makes | With tongue** || 10 ||

## Commentary (Sayana)
O worshipper, **praise** <note>original: īḷiṣva</note>—meaning laud—that Agni, **who** with his **flame** <note>original: arciṣā</note>, in the form of his fiery glow, **all** <note>original: viśvā</note>... <note>The commentary continues on the following page.</note>
