...[Agni] consumes all the forests and wild places; he "embraces" them, meaning he surrounds them on all sides. When he has burned those forests with his tongue of flame, he "makes them black," meaning he turns them the color of charcoal.

->॥ Now the eleventh verse ॥<-

## Hymn Text
The mortal man who honors the kindled fire to seek the favor of Indra; for his glory, the waters are made easy to cross. || 11 ||

**Word-for-word analysis:**
**Who | In the kindled [fire] | Honors | Favor | Of Indra | Mortal man | For glory | Easy to cross | The waters** || 11 ||

## Commentary (Sayana)
Whichever **mortal man** <note>original: martyaḥ</note> honors—meaning serves or offers—**the favor-bringing** <note>original: sumnam</note> (happiness-producing) oblation to **Indra** in the **kindled** (blazing) fire; for the **glory** <note>original: dyumnāya</note>—meaning for the shining food—of that mortal, Indra makes **the waters** <note>original: apaḥ</note> (in the form of rain) **easy to cross** <note>original: sutarāḥ</note> (easily obtainable). <note>Sayana notes a grammatical point: the possessive case "of Indra" is used here in the sense of the dative case "for Indra."</note>

->॥ Now the twelfth verse ॥<-

## Hymn Text
Bring us those food-rich refreshments and swift horses, so that we may bring Indra and Agni to the sacrifice. || 12 ||

**Word-for-word analysis:**
**Those | To us | Rich in food | Refreshments | Swift | Fulfill (give) | Horses | Indra | Agni | And | To bring** || 12 ||

## Commentary (Sayana)
O **Indra and Agni**, **those** two of you, fulfill—meaning grant or provide—**to us** the **food-rich** <note>original: vājavatīḥ</note> **refreshments** <note>original: iṣaḥ</note> (the desired rains). Alternatively, "Vaja" means strength; thus, refreshments full of strength. Also grant us **swift-going** <note>original: āśūn</note> **horses** <note>original: arvataḥ</note>. For what purpose? **To bring** <note>original: voḷhave</note>—meaning to convey or cause to arrive—**Indra and Agni** (yourselves) to the sacrificial oblations. 

Regarding the ritual use of this verse: it is used as the invitatory verse <term>Anuvakya: a verse recited by a priest to invite a deity to accept an offering</term> for the animal sacrifice dedicated to Indra and Agni. As it is said in the ritual manuals: <term>“O Indra and Agni, both of you to be called upon; today this pure, newly-born hymn of praise...”</term> <note>original reference: Ashvalayana Shrauta Sutra 3.7</note>.

---

->॥ This is the thirteenth verse of the hymn ॥<-

## Hymn Text
I call upon both Indra and Agni to be invoked; both together to be gladdened by the wealth of the offering; both givers of refreshments and riches; I call upon both for the attainment of strength. || 13 ||

**Word-for-word analysis:**
**Both | You two | Indra-Agni | To be invoked | Both | Of wealth | Together | To be gladdened | Both | Givers | Of refreshments | Of riches | Both | Of strength | For the attainment | I call | You two** || 13 ||

## Commentary (Sayana)
O **Indra and Agni**, who exist joined together as a pair, **I call** <note>original: huve</note> upon **you two**. For what purpose? **To be invoked** <note>original: āhuvadhyai</note>—to be called here before us. Likewise, I call you both **together** to be **gladdened** <note>original: mādayadhyai</note>—meaning to be satisfied—by the **wealth** <note>original: rādhasaḥ</note> (the effective oblation). If one asks why these two specifically should be called when all the gods exist, it is said: Because **both** of you are **the givers** of **refreshments** (foods) and **riches**...

## Hymn Text
Come to us with wealth consisting of cattle, horses, and riches. O divine friends, Indra and Agni, you who produce happiness, we call upon you for the sake of friendship. || 14 ||

## Commentary (Sayana)
O **Indra-Agni** <note>The dual deity of thunder/war and fire</note>, come toward us accompanied by **cattle** <note>original: gavyebhiḥ; groups of cows</note>, **horses** <note>original: ashvyaiḥ; groups of horses</note>, and **riches** <note>original: vasavyaiḥ; groups of wealth</note>. The remainder of the verse is addressed in the third person. You are **friends** <note>original: sakhāyau; those of equal renown</note>, you are **gods** <note>original: devau</note> endowed with qualities such as generosity, and you are **happiness-producing** <note>original: śambhuva; promoters of joy</note>. Such as you are, O Indra and Agni, we **call** <note>original: havāmahe; we invite</note> you for the sake of **friendship**.

## Hymn Text

## Commentary (Sayana)
O Indra and Agni, **hear** the **call** <note>original: havam; the hymn of invitation</note> of the **worshiper** <note>original: yajamānasya</note> who is **pressing** <note>original: sunvataḥ; performing the ritual extraction</note> the **Soma** <note>A sacred ritual drink</note>. Having heard it, **enjoy** <note>original: vītam; desire or consume</note> his **offerings**. Having desired them, **come** here. Having arrived, **drink** the **sweet** <note>original: madhu; honey-like</note> liquid consisting of **Soma**.

## Introductory Notes (Sukta 61)
The twelfth hymn of this section, beginning with the words "She gave" (*iyam adadāt*), consists of fourteen verses. The <term>Rishi</term> <note>the inspired seer or author</note> is **Bharadvaja**, and the deity is the goddess **Sarasvati**. Regarding the meters: the first three verses are in **Jagati** <note>a meter of 48 syllables</note>, as is the thirteenth verse; the fourteenth is in **Trishtubh** <note>44 syllables</note>, and the remaining verses are in **Gayatri** <note>24 syllables</note>. 

As stated in the <term>Anukramani</term> <note>the ancient index of the Veda</note>: "This hymn has six verses less than twenty (fourteen); it is dedicated to Sarasvati; it begins with three Jagatis and ends with a Trishtubh." 

On this matter, the sage Shaunaka says: "A twice-born man who, having purified himself in the morning, recites this first hymn dedicated to Sarasvati, becomes eloquent and wise." (Rigvidhana 2.23). 

In the ritual context of the sixth day of the <term>Parshnika</term> sacrifice, the triplet of verses starting with "She gave" is used in the **Prauga Shastra** <note>a specific set of recitations for the morning libation</note>. This is indicated in the ritual manuals: "The triplet 'She gave, the impetuous, the debt-remover' is for the Prauga." (Ashvalayana Shrauta Sutra 8.1).

<keywords>Indra-Agni, Sarasvati, Bharadvaja, Soma, Jagati meter, Gayatri meter, Prauga Shastra, ritual eloquence</keywords>

<meta>This page marks the beginning of the 61st hymn (Sukta) of the Sixth Mandala of the Rig Veda. The previous page concluded the 60th hymn dedicated to Indra and Agni. This new hymn is dedicated entirely to the goddess Sarasvati, who is praised here both as a powerful river and a divine granter of offspring. The commentary is provided by the 14th-century scholar Sayana.</meta>

-> ॥ Now the first verse ॥ <-

## Hymn Text

She gave the energetic Divodasa, the remover of debts, to the sacrificing Vadhryashva—she who thoroughly destroyed the many greedy hoarders. These, your gifts, are mighty, O Sarasvati. || 1 ||

---

**Word-for-word analysis:**
**She | Gave | The energetic | Debt-remover | Divodasa | To Vadhryashva | To the sacrificer | Who | The many | Thoroughly destroyed | The consumer/hoarder | The Pani | These | Your | Gifts | Mighty | O Sarasvati** || 1 ||

## Commentary (Sayana)
This goddess **Sarasvati** <note>In the Rig Veda, Sarasvati is both a river and the goddess of speech/wisdom</note> gave a son named **Divodasa** to the sage **Vadhryashva**, who had offered oblations. This son is described as **energetic** <note>original: rabhasam; fast or impetuous</note> and a **remover of debts** <note>original: ṛṇacyutam; one who clears the three spiritual debts to gods, sages, and ancestors, as well as worldly debts</note>. The connection is that she who **thoroughly destroyed** <note>original: ācakhāda; struck down or consumed</note> the **Pani** <note>original: paṇim; the Panis were a class of demons or stingy merchants who withheld wealth and cattle</note>—who are characterized as many and only interested in nourishing themselves—it is she who granted the son. Now, addressing the goddess directly, the poet praises her: O divine Sarasvati, these **gifts** <note>original: dātrāṇi; acts of giving</note> of yours, such as the granting of a son, are **mighty** <note>original: taviṣā; great or powerful</note>.

-> ॥ Now the second verse ॥ <-

## Hymn Text

With her powerful, parching waves, she breaks the ridges of the mountains like one digging for lotus stalks. Let us worship Sarasvati, the slayer of the Paravatas, for our protection with holy hymns and sacred works. || 2 ||

---

**Word-for-word analysis:**
**She | With powerful forces | Lotus-stalk digger | Like | Breaks | Ridge | Of mountains | With mighty | With waves | Slayer of the Paravatas | For protection | With holy hymns | Sarasvati | Near | We worship | With sacred works** || 2 ||

## Commentary (Sayana)
Sarasvati exists in two forms: as a deity and as a river. The previous verse praised her divine form; now the poet praises her in her river form. This river, Sarasvati, with her **powerful forces** <note>original: śuṣmaiḥ; forces that dry up or overpower</note> and her **mighty waves** <note>original: taviṣebhir ūrmibhiḥ</note>, breaks the **ridges** <note>original: sānu; the peaks or slopes</note> of the mountains adjacent to her banks. She does this **like one digging for lotus stalks** <note>original: bisakhā iva</note>; just as a person digs up the mud to find lotus roots, the river's force carves through the earth. We seek to **worship** <note>original: ā-vivāsema; to serve or attend upon</note> that Sarasvati for our **protection** <note>original: avase</note> through holy hymns and ritual actions. She is called the **slayer of the Paravatas** <note>original: pārāvataghnīm</note>, which means she destroys even the trees and obstacles in distant lands <note>original: parāvati; in a far-off place</note>. Alternatively, according to the *Nirukta* <note>An ancient text on Sanskrit etymology</note>, it means she strikes against her own "far and near" banks.

-> ॥ Now the third verse ॥ <-

## Hymn Text

O Sarasvati, strike down those who revile the gods, the offspring of the deceptive Brisaya. You found lands for the people to dwell in; O you who are rich in food, you flowed through the uneven terrains. || 3 ||

<vocab>
**Sarasvati**: The goddess and river of inspiration and flow.
**Divodasa**: A famous king in the Rig Veda, son of Vadhryashva.
**Vadhryashva**: A sage and king, father of Divodasa.
**Pani**: A term for stingy, non-sacrificing people or mythological hoarders.
**Bisakha**: One who digs for lotus stalks (*bisa*).
**Paravataghni**: Destroyer of the *Paravatas* (a specific tribe or those from afar).
**Nirukta**: Yaska's ancient treatise on the derivation of Vedic words.
**Vajinivati**: An epithet meaning "possessing food" or "possessing swift horses."
</vocab>

<summary>This page introduces the hymn to the goddess Sarasvati, depicting her as a powerful river that carves through mountains and a generous deity who grants a hero-son to the sage Vadhryashva. The verses emphasize her role in destroying the enemies of the Vedic people, specifically the Panis and the followers of Brisaya.</summary>
<keywords>Sarasvati, Divodasa, Vadhryashva, river goddess, Pani, mountain breaker, Vedic hymns, Sayana commentary</keywords>

<meta>This page continues the commentary on the 61st hymn of the Sixth Mandala of the Rig Veda, dedicated to the goddess Sarasvati. It concludes the commentary for verse 3 and provides the text and explanation for verses 4, 5, and 6. ## Hymn Text

O Sarasvati, strike down the revilers of the gods. Strike down the offspring of the all-pervading, deceitful Brisaya. Moreover, for the sake of the people, you found the lands; for them, you flowed with water, O you who are rich in food. || 3 ||

---

## Commentary (Sayana)

O **Sarasvati**, **strike down** <note>original: nibarhaya; destroy or kill</note> the **revilers of the gods**, the demons. Likewise, you destroyed the **offspring**—the son Vritra—of the all-encompassing, **deceitful Brisaya**. <note>original: bṛsayasya; Sayana identifies Brisaya as a name for Tvashtri, the divine smith, though here it refers to an adversarial figure</note>. The meaning is that Indra killed him only through your assistance. Furthermore, O **rich in food** <note>original: vājinīvati</note> Sarasvati, you **found** and obtained the **lands** <note>original: avanīḥ; the earth or rivers</note> that had been stolen by demons for the sake of **humanity** <note>original: kṣitibhyaḥ; for the people or settlers</note>. For these men, you **flowed with water** <note>original: viṣam; though usually meaning poison, Sayana interprets viṣam here as water, or alternatively as "deadly poison" for the enemies</note>.

Alternatively, the "peoples" <note>original: kṣitayaḥ</note> refers to the demon-folk; you took the lands away from them, and having killed them, you poured out **poison**—the cause of death—upon those demons.

---

## Hymn Text

-> ॥ Now the fourth verse ॥ <-

May the divine Sarasvati, rich in food, protect us with her nourishings—she, the protector of our prayers. || 4 ||

**Word-for-word analysis:**
**May [she] | Us | Divine | Sarasvati | With food/energies | Rich in food | Of prayers | The protector | Protect.** || 4 ||

---

## Commentary (Sayana)

The **divine** one, endowed with the qualities of generosity and light, is **rich in food**. <note>original: vājinīvati; Sayana breaks this down as 'vāja' meaning food or action, and the goddess being possessed of it</note>. She is the **protector** of those who meditate upon her and those who praise her. May such a Sarasvati **protect us** and thoroughly satisfy us **with food**.

---

## Hymn Text

-> ॥ Now the fifth verse ॥ <-

O divine Sarasvati, whoever calls upon you for the sake of wealth when it is contested, as one calls upon Indra in the battle against Vritra... || 5 ||

**Word-for-word analysis:**
**Who | You | Divine | Sarasvati | Calls upon | For wealth | Established/Contested | Indra | Like | In the Vritra-battle.** || 5 ||

---

## Commentary (Sayana)

O **divine Sarasvati**, the singer **who** praises and **calls upon you** in the **battle against Vritra** <note>original: vṛtratūrye; can mean a specific battle or a general metaphor for overcoming obstacles/enemies</note> for the sake of obtaining **established wealth**—calling upon you just **as** one calls upon **Indra**—[may you protect him]. <note>Sayana adds "protect him" to complete the grammatical thought of the verse</note>.

-> ॥ Thus ends the twentieth Varga of the eighth Adhyaya of the fourth Ashtaka ॥ <-

---

## Hymn Text

-> ॥ Now the sixth verse ॥ <-

O divine Sarasvati, protect us in battles, O powerful one; like Pushan, grant us wealth. || 6 ||

**Word-for-word analysis:**
**You | Divine | Sarasvati | Protect | In battles | O powerful one | Grant | Pushan-like | Our | Gift.** || 6 ||

---

## Commentary (Sayana)

O **divine** one, O **powerful one** <note>original: vājini; possessed of 'vāja' which can mean strength or food</note>, O Sarasvati, **protect** us **in battles**. Furthermore, **grant** <note>original: rada; literally 'dig' or 'bestow'</note> to **us** the **wealth** <note>original: sanim; a gift or share</note> that is worthy of being enjoyed, just **like Pushan** <note>The solar deity Pushan is often invoked as a provider of wealth and a guide for paths</note>, the nourishing god, does.

<summary>This page concludes the praise of Sarasvati's martial prowess in defeating the demon Brisaya's offspring and begins a series of prayers for her protection in battle and the granting of wealth, comparing her power to that of Indra and Pushan.</summary>

<page-num>844</page-num>
<header>॥ Rig Veda ॥ [Book 4, Chapter 8, Section 31.]</header>

-> ॥ Now the Seventh ॥ <-

## Hymn Text
And may that Sarasvati, the formidable one with a golden path, the slayer of enemies, desire our beautiful hymn. || 7 ||

**Word-for-word analysis:**
**And | that | our | Sarasvati | formidable | golden-pathed | enemy-slaying | desires | beautiful-hymn** || 7 ||

---

## Commentary (Sayana)
**And also** <note>original: utāpi ca</note>, may **that** well-known **Sarasvati**, who is **formidable**—meaning she causes fear in her enemies—**desire** or welcome **our beautiful hymn**, our excellent praise. She is described as **golden-pathed** <note>original: hiraṇyavartaniḥ</note>. A "path" <note>original: vartani</note> is that by which one moves, namely a chariot; therefore, her chariot is made of gold. She is also the **slayer of enemies** <note>original: vṛtraghnī</note>, the destroyer of those who obstruct <note>original: vṛtrāṇām</note>.

-> ॥ Now the Eighth ॥ <-

## Hymn Text
Whose power—limitless, unharmed, brilliant, ever-moving, surging—flows with a great roar. || 8 ||

**Word-for-word analysis:**
**Whose | endless | unharmed | brilliant | ever-moving | surging | power | flows | roaring** || 8 ||

---

## Commentary (Sayana)
**Whose**—referring to Sarasvati—**power** <note>original: amaḥ; strength or force</note> **flows** or exists, making a **great roar** <note>original: roruvat; a loud sound</note>. This power is **endless**, meaning it is without limit or measure. It is **unharmed** <note>original: ahutaḥ; literally 'un-struck', meaning it is not bent or hindered</note>. It is **brilliant** <note>original: tveṣaḥ; glowing</note> and **ever-moving**, meaning her course is unobstructed everywhere. It is **surging** <note>original: arṇavaḥ</note>, meaning it is full of water or is the provider of water. The connection to the phrase "she [carries] us [past] all" follows in the next verse.

-> ॥ Now the Ninth ॥ <-

## Hymn Text
May she, the possessor of truth, carry us past all enemies and [past] her other sisters, as the Sun carries us through the days. || 9 ||

**Word-for-word analysis:**
**She | us | all | past | enemies | sisters | other | truth-possessing | carried | days-like | Sun** || 9 ||

---

## Commentary (Sayana)
May **she**, Sarasvati, **carry us past** or lead us across **all** our **enemies** who surround us. Furthermore, may she who is the **possessor of truth** <note>original: ṛtāvarī; ṛta can mean the cosmic law or, as Sayana notes here, 'water'</note> lead us past the **other** rivers, her **sisters** who flow alongside her. 

<note>Grammatical note: Sayana mentions a Vedic variation where the plural ending is lengthened.</note>

Alternatively, the "water-rich sisters" refers to other rivers like the Ganges and others; may she lead us past our enemies through their aid. A comparison is given: **as the Sun**, the stimulator of all, moving constantly, carries us through the **days**. Just as the sun swiftly leads us through the passage of days, may she likewise lead us quickly.

## Critical Notes
In the **ten-night ritual** <term>Daśarātra: A major Soma sacrifice lasting ten days</term>, on the third day, during the **Prauga** <term>Prauga: A specific litany of seven triplets of verses addressed to different deities</term>, the triplet beginning with **"And to us, the dear one..."** <note>Rig Veda 6.61.1</note> is used for Sarasvati. This is indicated in the **Ashvalayana Shrauta Sutra** <note>9.10</note>: "The Ushnih-meter Prauga begins with 'And to us, the dear one, among the dear ones...'"

In the **purifying sacrifice** <term>Pavitreṣṭi: A ritual performed for purification</term>, the same verse is used as the **invitatory verse** <term>Anuvākyā: A verse recited by the Hotri priest to invite a deity to the offering</term> for the offering to Sarasvati. This is also indicated in the Ashvalayana Shrauta Sutra <note>2.12</note>: "And to us, the dear one, among the dear ones, these [oblations] are being offered with bows from you."

<header>Mandala 6, Chapter 5, Hymn 61.] || The Fourth Book (Ashtaka) ||</header>

## Hymn Text

-> ॥ The tenth verse of the first hymn of the triad ॥ <-

And may Sarasvati, our beloved among the beloved, having seven sisters, well-pleased, be worthy of praise. || 10 ||

**And | our | beloved | among the beloved | seven-sistered | well-pleased | Sarasvati | worthy of praise | be.** || 10 ||

---

## Commentary (Sayana)

**And also** <note>original: utāpi ca</note>, may the goddess **Sarasvati** be **worthy of praise** <note>original: stomyā; deserving of hymns</note>. She is described as **beloved** <note>original: priyā</note>, the most dear among those things that are **beloved** to us. She is **seven-sistered** <note>original: saptasvasā</note>, meaning she has the seven meters—such as the Gayatri—as her sisters; or, in her form as a river, the seven rivers—such as the Ganges—are her sisters. She is **well-pleased** <note>original: sujuṣṭā</note>, meaning she has been well-served or worshipped by the ancient seers <note>original: ṛṣis</note>. May such a goddess be the object of our hymns.

-> ॥ Thus ends the twenty-first section (varga) of the eighth chapter of the fourth book ॥ <-

---

## Hymn Text

-> ॥ Now the eleventh ॥ <-

Having filled the terrestrial regions and the wide atmosphere, may Sarasvati protect us from the reviler. || 11 ||

**Having filled | terrestrial | wide | region | atmosphere | Sarasvati | from the reviler | protect.** || 11 ||

---

## Commentary (Sayana)

The goddess **Sarasvati**, who has **filled** <note>original: āpapruṣī; pervaded or saturated</note> with her own brilliance the **terrestrial** <note>original: pārthivāni</note> realms—referring to the vast and extensive **regions** of the earth—and the **atmosphere** <note>original: antarikṣam; the space between heaven and earth</note>, may she **protect** us. Specifically, may she protect us **from the reviler** <note>original: nidaḥ</note>, meaning from the enemy who speaks ill of us.

---

## Hymn Text

-> ॥ Now the twelfth ॥ <-

Abiding in three places, seven-fold, nourishing the five peoples, may she be invoked in every battle. || 12 ||

**Abiding in three places | seven-fold | five | peoples | nourishing | in every battle | to be invoked | be.** || 12 ||

---

## Commentary (Sayana)

**Abiding in three places** <note>original: triṣadhasthā</note> means she exists simultaneously in the three worlds <note>the earth, atmosphere, and heaven</note>, pervading all three. She is **seven-fold** <note>original: saptadhātuḥ</note>, having seven parts or constituents, which refers again to either the seven meters (Gayatri, etc.) or the seven rivers (Ganges, etc.). She is **nourishing the five peoples** <note>original: pañca jātā vardhayantī</note>, causing the five classes of beings to prosper—this refers either to the four castes plus the Nishadas <note>an ancient group outside the traditional four-fold system</note>, or to the five divine beings like the Gandharvas. Such a **Sarasvati** is **to be invoked** <note>original: havyā; worthy of being called upon</note> **in every battle** <note>original: vāje vāje</note>, meaning in all conflicts or struggles.

---

## Hymn Text

-> ॥ Now the thirteenth ॥ <-

Sarasvati, who is distinguished by her greatness among these [rivers], who is the most active among the active, like a vast chariot constructed for power, she is to be praised by the wise one. || 13 ||

**Forth | who | by greatness | by great | among these | is distinguished | by her splendors | others | among the active | most active.**
**Chariot | like | vast | for power | constructed | to be praised | by the wise | Sarasvati.** || 13 ||

<note>This verse emphasizes Sarasvati's superiority over other rivers and her role as the primary object of wisdom and praise.</note>

<header>|| Rig Veda || [Book 4, Chapter 8, Section 32.]</header>

## Commentary (Sayana)
<note>This concludes the commentary on Rig Veda 6.61.13 from the previous page.</note>

Through her **greatness** <note>original: mahimnā; her majesty</note>, that is, through her high status, she is endowed with **splendor** <note>original: dyumnebhir; referring to either glorious fame or an abundance of food</note>. Among all these rivers and deities, **Sarasvati** is the one who is **distinctly known** <note>original: pra cekite; highly distinguished or celebrated</note>. Among the other **active** <note>original: apasām; referring to the swift-moving rivers</note> waters, she is the **most active** <note>original: apastamā; the swiftest or most powerful</note>. Like a chariot built for **pervading power** <note>original: vibhvane</note>, she is **vast** <note>original: bṛhatī</note>, expanded and made great with many virtues by the Creator, Prajapati. Such is Sarasvati, who is to be **approached with praise** <note>original: upastutyā</note> by the **wise** <note>original: cikituṣā; the one who knows</note>. She is indeed worthy of our hymns.

---

-> ॥ Now the fourteenth verse ॥ <-

## Hymn Text

O Sarasvati, lead us to better wealth; do not push us away. Do not overwhelm us with your waters. Be pleased with our friendship and our companionship. May we not go from you to lands that are unpleasant. ॥ 14 ॥

**Sarasvati | toward | us | lead | better wealth | do not | away | push | with water | do not | us | [over]power | strike | enjoy | our | friendship | companionship | and | do not | from you | lands | unpleasant | go.** ॥ 14 ॥

---

## Commentary (Sayana)

O **Sarasvati**, **lead** <note>original: abhineṣi; bring us toward</note> us to **better wealth** <note>original: vasyo; more excellent riches</note>. **Do not push us away** <note>original: māpa spharīḥ</note>; do not make us un-prosperous <note>The commentator notes that while 'sphāra' usually means growth or increase, the prefix 'apa' here reverses the meaning to imply a lack of growth</note>. Likewise, do not **strike** <note>original: mā dhak; do not burn or afflict</note> or oppress us with an excess of **water** <note>original: payasā</note> <note>A prayer to prevent the river from flooding or destroying crops</note>. Furthermore, **enjoy** <note>original: juṣasva; be pleased with or serve</note> our **friendship** <note>original: sakhyā; acts of a friend</note> and our **dwellings** <note>original: veśyā; our entryways or homes</note>. May we **not go** <note>original: mā ganma</note> from your presence to **unpleasant** <note>original: araṇāni; literally 'non-delightful' or inferior</note> **lands** <note>original: kṣetrāṇi</note>, but rather let us always reside in beautiful and fertile places.

-> ॥ Thus ends the thirty-second section of the eighth chapter of the fourth book ॥ <-
-> ॥ Thus ends the fifth lesson (Anuvaka) of the sixth Mandala ॥ <-

By the light of the meaning of the Veda, dispelling the darkness of the heart,
May the Great Lord Vidyatirtha grant the four goals of human life.
</center>

Thus, in the *Madhaviya Vedartha Prakasha* <note>The Light on the Meaning of the Vedas</note>, composed by the Great Teacher Sayana, the minister of the empire of the King Bukka I, the supreme king of kings and promoter of the Vedic path,
**the eighth chapter of the fourth book is completed.**

- **Sarasvati**: Here invoked as both a river that can flood and a goddess who provides fertile land and wealth.
- **Vasyas**: A comparative term for wealth, implying not just riches but a "better" or more prosperous state.
- **Prajapati**: The Creator deity mentioned in the commentary as the one who fashioned Sarasvati’s greatness.
- **Four goals of human life**: Known as the Purusharthas: Dharma (duty), Artha (prosperity), Kama (pleasure), and Moksha (liberation).
- **Sayana**: The 14th-century scholar whose commentary is the standard for understanding the Rig Veda.
</vocab>

-> Om <-

-> **Salutation to the auspicious Lord Ganesha** <-

**To Ganesha, whose mind is pure at the beginning of all endeavors,**
**Whom having bowed to, one becomes successful—to that elephant-faced one, I bow.**
**I salute Vidyatirtha Maheshvara, whose breath is the Vedas,**
**And who created the entire world from the Vedas.**

Now begins the First Chapter of the Fifth Volume <note>original: pañcamāṣṭaka; the fifth of eight major sections of the Rig Veda</note>. In the sixth section <note>original: anuvāka</note> of the Sixth Book <note>original: maṇḍala</note>, there are fourteen hymns. Among them, the first hymn, beginning with "I praise the two leaders," consists of eleven verses. Regarding this, the Systematic Index <note>original: anukramaṇikā; a traditional catalog of Vedic hymns</note> states: **"The hymn 'I praise' consists of eleven verses and is dedicated to the Ashvins."** The seer <note>original: rishi</note> of this book is Bharadvaja, the descendant of Brihaspati. Since the meter is not explicitly named, it is understood to be *Trishtubh* <note>a meter consisting of four lines of eleven syllables each</note>. The deities are the Ashvins <note>the twin physician-gods of the Vedic pantheon</note>. In the morning litany <note>original: prātaranuvāka</note>, during the ritual time for the Ashvins, there are two hymns beginning with this one. These same two are also used in the Ashvin-shastra <note>a specific recitation for the Ashvins in the Soma sacrifice</note>. This is indicated in the Ashvalayana Shrauta Sutra (4.15): "The hymn 'I praise the two leaders'..."

-> ॥ Here begins the first verse ॥ <-

---

## Hymn Text

I praise the two leaders of this heaven, the two rulers; I invoke the Ashvins, honoring them with hymns. They who, at the end of the night, swiftly drive away the enemies <note>or "the shadows"</note> from the ends of the earth, and encompass the vast, wide spaces. ॥ 1 ॥

**Pada-patha:**
I praise । the two leaders । of heaven । of this । the two rulers । the Ashvins । I invoke । honoring । with hymns ।
who । swiftly । the driving-away ones । at the breaking [of dawn] । of the earth । the ends । encompassing । around । wide । spaces ॥ 1 ॥

---

## Commentary (Sayana)

**Of heaven** <note>original: divo</note> refers to the celestial world. **The two leaders** <note>original: narā</note> means the guides or directors of this world. **The two rulers** <note>original: prasantā</note> refers to those who are powerful, the lords. **The Ashvins** <note>original: aśvinau</note>, those who are endowed with horses, **I praise** <note>original: stuṣe</note>. Through praises achieved by sung mantras and through weapons <note>shastras</note> achieved by worshipful mantras, **honoring** <note>original: jaramāṇaḥ</note> or offering praise, **I invoke** <note>original: huve</note>; that is, I call upon them. 

In response to the question "What are they like?", the text says: **Who** <note>original: yā</note>, meaning the two who **swiftly** <note>original: sadya</note> are **the driving-away ones** <note>original: usrā</note> of enemies. **At the breaking** <note>original: vyuṣi</note> means at the dawn or the completion of the night. **Of the earth** <note>original: kṣmaḥ</note>...

<meta>This page continues the commentary on the 62nd hymn of the Sixth Book of the Rig Veda. The previous page established the ritual context of this hymn, which is dedicated to the Ashvins—the divine twin physicians—and authored by the sage Bharadvaja. This page focuses on the second and third verses, describing the Ashvins' arrival at the sacrifice and their protection of the worshipper.</meta>

## Commentary (Sayana - Fragment)
...separating the surrounding ends, the vast spaces <note>original: varāṃsi</note>, and the darknesses that cover form. Alternatively, they spread the splendors <note>original: varāṃsi</note> by removing the darkness.

->॥ Here begins the second verse ॥<-

## Hymn Text
Those two, approaching the sacrifice with pure splendors, have made the brightness of the chariot shine through the regions of space. Measuring out many immeasurable spaces, they travel across the waters and the deserts with their horses. ॥ २ ॥

**Those two** | **the sacrifice** | **toward** | **with pure [splendors]** | **approaching** | **of the chariot** | **the brightness** | **they made shine** | **through regions of space**
**Many** | **spaces** | **immeasurable** | **measuring out** | **waters** | **deserts** | **they cross** | **travel** | **horses** ॥ २ ॥

---

## Commentary (Sayana)
Furthermore, **those two** <note>the famous Ashvins</note> **approaching our sacrifice** <note>our ritual act</note> with **pure** and stainless **regions** <note>meaning their own splendors or lights</note>. This is based on the authority of the ancient etymologist Yaska, who stated: "Light is called *rajas* from the root meaning to shine" <note>Nirukta 4.19; the term 'rajas' usually means atmosphere, but here is interpreted as light</note>. They **have made the brightness** <note>the radiance</note> **of the chariot**—their own chariot—**shine**. Additionally, **measuring out** or creating **many immeasurable spaces** <note>meaning the splendors that remove darkness</note>, you **cross** or cause your **horses** <note>original: añjān</note> to cross **the deserts** <note>waterless regions</note> while moving toward the waters.

---

->॥ Here begins the third verse ॥<-

## Hymn Text
Indeed, that journey of yours which reaches the goal adequately, they always carry the prayer with horses. With horses swift as thought and eager, to bring about the long sleep of the mortal who harms the giver. ॥ ३ ॥

**Those two** | **indeed** | **that** | **journey** | **which** | **adequately** | **reaches** | **prayers** | **they carry** | **always** | **with horses**
**Swift as thought** | **with eager [horses]** | **for lying down** | **around** | **the injurer** | **of the giver** | **of the mortal** ॥ ३ ॥

---

## Commentary (Sayana)
**Indeed, those two**—you two Ashvins—**when** you go to that **journey** <note>original: vartiḥ; referring to the path to the house of the worshipper</note> which is **adequate** <note>sufficiently prosperous</note> to support the worshipper. Furthermore, they **always carry** <note>convey to heaven</note> the **prayers** <note>the hymns of the chanters</note> with your **horses** that are **swift as thought** and **eager** <note>desirable or full of speed</note>. For the **mortal** human **who gives** <note>the pious worshipper</note>, let the **injurer** <note>the one who causes pain or the enemy</note> be made by you to enter a **long sleep** <note>literally "to lie down all around," meaning death or total incapacitation</note>.

---

->॥ Here begins the fourth verse ॥<-

## Hymn Text
May those two attend to the new prayer of the one praising them, they who are fond of being yoked together. Bringing nourishment, strength, and the desired prize, may the two youthful, non-deceiving ones perform the sacrifice for the sake of the honey-sweetness. ॥ ४ ॥

## Commentary (Sayana)

**Those two** <note>the two Ashvins</note> **having yoked horses** <note>original: yuyujānasaptī</note> to their chariot, **bringing radiance** <note>original: śubham</note> or beauty, **food** <note>original: pṛkṣam</note>—for *pṛkṣa* is listed among the names for food and milk—**refreshment** or vigor, and **strength** <note>the essence of food</note>, they **approach** <note>original: upabhūṣataḥ</note> or come toward the **praiseworthy hymn** <note>original: manma</note> of the **newer** or more recent **one who praises**. Alternatively, it means they stay near the hymn. Furthermore, may the **ancient** and eternal **Priest** <note>original: hotā</note>, the invoker of the gods, the **non-deceiving** and beloved Agni, **worship** <note>perform the sacrifice for</note> **those two youths** who are eternally young.

## Hymn Text

-> ॥ Here begins the fifth verse ॥ <-

I honor with a new song those two, the beautiful, performing many deeds, the ancient ones; who are most conducive to happiness for the one who recites and praises, and are of wondrous gifts to the singer. ॥ ५ ॥

## Commentary (Sayana)

**Who** <note>the two Ashvins</note> **have become** the **bringers of extreme happiness** <note>original: śambhaviṣṭhā</note>, or are happiness personified, for the person who **recites** the ritual hymns <note>shastras</note> and **praises** with songs <note>stotras</note>, and for the **singer** who offers extraordinary praises beyond the standard ritual songs. They are **of wonderful gifts** <note>giving marvelous things</note>. **Those two**, the **beautiful** or gracefully moving ones, **performing many deeds** or possessing many helpers, the **ancient** or eternal ones, the **miraculous** <note>original: dasrā</note> and lovely Ashvins—I **honor** or serve them with a **newer** or more recent **speech** <note>original: vacasā</note>, meaning a new hymn of praise.

**Ashvins** (Aśvinau): The twin Vedic deities, often portrayed as physicians of the gods who rescue those in distress.

**Dasra** (Dasrā): A common title for the Ashvins, meaning "performers of wonderful deeds" or "beautiful."

--- Page 918 ---
<meta>This page continues the commentary on the 73rd hymn of the Fifth Book of the Rig Veda, dedicated to the Ashvins. It concludes the description of the rescue of Bhujyu from the ocean and proceeds to describe the Ashvins' various miracles and a prayer for divine protection against the wrath of the gods.</meta>

...protecting [him], you two [the Ashvins] led [Bhujyu] out from the lap of the water, from the ocean, by dustless <note>original: areṇubhiḥ</note> paths in the atmosphere, with chariot-yoked birds <note>referring to the winged horses or actual birds that pulled the Ashvins' craft</note>. The expression "from the lap of the ocean" <note>original: samudrād anga</note> is used here in the sense of "he goes from his mother's house" <note>a grammatical comparison used by the commentator to explain the ablative case usage</note>.

---

-> ॥ Here begins the seventh verse ॥ <-

## Hymn Text

O charioteers, you two travel through the mountain with your victorious chariot. O showerers of benefits, you heard the call of Vadhrimati. Bestowing gifts, you filled the cow with milk for Shayu; thus, you two, who are ever-moving, maintain good favor. ॥ ७ ॥

**Pada Patha:**

Through | victorious | charioteers | travel | the mountain | heard | the call | O showerers | of Vadhrimati | bestowing gifts | for Shayu | filled | the cow | thus | moving | good favor | ever-active ॥ ७ ॥

---

## Commentary (Sayana)

**O charioteers** <note>original: rathyā</note>, O Ashvins mounted on your chariot, with your **victorious** <note>original: jyuṣā</note> chariot, **travel through** <note>original: vi yātam</note> or shatter the **mountain** <note>original: adrim</note> standing in your path. Here, the verb "to go" <note>yāti</note> implies the act of "striking" or "killing." This is supported by another Vedic passage:
> "O Nasatyas <note>another name for the Ashvins</note>, with your chariot that shatters, you traveled through the mountains, remaining ever-young." (Rig Veda 1.116.20)

Furthermore, **O showerers** <note>original: vṛṣaṇā</note> of desires, you **heard** <note>original: śrutam</note> the **call** <note>invocation</note> of **Vadhrimati** <note>a legendary woman whose name literally means "having a sterile husband"; she prayed to the Ashvins for a son</note> who desired a son. **Bestowing gifts** <note>original: daśasyantā</note> upon the chanters, you **filled** <note>original: pipyathuḥ</note> or caused to overflow with milk the **cow** belonging to **Shayu** <note>a protégé of the Ashvins who was given a cow that yielded milk though it was initially barren</note> as he praised you. This is also supported by another passage:
> "O Nasatyas, by your wondrous deeds, you filled the barren cow with milk for the exhausted Shayu." (Rig Veda 1.116.22)

In this manner, **maintaining good favor** <note>original: sumatiṃ cyavānā</note> or beautiful hymns, you are the **ever-active** <note>original: bhuraṇyū</note> ones who travel everywhere or sustain the sacrifice.

---

-> ॥ Here begins the eighth verse ॥ <-

## Hymn Text

Whatever great wrath of the gods exists in heaven and earth, even among mortals, O Adityas, Vasus, and Rudras, place that scorching calamity upon the one allied with demons. ॥ ८ ॥

**Pada Patha:**

Whatever | Heaven and Earth | ancient | is | great | wrath | of the gods | and | among mortals | that | Adityas | Vasus | Rudras | allied with demons | scorching | calamity | place ॥ ८ ॥

---

## Commentary (Sayana)

O **Heaven and Earth** <note>original: rodasī</note>, O **Adityas**, O **Vasus**, and O **sons of Rudra** <note>original: rudriyāsaḥ</note> (the Maruts), whatever **great** <note>original: bhūma</note> **wrath** <note>original: heḷaḥ</note> of the gods exists **among mortals** <note>original: martyatrā</note> who are the attendants of the Ashvins, **place** <note>original: dadhāta</note> that wrath—which is **scorching** <note>original: tapuḥ</note> or burning—as a **calamity** <note>original: agham</note> to strike the **one allied with demons** <note>original: rakṣoyuje</note>, meaning the master or instigator of demons. Alternatively, place that calamity upon the sacrificer who is associated with demons to destroy them.

<term>Rodasī</term> — A dual term referring to the combined entity of Heaven (Dyauṣ) and Earth (Pṛthivī).
<term>Adityas, Vasus, Rudras</term> — Three primary classes of Vedic deities representing different cosmic spheres.
<term>Heḷaḥ</term> — A specific Vedic word for divine anger or displeasure.
<term>Rakṣoyuj</term> — One who yokes or joins with <term>Rakshasas</term> (demons/evil spirits); an evildoer or sorcerer.

### [Mandala 6, Anuvaka 6, Sukta 62] | Fifth Ashtaka | Page 751

-> ॥ Here begins the ninth verse ॥ <-

## Hymn Text

He who duly honors these two kings, Mitra and Varuna shall take notice of him. He hurls a weapon against the deep-lurking demon, and even against the deceptive speech of the mortal enemy. ॥ ९ ॥

**Word-for-Word Analysis (Pada Patha):**

He who | [particle for emphasis] | the two kings | in due season | disposing | of the world | Mitra | Varuna | shall know | for the deep-seated | demon | a weapon | of his | for the treacherous | indeed | speech | of the mortal enemy ॥ ९ ॥

---

## Commentary (Sayana)

The man who **duly** <note>original: ṛtuthā; at the proper time</note> honors these two **kings** <note>original: rājānā; referring here to the Ashvins, though Mitra and Varuna are mentioned</note> of **the world** <note>original: rajasah; referring to all the worlds as explained by the ancient etymologist Yaska</note>, him **Mitra and Varuna** and other gods shall **know** <note>original: ciketat; take notice of or recognize</note>. This means the gods acknowledge such a worshipper. Furthermore, this worshipper **hurls** <note>original: asyati</note> a lethal **weapon** <note>original: hetim; a striking instrument</note> against the **deep-seated** <note>original: gambhīrāya; very powerful</note> **demon** <note>original: rakṣase</note>. <note>Note: Sayana points out a grammatical shift here from the third person to the second person</note>. He also hurls this weapon even against the **speech** <note>original: vacase cit</note> of the **mortal enemy** <note>original: ānavāya; a human adversary or descendant of Anu</note> who is **treacherous** <note>original: droghāya</note>, for such a person attacks the worshipper with malicious words.

---

-> ॥ Here begins the tenth verse ॥ <-

## Hymn Text

With your innermost wheels, come to our home with your glorious, hero-laden chariot for the sake of our children. With your hidden power, strike away the heads of the mortal who seeks to harm us. ॥ १० ॥

**Word-for-Word Analysis (Pada Patha):**

With the innermost | wheels | for progeny | the dwelling | glorious | come | with the hero-laden | chariot | with hidden | power | of the mortal | of those seeking to harm | even | the heads | strike off ॥ १० ॥

---

## Commentary (Sayana)

O Ashvins, with a **chariot** equipped with **innermost** <note>original: antaraiḥ; meaning wheels that are not inferior or are well-fitted</note> wheels, which is **glorious** <note>original: dyumat; shining</note> and **hero-laden** <note>original: nṛvatā; accompanied by a leader or charioteer; alternatively, Yaska suggests 'nara' can refer to horses</note>, come to our **dwelling** <note>original: vartiḥ</note> to grant us **progeny** <note>original: tanayāya; children</note>. Moreover, with **hidden** <note>original: sanutyena</note> **power** <note>original: tyajasā; interpreted here as wrath or defensive strength</note>, **strike off** <note>original: apivavṛktam</note> the **heads** <note>original: śīrṣā</note> of the **mortals** who are **seeking to harm** <note>original: vanuṣyatām; those who act as enemies</note> us. <note>original: vanuṣyati</note> is defined by Yaska as the act of killing or injuring.

---

-> ॥ Here begins the eleventh verse ॥ <-

## Hymn Text

Come from the highest, from the middle, or from the lowest regions with your yoked teams; for the singer, open the doors of the firm, cattle-filled enclosure... ॥ ११ ॥

## Hymn Text
<note>Rig Veda 6.72.11</note>
Come [O Ashvins] with your supreme, your middle, and your lowest teams of horses. From nearby, open the doors of the firmly closed cow-pen which is full of cattle. For the worshipper, be bestowers of wonderful gifts. ॥ ११ ॥

**Word-for-Word Analysis (Padapatha):**
Come | [with] supreme | and | [with] middle | with teams of horses | come | [with] lowest | from nearby | of the firm | indeed | of the one possessed of cattle | open | of the cow-pen | the doors | [for] the worshipper | O bestowers of wonderful gifts ॥ ११ ॥

---

## Commentary (Sayana)
O Ashvins, come towards us with your **teams of horses** <note>original: niyudbhiḥ; horses yoked to a chariot</note> that are **supreme** <note>original: paramābhiḥ; of the highest quality</note>, **middle** <note>original: madhyamābhiḥ; of moderate quality</note>, and even those that are **lowest** <note>original: avamābhiḥ; of lesser quality</note>. **Open** <note>original: vivartaṃ; unroll or throw open</note> the **doors** of the **cow-pen** <note>original: vrajasya; the enclosure where cattle are kept</note> which is **firmly closed** <note>original: dṛḷhasya</note> and **full of cattle**. Furthermore, for me, the one **praising** <note>original: gṛṇate</note> you, be **bestowers of wonderful gifts** <note>original: citrarātī; those who give varied and amazing wealth</note>.

->॥ Thus ends the second section (Varga) of the first chapter (Adhyaya) of the fifth book (Ashtaka) ॥<-

The second hymn, beginning with "Where are those two," consists of eleven verses and was seen by the sage **Bharadvaja** <note>One of the seven great seers (Saptarishi) associated with the Sixth Mandala of the Rig Veda</note>. The Index (Anukramani) states: "The hymn ending in 'kva tya' is in the **Trishtup** meter" <note>A Vedic meter consisting of four lines of eleven syllables each</note>. The eleventh verse is a single-footed Trishtup, while the rest are standard Trishtup. As the text mentions "for the two Ashvins," the deities of this hymn are the Ashvins. It is applied in the **Morning Prayer** <note>original: prātaranuvāka</note> and the **Ashvina-shastra** <note>A specific ritual recitation for the Ashvins</note> within the section designated for the Trishtup meter.

->॥ Here begins the first verse [of the new Sukta] ॥<-

## Hymn Text
<note>Rig Veda 6.73.1</note>
Where are those two beautiful ones, much-invoked today? Like a messenger, our devotional hymn has found them. O Nasatyas, what hymn has turned you toward us? For you both are the most beloved in this worshipper’s prayer. ॥ १ ॥

**Word-for-Word Analysis (Padapatha):**
Where | those two | beautiful | much-invoked | today | messenger | like | hymn of praise | has found | devotional | come | which | toward | O Nasatyas | has turned | most beloved | indeed | you two are | of this | in the prayer ॥ १ ॥

---

## Commentary (Sayana)
**Where** are **those two** Ashvins situated—those who are **beautiful** <note>original: valgū; charming or radiant</note> and **much-invoked** <note>original: puruhūtā; called upon by many worshippers</note>? Our **hymn of praise** <note>original: stomaḥ; referring to the liturgical chants</note>, which is **devotional** <note>original: namasvān; literally 'possessing bows' or accompanied by offerings</note>, has today **found** <note>original: avidat</note> them, like a **messenger** who has been sent out. This is the hymn which has **turned** the **Nasatyas** <note>An epithet of the Ashvins, often interpreted as 'those in whom there is no untruth' or 'the healers'</note> toward us. O Ashvins, you two are **indeed** the **most beloved** in the **prayer** <note>original: manman; the mental composition or meditation</note> of this worshipper.

->॥ Now follows the second verse ॥<-

## Hymn Text
<note>Rig Veda 6.73.2</note>
Come to my sacrifice, [O Ashvins], for you are being praised; drink the Soma juice. Travel around the path of the ritual so that neither the distant nor the near enemy may harm us. ॥ २ ॥

<vocab>
**Ashvinau** (अश्विनौ): The twin Vedic deities of the dawn, healing, and transitions.
**Puruhuta** (पुरुहूता): An epithet meaning "invoked by many," highlighting their popularity among worshippers.
**Nasatya** (नासत्या): A common name for the Ashvins; etymologically linked to truth or healing.
**Bharadvaja** (भरद्वाज): The primary Seer (Rishi) of the Sixth Mandala of the Rig Veda.
**Trishtup** (त्रिष्टुप्): A majestic poetic meter of 44 syllables used for powerful invocations.
**Stotra** (स्तोत्र): A hymn or song of praise performed during a sacrifice.
**Viniyoga** (विनियोग): The specific ritual context or application in which a mantra is recited.
</vocab>

Sayana provides the ritual context, identifying Bharadvaja as the seer and specifying the hymn's use in morning ceremonies.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the commentary on the 63rd hymn (Sukta) of the Sixth Mandala of the Rig Veda. The previous page began the second verse of this hymn, focusing on the invocation of the Ashvins, the divine twin physicians of the Vedic pantheon. This page concludes the second verse, provides the full text and commentary for the third verse, and begins the fourth. The commentary is by the 14th-century scholar Sayana, who provides a ritualistic and grammatical interpretation of the ancient Sanskrit verses.</meta>

[Page 853]

## Hymn Text

-> **Verse 2 (continued Word-for-Word Analysis)** <-

Enough | for me | come | to the invocation | for us | being praised | so that | you two may drink | the Soma juice | around | indeed | that | dwelling | you two go | from the injurer | not | which | distant | not | near | may harm ॥ २ ॥

---

## Commentary (Sayana)

O **Ashvins** <note>The twin gods of the dawn and healing</note>, may you both **come** <note>original: gantam</note> **enough** <note>original: aram; sufficiently</note> to **our** **invocation** <note>original: havanāya; the calling of the gods to the sacrifice</note>. **Being praised** <note>original: gṛṇānā</note> by us, **drink** the **Soma juice** <note>original: andhaḥ</note> **so that** <note>original: yathā</note> you are satisfied. **Go around** the **dwelling** <note>original: vartiḥ</note> of the **injurer** <note>original: riṣaḥ; the enemy who seeks to harm</note>, so **that** dwelling—whether **distant** <note>original: paraḥ</note> **or** even **near** <note>original: antaraḥ</note>—**may not harm** <note>original: tuturyāt</note> us. 

Alternatively, the interpretation is: go **around** **that dwelling of ours** to protect it from the **injurer**. May neither a **distant** nor a **near** enemy **harm** it. The intended meaning is: just as neither a distant nor a nearby enemy can harm our home, please provide us with such protection.

---

-> **॥ The Third Verse ॥** <-

## Hymn Text

For you two, the Soma has been prepared in the wide expanse; the sacred grass, most easy to traverse, has been strewn.
With outstretched hands, the priest desiring you has offered praise; the stones, reaching you, have prepared the juice. ॥ ३ ॥

-> **Word-for-Word Analysis** <-

Has been made | for you two | of the Soma juice | in the wide expanse | has been strewn | sacred grass | most easy to traverse |
With outstretched hands | desiring you two | has praised | towards | you two | reaching | the stones | have prepared ॥ ३ ॥

---

## Commentary (Sayana)

**For you two**, in the **wide expanse** <note>original: varīman</note> of the pressing-place, that which is required **of the Soma juice** <note>original: andhasaḥ</note> **has been made** <note>original: akāri</note>—that is, it has been prepared. The **sacred grass** <note>original: barhiḥ; the kusha grass used to carpet the sacrificial ground</note>, which is **most easy to traverse** <note>original: suprayaṇatamam; very soft and comfortable for the gods to sit upon</note>, **has been strewn** <note>original: astāri</note>. The priest (Hotar), **desiring you two** and with **outstretched hands** <note>original: uttānahastaḥ; a gesture of prayer or palms joined in reverence</note>, **has praised** <note>original: vavanda</note> you. The **stones** <note>original: adrayaḥ; the rocks used to crush the Soma stalks</note>, **reaching** <note>original: nakṣantaḥ; attaining or coming into contact with</note> you through the ritual, **have prepared** <note>original: āñjan; literally 'anointed', but here meaning they have made the juice ready for the gods</note>.

## Hymn Text

Agni has stood upright for you at the sacrifices; the sacrificial gift, moving forward, is bright with ghee.
The priest, with a dedicated mind and choosing his role, has yoked [the prayer], he who invokes you, O Nasatyas. ॥ ४ ॥

## Commentary (Sayana)

**Agni** <note>The god of fire and messenger to the gods</note> **has stood upright** for **you two** **in the sacrifices**. He rises and goes forward in the sacrificial rites; when kindled, he reaches the Ahavaniya altar. The **gift** <note>original: rātiḥ; the offering or wealth</note>, which is the oblation, is **moving** <note>original: jūrṇinī; going forward</note>... <note>Sayana begins a grammatical explanation of the word 'jūrṇinī' here, which continues on the next page.</note>

-> ॥ The Fifth Verse ॥ <-

**For glory, the daughter of the Sun mounted the chariot, O you two protectors of many, [the chariot] which has a hundred protections. Through your wisdom-powers, O wise ones, be present here, O leaders, O active ones, at the birth of the ones worthy of sacrifice.** ॥ ५ ॥

## Commentary (Sayana)

O **Purubhuja** <note>original: purubhujā</note>, O Ashvins, you who are the protectors of many, the daughter of the Sun named **Surya** mounted your **chariot**—which possesses **a hundred protections** <note>original: śatotim; meaning it has many means of protection or many paths</note>—for the sake of **glory** <note>original: śriye; to be resorted to or for the sake of beauty</note>. 

Furthermore, at the **birth** <note>original: janiman</note>—the manifestation—of the **gods worthy of sacrifice** <note>original: yajñiyānām</note> in this ritual, [become present] through your **wisdom-powers** <note>original: māyābhiḥ</note>. Because "Shachi" and "Maya" are listed among the synonyms for **wisdom** <note>original: prajñā</note> [in the ancient lexicons], you are **wise** <note>original: māyinau</note>, **leaders** <note>original: narā</note>, and **active ones** <note>original: nṛtū; literally 'dancers', signifying rhythmic, divine activity</note>. 

Alternatively: O wise ones, O leaders, O dancing Ashvins, at the birth and manifestation of the sacrificial gods, you have surpassed the very wise **Agni** <note>the god of fire</note> and other deities through your **wisdom-powers** or skillful deeds. This mythological event is clarified in the **Aitareya Brahmana** (4.7): "Prajapati <note>the Creator-progenitor deity</note> gave his daughter, Surya Savitri, to King **Soma** <note>the moon god, often identified with the sacred ritual drink</note>," and so on.

## Commentary (Sayana)

O **Nasatyas** <note>original: nāsatyau; a name for the Ashvins meaning 'truthful ones' or 'healers'</note>, may your **vayo**—the goers—the **vahishtha**—the most excellent carriers—the **ashvasho**—horses—**bring** <note>original: vahan-tu</note> you toward the **prayah**, the food in the form of Soma. ## Hymn Text

-> ॥ The Eighth Verse ॥ <-

**For great indeed is the gift you bestow, O protectors of many; cause nourishment to swell for us like a cow that does not stray. To you two, O sweet ones, belong the praiser and the beautiful hymn, and the juices which have come to the gift of food.** ॥ ८ ॥

**Word-for-Word Analysis:**
Great | indeed | for you two | O protectors of many | the gift | a cow | like | nourishment | cause to swell | not straying |

## Commentary (Sayana)

O **Purubhuja** <note>original: purubhujā; 'ones with great arms' or 'protectors of many'</note>, the **deshnam**—the wealth to be given—by you two is **puru**, truly great. For this reason, **pinvatam**—bestow upon us—**isham**, the food, like a **dhenu**, a cow that is pleasing and **asakram**, which does not stray from me to another. <note>The term 'asakra' is interpreted here via the ancient etymologist Yaska (Nirukta 6.29) as 'not moving away' or 'constant'.</note> Alternatively, the connection is: bestow the desired cow. Furthermore, the **stutah**—the praisers who sing your glories—are present. O **Madhvi** <note>original: mādhvī; 'sweet ones' or 'exhilarators'</note>, O Ashvins, the **sustutih**, the beautiful hymn, is performed by the chanters. The **rasah**, the Soma juices, are also present. These juices **agman**, have reached the place of sacrifice, aiming for the **ratim**, the act of giving to you both. The meaning is: having heard the beautiful hymn and having drunk the Soma juices at the sacrifice, grant the desires of the praisers.

## Commentary (Sayana on 6.63.9)

And furthermore, for me, as I perform the praise of the **Ashvins** <note>original: aśvinau; the twin celestial horsemen</note>, may there be the two reddish <note>original: rjre; meaning 'straight-going' or 'reddish'</note> and swift <note>original: raghvī</note> mares belonging to the king named **Puraya** <note>original: puraya</note>. Mandala 6, Anuvaka 6, Sukta 64.  ॥ Fifth Book ॥  857

And it is also recited: "Upwards for beauty..." In the morning litany <note>original: prātar-anuvāka; a series of recitations performed before sunrise</note> during the section dedicated to the Dawn, in the Trishtubh meter, and in the Ashvina-shastra <note>original: āśvina-śastra; a specific recitation for the Ashvins</note>, these two hymns starting with this one are used. It is indicated in the scriptures: "The two hymns beginning 'Upwards for beauty'..." (Ashvalayana Shrauta Sutra 4.14).

## Hymn Text

**Upward have the Dawns, glowing and bright, risen for the sake of beauty, like the waves of the waters. She makes all paths easy and pleasant to travel; the wealthy, bounteous goddess has become upright.** ॥ १ ॥

**Word-for-Word Analysis:**
Up | indeed | for beauty | the Dawns | shining | have stood | of the waters | like | waves | bright |
she makes | all | easy paths | easy to travel | has become | indeed | the excellent | bounteous one | wealthy one ॥ १ ॥

---

## Commentary (Sayana)

**Shining** <note>original: rocamānā</note> means glowing. **Bright** <note>original: ruśantaḥ</note> means white-colored. As the ancient etymologist **Yaska** says: "Rushad is a name for a color." The **Dawns** have risen for the **beauty** of the world—or so that the world may be seen—just like the **waves** of the **waters** rise up. Thereafter, the hymn speaks of the Dawn in the singular: **Ushas** <note>the Dawn</note> **makes all** places **easy paths** (well-marked roads) and **easy to travel** (reachable without difficulty). Furthermore, the **wealthy** Dawn has **become** the **bounteous** one, the excellent bestower of rewards.

---

->॥ Now the Second Verse ॥<-

## Hymn Text

**Auspicious one, you are seen; you shine far and wide. Your glowing rays have filled the sky. O radiant Goddess Dawn, shining with greatness, you reveal your form.** ॥ २ ॥

**Word-for-Word Analysis:**
Auspicious | you are seen | widely | far and wide | you shine | up | your | glowing | rays | the sky | have filled |
visible | the breast | you make | being adorned | O Dawn | O Goddess | shining | with greatness ॥ २ ॥

---

## Commentary (Sayana)

O **Goddess Dawn**, you are **seen** as **auspicious** and fortunate. You **shine** across a **wide** area. Your **glowing rays**—here "shochih" refers to the brilliance of the rays—have **filled** the sky and the atmosphere. Furthermore, O Goddess Dawn, **shining** and **being adorned** with your **greatness** (your light), you **reveal** your **breast**—that is, you make your own form manifest.

---

->॥ Now the Third Verse ॥<-

## Hymn Text

**The reddish, bright cows carry her, the fortunate one who spreads far and wide. Driving away enemies like an archer, the swift one pushes back the darkness like a porter.** ॥ ३ ॥

<note>VOL. III. 10 I</note>

<vocab>
- **Ushas**: The Goddess of Dawn, the deity of this hymn.
- **Maghoni**: Bounteous or wealthy, an epithet for the Dawn signifying the rewards she brings.
- **Dakshina**: Usually a sacrificial fee, but here used to describe the Dawn's role in enriching the world.
- **Rushantah**: Bright or white; refers to the color of the morning light.
- **Dyu**: The sky or the celestial realm.
- **Vakshah**: Literally "breast" or "chest," used here metaphorically to describe the Dawn revealing her physical presence or beauty to the world.
</vocab>

<meta>This page continues the commentary on Rig Veda, Mandala 6, Sukta 64, dedicated to Ushas, the Goddess of Dawn. The previous page introduced the hymn and the first two verses, describing the Dawn's rising like waves. This page concludes the third verse and covers verses four and five.</meta>

## Hymn Text

<note>Rig Veda 6.64.3 (Continued Word-for-Word Analysis)</note>
They carry | her | the red ones | glowing | cows (rays) | the fortunate one | broadly | spreading |
away | she goes | the powerful one | like a thrower | enemies | he drives away | darkness | swift | like | a carrier (leader) ॥ ३ ॥

---

## Commentary (Sayana)

The **red ones** <note>original: aruṇāsaḥ</note> are those of a reddish hue. The **glowing** <note>original: ruśantaḥ</note> are those who are shining. The **cows** <note>original: gāvaḥ</note> refer to the rays of light; this is because the word "cow" is listed among the synonyms for "rays" in the ancient lexicons. These rays carry her—the Goddess Dawn <note>Ushas</note>—who is **fortunate**, **broadly** extended, and **spreading** forth. This same Goddess Dawn drives **away** the **darkness**, just as a **powerful** hero or a **thrower** <note>of weapons</note> drives away **enemies**. She drives away the shadows just as a **swift** **carrier** <note>or leader of an army</note> overcomes his foes.

---

## Hymn Text

-> ॥ Now the Fourth Verse ॥ <-

**The going is easy and your paths are pleasant even in the mountains; you cross the waters in the windless space, O self-radiant one. O noble daughter of heaven, you of the broad path, bring us wealth for our enjoyment.** ॥ ४ ॥

<note>Word-for-Word Analysis (RV 6.64.4)</note>
Easy to travel | and | your | good paths | in the mountains | in the windless | the waters (space) | you cross | O self-radiant one |
she | to us | bring | O broad-pathed one | O noble one | wealth | of heaven | O daughter | for enjoyment ॥ ४ ॥

---

## Commentary (Sayana)

O Goddess Dawn, even in the **mountains** and in **difficult places** <note>original: durgeṣu</note> that are **windless** <note>original: avāte; interpreted here as a place lacking the usual means of movement</note>, your **paths** become **pleasant** and **easy to travel** for you. O **self-radiant one**, you **cross** the **waters**, by which is meant the mid-air or the atmosphere <note>original: apaḥ; listed in the Nighantu as a name for the atmosphere</note>, or perhaps you cross the literal waters of the ocean. O **daughter of heaven** <note>born from the sky</note>, O **noble** and beautiful one, you who possess a **broad path** <note>or a wide chariot</note>, bring to us that **wealth** which is to be desired.

---

## Hymn Text

-> ॥ Now the Fifth Verse ॥ <-

**Bring that wealth, you who are carried by oxen in the windless sky, O Dawn; you bring excellence according to your pleasure. You, the goddess, daughter of heaven, have appeared in your greatness, visible at the first invocation.** ॥ ५ ॥

<note>Word-for-Word Analysis (RV 6.64.5)</note>
She | bring | who | by oxen | windless | O Dawn | excellence | you carry | pleasure | according to |
you | of heaven | O daughter | who | indeed | goddess | at the first invocation | with greatness | visible | have become ॥ ५ ॥

---

## Commentary (Sayana)

O Dawn, bring that **excellence** <note>meaning wealth</note> to me. You are the one who, **according to your pleasure** <note>with affection</note>, carries rewards to the chanters, drawn by **oxen** <note>original: ukṣabhiḥ; these could be bulls or even horses</note> through the **windless** sky. Furthermore, O **daughter of heaven** <note>born of the atmosphere</note>, you are the **goddess** who, at the **first invocation** <note>original: pūrvahūtau; referring to the first call of the morning or the morning litany</note>, becomes **visible** and worthy of worship through your **greatness**.

<meta>This page concludes the commentary on Rig Veda Mandala 6, Hymn 64, and introduces the first verse of Hymn 65. The content continues the poetic and ritualistic description of Ushas, the Goddess of Dawn, including technical grammatical analysis and her role in the morning sacrifices. The previous page ended with the analysis of verse 5.</meta>

The construction is: "Thus you have become visible <note>original: darśatā</note> or beautiful to look upon." In the connection "the one who has become visible," because of the grammatical coordination <note term="sāmānādhikaraṇya">Grammatical agreement between words referring to the same thing</note> with the relative pronoun, the verb "have become" <note>original: bhūḥ</note> would not lose its Vedic accent.

-> ॥ Now the Sixth Verse ॥ <-

## Hymn Text
And even the **birds** fly up from their **nests**, and the **men** who **share in food** at your **dawning**. O **divine Dawn**, you **bring** much **wealth** to the **mortal** who **offers oblations**, remaining **near** [to him]. ॥ ६ ॥

**Word-for-Word Analysis:**
And | your | birds | even | from the nest | have flown up | men | and | who | sharing in food | at the dawning |
near | being | you bring | much | wealth | O Dawn | O Goddess | to the giver | to the mortal ॥ ६ ॥

---

## Commentary (Sayana)
O Goddess Dawn, when your **dawning** occurs, even the **birds** <note>original: vayaḥ</note> **fly up** from their **nests** or dwelling places. And those **men** who **share in food**—either those who partake in the sacrificial offerings or those who earn their sustenance—they too rise. <note>The commentator notes that the word "pitu" is listed among the synonyms for food in ancient lexicons.</note> Furthermore, O Goddess Dawn, you **bring** much excellent **wealth** to the **mortal** human who is a **giver** of oblations, while you are **near** to him.

-> ॥ Thus ends the fifth varga in the first chapter of the fifth book ॥ <-

---

The fourth hymn [of this section], beginning with "**This one**" <note>original: eṣā syā</note>, consists of six verses and was seen by the sage **Bharadvaja**. It is composed in the **Trishtubh** meter <note>A Vedic meter with four lines of eleven syllables each</note>. It is indexed by its opening words. Since it was stated in the previous hymn's introduction that it was "to the Dawn," this hymn is also understood to be dedicated to the deity **Ushas**. Its ritual use is prescribed in the morning litany <note term="Prātaranuvāka">The early morning recitation of the Rig Veda</note> and the Ashvin-shastra <note>A specific recitation for the Twin Gods of the Dawn</note>.

-> ॥ There, the First Verse ॥ <-

## Hymn Text
**This** very one, the **daughter** of **heaven**, has **awakened** the **human tribes**, **shining** for **us**. She who, with her **bright light**, has been **revealed** through the dark **nights**, setting aside even the **shadows** of **darkness**. ॥ १ ॥

**Word-for-Word Analysis:**
This | that | for us | daughter | born of heaven | the tribes | shining | human | she has awakened |
who | with light | bright | through the nights | has been revealed | setting aside | of darkness | even | the nights <note>shadows</note> ॥ १ ॥

---

## Commentary (Sayana)
**This** very one, **born of heaven** and therefore the **daughter of heaven**, is the Dawn. For **us**, she **shines**, dispelling the darkness, and has **awakened** the **human tribes** or inhabitants. <note>The scholar Yaska notes that the verb used here, 'jigarti', means to either utter or to illuminate.</note> In other words, she makes them visible. She, who is joined with a **bright**, shining **light**, is **revealed** or seen through the **nights**. <note>The commentator notes a phonetic shift in the word for nights, "ramyāsu," where the 'r' and 'y' sounds are interchanged.</note> She is seen setting aside the lights of the stars and the **shadows** of **darkness**.

<vocab>
- उषस् (Uṣas): The Goddess of Dawn, a central figure in early Vedic poetry.
- भरद्वाज (Bharadvāja): A renowned ancient sage (Rishi) to whom the sixth book of the Rig Veda is attributed.
- त्रैष्टुभ (Traiṣṭubha): One of the most common Vedic meters, often used for hymns of praise.
- पितृभाज (Pitṛbhāja): Interpreted here by Sayana as those who "share in food," derived from 'pitu' (nourishment).
- दिवोजा (Divojā): A compound meaning "sky-born" or "born of heaven."
- क्षिती (Kṣitī): Refers to the people or the dwelling places of the earth.
- सामानाधिकरण्य (Sāmānādhikaraṇya): A technical term for grammatical agreement between two words referring to the same object.
</vocab>

## Hymn Text

-> ॥ Now the Second [Verse] ॥ <-
The **Dawns**, with their **shining chariots**, move through the space with their **reddish horses**. Leading the **vanguard** of the **great sacrifice**, they drive away the **darkness** of the **night**. ॥ २ ॥
---
Through | that | space | with reddish | horses | wonderfully | shine | Dawns | with shining chariots |
vanguard | of sacrifice | great | leading | away | they | drive | darkness | of night ॥ २ ॥

## Commentary (Sayana)

**With shining chariots** <note term="chandra-rathāḥ">Those who possess chariots made of light or gold</note> means having radiant chariots. The sage Yaska states: **"Chandra" comes from the root meaning 'to shine'** <note>original: "candreścandateḥ kāntikarmaṇaḥ" (Nirukta 11.5)</note>. At that time, in the early morning, those Dawns, leading or preparing the **vanguard** (the foremost part or opening) of the **great** <note term="bṛhataḥ">literally 'swelling' or 'extensive'</note> sacrifice, move through the expanse with their **reddish horses** <note>original: aruṇa-yubhiḥ</note>, which are endowed with the color of the rising sun. They move extensively; they shine so as to appear **wonderful** (manifold or brightly colored). From the **night** <note term="ūrmyāyāḥ">The night, often personified as 'the undulating one'</note>—as the word "Urmya" is listed among the names for night in the ancient lexicons—they **drive away the darkness**; that is, they completely remove it.

---

## Hymn Text

-> ॥ Now the Third [Verse] ॥ <-
Bringing **fame**, **strength**, **nourishment**, and **vitality** to the **mortal** who **offers oblations**, O **Dawns**! You who are **wealthy** and **sovereign**, bestow **food** and **wealth** today upon the **worshipper** who possesses **heroic descendants**. ॥ ३ ॥
---
Fame | strength | food | vitality | bringing | down | to the giver | Dawns | to the mortal |
wealthy ones | with heroic sons | moving forward | food | bestow | to the worshipper | wealth | today ॥ ३ ॥

## Commentary (Sayana)

O Dawns, to the **mortal** who is a **giver** of oblations, you are **bringing** <note>original: vahantīḥ</note>—that is, carrying toward him—**fame** (or swiftness), **strength** (power), **food**, and **vitality** (sap or essence). You are **wealthy** <note term="maghonīḥ">Liberal or possessing great riches</note> and **moving forward**. **Today**, upon me, the **worshipper** who serves you, **bestow** <note term="ni-dhātta">place down or grant firmly</note> **food** <note>The commentator notes that the word "avas" is listed among the synonyms for food in the ancient lexicons</note> together with **heroic descendants** such as sons and grandsons, and also **wealth** <note>The word "ratnam" is listed among the synonyms for wealth/riches in the ancient lexicons</note>.

---

## Hymn Text

-> ॥ Now the Fourth [Verse] ॥ <-
For **indeed**, **now** your **wealth** exists for the **worshipper**; **now** for the **hero** who **offers**, O **Dawns**! **Now** for the **wise singer** who offers **hymns**; as in the **past**, you surely **bring** [these gifts] to someone **like me**. ॥ ४ ॥
---
Now | indeed | for you | to the worshipper | wealth | exists | now | to the hero | to the giver | Dawns |
now | to the wise | to the singer | which | hymns | down | indeed | to one like me | you bring | formerly | even ॥ ४ ॥

## Commentary (Sayana)

O Dawns, **now** <note>original: idā</note>—at this very moment—there is **wealth** <note term="ratnam">treasure or precious gifts</note> of yours to be given to the **worshipper** who serves you.

<vocab>
Ushas: The Goddess of Dawn.
Chandra-rathah: Having a chariot of light; shining-charioted.
Yajna: Sacrifice or sacred ritual.
Maghoni: Liberal, bountiful, or wealthy.
Ratna: Wealth, treasure, or a precious object.
Dashush: One who gives oblations; a pious worshipper.
Viravat: Accompanied by heroes or sons.
Nirukta: An ancient Sanskrit text on etymology and linguistics.
</vocab>

### [Mandala 6, Hymn 6, Verse 66] || Fifth Ashtaka || 961

Even now, at this very moment, there is a treasure of yours to be given to the hero who inspires, to the sacrificer who bestows oblations. Even now, there is a treasure of yours to be given to the wise sage who praises and sings. If in this sage there exist the hymns known as *Ukthas* <note term="ukthas">Specific chants or verses of praise used in the Soma sacrifice</note>, then bring that treasure to a sacrificer like me. Even in ancient times, treasure was given to me.

->॥ Now the Fifth [Verse] ॥<-

## Hymn Text
For even now, O Dawn of the mountain peaks, the Angirasas celebrate the herds of cattle; with their song and their prayer, they burst them open; the divine invocation of these leaders became true. ॥ ५ ॥

<note>Word-by-word breakdown (Pada-patha):</note>
Even now | indeed | your | O Dawn | O you of the mountain peaks | herds | of cattle | the Angirasas | celebrate | 
asunder | with the song | they burst | with the prayer | and | true | of the leaders | became | the divine invocation ॥ ५ ॥

---

## Commentary (Sayana)
O **Dawn of the mountain peaks** <note term="adri-sānu">Refers to the dawn appearing to rest upon the summits or "striking" the mountain tops with light</note>, by your grace, **even now** the **Angirasas** <note term="Angiras">A semi-mythical family of ancestral fire-priests</note> celebrate and release the **herds of cattle** <note>This refers to the Vedic myth of the Angirasas finding the cows (light/waters) hidden in the cave of Vala</note>. As another sacred text states: "O Angiras, you released the herd of cattle" (Rig Veda 2.23.18). With the **song** <note term="arkeṇa">venerable chant or ray of light</note> and the **prayer** <note term="brahmaṇā">the sacred hymn</note>, they **burst** asunder the darkness. For those **leaders**, the Angirasas, their **divine invocation** <note term="deva-hūtiḥ">the calling upon the gods</note> became **true**, meaning it yielded its intended result.

---

## Hymn Text
->॥ Now the Sixth [Verse] ॥<-
Shine forth, O Daughter of Heaven, as of old, upon us, O Bounteous One, as you did for Bharadvaja who serves you; grant to the singer wealth with noble sons; bestow upon us far-famed food. ॥ ६ ॥

<note>Word-by-word breakdown (Pada-patha):</note>
Shine forth | of Heaven | O Daughter | as of old | for us | as for Bharadvaja | for the worshiper | O Bounteous One | 
with noble sons | wealth | for the singer | grant | widely-renowned | upon | bestow | food | for us ॥ ६ ॥

---

## Commentary (Sayana)
O **Daughter of Heaven**, O Dawn, **shine forth** for our sake as you did for the **ancients**; dispel the darkness. O **Bounteous One** <note term="maghoni">The generous lady of wealth</note>, for the one who **serves** you **as did Bharadvaja**. The phrase "as for Bharadvaja" suggests there may be others with this name, or as the Brahmanas <note>The prose texts explaining Vedic ritual</note> state: "Life-breath indeed is Bharadvaja" <note>original: "prāṇo vai bharadvājaḥ"</note>. To me, who **sings** your praise, **grant wealth** that is **full of noble sons** <note term="suvīram">literally 'having good heroes,' referring to children and grandchildren</note>. Furthermore, **bestow upon us food** that is **widely-renowned** <note term="urugāyam">literally 'wide-striding' or 'gone toward by many'</note>; give us an abundance of it.

---
