->॥ Now the Fourth Verse ॥<-

## Hymn Text
Heaven and Earth are covered with ghee <note>original: *ghṛtena*; though literally clarified butter, the commentator explains it as water/rain in this context</note>, resting in ghee, touched by ghee, and increasing through ghee. They are wide and broad, placed in the forefront <note>honored</note> at the choice of the priest; the wise ones surely praise them for happiness and for the sake of the sacrifice. ॥ 4 ॥

**Word-by-word Analysis:**
With ghee. Heaven and Earth. Covered. Resting in ghee. Touched by ghee. 
Increasing through ghee. 
Wide. Broad. At the choice of the priest. Placed in the forefront. They. Indeed. 
The wise ones. Praise. Happiness. For the sacrifice. ॥ 4 ॥

## Commentary (Sayana)
Heaven and Earth are covered—that is, pervaded—by ghee, which here means water <note>original: *udakena*</note>. They are **resting in ghee** because they abide in the water, **touched by ghee** because they are in contact with water, and **increasing through ghee** because they cause the water to increase. They are both **wide** <note>original: *urvī*; meaning extensive</note> and **broad** <note>original: *pṛthvī*; meaning well-spread</note>. They are **placed in the forefront** by the sacrificers during the **choice of the priest**, which is to say, during the sacrifice. The **wise ones** <note>original: *viprāḥ*</note>, meaning the learned chanters of praise, seek from Heaven and Earth alone **happiness** <note>original: *sumnam*</note>—meaning joy or comfort—for the sake of the **sacrifice** <note>original: *iṣṭaye*; derived from a root meaning "to sacrifice"</note>. Indeed, when there is happiness and well-being, the sacrificial rites can proceed properly.

->॥ Now the Fifth Verse ॥<-

## Hymn Text
May Heaven and Earth mix sweetness for us—they who drip sweetness, yield sweetness, and whose laws are of sweetness. They who bestow the sacrifice, wealth, and divinity, along with great glory, food, and excellent strength upon us. ॥ 5 ॥

**Word-by-word Analysis:**
Sweetness. For us. Heaven and Earth. May they mix. Dripping sweetness. Yielding sweetness. 
Of sweet laws. 
Bestowing. Sacrifice. Wealth. And. Divinity. Great. Glory. Food. 
In us. Excellent strength. ॥ 5 ॥

## Commentary (Sayana)
Those two who are **dripping sweetness**, meaning they cause water to flow; **yielding sweetness**, meaning they milk out or provide water; and **of sweet laws**, meaning their actions are directed toward the production of water <note>Sayana consistently interprets "sweetness/honey" as the beneficial rain-water in this hymn</note>. They are the **divinities** <note>original: *devatā*</note>. May those two, Heaven and Earth, while **bestowing**—giving to us—the sacrifice, wealth <note>original: *draviṇam*</note>, great glory <note>original: *śravaḥ*</note>, food <note>original: *vājam*</note>, and excellent strength <note>original: *suvīryam*</note>, **mix** sweetness for us. That is, may they sprinkle us with sweetness <note>original: *madhunā mimikṣatām*; the grammar here uses a shortened case ending</note>.

## Hymn Text
May Heaven and Earth pour out nourishment for us—the Father and the Mother, who know all things and perform beautiful works. Acting in harmony, these two world-halves, who bring peace to all, shall send us gain, strength, and wealth. ॥ 6 ॥

---

Nourishment. For us. Heaven. And. Earth. And. May they pour out. Father. Mother. Knowing all <note>original: *viśva-vidā*</note>. Of beautiful works <note>original: *su-daṃsasā*</note>. 
Acting in harmony <note>original: *saṃrarāṇe*</note>. World-halves <note>original: *rodasī*</note>. Bringing peace to all <note>original: *viśva-śambhuvā*</note>. Gain. Strength. Wealth. 
For us. Together. May they send. ॥ 6 ॥

## Commentary (Sayana)
Heaven, acting as the Father because he is the shedder of rain, and Earth, acting as the Mother because she is the upholder of all, may both of them pour out—meaning grant—nourishment and food to us. Furthermore, may these two world-halves—Heaven and Earth—who are either "all-knowing" or "making all things known" <note>original: *viśvavidā*</note>, who are performers of excellent deeds, and who take delight in one another through a relationship of mutual benefit, send us gifts. These gifts include "gain" <note>original: *sanim*; such as children and followers</note>, "strength" <note>original: *vājam*</note>, and "wealth" <note>original: *rayim*</note>. Let them propel these blessings toward us.

-> ॥ Thus ends the fourteenth section of the first chapter of the fifth book ॥ <-

The tenth hymn of this section <note>Mandala 6, Hymn 71</note>, beginning with "Upwards that God," consists of six verses. The seer <note>Rishi</note> is Bharadvaja, and the deity is Savitar <note>the solar impeller</note>. The first three verses are in the *Jagati* metre <note>a 48-syllable rhythm</note>, and the last three are in the *Trishtubh* metre <note>a 44-syllable rhythm</note>. Thus it is stated in the Index <note>original: *Anukramani*</note>: **"Upwards that God is addressed to Savitar, with a mix of Trishtubh."** 

The ritual application <note>original: *viniyoga*</note> follows the nature of the signs in the text. In the *Chaturvimshika* day ceremony, during the recitation for the All-Gods <note>original: *Vaishvadeva-shastra*</note>, the first triplet <note>original: *tṛca*</note> of this hymn is inserted in the place of the hymn to Savitar. This is indicated in the ritual manuals: "Upwards that God Savitar with his golden [arms], these three verses belong to Heaven and Earth." <note>Aitareya Brahmana 7.4</note>. Also, in the *Brihaspati-sava* sacrifice, during the same recitation, this triplet takes the place of the Savitar hymn, as indicated: "One should stand up while reciting 'Upwards that God Savitar with his golden [arms].'" <note>Ashvalayana Shrauta Sutra 9.5</note>. On the fifth day of the *Vyulha* rite, this triplet is used to house the silent recitation <note>original: *nivid*</note> for Savitar. Furthermore, in the seasonal sacrifices to the All-Gods <note>original: *Vaishvadeva-parvan*</note>, the verse beginning with **"That desirable wealth today"** serves as the concluding prayer <note>original: *yājyā*</note> for the offering of the twelve-capacity cake to Savitar.

-> ॥ There, the First Verse ॥ <-

## Hymn Text
Upwards that God Savitar, the worker of good deeds, has stretched his golden arms to impel the sacrifice. The youthful and highly skilled one, at the foundation of the atmosphere, anoints his hands with butter <note>original: *ghṛtena*; symbolising the clarity and light of the sun</note>. ॥ 1 ॥

<vocab>
- **Savitar (Savitā):** The solar deity who impels and inspires life.
- **Heaven and Earth (Rodasī):** The dual cosmic parents.
- **Sky/Heaven (Dyauḥ):** The celestial masculine principle.
- **Earth (Pṛthivī):** The terrestrial feminine principle.
- **Ritual application (Viniyoga):** The specific point in a ceremony where a verse is chanted.
- **Vedic Index (Anukrānta):** Ancient catalogs listing the author, deity, and metre of each verse.
- **Triplet (Tṛca):** A group of three consecutive verses.
- **Concluding prayer (Yājyā):** The specific formula recited as an offering is poured into the fire.
</vocab>

## Hymn Text

<note>RV 6.071.01 (Word-by-word breakdown/Pada-patha only)</note>
Upwards | indeed | stands | the god | Savitar | golden | arms | he has extended | for the impulse <note>original: *savanāya*; refers to the sacrifice or the act of impelling</note> | of good intent | with clarified butter <note>original: *ghṛtena*; often symbolizes light or water in these contexts</note> | hands | he wipes/prepares | the adorable | youth | of good wisdom | of the atmosphere | in the support. ॥ 1 ॥

---

-> ॥ Now the Second Verse ॥ <-

<note>RV 6.071.02 (Combined Samhita and Pada-patha)</note>
May we be in the excellent impulse of the god Savitar, and in the granting of wealth. For you are the one who controls the resting and the stirring of every biped and every quadruped of the earth. ॥ 2 ॥

The god's | our | of Savitar | in the impulse | excellent | may we be | of wealth | and | in the granting |
Who | of all | biped | who | quadruped | in the resting | in the stirring | and | you are | of the earth. ॥ 2 ॥

---

-> ॥ Now the Third Verse ॥ <-

<note>RV 6.071.03</note>
With unharmable guards, O Savitar, with those that are auspicious, protect our household today. Golden-tongued one, protect us for a newer prosperity; let no speaker of evil have power over us. ॥ 3 ॥

With unharmable | O Savitar | with guards | you | with auspicious | today | around | protect | our | household |
Golden-tongued | for prosperity | for newer | protect | let no one | our | speaker of evil | have power. ॥ 3 ॥

---

## Commentary (Sayana)

**[Verse 1]** The "God" <note>original: *devaḥ*</note> is the shining one. "Of good intent" means he performs good works. He is that famous Savitar who has extended his two "golden" <note>original: *hiraṇmayau*</note> arms for the "impulse," which means for the purpose of sacrifice or for the sake of giving. He raises them up. Furthermore, the "adorable" one <note>original: *makhaḥ*</note>, who is the "youth" (eternally young), and "of good wisdom," stands in the "support of the atmosphere" <note>original: *rajaso vidharmaṇi*</note>—meaning he stays there to uphold the world or the waters—and he "wipes" or prepares his two hands which are filled with "clarified butter" or water. He impels them forward.

**[Verse 2]** May we be "in the impulse" <note>original: *savīmani*</note>—meaning in the procreation or the command—of that god Savitar, the impeller. This is as Yaska says: "In the impulse means in the procreation" <note>original: *Nirukta 6.9*</note>. And may we be "in the granting"—the giving—of "excellent" (highly praiseworthy) wealth. May we be capable of this. You are "independent" <note>original: *svatantraḥ*</note> in the "resting" (the state of staying) and the "stirring" (the state of activity) of all "bipeds" (human beings) and all "quadrupeds" (animals) of the earth.

**[Verse 3]** O Savitar, with "unharmable" (uninjured) "guards"—meaning his rays or his means of protection—which are "auspicious" (causing happiness), "protect" <note>original: *pari pāhi*</note> "our household" (our home or our wealth) "today."
<note>The commentator notes that the word *gaya* appears in the Nighantu—an ancient glossary—as a synonym for both 'house' and 'wealth'.</note>
You are "golden-tongued," meaning your speech is beneficial and charming. As Yaska explains: "Why is it called gold? Because it is beneficial and delightful" <note>original: *hita-ramaṇam*</note>. Protect us for a "newer prosperity" <note>original: *suvitāya navyase*</note>...

<vocab>
- <term>Savitar</term>: The solar deity representing the sun before its rise, characterized as the "Impeller" who stimulates all life and activity.
- <term>Savīmani</term>: A technical term for the divine command or the impulse that sets the world in motion.
- <term>Biped/Quadruped</term>: Vedic shorthand for the entire living world, distinguishing between humans (*dvipada*) and animals (*catuṣpada*).
- <term>Golden-tongued</term>: An epithet for Savitar suggesting that his commands (vibrations/rays) are as precious and perfect as gold.
- <term>Gaya</term>: A term that spans the meaning of family, home, and the resources (wealth) that sustain a household.
</vocab>

## Commentary (Sayana)

The **God** <note>original: *devaḥ*</note> is the shining one. **Domestic** <note>original: *damūnāḥ*</note> means one whose mind is focused on taming [the senses] or one whose mind is focused on giving. As **Yaska** <note>An ancient scholar of Vedic etymology (c. 4th-6th century BCE)</note> says: **"Damunas is one whose mind is taming, or giving, or restrained."** **Golden-handed** means having hands made of gold. **Iron-jawed** <note>original: *ayohanuḥ*</note> means having golden jaws; this is because "gold" is included in the list of names for iron or metal <note>original: *rukmamaya iti hiraṇyanāmnu pāṭhāt*; Sayana interprets 'iron' as a synonym for 'bright metal' or gold here</note>. **Adorable** means he is to be worshiped. **Joyous-tongued** means he possesses a voice of delight. **This** Savitar has stood up **at every dusk** <note>original: *pratidoṣam*</note>, meaning at the end of every night. Let him rise. He **sends** <note>original: *āsuvati*; impels or brings</note> to the **giver** <note>the sacrificer</note> **much** (abundant) **desirable wealth** <note>original: *vāmam*; that which is to be chosen or enjoyed</note>. **Yaska says: "Vamam means that which is desirable."**

## Commentary (Sayana)

May **Savitar**, like an **advocate** <note>original: *upavaktā*; a director of the sacrifice or one who speaks in favor of another</note> for us, **raise** his **two arms** which are **golden** and **beautifully shaped** <note>original: *supratīkā*; having lovely features</note>. He **ascends** the **heights** of the atmosphere and **heaven** all the way from the **earth**. Whatever **moving** <note>original: *patayat*; flying or moving</note> **great thing** <note>original: *abhvam*; a vast or monstrous entity, often referring to the darkness or the unformed world</note>—that is, the entire collection of objects that was hidden—he **causes to rest** <note>original: *arīramat*; he delights or settles them by his light</note>.

# Rig Veda — Book 5, Chapter 1, Section 16

## Hymn Text

<note>The word-by-word breakdown (Pada-patha) for Rig Veda 6.71.6</note>

Desirable | today | O Savitar | desirable | indeed | tomorrow | day by day | desirable | for us | grant |

## Commentary (Sayana)

<note>The 14th-century scholar Sayana explains the meaning of verse 6.71.6</note>

O Savitar <note>The Solar deity representing the impelling force of the sun</note>, grant us desirable wealth today. Indeed, bring it forth. And tomorrow, bring forth desirable wealth. Why say more? Every single day, bring forth desirable wealth. O God, because you are the giver of abundant and desirable wealth which is the very source of our dwelling, therefore, through this prayer <note>original: *dhiyā*; meaning a thought-directed hymn of praise</note>, may we be possessors of wealth. May it be so.

## Sukta Introduction

The eleventh hymn, beginning with "Indra and Soma, great [is] that [majesty]," consists of five verses. Its seer <note>original: *ṛṣi*; the poet-sage to whom the hymn was revealed</note> is Bharadvaja, its meter is Trishtubh <note>a rhythmic structure of 11 syllables per line</note>, and its deities are Indra and Soma together. The application of the hymn follows the indicators found within the text itself.

---

## Verse 1 (RV 6.72.1)

->॥ Here is the first verse ॥<-

### Hymn Text

<note>The connected recitation (Samhita-patha)</note>

O Indra and Soma, great is that majesty of yours; you two performed great primary deeds. You two found the Sun; you two found the light; you struck down all darkness and the mockers. ॥ 1 ॥

<note>The word-by-word breakdown (Pada-patha)</note>

O Indra and Soma | great | that | of you two | majesty | you two | great | primary | performed |
you two | the Sun | found | you two | the light | all | darknesses | struck down | the mockers | and ॥ 1 ॥

### Commentary (Sayana)

O Indra and Soma, that majesty <note>original: *mahitvam*; greatness</note> of yours is great. What is that majesty? The text says: You two performed great, primary <note>original: *prathamāni*; meaning the most important or original</note> deeds. As the ancient etymologist Yaska says: **"The word *Prathama* means the chief or foremost."** Furthermore, you two found <note>original: *vividathuḥ*; obtained or discovered</note> the Sun and brought him to the people. You two also found the light <note>original: *svaḥ*; interpreted here by Sayana as water</note>—this is because the word *Svar* is listed among the names for water in ancient lexicons. Additionally, you struck down <note>original: *ahatam*; destroyed</note> all darkness and the mockers <note>original: *nidaḥ*; those who revile or find fault, referring here to the demons or Asuras</note>.

---

## Verse 2 (RV 6.72.2)

->॥ Now the second verse ॥<-

### Hymn Text

<note>The connected recitation (Samhita-patha)</note>

O Indra and Soma, you cause the Dawn to shine; you lead up the Sun with his light. You propped up the sky with a pillar; you spread out the Earth, the Mother. ॥ 2 ॥

<note>The word-by-word breakdown (Pada-patha)</note>

O Indra and Soma | you cause to shine | the Dawn | up | the Sun | you lead | with light | with |
up | the sky | you propped | with a pillar | you spread out | the Earth | the Mother | wide ॥ 2 ॥

<note>Summary of Technical Terms:
**Savitar**: The solar deity often invoked at sunrise and sunset for prosperity.
**Indra-Soma**: A dual divinity representing the combined power of the King of Gods (Indra) and the sacred offering (Soma).
**Bharadvaja**: A famous Vedic sage, the primary seer of the 6th Book of the Rig Veda.
**Yaska**: An ancient scholar (c. 6th century BCE) whose work, the Nirukta, is the foundation for Vedic word-analysis.</note>

Mandal 6. Chapter 6. Hymn 72. ] ॥ Fifth Book ॥ 887

O Indra and Soma, you cause the dawn to dwell. You cause it to shine forth. The meaning is that you cause the dawn to break. Furthermore, you raise the sun along with its light and brilliance. Also, you have propped up the sky <note>the heavens</note> with a supporting pillar <note>original: *skambhanena*; a cosmic stay or prop</note> placed in the middle of the atmosphere. You made it firm. You spread out the Earth, who is the mother of the universe.

---

-> ॥ Here is the third verse ॥ <-

## Hymn Text
O Indra and Soma, you slew the serpent <note>original: *ahim*</note> who stood surrounding the waters; Vritra, indeed, you slew. Following your act, Heaven <note>the sky personified</note> gave its consent to you both. You sent forth the streams of the rivers; they filled many oceans ॥ 3 ॥

**Pada Patha:**
Indra-Soma । the serpent । the waters । surrounding । you two slew । Vritra । following । of you both । Heaven । consented ।
forth । the streams । you two sent । of the rivers । towards । the oceans । they filled । many ॥ 3 ॥

## Commentary (Sayana)
O Indra and Soma, you slew the serpent <note>original: *ahi*; explained here as the "striker of the world"</note> and the demon Vritra, who stood surrounding and obstructing the waters located in the clouds. At that time, Heaven <note>the sky</note> consented to the actions of you two. Furthermore, you sent forth the streams <note>original: *arṇāṃsi*; waters</note> of the rivers. Many <note>the word *purūṇi* is listed among the names for "many" in the ancient lexicon</note> oceans or water-receptacles were filled. You filled them with waters. Alternatively, "oceans" <note>original: *samudrāṇi*</note> refers to the waters themselves because they "flow together" <note>original: *samudanti*</note>. You filled them with essence. Thus says Yaska <note>an ancient authority on etymology</note>: "Why is it called *Samudra*? Because the waters flow from it, or because the waters run towards it, or because beings delight in it, or because it is a gatherer of water, or because it moistens" <note>original: *samudraḥ kasmāt...*</note>.

---

-> ॥ Here is the fourth verse ॥ <-

## Hymn Text
O Indra and Soma, you placed the cooked <note>ripe</note> milk inside the raw <note>uncooked</note> bodies of the cows; indeed, you placed it within their udders. You held the bright, white milk within these colorful, moving creatures, even though it was not tied down ॥ 4 ॥

**Pada Patha:**
Indra-Soma । the cooked । in the raw । inside । down । of the cows । indeed । they placed । in the udders ।
they two held । not tied down । in these । the bright । in the colorful । in the moving । inside ॥ 4 ॥

## Commentary (Sayana)
O Indra and Soma, you placed "cooked" milk <note>meaning ripe or refined by the animal's heat</note> inside the "raw" <note>unprocessed</note> udders of the cows. Furthermore, within these colorful cows of various hues—the word *Jagati* is listed among the names for "cow"—you held the "bright" white milk, which is not tied down <note>original: *anapinaddham*; meaning it is liquid and uncontained by any internal vessel or cord</note> by anything. You held it so that it does not leak out upon the earth on its own; this is the meaning. The word *Id* is used here as a filler particle.

<summary>This page describes Indra and Soma's cosmic role in releasing the waters by slaying Vritra and their miraculous creation of milk, which the poet describes as "cooked" substance placed within "raw" cows.</summary>

<meta>This page concludes the 72nd hymn of the 6th Mandala, addressed to the dual deity Indra-Soma, and begins the 73rd hymn addressed to Brihaspati. It marks the transition from Varga (section) 16 to Varga 17 of the first chapter in the fifth book (Ashtaka) of the Rig Veda.</meta>

## Hymn Text

-> ॥ Here is the fifth verse ॥ <-

**O Indra and Soma, you have quickly bestowed rescuing wealth that is accompanied by descendants and is worthy of renown. O mighty ones, you have extended toward mankind a strength that is beneficial to heroes and capable of overwhelming enemy armies ॥ 5 ॥**

-> **Word-by-Word Analysis** <-

**O Indra and Soma । you two । indeed । rescuing । accompanied by offspring । worthy of renown । you have given ।**
**you two । strength । beneficial to men । for the people । together । you have extended । army-overwhelming । O mighty ones ॥ 5 ॥**

---

## Commentary (Sayana)

**O Indra and Soma** <note>original: *indrāsomā*</note>, O dual deities, **you two** bestow quickly **wealth** <note>the word *rayim* is understood here</note> that is **rescuing** or delivering <note>original: *tarutram*</note>, **accompanied by offspring** or descendants <note>original: *apatyasācam*</note>, and **worthy of renown** or famous <note>original: *śrutyam*</note>. You grant this to us. Furthermore, **O mighty ones**, you who are powerful Indra and Soma, **you two** have **extended** or encompassed <note>original: *saṃvivyathuḥ*</note> a **strength** <note>original: *śuṣmam*</note> that is **beneficial to men** <note>original: *naryam*; helpful to heroes</note> and **overwhelming to enemy armies** <note>original: *pṛtanāṣaham*</note> for the sake of **mankind** or human beings. This is confirmed by the ancient lexicon where the terms *kṛṣṭayaḥ* and *carṣaṇayaḥ* are listed as names for "men."

-> ॥ Thus ends the sixteenth section of the first chapter of the fifth book ॥ <-

---

## Critical Notes

The twelfth hymn in this sequence, beginning with the words **"He who is the mountain-breaker"** <note>original: *yo adribhit*</note>, consists of three verses <note>a *tṛca*</note>. It is dedicated to the deity **Brihaspati** <note>The Lord of Prayer</note>, seen by the sage **Bharadvaja**, and composed in the **Trishtubh** meter <note>a rhythmic structure of 4 lines with 11 syllables each</note>. This is confirmed by the Index <note>original: *Anukramani*</note> which states: "The three verses beginning 'He who is the mountain-breaker' are dedicated to Brihaspati." In the *Abhiplava* rites <note>a six-day ritual cycle</note>, specifically during the third pressing of the Soma during the recitation of the *Brahmanacchamsi* priest, this hymn is used to conclude the praise. This is indicated in the ritual manuals <note>original: *Ashvalayana Shrauta Sutra 7.9*</note>: "The two hymns 'He who is the mountain-breaker' and 'From the sacrifice in heaven'..." It is also mentioned in the context of the **Vajapeya** <note>the "Drink of Strength" sacrifice</note> and the offerings of boiled rice <note>original: *caru*</note> to Brihaspati.

---

## Hymn Text

-> ॥ Therein, the first verse ॥ <-

**He who is the mountain-breaker, the first-born of Truth, the righteous Brihaspati, the descendant of Angiras, the possessor of the oblation; he who possesses double majesty, he sits in the heat of the sacrifice. Our father, the bull, roars aloud through the two worlds <note>Heaven and Earth</note> ॥ 1 ॥**

-> **Word-by-Word Analysis** <-

**He who । mountain-breaker । first-born । possessor of Truth । Brihaspati । descendant of Angiras । possessor of oblation ।**
**possessing double majesty । in the heat of the sacrifice । sits । father । our । through । the two worlds । the bull । roars aloud ॥ 1 ॥**

---

## Commentary (Sayana)

**He who** refers to Brihaspati, the **mountain-breaker** <note>original: *adribhit*</note>, meaning the shatterer of the rock-enclosures constructed by the Panis <note>demonic hoarders of light/cattle</note>, or the splitter of the clouds. This is supported by the lexicon where *adri* is listed as a name for "cloud." He is the **first-born** <note>original: *prathamajāḥ*</note>, born first from the vital power of Prajapati <note>the Creator</note>. He is **possessed of Truth** <note>original: *ṛtāvā*</note> or possessed of water. He is the **descendant of Angiras** <note>original: *āṅgirasaḥ*</note>, having been born afterward in that lineage. This is explained in the scripture: "Those which were glowing coals became the Angirasas; that which was rekindled from the cooled coals became Brihaspati" <note>original: *Aitareya Brahmana 3.34*</note>. He is the **possessor of the oblation** <note>original: *haviṣmān*</note>, meaning he receives a share of the sacrifice. He **possesses double majesty** <note>original: *dvibarhajmā*</note>, meaning his greatness extends over both worlds—

<summary>This page concludes the praise of Indra-Soma for granting heroic strength and descendants, and introduces a new hymn to Brihaspati. Brihaspati is characterized as a powerful, primordial deity ("mountain-breaker") associated with the Angiras lineage and essential to major sacrifices like the Vajapeya.</summary>

<keywords>Indra-Soma, Brihaspati, Bharadvaja, mountain-breaker, Angiras, Aitareya Brahmana, Vajapeya sacrifice, Trishtubh meter, Vedic ritual, descendants</keywords>

<meta>This page continues the commentary on the 73rd hymn of the 6th Mandala, which is dedicated to the deity Brihaspati. The previous page ended with the initial commentary on the first verse. This page concludes that commentary and presents the full text and explanation for verses 2 and 3, finishing the 17th section (varga) of the first chapter of the fifth book.</meta>

<header>Mandala 6. Hymn 73. Verse 3.] || Fifth Book || 889</header>

## Commentary (Sayana)

He whose movement is unimpeded, who exists in a preeminently radiant place, is our father and protector. That **Brihaspati** <note>original: *bṛhaspatiḥ*; the Lord of Prayer or Sacred Speech</note>, being a **showerer** <note>original: *vṛṣabhaḥ*; literally "the bull," symbolizing one who pours down rain or blessings</note>, **bellows** <note>original: *āroravīti*; cries out or roars</note> at the **two worlds** <note>original: *rodasī*; Heaven and Earth</note>. That is, he roars toward them.

---

## Hymn Text
-> ॥ Here is the second verse ॥ <-
**For the person who approaches him at the calling of the gods, Brihaspati has indeed created a place. Striking down the obstacles, he shatters the cities; conquering the enemies, he subdues the foes in battles ॥ 2 ॥**

**Word-by-Word Analysis:**
**For the person । indeed । who । approaches । indeed । a place । Brihaspati । at the calling of the gods । has made ।**
**striking । the obstacles । apart । the cities । he shatters । conquering । the enemies । the foes । in battles । subduing ॥ 2 ॥**

## Commentary (Sayana)
Furthermore, **Brihaspati** **creates** <note>original: *cakāra*</note> a **place** <note>original: *lokam*; a space or station</note> or position for the **person** <note>original: *janāya*</note> who **approaches** <note>original: *īvate*</note> or comes to him with praise, and who is present at the **calling of the gods** <note>original: *devahūtau*; the sacrifice where gods are invoked</note. The word *cit* is a filler used for poetic completion. He, **striking down** <note>original: *ghnan*</note> or warding off the **obstacles** <note>original: *vṛtrāṇi*; the "envelopers" or darknesses that block the light</note>, **conquering enemies** in **battles** <note>original: *pṛtsu*</note>, and **subduing** or overcoming **foes**, **shatters** <note>original: *vidardarīti*; tears apart repeatedly</note> the **cities** <note>original: *puraḥ*</note> belonging to the demons <note>the *asuras*</note>.

---

## Hymn Text
-> ॥ Here is the third verse ॥ <-
**Brihaspati has conquered the riches and the great cow-pens filled with cattle, for he is a shining god. Desiring to bestow the waters, unresisted, Brihaspati strikes the enemy of the sun's world with his hymns ॥ 3 ॥**

**Word-by-Word Analysis:**
**Brihaspati । completely । has conquered । the riches । the great । the cow-pens । filled with cattle । the god । he ।**
**the waters । desiring to bestow । the sun's world । unresisted । Brihaspati । strikes । the enemy । with hymns ॥ 3 ॥**

## Commentary (Sayana)
The **shining** <note>original: *devaḥ*</note> and famous **Brihaspati** has **conquered** <note>original: *samajayat*</note> the **riches** <note>original: *vasūni*</note>—which are the treasures of the **Panis** <note>a class of demons who hoard wealth</note>, the **Asuras**, or the demon **Vala**—as well as the **great cow-pens** <note>original: *vrajān*; enclosures</note> that are **filled with cattle** <note>original: *gomataḥ*</note>. This is supported by two scriptural passages: "Brihaspati took the marrow of Vala who was embodied in the form of a cow, as one extracts a joint" <note>Rig Veda 10.68.9</note>. And also: "Let the cows come forth, O Panis, to a wider place, leaving their concealment through the Law. Brihaspati, Soma, the pressing stones, and the wise sages have found them hidden" <note>Rig Veda 10.108.11</note>. Furthermore, **Brihaspati**, being **unresisted** <note>original: *apratītaḥ*; not gone against by anyone</note> and **desiring to bestow** <note>original: *siṣāsan*; wishing to share or distribute</note> the waters, **strikes** the **enemy** <note>original: *amitram*; the Asura</note> of the **sun's world** <note>original: *svaḥ*; heaven or the realm of light</note> using **hymns** <note>original: *arkaiḥ*; mantras used for worship</note>. **Yaska** <note>an ancient Vedic etymologist</note> explains: "The term *arka* refers to a mantra, because through it, they worship (*arcanti*)" <note>Nirukta 5.4</note>.

-> ॥ Thus ends the seventeenth section of the first chapter of the fifth book ॥ <-

# Rig Veda | Book 5, Chapter 1, Section 18.
**Page 890**

The thirteenth hymn, beginning with "Soma and Rudra," consists of four verses. It was seen by the sage **Bharadvaja**, is composed in the **Trishtubh** meter <note>a meter consisting of four lines of eleven syllables each</note>, and is dedicated to the dual deity **Soma-Rudra**. The ritual application is determined by its characteristic marks.

->॥ Here is the first verse ॥<-

## Hymn Text
**O Soma and Rudra, maintain in us the divine power; may our sacrifices reach you fully. Holding the seven treasures in every house, be a source of happiness to our bipeds and our quadrupeds ॥ 1 ॥**

**Word-by-Word Analysis:**
**O Soma and Rudra । maintain । divine power । forth । for you two । sacrifices । sufficiently । reach ।**
**in every house । seven । treasures । holding । happiness । for us । be । for the biped । happiness । for the quadruped ॥ 1 ॥**

---

## Commentary (Sayana)
**O Soma and Rudra** <note>original: *somārudrā*; the dual invocation of the deity of the sacred drink and the god of storms/remedies</note>, please **maintain** <note>original: *dhārayethām*</note> in us the **divine power** <note>original: *asuryam*; the vital strength or power belonging to the divine lords</note>. Furthermore, in **every house** <note>original: *dame dame*</note>, meaning in all our homes, may our **sacrifices** <note>original: *iṣṭayaḥ*</note> **reach** <note>original: *prāpnuvantu*</note> **you both** <note>original: *vām*</note> **sufficiently** <note>original: *aram*</note>. That is, may they pervade you completely. Also, you two, **holding** <note>original: *dadhānā*</note> the **seven treasures** <note>original: *sapta ratnā*</note>, **be** <note>original: *bhūtam*</note> **auspicious** <note>original: *śam*</note>—meaning bringers of happiness—to **us** <note>original: *naḥ*</note>. Be **auspicious** to our **bipeds** <note>original: *dvipade*; our children and servants</note> and **quadrupeds** <note>original: *catuṣpade*; our cattle and other animals</note> ॥

->॥ Now the second verse ॥<-

## Hymn Text
**O Soma and Rudra, drive away the spreading disease that has entered our household. Push misfortune far away from us; may we possess auspicious fame and food ॥ 2 ॥**

**Word-by-Word Analysis:**
**O Soma and Rudra । away । drive । spreading । disease । which । our । household । has entered ।**
**at a distance । push away । misfortune । far away । for us । auspicious । glory and food । let there be ॥ 2 ॥**

---

## Commentary (Sayana)
**O Soma and Rudra**, **drive away** <note>original: *vi vṛhatam*; pull apart or remove</note> the **disease** <note>original: *amīvām*</note> that **has entered** <note>original: *āviveśa*</note> **our** <note>original: *naḥ*</note> **household** <note>original: *gayam*; either the house itself or the living beings residing within</note>. This disease is **spreading** <note>original: *viṣūcīm*; going in all directions</note>. Furthermore, **push away** <note>original: *bādhethām*</note> **misfortune** <note>original: *nirṛtim*; personified destruction or ill-luck</note> so that it is **far** <note>original: *āre*</note> and **distant** <note>original: *parācaiḥ*</note>. May **auspicious** <note>original: *bhadrā*</note> **glory and food** <note>original: *sauśravasāni*; literally 'the state of having good fame,' implying both reputation and the abundance of food that supports it</note> **be** <note>original: *santu*</note> **ours** <note>original: *asme*</note>. The word *śravas* refers to both food and fame ॥

->॥ Now the third verse ॥<-

## Hymn Text
**O Soma and Rudra, place all these remedies within our bodies; loosen and set us free from the sin that is bound within our bodies ॥ 3 ॥**

<vocab>
- **Soma-Rudra**: The dual deity consisting of Soma (the moon/sacred plant) and Rudra (the fierce healer/storm god).
- **Asuryam**: Divine power or vitality; in the early Veda, this term refers to the power of the gods (Asuras).
- **Istayah**: Sacrifices, offerings, or the desires expressed through them.
- **Ratna**: Treasures, jewels, or precious gifts bestowed by the gods.
- **Dvipada**: Biped; a technical term for human beings.
- **Catuspada**: Quadruped; a technical term for domesticated animals or livestock.
- **Amiva**: Disease, affliction, or a personified spirit of sickness.
- **Gayam**: The household, including the family, wealth, and home.
- **Nirriti**: The personification of decay, death, or misfortune; the opposite of prosperity.
- **Bheshajani**: Medicines, cures, or spiritual remedies.
- **Enah**: Sin, error, or the negative consequences of an evil deed.
</vocab>

The verses specifically ask for the preservation of divine power in the home and the healing of both humans and animals.</summary>

## Hymn Text

**[Rig Veda 6.74.3 Word-by-Word Analysis]**
O Soma and Rudra । you two । these । in us । all । in our bodies । remedies । place ।
down । untie । release । whatever । our । is । in our bodies । bound । committed । sin । from us ॥ 3 ॥

-> ॥ Now the fourth verse ॥ <-

O Soma and Rudra, you who possess sharp weapons and sharp missiles, you who are most gracious, grant us great happiness here. Release us from the bond of Varuna <note>original: *varuṇasya pāśād*; Varuna's "noose" or "bond" usually symbolizes divine punishment, sin, or dropsy</note>, and protect us, being well-disposed toward us ॥ 4 ॥

**[Rig Veda 6.74.4 Word-by-Word Analysis]**
Sharp-weapons । sharp-missiles । most-gracious । Soma-Rudra । here । well ।
grant happiness । us ।
forth । us । release । Varuna's । from the bond । protect । us । well-disposed ॥ 4 ॥

## Commentary by Sayana

**[Commentary on 6.74.3]**
O **Soma and Rudra**, may you two **place** <note>original: *dhattam*; meaning to hold or bestow</note> **all these** well-known **remedies** <note>original: *bheṣajāni*; healing balms or medicines</note> **in our bodies**—that is, in our physical limbs. Furthermore, **whatever sin** <note>original: *enas*; error or transgression</note> **is** found **committed and bound in our bodies**, please **untie** <note>original: *avasyatam*; meaning to destroy or loosen</note> that sin. The sense is: make the bonds of our transgressions loose. And **release** it **from us**.

---

**[Commentary on 6.74.4]**
O **Soma and Rudra**, who are **possessors of sharp weapons** <note>original: *tigmāyudhau*; meaning those with shining bows</note> and **sharp missiles** <note>original: *tigmahetī*; those with pointed arrows</note>, and who are **most gracious** <note>original: *suśevau*; bestowers of excellent happiness</note>; you who are **well-disposed** <note>original: *sumanasyamānā*; desiring a beautiful mind or prayer, or being of good intent while being praised</note>, please **grant us great happiness** <note>original: *su mṛḷatam*; satisfy or gladden us exceedingly</note> in this world. **Release us from the bonds of Varuna** and **protect us**—guarding us from all calamities.

-> ॥ Thus ends the eighteenth section of the first chapter of the fifth book ॥ <-

**[Introduction to Hymn 6.75]**
The fourteenth hymn, beginning with "Of the cloud-like," consists of nineteen verses and was envisioned by the seer **Payu Bharadvaja** <note>Payu, of the Bharadvaja family, is the traditional author of this "Battle Hymn"</note>. According to the Index: "The hymn of nineteen verses starting with the cloud-like belongs to Payu Bharadvaja, who praised the **limbs of battle** <note>original: *saṅgrāmāṅgāni*; the various components and tools used in warfare</note> verse by verse." These include: **Armor** <note>original: *varma*</note>, the **Bow** <note>original: *dhanu*</note>, the **Bowstring** <note>original: *jyā*</note>, the **Ends of the Bow** <note>original: *ārtnī*</note>, the **Quiver** <note>original: *iṣudhi*</note> (dedicated to the **Jagati** meter in half-verses), the **Charioteer** <note>original: *sārathi*</note>, the **Reins** <note>original: *raśmīn*</note>, the **Horses** <note>original: *aśvān*</note>, the **Chariot** <note>original: *ratha*</note>, and the **Chariot-guards** <note>original: *rathagopān*</note>. The deities are as mentioned in the text: two verses for the **Arrows**, the **Whip** <note>original: *pratoda*</note>, the **Hand-guard** <note>original: *hastaghna*</note>, then more for the **Arrows** in the **Pankti** meter and others. The final verses are blessings for battle in the **Anushtubh** meter. Specifically, the 6th and 10th verses are in the Jagati meter; others like "the one who is ours" are in Anushtubh. The first verse praises the Armor, the second the Bow, the third the Bowstring, the fourth the Ends of the Bow, and the fifth the Quiver. Therefore, Armor and the others are the respective deities of these five verses. The first half of the sixth verse praises the Charioteer.

<meta>This page transitions from the conclusion of the hymn to Soma-Rudra (6.74) to the beginning of the famous "Battle Hymn" or "Hymn to the Weapons" (6.75). It includes the ritual instructions (viniyoga) for arming a king for war, as well as the first two verses praising the armor and the bow.</meta>

# Rig Veda

## Book 5, Chapter 1, Section 19

In the second half of the previous section, the rays of light are praised. In the seventh verse, the horses; in the eighth, the chariot; in the ninth, the chariot-guards. Therefore, those verses have those respective deities. In the verse "O Brahmanas," the deities are the Brahmanas, the Ancestors, Soma, Heaven and Earth, and Pushan, as indicated by the markers in the text. The eleventh and twelfth verses, being in the form of a praise of arrows, have the Arrow as their deity. In the thirteenth, the whip; in the fourteenth, the hand-guard <note>A leather guard worn on the forearm to protect against the bowstring</note>. The fifteenth and sixteenth have the Arrow as their deity. In the seventeenth, the deity is the battlefield, in the forms of Brahmanaspati and Aditi. In the eighteenth, the deities are Armor, Soma, and Varuna. In the final verse, the deities are the Gods and the Holy Word (Brahman).

One should arm a king for battle using this hymn. Thus says the teacher Ashvalayana: "When battle is joined, one should arm the king. Standing behind the chariot, he should give the armor to the king while reciting 'Like a thundercloud is his appearance.' He should have the king recite the next verse for the bow, and he himself should whisper the fourth. He should give the quiver with the fifth. As the king sets out, he recites the sixth. With the seventh, the horses. With the eighth, he has the king recite as he looks at the arrows. With 'Like a snake with its coils, he encircles the arm,' he binds the hand-guard." (Grihya Sutra 3.11.1).

Furthermore, "With 'Released, fly away,' he should discharge the arrows. Where the arrows fall among the combatants, he should recite 'Sharpened by prayer.'" (Grihya Sutra 3.11.1). For the ritual of starting and ending the study of the Vedas, or for the final offering of a mandala, the verse "He who is our own" is used. (Grihya Sutra 3.5).

---

## Hymn Text

-> ॥ Here is the first verse ॥ <-

Like a thundercloud <note>original: *jīmūtasya*; a dark, water-bearing cloud</note> is his appearance when the armored man <note>original: *varmī*; one wearing a coat of mail</note> goes into the lap of battles. Conquer with a body unpierced; let the greatness of the armor protect you ॥ 1 ॥

> **[Word-by-Word Analysis]**
> Of a thundercloud । like ॥ becomes ॥ the appearance ॥ when ॥ the armored one ॥ goes ॥ of battles । in the lap ॥
> With unpierced ॥ body ॥ conquer ॥ you ॥ that ॥ you ॥ of armor ॥ the greatness ॥ let it protect ॥ 1 ॥

---

## Commentary by Sayana

**[Commentary on 6.75.1]**
"In the lap of battles"—that is, when a battle is occurring—when this king, **the armored one** (the one wearing a coat of mail), **goes** forth, then the **appearance** (the form) of the king equipped with iron armor **becomes like a thundercloud**. The meaning is that his form becomes like the dark, imposing form of a cloud. O King, **conquer** your enemies **with a body unpierced** (unharmed by the weapons of foes). May **that greatness of the armor protect** (guard) **you**.

---

## Hymn Text

-> ॥ Now the second verse ॥ <-

With the bow let us win cows; with the bow let us win the race; with the bow let us win the fierce battles. The bow thwarts the enemy's desire; with the bow let us win all the regions ॥ 2 ॥

<meta>This page continues the "Battle Hymn" (Rig Veda 6.75), moving from the general praise of the bow into the specific praise of the bowstring and the ends of the bow. It follows the ritual instructions for arming a king for war.</meta>

[Mandala 6. Anuvaka 6. Hymn 75.] || Fifth Book || 793

## Hymn Text (Verse 2)

**[Word-by-word Analysis]**
With the bow | cows | with the bow | the battle | may we win | with the bow | fierce | battles | may we win |
The bow | of the enemy | frustration of desire | may it make | with the bow | all | directions | may we win || 2 ||

---

## Commentary (Sayana) on Verse 2

"With the bow" <note>original: *dhanvanā*</note>, that is, by means of the bow, "may we win the cows" belonging to the enemies. Let us bring them under our control. "With the bow, let us win the battle" <note>original: *āji* - literally a race or a contest</note>. "With the bow, let us win the fierce," meaning the violent and "battle-maddened" <note>original: *samadaḥ*</note> armies of the enemy. Regarding this, the ancient etymologist Yaska says: "**The word *samadaḥ* refers to battles, either from the root meaning 'to consume' or from the root meaning 'to be intoxicated with joy'**" <note>Nirukta 9.17</note>.

Furthermore, "the bow makes the enemy's desire to be gone" <note>original: *apakāmam*</note>; may it do so. Moreover, "with the bow, let us win all the directions," meaning let us conquer the enemies situated in every direction. Here, the word "directions" <note>original: *pradiś*</note> refers by association to the men standing within them, just as one might say "the benches are shouting" to mean the people on the benches are shouting. The repetition of the word "bow" and the verb "to win" is intended to show great respect and emphasis.

---

-> || Now the Third Verse || <-

## Hymn Text (Verse 3)

**[Full Verse]**
As if about to speak, she comes close to the ear, embracing her dear friend;
Like a maiden she whispers, stretched upon the bow—this bowstring, carrying us through the combat. || 3 ||

**[Word-by-word Analysis]**
As if about to speak | indeed | towards | she comes repeatedly | at the ear | dear | friend | embracing |
Like a maiden | she whispers | stretched | upon | the bow | bowstring | this | in combat | carrying across || 3 ||

---

## Commentary (Sayana) on Verse 3

In the two previous verses, the armor and the bow were praised. This verse is a praise of the <term>bowstring</term> <note>Sanskrit: *jyā*</note>. "This bowstring," which is "in the combat," meaning in the battle, "stretched upon the bow" <note>original: *dhanvan*</note>—the word "upon" is used here to indicate the location—and "carrying us across," meaning leading us to the end of the conflict. It "comes repeatedly" <note>original: *āganīganti*</note> to the "ear" of the royal archer as if "about to speak" a "dear" or pleasing word. The word "indeed" <note>original: *it*</note> is a filler for the meter.

She "whispers" <note>original: *śiṅkte*</note> or makes a sound like a "maiden" <note>original: *yoṣā*</note> or a young woman "embracing" her "friend" or husband. Regarding this, Yaska says: "**As if about to speak, she comes to the ear, embracing the arrow like a dear friend; like a maiden she whispers—making a sound—stretched upon the bow, this bowstring, carrying us through the combat**" <note>Nirukta 9.18</note>.

---

-> || Now the Fourth Verse || <-

## Hymn Text (Verse 4)

**[Full Verse]**
Coming together like two women at a meeting, like a mother carrying her son in her lap;
May these two bow-ends, acting in harmony and quivering, pierce the enemies and strike the foes. || 4 ||

**[Word-by-word Analysis]**
These two | approaching | as if at a meeting | women | like a mother | son | may they carry | in the lap |
Away | enemies | may they pierce | acting in harmony | the two bow-ends | these | quivering | the unfriendly || 4 ||

<meta>This page continues the commentary on Verse 4 of the "Battle Hymn" (Rig Veda 6.75), focusing on the tips of the bow, before moving to Verse 5 (the quiver) and the start of Verse 6 (the charioteer and reins).</meta>

894 || Rig Veda || [Ashtaka 5, Adhyaya 1, Varga 20]

## Commentary (Sayana)
[Continuation of commentary for Mandala 6, Sukta 75, verse 4]

In this section, the two tips of the bow are praised. These two tips <note>original: *dhanuḥ-koṭyau*</note>, like two women acting with a single mind, do not leave the side of their husband; acting in this way, coming together in the encounter, let them support the King as a mother supports her son. Furthermore, these two tips of the bow, acting in harmony and without conflict, are called the **ends of the bow** <note>original: *ārtnī*</note>.

<note>Linguistic note: The word *ārtnī* is derived from the root *ṛ* meaning 'to go'. By a grammatical rule, the suffix *ni* is added and the root undergoes a vowel change. The feminine ending *ṅīṣ* is then added to form the dual case.</note>

Let these two tips, vibrating and striking the enemies of this King, pierce through the foes. As the ancient etymologist Yaska says: "**Coming together like two women of one mind, let them support him in the encounter like a mother supports a son; may the two ends of the bow, acting in harmony, pierce the enemies**" <note>Nirukta 9.39</note>.

---

## Hymn Text
-> || Now the Fifth Verse || <-

The father of many, many are his sons; he makes a whistling sound, approaching the clash of battle. The quiver, bound upon the back, sent forth, wins all contests and all armies. || 5 ||

**Word-by-word Analysis:**
Of many | father | many | his | son | whistling sound | he makes | the clash | having approached |
quiver | contests | armies | and | all | on the back | bound | wins | sent forth || 5 ||

---

## Commentary (Sayana)
Here, the **quiver** <note>original: *iṣudhi*</note> is praised. The quiver is the "father of many" arrows. It is called a "father" because it is the cause of their protection. Because the word for quiver can be used in different genders, the feminine form "of many" <note>original: *bahvīnām*</note> is used here. The "son" of this quiver is the arrow, which is "many" or numerous. Indeed, many arrows are placed within a quiver. A quiver is so called because it is the "receptacle for arrows." As Yaska says: "**The quiver is the container of arrows**" <note>Nirukta 9.13</note>.

"He makes a whistling sound" <note>original: *chiścā kṛṇoti*</note>—this is an imitation of a sound. When the arrows are being drawn out, the quiver makes a *chishcha* sound. Furthermore, the quiver is "bound upon the back" of the bow-bearing King; having reached the battles and "being sent forth" <note>original: *prasūtaḥ*</note>—meaning acting as the source that impels the arrows—it conquers all "contests" <note>original: *saṃkāḥ* — literally those things that cause people to cry out together</note> and all "armies" <note>original: *pṛtanāḥ*</note>.

-> || Thus ends the nineteenth varga of the first chapter of the fifth book || <-

## Hymn Text
-> || Now the Sixth Verse || <-

Standing in the chariot, the skillful charioteer leads the horses forward to wherever he desires. Praise the greatness of the reins! The lines from behind follow the mind. || 6 ||

**Word-by-word Analysis:**
In the chariot | standing | he leads | the horses | forward | wherever | he desires | the skillful charioteer |
of the reins | the greatness | praise | the mind | from behind | after | they hold/guide | the reins || 6 ||

895 || Rig Veda || [Fifth Ashtaka, Adhyaya 6, Sukta 75]

## Commentary (Sayana) — Continued from previous page
[Concluding commentary on Mandala 6, Sukta 75, verse 6]

In the first half of this verse, the charioteer is praised; in the second half, the reins are praised. The **excellent charioteer** <note>original: *supārathiḥ*</note>, standing in the chariot, leads the horses that are positioned in front. He guides them wherever he desires to go. The reins <note>original: *raśmayaḥ*</note>, which act like fetters extending from the horses' necks to the back of the chariot, follow the mind <note>original: *manaḥ*</note> of the charioteer; that is, they remain under his control. O people, praise the greatness <note>original: *mahimānam*</note> of these reins <note>original: *abhīśūnām*</note>! As the ancient etymologist Yaska says: "**Standing in the chariot, the excellent charioteer leads the horses in front to wherever he wishes; honor the greatness of the reins, for they follow the mind of the one sitting behind**" <note>Nirukta 9.16</note>.

---

-> ॥ Now the Seventh Verse ॥ <-

## Hymn Text
The horses, with hoofs that scatter dust, making loud sounds, move swiftly with the chariots; trampling with their forefeet, they destroy the enemies, never retreating from the foes. || 7 ||

**Word-by-word Analysis:**
Loud | sounds | they make | hoofs scattering dust | horses | with chariots | together | moving swiftly |
trampling | with forefeet | those who are not friends | they destroy | enemies | not retreating || 7 ||

## Commentary (Sayana)
In this verse, the **horses** <note>original: *aśva*</note> are praised. The horses, described as "having hoofs that scatter dust" <note>original: *vṛṣapāṇayaḥ* — literally 'bull-hoofed,' signifying great power or the way they kick up earth</note>, make loud and intense sounds <note>original: *tīvrān ghoṣān*</note> while moving with great speed <note>original: *vājayan-taḥ*</note> alongside the chariots. Furthermore, without retreating <note>original: *anapavyayantaḥ*</note> or fleeing the battlefield, they destroy the harmful enemies <note>original: *amitrān*</note> by trampling them down with the tips of their front feet <note>original: *prapadaiḥ*</note>.

---

-> ॥ Now the Eighth Verse ॥ <-

## Hymn Text
The chariot-stand is called his "offering"; there his weapon and his armor are placed. Let us sit by that strong, pleasant chariot, always keeping happy minds. || 8 ||

**Word-by-word Analysis:**
Chariot-carrier | offering | his | name | where | weapon | placed | his | armor |
there | chariot | near | pleasant and strong | let us sit | all days | we | with happy minds || 8 ||

## Commentary (Sayana)
The **chariot-carrier** <note>original: *rathavāhanam* — likely a cart or platform used to transport the war-chariot to the battlefield to keep it from wear</note> of this King contains the wealth won after defeating enemies, which becomes like an offering <note>original: *haviḥ*</note>. It is "offering-like" because it increases the King's power just as a sacrificial offering increases the power of the fire-god Agni. The word "name" <note>original: *nāma*</note> here implies general recognition or consent. In that place where the King's weapons <note>original: *āyudham*</note>—such as his bow and arrows—and his armor <note>original: *varma*</note> are securely kept, let us, the protectors and descendants of the sage Bharadwaja, approach and sit near that pleasant and strengthening <note>original: *śagmam*</note> chariot. Let us remain there at all times, possessing joyful and well-disposed minds <note>original: *sumanasyamānāḥ*</note>.

<note>Grammatical note: The commentator notes that the word *taca* is an indeclinable form used here to represent various grammatical cases.</note>

<meta>This page continues the translation of Rig Veda Mandala 6, Sukta 75, a hymn dedicated to weapons and the implements of war. Having previously described the charioteer, horses, and armor, the text now transitions to praising the ancestral protectors and the spiritual forces that safeguard the warriors.</meta>

896 || Rig Veda || [Fifth Ashtaka, Adhyaya 1, Varga 20]

## Hymn Text

-> ॥ Now the Ninth Verse ॥ <-

The Fathers, who sit at the sweet feast, providers of strength, who support us in times of distress, powerful and profound; they have varied armies, the strength of arrows, and are never-failing; they are true heroes, great, and conquerors of enemy hosts. || 9 ||

**Word-by-word Analysis:**
Sitting at the sweet feast | Fathers | providers of strength | resting in distress | powerful | profound |
of varied armies | strength of arrows | invincible | true heroes | great | conquerors of hosts || 9 ||

---

## Commentary (Sayana)

In this verse, the **protectors of the chariot** <note>original: *rathagopa*</note> are praised. They are the **Fathers** <note>original: *pitaraḥ*</note>, the guardians of the chariot. They are **sitting at the sweet feast** <note>original: *svāduṣaṃsadaḥ*</note>, meaning they sit amidst the sweet food of the enemies, or rather, they consume and exhaust the enemies' food supplies. They are **providers of strength** <note>original: *vayodhā*</note>, the givers of nourishment. They are **resting in times of distress** <note>original: *kṛcchreśrita*, meaning they are resorted to or relied upon during calamities</note>. 

They are **powerful** <note>original: *śaktīvantaḥ*</note>. The word *shakti* refers to a specific type of weapon; thus, they are those who hold such weapons in their hands. Alternatively, *shakti* means strength, making them "the powerful ones." They are **profound** <note>original: *gabhīrā*</note>, meaning they are unassailable or difficult to overcome. They have **varied armies** <note>original: *citrasenā*, literally "beautiful or remarkable armies"</note> and the **strength of arrows** <note>original: *iṣubalā*</note>. 

They are **invincible** <note>original: *amṛdhrā*, those who cannot be harmed</note>. They are **true heroes** <note>original: *satovīrāḥ*</note>, those who have attained true valor. On this, the ancient etymologist Yaska says: "*Tiraḥ sataḥ* refers to one who has attained; *tiraḥ* means crossed over, and *sataḥ* means come together or attained" <note>Nirukta 3.14</note>. Finally, they are **great** <note>original: *uravo*</note> and **conquerors of enemy hosts** <note>original: *vrātasāhāḥ*</note>, the ones who defeat groups of foes.

---

## Hymn Text

-> ॥ Now the Tenth Verse ॥ <-

O Brahmins! O Fathers deserving of Soma! May Heaven and Earth be auspicious and sinless for us. May Pushan protect us from misfortune, O increasers of Truth! Protect us; let no evil-speaker have power over us. || 10 ||

**Word-by-word Analysis:**
Brahmins | Fathers | deserving of Soma | auspicious | for us | Heaven and Earth | sinless |
Pushan | us | may he protect | from misfortune | increasers of Truth | protect | let no | for us | evil-speaker | have power || 10 ||

---

## Commentary (Sayana)

**O Brahmins!** <note>original: *brāhmaṇāso*</note> and **O Fathers!** You are the **increasers of Truth** <note>original: *ṛtāvṛdha*, those who increase the sacrifice or the eternal truth</note>. You are **deserving of Soma** <note>original: *somyāḥ*</note>, meaning you are worthy of the Soma juice or you are the ones who prepare it. As Yaska says: "**Somyāḥ are those who prepare the Soma**" <note>Nirukta 11.18</note>.

**Protect us!** <note>original: *rakṣa*</note>. Although the word "protect" is in the singular in the original text, it is interpreted here as a plural command to match the subjects, as this is preferred over assuming missing words. Furthermore, may the sinless **Heaven and Earth** <note>original: *dyāvāpṛthivī*</note> be **auspicious** <note>original: *śive*, meaning makers of happiness</note> for us. 

May the deity **Pushan** <note>original: *pūṣā*, the nourisher</note> also **protect us from misfortune** <note>original: *duritāt*, from bad paths or sin</note>. Finally, let no **evil-speaker** <note>original: *aghaśaṃsaḥ*, an enemy who speaks or plots evil</note> among our foes **have power** <note>original: *īśata*</note> over us; may they never prevail.

-> ॥ Thus ends the twentieth varga of the first adhyaya of the fifth ashtaka ॥ <-

[Mandala 6, Hymn 6, Sukta 75] || Fifth Ashtaka || 897

->॥ Now the Eleventh Verse ॥<-

## Hymn Text
She clothes herself in fair wings; the deer is her tooth; bound together with cow-sinews, she flies forth when discharged. Where men rush together and flee apart, there may the arrows grant us shelter. || 11 ||

**Word-by-word Analysis:**
Fair-winged | she clothes herself | deer | her | tooth | with cow-sinews | bound together | flies | discharged | 
where | men | together | and | apart | and | rush | there | for us | arrows | shelter | grant. || 11 ||

---

## Commentary (Sayana)
In this verse, the arrows are praised. She **clothes herself in fair wings** <note>original: *suparṇaṃ vaste*</note>, meaning she possesses beautiful feathers at her end. This arrow holds these feathers. The **deer** <note>original: *mṛga*</note>, or rather a part of a deer such as the horn, becomes her **tooth** <note>original: *dantaḥ*</note>, for some arrows indeed have tips made of horn. Alternatively, **her tooth is a deer** in the sense that the arrow "hunts" or seeks out the enemies. Furthermore, she is **bound together with cow-sinews** <note>original: *gobhiḥ*</note>, meaning she is firmly tied with thongs made of cow-hide. Or, "cow" refers to the bowstring, and she is connected to it. Here there is a change in grammatical number. 

As the ancient text states: **"On every tree, the cow, being fixed, lows."** <note>Rig Veda 10.27.22</note>. The meaning of this is: on every "tree"—meaning every wooden bow—the "cow"—meaning the bowstring—being fixed, "lows" or makes a sound. Thus says Yaska <note>An ancient etymologist</note>: "On every tree means on every bow. A tree (*vṛkṣa*) is so called because it is 'cut' (*vrascana*) or because it 'covers the earth' (*vṛttvā kṣāṃ tiṣṭhati*). Earth (*kṣā*) comes from a root meaning 'to dwell.' The fixed cow lows, meaning it makes a sound. 'Lows' (*mimayat*) is a verb for making sound" <note>Nirukta 2.6</note>. 

**Discharged** <note>original: *prasūtā*</note>, or impelled, she **flies**. **Where** in battle **men rush together** in groups **and apart** individually, **there** in that place, may the **arrows grant us shelter** <note>original: *śarma yaṃsan*</note> or happiness. 

Yaska also explains this: "She clothes herself in fair wings" refers to the feathers. "The deer is her tooth" means it is made of deer-horn or it hunts. "Bound with cow-sinews she flies when discharged" is as explained. Where men rush together and flee, there may the arrows provide us with refuge or protection <note>Nirukta 9.19</note>. || 11 ||

---

->॥ Now the Twelfth Verse ॥<-

## Hymn Text
O straight-flying one, prosper us; let our bodies be as stone. May Soma speak in our favor; may Aditi grant us shelter. || 12 ||

**Word-by-word Analysis:**
O straight-flying one | around | increase/prosper | us | stone | let it be | our | body | 
Soma | in favor | let him speak | us | Aditi | shelter | let her grant. || 12 ||

---

## Commentary (Sayana)
**O straight-flying one** <note>original: *ṛjīte*</note>: The arrow is called *ṛjīti* because it goes straight. O Arrow, **prosper us** <note>original: *pari vṛdhi*</note>; increase us from all sides. Let **our bodies** <note>original: *tanūḥ*</note> **become stone** <note>original: *aśmā bhavatu*</note>; let them be firm and impenetrable like a rock. Furthermore, may **Soma speak in our favor** <note>original: *somo adhibravītu*</note>, speaking with partiality toward us to protect us. May **Aditi also grant us shelter** or happiness. || 12 ||

<meta>This page continues the translation of Rig Veda Mandala 6, Hymn 75. The previous page concluded the description of arrows (verses 11-12). This page moves to the specialized equipment of the chariot-warrior: the horse-whip (verse 13) and the leather hand-guard or bracer (verse 14) that protects the archer's arm from the snap of the bowstring.</meta>

->॥ Rig Veda ॥ [5.1.21]<-

->॥ Now the Thirteenth Verse ॥<-

## Hymn Text
It strikes the thighs of these [horses]; it lashes the flanks. O horse-whip, you who are wise, urge the horses in the battles. || 13 ||

**Strikes | the thighs | of these | the flanks | lashes |**
**horse-whip | wise | horses | in battles | urge. || 13 ||**

---

## Commentary (Sayana)
The **horse-whip** <note>original: *ashvājanī*</note> is that which drives the horses. With it, the charioteers of **great wisdom** <note>original: *pracetasaḥ*</note> strike the **thighs** <note>original: *sānu*</note> or the hind-parts of these horses. They **lash the flanks** <note>original: *jaghanān upajighnate*</note>. Therefore, O whip, urge the horses in the **battles** <note>original: *samatsu*</note> or conflicts. Thus, Yaska <note>the ancient etymologist</note> says:
> It strikes the thighs of these—meaning the moving limbs, the thighs. The word for thigh (*sakthi*) comes from a root meaning "to be attached," as the body is attached to it. They also strike the flanks. The word for flank/hindquarters (*jaghana*) comes from a root meaning "to strike repeatedly." O horse-whip of great wisdom, urge the horses in the encounters and battles. <note>Nirukta 9.20</note>

---

->॥ Now the Fourteenth Verse ॥<-

## Hymn Text
Like a snake with its coils, it encircles the arm, warding off the blow of the bowstring. May the hand-guard, knowing all ways, a man [like], protect the man [warrior] from all sides. || 14 ||

**Like a snake | with coils | around | goes | the arm | of the bowstring | the blow | warding off |**
**hand-guard | all | paths/wisdoms | knowing | man | the man | around | protect | from all sides. || 14 ||**

---

## Commentary (Sayana)
Here follows the praise of the **hand-guard** <note>original: *hastaghna*; a leather bracer or arm-guard</note> which is tied to the forearm of the archer. It is called *hastaghna* because it is located on the hand—specifically the forearm—where the bowstring strikes (*hanyate*). It **wards off** <note>original: *paribādhamānaḥ*</note> or prevents the **blow** <note>original: *hetim*</note> caused by the bowstring. It **encircles** <note>original: *paryeti*</note> the **arm** <note>meaning the forearm</note> with its **coils** <note>original: *bhogaiḥ*</note> or its leather body, **like a snake** <note>original: *ahiriva*</note>. Furthermore, this hand-guard is **knowing all ways** <note>original: *viśvā vayunāni vidvān*</note>, meaning it understands all that is to be known. This is because the word for "ways" <note>original: *vayuna*</note> is listed as a synonym for knowledge or wisdom. May this **manly** <note>original: *pumān*; brave or strong</note> object protect the **man** <note>the archer</note> from all sides. Thus, Yaska says:
> Like a snake with its coils, the hand-guard encircles the arm, being protected from the blow of the bowstring; knowing all wisdoms, it is "manly" because it is full of mind (*purumanā*) or from a root meaning "to be strong." <note>Nirukta 9.15</note>

<summary>This page describes the ritualized equipment of the Vedic warrior, specifically the horse-whip used to urge steeds in battle and the leather hand-guard that protects an archer's arm from the bowstring's recoil.</summary>
<keywords>Rig Veda, horse-whip (ashvajani), hand-guard (hastaghna), archery equipment, Vedic warfare, Sayana, Yaska, Nirukta, charioteer wisdom</keywords>

<meta>This page continues the translation of Rig Veda Mandala 6, Hymn 75. The previous page concluded the description of the warrior's protective gear, specifically the leather hand-guard used to protect the arm from the bowstring's snap (verse 14). This page moves into the consecration and description of the arrows themselves (verses 15-16) and a prayer for divine protection on the battlefield (verse 17).</meta>

-> ॥ Now the Fifteenth Verse ॥ <-

## Hymn Text
Poisoned with venom, tipped with deer-horn, its face is made of iron; to this arrow, the offspring of the Rain-cloud, the divine goddess, let there be great homage. || 15 ||

**Pada-patha:**
**Poisoned | which | deer-headed | of iron | whose | iron | mouth/tip |**
**this | Rain-cloud-seed | to the arrow | to the goddess | great | homage. || 15 ||**

---

## Commentary (Sayana)
Those arrows which are **poisoned** <note>original: *ālāktā*; smeared with a specific venom called *ālā*</note> and **deer-headed** <note>original: *ruruśīrṣṇī*; having a head made of deer-horn or shaped like a deer's head</note>. The word *ruru* comes from a root meaning "to strike" or "to kill." Alternatively, it simply means "having a head like a deer." Furthermore, the **mouth** <note>original: *mukham*; the tip</note> of this arrow is **made of iron** <note>original: *ayomaya*</note>. It is called the **offspring of the Rain-cloud** <note>original: *parjanyaretase*; literally 'the seed of Parjanya'</note> because the reed-stalk from which the arrow is made grows through the action of the rain. To this **divine arrow** <note>original: *iṣyai devyai*</note>, this **great homage** <note>original: *bṛhat namaḥ*</note> is offered.

-> ॥ Thus ends the twenty-first section (Varga) of the first lesson (Adhyaya) of the fifth book (Ashtaka) ॥ <-

---

-> ॥ Now the Sixteenth Verse ॥ <-

## Hymn Text
Released, fly far away, O arrow, sharpened by prayer; go to the enemies, fall upon them; do not leave a single one of them remaining. || 16 ||

**Pada-patha:**
**Released | far | fly | O arrow | prayer-sharpened |**
**go | enemies | forward | fall upon | do not | of them | any | even | up | leave/remain. || 16 ||**

---

## Commentary (Sayana)
O **arrow** <note>original: *śaravye*; a missile or arrow capable of injury</note>, you who are **sharpened by prayer** <note>original: *brahmasaṃśite*; made keen and effective through the power of mantras</note>, once you are **released** <note>original: *avasṛṣṭā*; shot from the bow</note>, you must **fly far away** <note>original: *parāpata*</note>. Go away from this place and **fall upon** <note>original: *prapadyasva*</note> the **enemies** <note>original: *amitrān*; the unfriendly ones</note>. Among those enemies, **do not leave any remaining** <note>original: *mā ... ucchiṣaḥ*</note>; do not allow even one to survive.

---

-> ॥ Now the Seventeenth Verse ॥ <-

## Hymn Text
Where the arrows fly together like boys with tufted hair, there may the Lord of Prayer and Aditi grant us protection; may she grant us protection always. || 17 ||

**Pada-patha:**
**Where | arrows | together-fly | boys | tufted-hair-like |**
**there | to us | of Prayer | the Lord | Aditi | protection | may grant | always | protection | may grant. || 17 ||**

---

## Commentary (Sayana)
In that battle **where** <note>original: *yatra*</note> the **arrows** <note>original: *bāṇāḥ*</note> **fly together** <note>original: *sampatanti*</note> like **boys with tufted hair** <note>original: *kumārā viśikhā iva*; an image comparing the feathered ends or the reed-tops of arrows to the unshorn hair of youths</note>, in that place may **Brahmanaspati** <note>the Lord of Prayer/Sacred Wisdom</note> grant us **protection** <note>original: *śarma*; peace or bliss</note>. May **Aditi** <note>the goddess of freedom and infinite space</note> also grant us protection **always** <note>original: *viśvāhā*; every day</note>. The repetition of the phrase "grant us protection" is intended to show great respect and earnestness.

# Rig Veda [Book 5, Lesson 1, Section 22]

-> ॥ Now the Eighteenth Verse ॥ <-

## Hymn Text

I cover your vital organs with armor; may King Soma clothe you with immortality. May Varuna make for you a space wider than the wide; may the gods rejoice in you as you conquer. || 18 ||

**Words:**
**Vital-organs | your | with armor | I cover | Soma | you | King | with immortality | afterward | may he clothe |**
**than the wide | wider | Varuna | for you | may he make | conquering | you | afterward | the gods | may they rejoice. || 18 ||**

---

## Commentary (Sayana)

O King, I **cover** your **vital organs** <note>original: *marmāṇi*; those vulnerable spots where, if wounded, one dies immediately</note> with **armor** <note>original: *varmaṇā*; a breastplate or coat of mail</note>. After this covering of the vitals, may **King Soma** <note>the deity associated with the sacred juice and the moon, often linked to health and longevity</note> **clothe you with immortality** <note>original: *amṛtena*; the nectar of the gods</note>. Furthermore, may **Varuna** <note>the god of cosmic law and the divine judge</note> also **make** for **you** a happiness that is **wider than the wide** <note>original: *urorvarīya*; meaning more extensive or vast</note>. May all the **gods** also **rejoice** in **you** as you are **conquering** <note>original: *jayantaṃ*; being victorious</note> the enemy.

---

-> ॥ Now the Nineteenth Verse ॥ <-

## Hymn Text

Whoever—be he one of our own or a stranger—desires to slay us, may all the gods destroy him. Prayer is my inner armor. || 19 ||

**Words:**
**Who | our | own | unfriendly/kinsman | who | and | outsider | desires to slay |**
**the gods | him | all | may they destroy | Prayer/Sacred Word | armor | my | inner. || 19 ||**

---

## Commentary (Sayana)

**Whoever** is **our own** <note>original: *svo*; a relative or kinsman</note> who has become **unfriendly** <note>original: *araṇo*; one who does not delight in us</note>, **and whoever** is an **outsider** <note>original: *niṣṭyo*; one who is a stranger or stays far away</note> who **desires to slay us**, may **all the gods** **destroy** <note>original: *dhūrvantu*; strike down or kill</note> that person. **Prayer** <note>original: *brahma*; the sacred mantra or spiritual power</note> exists as **my inner armor** <note>original: *antaraṃ varma*; a spiritual protection situated inside the physical armor</note> which wards off the arrows of the enemy.

---

-> ॥ Thus ends the twenty-second section (Varga) of the first lesson (Adhyaya) of the fifth book (Ashtaka) ॥ <-

-> ॥ Thus concludes the sixth sub-section (Anuvaka) of the sixth book (Mandala), and the entire Mandala, in the commentary on the Rig Veda composed by the teacher Sayana ॥ <-

# Rig Veda

->॥ Now the Seventh Book ॥<-

## Commentary (Sayana)

Now the Seventh Book begins. In this book, there are six sections <note>original: *anuvāka*; a traditional division of the Vedic text</note>. In the first section, there are seventeen hymns. Among them, the first hymn, beginning with the words "Agni, the men," consists of twenty-five verses. Here is the entry from the Index <note>original: *Anukramaṇikā*; a traditional register of the poets, meters, and deities of the Rig Veda</note>: **"Agni, five-additional; the first eighteen are Viraj meter."** It is stated that the Sage Vasishtha "saw" <note>Vedic poets are called "seers" (rishis) because they are said to have "seen" the eternal truths of the hymns</note> the Seventh Book; thus, the seer of this book is Vasishtha. The first eighteen verses are in the <term>Viraj<gloss>a poetic meter consisting of three lines of eleven syllables each</gloss></term> meter. The remaining verses, by the general rule of silence <note>original: *anādeśa-paribhāṣayā*; a rule of interpretation where if no meter is specified, a standard meter is assumed</note>, are in the <term>Trishtubh<gloss>a common Vedic meter consisting of four lines of eleven syllables each</gloss></term> meter. By the rule governing the beginning of a book, Agni is the deity.

In the <term>Vishvajit<gloss>a one-day sacrifice where the performer gives away all his possessions</gloss></term> sacrifice, this hymn is used as the <term>Ajya-shastra<gloss>a specific recitation involving clarified butter</gloss></term>. It is indicated in the scriptures: **"In the Vishvajit sacrifice, 'Agni, the men' is the Butter-praise."** <note>Reference to Ashvalayana Shrauta Sutra 8.9</note>. In the four-day rite called the Ashva-chaturvinsha, on the fourth day, this same hymn is the Butter-praise. For it is indicated: **"'Agni, the men' on the fourth day."** <note>Reference to Ashvalayana Shrauta Sutra 10.2</note>.

In the Vyuha Ten-Night rite, on the fourth day, this hymn is the <term>Jatavedasya-nividdhana<gloss>a recitation dedicated to Agni as the 'knower of all births'</gloss></term>. It is indicated: **"'Agni, the men' is the Agnimaruta recitation."** <note>Reference to Ashvalayana Shrauta Sutra 8.8</note>.

In the <term>Mahavrata<gloss>an elaborate 'Great Rite' performed at the end of the year</gloss></term>, this is also the Butter-praise. Likewise, it is indicated in the Fifth Aranyaka: **"The Butter-praise and the Prauga-praise are from the Vishvajit sacrifice."** <note>Reference to Aitareya Aranyaka 5.1</note>.

In the <term>Prataranuvaka<gloss>the Morning Litany, recited before sunrise</gloss></term>, the first triplet of verses should be inserted in place of the Anushtubh <note>a meter of four lines of eight syllables</note> verses that begin with "You, O Agni, of the riches." For it is indicated: **"On the tenth day, in place of the Anushtubh verses, use the triplet 'Agni, the men, with their meditations, from the two friction-sticks' in the rite for Agni."** <note>Reference to Ashvalayana Shrauta Sutra 8.12</note>. The first six verses on that same day in the Agnimaruta recitation serve as the "Praise-verses" and "Corresponding-verses" <note>original: *stotriyānurūpa*; specific technical roles for verses within a liturgical chant</note>. It is indicated: **"'Agni, the men, with their meditations, from the two friction-sticks' are the Praise-verse and Corresponding-verse."** <note>Reference to Ashvalayana Shrauta Sutra 8.12</note>.

This hymn is also used in the fire-offering at the start of a Book. In the Fire-Establishment ritual <note>original: *ādhāna*</note>, during the third offering, the verse **"Forward"** <note>referring to verse 3 of this hymn, *preḍḍho*</note> is the invitatory verse <note>original: *anuvākyā*</note> for the Svistakrit offering <note>an offering to Agni as the one who "makes the sacrifice well-offered"</note>. It is indicated: **"'Forward, O Agni' and 'These, O Agni' are the two concluding verses."** <note>Reference to Ashvalayana Shrauta Sutra 2.1</note>. This is similarly used as the invitatory verse for the Svistakrit in other rites like the Consecration.

In the Introductory Offering <note>original: *prāyaṇīyeṣṭi*</note>, the two verses beginning with **"He, indeed, Agni, the fires"** <note>referring to verses 14 and 15</note> are the sacrificial and invitatory verses for the Svistakrit. It is indicated: **"'He, indeed, Agni, the fires' and 'From this then others' are the two concluding verses."** <note>Reference to Ashvalayana Shrauta Sutra 4.3</note>.

In the third offering of the Fire-Establishment, the verse **"These, O Agni"** <note>referring to verse 2, *imo agne*</note> is the sacrificial verse for the Svistakrit. It is indicated: **"'These, O Agni' are the two concluding verses."** <note>Reference to Ashvalayana Shrauta Sutra 2.1</note>. Similarly, in the Consecration and other rites, this is the sacrificial verse for the Svistakrit. In the Morning Litany, within the section for Agni using the Trishtubh meter, and in the Ashvina-praise <note>recitation for the twin gods of the dawn</note>, the five verses beginning with **"You, O Agni, easily invoked"** <note>referring to verse 21</note> are used. It is indicated: **"You, O Agni, easily invoked, delightful to behold."** <note>Reference to Ashvalayana Shrauta Sutra 4.13</note>.

---
