## Commentary (Sayana)

And then, the thunder-armed Indra submerged Shruta, Kavasha, and Vriddha—these three—and likewise the Druhyu, in the waters, one after another. This means he caused them to drown. On this occasion, those who were "desiring you" <note>original: "tvāyataḥ"</note>, meaning those who sought you, and followed you with shouts of joy or praise—they, as friends, chose you for the sake of friendship and obtained that friendship. ## Hymn Text

-> ॥ Now the Thirteenth Verse ॥ <-

**Indra** suddenly shattered all their seven fortified cities with his might. He apportioned the wealth of the descendant of **Anu** to the **Tritsu** <note>The tribe of King Sudas</note>. May we overcome the **Puru** <note>A rival tribe</note> of **hostile speech** <note>original: "mṛdhravācam", implying either malicious or unintelligible language</note> in the assembly of battle. ॥ १३ ॥

## Commentary (Sayana)

Indra, by his power, suddenly shattered all the firm, fortified cities—the seven types of forts which served as the means of protection for Kavasha and the others. Furthermore, he distributed the "wealth" <note>original: "gayam", which can mean house or riches</note> of the Anava—the son or descendant of Anu—to the King named Tritsu, or to the assembly of the Tritsu people. He gave it to them; that is the meaning. Thus, while praising Indra, may we conquer the **Puru**—a human enemy of **hostile speech**—in the **assembly** <note>original: "vidathe", here meaning the conflict of battle</note>.

## Hymn Text

-> ॥ Now the Fourteenth Verse ॥ <-

The cattle-seeking **Anus** and **Druhyus** lay down in sleep—sixty hundreds, six thousands, and sixty-six heroes. All these are the heroic deeds performed by Indra. ॥ १४ ॥

> **Padapatha:** Down. Seeking-cattle. Anus. Druhyus. And. Sixty. Hundreds. They-slept. Six. Thousands. <column-break/> Sixty. Heroes. Above. Six. For-the-one-desiring-to-serve. All. Indeed. Of-Indra. Heroic-deeds. Performed. ॥ १४ ॥

## Commentary (Sayana)

The "cattle-seeking" ones—those desiring cows—the Anus (descendants of Anu) and the Druhyus (descendants of Druhyu), and their heroes, lay down completely <note>original: "ni suṣupuḥ", literally "slept soundly," a euphemism for death in battle</note>. Their numbers were sixty hundreds (meaning thousands), and six thousand, and sixty plus six more <note>This calculates to 6,666 casualties</note>. They fell for the sake of **Sudas**, who is "desirous of serving" <note>original: "duvoyu", referring to the King who performs the sacred rites</note>. This interpretation follows the traditional lists where "serving" refers to acts of worship. They lie down in the sleep of death.

## Hymn Text

-> ॥ Now the Fifteenth Verse ॥ <-

By **Indra’s** power, these [enemies], rushing together for battle like waters released flowing downward, fled. These **false friends** <note>original: "durmitrāsaḥ"</note>, while calculating their gains, abandoned all their possessions and wealth to **Sudas**. ॥ १५ ॥

## Commentary (Sayana)

Sometimes, those who were once protected by Indra are later oppressed by him. These enemies, acting as false friends <note>original: "durmitrāso", meaning bad or treacherous allies</note>, gathered for battle against Indra’s will. When Indra struck, they became eager to escape and fled just like water flowing downhill. ## Hymn Text

-> ॥ Now the Sixteenth Verse ॥ <-

**Indra** pushed the one who injures the hero [Sudas]—that one who ignores Indra and yet drinks the sacrificial offerings—down toward the earth. Indra struck down the fury of the furious; and the enemy, seeking a way, took the path of flight. ॥ १६ ॥

**[Word-by-word Analysis]**

## Commentary (Sayana)

Indra pushed the enemy toward the earth <note>original: "kṣām"</note>. This refers to the one who injures the heroic Sudas. The word "half" <note>original: "ardham"</note> is derived here from the root meaning "to injure." This enemy is described as "without Indra" <note>original: "anindram"</note>, meaning one who does not keep Indra in his mind or intellect; in other words, one who disregards Indra's power. Despite this, he is a "drinker of the cooked offerings" <note>original: "śṛtapām"</note> like milk. Indra pushed this defiant one away. Furthermore, Indra "measured" or struck down <note>original: "mimāya"</note> the wrath of the enemies who were acting out of fury. Then, the enemy of Sudas, seeking a way out, found the path of retreat and fled.

## Hymn Text (Continued)

-> [RV 7.18.17 Word-by-word Analysis] <-

With-a-poor-man | indeed | that | [particle] | one | he-performed | a-lion | indeed | with-a-goat | he-killed | down | the-edges | with-a-needle | he-cut | Indra | forth | he-gave | all | enjoyments | to-Sudas ॥ १७ ॥

## Commentary (Sayana)

**Indra** performed a primary deed of giving through a poor man <note>original: "ādhreṇa", meaning one who is destitute or weak</note>, namely **Sudas**. He caused it to be done. Even a **lion** <note>original: "siṃham", representing a powerful enemy</note> in its prime, he caused to be killed by a **goat** <note>original: "petvena"</note>. With a **needle** <note>original: "veśyā", here interpreted as a small tool or needle</note>, he cut or carved the edges <note>original: "sraktīḥ"</note> of the sacrificial posts. The meaning is that he performed the work of large tools using only a needle. One should not doubt these three acts as being "impossible," because **Indra’s** greatness is exceedingly high. He gave all enjoyments <note>original: "bhojanā", meaning objects of enjoyment or wealth</note> to King Sudas. ॥ १७ ॥

## Hymn Text

-> ॥ Now the Eighteenth Verse ॥ <-

Indeed, many enemies have submitted to you; find the subjection of even the arrogant **Bheda**. O **Indra**, strike with your sharp thunderbolt that mortal who commits sin against the one praising you. ॥ १८ ॥

-> [Word-by-word Analysis] <-

Many | indeed | enemies | have-submitted | to-you | of-Bheda | even | of-the-arrogant | find | subjection | mortals | sin | praising | who | does | sharp | on-him | [down] | strike | thunderbolt | Indra ॥ १८ ॥

## Commentary (Sayana)

O **Indra**, your many enemies have submitted <note>original: "raradhuḥ", meaning they came under control</note> to you. Furthermore, find the subjection <note>original: "randhim", meaning the act of bringing into one's power</note> of the arrogant **Bheda**. The name **Bheda** refers to an "atheist" <note>original: "nāstikaḥ"</note>—one who breaks <note>root: bhid</note> the boundaries of propriety. Or, it refers to a specific enemy of Sudas named Bheda. Find a way to subdue him. Whoever (like Bheda) commits sin against the mortals who are praising you, strike that Bheda with your sharp thunderbolt. 

Regarding the word **sharp** <note>original: "tigmam"</note>: it refers to one who incites the warrior's enthusiasm. As **Yaska** says: "Tigmam comes from the root *tej*, meaning the act of enthusiasm" <note>original: "Nirukta 10.6"</note>. Regarding the word **thunderbolt** <note>original: "vajra"</note>: it is that which "goes" <note>root: vraj</note> toward the enemy and is not struck back. <note>Note: Sayana here provides a grammatical derivation of the word 'Vajra' using the Unadi suffixes.</note> Strike him; the meaning is to hit Bheda with the thunderbolt. ॥ १८ ॥

## Commentary (Sayana)
[Continuation from previous page for Verse 19]

In this "all-attaining" <note>original: "sarvatātā," referring to a battle where everything is at stake</note> war, **Indra** destroyed the power of **Bheda**—who is described either as an "atheist" or a specific enemy leader of that name—on behalf of King **Sudas**. He effectively killed him. Like the river **Yamuna**, he brought satisfaction to the people; that is, everyone living on its banks was pleased by this victory. The **Tritsus** <note>the royal tribe of King Sudas</note> and their men were also protected. Furthermore, the **Aja**, **Shigru**, and **Yakshu** tribes brought offerings <note>original: "balim"</note> to Indra. These tributes consisted of the heads of horses killed in the battle, or perhaps they presented the choice horses they had captured as a gift to Indra. ॥ १९ ॥

## Hymn Text
-> ॥ Now the Twentieth Verse ॥ <-

O **Indra**, neither your ancient favors nor your riches can be counted, just as the many old and new dawns cannot be numbered. You struck down **Devaka**, the son of **Manyamana**, who thought highly of himself; by your own power, you shattered **Shambara** from the great mountain. ॥ २० ॥

**Word-by-word Analysis:**
Not | your | O Indra | favors | not | riches | for counting | many | dawns | not | new | Devaka | even | thinking highly of himself | you struck | down | by self | of the great [mountain] | Shambara | you shattered ॥ २० ॥

---

## Commentary (Sayana)

O **Indra**, your ancient <note>original: "purātanāḥ"</note> and beautiful thoughts <note>original: "sumatayaḥ"</note> and your riches <note>original: "rāyo dhanāni"</note> cannot be counted <note>original: "na saṃcakṣe"</note>, much like the infinite dawns. Neither your old nor your new favors can be calculated. Furthermore, you killed the enemy named **Devaka**, the son of **Manyamana**, who was arrogant. You personally shattered the demon **Shambara** <note>a famous mountain-dwelling foe of Indra</note> from the vast mountain.

-> ॥ This concludes the twenty-seventh section of the second chapter in the fifth book ॥ <-

---

## Hymn Text
-> ॥ Now the Twenty-first Verse ॥ <-

Those who, out of love for you, rejoiced even while leaving their homes—**Parashara**, **Shatayatu**, and **Vashishtha**—they do not forget your friendship, O bountiful one. Therefore, may bright days dawn for these patron-singers. ॥ २१ ॥

**Word-by-word Analysis:**
Forth | who | from home | rejoiced | for love of you | Parashara | Shatayatu | Vashishtha | not | your | of the bountiful one | friendship | they forget | then | for the patron-singers | bright days | [prefix] | may they dawn ॥ २१ ॥

## Commentary (Sayana)

O **Indra**, the sage **Parashara** is called "**Shatayatu**" because he provides much protection <note>original: "bahurakṣāḥ"</note>, or because he is the destroyer <note>original: "śātayitā"</note> of many demons <note>original: "rakṣasām"</note> who wish to harm him. Along with the sages **Shakti** and **Vashishtha**, these and others, out of love for you...

<vocab>
**Indra**: The king of the gods; **Sudas**: The king who won the Battle of the Ten Kings; **Yamuna**: A major river in India; **Tritsu**: The tribe of King Sudas; **Aja, Shigru, Yakshu**: Local tribes or clans; **Shambara**: A demonic figure representing drought or mountain fortresses; **Parashara/Vashishtha**: Famous Vedic sages and priests; **Shatayatu**: A title meaning 'destroyer of a hundred demons.'
</vocab>

<meta>This page concludes the commentary on Verse 21 and presents verses 22 and 23 of the 18th Hymn in the 7th Book (Mandala) of the Rig Veda. It focuses on the lavish gifts given to the sage Vasishtha by King Sudas following his victory in the "Battle of the Ten Kings."</meta>

By your will, he reached from house to house. <note>The commentator notes a grammatical point from Panini 2.3.28.1 regarding the use of the fifth case (ablative) to mean the second case (accusative).</note> Or rather, "from the house, in the house" <note>using the fifth case to mean the seventh (locative)</note>. Sages like **Parashara** and others greatly delighted in you and praised you. These patrons do not neglect <note>original: "na mṛṣanti," meaning they do not forget</note> your friendship, which consists of hymns of praise and sacrifice. They do not allow it to be forgotten. Because they do not forget, for these patrons and singers, "bright days" <note>original: "sudinā"</note> shall shine forth, dwell with them, or come to them. ॥

->|| Now the Twenty-Second Verse ||<-

## Hymn Text
Two hundred cows and two chariots with brides were the gifts from **Sudas**, the grandson of **Devavat** and son of **Pijavana**. O **Agni**, as one worthy of these gifts, I, **Vasishtha**, move around the sacrificial hall praising you, like a priest <note>original: "hotā," the invoking priest</note> singing hymns. ॥ २२ ॥

**Padapatha:**
Two | indeed | of the grandson | of Devavat | hundred | indeed | of the cow | two | chariots | with brides | of Sudas |
worthy | O Agni | of the son of Pijavana | gift | like a priest | the house | around | I go | praising ॥ २२ ॥

---

## Commentary (Sayana)
From the King **Sudas**, who is the son of **Pijavana** and the grandson of King **Devavat**, came the gift of two hundred cows and two chariots equipped with brides <note>or "maidens accompanying the gift"</note>. I, **Vasishtha**, being worthy <note>original: "arhan"</note> because I am the one praising **Indra** <note>original: "rebhan"</note>, move around the sacrificial house <note>original: "sadma"</note> like a *Hotar* priest who performs the *Vashat* call. 

<note>Translator's note: Sayana clarifies that although Agni is addressed here, it is to honor him as the chief of the gods and the witness of the sacrifice, rather than indicating that this specific verse is dedicated to him; the entire hymn remains dedicated to Indra.</note>

->|| Now the Twenty-Third Verse ||<-

## Hymn Text
Four horses, the gifts of the son of **Pijavana**, adorned with gold and moving straight, carry me comfortably even in difficult places. These horses of **Sudas**, standing firm on the earth, carry me—as if I were their own son—toward food and renown. ॥ २३ ॥

**Padapatha:**
Four | me | of the son of Pijavana | gifts | with good speed | adorned with gold | in the void [or difficulty] |
straight-going | me | standing on the earth | of Sudas | son | for the son | for renown [or food] | they carry ॥ २३ ॥

---

## Commentary (Sayana)
The gifts of King **Sudas** (the son of **Pijavana**) include four horses. These horses are described as <term>smadiṣṭayaḥ</term> <note>meaning they are accompanied by the king's excellent generosity and faith</note> and <term>kṛśaninaḥ</term> <note>meaning they are decorated with gold ornaments</note>. Even in <term>nireke</term> <note>meaning a difficult path or a place of scarcity</note>, these horses move straight and are well-established upon the earth. These four horses, which were given as gifts, carry me (**Vasishtha**) as I sit in the chariot. They carry me like a father carries a son <note>original: "tokam," meaning "offspring"</note> toward "shravas" <note>which can mean either "food" or "fame"</note>. 

<note>Note: The commentator mentions that the word "me" (me) is repeated in the verse for the sake of completing the meter.</note>

<summary>This page describes the generous rewards (cows, chariots with brides, and gold-adorned horses) given by King Sudas to the sage Vasishtha after their military success. The commentary explains the king's lineage and justifies the sage's receipt of such wealth as a reward for his spiritual service.</summary>

## Hymn Text

-> ॥ Now the Twenty-Fourth Verse ॥ <-

Whose glory fills the two vast worlds, heaven and earth; he, the distributor, has shared wealth among the leaders one by one. Like rivers flowing toward the ocean, all people praise Indra because of him, who struck down the enemy Yudhyamadhi in the encounter. ॥ २४ ॥

**Word-for-Word Breakdown:**
Whose | glory | heaven and earth <note>original: "rodasī"</note> | within | the two vast ones | from head to head <note>meaning: to each leader or chief</note> | distributed | the distributor | fame | indeed | Indra | like | the flowing rivers | they praise | down | the enemy Yudhyamadhi | he struck | in the encounter ॥ २४ ॥

---

## Commentary (Sayana)

The fame <note>original: "shravas"</note> of this King Sudas dwells within the two vast worlds, heaven and earth. This means his renown pervades the space between them. Furthermore, Sudas, acting as a distributor of wealth, gave riches to every prominent person <note>original: "shirshno-shirshno," literally "from head to head," meaning to each excellence or leader</note>. Regarding this Sudas, all the people praise him just as they praise **Indra**. Moreover, just as rivers flow into the sea, praises flow to him. In the battle <note>original: "abhīke"</note>, he struck down <note>original: "nyashishāt"</note> the adversary named **Yudhyamadhi**.

---

## Hymn Text

-> ॥ Now the Twenty-Fifth Verse ॥ <-

O heroic **Maruts**, attend to this King Sudas just as you attended to his father **Divodasa**. Protect the prayer and the home of the son of **Pijavana**; may his dominion be indestructible, unaging, and desired by those who serve. ॥ २५ ॥

**Word-for-Word Breakdown:**
This | O heroes | Maruts | attend/serve | after | Divodasa | like | the father | of Sudas | protect | of the son of Pijavana | the prayer or home | indestructible | dominion | unaging | desiring service ॥ २५ ॥

---

## Commentary (Sayana)

O leaders, O **Maruts** <note>the storm deities and companions of Indra</note>, attend to this King Sudas just as you once attended to his father **Divodasa**. <note>The commentator notes that Divodasa is another name for Pijavana, the father of Sudas.</note> Furthermore, protect the prayer <note>original: "ketam," which can mean a sacred hymn or a dwelling</note> of this son of Pijavana. Also, may the dominion and strength of this Sudas be indestructible <note>original: "dūnāsham"</note> and unaging—that is, never-failing.

-> ॥ This concludes the twenty-eighth section <note>varga</note> of the second chapter <note>adhyaya</note> of the fifth book <note>ashtaka</note> ॥ <-

---

## Commentary (Introduction to Hymn 19)

The second hymn, beginning with "He who has sharp horns" <note>original: "yas tigma-shṛnga"</note>, consists of eleven verses. The seer is **Vasishtha**, the meter is **Trishtubh**, and the deity is **Indra**. This is confirmed by the Index <note>original: "Anukramani"</note>. In the ritual context, this hymn is used on the fifth day of the *Abhilavika* ceremony as the formula for the *Nivid* <note>a specific short invocation</note>. This is indicated in the liturgical texts: "With what splendor... He who has sharp horns..." is used during the midday libation <note>original: "Madhyandina Savana"</note>. It is also used during the *Vishuvat* day <note>the solstice or middle day of a year-long sacrifice</note> in the *Nishkevalya* ritual.

<vocab>
**Maruts**: Storm deities who are often depicted as a troop of young warriors.
**Divodasa**: A famous king and ancestor (or father) of Sudas.
**Sudas**: The king of the Tritsu clan, famous for his victory in the Battle of the Ten Kings.
**Paijavana**: A patronymic meaning "son of Pijavana."
**Vasishtha**: One of the most famous Vedic sages, the primary seer of the 7th Book of the Rig Veda.
**Indra**: The king of the gods and the primary deity of the Rig Veda.
**Heaven and Earth**: Termed "Rodasi," viewed as the two parents of the universe.
**Dominion**: Termed "Kshatram," referring to the power and authority of a ruler.
**Madhyandina Savana**: The midday pressing of the Soma juice during a sacrifice.
**Abhilavika**: A six-day sacrificial cycle within a larger Soma sacrifice.
</vocab>

<summary>This page concludes the 18th hymn with final praises for King Sudas's generosity and victory over enemies like Yudhyamadhi, followed by an invocation to the Maruts. It then introduces the 19th hymn dedicated to Indra, detailing its poetic structure and ritual applications.</summary>
<keywords>Sudas, Maruts, Divodasa, Indra, Vasishtha, victory, wealth distribution, Vedic ritual, liturgy, fame</keywords>

<meta>This page continues from the conclusion of Hymn 18, which celebrated the victory of King Sudas. Here, the text transitions to Hymn 19 of the 7th Book (Mandala), shifting focus to Indra’s general martial power and his legendary protection of the sage-warrior Kutsa.</meta>

### Book 7. Chapter 2. Hymn 19. || Fifth Volume || Page 969

In the *Mahavrata* <note>A major Vedic rite performed at the winter solstice</note> ceremony, specifically in the *Nishkevalya* litany, this hymn is used. It is indicated by the citation: "He who is a fierce bull with sharp horns, born for strength and self-power." (Aitareya Aranyaka 5.8). Furthermore, in the sacrifice for one desiring long life (*Ayushyakama-ishti*), the verse "May we not, O powerful one..." is used as the offering prayer for Indra. This is indicated by: "May we not, O powerful one, be in your exclusion; protect us, O Agni, with your protections." (Ashvalayana Shrauta Sutra 2.10).

---

-> ॥ Now the First Verse ॥ <-

## Hymn Text
He who is like a fierce bull with sharp horns, who alone makes all people tremble; he who is the giver of the eternal wealth from the house of the non-sacrificer to the one who presses [Soma] exceedingly well. ॥ १ ॥

**Word-for-Word Breakdown:**
He who | sharp-horned <note>original: "tigma-shringa"</note> | bull | like <note>original: "na" - here used for comparison</note> | fierce | alone | people/enemies | makes tremble | forth | all |
He who | eternal | of the non-sacrificer | of the house/wealth | the giver | you are | to the one who presses [Soma] well | wealth ॥ १ ॥

---

## Commentary (Sayana)
That Indra, being fierce like a bull with sharp or piercing horns, acting alone and without assistance, makes all people—meaning all enemy populations—flee from their places. Furthermore, it is understood that Indra is the one who carries away the wealth or the house of the person who does not offer sacrifices (*adashushah*), though that wealth be vast and eternal. O Indra, you are the giver (*prayanta*) of that wealth (*vedas*) to the person who performs the pressing of Soma juice (*sushvitara*) with great excellence. 

<term>Because it ends with the suffix -trin</term>, the genitive case is absent here. Since the verb "you are" (*asi*) is an accented verb and follows the relative pronoun "who" (*yat*), it cannot be unaccented; therefore, the connection is made by supplying another verb associated with the relative pronoun.

---

-> ॥ Now the Second Verse ॥ <-

## Hymn Text
O Indra, you indeed protected **Kutsa**, serving him with your own person in the battle. When you subdued the **Dasa** <note>A class of enemies or demons</note> **Shushna** and **Kuyava** for this son of Arjuni, while bestowing favor upon him. ॥ २ ॥

**Word-for-Word Breakdown:**
You | indeed | that | Indra | Kutsa | protected | serving/desiring to hear | with the body | in the battle |
The Dasa | when | Shushna | Kuyava | down | for him | you subdued | for the son of Arjuni | bestowing/favoring ॥ २ ॥

---

## Commentary (Sayana)
O Indra, you indeed <note>original: "ha"</note> at that time <note>original: "tyat"</note> protected **Kutsa** (*avah*). You did this by serving him or attending to him with your own physical body (*tanva*) in the battle (*samarye*) which was filled with mortal warriors (*maryaih*). When did this happen? It was when you were favoring the son of **Arjuni** <note>Arjuni is the mother of Kutsa, thus he is called Arjuneya</note>, giving him wealth, and when you completely subdued (*nyarandhayah*) the Dasa-demon named **Shushna** and the demon **Kuyava**.

<summary>This page introduces Hymn 19 of Book 7, establishing its liturgical use in the Mahavrata rite. The verses and commentary describe Indra as a powerful, bull-like deity who strips wealth from non-believers to reward Soma-pressers and specifically protects the hero Kutsa against the demons Shushna and Kuyava.</summary>
<keywords>Indra, Kutsa, Shushna, Kuyava, Mahavrata, Soma, Arjuneya, Vedic Sacrifice, Sanskrit Commentary</keywords>

# Rig Veda || Mandala 5. Anuvaka 2. Varga 29. || Page 970

## Hymn Text

-> ॥ Now the Third Verse ॥ <-

You, O bold one, with your crushing power, protected Vitahavya and Sudas with all your protections. You protected Trasadasyu, the son of Purukutsa, and Puru in the winning of land and in the slaying of enemies. ॥ ३ ॥

**Word-for-Word Breakdown:**
You | O bold one <note>original: "dhṛṣṇo"</note> | with crushing [power] | Vitahavya | forth | protected | with all | protections | Sudas |
forth | the son of Purukutsa | Trasadasyu | protected | in the winning of land | in the slaying of enemies | Puru ॥ ३ ॥

---

## Commentary (Sayana)

O **bold one** <note>original: "dhṛṣṇo"</note>, subduer of enemies, with your **crushing** <note>original: "dhṛṣatā"</note> thunderbolt or strength, you **protected** <note>original: "prāvaḥ"</note>—that is, you guarded exceedingly—the King **Sudas** and **Vitahavya**, who had offered or prepared the sacrificial oblations, with **all** <note>original: "viśvābhiḥ"</note> your **protections** <note>original: "ūtibhiḥ"</note>. Furthermore, in **the slaying of enemies** <note>original: "vṛtra-hatyeṣu"</note>, specifically in battles fought for the sake of **winning land** <note>original: "kṣetra-sātā"</note> or dividing territory, you protected **Trasadasyu**, the **son of Purukutsa** <note>original: "paurukutsim"</note>, as well as **Puru**.

---

## Hymn Text

-> ॥ Now the Fourth Verse ॥ <-

O Indra, mindful of men, you slay many enemies with your men at the feast of the gods. You, Lord of the bay horses, lulled the enemies Cumuri and Dhuni to sleep for the sake of Dabhiti, using your easy-slaying [weapon]. ॥ ४ ॥

**Word-for-Word Breakdown:**
Him/That | by men | mindful of men | in the feast of the gods | many | enemies | O Lord of bay horses | you slay |
You | down | enemy | Cumuri | Dhuni | and | lulled to sleep | for Dabhiti | easy-slaying ॥ ४ ॥

---

## Commentary (Sayana)

O **mindful of men** <note>original: "nṛmaṇo"</note>, you who are to be meditated upon or praised by men (the leaders and chanters of the sacrifice); or alternatively, one whose mind is fixed upon men. When the **feast of the gods** <note>original: "devavītau"</note> occurs—meaning during the performance of a sacrifice or in a battle (which is called a "feast of gods" because those desiring victory go there)—you **slay** <note>original: "haṃsi"</note>, or rather you have killed, **many enemies** <note>original: "bhūrīṇi vṛtrā"</note> alongside your men, the Maruts <note>The storm-deities who are Indra's constant companions</note>. Furthermore, O **Indra, Lord of the bay horses** <note>original: "haryaśva"</note>, for the sake of the royal sage named **Dabhiti**, you **lulled to sleep** <note>original: "asvāpayaḥ"</note>—meaning you utterly destroyed—the **enemies** <note>original: "dasyum"</note> known as **Cumuri** and **Dhuni** with your **easy-slaying** <note>original: "suhantu"</note> thunderbolt.

---

## Hymn Text

-> ॥ Now the Fifth Verse ॥ <-

O thunderbolt-handed one, these are your exploits: that you [shattered] ninety and nine cities in a single day. At the hundredth stronghold you entered; you slew Vritra and also slew Namuci. ॥ ५ ॥

**Word-for-Word Breakdown:**
Your | exploits | O thunderbolt-handed | those | nine | that | cities | ninety | and | in a day |
in the dwelling/stronghold | the hundredth | you entered | you slew | and | Vritra | Namuci | and | you slew ॥ ५ ॥

<vocab>
**Bold/Subduer** <note>original: "dhṛṣṇu"</note>: An epithet for Indra's overpowering nature.
**Sudas** <note>original: "sudāsa"</note>: A famous Vedic king of the Tritsu clan.
**Trasadasyu** <note>original: "trasadasyu"</note>: A king whose name literally means "he who makes the Dasyus (enemies) tremble."
**Son of Purukutsa** <note>original: "paurukutsi"</note>: A patronymic referring to Trasadasyu.
**Slaying of enemies** <note>original: "vṛtra-hatya"</note>: While "Vritra" is a specific demon, the term often refers to the destruction of any obstacle or foe.
**Mindful of men** <note>original: "nṛmaṇas"</note>: One who cares for or is praised by human worshippers.
**Lord of bay horses** <note>original: "haryaśva"</note>: A standard title for Indra, whose chariot is pulled by two tawny steeds.
**Enemy/demon** <note>original: "dasyu"</note>: Often referring to non-sacrificing enemies or chaotic forces.
**Cumuri and Dhuni** <note>original: "cumuri, dhuni"</note>: Specific tribal chieftains or demons defeated by Indra.
**Dabhiti** <note>original: "dabhīti"</note>: A king and sage whom Indra befriended.
**Namuci** <note>original: "namuci"</note>: A prominent demon in Vedic mythology known for being difficult to kill.
</vocab>

It emphasizes Indra's martial cooperation with the Maruts and his use of the thunderbolt to "lay to sleep" (slay) his foes.</summary>

# Mandala 1. Anuvaka 4. Hymn 54. | Fifth Ashtaka | Page 971

## Commentary (Sayana) - Continued from Verse 5

O wielder of the thunderbolt <note>original: "vajrahasta"</note>, such are your **strengths** <note>original: "cyautnāni"</note>. When you simultaneously shattered the **ninety-nine cities** of the demon **Shambara**, then, to establish your dwelling, you entered the **hundredth city**. You also slew the serpent-demon **Vritra**, and furthermore, you destroyed the demon **Namuci**.

-> ॥ This concludes the nineteenth section <note>original: "varga"</note> of the second chapter of the fifth book ॥ <-

---

## Hymn Text - Verse 6

-> ॥ Now the Sixth Verse ॥ <-

**Eternal are those enjoyments, O Indra, for the giver of oblations, for the donor, for the generous Sudas. For you, the showerer of benefits, I yoke the two vigorous bay horses; let our prayers reach the powerful strength.** ॥ ६ ॥

**Padapatha:**

Eternal | those | for you | Indra | enjoyments | for the one who has offered oblations | for the donor | for the generous Sudas |
for the showerer | for you | two bay horses | vigorous | I yoke | let them reach | prayers | O you of many deeds | strength ॥ ६ ॥

## Commentary (Sayana)

O Indra, those **enjoyments** <note>original: "bhojanāni"</note> or pleasurable riches given by you to the **generous Sudas**—the sacrificer who is a **giver of oblations** <note>original: "rātahavyāya"</note>—have become **eternal** <note>original: "sanā"</note> or everlasting. O **Indra of many deeds** <note>original: "puruśāka"</note>, for you, the **showerer** <note>original: "vṛṣṇe"</note> of desires, I **yoke** <note>original: "yunajmi"</note>—meaning I join to your chariot—the two **vigorous** <note>original: "vṛṣaṇā"</note> **bay horses** <note>original: "harī"</note> in order to bring you here. Let our **prayers** <note>original: "brahmāṇi"</note> or hymns also **reach** <note>original: "vyantu"</note> that mighty **strength** <note>original: "vājam"</note>.

---

## Hymn Text - Verse 7

-> ॥ Now the Seventh Verse ॥ <-

**In this search of yours, O Mighty One, let us not be abandoned to evil, O Lord of the bay horses. Protect us with your shields that cannot be harmed; let us be dear among your wise worshippers.** ॥ ७ ॥

**Padapatha:**

Not | your | in this | O Mighty One | search / praise | to evil | many / abundance | O Lord of the bay horses | to be abandoned |
protect | us | with un-tearable / unharmed | shields / protections | your | dear ones | among the wise / patrons | let us be ॥ ७ ॥

## Commentary (Sayana)

O **Mighty One** <note>original: "sahasāvan"</note>, O Indra, **Lord of the bay horses** <note>original: "harivaḥ"</note>, in this **searching** <note>original: "pariṣṭau"</note> or investigation conducted by us through this hymn, let us **not** <note>original: "mā"</note> be **abandoned** <note>original: "parādai"</note> to **evil** <note>original: "aghāya"</note>. Furthermore, **protect** <note>original: "trāyasva"</note> us with **shields** <note>original: "varūthaiḥ"</note>—called so because they ward off <note>original: "vārayanti"</note> calamities—that are **unharmed** <note>original: "avṛkebhiḥ"</note> or unobstructed. Among your **wise worshippers** <note>original: "sūriṣu"</note>, let us **be** <note>original: "syāma"</note> the **dear ones** <note>original: "priyāsaḥ"</note>.

# Rig-Veda || [Book 5, Chapter 2, Section 30]

## Hymn Text

-> ॥ Now the Eighth Verse ॥ <-

**O Bountiful One <note>original: "maghavan"</note>, in your praise may we, the leaders of the people and your friends, find delight in your protection. Sharpen your weapons against Turvasha and Yadu, seeking to bring praiseworthy happiness to Atithigva.** ॥ ८ ॥

**Word-by-word Breakdown:**
Dear ones | indeed | your | O Bountiful One | in praise | leaders | may we rejoice | in protection | friends |
subdue | Turvasha | subdue | Yadu | sharpen | for Atithigva | praiseworthy | intending to do ॥ ८ ॥

---

## Commentary (Sayana)

O **Bountiful** <note>original: "maghavan"</note> wealthy Indra, in **your praise** <note>original: "te abhiṣṭau"</note>, we who are **leaders** <note>original: "naraḥ"</note> of the singers and your **friends** <note>original: "sakhāyaḥ"</note>—sharing the same fame and being **dear** <note>original: "priyāsaḥ"</note> to you—may we **rejoice** <note>original: "madema"</note> within our own **protection** <note>original: "śaraṇe"</note> or home. Furthermore, while you are **intending to provide** <note>original: "kariṣyan"</note> **praiseworthy** <note>original: "śaṃsyam"</note> happiness **for Atithigva** <note>The name Atithigva literally means "he who goes to worshipful guests," identifying him as a hospitable ruler, likely Sudas or Divodasa</note>, **subdue** <note>original: "ni śiśīhi"</note> the king **Turvasha**; bring him under your control. Likewise, **subdue** the king **Yadu** <note>original: "yādam"</note>.

---

## Hymn Text

-> ॥ Now the Ninth Verse ॥ <-

**Even now, O Bountiful One, the leaders of men, the reciters of hymns, chant their prayers in your praise. They who, through their invocations to you, have made even the Panis generous—select us for that same alliance.** ॥ ९ ॥

**Word-by-word Breakdown:**
Immediately | even | now | your | O Bountiful One | in praise | leaders | they chant | reciters of hymns | prayers |
who | your | with invocations | [particle of distinction] | the Panis | they have made to give | us | choose | for alliance | for that ॥ ९ ॥

---

## Commentary (Sayana)

O **Bountiful** <note>original: "maghavan"</note> wealthy Indra, in **your praise** <note>original: "te abhiṣṭau"</note> **now** <note>original: "nu"</note>, **those leaders of men who are reciters of hymns** <note>original: "ye nara ukthaśāsa"</note> **chant** <note>original: "śaṃsanti"</note> their **prayers** <note>original: "ukthā"</note>—the laudatory chants—**at this very moment** <note>original: "sadyaś cit"</note>. Furthermore, through **your invocations** <note>original: "te havebhiḥ"</note> or sacrificial songs, they have even made the **Panis** <note>original: "paṇīn"</note>—those miserly merchants who do not give—**bestow wealth** <note>original: "vyadaśan"</note>. This means they cause the misers to give up their riches specifically. **Choose us** <note>original: "asmān vṛṇīṣva"</note> **for that same alliance** <note>original: "tasmai yujyāya"</note> or partnership to continue that friendship.

---

## Hymn Text

-> ॥ Now the Tenth Verse ॥ <-

**These hymns, O most manly of men, are offered to you by these people, directing our devotion to you and granting wealth. In the slaying of Vritra, O Indra, be gracious to them—a friend, a hero, and the protector of men.** ॥ १० ॥

**Word-by-word Breakdown:**
These | hymns | of men | O most manly | to you | directed toward us | giving | riches |
of them | O Indra | in the slaying of Vritra | gracious | be | friend | and | hero | protector | and | of men ॥ १० ॥

<summary>In these final verses of the hymn, the poet appeals to Indra as a friend and protector, asking him to subdue rival kings Turvasha and Yadu while rewarding the hospitable Atithigva. The text also highlights the power of hymns to compel even the miserly Panis to become donors, concluding with a plea for Indra's grace during the battle against Vritra.</summary>
<keywords>Indra, Maghavan, Atithigva, Turvasha, Yadu, Panis, Vritra, Sayana, Vedic hymns, ritual alliance</keywords>

<meta>Continuity Note: The previous page concluded a hymn in Mandala 1. This page, numbered 973, transitions to the conclusion of Mandala 7, Hymn 19. It specifically contains the final verse (verse 11) and the closing formal colophon for the second chapter of the fifth book (Ashtaka) of the Rig Veda.</meta>

# Rig-Veda || [Book 5, Chapter 2, Section 20] || Page 973

## Commentary (Sayana)
<note>This section concludes the commentary on the previous verse.</note>
O **Best of Leaders** <note>original: "nṛtama"</note>, Indra! To you, these **praises** <note>original: "stomāḥ"</note> from the **leaders** <note>original: "narām"</note> of men, who offer **worthy** <note>original: "mạnhanīyāni"</note> **oblations** <note>original: "havīṃṣi"</note>, have become directed toward us. In the **slaying of Vritra** <note>original: "vṛtrahatye"</note>—that is, in battle—be **auspicious** <note>original: "śivaḥ"</note>, a bringer of welfare to those men. Be a **friend** <note>original: "sakhā"</note> and be a **protector** <note>original: "avitā"</note>.

---

## Hymn Text
-> ॥ Now the Eleventh Verse ॥ <-

**Now, O Heroic Indra, being praised, increased in your body through your protection and impelled by our prayer, bestow riches upon us; bestow upon us household members. Do you all protect us always with your blessings.** ॥ ११ ॥

-> Now | Indra | Hero | being praised | with protection | impelled by prayer | with the body | grow |
bestow | upon us | riches | bestow | household members | You | protect | with blessings | always | us ॥ ११ ॥ <-

---

## Commentary (Sayana)
O **Heroic Indra** <note>original: "śūrendra"</note>, **now** <note>original: "nu"</note>, on this day, as you are **being praised** <note>original: "stavamānaḥ"</note> and **impelled by prayer** <note>original: "brahmajūtaḥ"</note>—meaning encouraged by this sacred hymn—**grow** <note>original: "vavṛdhasva"</note> in your **body** <note>original: "tanvā"</note> or physical form. Furthermore, **bestow** <note>original: "upa mimīhi"</note>—or grant—**riches** <note>original: "vājān"</note>—meaning food or spoils—unto us. Also, **bestow household members** <note>original: "stīn"</note> or homes. The rest of the verse is clear.

-> ॥ This concludes the twentieth section of the second chapter of the fifth book ॥ <-

**By the illumination of the meaning of the Veda, may Vidyatirtha-Maheshvara—who removes the darkness of the heart—grant the four goals of human life.** <note>The "four goals" refers to the Purusharthas: Dharma (duty), Artha (prosperity), Kama (pleasure), and Moksha (liberation). Vidyatirtha was likely the spiritual preceptor of Sayana.</note>

Thus ends the second chapter of the fifth book in the **Commentary on the Rig-Veda Sanhita** <note>original: "Ṛg-saṃhitā-bhāṣya"</note>, titled **The Illumination of the Vedic Meaning** <note>original: "Vedārtha-prakāśa"</note>, composed by the great teacher **Sayana** <note>original: "Sāyaṇācārya"</note>, who served as the prime minister under the empire of the illustrious **King Bukka I** <note>original: "Vīra-bukka-bhūpāla"</note>, the supreme sovereign and promoter of the Vedic path.

---

<summary>This page concludes Mandala 7, Hymn 19 with a prayer for Indra to increase his power through hymns and provide the community with food and shelter. It also contains the formal colophon marking the end of the chapter and honoring the commentator Sayana and his royal patron, King Bukka I.</summary>
<keywords>Indra, Sayana, King Bukka I, Veda commentary, prayer for prosperity, household, Vidyatirtha, Vijayanagara Empire</keywords>

<meta>Continuity: While the previous page provided concluded a hymn in Mandala 7, this page transitions to the Ninth Mandala, specifically the start of the Second Chapter (Anuvaka 2). This Mandala is entirely dedicated to Soma Pavamana (the Purifying Soma). These verses belong to an 'Apri' hymn, which is a specific type of invocatory song used in rituals. Unlike most Apri hymns addressed to the Fire God (Agni), this one is addressed to the deified Soma juice.</meta>

# Rig-Veda || [Book 9, Hymn 5, Part 2, Section 1] || Page 619

## Hymn Text

-> ॥ Second Chapter ॥ <-
-> ॥ Fifth Hymn ॥ <-

**Kindled today, you shine as a god; worship the gods. Bring that which is worthy of sacrifice and impel the juice that causes exhilaration.** ॥ १ ॥

---

## Commentary (Sayana)

**'Kindled'** <note>original: "samiddhaḥ"</note>: Brightly lit or thoroughly burning. **'Today'** <note>original: "adya"</note>: At this time. **'You shine'** <note>original: "rājasi"</note>: You are radiant. **'God'** <note>original: "devaḥ"</note>: You, who are endowed with qualities such as generosity, **'worship'** <note>original: "yaja"</note> or honor the **'gods'** <note>original: "devān"</note> in their **'presence'** <note>original: "upa"</note>. **'He'** <note>original: "saḥ"</note>: You, being such a one, **'convey'** <note>original: "vahasva"</note> or bring this Soma which is **'worthy of sacrifice'** <note>original: "yajñiyaṃ"</note>. Furthermore, **'impel'** <note>original: "codayasva"</note> or stimulate this juice, the **'bringer of exhilaration'** <note>original: "madacyutaṃ"</note>—that which causes the flow of ritual joy. ॥ १ ॥

---

## Hymn Text

**O Child of the Self, flow in a stream of sweetness for our joy, where the gods have given their offerings.** ॥ २ ॥

---

## Commentary (Sayana)

**'Child of the Self'** <note>original: "tanūnapāt"</note>: O <term>Tanunapat</term> <note>A title meaning 'son of one's own self,' usually applied to Agni but here to Soma</note> Soma! **'Flow'** <note>original: "pavasva"</note> or trickle as a **'sweet'** <note>original: "madhu"</note> delicious juice in a **'stream'** <note>original: "dhārayā"</note> **'for joy'** <note>original: "made"</note> or for the sake of spiritual exhilaration. **'Where'** <note>original: "yatra"</note>: In the presence of which Soma the **'gods'** <note>original: "devāḥ"</note> **'and'** <note>original: "ca"</note> others **'gave'** <note>original: "dāśate"</note> or presented their ritual offerings. ॥ २ ॥

---

## Hymn Text

**Praised by men, being purified, you are the best of settlers among the people, O Creator. Soma takes his seat in the vessels.** ॥ ३ ॥

---

## Commentary (Sayana)

**'Praised by men'** <note>original: "narāśaṃsaḥ"</note>: O **'Creator'** <note>original: "vedhaḥ"</note> or Ordainer, Soma! As you are **'being purified'** <note>original: "punānaḥ"</note>, you are the one **'praised by men'** <note>original: "narāśaṃsaḥ"</note>—the one who should be celebrated by human leaders. Being the **'best of settlers'** <note>original: "vasiṣṭhaḥ"</note>—the most excellent among those who provide a dwelling or cause others to dwell—you take your **'place'** <note>original: "sādanaṃ"</note> or seat **'in the vessels'** <note>original: "camūṣu"</note> (the ritual jars), aiming toward the **'food'** <note>original: "prayaḥ"</note> or sustenance **'among the people'** <note>original: "vikṣu"</note> or subjects. ॥ ३ ॥

---

<summary>This page contains the opening three verses of an Apri hymn from the Ninth Mandala of the Rig Veda, where Soma is invoked with titles like Tanunapat and Narashamsa. Sayana’s commentary explains these verses in the context of the Soma sacrifice, describing the juice’s purification and its role in inviting the gods.</summary>
<keywords>Rig Veda, Soma Pavamana, Sayana, Apri Hymn, Tanunapat, Narashamsa, Vedic Ritual, Sanskrit Commentary</keywords>

### Critical Notes
- The "......" marks in the original table signify that the information is identical to the entry immediately above it.
- In Hymn 61, the Sage/Deity attribution is notably complex. It involves the poet Shyavashva addressing not just the Storm Gods (Maruts) but also praising human patrons like the King Taranta and his queen Sashiyasi.
- Page numbers ("Pag.") correspond to the specific page in Max Müller's printed edition of the Rig Veda.
